A 52-year-old man presented to our dermatology clinic for evaluation of several bluish nodules of the right hand and wrist (figure) that had gradually increased in number over the previous 31 years. The lesions were asymptomatic but had been causing the patient embarrassment and had started affecting his social interactions. No one in his family had a history of similar lesions. During adolescence he had had surgical excision of several painful enchondromas involving the proximal phalanx of the right fifth finger and three chondrosarcomas of the metacarpo-phalangeal joints of the right hand, but at the time he had no evidence of cutaneous lesions and therefore had been diagnosed as having Ollier disease (enchondromatosis).On examination he had several hard, painless, compressible, angiomatous, subcutaneous nodules on the fingers of the right hand, consistent with a diagnosis of enchondromas, which was confirmed on radiography (figure). Histology of one of the skin lesions showed typical features of cavernous haemangioma—ie, large blood-filled spaces lined by tumour endothelial cells separated by fibrous tissue. Human herpesvirus type 8 and D2-40 immunohistochemical stains were negative. On the basis of clinical and histological findings we made a diagnosis of Maffucci syndrome. We referred the patient to our plastic surgery department for excision of the largest angiomas, and he has follow-up every 6 months to assess new or changing lesions and check for possible chondrosarcomas.
Maffucci syndrome is a rare, sporadic genodermatosis affecting both males and females, which is associated with postzygotic somatic mutations in isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 and 2 genes. Although cases of late-onset Maffucci syndrome have been reported, it usually manifests around age 4–5 years, affecting the hands or feet in a unilateral or asymmetrical fashion. Clinically, it is characterised by the combination of benign enlargements of cartilage (enchondromas) and multiple angiomatous skin lesions—usually cavernous haemangiomas, but patients can also present with lymphangiomas and spindle cell haemangioendotheliomas. Treatment is usually necessary only for aesthetic or functional problems. Surgery is the most common therapeutic approach for both cartilaginous and cutaneous lesions. Possible complications include spontaneous fractures, malignant transformation of angiomatous lesions, and sarcomatous degeneration of enchondromas—with a lifetime risk of about 100%. Prompt identification of Maffucci syndrome can help to identify and treat possible chondrosarcomas in a timely fashion. The principal differential diagnoses are Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome, Kaposi sarcoma, glomuvenous malformations, Proteus syndrome, blue rubber bleb naevus syndrome, and Ollier disease, which is frequently confused with Maffucci syndrome. Ollier disease does not present with angiomatous lesions but only enchondromas, which have a much lower risk of malignant transformation (about 25% of cases) compared with patients who have Maffucci syndrome.

A 52-year-old man presented to our dermatology clinic for evaluation of several bluish nodules of the right hand and wrist (figure) that had gradually increased in number over the previous 31 years. The lesions were asymptomatic but had been causing the patient embarrassment and had started affecting his social interactions. No one in his family had a history of similar lesions. During adolescence he had had surgical excision of several painful enchondromas involving the proximal phalanx of the right fifth finger and three chondrosarcomas of the metacarpo-phalangeal joints of the right hand, but at the time he had no evidence of cutaneous lesions and therefore had been diagnosed as having Ollier disease (enchondromatosis).On examination he had several hard, painless, compressible, angiomatous, subcutaneous nodules on the fingers of the right hand, consistent with a diagnosis of enchondromas, which was confirmed on radiography (figure). Histology of one of the skin lesions showed typical features of cavernous haemangioma—ie, large blood-filled spaces lined by tumour endothelial cells separated by fibrous tissue. Human herpesvirus type 8 and D2-40 immunohistochemical stains were negative. On the basis of clinical and histological findings we made a diagnosis of Maffucci syndrome. We referred the patient to our plastic surgery department for excision of the largest angiomas, and he has follow-up every 6 months to assess new or changing lesions and check for possible chondrosarcomas.
Maffucci syndrome is a rare, sporadic genodermatosis affecting both males and females, which is associated with postzygotic somatic mutations in isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 and 2 genes. Although cases of late-onset Maffucci syndrome have been reported, it usually manifests around age 4–5 years, affecting the hands or feet in a unilateral or asymmetrical fashion. Clinically, it is characterised by the combination of benign enlargements of cartilage (enchondromas) and multiple angiomatous skin lesions—usually cavernous haemangiomas, but patients can also present with lymphangiomas and spindle cell haemangioendotheliomas. Treatment is usually necessary only for aesthetic or functional problems. Surgery is the most common therapeutic approach for both cartilaginous and cutaneous lesions. Possible complications include spontaneous fractures, malignant transformation of angiomatous lesions, and sarcomatous degeneration of enchondromas—with a lifetime risk of about 100%. Prompt identification of Maffucci syndrome can help to identify and treat possible chondrosarcomas in a timely fashion. The principal differential diagnoses are Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome, Kaposi sarcoma, glomuvenous malformations, Proteus syndrome, blue rubber bleb naevus syndrome, and Ollier disease, which is frequently confused with Maffucci syndrome. Ollier disease does not present with angiomatous lesions but only enchondromas, which have a much lower risk of malignant transformation (about 25% of cases) compared with patients who have Maffucci syndrome.

A 37-year-old Han woman from China presented with a transient episode of syncope and an 8-year history of recurrent dizziness accompanied by intermittent leg weakness. She reported being a non-smoker and had no noteworthy medical or family history. Physical examination revealed auscultatory bruits over the bilateral carotid arteries, with no muscular tenderness and typical muscle strength in all four limbs. Laboratory tests revealed elevated concentrations of C-reactive protein (5·9 mg/L; reference range: <5 mg/L) and serum creatine kinase (4152 U/L; reference range: 25–192 U/L). Other laboratory tests, including complete blood counts, routine urinalysis, blood glucose concentration, lipid profile, creatine kinase isoenzymes (creatine kinase myocardial band), renal and hepatic function, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were unremarkable. The patient tested negative for autoantibodies, including antinuclear antibodies, anti-extractable nuclear antigen antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies. CT angiography showed multifocal vascular lesions, including stenosis, occlusion, and dilatation of the bilateral common carotid arteries, the left internal carotid artery, and the bilateral vertebral arteries (figure A). No involvement of the leg or renal arteries was noted. Infectious serologies for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B and C, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis were all negative, and no infectious cause was identified.
No substantial evidence supported diagnoses of fibromuscular dysplasia or early-onset atherosclerosis. Consequently, the patient was diagnosed with Takayasu's arteritis and treatment was initiated with prednisolone (30 mg/day for 1 month, gradually tapered to 7·5 mg/day), methotrexate (15 mg/week), and tocilizumab (400 mg/month). Follow-up vascular imaging done at 3 and 12 months after initial therapy showed a gradual improvement of Takayasu's arteritis, and prednisolone was maintained at a daily dose of 7·5 mg. Methotrexate was tapered to 12·5 mg/week after 12 months of initial therapy and tocilizumab was maintained at a monthly dose of 400 mg. However, the patient persistently reported recurrent exertional weakness in both legs, which occurred a few minutes after starting exercise (eg, yoga) and improved after a short period of rest. Notably, during the follow-up, elevated creatine kinase continuously fluctuated, up to 30 320 U/L. A comprehensive neuromuscular evaluation excluded myositis or vascular insufficiency, supported by negative testing for myositis-specific antibodies and typical electromyography, ultrasonography of blood vessels, and muscle MRI of both legs. Therefore, the elevated serum creatine kinase concentration was suspected to be associated with genetic-related diseases. The patient declined an invasive muscle biopsy. Therefore, whole-exome sequencing was done and a homozygous pathogenic PYGM variant (2111C→T, Ala704Val; figure B) was identified. A diagnosis of Takayasu's arteritis concurrent with glycogen storage disease type 5 was made.
Takayasu's arteritis, a chronic granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis, shows a striking epidemiological predilection for young women in Asia, with an annual incidence of about 1–2 cases per million people worldwide. Glycogen storage disease type 5, also known as McArdle disease, is a rare autosomal recessive metabolic disease, presenting with exercise intolerance and a high concentration of serum creatine kinase, with an average incidence of 1 per 100 000 people in the USA and Europe. Only a small number of cases have been reported in China. Takayasu's arteritis and glycogen storage disease type 5 are distinct entities, with no previously reported association. In this patient, vascular imaging done at baseline and during follow-up consistently showed no involvement of the leg vessels, suggesting that ischaemic muscle injury secondary to Takayasu's arteritis was unlikely to account for the elevated creatine kinase concentration. Although myositis was previously reported as an atypical manifestation of juvenile Takayasu's arteritis, this was ruled out in this patient because of negative testing for myositis-specific antibodies, normal electromyography, and unremarkable muscle MRI of both legs. Despite the absence of histological verification with muscle biopsy, the diagnosis of glycogen storage disease type 5 is strongly supported by the presence of characteristic clinical features, including recurrent exercise-induced symptoms with a typical so-called second wind, intermittently elevated creatine kinase concentrations, and the identification of a homozygous pathogenic PYGM variant (2111C→T, Ala704Val), which was previously reported in glycogen storage disease type 5. Notably, PYGM mutations have substantial geographical and ethnic variability. In White populations, the most frequent pathogenic variant is 148C→T, Arg50Ter, accounting for more than 50% of mutant alleles. By contrast, this variant is rarely observed in people from Asia, emphasising the importance of whole-exome sequencing for the diagnosis of glycogen storage disease type 5 in these populations.
In this Clinical Picture, we present a patient with Takayasu's arteritis and concurrent glycogen storage disease type 5, which has never been reported before. This case highlights the diagnostic complexity that can arise when autoimmune and inherited metabolic disorders coexist, underscoring the need for multidisciplinary evaluation.

A 37-year-old Han woman from China presented with a transient episode of syncope and an 8-year history of recurrent dizziness accompanied by intermittent leg weakness. She reported being a non-smoker and had no noteworthy medical or family history. Physical examination revealed auscultatory bruits over the bilateral carotid arteries, with no muscular tenderness and typical muscle strength in all four limbs. Laboratory tests revealed elevated concentrations of C-reactive protein (5·9 mg/L; reference range: <5 mg/L) and serum creatine kinase (4152 U/L; reference range: 25–192 U/L). Other laboratory tests, including complete blood counts, routine urinalysis, blood glucose concentration, lipid profile, creatine kinase isoenzymes (creatine kinase myocardial band), renal and hepatic function, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were unremarkable. The patient tested negative for autoantibodies, including antinuclear antibodies, anti-extractable nuclear antigen antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies. CT angiography showed multifocal vascular lesions, including stenosis, occlusion, and dilatation of the bilateral common carotid arteries, the left internal carotid artery, and the bilateral vertebral arteries (figure A). No involvement of the leg or renal arteries was noted. Infectious serologies for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B and C, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis were all negative, and no infectious cause was identified.
No substantial evidence supported diagnoses of fibromuscular dysplasia or early-onset atherosclerosis. Consequently, the patient was diagnosed with Takayasu's arteritis and treatment was initiated with prednisolone (30 mg/day for 1 month, gradually tapered to 7·5 mg/day), methotrexate (15 mg/week), and tocilizumab (400 mg/month). Follow-up vascular imaging done at 3 and 12 months after initial therapy showed a gradual improvement of Takayasu's arteritis, and prednisolone was maintained at a daily dose of 7·5 mg. Methotrexate was tapered to 12·5 mg/week after 12 months of initial therapy and tocilizumab was maintained at a monthly dose of 400 mg. However, the patient persistently reported recurrent exertional weakness in both legs, which occurred a few minutes after starting exercise (eg, yoga) and improved after a short period of rest. Notably, during the follow-up, elevated creatine kinase continuously fluctuated, up to 30 320 U/L. A comprehensive neuromuscular evaluation excluded myositis or vascular insufficiency, supported by negative testing for myositis-specific antibodies and typical electromyography, ultrasonography of blood vessels, and muscle MRI of both legs. Therefore, the elevated serum creatine kinase concentration was suspected to be associated with genetic-related diseases. The patient declined an invasive muscle biopsy. Therefore, whole-exome sequencing was done and a homozygous pathogenic PYGM variant (2111C→T, Ala704Val; figure B) was identified. A diagnosis of Takayasu's arteritis concurrent with glycogen storage disease type 5 was made.
Takayasu's arteritis, a chronic granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis, shows a striking epidemiological predilection for young women in Asia, with an annual incidence of about 1–2 cases per million people worldwide. Glycogen storage disease type 5, also known as McArdle disease, is a rare autosomal recessive metabolic disease, presenting with exercise intolerance and a high concentration of serum creatine kinase, with an average incidence of 1 per 100 000 people in the USA and Europe. Only a small number of cases have been reported in China. Takayasu's arteritis and glycogen storage disease type 5 are distinct entities, with no previously reported association. In this patient, vascular imaging done at baseline and during follow-up consistently showed no involvement of the leg vessels, suggesting that ischaemic muscle injury secondary to Takayasu's arteritis was unlikely to account for the elevated creatine kinase concentration. Although myositis was previously reported as an atypical manifestation of juvenile Takayasu's arteritis, this was ruled out in this patient because of negative testing for myositis-specific antibodies, normal electromyography, and unremarkable muscle MRI of both legs. Despite the absence of histological verification with muscle biopsy, the diagnosis of glycogen storage disease type 5 is strongly supported by the presence of characteristic clinical features, including recurrent exercise-induced symptoms with a typical so-called second wind, intermittently elevated creatine kinase concentrations, and the identification of a homozygous pathogenic PYGM variant (2111C→T, Ala704Val), which was previously reported in glycogen storage disease type 5. Notably, PYGM mutations have substantial geographical and ethnic variability. In White populations, the most frequent pathogenic variant is 148C→T, Arg50Ter, accounting for more than 50% of mutant alleles. By contrast, this variant is rarely observed in people from Asia, emphasising the importance of whole-exome sequencing for the diagnosis of glycogen storage disease type 5 in these populations.
In this Clinical Picture, we present a patient with Takayasu's arteritis and concurrent glycogen storage disease type 5, which has never been reported before. This case highlights the diagnostic complexity that can arise when autoimmune and inherited metabolic disorders coexist, underscoring the need for multidisciplinary evaluation.

input:
A 37-year-old Han woman from China presented with a transient episode of syncope and an 8-year history of recurrent dizziness accompanied by intermittent leg weakness. She reported being a non-smoker and had no noteworthy medical or family history. Physical examination revealed auscultatory bruits over the bilateral carotid arteries, with no muscular tenderness and typical muscle strength in all four limbs. Laboratory tests revealed elevated concentrations of C-reactive protein (5·9 mg/L; reference range: <5 mg/L) and serum creatine kinase (4152 U/L; reference range: 25–192 U/L). Other laboratory tests, including complete blood counts, routine urinalysis, blood glucose concentration, lipid profile, creatine kinase isoenzymes (creatine kinase myocardial band), renal and hepatic function, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were unremarkable. The patient tested negative for autoantibodies, including antinuclear antibodies, anti-extractable nuclear antigen antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies. CT angiography showed multifocal vascular lesions, including stenosis, occlusion, and dilatation of the bilateral common carotid arteries, the left internal carotid artery, and the bilateral vertebral arteries (figure A). No involvement of the leg or renal arteries was noted. Infectious serologies for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B and C, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis were all negative, and no infectious cause was identified.
No substantial evidence supported diagnoses of fibromuscular dysplasia or early-onset atherosclerosis. Consequently, the patient was diagnosed with Takayasu's arteritis and treatment was initiated with prednisolone (30 mg/day for 1 month, gradually tapered to 7·5 mg/day), methotrexate (15 mg/week), and tocilizumab (400 mg/month). Follow-up vascular imaging done at 3 and 12 months after initial therapy showed a gradual improvement of Takayasu's arteritis, and prednisolone was maintained at a daily dose of 7·5 mg. Methotrexate was tapered to 12·5 mg/week after 12 months of initial therapy and tocilizumab was maintained at a monthly dose of 400 mg. However, the patient persistently reported recurrent exertional weakness in both legs, which occurred a few minutes after starting exercise (eg, yoga) and improved after a short period of rest. Notably, during the follow-up, elevated creatine kinase continuously fluctuated, up to 30 320 U/L. A comprehensive neuromuscular evaluation excluded myositis or vascular insufficiency, supported by negative testing for myositis-specific antibodies and typical electromyography, ultrasonography of blood vessels, and muscle MRI of both legs. Therefore, the elevated serum creatine kinase concentration was suspected to be associated with genetic-related diseases. The patient declined an invasive muscle biopsy. Therefore, whole-exome sequencing was done and a homozygous pathogenic PYGM variant (2111C→T, Ala704Val; figure B) was identified. A diagnosis of Takayasu's arteritis concurrent with glycogen storage disease type 5 was made.
Takayasu's arteritis, a chronic granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis, shows a striking epidemiological predilection for young women in Asia, with an annual incidence of about 1–2 cases per million people worldwide. Glycogen storage disease type 5, also known as McArdle disease, is a rare autosomal recessive metabolic disease, presenting with exercise intolerance and a high concentration of serum creatine kinase, with an average incidence of 1 per 100 000 people in the USA and Europe. Only a small number of cases have been reported in China. Takayasu's arteritis and glycogen storage disease type 5 are distinct entities, with no previously reported association. In this patient, vascular imaging done at baseline and during follow-up consistently showed no involvement of the leg vessels, suggesting that ischaemic muscle injury secondary to Takayasu's arteritis was unlikely to account for the elevated creatine kinase concentration. Although myositis was previously reported as an atypical manifestation of juvenile Takayasu's arteritis, this was ruled out in this patient because of negative testing for myositis-specific antibodies, normal electromyography, and unremarkable muscle MRI of both legs. Despite the absence of histological verification with muscle biopsy, the diagnosis of glycogen storage disease type 5 is strongly supported by the presence of characteristic clinical features, including recurrent exercise-induced symptoms with a typical so-called second wind, intermittently elevated creatine kinase concentrations, and the identification of a homozygous pathogenic PYGM variant (2111C→T, Ala704Val), which was previously reported in glycogen storage disease type 5. Notably, PYGM mutations have substantial geographical and ethnic variability. In White populations, the most frequent pathogenic variant is 148C→T, Arg50Ter, accounting for more than 50% of mutant alleles. By contrast, this variant is rarely observed in people from Asia, emphasising the importance of whole-exome sequencing for the diagnosis of glycogen storage disease type 5 in these populations.
In this Clinical Picture, we present a patient with Takayasu's arteritis and concurrent glycogen storage disease type 5, which has never been reported before. This case highlights the diagnostic complexity that can arise when autoimmune and inherited metabolic disorders coexist, underscoring the need for multidisciplinary evaluation.

A man aged 57 years, who had had herpes zoster 10 years previously, visited our emergency room with a tingling ache in his right lower back. Physical examination revealed neither eruption nor trauma on the body surface. However, an abdominal wall protrusion was observed on his right side, especially while he was standing (figure). Abdominal imaging using contrasted computer tomography did not reveal any abnormalities.Abdominal muscle paralysis was considered as the possible diagnosis and 60 mg loxoprofen, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, was administered for his back pain once daily for 5 days. 5 days after the initial visit, dome-shaped papules with overlying small, dark-coloured vesicles appeared on his trunk and extremities, suggesting disseminated herpes zoster. The patient was treated with 1000 mg oral valacyclovir three times daily for 7 days, along with the same regimen of loxoprofen as already described. The vesicular papules dried up after 5 days and became brown scabs within a week. The protruding abdominal wall flattened within a month, and the patient's lower back pain gradually abated within a couple of months.
Herpes zoster is characterised by the reactivation of the varicella zoster virus, which causes a vesicular rash, typically restricted to a single dermatome. However, some patients develop disseminated herpes zoster; these patients are more likely to be immunosuppressed. It is rare for this condition to occur in an immunocompetent host, as it did in this case.
Post-herpetic abdominal pseudohernia is uncommon, occurring in 2% of patients with herpes zoster. Although pseudohernia should be suspected when a patient develops abdominal paresis coincident with or after a herpetic rash, abdominal paresis can also very rarely precede a rash. Awareness of this clinical condition might help physicians anticipate herpes zoster, allowing prompt treatment.

Post-herpetic abdominal pseudohernia is uncommon, occurring in 2% of patients with herpes zoster. Although pseudohernia should be suspected when a patient develops abdominal paresis coincident with or after a herpetic rash, abdominal paresis can also very rarely precede a rash. Awareness of this clinical condition might help physicians anticipate herpes zoster, allowing prompt treatment.

A 57-year-old man presented with dyspnoea and haemoptysis. He had a history of amyloid light-chain systemic amyloidosis with renal involvement and a remote history of pulmonary emboli. He was also currently taking lenalidomide. A ventilation-perfusion lung scan was indeterminate for an acute pulmonary embolus (figure). Therefore, he was empirically anticoagulated with warfarin. Shortly after, he developed significant epistaxis, gingival bleeding, and large bilateral flank ecchymoses (figure). His international normalised ratio was slightly high (4·5). The clinical presentation was most consistent with warfarin toxicity superimposed on the multifactorial haemostatic abnormalities of systemic amyloidosis. However, the Grey Turner sign suggested a large retroperitoneal haematoma. Warfarin was discontinued, an inferior vena cava filter was placed, and he was transfused several units of blood before eventually being discharged.
Originally described by Grey Turner in 1920 as a sign of haemorrhagic pancreatitis, flank ecchymoses are caused by blood tracking subcutaneously from a retroperitoneal or intraperitoneal source.

Shortly after, he developed significant epistaxis, gingival bleeding, and large bilateral flank ecchymoses (figure). His international normalised ratio was slightly high (4·5). The clinical presentation was most consistent with warfarin toxicity superimposed on the multifactorial haemostatic abnormalities of systemic amyloidosis. However, the Grey Turner sign suggested a large retroperitoneal haematoma. Warfarin was discontinued, an inferior vena cava filter was placed, and he was transfused several units of blood before eventually being discharged.
Originally described by Grey Turner in 1920 as a sign of haemorrhagic pancreatitis, flank ecchymoses are caused by blood tracking subcutaneously from a retroperitoneal or intraperitoneal source.

A 26-year-old woman with a 2-year history of swelling of her eyelids and reduced vision was referred to our clinic by an ophthalmologist because of increased myopia, decreased visual acuity, scattered pale dots of the maculae, and suspected angioedema.
The patient had been diagnosed with attention deficit disorder and had been prescribed methylphenidate since adolescence. 5 years before we saw her, she reported having occasional episodes of dizziness thought to be caused by anaemia—investigations at that stage had found an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR; 134 mm/h; typical rate 0–20) and a normocytic anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 9·5 g/dL; typical range 11·7–15·5). The patient had been found to have hepatitis C genotype 3 but was temporarily lost to follow-up.
On examination, we found the patient to be generally well but lethargic; she was thin with a BMI of 13·9 kg/m2 (typical range 18·5–25·0). She had bilateral upper and lower palpebral oedema (figure 1) and diminished visual acuity. Oedema was noted also in the face and lips; but despite slight distal lower extremity hyperalgesia and uncertainty of balance and side steps in tandem walk, there were no other abnormalities found.Fundoscopic examination showed abundant pale dots around the maculae and peripherally in the retinae (figure 2) indicating a crystal retinopathy; optical coherence tomography confirmed the diagnosis showing numerous retinal white dots, oedema of both fovea, and submacular cysts (figure 2).Laboratory investigations found that both the anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 8·2 g/dL) and the elevated ESR (129 mm/h) persisted. A comprehensive metabolic panel—which included tests for plasma C-reactive protein concentration, sodium concentration, potassium concentration, creatinine concentration, calcium concentration, glucose concentration, alanine aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, thromboplastin time, amylase, cortisol, free thyroxine, thyroid stimulating hormone, angiotensin converting enzyme, and immunoglobulin subclass analysis—and urinalysis found no abnormalities. Tests for infectious mononucleosis and HIV were negative; plasma albumin was 31 g/L (normal range 36–48) and prealbumin 0·13 g/L (normal range 0·23–0·37).
18fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT of the whole body showed no signs of systemic disease, infection, or cancer. An electrocardiogram showed inverted T waves in the anterior leads; an echocardiogram showed mild enlargement of the right heart with a small pericardial effusion. Systolic flattening of the interventricular septum was present. Trace tricuspid regurgitation was seen. Right heart catheterisation confirmed precapillary pulmonary hypertension.
Histopathological analysis of a sample of a bone marrow biopsy showed abundant foamy macrophage infiltration characterised by clear cytoplasm (figure 2); additionally, histiocytes in the bone marrow contained dark pigmented fragments—consistent with titanium deposits that can be associated with intravenous substance use. Furthermore, serum chitotriosidase activity was elevated (1036 nmol/h per mL; typical range 0–195), indicating possible increased macrophage activity or any of several lysosomal storage disorders. Neuropsychiatric assessment showed the patient had impairments of both short-term memory and executive functioning.
Brain MRI with contrast showed diffuse dural thickening and enhancement without any focal pathology of the brain (figure 2). Histopathologic examination of a sample obtained from dural biopsy indicated clusters of CD68-positive macrophages (figure 2); analyses of samples of biopsies from the skin and of biopsies obtained during a gastroscopy were normal.
At this stage our working diagnoses included chronic hepatitis C, severe protein energy malnutrition, secondary pulmonary hypertension, talc retinopathy, secondary histiocytosis, pachymeningitis, amyloidosis, and IgG4 disease.
Whole exome sequencing ruled out inherited causes of primary or secondary histiocytosis. On closer questioning, the patient said she had been intravenously injecting methylphenidate hydrochloride by dissolving the core of the tablets in water. Methylphenidate tablets contain titanium and high molecular weight polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) as an adjuvant—a substance associated with histiocytosis when used parenterally. A diagnosis of PVP histiocytosis was made. The patient was counselled and informed of the diagnosis and advised to avoid intravenous substance use. At follow-up 1 year later, she was more alert than before, and her appetite had improved; ESR had decreased ranging from 26 mm/h to 38 mm/h suggesting discontinuation of active intravenous substance use.
Bilateral swelling of the eyelids or periorbital oedema can be caused by nephrotic syndrome, thyroid eye disease, systemic infections such as mononucleosis, atopic or allergic swelling, sarcoidosis, dermatomyositis, lymphoma, IgG4 disease, and various histiocytoses. PVP is widely used in prescription drugs. Moderate and high molecular weight PVP is only used in oral preparations; when used intravenously patients may have renal insufficiency, anaemia, pathological fractures, and abdominal complaints. PVP can be deposited in most organs leading to severe dysfunction. Earlier intravenous abuse of oral PVP containing buprenorphine and methadone preparations, for maintenance therapy for opioid dependence, has been reported to cause severe, and even lethal PVP histiocytosis.

A 26-year-old woman with a 2-year history of swelling of her eyelids and reduced vision was referred to our clinic by an ophthalmologist because of increased myopia, decreased visual acuity, scattered pale dots of the maculae, and suspected angioedema.
The patient had been diagnosed with attention deficit disorder and had been prescribed methylphenidate since adolescence. 5 years before we saw her, she reported having occasional episodes of dizziness thought to be caused by anaemia—investigations at that stage had found an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR; 134 mm/h; typical rate 0–20) and a normocytic anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 9·5 g/dL; typical range 11·7–15·5). The patient had been found to have hepatitis C genotype 3 but was temporarily lost to follow-up.
On examination, we found the patient to be generally well but lethargic; she was thin with a BMI of 13·9 kg/m2 (typical range 18·5–25·0). She had bilateral upper and lower palpebral oedema (figure 1) and diminished visual acuity. Oedema was noted also in the face and lips; but despite slight distal lower extremity hyperalgesia and uncertainty of balance and side steps in tandem walk, there were no other abnormalities found.Fundoscopic examination showed abundant pale dots around the maculae and peripherally in the retinae (figure 2) indicating a crystal retinopathy; optical coherence tomography confirmed the diagnosis showing numerous retinal white dots, oedema of both fovea, and submacular cysts (figure 2).Laboratory investigations found that both the anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 8·2 g/dL) and the elevated ESR (129 mm/h) persisted. A comprehensive metabolic panel—which included tests for plasma C-reactive protein concentration, sodium concentration, potassium concentration, creatinine concentration, calcium concentration, glucose concentration, alanine aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, thromboplastin time, amylase, cortisol, free thyroxine, thyroid stimulating hormone, angiotensin converting enzyme, and immunoglobulin subclass analysis—and urinalysis found no abnormalities. Tests for infectious mononucleosis and HIV were negative; plasma albumin was 31 g/L (normal range 36–48) and prealbumin 0·13 g/L (normal range 0·23–0·37).
18fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT of the whole body showed no signs of systemic disease, infection, or cancer. An electrocardiogram showed inverted T waves in the anterior leads; an echocardiogram showed mild enlargement of the right heart with a small pericardial effusion. Systolic flattening of the interventricular septum was present. Trace tricuspid regurgitation was seen. Right heart catheterisation confirmed precapillary pulmonary hypertension.
Histopathological analysis of a sample of a bone marrow biopsy showed abundant foamy macrophage infiltration characterised by clear cytoplasm (figure 2); additionally, histiocytes in the bone marrow contained dark pigmented fragments—consistent with titanium deposits that can be associated with intravenous substance use. Furthermore, serum chitotriosidase activity was elevated (1036 nmol/h per mL; typical range 0–195), indicating possible increased macrophage activity or any of several lysosomal storage disorders. Neuropsychiatric assessment showed the patient had impairments of both short-term memory and executive functioning.
Brain MRI with contrast showed diffuse dural thickening and enhancement without any focal pathology of the brain (figure 2). Histopathologic examination of a sample obtained from dural biopsy indicated clusters of CD68-positive macrophages (figure 2); analyses of samples of biopsies from the skin and of biopsies obtained during a gastroscopy were normal.

Whole exome sequencing ruled out inherited causes of primary or secondary histiocytosis. On closer questioning, the patient said she had been intravenously injecting methylphenidate hydrochloride by dissolving the core of the tablets in water. Methylphenidate tablets contain titanium and high molecular weight polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) as an adjuvant—a substance associated with histiocytosis when used parenterally. A diagnosis of PVP histiocytosis was made. The patient was counselled and informed of the diagnosis and advised to avoid intravenous substance use. At follow-up 1 year later, she was more alert than before, and her appetite had improved; ESR had decreased ranging from 26 mm/h to 38 mm/h suggesting discontinuation of active intravenous substance use.

PVP is widely used in prescription drugs. Moderate and high molecular weight PVP is only used in oral preparations; when used intravenously patients may have renal insufficiency, anaemia, pathological fractures, and abdominal complaints. PVP can be deposited in most organs leading to severe dysfunction. Earlier intravenous abuse of oral PVP containing buprenorphine and methadone preparations, for maintenance therapy for opioid dependence, has been reported to cause severe, and even lethal PVP histiocytosis.

The patient's medical history was unremarkable apart from a cholelithiasis-related cholecystectomy which had been done 12 years earlier.On examination, we found the patient to be generally well; her pulse was 75 beats per min and blood pressure 145/80 mm Hg. She was febrile with a temperature of 38·0°C; she had diffuse left-sided abdominal tenderness.
Laboratory investigations found a mildly elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration of 16 mg/dL (normal <6) and a raised white blood cell (WBC) count of 12·6 × 109 per L (normal range 4–11); carcinoembryonic antigen concentration was within normal range (1·2 ng/mL; typical value for non-smoker or ex-smoker <3·8 and for smokers <5·5).
A CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed a 3·3 cm × 2·8 cm × 8·0 cm intramural peripherally enhancing hypodense lesion together with pericolic fat stranding and haziness which had caused mild upstream large bowel distention—we presumed it was an abscess in the large bowel wall; features—colonic wall outpouchings—consistent with a diagnosis of acute diverticulitis were also seen (figure). Importantly, no extraluminal air was seen. Considering the patient's clinical condition, particularly the absence of signs of peritonitis, we decided to manage her conservatively; she was started on intravenous fluids and treated empirically with piperacillin and tazobactam. Over the next few days, the patient's symptoms improved; her temperature, WBC count, and CRP concentration reduced. A repeat CT scan 7 days after admission showed almost complete resolution of original findings—indicating spontaneous resolution of the abscess and further confirming the initial diagnosis (figure). The patient was allowed home 8 days after admission and prescribed oral antimicrobial treatment (ciprofloxacin and metronidazole).
6 weeks later, an outpatient colonoscopy showed mild residual stenosis at the site of the previous intramural abscess with no other abnormalities; the patient reported no symptoms or difficulty passing faeces.
Abscesses complicate 15–30% of acute diverticulitis cases; intramural lesions are infrequently reported. Secondary partial intestinal obstruction may occur, but severe obstruction is rare. In most cases, abscesses spontaneously resolve. Conservative treatment is favoured in smaller-sized abscesses (<3–4 cm); further intervention may be needed for larger ones.
The treatment approach depends upon abscess location and the overall medical condition of the patient; conservative management is preferable. The differential diagnosis of such a lesion should include various types of colitis-related abscesses, inflammatory bowel disease, contained perforations, infected enteric duplication cysts, and, most significantly, colon cancer. Importantly, in patients with radiologically confirmed acute diverticulitis, colonic cancer has been found to have a 1-year incidence rate ranging from 1·6% to 2·7%. To exclude an underlying colonic malignancy, patients with acute diverticulitis are advised to undergo colonoscopy approximately 6–8 weeks following their episode.

A 60-year-old woman presented to our emergency department with a 4-day history of mild, diffuse abdominal pain and discomfort in her abdomen. The patient's medical history was unremarkable apart from a cholelithiasis-related cholecystectomy which had been done 12 years earlier.On examination, we found the patient to be generally well; her pulse was 75 beats per min and blood pressure 145/80 mm Hg. She was febrile with a temperature of 38·0°C; she had diffuse left-sided abdominal tenderness.
Laboratory investigations found a mildly elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration of 16 mg/dL (normal <6) and a raised white blood cell (WBC) count of 12·6 × 109 per L (normal range 4–11); carcinoembryonic antigen concentration was within normal range (1·2 ng/mL; typical value for non-smoker or ex-smoker <3·8 and for smokers <5·5).
A CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed a 3·3 cm × 2·8 cm × 8·0 cm intramural peripherally enhancing hypodense lesion together with pericolic fat stranding and haziness which had caused mild upstream large bowel distention—we presumed it was an abscess in the large bowel wall; features—colonic wall outpouchings—consistent with a diagnosis of acute diverticulitis were also seen (figure). Importantly, no extraluminal air was seen. Considering the patient's clinical condition, particularly the absence of signs of peritonitis, we decided to manage her conservatively; she was started on intravenous fluids and treated empirically with piperacillin and tazobactam. Over the next few days, the patient's symptoms improved; her temperature, WBC count, and CRP concentration reduced. A repeat CT scan 7 days after admission showed almost complete resolution of original findings—indicating spontaneous resolution of the abscess and further confirming the initial diagnosis (figure). The patient was allowed home 8 days after admission and prescribed oral antimicrobial treatment (ciprofloxacin and metronidazole).
6 weeks later, an outpatient colonoscopy showed mild residual stenosis at the site of the previous intramural abscess with no other abnormalities; the patient reported no symptoms or difficulty passing faeces.
Abscesses complicate 15–30% of acute diverticulitis cases; intramural lesions are infrequently reported. Secondary partial intestinal obstruction may occur, but severe obstruction is rare. In most cases, abscesses spontaneously resolve. Conservative treatment is favoured in smaller-sized abscesses (<3–4 cm); further intervention may be needed for larger ones.
The treatment approach depends upon abscess location and the overall medical condition of the patient; conservative management is preferable. The differential diagnosis of such a lesion should include various types of colitis-related abscesses, inflammatory bowel disease, contained perforations, infected enteric duplication cysts, and, most significantly, colon cancer. Importantly, in patients with radiologically confirmed acute diverticulitis, colonic cancer has been found to have a 1-year incidence rate ranging from 1·6% to 2·7%. To exclude an underlying colonic malignancy, patients with acute diverticulitis are advised to undergo colonoscopy approximately 6–8 weeks following their episode.

Early pericardiectomy is strongly encouraged in patients suspected of having tuberculous pericarditis with massive calcification, before signs of cardiac tamponade occur.

input: A 48-year-old man was referred to our institution because of shortness of breath and symptoms related to right ventricular dysfunction. His medical history included tuberculosis as a child. Chest radiography showed a calcific ring located at the heart base. Transthoracic echocardiography showed signs of cardiac tamponade. High resolution CT scan showed the calcific ring at the cardiac base reproducing “el corazón espinado” (the sacred heart wrapped in thorns), with incomplete compression at the level of the inferior vena cava. The patient underwent successful pericardectomy (removal of the pericardium). Despite repeated attempts, the diaphragmatic layer of the calcified pericardium was not removed, because of deep penetration of the calcification inside the myocardium of the inferior right and left ventricles. Histology confirmed the tuberculous cause. Chronic calcific pericarditis is an uncommon form of pericardial inflammation. The cause is idiopathic in most cases; tuberculosis is the second most common cause of this syndrome. Pericardial calcifications occur in nearly half the people affected by chronic pericarditis and are often indicative of infective origin. Early pericardiectomy is strongly encouraged in patients suspected of having tuberculous pericarditis with massive calcification, before signs of cardiac tamponade occur.

A 64-year-old man presented with high fever (38–39°C oral temperature), severe joint pains with explosive onset, and substantial weight loss (4 kg in 1 month). On examination, he had dorsal oedema on the hands (figure) and symmetrically tender and swollen joints (ie, proximal interphalangeal joints, metacarpophalangeal joints, wrists, elbows, and knees). Additionally, he had generalised lymphadenopathy (bilateral upper cervical, left lower cervical, right supraclavicular, bilateral inguinal) and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory investigations were notable for anaemia (haemoglobin 8 g/dL), hypoalbuminaemia (2·8 g/dL), hyperglobulinaemia (5·2 g/dL), increased erythrocyte sedimentation (35 mm/h), and increased concentrations of C-reactive protein (11·3 mg/dL). Tests for antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and anticyclic citrullinated peptide were negative. PET scanning with 18-fluorodeoxyglucose showed avid lymph nodes on both sides of the diaphragm and uptake in both shoulders and the right wrist (figure). A cervical lymph node was excised for haematoxylin and eosin staining that showed architectural effacement by lymphoid cells (positive for PD-1 and CD3) surrounding an arborising network of high endothelial venules, which was suggestive of angio-immunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (figure). The patient was transferred to the haematology unit where chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (known as the CHOP regimen) was initiated, which resolved the fever and arthritis.Many aetiologies can cause fever with polyarthritis: infections (viral infections, infective endocarditis, Lyme disease), para-infections (rheumatic fever, reactive arthritis), true arthritis (adult-onset Still's disease), connective-tissue diseases (systemic lupus erythematosus), vasculitis (giant-cell arteritis, ANCA-associated vasculitis), and paraneoplastic arthritis. Paraneoplastic arthritis is arthritis secondary to solid-organ (particularly carcinomas) or lympho-reticular malignancy, which is not due to direct tumour infiltration. Important clues for paraneoplastic arthritis include advanced age, explosive onset, severe pain disproportionate to the pathological findings on examination, unresponsiveness to disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), substantial weight loss, highly increased acute-phase reactants, and seronegativity for rheumatoid factor, anticyclic citrullinated peptide, and antinuclear antibodies. Specific patterns such as asymmetric arthritis, lower-limb predominance, sparing of small joints, palmar fasciitis, and remitting seronegative symmetric synovitis with pitting oedema should alert the clinician to investigate for an underlying malignancy.
In this man's case, the underlying malignancy was angio-immunoblastic T-cell lymphoma. Although an uncommon non-Hodgkin lymphoma overall (1–2% of all patients diagnosed with lymphoma globally), it is common in patients with peripheral T-cell lymphomas (18% prevalence) and typically occurs in older people (median age 65 years). Angio-immunoblastic T-cell lymphoma is notorious for immune-activation features such as rash, arthritis, cytopenia, polychondritis, hypergammaglobulinaemia, and even positive autoantibodies. These symptoms are thought to be secondary to increased serum concentrations of pro-inflammatory cytokines, notably TNFα and interleukin-6 secreted by the tumour cells. The case highlights the importance of clues such as disease onset at an older age, explosive-onset joint pain, weight loss, and a thorough general examination (to detect lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly) to make an accurate diagnosis of paraneoplastic arthritis.

input:
A 64-year-old man presented with high fever (38–39°C oral temperature), severe joint pains with explosive onset, and substantial weight loss (4 kg in 1 month). On examination, he had dorsal oedema on the hands (figure) and symmetrically tender and swollen joints (ie, proximal interphalangeal joints, metacarpophalangeal joints, wrists, elbows, and knees). Additionally, he had generalised lymphadenopathy (bilateral upper cervical, left lower cervical, right supraclavicular, bilateral inguinal) and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory investigations were notable for anaemia (haemoglobin 8 g/dL), hypoalbuminaemia (2·8 g/dL), hyperglobulinaemia (5·2 g/dL), increased erythrocyte sedimentation (35 mm/h), and increased concentrations of C-reactive protein (11·3 mg/dL). Tests for antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and anticyclic citrullinated peptide were negative. PET scanning with 18-fluorodeoxyglucose showed avid lymph nodes on both sides of the diaphragm and uptake in both shoulders and the right wrist (figure). A cervical lymph node was excised for haematoxylin and eosin staining that showed architectural effacement by lymphoid cells (positive for PD-1 and CD3) surrounding an arborising network of high endothelial venules, which was suggestive of angio-immunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (figure). The patient was transferred to the haematology unit where chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (known as the CHOP regimen) was initiated, which resolved the fever and arthritis.Many aetiologies can cause fever with polyarthritis: infections (viral infections, infective endocarditis, Lyme disease), para-infections (rheumatic fever, reactive arthritis), true arthritis (adult-onset Still's disease), connective-tissue diseases (systemic lupus erythematosus), vasculitis (giant-cell arteritis, ANCA-associated vasculitis), and paraneoplastic arthritis. Paraneoplastic arthritis is arthritis secondary to solid-organ (particularly carcinomas) or lympho-reticular malignancy, which is not due to direct tumour infiltration. Important clues for paraneoplastic arthritis include advanced age, explosive onset, severe pain disproportionate to the pathological findings on examination, unresponsiveness to disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), substantial weight loss, highly increased acute-phase reactants, and seronegativity for rheumatoid factor, anticyclic citrullinated peptide, and antinuclear antibodies. Specific patterns such as asymmetric arthritis, lower-limb predominance, sparing of small joints, palmar fasciitis, and remitting seronegative symmetric synovitis with pitting oedema should alert the clinician to investigate for an underlying malignancy.
In this man's case, the underlying malignancy was angio-immunoblastic T-cell lymphoma. Although an uncommon non-Hodgkin lymphoma overall (1–2% of all patients diagnosed with lymphoma globally), it is common in patients with peripheral T-cell lymphomas (18% prevalence) and typically occurs in older people (median age 65 years). Angio-immunoblastic T-cell lymphoma is notorious for immune-activation features such as rash, arthritis, cytopenia, polychondritis, hypergammaglobulinaemia, and even positive autoantibodies. These symptoms are thought to be secondary to increased serum concentrations of pro-inflammatory cytokines, notably TNFα and interleukin-6 secreted by the tumour cells. The case highlights the importance of clues such as disease onset at an older age, explosive-onset joint pain, weight loss, and a thorough general examination (to detect lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly) to make an accurate diagnosis of paraneoplastic arthritis.

A 46-year-old woman attended our emergency department reporting a 3-month history of dyspnoea and, in the last 2 weeks, lower limb oedema. The patient had a history of rheumatoid arthritis, which had been diagnosed 13 years before, and had been treated with oral hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice a day. 1 year earlier, she had presented with syncope; an electrocardiogram (ECG) had showed paroxysmal third-degree atrioventricular block, and a dual-chamber pacemaker had been fitted. An echocardiogram had shown normal biventricular systolic function and mild to moderate left ventricular hypertrophy with an interventricular septum diameter of 13 mm (normal range 6–9); no further investigations were done.
On examination, at our hospital, the patient was generally unwell; her blood pressure was 80/40 mm Hg, she had peripheral oedema, jugular venous distension, pulmonary crackles, and cold extremities. An ECG showed atrial fibrillation with ventricular pacing at 69 beats per min (appendix). Laboratory tests showed a significantly raised N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide concentration of 31 255 ng/L (normal range 0–86) and high-sensitivity cardiac troponin concentration of 543 ng/L (normal range 0–14); and signs of hepatic injury with alanine aminotransferase concentration of 126 U/L (normal range 3–45), aspartate aminotransferase concentration of 92 U/L (normal range 0–40), total bilirubin concentration of 2·51 mg/dL (normal range 0·25–1). Echocardiography showed severe biventricular systolic dysfunction—left ventricular ejection fraction of 20%—and a restrictive filling pattern. Severe concentric hypertrophy was evident with an interventricular septum diameter of 17 mm and heterogeneous myocardial texture (figure).
The differential diagnoses we considered included inflammatory and infiltrative cardiomyopathies—specifically reactive systemic (AA) amyloidosis related to the long-lasting autoimmune disorder—or a hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy.
Inotropic support was immediately started, the hydroxychloroquine was discontinued, and the patient was admitted to our intensive care unit. Despite all these measures, 3 days after admission, the patient developed cardiogenic shock and required haemodynamic support with venous-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.
An endomyocardial biopsy was done with the patient on temporary mechanical support; we hoped the results would inform ongoing treatment. Histopathological examination of a sample obtained at biopsy showed vacuolisation of multiple cardiomyocytes with no inflammatory infiltrate; no amyloid was found (figure). Transmission electron microscopy showed lamellar lysosomal structures—myeloid bodies—and curvilinear inclusions consistent with drug-induced myocardial toxicity. Considering these classic findings, a diagnosis of hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy was made.
8 days after admission, despite maximal pharmacological and mechanical support, the patient died due to refractory cardiogenic shock while heart transplantation screening was ongoing. The results of metabolic testing, available after the patient's death, showed no evidence of lysosomal storage disorders—including Fabry's disease and mucopolysaccharidoses. Additionally, the heart post-mortem showed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy: septal thickness 16 mm (normal value 13·6 mm [SD 2·0 mm]) and an increased thickness of the right ventricle free wall of 8 mm (normal value 3·8 mm [SD 0·9 mm]). The cardiac mass was also increased (weight 500 g; typical range 190–360; figure).
Chronic use of hydroxychloroquine can result in a drug-induced cardiomyopathy characterised by concentric hypertrophy and conduction abnormalities. Early clinical suspicion is essential, since the condition is potentially reversible. Delay in discontinuation of the drug may not improve the pathology, especially in patients—as in this case—with advanced heart failure.

An echocardiogram had shown normal biventricular systolic function and mild to moderate left ventricular hypertrophy with an interventricular septum diameter of 13 mm (normal range 6–9); no further investigations were done.
On examination, at our hospital, the patient was generally unwell; her blood pressure was 80/40 mm Hg, she had peripheral oedema, jugular venous distension, pulmonary crackles, and cold extremities. An ECG showed atrial fibrillation with ventricular pacing at 69 beats per min (appendix). Laboratory tests showed a significantly raised N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide concentration of 31 255 ng/L (normal range 0–86) and high-sensitivity cardiac troponin concentration of 543 ng/L (normal range 0–14); and signs of hepatic injury with alanine aminotransferase concentration of 126 U/L (normal range 3–45), aspartate aminotransferase concentration of 92 U/L (normal range 0–40), total bilirubin concentration of 2·51 mg/dL (normal range 0·25–1). Echocardiography showed severe biventricular systolic dysfunction—left ventricular ejection fraction of 20%—and a restrictive filling pattern. Severe concentric hypertrophy was evident with an interventricular septum diameter of 17 mm and heterogeneous myocardial texture (figure).
The differential diagnoses we considered included inflammatory and infiltrative cardiomyopathies—specifically reactive systemic (AA) amyloidosis related to the long-lasting autoimmune disorder—or a hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy.
Inotropic support was immediately started, the hydroxychloroquine was discontinued, and the patient was admitted to our intensive care unit. Despite all these measures, 3 days after admission, the patient developed cardiogenic shock and required haemodynamic support with venous-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.
An endomyocardial biopsy was done with the patient on temporary mechanical support; we hoped the results would inform ongoing treatment. Histopathological examination of a sample obtained at biopsy showed vacuolisation of multiple cardiomyocytes with no inflammatory infiltrate; no amyloid was found (figure). Transmission electron microscopy showed lamellar lysosomal structures—myeloid bodies—and curvilinear inclusions consistent with drug-induced myocardial toxicity. Considering these classic findings, a diagnosis of hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy was made.
8 days after admission, despite maximal pharmacological and mechanical support, the patient died due to refractory cardiogenic shock while heart transplantation screening was ongoing. The results of metabolic testing, available after the patient's death, showed no evidence of lysosomal storage disorders—including Fabry's disease and mucopolysaccharidoses. A 64-year-old woman presented to our hospital with abdominal pain, chronic constipation, muscle cramps, mood changes, and fatigue. She said the problems had been present for many years.The patient had recently been diagnosed with osteoporosis—using dual energy x-ray absorptiometry bone mineral density (BMD) T scores at the spine, hip, and distal radius were –3·1, –1·5, and –3·3, respectively—defined as BMD T score of –2·5 or less.
A physical examination was unremarkable, but laboratory investigations showed hypercalcaemia with a calcium concentration of 3·18 mmol/L (normal 2·15–2·55) and an elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) concentration of 323·7 pg/mL (normal 10·0–65·0). Subsequently, after correction of vitamin D deficiency, which had been 21 ng/mL (normal 30–100) and improved to 45 ng/mL, to rule out a potential secondary hyperparathyroidism, we made a diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism. Additionally, because of a history of possible brain calcifications we did a CT scan of the patient's head which showed diffuse calvarial thickening (figure; appendix), a finding known to occur in hyperparathyroidism—more commonly in secondary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism of renal failure—and presumed to be an effect of chronically elevated PTH levels on osteogenic progenitor cells in the intramembranous calvarial bone.
The patient then had explorative surgery in her neck during which a single hyperplastic parathyroid gland was identified and removed.
She had normal calcium and PTH concentration in the time after the operation; 2 years after surgery her BMD T scores at the spine and distal radius had improved to –2·4 and –3·0, respectively; the hip T-score remained the same at –1·5. Additionally, during this postoperative time, the patient was only taking daily vitamin D and calcium supplementation as needed.
The binding of PTH to its receptor activates and increases intracellular cAMP levels; although continuously elevated PTH has a catabolic effect on appendicular bone—as evidenced by our patient's osteoporosis—it can have a proliferative, expansile effect on calvarial bones.
The x-ray findings described in this case are similar to patients with other conditions with either elevated PTH or cAMP signalling: firstly, pseudohypoparathyroidism (figure; appendix)—where renal PTH resistance at the kidney, but not the bone, leads to compensatory elevated PTH blood levels; secondly, treatment of hypoparathyroidism with pharmacologic doses of PTH (figure; appendix); and finally, fibrous dysplasia—which is caused by gain-of-function mutations in the Gαs protein immediately downstream of PTH and associated with increased intracellular cAMP signalling (figure; appendix).
The unifying pathophysiology of these conditions—increased cAMP signalling in intramembranous bones—highlights the different effects of PTH signalling on various skeletal compartments.

**Pathophysiology:**

| Bone Type | PTH Effect | Mechanism |
|-----------|------------|-----------|
| Appendicular (endochondral) | Catabolic | Continuous PTH stimulates RANKL, activates osteoclasts, net bone loss |

A 64-year-old woman presented to our hospital with abdominal pain, chronic constipation, muscle cramps, mood changes, and fatigue. She said the problems had been present for many years.The patient had recently been diagnosed with osteoporosis—using dual energy x-ray absorptiometry bone mineral density (BMD) T scores at the spine, hip, and distal radius were –3·1, –1·5, and –3·3, respectively—defined as BMD T score of –2·5 or less.
A physical examination was unremarkable, but laboratory investigations showed hypercalcaemia with a calcium concentration of 3·18 mmol/L (normal 2·15–2·55) and an elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) concentration of 323·7 pg/mL (normal 10·0–65·0). Subsequently, after correction of vitamin D deficiency, which had been 21 ng/mL (normal 30–100) and improved to 45 ng/mL, to rule out a potential secondary hyperparathyroidism, we made a diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism. Additionally, because of a history of possible brain calcifications we did a CT scan of the patient's head which showed diffuse calvarial thickening (figure; appendix), a finding known to occur in hyperparathyroidism—more commonly in secondary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism of renal failure—and presumed to be an effect of chronically elevated PTH levels on osteogenic progenitor cells in the intramembranous calvarial bone.
The patient then had explorative surgery in her neck during which a single hyperplastic parathyroid gland was identified and removed.
She had normal calcium and PTH concentration in the time after the operation; 2 years after surgery her BMD T scores at the spine and distal radius had improved to –2·4 and –3·0, respectively; the hip T-score remained the same at –1·5. Additionally, during this postoperative time, the patient was only taking daily vitamin D and calcium supplementation as needed.
The binding of PTH to its receptor activates and increases intracellular cAMP levels; although continuously elevated PTH has a catabolic effect on appendicular bone—as evidenced by our patient's osteoporosis—it can have a proliferative, expansile effect on calvarial bones.
The x-ray findings described in this case are similar to patients with other conditions with either elevated PTH or cAMP signalling: firstly, pseudohypoparathyroidism (figure; appendix)—where renal PTH resistance at the kidney, but not the bone, leads to compensatory elevated PTH blood levels; secondly, treatment of hypoparathyroidism with pharmacologic doses of PTH (figure; appendix); and finally, fibrous dysplasia—which is caused by gain-of-function mutations in the Gαs protein immediately downstream of PTH and associated with increased intracellular cAMP signalling (figure; appendix).
The unifying pathophysiology of these conditions—increased cAMP signalling in intramembranous bones—highlights the different effects of PTH signalling on various skeletal compartments.
Recognising these radiological findings may alert clinicians to consider the different diagnoses when these images are incidentally observed—especially given the expanding use of parathyroid hormone analogues for the management of osteoporosis and hypoparathyroidism, which may increase the incidence of such x-ray images (video).

input:
A 64-year-old woman presented to our hospital with abdominal pain, chronic constipation, muscle cramps, mood changes, and fatigue. She said the problems had been present for many years.The patient had recently been diagnosed with osteoporosis—using dual energy x-ray absorptiometry bone mineral density (BMD) T scores at the spine, hip, and distal radius were –3·1, –1·5, and –3·3, respectively—defined as BMD T score of –2·5 or less.
A physical examination was unremarkable, but laboratory investigations showed hypercalcaemia with a calcium concentration of 3·18 mmol/L (normal 2·15–2·55) and an elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) concentration of 323·7 pg/mL (normal 10·0–65·0). Subsequently, after correction of vitamin D deficiency, which had been 21 ng/mL (normal 30–100) and improved to 45 ng/mL, to rule out a potential secondary hyperparathyroidism, we made a diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism. Additionally, because of a history of possible brain calcifications we did a CT scan of the patient's head which showed diffuse calvarial thickening (figure; appendix), a finding known to occur in hyperparathyroidism—more commonly in secondary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism of renal failure—and presumed to be an effect of chronically elevated PTH levels on osteogenic progenitor cells in the intramembranous calvarial bone.
The patient then had explorative surgery in her neck during which a single hyperplastic parathyroid gland was identified and removed.
She had normal calcium and PTH concentration in the time after the operation; 2 years after surgery her BMD T scores at the spine and distal radius had improved to –2·4 and –3·0, respectively; the hip T-score remained the same at –1·5. Additionally, during this postoperative time, the patient was only taking daily vitamin D and calcium supplementation as needed.
The binding of PTH to its receptor activates and increases intracellular cAMP levels; although continuously elevated PTH has a catabolic effect on appendicular bone—as evidenced by our patient's osteoporosis—it can have a proliferative, expansile effect on calvarial bones.
The x-ray findings described in this case are similar to patients with other conditions with either elevated PTH or cAMP signalling: firstly, pseudohypoparathyroidism (figure; appendix)—where renal PTH resistance at the kidney, but not the bone, leads to compensatory elevated PTH blood levels; secondly, treatment of hypoparathyroidism with pharmacologic doses of PTH (figure; appendix); and finally, fibrous dysplasia—which is caused by gain-of-function mutations in the Gαs protein immediately downstream of PTH and associated with increased intracellular cAMP signalling (figure; appendix).
The unifying pathophysiology of these conditions—increased cAMP signalling in intramembranous bones—highlights the different effects of PTH signalling on various skeletal compartments.
Recognising these radiological findings may alert clinicians to consider the different diagnoses when these images are incidentally observed—especially given the expanding use of parathyroid hormone analogues for the management of osteoporosis and hypoparathyroidism, which may increase the incidence of such x-ray images (video).

input: A 60-year-old Japanese man was referred to our hospital because of an abnormal endoscopic finding in the oesophagus at a regular health check. He reported receiving no medication and had no history of alcohol misuse. The patient was a former smoker and reported sometimes feeling heartburn. Laboratory data revealed no pronounced abnormalities. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed short segment Barrett's oesophagus and a whitish elevated lesion adjacent to the Barrett's oesophagus lesion (figure, A). Vessel structures could not be seen by magnified narrow band imaging, because of a whitish plaque (figure, B). Chromoendoscopy with Lugol's iodine solution showed decreased staining of the lesion (figure, C). A biopsy was done, and histology confirmed cell proliferation of the squamous epithelium. Although cellular atypicality was mild, we considered the lesion to be potentially malignant. Therefore, an endoscopic submucosal dissection was done for an en-bloc complete resection and diagnosis. Histology showed papillary growth and nests of well differentiated squamous epithelium pushing into the underlying stroma, which is typical of oesophageal verrucous carcinoma (figure, D). Pathological examination revealed tumour depth invasion into the lamina propria mucosa (stage T1a) without lymphovascular invasion. The patient was monitored closely and no recurrence had occurred at 3 months after the endoscopic submucosal dissection.Oesophageal verrucous carcinoma is a very rare malignancy. Although, the cause of such lesions is debated, it has been suggested that oesophageal verrucous carcinoma is associated with achalasia, acid reflux, and alcohol and nicotine misuse. The common endoscopic appearance of most oesophageal verrucous carcinomas is an elevated whitish plaque that is clearly circumscribed. Oesophageal verrucous carcinomas are difficult to diagnose before surgical resection. Accurate diagnosis is often delayed because the endoscopic finding of a whitish plaque is similar to a Candida infection and squamous cell papilloma. In addition, superficial biopsies are frequently false negative for malignancy because of highly differentiated histology. Endoscopic resection can be curative for oesophageal verrucous carcinoma restricted to the epithelium and the lamina propria mucosa. A lack of recognition of oesophageal verrucous carcinoma leads to a delay in diagnosis and progression of the disease. To improve the chance of curative treatment, endoscopists need to recognise the macroscopic findings and frequent difficulties associated with diagnosis of oesophageal verrucous carcinoma.

Chromoendoscopy with Lugol's iodine solution showed decreased staining of the lesion (figure, C). A biopsy was done, and histology confirmed cell proliferation of the squamous epithelium. Although cellular atypicality was mild, we considered the lesion to be potentially malignant. Therefore, an endoscopic submucosal dissection was done for an en-bloc complete resection and diagnosis. Histology showed papillary growth and nests of well differentiated squamous epithelium pushing into the underlying stroma, which is typical of oesophageal verrucous carcinoma (figure, D). Pathological examination revealed tumour depth invasion into the lamina propria mucosa (stage T1a) without lymphovascular invasion. Although, the cause of such lesions is debated, it has been suggested that oesophageal verrucous carcinoma is associated with achalasia, acid reflux, and alcohol and nicotine misuse. The common endoscopic appearance of most oesophageal verrucous carcinomas is an elevated whitish plaque that is clearly circumscribed. Oesophageal verrucous carcinomas are difficult to diagnose before surgical resection. Accurate diagnosis is often delayed because the endoscopic finding of a whitish plaque is similar to a Candida infection and squamous cell papilloma. In addition, superficial biopsies are frequently false negative for malignancy because of highly differentiated histology. Endoscopic resection can be curative for oesophageal verrucous carcinoma restricted to the epithelium and the lamina propria mucosa. A lack of recognition of oesophageal verrucous carcinoma leads to a delay in diagnosis and progression of the disease. A 43-year-old man who developed numbness and impaired fine motor skills in his left arm lasting approximately 10 min while chanting during a football match, attended our emergency room. The patient, who was visiting Germany for the UEFA European Football Championship, explained that the problems started at the end of the first half. He said he had been chanting continuously during the game. Despite complete resolution of the symptoms, he was concerned enough to seek help, and at half-time he came to our hospital by ambulance. We decided to admit him to our stroke unit for further investigations. He had no medical history; he said he had consumed a moderate amount of alcohol. He was a non-smoker.
On examination the patient was generally fit and well; his pulse was 92 beats per min, blood pressure was 140/90 mm Hg, and his oxygen saturation was 94%. Physical examination found no abnormalities.
Laboratory investigations showed a mildly elevated LDL cholesterol (142 mg/dL; normal range <115). A coagulopathy was excluded: clotting factors II and V were within normal range, tests for antiphospholipid syndrome were negative, antithrombin III activity was in normal range, and protein S and C levels were normal. The patient's homocysteine serum concentration was slightly elevated (15 μmol/L; typical range 3·7–13·9), genotyping found the wild-type variant of the MTHFR gene.
MRI showed a small acute embolic ischaemic lesion in the postcentral gyrus of the right hemisphere (figure 1); doppler and duplex sonography of extracranial and intracranial vessels and multimodal imaging—including magnetic resonance angiography—ruled out any atherosclerotic plaques, dissection, or vasculitis (figure 1). Electrocardiogram monitoring during more than 72 h of telemetry found no abnormalities.
Transoesophageal echocardiography showed a patent foramen ovale (PFO) with spontaneous passage of bubbles and accentuation with Valsalva manoeuvre; no septal aneurysm was seen (figure 2). Atrial size and valvular structures were normal, and no intracardiac thrombi were seen. The Risk of Paradoxical Embolism score was 8—indicating an 84% chance that a stroke is PFO-related. Venous ultrasound imaging showed no deep vein thromboses in the legs, pelvis, or vena cava. The patient left the hospital after 3 days with a prescription for an antithrombotic treatment. He took a flight back to his home country a day later.
The role of a PFO in young patients with acute ischaemic stroke has been the subject of much debate: several studies have shown PFO closure may reduce risk of recurrent strokes in young patients with cryptogenic stroke. A possible pathophysiologic mechanism is paradoxical embolism through the PFO facilitated by intrathoracic pressure elevation during pressing or coughing. We hypothesise that a paradoxical embolism in our patient was possibly provoked by continuous chanting—a provoking factor not previously reported—and we therefore advised him to avoid intensive chanting until interventional PFO closure.

A 43-year-old man who developed numbness and impaired fine motor skills in his left arm lasting approximately 10 min while chanting during a football match, attended our emergency room. The patient, who was visiting Germany for the UEFA European Football Championship, explained that the problems started at the end of the first half. He said he had been chanting continuously during the game. Despite complete resolution of the symptoms, he was concerned enough to seek help, and at half-time he came to our hospital by ambulance. We decided to admit him to our stroke unit for further investigations. He had no medical history; he said he had consumed a moderate amount of alcohol. He was a non-smoker.
On examination the patient was generally fit and well; his pulse was 92 beats per min, blood pressure was 140/90 mm Hg, and his oxygen saturation was 94%. Physical examination found no abnormalities.
Laboratory investigations showed a mildly elevated LDL cholesterol (142 mg/dL; normal range <115). A coagulopathy was excluded: clotting factors II and V were within normal range, tests for antiphospholipid syndrome were negative, antithrombin III activity was in normal range, and protein S and C levels were normal. The patient's homocysteine serum concentration was slightly elevated (15 μmol/L; typical range 3·7–13·9), genotyping found the wild-type variant of the MTHFR gene.
MRI showed a small acute embolic ischaemic lesion in the postcentral gyrus of the right hemisphere (figure 1); doppler and duplex sonography of extracranial and intracranial vessels and multimodal imaging—including magnetic resonance angiography—ruled out any atherosclerotic plaques, dissection, or vasculitis (figure 1). Electrocardiogram monitoring during more than 72 h of telemetry found no abnormalities.
Transoesophageal echocardiography showed a patent foramen ovale (PFO) with spontaneous passage of bubbles and accentuation with Valsalva manoeuvre; no septal aneurysm was seen (figure 2). Atrial size and valvular structures were normal, and no intracardiac thrombi were seen. The Risk of Paradoxical Embolism score was 8—indicating an 84% chance that a stroke is PFO-related. Venous ultrasound imaging showed no deep vein thromboses in the legs, pelvis, or vena cava. The patient left the hospital after 3 days with a prescription for an antithrombotic treatment. He took a flight back to his home country a day later.
The role of a PFO in young patients with acute ischaemic stroke has been the subject of much debate: several studies have shown PFO closure may reduce risk of recurrent strokes in young patients with cryptogenic stroke. A possible pathophysiologic mechanism is paradoxical embolism through the PFO facilitated by intrathoracic pressure elevation during pressing or coughing. We hypothesise that a paradoxical embolism in our patient was possibly provoked by continuous chanting—a provoking factor not previously reported—and we therefore advised him to avoid intensive chanting until interventional PFO closure.
