A 43-year-old man who developed numbness and impaired fine motor skills in his left arm lasting approximately 10 min while chanting during a football match, attended our emergency room. The patient, who was visiting Germany for the UEFA European Football Championship, explained that the problems started at the end of the first half. He said he had been chanting continuously during the game. Despite complete resolution of the symptoms, he was concerned enough to seek help, and at half-time he came to our hospital by ambulance. We decided to admit him to our stroke unit for further investigations. He had no medical history; he said he had consumed a moderate amount of alcohol. He was a non-smoker.
On examination the patient was generally fit and well; his pulse was 92 beats per min, blood pressure was 140/90 mm Hg, and his oxygen saturation was 94%. Physical examination found no abnormalities.
Laboratory investigations showed a mildly elevated LDL cholesterol (142 mg/dL; normal range <115). A coagulopathy was excluded: clotting factors II and V were within normal range, tests for antiphospholipid syndrome were negative, antithrombin III activity was in normal range, and protein S and C levels were normal. The patient's homocysteine serum concentration was slightly elevated (15 μmol/L; typical range 3·7–13·9), genotyping found the wild-type variant of the MTHFR gene.
MRI showed a small acute embolic ischaemic lesion in the postcentral gyrus of the right hemisphere (figure 1); doppler and duplex sonography of extracranial and intracranial vessels and multimodal imaging—including magnetic resonance angiography—ruled out any atherosclerotic plaques, dissection, or vasculitis (figure 1). Electrocardiogram monitoring during more than 72 h of telemetry found no abnormalities.
Transoesophageal echocardiography showed a patent foramen ovale (PFO) with spontaneous passage of bubbles and accentuation with Valsalva manoeuvre; no septal aneurysm was seen (figure 2). Atrial size and valvular structures were normal, and no intracardiac thrombi were seen. The Risk of Paradoxical Embolism score was 8—indicating an 84% chance that a stroke is PFO-related. Venous ultrasound imaging showed no deep vein thromboses in the legs, pelvis, or vena cava. The patient left the hospital after 3 days with a prescription for an antithrombotic treatment. He took a flight back to his home country a day later.
The role of a PFO in young patients with acute ischaemic stroke has been the subject of much debate: several studies have shown PFO closure may reduce risk of recurrent strokes in young patients with cryptogenic stroke. A possible pathophysiologic mechanism is paradoxical embolism through the PFO facilitated by intrathoracic pressure elevation during pressing or coughing. We hypothesise that a paradoxical embolism in our patient was possibly provoked by continuous chanting—a provoking factor not previously reported—and we therefore advised him to avoid intensive chanting until interventional PFO closure.

A 10-year-old girl was referred to the Ophthalmology Department at Cantonal Hospital St Gallen, Switzerland, for intermittent divergent strabismus. Ophthalmologic examination revealed prominent bilateral corneal nerve fibres (figure A and B; white arrows) and multiple nodules along the eyelid margins (figure A and C; black arrows). She also had distinct facial features that included a narrow face, prominent chin, bulging lips, and nodules on the tongue and ears (appendix p 1). During planned strabismus surgery, a biopsy of one eyelid nodule was performed due to the unusual appearance of these lesions. Histological analysis revealed a neuroma, which prompted further systemic evaluation and led to the diagnosis of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B (MEN2B), an autosomal dominant tumour predisposition syndrome.
Urgent paediatric evaluation did not find biochemical evidence of phaeochromocytoma, but found elevated tumour markers calcitonin (129 ng/l; normal range <3 ng/l) and carcinoembryonic antigen (3·2 ug/l; normal range <3·2 μg/l) and a suspicious sonographic thyroid nodule (appendix p 2), which indicated a medullary thyroid carcinoma. The diagnosis of MEN2B was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, revealing the de novo, pathological, heterozygous RET proto-oncogene mutation Met918Thr. This is a high risk mutation that has an 100% incidence for aggressive early-onset medullary thyroid carcinoma, and prophylactic thyroidectomy is recommended after diagnosis. The patient did not show signs of dry eyes in infancy or throughout childhood, and did not have any dental, urinary, or skeletal atypicalities. Moreover, her growth variables and cognitive development (intelligent quotient) were within the normal range.
Our patient underwent a complete thyroidectomy with central lymphadenectomy, which would have been performed in the first year of life if the RET mutation had been known about. Histological analysis confirmed medullary thyroid carcinoma with lymphogenic metastasis and focal angioinvasion. After surgery, her carcinoembryonic antigen levels normalised (below 3·2 μg/l), but her calcitonin levels only dropped by 50% (63 ng/l). A cervicolateral lymphadenectomy was performed 3 months later, and incomplete biochemical control was reached with a minimum calcitonin level of 4·6 ng/l. One year later, the patient is healthy and taking daily L-thyroxine 112 ug, with no long-term surgical complications.
An intestinal endoscopy was given due to long-standing flatulence and revealed ganglioneuromatosis, which will be observed clinically. Follow up also includes regular screening for phaeochromocytoma and medullary thyroid carcinoma metastases.
Prominent corneal nerves and the development of multiple mucosal and cutaneous nodules in childhood should raise suspicion of MEN2B, warranting urgent investigation to manage early-onset medullary thyroid carcinoma.

input:
A 10-year-old girl was referred to the Ophthalmology Department at Cantonal Hospital St Gallen, Switzerland, for intermittent divergent strabismus. Ophthalmologic examination revealed prominent bilateral corneal nerve fibres (figure A and B; white arrows) and multiple nodules along the eyelid margins (figure A and C; black arrows). She also had distinct facial features that included a narrow face, prominent chin, bulging lips, and nodules on the tongue and ears (appendix p 1). During planned strabismus surgery, a biopsy of one eyelid nodule was performed due to the unusual appearance of these lesions. Histological analysis revealed a neuroma, which prompted further systemic evaluation and led to the diagnosis of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B (MEN2B), an autosomal dominant tumour predisposition syndrome.
Urgent paediatric evaluation did not find biochemical evidence of phaeochromocytoma, but found elevated tumour markers calcitonin (129 ng/l; normal range <3 ng/l) and carcinoembryonic antigen (3·2 ug/l; normal range <3·2 μg/l) and a suspicious sonographic thyroid nodule (appendix p 2), which indicated a medullary thyroid carcinoma. The diagnosis of MEN2B was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, revealing the de novo, pathological, heterozygous RET proto-oncogene mutation Met918Thr. This is a high risk mutation that has an 100% incidence for aggressive early-onset medullary thyroid carcinoma, and prophylactic thyroidectomy is recommended after diagnosis. The patient did not show signs of dry eyes in infancy or throughout childhood, and did not have any dental, urinary, or skeletal atypicalities. Moreover, her growth variables and cognitive development (intelligent quotient) were within the normal range.
Our patient underwent a complete thyroidectomy with central lymphadenectomy, which would have been performed in the first year of life if the RET mutation had been known about. Histological analysis confirmed medullary thyroid carcinoma with lymphogenic metastasis and focal angioinvasion. After surgery, her carcinoembryonic antigen levels normalised (below 3·2 μg/l), but her calcitonin levels only dropped by 50% (63 ng/l). A cervicolateral lymphadenectomy was performed 3 months later, and incomplete biochemical control was reached with a minimum calcitonin level of 4·6 ng/l. One year later, the patient is healthy and taking daily L-thyroxine 112 ug, with no long-term surgical complications.
An intestinal endoscopy was given due to long-standing flatulence and revealed ganglioneuromatosis, which will be observed clinically. Follow up also includes regular screening for phaeochromocytoma and medullary thyroid carcinoma metastases.
Prominent corneal nerves and the development of multiple mucosal and cutaneous nodules in childhood should raise suspicion of MEN2B, warranting urgent investigation to manage early-onset medullary thyroid carcinoma.

input:
A 10-year-old girl was referred to the Ophthalmology Department at Cantonal Hospital St Gallen, Switzerland, for intermittent divergent strabismus. Ophthalmologic examination revealed prominent bilateral corneal nerve fibres (figure A and B; white arrows) and multiple nodules along the eyelid margins (figure A and C; black arrows). She also had distinct facial features that included a narrow face, prominent chin, bulging lips, and nodules on the tongue and ears (appendix p 1). During planned strabismus surgery, a biopsy of one eyelid nodule was performed due to the unusual appearance of these lesions. Histological analysis revealed a neuroma, which prompted further systemic evaluation and led to the diagnosis of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B (MEN2B), an autosomal dominant tumour predisposition syndrome.
Urgent paediatric evaluation did not find biochemical evidence of phaeochromocytoma, but found elevated tumour markers calcitonin (129 ng/l; normal range <3 ng/l) and carcinoembryonic antigen (3·2 ug/l; normal range <3·2 μg/l) and a suspicious sonographic thyroid nodule (appendix p 2), which indicated a medullary thyroid carcinoma. The diagnosis of MEN2B was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, revealing the de novo, pathological, heterozygous RET proto-oncogene mutation Met918Thr. This is a high risk mutation that has an 100% incidence for aggressive early-onset medullary thyroid carcinoma, and prophylactic thyroidectomy is recommended after diagnosis. The patient did not show signs of dry eyes in infancy or throughout childhood, and did not have any dental, urinary, or skeletal atypicalities. Moreover, her growth variables and cognitive development (intelligent quotient) were within the normal range.
Our patient underwent a complete thyroidectomy with central lymphadenectomy, which would have been performed in the first year of life if the RET mutation had been known about. Histological analysis confirmed medullary thyroid carcinoma with lymphogenic metastasis and focal angioinvasion. After surgery, her carcinoembryonic antigen levels normalised (below 3·2 μg/l), but her calcitonin levels only dropped by 50% (63 ng/l). A cervicolateral lymphadenectomy was performed 3 months later, and incomplete biochemical control was reached with a minimum calcitonin level of 4·6 ng/l. One year later, the patient is healthy and taking daily L-thyroxine 112 ug, with no long-term surgical complications.
An intestinal endoscopy was given due to long-standing flatulence and revealed ganglioneuromatosis, which will be observed clinically. Follow up also includes regular screening for phaeochromocytoma and medullary thyroid carcinoma metastases.
Prominent corneal nerves and the development of multiple mucosal and cutaneous nodules in childhood should raise suspicion of MEN2B, warranting urgent investigation to manage early-onset medullary thyroid carcinoma.

On admission, a 12-lead ECG showed sinus tachycardia without evidence of ischaemia. Biomarkers of myocardial necrosis were negative. A portable chest radiograph and a bedside transthoracic echocardiogram showed pathognomonic findings of acute type A aortic dissection (figure; videos). The patient underwent urgent repair of the aortic root. The patient survived the immediate postoperative course despite complications of haemodynamic instability, hypotension, and acute renal failure, but later succumbed to multiorgan failure.
Delayed presentation of acute aortic syndrome is plagued by high mortality and morbidity. The location of the intimal tear in acute type A aortic dissection is in the immediate vicinity of the sinuses of Valsalva 65% of the time. The sensitivity and specificity of chest radiography is 81% and 89%, respectively. The sensitivity of transthoracic echocardiography is between 78% and 100%; its specificity ranges from 87% to 96%. Transthoracic echocardiography is a valuable diagnostic tool in cases when more sensitive techniques (transoesophageal echocardiography, CT, magnetic resonance angiography) are not readily available or are impractical.

A 69-year-old woman with a history of myocardial infarction came to hospital after more than 24 h of intermittent chest pain, shortness of breath, and diaphoresis. On admission, a 12-lead ECG showed sinus tachycardia without evidence of ischaemia. Biomarkers of myocardial necrosis were negative. A portable chest radiograph and a bedside transthoracic echocardiogram showed pathognomonic findings of acute type A aortic dissection (figure; videos). The patient underwent urgent repair of the aortic root. The patient survived the immediate postoperative course despite complications of haemodynamic instability, hypotension, and acute renal failure, but later succumbed to multiorgan failure.
Delayed presentation of acute aortic syndrome is plagued by high mortality and morbidity. The location of the intimal tear in acute type A aortic dissection is in the immediate vicinity of the sinuses of Valsalva 65% of the time. The sensitivity and specificity of chest radiography is 81% and 89%, respectively. The sensitivity of transthoracic echocardiography is between 78% and 100%; its specificity ranges from 87% to 96%. Transthoracic echocardiography is a valuable diagnostic tool in cases when more sensitive techniques (transoesophageal echocardiography, CT, magnetic resonance angiography) are not readily available or are impractical.

A 7-year-old girl, with early-onset sarcoidosis, attended our clinic for a routine follow-up eye examination. She had reported no recent visual problems.The patient had been diagnosed with sarcoidosis 3 years earlier, after she developed problems walking, red eyes, rashes on her face and arms, and a fever. She had an elevated angiotensin converting enzyme concentration and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 52 mm/h. Synovial biopsy showed a non-necrotising granuloma and genetic testing found a novel mutation of unknown significance in the NOD2 gene. The patient was treated with methotrexate and adalimumab.
On examination, we found that she had reduced visual acuity in both eyes: 20/40 in the right and 20/60 in the left (typical 20/20). A slit-lamp examination showed bilateral anterior chamber inflammation and large off-white deposits on the inner corneal surface known as mutton-fat keratic precipitates (figure). Anterior-segment optical coherence tomography showed inflammatory cells in both eyes and the keratic precipitates (figure). Laboratory investigations showed a raised ESR of 41 mm/h.
We started the patient on topical corticosteroids (dexamethasone eye drops) and provided the family with advice about concordance. At follow-up 4 weeks later, both the patient's vision and the anterior chamber inflammation had improved. The patient's concordance with the methotrexate and adalimumab had also improved: previously doses had been omitted based on the assumption that a long period without symptoms was due to remission rather than simply control of the disease process.
Sarcoidosis is a rare, multisystem, chronic inflammatory disorder most commonly affecting the lungs (in adults) and skin (in children). Early onset, defined as before the age of 4 years, typically presents with a triad of skin, joint, and eye problems, and may be caused by mutations of the NOD2 gene. Eye signs in both early and later presentations in childhood include anterior uveitis, vitritis, choroiditis, and retinal vasculitis.
Anterior uveitis may be asymptomatic in children up until the development of irreversible sight-threatening complications. Although anterior chamber inflammation is often difficult to detect, mutton-fat keratic precipitates can be seen with the naked eye. A 7-year-old girl, with early-onset sarcoidosis, attended our clinic for a routine follow-up eye examination. She had reported no recent visual problems.The patient had been diagnosed with sarcoidosis 3 years earlier, after she developed problems walking, red eyes, rashes on her face and arms, and a fever. She had an elevated angiotensin converting enzyme concentration and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 52 mm/h. Synovial biopsy showed a non-necrotising granuloma and genetic testing found a novel mutation of unknown significance in the NOD2 gene. The patient was treated with methotrexate and adalimumab.
On examination, we found that she had reduced visual acuity in both eyes: 20/40 in the right and 20/60 in the left (typical 20/20). A slit-lamp examination showed bilateral anterior chamber inflammation and large off-white deposits on the inner corneal surface known as mutton-fat keratic precipitates (figure). Anterior-segment optical coherence tomography showed inflammatory cells in both eyes and the keratic precipitates (figure). Laboratory investigations showed a raised ESR of 41 mm/h.
We started the patient on topical corticosteroids (dexamethasone eye drops) and provided the family with advice about concordance. At follow-up 4 weeks later, both the patient's vision and the anterior chamber inflammation had improved. The patient's concordance with the methotrexate and adalimumab had also improved: previously doses had been omitted based on the assumption that a long period without symptoms was due to remission rather than simply control of the disease process.
Sarcoidosis is a rare, multisystem, chronic inflammatory disorder most commonly affecting the lungs (in adults) and skin (in children). Early onset, defined as before the age of 4 years, typically presents with a triad of skin, joint, and eye problems, and may be caused by mutations of the NOD2 gene. Eye signs in both early and later presentations in childhood include anterior uveitis, vitritis, choroiditis, and retinal vasculitis.
Anterior uveitis may be asymptomatic in children up until the development of irreversible sight-threatening complications. Although anterior chamber inflammation is often difficult to detect, mutton-fat keratic precipitates can be seen with the naked eye. The presence of these large deposits—aggregates of polymorphonuclear cells, lymphocytes, and epithelioid cells—suggests granulomatous disease indicating differential diagnoses and investigations.

A 44-year-old man with a 1-month history of confusion attended our neurology clinic. The patient's parents reported that their son, who had Down syndrome and was socially competent, had shown subtle changes in his behaviour; he was irritable, subject to mood swings, and more demanding of his family's attention. The patient had no vascular risk factors and was not prescribed any medication.
On initial assessment, the patient was generally well; temperature was 36·3°C, pulse was 62 beats per min and regular, and blood pressure was 110/75 mm Hg. Neurological examination showed a right hemineglect and mild right hemiparesis.
Laboratory investigations—including a complete blood count and coagulation parameters—were within typical range.
MRI of the head (figure) showed multiple lobar cortico-subcortical haemorrhages in both hemispheres and ubiquitous brain microbleeds throughout the cerebral cortex and cerebellum.
The patient was admitted to the neurology ward for observation and supportive treatment. Genotyping for APOE showed ɛ2/ɛ3. The patient's clinical course was uncomplicated, and he was allowed home after 7 days. At follow-up 3 months later, he was recovering well, with mild bradypsychia. A CT scan of the head showed resolution of the intracerebral haemorrhages.
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is a form of cerebrovascular pathology characterised by the deposition of amyloid β in the leptomeningeal and cortical blood vessels; it can result in cognitive impairment and—as vascular amyloid deposits are thought to weaken blood vessels—symptomatic lobar intracerebral haemorrhages as well as bleeding into smaller regions of the brain giving cerebral microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis. The dysfunction of vascular physiology associated with cerebral amyloid angiopathy—although not explicitly causative—is likely to impair glymphatic clearance, potentially leading to increased amyloid β accumulation and further degeneration of vessel walls. While direct visualisation of vascular amyloid β in cerebral amyloid angiopathy requires brain biopsy or autopsy, a set of clinical and MRI-based diagnostic criteria—the Boston criteria version 2.0 for cerebral amyloid angiopathy—have been validated so that the diagnosis can be made without brain tissue analysis.
People with Down syndrome may develop cerebral amyloid angiopathy due to overexpression of the amyloid precursor protein gene and subsequent increase of amyloid β in the brain; they are also at higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is a major feature of the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease and has been considered the disease's pathological hallmark. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is part of the natural history of the development of Alzheimer's disease in people with Down syndrome.

A 7-year-old girl, with early-onset sarcoidosis, attended our clinic for a routine follow-up eye examination. She had reported no recent visual problems.The patient had been diagnosed with sarcoidosis 3 years earlier, after she developed problems walking, red eyes, rashes on her face and arms, and a fever. She had an elevated angiotensin converting enzyme concentration and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 52 mm/h. Synovial biopsy showed a non-necrotising granuloma and genetic testing found a novel mutation of unknown significance in the NOD2 gene. The patient was treated with methotrexate and adalimumab.
On examination, we found that she had reduced visual acuity in both eyes: 20/40 in the right and 20/60 in the left (typical 20/20). A slit-lamp examination showed bilateral anterior chamber inflammation and large off-white deposits on the inner corneal surface known as mutton-fat keratic precipitates (figure). Anterior-segment optical coherence tomography showed inflammatory cells in both eyes and the keratic precipitates (figure). Laboratory investigations showed a raised ESR of 41 mm/h.
We started the patient on topical corticosteroids (dexamethasone eye drops) and provided the family with advice about concordance. At follow-up 4 weeks later, both the patient's vision and the anterior chamber inflammation had improved. The patient's concordance with the methotrexate and adalimumab had also improved: previously doses had been omitted based on the assumption that a long period without symptoms was due to remission rather than simply control of the disease process.
Sarcoidosis is a rare, multisystem, chronic inflammatory disorder most commonly affecting the lungs (in adults) and skin (in children). Early onset, defined as before the age of 4 years, typically presents with a triad of skin, joint, and eye problems, and may be caused by mutations of the NOD2 gene. Eye signs in both early and later presentations in childhood include anterior uveitis, vitritis, choroiditis, and retinal vasculitis.
Anterior uveitis may be asymptomatic in children up until the development of irreversible sight-threatening complications. Although anterior chamber inflammation is often difficult to detect, mutton-fat keratic precipitates can be seen with the naked eye. The presence of these large deposits—aggregates of polymorphonuclear cells, lymphocytes, and epithelioid cells—suggests granulomatous disease indicating differential diagnoses and investigations.
Clinical features are key to identifying the underlying granulomatous disorder when mutton-fat keratic precipitates are seen. Prompt diagnosis and management of the associated systemic disease, with coordinated care involving specialists, affords the best opportunity of disease control, and reduced burden of avoidable later-life morbidity and disability.

A 44-year-old man with a 1-month history of confusion attended our neurology clinic. The patient's parents reported that their son, who had Down syndrome and was socially competent, had shown subtle changes in his behaviour; he was irritable, subject to mood swings, and more demanding of his family's attention. The patient had no vascular risk factors and was not prescribed any medication.
On initial assessment, the patient was generally well; temperature was 36·3°C, pulse was 62 beats per min and regular, and blood pressure was 110/75 mm Hg. Neurological examination showed a right hemineglect and mild right hemiparesis.
Laboratory investigations—including a complete blood count and coagulation parameters—were within typical range.
MRI of the head (figure) showed multiple lobar cortico-subcortical haemorrhages in both hemispheres and ubiquitous brain microbleeds throughout the cerebral cortex and cerebellum.
The patient was admitted to the neurology ward for observation and supportive treatment. Genotyping for APOE showed ɛ2/ɛ3. The patient's clinical course was uncomplicated, and he was allowed home after 7 days. At follow-up 3 months later, he was recovering well, with mild bradypsychia. A CT scan of the head showed resolution of the intracerebral haemorrhages.
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is a form of cerebrovascular pathology characterised by the deposition of amyloid β in the leptomeningeal and cortical blood vessels; it can result in cognitive impairment and—as vascular amyloid deposits are thought to weaken blood vessels—symptomatic lobar intracerebral haemorrhages as well as bleeding into smaller regions of the brain giving cerebral microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis. The dysfunction of vascular physiology associated with cerebral amyloid angiopathy—although not explicitly causative—is likely to impair glymphatic clearance, potentially leading to increased amyloid β accumulation and further degeneration of vessel walls. While direct visualisation of vascular amyloid β in cerebral amyloid angiopathy requires brain biopsy or autopsy, a set of clinical and MRI-based diagnostic criteria—the Boston criteria version 2.0 for cerebral amyloid angiopathy—have been validated so that the diagnosis can be made without brain tissue analysis.
People with Down syndrome may develop cerebral amyloid angiopathy due to overexpression of the amyloid precursor protein gene and subsequent increase of amyloid β in the brain; they are also at higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is a major feature of the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease and has been considered the disease's pathological hallmark. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is part of the natural history of the development of Alzheimer's disease in people with Down syndrome.

A 57-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease from type 2 diabetes was assessed at our specialist unit for a kidney transplant to be donated by his brother. The patient was unsensitised and blood group O; his 59-year-old brother was the same blood type and two-haplotype HLA-matched. Both the patient and his brother were enrolled into our immunological tolerance protocol, which combines a haematopoietic stem-cell transplant with a kidney transplant with the goal of inducing sustained mixed chimerism—a state where the recipient's haematopoietic system has a mixture of both host and donor cells.Notably, the requirements for tacrolimus withdrawal include a stable mixed chimerism of greater than 5% of donor cells, no evidence of rejection on a series of renal biopsies, and no evidence of graft-versus-host disease.
Initially, the donor's haematopoietic stem cells were mobilised using granulocyte colony-stimulating factor. Peripheral blood apheresis was then done, and CD34+ and CD3+ cell products were isolated and cryopreserved.
On day 0, we did a left-sided donor nephrectomy and kidney transplant; the recipient was immediately started on tacrolimus and prednisone.
On day 1, the donor was allowed home and the recipient underwent conditioning with total lymphoid irradiation and an intravenous infusion of rabbit anti-thymocyte globulins.
On day 5, the recipient was allowed home; his urine output at that stage was 3·4 L per 24 h (normal >30–50 cc/kg per day) and his serum creatinine concentration was 0·89 mg/dL (normal 0·74–1·35).
On day 11, the prednisone tapering off was complete.
On day 12, donor CD34+ and CD3+ cell products and haematopoietic stem cells were infused, and mycophenolate mofetil was started and continued for one month.
At 3 months, repeated tests for levels of donor chimerism were sent to guide the tapering and withdrawal of the immunosuppression.
The tacrolimus tapering schedule continued until it was finally stopped at one year, at which point the recipient had a sustained mixed chimerism of 7% donor cells and stable renal function with a serum creatinine concentration of 0·87 mg/dL: we were able to pronounce the patient immunosuppression-free (figure; appendix).
2 months after stopping all immunosuppressive therapy, the patient was well and his kidney function remained stable.
Immune tolerance induction for patients undergoing kidney transplant offers the potential to mitigate the deleterious effects of long-term immunosuppression—including cardiovascular diseases, hypertension, diabetes, and nephrotoxicity—for well selected patients. Ongoing trials are investigating the induction of immune tolerance in both living HLA-mismatched and deceased donor kidney transplants (video).

A 44-year-old man with a 1-month history of confusion attended our neurology clinic. The patient's parents reported that their son, who had Down syndrome and was socially competent, had shown subtle changes in his behaviour; he was irritable, subject to mood swings, and more demanding of his family's attention. The patient had no vascular risk factors and was not prescribed any medication.
On initial assessment, the patient was generally well; temperature was 36·3°C, pulse was 62 beats per min and regular, and blood pressure was 110/75 mm Hg. Neurological examination showed a right hemineglect and mild right hemiparesis.
Laboratory investigations—including a complete blood count and coagulation parameters—were within typical range.
MRI of the head (figure) showed multiple lobar cortico-subcortical haemorrhages in both hemispheres and ubiquitous brain microbleeds throughout the cerebral cortex and cerebellum.
The patient was admitted to the neurology ward for observation and supportive treatment. Genotyping for APOE showed ɛ2/ɛ3. The patient's clinical course was uncomplicated, and he was allowed home after 7 days. At follow-up 3 months later, he was recovering well, with mild bradypsychia. A CT scan of the head showed resolution of the intracerebral haemorrhages.
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is a form of cerebrovascular pathology characterised by the deposition of amyloid β in the leptomeningeal and cortical blood vessels; it can result in cognitive impairment and—as vascular amyloid deposits are thought to weaken blood vessels—symptomatic lobar intracerebral haemorrhages as well as bleeding into smaller regions of the brain giving cerebral microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis. The dysfunction of vascular physiology associated with cerebral amyloid angiopathy—although not explicitly causative—is likely to impair glymphatic clearance, potentially leading to increased amyloid β accumulation and further degeneration of vessel walls. While direct visualisation of vascular amyloid β in cerebral amyloid angiopathy requires brain biopsy or autopsy, a set of clinical and MRI-based diagnostic criteria—the Boston criteria version 2.0 for cerebral amyloid angiopathy—have been validated so that the diagnosis can be made without brain tissue analysis.
People with Down syndrome may develop cerebral amyloid angiopathy due to overexpression of the amyloid precursor protein gene and subsequent increase of amyloid β in the brain; they are also at higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is a major feature of the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease and has been considered the disease's pathological hallmark. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is part of the natural history of the development of Alzheimer's disease in people with Down syndrome.

A 57-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease from type 2 diabetes was assessed at our specialist unit for a kidney transplant to be donated by his brother. The patient was unsensitised and blood group O; his 59-year-old brother was the same blood type and two-haplotype HLA-matched. Both the patient and his brother were enrolled into our immunological tolerance protocol, which combines a haematopoietic stem-cell transplant with a kidney transplant with the goal of inducing sustained mixed chimerism—a state where the recipient's haematopoietic system has a mixture of both host and donor cells.Notably, the requirements for tacrolimus withdrawal include a stable mixed chimerism of greater than 5% of donor cells, no evidence of rejection on a series of renal biopsies, and no evidence of graft-versus-host disease.
Initially, the donor's haematopoietic stem cells were mobilised using granulocyte colony-stimulating factor. Peripheral blood apheresis was then done, and CD34+ and CD3+ cell products were isolated and cryopreserved.
On day 0, we did a left-sided donor nephrectomy and kidney transplant; the recipient was immediately started on tacrolimus and prednisone.
On day 1, the donor was allowed home and the recipient underwent conditioning with total lymphoid irradiation and an intravenous infusion of rabbit anti-thymocyte globulins.
On day 5, the recipient was allowed home; his urine output at that stage was 3·4 L per 24 h (normal >30–50 cc/kg per day) and his serum creatinine concentration was 0·89 mg/dL (normal 0·74–1·35).
On day 11, the prednisone tapering off was complete.
On day 12, donor CD34+ and CD3+ cell products and haematopoietic stem cells were infused, and mycophenolate mofetil was started and continued for one month.
At 3 months, repeated tests for levels of donor chimerism were sent to guide the tapering and withdrawal of the immunosuppression.
The tacrolimus tapering schedule continued until it was finally stopped at one year, at which point the recipient had a sustained mixed chimerism of 7% donor cells and stable renal function with a serum creatinine concentration of 0·87 mg/dL: we were able to pronounce the patient immunosuppression-free (figure; appendix).
2 months after stopping all immunosuppressive therapy, the patient was well and his kidney function remained stable.
Immune tolerance induction for patients undergoing kidney transplant offers the potential to mitigate the deleterious effects of long-term immunosuppression—including cardiovascular diseases, hypertension, diabetes, and nephrotoxicity—for well selected patients. Ongoing trials are investigating the induction of immune tolerance in both living HLA-mismatched and deceased donor kidney transplants (video).

A 57-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease from type 2 diabetes was assessed at our specialist unit for a kidney transplant to be donated by his brother. The patient was unsensitised and blood group O; his 59-year-old brother was the same blood type and two-haplotype HLA-matched. Both the patient and his brother were enrolled into our immunological tolerance protocol, which combines a haematopoietic stem-cell transplant with a kidney transplant with the goal of inducing sustained mixed chimerism—a state where the recipient's haematopoietic system has a mixture of both host and donor cells.Notably, the requirements for tacrolimus withdrawal include a stable mixed chimerism of greater than 5% of donor cells, no evidence of rejection on a series of renal biopsies, and no evidence of graft-versus-host disease.
Initially, the donor's haematopoietic stem cells were mobilised using granulocyte colony-stimulating factor. Peripheral blood apheresis was then done, and CD34+ and CD3+ cell products were isolated and cryopreserved.
On day 0, we did a left-sided donor nephrectomy and kidney transplant; the recipient was immediately started on tacrolimus and prednisone.
On day 1, the donor was allowed home and the recipient underwent conditioning with total lymphoid irradiation and an intravenous infusion of rabbit anti-thymocyte globulins.
On day 5, the recipient was allowed home; his urine output at that stage was 3·4 L per 24 h (normal >30–50 cc/kg per day) and his serum creatinine concentration was 0·89 mg/dL (normal 0·74–1·35).
On day 11, the prednisone tapering off was complete.
On day 12, donor CD34+ and CD3+ cell products and haematopoietic stem cells were infused, and mycophenolate mofetil was started and continued for one month.
At 3 months, repeated tests for levels of donor chimerism were sent to guide the tapering and withdrawal of the immunosuppression.
The tacrolimus tapering schedule continued until it was finally stopped at one year, at which point the recipient had a sustained mixed chimerism of 7% donor cells and stable renal function with a serum creatinine concentration of 0·87 mg/dL: we were able to pronounce the patient immunosuppression-free (figure; appendix).
2 months after stopping all immunosuppressive therapy, the patient was well and his kidney function remained stable.
Immune tolerance induction for patients undergoing kidney transplant offers the potential to mitigate the deleterious effects of long-term immunosuppression—including cardiovascular diseases, hypertension, diabetes, and nephrotoxicity—for well selected patients. Ongoing trials are investigating the induction of immune tolerance in both living HLA-mismatched and deceased donor kidney transplants (video).

input: A 14-year-old boy came to our clinic with lumps in his oral cavity. His mother informed us that the lesions had appeared spontaneously 13 years before. The boy had taken numerous drugs for the condition without effect. Another 8-year-old son had similar lesions. The patient was of North American Indian descent. Oral examination showed several papulonodular lesions on the cheek mucosa, lip mucosa, and tongue (figure). The lesions were painless to palpation, soft, of different diameter, and similar in colour to normal mucosa. The clinical diagnosis was focal epithelial hyperplasia (FEH), a rare benign condition caused by human papillomavirus subtype 13 or 32. An incisional biopsy was done. Microscopic analysis showed parakeratosis, acanthosis, epithelial hyperplasia, and koilocytic cells (figure), which confirmed FEH. The patient had therapy with CO2 laser ablation; however, it is not possible to predict when FEH lesions will recur or where new lesions will be seen.

input:
A 51-year-old woman with a 3-year history of painful hips presented to our mineral metabolism service having been referred by her general practitioner. The pain was present at rest and made worse by more vigorous movement; she used crutches to walk.Regarding her medical history, the patient had transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia intermedia and had been having regular red blood cell transfusions since she was 40 days old; she had a splenectomy aged 29 years. She reported that she was currently receiving two units of filtered red blood cells every 15 days; her mean pre-transfusion haemoglobin concentration for the past 12 months was between 9·5 and 10·0 g/dL. Genotypically, she had compound heterozygous mutations: intervening segments (IVS)-I–110 (G>A) and IVS-I–6 (T>C). Additionally, she had diabetes mellitus. Both the patient's parents had microcytic anaemia. She was being prescribed deferasirox, cholecalciferol, proton pump inhibitors, and ultralong acting insulin.
On examination we found her to be generally well; she had pain on flexion, internal rotation, and adduction of both hips that limited her range of movements.
Laboratory investigations done prior to our consultation showed a haemoglobin concentration of 9·5 g/dL, haematocrit 27·5%, red blood cell count 3·26 × 1012 per L, serum iron concentration 208 μg/dL (normal range 60–170), and ferritin concentration 590 μg/L (normal range 24–336).
An x-ray of the patient's hips showed flattening of both the femoral heads—particularly apparent on the left hip—and a T2-weighted MRI showed heterogeneous signal intensity with geodic cavities and marrow oedema, findings indicative of bilateral avascular necrosis of both hips. We recommended the patient have bilateral hip replacement but she did not want to have any surgical intervention. The patient continues to manage her pain with analgesics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatories.
Several skeletal abnormalities have been documented in β-thalassaemia and avascular necrosis of the head of the femur is quite rare. It is more commonly seen in patients with sickle cell disease—where the prevalence may be up to 22%. Even rarer is the finding—as seen in our patient—of bilateral osteonecrosis. Multiple microfractures, local hypoxia, and medullary expansion with possible arterial compression represent the most important pathophysiological mechanisms underlying skeletal necrosis.

A 51-year-old woman with a 3-year history of painful hips presented to our mineral metabolism service having been referred by her general practitioner. The pain was present at rest and made worse by more vigorous movement; she used crutches to walk.Regarding her medical history, the patient had transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia intermedia and had been having regular red blood cell transfusions since she was 40 days old; she had a splenectomy aged 29 years. She reported that she was currently receiving two units of filtered red blood cells every 15 days; her mean pre-transfusion haemoglobin concentration for the past 12 months was between 9·5 and 10·0 g/dL. Genotypically, she had compound heterozygous mutations: intervening segments (IVS)-I–110 (G>A) and IVS-I–6 (T>C). Additionally, she had diabetes mellitus. Both the patient's parents had microcytic anaemia. She was being prescribed deferasirox, cholecalciferol, proton pump inhibitors, and ultralong acting insulin.
On examination we found her to be generally well; she had pain on flexion, internal rotation, and adduction of both hips that limited her range of movements.
Laboratory investigations done prior to our consultation showed a haemoglobin concentration of 9·5 g/dL, haematocrit 27·5%, red blood cell count 3·26 × 1012 per L, serum iron concentration 208 μg/dL (normal range 60–170), and ferritin concentration 590 μg/L (normal range 24–336).
An x-ray of the patient's hips showed flattening of both the femoral heads—particularly apparent on the left hip—and a T2-weighted MRI showed heterogeneous signal intensity with geodic cavities and marrow oedema, findings indicative of bilateral avascular necrosis of both hips. We recommended the patient have bilateral hip replacement but she did not want to have any surgical intervention. The patient continues to manage her pain with analgesics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatories.
Several skeletal abnormalities have been documented in β-thalassaemia and avascular necrosis of the head of the femur is quite rare. It is more commonly seen in patients with sickle cell disease—where the prevalence may be up to 22%. Even rarer is the finding—as seen in our patient—of bilateral osteonecrosis. Multiple microfractures, local hypoxia, and medullary expansion with possible arterial compression represent the most important pathophysiological mechanisms underlying skeletal necrosis.

A 51-year-old woman with a 3-year history of painful hips presented to our mineral metabolism service having been referred by her general practitioner. The pain was present at rest and made worse by more vigorous movement; she used crutches to walk.Regarding her medical history, the patient had transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia intermedia and had been having regular red blood cell transfusions since she was 40 days old; she had a splenectomy aged 29 years. She reported that she was currently receiving two units of filtered red blood cells every 15 days; her mean pre-transfusion haemoglobin concentration for the past 12 months was between 9·5 and 10·0 g/dL. Genotypically, she had compound heterozygous mutations: intervening segments (IVS)-I–110 (G>A) and IVS-I–6 (T>C). Additionally, she had diabetes mellitus. Both the patient's parents had microcytic anaemia. She was being prescribed deferasirox, cholecalciferol, proton pump inhibitors, and ultralong acting insulin.
On examination we found her to be generally well; she had pain on flexion, internal rotation, and adduction of both hips that limited her range of movements.
Laboratory investigations done prior to our consultation showed a haemoglobin concentration of 9·5 g/dL, haematocrit 27·5%, red blood cell count 3·26 × 1012 per L, serum iron concentration 208 μg/dL (normal range 60–170), and ferritin concentration 590 μg/L (normal range 24–336).
An x-ray of the patient's hips showed flattening of both the femoral heads—particularly apparent on the left hip—and a T2-weighted MRI showed heterogeneous signal intensity with geodic cavities and marrow oedema, findings indicative of bilateral avascular necrosis of both hips. We recommended the patient have bilateral hip replacement but she did not want to have any surgical intervention. The patient continues to manage her pain with analgesics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatories.
Several skeletal abnormalities have been documented in β-thalassaemia and avascular necrosis of the head of the femur is quite rare. It is more commonly seen in patients with sickle cell disease—where the prevalence may be up to 22%. Even rarer is the finding—as seen in our patient—of bilateral osteonecrosis. Multiple microfractures, local hypoxia, and medullary expansion with possible arterial compression represent the most important pathophysiological mechanisms underlying skeletal necrosis.

A 58-year-old man, who after reporting several days of abdominal pain was found to have acute kidney injury, was transferred to our unit from a regional hospital.In the preceding 6 months, the patient had been diagnosed with frontotemporal dementia; he had no personal or family history of nephrolithiasis, bowel disease, or weight loss. Notably, the year before this presentation, his kidney function had been found to be normal with the serum creatinine concentration recorded as 71 μmol/L (normal range 60–115).
On examination, the patient was clinically well with a blood pressure of 122/66 mm Hg, heart rate of 95 beats per min, respiratory rate of 18 breaths per min, and an oxygen saturation of 95% on room air.
Laboratory investigations confirmed acute kidney injury—his serum creatinine concentration was 703 μmol/L with preserved urinary output; his remaining serum biochemistry was unremarkable. The urinary protein/creatinine ratio was 39 mg/mmol (normal range 0–12·5).
The patient was admitted to the nephrology ward for a kidney biopsy which showed acute tubular injury with abundant intratubular calcium oxalate crystals; the background kidney was healthy, with little scarring, and only 1/14 obsolete glomeruli (figure).
A detailed dietary history found that the patient had been eating 500–1000 g of almonds daily over the last four years—corresponding to approximately 2–4 g of oxalate per day. He had no evidence of malabsorption; his faecal elastase concentration was >500 ug/g (typical range 200 to less than 500).
A CT of the kidney, ureter, and bladder showed a non-obstructing 1·4 cm calculus in the lower pole of the right kidney and a non-obstructing 0·6 cm calculus in the distal left ureter (figure). We concluded the patient had a diet-related secondary hyperoxaluria; frontotemporal dementia is associated with unusual, compulsive eating habits.
As he was asymptomatic, we decided to manage him conservatively; the patient was started on a low-oxalate, high-calcium diet with a high fluid intake and reviewed regularly. At his last appointment, the patient's laboratory results showed his serum creatinine concentration was improving (478 μmol/L).
Hyperoxaluria causes calcium oxalate stones by raising urinary saturation of calcium oxalate; hyperoxaluria can result from ingestion of oxalate-rich foods, such as rhubarb, spinach, beetroot, almonds—as in our case—and chocolate. Hyperoxaluria is less common than hypercalciuria as a cause of calcium oxalate stones.
Non-obstructive kidney stones of less than 15 mm can be treated conservatively and monitored closely; an increase in the size of the stone or complications, such as infections, may result in a more proactive approach.

A 58-year-old man, who after reporting several days of abdominal pain was found to have acute kidney injury, was transferred to our unit from a regional hospital.In the preceding 6 months, the patient had been diagnosed with frontotemporal dementia; he had no personal or family history of nephrolithiasis, bowel disease, or weight loss. Notably, the year before this presentation, his kidney function had been found to be normal with the serum creatinine concentration recorded as 71 μmol/L (normal range 60–115).
On examination, the patient was clinically well with a blood pressure of 122/66 mm Hg, heart rate of 95 beats per min, respiratory rate of 18 breaths per min, and an oxygen saturation of 95% on room air.
Laboratory investigations confirmed acute kidney injury—his serum creatinine concentration was 703 μmol/L with preserved urinary output; his remaining serum biochemistry was unremarkable. The urinary protein/creatinine ratio was 39 mg/mmol (normal range 0–12·5).
The patient was admitted to the nephrology ward for a kidney biopsy which showed acute tubular injury with abundant intratubular calcium oxalate crystals; the background kidney was healthy, with little scarring, and only 1/14 obsolete glomeruli (figure).
A detailed dietary history found that the patient had been eating 500–1000 g of almonds daily over the last four years—corresponding to approximately 2–4 g of oxalate per day. He had no evidence of malabsorption; his faecal elastase concentration was >500 ug/g (typical range 200 to less than 500).
A CT of the kidney, ureter, and bladder showed a non-obstructing 1·4 cm calculus in the lower pole of the right kidney and a non-obstructing 0·6 cm calculus in the distal left ureter (figure). We concluded the patient had a diet-related secondary hyperoxaluria; frontotemporal dementia is associated with unusual, compulsive eating habits.
As he was asymptomatic, we decided to manage him conservatively; the patient was started on a low-oxalate, high-calcium diet with a high fluid intake and reviewed regularly. At his last appointment, the patient's laboratory results showed his serum creatinine concentration was improving (478 μmol/L).
Hyperoxaluria causes calcium oxalate stones by raising urinary saturation of calcium oxalate; hyperoxaluria can result from ingestion of oxalate-rich foods, such as rhubarb, spinach, beetroot, almonds—as in our case—and chocolate. Hyperoxaluria is less common than hypercalciuria as a cause of calcium oxalate stones.
Non-obstructive kidney stones of less than 15 mm can be treated conservatively and monitored closely; an increase in the size of the stone or complications, such as infections, may result in a more proactive approach.

A 58-year-old man, who after reporting several days of abdominal pain was found to have acute kidney injury, was transferred to our unit from a regional hospital.In the preceding 6 months, the patient had been diagnosed with frontotemporal dementia; he had no personal or family history of nephrolithiasis, bowel disease, or weight loss. Notably, the year before this presentation, his kidney function had been found to be normal with the serum creatinine concentration recorded as 71 μmol/L (normal range 60–115).
On examination, the patient was clinically well with a blood pressure of 122/66 mm Hg, heart rate of 95 beats per min, respiratory rate of 18 breaths per min, and an oxygen saturation of 95% on room air.
Laboratory investigations confirmed acute kidney injury—his serum creatinine concentration was 703 μmol/L with preserved urinary output; his remaining serum biochemistry was unremarkable. The urinary protein/creatinine ratio was 39 mg/mmol (normal range 0–12·5).
The patient was admitted to the nephrology ward for a kidney biopsy which showed acute tubular injury with abundant intratubular calcium oxalate crystals; the background kidney was healthy, with little scarring, and only 1/14 obsolete glomeruli (figure).
A detailed dietary history found that the patient had been eating 500–1000 g of almonds daily over the last four years—corresponding to approximately 2–4 g of oxalate per day. He had no evidence of malabsorption; his faecal elastase concentration was >500 ug/g (typical range 200 to less than 500).
A CT of the kidney, ureter, and bladder showed a non-obstructing 1·4 cm calculus in the lower pole of the right kidney and a non-obstructing 0·6 cm calculus in the distal left ureter (figure). We concluded the patient had a diet-related secondary hyperoxaluria; frontotemporal dementia is associated with unusual, compulsive eating habits.
As he was asymptomatic, we decided to manage him conservatively; the patient was started on a low-oxalate, high-calcium diet with a high fluid intake and reviewed regularly. At his last appointment, the patient's laboratory results showed his serum creatinine concentration was improving (478 μmol/L).
Hyperoxaluria causes calcium oxalate stones by raising urinary saturation of calcium oxalate; hyperoxaluria can result from ingestion of oxalate-rich foods, such as rhubarb, spinach, beetroot, almonds—as in our case—and chocolate. Hyperoxaluria is less common than hypercalciuria as a cause of calcium oxalate stones.
Non-obstructive kidney stones of less than 15 mm can be treated conservatively and monitored closely; an increase in the size of the stone or complications, such as infections, may result in a more proactive approach.

A 70-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital reporting puffy eyelids and swelling of both legs. She had a 7-year history of nephrotic syndrome and hypertension.On examination, she had swollen eyelids and oedema in both legs; her blood pressure was 172/81 mm Hg.
Laboratory investigations showed serum albumin concentration of 2·9 g/dL (normal 4·1–5·1), creatinine 0·81 mg/dL (0·46–0·79), and LDL cholesterol 296 mg/dL (65–163). Urinalysis showed severe proteinuria of 9·3 g/gCr (<0·3) with greater than 100 red blood cells per high-power field and greater than 50 white blood cell per high-power field in the urine sediment.
Tests for hepatitis B and C viruses, cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and double-stranded DNA antibodies were negative; free light chain κ was 27·4 mg/L (normal 3·3–19·4), free light chain λ was 15·6 mg/L (5·7–26·3), and free light chain κ:λ ratio was 1·76 (0·26–1·65).
Cryoglobulin was negative. Malignancy screenings were all negative. Bone marrow biopsy specimen was normal. Renal biopsy was performed; light microscopy revealed membranoproliferative pattern of the glomeruli (figure). Immunofluorescence microscopy revealed the presence of IgG, C3, and C1q in the mesangium with aggregates in the capillary wall. Electron microscopy revealed microtubules with a diameter of almost 40 nm and a distinct hollow core (figure). Based on these findings, immunotactoid glomerulopathy (ITG) associated with monoclonal gammopathy was diagnosed. Oral prednisolone (40 mg/day) administered initially, normalised the urine sediment; remission of proteinuria was incomplete. Intravenous rituximab facilitated complete remission after 1 month.
ITG is a rare glomerular disease encountered in 0·06% of native kidney biopsies; its management remains poorly defined. ITG is characterised by electron microscopic findings of deposits comprising straight, long microtubules with hollow cores and a diameter of greater than 30 nm. Cryoglobulinaemic glomerulonephritis—which should be distinguished from ITG—has deposits comprising short, curved microtubules or fibrillary substructures of diameters less than 30 nm.
ITG has IgG monoclonal and polyclonal variants: the monoclonal type has a higher incidence of haematological conditions—including lymphoma, multiple myeloma, and monoclonal gammopathy. Monoclonal ITG is more commonly treated with clone-directed therapy and associated with frequent remissions and less end-stage kidney disease; it should therefore be subclassified into monoclonal and polyclonal variants. Recently—as seen in our case—improved prognosis in ITG may be possible due to rituximab-based therapy (video).

A 25-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 2-week history of persistent vomiting, abdominal distension, and weight loss.
4 months earlier, she had presented to the local district hospital because her work colleagues had thought she looked pale. The patient had been found to be anaemic with a haemoglobin concentration of 4·7 g/dL and a peripheral blood smear suggestive of a hypochromic microcytic anaemia. She had no other medical history. She was transfused 2 units of blood; she was investigated at the outpatient clinic but was not referred for endoscopic assessment.
On examination, we found the patient to be pale and cachectic. Her blood pressure was 122/74 mm Hg, heart rate was 100 beats per min, temperature was 37·0°C, and oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. On palpation of her abdomen, we felt a discernible, non-tender right upper quadrant mass; she had no other abnormal findings.
Investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8·1 g/dL, platelet count of 565 × 109 per L (normal 150–400), and white cell count of 10·5 × 109 per L; the mean corpuscular volume was 77·2 fL (normal 80–94) and the mean corpuscular haemoglobin was 23·1 pg per cell—suggestive of iron deficiency anaemia. The patient's renal and liver function tests were unremarkable.
An abdominal CT scan showed—on axial view—a target-like lesion (figure) and—on coronal view—a sausage-shaped lesion at the third part of duodenum; the stomach appeared distended. An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed a grossly elongated stomach with external compression at the second part of the duodenum.
We carried out an exploratory laparotomy and found a duodenojejunal intussusception. We were unable to manually reduce the lesion, and so carried out a segmental resection of third part of the duodenum and proximal jejunum with a side-to-side duodenojejunal anastomosis at the second part of the duodenum. Analysis of the excised lesion showed a 6 cm × 5 cm well-encapsulated and pedunculated tumour of the third part of the duodenum which acted as the intussusceptum telescoping into the proximal jejunum—the intussuscipiens (appendix). Histological analysis of samples of the tumour showed a poorly differentiated extra-skeletal Ewing sarcoma of the duodenum. Immunohistochemistry stains demonstrated strong and diffuse nuclear immunoreactivity to NKX2-2 and ERG, with membranous immunoreactivity to CD99, and an absence of nuclear immunoreactivity to FLI1: supporting a possible fusion of the EWSRI gene on chromosome 22q12 with the gene encoding the transcription factor ERG (appendix). The tumour cells exhibited no immunoreactivity to cytokeratin AE1/AE3, CD20, CD3, LCA, TdT, synaptophysin, chromogranin, desmin, myogenin, S100, and α-smooth muscle actin.
Postoperatively, the patient recovered well and was discharged after a week. One month later, she returned reporting persistent abdominal and lower back pain. An abdominal CT showed enlarged coeliac, para-caval, and para-aortic lymph nodes with no lung metastases in the lower half of the thorax. Skeletal x-rays of the axial and cortical bones displayed no osteolytic bone lesions. The patient was urgently transferred to the oncology clinic but died before treatment was commenced.
Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma of the small intestine is an extremely rare tumour with poor prognosis. However, if detected early, it may be successfully treated with surgical resection and adjuvant chemotherapy. Young adults presenting with recurrent vomiting, weight loss, an abdominal mass, and anaemia should raise the suspicion of an aggressive malignancy (video).

A 25-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 2-week history of persistent vomiting, abdominal distension, and weight loss.
4 months earlier, she had presented to the local district hospital because her work colleagues had thought she looked pale. The patient had been found to be anaemic with a haemoglobin concentration of 4·7 g/dL and a peripheral blood smear suggestive of a hypochromic microcytic anaemia. She had no other medical history. She was transfused 2 units of blood; she was investigated at the outpatient clinic but was not referred for endoscopic assessment.
On examination, we found the patient to be pale and cachectic. Her blood pressure was 122/74 mm Hg, heart rate was 100 beats per min, temperature was 37·0°C, and oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. On palpation of her abdomen, we felt a discernible, non-tender right upper quadrant mass; she had no other abnormal findings.
Investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8·1 g/dL, platelet count of 565 × 109 per L (normal 150–400), and white cell count of 10·5 × 109 per L; the mean corpuscular volume was 77·2 fL (normal 80–94) and the mean corpuscular haemoglobin was 23·1 pg per cell—suggestive of iron deficiency anaemia. The patient's renal and liver function tests were unremarkable.
An abdominal CT scan showed—on axial view—a target-like lesion (figure) and—on coronal view—a sausage-shaped lesion at the third part of duodenum; the stomach appeared distended. An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed a grossly elongated stomach with external compression at the second part of the duodenum.
We carried out an exploratory laparotomy and found a duodenojejunal intussusception. We were unable to manually reduce the lesion, and so carried out a segmental resection of third part of the duodenum and proximal jejunum with a side-to-side duodenojejunal anastomosis at the second part of the duodenum. Analysis of the excised lesion showed a 6 cm × 5 cm well-encapsulated and pedunculated tumour of the third part of the duodenum which acted as the intussusceptum telescoping into the proximal jejunum—the intussuscipiens (appendix). Histological analysis of samples of the tumour showed a poorly differentiated extra-skeletal Ewing sarcoma of the duodenum. Immunohistochemistry stains demonstrated strong and diffuse nuclear immunoreactivity to NKX2-2 and ERG, with membranous immunoreactivity to CD99, and an absence of nuclear immunoreactivity to FLI1: supporting a possible fusion of the EWSRI gene on chromosome 22q12 with the gene encoding the transcription factor ERG (appendix). The tumour cells exhibited no immunoreactivity to cytokeratin AE1/AE3, CD20, CD3, LCA, TdT, synaptophysin, chromogranin, desmin, myogenin, S100, and α-smooth muscle actin.
Postoperatively, the patient recovered well and was discharged after a week. One month later, she returned reporting persistent abdominal and lower back pain. An abdominal CT showed enlarged coeliac, para-caval, and para-aortic lymph nodes with no lung metastases in the lower half of the thorax. Skeletal x-rays of the axial and cortical bones displayed no osteolytic bone lesions. The patient was urgently transferred to the oncology clinic but died before treatment was commenced.
Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma of the small intestine is an extremely rare tumour with poor prognosis. However, if detected early, it may be successfully treated with surgical resection and adjuvant chemotherapy. Young adults presenting with recurrent vomiting, weight loss, an abdominal mass, and anaemia should raise the suspicion of an aggressive malignancy (video).

A 25-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 2-week history of persistent vomiting, abdominal distension, and weight loss.
4 months earlier, she had presented to the local district hospital because her work colleagues had thought she looked pale. The patient had been found to be anaemic with a haemoglobin concentration of 4·7 g/dL and a peripheral blood smear suggestive of a hypochromic microcytic anaemia. She had no other medical history. She was transfused 2 units of blood; she was investigated at the outpatient clinic but was not referred for endoscopic assessment.
On examination, we found the patient to be pale and cachectic. Her blood pressure was 122/74 mm Hg, heart rate was 100 beats per min, temperature was 37·0°C, and oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. On palpation of her abdomen, we felt a discernible, non-tender right upper quadrant mass; she had no other abnormal findings.
Investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8·1 g/dL, platelet count of 565 × 109 per L (normal 150–400), and white cell count of 10·5 × 109 per L; the mean corpuscular volume was 77·2 fL (normal 80–94) and the mean corpuscular haemoglobin was 23·1 pg per cell—suggestive of iron deficiency anaemia. The patient's renal and liver function tests were unremarkable.
An abdominal CT scan showed—on axial view—a target-like lesion (figure) and—on coronal view—a sausage-shaped lesion at the third part of duodenum; the stomach appeared distended. An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed a grossly elongated stomach with external compression at the second part of the duodenum.
We carried out an exploratory laparotomy and found a duodenojejunal intussusception. We were unable to manually reduce the lesion, and so carried out a segmental resection of third part of the duodenum and proximal jejunum with a side-to-side duodenojejunal anastomosis at the second part of the duodenum. Analysis of the excised lesion showed a 6 cm × 5 cm well-encapsulated and pedunculated tumour of the third part of the duodenum which acted as the intussusceptum telescoping into the proximal jejunum—the intussuscipiens (appendix). Histological analysis of samples of the tumour showed a poorly differentiated extra-skeletal Ewing sarcoma of the duodenum. Immunohistochemistry stains demonstrated strong and diffuse nuclear immunoreactivity to NKX2-2 and ERG, with membranous immunoreactivity to CD99, and an absence of nuclear immunoreactivity to FLI1: supporting a possible fusion of the EWSRI gene on chromosome 22q12 with the gene encoding the transcription factor ERG (appendix). The tumour cells exhibited no immunoreactivity to cytokeratin AE1/AE3, CD20, CD3, LCA, TdT, synaptophysin, chromogranin, desmin, myogenin, S100, and α-smooth muscle actin.
Postoperatively, the patient recovered well and was discharged after a week. One month later, she returned reporting persistent abdominal and lower back pain. An abdominal CT showed enlarged coeliac, para-caval, and para-aortic lymph nodes with no lung metastases in the lower half of the thorax. Skeletal x-rays of the axial and cortical bones displayed no osteolytic bone lesions. The patient was urgently transferred to the oncology clinic but died before treatment was commenced.
Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma of the small intestine is an extremely rare tumour with poor prognosis. However, if detected early, it may be successfully treated with surgical resection and adjuvant chemotherapy. Young adults presenting with recurrent vomiting, weight loss, an abdominal mass, and anaemia should raise the suspicion of an aggressive malignancy (video).

A 66-year-old man attended our hospital for endoscopic surveillance of a 20 mm gastric antral ulcer. 4 weeks earlier, the patient had presented with haematemesis and melena; a Forrest IB gastric ulcer—active oozing—was found at gastroscopy, and was treated by adrenaline injection, bipolar coagulation, and endoscopic hemoclipping (figure).The patient had a medical history of oesophageal cancer—surgically treated by an Ivor Lewis oesophagectomy 5 years earlier—and common variable immunodeficiency, for which he was receiving monthly intravenous immunoglobulin.
The ulcer had first been discovered 3 months earlier during routine surveillance endoscopy of the oesophagectomy anastomosis. Analysis of samples of biopsies taken during both gastroscopies had shown no evidence of malignancy or Helicobacter pylori; IgG testing for H pylori was also negative. Notably, the patient did not have a history of alcohol misuse or use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatories. He had received all childhood vaccinations—including measles—and he reported no recent contact with cats or other pets. During the period of surveillance, the ulcer had failed to heal and it continued to actively bleed despite confirmed concordance of the patient to a high dose of a proton pump inhibitor twice daily and sucralfate four times a day.
On examination, we found the patient to be alert and well looking. His abdomen was soft, with no tenderness or signs of upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 110 g/L (normal 138–172), which did not change during the admission. We took additional biopsies from the ulcer's edge and the patient remained on our ward for further monitoring and treatment with a proton pump inhibitor given intravenously.
Histopathological analysis of samples of the gastric ulcer biopsies showed chronic active inflammatory changes with multiple inclusion bodies in the mucosal epithelial lining, stromal cells, and capillaries (figure). The inclusion bodies were characterised by enlarged nuclei containing bright granular aggregates, surrounded by clear halo and typical owl's-eye morphology. Cytomegalovirus was confirmed as the cause on immunohistochemistry. No helicobacter organisms, dysplasia, or signs of malignancy were seen. Furthermore, the patient had a detectable viral load for cytomegalovirus of 1812 IU/mL; immunoglobulin levels demonstrated an IgG of 4·23 (normal 6·0–16·0 g/L), IgA <0·10 (normal 0·8–3·0 g/L), and IgM <0·20 (normal 0·4–2·5 g/L).
We started treatment with valganciclovir; 1 week later viral load for cytomegalovirus was 332 IU/mL, 270 IU/mL after 2 weeks, and after 4 months, the ulcer had healed completely. The patient had no further episodes of upper gastrointestinal bleeding, with undetectable levels of viral load of cytomegalovirus.
Common variable immunodeficiency is characterised by reduced serum levels of immunoglobulins with reduced or absent specific antibody production.
Cytomegalovirus-related gastric ulcers are not uncommon as a cause of gastrointestinal bleeding; a global deficiency in immunoglobulin—as in our case—and specifically of IgA, will result in a greater susceptibility of patients becoming infected with the virus. Infectious causes—including cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, measles virus, varicella zoster virus, Toxoplasma gondii, and Epstein-Barr virus—should be considered as a possible cause of a gastric ulcer that fails to heal in immunocompromised patients (video).

A 66-year-old man attended our hospital for endoscopic surveillance of a 20 mm gastric antral ulcer. 4 weeks earlier, the patient had presented with haematemesis and melena; a Forrest IB gastric ulcer—active oozing—was found at gastroscopy, and was treated by adrenaline injection, bipolar coagulation, and endoscopic hemoclipping (figure).The patient had a medical history of oesophageal cancer—surgically treated by an Ivor Lewis oesophagectomy 5 years earlier—and common variable immunodeficiency, for which he was receiving monthly intravenous immunoglobulin.
The ulcer had first been discovered 3 months earlier during routine surveillance endoscopy of the oesophagectomy anastomosis. Analysis of samples of biopsies taken during both gastroscopies had shown no evidence of malignancy or Helicobacter pylori; IgG testing for H pylori was also negative. Notably, the patient did not have a history of alcohol misuse or use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatories. He had received all childhood vaccinations—including measles—and he reported no recent contact with cats or other pets. During the period of surveillance, the ulcer had failed to heal and it continued to actively bleed despite confirmed concordance of the patient to a high dose of a proton pump inhibitor twice daily and sucralfate four times a day.
On examination, we found the patient to be alert and well looking. His abdomen was soft, with no tenderness or signs of upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 110 g/L (normal 138–172), which did not change during the admission. We took additional biopsies from the ulcer's edge and the patient remained on our ward for further monitoring and treatment with a proton pump inhibitor given intravenously.
Histopathological analysis of samples of the gastric ulcer biopsies showed chronic active inflammatory changes with multiple inclusion bodies in the mucosal epithelial lining, stromal cells, and capillaries (figure). The inclusion bodies were characterised by enlarged nuclei containing bright granular aggregates, surrounded by clear halo and typical owl's-eye morphology. Cytomegalovirus was confirmed as the cause on immunohistochemistry. No helicobacter organisms, dysplasia, or signs of malignancy were seen. Furthermore, the patient had a detectable viral load for cytomegalovirus of 1812 IU/mL; immunoglobulin levels demonstrated an IgG of 4·23 (normal 6·0–16·0 g/L), IgA <0·10 (normal 0·8–3·0 g/L), and IgM <0·20 (normal 0·4–2·5 g/L).
We started treatment with valganciclovir; 1 week later viral load for cytomegalovirus was 332 IU/mL, 270 IU/mL after 2 weeks, and after 4 months, the ulcer had healed completely. The patient had no further episodes of upper gastrointestinal bleeding, with undetectable levels of viral load of cytomegalovirus.
Common variable immunodeficiency is characterised by reduced serum levels of immunoglobulins with reduced or absent specific antibody production.
Cytomegalovirus-related gastric ulcers are not uncommon as a cause of gastrointestinal bleeding; a global deficiency in immunoglobulin—as in our case—and specifically of IgA, will result in a greater susceptibility of patients becoming infected with the virus. Infectious causes—including cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, measles virus, varicella zoster virus, Toxoplasma gondii, and Epstein-Barr virus—should be considered as a possible cause of a gastric ulcer that fails to heal in immunocompromised patients (video).

input:
The differential diagnosis of transient monocular vision loss (TMVL), based on clinical history alone, is a common clinical problem. A 66-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of recurrent right TMVL. He had more than 15 episodes without provocation. He described multiple islands of visual loss that coalesced to complete monocular blindness—persisting for several minutes—followed by recovery in a reverse manner. While venous access was being obtained for fluorescein angiography (FA), the patient reported onset of an attack. The examination was thus fortuitously done during vision loss.Normally, following intravenous injection, the dye passes through the short posterior ciliary arteries and appears in the optic disc and choroid within 8–12 s, depending on the age, cardiovascular status of the patient, and speed of dye injection. The arterial retinal circulation appears 11–18 s after injection. However, in our patient, FA of the right eye showed slightly delayed filling of the central retinal artery and severely delayed filling of the nasal choroid and prelaminar region of the optic disc (figure). The circulation of the left eye was normal. Examination 1 week later confirmed retinal circulation was normal between attacks (figure). A diagnosis of vasospasm was made and after treatment with nifedipine 5 mg twice a day, the attacks ceased. The patient remained attack free at 8 months' follow-up.
Many attempts have been made to classify TMVL from patients' descriptions to distinguish embolic from non-embolic attacks. Further, it has been speculated that the reticulated, patchy pattern of TMVL corresponds to interruption of the choroidal circulation—related to its lobular arrangement. This will very rarely occur due to thromboembolism because of the extensive anastomoses between the posterior ciliary arteries supplying the choroid. However, whereas vasospasm of the central retinal artery has been directly observed, choroidal perfusion abnormalities can usually only be identified by FA, and no photographic evidence for this assertion has been published. Our Clinical Picture provides the first direct confirmation for the proposed theory that the reticulated pattern of TMVL is a signature of transient ischaemia of the choroidal lobular circulation. Clearly, such cases should be managed as vasospasm.
