input:
The differential diagnosis of transient monocular vision loss (TMVL), based on clinical history alone, is a common clinical problem. A 66-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of recurrent right TMVL. He had more than 15 episodes without provocation. He described multiple islands of visual loss that coalesced to complete monocular blindness—persisting for several minutes—followed by recovery in a reverse manner. While venous access was being obtained for fluorescein angiography (FA), the patient reported onset of an attack. The examination was thus fortuitously done during vision loss.Normally, following intravenous injection, the dye passes through the short posterior ciliary arteries and appears in the optic disc and choroid within 8–12 s, depending on the age, cardiovascular status of the patient, and speed of dye injection. The arterial retinal circulation appears 11–18 s after injection. However, in our patient, FA of the right eye showed slightly delayed filling of the central retinal artery and severely delayed filling of the nasal choroid and prelaminar region of the optic disc (figure). The circulation of the left eye was normal. Examination 1 week later confirmed retinal circulation was normal between attacks (figure). A diagnosis of vasospasm was made and after treatment with nifedipine 5 mg twice a day, the attacks ceased. The patient remained attack free at 8 months' follow-up.
Many attempts have been made to classify TMVL from patients' descriptions to distinguish embolic from non-embolic attacks. Further, it has been speculated that the reticulated, patchy pattern of TMVL corresponds to interruption of the choroidal circulation—related to its lobular arrangement. This will very rarely occur due to thromboembolism because of the extensive anastomoses between the posterior ciliary arteries supplying the choroid. However, whereas vasospasm of the central retinal artery has been directly observed, choroidal perfusion abnormalities can usually only be identified by FA, and no photographic evidence for this assertion has been published. Our Clinical Picture provides the first direct confirmation for the proposed theory that the reticulated pattern of TMVL is a signature of transient ischaemia of the choroidal lobular circulation. Clearly, such cases should be managed as vasospasm.

A 66-year-old man attended our hospital for endoscopic surveillance of a 20 mm gastric antral ulcer. 4 weeks earlier, the patient had presented with haematemesis and melena; a Forrest IB gastric ulcer—active oozing—was found at gastroscopy, and was treated by adrenaline injection, bipolar coagulation, and endoscopic hemoclipping (figure).The patient had a medical history of oesophageal cancer—surgically treated by an Ivor Lewis oesophagectomy 5 years earlier—and common variable immunodeficiency, for which he was receiving monthly intravenous immunoglobulin.
The ulcer had first been discovered 3 months earlier during routine surveillance endoscopy of the oesophagectomy anastomosis. Analysis of samples of biopsies taken during both gastroscopies had shown no evidence of malignancy or Helicobacter pylori; IgG testing for H pylori was also negative. Notably, the patient did not have a history of alcohol misuse or use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatories. He had received all childhood vaccinations—including measles—and he reported no recent contact with cats or other pets. During the period of surveillance, the ulcer had failed to heal and it continued to actively bleed despite confirmed concordance of the patient to a high dose of a proton pump inhibitor twice daily and sucralfate four times a day.
On examination, we found the patient to be alert and well looking. His abdomen was soft, with no tenderness or signs of upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 110 g/L (normal 138–172), which did not change during the admission. We took additional biopsies from the ulcer's edge and the patient remained on our ward for further monitoring and treatment with a proton pump inhibitor given intravenously.
Histopathological analysis of samples of the gastric ulcer biopsies showed chronic active inflammatory changes with multiple inclusion bodies in the mucosal epithelial lining, stromal cells, and capillaries (figure). The inclusion bodies were characterised by enlarged nuclei containing bright granular aggregates, surrounded by clear halo and typical owl's-eye morphology. Cytomegalovirus was confirmed as the cause on immunohistochemistry. No helicobacter organisms, dysplasia, or signs of malignancy were seen. Furthermore, the patient had a detectable viral load for cytomegalovirus of 1812 IU/mL; immunoglobulin levels demonstrated an IgG of 4·23 (normal 6·0–16·0 g/L), IgA <0·10 (normal 0·8–3·0 g/L), and IgM <0·20 (normal 0·4–2·5 g/L).
We started treatment with valganciclovir; 1 week later viral load for cytomegalovirus was 332 IU/mL, 270 IU/mL after 2 weeks, and after 4 months, the ulcer had healed completely. The patient had no further episodes of upper gastrointestinal bleeding, with undetectable levels of viral load of cytomegalovirus.
Common variable immunodeficiency is characterised by reduced serum levels of immunoglobulins with reduced or absent specific antibody production.
Cytomegalovirus-related gastric ulcers are not uncommon as a cause of gastrointestinal bleeding; a global deficiency in immunoglobulin—as in our case—and specifically of IgA, will result in a greater susceptibility of patients becoming infected with the virus. Infectious causes—including cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, measles virus, varicella zoster virus, Toxoplasma gondii, and Epstein-Barr virus—should be considered as a possible cause of a gastric ulcer that fails to heal in immunocompromised patients (video).

input: A 15-year-old girl presented with short stature; her height was 1·42 m (3 cm below third percentile) and her bodyweight was 41·8 kg (around 50th percentile). She had a round face and several subcutaneous nodules over her forehead, hands, and knees. She had hypoplasia of her fourth and fifth metacarpals bilaterally (figure). Serum calcium and parathormone concentrations were normal. Genetic testing showed that she was heterozygous for a non-sense mutation affecting GNAS, confirming the diagnosis of pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism. GNAS encodes the α-chain of the heterotrimeric G-protein Gs, which couples receptors for many hormones and neurotransmitters to activation of adenylyl cyclase. Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism is indicative of genomic imprinting. Patients who inherit the mutation from the paternal allele develop pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism, whereas inheritance from the maternal allele leads to pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism and renal resistance to parathormone and hypocalcaemia. Brachydactyly is due to premature closure of the epiphyses in the metacarpals.

The differential diagnosis of transient monocular vision loss (TMVL), based on clinical history alone, is a common clinical problem. A 66-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of recurrent right TMVL. He had more than 15 episodes without provocation. He described multiple islands of visual loss that coalesced to complete monocular blindness—persisting for several minutes—followed by recovery in a reverse manner. While venous access was being obtained for fluorescein angiography (FA), the patient reported onset of an attack. The examination was thus fortuitously done during vision loss.Normally, following intravenous injection, the dye passes through the short posterior ciliary arteries and appears in the optic disc and choroid within 8–12 s, depending on the age, cardiovascular status of the patient, and speed of dye injection. The arterial retinal circulation appears 11–18 s after injection. However, in our patient, FA of the right eye showed slightly delayed filling of the central retinal artery and severely delayed filling of the nasal choroid and prelaminar region of the optic disc (figure). The circulation of the left eye was normal. Examination 1 week later confirmed retinal circulation was normal between attacks (figure). A diagnosis of vasospasm was made and after treatment with nifedipine 5 mg twice a day, the attacks ceased. The patient remained attack free at 8 months' follow-up.
Many attempts have been made to classify TMVL from patients' descriptions to distinguish embolic from non-embolic attacks. Further, it has been speculated that the reticulated, patchy pattern of TMVL corresponds to interruption of the choroidal circulation—related to its lobular arrangement. This will very rarely occur due to thromboembolism because of the extensive anastomoses between the posterior ciliary arteries supplying the choroid. However, whereas vasospasm of the central retinal artery has been directly observed, choroidal perfusion abnormalities can usually only be identified by FA, and no photographic evidence for this assertion has been published. Our Clinical Picture provides the first direct confirmation for the proposed theory that the reticulated pattern of TMVL is a signature of transient ischaemia of the choroidal lobular circulation. Clearly, such cases should be managed as vasospasm.

Patients who inherit the mutation from the paternal allele develop pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism, whereas inheritance from the maternal allele leads to pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism and renal resistance to parathormone and hypocalcaemia. input: A 69-year-old woman with a 27-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presented to the rheumatology clinic at Kochi Medical School hospital, Japan, with polyarthralgia of both hands and painless subcutaneous nodules on her right hand that had slowly grown over a year. Physical examination revealed arthritis mutilans with ulnar deviation and yellow masses on the metacarpophalangeal joints of the fingers of the right hand (figure A). There were no abnormal findings in any part of the body other than the joints, such as the eyelids and trunk. Laboratory investigations revealed that the levels of C-reactive protein (CRP) and rheumatoid factor were 1·78 mg/dL (normal range <0·15 mg/dL) and 1 096·0 IU/mL (<15 IU/mL), respectively. Hyperlipidaemia, cryoglobulinemia, hypocomplementemia, and monoclonal paraproteins were not detected. We performed a bone marrow biopsy, which was normocellular. An x-ray revealed severe erosion and deformities of the hand bones and punched-out bony radiolucencies associated with the subcutaneous nodular lesions (figure B). A skin biopsy specimen of the subcutaneous mass showed areas of cholesterol clefts and necrobiosis surrounded by foamy histiocytes, lymphocytes, Touton giant cells, and foreign body-type multinucleated giant cells (figure C–F). These findings confirmed a diagnosis of pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodule. Pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodules are an unusual form of rheumatoid nodule resembling tendon xanthomas, are often mistakenly diagnosed as xanthomatosis, and have been previously regarded by investigators as subcutaneous xanthogranuloma, observed in the juxta-articular sites of the hand, wrist, elbow, knee, foot, and acromioclavicular joints. Pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodules are distinguished from xanthomatosis by x-ray findings of demonstrable punched-out bony radiolucencies, which are not present in xanthomatosis. Cholesterol clefts surrounded by granulomatous reactions can also be observed in rheumatoid synovial fluid and bursitis, sometimes presenting as migrating chylous cysts. Pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodule and xanthomatosis are easily misdiagnosed because their histopathological findings are similar. However, xanthomatosis is often associated with hyperlipidaemia, cryoglobulinemia, hypocomplementemia, and monoclonal paraproteins, whereas pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodule is not accompanied by these diseases and is found in the juxta-articular sites with punched-out bony radiolucencies. After initiating treatment with 6 mg oral methotrexate per week, the concentrations of CRP reduced to 0·63 mg/dL, polyarthralgia improved, and the pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodules shrank.

GNAS encodes the α-chain of the heterotrimeric G-protein Gs, which couples receptors for many hormones and neurotransmitters to activation of adenylyl cyclase. Patients who inherit the mutation from the paternal allele develop pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism, whereas inheritance from the maternal allele leads to pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism and renal resistance to parathormone and hypocalcaemia. input: A 69-year-old woman with a 27-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presented to the rheumatology clinic at Kochi Medical School hospital, Japan, with polyarthralgia of both hands and painless subcutaneous nodules on her right hand that had slowly grown over a year. Physical examination revealed arthritis mutilans with ulnar deviation and yellow masses on the metacarpophalangeal joints of the fingers of the right hand (figure A). There were no abnormal findings in any part of the body other than the joints, such as the eyelids and trunk. Laboratory investigations revealed that the levels of C-reactive protein (CRP) and rheumatoid factor were 1·78 mg/dL (normal range <0·15 mg/dL) and 1 096·0 IU/mL (<15 IU/mL), respectively. Hyperlipidaemia, cryoglobulinemia, hypocomplementemia, and monoclonal paraproteins were not detected. We performed a bone marrow biopsy, which was normocellular. An x-ray revealed severe erosion and deformities of the hand bones and punched-out bony radiolucencies associated with the subcutaneous nodular lesions (figure B). A skin biopsy specimen of the subcutaneous mass showed areas of cholesterol clefts and necrobiosis surrounded by foamy histiocytes, lymphocytes, Touton giant cells, and foreign body-type multinucleated giant cells (figure C–F). These findings confirmed a diagnosis of pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodule. Pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodules are an unusual form of rheumatoid nodule resembling tendon xanthomas, are often mistakenly diagnosed as xanthomatosis, and have been previously regarded by investigators as subcutaneous xanthogranuloma, observed in the juxta-articular sites of the hand, wrist, elbow, knee, foot, and acromioclavicular joints. Pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodules are distinguished from xanthomatosis by x-ray findings of demonstrable punched-out bony radiolucencies, which are not present in xanthomatosis. Cholesterol clefts surrounded by granulomatous reactions can also be observed in rheumatoid synovial fluid and bursitis, sometimes presenting as migrating chylous cysts. Pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodule and xanthomatosis are easily misdiagnosed because their histopathological findings are similar. However, xanthomatosis is often associated with hyperlipidaemia, cryoglobulinemia, hypocomplementemia, and monoclonal paraproteins, whereas pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodule is not accompanied by these diseases and is found in the juxta-articular sites with punched-out bony radiolucencies. After initiating treatment with 6 mg oral methotrexate per week, the concentrations of CRP reduced to 0·63 mg/dL, polyarthralgia improved, and the pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodules shrank.

A 17-year-old boy was referred to the ophthalmology service at St Thomas' Hospital (London, UK) with bilateral red eyes, bilateral eye pain independent of eye movement that disturbed his sleep, photophobia, and mild, subjective blurring of vision. He had become infected with SARS-CoV-2 5 weeks before referral and had been diagnosed with paediatric inflammatory multisystem syndrome temporally associated with COVID-19 (PIMS-TS) and associated myocarditis.His Snellen visual acuity was excellent: 6/4 unaided in both eyes. He had bilateral, diffuse episcleral and deep scleral injection (vasodilatation with hyperaemia) that did not blanch with topical 10% phenylephrine; a bilateral anterior chamber grading of 2+ (16–25 cells in a 1 mm × 1 mm field); no vitritis, retinitis, or vasculitis; and an otherwise unremarkable fundal examination (figure A, B). A B-scan ultrasound did not show any posterior scleritis. He was diagnosed with bilateral, diffuse, anterior non-necrotising scleritis with anterior uveitis.
Before his ophthalmology referral, the patient had been treated for PIMS-TS with a 3-day course of intravenous methylprednisolone (950 mg/day). He subsequently developed fever, had a rising C-reactive protein concentration 1 week post-admission (from 47 mg/L to 94 mg/L over the course of 1 day), and received 800 mg of intravenous tocilizumab on the day of his referral. After attending the ophthalmology service, he started a course of oral prednisolone (starting dose 40 mg/day for 17 days), guttae 0·1% dexamethasone (eye drops to both eyes at an initial schedule of once every 2 h for 3 days), and a 1-week course of guttae 1% cyclopentolate (eye drops to both eyes twice daily). Treatment (prednisolone and guttae 0·1% dexamethasone) was tapered over a 6-week period. 7 days after ophthalmology referral and review, the patient's symptoms had resolved and he had normal vision and no ongoing inflammation.
10 days after referral, the patient presented with a right facial (VIIth) nerve palsy and his prescribed regimen of prednisolone (40 mg/day, before tapering) was not changed. Neuroimaging showed mild inflammation of the right tympanic facial nerve (figure 1C). Prompt resolution of facial weakness occurred within 4 weeks.
It is imperative not to misdiagnose the potentially sight-threatening conditions of scleritis and uveitis as conjunctivitis, which is the commonly known ophthalmic association in PIMS-TS.

A 17-year-old boy was referred to the ophthalmology service at St Thomas' Hospital (London, UK) with bilateral red eyes, bilateral eye pain independent of eye movement that disturbed his sleep, photophobia, and mild, subjective blurring of vision. He had become infected with SARS-CoV-2 5 weeks before referral and had been diagnosed with paediatric inflammatory multisystem syndrome temporally associated with COVID-19 (PIMS-TS) and associated myocarditis.His Snellen visual acuity was excellent: 6/4 unaided in both eyes. He had bilateral, diffuse episcleral and deep scleral injection (vasodilatation with hyperaemia) that did not blanch with topical 10% phenylephrine; a bilateral anterior chamber grading of 2+ (16–25 cells in a 1 mm × 1 mm field); no vitritis, retinitis, or vasculitis; and an otherwise unremarkable fundal examination (figure A, B). A B-scan ultrasound did not show any posterior scleritis. He was diagnosed with bilateral, diffuse, anterior non-necrotising scleritis with anterior uveitis.
Before his ophthalmology referral, the patient had been treated for PIMS-TS with a 3-day course of intravenous methylprednisolone (950 mg/day). He subsequently developed fever, had a rising C-reactive protein concentration 1 week post-admission (from 47 mg/L to 94 mg/L over the course of 1 day), and received 800 mg of intravenous tocilizumab on the day of his referral. After attending the ophthalmology service, he started a course of oral prednisolone (starting dose 40 mg/day for 17 days), guttae 0·1% dexamethasone (eye drops to both eyes at an initial schedule of once every 2 h for 3 days), and a 1-week course of guttae 1% cyclopentolate (eye drops to both eyes twice daily). Treatment (prednisolone and guttae 0·1% dexamethasone) was tapered over a 6-week period. 7 days after ophthalmology referral and review, the patient's symptoms had resolved and he had normal vision and no ongoing inflammation.
10 days after referral, the patient presented with a right facial (VIIth) nerve palsy and his prescribed regimen of prednisolone (40 mg/day, before tapering) was not changed. Neuroimaging showed mild inflammation of the right tympanic facial nerve (figure 1C). Prompt resolution of facial weakness occurred within 4 weeks.
It is imperative not to misdiagnose the potentially sight-threatening conditions of scleritis and uveitis as conjunctivitis, which is the commonly known ophthalmic association in PIMS-TS.

Her family reported that the day before admission she had appeared more tired and weak with altered mental status, but before that had been in normal health. On examination she had Glasgow coma score (GCS) of 3, a temperature of 39·4°C, tachycardia, and systolic blood pressure ranging from 170–200 mm Hg. She had weakness in her legs bilaterally, but review of systems was otherwise negative. In view of her low GCS score she was intubated for airway protection, and required vasopressors because she was hypotensive, febrile, tachycardic, and not responding to fluids. A CT scan of her head and subsequent MRI showed profound hydrocephalus (figure).An external ventricular drain was fitted for possible acute hydrocephalus, but her intracranial pressure was found to be 5 mm Hg (normal 5–15 mm Hg) and remained 5–10 mm Hg so the drain was removed 2 days later. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tests were normal. We made a diagnosis of sepsis secondary to pneumonia, on the basis of chest radiographs showing consolidation and blood culture results, as the cause of her altered mental status, which returned to normal after treatment with antibiotics. She was discharged to a rehabilitation facility and has now returned to her normal baseline. In view of her previously normal medical history the clinical team decided her hydrocephalus had probably been present since birth.
This case shows the brain's ability to maintain normal mental status and function in spite of profound chronic hydrocephalus. In contrast to normal pressure hydrocephalus, compensated hydrocephalus can be asymptomatic until an external insult, such as an infection as in this case, and can lead to syncope or even sudden death. Compensated hydrocephalus, also known as hydrocephalus ex vacuo, is a form of communicating hydrocephalus—ie, one that does not obstruct the flow of CSF. Compensated hydrocephalus is usually seen in elderly people as the result of brain volume loss due to ageing or a disorder that causes the brain to shrink, such as Alzheimer's disease, leukodystrophy, or encephalomalacia resulting from focal damage caused by a stroke or traumatic brain injury. Clinicians should be aware of this condition that might be found incidentally on imaging in asymptomatic patients. Unless dictated by clinical examination, as in this case, additional work-up is not necessary.

A 62-year-old woman with a medical history of hypertension and well-controlled diabetes mellitus type 2 was found unresponsive on the floor at home by her family. Her family reported that the day before admission she had appeared more tired and weak with altered mental status, but before that had been in normal health. On examination she had Glasgow coma score (GCS) of 3, a temperature of 39·4°C, tachycardia, and systolic blood pressure ranging from 170–200 mm Hg. She had weakness in her legs bilaterally, but review of systems was otherwise negative. In view of her low GCS score she was intubated for airway protection, and required vasopressors because she was hypotensive, febrile, tachycardic, and not responding to fluids. A CT scan of her head and subsequent MRI showed profound hydrocephalus (figure).An external ventricular drain was fitted for possible acute hydrocephalus, but her intracranial pressure was found to be 5 mm Hg (normal 5–15 mm Hg) and remained 5–10 mm Hg so the drain was removed 2 days later. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tests were normal. We made a diagnosis of sepsis secondary to pneumonia, on the basis of chest radiographs showing consolidation and blood culture results, as the cause of her altered mental status, which returned to normal after treatment with antibiotics. She was discharged to a rehabilitation facility and has now returned to her normal baseline. In view of her previously normal medical history the clinical team decided her hydrocephalus had probably been present since birth.
This case shows the brain's ability to maintain normal mental status and function in spite of profound chronic hydrocephalus. In contrast to normal pressure hydrocephalus, compensated hydrocephalus can be asymptomatic until an external insult, such as an infection as in this case, and can lead to syncope or even sudden death. Compensated hydrocephalus, also known as hydrocephalus ex vacuo, is a form of communicating hydrocephalus—ie, one that does not obstruct the flow of CSF. Compensated hydrocephalus is usually seen in elderly people as the result of brain volume loss due to ageing or a disorder that causes the brain to shrink, such as Alzheimer's disease, leukodystrophy, or encephalomalacia resulting from focal damage caused by a stroke or traumatic brain injury. Clinicians should be aware of this condition that might be found incidentally on imaging in asymptomatic patients. Unless dictated by clinical examination, as in this case, additional work-up is not necessary.

input: A 61-year-old man presented with bilateral, asymptomatic, indurated non-pitting verrucous plaques and nodules on his extremities and buttocks. He was diagnosed with Graves' disease 20 years ago. The patient developed hypothyroidism secondary to radioactive iodine ablation of the thyroid 4 years prior to presenting to us and received levothyroxine replacement therapy, after which he attained a sustained euthyroid state. However, he developed an asymptomatic rash over his extremities and buttock, which worsened gradually. On physical examination, several plaques that were leathery in texture and nodules were observed on his extremities and buttock (figure A–D). The results of thyroid-function tests were normal (free tri-iodothyronine [T3] 3·83 pg/mL, local reference 1·80–4·10; free thyroxine [T4] 1·23 ng/dL, local reference 0·81–1·89) except for a thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration of 0·094 μIU/mL (local reference 0·38–4·34) and thyrotrophin receptor antibody concentration of 280·51 IU/L (local reference <13). Results of liver and kidney function tests were normal, and concentrations of calcium, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3, 25-hydroxyvitamin D3, parathyroid hormone, urinary calcium, and urine phosphorus were within normal limits. On histological examination of skin lesion biopsy specimens stained with haematoxylin and eosin and alcian blue, abundant deposition of mucin was seen in the dermis (figure E, F). The final diagnosis according to the pathology report was myxedema. Despite application of potent topical corticosteroids, occlusive or compressive therapy, and multipoint subcutaneous injection of long-acting glucocorticoid, the skin lesions showed no obvious signs of remission after 6 months of treatment.Myxedema results from the accumulation in the dermis of glycosaminoglycan secreted by fibroblasts. The pathogenesis of the extrathyroidal manifestations of myxedema involves fibroblast activation and increased glycosaminoglycan production. Some studies postulate that the destruction of the thyroid gland by therapeutic drugs (especially iodine-131) results in the release of an antigen from thyroid cells that then stimulates the production of the thyrotrophin receptor antibody. The fibroblast in the orbital area and pretibial dermis share antigenic sites that underlie the autoimmune process that causes Graves' disease. Thereby crossreaction contributes to the development of myxedema occurring long after euthyroid status is achieved through treatment. Although myxedema does not seem to be related to the concentrations of T3 and T4, only four cases of euthyroid patients being diagnosed with myxedema have been reported in the literature.

input: A 61-year-old man presented with bilateral, asymptomatic, indurated non-pitting verrucous plaques and nodules on his extremities and buttocks. He was diagnosed with Graves' disease 20 years ago. The patient developed hypothyroidism secondary to radioactive iodine ablation of the thyroid 4 years prior to presenting to us and received levothyroxine replacement therapy, after which he attained a sustained euthyroid state. However, he developed an asymptomatic rash over his extremities and buttock, which worsened gradually. On physical examination, several plaques that were leathery in texture and nodules were observed on his extremities and buttock (figure A–D). The results of thyroid-function tests were normal (free tri-iodothyronine [T3] 3·83 pg/mL, local reference 1·80–4·10; free thyroxine [T4] 1·23 ng/dL, local reference 0·81–1·89) except for a thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration of 0·094 μIU/mL (local reference 0·38–4·34) and thyrotrophin receptor antibody concentration of 280·51 IU/L (local reference <13). Results of liver and kidney function tests were normal, and concentrations of calcium, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3, 25-hydroxyvitamin D3, parathyroid hormone, urinary calcium, and urine phosphorus were within normal limits. On histological examination of skin lesion biopsy specimens stained with haematoxylin and eosin and alcian blue, abundant deposition of mucin was seen in the dermis (figure E, F). The final diagnosis according to the pathology report was myxedema. Despite application of potent topical corticosteroids, occlusive or compressive therapy, and multipoint subcutaneous injection of long-acting glucocorticoid, the skin lesions showed no obvious signs of remission after 6 months of treatment.Myxedema results from the accumulation in the dermis of glycosaminoglycan secreted by fibroblasts. The pathogenesis of the extrathyroidal manifestations of myxedema involves fibroblast activation and increased glycosaminoglycan production. Some studies postulate that the destruction of the thyroid gland by therapeutic drugs (especially iodine-131) results in the release of an antigen from thyroid cells that then stimulates the production of the thyrotrophin receptor antibody. The fibroblast in the orbital area and pretibial dermis share antigenic sites that underlie the autoimmune process that causes Graves' disease. Thereby crossreaction contributes to the development of myxedema occurring long after euthyroid status is achieved through treatment. Although myxedema does not seem to be related to the concentrations of T3 and T4, only four cases of euthyroid patients being diagnosed with myxedema have been reported in the literature.

A 24-year-old man presented to our clinic reporting severe anal pain and a pustular rash on his trunk, arms, penis, and fingers. The patient said the pain started 3 days after he had condomless penetrative and receptive anal intercourse with a man; he then developed a fever, chills, and inguinal lymphadenopathy. The skin lesions appeared approximately 8 days after the sexual activity: 2 days before he attended our clinic. The patient was previously fit and well with no medical history.On examination, we found him to be in obvious distress because of the anal pain; his temperature was 37·1°C, heart rate was 98 beats per min, and blood pressure was 140/98 mm Hg. He had approximately 10 vesicular lesions, without surrounding erythema, containing yellow fluid, and measuring between 2 mm and 3 mm on his trunk, arms, penis, and fingers; his penis was oedematous.
Laboratory investigations showed a C-reactive protein concentration of 16 mg/L, which increased to approximately 7 times this concentration on day 2 of his hospital stay. Anorectoscopy showed ulcerating lesions adjacent to the pectinate line of the anal canal (appendix). Anorectal and oropharyngeal swabs tested positive for monkeypox virus by PCR.
Histopathological analysis of tissue samples taken from the anal lesions (appendix) showed prominent inflammation and regional disruption of the crypt epithelium, specifically loss of columnar cell shape. Notably, balloon-like expansion of epithelial cells and regular eosinophilic plasma inclusions, typical of poxvirus infections of the skin, were absent. Immunohistochemistry for cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, and nucleic acid amplification tests for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoea were negative.
Paraffin-embedded biopsy samples were processed for thin-section electron microscopy (EM) to investigate whether cells are infected by monkeypox virus and whether they propagate the virus. Ultrathin sections of the samples were analysed by transmission EM. One section was entirely digitalised at high resolution by EM—so called large-scale scanning-transmission EM—to allow microscope-independent analysis by pan-and-zoom viewing at the computer screen. EM showed both mature and immature virus particles—indicating virus replication—organised in specific cytoplasmic areas of epithelial cells of colonic crypts and of interstitial cells (figure).
The patient was admitted to the infectious disease ward, because of anal pain, and prescribed a combination of morphine, metamizole, and gabapentin, which controlled his symptoms. He was allowed home, 8 days later, when his condition had improved. He had no antiviral treatment.

He had approximately 10 vesicular lesions, without surrounding erythema, containing yellow fluid, and measuring between 2 mm and 3 mm on his trunk, arms, penis, and fingers; his penis was oedematous.

Anorectoscopy showed ulcerating lesions adjacent to the pectinate line of the anal canal (appendix). Anorectal and oropharyngeal swabs tested positive for monkeypox virus by PCR.

Ultrathin sections of the samples were analysed by transmission EM. One section was entirely digitalised at high resolution by EM—so called large-scale scanning-transmission EM—to allow microscope-independent analysis by pan-and-zoom viewing at the computer screen. EM showed both mature and immature virus particles—indicating virus replication—organised in specific cytoplasmic areas of epithelial cells of colonic crypts and of interstitial cells (figure).
The patient was admitted to the infectious disease ward, because of anal pain, and prescribed a combination of morphine, metamizole, and gabapentin, which controlled his symptoms. He was allowed home, 8 days later, when his condition had improved. He had no antiviral treatment.

A 47-year-old woman presented to our clinic with a 1-month history of a painful, itching, non-healing, and oozing lesion on the left side of her neck (figure). In addition to the lesion, she reported having disturbed sleep because of pain and pruritus in the affected area. The problem developed between 4 and 5 weeks after a trip to the Mediterranean coast of southern Turkey. An oral antibiotic and iodine ointment had failed to make any improvement.On clinical examination, the lesion was a single ulcer with yellow exudate and an indurated erythematous margin. The patient also had palpable, indolent lymphadenopathy of the submental lymph nodes. A bacterial swab showed coagulase-negative staphylococci. Initially, we suspected that the patient might have cutaneous leishmaniasis and we took two punch biopsy samples from both the centre and margin of the lesion for PCR and histological analyses. Haematoxylin and eosin staining of the central biopsy showed plasma-cell-rich granulation tissue. Immunohistochemical staining for Treponema pallidum showed spirochetes (figure). Laboratory test results showed a positive non-treponemal venereal disease research laboratory test titre of 1:8, as well as positive specific assays—the T pallidum particle agglutination assay, IgM immunoblot, and IgG ELISA. On further inquiry, the patient explained that she had unprotected sexual intercourse during her holiday. She reported that her partner had wounds on the lips that may have been the source of infection. A diagnosis of a primary syphilitic chancre was made, and the patient was treated with benzylpenicillin at 2 400 000 IU, intramuscularly. The ulceration resolved 3 weeks after treatment.
Primary syphilis usually consists of a single, painless, non-itching, sharply bordered ulceration—called a chancre—with regional lymphadenopathy. Syphilitic chancres can show great clinical variability: less than 10% are extragenital occurring in any location. Most of these cases have been described on the abdomen, breasts, fingers, and in and around the mouth. A syphilitic chancre should, therefore, be a diagnostic consideration—albeit in some places an unlikely possibility—in any non-healing, indurated ulcer found anywhere on the body.

A 47-year-old woman presented to our clinic with a 1-month history of a painful, itching, non-healing, and oozing lesion on the left side of her neck (figure). In addition to the lesion, she reported having disturbed sleep because of pain and pruritus in the affected area. The problem developed between 4 and 5 weeks after a trip to the Mediterranean coast of southern Turkey. An oral antibiotic and iodine ointment had failed to make any improvement.On clinical examination, the lesion was a single ulcer with yellow exudate and an indurated erythematous margin. The patient also had palpable, indolent lymphadenopathy of the submental lymph nodes. A bacterial swab showed coagulase-negative staphylococci. Initially, we suspected that the patient might have cutaneous leishmaniasis and we took two punch biopsy samples from both the centre and margin of the lesion for PCR and histological analyses. Haematoxylin and eosin staining of the central biopsy showed plasma-cell-rich granulation tissue. Immunohistochemical staining for Treponema pallidum showed spirochetes (figure). Laboratory test results showed a positive non-treponemal venereal disease research laboratory test titre of 1:8, as well as positive specific assays—the T pallidum particle agglutination assay, IgM immunoblot, and IgG ELISA. On further inquiry, the patient explained that she had unprotected sexual intercourse during her holiday. She reported that her partner had wounds on the lips that may have been the source of infection. A diagnosis of a primary syphilitic chancre was made, and the patient was treated with benzylpenicillin at 2 400 000 IU, intramuscularly. The ulceration resolved 3 weeks after treatment.
Primary syphilis usually consists of a single, painless, non-itching, sharply bordered ulceration—called a chancre—with regional lymphadenopathy. Syphilitic chancres can show great clinical variability: less than 10% are extragenital occurring in any location. Most of these cases have been described on the abdomen, breasts, fingers, and in and around the mouth. A syphilitic chancre should, therefore, be a diagnostic consideration—albeit in some places an unlikely possibility—in any non-healing, indurated ulcer found anywhere on the body.

input:
A 47-year-old woman presented to our clinic with a 1-month history of a painful, itching, non-healing, and oozing lesion on the left side of her neck (figure). In addition to the lesion, she reported having disturbed sleep because of pain and pruritus in the affected area. The problem developed between 4 and 5 weeks after a trip to the Mediterranean coast of southern Turkey. An oral antibiotic and iodine ointment had failed to make any improvement.On clinical examination, the lesion was a single ulcer with yellow exudate and an indurated erythematous margin. The patient also had palpable, indolent lymphadenopathy of the submental lymph nodes. A bacterial swab showed coagulase-negative staphylococci. Initially, we suspected that the patient might have cutaneous leishmaniasis and we took two punch biopsy samples from both the centre and margin of the lesion for PCR and histological analyses. Haematoxylin and eosin staining of the central biopsy showed plasma-cell-rich granulation tissue. Immunohistochemical staining for Treponema pallidum showed spirochetes (figure). Laboratory test results showed a positive non-treponemal venereal disease research laboratory test titre of 1:8, as well as positive specific assays—the T pallidum particle agglutination assay, IgM immunoblot, and IgG ELISA. On further inquiry, the patient explained that she had unprotected sexual intercourse during her holiday. She reported that her partner had wounds on the lips that may have been the source of infection. A diagnosis of a primary syphilitic chancre was made, and the patient was treated with benzylpenicillin at 2 400 000 IU, intramuscularly. The ulceration resolved 3 weeks after treatment.
Primary syphilis usually consists of a single, painless, non-itching, sharply bordered ulceration—called a chancre—with regional lymphadenopathy. Syphilitic chancres can show great clinical variability: less than 10% are extragenital occurring in any location. Most of these cases have been described on the abdomen, breasts, fingers, and in and around the mouth. A syphilitic chancre should, therefore, be a diagnostic consideration—albeit in some places an unlikely possibility—in any non-healing, indurated ulcer found anywhere on the body.

A 45-year-old woman presented to our emergency department with a 4-h history of diplopia and vertigo.
The patient had been found to have a bicuspid aortic valve without any significant dysfunction; the bicuspid valve had been diagnosed when she was aged 25 years by transthoracic echocardiography when investigated for a systolic murmur. The patient was a non-smoker; she had previously been fit and well, and she was taking no medications.
On examination after admission, she was well and alert; her temperature was 36·7°C, blood pressure 186/105 mm Hg, and pulse rate 83 beats per min. She had ataxia in her arms.
An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm. Laboratory investigations showed a mildly increased C-reactive protein concentration of 18 mg/L (normal <5); leukocytes and procalcitonin concentration were in normal range.
A brain MRI showed cerebellar bilateral ischaemic lesions; and transoesophageal echocardiography showed findings consistent with a marked thickening of the aortic leaflets with hypoechogenic masses, which was causing mild aortic regurgitation (figure; video).The hospital endocarditis team assessed the patient; empirical treatment with antibiotics—amoxicillin and ceftriaxone—was started after collection of four samples for blood cultures. Additionally, serological testing for bacteria—including Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella spp, Aspergillus spp, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Brucella spp, and Legionellla pneumophilia—causing blood culture-negative endocarditis, was carried out.
Antibiotics were stopped after 3 weeks—given from day 1 of the admission to day 21—after all microbiological results came back negative. Assays for antiphospholipid, rheumatic factor, and antinuclear antibodies were also negative; moreover, a workup for disseminated intravascular coagulation was also negative.
To investigate for possible peripheral emboli, a thoracic CT scan was done which showed a left inferior lung mass with mediastinal and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy (figure). An 18fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT showed intense metabolic fixation of all tumour targets (figure). After lymphadenomectomy puncture, histopathological analysis of samples of a transthoracic needle biopsy of the lesion showed a solid architecture invasive adenocarcinoma; mucin-secreting cells were strongly positive for tumour marker thyroid transcription factor-1 and intensely positive (3+ in 100% of cells) for ALK-EML4 on immunohistochemical analysis. Fluorescence in situ hybridisation analysis found an ALK gene rearrangement in 93% of the nuclei, characterised by supernumerary red signals.
A diagnosis of marantic endocarditis was made and tyrosine kinase inhibitor treatment with crizotinib—an ALK inhibitor—was initiated on day 19. The patient described a transient visual disturbance 48 h later. Brain MRI showed additional small ischaemic lesions; owing to the perceived risk of intracranial bleeding due to recent brain infarcts, anticoagulation was not initiated. No subsequent neurological events were noted.
2 months after crizotinib initiation, the heart valve lesions had disappeared with no perforation or deterioration of function (figure; video). An 18F-FDG PET/CT confirmed a complete metabolic response (figure).
At 7-year follow-up, the patient is alive and well without cancer or evidence of marantic endocarditis.
Advanced malignancy is associated with marantic endocarditis, although it may be found with autoimmune diseases including systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis. Treatment of the underlying cause—in our case the malignancy—may lead to resolution of the valvular lesions.

The patient was a non-smoker; she had previously been fit and well, and she was taking no medications.

An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm. Laboratory investigations showed a mildly increased C-reactive protein concentration of 18 mg/L (normal <5); leukocytes and procalcitonin concentration were in normal range.

Additionally, serological testing for bacteria—including Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella spp, Aspergillus spp, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Brucella spp, and Legionellla pneumophilia—causing blood culture-negative endocarditis, was carried out.
Antibiotics were stopped after 3 weeks—given from day 1 of the admission to day 21—after all microbiological results came back negative. Assays for antiphospholipid, rheumatic factor, and antinuclear antibodies were also negative; moreover, a workup for disseminated intravascular coagulation was also negative.
To investigate for possible peripheral emboli, a thoracic CT scan was done which showed a left inferior lung mass with mediastinal and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy (figure). An 18fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT showed intense metabolic fixation of all tumour targets (figure). After lymphadenomectomy puncture, histopathological analysis of samples of a transthoracic needle biopsy of the lesion showed a solid architecture invasive adenocarcinoma; mucin-secreting cells were strongly positive for tumour marker thyroid transcription factor-1 and intensely positive (3+ in 100% of cells) for ALK-EML4 on immunohistochemical analysis. Fluorescence in situ hybridisation analysis found an ALK gene rearrangement in 93% of the nuclei, characterised by supernumerary red signals.
A diagnosis of marantic endocarditis was made and tyrosine kinase inhibitor treatment with crizotinib—an ALK inhibitor—was initiated on day 19. The patient described a transient visual disturbance 48 h later. Brain MRI showed additional small ischaemic lesions; owing to the perceived risk of intracranial bleeding due to recent brain infarcts, anticoagulation was not initiated. No subsequent neurological events were noted.
2 months after crizotinib initiation, the heart valve lesions had disappeared with no perforation or deterioration of function (figure; video). An 18F-FDG PET/CT confirmed a complete metabolic response (figure).
At 7-year follow-up, the patient is alive and well without cancer or evidence of marantic endocarditis.

An 81-year-old man was referred to our clinic with a 1-year history of shortness of breath on exertion. The patient also had a history of cryptogenic liver cirrhosis and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.On examination we found him to have a pan-systolic murmur, fine bilateral basal crackles on chest auscultation, heart rate 73 beats per min, and respiratory rate 17 breaths per min. Oxygen saturation was 96% on room air.
Laboratory investigations showed normal white blood cell count and C-reactive protein concentration. Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with first-degree heart block. An echocardiogram showed normal left ventricular size and function with possible bi-leaflet mitral valve prolapse resulting in severe mitral regurgitation (appendix). Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) showed a central jet of mitral regurgitation caused by annular dilatation and non-coaptation of the mitral valve leaflets (figure); using both the standard method—defined as the left ventricular stroke volume minus the aortic net flow—and four-dimensional (4D) flow advanced techniques, the mitral regurgitation was found to be 5 mL (<30 mL is mild; appendix). Additionally, the mitral regurgitation jet was seen swirling around the left atrium, thus leading to an overestimation of the regurgitation using a speckle-doppler trace (figure; video). Furthermore, moderate left ventricular systolic impairment, with a non-ischaemic fibrosis pattern in the lateral and anterior walls, was seen; on T1 mapping, there was globally increased T1 signal and raised extracellular volume (figure). Taken together, the findings suggested non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy secondary to cardiac sarcoidosis—and on discussion with the respiratory team, it became apparent that the patient had, 20 years earlier, indeed been treated abroad for sarcoidosis of the lung.
We consequently decided to defer the planned mitral valve surgery, as it was evident—with the information gleaned from the CMR—that the patient had a primary cardiomyopathy and that his symptoms were unrelated to the mild mitral regurgitation. A respiratory review concluded the problem was chronic and recommended close monitoring of the disease.
Multiparametric CMR imaging is invaluable not only for the accurate assessment of function and sub-phenotyping the aetiology of cardiomyopathy, but also, using 4D flow methods, for more precise quantification of mitral regurgitation that might—as shown in our case—completely change the course of clinical management.

input:
An 81-year-old man was referred to our clinic with a 1-year history of shortness of breath on exertion. The patient also had a history of cryptogenic liver cirrhosis and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.On examination we found him to have a pan-systolic murmur, fine bilateral basal crackles on chest auscultation, heart rate 73 beats per min, and respiratory rate 17 breaths per min. Oxygen saturation was 96% on room air.
Laboratory investigations showed normal white blood cell count and C-reactive protein concentration. Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with first-degree heart block. An echocardiogram showed normal left ventricular size and function with possible bi-leaflet mitral valve prolapse resulting in severe mitral regurgitation (appendix). Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) showed a central jet of mitral regurgitation caused by annular dilatation and non-coaptation of the mitral valve leaflets (figure); using both the standard method—defined as the left ventricular stroke volume minus the aortic net flow—and four-dimensional (4D) flow advanced techniques, the mitral regurgitation was found to be 5 mL (<30 mL is mild; appendix). Additionally, the mitral regurgitation jet was seen swirling around the left atrium, thus leading to an overestimation of the regurgitation using a speckle-doppler trace (figure; video). Furthermore, moderate left ventricular systolic impairment, with a non-ischaemic fibrosis pattern in the lateral and anterior walls, was seen; on T1 mapping, there was globally increased T1 signal and raised extracellular volume (figure). Taken together, the findings suggested non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy secondary to cardiac sarcoidosis—and on discussion with the respiratory team, it became apparent that the patient had, 20 years earlier, indeed been treated abroad for sarcoidosis of the lung.
We consequently decided to defer the planned mitral valve surgery, as it was evident—with the information gleaned from the CMR—that the patient had a primary cardiomyopathy and that his symptoms were unrelated to the mild mitral regurgitation. A respiratory review concluded the problem was chronic and recommended close monitoring of the disease.
Multiparametric CMR imaging is invaluable not only for the accurate assessment of function and sub-phenotyping the aetiology of cardiomyopathy, but also, using 4D flow methods, for more precise quantification of mitral regurgitation that might—as shown in our case—completely change the course of clinical management.

An 81-year-old man was referred to our clinic with a 1-year history of shortness of breath on exertion. The patient also had a history of cryptogenic liver cirrhosis and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.On examination we found him to have a pan-systolic murmur, fine bilateral basal crackles on chest auscultation, heart rate 73 beats per min, and respiratory rate 17 breaths per min. Oxygen saturation was 96% on room air.
Laboratory investigations showed normal white blood cell count and C-reactive protein concentration. Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with first-degree heart block. An echocardiogram showed normal left ventricular size and function with possible bi-leaflet mitral valve prolapse resulting in severe mitral regurgitation (appendix). Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) showed a central jet of mitral regurgitation caused by annular dilatation and non-coaptation of the mitral valve leaflets (figure); using both the standard method—defined as the left ventricular stroke volume minus the aortic net flow—and four-dimensional (4D) flow advanced techniques, the mitral regurgitation was found to be 5 mL (<30 mL is mild; appendix). Additionally, the mitral regurgitation jet was seen swirling around the left atrium, thus leading to an overestimation of the regurgitation using a speckle-doppler trace (figure; video). Furthermore, moderate left ventricular systolic impairment, with a non-ischaemic fibrosis pattern in the lateral and anterior walls, was seen; on T1 mapping, there was globally increased T1 signal and raised extracellular volume (figure). Taken together, the findings suggested non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy secondary to cardiac sarcoidosis—and on discussion with the respiratory team, it became apparent that the patient had, 20 years earlier, indeed been treated abroad for sarcoidosis of the lung.
We consequently decided to defer the planned mitral valve surgery, as it was evident—with the information gleaned from the CMR—that the patient had a primary cardiomyopathy and that his symptoms were unrelated to the mild mitral regurgitation. A respiratory review concluded the problem was chronic and recommended close monitoring of the disease.
Multiparametric CMR imaging is invaluable not only for the accurate assessment of function and sub-phenotyping the aetiology of cardiomyopathy, but also, using 4D flow methods, for more precise quantification of mitral regurgitation that might—as shown in our case—completely change the course of clinical management.

A 58-year-old woman presented as an emergency with a 4-month history of intermittent upper abdominal pain, distension, and vomiting.She had a history of a hernia which had been repaired and augmented with prosthetic mesh 4 years earlier.
On examination, we found the patient to be apyrexial but not distressed. Her abdomen was slightly distended; she had normal bowel sounds with a non-tender fullness at the umbilicus—at the site of the earlier hernia repair—with no discharge.
Laboratory investigations showed a normal white cell count of 11·3 × 109 per L with a haemoglobin concentration of 14·6 g/dL (normal 13·0–16·5); her serum C-reactive protein concentration and renal function were both normal. An initial unprepared contrast enhanced CT showed gallstones and it also raised the possibility of a fistula between the small bowel and the mesh, because the mesh appeared adjacent to the slightly distended gut (figure). We managed the patient conservatively with intravenous fluids and kept her nil by mouth and her symptoms settled within 12 h.
However, 2 months later, at an outpatient appointment review, she continued to report pain and abdominal distention; a fully prepared CT suggested a stricture in the distal transverse colon. We carried out a colonoscopy and a biopsy which indicated that the lesion was malignant. We then did an open extended right hemicolectomy, cholecystectomy, and a segmental small bowel resection when we found the mesh from the earlier hernial repair intra-luminal (figure). Histopathological examination of a sample of the excised lesion showed a T4aN2a adenocarcinoma; the patient was then given adjuvant chemotherapy. At 12 months’ follow-up she remains symptom free.
Repairs of abdominal wall hernias are currently frequently augmented with prosthetic biomaterials—such as mesh—and this has resulted in minimal tension reconstruction and a lower later recurrence rate. However, the use of such prostheses, irrespective of type or size, may be associated with various complications including migration and visceral fistulation to the bladder, colon, or small bowel. The incidence of such fistulation—albeit clinically uncommon—remains uncertain, as not all cases give rise to symptoms. It is likely that many cases go unreported for a variety of reasons—including the possibility of litigation.
In the radiological report of our patient's initial CT scan, the presence of the mesh was considered incidental as she was not systemically unwell, she had few local symptoms, and the scan had shown gallstones. However, if symptoms persist—even causing only minimal discomfort, as in our patient—careful re-imaging is essential. Finally, although the migration of mesh into the gut lumen may be more common than is appreciated, it is crucial to consider that it might obscure more significant intra-abdominal pathologies, such as adenocarcinomas of the gut (video).

A 58-year-old woman presented as an emergency with a 4-month history of intermittent upper abdominal pain, distension, and vomiting.She had a history of a hernia which had been repaired and augmented with prosthetic mesh 4 years earlier.
On examination, we found the patient to be apyrexial but not distressed. Her abdomen was slightly distended; she had normal bowel sounds with a non-tender fullness at the umbilicus—at the site of the earlier hernia repair—with no discharge.
Laboratory investigations showed a normal white cell count of 11·3 × 109 per L with a haemoglobin concentration of 14·6 g/dL (normal 13·0–16·5); her serum C-reactive protein concentration and renal function were both normal. An initial unprepared contrast enhanced CT showed gallstones and it also raised the possibility of a fistula between the small bowel and the mesh, because the mesh appeared adjacent to the slightly distended gut (figure). We managed the patient conservatively with intravenous fluids and kept her nil by mouth and her symptoms settled within 12 h.
However, 2 months later, at an outpatient appointment review, she continued to report pain and abdominal distention; a fully prepared CT suggested a stricture in the distal transverse colon. We carried out a colonoscopy and a biopsy which indicated that the lesion was malignant. We then did an open extended right hemicolectomy, cholecystectomy, and a segmental small bowel resection when we found the mesh from the earlier hernial repair intra-luminal (figure). Histopathological examination of a sample of the excised lesion showed a T4aN2a adenocarcinoma; the patient was then given adjuvant chemotherapy. At 12 months’ follow-up she remains symptom free.
Repairs of abdominal wall hernias are currently frequently augmented with prosthetic biomaterials—such as mesh—and this has resulted in minimal tension reconstruction and a lower later recurrence rate. However, the use of such prostheses, irrespective of type or size, may be associated with various complications including migration and visceral fistulation to the bladder, colon, or small bowel. The incidence of such fistulation—albeit clinically uncommon—remains uncertain, as not all cases give rise to symptoms. It is likely that many cases go unreported for a variety of reasons—including the possibility of litigation.
In the radiological report of our patient's initial CT scan, the presence of the mesh was considered incidental as she was not systemically unwell, she had few local symptoms, and the scan had shown gallstones. However, if symptoms persist—even causing only minimal discomfort, as in our patient—careful re-imaging is essential. Finally, although the migration of mesh into the gut lumen may be more common than is appreciated, it is crucial to consider that it might obscure more significant intra-abdominal pathologies, such as adenocarcinomas of the gut (video).

A 58-year-old woman presented as an emergency with a 4-month history of intermittent upper abdominal pain, distension, and vomiting.She had a history of a hernia which had been repaired and augmented with prosthetic mesh 4 years earlier.
On examination, we found the patient to be apyrexial but not distressed. Her abdomen was slightly distended; she had normal bowel sounds with a non-tender fullness at the umbilicus—at the site of the earlier hernia repair—with no discharge.
Laboratory investigations showed a normal white cell count of 11·3 × 109 per L with a haemoglobin concentration of 14·6 g/dL (normal 13·0–16·5); her serum C-reactive protein concentration and renal function were both normal. An initial unprepared contrast enhanced CT showed gallstones and it also raised the possibility of a fistula between the small bowel and the mesh, because the mesh appeared adjacent to the slightly distended gut (figure). We managed the patient conservatively with intravenous fluids and kept her nil by mouth and her symptoms settled within 12 h.
However, 2 months later, at an outpatient appointment review, she continued to report pain and abdominal distention; a fully prepared CT suggested a stricture in the distal transverse colon. We carried out a colonoscopy and a biopsy which indicated that the lesion was malignant. We then did an open extended right hemicolectomy, cholecystectomy, and a segmental small bowel resection when we found the mesh from the earlier hernial repair intra-luminal (figure). Histopathological examination of a sample of the excised lesion showed a T4aN2a adenocarcinoma; the patient was then given adjuvant chemotherapy. At 12 months’ follow-up she remains symptom free.
Repairs of abdominal wall hernias are currently frequently augmented with prosthetic biomaterials—such as mesh—and this has resulted in minimal tension reconstruction and a lower later recurrence rate. However, the use of such prostheses, irrespective of type or size, may be associated with various complications including migration and visceral fistulation to the bladder, colon, or small bowel. The incidence of such fistulation—albeit clinically uncommon—remains uncertain, as not all cases give rise to symptoms. It is likely that many cases go unreported for a variety of reasons—including the possibility of litigation.
In the radiological report of our patient's initial CT scan, the presence of the mesh was considered incidental as she was not systemically unwell, she had few local symptoms, and the scan had shown gallstones. However, if symptoms persist—even causing only minimal discomfort, as in our patient—careful re-imaging is essential. Finally, although the migration of mesh into the gut lumen may be more common than is appreciated, it is crucial to consider that it might obscure more significant intra-abdominal pathologies, such as adenocarcinomas of the gut (video).

A 40-year-old man presented to our emergency department with acute upper abdominal pain 8 h after ingestion of sushi. During physical examination, he was found to have tenderness in the epigastric region. Abdominal CT showed diffuse thickening of the wall of the gastric body with surrounding fat stranding. Emergency gastroscopy identified a 15 mm long larva of the nematode Anisakis simplex penetrating the inflamed body of the stomach (figure). Disinfestation rapidly resolved the patient's symptoms.Anisakiasis is a gastrointestinal infection caused in human beings by nematode larvae belonging to the family Anisakidae. The disease is caused by Anisakis spp and Pseudoterranova decipiens, which are present in both raw fish and raw squid. When the host animal dies, the larvae migrate from the viscera to the muscle. Human infestation results from accidental ingestion of the larvae. Sources of human infections differ between countries. The larvae penetrate the gastrointestinal mucosa—leading to an inflammatory response with a generalised immunoglobulin E (IgE)—mediated allergic reaction—and this results in an ulcer, an eosinophilic granuloma, or even gastrointestinal perforation. Depending on the site affected, anisakiasis is divided into gastric, intestinal, and ectopic. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, nausea, and diarrhoea, which may be complicated with urticaria or anaphylaxis. Involvement of the small intestine occasionally produces intestinal obstruction. Gastric anisakiasis and intestinal anisakiasis typically occur 1–12 h and 12–48 h after ingestion, respectively. Although patients may have no awareness of the relationship between symptoms and foods, a history of recent consumption of raw seafood is an important clue to the diagnosis. Eosinophilia may develop a few weeks after disease onset, and the specific IgE antibody test is useful when endoscopic diagnosis is not possible. Endoscopic disinfestation is the only definitive treatment, though conservative management usually resolves symptoms within a few weeks due to the death of the larvae that occurs after a few days.
Early evisceration, thorough cooking, and deep freezing of seafood are recommended to prevent the disease. Many cases of anisakiasis are reported in Japan because the raw flesh of fish and squid is commonly sold without evisceration or deep freezing; keeping the guts in situ supposedly helps maintain a good appearance of the produce, and deep freezing leads to a deterioration in taste. Anisakiasis should always be considered as a differential diagnosis in patients with acute gastrointestinal symptoms because of the continuing and growing worldwide trend of eating raw seafood.

Additional diagnostic tests showed insufficiency of the gonadotropic axis, but the thyrotropic and somatotropic axes were intact. However, a MRI scan of the sella did not reveal any specific cause of partial hypopituitarism. No other endocrinopathies or diabetes were detected. The patient also reported painless stiffness of both ears over the past 10 years. On inspection, his ears appeared normal, but on palpation they were found to have a stone-like hardness. However, to date, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear and no treatment is currently available to reverse calcification or ossification.
At the 1 month follow-up visit after discharge from hospital, the patient had responded well to regular glucocorticoid replacement. His weight had increased to 55 kg and the percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube could be removed. However, both ears remained petrified. A 75-year-old man was admitted to our Department of Endocrinology with a 2 month history of recurrent pneumonia, somnolence, and progressive cachexia requiring enteral nutrition via a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube. His wife reported that the man had had recurrent episodes of weakness during stressful situations over the past 20 years. Clinical examination of the patient revealed somnolence, hypotension (blood pressure <100/60 mm Hg), and cachexia (weight 50 kg, height 174 cm, BMI 16·5 kg/m2). Laboratory analysis showed hyponatraemia (serum sodium 124 mmol/L [reference 136–145 mmol/L]) and concomitant borderline hyperkalaemia (serum potassium 4·94 mmol/L [reference 3·40–4·40 mmol/L]). Low morning serum cortisol (123 nmol/L [reference 133–537 nmol/L between 0600 h and 1000 h]) and low adrenocorticotropic hormone (2·06 ng/L [reference 7·2–63·3 ng/L between 0600 h and 1000 h]) and negative results for adrenal autoantibodies confirmed secondary adrenal insufficiency. Glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement was initiated and the clinical condition of the patient improved rapidly. Additional diagnostic tests showed insufficiency of the gonadotropic axis, but the thyrotropic and somatotropic axes were intact. However, a MRI scan of the sella did not reveal any specific cause of partial hypopituitarism. No other endocrinopathies or diabetes were detected. The patient also reported painless stiffness of both ears over the past 10 years. On inspection, his ears appeared normal, but on palpation they were found to have a stone-like hardness. An x-ray (figure, A) and a 3D reconstruction from a CT scan (figure, B) showed ossification of the auricular cartilage, including helix, antihelix, and antitragus. There were no other manifestations of pathological ossification.Rheumatological and immunological work-up showed no remarkable findings, nor was there a history of frostbite or traumatic brain injury. Pathological calcification and, even more rarely, ossification can occur on a background of dystrophic calcification or Albright hereditary osteodystrophy and fibrodysplasia ossificans. Endocrinopathies (eg, adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, and acromegaly), metabolic disease (eg, diabetes), mechanical or hypothermic trauma, and inflammatory disease (eg, perichondritis and systemic chondromalacia) have been reported to be associated with petrified ears. However, to date, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear and no treatment is currently available to reverse calcification or ossification.
At the 1 month follow-up visit after discharge from hospital, the patient had responded well to regular glucocorticoid replacement. His weight had increased to 55 kg and the percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube could be removed. However, both ears remained petrified. Despite being a rare occurrence, petrified ears can be diagnosed easily during physical examination and might suggest long-term clinical or subclinical adrenal insufficiency.

A 27-year-old woman attended our accident and emergency unit reporting fatigue and recurrent pain in the right side of her chest; the tiredness, which had been present for several years, had recently worsened.The patient had been diagnosed with anorexia nervosa (AN) at the age of 17 years; she severely restricted her diet, resulting in significant weight loss. She was prescribed antidepressants and hormone replacement therapy for previously disturbed periods.
On examination she was very unwell and markedly cachectic; her pulse was 98 beats per min, her blood pressure was 68/45 mm Hg, and her oxygen saturation was 90% and BMI was 10 kg/m2. Laboratory investigations showed a pancytopenia with a white blood cell count of 2·07 × 109 per L (normal 3·5–11·0), haemoglobin concentration of 10 g/dL (normal 12–16), and a platelet count of 78·0 × 109 per L (normal 150–440). The patient's serum glucose concentration was 51 mg/dL (normal 70–100); liver function tests were as follows: alanine aminotransferase 347 units per L (normal <33), aspartate transaminase 173 units per L (normal <32), and lactate dehydrogenase 293 units per L (normal 135–214).
An initial CT scan of the patient's chest showed an apical condensation; on subsequent scans the lesion appeared with some excavation (figure). No signs of a pulmonary embolism were seen. Investigations for common viral, fungal, and bacterial causes of lung infections—including tuberculosis—were negative. A sample obtained from a lung biopsy, which we decided to do because the patient's chest pain was worsening, showed inflammatory changes surrounding an unknown material, indicating inhalation of a foreign body. No signs of malignancy were seen.
We prescribed amoxicillin and clavulanate and commenced enteral feeding. After 4 weeks in hospital the pancytopenia was still present, so we did a bone marrow aspirate which showed some hypocellular spicules with an increase in adipocytes surrounded by abundant extracellular pinkish material—indicating gelatinous transformation (figure).
The patient was commenced on enteral nutrition with a progressive energetic regimen and concomitant correction of fluid and electrolyte imbalances; her weight increased from 32·5 kg to 39·5 kg and her BMI from 10 kg/m2 to 12 kg/m2. After 2 months of treatment the white cell count and platelet count had returned to normal levels. The patient then went to a specialised centre to continue with psychiatric and nutritional care.
The severity of AN is determined by the BMI: less than or equal to 17 kg/m2 is considered mild, 16 kg/m2 to 16·99 kg/m2 is moderate, 15 kg/m2 to 15·99 kg/m2 is severe, and less than 15 kg/m2 is extreme. Patients with a very low BMI—as in our case—are at high risk of developing the refeeding syndrome which occurs when rapid and inappropriate feeding is initiated after a long period of starvation. AN is also associated with an increased risk of gelatinous bone marrow transformation, which is reversible with treatment (video).

She was prescribed antidepressants and hormone replacement therapy for previously disturbed periods.
On examination she was very unwell and markedly cachectic; her pulse was 98 beats per min, her blood pressure was 68/45 mm Hg, and her oxygen saturation was 90% and BMI was 10 kg/m2. Laboratory investigations showed a pancytopenia with a white blood cell count of 2·07 × 109 per L (normal 3·5–11·0), haemoglobin concentration of 10 g/dL (normal 12–16), and a platelet count of 78·0 × 109 per L (normal 150–440). The patient's serum glucose concentration was 51 mg/dL (normal 70–100); liver function tests were as follows: alanine aminotransferase 347 units per L (normal <33), aspartate transaminase 173 units per L (normal <32), and lactate dehydrogenase 293 units per L (normal 135–214).
An initial CT scan of the patient's chest showed an apical condensation; on subsequent scans the lesion appeared with some excavation (figure). No signs of a pulmonary embolism were seen. Investigations for common viral, fungal, and bacterial causes of lung infections—including tuberculosis—were negative. A sample obtained from a lung biopsy, which we decided to do because the patient's chest pain was worsening, showed inflammatory changes surrounding an unknown material, indicating inhalation of a foreign body. No signs of malignancy were seen.
We prescribed amoxicillin and clavulanate and commenced enteral feeding. After 4 weeks in hospital the pancytopenia was still present, so we did a bone marrow aspirate which showed some hypocellular spicules with an increase in adipocytes surrounded by abundant extracellular pinkish material—indicating gelatinous transformation (figure).
The patient was commenced on enteral nutrition with a progressive energetic regimen and concomitant correction of fluid and electrolyte imbalances; her weight increased from 32·5 kg to 39·5 kg and her BMI from 10 kg/m2 to 12 kg/m2. After 2 months of treatment the white cell count and platelet count had returned to normal levels. The patient then went to a specialised centre to continue with psychiatric and nutritional care.

input:
A 75-year-old man presented with a 12-month history of increasing pain in his right knee; he said that intermittently he had “popping” sensations and episodic locking of the joint that prevented full extension. The patient also reported feeling like objects were moving inside his knee; 10 years earlier, he had a partial medial meniscectomy on the same knee. In addition, the patient reported that 3 years before, he had similar transient symptoms in his left knee; an MRI at that time had shown a loose body of similar signal intensity to bone and cartilage in proton density-weighted spectral attenuated inversion-recovery sequences (figure).On examination, we found the patient to be generally well. He had a 10 degree (normal 0) fixed flexion deformity of the right knee with full flexion limited to 100 degrees (normal 135).
X-rays showed popcorn-shaped loose bodies in the supra-patellar pouch and osteoarthritis in the knee, consistent with synovial osteochondromatosis (figure).
A total right knee replacement was done because of the extent of the osteoarthritis in the joint; intra-operatively the loose bodies were removed (figure).
Postoperatively, the patient's pain and function of his right knee had significantly improved. At follow-up 18 months later, his function was normal with a range of movements from 0 to 120 degrees and his pain had resolved.
Pseudo-locking of the knee occurs when pain inhibits movement of the joint; this can be caused by pain from trauma, arthritis, inflammatory conditions, and abnormalities of the patella. Mechanical locking, which is also known as true locking, results from a physical block to full extension of the knee, which most frequently results from a meniscal tear of a loose body in the joint. Loose bodies can be cartilaginous or osseous.
Synovial osteochondromatosis is predominantly a benign condition which occurs when foci of synovium undergo metaplasia into cartilage-producing tissue. The metaplastic nidus produces sessile nodules which may ossify but ultimately bud off into the joint, forming loose bodies. When ossified, they are radio-opaque and display a characteristic popcorn appearance. The diagnosis can typically be made on plain x-rays; on MRI they appear as loose bodies of a similar signal to cartilage. Histologically, the condition is characterised by multiple hyaline cartilage nodules within the synovium. Nodules that have budded off from the synovium may cause third-body wear which accelerates and aggravates arthritis. They may also cause the mechanical symptom of locking. The condition can affect any joint, but the knee is the most common.
Treatment involves arthroscopic retrieval or total joint replacement in cases with concomitant osteoarthritis. Notably, malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma is very rare.
