A 75-year-old man presented with a 12-month history of increasing pain in his right knee; he said that intermittently he had “popping” sensations and episodic locking of the joint that prevented full extension. The patient also reported feeling like objects were moving inside his knee; 10 years earlier, he had a partial medial meniscectomy on the same knee. In addition, the patient reported that 3 years before, he had similar transient symptoms in his left knee; an MRI at that time had shown a loose body of similar signal intensity to bone and cartilage in proton density-weighted spectral attenuated inversion-recovery sequences (figure).On examination, we found the patient to be generally well. He had a 10 degree (normal 0) fixed flexion deformity of the right knee with full flexion limited to 100 degrees (normal 135).
X-rays showed popcorn-shaped loose bodies in the supra-patellar pouch and osteoarthritis in the knee, consistent with synovial osteochondromatosis (figure).
A total right knee replacement was done because of the extent of the osteoarthritis in the joint; intra-operatively the loose bodies were removed (figure).
Postoperatively, the patient's pain and function of his right knee had significantly improved. At follow-up 18 months later, his function was normal with a range of movements from 0 to 120 degrees and his pain had resolved.
Pseudo-locking of the knee occurs when pain inhibits movement of the joint; this can be caused by pain from trauma, arthritis, inflammatory conditions, and abnormalities of the patella. Mechanical locking, which is also known as true locking, results from a physical block to full extension of the knee, which most frequently results from a meniscal tear of a loose body in the joint. Loose bodies can be cartilaginous or osseous.
Synovial osteochondromatosis is predominantly a benign condition which occurs when foci of synovium undergo metaplasia into cartilage-producing tissue. The metaplastic nidus produces sessile nodules which may ossify but ultimately bud off into the joint, forming loose bodies. When ossified, they are radio-opaque and display a characteristic popcorn appearance. The diagnosis can typically be made on plain x-rays; on MRI they appear as loose bodies of a similar signal to cartilage. input:
A 75-year-old man presented with a 12-month history of increasing pain in his right knee; he said that intermittently he had “popping” sensations and episodic locking of the joint that prevented full extension. The patient also reported feeling like objects were moving inside his knee; 10 years earlier, he had a partial medial meniscectomy on the same knee. In addition, the patient reported that 3 years before, he had similar transient symptoms in his left knee; an MRI at that time had shown a loose body of similar signal intensity to bone and cartilage in proton density-weighted spectral attenuated inversion-recovery sequences (figure).On examination, we found the patient to be generally well. He had a 10 degree (normal 0) fixed flexion deformity of the right knee with full flexion limited to 100 degrees (normal 135).
X-rays showed popcorn-shaped loose bodies in the supra-patellar pouch and osteoarthritis in the knee, consistent with synovial osteochondromatosis (figure).
A total right knee replacement was done because of the extent of the osteoarthritis in the joint; intra-operatively the loose bodies were removed (figure).
Postoperatively, the patient's pain and function of his right knee had significantly improved. At follow-up 18 months later, his function was normal with a range of movements from 0 to 120 degrees and his pain had resolved.
Pseudo-locking of the knee occurs when pain inhibits movement of the joint; this can be caused by pain from trauma, arthritis, inflammatory conditions, and abnormalities of the patella. Mechanical locking, which is also known as true locking, results from a physical block to full extension of the knee, which most frequently results from a meniscal tear of a loose body in the joint. Loose bodies can be cartilaginous or osseous.
Synovial osteochondromatosis is predominantly a benign condition which occurs when foci of synovium undergo metaplasia into cartilage-producing tissue. The metaplastic nidus produces sessile nodules which may ossify but ultimately bud off into the joint, forming loose bodies. When ossified, they are radio-opaque and display a characteristic popcorn appearance. The diagnosis can typically be made on plain x-rays; on MRI they appear as loose bodies of a similar signal to cartilage. Histologically, the condition is characterised by multiple hyaline cartilage nodules within the synovium. Nodules that have budded off from the synovium may cause third-body wear which accelerates and aggravates arthritis. They may also cause the mechanical symptom of locking. The condition can affect any joint, but the knee is the most common.
Treatment involves arthroscopic retrieval or total joint replacement in cases with concomitant osteoarthritis. Notably, malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma is very rare.

On the basis of the history and this radiographic finding, the band was deflated in the emergency department, and the patient was given urgent laparoscopic band removal. With the increase in obesity surgery it is important to highlight such complications, as emergency deflation and band removal is necessary to prevent necrosis of the herniated stomach.

A 59-year-old man attended our emergency department reporting a sudden onset of a severe headache and photophobia. He had no medical history.On examination, the patient appeared unwell and was covering his eyes with his hands; his blood pressure was 180/90 mm Hg and his heart rate 90 beats per min. He had neck stiffness and both Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs were positive. He had no other neurological deficits and his consciousness was unaffected.
A CT scan of the patient's head showed a diffuse subarachnoid haemorrhage predominantly in the basal cisterns (figure). CT angiography showed a left posterior inferior cerebellar artery aneurysm.
The patient was transferred to the neuroradiology department for embolisation; percutaneous left vertebral artery angiography, accessed through the femoral artery, confirmed an irregularly shaped saccular aneurysm along the proximal aspect of the left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (figure).
During three-dimensional (3D) rotational angiography, we noticed that, after a bolus injection of contrast agent, a large amount of it appeared to have extravasated from an aneurysmal lump—indicative of an aneurysm rupture (figure; video). We urgently proceeded to measurements using 3D rotational angiography, microcatheter placement, and then endovascular coiling. The final angiography showed near complete obliteration of the source of the leak with a small neck remnant (figure). A CT scan showed contrast extravasation in the basal cisterns, but no compressing haematoma or hydrocephalus (figure).
After the procedure, the patient was extubated in the operating room; he was then monitored and cared for on the neurovascular intensive care unit. His postoperative course was excellent, and he was allowed home 10 days later.
Follow-up was planned for 6 months after the surgery, when the aneurysm was to be assessed by repeating an angiogram.
Patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage must be diagnosed and treated in a timely manner to ensure best outcomes. About 70% present with headache, of which 50% present with the so-called thunderclap headache. Notably, headache is the only symptom in about half of all cases; nausea, vomiting, and loss of consciousness may also be present.
Rebleeding—and indeed rupture—is an important complication of cerebral aneurysms, occurring in 8–23% of cases within 72 h, of which 50–90% occur within the first 6 h, which can result in severe brain damage or death. Rebleeding has a mortality of 20–60%. Rebleeding or rupture on the table or during operation is not an unusual occurrence. Risk factors for rebleeding include a poor neurological grade, admission hypertension, and a large aneurysm; the use of antiplatelet drugs may also be associated.
The high mortality rate and the relatively frequent complication of rebleeding indicate that aneurysm repair—either by clipping or inserting a coil—should be carried out as soon as possible after presentation. Guidelines recommend intervention as early as possible or within 72 h in all but the most severe cases.

A 59-year-old man attended our emergency department reporting a sudden onset of a severe headache and photophobia. He had no medical history.On examination, the patient appeared unwell and was covering his eyes with his hands; his blood pressure was 180/90 mm Hg and his heart rate 90 beats per min. He had neck stiffness and both Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs were positive. He had no other neurological deficits and his consciousness was unaffected.
A CT scan of the patient's head showed a diffuse subarachnoid haemorrhage predominantly in the basal cisterns (figure). CT angiography showed a left posterior inferior cerebellar artery aneurysm.
The patient was transferred to the neuroradiology department for embolisation; percutaneous left vertebral artery angiography, accessed through the femoral artery, confirmed an irregularly shaped saccular aneurysm along the proximal aspect of the left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (figure).
During three-dimensional (3D) rotational angiography, we noticed that, after a bolus injection of contrast agent, a large amount of it appeared to have extravasated from an aneurysmal lump—indicative of an aneurysm rupture (figure; video). We urgently proceeded to measurements using 3D rotational angiography, microcatheter placement, and then endovascular coiling. The final angiography showed near complete obliteration of the source of the leak with a small neck remnant (figure). A CT scan showed contrast extravasation in the basal cisterns, but no compressing haematoma or hydrocephalus (figure).
After the procedure, the patient was extubated in the operating room; he was then monitored and cared for on the neurovascular intensive care unit. His postoperative course was excellent, and he was allowed home 10 days later.
Follow-up was planned for 6 months after the surgery, when the aneurysm was to be assessed by repeating an angiogram.
Patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage must be diagnosed and treated in a timely manner to ensure best outcomes. About 70% present with headache, of which 50% present with the so-called thunderclap headache. Notably, headache is the only symptom in about half of all cases; nausea, vomiting, and loss of consciousness may also be present.
Rebleeding—and indeed rupture—is an important complication of cerebral aneurysms, occurring in 8–23% of cases within 72 h, of which 50–90% occur within the first 6 h, which can result in severe brain damage or death. Rebleeding has a mortality of 20–60%. Rebleeding or rupture on the table or during operation is not an unusual occurrence. Risk factors for rebleeding include a poor neurological grade, admission hypertension, and a large aneurysm; the use of antiplatelet drugs may also be associated.
The high mortality rate and the relatively frequent complication of rebleeding indicate that aneurysm repair—either by clipping or inserting a coil—should be carried out as soon as possible after presentation. Guidelines recommend intervention as early as possible or within 72 h in all but the most severe cases.

A 59-year-old man attended our emergency department reporting a sudden onset of a severe headache and photophobia. He had no medical history.On examination, the patient appeared unwell and was covering his eyes with his hands; his blood pressure was 180/90 mm Hg and his heart rate 90 beats per min. He had neck stiffness and both Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs were positive. He had no other neurological deficits and his consciousness was unaffected.
A CT scan of the patient's head showed a diffuse subarachnoid haemorrhage predominantly in the basal cisterns (figure). CT angiography showed a left posterior inferior cerebellar artery aneurysm.
The patient was transferred to the neuroradiology department for embolisation; percutaneous left vertebral artery angiography, accessed through the femoral artery, confirmed an irregularly shaped saccular aneurysm along the proximal aspect of the left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (figure).
During three-dimensional (3D) rotational angiography, we noticed that, after a bolus injection of contrast agent, a large amount of it appeared to have extravasated from an aneurysmal lump—indicative of an aneurysm rupture (figure; video). We urgently proceeded to measurements using 3D rotational angiography, microcatheter placement, and then endovascular coiling. The final angiography showed near complete obliteration of the source of the leak with a small neck remnant (figure). A CT scan showed contrast extravasation in the basal cisterns, but no compressing haematoma or hydrocephalus (figure).
After the procedure, the patient was extubated in the operating room; he was then monitored and cared for on the neurovascular intensive care unit. His postoperative course was excellent, and he was allowed home 10 days later.
Follow-up was planned for 6 months after the surgery, when the aneurysm was to be assessed by repeating an angiogram.
Patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage must be diagnosed and treated in a timely manner to ensure best outcomes. About 70% present with headache, of which 50% present with the so-called thunderclap headache. Notably, headache is the only symptom in about half of all cases; nausea, vomiting, and loss of consciousness may also be present.
Rebleeding—and indeed rupture—is an important complication of cerebral aneurysms, occurring in 8–23% of cases within 72 h, of which 50–90% occur within the first 6 h, which can result in severe brain damage or death. Rebleeding has a mortality of 20–60%. Rebleeding or rupture on the table or during operation is not an unusual occurrence. Risk factors for rebleeding include a poor neurological grade, admission hypertension, and a large aneurysm; the use of antiplatelet drugs may also be associated.
The high mortality rate and the relatively frequent complication of rebleeding indicate that aneurysm repair—either by clipping or inserting a coil—should be carried out as soon as possible after presentation. Guidelines recommend intervention as early as possible or within 72 h in all but the most severe cases.

A 31-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 1-week history of fever, myalgia, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. She had no significant medical history, history of recent travel, or alcohol use. She reported no genitourinary symptoms, rashes, oral ulcerations, or pharyngitis. She did say that she had been recently sexually active with a new male partner.On examination, we found the patient to be febrile (temperature 38·2°C). She was tachycardic (heart rate 120 beats per min), tachypnoeic (respiratory rate 44 breaths per min), and she was tender in her right upper quadrant. She was not jaundiced and there were no mucocutaneous lesions seen anywhere.
Laboratory investigations showed a hepatitic picture: alanine aminotransferase was 629 units per L (normal <35), aspartate aminotransferase 634 units per L (normal <30), gamma-glutamyl transferase 182 units per L (normal <38), alkaline phosphatase 143 units per mL (normal <110), and a total bilirubin concentration within normal limits. The patient's C-reactive protein concentration was 192 mg/L (normal <3).
An abdominal ultrasound showed pericholecystic fluid and biliary sludge in a thin-walled gallbladder.
We admitted her with presumed diagnosis of cholecystitis. However, during abdominal laparoscopy, we found numerous vesicles across the surface of the liver—with no evidence of cholecystitis (figure).
Histological analysis of a liver biopsy sample showed a lobular parenchymal lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate; herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) was detected by PCR (AusDiagnostics, Sydney, NSW, Australia).
She was treated with intravenous acyclovir followed by oral valacyclovir for 6 weeks after which she made complete recovery; laboratory investigations returned to normal levels. Notably, having been seronegative at presentation, the patient was found to have seroconverted after 4 weeks showing convalescent type-specific serology—HSV-2 IgG. Subsequent testing of her asymptomatic partner found that he was also HSV-2 IgG positive.
Hepatitis A, B, C, D, and E are the most frequent causes of viral hepatitis. Primary HSV-2 should be considered as a cause of acute hepatitis—even in the absence of jaundice or mucocutaneous lesions and if the patient is immunocompetent. A viral prodrome with a headache and fever is common. Transmission may occur via asymptomatic viral shedding in sexually active individuals. In the acute stages of the illness, PCR is the diagnostic method of choice as patients have usually not seroconverted. The high mortality of patients with untreated HSV-2 hepatitis is greatly reduced with early intravenous acyclovir treatment.

A 31-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 1-week history of fever, myalgia, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. She had no significant medical history, history of recent travel, or alcohol use. She reported no genitourinary symptoms, rashes, oral ulcerations, or pharyngitis. She did say that she had been recently sexually active with a new male partner.On examination, we found the patient to be febrile (temperature 38·2°C). She was tachycardic (heart rate 120 beats per min), tachypnoeic (respiratory rate 44 breaths per min), and she was tender in her right upper quadrant. She was not jaundiced and there were no mucocutaneous lesions seen anywhere.
Laboratory investigations showed a hepatitic picture: alanine aminotransferase was 629 units per L (normal <35), aspartate aminotransferase 634 units per L (normal <30), gamma-glutamyl transferase 182 units per L (normal <38), alkaline phosphatase 143 units per mL (normal <110), and a total bilirubin concentration within normal limits. The patient's C-reactive protein concentration was 192 mg/L (normal <3).
An abdominal ultrasound showed pericholecystic fluid and biliary sludge in a thin-walled gallbladder.
We admitted her with presumed diagnosis of cholecystitis. However, during abdominal laparoscopy, we found numerous vesicles across the surface of the liver—with no evidence of cholecystitis (figure).
Histological analysis of a liver biopsy sample showed a lobular parenchymal lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate; herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) was detected by PCR (AusDiagnostics, Sydney, NSW, Australia).
She was treated with intravenous acyclovir followed by oral valacyclovir for 6 weeks after which she made complete recovery; laboratory investigations returned to normal levels. Notably, having been seronegative at presentation, the patient was found to have seroconverted after 4 weeks showing convalescent type-specific serology—HSV-2 IgG. Subsequent testing of her asymptomatic partner found that he was also HSV-2 IgG positive.
Hepatitis A, B, C, D, and E are the most frequent causes of viral hepatitis. Primary HSV-2 should be considered as a cause of acute hepatitis—even in the absence of jaundice or mucocutaneous lesions and if the patient is immunocompetent. A viral prodrome with a headache and fever is common. Transmission may occur via asymptomatic viral shedding in sexually active individuals. In the acute stages of the illness, PCR is the diagnostic method of choice as patients have usually not seroconverted. The high mortality of patients with untreated HSV-2 hepatitis is greatly reduced with early intravenous acyclovir treatment.

A 4-month-old girl presented to our emergency department with a low-grade fever and a persistent cough—her parents reported a daily productive cough and said the child's stools had become greenish and greasy in recent weeks. The infant was the second child of non-consanguineous parents, born full-term after an unremarkable pregnancy; birthweight was 3·8 kg and meconium was passed on the first day of life.Examination showed insufficient weight gain: the child's weight (4·5 kg) was less than the third percentile on the normal growth curve. On chest auscultation, we heard bilateral crackles. The infant's social interactions and axial tone were good. However, she had a continuous large amplitude action tremor involving all limbs and head (video); the tremor increased at the beginning of the movement and was enhanced by sudden acoustic stimuli. Spontaneous movements were reduced—especially in the lower limbs. Antigravity limb movements were reduced: she could move her arms towards an object in front of her but was unable to reach it.
Laboratory investigations showed normal electrolytes, glucose concentration, and liver enzymes. A depletion of the fat-soluble vitamins was identified—notably vitamin E was 3 μmol/L (normal range 10–20). An x-ray showed bronchovascular markings.
We conducted a sweat test and diagnosed cystic fibrosis, confirmed by genetic analysis—cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene homozygous F508del mutation. We started the patient on pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy and polyvitamin supplementation. 1 week later, the patient's motor function had improved: spontaneous movements had increased, and the tremor had almost disappeared (figure). She could play with her hands and feet and grasp objects. 1 month later, her vitamin E blood concentration was in normal range and neurological examination was normal (video).
Vitamin E deficiency is associated with movement disorders—including ataxia and tremor; neurological symptoms develop after severe and prolonged deficiency. Monitoring and supplementation of vitamin E in patients with cystic fibrosis means that neurological symptoms are rare. In Italy—where our patient was born—screening has been mandatory since 1992. The patient did have expanded newborn screening, but results were negative for all screened diseases: blood concentration of immunoreactive trypsinogen was 49 ng/mL (cutoff value 62). False negatives, while rare, can occur in patients with the more severe class III mutations.
Finally, infants with a history of persistent coughing, unwellness, and a tremor should raise suspicions of having cystic fibrosis—even if all newborn screening tests are negative.

A 31-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 1-week history of fever, myalgia, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. She had no significant medical history, history of recent travel, or alcohol use. She reported no genitourinary symptoms, rashes, oral ulcerations, or pharyngitis. She did say that she had been recently sexually active with a new male partner.On examination, we found the patient to be febrile (temperature 38·2°C). She was tachycardic (heart rate 120 beats per min), tachypnoeic (respiratory rate 44 breaths per min), and she was tender in her right upper quadrant. She was not jaundiced and there were no mucocutaneous lesions seen anywhere.
Laboratory investigations showed a hepatitic picture: alanine aminotransferase was 629 units per L (normal <35), aspartate aminotransferase 634 units per L (normal <30), gamma-glutamyl transferase 182 units per L (normal <38), alkaline phosphatase 143 units per mL (normal <110), and a total bilirubin concentration within normal limits. The patient's C-reactive protein concentration was 192 mg/L (normal <3).
An abdominal ultrasound showed pericholecystic fluid and biliary sludge in a thin-walled gallbladder.
We admitted her with presumed diagnosis of cholecystitis. However, during abdominal laparoscopy, we found numerous vesicles across the surface of the liver—with no evidence of cholecystitis (figure).
Histological analysis of a liver biopsy sample showed a lobular parenchymal lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate; herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) was detected by PCR (AusDiagnostics, Sydney, NSW, Australia).
She was treated with intravenous acyclovir followed by oral valacyclovir for 6 weeks after which she made complete recovery; laboratory investigations returned to normal levels. Notably, having been seronegative at presentation, the patient was found to have seroconverted after 4 weeks showing convalescent type-specific serology—HSV-2 IgG. Subsequent testing of her asymptomatic partner found that he was also HSV-2 IgG positive.
Hepatitis A, B, C, D, and E are the most frequent causes of viral hepatitis. Primary HSV-2 should be considered as a cause of acute hepatitis—even in the absence of jaundice or mucocutaneous lesions and if the patient is immunocompetent. A viral prodrome with a headache and fever is common. Transmission may occur via asymptomatic viral shedding in sexually active individuals. In the acute stages of the illness, PCR is the diagnostic method of choice as patients have usually not seroconverted. The high mortality of patients with untreated HSV-2 hepatitis is greatly reduced with early intravenous acyclovir treatment.

A 4-month-old girl presented to our emergency department with a low-grade fever and a persistent cough—her parents reported a daily productive cough and said the child's stools had become greenish and greasy in recent weeks. The infant was the second child of non-consanguineous parents, born full-term after an unremarkable pregnancy; birthweight was 3·8 kg and meconium was passed on the first day of life.Examination showed insufficient weight gain: the child's weight (4·5 kg) was less than the third percentile on the normal growth curve. On chest auscultation, we heard bilateral crackles. The infant's social interactions and axial tone were good. However, she had a continuous large amplitude action tremor involving all limbs and head (video); the tremor increased at the beginning of the movement and was enhanced by sudden acoustic stimuli. Spontaneous movements were reduced—especially in the lower limbs. Antigravity limb movements were reduced: she could move her arms towards an object in front of her but was unable to reach it.
Laboratory investigations showed normal electrolytes, glucose concentration, and liver enzymes. A depletion of the fat-soluble vitamins was identified—notably vitamin E was 3 μmol/L (normal range 10–20). An x-ray showed bronchovascular markings.
We conducted a sweat test and diagnosed cystic fibrosis, confirmed by genetic analysis—cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene homozygous F508del mutation. We started the patient on pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy and polyvitamin supplementation. 1 week later, the patient's motor function had improved: spontaneous movements had increased, and the tremor had almost disappeared (figure). She could play with her hands and feet and grasp objects. 1 month later, her vitamin E blood concentration was in normal range and neurological examination was normal (video).
Vitamin E deficiency is associated with movement disorders—including ataxia and tremor; neurological symptoms develop after severe and prolonged deficiency. Monitoring and supplementation of vitamin E in patients with cystic fibrosis means that neurological symptoms are rare. In Italy—where our patient was born—screening has been mandatory since 1992. The patient did have expanded newborn screening, but results were negative for all screened diseases: blood concentration of immunoreactive trypsinogen was 49 ng/mL (cutoff value 62). False negatives, while rare, can occur in patients with the more severe class III mutations.
Finally, infants with a history of persistent coughing, unwellness, and a tremor should raise suspicions of having cystic fibrosis—even if all newborn screening tests are negative.

A 55-year-old, right-handed man with a history of treatment-resistant epilepsy, which began when he was 3 years old, attended our specialist centre for surgical assessment.
The patient's main symptoms were twitching of his left leg with altered, uncomfortable sensation; he had an average of 10–15 episodes a week, each lasting approximately 20 s. He reported no impairment of consciousness. The patient also reported infrequent episodes of sudden-onset myoclonic jerks and numbness in his left leg followed by spasms of both legs with impaired consciousness throughout the whole attack. He had continued to have seizures despite treatment with multiple antiseizure medications. The patient reported no family history of seizures.
On examination, he was generally well; his left lower limb muscle strength was grade 3, with a slight decrease in muscle tone noted. Neuropsychiatric assessment showed no abnormal findings.
Laboratory investigations—including a complete blood count, liver function tests, kidney function tests, coagulation screen, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis—were all within typical range. A CT and MRI of the patient's brain had previously, at the local hospital, been reported as showing no abnormalities. However, we did a T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery MRI which showed a hyperintense lesion in the patient's right central posterior gyrus (figure 1). Repeated scalp electroencephalograms showed epileptic discharges in the right parietal and frontal lobes.We conducted stereotactic electroencephalography with three main targets in the right anterior central gyrus, posterior central gyrus, and superior parietal lobule in preparation for resective surgery; the initial area of abnormal epileptiform discharges—captured by deep electrodes placed in the right central posterior gyrus region—was consistent with the lesion seen on MRI (figure 1).
A multidisciplinary team meeting concluded that resection of the epileptogenic zone in the right central posterior gyrus was appropriate. Intraoperative electrocorticography was done to confirm that the planned scope of cortical resection was accurate and sufficient. Cortical electrical stimulation was used to identify the central anterior gyrus and avoid causing neurological damage during surgery (figure 1). The patient recovered well postoperatively and had no neurological deficits. Immunohistochemical analysis of a sample of tissue removed during surgery showed dysmorphic neurons, balloon cells, and glial cells (figure 2). We diagnosed focal cortical dysplasia type IIb-associated right parietal lobe epilepsy—classified by the International League Against Epilepsy Task Force. At follow-up, 4 months after surgery, the patient was seizure free and prescribed oral oxcarbazepine (0·6 g twice a day)—classified as IA on the Engel Outcome Scale.
Focal cortical dysplasia commonly presents with epilepsy; seizures can begin at any age, but usually develop in early childhood—as in our patient. Resective surgery for drug-resistant seizures has low rates of morbidity and mortality when done in specialised centres. Despite the effectiveness of surgery in controlling intractable seizures it is currently underutilised as a treatment. Timely referral to specialised units, at least for a comprehensive surgical assessment, is recommended in all cases of drug-resistant epilepsy.

A 55-year-old, right-handed man with a history of treatment-resistant epilepsy, which began when he was 3 years old, attended our specialist centre for surgical assessment.
The patient's main symptoms were twitching of his left leg with altered, uncomfortable sensation; he had an average of 10–15 episodes a week, each lasting approximately 20 s. He reported no impairment of consciousness. The patient also reported infrequent episodes of sudden-onset myoclonic jerks and numbness in his left leg followed by spasms of both legs with impaired consciousness throughout the whole attack. He had continued to have seizures despite treatment with multiple antiseizure medications. The patient reported no family history of seizures.
On examination, he was generally well; his left lower limb muscle strength was grade 3, with a slight decrease in muscle tone noted. Neuropsychiatric assessment showed no abnormal findings.
Laboratory investigations—including a complete blood count, liver function tests, kidney function tests, coagulation screen, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis—were all within typical range. A CT and MRI of the patient's brain had previously, at the local hospital, been reported as showing no abnormalities. However, we did a T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery MRI which showed a hyperintense lesion in the patient's right central posterior gyrus (figure 1). Repeated scalp electroencephalograms showed epileptic discharges in the right parietal and frontal lobes.We conducted stereotactic electroencephalography with three main targets in the right anterior central gyrus, posterior central gyrus, and superior parietal lobule in preparation for resective surgery; the initial area of abnormal epileptiform discharges—captured by deep electrodes placed in the right central posterior gyrus region—was consistent with the lesion seen on MRI (figure 1).
A multidisciplinary team meeting concluded that resection of the epileptogenic zone in the right central posterior gyrus was appropriate. Intraoperative electrocorticography was done to confirm that the planned scope of cortical resection was accurate and sufficient. Cortical electrical stimulation was used to identify the central anterior gyrus and avoid causing neurological damage during surgery (figure 1). The patient recovered well postoperatively and had no neurological deficits. Immunohistochemical analysis of a sample of tissue removed during surgery showed dysmorphic neurons, balloon cells, and glial cells (figure 2). We diagnosed focal cortical dysplasia type IIb-associated right parietal lobe epilepsy—classified by the International League Against Epilepsy Task Force. At follow-up, 4 months after surgery, the patient was seizure free and prescribed oral oxcarbazepine (0·6 g twice a day)—classified as IA on the Engel Outcome Scale.
Focal cortical dysplasia commonly presents with epilepsy; seizures can begin at any age, but usually develop in early childhood—as in our patient. Resective surgery for drug-resistant seizures has low rates of morbidity and mortality when done in specialised centres. Despite the effectiveness of surgery in controlling intractable seizures it is currently underutilised as a treatment. Timely referral to specialised units, at least for a comprehensive surgical assessment, is recommended in all cases of drug-resistant epilepsy.

A 4-month-old girl presented to our emergency department with a low-grade fever and a persistent cough—her parents reported a daily productive cough and said the child's stools had become greenish and greasy in recent weeks. The infant was the second child of non-consanguineous parents, born full-term after an unremarkable pregnancy; birthweight was 3·8 kg and meconium was passed on the first day of life.Examination showed insufficient weight gain: the child's weight (4·5 kg) was less than the third percentile on the normal growth curve. On chest auscultation, we heard bilateral crackles. The infant's social interactions and axial tone were good. However, she had a continuous large amplitude action tremor involving all limbs and head (video); the tremor increased at the beginning of the movement and was enhanced by sudden acoustic stimuli. Spontaneous movements were reduced—especially in the lower limbs. Antigravity limb movements were reduced: she could move her arms towards an object in front of her but was unable to reach it.
Laboratory investigations showed normal electrolytes, glucose concentration, and liver enzymes. A depletion of the fat-soluble vitamins was identified—notably vitamin E was 3 μmol/L (normal range 10–20). An x-ray showed bronchovascular markings.
We conducted a sweat test and diagnosed cystic fibrosis, confirmed by genetic analysis—cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene homozygous F508del mutation. We started the patient on pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy and polyvitamin supplementation. 1 week later, the patient's motor function had improved: spontaneous movements had increased, and the tremor had almost disappeared (figure). She could play with her hands and feet and grasp objects. 1 month later, her vitamin E blood concentration was in normal range and neurological examination was normal (video).
Vitamin E deficiency is associated with movement disorders—including ataxia and tremor; neurological symptoms develop after severe and prolonged deficiency. Monitoring and supplementation of vitamin E in patients with cystic fibrosis means that neurological symptoms are rare. In Italy—where our patient was born—screening has been mandatory since 1992. The patient did have expanded newborn screening, but results were negative for all screened diseases: blood concentration of immunoreactive trypsinogen was 49 ng/mL (cutoff value 62). False negatives, while rare, can occur in patients with the more severe class III mutations.
Finally, infants with a history of persistent coughing, unwellness, and a tremor should raise suspicions of having cystic fibrosis—even if all newborn screening tests are negative.

A 55-year-old, right-handed man with a history of treatment-resistant epilepsy, which began when he was 3 years old, attended our specialist centre for surgical assessment.
The patient's main symptoms were twitching of his left leg with altered, uncomfortable sensation; he had an average of 10–15 episodes a week, each lasting approximately 20 s. He reported no impairment of consciousness. The patient also reported infrequent episodes of sudden-onset myoclonic jerks and numbness in his left leg followed by spasms of both legs with impaired consciousness throughout the whole attack. He had continued to have seizures despite treatment with multiple antiseizure medications. The patient reported no family history of seizures.
On examination, he was generally well; his left lower limb muscle strength was grade 3, with a slight decrease in muscle tone noted. Neuropsychiatric assessment showed no abnormal findings.
Laboratory investigations—including a complete blood count, liver function tests, kidney function tests, coagulation screen, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis—were all within typical range. A CT and MRI of the patient's brain had previously, at the local hospital, been reported as showing no abnormalities. However, we did a T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery MRI which showed a hyperintense lesion in the patient's right central posterior gyrus (figure 1). Repeated scalp electroencephalograms showed epileptic discharges in the right parietal and frontal lobes.We conducted stereotactic electroencephalography with three main targets in the right anterior central gyrus, posterior central gyrus, and superior parietal lobule in preparation for resective surgery; the initial area of abnormal epileptiform discharges—captured by deep electrodes placed in the right central posterior gyrus region—was consistent with the lesion seen on MRI (figure 1).
A multidisciplinary team meeting concluded that resection of the epileptogenic zone in the right central posterior gyrus was appropriate. Intraoperative electrocorticography was done to confirm that the planned scope of cortical resection was accurate and sufficient. Cortical electrical stimulation was used to identify the central anterior gyrus and avoid causing neurological damage during surgery (figure 1). The patient recovered well postoperatively and had no neurological deficits. Immunohistochemical analysis of a sample of tissue removed during surgery showed dysmorphic neurons, balloon cells, and glial cells (figure 2). We diagnosed focal cortical dysplasia type IIb-associated right parietal lobe epilepsy—classified by the International League Against Epilepsy Task Force. At follow-up, 4 months after surgery, the patient was seizure free and prescribed oral oxcarbazepine (0·6 g twice a day)—classified as IA on the Engel Outcome Scale.
Focal cortical dysplasia commonly presents with epilepsy; seizures can begin at any age, but usually develop in early childhood—as in our patient. Resective surgery for drug-resistant seizures has low rates of morbidity and mortality when done in specialised centres. Despite the effectiveness of surgery in controlling intractable seizures it is currently underutilised as a treatment. Timely referral to specialised units, at least for a comprehensive surgical assessment, is recommended in all cases of drug-resistant epilepsy.

A 4-year-old boy was brought to our hospital with an 18-month history of progressive swelling in his neck. His parents said that over the previous few months he had begun to snore. Before he was seen by us he had been treated empirically at another hospital for extra-pulmonary tuberculosis without any improvement of his symptoms.On examination he had widespread lymphadenopathy, most markedly in the neck and axilla (figure); the nodes in the neck were suppurative. He had hepatosplenomegaly but was not malnourished. Our initial differential diagnosis was tuberculosis, filariasis, or lymphoma. Blood tests showed the boy to be anaemic, with a haemoglobin concentration of 7·3 g/dL. He had a raised platelet count (1000 × 109 per L), a significantly raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and raised lactate-dehydrogenase levels. Blood cultures and an HIV test were negative. We did a lymph node biopsy, bone marrow aspiration, and CT scan of his head and neck. The lymph node biopsy result showed granulomatous infiltration with negative infective stains and the bone marrow was normal. A CT scan of the boy's head showed widespread lymphadenopathy, and a lytic lesion in the skull (figure). Considering all the information together, we made a provisional diagnosis of a histiocytic disease such as Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH); the degree of lymphadenopathy was phenotypically consistent with Rosai-Dorfman-Destombes (RDD) disease. Full histological analysis, including immunological staining, was not available in Kenya; however, our local expert's opinion was that the pathology was consistent with the provisional diagnosis. So due to the severity and duration of the patient's symptoms, he was started on treatment with prednisone 40 mg/m2 daily for 4 weeks, tapered over 2 weeks, and vinblastine 6 mg/m2 per week for 6 weeks.
Happily, over the next 6 months, the boy's symptoms dramatically improved on continuation therapy: vinblastine, prednisone, and mercaptopurine (figure). We will continue treatment until he has completed a total of 52 weeks of chemotherapy.
In the process of reviewing the case for publication in The Lancet, the histology was examined by an expert in France, who confirmed that our patient did indeed have a rare form of mixed type histiocytosis—LCH and RDD. All the boy's histocytes strongly expressed S100, with around 30% of these cells also expressing CD1a or CD207.
Histiocytosis encompasses a range of conditions in which there is abnormal proliferation or differentiation and function of the mononuclear phagocyte system. LCH is the most common histiocyte disorder, with clinical presentations ranging from multisystem disease to single indolent lesions. RDD is also called sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy due to its propensity to cause large lymphadenopathy, and has a wide range of clinical presentations. Mixed type histiocytosis—as in our patient—is an unusual but well documented occurrence. Usually, treatment for histiocytosis is tailored to the individual. However, in severe, multifocal disease and in low-income and middle-income settings where sophisticated histopathological analysis may not be available, it might be appropriate to treat patients with chemotherapy empirically.

A 4-year-old boy was brought to our hospital with an 18-month history of progressive swelling in his neck. His parents said that over the previous few months he had begun to snore. Before he was seen by us he had been treated empirically at another hospital for extra-pulmonary tuberculosis without any improvement of his symptoms.On examination he had widespread lymphadenopathy, most markedly in the neck and axilla (figure); the nodes in the neck were suppurative. He had hepatosplenomegaly but was not malnourished. Our initial differential diagnosis was tuberculosis, filariasis, or lymphoma. Blood tests showed the boy to be anaemic, with a haemoglobin concentration of 7·3 g/dL. He had a raised platelet count (1000 × 109 per L), a significantly raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and raised lactate-dehydrogenase levels. Blood cultures and an HIV test were negative. We did a lymph node biopsy, bone marrow aspiration, and CT scan of his head and neck. The lymph node biopsy result showed granulomatous infiltration with negative infective stains and the bone marrow was normal. A CT scan of the boy's head showed widespread lymphadenopathy, and a lytic lesion in the skull (figure). Considering all the information together, we made a provisional diagnosis of a histiocytic disease such as Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH); the degree of lymphadenopathy was phenotypically consistent with Rosai-Dorfman-Destombes (RDD) disease. Full histological analysis, including immunological staining, was not available in Kenya; however, our local expert's opinion was that the pathology was consistent with the provisional diagnosis. So due to the severity and duration of the patient's symptoms, he was started on treatment with prednisone 40 mg/m2 daily for 4 weeks, tapered over 2 weeks, and vinblastine 6 mg/m2 per week for 6 weeks.
Happily, over the next 6 months, the boy's symptoms dramatically improved on continuation therapy: vinblastine, prednisone, and mercaptopurine (figure). We will continue treatment until he has completed a total of 52 weeks of chemotherapy.
In the process of reviewing the case for publication in The Lancet, the histology was examined by an expert in France, who confirmed that our patient did indeed have a rare form of mixed type histiocytosis—LCH and RDD. All the boy's histocytes strongly expressed S100, with around 30% of these cells also expressing CD1a or CD207.
Histiocytosis encompasses a range of conditions in which there is abnormal proliferation or differentiation and function of the mononuclear phagocyte system. LCH is the most common histiocyte disorder, with clinical presentations ranging from multisystem disease to single indolent lesions. RDD is also called sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy due to its propensity to cause large lymphadenopathy, and has a wide range of clinical presentations. Mixed type histiocytosis—as in our patient—is an unusual but well documented occurrence. Usually, treatment for histiocytosis is tailored to the individual. However, in severe, multifocal disease and in low-income and middle-income settings where sophisticated histopathological analysis may not be available, it might be appropriate to treat patients with chemotherapy empirically.

A 52-year-old woman with a 10-day history of a fever and who had, for the past 4 days, an impaired level of consciousness attended our hospital.She had a medical history of autoimmune encephalitis and urinary tract infections.
On examination we found her to be unwell, with a respiratory rate of 20 breaths per min, pulse rate of 103 beats per min, a temperature of 38·11°C, blood oxygen saturation of 95%, and a blood pressure of 136/93 mm Hg.
A chest CT showed inflammation in both lungs and the patient was then intubated using an endotracheal tube.
Laboratory investigations showed a raised white blood cell count of 14·20 × 109 per L (normal 4·5–11·0); absolute neutrophil count was 13·83 × 109 per L (normal 1·8–7·5) with a percentage of 97·3%.
Sequencing of a strain isolated from the patient's sputum showed that she had a lung infection caused by the Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase (KPC)-producing KPC-2 strain.
We commenced treatment with antibacterial drugs: polymyxin B plus the cefoperazone-sulbactam combination for 8 days, followed by tigecycline plus fosfomycin for 2 days, and then ceftazidime-avibactam for 21 days. However, 3 days after stopping the ceftazidime-avibactam combination and replacing it with fosfomycin monotherapy, the patient's temperature increased again. Further laboratory investigations showed a white blood cell count of 10·46 × 109 per L, with an absolute neutrophil count of 8·63 × 109 per L; neutrophils were 82·4%.
Carbapenem-resistant K pneumoniae was still cultured from a sample of the patient's sputum.
We then re-sequenced the bacteria which showed that one of the genes encoding carbapenemases—the KPC-2 genotype—had evolved, in vivo, from blaKPC-2 to blaKPC-76 through a 7-amino acid tandem repeat, between amino acids 262 and 268 (262V-268N dup), and a D179Y substitution mutation. We presumed the change had resulted in the treatment failure.
Additionally, antimicrobial susceptibility testing indicated that the K pneumoniae had changed its antimicrobial susceptibility profile: initially it had the characteristic growth of classic KPC-2 (figure), which is susceptible to the ceftazidime-avibactam and aztreonam-avibactam combinations; and after 3 weeks, the profile had changed to the New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase-producing K pneumoniae, which is resistant to the ceftazidime-avibactam combination but susceptible to aztreonam-avibactam (figure).
The patient was then given the ceftazidime-avibactam combination plus amikacin, and then was switched to tigecycline plus meropenem; her symptoms improved, and her vital signs stabilised. She was then transferred to a rehabilitation facility for further treatment.
At the molecular level, nucleotide deletions, mutations, insertions, and tandem repeats are the mechanisms most commonly responsible for bacterial resistance to ceftazidime-avibactam.
The newer antibiotic combinations, such as carbapenem, meropenem, and the cyclic boronic acid β-lactamase inhibitor, vaborbactam, can be considered as salvage therapies for the treatment of infections caused by emerging strains with novel KPC-variants—although these agents have not yet been marketed for clinical use in many countries.

A 52-year-old woman with a 10-day history of a fever and who had, for the past 4 days, an impaired level of consciousness attended our hospital.She had a medical history of autoimmune encephalitis and urinary tract infections.
On examination we found her to be unwell, with a respiratory rate of 20 breaths per min, pulse rate of 103 beats per min, a temperature of 38·11°C, blood oxygen saturation of 95%, and a blood pressure of 136/93 mm Hg.
A chest CT showed inflammation in both lungs and the patient was then intubated using an endotracheal tube.
Laboratory investigations showed a raised white blood cell count of 14·20 × 109 per L (normal 4·5–11·0); absolute neutrophil count was 13·83 × 109 per L (normal 1·8–7·5) with a percentage of 97·3%.
Sequencing of a strain isolated from the patient's sputum showed that she had a lung infection caused by the Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase (KPC)-producing KPC-2 strain.
We commenced treatment with antibacterial drugs: polymyxin B plus the cefoperazone-sulbactam combination for 8 days, followed by tigecycline plus fosfomycin for 2 days, and then ceftazidime-avibactam for 21 days. However, 3 days after stopping the ceftazidime-avibactam combination and replacing it with fosfomycin monotherapy, the patient's temperature increased again. Further laboratory investigations showed a white blood cell count of 10·46 × 109 per L, with an absolute neutrophil count of 8·63 × 109 per L; neutrophils were 82·4%.
Carbapenem-resistant K pneumoniae was still cultured from a sample of the patient's sputum.
We then re-sequenced the bacteria which showed that one of the genes encoding carbapenemases—the KPC-2 genotype—had evolved, in vivo, from blaKPC-2 to blaKPC-76 through a 7-amino acid tandem repeat, between amino acids 262 and 268 (262V-268N dup), and a D179Y substitution mutation. We presumed the change had resulted in the treatment failure.

The patient was then given the ceftazidime-avibactam combination plus amikacin, and then was switched to tigecycline plus meropenem; her symptoms improved, and her vital signs stabilised. She was then transferred to a rehabilitation facility for further treatment.
At the molecular level, nucleotide deletions, mutations, insertions, and tandem repeats are the mechanisms most commonly responsible for bacterial resistance to ceftazidime-avibactam.
The newer antibiotic combinations, such as carbapenem, meropenem, and the cyclic boronic acid β-lactamase inhibitor, vaborbactam, can be considered as salvage therapies for the treatment of infections caused by emerging strains with novel KPC-variants—although these agents have not yet been marketed for clinical use in many countries.

A 52-year-old woman with a 10-day history of a fever and who had, for the past 4 days, an impaired level of consciousness attended our hospital.She had a medical history of autoimmune encephalitis and urinary tract infections.
On examination we found her to be unwell, with a respiratory rate of 20 breaths per min, pulse rate of 103 beats per min, a temperature of 38·11°C, blood oxygen saturation of 95%, and a blood pressure of 136/93 mm Hg.
A chest CT showed inflammation in both lungs and the patient was then intubated using an endotracheal tube.
Laboratory investigations showed a raised white blood cell count of 14·20 × 109 per L (normal 4·5–11·0); absolute neutrophil count was 13·83 × 109 per L (normal 1·8–7·5) with a percentage of 97·3%.
Sequencing of a strain isolated from the patient's sputum showed that she had a lung infection caused by the Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase (KPC)-producing KPC-2 strain.
We commenced treatment with antibacterial drugs: polymyxin B plus the cefoperazone-sulbactam combination for 8 days, followed by tigecycline plus fosfomycin for 2 days, and then ceftazidime-avibactam for 21 days. However, 3 days after stopping the ceftazidime-avibactam combination and replacing it with fosfomycin monotherapy, the patient's temperature increased again. Further laboratory investigations showed a white blood cell count of 10·46 × 109 per L, with an absolute neutrophil count of 8·63 × 109 per L; neutrophils were 82·4%.
Carbapenem-resistant K pneumoniae was still cultured from a sample of the patient's sputum.
We then re-sequenced the bacteria which showed that one of the genes encoding carbapenemases—the KPC-2 genotype—had evolved, in vivo, from blaKPC-2 to blaKPC-76 through a 7-amino acid tandem repeat, between amino acids 262 and 268 (262V-268N dup), and a D179Y substitution mutation. We presumed the change had resulted in the treatment failure.
Additionally, antimicrobial susceptibility testing indicated that the K pneumoniae had changed its antimicrobial susceptibility profile: initially it had the characteristic growth of classic KPC-2 (figure), which is susceptible to the ceftazidime-avibactam and aztreonam-avibactam combinations; and after 3 weeks, the profile had changed to the New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase-producing K pneumoniae, which is resistant to the ceftazidime-avibactam combination but susceptible to aztreonam-avibactam (figure).
The patient was then given the ceftazidime-avibactam combination plus amikacin, and then was switched to tigecycline plus meropenem; her symptoms improved, and her vital signs stabilised. She was then transferred to a rehabilitation facility for further treatment.
At the molecular level, nucleotide deletions, mutations, insertions, and tandem repeats are the mechanisms most commonly responsible for bacterial resistance to ceftazidime-avibactam.
The newer antibiotic combinations, such as carbapenem, meropenem, and the cyclic boronic acid β-lactamase inhibitor, vaborbactam, can be considered as salvage therapies for the treatment of infections caused by emerging strains with novel KPC-variants—although these agents have not yet been marketed for clinical use in many countries.

A 26-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 6-month history of dry, itchy eyes, and poor vision at night. She also reported dry, itchy skin, and brittle nails.She was a teetotaller and had no history of bowel surgery. On examination, we found no evidence of malabsorption, chronic liver disease, cholestasis, or pancreatic disease; a physical examination was unremarkable apart from abnormalities in her eyes. The patient's unaided visual acuity was 6/6 in both eyes and she had symmetrical, triangular, foamy, keratinised patches over her bulbar conjunctiva, adjoining the temporal limbus of both eyes (figure). The cornea was normal and a fundoscopic examination found no abnormalities.
We concluded the lesions were Bitot's spots—indicative of xerophthalmia stage X1B, according to the WHO classification.
Laboratory investigations—including full blood count, liver function tests, and renal function tests—were normal. Microscopic examination of a sample of the patient's stool was negative for ova, parasites, and cysts for Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm), Giardia duodenalis (giardiasis), Trichuris trichiura (whipworm), Entamoeba histolytica (amoebiasis), and Ancylostoma duodenale (hookworm).
We prescribed oral vitamin A 10 000 U/day for 3 months and lubricating eye drops. The patient's symptoms and signs resolved within 1 month of starting therapy. As a woman of childbearing age, we advised her to try and maintain a varied, healthy diet—specifically rich in fruits and vegetables. We also counselled her to seek medical advice if she was planning to have children in order to prevent recurrence of vitamin A deficiency (VAD) in her or its development in her offspring.
Keratin admixed with Corynebacterium xerosis from the stratum corneum of the conjunctiva along with metaplasia of conjunctival epithelium due to VAD may produce Bitot's spots. The foamy appearance may be due to gas produced by the bacteria. Histopathological examination normally shows keratinisation, inflammatory infiltrates, with the accumulation of Gram-positive bacilli. The prevalence of subclinical VAD in India is about 61%, which is one of the highest in the world. Bitot's spots represent the pathognomonic clinical finding which can be used to estimate the prevalence of VAD. In low-income and middle-income countries (LMICs), primary VAD is usually attributed to malnourishment with an increased susceptibility occurring during pregnancy and lactation. Young children are also at increased risk because of high nutritional demands.
Globally, nearly 4·5 billion people are at risk of VAD due to intestinal parasite infections. Gender difference in access to eye care services may be responsible for the higher incidence of blindness in women in LMICs.
Bitot's spots respond rapidly to vitamin A supplements and indicate a level of VAD that can be reversed without the development of blindness; the finding should therefore prompt immediate treatment. If xerophthalmia and blindness ensue, then mortality can be as high as 40% within the first year of diagnosis (video).

The cornea was normal and a fundoscopic examination found no abnormalities.
We concluded the lesions were Bitot's spots—indicative of xerophthalmia stage X1B, according to the WHO classification.
Laboratory investigations—including full blood count, liver function tests, and renal function tests—were normal. Microscopic examination of a sample of the patient's stool was negative for ova, parasites, and cysts for Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm), Giardia duodenalis (giardiasis), Trichuris trichiura (whipworm), Entamoeba histolytica (amoebiasis), and Ancylostoma duodenale (hookworm).

A 63-year-old man attended our department reporting a 3-month history of diffuse pain in both hands. He had been investigated for primary hyperparathyroidism because of previous episodes of hypercalcaemia—the last time had necessitated hospitalisation—despite taking high doses of a calcimimetic (cinacalcet). The patient's maximum serum calcium concentration had been 13·3 mg/dL (normal range 8·5–10·5). His parathyroid hormone (286 pg/mL; normal range 12–88) and 24-h urine test for calcium (491·8 mg; normal range 100–300) had also been raised; imaging studies had been inconclusive for parathyroid hyperfunction.On examination, the patient had bone tenderness on palpation, but no associated erythema. He was cognitively intact.
x-rays of his hands (figure) showed subperiosteal resorption of the radial side of the middle phalanges; an expansive cystic lesion with thinning of the overlying cortical bone and slight trabeculation—suggestive of brown tumour because of the diaphyseal location—on the third middle phalanx of the right hand; and lucent striations—so called cortical tunnelling—within the cortex of the long axis of the ulnar side of both fifth metacarpals. Notably, no cystic lesions were found elsewhere in the skeleton.
Taken together, these findings indicated osteitis fibrosa cystica: the pathognomonic skeletal features of primary hyperparathyroidism. Moreover, laboratory investigations showed a slight increase in alkaline phosphatase concentration (124 units per L; normal range 30–120) and bone densitometry showed osteopenia in his lumbar vertebrae, hip, and the bones of his distal forearms.
However, a hemiparathyroidectomy carried out 6 months later failed to resolve the patient's hyperparathyroidism. Consequently, he had to continue treatment with cinacalcet. 14 months later, a right thyroid nodule was identified by neck ultrasound. During the subsequent hemithyroidectomy, an ectopic parathyroid gland was discovered and removed, which resulted in an improvement in the calcium and parathyroid hormone concentrations, measured during the operation. Histology showed a clear cell parathyroid adenoma. Although no improvement in skeletal changes was observed on an x-ray, performed 6 months after surgery, the serum calcium concentration had normalised.
Osteitis fibrosa cystica is uncommon and usually found in severe or neglected cases of chronic exposure to high parathyroid hormone concentrations. The findings may be mistaken for malignant disease, especially when cystic lesions and hypercalcaemia are both present; in this context, the presence of an unsuppressed parathyroid hormone concentration suggests hyperparathyroidism rather than malignancy (video).

A 63-year-old man attended our department reporting a 3-month history of diffuse pain in both hands. He had been investigated for primary hyperparathyroidism because of previous episodes of hypercalcaemia—the last time had necessitated hospitalisation—despite taking high doses of a calcimimetic (cinacalcet). The patient's maximum serum calcium concentration had been 13·3 mg/dL (normal range 8·5–10·5). His parathyroid hormone (286 pg/mL; normal range 12–88) and 24-h urine test for calcium (491·8 mg; normal range 100–300) had also been raised; imaging studies had been inconclusive for parathyroid hyperfunction.On examination, the patient had bone tenderness on palpation, but no associated erythema. He was cognitively intact.
x-rays of his hands (figure) showed subperiosteal resorption of the radial side of the middle phalanges; an expansive cystic lesion with thinning of the overlying cortical bone and slight trabeculation—suggestive of brown tumour because of the diaphyseal location—on the third middle phalanx of the right hand; and lucent striations—so called cortical tunnelling—within the cortex of the long axis of the ulnar side of both fifth metacarpals. Notably, no cystic lesions were found elsewhere in the skeleton.
Taken together, these findings indicated osteitis fibrosa cystica: the pathognomonic skeletal features of primary hyperparathyroidism. Moreover, laboratory investigations showed a slight increase in alkaline phosphatase concentration (124 units per L; normal range 30–120) and bone densitometry showed osteopenia in his lumbar vertebrae, hip, and the bones of his distal forearms.
However, a hemiparathyroidectomy carried out 6 months later failed to resolve the patient's hyperparathyroidism. Consequently, he had to continue treatment with cinacalcet. 14 months later, a right thyroid nodule was identified by neck ultrasound. During the subsequent hemithyroidectomy, an ectopic parathyroid gland was discovered and removed, which resulted in an improvement in the calcium and parathyroid hormone concentrations, measured during the operation. Histology showed a clear cell parathyroid adenoma. Although no improvement in skeletal changes was observed on an x-ray, performed 6 months after surgery, the serum calcium concentration had normalised.
Osteitis fibrosa cystica is uncommon and usually found in severe or neglected cases of chronic exposure to high parathyroid hormone concentrations. The findings may be mistaken for malignant disease, especially when cystic lesions and hypercalcaemia are both present; in this context, the presence of an unsuppressed parathyroid hormone concentration suggests hyperparathyroidism rather than malignancy (video).

An 86-year-old woman with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis—reporting progressive dyspnoea, rated as Class II on the New York Heart Association Functional Classification, for the previous few months—had a transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) in our unit. The patient's valve was replaced with an aortic valve bio prosthesis (Evolut PRO/PRO+ 29 mm [Medtronic Evolut™]).
Immediately after the valve had been replaced, continuous electrocardiogram monitoring showed ST-segment elevation in all antero-septal leads. A coronary angiogram showed complete occlusion of the distal part of the left anterior descending artery (figure 1).We then did a mechanical embolectomy—using a stent retriever (enVast 4·5 × 37 mm [enVast™]) combined with vacuum-assisted aspiration—which resulted in the immediate restoration of blood flow in the blocked artery; no residual material was seen in the vessel on repeat angiography (figure 1).
The extracted material was amber-coloured, calcified, and 2 mm in size; histopathological examination showed that it was mostly composed of collagen, proteoglycans, and extracellular matrix—compatible with a fragment of a leaflet from the patient's original aortic valve (figure 2). Additionally, substrates appeared non-birefringent under polarised light, confirming the absence of polymer-coated device fragments.The patient's chest pain promptly resolved; concentration of high-sensitivity troponin peaked at 24 h (202 ng/L; normal value <14). The patient remained asymptomatic for 1 day after the operation.
On day 2 postoperatively, she developed severe abdominal pain; an abdominal CT scan showed patency of both the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries with radiological signs of intestinal ischaemia. The patient had abdominal surgery which was complicated by multiple-organ failure; she died 4 days after the index TAVR.
Embolisation of aortic valve debris is a feared complication during TAVR, typically resulting in cerebrovascular accidents, and mesenteric or peripheral ischaemia. Histological analysis of captured material from cerebral protective devices has previously been done.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report showing that embolisation of aortic valve debris—confirmed by histological examination—into coronary circulation can be extracted with a stent retriever. Coronary embolisation during TAVR is unpredictable and no effective preventive measures exist; conventional angioplasty is often unsuccessful because of the presence of the calcified, non-friable material inside the vessel.

An 86-year-old woman with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis—reporting progressive dyspnoea, rated as Class II on the New York Heart Association Functional Classification, for the previous few months—had a transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) in our unit. The patient's valve was replaced with an aortic valve bio prosthesis (Evolut PRO/PRO+ 29 mm [Medtronic Evolut™]).
Immediately after the valve had been replaced, continuous electrocardiogram monitoring showed ST-segment elevation in all antero-septal leads. A coronary angiogram showed complete occlusion of the distal part of the left anterior descending artery (figure 1).We then did a mechanical embolectomy—using a stent retriever (enVast 4·5 × 37 mm [enVast™]) combined with vacuum-assisted aspiration—which resulted in the immediate restoration of blood flow in the blocked artery; no residual material was seen in the vessel on repeat angiography (figure 1).
The extracted material was amber-coloured, calcified, and 2 mm in size; histopathological examination showed that it was mostly composed of collagen, proteoglycans, and extracellular matrix—compatible with a fragment of a leaflet from the patient's original aortic valve (figure 2). Additionally, substrates appeared non-birefringent under polarised light, confirming the absence of polymer-coated device fragments.The patient's chest pain promptly resolved; concentration of high-sensitivity troponin peaked at 24 h (202 ng/L; normal value <14). The patient remained asymptomatic for 1 day after the operation.
On day 2 postoperatively, she developed severe abdominal pain; an abdominal CT scan showed patency of both the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries with radiological signs of intestinal ischaemia. The patient had abdominal surgery which was complicated by multiple-organ failure; she died 4 days after the index TAVR.
Embolisation of aortic valve debris is a feared complication during TAVR, typically resulting in cerebrovascular accidents, and mesenteric or peripheral ischaemia. Histological analysis of captured material from cerebral protective devices has previously been done.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report showing that embolisation of aortic valve debris—confirmed by histological examination—into coronary circulation can be extracted with a stent retriever. Coronary embolisation during TAVR is unpredictable and no effective preventive measures exist; conventional angioplasty is often unsuccessful because of the presence of the calcified, non-friable material inside the vessel.

input: A 45-year-old man presented to the rheumatology outpatient unit with bilateral swelling of the hands from the proximal segments of the fingers to the wrist that developed gradually over the past 3 years (figure). The oedema was non-pitting and was not affected by raising the hands. Function of the hands and fingers was not impaired. He had no generalised or pretibial oedema. The patient reported drinking 1–1·5 L of wine per day; medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Blood tests and an ultrasound scan confirmed hepatitis (alanine aminotransferase [ALT] 175 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase [AST] 170 IU/L, albumin 4·68 mg/dL) with a positive antibody test for hepatitis C virus; hepatitis B virus and HIV tests were negative. Rheumatoid factor was 29 IU/mL (normal <14 IU/mL); anti-nuclear antibodies, anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies, complement, protein electrophoresis, and total bilirubin were normal. On further questioning he admitted that he had been injecting high-dose sublingual buprenorphine for more than 5 years, preferentially in the wrist either into or around the veins, three to four times a day.Puffy hand syndrome is a complication of intravenous drug misuse. Users themselves are often aware of the risk, particularly from hand injections, but most physicians, including addiction specialists and general practitioners, rarely encounter this presentation and might not be familiar with it. The frequency of puffy hand syndrome is unknown. The pathogenesis of the oedema probably includes venous and lymphatic insufficiency, and the direct toxicity of injected drugs. Biopsy samples of skin and subcutaneous tissue and lymphangiograms can show destruction of the lymphatics that leads to fibrosis of the subcutaneous tissue, probably due to soluble compounds of the drugs that damage lymphatic vessels. Treatment with low-stretch bandaging and the wearing of elastic garments help to decrease the volume in puffy hand syndrome.

input:
An 86-year-old woman with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis—reporting progressive dyspnoea, rated as Class II on the New York Heart Association Functional Classification, for the previous few months—had a transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) in our unit. The patient's valve was replaced with an aortic valve bio prosthesis (Evolut PRO/PRO+ 29 mm [Medtronic Evolut™]).
Immediately after the valve had been replaced, continuous electrocardiogram monitoring showed ST-segment elevation in all antero-septal leads. A coronary angiogram showed complete occlusion of the distal part of the left anterior descending artery (figure 1).We then did a mechanical embolectomy—using a stent retriever (enVast 4·5 × 37 mm [enVast™]) combined with vacuum-assisted aspiration—which resulted in the immediate restoration of blood flow in the blocked artery; no residual material was seen in the vessel on repeat angiography (figure 1).
The extracted material was amber-coloured, calcified, and 2 mm in size; histopathological examination showed that it was mostly composed of collagen, proteoglycans, and extracellular matrix—compatible with a fragment of a leaflet from the patient's original aortic valve (figure 2). Additionally, substrates appeared non-birefringent under polarised light, confirming the absence of polymer-coated device fragments.The patient's chest pain promptly resolved; concentration of high-sensitivity troponin peaked at 24 h (202 ng/L; normal value <14). The patient remained asymptomatic for 1 day after the operation.
On day 2 postoperatively, she developed severe abdominal pain; an abdominal CT scan showed patency of both the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries with radiological signs of intestinal ischaemia. The patient had abdominal surgery which was complicated by multiple-organ failure; she died 4 days after the index TAVR.
Embolisation of aortic valve debris is a feared complication during TAVR, typically resulting in cerebrovascular accidents, and mesenteric or peripheral ischaemia. Histological analysis of captured material from cerebral protective devices has previously been done.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report showing that embolisation of aortic valve debris—confirmed by histological examination—into coronary circulation can be extracted with a stent retriever. Coronary embolisation during TAVR is unpredictable and no effective preventive measures exist; conventional angioplasty is often unsuccessful because of the presence of the calcified, non-friable material inside the vessel.

A 19-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever. He had no medical history. On examination his temperature was 38·8°C, he was dehydrated and tachycardic, and he had postural hypotension: his blood pressure was 110/40 mm Hg supine and 88/36 mm Hg standing. On palpation of his abdomen, the patient reported widespread pain with equivocal rebound tenderness. We also noted diffuse darkening of the mucous membranes and skin, which the patient said had gradually increased over the past 7 years. The hyperpigmentation was more pronounced on the skin over the patient's joints, hands and feet nail beds, gingivae, and the dorsum of the tongue (figure).Laboratory tests showed a sodium concentration of 116 mmol/L, a potassium concentration of 5·3 mmol/L, a low morning serum cortisol concentration of 63·4 nmol/L (normal range 172–496), and a high plasma adrenocorticotropic hormone concentration of 440 pmol/L (normal range 1·5–13·9). We started the patient on an intravenous saline drip and gave him a bolus of 100 mg of hydrocortisone intravenously. After 24 h the patient's symptoms improved, and after 6 days his electrolytes normalised.
Further investigations found no HIV antibodies, no antibodies against 21-hydroxylase, no antibodies to Paracoccidioides brasiliensis (also known as South American blastomycosis), and a negative tuberculin test. However, the patient's serum concentration of hexacosanoic acid—a very long chain fatty acid (VLCFA)—was 2·82 μmol/L (normal range 0·22–0·88).
Molecular sequencing found a missense mutation in exon 6 of the ABCD1 gene—the R518Q mutation—in both the patient and his mother confirming the diagnosis of X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy. Additionally, when we repeated a neurological examination, we found the patient to have a previously unnoticed, slight left hemiparesis with preserved deep tendon reflexes, muscle tone, and normal sensation. After 9 days in the hospital, the patient went home taking oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone.
The characteristic mucocutaneous manifestations of Addison's disease (AD) are the crucial clue in diagnosing this life-threatening condition: ideally, they should be engrained into every clinician's visual memory—the other signs and symptoms of AD are non-specific.
X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy is a rare genetic disorder characterised by intracellular accumulation of VLCFA. Phenotypes range from a severe progressive cerebral form in boys to a myelopathy form in adults. AD may occur throughout the lifespan, independently of the neurological presentations; it is seen as an isolated manifestation in up to 10% of cases. X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy must be considered as a differential diagnosis of AD in young men—even if neurological symptoms are not obvious at initial examination, as we found in our patient (video).
