A 65-year-old woman attended our hospital with a 1-day history of fever and falls, saying that her legs had given out from under her. The patient's symptoms began within 1 day of the first dose of the mRNA-1273 SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. She had a medical history of hypertension and diabetes.On examination in the emergency department, the patient's temperature was 39·1°C, her respiratory rate was 25 breaths per min, and her heart rate was 88 beats per min. As she met the criteria for systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), an extensive infection work-up was initiated and she was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Laboratory investigations found a D-dimer concentration of 5267 ng/mL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 69 mm/h, and a C-reactive protein concentration of 63·4 mg/L. The patient's white blood cell count, lactate, urinalysis, respiratory pathogen panel—including SARS-CoV-2—and urine and blood cultures were unremarkable. Due to concerns of exposure to SARS-CoV-2, the PCR test was repeated after 24 h, but this was again negative.
CT of the patient's chest showed multiple pulmonary nodules measuring up to 1·1 cm. A small filling defect in a distal subsegmental pulmonary artery was also seen, which we thought was inconsistent with an acute pulmonary embolism and probably artifactual. Doppler ultrasounds of the patient's lower limbs were normal; her head CT was also normal.
4 days after presentation, 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT was done to characterise the pulmonary nodules; it showed uptake in the fat stranding posterior to the right deltoid (figure); moderately increased uptake within multiple right axillary lymph nodes (figure); and diffusely increased splenic uptake (figure). The pulmonary nodules had no uptake—indicating that they were probably benign.
The patient's symptoms resolved 3 days after the vaccination. Given the imaging findings, the temporal relationship of the symptoms to the vaccination, and negative test results from an extensive work-up for malignant and infectious causes, we believe, the diagnosis was a local and systemic immune response following vaccination. However possible masking effects of broad-spectrum antibiotics cannot be excluded.
The high D-dimer concentration probably reflected significant concomitant coagulation and fibrinolysis associated with SIRS.
The local response was demonstrated by hypermetabolism within the axillary lymph nodes draining the site of intramuscular injection; diffusely increased splenic activity suggests a systemic response—corroborated by elevated inflammatory markers.
As the global vaccination effort continues, more patients will undoubtedly require assessment and investigation shortly after immunisation. Imaging and laboratory findings consistent with a systemic immune response might result in further unnecessary evaluation or interventions. However, findings overlap with other diseases—notably those of the 18F-FDG PET/CT scan in patients with malignancies. Recognition of the clinical and imaging features of the systemic immune response to vaccination might become essential in the coming months (video).

A 19-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever. He had no medical history. On examination his temperature was 38·8°C, he was dehydrated and tachycardic, and he had postural hypotension: his blood pressure was 110/40 mm Hg supine and 88/36 mm Hg standing. On palpation of his abdomen, the patient reported widespread pain with equivocal rebound tenderness. We also noted diffuse darkening of the mucous membranes and skin, which the patient said had gradually increased over the past 7 years. The hyperpigmentation was more pronounced on the skin over the patient's joints, hands and feet nail beds, gingivae, and the dorsum of the tongue (figure).Laboratory tests showed a sodium concentration of 116 mmol/L, a potassium concentration of 5·3 mmol/L, a low morning serum cortisol concentration of 63·4 nmol/L (normal range 172–496), and a high plasma adrenocorticotropic hormone concentration of 440 pmol/L (normal range 1·5–13·9). We started the patient on an intravenous saline drip and gave him a bolus of 100 mg of hydrocortisone intravenously. After 24 h the patient's symptoms improved, and after 6 days his electrolytes normalised.
Further investigations found no HIV antibodies, no antibodies against 21-hydroxylase, no antibodies to Paracoccidioides brasiliensis (also known as South American blastomycosis), and a negative tuberculin test. However, the patient's serum concentration of hexacosanoic acid—a very long chain fatty acid (VLCFA)—was 2·82 μmol/L (normal range 0·22–0·88).
Molecular sequencing found a missense mutation in exon 6 of the ABCD1 gene—the R518Q mutation—in both the patient and his mother confirming the diagnosis of X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy. Additionally, when we repeated a neurological examination, we found the patient to have a previously unnoticed, slight left hemiparesis with preserved deep tendon reflexes, muscle tone, and normal sensation. After 9 days in the hospital, the patient went home taking oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone.
The characteristic mucocutaneous manifestations of Addison's disease (AD) are the crucial clue in diagnosing this life-threatening condition: ideally, they should be engrained into every clinician's visual memory—the other signs and symptoms of AD are non-specific.
X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy is a rare genetic disorder characterised by intracellular accumulation of VLCFA. Phenotypes range from a severe progressive cerebral form in boys to a myelopathy form in adults. AD may occur throughout the lifespan, independently of the neurological presentations; it is seen as an isolated manifestation in up to 10% of cases. X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy must be considered as a differential diagnosis of AD in young men—even if neurological symptoms are not obvious at initial examination, as we found in our patient (video).

A 65-year-old woman attended our hospital with a 1-day history of fever and falls, saying that her legs had given out from under her. The patient's symptoms began within 1 day of the first dose of the mRNA-1273 SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. She had a medical history of hypertension and diabetes.On examination in the emergency department, the patient's temperature was 39·1°C, her respiratory rate was 25 breaths per min, and her heart rate was 88 beats per min. As she met the criteria for systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), an extensive infection work-up was initiated and she was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Laboratory investigations found a D-dimer concentration of 5267 ng/mL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 69 mm/h, and a C-reactive protein concentration of 63·4 mg/L. The patient's white blood cell count, lactate, urinalysis, respiratory pathogen panel—including SARS-CoV-2—and urine and blood cultures were unremarkable. Due to concerns of exposure to SARS-CoV-2, the PCR test was repeated after 24 h, but this was again negative.
CT of the patient's chest showed multiple pulmonary nodules measuring up to 1·1 cm. A small filling defect in a distal subsegmental pulmonary artery was also seen, which we thought was inconsistent with an acute pulmonary embolism and probably artifactual. Doppler ultrasounds of the patient's lower limbs were normal; her head CT was also normal.
4 days after presentation, 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT was done to characterise the pulmonary nodules; it showed uptake in the fat stranding posterior to the right deltoid (figure); moderately increased uptake within multiple right axillary lymph nodes (figure); and diffusely increased splenic uptake (figure). The pulmonary nodules had no uptake—indicating that they were probably benign.
The patient's symptoms resolved 3 days after the vaccination. Given the imaging findings, the temporal relationship of the symptoms to the vaccination, and negative test results from an extensive work-up for malignant and infectious causes, we believe, the diagnosis was a local and systemic immune response following vaccination. However possible masking effects of broad-spectrum antibiotics cannot be excluded.
The high D-dimer concentration probably reflected significant concomitant coagulation and fibrinolysis associated with SIRS.
The local response was demonstrated by hypermetabolism within the axillary lymph nodes draining the site of intramuscular injection; diffusely increased splenic activity suggests a systemic response—corroborated by elevated inflammatory markers.
As the global vaccination effort continues, more patients will undoubtedly require assessment and investigation shortly after immunisation. Imaging and laboratory findings consistent with a systemic immune response might result in further unnecessary evaluation or interventions. However, findings overlap with other diseases—notably those of the 18F-FDG PET/CT scan in patients with malignancies. Recognition of the clinical and imaging features of the systemic immune response to vaccination might become essential in the coming months (video).

A 65-year-old woman attended our hospital with a 1-day history of fever and falls, saying that her legs had given out from under her. The patient's symptoms began within 1 day of the first dose of the mRNA-1273 SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. She had a medical history of hypertension and diabetes.On examination in the emergency department, the patient's temperature was 39·1°C, her respiratory rate was 25 breaths per min, and her heart rate was 88 beats per min. As she met the criteria for systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), an extensive infection work-up was initiated and she was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Laboratory investigations found a D-dimer concentration of 5267 ng/mL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 69 mm/h, and a C-reactive protein concentration of 63·4 mg/L. The patient's white blood cell count, lactate, urinalysis, respiratory pathogen panel—including SARS-CoV-2—and urine and blood cultures were unremarkable. Due to concerns of exposure to SARS-CoV-2, the PCR test was repeated after 24 h, but this was again negative.
CT of the patient's chest showed multiple pulmonary nodules measuring up to 1·1 cm. A small filling defect in a distal subsegmental pulmonary artery was also seen, which we thought was inconsistent with an acute pulmonary embolism and probably artifactual. Doppler ultrasounds of the patient's lower limbs were normal; her head CT was also normal.
4 days after presentation, 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT was done to characterise the pulmonary nodules; it showed uptake in the fat stranding posterior to the right deltoid (figure); moderately increased uptake within multiple right axillary lymph nodes (figure); and diffusely increased splenic uptake (figure). The pulmonary nodules had no uptake—indicating that they were probably benign.
The patient's symptoms resolved 3 days after the vaccination. Given the imaging findings, the temporal relationship of the symptoms to the vaccination, and negative test results from an extensive work-up for malignant and infectious causes, we believe, the diagnosis was a local and systemic immune response following vaccination. However possible masking effects of broad-spectrum antibiotics cannot be excluded.
The high D-dimer concentration probably reflected significant concomitant coagulation and fibrinolysis associated with SIRS.
The local response was demonstrated by hypermetabolism within the axillary lymph nodes draining the site of intramuscular injection; diffusely increased splenic activity suggests a systemic response—corroborated by elevated inflammatory markers.
As the global vaccination effort continues, more patients will undoubtedly require assessment and investigation shortly after immunisation. Imaging and laboratory findings consistent with a systemic immune response might result in further unnecessary evaluation or interventions. However, findings overlap with other diseases—notably those of the 18F-FDG PET/CT scan in patients with malignancies. Recognition of the clinical and imaging features of the systemic immune response to vaccination might become essential in the coming months (video).

A 53-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 4-week history of abdominal pain, jaundice, and pruritus.The patient had a history of gout; his alcohol consumption was 7 drinks per week, and he had a 10-pack-year smoking history which ended when he quit 8 months earlier. He had no history of recent travel or contact with any ill people.
On examination, he had scleral icterus, a soft non-tender abdomen with no palpable masses or organomegaly; he had no stigmata of chronic liver disease or palpable lymphadenopathy. He was afebrile with vital signs in normal range.
Laboratory investigations showed a white blood cell count of 7·1 × 109 cells per L, haemoglobin concentration 123 g/L, creatinine concentration 82 μmol/L, alkaline phosphatase of 510 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 825 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 180 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 298 U/L, and a total bilirubin of 169 μmol/L. Serum protein electrophoresis demonstrated a mild polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. The serum IgG4 concentration was mildly elevated at 2·05 g/L; the IgG1 was elevated at 11·9 g/L and IgG3 was elevated at 2·03g/L. Tumour markers were normal. Ferritin was raised at 707 μg/L, transferrin saturation was 12%. Hepatitis B, C, HIV, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus serology were all negative. CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed marked intrahepatic and extrahepatic duct dilation; there were no intraluminal or adjacent extrinsic lesions, but the pancreas was diffusely enlarged, and there was bilateral renal enlargement with poorly enhancing nodules. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography demonstrated a distal common bile duct stricture (appendix), and histopathological examination of biopsy samples of the pancreas obtained by fine needle showed active and chronic inflammation; no IgG4-positive plasma cells or malignancy were identified. Our working diagnosis at that stage was an autoimmune pancreatitis and the patient was prescribed prednisone; initially his condition improved, and he showed a good response. However, six months later, he returned reporting fatigue and weight loss. Laboratory investigations showed a C-reactive protein concentration of 45 mg/L and creatinine concentration of 200 μmol/L.
A repeat CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed noticeable changes when compared with the earlier imaging, extensive lymphadenopathy, a bulky pancreatic head, hepatomegaly, and bilateral nephromegaly, were observed.
Histopathological analysis of a sample of a cervical lymph node obtained after an excisional biopsy showed expansion of the sinuses by histiocytes (appendix), with lymphocytic emperipolesis (figure). Immunohistochemistry demonstrated the histiocytes were positive for CD68 and S100, and negative for CD1a. The clinical presentation and histological findings were consistent with Rosai-Dorfman-Destombes (RDD) disease. He was prescribed rituximab, which led to the complete resolution of his symptoms. At follow-up one year later, he remained in complete clinical, radiological, and biochemical remission.
Obstructive jaundice results from a disruption in the flow of bile due to complete or partial obstruction of the extrahepatic biliary system. Common causes in mid-life include choledocholithiasis, choledochal cysts, bile duct strictures secondary to chronic pancreatitis or primary sclerosing cholangitis, pancreatic cancer, and cholangiocarcinoma. RDD is a rare histiocytic neoplasm that classically presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy. Pancreatic RDD can be mass-forming and may mimic malignancy, infection, or autoimmune pancreatitis—both non-IgG4-related and IgG4-related (video).

A 53-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 4-week history of abdominal pain, jaundice, and pruritus.The patient had a history of gout; his alcohol consumption was 7 drinks per week, and he had a 10-pack-year smoking history which ended when he quit 8 months earlier. He had no history of recent travel or contact with any ill people.
On examination, he had scleral icterus, a soft non-tender abdomen with no palpable masses or organomegaly; he had no stigmata of chronic liver disease or palpable lymphadenopathy. He was afebrile with vital signs in normal range.
Laboratory investigations showed a white blood cell count of 7·1 × 109 cells per L, haemoglobin concentration 123 g/L, creatinine concentration 82 μmol/L, alkaline phosphatase of 510 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 825 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 180 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 298 U/L, and a total bilirubin of 169 μmol/L. Serum protein electrophoresis demonstrated a mild polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. The serum IgG4 concentration was mildly elevated at 2·05 g/L; the IgG1 was elevated at 11·9 g/L and IgG3 was elevated at 2·03g/L. Tumour markers were normal. Ferritin was raised at 707 μg/L, transferrin saturation was 12%. Hepatitis B, C, HIV, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus serology were all negative. CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed marked intrahepatic and extrahepatic duct dilation; there were no intraluminal or adjacent extrinsic lesions, but the pancreas was diffusely enlarged, and there was bilateral renal enlargement with poorly enhancing nodules. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography demonstrated a distal common bile duct stricture (appendix), and histopathological examination of biopsy samples of the pancreas obtained by fine needle showed active and chronic inflammation; no IgG4-positive plasma cells or malignancy were identified. Our working diagnosis at that stage was an autoimmune pancreatitis and the patient was prescribed prednisone; initially his condition improved, and he showed a good response. However, six months later, he returned reporting fatigue and weight loss. Laboratory investigations showed a C-reactive protein concentration of 45 mg/L and creatinine concentration of 200 μmol/L.
A repeat CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed noticeable changes when compared with the earlier imaging, extensive lymphadenopathy, a bulky pancreatic head, hepatomegaly, and bilateral nephromegaly, were observed.
Histopathological analysis of a sample of a cervical lymph node obtained after an excisional biopsy showed expansion of the sinuses by histiocytes (appendix), with lymphocytic emperipolesis (figure). Immunohistochemistry demonstrated the histiocytes were positive for CD68 and S100, and negative for CD1a. The clinical presentation and histological findings were consistent with Rosai-Dorfman-Destombes (RDD) disease. He was prescribed rituximab, which led to the complete resolution of his symptoms. At follow-up one year later, he remained in complete clinical, radiological, and biochemical remission.
Obstructive jaundice results from a disruption in the flow of bile due to complete or partial obstruction of the extrahepatic biliary system. Common causes in mid-life include choledocholithiasis, choledochal cysts, bile duct strictures secondary to chronic pancreatitis or primary sclerosing cholangitis, pancreatic cancer, and cholangiocarcinoma. RDD is a rare histiocytic neoplasm that classically presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy. Pancreatic RDD can be mass-forming and may mimic malignancy, infection, or autoimmune pancreatitis—both non-IgG4-related and IgG4-related (video).

input:
A 53-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 4-week history of abdominal pain, jaundice, and pruritus.The patient had a history of gout; his alcohol consumption was 7 drinks per week, and he had a 10-pack-year smoking history which ended when he quit 8 months earlier. He had no history of recent travel or contact with any ill people.
On examination, he had scleral icterus, a soft non-tender abdomen with no palpable masses or organomegaly; he had no stigmata of chronic liver disease or palpable lymphadenopathy. He was afebrile with vital signs in normal range.
Laboratory investigations showed a white blood cell count of 7·1 × 109 cells per L, haemoglobin concentration 123 g/L, creatinine concentration 82 μmol/L, alkaline phosphatase of 510 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 825 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 180 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 298 U/L, and a total bilirubin of 169 μmol/L. Serum protein electrophoresis demonstrated a mild polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. The serum IgG4 concentration was mildly elevated at 2·05 g/L; the IgG1 was elevated at 11·9 g/L and IgG3 was elevated at 2·03g/L. Tumour markers were normal. Ferritin was raised at 707 μg/L, transferrin saturation was 12%. Hepatitis B, C, HIV, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus serology were all negative. CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed marked intrahepatic and extrahepatic duct dilation; there were no intraluminal or adjacent extrinsic lesions, but the pancreas was diffusely enlarged, and there was bilateral renal enlargement with poorly enhancing nodules. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography demonstrated a distal common bile duct stricture (appendix), and histopathological examination of biopsy samples of the pancreas obtained by fine needle showed active and chronic inflammation; no IgG4-positive plasma cells or malignancy were identified. Our working diagnosis at that stage was an autoimmune pancreatitis and the patient was prescribed prednisone; initially his condition improved, and he showed a good response. However, six months later, he returned reporting fatigue and weight loss. Laboratory investigations showed a C-reactive protein concentration of 45 mg/L and creatinine concentration of 200 μmol/L.
A repeat CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed noticeable changes when compared with the earlier imaging, extensive lymphadenopathy, a bulky pancreatic head, hepatomegaly, and bilateral nephromegaly, were observed.
Histopathological analysis of a sample of a cervical lymph node obtained after an excisional biopsy showed expansion of the sinuses by histiocytes (appendix), with lymphocytic emperipolesis (figure). Immunohistochemistry demonstrated the histiocytes were positive for CD68 and S100, and negative for CD1a. The clinical presentation and histological findings were consistent with Rosai-Dorfman-Destombes (RDD) disease. He was prescribed rituximab, which led to the complete resolution of his symptoms. At follow-up one year later, he remained in complete clinical, radiological, and biochemical remission.
Obstructive jaundice results from a disruption in the flow of bile due to complete or partial obstruction of the extrahepatic biliary system. Common causes in mid-life include choledocholithiasis, choledochal cysts, bile duct strictures secondary to chronic pancreatitis or primary sclerosing cholangitis, pancreatic cancer, and cholangiocarcinoma. RDD is a rare histiocytic neoplasm that classically presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy. Pancreatic RDD can be mass-forming and may mimic malignancy, infection, or autoimmune pancreatitis—both non-IgG4-related and IgG4-related (video).

A 40-year-old woman was referred to our clinic by her optometrist because she had lesions on her retina suggestive of age-related macular degeneration (AMD). She was otherwise well: with no systemic or visual symptoms.In her medical history, the patient had no previous problems with her eyesight. However, at the age of 10 years, she had developed end-stage renal disease—initially diagnosed as post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis—which eventually resulted in her having a right kidney transplant when she was 22 years old. 6 years later, aged 28 years, she developed signs of rejection and required hospitalisation. At that stage, a kidney biopsy led to a diagnosis of dense deposit disease (DDD). She received a second kidney transplant at age 39 years.
She had been prescribed a combination of immunosuppressive drugs—prednisolone, mycophenolate, and tacrolimus—for the past 2 years, and her blood pressure had remained stable without pharmacotherapy.
On examination, we found her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Fundus examination showed drusen-like deposits in the macula and numerous lesions in the peripheral retina of both eyes (figure). Optical coherence tomography showed subretinal dome-shaped deposits—known as drusen—in the peripheral retina, with some encroaching in the macular region of both eyes (figure). Drusen is the plural form of druse, a German word meaning node or geode.
Considering the situation in the round, including the patient's age and medical history, and the appearance and distribution of the fundus lesions, we concluded that the drusen were a feature of DDD rather than AMD. The patient continues to be followed up by both her nephrologist and ophthalmologist.
DDD, which was previously known as type II membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, is classified as either complement or immune complex mediated; DDD is considered a subtype of complement C3-mediated glomerulopathy. Patients with DDD have diffuse, dense deposits in the glomerular basement membrane, and unlike other forms of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, they also typically have drusen deposits in Bruch's membrane of the eye. It is a rare disease that usually presents in children aged 5–15 years old and eventually leads to end-stage renal disease.
Drusen in patients with DDD typically develop after more than 20 years, and although the retinal lesions do not directly cause visual impairment, vision can deteriorate, most commonly due to macular detachment, central serous chorioretinopathy, or choroidal neovascularisation similar to patients with AMD.
Anyone under the age of 50 years found to have retinal drusen should therefore be assessed for renal disease at the time of presentation, and should have regular ophthalmic examinations to monitor for the development of potential vision-threatening changes (video).

A woman aged 28 years with systemic lupus erythematous and abnormal kidney function, treated with 4·5 mg/kg hydroxychloroquine daily for 15 years (cumulative dose 1369 g), presented with bilateral progressive central vision loss for 2 months. The patient had no known previous exposure to chloroquine. Best corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in her right eye and 20/30 in her left eye. Funduscopy showed a concentric hypopigmentation around both foveas (figure). Spectral domain optical coherence tomography of the macula revealed photoreceptor layer and retinal pigmented epithelium loss, and automated 24-2 visual fields showed bilateral central scotomas (figure). These findings were consistent with bull's eye maculopathy, a classic feature of advanced hydroxychloroquine toxicity. 3 months after medication was stopped, the patient's visual acuity had remained stable, and no other complaints were reported.Hydroxychloroquine is an antimalarial drug commonly used in the treatment of systemic lupus erythematous, rheumatoid arthritis, and other connective tissue disorders. Its toxic effect on the retina is due to its ability to bind melanin in the retinal pigmented epithelium. Early toxicity might be asymptomatic or the patient might complain of colour vision changes and paracentral scotomas. When the classic fundus findings are present, as in our patient, the scotomas might not resolve and the retinal damage might progress despite discontinuation of the drug. The dose (>5·0 mg/kg) and duration of treatment (>5 years), and concomitant renal disease and tamoxifen use are important risk factors for the development of maculopathy.
In 2016, the American Academy of Ophthalmology recommended a baseline fundus examination to be done during the first year of starting the drug and annual screening after 5 years of treatment, using automated visual fields plus spectral domain optical coherence tomography for patients on acceptable doses (ie, <5·0 mg/kg) and without major risk factors. Hence, it is hoped that with proper dosage and regular screening, bull's eye maculopathy will rarely occur.

input:
A woman aged 28 years with systemic lupus erythematous and abnormal kidney function, treated with 4·5 mg/kg hydroxychloroquine daily for 15 years (cumulative dose 1369 g), presented with bilateral progressive central vision loss for 2 months. The patient had no known previous exposure to chloroquine. Best corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in her right eye and 20/30 in her left eye. Funduscopy showed a concentric hypopigmentation around both foveas (figure). Spectral domain optical coherence tomography of the macula revealed photoreceptor layer and retinal pigmented epithelium loss, and automated 24-2 visual fields showed bilateral central scotomas (figure). These findings were consistent with bull's eye maculopathy, a classic feature of advanced hydroxychloroquine toxicity. 3 months after medication was stopped, the patient's visual acuity had remained stable, and no other complaints were reported.Hydroxychloroquine is an antimalarial drug commonly used in the treatment of systemic lupus erythematous, rheumatoid arthritis, and other connective tissue disorders. Its toxic effect on the retina is due to its ability to bind melanin in the retinal pigmented epithelium. Early toxicity might be asymptomatic or the patient might complain of colour vision changes and paracentral scotomas. When the classic fundus findings are present, as in our patient, the scotomas might not resolve and the retinal damage might progress despite discontinuation of the drug. The dose (>5·0 mg/kg) and duration of treatment (>5 years), and concomitant renal disease and tamoxifen use are important risk factors for the development of maculopathy.
In 2016, the American Academy of Ophthalmology recommended a baseline fundus examination to be done during the first year of starting the drug and annual screening after 5 years of treatment, using automated visual fields plus spectral domain optical coherence tomography for patients on acceptable doses (ie, <5·0 mg/kg) and without major risk factors. Hence, it is hoped that with proper dosage and regular screening, bull's eye maculopathy will rarely occur.

A woman aged 28 years with systemic lupus erythematous and abnormal kidney function, treated with 4·5 mg/kg hydroxychloroquine daily for 15 years (cumulative dose 1369 g), presented with bilateral progressive central vision loss for 2 months. The patient had no known previous exposure to chloroquine. Best corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in her right eye and 20/30 in her left eye. Funduscopy showed a concentric hypopigmentation around both foveas (figure). Spectral domain optical coherence tomography of the macula revealed photoreceptor layer and retinal pigmented epithelium loss, and automated 24-2 visual fields showed bilateral central scotomas (figure). These findings were consistent with bull's eye maculopathy, a classic feature of advanced hydroxychloroquine toxicity. 3 months after medication was stopped, the patient's visual acuity had remained stable, and no other complaints were reported.Hydroxychloroquine is an antimalarial drug commonly used in the treatment of systemic lupus erythematous, rheumatoid arthritis, and other connective tissue disorders. Its toxic effect on the retina is due to its ability to bind melanin in the retinal pigmented epithelium. Early toxicity might be asymptomatic or the patient might complain of colour vision changes and paracentral scotomas. When the classic fundus findings are present, as in our patient, the scotomas might not resolve and the retinal damage might progress despite discontinuation of the drug. The dose (>5·0 mg/kg) and duration of treatment (>5 years), and concomitant renal disease and tamoxifen use are important risk factors for the development of maculopathy.
In 2016, the American Academy of Ophthalmology recommended a baseline fundus examination to be done during the first year of starting the drug and annual screening after 5 years of treatment, using automated visual fields plus spectral domain optical coherence tomography for patients on acceptable doses (ie, <5·0 mg/kg) and without major risk factors. Hence, it is hoped that with proper dosage and regular screening, bull's eye maculopathy will rarely occur.

Skin biopsy and radiographic features are helpful in the diagnosis; but negative results do not necessarily exclude the diagnosis. Although the pathogenesis remains unclear, several comorbid conditions are known to increase its development. Associated risk factors in our patient were: end-stage renal disease, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and oral anticoagulation with phenprocoumon. Recent reports indicate that low parathyroid hormone levels in association with adynamic bone diseases can also be associated with calciphylaxis. Unfortunately, there is still no standardised treatment for calciphylaxis. Based on previous reports, phenprocoumon was withdrawn in our patient and he was treated with cinacalcet, daily haemodialysis, sodium thiosulfate, and bisphosphonate. After 4 weeks, skin condition improved and the patient was discharged home.

A 37-year-old man living in northwest Ohio, USA, presented with a cough, haemoptysis, and weight loss, all observed for 2 months. The patient emigrated from Taiwan at the age of 3 years and now works in a parcel warehouse. He had no history of incarceration or travel outside of the USA.Chest x-ray and contrast-enhanced CT (appendix) showed a left upper lobe lesion with associated mediastinal lymphadenopathy. A transbronchial biopsy with mycobacterial and fungal stains and cultures was negative, and histopathology showed non-caseating granulomatous inflammation. A four-drug regimen (daily standard weight-based dosing of rifampicin [600 mg], isoniazid [300 mg], ethambutol [1600 mg], and pyrazinamide [2000 mg]) was started for suspected pulmonary tuberculosis.
After completing 6 months of therapy for tuberculosis, the patient was readmitted to hospital, this time complaining of multiple tender, cutaneous lesions on his face, torso, and extremities; some were verrucous and others nodular (figure). He also had headaches, nausea, and vomiting. Haemogram results showed a white blood cell count of 22 000 cells per μL with 91% segmented neutrophils. An ELISA test for HIV was negative. The chest CT revealed near complete resolution of the lung lesion; however, a CT of the head and neck (appendix) showed numerous white matter ring-enhancing lesions bilaterally in the frontal lobe, parietal lobe, temporal lobe, and cerebellar hemispheres, as well as a retropharyngeal abscess.
Subcutaneous nodules were drained and histopathology showed broad-based, thick-walled budding yeast suggestive of Blastomyces dermatitidis. Urine antigen testing for B dermatitidis was positive, and fungal cultures from surgical specimens grew B dermatitidis after 1 week.
4 weeks of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B at a dose of 5 mg/kg per day, followed by 12 months of oral voriconazole (300 mg twice daily), led to resolution of skin and brain lesions. Voriconazole has become one of the preferred options for oral stepdown when CNS drug penetration is desired. Disseminated cases of blastomycosis should include CNS imaging even in the absence of CNS-related symptoms. Diagnosis might require multiple testing modalities for improved sensitivity.

A 37-year-old man living in northwest Ohio, USA, presented with a cough, haemoptysis, and weight loss, all observed for 2 months. The patient emigrated from Taiwan at the age of 3 years and now works in a parcel warehouse. He had no history of incarceration or travel outside of the USA.Chest x-ray and contrast-enhanced CT (appendix) showed a left upper lobe lesion with associated mediastinal lymphadenopathy. A transbronchial biopsy with mycobacterial and fungal stains and cultures was negative, and histopathology showed non-caseating granulomatous inflammation. A four-drug regimen (daily standard weight-based dosing of rifampicin [600 mg], isoniazid [300 mg], ethambutol [1600 mg], and pyrazinamide [2000 mg]) was started for suspected pulmonary tuberculosis.
After completing 6 months of therapy for tuberculosis, the patient was readmitted to hospital, this time complaining of multiple tender, cutaneous lesions on his face, torso, and extremities; some were verrucous and others nodular (figure). He also had headaches, nausea, and vomiting. Haemogram results showed a white blood cell count of 22 000 cells per μL with 91% segmented neutrophils. An ELISA test for HIV was negative. The chest CT revealed near complete resolution of the lung lesion; however, a CT of the head and neck (appendix) showed numerous white matter ring-enhancing lesions bilaterally in the frontal lobe, parietal lobe, temporal lobe, and cerebellar hemispheres, as well as a retropharyngeal abscess.
Subcutaneous nodules were drained and histopathology showed broad-based, thick-walled budding yeast suggestive of Blastomyces dermatitidis. Urine antigen testing for B dermatitidis was positive, and fungal cultures from surgical specimens grew B dermatitidis after 1 week.
4 weeks of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B at a dose of 5 mg/kg per day, followed by 12 months of oral voriconazole (300 mg twice daily), led to resolution of skin and brain lesions. Voriconazole has become one of the preferred options for oral stepdown when CNS drug penetration is desired. Disseminated cases of blastomycosis should include CNS imaging even in the absence of CNS-related symptoms. Diagnosis might require multiple testing modalities for improved sensitivity.

A 37-year-old man living in northwest Ohio, USA, presented with a cough, haemoptysis, and weight loss, all observed for 2 months. The patient emigrated from Taiwan at the age of 3 years and now works in a parcel warehouse. He had no history of incarceration or travel outside of the USA.Chest x-ray and contrast-enhanced CT (appendix) showed a left upper lobe lesion with associated mediastinal lymphadenopathy. A transbronchial biopsy with mycobacterial and fungal stains and cultures was negative, and histopathology showed non-caseating granulomatous inflammation. A four-drug regimen (daily standard weight-based dosing of rifampicin [600 mg], isoniazid [300 mg], ethambutol [1600 mg], and pyrazinamide [2000 mg]) was started for suspected pulmonary tuberculosis.
After completing 6 months of therapy for tuberculosis, the patient was readmitted to hospital, this time complaining of multiple tender, cutaneous lesions on his face, torso, and extremities; some were verrucous and others nodular (figure). He also had headaches, nausea, and vomiting. Haemogram results showed a white blood cell count of 22 000 cells per μL with 91% segmented neutrophils. An ELISA test for HIV was negative. The chest CT revealed near complete resolution of the lung lesion; however, a CT of the head and neck (appendix) showed numerous white matter ring-enhancing lesions bilaterally in the frontal lobe, parietal lobe, temporal lobe, and cerebellar hemispheres, as well as a retropharyngeal abscess.
Subcutaneous nodules were drained and histopathology showed broad-based, thick-walled budding yeast suggestive of Blastomyces dermatitidis. Urine antigen testing for B dermatitidis was positive, and fungal cultures from surgical specimens grew B dermatitidis after 1 week.
4 weeks of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B at a dose of 5 mg/kg per day, followed by 12 months of oral voriconazole (300 mg twice daily), led to resolution of skin and brain lesions. Voriconazole has become one of the preferred options for oral stepdown when CNS drug penetration is desired. Disseminated cases of blastomycosis should include CNS imaging even in the absence of CNS-related symptoms. Diagnosis might require multiple testing modalities for improved sensitivity.

input: A 28-year-old woman came to our clinic saying she had blurred vision in her right eye. 22 h earlier, she had noticed areas of darkness in the lower half of her right visual field. Her medical history was unremarkable apart from her reporting that she had recurrent tonsillitis as a child. Corrected visual acuity was 20/80 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left. Slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment showed no abnormalities, with normal pupillary reactions. However, slit lamp biomicroscopy and fundus examination in the right eye showed intra-retinal oedema with retinal whitening in the superior area (figure). Fluorescein angiography showed an arterial filling defect along the superotemporal arcade (figure). A diagnosis of right eye superotemporal branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) was made. A cardiology review was sought as part of the mandatory systemic investigations required in such cases. Our cardiology colleagues reported that the patient's electrocardiogram was normal but that her echocardiogram showed moderate mitral stenosis. An analysis of her urine found no abnormalities. Her fasting blood glucose, blood cholesterol, and serum triglyceride concentrations were normal, and a full blood count showed values within the normal range. Also, both her erythrocyte sedimentation rate and serum C-reactive protein concentration were normal. The patient was treated with acetyl salicylate 75 mg once a day and spironolactone 25 mg once a day. She was seen again 12 months later, and her visual fields had improved and she had no further problems.The incidence of retinal arterial obstruction in patients under the age of 30 years has been estimated at less than one in 50 000 outpatients. The causes of retinal arterial occlusion in young adults—different from those in older individuals—include systemic vasculitis, migraine, sickle-cell haemoglobinopathy, myeloproliferative disorders, hypercoagulable states, use of oral contraceptives, and intravenous drug abuse. Valvular heart disease—originating from rheumatic fever—remains an important cause of BRAO that should be borne in mind, although rates are declining in developed countries.

input: A 28-year-old woman came to our clinic saying she had blurred vision in her right eye. 22 h earlier, she had noticed areas of darkness in the lower half of her right visual field. Her medical history was unremarkable apart from her reporting that she had recurrent tonsillitis as a child. Corrected visual acuity was 20/80 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left. Slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment showed no abnormalities, with normal pupillary reactions. However, slit lamp biomicroscopy and fundus examination in the right eye showed intra-retinal oedema with retinal whitening in the superior area (figure). Fluorescein angiography showed an arterial filling defect along the superotemporal arcade (figure). A diagnosis of right eye superotemporal branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) was made. A cardiology review was sought as part of the mandatory systemic investigations required in such cases. Our cardiology colleagues reported that the patient's electrocardiogram was normal but that her echocardiogram showed moderate mitral stenosis. An analysis of her urine found no abnormalities. Her fasting blood glucose, blood cholesterol, and serum triglyceride concentrations were normal, and a full blood count showed values within the normal range. Also, both her erythrocyte sedimentation rate and serum C-reactive protein concentration were normal. The patient was treated with acetyl salicylate 75 mg once a day and spironolactone 25 mg once a day. She was seen again 12 months later, and her visual fields had improved and she had no further problems.The incidence of retinal arterial obstruction in patients under the age of 30 years has been estimated at less than one in 50 000 outpatients. The causes of retinal arterial occlusion in young adults—different from those in older individuals—include systemic vasculitis, migraine, sickle-cell haemoglobinopathy, myeloproliferative disorders, hypercoagulable states, use of oral contraceptives, and intravenous drug abuse. Valvular heart disease—originating from rheumatic fever—remains an important cause of BRAO that should be borne in mind, although rates are declining in developed countries.

A 77-year-old man presented to our neurology clinic reporting short episodes of unsteadiness followed by loss of consciousness brought on by standing from a sitting position. The problem had been present for 2 weeks and had led to frequent falls. He had a history of hypertension—treated with amlodipine, atenolol, and perindopril—and hypercholesterolaemia—treated with ezetimibe. He was a non-smoker.A neurological examination was unremarkable. A working diagnosis of orthostatic hypotension was made, and the perindopril was stopped.
3 days later, the patient returned, reporting difficulties speaking and more severe gait problems. On examination, he was mildly dysarthric, with a broad-based gait, and impaired tandem walking.
A CT scan showed subacute ischaemia in the left cerebellar hemisphere. We diagnosed a cerebellar infarction and started the patient on aspirin.
Diffusion-weighted MRI showed ischaemic foci in both cerebellar hemispheres (figure) and the right occipital lobe; there was contrast enhancement of the vessels walls of both vertebral arteries, where MR angiography also demonstrated luminal narrowing (figure; appendix). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 23mm/h and the serum C-reactive protein concentration was 8 mg/L; all specific autoantibody tests were negative.
A duplex ultrasound of the vertebral arteries showed luminal narrowing with elevated flow velocities of >300 cm/s (normal <75) and longitudinal, hypoechogenic vessel wall thickening. Axial imaging showed a concentric, hypoechogenic signal—the so-called halo sign—in the vertebral artery (figure). Ultrasonography of the right temporal artery also showed a bilateral halo sign (appendix).
Upon discussion of the results with the patient, he reported that he had previously experienced jaw claudication and tenderness over the temporal artery 2 years earlier; at the time he had been treated with prednisone.
A biopsy of the right temporal artery established a diagnosis of giant-cell arteritis (GCA; appendix). Corticosteroid therapy was started, and 1 week later the patient reported improvement of his symptoms.
GCA can present in a wide variety of ways; the typical symptoms are headache, claudication of the jaw and tongue, loss of vision in one eye, fever, myalgia, weight loss, anorexia, and fatigue. Rarely, GCA presents with symptoms of a posterior circulation stroke because of vertebral artery involvement. Distinguishing GCA from other vessel wall abnormalities on duplex ultrasound is key: atherosclerosis or dissection—which can be similarly hypoechogenic—are usually eccentric rather than concentric. As vertebral artery imaging is routine in the evaluation of large vessel disease after a stroke, recognition of the halo sign—even in the absence of systemic inflammatory markers—should raise the suspicion of GCA (video).

A 77-year-old man presented to our neurology clinic reporting short episodes of unsteadiness followed by loss of consciousness brought on by standing from a sitting position. The problem had been present for 2 weeks and had led to frequent falls. He had a history of hypertension—treated with amlodipine, atenolol, and perindopril—and hypercholesterolaemia—treated with ezetimibe. He was a non-smoker.A neurological examination was unremarkable. A working diagnosis of orthostatic hypotension was made, and the perindopril was stopped.
3 days later, the patient returned, reporting difficulties speaking and more severe gait problems. On examination, he was mildly dysarthric, with a broad-based gait, and impaired tandem walking.
A CT scan showed subacute ischaemia in the left cerebellar hemisphere. We diagnosed a cerebellar infarction and started the patient on aspirin.
Diffusion-weighted MRI showed ischaemic foci in both cerebellar hemispheres (figure) and the right occipital lobe; there was contrast enhancement of the vessels walls of both vertebral arteries, where MR angiography also demonstrated luminal narrowing (figure; appendix). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 23mm/h and the serum C-reactive protein concentration was 8 mg/L; all specific autoantibody tests were negative.
A duplex ultrasound of the vertebral arteries showed luminal narrowing with elevated flow velocities of >300 cm/s (normal <75) and longitudinal, hypoechogenic vessel wall thickening. Axial imaging showed a concentric, hypoechogenic signal—the so-called halo sign—in the vertebral artery (figure). Ultrasonography of the right temporal artery also showed a bilateral halo sign (appendix).
Upon discussion of the results with the patient, he reported that he had previously experienced jaw claudication and tenderness over the temporal artery 2 years earlier; at the time he had been treated with prednisone.
A biopsy of the right temporal artery established a diagnosis of giant-cell arteritis (GCA; appendix). Corticosteroid therapy was started, and 1 week later the patient reported improvement of his symptoms.
GCA can present in a wide variety of ways; the typical symptoms are headache, claudication of the jaw and tongue, loss of vision in one eye, fever, myalgia, weight loss, anorexia, and fatigue. Rarely, GCA presents with symptoms of a posterior circulation stroke because of vertebral artery involvement. Distinguishing GCA from other vessel wall abnormalities on duplex ultrasound is key: atherosclerosis or dissection—which can be similarly hypoechogenic—are usually eccentric rather than concentric. As vertebral artery imaging is routine in the evaluation of large vessel disease after a stroke, recognition of the halo sign—even in the absence of systemic inflammatory markers—should raise the suspicion of GCA (video).

input:
A 77-year-old man presented to our neurology clinic reporting short episodes of unsteadiness followed by loss of consciousness brought on by standing from a sitting position. The problem had been present for 2 weeks and had led to frequent falls. He had a history of hypertension—treated with amlodipine, atenolol, and perindopril—and hypercholesterolaemia—treated with ezetimibe. He was a non-smoker.A neurological examination was unremarkable. A working diagnosis of orthostatic hypotension was made, and the perindopril was stopped.
3 days later, the patient returned, reporting difficulties speaking and more severe gait problems. On examination, he was mildly dysarthric, with a broad-based gait, and impaired tandem walking.
A CT scan showed subacute ischaemia in the left cerebellar hemisphere. We diagnosed a cerebellar infarction and started the patient on aspirin.
Diffusion-weighted MRI showed ischaemic foci in both cerebellar hemispheres (figure) and the right occipital lobe; there was contrast enhancement of the vessels walls of both vertebral arteries, where MR angiography also demonstrated luminal narrowing (figure; appendix). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 23mm/h and the serum C-reactive protein concentration was 8 mg/L; all specific autoantibody tests were negative.
A duplex ultrasound of the vertebral arteries showed luminal narrowing with elevated flow velocities of >300 cm/s (normal <75) and longitudinal, hypoechogenic vessel wall thickening. Axial imaging showed a concentric, hypoechogenic signal—the so-called halo sign—in the vertebral artery (figure). Ultrasonography of the right temporal artery also showed a bilateral halo sign (appendix).
Upon discussion of the results with the patient, he reported that he had previously experienced jaw claudication and tenderness over the temporal artery 2 years earlier; at the time he had been treated with prednisone.
A biopsy of the right temporal artery established a diagnosis of giant-cell arteritis (GCA; appendix). Corticosteroid therapy was started, and 1 week later the patient reported improvement of his symptoms.
GCA can present in a wide variety of ways; the typical symptoms are headache, claudication of the jaw and tongue, loss of vision in one eye, fever, myalgia, weight loss, anorexia, and fatigue. Rarely, GCA presents with symptoms of a posterior circulation stroke because of vertebral artery involvement. Distinguishing GCA from other vessel wall abnormalities on duplex ultrasound is key: atherosclerosis or dissection—which can be similarly hypoechogenic—are usually eccentric rather than concentric. As vertebral artery imaging is routine in the evaluation of large vessel disease after a stroke, recognition of the halo sign—even in the absence of systemic inflammatory markers—should raise the suspicion of GCA (video).

A 21-year-old man presented to the Lausanne University Hospital (CHUV) in August, 2020, with reddened skin lesions on the forehead and upper torso, clinically suggestive of skin lymphoma. Skin biopsy, bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy, and PET-CT with 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) subsequently led to a diagnosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, of mature T-cell phenotype, with skin infiltration. After diagnosis, the patient was enrolled in the GRAAL-2014/T clinical trial (NCT02619630).The patient also had type 1 diabetes and was on insulin-pump therapy. He had interrupted his insulin infusion (basal and bolus) for 48 h because of frequent hypoglycaemia. Initial laboratory values showed glucose of 6·5 mmol/L (117 mg/dL), metabolic acidosis (pH 7·28, lactate 11·8 mmol/L, bicarbonate 15 mmol/L), and high concentrations of ketones bodies, consistent with euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis.
PET scan images (figure) showed both entities: intense 18F-FDG uptake in the acute lymphoblastic leukaemia-infiltrated scalp (maximum standardised uptake value [SUV] 15·2), and reduced brain 18F-FDG uptake (SUV 4·7) indicative of ketone body metabolism. Intravenous insulin with glucose, fluid, and electrolyte replacement, led to the resolution of diabetic ketoacidosis within 48 h; lactatemia fully normalised with chemotherapy (oral prednisone [60 mg/m2 per day on days 1–14]; intravenous vincristine [2 mg per day on days 1, 8, 15, and 22]; intravenous daunorubicin [50 mg/m2 per day on days 1–3 and 30 mg/m2 per day on days 15 and 16]; intravenous cyclophosphamide [750mg/m2 per day on days 1 and 15]; and intravenous L-asparaginase [6000 UI/m2 per day on days 8, 10, 12, 20, 22, 24, 26, and 28]). PET scan obtained after the first induction (appendix) showed haematological remission (confirmed by marrow examination) and restored brain glucose metabolism.
Causes of euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis involve processes that impair hepatic glycogen storage or cause glucose consumption or wasting, such as sodium-glucose-transporter-2 inhibitor induced glycosuria or foetal glucose consumption in late-term pregnancy. To our knowledge, this is the first report of euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis caused by high glucose uptake in aggressive neoplasia. Tumour aerobic glycolysis (Warburg effect), further contributed to metabolic acidosis through lactate release.
With mild symptoms and normal glucose concentration, euglycaemic ketoacidosis might be overlooked. Euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis can accompany high-grade haematological malignancy, where 18F-FDG PET shows both diagnoses. Haemato-oncologists should be aware of this presentation in diabetic patients to expedite diagnosis and avoid detrimental delay in management.

Skin biopsy, bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy, and PET-CT with 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) subsequently led to a diagnosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, of mature T-cell phenotype, with skin infiltration. After diagnosis, the patient was enrolled in the GRAAL-2014/T clinical trial (NCT02619630).The patient also had type 1 diabetes and was on insulin-pump therapy. He had interrupted his insulin infusion (basal and bolus) for 48 h because of frequent hypoglycaemia. Initial laboratory values showed glucose of 6·5 mmol/L (117 mg/dL), metabolic acidosis (pH 7·28, lactate 11·8 mmol/L, bicarbonate 15 mmol/L), and high concentrations of ketones bodies, consistent with euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis.
PET scan images (figure) showed both entities: intense 18F-FDG uptake in the acute lymphoblastic leukaemia-infiltrated scalp (maximum standardised uptake value [SUV] 15·2), and reduced brain 18F-FDG uptake (SUV 4·7) indicative of ketone body metabolism. PET scan obtained after the first induction (appendix) showed haematological remission (confirmed by marrow examination) and restored brain glucose metabolism.
Causes of euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis involve processes that impair hepatic glycogen storage or cause glucose consumption or wasting, such as sodium-glucose-transporter-2 inhibitor induced glycosuria or foetal glucose consumption in late-term pregnancy. To our knowledge, this is the first report of euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis caused by high glucose uptake in aggressive neoplasia. Tumour aerobic glycolysis (Warburg effect), further contributed to metabolic acidosis through lactate release.
With mild symptoms and normal glucose concentration, euglycaemic ketoacidosis might be overlooked. Euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis can accompany high-grade haematological malignancy, where 18F-FDG PET shows both diagnoses. Haemato-oncologists should be aware of this presentation in diabetic patients to expedite diagnosis and avoid detrimental delay in management.

input: A 39-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 2-month history of painful nodules in his umbilicus. He had been diagnosed with gastric ring cell carcinoma of the stomach with extensive metastasis 9 months earlier. An ill-defined, firm, indurated plaque, with multiple nodules in and around the umbilicus (figure), was found on examination. A skin biopsy sample showed extensive infiltration of the dermis by signet ring cells (figure). A diagnosis of Sister Mary Joseph's nodule was made: the lesion in the umbilicus was caused by metastases from the gastric carcinoma. A CT scan of his abdomen showed thickening of the gastric wall and a mass forming posteriorly (figure). He was given intravenous chemotherapy every 2 weeks: fluorouracil 2400 mg/m2, oxaliplatin 70 mg/m2, and docetaxel 50 mg/m2, for eight cycles. He was then given one cycle of the combined oral treatment, 25 mg/m2 twice a day, of tegafur, gimeracil, and oteracil for 28 consecutive days; this was followed by 14 days of rest. However, the primary tumour remained unchanged. The patient decided not to continue with chemotherapy and died of multiorgan metastasis 4 months later.Sister Mary Joseph's nodule—a condition generally associated with a poor prognosis—refers to the umbilical metastasis of an abdominal malignancy. Stomach and colon cancers are the most common sources of the condition in men, and in women the ovaries are most frequently the origin. In up to 30% of cases, the umbilical nodule may be the first and only sign of an advanced intra-abdominal malignancy. Clearly, many other diseases can present with umbilical lesions—including hernias, endometriosis, urachal duct cysts, abscesses, pyogenic granuloma, lymphangioma, and epidermoid cysts. The English surgeon Sir Hamilton Bailey named the sinister malignant manifestation after Sister Mary Joseph (1856–1939), a nurse at St Mary's Hospital in Rochester, MN, USA, who noted the association between periumbilical nodules and intra-abdominal cancer.

input: A 39-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 2-month history of painful nodules in his umbilicus. He had been diagnosed with gastric ring cell carcinoma of the stomach with extensive metastasis 9 months earlier. An ill-defined, firm, indurated plaque, with multiple nodules in and around the umbilicus (figure), was found on examination. A skin biopsy sample showed extensive infiltration of the dermis by signet ring cells (figure). A diagnosis of Sister Mary Joseph's nodule was made: the lesion in the umbilicus was caused by metastases from the gastric carcinoma. A CT scan of his abdomen showed thickening of the gastric wall and a mass forming posteriorly (figure). He was given intravenous chemotherapy every 2 weeks: fluorouracil 2400 mg/m2, oxaliplatin 70 mg/m2, and docetaxel 50 mg/m2, for eight cycles. He was then given one cycle of the combined oral treatment, 25 mg/m2 twice a day, of tegafur, gimeracil, and oteracil for 28 consecutive days; this was followed by 14 days of rest. However, the primary tumour remained unchanged. The patient decided not to continue with chemotherapy and died of multiorgan metastasis 4 months later.Sister Mary Joseph's nodule—a condition generally associated with a poor prognosis—refers to the umbilical metastasis of an abdominal malignancy. Stomach and colon cancers are the most common sources of the condition in men, and in women the ovaries are most frequently the origin. In up to 30% of cases, the umbilical nodule may be the first and only sign of an advanced intra-abdominal malignancy. Clearly, many other diseases can present with umbilical lesions—including hernias, endometriosis, urachal duct cysts, abscesses, pyogenic granuloma, lymphangioma, and epidermoid cysts. The English surgeon Sir Hamilton Bailey named the sinister malignant manifestation after Sister Mary Joseph (1856–1939), a nurse at St Mary's Hospital in Rochester, MN, USA, who noted the association between periumbilical nodules and intra-abdominal cancer.

input: A 39-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 2-month history of painful nodules in his umbilicus. He had been diagnosed with gastric ring cell carcinoma of the stomach with extensive metastasis 9 months earlier. An ill-defined, firm, indurated plaque, with multiple nodules in and around the umbilicus (figure), was found on examination. A skin biopsy sample showed extensive infiltration of the dermis by signet ring cells (figure). A diagnosis of Sister Mary Joseph's nodule was made: the lesion in the umbilicus was caused by metastases from the gastric carcinoma. A CT scan of his abdomen showed thickening of the gastric wall and a mass forming posteriorly (figure). He was given intravenous chemotherapy every 2 weeks: fluorouracil 2400 mg/m2, oxaliplatin 70 mg/m2, and docetaxel 50 mg/m2, for eight cycles. He was then given one cycle of the combined oral treatment, 25 mg/m2 twice a day, of tegafur, gimeracil, and oteracil for 28 consecutive days; this was followed by 14 days of rest. However, the primary tumour remained unchanged. The patient decided not to continue with chemotherapy and died of multiorgan metastasis 4 months later.Sister Mary Joseph's nodule—a condition generally associated with a poor prognosis—refers to the umbilical metastasis of an abdominal malignancy. Stomach and colon cancers are the most common sources of the condition in men, and in women the ovaries are most frequently the origin. In up to 30% of cases, the umbilical nodule may be the first and only sign of an advanced intra-abdominal malignancy. Clearly, many other diseases can present with umbilical lesions—including hernias, endometriosis, urachal duct cysts, abscesses, pyogenic granuloma, lymphangioma, and epidermoid cysts. The English surgeon Sir Hamilton Bailey named the sinister malignant manifestation after Sister Mary Joseph (1856–1939), a nurse at St Mary's Hospital in Rochester, MN, USA, who noted the association between periumbilical nodules and intra-abdominal cancer.

input: A 76-year-old woman was referred to University Medical Center Utrecht (Utrecht, Netherlands) in August, 2016, for surgical resection of a tumour of the appendix (figure, A). CT scan showed homogeneous enhancing mass at the tip of the appendix, and because of the location and arterial enhancement, the lesion was thought to be a neuroendocrine tumour. To rule out metastases before surgery, a 68Ga-HA-DOTATATE PET–CT scan was done, showing intense tracer accumulation in the suspected lesion (maximum standardised uptake value of 29·8; figure, B) without any signs of metastases. After laparoscopic surgical resection, histopathological examination showed a sharply demarcated tumour composed of spindle cells with elongated nuclei without overt atypia and low mitotic and proliferative activity (Ki-67-positive cells <2%; figure, C). DNA sequencing showed a mutation in exon 11 of KIT proto-oncogene receptor tyrosine kinase (KIT; Gln575_Leu576delinsHis) and the tumour was strongly positive for c-KIT and anoctamin-1 consistent with criteria for gastrointestinal stromal tumour. Because of the positive PET scan, somatostatin receptor type 2 (SSTR2A) immunohistochemistry was done, which showed strong positivity for SSTR2A in the tumour (figure, D). Surgery was completed without any complications and the patient recovered quickly. Follow-up imaging will be done in March, 2017, in accordance with our national guideline for low-risk gastrointestinal stromal tumour.High expression of somatostatin receptors can be found in up to 81·9% (receptor subtype one) and 87·6% (subtype two) of gastrointestinal stromal tumours, and is therefore a much more reliable marker than immunohistochemical evidence of neuroendocrine differentiation, which might be seen in about 15% of tumours. Several gastrointestinal stromal tumours have also shown high uptake in 111In-pentetreotide scintigraphy. However, to our knowledge, no case of gastrointestinal stromal tumour detected by 68Ga-HA-DOTATATE has been described before. In malignant or high-grade gastrointestinal stromal tumours, 18fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET–CT is useful for detection, therapy response monitoring, and prognostication, but has little value in gastrointestinal stromal tumours with a low proliferative index. Somatostatin receptor-targeted PET–CT might be a valuable extension of the diagnostic repertoire and could also be used to select patients with metastasis for peptide receptor radionuclide therapy when no further surgical or chemotherapeutic options are available.

input:
A 2-month-old infant with a 1-month history of a generalised persistent blistering rash (figure) and a 4-day history of vomiting and poor oral intake attended our hospital with her mother.
Notably, the patient's mother had a standard prenatal infectious diseases screening test, done 3 months into the pregnancy, in Japan; the test—for hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, human T-cell leukaemia virus type-1, and HIV—was negative. Specifically, both a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test and a Treponema pallidum latex assay (TPLA) test were negative. During the pregnancy, the mother had regular antenatal check-ups and as no abnormalities were noted, no additional tests were done.
On examination, the infant was generally unwell; she had a macular, bullous rash on her arms, hands, legs, and abdomen—the lesions were worse peripherally. Body temperature was 36·7°C, blood pressure was 102/51 mm Hg, heart rate was 155 beats per min, and oxygen saturation was 99% on room air; she had hepatosplenomegaly.
Laboratory investigations showed anaemia (haemoglobin concentration was 8·5 g/dL; typical range 9·0–13·5), thrombocytopaenia (platelet count was 11·3 × 104 per μL; typical rang 27·0–88·0), elevated liver enzyme levels (aspartate transaminase concentration 146 U/L [typical range 21–64]; alanine transaminase concentration 170 U/L [typical range 12–50]), and hypoalbuminaemia (albumin concentration 1·9 g/dL; typical range 3·1–4·3).
X-rays showed periosteal thickening of the long-bones periosteal thickening (figure).
Importantly, both mother and child were positive on RPR and TPLA tests—confirming a diagnosis of congenital syphilis in the infant. Furthermore, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, which showed three white blood cells (typical range zero to five), was negative on RPR test. Ophthalmological and auditory examinations showed no atypical findings.
The infant was treated with parenteral crystalline penicillin but developed respiratory failure and metabolic acidosis because of a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction; she was admitted to our intensive care unit where her condition gradually improved, and she completed a 10-day course of antibiotic therapy. The rash improved (figure), and the infant showed no developmental problems. Repeat x-rays, 2 months after admission, showed ossification of the thickened areas of the long bones (figure).
Following the global resurgence in syphilis, Japan implemented a programme to increase rates of prenatal care attendance and screening for the disease. However, pregnant women may contract syphilis after the initial screening necessitating additional prenatal follow-up—including supplementary and repeat screening tests. Newborns may also require testing at the time of birth.

A 2-month-old infant with a 1-month history of a generalised persistent blistering rash (figure) and a 4-day history of vomiting and poor oral intake attended our hospital with her mother.
Notably, the patient's mother had a standard prenatal infectious diseases screening test, done 3 months into the pregnancy, in Japan; the test—for hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, human T-cell leukaemia virus type-1, and HIV—was negative. Specifically, both a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test and a Treponema pallidum latex assay (TPLA) test were negative. During the pregnancy, the mother had regular antenatal check-ups and as no abnormalities were noted, no additional tests were done.
On examination, the infant was generally unwell; she had a macular, bullous rash on her arms, hands, legs, and abdomen—the lesions were worse peripherally. Body temperature was 36·7°C, blood pressure was 102/51 mm Hg, heart rate was 155 beats per min, and oxygen saturation was 99% on room air; she had hepatosplenomegaly.
Laboratory investigations showed anaemia (haemoglobin concentration was 8·5 g/dL; typical range 9·0–13·5), thrombocytopaenia (platelet count was 11·3 × 104 per μL; typical rang 27·0–88·0), elevated liver enzyme levels (aspartate transaminase concentration 146 U/L [typical range 21–64]; alanine transaminase concentration 170 U/L [typical range 12–50]), and hypoalbuminaemia (albumin concentration 1·9 g/dL; typical range 3·1–4·3).
X-rays showed periosteal thickening of the long-bones periosteal thickening (figure).
Importantly, both mother and child were positive on RPR and TPLA tests—confirming a diagnosis of congenital syphilis in the infant. Furthermore, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, which showed three white blood cells (typical range zero to five), was negative on RPR test. Ophthalmological and auditory examinations showed no atypical findings.
The infant was treated with parenteral crystalline penicillin but developed respiratory failure and metabolic acidosis because of a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction; she was admitted to our intensive care unit where her condition gradually improved, and she completed a 10-day course of antibiotic therapy. The rash improved (figure), and the infant showed no developmental problems. Repeat x-rays, 2 months after admission, showed ossification of the thickened areas of the long bones (figure).
Following the global resurgence in syphilis, Japan implemented a programme to increase rates of prenatal care attendance and screening for the disease. However, pregnant women may contract syphilis after the initial screening necessitating additional prenatal follow-up—including supplementary and repeat screening tests. Newborns may also require testing at the time of birth.

A 58-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 10-h history of acute lower abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The patient was otherwise healthy with no significant medical history.On examination, she had generalised, mild abdominal tenderness especially in the left lower quadrant where there was guarding and rebound tenderness; her vital signs were normal—blood pressure 127/66 mm Hg, temperature 37·3 oC, heart rate of 59 beats per min, and respiratory rate was 12 breaths per min.
Blood tests showed elevated white blood cell count of 12·4 × 109 per mL and serum C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration of 22 mg/L. An abdominal CT confirmed a diagnosis of acute left-sided colonic diverticulitis and showed intraperitoneal free air.
We decided to manage the case conservatively, and gave the patient intravenous piperacillin and tazobactam (4 g and 0·5 g) three times a day; she was also allowed a light diet. After an initial increase in serum CRP concentration, there followed a decline: 22 mg/L to 190 mg/L to 300 mg/L to 250 mg/L to 180 mg/L; the decrease was accompanied by an improvement in the patient's clinical state. She was allowed home after 5 days in the hospital and the intravenous antibiotics were switched to oral; she went on to make an event-free recovery. At routine colonoscopy, 3 months later, there were no signs of malignancy.
Left-sided colonic diverticulosis is common in western countries. The lifetime risk for acute diverticulitis is approximately 5–25% in patients with diverticulosis. CT has become the gold standard method of diagnosing diverticulitis and its complications; distant free air is a radiological sign of a free perforation.
Acute uncomplicated diverticulitis has a mild natural course and is usually managed without antibiotics. In cases of sepsis, immunosuppression, or CT-proven complications—the presence of abscesses or extraluminal air—antibiotics are indicated. Perforation with generalised peritonitis—as seen in our case—is associated with high morbidity and mortality—and traditionally, free air alone was an indication for laparotomy with resection of the affected colon segment and end-colostomy. However, in recent years, the trend has been towards a more conservative approach; the latest evidence shows that such a move has resulted in fewer patients requiring a stoma. Further, many immunocompetent, haemodynamically stable patients with acute perforated diverticulitis and extraluminal air can be treated conservatively especially if there is only pericolic air. Immediate surgery is indicated in septic patients and if there are clinical signs of generalised peritonitis or treatment failure. Laparoscopic peritoneal lavage without resection is safe in selected patients with purulent peritonitis; alternatively, resection is recommended—and, depending on the patient's condition, a primary anastomosis or an end colostomy should be performed (video).

A 58-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 10-h history of acute lower abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The patient was otherwise healthy with no significant medical history.On examination, she had generalised, mild abdominal tenderness especially in the left lower quadrant where there was guarding and rebound tenderness; her vital signs were normal—blood pressure 127/66 mm Hg, temperature 37·3 oC, heart rate of 59 beats per min, and respiratory rate was 12 breaths per min.
Blood tests showed elevated white blood cell count of 12·4 × 109 per mL and serum C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration of 22 mg/L. An abdominal CT confirmed a diagnosis of acute left-sided colonic diverticulitis and showed intraperitoneal free air.
We decided to manage the case conservatively, and gave the patient intravenous piperacillin and tazobactam (4 g and 0·5 g) three times a day; she was also allowed a light diet. After an initial increase in serum CRP concentration, there followed a decline: 22 mg/L to 190 mg/L to 300 mg/L to 250 mg/L to 180 mg/L; the decrease was accompanied by an improvement in the patient's clinical state. She was allowed home after 5 days in the hospital and the intravenous antibiotics were switched to oral; she went on to make an event-free recovery. At routine colonoscopy, 3 months later, there were no signs of malignancy.
Left-sided colonic diverticulosis is common in western countries. The lifetime risk for acute diverticulitis is approximately 5–25% in patients with diverticulosis. CT has become the gold standard method of diagnosing diverticulitis and its complications; distant free air is a radiological sign of a free perforation.
Acute uncomplicated diverticulitis has a mild natural course and is usually managed without antibiotics. In cases of sepsis, immunosuppression, or CT-proven complications—the presence of abscesses or extraluminal air—antibiotics are indicated. Perforation with generalised peritonitis—as seen in our case—is associated with high morbidity and mortality—and traditionally, free air alone was an indication for laparotomy with resection of the affected colon segment and end-colostomy. However, in recent years, the trend has been towards a more conservative approach; the latest evidence shows that such a move has resulted in fewer patients requiring a stoma. Further, many immunocompetent, haemodynamically stable patients with acute perforated diverticulitis and extraluminal air can be treated conservatively especially if there is only pericolic air. Immediate surgery is indicated in septic patients and if there are clinical signs of generalised peritonitis or treatment failure. Laparoscopic peritoneal lavage without resection is safe in selected patients with purulent peritonitis; alternatively, resection is recommended—and, depending on the patient's condition, a primary anastomosis or an end colostomy should be performed (video).
