A 58-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 10-h history of acute lower abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The patient was otherwise healthy with no significant medical history.On examination, she had generalised, mild abdominal tenderness especially in the left lower quadrant where there was guarding and rebound tenderness; her vital signs were normal—blood pressure 127/66 mm Hg, temperature 37·3 oC, heart rate of 59 beats per min, and respiratory rate was 12 breaths per min.
Blood tests showed elevated white blood cell count of 12·4 × 109 per mL and serum C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration of 22 mg/L. An abdominal CT confirmed a diagnosis of acute left-sided colonic diverticulitis and showed intraperitoneal free air.
We decided to manage the case conservatively, and gave the patient intravenous piperacillin and tazobactam (4 g and 0·5 g) three times a day; she was also allowed a light diet. After an initial increase in serum CRP concentration, there followed a decline: 22 mg/L to 190 mg/L to 300 mg/L to 250 mg/L to 180 mg/L; the decrease was accompanied by an improvement in the patient's clinical state. She was allowed home after 5 days in the hospital and the intravenous antibiotics were switched to oral; she went on to make an event-free recovery. At routine colonoscopy, 3 months later, there were no signs of malignancy.
Left-sided colonic diverticulosis is common in western countries. The lifetime risk for acute diverticulitis is approximately 5–25% in patients with diverticulosis. CT has become the gold standard method of diagnosing diverticulitis and its complications; distant free air is a radiological sign of a free perforation.
Acute uncomplicated diverticulitis has a mild natural course and is usually managed without antibiotics. In cases of sepsis, immunosuppression, or CT-proven complications—the presence of abscesses or extraluminal air—antibiotics are indicated. Perforation with generalised peritonitis—as seen in our case—is associated with high morbidity and mortality—and traditionally, free air alone was an indication for laparotomy with resection of the affected colon segment and end-colostomy. However, in recent years, the trend has been towards a more conservative approach; the latest evidence shows that such a move has resulted in fewer patients requiring a stoma. Further, many immunocompetent, haemodynamically stable patients with acute perforated diverticulitis and extraluminal air can be treated conservatively especially if there is only pericolic air. Immediate surgery is indicated in septic patients and if there are clinical signs of generalised peritonitis or treatment failure. Laparoscopic peritoneal lavage without resection is safe in selected patients with purulent peritonitis; alternatively, resection is recommended—and, depending on the patient's condition, a primary anastomosis or an end colostomy should be performed (video).

A 32-year-old man presented to our dermatology clinic with a 5-year history of increasing skin folds on his scalp, excessive sweating, joint pain, and development of a deep voice. The patient's medical history was significant for acne keloidalis nuchae which had been treated with antibiotics, isotretinoin, and surgical excision with primary closure of the residual lesions, one year before we saw him.On examination, we found the patient to be generally well; he had thickening of the skin on his scalp with prominent ridges and furrows (figure). He had coarse facial features (figure), acanthosis nigricans of the skin in his neck, axillae, and knuckles. Notably, his feet, hands, and tongue were enlarged. We found no other abnormal signs, and on further questioning, he reported no headaches, seizures, or visual disturbances.
We made a working diagnosis of cutis verticis gyrate (CVG) due to acromegaly.
Laboratory investigations found a raised insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) concentration of 634 μg/L (normal 64–243), a raised growth hormone (GH) concentration of 9·4 μg/L (normal <3), unsuppressed post-glucose GH of 8·92 ng/mL (normal <1), free thyroxine of 1·44 ng/dL (normal 0·93–1·7), thyroid-stimulating-hormone 1·44 μUI/mL (normal 0·27–4·2), HbA1c 5·8% (normal <5·6), and glucose of 110 mg/dL (normal <100).
MRI of the patient's head showed a pituitary macroadenoma measuring 14 mm × 13 mm × 13 mm (figure)—establishing the diagnosis of acromegaly.
The patient was referred to our surgical department and had a transsphenoidal resection of the tumour. After surgery, a repeat MRI showed no residual tumour. At follow-up 3 months later, the patient reported improvement of the hyperhidrosis, amelioration of the joint pain, and decreased macroglossia; IGF1 and GH levels were normal.
Acromegaly commonly presents with facial and acral dysmorphic features; other features include a headache, fatigue, and hyperhidrosis. Hypertension occurs in 20–50% of people with the condition. CVG refers to the thickening of the skin on the scalp creating furrows and ridges; it may present as an isolated finding or secondary to conditions such as pachydermoperiostosis, cerebriform intradermal nevus, Noonan syndrome, myxoedema, or—as in our patient—acromegaly. CVG is observed in 14–30% of patients with acromegaly and can be the first clinical manifestation. Pathogenesis of CVG in acromegaly is thought, acting through GH and IGF1, mainly over dermal fibroblasts, to increase deposition of glycosaminoglycans by mesenchymal cells, which produces skin changes. Improvement of CVG after a surgical intervention or medication for acromegaly supports this hypothesis.
Patients presenting with CVG require a full investigation since it may be the superficial clue to a serious systemic disease like acromegaly.

An 80-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 4-day history of a throbbing pain in the front part of his head that was not relieved by analgesics. The pain had developed gradually and was not associated with any weakness in his arms or legs, numbness or visual symptoms. His medical history included a diagnosis of an intracranial epidermoid cyst, hypertension, and depression. A full clinical neurological examination showed no abnormalities. A CT scan of his head (appendix) showed no additional changes to those seen in a CT scan and an MRI (figure and appendix) done 4 months earlier; at the time when the epidermoid cyst was first found, it was a 9 cm × 7·5 cm mass in the left parietal region, thinning and scalloping of the skull vault, and a slight midline shift to the right. No acute bleeds or infarcts were found. The patient was told his symptoms were due to the epidermoid cyst. At the time the cyst was first diagnosed, it was jointly decided by the patient and us to avoid any surgical interventions because epidermoid cysts are usually slow growing, benign, and asymptomatic.In such cases it is important to differentiate an epidermoid cyst from a dermoid cyst: the CT scans in this case showed a lesion of low density, which might have been fat—typically associated with dermoid cysts. An MRI with the appropriate enhancement was needed to differentiate the two. T1-weighted MRI showed strands of high signal in the lesion, which could also have represented fat (figure). However, the diffusion-weighted MRI (figure inset), which showed restricted diffusion, confirmed the diagnosis.
Furthermore, these striking images—in a patient with no neurological signs—show how a large lesion can be accommodated by a relatively atrophic brain with increased cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) filled spaces and the clinical relevance of the Monro–Kellie doctrine. Normal intracranial pressure is maintained in the presence of an expanding intracranial mass—firstly, as CSF is forced out of the ventricles and secondly, as intracranial venous volume reduces, both effects resulting in the creation of up to 150 mL of space. Essentially, the changes in the CSF and venous blood volume buffer the effect of an expanding intracranial mass within the rigid skull. Neurological symptoms—such as headaches, visual disturbances, and sensorimotor deficits—only develop when these mechanisms are exhausted, and at this point surgery may be indicated.

input: A 51-year-old man who had been receiving haemodialysis for 15 years was referred to the Toranomon Hospital (Tokyo, Japan) with progressive calcified nodules on his fingers. He had been undergoing haemodialysis three times per week, for a total of 12 h per week. The patient had been deemed to have end-stage renal disease of unknown cause. He had undergone a parathyroidectomy 2 years before the referral because he was believed to have progressive extraskeletal calcification caused by hyperparathyroidism with constant hypercalcaemia that was refractory to medical treatment; laboratory findings were compatible with secondary hyperparathyroidism. Since the parathyroidectomy, laboratory findings had returned to normal, but the nodules had progressed and made him unable to grip. A family history could not be obtained because the patient was an orphan, but through a careful interview we identified a past medical history of recurrent urolithiasis, which was judged to be the leading cause of the end-stage renal disease. Physical examination showed clubbed fingers with exposed calcified masses (figure A). Radiography showed prominent bilateral calcified deposits (figure B) and nephrocalcinosis. Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry-based plasma metabolomic assessment showed substantially increased concentrations of oxalate (316 μmol/L) and glycerate (50·2 μmol/L; normal is <10 μmol/L for both), but glycolate concentration was almost normal at 13·3 μmol/L (normal is <12 μmol/L), suggesting the possibility of primary hyperoxaluria type 2. Genetic analysis showed a missense mutation, 181G→A (Asp61Asn), of GRHPR in exon 2. We therefore diagnosed the patient as having primary hyperoxaluria type 2 and started intensive haemodialysis (25 h per week, Monday to Friday, for 2 years so far) in preparation for renal transplantation. The patient is currently on a waiting list for renal transplantation.Primary hyperoxaluria type 2 is a rare autosomal recessive disease caused by mutation of GRHPR, the gene encoding the enzyme glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase, which results in hyperoxaluria, recurrent urolithiasis, progressive nephrocalcinosis, end-stage renal disease, and, eventually, systemic oxalate deposition. Primary hyperoxaluria type 2, especially when associated with renal failure and caused by plasma oxalate concentrations exceeding the supersaturation index of oxalate in plasma (30 μmol/L), should be identified early because severe manifestations, as seen in our patient, can be prevented with early diagnosis, intensive management of dialysis, and timely transplantation.

An 80-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 4-day history of a throbbing pain in the front part of his head that was not relieved by analgesics. The pain had developed gradually and was not associated with any weakness in his arms or legs, numbness or visual symptoms. His medical history included a diagnosis of an intracranial epidermoid cyst, hypertension, and depression. A full clinical neurological examination showed no abnormalities. A CT scan of his head (appendix) showed no additional changes to those seen in a CT scan and an MRI (figure and appendix) done 4 months earlier; at the time when the epidermoid cyst was first found, it was a 9 cm × 7·5 cm mass in the left parietal region, thinning and scalloping of the skull vault, and a slight midline shift to the right. No acute bleeds or infarcts were found. The patient was told his symptoms were due to the epidermoid cyst. At the time the cyst was first diagnosed, it was jointly decided by the patient and us to avoid any surgical interventions because epidermoid cysts are usually slow growing, benign, and asymptomatic.In such cases it is important to differentiate an epidermoid cyst from a dermoid cyst: the CT scans in this case showed a lesion of low density, which might have been fat—typically associated with dermoid cysts. An MRI with the appropriate enhancement was needed to differentiate the two. T1-weighted MRI showed strands of high signal in the lesion, which could also have represented fat (figure). However, the diffusion-weighted MRI (figure inset), which showed restricted diffusion, confirmed the diagnosis.
Furthermore, these striking images—in a patient with no neurological signs—show how a large lesion can be accommodated by a relatively atrophic brain with increased cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) filled spaces and the clinical relevance of the Monro–Kellie doctrine. Normal intracranial pressure is maintained in the presence of an expanding intracranial mass—firstly, as CSF is forced out of the ventricles and secondly, as intracranial venous volume reduces, both effects resulting in the creation of up to 150 mL of space. Essentially, the changes in the CSF and venous blood volume buffer the effect of an expanding intracranial mass within the rigid skull. Neurological symptoms—such as headaches, visual disturbances, and sensorimotor deficits—only develop when these mechanisms are exhausted, and at this point surgery may be indicated.

input: A 51-year-old man who had been receiving haemodialysis for 15 years was referred to the Toranomon Hospital (Tokyo, Japan) with progressive calcified nodules on his fingers. He had been undergoing haemodialysis three times per week, for a total of 12 h per week. The patient had been deemed to have end-stage renal disease of unknown cause. He had undergone a parathyroidectomy 2 years before the referral because he was believed to have progressive extraskeletal calcification caused by hyperparathyroidism with constant hypercalcaemia that was refractory to medical treatment; laboratory findings were compatible with secondary hyperparathyroidism. Since the parathyroidectomy, laboratory findings had returned to normal, but the nodules had progressed and made him unable to grip. A family history could not be obtained because the patient was an orphan, but through a careful interview we identified a past medical history of recurrent urolithiasis, which was judged to be the leading cause of the end-stage renal disease. Physical examination showed clubbed fingers with exposed calcified masses (figure A). Radiography showed prominent bilateral calcified deposits (figure B) and nephrocalcinosis. Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry-based plasma metabolomic assessment showed substantially increased concentrations of oxalate (316 μmol/L) and glycerate (50·2 μmol/L; normal is <10 μmol/L for both), but glycolate concentration was almost normal at 13·3 μmol/L (normal is <12 μmol/L), suggesting the possibility of primary hyperoxaluria type 2. Genetic analysis showed a missense mutation, 181G→A (Asp61Asn), of GRHPR in exon 2. We therefore diagnosed the patient as having primary hyperoxaluria type 2 and started intensive haemodialysis (25 h per week, Monday to Friday, for 2 years so far) in preparation for renal transplantation. The patient is currently on a waiting list for renal transplantation.Primary hyperoxaluria type 2 is a rare autosomal recessive disease caused by mutation of GRHPR, the gene encoding the enzyme glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase, which results in hyperoxaluria, recurrent urolithiasis, progressive nephrocalcinosis, end-stage renal disease, and, eventually, systemic oxalate deposition. Primary hyperoxaluria type 2, especially when associated with renal failure and caused by plasma oxalate concentrations exceeding the supersaturation index of oxalate in plasma (30 μmol/L), should be identified early because severe manifestations, as seen in our patient, can be prevented with early diagnosis, intensive management of dialysis, and timely transplantation.

input: A 51-year-old man who had been receiving haemodialysis for 15 years was referred to the Toranomon Hospital (Tokyo, Japan) with progressive calcified nodules on his fingers. He had been undergoing haemodialysis three times per week, for a total of 12 h per week. The patient had been deemed to have end-stage renal disease of unknown cause. He had undergone a parathyroidectomy 2 years before the referral because he was believed to have progressive extraskeletal calcification caused by hyperparathyroidism with constant hypercalcaemia that was refractory to medical treatment; laboratory findings were compatible with secondary hyperparathyroidism. Since the parathyroidectomy, laboratory findings had returned to normal, but the nodules had progressed and made him unable to grip. A family history could not be obtained because the patient was an orphan, but through a careful interview we identified a past medical history of recurrent urolithiasis, which was judged to be the leading cause of the end-stage renal disease. Physical examination showed clubbed fingers with exposed calcified masses (figure A). Radiography showed prominent bilateral calcified deposits (figure B) and nephrocalcinosis. Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry-based plasma metabolomic assessment showed substantially increased concentrations of oxalate (316 μmol/L) and glycerate (50·2 μmol/L; normal is <10 μmol/L for both), but glycolate concentration was almost normal at 13·3 μmol/L (normal is <12 μmol/L), suggesting the possibility of primary hyperoxaluria type 2. Genetic analysis showed a missense mutation, 181G→A (Asp61Asn), of GRHPR in exon 2. We therefore diagnosed the patient as having primary hyperoxaluria type 2 and started intensive haemodialysis (25 h per week, Monday to Friday, for 2 years so far) in preparation for renal transplantation. The patient is currently on a waiting list for renal transplantation.Primary hyperoxaluria type 2 is a rare autosomal recessive disease caused by mutation of GRHPR, the gene encoding the enzyme glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase, which results in hyperoxaluria, recurrent urolithiasis, progressive nephrocalcinosis, end-stage renal disease, and, eventually, systemic oxalate deposition. Primary hyperoxaluria type 2, especially when associated with renal failure and caused by plasma oxalate concentrations exceeding the supersaturation index of oxalate in plasma (30 μmol/L), should be identified early because severe manifestations, as seen in our patient, can be prevented with early diagnosis, intensive management of dialysis, and timely transplantation.

A 69-year old man, from Lombardy, Italy, was admitted to our unit because of acute respiratory distress syndrome that required mechanical ventilation; he was in Nice, France, on holiday. He had previously been fit and well; he had a history of hypertension controlled with bisoprolol 2·5 mg/day. He initially reported vomiting and diarrhoea, and 7 days afterwards, he came to our emergency department with a cough, fever of 39°C, and dyspnoea. He was immediately transferred to our intensive care unit (ICU) because of the respiratory distress syndrome and severe hypoxia. Investigations found a haemoglobin concentration of 15·4 g/dL, a platelet count of 187 × 109 per L, and a leucocyte count of 14·9 × 109 per L (neutrophils 89%, lymphocytes 7%, monocytes 4%, and no eosinophils or basophils 0%). His blood pH was 7·27, partial pressure of carbon dioxide was 45·3 mm Hg, partial pressure of oxygen was 146 mm Hg, and peripheral oxygen saturation was 98·2%.A CT of his chest showed bilateral ground-glass opacities and condensations (figure; video). PCR of swabs taken from his upper respiratory tract showed severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-Cov-2) confirming a diagnosis of coronavirus disease 19 (COVID-19). Multiplex PCR was negative for other viruses using BioFire FilmArray Respiratory Panel 2 plus (bioMérieux, Marcy l'Etoile, France) and no bacterial infections were found. An electrocardiogram (ECG), done on admission to the ICU, showed signs of left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) and diffuse inverted T waves (figure)—a previous ECG showed inverted T waves in anterior leads only. High-sensitivity cardiac troponin I concentration was raised at 9002 ng/L (normal <40). Transthoracic echocardiography showed mild LVH; the left ventricular ejection fraction and wall motion were within normal limits (figure; video). The patient was known to have LVH which was probably caused by his chronic hypertension.
Antiplatelet therapy—aspirin—and anticoagulation therapy—fondaparinux—were started because we suspected a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction: his Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events (GRACE) score was greater than 140. However, coronary angiography showed no disease, but cardiovascular magnetic resonance scanning showed subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement of the apex and inferolateral wall—suggestive of myocarditis (figure; video). We decided not to do an endomyocardial biopsy because the patient showed no signs of heart failure or arrhythmias. Additional tests for common causes of myocarditis—including parvovirus B19, human herpes virus, Epstein-Barr virus, enterovirus, cytomegalovirus, adenovirus, HIV, and hepatitis C virus—were negative. We therefore concluded that SARS-CoV-2 infection was the most likely cause of our patient's myocarditis. We gave the patient hydrocortisone at day 11 for 9 days with the aim of reducing inflammation—particularly of the myocardium. The patient was weaned off mechanical ventilation and discharged from the ICU after 3 weeks.
We believe this comprehensive description of myocarditis associated with COVID-19 confirms the importance of recent data reporting acute cardiac injury in almost a fifth of patients, with a 50% survival rate. It is recommended that troponin is not routinely measured in patients with COVID-19. However, physicians need to pay heed to the possibility of myocarditis in cases of COVID-19: in cases with high GRACE scores and dynamic ECG changes, usual guidelines to exclude the possibility of an acute myocardial infarction, including measuring troponin and doing an angiogram within 24 h, need to be followed (video).

A 69-year old man, from Lombardy, Italy, was admitted to our unit because of acute respiratory distress syndrome that required mechanical ventilation; he was in Nice, France, on holiday. He had previously been fit and well; he had a history of hypertension controlled with bisoprolol 2·5 mg/day. He initially reported vomiting and diarrhoea, and 7 days afterwards, he came to our emergency department with a cough, fever of 39°C, and dyspnoea. He was immediately transferred to our intensive care unit (ICU) because of the respiratory distress syndrome and severe hypoxia. Investigations found a haemoglobin concentration of 15·4 g/dL, a platelet count of 187 × 109 per L, and a leucocyte count of 14·9 × 109 per L (neutrophils 89%, lymphocytes 7%, monocytes 4%, and no eosinophils or basophils 0%). His blood pH was 7·27, partial pressure of carbon dioxide was 45·3 mm Hg, partial pressure of oxygen was 146 mm Hg, and peripheral oxygen saturation was 98·2%.A CT of his chest showed bilateral ground-glass opacities and condensations (figure; video). PCR of swabs taken from his upper respiratory tract showed severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-Cov-2) confirming a diagnosis of coronavirus disease 19 (COVID-19). Multiplex PCR was negative for other viruses using BioFire FilmArray Respiratory Panel 2 plus (bioMérieux, Marcy l'Etoile, France) and no bacterial infections were found. An electrocardiogram (ECG), done on admission to the ICU, showed signs of left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) and diffuse inverted T waves (figure)—a previous ECG showed inverted T waves in anterior leads only. High-sensitivity cardiac troponin I concentration was raised at 9002 ng/L (normal <40). Transthoracic echocardiography showed mild LVH; the left ventricular ejection fraction and wall motion were within normal limits (figure; video). The patient was known to have LVH which was probably caused by his chronic hypertension.
Antiplatelet therapy—aspirin—and anticoagulation therapy—fondaparinux—were started because we suspected a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction: his Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events (GRACE) score was greater than 140. However, coronary angiography showed no disease, but cardiovascular magnetic resonance scanning showed subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement of the apex and inferolateral wall—suggestive of myocarditis (figure; video). We decided not to do an endomyocardial biopsy because the patient showed no signs of heart failure or arrhythmias. Additional tests for common causes of myocarditis—including parvovirus B19, human herpes virus, Epstein-Barr virus, enterovirus, cytomegalovirus, adenovirus, HIV, and hepatitis C virus—were negative. We therefore concluded that SARS-CoV-2 infection was the most likely cause of our patient's myocarditis. We gave the patient hydrocortisone at day 11 for 9 days with the aim of reducing inflammation—particularly of the myocardium. The patient was weaned off mechanical ventilation and discharged from the ICU after 3 weeks.
We believe this comprehensive description of myocarditis associated with COVID-19 confirms the importance of recent data reporting acute cardiac injury in almost a fifth of patients, with a 50% survival rate. It is recommended that troponin is not routinely measured in patients with COVID-19. However, physicians need to pay heed to the possibility of myocarditis in cases of COVID-19: in cases with high GRACE scores and dynamic ECG changes, usual guidelines to exclude the possibility of an acute myocardial infarction, including measuring troponin and doing an angiogram within 24 h, need to be followed (video).

An electrocardiogram (ECG), done on admission to the ICU, showed signs of left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) and diffuse inverted T waves (figure)—a previous ECG showed inverted T waves in anterior leads only. High-sensitivity cardiac troponin I concentration was raised at 9002 ng/L (normal <40). Transthoracic echocardiography showed mild LVH; the left ventricular ejection fraction and wall motion were within normal limits (figure; video). The patient was known to have LVH which was probably caused by his chronic hypertension.
Antiplatelet therapy—aspirin—and anticoagulation therapy—fondaparinux—were started because we suspected a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction: his Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events (GRACE) score was greater than 140. However, coronary angiography showed no disease, but cardiovascular magnetic resonance scanning showed subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement of the apex and inferolateral wall—suggestive of myocarditis (figure; video). We therefore concluded that SARS-CoV-2 infection was the most likely cause of our patient's myocarditis. We gave the patient hydrocortisone at day 11 for 9 days with the aim of reducing inflammation—particularly of the myocardium. The patient was weaned off mechanical ventilation and discharged from the ICU after 3 weeks.

A 56-year-old man was referred to our specialist unit after presenting to his primary care clinic with a dry cough and breathlessness on exertion that were slowly worsening. He had been a smoker for 7 years but quit over a decade earlier. Also, he had worked for 8 years in underground coal mines, in Kentucky, USA. He left the profession when he was 26 years old following the collapse of a wall in the mine that left him disabled after a head injury and the development of seizures. During his time in the industry, he had worked exclusively at the coal face, primarily drilling and bolting into the ceiling of the mine to prevent collapses—known in the trade as a roof bolter. He said he wore a dust mask inconsistently because it made breathing difficult.The patient's vital signs were within normal limits and a physical examination was unremarkable. Pulmonary function testing showed moderate obstruction without a bronchodilator response: forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) to forced vital capacity (FVC) ratio was low at 0·58 (National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey III fifth percentile lower limit of normal [LLN] 0·67), with a low FEV1 of 1·97 L, 59% predicted (LLN 2·58 L), a normal FVC of 3·52 L, 81% predicted (LLN 3·41 L), a normal total lung capacity of 6·58 L, 107% predicted (LLN 5·06 L), and a normal diffusion of 25·3m L/mm Hg per min, 88% predicted (LLN 17·69 m L/mm Hg per min).
CT scan of the patient's chest showed numerous bilateral pulmonary nodules and an irregular right upper lobe mass with mediastinal lymphadenopathy (figure). A PET scan showed the lung mass and mediastinal lymph nodes with heterogeneous hypermetabolic uptake (appendix). Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and endobronchial ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration of his mediastinal lymph nodes showed no infection, granuloma, or cancer. However, it did show anthracotic pigment laden macrophages. Coal workers' pneumoconiosis (CWP) was suspected, but because of his relatively young age and short mining tenure, a transthoracic, CT-guided biopsy of his lung mass was done. Histopathological examination showed areas of focal collagenous fibrosis associated with anthracosis and polarised silicate particles; there was no evidence of cancer, granulomas, vasculitis, or infection (figure). We therefore made a definitive diagnosis of CWP and progressive massive fibrosis (PMF).
PET scans—as our patient's imaging illustrates—may fail to reliably distinguish PMF from malignancy as both are commonly hypermetabolic. Historically, CWP and PMF develop in miners with mining tenures of 25 years or more. However, in recent years, rates of severe disease have been increasing in younger miners with short mining tenures, despite improved health and safety regulations. Current mining practices—including digging for thinner and harder to reach seams leading to increased cutting of rock and therefore higher exposure to silica—may be a contributing factor. CWP and PMF should be considered in the differential diagnosis in both current and former coal miners presenting with respiratory problems regardless of age or the duration of coal mine employment. Early detection is crucial to prevent further dust exposure and delay progression of disease; effective treatments are lacking, and morbidity is irreversible (video).

A 56-year-old man was referred to our specialist unit after presenting to his primary care clinic with a dry cough and breathlessness on exertion that were slowly worsening. He had been a smoker for 7 years but quit over a decade earlier. Also, he had worked for 8 years in underground coal mines, in Kentucky, USA. He left the profession when he was 26 years old following the collapse of a wall in the mine that left him disabled after a head injury and the development of seizures. During his time in the industry, he had worked exclusively at the coal face, primarily drilling and bolting into the ceiling of the mine to prevent collapses—known in the trade as a roof bolter. He said he wore a dust mask inconsistently because it made breathing difficult.The patient's vital signs were within normal limits and a physical examination was unremarkable. Pulmonary function testing showed moderate obstruction without a bronchodilator response: forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) to forced vital capacity (FVC) ratio was low at 0·58 (National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey III fifth percentile lower limit of normal [LLN] 0·67), with a low FEV1 of 1·97 L, 59% predicted (LLN 2·58 L), a normal FVC of 3·52 L, 81% predicted (LLN 3·41 L), a normal total lung capacity of 6·58 L, 107% predicted (LLN 5·06 L), and a normal diffusion of 25·3m L/mm Hg per min, 88% predicted (LLN 17·69 m L/mm Hg per min).
CT scan of the patient's chest showed numerous bilateral pulmonary nodules and an irregular right upper lobe mass with mediastinal lymphadenopathy (figure). A PET scan showed the lung mass and mediastinal lymph nodes with heterogeneous hypermetabolic uptake (appendix). Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and endobronchial ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration of his mediastinal lymph nodes showed no infection, granuloma, or cancer. However, it did show anthracotic pigment laden macrophages. Coal workers' pneumoconiosis (CWP) was suspected, but because of his relatively young age and short mining tenure, a transthoracic, CT-guided biopsy of his lung mass was done. Histopathological examination showed areas of focal collagenous fibrosis associated with anthracosis and polarised silicate particles; there was no evidence of cancer, granulomas, vasculitis, or infection (figure). We therefore made a definitive diagnosis of CWP and progressive massive fibrosis (PMF).
PET scans—as our patient's imaging illustrates—may fail to reliably distinguish PMF from malignancy as both are commonly hypermetabolic. Historically, CWP and PMF develop in miners with mining tenures of 25 years or more. However, in recent years, rates of severe disease have been increasing in younger miners with short mining tenures, despite improved health and safety regulations. Current mining practices—including digging for thinner and harder to reach seams leading to increased cutting of rock and therefore higher exposure to silica—may be a contributing factor. CWP and PMF should be considered in the differential diagnosis in both current and former coal miners presenting with respiratory problems regardless of age or the duration of coal mine employment. Early detection is crucial to prevent further dust exposure and delay progression of disease; effective treatments are lacking, and morbidity is irreversible (video).

A 29-year-old woman presented with a 23-year history of multiple joint swelling and intermittent pain. Physical examination showed large, soft, and fluctuant soft tissue swelling of the hands, wrists, elbows, knees, and ankles, bilaterally (figure A; appendix p 2). Symmetric tense knee effusions restricted her range of motion. She had previously had multiple recurrences of panuveitis, cataract, and secondary glaucoma in both eyes for 7 years, with retinal detachment leading to blindness in her left eye. 9 years earlier, she had undergone knee synovectomy, and histopathological examination showed extensive infiltration of mature adipose tissue, consistent with lipoma arborescens. Noncaseating granulomas were also observed at higher magnification (figure B). MRI of the knee at that time showed diffuse villous and frond-like intra-articular fatty masses in the suprapatellar bursa, with associated marked joint effusion (appendix p 3). Her father had displayed almost identical symptoms and had died 19 years previously, at the age of 34 years.
Immunological tests showed no abnormalities. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was slightly elevated, at 34 mm/h. MRI of the right hand revealed multiple lobulations along the tendons, with joint effusions (figures C and D, appendix p 4); the signal intensity of the frond-like lobules was high on T1-weighted images (figure C) and very low on fat-saturated T2-weighted images (figure D), indicating their fatty composition. Whole-exome sequencing revealed a novel heterozygous missense frameshift mutation in NOD2 (1066G>C [Glu356Gln]), which was predicted to be damaging by in silico analysis (appendix p 5). The patient recalled having scaly erythematous lesions in childhood. A diagnosis of Blau syndrome was made. Genetic analysis could not be done on the father, but, given his medical history, it is highly probable that he had a severe form of Blau syndrome.
Blau syndrome is an autoinflammatory granulomatosis disease resulting from mutations in NOD2 and characterised by skin, joint, and eye disorders. Joint manifestations are chronic and symmetrical polyarthritis, which usually start within the first decade of life, with marked soft-tissue swelling, especially in the wrists and ankles, due to synovial granulomatous inflammation. Ocular involvement usually occurs later than other symptoms but accounts for the highest morbidity.
Lipoma arborescens is a rare disorder that results in the growth of fatty tissue within the joint linings, often leading to swelling, pain, and restricted movement, primarily affecting the knee, although it can involve multiple joints. Hand involvement, early childhood onset, and familial inheritance in lipoma arborescens are very rare, suggesting a possible misdiagnosis. Joint involvement in Blau syndrome presenting as lipoma arborescens has only been documented once but cases might be underestimated due to the lack of genetic confirmation. Hence, Blau syndrome should be looked for in lipoma arborescens cases with uveitis, familial history, hand joint involvement, or early onset.
If the condition had been identified sooner, blindness might have been averted in the patient, highlighting the importance of early recognition and treatment. In this case, the patient was treated with glucocorticoids and thalidomide, resulting in pain relief and stabilisation. Glucocorticoids were tapered gradually, with the addition of tofacitinib.

A 29-year-old woman presented with a 23-year history of multiple joint swelling and intermittent pain. Physical examination showed large, soft, and fluctuant soft tissue swelling of the hands, wrists, elbows, knees, and ankles, bilaterally (figure A; appendix p 2). Symmetric tense knee effusions restricted her range of motion. She had previously had multiple recurrences of panuveitis, cataract, and secondary glaucoma in both eyes for 7 years, with retinal detachment leading to blindness in her left eye. 9 years earlier, she had undergone knee synovectomy, and histopathological examination showed extensive infiltration of mature adipose tissue, consistent with lipoma arborescens. Noncaseating granulomas were also observed at higher magnification (figure B). MRI of the knee at that time showed diffuse villous and frond-like intra-articular fatty masses in the suprapatellar bursa, with associated marked joint effusion (appendix p 3). Her father had displayed almost identical symptoms and had died 19 years previously, at the age of 34 years.
Immunological tests showed no abnormalities. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was slightly elevated, at 34 mm/h. MRI of the right hand revealed multiple lobulations along the tendons, with joint effusions (figures C and D, appendix p 4); the signal intensity of the frond-like lobules was high on T1-weighted images (figure C) and very low on fat-saturated T2-weighted images (figure D), indicating their fatty composition. Whole-exome sequencing revealed a novel heterozygous missense frameshift mutation in NOD2 (1066G>C [Glu356Gln]), which was predicted to be damaging by in silico analysis (appendix p 5). The patient recalled having scaly erythematous lesions in childhood. A diagnosis of Blau syndrome was made. Genetic analysis could not be done on the father, but, given his medical history, it is highly probable that he had a severe form of Blau syndrome.
Blau syndrome is an autoinflammatory granulomatosis disease resulting from mutations in NOD2 and characterised by skin, joint, and eye disorders. Joint manifestations are chronic and symmetrical polyarthritis, which usually start within the first decade of life, with marked soft-tissue swelling, especially in the wrists and ankles, due to synovial granulomatous inflammation. Ocular involvement usually occurs later than other symptoms but accounts for the highest morbidity.
Lipoma arborescens is a rare disorder that results in the growth of fatty tissue within the joint linings, often leading to swelling, pain, and restricted movement, primarily affecting the knee, although it can involve multiple joints. Hand involvement, early childhood onset, and familial inheritance in lipoma arborescens are very rare, suggesting a possible misdiagnosis. Joint involvement in Blau syndrome presenting as lipoma arborescens has only been documented once but cases might be underestimated due to the lack of genetic confirmation. Hence, Blau syndrome should be looked for in lipoma arborescens cases with uveitis, familial history, hand joint involvement, or early onset.
If the condition had been identified sooner, blindness might have been averted in the patient, highlighting the importance of early recognition and treatment. In this case, the patient was treated with glucocorticoids and thalidomide, resulting in pain relief and stabilisation. Glucocorticoids were tapered gradually, with the addition of tofacitinib.

A 56-year-old man was referred to our specialist unit after presenting to his primary care clinic with a dry cough and breathlessness on exertion that were slowly worsening. He had been a smoker for 7 years but quit over a decade earlier. Also, he had worked for 8 years in underground coal mines, in Kentucky, USA. He left the profession when he was 26 years old following the collapse of a wall in the mine that left him disabled after a head injury and the development of seizures. During his time in the industry, he had worked exclusively at the coal face, primarily drilling and bolting into the ceiling of the mine to prevent collapses—known in the trade as a roof bolter. He said he wore a dust mask inconsistently because it made breathing difficult.The patient's vital signs were within normal limits and a physical examination was unremarkable. Pulmonary function testing showed moderate obstruction without a bronchodilator response: forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) to forced vital capacity (FVC) ratio was low at 0·58 (National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey III fifth percentile lower limit of normal [LLN] 0·67), with a low FEV1 of 1·97 L, 59% predicted (LLN 2·58 L), a normal FVC of 3·52 L, 81% predicted (LLN 3·41 L), a normal total lung capacity of 6·58 L, 107% predicted (LLN 5·06 L), and a normal diffusion of 25·3m L/mm Hg per min, 88% predicted (LLN 17·69 m L/mm Hg per min).
CT scan of the patient's chest showed numerous bilateral pulmonary nodules and an irregular right upper lobe mass with mediastinal lymphadenopathy (figure). A PET scan showed the lung mass and mediastinal lymph nodes with heterogeneous hypermetabolic uptake (appendix). Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and endobronchial ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration of his mediastinal lymph nodes showed no infection, granuloma, or cancer. However, it did show anthracotic pigment laden macrophages. Coal workers' pneumoconiosis (CWP) was suspected, but because of his relatively young age and short mining tenure, a transthoracic, CT-guided biopsy of his lung mass was done. Histopathological examination showed areas of focal collagenous fibrosis associated with anthracosis and polarised silicate particles; there was no evidence of cancer, granulomas, vasculitis, or infection (figure). We therefore made a definitive diagnosis of CWP and progressive massive fibrosis (PMF).
PET scans—as our patient's imaging illustrates—may fail to reliably distinguish PMF from malignancy as both are commonly hypermetabolic. Historically, CWP and PMF develop in miners with mining tenures of 25 years or more. However, in recent years, rates of severe disease have been increasing in younger miners with short mining tenures, despite improved health and safety regulations. Current mining practices—including digging for thinner and harder to reach seams leading to increased cutting of rock and therefore higher exposure to silica—may be a contributing factor. CWP and PMF should be considered in the differential diagnosis in both current and former coal miners presenting with respiratory problems regardless of age or the duration of coal mine employment. Early detection is crucial to prevent further dust exposure and delay progression of disease; effective treatments are lacking, and morbidity is irreversible (video).

A 29-year-old woman presented with a 23-year history of multiple joint swelling and intermittent pain. Physical examination showed large, soft, and fluctuant soft tissue swelling of the hands, wrists, elbows, knees, and ankles, bilaterally (figure A; appendix p 2). Symmetric tense knee effusions restricted her range of motion. She had previously had multiple recurrences of panuveitis, cataract, and secondary glaucoma in both eyes for 7 years, with retinal detachment leading to blindness in her left eye. 9 years earlier, she had undergone knee synovectomy, and histopathological examination showed extensive infiltration of mature adipose tissue, consistent with lipoma arborescens. Noncaseating granulomas were also observed at higher magnification (figure B). MRI of the knee at that time showed diffuse villous and frond-like intra-articular fatty masses in the suprapatellar bursa, with associated marked joint effusion (appendix p 3). Her father had displayed almost identical symptoms and had died 19 years previously, at the age of 34 years.
Immunological tests showed no abnormalities. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was slightly elevated, at 34 mm/h. MRI of the right hand revealed multiple lobulations along the tendons, with joint effusions (figures C and D, appendix p 4); the signal intensity of the frond-like lobules was high on T1-weighted images (figure C) and very low on fat-saturated T2-weighted images (figure D), indicating their fatty composition. Whole-exome sequencing revealed a novel heterozygous missense frameshift mutation in NOD2 (1066G>C [Glu356Gln]), which was predicted to be damaging by in silico analysis (appendix p 5). The patient recalled having scaly erythematous lesions in childhood. A diagnosis of Blau syndrome was made. Genetic analysis could not be done on the father, but, given his medical history, it is highly probable that he had a severe form of Blau syndrome.
Blau syndrome is an autoinflammatory granulomatosis disease resulting from mutations in NOD2 and characterised by skin, joint, and eye disorders. Joint manifestations are chronic and symmetrical polyarthritis, which usually start within the first decade of life, with marked soft-tissue swelling, especially in the wrists and ankles, due to synovial granulomatous inflammation. Ocular involvement usually occurs later than other symptoms but accounts for the highest morbidity.
Lipoma arborescens is a rare disorder that results in the growth of fatty tissue within the joint linings, often leading to swelling, pain, and restricted movement, primarily affecting the knee, although it can involve multiple joints. Hand involvement, early childhood onset, and familial inheritance in lipoma arborescens are very rare, suggesting a possible misdiagnosis. Joint involvement in Blau syndrome presenting as lipoma arborescens has only been documented once but cases might be underestimated due to the lack of genetic confirmation. Hence, Blau syndrome should be looked for in lipoma arborescens cases with uveitis, familial history, hand joint involvement, or early onset.
If the condition had been identified sooner, blindness might have been averted in the patient, highlighting the importance of early recognition and treatment. In this case, the patient was treated with glucocorticoids and thalidomide, resulting in pain relief and stabilisation. Glucocorticoids were tapered gradually, with the addition of tofacitinib.

A 51-year-old woman presented to our emergency room with a 4-day history of fever, chills, abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhoea.1 week before these problems began, the patient had a nevus removed from her right arm. The dermatologists were concerned it may have been a melanoma; she had a history of primary biliary cholangitis treated with ursodeoxycholic acid.
On examination, we found the patient to be unwell but responsive; her blood pressure was 85/59 mm Hg, her pulse was 107 beats per min, temperature was 39·0°C, respiratory rate 27 breaths per min, and oxygen saturation was 94%.
A CT scan of the patient's chest showed air space opacities with air bronchogram indicating a pneumonia in the left and right lower lobes (figure); a CT of the abdomen showed circumferential wall thickening of the right colon and surrounding fat stranding, indicating colitis. Blood cultures grew Streptococcus pyogenes.
10 h after admission, the patient's condition deteriorated and she developed septic shock; she was given intravenous antibiotics, crystalloid fluid, and norepinephrine, and transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU). 24 h after admission, she went into cardiogenic shock with a decreased left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 25% with hypokinesis of the basal and midventricular segments—typical of an inverted takotsubo cardiomyopathy (appendix); on admission her LVEF had been 50%.
Troponin blood concentration was 104 819 ng/L (normal <74). Coronary angiography showed no abnormalities. We made a diagnosis of septic cardiomyopathy, and the patient was treated with dobutamine. After some initial improvement her condition worsened and she was readmitted to the ICU because of pulmonary oedema and a persistent fever (temperature was 38·8°C): LVEF was still decreased at 25%. A whole-body CT scan showed diffuse myocardial calcifications of the left ventricle (figure) but no focus of secondary pulmonary or abdominal infection.
Histopathological examination of a sample obtained at endomyocardial biopsy confirmed myocardial calcifications (figure). Considering the findings in the round, we made a diagnosis of diffuse myocardial calcifications following severe streptococcal sepsis, and high-dose—2 mg/kg—corticosteroids were started. The fever abated and the patient's clinical status improved; she was allowed home 3 months after admission. Corticosteroids were decreased and stopped at 3 months and the patient was treated with dapagliflozin, ramipril, and a cardioverter-defibrillator was implanted. 10 months after initial presentation, she was asymptomatic and her LVEF was 40%; the microcalcifications were still present (appendix).
Diffuse myocardial calcifications following severe sepsis are uncommon and associated with a poor prognosis. High-dose pulses of corticosteroids are recommended but evidence for effectiveness remains weak in the absence of prospective clinical trials (video).

A 51-year-old woman presented to our emergency room with a 4-day history of fever, chills, abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhoea.1 week before these problems began, the patient had a nevus removed from her right arm. The dermatologists were concerned it may have been a melanoma; she had a history of primary biliary cholangitis treated with ursodeoxycholic acid.
On examination, we found the patient to be unwell but responsive; her blood pressure was 85/59 mm Hg, her pulse was 107 beats per min, temperature was 39·0°C, respiratory rate 27 breaths per min, and oxygen saturation was 94%.
A CT scan of the patient's chest showed air space opacities with air bronchogram indicating a pneumonia in the left and right lower lobes (figure); a CT of the abdomen showed circumferential wall thickening of the right colon and surrounding fat stranding, indicating colitis. Blood cultures grew Streptococcus pyogenes.
10 h after admission, the patient's condition deteriorated and she developed septic shock; she was given intravenous antibiotics, crystalloid fluid, and norepinephrine, and transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU). 24 h after admission, she went into cardiogenic shock with a decreased left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 25% with hypokinesis of the basal and midventricular segments—typical of an inverted takotsubo cardiomyopathy (appendix); on admission her LVEF had been 50%.
Troponin blood concentration was 104 819 ng/L (normal <74). Coronary angiography showed no abnormalities. We made a diagnosis of septic cardiomyopathy, and the patient was treated with dobutamine. After some initial improvement her condition worsened and she was readmitted to the ICU because of pulmonary oedema and a persistent fever (temperature was 38·8°C): LVEF was still decreased at 25%. A whole-body CT scan showed diffuse myocardial calcifications of the left ventricle (figure) but no focus of secondary pulmonary or abdominal infection.
Histopathological examination of a sample obtained at endomyocardial biopsy confirmed myocardial calcifications (figure). Considering the findings in the round, we made a diagnosis of diffuse myocardial calcifications following severe streptococcal sepsis, and high-dose—2 mg/kg—corticosteroids were started. The fever abated and the patient's clinical status improved; she was allowed home 3 months after admission. Corticosteroids were decreased and stopped at 3 months and the patient was treated with dapagliflozin, ramipril, and a cardioverter-defibrillator was implanted. 10 months after initial presentation, she was asymptomatic and her LVEF was 40%; the microcalcifications were still present (appendix).
Diffuse myocardial calcifications following severe sepsis are uncommon and associated with a poor prognosis. High-dose pulses of corticosteroids are recommended but evidence for effectiveness remains weak in the absence of prospective clinical trials (video).

She reported hyperpigmented lesions on her arms and face on a background of mostly hypopigmented skin, creating a leopard-like appearance (figure A). The lesions first appeared 9 months earlier, and the dark pigment intensified over time. Her history included vitiligo and primary adrenal insufficiency, for which she received glucocorticoid replacement therapy with delayed-release hydrocortisone (10 mg orally per day; 0·11 mg per kg body weight [87 kg]) and fludrocortisone (0·1 mg orally per day). Serum electrolytes were normal; C-reactive protein was raised to 40 mg/L (reference: <5 mg/L); and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated at 46 mm/h (reference: <30 mm/h after 1 h), while complete blood count was within the normal range. Serum cortisol was 17 nmol/L (reference: 124–662 nmol/L) and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) was 274 pmol/L (reference: 2·6–10·1 pmol/L). Based on her presentation, we suspected inadequate glucocorticoid replacement because of enhanced glucocorticoid demand. Hydrocortisone was increased to 40 mg per day. A CT scan showed splenomegaly and diffuse lymphadenopathy (figure B). Surgical extirpation and histopathological analysis of an axillary lymph node revealed follicular lymphoma (stage 3B). The insidious development of lymphoma might have enhanced the patient's glucocorticoid requirement, as reflected by her symptoms and elevated concentrations of ACTH. Cosecretion of α-melanocyte-stimulating hormone with ACTH, both from the common precursor POMC, enhanced the contrast of hyperpigmented islands on vitiligous skin. After treatment with bendamustine and rituximab (R-Bendamustine protocol: 3 cycles, cumulative dose of bendamustine at 1080 mg [IV], cumulative dose of rituximab at 2250 mg [IV]), lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly had disappeared and the patient was free of symptoms when on hydrocortisone (20 mg per day).Patients with inadequate glucocorticoid replacement generally present with fatigue, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea, as well as hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia. In severe cases, adrenal crisis might occur and rapid intravenous replacement of glucocorticoids is required. As for the patient described here, cutaneous hyperpigmentation might also indicate an increased glucocorticoid demand compared with the replacement dose. Thus, inspection of the skin might be a useful diagnostic tool in patients with primary adrenal insufficiency, including mucosal membranes, scars, and skin creases. However, in patients with underlying skin conditions, the presentation of the characteristic hyperpigmentation might vary and could be misinterpreted as part of the skin disease if not carefully examined. If a patient with primary adrenal insufficiency who is on glucocorticoid-replacement therapy develops hyperpigmentation, possible causes of the increased glucocorticoid demand need to be investigated, including malignancies, infection, or autoimmune disease. Here, we were able to diagnose lymphoma as the underlying cause of the increased glucocorticoid requirement.

A 51-year-old woman presented to our emergency room with a 4-day history of fever, chills, abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhoea.1 week before these problems began, the patient had a nevus removed from her right arm. The dermatologists were concerned it may have been a melanoma; she had a history of primary biliary cholangitis treated with ursodeoxycholic acid.
On examination, we found the patient to be unwell but responsive; her blood pressure was 85/59 mm Hg, her pulse was 107 beats per min, temperature was 39·0°C, respiratory rate 27 breaths per min, and oxygen saturation was 94%.
A CT scan of the patient's chest showed air space opacities with air bronchogram indicating a pneumonia in the left and right lower lobes (figure); a CT of the abdomen showed circumferential wall thickening of the right colon and surrounding fat stranding, indicating colitis. Blood cultures grew Streptococcus pyogenes.
10 h after admission, the patient's condition deteriorated and she developed septic shock; she was given intravenous antibiotics, crystalloid fluid, and norepinephrine, and transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU). 24 h after admission, she went into cardiogenic shock with a decreased left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 25% with hypokinesis of the basal and midventricular segments—typical of an inverted takotsubo cardiomyopathy (appendix); on admission her LVEF had been 50%.
Troponin blood concentration was 104 819 ng/L (normal <74). Coronary angiography showed no abnormalities. We made a diagnosis of septic cardiomyopathy, and the patient was treated with dobutamine. After some initial improvement her condition worsened and she was readmitted to the ICU because of pulmonary oedema and a persistent fever (temperature was 38·8°C): LVEF was still decreased at 25%. A whole-body CT scan showed diffuse myocardial calcifications of the left ventricle (figure) but no focus of secondary pulmonary or abdominal infection.
Histopathological examination of a sample obtained at endomyocardial biopsy confirmed myocardial calcifications (figure). Considering the findings in the round, we made a diagnosis of diffuse myocardial calcifications following severe streptococcal sepsis, and high-dose—2 mg/kg—corticosteroids were started. The fever abated and the patient's clinical status improved; she was allowed home 3 months after admission. Corticosteroids were decreased and stopped at 3 months and the patient was treated with dapagliflozin, ramipril, and a cardioverter-defibrillator was implanted. 10 months after initial presentation, she was asymptomatic and her LVEF was 40%; the microcalcifications were still present (appendix).
Diffuse myocardial calcifications following severe sepsis are uncommon and associated with a poor prognosis. High-dose pulses of corticosteroids are recommended but evidence for effectiveness remains weak in the absence of prospective clinical trials (video).

If a patient with primary adrenal insufficiency who is on glucocorticoid-replacement therapy develops hyperpigmentation, possible causes of the increased glucocorticoid demand need to be investigated, including malignancies, infection, or autoimmune disease. input: A 58-year-old woman presented with fever and fatigue for the past 4 weeks. She reported hyperpigmented lesions on her arms and face on a background of mostly hypopigmented skin, creating a leopard-like appearance (figure A). The lesions first appeared 9 months earlier, and the dark pigment intensified over time. Her history included vitiligo and primary adrenal insufficiency, for which she received glucocorticoid replacement therapy with delayed-release hydrocortisone (10 mg orally per day; 0·11 mg per kg body weight [87 kg]) and fludrocortisone (0·1 mg orally per day). Serum electrolytes were normal; C-reactive protein was raised to 40 mg/L (reference: <5 mg/L); and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated at 46 mm/h (reference: <30 mm/h after 1 h), while complete blood count was within the normal range. Serum cortisol was 17 nmol/L (reference: 124–662 nmol/L) and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) was 274 pmol/L (reference: 2·6–10·1 pmol/L). Based on her presentation, we suspected inadequate glucocorticoid replacement because of enhanced glucocorticoid demand. Hydrocortisone was increased to 40 mg per day. A CT scan showed splenomegaly and diffuse lymphadenopathy (figure B). Surgical extirpation and histopathological analysis of an axillary lymph node revealed follicular lymphoma (stage 3B). The insidious development of lymphoma might have enhanced the patient's glucocorticoid requirement, as reflected by her symptoms and elevated concentrations of ACTH. Cosecretion of α-melanocyte-stimulating hormone with ACTH, both from the common precursor POMC, enhanced the contrast of hyperpigmented islands on vitiligous skin. After treatment with bendamustine and rituximab (R-Bendamustine protocol: 3 cycles, cumulative dose of bendamustine at 1080 mg [IV], cumulative dose of rituximab at 2250 mg [IV]), lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly had disappeared and the patient was free of symptoms when on hydrocortisone (20 mg per day).Patients with inadequate glucocorticoid replacement generally present with fatigue, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea, as well as hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia. In severe cases, adrenal crisis might occur and rapid intravenous replacement of glucocorticoids is required. As for the patient described here, cutaneous hyperpigmentation might also indicate an increased glucocorticoid demand compared with the replacement dose. Thus, inspection of the skin might be a useful diagnostic tool in patients with primary adrenal insufficiency, including mucosal membranes, scars, and skin creases. However, in patients with underlying skin conditions, the presentation of the characteristic hyperpigmentation might vary and could be misinterpreted as part of the skin disease if not carefully examined. If a patient with primary adrenal insufficiency who is on glucocorticoid-replacement therapy develops hyperpigmentation, possible causes of the increased glucocorticoid demand need to be investigated, including malignancies, infection, or autoimmune disease. Here, we were able to diagnose lymphoma as the underlying cause of the increased glucocorticoid requirement.

A previously well 79-year-old woman presented with the acute onset of coffee-ground emesis. She had no previous history of alcohol intake, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug use, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or ingestion of corrosive agents. Urgent oesophagogastroduodenoscopy was done. She was kept nil-orally and commenced on an intravenous proton-pump inhibitor, fluconazole, and broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a diffuse black appearance of the mucosa from the mid-oesophagus to the gastro-oesophageal junction (figure A), where there was a clearly demarcated boundary with normal mucosa (figure B)—a finding consistent with a diagnosis of acute oesophageal necrosis. This condition is also known as Gurvits' syndrome or black oesophagus. Acute oesophageal necrosis is a rare clinical entity that usually presents with either frank haematemesis or coffee-ground emesis. It has a characteristic endoscopic appearance of circumferential, friable, black-coloured mucosa in the distal oesophagus that ends clearly and abruptly at the gastro-oesophageal junction. It is thought to be caused by oesophageal ischaemia. Multiple factors might be involved, including haemodynamic compromise, malnutrition, drug ingestion, and underlying cardiovascular or renal disease. Although the oesophagus is largely protected from ischaemia by its complex and intricate anastomotic vascular network, there is a watershed area in the distal oesophagus that is more susceptible to ischaemic injury. Management of acute oesophageal necrosis generally involves resuscitation, supportive measures, and treatment of any coexisting illness. Antimicrobial therapy is usually unnecessary, except in the setting of oesophageal perforation, positive cultures, or suspected sepsis. Although complications of perforation and stricture formation are uncommon, acute oesophageal necrosis carries a high overall mortality risk due to its association with other comorbidities and critical illness. However, acute oesophageal necrosis in an otherwise healthy patient often resolves spontaneously and is associated with a more favourable outcome.Repeat oesophagogastroduodenoscopy of our patient 72 h later revealed complete resolution of the initial endoscopic findings (figure C). Our patient was subsequently discharged home following resolution of the injury and remains well at 6-month follow-up.

A previously well 79-year-old woman presented with the acute onset of coffee-ground emesis. She had no previous history of alcohol intake, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug use, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or ingestion of corrosive agents. Urgent oesophagogastroduodenoscopy was done. She was kept nil-orally and commenced on an intravenous proton-pump inhibitor, fluconazole, and broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a diffuse black appearance of the mucosa from the mid-oesophagus to the gastro-oesophageal junction (figure A), where there was a clearly demarcated boundary with normal mucosa (figure B)—a finding consistent with a diagnosis of acute oesophageal necrosis. This condition is also known as Gurvits' syndrome or black oesophagus. Acute oesophageal necrosis is a rare clinical entity that usually presents with either frank haematemesis or coffee-ground emesis. It has a characteristic endoscopic appearance of circumferential, friable, black-coloured mucosa in the distal oesophagus that ends clearly and abruptly at the gastro-oesophageal junction. It is thought to be caused by oesophageal ischaemia. Multiple factors might be involved, including haemodynamic compromise, malnutrition, drug ingestion, and underlying cardiovascular or renal disease. Although the oesophagus is largely protected from ischaemia by its complex and intricate anastomotic vascular network, there is a watershed area in the distal oesophagus that is more susceptible to ischaemic injury. Management of acute oesophageal necrosis generally involves resuscitation, supportive measures, and treatment of any coexisting illness. Antimicrobial therapy is usually unnecessary, except in the setting of oesophageal perforation, positive cultures, or suspected sepsis. Although complications of perforation and stricture formation are uncommon, acute oesophageal necrosis carries a high overall mortality risk due to its association with other comorbidities and critical illness. However, acute oesophageal necrosis in an otherwise healthy patient often resolves spontaneously and is associated with a more favourable outcome.Repeat oesophagogastroduodenoscopy of our patient 72 h later revealed complete resolution of the initial endoscopic findings (figure C). Our patient was subsequently discharged home following resolution of the injury and remains well at 6-month follow-up.

A 28-year-old man presented to our rheumatology department with a 10-year history of progressive facial and truncal rash and mild muscle weakness. He had previously presented with these symptoms at a local dermatology clinic at age 18 years. After this initial examination, the patient was diagnosed with dermatomyositis and given combined treatment with prednisone, methotrexate, and hydroxychloroquine. This treatment resulted in improved muscle weakness after a few months; however, the patient had mild hepatotoxicity and so methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine were discontinued. He also reported recurrence of cutaneous involvement, which prompted re-referral and re-evaluation at our department 10 years later.
On re-examination, physical examination revealed a violaceous heliotrope rash on the eyelids and malar area, accompanied by a striking reticular erythematous eruption on the neck and back (figure 1A). Muscle involvement was assessed by use of the Manual Muscle Testing-8 scale, yielding a score of 150 (ie, normal muscle strength).
Histopathological evaluation of the reticular rash biopsy sample revealed interface dermatitis on haematoxylin and eosin staining (figure 1B), along with basement membrane thickening highlighted by periodic acid-Schiff staining (figure 1C). Laboratory investigations showed creatine kinase concentrations within the normal range (64 U/L; reference range 50–310 U/L) and exclusive anti-transcriptional intermediary factor 1-γ (anti-TIF1-γ) antibody positivity, detected by immunoblot, with negative results for other myositis-specific autoantibodies. In China, there are currently no commercially available ELISA kits for anti-TIF1-γ antibody detection that have been approved by the China Food and Drug Administration. Muscle MRI showed no inflammation or oedema, and high-resolution pulmonary CT revealed no interstitial lung disease. Extensive malignancy screening, including whole-body PET–CT and gastrointestinal endoscopy, showed no occult neoplasms. Peripheral blood PCR revealed elevated interferon-stimulated genes (MX1 and IFI44), confirming a type I interferon signature. Immunohistochemical and immunofluorescence analysis revealed MX1 expression in the basal epidermis and perivascular regions.
When the patient was first diagnosed at his local dermatology clinic at age 18 years, his clinical manifestations were characterised by prominent cutaneous features without evidence of calcinosis, which is suggestive of cancer-associated adult dermatomyositis. However, detection of myositis-specific autoantibodies, including anti-TIF1-γ, was unavailable at the time. Upon re-evaluation 10 years later, and taking into account the patient's history, symptoms, laboratory examination, and cutaneous biopsy findings, the diagnosis of dermatomyositis was confirmed. Baricitinib (4 mg per day) combined with prednisone (0·8 mg/kg per day) were initiated. At 24 weeks follow-up at our department, Cutaneous Disease Area and Severity Index scores improved by 60% (scores reduced from 25 to 10), with reduced erythema intensity and extent of rash. As there was no progression of muscle weakness, interstitial lung disease, or malignancy after 24 weeks, prednisone was tapered to 7·5 mg per day.
Anti-TIF1-γ antibodies are strongly associated with malignancy, with peak risk 3–5 years before and after disease onset. Characteristic cutaneous findings of anti-TIF1-γ positive dermatomyositis, including facial rash, V-neck and back rash, periungual telangiectasias, heliotrope rash, Gottron's sign, palatal patch, and diffuse photoerythema, are well documented. However, reticular rash, a rare manifestation as seen in this patient, expands the spectrum of cutaneous manifestations. Emerging evidence implicates type I interferon dysregulation in pathogenesis, and Janus kinase inhibitors might be of benefit to patients with refractory cutaneous dermatomyositis.

A 28-year-old man presented to our rheumatology department with a 10-year history of progressive facial and truncal rash and mild muscle weakness. He had previously presented with these symptoms at a local dermatology clinic at age 18 years. After this initial examination, the patient was diagnosed with dermatomyositis and given combined treatment with prednisone, methotrexate, and hydroxychloroquine. This treatment resulted in improved muscle weakness after a few months; however, the patient had mild hepatotoxicity and so methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine were discontinued. He also reported recurrence of cutaneous involvement, which prompted re-referral and re-evaluation at our department 10 years later.
On re-examination, physical examination revealed a violaceous heliotrope rash on the eyelids and malar area, accompanied by a striking reticular erythematous eruption on the neck and back (figure 1A). Muscle involvement was assessed by use of the Manual Muscle Testing-8 scale, yielding a score of 150 (ie, normal muscle strength).
Histopathological evaluation of the reticular rash biopsy sample revealed interface dermatitis on haematoxylin and eosin staining (figure 1B), along with basement membrane thickening highlighted by periodic acid-Schiff staining (figure 1C). Laboratory investigations showed creatine kinase concentrations within the normal range (64 U/L; reference range 50–310 U/L) and exclusive anti-transcriptional intermediary factor 1-γ (anti-TIF1-γ) antibody positivity, detected by immunoblot, with negative results for other myositis-specific autoantibodies. In China, there are currently no commercially available ELISA kits for anti-TIF1-γ antibody detection that have been approved by the China Food and Drug Administration. Muscle MRI showed no inflammation or oedema, and high-resolution pulmonary CT revealed no interstitial lung disease. Extensive malignancy screening, including whole-body PET–CT and gastrointestinal endoscopy, showed no occult neoplasms. Peripheral blood PCR revealed elevated interferon-stimulated genes (MX1 and IFI44), confirming a type I interferon signature. Immunohistochemical and immunofluorescence analysis revealed MX1 expression in the basal epidermis and perivascular regions.
When the patient was first diagnosed at his local dermatology clinic at age 18 years, his clinical manifestations were characterised by prominent cutaneous features without evidence of calcinosis, which is suggestive of cancer-associated adult dermatomyositis. However, detection of myositis-specific autoantibodies, including anti-TIF1-γ, was unavailable at the time. Upon re-evaluation 10 years later, and taking into account the patient's history, symptoms, laboratory examination, and cutaneous biopsy findings, the diagnosis of dermatomyositis was confirmed. Baricitinib (4 mg per day) combined with prednisone (0·8 mg/kg per day) were initiated. At 24 weeks follow-up at our department, Cutaneous Disease Area and Severity Index scores improved by 60% (scores reduced from 25 to 10), with reduced erythema intensity and extent of rash. As there was no progression of muscle weakness, interstitial lung disease, or malignancy after 24 weeks, prednisone was tapered to 7·5 mg per day.
Anti-TIF1-γ antibodies are strongly associated with malignancy, with peak risk 3–5 years before and after disease onset. Characteristic cutaneous findings of anti-TIF1-γ positive dermatomyositis, including facial rash, V-neck and back rash, periungual telangiectasias, heliotrope rash, Gottron's sign, palatal patch, and diffuse photoerythema, are well documented. However, reticular rash, a rare manifestation as seen in this patient, expands the spectrum of cutaneous manifestations. Emerging evidence implicates type I interferon dysregulation in pathogenesis, and Janus kinase inhibitors might be of benefit to patients with refractory cutaneous dermatomyositis.

A 5-year-old migrant boy from Syria came to our clinic complaining of a worsening cough that had started about 6 months earlier. On clinical examination, he was found to be hyperpyrexic and tachypnoeic with sternal recessions and decreased air entry on his right side. Laboratory investigations showed a raised C-reactive protein level of 247 mg/L (normal value <5·0 mg/L) and a leucocytosis (28·4 × 109 per L) without eosinophilia. Chest x-ray showed a large, ill-defined, radiolucent, cavernous lesion in the right upper lobe with a radiopaque mass in its lower part (figure). Our initial differential diagnosis included a possible bacterial infection that had subsequently developed into an abscess, Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, or cystic echinococcosis. The patient was started on antibiotics—piperacillin and tazobactam initially, with linezolid added to cover any presumed infection with community-associated methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). A contrast-enhanced, chest CT scan (coronal reconstruction) showed a large cystic mass with a thick, contrast-enhancing wall in the right upper lobe (figure). A corresponding lung window CT scan reconstruction showed marked consolidation of the adjacent lung parenchyma, with curvilinear septa within the lesion—the so-called water-lily sign (figure). These findings were highly suggestive of a ruptured Echinococcus granulosus hydatid cyst in the right upper lobe of the lung.Microbiological examination of bronchial alveolar lavage samples grew Haemophilus influenzae but no MRSA. Linezolid was therefore stopped. Additionally, no evidence of mycobacterial infection was found. However, 1 week after admission, the initially negative serology for echinococcosis became strongly positive and the patient developed eosinophilia. Additional investigations found a solitary hydatid cyst in the patient's liver. He was therefore diagnosed with cystic echinococcosis with both pulmonary and hepatic manifestations. As the imaging and the seroconversion provided good evidence of recent cyst rupture, the risk of further spillage of the contents of a cyst was considered high, so the patient was started on anthelmintic therapy—oral albendazone—prior to surgical resection. The patient finally went home well on albendazole.
Acute rupture of pulmonary E granulosus cysts with or without superimposed bacterial infection can mimic other pulmonary infections. In the context of recent and continued migration of people from areas where the disease is endemic, it is important to consider this rare clinical entity in children and adults. Of note, serology is frequently negative even in the presence of large, non-ruptured hydatic cysts and the optimal time to start albendazole treatment remains uncertain.
