input:
A 5-year-old migrant boy from Syria came to our clinic complaining of a worsening cough that had started about 6 months earlier. On clinical examination, he was found to be hyperpyrexic and tachypnoeic with sternal recessions and decreased air entry on his right side. Laboratory investigations showed a raised C-reactive protein level of 247 mg/L (normal value <5·0 mg/L) and a leucocytosis (28·4 × 109 per L) without eosinophilia. Chest x-ray showed a large, ill-defined, radiolucent, cavernous lesion in the right upper lobe with a radiopaque mass in its lower part (figure). Our initial differential diagnosis included a possible bacterial infection that had subsequently developed into an abscess, Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, or cystic echinococcosis. The patient was started on antibiotics—piperacillin and tazobactam initially, with linezolid added to cover any presumed infection with community-associated methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). A contrast-enhanced, chest CT scan (coronal reconstruction) showed a large cystic mass with a thick, contrast-enhancing wall in the right upper lobe (figure). A corresponding lung window CT scan reconstruction showed marked consolidation of the adjacent lung parenchyma, with curvilinear septa within the lesion—the so-called water-lily sign (figure). These findings were highly suggestive of a ruptured Echinococcus granulosus hydatid cyst in the right upper lobe of the lung.Microbiological examination of bronchial alveolar lavage samples grew Haemophilus influenzae but no MRSA. Linezolid was therefore stopped. Additionally, no evidence of mycobacterial infection was found. However, 1 week after admission, the initially negative serology for echinococcosis became strongly positive and the patient developed eosinophilia. Additional investigations found a solitary hydatid cyst in the patient's liver. He was therefore diagnosed with cystic echinococcosis with both pulmonary and hepatic manifestations. As the imaging and the seroconversion provided good evidence of recent cyst rupture, the risk of further spillage of the contents of a cyst was considered high, so the patient was started on anthelmintic therapy—oral albendazone—prior to surgical resection. The patient finally went home well on albendazole.
Acute rupture of pulmonary E granulosus cysts with or without superimposed bacterial infection can mimic other pulmonary infections. In the context of recent and continued migration of people from areas where the disease is endemic, it is important to consider this rare clinical entity in children and adults. Of note, serology is frequently negative even in the presence of large, non-ruptured hydatic cysts and the optimal time to start albendazole treatment remains uncertain.

A 5-year-old migrant boy from Syria came to our clinic complaining of a worsening cough that had started about 6 months earlier. On clinical examination, he was found to be hyperpyrexic and tachypnoeic with sternal recessions and decreased air entry on his right side. Laboratory investigations showed a raised C-reactive protein level of 247 mg/L (normal value <5·0 mg/L) and a leucocytosis (28·4 × 109 per L) without eosinophilia. Chest x-ray showed a large, ill-defined, radiolucent, cavernous lesion in the right upper lobe with a radiopaque mass in its lower part (figure). Our initial differential diagnosis included a possible bacterial infection that had subsequently developed into an abscess, Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, or cystic echinococcosis. The patient was started on antibiotics—piperacillin and tazobactam initially, with linezolid added to cover any presumed infection with community-associated methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). A contrast-enhanced, chest CT scan (coronal reconstruction) showed a large cystic mass with a thick, contrast-enhancing wall in the right upper lobe (figure). A corresponding lung window CT scan reconstruction showed marked consolidation of the adjacent lung parenchyma, with curvilinear septa within the lesion—the so-called water-lily sign (figure). These findings were highly suggestive of a ruptured Echinococcus granulosus hydatid cyst in the right upper lobe of the lung.Microbiological examination of bronchial alveolar lavage samples grew Haemophilus influenzae but no MRSA. Linezolid was therefore stopped. Additionally, no evidence of mycobacterial infection was found. However, 1 week after admission, the initially negative serology for echinococcosis became strongly positive and the patient developed eosinophilia. Additional investigations found a solitary hydatid cyst in the patient's liver. He was therefore diagnosed with cystic echinococcosis with both pulmonary and hepatic manifestations. As the imaging and the seroconversion provided good evidence of recent cyst rupture, the risk of further spillage of the contents of a cyst was considered high, so the patient was started on anthelmintic therapy—oral albendazone—prior to surgical resection. The patient finally went home well on albendazole.
Acute rupture of pulmonary E granulosus cysts with or without superimposed bacterial infection can mimic other pulmonary infections. In the context of recent and continued migration of people from areas where the disease is endemic, it is important to consider this rare clinical entity in children and adults. Of note, serology is frequently negative even in the presence of large, non-ruptured hydatic cysts and the optimal time to start albendazole treatment remains uncertain.

input: A 44-year-old man presented with bloody diarrhoea and a non-healing, rapidly advancing, painful ulceration wound on his left foot. He had received empirical antibiotics for the previous 2 weeks, with no improvement. The patient had a history of ulcerative colitis, but he discontinued maintenance therapy. Physical examination revealed a large painful ulcer with an undermined border that was violet and gunmetal grey in colour; the extensor tendons were exposed (figure, A). Biopsy showed a dense infiltrate of neutrophils in the dermis, acanthosis of the overlying epidermis, and papillary dermal oedema with necrosis. Microbiological cultures and special staining for microorganisms were negative. A colonoscopy showed severe ulcerative colitis. The diagnosis of ulcerative pyoderma gangrenosum associated with ulcerative colitis was made. Treatment with infliximab was started and negative-pressure dressing was applied. We observed remission of intestinal symptoms and improvement of lesion after only one administration of infliximab (figure, B).Pyoderma gangrenosum is the second most common dermatological manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease after erythema nodosum. The lesions initially appear as single or multiple erythematous papules or pustules that are often preceded by trauma to the skin. They occur most commonly on the legs but can develop on any area of the body, including the abdominal wall adjacent to the stoma after colectomy or surgical scars. Subsequent necrosis of the dermis leads to the development of deep ulcerations, which contain purulent material that is usually sterile on culture. Pyoderma gangrenosum is usually diagnosed clinically based on the characteristic appearance of the lesions following exclusion of other possible skin diseases. Biopsy reveals non-specific findings consistent with a sterile abscess; it can be helpful to exclude other skin disorders. A biopsy could be indicated in patients without a history of pyoderma gangrenosum and in patients with established pyoderma gangrenosum who present with lesions with atypical features or lesions that fail to respond, as expected, to therapy. Biopsy should be accompanied by tissue culture (bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial) to exclude infection. Traditionally, the most commonly used drugs to manage pyoderma gangrenosum were systemic corticosteroids and ciclosporin. However, infliximab has changed the management of pyoderma gangrenosum; therefore, use of infliximab should be considered if a rapid response to corticosteroids cannot be achieved.

input: A 44-year-old man presented with bloody diarrhoea and a non-healing, rapidly advancing, painful ulceration wound on his left foot. He had received empirical antibiotics for the previous 2 weeks, with no improvement. The patient had a history of ulcerative colitis, but he discontinued maintenance therapy. Physical examination revealed a large painful ulcer with an undermined border that was violet and gunmetal grey in colour; the extensor tendons were exposed (figure, A). Biopsy showed a dense infiltrate of neutrophils in the dermis, acanthosis of the overlying epidermis, and papillary dermal oedema with necrosis. Microbiological cultures and special staining for microorganisms were negative. A colonoscopy showed severe ulcerative colitis. The diagnosis of ulcerative pyoderma gangrenosum associated with ulcerative colitis was made. Treatment with infliximab was started and negative-pressure dressing was applied. We observed remission of intestinal symptoms and improvement of lesion after only one administration of infliximab (figure, B).Pyoderma gangrenosum is the second most common dermatological manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease after erythema nodosum. The lesions initially appear as single or multiple erythematous papules or pustules that are often preceded by trauma to the skin. They occur most commonly on the legs but can develop on any area of the body, including the abdominal wall adjacent to the stoma after colectomy or surgical scars. Subsequent necrosis of the dermis leads to the development of deep ulcerations, which contain purulent material that is usually sterile on culture. Pyoderma gangrenosum is usually diagnosed clinically based on the characteristic appearance of the lesions following exclusion of other possible skin diseases. Biopsy reveals non-specific findings consistent with a sterile abscess; it can be helpful to exclude other skin disorders. A biopsy could be indicated in patients without a history of pyoderma gangrenosum and in patients with established pyoderma gangrenosum who present with lesions with atypical features or lesions that fail to respond, as expected, to therapy. Biopsy should be accompanied by tissue culture (bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial) to exclude infection. Traditionally, the most commonly used drugs to manage pyoderma gangrenosum were systemic corticosteroids and ciclosporin. However, infliximab has changed the management of pyoderma gangrenosum; therefore, use of infliximab should be considered if a rapid response to corticosteroids cannot be achieved.

A 64-year-old man hospitalised for observation after treatment with chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cells targeting the B-cell maturation antigen reported a 4-day history of indentations developing over the top of his head; he had not been involved in any recent trauma and he did not have any pain (figure).The patient had a history of refractory high-risk κ light chain multiple myeloma with known bone plasmacytomas in his skull and spine: 5 years ago, he was diagnosed with multiple myeloma, presenting with back pain. Imaging had shown compression fractures of T4, L3, and L5. Laboratory investigations had shown hypercalcaemia (14·4 mg/dL; normal range 8·8–10·2) and renal failure (serum creatinine concentration 2·04 mg/dL; normal range 0·74–1·35). A urine protein electrophoresis showed 623 mg per 24 h of urine with a monoclonal band (M-spike); serum free light chain ratio was greater than 1000 (normal range 0·26–1·65), and his baseline bone marrow biopsy showed 55% involvement by κ light chain restricted plasma cells with the presence of t(11;14) seen by fluorescent in-situ hybridisation. Since the initial presentation, the patient had received more than 4 lines of systemic therapy, which included a failed autologous stem-cell transplantation. We therefore felt he was a good candidate for autologous CAR T-cells.
On examination, we found the patient to be well; his vital signs were within normal limits. Over his calvarium, we found 2 depressions—one on the left frontal skull and the other on the right parietal skull—each approximately 20 mm × 30 mm. They were soft and non-pulsatile. While monitoring the depressions, we noticed that his myeloma-related laboratory tests improved.
A CT scan of the patient's head showed 2 lesions over the calvarium (figure), corresponding to the lesions previously noted at the time he was diagnosed with multiple myeloma. No intracranial extension, mass effect, or midline shift were seen; no new or enlarging lytic lesions had developed.
At follow-up 4 months post CAR T-cells, the patient reported continued improvement of his calvarium lesions with connective tissue. We plan to continue to monitor the patient periodically, hoping for additional clinical and radiographic improvement. Laboratory investigations have shown improvement of serological markers—including normal creatinine and calcium concentrations.
We believe that the soft tissue and bony component of the multiple myeloma lesions had reduced in size due to effective treatment of the myeloma, as the skull indentations developed shortly after the CAR T-cells were infused, which correlated with serological evidence of improvement in the myeloma markers.
As multiple myeloma is known to have a predilection to affect bone structures and novel cellular therapies are becoming more available, clinicians need to be aware of the potential effect of CAR T-cells in patients with skeletal involvement, as abnormalities may represent response to therapy instead of progression of disease.

A 64-year-old man hospitalised for observation after treatment with chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cells targeting the B-cell maturation antigen reported a 4-day history of indentations developing over the top of his head; he had not been involved in any recent trauma and he did not have any pain (figure).The patient had a history of refractory high-risk κ light chain multiple myeloma with known bone plasmacytomas in his skull and spine: 5 years ago, he was diagnosed with multiple myeloma, presenting with back pain. Imaging had shown compression fractures of T4, L3, and L5. Laboratory investigations had shown hypercalcaemia (14·4 mg/dL; normal range 8·8–10·2) and renal failure (serum creatinine concentration 2·04 mg/dL; normal range 0·74–1·35). A urine protein electrophoresis showed 623 mg per 24 h of urine with a monoclonal band (M-spike); serum free light chain ratio was greater than 1000 (normal range 0·26–1·65), and his baseline bone marrow biopsy showed 55% involvement by κ light chain restricted plasma cells with the presence of t(11;14) seen by fluorescent in-situ hybridisation. Since the initial presentation, the patient had received more than 4 lines of systemic therapy, which included a failed autologous stem-cell transplantation. We therefore felt he was a good candidate for autologous CAR T-cells.
On examination, we found the patient to be well; his vital signs were within normal limits. Over his calvarium, we found 2 depressions—one on the left frontal skull and the other on the right parietal skull—each approximately 20 mm × 30 mm. They were soft and non-pulsatile. While monitoring the depressions, we noticed that his myeloma-related laboratory tests improved.
A CT scan of the patient's head showed 2 lesions over the calvarium (figure), corresponding to the lesions previously noted at the time he was diagnosed with multiple myeloma. No intracranial extension, mass effect, or midline shift were seen; no new or enlarging lytic lesions had developed.
At follow-up 4 months post CAR T-cells, the patient reported continued improvement of his calvarium lesions with connective tissue. We plan to continue to monitor the patient periodically, hoping for additional clinical and radiographic improvement. Laboratory investigations have shown improvement of serological markers—including normal creatinine and calcium concentrations.
We believe that the soft tissue and bony component of the multiple myeloma lesions had reduced in size due to effective treatment of the myeloma, as the skull indentations developed shortly after the CAR T-cells were infused, which correlated with serological evidence of improvement in the myeloma markers.
As multiple myeloma is known to have a predilection to affect bone structures and novel cellular therapies are becoming more available, clinicians need to be aware of the potential effect of CAR T-cells in patients with skeletal involvement, as abnormalities may represent response to therapy instead of progression of disease.

A 64-year-old man hospitalised for observation after treatment with chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cells targeting the B-cell maturation antigen reported a 4-day history of indentations developing over the top of his head; he had not been involved in any recent trauma and he did not have any pain (figure).The patient had a history of refractory high-risk κ light chain multiple myeloma with known bone plasmacytomas in his skull and spine: 5 years ago, he was diagnosed with multiple myeloma, presenting with back pain. Imaging had shown compression fractures of T4, L3, and L5. Laboratory investigations had shown hypercalcaemia (14·4 mg/dL; normal range 8·8–10·2) and renal failure (serum creatinine concentration 2·04 mg/dL; normal range 0·74–1·35). A urine protein electrophoresis showed 623 mg per 24 h of urine with a monoclonal band (M-spike); serum free light chain ratio was greater than 1000 (normal range 0·26–1·65), and his baseline bone marrow biopsy showed 55% involvement by κ light chain restricted plasma cells with the presence of t(11;14) seen by fluorescent in-situ hybridisation. Since the initial presentation, the patient had received more than 4 lines of systemic therapy, which included a failed autologous stem-cell transplantation. We therefore felt he was a good candidate for autologous CAR T-cells.
On examination, we found the patient to be well; his vital signs were within normal limits. Over his calvarium, we found 2 depressions—one on the left frontal skull and the other on the right parietal skull—each approximately 20 mm × 30 mm. They were soft and non-pulsatile. While monitoring the depressions, we noticed that his myeloma-related laboratory tests improved.
A CT scan of the patient's head showed 2 lesions over the calvarium (figure), corresponding to the lesions previously noted at the time he was diagnosed with multiple myeloma. No intracranial extension, mass effect, or midline shift were seen; no new or enlarging lytic lesions had developed.
At follow-up 4 months post CAR T-cells, the patient reported continued improvement of his calvarium lesions with connective tissue. We plan to continue to monitor the patient periodically, hoping for additional clinical and radiographic improvement. Laboratory investigations have shown improvement of serological markers—including normal creatinine and calcium concentrations.
We believe that the soft tissue and bony component of the multiple myeloma lesions had reduced in size due to effective treatment of the myeloma, as the skull indentations developed shortly after the CAR T-cells were infused, which correlated with serological evidence of improvement in the myeloma markers.
As multiple myeloma is known to have a predilection to affect bone structures and novel cellular therapies are becoming more available, clinicians need to be aware of the potential effect of CAR T-cells in patients with skeletal involvement, as abnormalities may represent response to therapy instead of progression of disease.

Under antiretroviral therapy, the HIV viral load was below the limit of detection, and his CD4+ T-cell count was 802 cells per μL. Given the rising number of monkeypox cases in Europe at that time and the patient's history of unprotected sexual contact with a man 1 week before symptom onset, an infection with monkeypox virus was suspected. Specimens from two different skin lesions yielded a positive PCR result (cycle threshold values of 20 and 21) for monkeypox virus. The patient was discharged and self-isolated.11 days later a follow-up examination was scheduled, the rash and lymphadenopathy had completely resolved, but a marked swelling of the right knee was noted (figure B). Arthrocentesis was performed, resulting in aspiration of 60 mL of cloudy synovial fluid. Analysis of the synovial fluid showed a cell count of 16 127 cells per μL with 88·5% mononuclear cells (lymphocytes) and 11·5% neutrophil granulocytes. The synovial fluid PCR yielded a positive result for monkeypox virus (cycle threshold value of 27). Laboratory test results were unremarkable apart from a slightly elevated C-reactive protein of 18 mg/L.
Bacterial cultures and broad-range PCR of synovial fluid, serological testing for rheumatoid factor, anti-citrullinated protein antibodies and antinuclear antibodies, human leukocyte antigen B27, and PCR for Lyme disease were all negative. A second arthrocentesis was needed 8 days later due to reoccurrence of effusion. PCR of synovial fluid was again positive for monkeypox virus (cycle threshold value of 33), whereas PCR of whole-blood was negative for monkeypox virus. MRI showed synovitis, joint effusion, and a marked oedema of the medial femoral condyle with a subchondral demarcation zone of 1 cm, compatible with the diagnosis of arthritis and osteomyelitis (figure C–E). Treatment with non-steroidal-anti-inflammatory drugs led to improvement of arthralgia and swelling within 3 weeks.
Viruses are common triggers of arthritis, but viral bone infection has only rarely been reported. However, viral osteomyelitis was a typical complication of smallpox. Referred to as osteomyelitis variolosa, it affected 2–5% of children and 0·25–0·50% of all patients infected with smallpox. No cases of monkeypox-related arthritis or osteomyelitis have been described in the literature so far. Considering that variola virus and monkeypox virus are closely related, we believe that monkeypox virus might lead to arthritis and potentially osteomyelitis.

input: A 44-year-old man presented with bloody diarrhoea and a non-healing, rapidly advancing, painful ulceration wound on his left foot. He had received empirical antibiotics for the previous 2 weeks, with no improvement. The patient had a history of ulcerative colitis, but he discontinued maintenance therapy. Physical examination revealed a large painful ulcer with an undermined border that was violet and gunmetal grey in colour; the extensor tendons were exposed (figure, A). Biopsy showed a dense infiltrate of neutrophils in the dermis, acanthosis of the overlying epidermis, and papillary dermal oedema with necrosis. Microbiological cultures and special staining for microorganisms were negative. A colonoscopy showed severe ulcerative colitis. The diagnosis of ulcerative pyoderma gangrenosum associated with ulcerative colitis was made. Treatment with infliximab was started and negative-pressure dressing was applied. We observed remission of intestinal symptoms and improvement of lesion after only one administration of infliximab (figure, B).Pyoderma gangrenosum is the second most common dermatological manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease after erythema nodosum. The lesions initially appear as single or multiple erythematous papules or pustules that are often preceded by trauma to the skin. They occur most commonly on the legs but can develop on any area of the body, including the abdominal wall adjacent to the stoma after colectomy or surgical scars. Subsequent necrosis of the dermis leads to the development of deep ulcerations, which contain purulent material that is usually sterile on culture. Pyoderma gangrenosum is usually diagnosed clinically based on the characteristic appearance of the lesions following exclusion of other possible skin diseases. Biopsy reveals non-specific findings consistent with a sterile abscess; it can be helpful to exclude other skin disorders. A biopsy could be indicated in patients without a history of pyoderma gangrenosum and in patients with established pyoderma gangrenosum who present with lesions with atypical features or lesions that fail to respond, as expected, to therapy. Biopsy should be accompanied by tissue culture (bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial) to exclude infection. Traditionally, the most commonly used drugs to manage pyoderma gangrenosum were systemic corticosteroids and ciclosporin. However, infliximab has changed the management of pyoderma gangrenosum; therefore, use of infliximab should be considered if a rapid response to corticosteroids cannot be achieved.

A 31-year-old HIV-positive man presented to the hospital on June 30, 2022, with a vesicular rash (figure A), perianal lesions, swollen inguinal lymph nodes, and arthralgia of the right knee. Under antiretroviral therapy, the HIV viral load was below the limit of detection, and his CD4+ T-cell count was 802 cells per μL. Given the rising number of monkeypox cases in Europe at that time and the patient's history of unprotected sexual contact with a man 1 week before symptom onset, an infection with monkeypox virus was suspected. Specimens from two different skin lesions yielded a positive PCR result (cycle threshold values of 20 and 21) for monkeypox virus. The patient was discharged and self-isolated.11 days later a follow-up examination was scheduled, the rash and lymphadenopathy had completely resolved, but a marked swelling of the right knee was noted (figure B). Arthrocentesis was performed, resulting in aspiration of 60 mL of cloudy synovial fluid. Analysis of the synovial fluid showed a cell count of 16 127 cells per μL with 88·5% mononuclear cells (lymphocytes) and 11·5% neutrophil granulocytes. The synovial fluid PCR yielded a positive result for monkeypox virus (cycle threshold value of 27). Laboratory test results were unremarkable apart from a slightly elevated C-reactive protein of 18 mg/L.
Bacterial cultures and broad-range PCR of synovial fluid, serological testing for rheumatoid factor, anti-citrullinated protein antibodies and antinuclear antibodies, human leukocyte antigen B27, and PCR for Lyme disease were all negative. A second arthrocentesis was needed 8 days later due to reoccurrence of effusion. PCR of synovial fluid was again positive for monkeypox virus (cycle threshold value of 33), whereas PCR of whole-blood was negative for monkeypox virus. MRI showed synovitis, joint effusion, and a marked oedema of the medial femoral condyle with a subchondral demarcation zone of 1 cm, compatible with the diagnosis of arthritis and osteomyelitis (figure C–E). Treatment with non-steroidal-anti-inflammatory drugs led to improvement of arthralgia and swelling within 3 weeks.
Viruses are common triggers of arthritis, but viral bone infection has only rarely been reported. However, viral osteomyelitis was a typical complication of smallpox. Referred to as osteomyelitis variolosa, it affected 2–5% of children and 0·25–0·50% of all patients infected with smallpox. No cases of monkeypox-related arthritis or osteomyelitis have been described in the literature so far. Considering that variola virus and monkeypox virus are closely related, we believe that monkeypox virus might lead to arthritis and potentially osteomyelitis.

input:
A 31-year-old HIV-positive man presented to the hospital on June 30, 2022, with a vesicular rash (figure A), perianal lesions, swollen inguinal lymph nodes, and arthralgia of the right knee. Under antiretroviral therapy, the HIV viral load was below the limit of detection, and his CD4+ T-cell count was 802 cells per μL. Given the rising number of monkeypox cases in Europe at that time and the patient's history of unprotected sexual contact with a man 1 week before symptom onset, an infection with monkeypox virus was suspected. Specimens from two different skin lesions yielded a positive PCR result (cycle threshold values of 20 and 21) for monkeypox virus. The patient was discharged and self-isolated.11 days later a follow-up examination was scheduled, the rash and lymphadenopathy had completely resolved, but a marked swelling of the right knee was noted (figure B). Arthrocentesis was performed, resulting in aspiration of 60 mL of cloudy synovial fluid. Analysis of the synovial fluid showed a cell count of 16 127 cells per μL with 88·5% mononuclear cells (lymphocytes) and 11·5% neutrophil granulocytes. The synovial fluid PCR yielded a positive result for monkeypox virus (cycle threshold value of 27). Laboratory test results were unremarkable apart from a slightly elevated C-reactive protein of 18 mg/L.
Bacterial cultures and broad-range PCR of synovial fluid, serological testing for rheumatoid factor, anti-citrullinated protein antibodies and antinuclear antibodies, human leukocyte antigen B27, and PCR for Lyme disease were all negative. A second arthrocentesis was needed 8 days later due to reoccurrence of effusion. PCR of synovial fluid was again positive for monkeypox virus (cycle threshold value of 33), whereas PCR of whole-blood was negative for monkeypox virus. MRI showed synovitis, joint effusion, and a marked oedema of the medial femoral condyle with a subchondral demarcation zone of 1 cm, compatible with the diagnosis of arthritis and osteomyelitis (figure C–E). Treatment with non-steroidal-anti-inflammatory drugs led to improvement of arthralgia and swelling within 3 weeks.
Viruses are common triggers of arthritis, but viral bone infection has only rarely been reported. However, viral osteomyelitis was a typical complication of smallpox. Referred to as osteomyelitis variolosa, it affected 2–5% of children and 0·25–0·50% of all patients infected with smallpox. No cases of monkeypox-related arthritis or osteomyelitis have been described in the literature so far. Considering that variola virus and monkeypox virus are closely related, we believe that monkeypox virus might lead to arthritis and potentially osteomyelitis.

A 57-year-old native English-speaking man attended our department with a 5-week history of progressively becoming unable to understand words—despite hearing them. Much to his distress, he also reported hearing a constant noise which he said sounded “like trucks”.18 months earlier, the patient had presented with dysphagia due to an inoperable adenocarcinoma in the oesophagogastric junction which had been treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy; he had no other relevant medical history and no previous hearing difficulties.
On examination we found the patient to be healthy with normal vital signs. Left and right external auditory canals were normal with intact and mobile tympanic membranes. We found he could identify and distinguish syllables, rhythms, voices, musical instruments, and individual environmental sounds even without visual cues, but he could not discern their content or structure, describing what he heard as being “all mushed together”. He reported no difficulties with reading, writing, or cognition. He also had vertical diplopia on downward gaze and to either side—indicating mild bilateral fourth nerve palsies; he had normal pupils, eyelids, convergence, and vertical eye movements.
While pure-tone audiometry showed only a mild to moderate bilaterally, almost symmetrical, sensorineural hearing loss (figure), he was unable to understand speech in either ear, even at 100 decibels hearing level (dB HL)—which is as loud as a nightclub (figure). T1-weighted sagittal MRI showed a contrast-enhancing 20 mm mass in the quadrigeminal cistern compressing the midbrain tectum and including both inferior colliculi (figure). The lesion—which we assumed to be metastatic—was treated with stereotactic radiotherapy.
Since his pure-tone audiometric abnormalities—a mild to moderate pure-tone hearing loss—could not account for his profound speech comprehension impairment, we made the diagnosis of word deafness due to the mass compressing the inferior colliculi. We were able to teach the patient and his family to communicate using a smartphone voice-to-text translator.
3 months later, a repeat MRI showed that the mass had reduced in size and enhancement. We repeated the pure-tone audiometry which was essentially unchanged: speech comprehension was now normal with his left ear and mildly impaired in his right at 40 db HL—like in a quiet library (figure). The patient died 2 months later.
Pure tones used in audiometry are simple sounds without the complex structure of speech, which has rapid, unpredictable fluctuations in frequency, amplitude, and timing. The cochlea converts sound into neural signals that ascend from the cochlear nuclei, via the lateral lemnisci, to the inferior colliculi and then to the medial geniculate nuclei and on to the auditory cortex.
The auditory pathway processes sound timing and frequency extracting features that indicate what and where the sound is. The inferior colliculi begin to integrate the features that create an auditory object: the assignment of a sound to a specific source.
A general inability to perceive and identify the nature of any sounds is called auditory agnosia; although patients can hear pure tones, all complex sounds lose meaning, such that they cannot recognise or understand speech, music, or environmental sounds. The usual cause is bilateral temporal lobe lesions. A specific inability to understand speech, despite intact hearing of pure tones and intact language comprehension, is called verbal auditory agnosia (or word deafness); only speech sounds lose meaning, probably due to impaired processing of their rapidly changing acoustic content. The usual cause is bilateral lesions of the superior temporal gyrus or their projections, or—like our case—a single brainstem lesion of the inferior colliculi.
Testing hearing with speech, as well as with pure tones, evaluates the full bandwidth of the auditory pathway. It is important to bear in mind that if patients complain that they can’t hear, sometimes the problem is not in the ear (video).

A 57-year-old native English-speaking man attended our department with a 5-week history of progressively becoming unable to understand words—despite hearing them. Much to his distress, he also reported hearing a constant noise which he said sounded “like trucks”.18 months earlier, the patient had presented with dysphagia due to an inoperable adenocarcinoma in the oesophagogastric junction which had been treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy; he had no other relevant medical history and no previous hearing difficulties.
On examination we found the patient to be healthy with normal vital signs. Left and right external auditory canals were normal with intact and mobile tympanic membranes. We found he could identify and distinguish syllables, rhythms, voices, musical instruments, and individual environmental sounds even without visual cues, but he could not discern their content or structure, describing what he heard as being “all mushed together”. He reported no difficulties with reading, writing, or cognition. He also had vertical diplopia on downward gaze and to either side—indicating mild bilateral fourth nerve palsies; he had normal pupils, eyelids, convergence, and vertical eye movements.
While pure-tone audiometry showed only a mild to moderate bilaterally, almost symmetrical, sensorineural hearing loss (figure), he was unable to understand speech in either ear, even at 100 decibels hearing level (dB HL)—which is as loud as a nightclub (figure). T1-weighted sagittal MRI showed a contrast-enhancing 20 mm mass in the quadrigeminal cistern compressing the midbrain tectum and including both inferior colliculi (figure). The lesion—which we assumed to be metastatic—was treated with stereotactic radiotherapy.
Since his pure-tone audiometric abnormalities—a mild to moderate pure-tone hearing loss—could not account for his profound speech comprehension impairment, we made the diagnosis of word deafness due to the mass compressing the inferior colliculi. We were able to teach the patient and his family to communicate using a smartphone voice-to-text translator.
3 months later, a repeat MRI showed that the mass had reduced in size and enhancement. We repeated the pure-tone audiometry which was essentially unchanged: speech comprehension was now normal with his left ear and mildly impaired in his right at 40 db HL—like in a quiet library (figure). The patient died 2 months later.
Pure tones used in audiometry are simple sounds without the complex structure of speech, which has rapid, unpredictable fluctuations in frequency, amplitude, and timing. The cochlea converts sound into neural signals that ascend from the cochlear nuclei, via the lateral lemnisci, to the inferior colliculi and then to the medial geniculate nuclei and on to the auditory cortex.
The auditory pathway processes sound timing and frequency extracting features that indicate what and where the sound is. The inferior colliculi begin to integrate the features that create an auditory object: the assignment of a sound to a specific source.
A general inability to perceive and identify the nature of any sounds is called auditory agnosia; although patients can hear pure tones, all complex sounds lose meaning, such that they cannot recognise or understand speech, music, or environmental sounds. The usual cause is bilateral temporal lobe lesions. A specific inability to understand speech, despite intact hearing of pure tones and intact language comprehension, is called verbal auditory agnosia (or word deafness); only speech sounds lose meaning, probably due to impaired processing of their rapidly changing acoustic content. The usual cause is bilateral lesions of the superior temporal gyrus or their projections, or—like our case—a single brainstem lesion of the inferior colliculi.
Testing hearing with speech, as well as with pure tones, evaluates the full bandwidth of the auditory pathway. It is important to bear in mind that if patients complain that they can’t hear, sometimes the problem is not in the ear (video).

A 17-year-old German student with acute abdominal pain attended a regional hospital in northern Germany. During interview, he said that 2 weeks earlier his ejaculate had changed to a yellowish brown colour. Laboratory analysis showed leucocytosis (21·9 × 109 per L) with a marked eosinophilia (78%, 15·3 × 109 per L) and slightly elevated liver enzymes (alanine aminotransferase 101 U/L). An acute appendicitis was suspected and laparoscopic appendectomy was performed.Unexpectedly, intraoperative macroscopic inspection of the liver showed raised white spots on its surface (figure). A biopsy of the liver was done and necrotic granulomas with mainly eosinophils were seen.
A CT scan of the thorax and abdomen after the appendectomy showed nodular pulmonary infiltrates (figure) and hepatomegaly without any specific lesions. The patient was then referred to our hospital, where in a further interview, he said he had recently completed a 2-month trip to Malawi, where he had frequently been in contact with the fresh water in Lake Malawi; the last time was 5 months before the onset of his symptoms.
We diagnosed Schistosoma haematobium using multiplex real-time PCR of the ejaculate and blood. Examination of the ejaculate under light microscope showed vital S haematobium eggs (figure). Re-examination of histopathological samples from the appendix and the liver (figure) showed granulomas with a predominance of eosinophils surrounding S haematobium eggs.
The antiparasitic drug praziquantel was administered at a dose of 40 mg/kg, orally, for 3 days and the patient made a full clinical recovery.
Schistosomiasis affects more than 250 million people worldwide. Global travel and migration have led to an increase in cases presenting in non-endemic regions. The lengthy delay between exposure and the development of non-specific symptoms means that the disease is commonly misdiagnosed at initial presentation. The discovery of macroscopic white spots on the liver and the accidental detection of S haematobium eggs on liver biopsy are uncommon presentations of S haematobium.
When taking a medical history, questions about travel and migration are—as always—of paramount importance.

input:
A 17-year-old German student with acute abdominal pain attended a regional hospital in northern Germany. During interview, he said that 2 weeks earlier his ejaculate had changed to a yellowish brown colour. Laboratory analysis showed leucocytosis (21·9 × 109 per L) with a marked eosinophilia (78%, 15·3 × 109 per L) and slightly elevated liver enzymes (alanine aminotransferase 101 U/L). An acute appendicitis was suspected and laparoscopic appendectomy was performed.Unexpectedly, intraoperative macroscopic inspection of the liver showed raised white spots on its surface (figure). A biopsy of the liver was done and necrotic granulomas with mainly eosinophils were seen.
A CT scan of the thorax and abdomen after the appendectomy showed nodular pulmonary infiltrates (figure) and hepatomegaly without any specific lesions. The patient was then referred to our hospital, where in a further interview, he said he had recently completed a 2-month trip to Malawi, where he had frequently been in contact with the fresh water in Lake Malawi; the last time was 5 months before the onset of his symptoms.
We diagnosed Schistosoma haematobium using multiplex real-time PCR of the ejaculate and blood. Examination of the ejaculate under light microscope showed vital S haematobium eggs (figure). Re-examination of histopathological samples from the appendix and the liver (figure) showed granulomas with a predominance of eosinophils surrounding S haematobium eggs.
The antiparasitic drug praziquantel was administered at a dose of 40 mg/kg, orally, for 3 days and the patient made a full clinical recovery.
Schistosomiasis affects more than 250 million people worldwide. Global travel and migration have led to an increase in cases presenting in non-endemic regions. The lengthy delay between exposure and the development of non-specific symptoms means that the disease is commonly misdiagnosed at initial presentation. The discovery of macroscopic white spots on the liver and the accidental detection of S haematobium eggs on liver biopsy are uncommon presentations of S haematobium.
When taking a medical history, questions about travel and migration are—as always—of paramount importance.

input:
A 17-year-old German student with acute abdominal pain attended a regional hospital in northern Germany. During interview, he said that 2 weeks earlier his ejaculate had changed to a yellowish brown colour. Laboratory analysis showed leucocytosis (21·9 × 109 per L) with a marked eosinophilia (78%, 15·3 × 109 per L) and slightly elevated liver enzymes (alanine aminotransferase 101 U/L). An acute appendicitis was suspected and laparoscopic appendectomy was performed.Unexpectedly, intraoperative macroscopic inspection of the liver showed raised white spots on its surface (figure). A biopsy of the liver was done and necrotic granulomas with mainly eosinophils were seen.
A CT scan of the thorax and abdomen after the appendectomy showed nodular pulmonary infiltrates (figure) and hepatomegaly without any specific lesions. The patient was then referred to our hospital, where in a further interview, he said he had recently completed a 2-month trip to Malawi, where he had frequently been in contact with the fresh water in Lake Malawi; the last time was 5 months before the onset of his symptoms.
We diagnosed Schistosoma haematobium using multiplex real-time PCR of the ejaculate and blood. Examination of the ejaculate under light microscope showed vital S haematobium eggs (figure). Re-examination of histopathological samples from the appendix and the liver (figure) showed granulomas with a predominance of eosinophils surrounding S haematobium eggs.
The antiparasitic drug praziquantel was administered at a dose of 40 mg/kg, orally, for 3 days and the patient made a full clinical recovery.
Schistosomiasis affects more than 250 million people worldwide. Global travel and migration have led to an increase in cases presenting in non-endemic regions. The lengthy delay between exposure and the development of non-specific symptoms means that the disease is commonly misdiagnosed at initial presentation. The discovery of macroscopic white spots on the liver and the accidental detection of S haematobium eggs on liver biopsy are uncommon presentations of S haematobium.
When taking a medical history, questions about travel and migration are—as always—of paramount importance.

A 50-year-old man attended our specialised clinic reporting swelling, paraesthesia, discolouration, and fatigue in both arms while doing physical activity. The patient said the problem was particularly bad when lifting objects above his shoulders; his right side was worse than his left.Notably in his medical history, the patient, aged 32 years, was diagnosed with deep venous thrombosis in his left arm which developed after a period of strenuous physical activity; lifelong anticoagulant treatment was initiated at that time and he was switched to apixaban 3 months before we saw him. Also, aged 46 years, he had a further thrombosis in his right subclavian vein; it was successfully treated with thrombolysis followed by 2 years of fenprocoumon. Thrombophilia screening was negative, and a CT scan found no predisposing factors for thrombosis and no skeletal anomalies—including cervical ribs or anomalies of the clavicular bones. Additionally, no soft tissue abnormalities were identified. After the second episode, the treating physicians felt that both thromboses were primary—or spontaneous—since no trauma had been involved and the first episode had developed after vigorous activity.
Examination of the patient at our specialist centre found him to be fit and healthy looking; his heart rate was 81 beats per min and regular, and his blood pressure was 127/72 mm Hg. A cardiovascular examination found no murmurs or gallops and intact radial and ulnar pulses. Neurological examination was normal; we found no swelling, skin discolouration, or other evidence of venous obstruction at rest. The Eden test—or military brace test—provoked his complaints and both cephalic veins became distended.
An x-ray of the thoracic aperture showed no cervical ribs or bony anomalies of the first rib; venography in four positions showed no abnormalities at the costoclavicular junctions in the neutral position, abduction, or adduction. In a military attitude position, significant effacement of the veins was seen at the site of the pectoralis minor on both sides—indicating thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS; figure).
A 2-stage trans-axillary pectoral minor tenectomy was done and the patient immediately reported relief of his symptoms. Postoperative venography showed no further compression (appendix) and the anticoagulation was stopped. 1 year after surgery, the patient was asymptomatic—even during strenuous activities.
TOS disorders result from compression of either nerves, veins, or arteries in the thoracic outlet. Venous TOS is caused by repetitive extrinsic compression and resultant injury to the subclavian vein at the bony thoracic outlet. Symptoms in the arms are caused by intermittent positional obstruction without thrombosis—known as McCleery syndrome—or with acute or chronic thrombosis—known as effort thrombosis or Paget-von Schröetter syndrome. Compression of the subclavian vein usually occurs at the junction of the first rib and the clavicle: costoclavicular junction. Obstruction by the pectoralis minor muscle at the retropectoralis space—as seen in our patient—is relatively rare.
Patients with positional intermittent subclavian vein obstruction will present with episodic arm discolouration and swelling, usually elicited by either exercise or arm elevation; venograms can be normal at rest. Investigation using venography—rather than CT or MRI—we believe, is preferable since it facilitates communication between the radiologist and patient making it easier to elicit symptoms, and at the same time, observing the compression. If dynamic positioning shows no compression at the costoclavicular junction, the possibility of obstruction by the pectoralis minor muscle must be considered (video).

A 50-year-old man attended our specialised clinic reporting swelling, paraesthesia, discolouration, and fatigue in both arms while doing physical activity. The patient said the problem was particularly bad when lifting objects above his shoulders; his right side was worse than his left.Notably in his medical history, the patient, aged 32 years, was diagnosed with deep venous thrombosis in his left arm which developed after a period of strenuous physical activity; lifelong anticoagulant treatment was initiated at that time and he was switched to apixaban 3 months before we saw him. Also, aged 46 years, he had a further thrombosis in his right subclavian vein; it was successfully treated with thrombolysis followed by 2 years of fenprocoumon. Thrombophilia screening was negative, and a CT scan found no predisposing factors for thrombosis and no skeletal anomalies—including cervical ribs or anomalies of the clavicular bones. Additionally, no soft tissue abnormalities were identified. After the second episode, the treating physicians felt that both thromboses were primary—or spontaneous—since no trauma had been involved and the first episode had developed after vigorous activity.
Examination of the patient at our specialist centre found him to be fit and healthy looking; his heart rate was 81 beats per min and regular, and his blood pressure was 127/72 mm Hg. A cardiovascular examination found no murmurs or gallops and intact radial and ulnar pulses. Neurological examination was normal; we found no swelling, skin discolouration, or other evidence of venous obstruction at rest. The Eden test—or military brace test—provoked his complaints and both cephalic veins became distended.
An x-ray of the thoracic aperture showed no cervical ribs or bony anomalies of the first rib; venography in four positions showed no abnormalities at the costoclavicular junctions in the neutral position, abduction, or adduction. In a military attitude position, significant effacement of the veins was seen at the site of the pectoralis minor on both sides—indicating thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS; figure).
A 2-stage trans-axillary pectoral minor tenectomy was done and the patient immediately reported relief of his symptoms. Postoperative venography showed no further compression (appendix) and the anticoagulation was stopped. 1 year after surgery, the patient was asymptomatic—even during strenuous activities.
TOS disorders result from compression of either nerves, veins, or arteries in the thoracic outlet. Venous TOS is caused by repetitive extrinsic compression and resultant injury to the subclavian vein at the bony thoracic outlet. Symptoms in the arms are caused by intermittent positional obstruction without thrombosis—known as McCleery syndrome—or with acute or chronic thrombosis—known as effort thrombosis or Paget-von Schröetter syndrome. Compression of the subclavian vein usually occurs at the junction of the first rib and the clavicle: costoclavicular junction. Obstruction by the pectoralis minor muscle at the retropectoralis space—as seen in our patient—is relatively rare.
Patients with positional intermittent subclavian vein obstruction will present with episodic arm discolouration and swelling, usually elicited by either exercise or arm elevation; venograms can be normal at rest. Investigation using venography—rather than CT or MRI—we believe, is preferable since it facilitates communication between the radiologist and patient making it easier to elicit symptoms, and at the same time, observing the compression. If dynamic positioning shows no compression at the costoclavicular junction, the possibility of obstruction by the pectoralis minor muscle must be considered (video).

A 50-year-old man attended our specialised clinic reporting swelling, paraesthesia, discolouration, and fatigue in both arms while doing physical activity. The patient said the problem was particularly bad when lifting objects above his shoulders; his right side was worse than his left.Notably in his medical history, the patient, aged 32 years, was diagnosed with deep venous thrombosis in his left arm which developed after a period of strenuous physical activity; lifelong anticoagulant treatment was initiated at that time and he was switched to apixaban 3 months before we saw him. Also, aged 46 years, he had a further thrombosis in his right subclavian vein; it was successfully treated with thrombolysis followed by 2 years of fenprocoumon. Thrombophilia screening was negative, and a CT scan found no predisposing factors for thrombosis and no skeletal anomalies—including cervical ribs or anomalies of the clavicular bones. Additionally, no soft tissue abnormalities were identified. After the second episode, the treating physicians felt that both thromboses were primary—or spontaneous—since no trauma had been involved and the first episode had developed after vigorous activity.
Examination of the patient at our specialist centre found him to be fit and healthy looking; his heart rate was 81 beats per min and regular, and his blood pressure was 127/72 mm Hg. A cardiovascular examination found no murmurs or gallops and intact radial and ulnar pulses. Neurological examination was normal; we found no swelling, skin discolouration, or other evidence of venous obstruction at rest. The Eden test—or military brace test—provoked his complaints and both cephalic veins became distended.
An x-ray of the thoracic aperture showed no cervical ribs or bony anomalies of the first rib; venography in four positions showed no abnormalities at the costoclavicular junctions in the neutral position, abduction, or adduction. In a military attitude position, significant effacement of the veins was seen at the site of the pectoralis minor on both sides—indicating thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS; figure).
A 2-stage trans-axillary pectoral minor tenectomy was done and the patient immediately reported relief of his symptoms. Postoperative venography showed no further compression (appendix) and the anticoagulation was stopped. 1 year after surgery, the patient was asymptomatic—even during strenuous activities.
TOS disorders result from compression of either nerves, veins, or arteries in the thoracic outlet. Venous TOS is caused by repetitive extrinsic compression and resultant injury to the subclavian vein at the bony thoracic outlet. Symptoms in the arms are caused by intermittent positional obstruction without thrombosis—known as McCleery syndrome—or with acute or chronic thrombosis—known as effort thrombosis or Paget-von Schröetter syndrome. Compression of the subclavian vein usually occurs at the junction of the first rib and the clavicle: costoclavicular junction. Obstruction by the pectoralis minor muscle at the retropectoralis space—as seen in our patient—is relatively rare.
Patients with positional intermittent subclavian vein obstruction will present with episodic arm discolouration and swelling, usually elicited by either exercise or arm elevation; venograms can be normal at rest. Investigation using venography—rather than CT or MRI—we believe, is preferable since it facilitates communication between the radiologist and patient making it easier to elicit symptoms, and at the same time, observing the compression. If dynamic positioning shows no compression at the costoclavicular junction, the possibility of obstruction by the pectoralis minor muscle must be considered (video).

A 43-year-old Australian-born, white man was referred to our unit because of increasing pain in both his ankles. The pain had developed approximately 7 days earlier. 3 days before the pain started, he had been admitted to hospital with cellulitis of his upper arm; he had been treated for septicaemia and acute kidney injury caused by an infection with Streptococcus pyogenes.In his medical history, the patient had been diagnosed with X-linked phosphataemia as a child; he had a family history of the disease, an Arnold-Chiari I malformation, and been treated with 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) and phosphate supplements, which he stopped taking from early adulthood. The patient had also been previously treated successfully with interferon for a hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection when he was 35 years old.
On examination we found moderate, bilateral ankle effusions, pain on both active and passive movement of the joints and marked bone deformity of his feet—he had pes planus and hypertrophic growth of the midfoot region. He also had tenderness at the plantar fascial insertions but no gouty tophi.
x-rays of his feet showed significant heterotrophic ossification of the entheses of all hind and midfoot bones (figure) and fluid analysis from an ankle joint aspirate showed monosodium urate crystals.
We therefore attributed his symptoms to a gout flare precipitated by acute kidney injury and septicaemia. We treated him with colchicine and the pain reduced; we later confirmed that the gout flare had resolved with a dual-energy CT scan that showed no urate crystals. Despite the negative finding on the dual-energy CT scan, the patient continued to experience arthralgia in his ankles. We carried out further investigations to clarify the additional, underlying aetiology—namely, the X-linked hypophosphataemia. The serum phosphate concentration was low (0·63 mmol/L; normal 0·75–1·50) and the calcitriol concentration was also low (19 pmol/L; normal 48–190); additional investigations were normal (appendix). CT scans of the patient's feet, ankles, and pelvis showed extensive enthesopathy (figure).
X-linked hypophosphataemia is a rare disorder often identified in childhood. Problems arise from inactivating mutations of the phosphate regulating endopeptidase homolog, X-linked (PHEX) gene. Hypophosphataemia is caused by poor absorption of phosphate in the intestine and impaired renal tubular reabsorption, with normal serum calcium, parathyroid hormone, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels. The calcitriol is often low or normal in X-linked hypophosphataemia: findings that would be unexpected in cases where there is an increased level of calcitriol.
Patients have a range of medical problems depending on age. In children, problems include delayed and disproportionate growth, craniosynostosis, and rickets. In adults, problems include inappropriate mineralisation of fibrocartilage—tendons insert into bone leading to the development of spurs or enthesophytes, which results in joint stiffness and pain or enthesopathy—as in our patient. Adult patients mainly complain of arthralgia of the knees, hip, and back. Traditional treatment with oral phosphate and calcitriol may improve the rate of growth and mineralisation in childhood but fails to stop the progressive enthesopathy and arthropathy found in adulthood. Arthralgia may develop because of degenerative arthropathy which is a consequence of the progressive enthesopathy altering the architecture and mechanics of the foot.
Enthesopathy can occur in psoriatic arthritis, heavy metal exposure, skeletal fluorosis, hyperparathyroidism, and other heritable forms of hypophosphataemia. HCV-related osteosclerosis—which was included in the differential diagnoses in this case—can cause bone pain; however, it is not associated with enthesopathy and is characterised by accelerated bone turnover (video).

A 2-year-old boy presented for severe frostbite after being outside on a cold day (mean temperature –18°C). The child had reportedly spent 20–30 minutes outside and was found without gloves. Eight fingers (1–5 on the right hand, and 1, 2, and 5 on the left hand) first appeared pale, then developed severe blisters. He was admitted for wound care, surgical debridement of necrotic skin, and pain control. At first, radiographs of the hands were typical (appendix). The patient was discharged home after 2 weeks, following a favourable evolution. 1 year later, he presented with widened interphalangeal joints in the eight fingers affected by frostbite. On x-ray, there was substantial damage to the metaphyses and epiphyses (figure A). Conservative treatment (occupational therapy and splinting) was started. During follow up, joint damage progressed to deformity and growth restrictions in the affected fingers (appendix). At the age of 17 years, there is substantial joint and bone damage, finger shortening, and nail dystrophy in the eight fingers affected by frostbite (figure B and C). The patient does not report any joint pain or stiffness and has a near-typical functional status.
Frostbite is cold-induced tissue damage, with lack of supervision and alcohol and drug use as common risk factors in children and adolescents. Short-term complications include severe pain, infections, and tissue necrosis (ranging from skin blisters to extensive gangrene). Long-term sequelae include neuropathic pain, vasospasm, nails dystrophy, and risk for squamous cell-carcinoma. Additionally, frostbite arthropathy can appear months to years after the acute episode. In an immature skeleton, frostbite arthropathy can exceptionally result in physeal, growth plate, and epiphyseal destruction of affected phalanges. The frequency of this complication is unknown, with only a few historical cases published. Physicians should be aware of this rare complication of severe paediatric frostbite, which can occur even after an initially favourable evolution. In the absence of curative treatment, prevention of cold-induced injuries (especially in at-risk familial and environmental contexts) remains crucial.

A 2-year-old boy presented for severe frostbite after being outside on a cold day (mean temperature –18°C). The child had reportedly spent 20–30 minutes outside and was found without gloves. Eight fingers (1–5 on the right hand, and 1, 2, and 5 on the left hand) first appeared pale, then developed severe blisters. He was admitted for wound care, surgical debridement of necrotic skin, and pain control. At first, radiographs of the hands were typical (appendix). The patient was discharged home after 2 weeks, following a favourable evolution. 1 year later, he presented with widened interphalangeal joints in the eight fingers affected by frostbite. On x-ray, there was substantial damage to the metaphyses and epiphyses (figure A). Conservative treatment (occupational therapy and splinting) was started. During follow up, joint damage progressed to deformity and growth restrictions in the affected fingers (appendix). At the age of 17 years, there is substantial joint and bone damage, finger shortening, and nail dystrophy in the eight fingers affected by frostbite (figure B and C). The patient does not report any joint pain or stiffness and has a near-typical functional status.
Frostbite is cold-induced tissue damage, with lack of supervision and alcohol and drug use as common risk factors in children and adolescents. Short-term complications include severe pain, infections, and tissue necrosis (ranging from skin blisters to extensive gangrene). Long-term sequelae include neuropathic pain, vasospasm, nails dystrophy, and risk for squamous cell-carcinoma. Additionally, frostbite arthropathy can appear months to years after the acute episode. In an immature skeleton, frostbite arthropathy can exceptionally result in physeal, growth plate, and epiphyseal destruction of affected phalanges. The frequency of this complication is unknown, with only a few historical cases published. Physicians should be aware of this rare complication of severe paediatric frostbite, which can occur even after an initially favourable evolution. In the absence of curative treatment, prevention of cold-induced injuries (especially in at-risk familial and environmental contexts) remains crucial.

A 2-year-old boy presented for severe frostbite after being outside on a cold day (mean temperature –18°C). The child had reportedly spent 20–30 minutes outside and was found without gloves. Eight fingers (1–5 on the right hand, and 1, 2, and 5 on the left hand) first appeared pale, then developed severe blisters. He was admitted for wound care, surgical debridement of necrotic skin, and pain control. At first, radiographs of the hands were typical (appendix). The patient was discharged home after 2 weeks, following a favourable evolution. 1 year later, he presented with widened interphalangeal joints in the eight fingers affected by frostbite. On x-ray, there was substantial damage to the metaphyses and epiphyses (figure A). Conservative treatment (occupational therapy and splinting) was started. During follow up, joint damage progressed to deformity and growth restrictions in the affected fingers (appendix). At the age of 17 years, there is substantial joint and bone damage, finger shortening, and nail dystrophy in the eight fingers affected by frostbite (figure B and C). The patient does not report any joint pain or stiffness and has a near-typical functional status.
Frostbite is cold-induced tissue damage, with lack of supervision and alcohol and drug use as common risk factors in children and adolescents. Short-term complications include severe pain, infections, and tissue necrosis (ranging from skin blisters to extensive gangrene). Long-term sequelae include neuropathic pain, vasospasm, nails dystrophy, and risk for squamous cell-carcinoma. Additionally, frostbite arthropathy can appear months to years after the acute episode. In an immature skeleton, frostbite arthropathy can exceptionally result in physeal, growth plate, and epiphyseal destruction of affected phalanges. The frequency of this complication is unknown, with only a few historical cases published. Physicians should be aware of this rare complication of severe paediatric frostbite, which can occur even after an initially favourable evolution. In the absence of curative treatment, prevention of cold-induced injuries (especially in at-risk familial and environmental contexts) remains crucial.

A 27-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 4-month history of bilateral frontal headache, irritability, frontal lobe signs, bilateral proptosis, and nasal obstruction. He had no other signs or symptoms of a systemic illness. Rhinoscopy showed a soft tissue mass obstructing both nasal airways. A CT scan of his head showed hyperdense lesions involving both the paranasal sinuses (figure), with expansions into the frontal interdiploë spaces, and some calcification (figure). An MRI scan of the brain showed a soft tissue mass extending along the anterior cranial fossa floor up to the sellar and parasellar regions (figure). Endoscopic biopsy was inconclusive; however, because of raised intracranial pressure, the patient was taken to surgery for craniotomy and excision of the lesion.During the operation, an extradural grey-coloured, foul smelling, soft tissue mass was seen carpeting the cranial fossa floor over both frontal lobes and extending up into the air sinuses. The extradural mass, which was found to be exerting pressure on the brain by compressing the frontal lobes without any macroscopic invasion of the dura, was excised completely. The intracranial pressure was reduced on completion of the operation.
Histopathological examination of the lesion showed septate fungal hyphae most consistent with Aspergillus spp.
In the immediate postoperative period, the patient was conscious and had no additional neurological deficits; he was also started on voriconazole. However, 24 h post-operatively, the patient suddenly became unresponsive and needed mechanical ventilation. He remained unconscious and on the fourth day after the operation, he developed diffuse ischaemic changes—possible global ischaemia—throughout the brain and died.
Unexpected deaths have been widely reported in cases of intracranial aspergillosis, but sudden deterioration on the first postoperative day is unusual. Systemic antifungal chemotherapy should be started prior to any surgical intervention. Such clinical and radiological presentations will, in our opinion, continue taking even the most experienced clinicians by surprise.

A 27-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 4-month history of bilateral frontal headache, irritability, frontal lobe signs, bilateral proptosis, and nasal obstruction. He had no other signs or symptoms of a systemic illness. Rhinoscopy showed a soft tissue mass obstructing both nasal airways. A CT scan of his head showed hyperdense lesions involving both the paranasal sinuses (figure), with expansions into the frontal interdiploë spaces, and some calcification (figure). An MRI scan of the brain showed a soft tissue mass extending along the anterior cranial fossa floor up to the sellar and parasellar regions (figure). Endoscopic biopsy was inconclusive; however, because of raised intracranial pressure, the patient was taken to surgery for craniotomy and excision of the lesion.During the operation, an extradural grey-coloured, foul smelling, soft tissue mass was seen carpeting the cranial fossa floor over both frontal lobes and extending up into the air sinuses. The extradural mass, which was found to be exerting pressure on the brain by compressing the frontal lobes without any macroscopic invasion of the dura, was excised completely. The intracranial pressure was reduced on completion of the operation.
Histopathological examination of the lesion showed septate fungal hyphae most consistent with Aspergillus spp.
In the immediate postoperative period, the patient was conscious and had no additional neurological deficits; he was also started on voriconazole. However, 24 h post-operatively, the patient suddenly became unresponsive and needed mechanical ventilation. He remained unconscious and on the fourth day after the operation, he developed diffuse ischaemic changes—possible global ischaemia—throughout the brain and died.
Unexpected deaths have been widely reported in cases of intracranial aspergillosis, but sudden deterioration on the first postoperative day is unusual. Systemic antifungal chemotherapy should be started prior to any surgical intervention. Such clinical and radiological presentations will, in our opinion, continue taking even the most experienced clinicians by surprise.

A 2-year-old boy presented to our unit with swelling of the left side of his face and mouth. He had been investigated before we saw him, and imaging was consistent with recurrence of a giant cell tumour in the left maxilla. 2 months earlier, the patient had a subtotal resection of the mass; he had initially presented aged 1 year and 11 months with a painless swelling of the left side of his mouth. On examination the patient was generally well; he had a 2 cm × 2 cm reddish purple bulging lesion on the left palate.A CT scan, with contrast, of the maxillofacial region showed that the tumour had invaded the left nasal cavity, maxillary and ethmoid sinuses, and raised the floor of the left orbit.
We started the patient on high-dose denosumab— 1·7 mg/kg given subcutaneously every 4 weeks—which was continued after he had been allowed home. The size of the tumour reduced substantially.
After 7 months of treatment, the boy developed pain in his left knee; an x-ray showed dense sclerosis about the distal femoral, proximal tibial, and fibular metaphyses along with two atypical stress fractures (figure). An x-ray of his left hand showed diffuse sclerosis with an asymptomatic atypical stress fracture of the metaphysis of the distal ulna (figure).
Because of propitious response seen on the tumour by the treatment, together with the observed metaphyseal sclerosis and concern for atypical stress fractures, we decided to stop the denosumab and do a further surgical resection of the lesion.
Follow-up will involve the patient being seen every 3 months with serial imaging to monitor for tumour recurrence.
Giant cell tumours are rare benign primary bone neoplasms composed of neoplastic primitive mesenchymal stromal cells that overexpress receptor activator of nuclear factor-kappa β ligand (RANKL) which promotes formation of osteoclast-like giant cells that create osteolytic lesions. Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL that suppresses osteoclastogenesis and inhibits bone resorption. In neoplastic disorders such as giant cell tumours of bone, denosumab may also promote osteoblastic differentiation resulting in mineralisation of the lesion. Sclerotic bands are a manifestation of antiresorptive therapy in children before closure of the epiphyseal growth plates, and result from disruption in osteoclastic resorption of growth plate cartilage. The extent of sclerosis varies depending on the patient's age, growth rate, and antiresorptive regimen. Denosumab has potent anti-osteoclastic effects, and oncologic doses may result in bone turnover suppression—particularly in young children with rapid skeletal growth—which may result in stress fractures, as seen in our patient. Children treated with denosumab should undergo clinical monitoring for potential adverse metaphyseal effects. Radiographic assessment may be helpful in evaluating metaphyseal changes and should be done in any patient presenting with bone pain (video).

A 2-year-old boy presented to our unit with swelling of the left side of his face and mouth. He had been investigated before we saw him, and imaging was consistent with recurrence of a giant cell tumour in the left maxilla. 2 months earlier, the patient had a subtotal resection of the mass; he had initially presented aged 1 year and 11 months with a painless swelling of the left side of his mouth. On examination the patient was generally well; he had a 2 cm × 2 cm reddish purple bulging lesion on the left palate.A CT scan, with contrast, of the maxillofacial region showed that the tumour had invaded the left nasal cavity, maxillary and ethmoid sinuses, and raised the floor of the left orbit.
We started the patient on high-dose denosumab— 1·7 mg/kg given subcutaneously every 4 weeks—which was continued after he had been allowed home. The size of the tumour reduced substantially.
After 7 months of treatment, the boy developed pain in his left knee; an x-ray showed dense sclerosis about the distal femoral, proximal tibial, and fibular metaphyses along with two atypical stress fractures (figure). An x-ray of his left hand showed diffuse sclerosis with an asymptomatic atypical stress fracture of the metaphysis of the distal ulna (figure).
Because of propitious response seen on the tumour by the treatment, together with the observed metaphyseal sclerosis and concern for atypical stress fractures, we decided to stop the denosumab and do a further surgical resection of the lesion.
Follow-up will involve the patient being seen every 3 months with serial imaging to monitor for tumour recurrence.
Giant cell tumours are rare benign primary bone neoplasms composed of neoplastic primitive mesenchymal stromal cells that overexpress receptor activator of nuclear factor-kappa β ligand (RANKL) which promotes formation of osteoclast-like giant cells that create osteolytic lesions. Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL that suppresses osteoclastogenesis and inhibits bone resorption. In neoplastic disorders such as giant cell tumours of bone, denosumab may also promote osteoblastic differentiation resulting in mineralisation of the lesion. Sclerotic bands are a manifestation of antiresorptive therapy in children before closure of the epiphyseal growth plates, and result from disruption in osteoclastic resorption of growth plate cartilage. The extent of sclerosis varies depending on the patient's age, growth rate, and antiresorptive regimen. Denosumab has potent anti-osteoclastic effects, and oncologic doses may result in bone turnover suppression—particularly in young children with rapid skeletal growth—which may result in stress fractures, as seen in our patient. Children treated with denosumab should undergo clinical monitoring for potential adverse metaphyseal effects. Radiographic assessment may be helpful in evaluating metaphyseal changes and should be done in any patient presenting with bone pain (video).

A 95-year-old woman attended our oral medicine department reporting a painful white plaque on the left margin of her tongue. The patient had been seen by her dentist 8 months earlier, who concluded that the small, nodular, white patch (figure), opposite a broken tooth, had been caused by trauma; he polished the broken tooth and arranged no follow-up appointments. However, 8 months later, the patient went back to her dentist because of persistent pain; the white patch had progressed, and the dentist referred her to us.The patient had a history of hypertension treated with candesartan; she reported no tobacco use or alcohol consumption.
On examination, she was generally well; in her mouth the original white plaque had developed an ulcerated lichenoid appearance, and three new plaques were present on her tongue (figure). Regional lymph nodes in the neck were not palpable. Two biopsies were taken and each examined at three levels: the first showed squamous cell carcinomatous proliferation—essentially in situ, locally ulcerated, with focal budding of the basal layer and micro-infiltrative subepithelial small clumps or squamous epithelial cells (figure); the second biopsy found an acanthotic leukokeratotic mucosa with sparse subepithelial lymphocytic inflammation, and a few apoptotic bodies (figure). Well differentiated micro-invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue was diagnosed. The second biopsy also showed lichenoid inflammation.
The patient had a partial glossectomy and a sentinel lymph node biopsy which showed no signs of metastasis; no adjuvant treatment was indicated. At her last follow-up 1 year after surgery, the patient was in clinical remission.
Late diagnosis of oral cancers—as with many malignancies—results in poorer prognosis. Notably, oral traumatic lesions typically resolve within 4 weeks once the causative agent is removed.
All new oral white and red patches, whether they appear malignant or not, should be monitored and investigated. Importantly, any plaque, patch, ulcer, lump, or anything that appears atypical needs to be explored and the aetiology found; many head and neck cancers present initially with lesions in the oral cavity. The persistence of pain and any persistent or progressive lesion should be biopsied to avoid missing an oral squamous cell carcinoma or misdiagnosing a lesion that appears to be benign. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), in the UK, guidelines recommend that any non-healing oral ulcer or a lump on the tongue should be referred to a specialist so that patients with a suspected cancer are seen within 2 weeks.
Contributors
We were all involved with the patient's care. EV, DM, and SW devised the article. EV and DM gathered the data. EV, DM, and BHB did the investigations. EV and DM wrote the original draft. SW reviewed and edited the paper. Written consent for publication was obtained from the patient.
