A 37-year-old man presented to our emergency room with a sudden onset of partial loss of vision and diplopia while driving home 2 h earlier. The patient was previously fit and well and had no medical history.On examination we found him to be alert and oriented. Temperature was 37·6°C, pulse was 93 beats per min, and blood pressure was 130/89 mm Hg supine and 120/75 mm Hg erect. Neurological examination showed the patient to have decreased visual acuity in both eyes with a bitemporal hemianopia; we observed no oculomotor palsies and no sensory or motor deficits.
Laboratory investigations showed no abnormalities.
Brain MRI showed a partially cystic sellar and suprasellar mass that was hyperintense on T1-weighted images and hypointense on T2-weighted images without clear contrast enhancement. The optic chiasm was compressed and displaced by the lesion (figure).
Endocrinological work-up showed a slightly elevated serum prolactin concentration of 30 ng/mL (normal <20 in men); all other pituitary function studies—including thyroid-stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, adrenocorticotropic hormone, cortisol, insulin-like growth factor 1, testosterone, follicle-stimulating hormone, and luteinising hormone—were within normal ranges.
We then embarked upon a transsphenoidal endoscopic resection of what we thought was a pituitary adenoma in a patient with pituitary apoplexy. However, on removal of the sella floor, the classic white-greyish discolouration of the dura was not evident: the sella had a more purplish appearance—and although this might have been attributable to intrasellar haemorrhage, a small scratch of this layer produced a mass with yellow crystalline-like fluid. Progressive resection was performed using sharp dissection and curettes, and no evidence of haemorrhage was found; after near complete resection, a dural layer came, surprisingly, into view. A 4 mm 45° endoscope was inserted for verification and this confirmed that the dural layer was intact with no intraoperative cerebrospinal fluid leakage. Further, we observed no cavernous sinus invasion or mass remnant. Postoperatively, the patient had complete resolution of his diplopia and visual deficit and no evidence of diabetes insipidus.
Histopathological examination showed the tumour consisted of fibrous tissue with cholesterol clefts, lympho-plasma-cellular infiltrates, marked haemosiderin deposits, multinucleated giant cells, granular necrotic debris, and accumulations of foamy macrophages; no epithelial cells positive for epithelial membrane antigen or cytokeratin were observed in any part of the tumour. A xanthogranuloma was therefore confirmed.
The patient was well with no neurological deficits or evidence of disease recurrence 12 months postoperatively.
Pituitary apoplexy—a clinical syndrome secondary to sudden haemorrhage or infarction—occurs in approximately 7% of pituitary adenomas; a severe headache, often accompanied by visual disturbances, is commonly the presenting complaint. Xanthogranulomas of the sellar region are extremely rare and might be misdiagnosed as macroadenomas presenting with pituitary apoplexy if—as in our case—the lesion is an intrasellar, extradural xanthogranuloma with suprasellar extension (video).

A 37-year-old man presented to our emergency room with a sudden onset of partial loss of vision and diplopia while driving home 2 h earlier. The patient was previously fit and well and had no medical history.On examination we found him to be alert and oriented. Temperature was 37·6°C, pulse was 93 beats per min, and blood pressure was 130/89 mm Hg supine and 120/75 mm Hg erect. Neurological examination showed the patient to have decreased visual acuity in both eyes with a bitemporal hemianopia; we observed no oculomotor palsies and no sensory or motor deficits.
Laboratory investigations showed no abnormalities.
Brain MRI showed a partially cystic sellar and suprasellar mass that was hyperintense on T1-weighted images and hypointense on T2-weighted images without clear contrast enhancement. The optic chiasm was compressed and displaced by the lesion (figure).
Endocrinological work-up showed a slightly elevated serum prolactin concentration of 30 ng/mL (normal <20 in men); all other pituitary function studies—including thyroid-stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, adrenocorticotropic hormone, cortisol, insulin-like growth factor 1, testosterone, follicle-stimulating hormone, and luteinising hormone—were within normal ranges.
We then embarked upon a transsphenoidal endoscopic resection of what we thought was a pituitary adenoma in a patient with pituitary apoplexy. However, on removal of the sella floor, the classic white-greyish discolouration of the dura was not evident: the sella had a more purplish appearance—and although this might have been attributable to intrasellar haemorrhage, a small scratch of this layer produced a mass with yellow crystalline-like fluid. Progressive resection was performed using sharp dissection and curettes, and no evidence of haemorrhage was found; after near complete resection, a dural layer came, surprisingly, into view. A 4 mm 45° endoscope was inserted for verification and this confirmed that the dural layer was intact with no intraoperative cerebrospinal fluid leakage. Further, we observed no cavernous sinus invasion or mass remnant. Postoperatively, the patient had complete resolution of his diplopia and visual deficit and no evidence of diabetes insipidus.
Histopathological examination showed the tumour consisted of fibrous tissue with cholesterol clefts, lympho-plasma-cellular infiltrates, marked haemosiderin deposits, multinucleated giant cells, granular necrotic debris, and accumulations of foamy macrophages; no epithelial cells positive for epithelial membrane antigen or cytokeratin were observed in any part of the tumour. A xanthogranuloma was therefore confirmed.
The patient was well with no neurological deficits or evidence of disease recurrence 12 months postoperatively.
Pituitary apoplexy—a clinical syndrome secondary to sudden haemorrhage or infarction—occurs in approximately 7% of pituitary adenomas; a severe headache, often accompanied by visual disturbances, is commonly the presenting complaint. Xanthogranulomas of the sellar region are extremely rare and might be misdiagnosed as macroadenomas presenting with pituitary apoplexy if—as in our case—the lesion is an intrasellar, extradural xanthogranuloma with suprasellar extension (video).

A 40-year-old woman presented to her local emergency department following a syncopal episode which had been preceded by abrupt onset of chest discomfort, dyspnoea, and light-headedness.Two weeks before, the patient had liposuction and abdominoplasty; one week postoperatively, she had developed swelling of her left leg which was painful mainly on walking. She was prescribed an oestrogen-containing oral contraceptive.
On initial examination, the patient was alert but uncomfortable; blood pressure was 145/86 mm Hg, pulse 130 beats per min, temperature 37oC, respiratory rate 21 breaths per min, and oxygen saturation 96% on ambient air. Laboratory investigations showed a raised high-sensitivity troponin level (155 ng/L; normal <9). CT pulmonary angiography (CT-PA) showed a pulmonary embolism involving the pulmonary trunk and main pulmonary arteries, with right ventricular strain. Intravenous unfractionated heparin was started, and she was transferred to our institution.
On arrival, the patient reported worsening chest discomfort and breathlessness. After discussion with our hospital's multidisciplinary Pulmonary Embolism Response Team, a catheter-directed pulmonary embolectomy was done. The patient's discomfort and breathlessness improved. Transthoracic echocardiography showed mild right ventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction; duplex venous ultrasonography found extensive proximal deep venous thromboses in both legs.
Within 48 h, the patient developed recrudescent chest discomfort and breathlessness. A repeat CT-PA showed a new thromboembolus extending from the right ventricle to the right pulmonary artery (figure). Both atria also appeared to be involved (appendix). Transthoracic echocardiography confirmed a thrombus in both atria, which appeared to traverse the interatrial septum (figure; video).
During preparation for urgent surgical embolectomy, causes for the repeat embolus were considered. Specifically, a hypercoagulable state caused by heparin-induced thrombocytopenia—although partial thromboplastin times were intermittently below the target level during treatment with unfractionated heparin—since the patient's platelet count had fallen from 180 × 109 per L (typical range 150–450) to 125 × 109 per L. A 4Ts score, which categorises disease likelihood in the domains of thrombocytopenia, timing of platelet count fall, thrombosis or other sequelae, and other causes of thrombocytopenia, was calculated to be 5—indicating an intermediate probability of disease. A platelet factor 4 antibody immunoassay was positive. We therefore decided to change the unfractionated heparin to bivalirudin while further tests were awaited.
An intraoperative transoesophageal echocardiogram showed contiguous thrombus extending from the right to the left atria via a patent foramen ovale (figure). Gross examination after cardiopulmonary bypass confirmed these findings: an intracardiac and pulmonary artery embolectomy, combined with patent foramen ovale closure, was done (appendix).
The patient's postoperative course was unremarkable. A serotonin-release assay was negative, excluding heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and bivalirudin was changed to apixaban.
At outpatient follow-up, the patient reported feeling well and had no dyspnoea. Antiphospholipid autoantibody and inherited thrombophilia testing were negative.
Our case, we believe, has two important take-home messages. Firstly, inherited and acquired hypercoagulable conditions need to be excluded in cases of rapid, in-hospital recurrence of pulmonary embolism. Secondly, management of intracardiac thrombus-in-transit is clinically challenging; surgical embolectomy, when available, is preferable to prevent further systemic emboli—particularly in cases with concomitant pulmonary emboli, involvement of the left side of the heart, or an intracardiac communication.

A 40-year-old woman presented to her local emergency department following a syncopal episode which had been preceded by abrupt onset of chest discomfort, dyspnoea, and light-headedness.Two weeks before, the patient had liposuction and abdominoplasty; one week postoperatively, she had developed swelling of her left leg which was painful mainly on walking. She was prescribed an oestrogen-containing oral contraceptive.
On initial examination, the patient was alert but uncomfortable; blood pressure was 145/86 mm Hg, pulse 130 beats per min, temperature 37oC, respiratory rate 21 breaths per min, and oxygen saturation 96% on ambient air. Laboratory investigations showed a raised high-sensitivity troponin level (155 ng/L; normal <9). CT pulmonary angiography (CT-PA) showed a pulmonary embolism involving the pulmonary trunk and main pulmonary arteries, with right ventricular strain. Intravenous unfractionated heparin was started, and she was transferred to our institution.
On arrival, the patient reported worsening chest discomfort and breathlessness. After discussion with our hospital's multidisciplinary Pulmonary Embolism Response Team, a catheter-directed pulmonary embolectomy was done. The patient's discomfort and breathlessness improved. Transthoracic echocardiography showed mild right ventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction; duplex venous ultrasonography found extensive proximal deep venous thromboses in both legs.
Within 48 h, the patient developed recrudescent chest discomfort and breathlessness. A repeat CT-PA showed a new thromboembolus extending from the right ventricle to the right pulmonary artery (figure). Both atria also appeared to be involved (appendix). Transthoracic echocardiography confirmed a thrombus in both atria, which appeared to traverse the interatrial septum (figure; video).
During preparation for urgent surgical embolectomy, causes for the repeat embolus were considered. Specifically, a hypercoagulable state caused by heparin-induced thrombocytopenia—although partial thromboplastin times were intermittently below the target level during treatment with unfractionated heparin—since the patient's platelet count had fallen from 180 × 109 per L (typical range 150–450) to 125 × 109 per L. A 4Ts score, which categorises disease likelihood in the domains of thrombocytopenia, timing of platelet count fall, thrombosis or other sequelae, and other causes of thrombocytopenia, was calculated to be 5—indicating an intermediate probability of disease. A platelet factor 4 antibody immunoassay was positive. We therefore decided to change the unfractionated heparin to bivalirudin while further tests were awaited.
An intraoperative transoesophageal echocardiogram showed contiguous thrombus extending from the right to the left atria via a patent foramen ovale (figure). Gross examination after cardiopulmonary bypass confirmed these findings: an intracardiac and pulmonary artery embolectomy, combined with patent foramen ovale closure, was done (appendix).
The patient's postoperative course was unremarkable. A serotonin-release assay was negative, excluding heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and bivalirudin was changed to apixaban.
At outpatient follow-up, the patient reported feeling well and had no dyspnoea. Antiphospholipid autoantibody and inherited thrombophilia testing were negative.
Our case, we believe, has two important take-home messages. Firstly, inherited and acquired hypercoagulable conditions need to be excluded in cases of rapid, in-hospital recurrence of pulmonary embolism. Secondly, management of intracardiac thrombus-in-transit is clinically challenging; surgical embolectomy, when available, is preferable to prevent further systemic emboli—particularly in cases with concomitant pulmonary emboli, involvement of the left side of the heart, or an intracardiac communication.

A full-term infant, weighing 2820 g, born to a 33-year-old healthy primigravida, was referred to us after delivery by emergency caesarean section, because of decreased foetal movements. The baby was also reported to have reduced activity after birth.On examination, we found the patient to be pale. He had delayed capillary refill. Hydrops, jaundice, and hepatosplenomegaly were absent.
Laboratory investigations showed anaemia with a haemoglobin concentration of 5·5 g/dL (reference range 12·5–19·5), a raised mean corpuscular volume of 125·9 fL (reference range 91·3–120·0), and an increased reticulocyte count of 22·8% (reference range 2·0–5·4).
Congenital infection screening tests and neonatal screening tests showed no positive findings (appendix). The infant's mother did not have a history of haemoglobinopathies and had the same blood type as her baby: type O positive. The Coombs test was negative. Abdominal and brain sonography showed no haemorrhages.
Polychromasia was found in a peripheral blood smear. The Kleihauer-Betke test showed approximately 10% (reference range 0·0–0·5) of fetal red blood cells (RBCs) in the mother's blood (figure); substantially higher than the typical value.
Considering this information, we diagnosed fetal-maternal haemorrhage (FMH). We subsequently transfused the infant packed RBCs and he was allowed home, fit and well, 21 days after birth.
FMH is characterised by the passage of fetal blood into the mother's circulation either before or at birth. Although fetal problems, placental abnormalities, direct trauma to the abdomen, previous FMH, obstetrical intervention, obstetrical complications, and substance misuse are recognised risk factors for FMH. The cause, in most cases, is unknown. Additionally, depending on the amount of fetal blood loss, and whether it is acute or chronic, the clinical manifestations of FMH can be categorised as asymptomatic or symptomatic with decreased or absent fetal movement, stillbirth, non-immune hydrops fetalis, neonatal anaemia, sinusoidal fetal heart rate pattern, and tachyarrhythmia.
The Kleihauer-Betke acid elution test is one of the diagnostic tools of FMH, which results in fetal RBCs remaining pink and adult RBCs becoming colourless—known as ghost cells. The difference in colour is explained by haemoglobin F being stable—compared to haemoglobin A which is unstable—at a low pH. Management options include intrauterine transfusion, emergency delivery by caesarean section, and neonatal transfusion.

Abdominal and brain sonography showed no haemorrhages.
Polychromasia was found in a peripheral blood smear. The Kleihauer-Betke test showed approximately 10% (reference range 0·0–0·5) of fetal red blood cells (RBCs) in the mother's blood (figure); substantially higher than the typical value.
Considering this information, we diagnosed fetal-maternal haemorrhage (FMH). We subsequently transfused the infant packed RBCs and he was allowed home, fit and well, 21 days after birth.
FMH is characterised by the passage of fetal blood into the mother's circulation either before or at birth. Although fetal problems, placental abnormalities, direct trauma to the abdomen, previous FMH, obstetrical intervention, obstetrical complications, and substance misuse are recognised risk factors for FMH. The cause, in most cases, is unknown. The Kleihauer-Betke acid elution test is one of the diagnostic tools of FMH, which results in fetal RBCs remaining pink and adult RBCs becoming colourless—known as ghost cells. The difference in colour is explained by haemoglobin F being stable—compared to haemoglobin A which is unstable—at a low pH. Management options include intrauterine transfusion, emergency delivery by caesarean section, and neonatal transfusion.

A 34-year-old man was brought to our Emergency Department after a truck ran over the right side of his body while he was out walking. He had no medical history.On examination, the patient's vital signs were stable; he had tenderness over his right shoulder, mild tenderness and bruising over the right hip, and abrasions over the right side of his arm, chest, abdomen, and right flank. His pelvis was stable, and movements of the right hip joint were unaffected.
Laboratory investigations were within normal range. No fractures were seen on x-rays of the patient's chest, pelvis, right shoulder, and right femur. A whole-body CT scan showed subcutaneous haematomas about 3·5 cm × 3·0 cm in the right infra-axillary region, right lateral abdominal wall, and pelvis.
We admitted the patient under the trauma service; an MRI of his right shoulder showed an acute contusion of the right supraspinatus muscle and right acromioclavicular joint. The patient was allowed home after an orthopaedic review with a plan of conservative treatment: analgesia and outpatient physiotherapy.
At follow-up with his general practitioner, 3 weeks later, the patient had an ill-defined soft, fluctuant swelling over his right flank and a fluctuant, non-tender swelling around the right hip with no abnormalities of the overlying skin.
At further assessment, 5 weeks after the accident, the swelling over the patient's right flank had resolved, but the one over his right hip area had grown larger. An MRI of the right hip showed a large 14 cm × 9·5 cm × 26 cm fluid signal collection with multiple fat locules within the deep subcutaneous tissue of the right posterolateral proximal thigh and hip, immediately superficial to the intact deep fascia (figure). The findings were consistent with a diagnosis of a Morel-Lavallée lesion.
The patient underwent open debridement; a mixture of blood and serous fluid was drained from the lesion and multiple pseudo-polyps, that had formed as a result of fat necrosis, were excised along with the capsule of the cavity. The cavity was washed out and the incision was closed.
The patient was allowed home. At postoperative follow-up in the trauma clinic, 4 weeks later, the lesion had completely resolved.
A Morel-Lavallée lesion is a rare, closed, internal degloving soft-tissue injury usually resulting from trauma. Lesions can present acutely after the trauma or they can develop a few days or weeks after the injury; they are often missed initially—as in our case. They develop by shearing forces which lead to separation of the skin and subcutaneous tissues from the underlying fascia, leading to fluid accumulation in the perifascial space.
In approximately 8% of cases, Morel-Lavallée lesions are associated with underlying pelvic or acetabular fractures—although the true incidence may be higher in such patients. When the lesion is small, it may be overlooked. Additionally, Morel-Lavallée lesions are sometimes misdiagnosed as a post-traumatic muscle contusion, haematomas, or myositis ossificans. Early recognition of the condition prevents the development of complications such as infections or skin necrosis. MRI is the investigation of choice, aiding diagnosis, and guiding management.

A 40-year-old woman presented to her local emergency department following a syncopal episode which had been preceded by abrupt onset of chest discomfort, dyspnoea, and light-headedness.Two weeks before, the patient had liposuction and abdominoplasty; one week postoperatively, she had developed swelling of her left leg which was painful mainly on walking. She was prescribed an oestrogen-containing oral contraceptive.
On initial examination, the patient was alert but uncomfortable; blood pressure was 145/86 mm Hg, pulse 130 beats per min, temperature 37oC, respiratory rate 21 breaths per min, and oxygen saturation 96% on ambient air. Laboratory investigations showed a raised high-sensitivity troponin level (155 ng/L; normal <9). CT pulmonary angiography (CT-PA) showed a pulmonary embolism involving the pulmonary trunk and main pulmonary arteries, with right ventricular strain. Intravenous unfractionated heparin was started, and she was transferred to our institution.
On arrival, the patient reported worsening chest discomfort and breathlessness. After discussion with our hospital's multidisciplinary Pulmonary Embolism Response Team, a catheter-directed pulmonary embolectomy was done. The patient's discomfort and breathlessness improved. Transthoracic echocardiography showed mild right ventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction; duplex venous ultrasonography found extensive proximal deep venous thromboses in both legs.
Within 48 h, the patient developed recrudescent chest discomfort and breathlessness. A repeat CT-PA showed a new thromboembolus extending from the right ventricle to the right pulmonary artery (figure). Both atria also appeared to be involved (appendix). Transthoracic echocardiography confirmed a thrombus in both atria, which appeared to traverse the interatrial septum (figure; video).
During preparation for urgent surgical embolectomy, causes for the repeat embolus were considered. Specifically, a hypercoagulable state caused by heparin-induced thrombocytopenia—although partial thromboplastin times were intermittently below the target level during treatment with unfractionated heparin—since the patient's platelet count had fallen from 180 × 109 per L (typical range 150–450) to 125 × 109 per L. A 4Ts score, which categorises disease likelihood in the domains of thrombocytopenia, timing of platelet count fall, thrombosis or other sequelae, and other causes of thrombocytopenia, was calculated to be 5—indicating an intermediate probability of disease. A platelet factor 4 antibody immunoassay was positive. We therefore decided to change the unfractionated heparin to bivalirudin while further tests were awaited.
An intraoperative transoesophageal echocardiogram showed contiguous thrombus extending from the right to the left atria via a patent foramen ovale (figure). Gross examination after cardiopulmonary bypass confirmed these findings: an intracardiac and pulmonary artery embolectomy, combined with patent foramen ovale closure, was done (appendix).
The patient's postoperative course was unremarkable. A serotonin-release assay was negative, excluding heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and bivalirudin was changed to apixaban.
At outpatient follow-up, the patient reported feeling well and had no dyspnoea. Antiphospholipid autoantibody and inherited thrombophilia testing were negative.
Our case, we believe, has two important take-home messages. Firstly, inherited and acquired hypercoagulable conditions need to be excluded in cases of rapid, in-hospital recurrence of pulmonary embolism. Secondly, management of intracardiac thrombus-in-transit is clinically challenging; surgical embolectomy, when available, is preferable to prevent further systemic emboli—particularly in cases with concomitant pulmonary emboli, involvement of the left side of the heart, or an intracardiac communication.

A 34-year-old man was brought to our Emergency Department after a truck ran over the right side of his body while he was out walking. He had no medical history.On examination, the patient's vital signs were stable; he had tenderness over his right shoulder, mild tenderness and bruising over the right hip, and abrasions over the right side of his arm, chest, abdomen, and right flank. His pelvis was stable, and movements of the right hip joint were unaffected.
Laboratory investigations were within normal range. No fractures were seen on x-rays of the patient's chest, pelvis, right shoulder, and right femur. A whole-body CT scan showed subcutaneous haematomas about 3·5 cm × 3·0 cm in the right infra-axillary region, right lateral abdominal wall, and pelvis.
We admitted the patient under the trauma service; an MRI of his right shoulder showed an acute contusion of the right supraspinatus muscle and right acromioclavicular joint. The patient was allowed home after an orthopaedic review with a plan of conservative treatment: analgesia and outpatient physiotherapy.
At follow-up with his general practitioner, 3 weeks later, the patient had an ill-defined soft, fluctuant swelling over his right flank and a fluctuant, non-tender swelling around the right hip with no abnormalities of the overlying skin.
At further assessment, 5 weeks after the accident, the swelling over the patient's right flank had resolved, but the one over his right hip area had grown larger. An MRI of the right hip showed a large 14 cm × 9·5 cm × 26 cm fluid signal collection with multiple fat locules within the deep subcutaneous tissue of the right posterolateral proximal thigh and hip, immediately superficial to the intact deep fascia (figure). The findings were consistent with a diagnosis of a Morel-Lavallée lesion.
The patient underwent open debridement; a mixture of blood and serous fluid was drained from the lesion and multiple pseudo-polyps, that had formed as a result of fat necrosis, were excised along with the capsule of the cavity. The cavity was washed out and the incision was closed.
The patient was allowed home. At postoperative follow-up in the trauma clinic, 4 weeks later, the lesion had completely resolved.
A Morel-Lavallée lesion is a rare, closed, internal degloving soft-tissue injury usually resulting from trauma. Lesions can present acutely after the trauma or they can develop a few days or weeks after the injury; they are often missed initially—as in our case. They develop by shearing forces which lead to separation of the skin and subcutaneous tissues from the underlying fascia, leading to fluid accumulation in the perifascial space.
In approximately 8% of cases, Morel-Lavallée lesions are associated with underlying pelvic or acetabular fractures—although the true incidence may be higher in such patients. When the lesion is small, it may be overlooked. Additionally, Morel-Lavallée lesions are sometimes misdiagnosed as a post-traumatic muscle contusion, haematomas, or myositis ossificans. Early recognition of the condition prevents the development of complications such as infections or skin necrosis. MRI is the investigation of choice, aiding diagnosis, and guiding management.

A 34-year-old man was brought to our Emergency Department after a truck ran over the right side of his body while he was out walking. He had no medical history.On examination, the patient's vital signs were stable; he had tenderness over his right shoulder, mild tenderness and bruising over the right hip, and abrasions over the right side of his arm, chest, abdomen, and right flank. His pelvis was stable, and movements of the right hip joint were unaffected.
Laboratory investigations were within normal range. No fractures were seen on x-rays of the patient's chest, pelvis, right shoulder, and right femur. A whole-body CT scan showed subcutaneous haematomas about 3·5 cm × 3·0 cm in the right infra-axillary region, right lateral abdominal wall, and pelvis.
We admitted the patient under the trauma service; an MRI of his right shoulder showed an acute contusion of the right supraspinatus muscle and right acromioclavicular joint. The patient was allowed home after an orthopaedic review with a plan of conservative treatment: analgesia and outpatient physiotherapy.
At follow-up with his general practitioner, 3 weeks later, the patient had an ill-defined soft, fluctuant swelling over his right flank and a fluctuant, non-tender swelling around the right hip with no abnormalities of the overlying skin.
At further assessment, 5 weeks after the accident, the swelling over the patient's right flank had resolved, but the one over his right hip area had grown larger. An MRI of the right hip showed a large 14 cm × 9·5 cm × 26 cm fluid signal collection with multiple fat locules within the deep subcutaneous tissue of the right posterolateral proximal thigh and hip, immediately superficial to the intact deep fascia (figure). The findings were consistent with a diagnosis of a Morel-Lavallée lesion.
The patient underwent open debridement; a mixture of blood and serous fluid was drained from the lesion and multiple pseudo-polyps, that had formed as a result of fat necrosis, were excised along with the capsule of the cavity. The cavity was washed out and the incision was closed.
The patient was allowed home. At postoperative follow-up in the trauma clinic, 4 weeks later, the lesion had completely resolved.
A Morel-Lavallée lesion is a rare, closed, internal degloving soft-tissue injury usually resulting from trauma. Lesions can present acutely after the trauma or they can develop a few days or weeks after the injury; they are often missed initially—as in our case. They develop by shearing forces which lead to separation of the skin and subcutaneous tissues from the underlying fascia, leading to fluid accumulation in the perifascial space.
In approximately 8% of cases, Morel-Lavallée lesions are associated with underlying pelvic or acetabular fractures—although the true incidence may be higher in such patients. When the lesion is small, it may be overlooked. Additionally, Morel-Lavallée lesions are sometimes misdiagnosed as a post-traumatic muscle contusion, haematomas, or myositis ossificans. Early recognition of the condition prevents the development of complications such as infections or skin necrosis. MRI is the investigation of choice, aiding diagnosis, and guiding management.

input:
A 16-year-old girl attended our outpatient clinic complaining about a hard lump on the second toe of her left foot. She said it had been present for 6 years, but that in the past 3 months it had become moderately painful and that the pain was aggravated by walking. She said that the lump had not increased in size. She reported no history of trauma and no relevant medical history.On examination, the patient was fit and well, and all vital signs were within normal limits. The lump was firm and round and located on the proximal phalanx of her second toe of her left foot; there were no overlying skin changes. The lesion was hard, fixed to the bone, and non-tender on palpation; there were no signs of local inflammation. Neuromuscular examination of the lower limbs was unremarkable: we found no other palpable masses.
x-ray showed a 1–1·8 cm well circumscribed, lucent, central medullary lesion within the diaphysis of the proximal phalanx. Cortical expansion and thinning were also present (figure). We saw no fractures on the x-ray.
Laboratory investigations—including inflammatory markers, a full blood count, and calcium and phosphate concentrations—were all within normal limits.
We decided to surgically excise the lesion with intramedullary curettage and subsequent bone grafting because the lesion was painful, and no fracture was seen on the x-rays.
Histological examination of the lesion undertaken postoperatively showed lobules of hyaline cartilage encased by normal bone and fibrous tissue, consistent with a diagnosis of an enchondroma. Cellularity was within normal limits and without atypical cells or mitotic figures (figure).
At follow-up 3 weeks later, the surgical incision had healed well and the patient said the pain had gone.
Enchondromas are benign cartilage-forming tumours that usually develop in the medulla—marrow cavity—of long bones. They typically present during the second decade of life, but they can present at any age. Enchondromas are often an incidental finding because they are usually asymptomatic. However, when pain is the presenting symptom, a chondrosarcoma should be at the top of the differential diagnosis list—especially if the lesion is on the hands or feet. Additionally, fractures should be excluded first. Treatment depends upon the presence of symptoms and size of the lesion: localised asymptomatic enchondromas which are small enough not to provoke pathological fractures and show no signs of increasing in size can be kept under regular observation with repeated radiographical check-ups—usually annually. Symptomatic, large, or rapidly growing enchondromas can be managed surgically (video).

A 66-year-old man attended our hospital reporting a 1-year history of progressively worsening difficulties with walking, falls, a tremor, and erectile dysfunction. Additionally, he believed he had become more impulsive, anxious, and he reported feeling resentment towards others. The patient had no notable medical or family history.On examination we found him to be generally well; neurological evaluation showed a mixed cerebellar and sensory ataxic gait with a positive Romberg sign. In addition, the patient had difficulty standing with both feet together, and walking during the tandem walk test (video).
Dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia, as well as a bilateral postural and action tremor—further cerebellar signs—were noted. We also found the patient to have global areflexia and pallhypesthesia in both feet. Notably, during examination and interview, the patient made several out of place comments and jokes and laughed inappropriately. He scored 20/30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment—he had completed 11 years of full-time education—but showed no impairment of daily functional activities.
MRI of his brain showed diffuse cerebral and cerebellar atrophy with symmetrical middle cerebellar peduncle and periventricular hyperintensities, and diffuse corpus callosum thinning with hyperintensities (figure; appendix). Electrophysiological studies showed a sensory-motor polyneuropathy pattern with predominantly sensory involvement. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal.
Laboratory investigations—including full blood count, liver function tests, kidney function tests, thyroid and parathyroid function tests, folate, vitamins B12 and E, cholesterol, ceruloplasmin, C-reactive protein concentration, and autoantibodies were all within typical range.
Considering the findings together, we proceeded to genetic testing for the fragile X syndrome, which showed 111 CGG trinucleotide repeats in the fragile X mental retardation 1 protein (FMR1) gene, confirming a diagnosis of fragile X-associated tremor or ataxia syndrome (FXTAS).
We explained the diagnosis and symptoms of the condition to the patient and he was managed with physiotherapy focusing upon gait and balance training and on prevention of falls; he received advice from an occupational therapist and a clinical geneticist.
Fragile X syndrome and FXTAS are caused by the expansion of the CGG trinucleotide in the FMR1 gene, which is also known as the fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP) gene. A mutation in the FMR1 gene of more than 200 CGG trinucleotide repeats leads to the absence of the FMR1 mRNA protein and results in developmental delay, intellectual disability, and autism spectrum disorder—a condition referred to as fragile X syndrome. When a premutation occurs—with between 55 and 200 CGG repeats—the FMR1 gene expresses high levels of mRNA, which results in toxicity and consequently the neurodegenerative condition of FXTAS. Management involves symptomatic therapy: medications, psychological counselling, and rehabilitative treatments. Genetic counselling should be given to all individuals with FXTAS and family members.

A 66-year-old man attended our hospital reporting a 1-year history of progressively worsening difficulties with walking, falls, a tremor, and erectile dysfunction. Additionally, he believed he had become more impulsive, anxious, and he reported feeling resentment towards others. The patient had no notable medical or family history.On examination we found him to be generally well; neurological evaluation showed a mixed cerebellar and sensory ataxic gait with a positive Romberg sign. In addition, the patient had difficulty standing with both feet together, and walking during the tandem walk test (video).
Dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia, as well as a bilateral postural and action tremor—further cerebellar signs—were noted. We also found the patient to have global areflexia and pallhypesthesia in both feet. Notably, during examination and interview, the patient made several out of place comments and jokes and laughed inappropriately. He scored 20/30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment—he had completed 11 years of full-time education—but showed no impairment of daily functional activities.
MRI of his brain showed diffuse cerebral and cerebellar atrophy with symmetrical middle cerebellar peduncle and periventricular hyperintensities, and diffuse corpus callosum thinning with hyperintensities (figure; appendix). Electrophysiological studies showed a sensory-motor polyneuropathy pattern with predominantly sensory involvement. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal.
Laboratory investigations—including full blood count, liver function tests, kidney function tests, thyroid and parathyroid function tests, folate, vitamins B12 and E, cholesterol, ceruloplasmin, C-reactive protein concentration, and autoantibodies were all within typical range.
Considering the findings together, we proceeded to genetic testing for the fragile X syndrome, which showed 111 CGG trinucleotide repeats in the fragile X mental retardation 1 protein (FMR1) gene, confirming a diagnosis of fragile X-associated tremor or ataxia syndrome (FXTAS).
We explained the diagnosis and symptoms of the condition to the patient and he was managed with physiotherapy focusing upon gait and balance training and on prevention of falls; he received advice from an occupational therapist and a clinical geneticist.
Fragile X syndrome and FXTAS are caused by the expansion of the CGG trinucleotide in the FMR1 gene, which is also known as the fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP) gene. A mutation in the FMR1 gene of more than 200 CGG trinucleotide repeats leads to the absence of the FMR1 mRNA protein and results in developmental delay, intellectual disability, and autism spectrum disorder—a condition referred to as fragile X syndrome. When a premutation occurs—with between 55 and 200 CGG repeats—the FMR1 gene expresses high levels of mRNA, which results in toxicity and consequently the neurodegenerative condition of FXTAS. Management involves symptomatic therapy: medications, psychological counselling, and rehabilitative treatments. Genetic counselling should be given to all individuals with FXTAS and family members.

A thyroid biopsy performed under ultrasound showed massive invasion by a diffuse lymphoid proliferation. The patient was treated according to the paediatric French-American-British/Lymphomes Malins B-based chemotherapy (risk group B) combined with rituximab, despite being classified as stage I according to the St Jude system and having an lactate dehydrogenase level less than twice the upper normal limit. This treatment led to a complete response after two cycles, which was sustained 6 months after the end of therapy.Primary thyroid lymphomas are extremely rare and account for 2% of extra-nodal lymphomas. DLBCL is the most common histological subtype. These lymphomas classically affect older women and generally occur in the setting of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. To our knowledge, only two paediatric cases of primary thyroid lymphoma have been reported.

A 66-year-old man attended our hospital reporting a 1-year history of progressively worsening difficulties with walking, falls, a tremor, and erectile dysfunction. Additionally, he believed he had become more impulsive, anxious, and he reported feeling resentment towards others. The patient had no notable medical or family history.On examination we found him to be generally well; neurological evaluation showed a mixed cerebellar and sensory ataxic gait with a positive Romberg sign. In addition, the patient had difficulty standing with both feet together, and walking during the tandem walk test (video).
Dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia, as well as a bilateral postural and action tremor—further cerebellar signs—were noted. We also found the patient to have global areflexia and pallhypesthesia in both feet. Notably, during examination and interview, the patient made several out of place comments and jokes and laughed inappropriately. He scored 20/30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment—he had completed 11 years of full-time education—but showed no impairment of daily functional activities.
MRI of his brain showed diffuse cerebral and cerebellar atrophy with symmetrical middle cerebellar peduncle and periventricular hyperintensities, and diffuse corpus callosum thinning with hyperintensities (figure; appendix). Electrophysiological studies showed a sensory-motor polyneuropathy pattern with predominantly sensory involvement. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal.
Laboratory investigations—including full blood count, liver function tests, kidney function tests, thyroid and parathyroid function tests, folate, vitamins B12 and E, cholesterol, ceruloplasmin, C-reactive protein concentration, and autoantibodies were all within typical range.
Considering the findings together, we proceeded to genetic testing for the fragile X syndrome, which showed 111 CGG trinucleotide repeats in the fragile X mental retardation 1 protein (FMR1) gene, confirming a diagnosis of fragile X-associated tremor or ataxia syndrome (FXTAS).
We explained the diagnosis and symptoms of the condition to the patient and he was managed with physiotherapy focusing upon gait and balance training and on prevention of falls; he received advice from an occupational therapist and a clinical geneticist.
Fragile X syndrome and FXTAS are caused by the expansion of the CGG trinucleotide in the FMR1 gene, which is also known as the fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP) gene. A mutation in the FMR1 gene of more than 200 CGG trinucleotide repeats leads to the absence of the FMR1 mRNA protein and results in developmental delay, intellectual disability, and autism spectrum disorder—a condition referred to as fragile X syndrome. When a premutation occurs—with between 55 and 200 CGG repeats—the FMR1 gene expresses high levels of mRNA, which results in toxicity and consequently the neurodegenerative condition of FXTAS. Management involves symptomatic therapy: medications, psychological counselling, and rehabilitative treatments. Genetic counselling should be given to all individuals with FXTAS and family members.

A 17-year-old boy with no personal or family history presented at St Louis Hospital in Paris in October, 2024 with a thyroid goitre that progressed over several weeks, rapidly causing dysphonia. A CT showed invasion of the thyroid gland by a lobulated structure infiltrating both lobes and the isthmus, measured at 75โ€ร—โ€46 mm (figure A). Biological investigations showed no abnormalities (normal complete blood count, and normal thyroid-stimulating hormone, thyroglobulin, and calcitonin levels). Thyroid fine needle aspiration disclosed the presence of large cells with dispersed chromatin (figure B). A thyroid biopsy performed under ultrasound showed massive invasion by a diffuse lymphoid proliferation. The cells were large, with regular nucleolated nucleus and moderately abundant cytoplasm (appendix). Immunohistochemistry showed that these cells expressed CD20, CD10, and BLC6 but not BLC2, MUM1, TdT, or MYC. The Ki67 proliferation index was 80%. Overall, these data confirmed a diagnosis of diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL) with a germinal centre phenotype. [18F]-fluorodeoxyglucose PET-CT showed intense hypermetabolism of the thyroid mass (standardised uptake value maximum of 20ยท8) without distant involvement (appendix). The lactate dehydrogenase level was normal (196 IU/L [normal laboratory range: 135โ€“225 IU/L]). The patient was treated according to the paediatric French-American-British/Lymphomes Malins B-based chemotherapy (risk group B) combined with rituximab, despite being classified as stage I according to the St Jude system and having an lactate dehydrogenase level less than twice the upper normal limit. This decision was made due to the rarity of this malignancy in a paediatric setting and the routine use of rituximab as first-line therapy in adult DLBCL. This treatment led to a complete response after two cycles, which was sustained 6 months after the end of therapy.Primary thyroid lymphomas are extremely rare and account for 2% of extra-nodal lymphomas. DLBCL is the most common histological subtype. These lymphomas classically affect older women and generally occur in the setting of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. To our knowledge, only two paediatric cases of primary thyroid lymphoma have been reported.
This rare case highlights the importance of promptly performing fine needle aspiration in the presence of a thyroid goitre, even in paediatric patients and without a previous history of thyroiditis, because it can rapidly suggest a high-grade lymphoma, which will subsequently need to be confirmed by histological analysis.

A 77-year-old man attended our hospital reporting a sudden onset of shortness of breath and a fever.14 days earlier, the patient had posterior wall isolation, pulmonary vein isolation, and linear mitral isthmus ablation for drug-refractory atrial fibrillation. Following the procedure, he was complication-free and had been allowed home; he had been prescribed anticoagulation therapy and a proton pump inhibitor.
On examination, the patient was frail but not in a critical state; his blood pressure was 148/68 mm Hg, his pulse was 90 beats per min, and his oxygen saturation was 95% on room air, and his temperature was 38·0°C. Laboratory investigations showed a white blood cell count of 18·8 × 109 per L (typical range 4·5–11·0), C-reactive protein concentration 18·61 mg/dL (typical range <0·3), brain natriuretic peptide 78 pg/mL (typical <18·4), and troponin I 15 pg/mL (typical 26·2 or less). An electrocardiogram showed widespread ST segment elevation and PR segment depression.
A chest CT showed a pericardial effusion with a tiny low-density area—suggesting there was air within the pericardium (figure). The day after his presentation, we did a pericardiocentesis because of haemodynamic instability. However, air continued to be drawn from the pericardial drainage, and a pneumopericardium on the posterior wall of the left atrium was confirmed (figure), indicating a possible oesophageal communication. Endoscopy—using carbon dioxide insufflation to avoid an air embolism in the case of an atrio-oesophagus fistula—showed a 1·5 cm fistula at the level of the mid-oesophagus (figure) on the left atrial wall with the beating heart visible through the fistula, confirming a diagnosis of a pericardial-oesophageal fistula.
We then carried out an emergency thoracoscopic esophagectomy in order to repair the defect in the oesophagus. The patient recovered well and was allowed home after 6 weeks.
Pulmonary vein isolation remains the standard form of catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation; inclusion of posterior wall isolation, as an adjunct to pulmonary vein isolation, is increasing. However, one of the problems with posterior wall ablation is the risk of damage to the oesophagus. Oesophageal fistula after ablation for atrial fibrillation is rare—with an incidence of less than 0·1%—but can be fatal. Importantly, to prevent oesophageal complications the amount of energy delivered to the posterior wall should be limited as much as possible. Symptoms of oesophageal perforation usually, if they are going to, develop within a few weeks of the ablation procedure; patients mainly present with pyrexia and chest pain—as in our patient. Early identification leads to appropriate management and a greater likelihood of successful treatment.

A 77-year-old man attended our hospital reporting a sudden onset of shortness of breath and a fever.14 days earlier, the patient had posterior wall isolation, pulmonary vein isolation, and linear mitral isthmus ablation for drug-refractory atrial fibrillation. Following the procedure, he was complication-free and had been allowed home; he had been prescribed anticoagulation therapy and a proton pump inhibitor.
On examination, the patient was frail but not in a critical state; his blood pressure was 148/68 mm Hg, his pulse was 90 beats per min, and his oxygen saturation was 95% on room air, and his temperature was 38·0°C. Laboratory investigations showed a white blood cell count of 18·8 × 109 per L (typical range 4·5–11·0), C-reactive protein concentration 18·61 mg/dL (typical range <0·3), brain natriuretic peptide 78 pg/mL (typical <18·4), and troponin I 15 pg/mL (typical 26·2 or less). An electrocardiogram showed widespread ST segment elevation and PR segment depression.
A chest CT showed a pericardial effusion with a tiny low-density area—suggesting there was air within the pericardium (figure). The day after his presentation, we did a pericardiocentesis because of haemodynamic instability. However, air continued to be drawn from the pericardial drainage, and a pneumopericardium on the posterior wall of the left atrium was confirmed (figure), indicating a possible oesophageal communication. Endoscopy—using carbon dioxide insufflation to avoid an air embolism in the case of an atrio-oesophagus fistula—showed a 1·5 cm fistula at the level of the mid-oesophagus (figure) on the left atrial wall with the beating heart visible through the fistula, confirming a diagnosis of a pericardial-oesophageal fistula.
We then carried out an emergency thoracoscopic esophagectomy in order to repair the defect in the oesophagus. The patient recovered well and was allowed home after 6 weeks.
Pulmonary vein isolation remains the standard form of catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation; inclusion of posterior wall isolation, as an adjunct to pulmonary vein isolation, is increasing. However, one of the problems with posterior wall ablation is the risk of damage to the oesophagus. Oesophageal fistula after ablation for atrial fibrillation is rare—with an incidence of less than 0·1%—but can be fatal. Importantly, to prevent oesophageal complications the amount of energy delivered to the posterior wall should be limited as much as possible. Symptoms of oesophageal perforation usually, if they are going to, develop within a few weeks of the ablation procedure; patients mainly present with pyrexia and chest pain—as in our patient. Early identification leads to appropriate management and a greater likelihood of successful treatment.

A 17-year-old boy with no personal or family history presented at St Louis Hospital in Paris in October, 2024 with a thyroid goitre that progressed over several weeks, rapidly causing dysphonia. A CT showed invasion of the thyroid gland by a lobulated structure infiltrating both lobes and the isthmus, measured at 75โ€ร—โ€46 mm (figure A). Biological investigations showed no abnormalities (normal complete blood count, and normal thyroid-stimulating hormone, thyroglobulin, and calcitonin levels). Thyroid fine needle aspiration disclosed the presence of large cells with dispersed chromatin (figure B). A thyroid biopsy performed under ultrasound showed massive invasion by a diffuse lymphoid proliferation. The cells were large, with regular nucleolated nucleus and moderately abundant cytoplasm (appendix). Immunohistochemistry showed that these cells expressed CD20, CD10, and BLC6 but not BLC2, MUM1, TdT, or MYC. The Ki67 proliferation index was 80%. Overall, these data confirmed a diagnosis of diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL) with a germinal centre phenotype. [18F]-fluorodeoxyglucose PET-CT showed intense hypermetabolism of the thyroid mass (standardised uptake value maximum of 20ยท8) without distant involvement (appendix). The lactate dehydrogenase level was normal (196 IU/L [normal laboratory range: 135โ€“225 IU/L]). The patient was treated according to the paediatric French-American-British/Lymphomes Malins B-based chemotherapy (risk group B) combined with rituximab, despite being classified as stage I according to the St Jude system and having an lactate dehydrogenase level less than twice the upper normal limit. This decision was made due to the rarity of this malignancy in a paediatric setting and the routine use of rituximab as first-line therapy in adult DLBCL. This treatment led to a complete response after two cycles, which was sustained 6 months after the end of therapy.Primary thyroid lymphomas are extremely rare and account for 2% of extra-nodal lymphomas. DLBCL is the most common histological subtype. These lymphomas classically affect older women and generally occur in the setting of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. To our knowledge, only two paediatric cases of primary thyroid lymphoma have been reported.
This rare case highlights the importance of promptly performing fine needle aspiration in the presence of a thyroid goitre, even in paediatric patients and without a previous history of thyroiditis, because it can rapidly suggest a high-grade lymphoma, which will subsequently need to be confirmed by histological analysis.

CT scan showed bone destruction involving the palate.Under local anaesthesic, a biopsy was performed and the histopathological diagnosis, according to the 2016 revision of the WHO classification of lymphoid neoplasms, was Epstein–Barr virus (EBV)-positive, B-cell lymphoma, Burkitt's lymphoma subtype (CD20+, CD3–, EBV+, MUM1+ Bcl6–, CD10–,CD30+,CD15–, Ki67 45%).
The patient was transferred to the oncohaematology unit at the hospital to receive treatment with radiotherapy (total dose of 45 Gy given over 4 weeks, administered in a continous course over 4 days per week in doses of 2·5 Gy per fraction) and chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone [CHOP], given in eight cycles for 3 weeks. Despite the biologically aggressive behaviour of the tumour, at 18 months follow-up, the disease seemed to be in remission.
Burkitt's lymphoma is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma with a poor prognosis. This type of lymphoma is rare outside Africa where is endemic. WHO classifies three variants of Burkitt's lymphoma: endemic, sporadic, and immunodeficiency-associated types. The endemic form develops most frequently in young people in Africa (children, adolescents, and young adults less than 40 years of age) and is associated with Epstein–Barr virus infection. It typically involves the mandible, maxilla, and abdomen. The sporadic form has no geographical predilection and develops most often in adults, most commonly presenting as an abdominal mass and rarely presenting in the orofacial region. Only a small subset of non-endemic Burkitt's lymphomas are Epstein–Barr virus positive. The immunodeficiency-related variant usually is associated with HIV infection and rarely involves the orofacial region.

The physician must be able to recognise this disease, to have an adequate degree of suspicion to consider this option in the differential diagnosis with other tumours or inflammatory diseases, and to understand the steps necessary to treat this aggressive malignancy.

The mass had developed about 6 months previously and had grown rapidly. The initial suspected diagnosis was squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity. No specific other symptoms were reported and her blood tests were almost normal, with the exception of a non-specific state of malnutrition due to a reduced food intake, and anaemia due to malnutrition and bleeding from the tumour. Blood tests also showed her to be immunocompetent. CT scan showed bone destruction involving the palate.Under local anaesthesic, a biopsy was performed and the histopathological diagnosis, according to the 2016 revision of the WHO classification of lymphoid neoplasms, was Epstein–Barr virus (EBV)-positive, B-cell lymphoma, Burkitt's lymphoma subtype (CD20+, CD3–, EBV+, MUM1+ Bcl6–, CD10–,CD30+,CD15–, Ki67 45%).
The patient was transferred to the oncohaematology unit at the hospital to receive treatment with radiotherapy (total dose of 45 Gy given over 4 weeks, administered in a continous course over 4 days per week in doses of 2·5 Gy per fraction) and chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone [CHOP], given in eight cycles for 3 weeks. Despite the biologically aggressive behaviour of the tumour, at 18 months follow-up, the disease seemed to be in remission.
Burkitt's lymphoma is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma with a poor prognosis. This type of lymphoma is rare outside Africa where is endemic. WHO classifies three variants of Burkitt's lymphoma: endemic, sporadic, and immunodeficiency-associated types. The endemic form develops most frequently in young people in Africa (children, adolescents, and young adults less than 40 years of age) and is associated with Epstein–Barr virus infection. It typically involves the mandible, maxilla, and abdomen. The sporadic form has no geographical predilection and develops most often in adults, most commonly presenting as an abdominal mass and rarely presenting in the orofacial region. Only a small subset of non-endemic Burkitt's lymphomas are Epstein–Barr virus positive. The immunodeficiency-related variant usually is associated with HIV infection and rarely involves the orofacial region.
Because Burkitt's lymphoma grows rapidly. timely diagnosis and treatment are important. The physician must be able to recognise this disease, to have an adequate degree of suspicion to consider this option in the differential diagnosis with other tumours or inflammatory diseases, and to understand the steps necessary to treat this aggressive malignancy.

input:
A 71-year-old woman attended our hospital with a 2-week history of fluctuating confusion.
The patient, who lived in the German state of Bavaria, close to agricultural areas, had no medical history; she was prescribed no regular medications.
On examination at admission, the patient was well and orientated; her vital signs were within typical range. Neurology examination was within normal limits.
Laboratory investigations on admission for systemic infection, liver function, and kidney function were within typical range.
A chest x-ray showed no abnormalities; an electrocardiogram showed a right bundle branch block and electroencephalography showed no epileptiform discharges.
2 days after admission, the patient rapidly became increasingly encephalopathic; she developed aphasia, atactic movements, and fluctuating vigilance resulting in a state of unresponsive wakefulness syndrome on day 16 after admission.
Brain MRIs on days 2, 5, and 14 after admission showed no abnormalities (figure 1).Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) on days 2, 5, and 20 after admission showed repeatedly raised total protein concentration ranging from 0·41 to 0·57 g/L (typical range 0·15–0·45); all other measurements were within normal range or unclear with regard to diagnosis (appendix; table 1).
Since MRIs and further tests were not conclusive, 18fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT of the brain was done on day 8 which showed marked hypermetabolism in the basal ganglia, the temporomesial lobes, and the cerebellum; frontal and parietal lateral cortex showed distinct hypometabolism (figure 2).
On day 19 after admission, a whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT showed progression of the abnormalities found in the initial scan (figure 2).
Considering a probable autoimmune pathology, the patient was treated with high-dose glucocorticoids—increasing to a maximum of 4 g methylprednisolone after 5 days and then tapering down—and intravenous immunoglobulins (2 g/kg of bodyweight) without any clinical response.
On day 34 after admission, T2 FLAIR and diffusion-weighted MRIs showed hyperintensities in the basal ganglia and head of the caudate nucleus (figure 1) indicating possible Borna disease virus 1 (BoDV-1) encephalitis.
Retrospective analysis, done on day 37 after admission, of CSF taken on days 5 and 20 after admission using reverse-transcription quantitative polymerase-chain-reaction (RT-qPCR) was positive for BoDV-1 RNA with quantification cycle values of 34·3 and 32·5, respectively.
Testing for BoDV-1-antibodies was negative until day 35 after admission; seroconversion occurred on day 42 (indirect immunofluorescence antibody test 1:1280, line blot BoDV-1-phosphoprotein 14 arbitrary units [AU], BoDV-1-nucleoprotein 22 AU; appendix, table 2).
On day 49 after admission, the patient died. Post-mortem histology, BoDV-1-specific immunohistochemistry (appendix, figure 2), and RT-qPCR on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue confirmed BoDV-1 encephalitis. A timeline was constructed of the patient's case (appendix, figure 1).
18F-FDG PET/CT findings may aid the diagnosis of patients with unexplained encephalitis and may—as in our patient—precede MRI changes. In Rasmussen encephalitis and anti-leucine glioma-inactivated protein 1 autoimmune encephalitis, for example, brain MRI has been reported as being less sensitive when compared to 18F-FDG PET/CT. In herpes simplex virus encephalitis, temporal lobe, ventral striatal, and septal abnormalities have been described on 18F-FDG PET/CT. And in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, 18F-FDG PET/CT may show hypometabolism in the basal ganglia, the occipital, frontal and parietal lobes, and in regions of the brain specifically related to clinical signs.
BoDV-1 infection is a potentially lethal zoonosis in endemic regions with reported spillover infections in horses and sheep. BoDV-1 infection can result in fatal encephalitis; all severe encephalitis cases of unknown cause should be tested for bornaviruses—especially in endemic regions.

A 71-year-old woman attended our hospital with a 2-week history of fluctuating confusion.
The patient, who lived in the German state of Bavaria, close to agricultural areas, had no medical history; she was prescribed no regular medications.
On examination at admission, the patient was well and orientated; her vital signs were within typical range. Neurology examination was within normal limits.
Laboratory investigations on admission for systemic infection, liver function, and kidney function were within typical range.
A chest x-ray showed no abnormalities; an electrocardiogram showed a right bundle branch block and electroencephalography showed no epileptiform discharges.
2 days after admission, the patient rapidly became increasingly encephalopathic; she developed aphasia, atactic movements, and fluctuating vigilance resulting in a state of unresponsive wakefulness syndrome on day 16 after admission.
Brain MRIs on days 2, 5, and 14 after admission showed no abnormalities (figure 1).Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) on days 2, 5, and 20 after admission showed repeatedly raised total protein concentration ranging from 0·41 to 0·57 g/L (typical range 0·15–0·45); all other measurements were within normal range or unclear with regard to diagnosis (appendix; table 1).
Since MRIs and further tests were not conclusive, 18fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT of the brain was done on day 8 which showed marked hypermetabolism in the basal ganglia, the temporomesial lobes, and the cerebellum; frontal and parietal lateral cortex showed distinct hypometabolism (figure 2).
On day 19 after admission, a whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT showed progression of the abnormalities found in the initial scan (figure 2).
Considering a probable autoimmune pathology, the patient was treated with high-dose glucocorticoids—increasing to a maximum of 4 g methylprednisolone after 5 days and then tapering down—and intravenous immunoglobulins (2 g/kg of bodyweight) without any clinical response.
On day 34 after admission, T2 FLAIR and diffusion-weighted MRIs showed hyperintensities in the basal ganglia and head of the caudate nucleus (figure 1) indicating possible Borna disease virus 1 (BoDV-1) encephalitis.
Retrospective analysis, done on day 37 after admission, of CSF taken on days 5 and 20 after admission using reverse-transcription quantitative polymerase-chain-reaction (RT-qPCR) was positive for BoDV-1 RNA with quantification cycle values of 34·3 and 32·5, respectively.
Testing for BoDV-1-antibodies was negative until day 35 after admission; seroconversion occurred on day 42 (indirect immunofluorescence antibody test 1:1280, line blot BoDV-1-phosphoprotein 14 arbitrary units [AU], BoDV-1-nucleoprotein 22 AU; appendix, table 2).
On day 49 after admission, the patient died. Post-mortem histology, BoDV-1-specific immunohistochemistry (appendix, figure 2), and RT-qPCR on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue confirmed BoDV-1 encephalitis. A timeline was constructed of the patient's case (appendix, figure 1).
18F-FDG PET/CT findings may aid the diagnosis of patients with unexplained encephalitis and may—as in our patient—precede MRI changes. In Rasmussen encephalitis and anti-leucine glioma-inactivated protein 1 autoimmune encephalitis, for example, brain MRI has been reported as being less sensitive when compared to 18F-FDG PET/CT. In herpes simplex virus encephalitis, temporal lobe, ventral striatal, and septal abnormalities have been described on 18F-FDG PET/CT. And in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, 18F-FDG PET/CT may show hypometabolism in the basal ganglia, the occipital, frontal and parietal lobes, and in regions of the brain specifically related to clinical signs.
BoDV-1 infection is a potentially lethal zoonosis in endemic regions with reported spillover infections in horses and sheep. BoDV-1 infection can result in fatal encephalitis; all severe encephalitis cases of unknown cause should be tested for bornaviruses—especially in endemic regions.

A 77-year-old man attended our hospital reporting a sudden onset of shortness of breath and a fever.14 days earlier, the patient had posterior wall isolation, pulmonary vein isolation, and linear mitral isthmus ablation for drug-refractory atrial fibrillation. Following the procedure, he was complication-free and had been allowed home; he had been prescribed anticoagulation therapy and a proton pump inhibitor.
On examination, the patient was frail but not in a critical state; his blood pressure was 148/68 mm Hg, his pulse was 90 beats per min, and his oxygen saturation was 95% on room air, and his temperature was 38·0°C. Laboratory investigations showed a white blood cell count of 18·8 × 109 per L (typical range 4·5–11·0), C-reactive protein concentration 18·61 mg/dL (typical range <0·3), brain natriuretic peptide 78 pg/mL (typical <18·4), and troponin I 15 pg/mL (typical 26·2 or less). An electrocardiogram showed widespread ST segment elevation and PR segment depression.
A chest CT showed a pericardial effusion with a tiny low-density area—suggesting there was air within the pericardium (figure). The day after his presentation, we did a pericardiocentesis because of haemodynamic instability. However, air continued to be drawn from the pericardial drainage, and a pneumopericardium on the posterior wall of the left atrium was confirmed (figure), indicating a possible oesophageal communication. Endoscopy—using carbon dioxide insufflation to avoid an air embolism in the case of an atrio-oesophagus fistula—showed a 1·5 cm fistula at the level of the mid-oesophagus (figure) on the left atrial wall with the beating heart visible through the fistula, confirming a diagnosis of a pericardial-oesophageal fistula.
We then carried out an emergency thoracoscopic esophagectomy in order to repair the defect in the oesophagus. The patient recovered well and was allowed home after 6 weeks.
Pulmonary vein isolation remains the standard form of catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation; inclusion of posterior wall isolation, as an adjunct to pulmonary vein isolation, is increasing. However, one of the problems with posterior wall ablation is the risk of damage to the oesophagus. Oesophageal fistula after ablation for atrial fibrillation is rare—with an incidence of less than 0·1%—but can be fatal. Importantly, to prevent oesophageal complications the amount of energy delivered to the posterior wall should be limited as much as possible. Symptoms of oesophageal perforation usually, if they are going to, develop within a few weeks of the ablation procedure; patients mainly present with pyrexia and chest pain—as in our patient. Early identification leads to appropriate management and a greater likelihood of successful treatment.

A 23-year-old woman was referred to our hospital for a recurrent discharge of something resembling a white string from her anus. She explained that the problem had started 4 months ago and that she had no other symptoms. She said she had eaten raw fish as sashimi approximately 6 months earlier and that the discharge had started 2 months later. A physical examination found no abnormalities and the blood test results were all normal. However, based on her history, we suspected she had diphyllobothriasis and did a screening abdominal ultrasound scan, which showed a hyperechoic strand-like structure floating freely and moving autonomously in her intestinal tract (figure; videos 1 and 2). A subsequent capsule endoscopy showed a tapeworm (figure); a coprological examination was positive, confirming the diagnosis of diphyllobothriasis. We treated the patient with diatrizoate (Gastrografin, Bayer, Reading, UK) given through a duodenal tube to ensure that the scolex of the cestode was expelled: the complete, uninjured tapeworm measured 210 cm in length when we examined it outside the patient's body (figure). Mitochondrial DNA analysis of the COX-1 and NAD-3 gene sequences identified the causative cestode as Diphyllobothrium nihonkaiense—based on comparisons with homologous sequences in GenBank.D nihonkaiense is the principal cestode causing diphyllobothriasis in Japan. It can infect anyone—regardless of immune status—who eats raw or undercooked fish harbouring infective larvae: once infected, the patient then becomes the worm's second intermediate host. Presenting symptoms include diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and bloating—although up to 30% of patients report no problems.
Oral praziquantel remains the first-line treatment, with the introduction of the radio-opaque contrast medium Gastrografin into the duodenum via a tube the second choice: using Gastrografin ensures complete deworming—ie, discharge of the whole organism, including the scolex—as in our case. Diphyllobothriasis is typically diagnosed by detecting the cestode's ova or proglottids in the patient's faeces. However, the examination of stool samples for the ova is not routinely done in many clinics or hospitals; the detection is sometimes difficult and not definitive. Moreover, once a large part of the worm's body is excreted, the ova are undetectable for some time afterwards. Capsule endoscopy has been reported as a useful alternative for diagnosing diphyllobothriasis, but it is expensive and carries the risk of capsule retention—occurring in approximately 2% of all patients undergoing small bowel capsule endoscopy. In our patient, the abdominal ultrasound vividly showed the tapeworm moving in the intestinal fluid in the gut. And although intestinal gas may sometimes prevent visualisation of the worm, we believe that an abdominal ultrasound scan offers a practical, real-time, non-invasive way of screening for diphyllobothriasis.

A 71-year-old woman attended our hospital with a 2-week history of fluctuating confusion.
The patient, who lived in the German state of Bavaria, close to agricultural areas, had no medical history; she was prescribed no regular medications.
On examination at admission, the patient was well and orientated; her vital signs were within typical range. Neurology examination was within normal limits.
Laboratory investigations on admission for systemic infection, liver function, and kidney function were within typical range.
A chest x-ray showed no abnormalities; an electrocardiogram showed a right bundle branch block and electroencephalography showed no epileptiform discharges.
2 days after admission, the patient rapidly became increasingly encephalopathic; she developed aphasia, atactic movements, and fluctuating vigilance resulting in a state of unresponsive wakefulness syndrome on day 16 after admission.
Brain MRIs on days 2, 5, and 14 after admission showed no abnormalities (figure 1).Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) on days 2, 5, and 20 after admission showed repeatedly raised total protein concentration ranging from 0·41 to 0·57 g/L (typical range 0·15–0·45); all other measurements were within normal range or unclear with regard to diagnosis (appendix; table 1).
Since MRIs and further tests were not conclusive, 18fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT of the brain was done on day 8 which showed marked hypermetabolism in the basal ganglia, the temporomesial lobes, and the cerebellum; frontal and parietal lateral cortex showed distinct hypometabolism (figure 2).
On day 19 after admission, a whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT showed progression of the abnormalities found in the initial scan (figure 2).
Considering a probable autoimmune pathology, the patient was treated with high-dose glucocorticoids—increasing to a maximum of 4 g methylprednisolone after 5 days and then tapering down—and intravenous immunoglobulins (2 g/kg of bodyweight) without any clinical response.
On day 34 after admission, T2 FLAIR and diffusion-weighted MRIs showed hyperintensities in the basal ganglia and head of the caudate nucleus (figure 1) indicating possible Borna disease virus 1 (BoDV-1) encephalitis.
Retrospective analysis, done on day 37 after admission, of CSF taken on days 5 and 20 after admission using reverse-transcription quantitative polymerase-chain-reaction (RT-qPCR) was positive for BoDV-1 RNA with quantification cycle values of 34·3 and 32·5, respectively.
Testing for BoDV-1-antibodies was negative until day 35 after admission; seroconversion occurred on day 42 (indirect immunofluorescence antibody test 1:1280, line blot BoDV-1-phosphoprotein 14 arbitrary units [AU], BoDV-1-nucleoprotein 22 AU; appendix, table 2).
On day 49 after admission, the patient died. Post-mortem histology, BoDV-1-specific immunohistochemistry (appendix, figure 2), and RT-qPCR on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue confirmed BoDV-1 encephalitis. A timeline was constructed of the patient's case (appendix, figure 1).
18F-FDG PET/CT findings may aid the diagnosis of patients with unexplained encephalitis and may—as in our patient—precede MRI changes. In Rasmussen encephalitis and anti-leucine glioma-inactivated protein 1 autoimmune encephalitis, for example, brain MRI has been reported as being less sensitive when compared to 18F-FDG PET/CT. In herpes simplex virus encephalitis, temporal lobe, ventral striatal, and septal abnormalities have been described on 18F-FDG PET/CT. And in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, 18F-FDG PET/CT may show hypometabolism in the basal ganglia, the occipital, frontal and parietal lobes, and in regions of the brain specifically related to clinical signs.
BoDV-1 infection is a potentially lethal zoonosis in endemic regions with reported spillover infections in horses and sheep. BoDV-1 infection can result in fatal encephalitis; all severe encephalitis cases of unknown cause should be tested for bornaviruses—especially in endemic regions.
