A 23-year-old woman was referred to our hospital for a recurrent discharge of something resembling a white string from her anus. She explained that the problem had started 4 months ago and that she had no other symptoms. She said she had eaten raw fish as sashimi approximately 6 months earlier and that the discharge had started 2 months later. A physical examination found no abnormalities and the blood test results were all normal. However, based on her history, we suspected she had diphyllobothriasis and did a screening abdominal ultrasound scan, which showed a hyperechoic strand-like structure floating freely and moving autonomously in her intestinal tract (figure; videos 1 and 2). A subsequent capsule endoscopy showed a tapeworm (figure); a coprological examination was positive, confirming the diagnosis of diphyllobothriasis. We treated the patient with diatrizoate (Gastrografin, Bayer, Reading, UK) given through a duodenal tube to ensure that the scolex of the cestode was expelled: the complete, uninjured tapeworm measured 210 cm in length when we examined it outside the patient's body (figure). Mitochondrial DNA analysis of the COX-1 and NAD-3 gene sequences identified the causative cestode as Diphyllobothrium nihonkaiense—based on comparisons with homologous sequences in GenBank.D nihonkaiense is the principal cestode causing diphyllobothriasis in Japan. It can infect anyone—regardless of immune status—who eats raw or undercooked fish harbouring infective larvae: once infected, the patient then becomes the worm's second intermediate host. Presenting symptoms include diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and bloating—although up to 30% of patients report no problems.
Oral praziquantel remains the first-line treatment, with the introduction of the radio-opaque contrast medium Gastrografin into the duodenum via a tube the second choice: using Gastrografin ensures complete deworming—ie, discharge of the whole organism, including the scolex—as in our case. Diphyllobothriasis is typically diagnosed by detecting the cestode's ova or proglottids in the patient's faeces. However, the examination of stool samples for the ova is not routinely done in many clinics or hospitals; the detection is sometimes difficult and not definitive. Moreover, once a large part of the worm's body is excreted, the ova are undetectable for some time afterwards. Capsule endoscopy has been reported as a useful alternative for diagnosing diphyllobothriasis, but it is expensive and carries the risk of capsule retention—occurring in approximately 2% of all patients undergoing small bowel capsule endoscopy. In our patient, the abdominal ultrasound vividly showed the tapeworm moving in the intestinal fluid in the gut. And although intestinal gas may sometimes prevent visualisation of the worm, we believe that an abdominal ultrasound scan offers a practical, real-time, non-invasive way of screening for diphyllobothriasis.

A 37-year-old woman, who was 35 weeks into a singleton pregnancy, was admitted to our hospital for a planned caesarean hysterectomy.Previously, she had two children, both delivered by caesarean section; this was her third pregnancy. She had no other notable medical history.
At 20 weeks' gestation, an ultrasound scan had shown a low-lying anterior placenta.
At 32 weeks, a repeat ultrasound scan showed placenta praevia with heterogeneity of the placental tissue—some lacunae were seen (figure). Additionally, a placental bulge was identified anteriorly, with deficient overlying myometrium: findings suggestive of placenta accreta spectrum (PAS).
An MRI confirmed the thin myometrium with underlying lacunae, loss of tissue planes at the site of the previous caesarean scar, and large varices in the uterovesical fold.
Laboratory investigations showed a preoperative haemoglobin concentration of 130 g/L (typical range 120–160); the platelet count, clotting screen, and renal function were within typical range.
The patient had an elective caesarean hysterectomy at 35 weeks and 4 days' gestation—a balance having been made between fetal maturity and the risk of an unplanned emergency delivery.
At surgery, the findings correlated with the pre-operative imaging; specifically, we found neovascularisation in the uterovesical fold (figure). The myometrium was particularly deficient and ruptured during uterovesical dissection. We delivered the baby girl via a fundal incision and closed the uterus, leaving the placenta in situ; we then did a total hysterectomy.
The patient, who had a blood loss of 2·5 L, was initially managed with high-dependency care, and made an uncomplicated recovery; mother and baby were allowed home after 5 days.
Gross morphology of the formalin-fixed excised uterus showed the placenta covering the cervix and an extremely thin myometrium anteriorly (figure); the site of the rupture was found with placental tissue visible through the defect. Histopathological examination of a sample of the uterus showed placental villi directly adjacent to myometrial fibres with no intervening decidua (figure). Loss of a typical placental contour, deep infiltrating trophoblast cells, and remodelling of deep uterine blood vessels were noted in additional sections—confirming morbid adherence of the placenta to the uterus.
In PAS, the placenta is abnormally adherent to the uterus, preventing spontaneous separation of the placenta after the birth; subsequent haemorrhage can result in maternal morbidity and mortality. Good outcomes depend upon identifying PAS prior to caesarean section, and appropriate intra-operative management.
Current classification delineates three main clinical grades of PAS: grade 1 is where the placenta is abnormally adherent with trophoblast attached to the myometrium; grade 2 is where the placenta is abnormally invasive with trophoblast invasion into the myometrium; and grade 3 is where the placenta is abnormally invasive with trophoblast breaching myometrial serosa.
The major risk factor for PAS is myometrial scarring, and as rates of caesarean section increase globally, the prevalence of PAS will continue to rise. Patients having a caesarean section should be informed about this potential future complication. Caesarean sections for PAS are best done electively by a multidisciplinary team to prevent extensive blood loss and adjacent organ injury (video).

A 23-year-old woman was referred to our hospital for a recurrent discharge of something resembling a white string from her anus. She explained that the problem had started 4 months ago and that she had no other symptoms. She said she had eaten raw fish as sashimi approximately 6 months earlier and that the discharge had started 2 months later. A physical examination found no abnormalities and the blood test results were all normal. However, based on her history, we suspected she had diphyllobothriasis and did a screening abdominal ultrasound scan, which showed a hyperechoic strand-like structure floating freely and moving autonomously in her intestinal tract (figure; videos 1 and 2). A subsequent capsule endoscopy showed a tapeworm (figure); a coprological examination was positive, confirming the diagnosis of diphyllobothriasis. We treated the patient with diatrizoate (Gastrografin, Bayer, Reading, UK) given through a duodenal tube to ensure that the scolex of the cestode was expelled: the complete, uninjured tapeworm measured 210 cm in length when we examined it outside the patient's body (figure). A 37-year-old woman, who was 35 weeks into a singleton pregnancy, was admitted to our hospital for a planned caesarean hysterectomy.Previously, she had two children, both delivered by caesarean section; this was her third pregnancy. She had no other notable medical history.
At 20 weeks' gestation, an ultrasound scan had shown a low-lying anterior placenta.
At 32 weeks, a repeat ultrasound scan showed placenta praevia with heterogeneity of the placental tissue—some lacunae were seen (figure). Additionally, a placental bulge was identified anteriorly, with deficient overlying myometrium: findings suggestive of placenta accreta spectrum (PAS).
An MRI confirmed the thin myometrium with underlying lacunae, loss of tissue planes at the site of the previous caesarean scar, and large varices in the uterovesical fold.
Laboratory investigations showed a preoperative haemoglobin concentration of 130 g/L (typical range 120–160); the platelet count, clotting screen, and renal function were within typical range.
The patient had an elective caesarean hysterectomy at 35 weeks and 4 days' gestation—a balance having been made between fetal maturity and the risk of an unplanned emergency delivery.
At surgery, the findings correlated with the pre-operative imaging; specifically, we found neovascularisation in the uterovesical fold (figure). The myometrium was particularly deficient and ruptured during uterovesical dissection. We delivered the baby girl via a fundal incision and closed the uterus, leaving the placenta in situ; we then did a total hysterectomy.
The patient, who had a blood loss of 2·5 L, was initially managed with high-dependency care, and made an uncomplicated recovery; mother and baby were allowed home after 5 days.
Gross morphology of the formalin-fixed excised uterus showed the placenta covering the cervix and an extremely thin myometrium anteriorly (figure); the site of the rupture was found with placental tissue visible through the defect. Histopathological examination of a sample of the uterus showed placental villi directly adjacent to myometrial fibres with no intervening decidua (figure). Loss of a typical placental contour, deep infiltrating trophoblast cells, and remodelling of deep uterine blood vessels were noted in additional sections—confirming morbid adherence of the placenta to the uterus.
In PAS, the placenta is abnormally adherent to the uterus, preventing spontaneous separation of the placenta after the birth; subsequent haemorrhage can result in maternal morbidity and mortality. Good outcomes depend upon identifying PAS prior to caesarean section, and appropriate intra-operative management.
Current classification delineates three main clinical grades of PAS: grade 1 is where the placenta is abnormally adherent with trophoblast attached to the myometrium; grade 2 is where the placenta is abnormally invasive with trophoblast invasion into the myometrium; and grade 3 is where the placenta is abnormally invasive with trophoblast breaching myometrial serosa.
The major risk factor for PAS is myometrial scarring, and as rates of caesarean section increase globally, the prevalence of PAS will continue to rise. Patients having a caesarean section should be informed about this potential future complication. Caesarean sections for PAS are best done electively by a multidisciplinary team to prevent extensive blood loss and adjacent organ injury (video).

A 62-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol abuse was admitted to our hospital with chronic diarrhoea, confusion, and weakness in both legs. Initial physical examination showed marked cachexia and decreased strength in both lower limbs. His sensation was intact. Laboratory testing showed several electrolyte abnormalities—presumed to be due to his diarrhoea—including hyponatraemia (130 mmol/L); this was gradually corrected over the course of 4 days, using 0·9% sodium chloride. At the end of this period, the sodium was 140 mmol/L (normal range 135–145 mmol/L). Over the next few days, he continued to be encephalopathic and eventually lost motor function of his arms and legs; his pupils continued to be reactive to light and the function of his extraocular muscles remained intact. An MRI scan of his brain showed restricted diffusion and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) showed a corresponding abnormality in the central pons that was consistent with a diagnosis of central pontine demyelination (figure). Sadly, the patient died in the intensive care unit after his family decided to pursue palliative care.
Osmotic demyelination syndrome—also known as central pontine myelinolysis or extrapontine myelinolysis—usually occurs after rapid correction of sodium abnormalities, although it might be seen secondary to chronic alcohol use, other severe electrolyte disturbances, and malnutrition. According to one theory, the lack of sufficient energy in malnourished patients leads to suboptimal functioning of the Na+/K+ATPase pump, which subsequently results in imbalances in sodium homoeostasis in the brain. A high degree of clinical suspicion that it is likely to occur in patients with chronic alcohol use and those who are malnourished might help to prevent the development of osmotic demyelination syndrome. Treatment is usually just supportive management. However, there have been some case reports of successful treatment with plasma exchange, methylprednisone, and immunoglobulins. MRI usually confirms the diagnosis, and the FLAIR sequence is used to suppress the effects of cerebrospinal fluid on the image—this is especially helpful in showing subtle changes at the periphery of the cerebral hemispheres and in the periventricular region.

A 37-year-old woman, who was 35 weeks into a singleton pregnancy, was admitted to our hospital for a planned caesarean hysterectomy.Previously, she had two children, both delivered by caesarean section; this was her third pregnancy. She had no other notable medical history.
At 20 weeks' gestation, an ultrasound scan had shown a low-lying anterior placenta.
At 32 weeks, a repeat ultrasound scan showed placenta praevia with heterogeneity of the placental tissue—some lacunae were seen (figure). Additionally, a placental bulge was identified anteriorly, with deficient overlying myometrium: findings suggestive of placenta accreta spectrum (PAS).
An MRI confirmed the thin myometrium with underlying lacunae, loss of tissue planes at the site of the previous caesarean scar, and large varices in the uterovesical fold.
Laboratory investigations showed a preoperative haemoglobin concentration of 130 g/L (typical range 120–160); the platelet count, clotting screen, and renal function were within typical range.
The patient had an elective caesarean hysterectomy at 35 weeks and 4 days' gestation—a balance having been made between fetal maturity and the risk of an unplanned emergency delivery.
At surgery, the findings correlated with the pre-operative imaging; specifically, we found neovascularisation in the uterovesical fold (figure). The myometrium was particularly deficient and ruptured during uterovesical dissection. We delivered the baby girl via a fundal incision and closed the uterus, leaving the placenta in situ; we then did a total hysterectomy.
The patient, who had a blood loss of 2·5 L, was initially managed with high-dependency care, and made an uncomplicated recovery; mother and baby were allowed home after 5 days.
Gross morphology of the formalin-fixed excised uterus showed the placenta covering the cervix and an extremely thin myometrium anteriorly (figure); the site of the rupture was found with placental tissue visible through the defect. Histopathological examination of a sample of the uterus showed placental villi directly adjacent to myometrial fibres with no intervening decidua (figure). Loss of a typical placental contour, deep infiltrating trophoblast cells, and remodelling of deep uterine blood vessels were noted in additional sections—confirming morbid adherence of the placenta to the uterus.
In PAS, the placenta is abnormally adherent to the uterus, preventing spontaneous separation of the placenta after the birth; subsequent haemorrhage can result in maternal morbidity and mortality. Good outcomes depend upon identifying PAS prior to caesarean section, and appropriate intra-operative management.
Current classification delineates three main clinical grades of PAS: grade 1 is where the placenta is abnormally adherent with trophoblast attached to the myometrium; grade 2 is where the placenta is abnormally invasive with trophoblast invasion into the myometrium; and grade 3 is where the placenta is abnormally invasive with trophoblast breaching myometrial serosa.
The major risk factor for PAS is myometrial scarring, and as rates of caesarean section increase globally, the prevalence of PAS will continue to rise. Patients having a caesarean section should be informed about this potential future complication. Caesarean sections for PAS are best done electively by a multidisciplinary team to prevent extensive blood loss and adjacent organ injury (video).

A 62-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol abuse was admitted to our hospital with chronic diarrhoea, confusion, and weakness in both legs. Initial physical examination showed marked cachexia and decreased strength in both lower limbs. His sensation was intact. Laboratory testing showed several electrolyte abnormalities—presumed to be due to his diarrhoea—including hyponatraemia (130 mmol/L); this was gradually corrected over the course of 4 days, using 0·9% sodium chloride. At the end of this period, the sodium was 140 mmol/L (normal range 135–145 mmol/L). Over the next few days, he continued to be encephalopathic and eventually lost motor function of his arms and legs; his pupils continued to be reactive to light and the function of his extraocular muscles remained intact. An MRI scan of his brain showed restricted diffusion and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) showed a corresponding abnormality in the central pons that was consistent with a diagnosis of central pontine demyelination (figure). Sadly, the patient died in the intensive care unit after his family decided to pursue palliative care.
Osmotic demyelination syndrome—also known as central pontine myelinolysis or extrapontine myelinolysis—usually occurs after rapid correction of sodium abnormalities, although it might be seen secondary to chronic alcohol use, other severe electrolyte disturbances, and malnutrition. According to one theory, the lack of sufficient energy in malnourished patients leads to suboptimal functioning of the Na+/K+ATPase pump, which subsequently results in imbalances in sodium homoeostasis in the brain. A high degree of clinical suspicion that it is likely to occur in patients with chronic alcohol use and those who are malnourished might help to prevent the development of osmotic demyelination syndrome. Treatment is usually just supportive management. However, there have been some case reports of successful treatment with plasma exchange, methylprednisone, and immunoglobulins. MRI usually confirms the diagnosis, and the FLAIR sequence is used to suppress the effects of cerebrospinal fluid on the image—this is especially helpful in showing subtle changes at the periphery of the cerebral hemispheres and in the periventricular region.

A 2-month-old baby boy, who had noisy breathing since birth that increased in volume during feeding and times of agitation, was referred to our unit for assessment (video).The baby had been born at full term by vaginal delivery; there was no history of infection, foreign body aspiration, intubation, or other airway injury. Investigations previously done included a laryngoscopy, which showed no evidence of laryngomalacia or other abnormalities, an unremarkable barium swallow, and a chest x-ray that showed a left-sided aortic arch.
On examination the patient was in mild respiratory distress. He had wheezing and stridor and was mildly tachypnoeic with a respiratory rate of 68 breaths per min (normal in a 2-month-old: 30–60). His temperature was 36·4°C.
Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal intracardiac anatomy and a left-sided aortic arch with normal branching of the head and neck vessels. However, the left pulmonary artery had an anomalous course (figure): a CT angiogram showed the left pulmonary artery originated from the right pulmonary artery—confirming the suspected diagnosis of a pulmonary artery sling (figure; appendix).
A rigid bronchoscopy showed a long segment of tracheal stenosis, with complete tracheal rings in the distal half of the trachea. Additionally, external compression of the carina by the left pulmonary artery was noted (figure; appendix).
We referred to a specialist centre for an operation to reimplant the left pulmonary artery into the main pulmonary artery; a slide tracheoplasty, which involved dividing and reconstructing part of the trachea to create a wider airway, was also done.
The baby was allowed home after 3 weeks. At follow-up, 2 months later, our patient was well without any symptoms.
Congenital stridor—a sign of upper airway obstruction—results from several conditions including laryngomalacia, vocal cord paralysis, and laryngeal webs. Stridor may also occur due to extrinsic compression on the airway by vascular rings: a double aortic arch or right aortic arch with an aberrant left subclavian artery.
Pulmonary artery sling is a rare vascular anomaly causing external airway obstruction. In contrast to a vascular ring, which may cause respiratory and feeding problems, a sling does not encircle the trachea and oesophagus. Rather, the left pulmonary artery arises from the posterior aspect of the right pulmonary artery, passes over the right main-stem bronchus, turns to the left, and courses between the trachea and oesophagus, before reaching the left pulmonary hilum.
When a sling is suspected, advanced imaging modalities confirm the diagnosis and delineate the anatomy. A bronchoscopy is necessary to evaluate the airway because associated anomalies of the tracheobronchial tree are common and approximately 50% of patients have tracheal stenosis. Additionally, patients frequently have concomitant cardiac lesions such as tetralogy of Fallot, which can be repaired simultaneously.

A 62-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol abuse was admitted to our hospital with chronic diarrhoea, confusion, and weakness in both legs. Initial physical examination showed marked cachexia and decreased strength in both lower limbs. His sensation was intact. Laboratory testing showed several electrolyte abnormalities—presumed to be due to his diarrhoea—including hyponatraemia (130 mmol/L); this was gradually corrected over the course of 4 days, using 0·9% sodium chloride. At the end of this period, the sodium was 140 mmol/L (normal range 135–145 mmol/L). Over the next few days, he continued to be encephalopathic and eventually lost motor function of his arms and legs; his pupils continued to be reactive to light and the function of his extraocular muscles remained intact. An MRI scan of his brain showed restricted diffusion and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) showed a corresponding abnormality in the central pons that was consistent with a diagnosis of central pontine demyelination (figure). Sadly, the patient died in the intensive care unit after his family decided to pursue palliative care.
Osmotic demyelination syndrome—also known as central pontine myelinolysis or extrapontine myelinolysis—usually occurs after rapid correction of sodium abnormalities, although it might be seen secondary to chronic alcohol use, other severe electrolyte disturbances, and malnutrition. According to one theory, the lack of sufficient energy in malnourished patients leads to suboptimal functioning of the Na+/K+ATPase pump, which subsequently results in imbalances in sodium homoeostasis in the brain. A high degree of clinical suspicion that it is likely to occur in patients with chronic alcohol use and those who are malnourished might help to prevent the development of osmotic demyelination syndrome. Treatment is usually just supportive management. However, there have been some case reports of successful treatment with plasma exchange, methylprednisone, and immunoglobulins. MRI usually confirms the diagnosis, and the FLAIR sequence is used to suppress the effects of cerebrospinal fluid on the image—this is especially helpful in showing subtle changes at the periphery of the cerebral hemispheres and in the periventricular region.

A 2-month-old baby boy, who had noisy breathing since birth that increased in volume during feeding and times of agitation, was referred to our unit for assessment (video).The baby had been born at full term by vaginal delivery; there was no history of infection, foreign body aspiration, intubation, or other airway injury. Investigations previously done included a laryngoscopy, which showed no evidence of laryngomalacia or other abnormalities, an unremarkable barium swallow, and a chest x-ray that showed a left-sided aortic arch.
On examination the patient was in mild respiratory distress. He had wheezing and stridor and was mildly tachypnoeic with a respiratory rate of 68 breaths per min (normal in a 2-month-old: 30–60). His temperature was 36·4°C.
Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal intracardiac anatomy and a left-sided aortic arch with normal branching of the head and neck vessels. However, the left pulmonary artery had an anomalous course (figure): a CT angiogram showed the left pulmonary artery originated from the right pulmonary artery—confirming the suspected diagnosis of a pulmonary artery sling (figure; appendix).
A rigid bronchoscopy showed a long segment of tracheal stenosis, with complete tracheal rings in the distal half of the trachea. Additionally, external compression of the carina by the left pulmonary artery was noted (figure; appendix).
We referred to a specialist centre for an operation to reimplant the left pulmonary artery into the main pulmonary artery; a slide tracheoplasty, which involved dividing and reconstructing part of the trachea to create a wider airway, was also done.
The baby was allowed home after 3 weeks. At follow-up, 2 months later, our patient was well without any symptoms.
Congenital stridor—a sign of upper airway obstruction—results from several conditions including laryngomalacia, vocal cord paralysis, and laryngeal webs. Stridor may also occur due to extrinsic compression on the airway by vascular rings: a double aortic arch or right aortic arch with an aberrant left subclavian artery.
Pulmonary artery sling is a rare vascular anomaly causing external airway obstruction. In contrast to a vascular ring, which may cause respiratory and feeding problems, a sling does not encircle the trachea and oesophagus. Rather, the left pulmonary artery arises from the posterior aspect of the right pulmonary artery, passes over the right main-stem bronchus, turns to the left, and courses between the trachea and oesophagus, before reaching the left pulmonary hilum.
When a sling is suspected, advanced imaging modalities confirm the diagnosis and delineate the anatomy. A bronchoscopy is necessary to evaluate the airway because associated anomalies of the tracheobronchial tree are common and approximately 50% of patients have tracheal stenosis. Additionally, patients frequently have concomitant cardiac lesions such as tetralogy of Fallot, which can be repaired simultaneously.

A 26-year-old woman, 10 weeks pregnant, attended our hospital with a 1-week history of gradually progressive abdominal discomfort, lethargy, and nausea.On examination, she was pale; blood pressure was 124/74 mm Hg and pulse was 106 beats per min. The patient's spleen was enlarged and extended down to the pelvic brim. She had no abdominal tenderness, vaginal bleeding, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or signs of chronic liver disease including jaundice, clubbing, or ascites.
Abdominal ultrasound with colour Doppler showed a viable intrauterine pregnancy and splenomegaly—measuring 23 cm in oblique craniocaudal length—with peri splenic varices (figure).
Laboratory investigations showed iron-deficiency anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 7·4 g/dL; normal 11·4–14·7), a leukocyte count of 4·2 × 109 per L (3·84–10·0), platelet count of 206 × 109 per L (164–387), and a lactate dehydrogenase concentration of 547 U/L (250–580).
Liver function tests and investigations for thalassaemia, chronic viral and autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis, and Wilson's disease were negative.
Peripheral blood film showed teardrop-shaped red cells without blasts. Bone marrow biopsy showed a hypercellular marrow with relative myeloid hyperplasia, megakaryocytic proliferation with atypia, and minimal fibrosis (WHO grade 1/3). DNA sequencing showed a JAK2-V617F mutation with a 31% median allele burden; no BCR-ABL1 fusion gene was found. Cytogenetic analyses showed a 46,XX karyotype. No features of malignancy, lymphoproliferative, or other chronic myeloid disorders were seen.
Taken together with the splenomegaly, we diagnosed pre-fibrotic primary myelofibrosis, using the revised WHO 2016, criteria and scored the patient 0 (indicating a good prognosis) on the Dynamic International Prognostic Scoring System plus.
We started her on aspirin 150 mg once daily, as prophylaxis against myelofibrosis-associated pre-eclampsia, but stopped it when she developed haematemesis at 16 weeks’ gestation. An emergency endoscopy showed large oesophageal and gastric varices due to noncirrhotic portal hypertension.
Following endoscopic variceal ligation, we started propranolol 20 mg twice daily to prevent further bleeding; the patient was then monitored for fetal growth restriction.
From 26 weeks’ gestation, we prescribed 45 μg weekly of pegylated interferon alfa-2a, increasing to 90 μg a week from 29 weeks’ gestation, to reduce the size of the spleen.
At 34 weeks’ gestation, ultrasound scans showed fetal growth restriction. The spleen was 17 cm and had regressed away from the pelvic brim, allowing us to deliver a baby girl, weighing 2080 g with normal Apgar scores, by a lower-segment caesarean section using a Pfannenstiel incision (figure). We did not see the spleen when entering the peritoneal cavity. Mother and baby were allowed home 4 days after the delivery.
We prescribed the patient 40 mg once a day of enoxaparin for 6 weeks—to prevent post-partum thrombosis after an endoscopy, on the day after the caesarean section, showed small varices.
Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) are rare in pregnancy; they are associated with thrombosis, pre-eclampsia, fetal growth restriction, and stillbirth. Interferon alfa-2a is recommended for cytoreduction in pregnancy if high cell counts, multiple symptoms, or a history of thrombosis or poor obstetric outcomes is found. Unlike Janus kinase 2 inhibitors and hydroxyurea, interferon alfa-2a does not cross the placenta and has a proven fetal safety profile; it can reduce spleen size by at least 50% in about half of non-pregnant patients with MPN. Splenomegaly—a cause of obstetric haemorrhage currently unaddressed in existing guidelines—may rupture in labour or obstruct surgical incisions during caesarean section. Interferon alfa-2a might be considered for newly detected or persisting splenomegaly in pregnant patients with MPN, even in the absence of indications for cytoreduction. Ideally, patients should be monitored, in a multidisciplinary setting, for dose-limiting haematologic toxicities and other complications (appendix). Finally, the possibility of portal hypertension in MPN should be considered if splenic varices are detected on ultrasound; elective gastroscopy might avoid unforeseen episodes of acute variceal bleeding as the pregnancy advances.

A 2-month-old baby boy, who had noisy breathing since birth that increased in volume during feeding and times of agitation, was referred to our unit for assessment (video).The baby had been born at full term by vaginal delivery; there was no history of infection, foreign body aspiration, intubation, or other airway injury. Investigations previously done included a laryngoscopy, which showed no evidence of laryngomalacia or other abnormalities, an unremarkable barium swallow, and a chest x-ray that showed a left-sided aortic arch.
On examination the patient was in mild respiratory distress. He had wheezing and stridor and was mildly tachypnoeic with a respiratory rate of 68 breaths per min (normal in a 2-month-old: 30–60). His temperature was 36·4°C.
Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal intracardiac anatomy and a left-sided aortic arch with normal branching of the head and neck vessels. However, the left pulmonary artery had an anomalous course (figure): a CT angiogram showed the left pulmonary artery originated from the right pulmonary artery—confirming the suspected diagnosis of a pulmonary artery sling (figure; appendix).
A rigid bronchoscopy showed a long segment of tracheal stenosis, with complete tracheal rings in the distal half of the trachea. Additionally, external compression of the carina by the left pulmonary artery was noted (figure; appendix).
We referred to a specialist centre for an operation to reimplant the left pulmonary artery into the main pulmonary artery; a slide tracheoplasty, which involved dividing and reconstructing part of the trachea to create a wider airway, was also done.
The baby was allowed home after 3 weeks. At follow-up, 2 months later, our patient was well without any symptoms.
Congenital stridor—a sign of upper airway obstruction—results from several conditions including laryngomalacia, vocal cord paralysis, and laryngeal webs. Stridor may also occur due to extrinsic compression on the airway by vascular rings: a double aortic arch or right aortic arch with an aberrant left subclavian artery.
Pulmonary artery sling is a rare vascular anomaly causing external airway obstruction. In contrast to a vascular ring, which may cause respiratory and feeding problems, a sling does not encircle the trachea and oesophagus. Rather, the left pulmonary artery arises from the posterior aspect of the right pulmonary artery, passes over the right main-stem bronchus, turns to the left, and courses between the trachea and oesophagus, before reaching the left pulmonary hilum.
When a sling is suspected, advanced imaging modalities confirm the diagnosis and delineate the anatomy. A bronchoscopy is necessary to evaluate the airway because associated anomalies of the tracheobronchial tree are common and approximately 50% of patients have tracheal stenosis. Additionally, patients frequently have concomitant cardiac lesions such as tetralogy of Fallot, which can be repaired simultaneously.

An 80-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of acute-onset severe polyarthralgia of the hands, feet, elbows, and shoulders with associated swelling of the dorsum of the hands and feet. The patient had a preceding history of anorexia and weight loss for 2 months associated with fatigue and prolonged morning stiffness. On examination she had marked stiffness of the neck and shoulders and required high back support (figure A). The patient's hands and feet were swollen with pitting oedema giving a boxing glove appearance of the hands (figure B–D). There was tenderness in the wrists and hands over the metacarpophalangeal joints and proximal interphalangeal joints with reduced range of motion. X-ray of the hands revealed soft tissue swelling with no joint erosions and x-ray of the spine revealed age related degenerative changes with no evidence of an axial spondyloarthopathy. Ultrasound of the shoulders and hands showed subdeltoid and subacromial bursitis with minimal fluid and extensor synovitis in both hands.The patient's blood results showed anaemia, markedly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (100 mm/hr) and C-reactive protein (50 mg/L); tests for rheumatoid factor, anticitrullinated protein antibody, antinuclear antibody, HLA B27, and multiple myeloma screen were all negative. Joint aspirate of the left wrist did not reveal any evidence of a crystal-related arthropathy. A diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica with remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis and pitting oedema (RS3PE) was made. The patient was started on 20 mg of prednisone per day; however, there was no appreciable response to treatment, and the patient's joint pains, stiffness, and swelling persisted.
The patient's 2-month history of anorexia and weight loss and, particularly, unresponsiveness to moderate dose steroids raised the possibility of a malignancy. On further evaluation and after doing an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, colonoscopy, and ultrasound of the abdomen, the patient was diagnosed with a metastatic, poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the colon, indicating that her steroid resistant polymyalgia rheumatica with RS3PE was paraneoplastic in origin. Paraneoplastic RS3PE often does not respond to steroids alone and should be targeted by treating the underlying malignancy.
RS3PE is an uncommon condition that is characterised as an acute polysynovitis associated with pitting oedema that tends to affect individuals who are older than 50 years. This condition can occur in isolation or be associated with other connective tissue diseases, malignancies, or, more rarely, infections or drugs. Polymyalgia rheumatica RS3PE is very sensitive to low-to-moderate doses of steroids, with a starting dose of prednisone of 15 to 20 mg/day typically showing a substantial response within 24–48 hours of treatment initiation. Methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine, medications that can be useful in patients with steroid resistance, have been studied in these patients; however, the response to steroids has been more pronounced and robust.
The absence of a response to moderate dose of steroids should call into question the diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica RS3PE or suggest a secondary cause of the disease. Before labelling a case as steroid resistant, a search for a secondary cause of the disease—especially a malignancy—should be made, because paraneoplastic RS3PE is not uncommon. In 20–50% of cases, RS3PE has been associated with a malignancy. 75% of cases of paraneoplastic RS3PE are due to solid tumours.

A 26-year-old woman, 10 weeks pregnant, attended our hospital with a 1-week history of gradually progressive abdominal discomfort, lethargy, and nausea.On examination, she was pale; blood pressure was 124/74 mm Hg and pulse was 106 beats per min. The patient's spleen was enlarged and extended down to the pelvic brim. She had no abdominal tenderness, vaginal bleeding, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or signs of chronic liver disease including jaundice, clubbing, or ascites.
Abdominal ultrasound with colour Doppler showed a viable intrauterine pregnancy and splenomegaly—measuring 23 cm in oblique craniocaudal length—with peri splenic varices (figure).
Laboratory investigations showed iron-deficiency anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 7·4 g/dL; normal 11·4–14·7), a leukocyte count of 4·2 × 109 per L (3·84–10·0), platelet count of 206 × 109 per L (164–387), and a lactate dehydrogenase concentration of 547 U/L (250–580).
Liver function tests and investigations for thalassaemia, chronic viral and autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis, and Wilson's disease were negative.
Peripheral blood film showed teardrop-shaped red cells without blasts. Bone marrow biopsy showed a hypercellular marrow with relative myeloid hyperplasia, megakaryocytic proliferation with atypia, and minimal fibrosis (WHO grade 1/3). DNA sequencing showed a JAK2-V617F mutation with a 31% median allele burden; no BCR-ABL1 fusion gene was found. Cytogenetic analyses showed a 46,XX karyotype. No features of malignancy, lymphoproliferative, or other chronic myeloid disorders were seen.
Taken together with the splenomegaly, we diagnosed pre-fibrotic primary myelofibrosis, using the revised WHO 2016, criteria and scored the patient 0 (indicating a good prognosis) on the Dynamic International Prognostic Scoring System plus.
We started her on aspirin 150 mg once daily, as prophylaxis against myelofibrosis-associated pre-eclampsia, but stopped it when she developed haematemesis at 16 weeks’ gestation. An emergency endoscopy showed large oesophageal and gastric varices due to noncirrhotic portal hypertension.
Following endoscopic variceal ligation, we started propranolol 20 mg twice daily to prevent further bleeding; the patient was then monitored for fetal growth restriction.
From 26 weeks’ gestation, we prescribed 45 μg weekly of pegylated interferon alfa-2a, increasing to 90 μg a week from 29 weeks’ gestation, to reduce the size of the spleen.
At 34 weeks’ gestation, ultrasound scans showed fetal growth restriction. The spleen was 17 cm and had regressed away from the pelvic brim, allowing us to deliver a baby girl, weighing 2080 g with normal Apgar scores, by a lower-segment caesarean section using a Pfannenstiel incision (figure). We did not see the spleen when entering the peritoneal cavity. Mother and baby were allowed home 4 days after the delivery.
We prescribed the patient 40 mg once a day of enoxaparin for 6 weeks—to prevent post-partum thrombosis after an endoscopy, on the day after the caesarean section, showed small varices.
Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) are rare in pregnancy; they are associated with thrombosis, pre-eclampsia, fetal growth restriction, and stillbirth. Interferon alfa-2a is recommended for cytoreduction in pregnancy if high cell counts, multiple symptoms, or a history of thrombosis or poor obstetric outcomes is found. Unlike Janus kinase 2 inhibitors and hydroxyurea, interferon alfa-2a does not cross the placenta and has a proven fetal safety profile; it can reduce spleen size by at least 50% in about half of non-pregnant patients with MPN. Splenomegaly—a cause of obstetric haemorrhage currently unaddressed in existing guidelines—may rupture in labour or obstruct surgical incisions during caesarean section. Interferon alfa-2a might be considered for newly detected or persisting splenomegaly in pregnant patients with MPN, even in the absence of indications for cytoreduction. Ideally, patients should be monitored, in a multidisciplinary setting, for dose-limiting haematologic toxicities and other complications (appendix). Finally, the possibility of portal hypertension in MPN should be considered if splenic varices are detected on ultrasound; elective gastroscopy might avoid unforeseen episodes of acute variceal bleeding as the pregnancy advances.

An 80-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of acute-onset severe polyarthralgia of the hands, feet, elbows, and shoulders with associated swelling of the dorsum of the hands and feet. The patient had a preceding history of anorexia and weight loss for 2 months associated with fatigue and prolonged morning stiffness. On examination she had marked stiffness of the neck and shoulders and required high back support (figure A). The patient's hands and feet were swollen with pitting oedema giving a boxing glove appearance of the hands (figure B–D). There was tenderness in the wrists and hands over the metacarpophalangeal joints and proximal interphalangeal joints with reduced range of motion. X-ray of the hands revealed soft tissue swelling with no joint erosions and x-ray of the spine revealed age related degenerative changes with no evidence of an axial spondyloarthopathy. Ultrasound of the shoulders and hands showed subdeltoid and subacromial bursitis with minimal fluid and extensor synovitis in both hands.The patient's blood results showed anaemia, markedly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (100 mm/hr) and C-reactive protein (50 mg/L); tests for rheumatoid factor, anticitrullinated protein antibody, antinuclear antibody, HLA B27, and multiple myeloma screen were all negative. Joint aspirate of the left wrist did not reveal any evidence of a crystal-related arthropathy. A diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica with remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis and pitting oedema (RS3PE) was made. The patient was started on 20 mg of prednisone per day; however, there was no appreciable response to treatment, and the patient's joint pains, stiffness, and swelling persisted.
The patient's 2-month history of anorexia and weight loss and, particularly, unresponsiveness to moderate dose steroids raised the possibility of a malignancy. On further evaluation and after doing an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, colonoscopy, and ultrasound of the abdomen, the patient was diagnosed with a metastatic, poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the colon, indicating that her steroid resistant polymyalgia rheumatica with RS3PE was paraneoplastic in origin. Paraneoplastic RS3PE often does not respond to steroids alone and should be targeted by treating the underlying malignancy.
RS3PE is an uncommon condition that is characterised as an acute polysynovitis associated with pitting oedema that tends to affect individuals who are older than 50 years. This condition can occur in isolation or be associated with other connective tissue diseases, malignancies, or, more rarely, infections or drugs. Polymyalgia rheumatica RS3PE is very sensitive to low-to-moderate doses of steroids, with a starting dose of prednisone of 15 to 20 mg/day typically showing a substantial response within 24–48 hours of treatment initiation. Methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine, medications that can be useful in patients with steroid resistance, have been studied in these patients; however, the response to steroids has been more pronounced and robust.
The absence of a response to moderate dose of steroids should call into question the diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica RS3PE or suggest a secondary cause of the disease. Before labelling a case as steroid resistant, a search for a secondary cause of the disease—especially a malignancy—should be made, because paraneoplastic RS3PE is not uncommon. In 20–50% of cases, RS3PE has been associated with a malignancy. 75% of cases of paraneoplastic RS3PE are due to solid tumours.

On examination she had marked stiffness of the neck and shoulders and required high back support (figure A). The patient's hands and feet were swollen with pitting oedema giving a boxing glove appearance of the hands (figure B–D). There was tenderness in the wrists and hands over the metacarpophalangeal joints and proximal interphalangeal joints with reduced range of motion. X-ray of the hands revealed soft tissue swelling with no joint erosions and x-ray of the spine revealed age related degenerative changes with no evidence of an axial spondyloarthopathy. Ultrasound of the shoulders and hands showed subdeltoid and subacromial bursitis with minimal fluid and extensor synovitis in both hands.The patient's blood results showed anaemia, markedly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (100 mm/hr) and C-reactive protein (50 mg/L); tests for rheumatoid factor, anticitrullinated protein antibody, antinuclear antibody, HLA B27, and multiple myeloma screen were all negative. Joint aspirate of the left wrist did not reveal any evidence of a crystal-related arthropathy. A diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica with remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis and pitting oedema (RS3PE) was made. The patient was started on 20 mg of prednisone per day; however, there was no appreciable response to treatment, and the patient's joint pains, stiffness, and swelling persisted.
The patient's 2-month history of anorexia and weight loss and, particularly, unresponsiveness to moderate dose steroids raised the possibility of a malignancy. On further evaluation and after doing an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, colonoscopy, and ultrasound of the abdomen, the patient was diagnosed with a metastatic, poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the colon, indicating that her steroid resistant polymyalgia rheumatica with RS3PE was paraneoplastic in origin. Paraneoplastic RS3PE often does not respond to steroids alone and should be targeted by treating the underlying malignancy.
RS3PE is an uncommon condition that is characterised as an acute polysynovitis associated with pitting oedema that tends to affect individuals who are older than 50 years. This condition can occur in isolation or be associated with other connective tissue diseases, malignancies, or, more rarely, infections or drugs. Polymyalgia rheumatica RS3PE is very sensitive to low-to-moderate doses of steroids, with a starting dose of prednisone of 15 to 20 mg/day typically showing a substantial response within 24–48 hours of treatment initiation. Methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine, medications that can be useful in patients with steroid resistance, have been studied in these patients; however, the response to steroids has been more pronounced and robust.
The absence of a response to moderate dose of steroids should call into question the diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica RS3PE or suggest a secondary cause of the disease. Before labelling a case as steroid resistant, a search for a secondary cause of the disease—especially a malignancy—should be made, because paraneoplastic RS3PE is not uncommon. In 20–50% of cases, RS3PE has been associated with a malignancy. 75% of cases of paraneoplastic RS3PE are due to solid tumours.

A 27-year-old man came to our emergency department with shortness of breath, a cough, and a globus sensation, which had all started earlier in the day. He also complained of an itchy rash on his neck, chest, and arms, which had developed 2 weeks earlier. During the previous 6 weeks, he had been repeatedly exposed to tear gas while working as a photojournalist at different protests around Hong Kong; the last exposure was 11 days before he came to see us. He said he had worn a full-face respirator during recent episodes.The patient had attended our department on three previous occasions because of the rash. He had been given oral prednisolone, antihistamines, and topical steroids but his symptoms had not improved. He had a history of allergic rhinitis; he had no history of asthma or bronchitis.
On examination we found the patient to have a blanchable, maculopapular rash over his neck, upper trunk, and arms—consistent with an allergic contact dermatitis (figure). His respiratory rate was 18 breaths per min and his oxygen saturation was 100% on room air; there was no evidence of angio-edema involving the upper airway. His lung fields were clear on auscultation.
Blood investigations showed no abnormalities: the patient's absolute eosinophil count and serum IgE concentration were normal.
A chest x-ray and thoracic CT showed no abnormalities. Bronchoscopy showed mild pharyngitis but severe tracheobronchitis (figure; video). No pathogens were detected with PCR or culture of the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. We decided not to do a bronchial biopsy of the severely inflamed bronchi because we were concerned about the risk of bleeding caused by the procedure. Lung function tests showed normal spirometry but a significant bronchodilator response: an increase of 19%, 640 mL in forced expiratory volume in 1 s, and a slightly reduced oxygen diffusion capacity of 71% (normal range 75–125%).
Considering the patient's presentation in the round we believe the patient had severe tracheobronchitis and an allergic contact dermatitis due to repeated exposure to tear gas. The patient was admitted and given intravenous hydrocortisone, inhaled fluticasone and vilanterol, and 50 mg/day of oral prednisolone. His condition improved and he went home after 4 days.
At follow-up 6 weeks later, the patient's shortness of breath had improved but he still had the cough. We repeated the bronchoscopy, which showed improvement in the tracheobronchitis (figure).
Lung function tests showed a significant bronchodilator response only in small airways: an increase of 18% in forced expiratory flow between 25% and 75% of the forced vital capacity (appendix).
We recommended that he continue with the inhaled fluticasone and vilanterol. Notably, the patient's skin rash recurred following re-exposure to tear gas. He was given three more short courses of oral prednisolone. 4 months later at a follow-up appointment his dermatological and respiratory symptoms had resolved.
o-Chlorobenzylidene malononitrile (CS) has become the most commonly used tear gas agent—often deployed by producing microparticles 3–10 μm in size with pyrotechnic devices like grenades or canisters. CS is a potent agonist of the transient receptor potential cation channel A1, which is expressed in nociceptors in the skin and mucous membranes; it triggers pain and an acute inflammatory reaction. Exposure also causes immediate intense irritation of the eyes, nose, mouth, skin, respiratory tract, and gastrointestinal tract in a dose-dependent manner—these effects lead the individual to be temporarily incapacitated.
Repeated exposure has been associated with chronic bronchitis and allergic contact dermatitis which—as in our patient—may occur despite a normal eosinophil count and serum IgE concentration.

input:
A 27-year-old man came to our emergency department with shortness of breath, a cough, and a globus sensation, which had all started earlier in the day. He also complained of an itchy rash on his neck, chest, and arms, which had developed 2 weeks earlier. During the previous 6 weeks, he had been repeatedly exposed to tear gas while working as a photojournalist at different protests around Hong Kong; the last exposure was 11 days before he came to see us. He said he had worn a full-face respirator during recent episodes.The patient had attended our department on three previous occasions because of the rash. He had been given oral prednisolone, antihistamines, and topical steroids but his symptoms had not improved. He had a history of allergic rhinitis; he had no history of asthma or bronchitis.
On examination we found the patient to have a blanchable, maculopapular rash over his neck, upper trunk, and arms—consistent with an allergic contact dermatitis (figure). His respiratory rate was 18 breaths per min and his oxygen saturation was 100% on room air; there was no evidence of angio-edema involving the upper airway. His lung fields were clear on auscultation.
Blood investigations showed no abnormalities: the patient's absolute eosinophil count and serum IgE concentration were normal.
A chest x-ray and thoracic CT showed no abnormalities. Bronchoscopy showed mild pharyngitis but severe tracheobronchitis (figure; video). No pathogens were detected with PCR or culture of the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. We decided not to do a bronchial biopsy of the severely inflamed bronchi because we were concerned about the risk of bleeding caused by the procedure. Lung function tests showed normal spirometry but a significant bronchodilator response: an increase of 19%, 640 mL in forced expiratory volume in 1 s, and a slightly reduced oxygen diffusion capacity of 71% (normal range 75–125%).
Considering the patient's presentation in the round we believe the patient had severe tracheobronchitis and an allergic contact dermatitis due to repeated exposure to tear gas. The patient was admitted and given intravenous hydrocortisone, inhaled fluticasone and vilanterol, and 50 mg/day of oral prednisolone. His condition improved and he went home after 4 days.
At follow-up 6 weeks later, the patient's shortness of breath had improved but he still had the cough. We repeated the bronchoscopy, which showed improvement in the tracheobronchitis (figure).
Lung function tests showed a significant bronchodilator response only in small airways: an increase of 18% in forced expiratory flow between 25% and 75% of the forced vital capacity (appendix).
We recommended that he continue with the inhaled fluticasone and vilanterol. Notably, the patient's skin rash recurred following re-exposure to tear gas. He was given three more short courses of oral prednisolone. 4 months later at a follow-up appointment his dermatological and respiratory symptoms had resolved.
o-Chlorobenzylidene malononitrile (CS) has become the most commonly used tear gas agent—often deployed by producing microparticles 3–10 μm in size with pyrotechnic devices like grenades or canisters. CS is a potent agonist of the transient receptor potential cation channel A1, which is expressed in nociceptors in the skin and mucous membranes; it triggers pain and an acute inflammatory reaction. Exposure also causes immediate intense irritation of the eyes, nose, mouth, skin, respiratory tract, and gastrointestinal tract in a dose-dependent manner—these effects lead the individual to be temporarily incapacitated.
Repeated exposure has been associated with chronic bronchitis and allergic contact dermatitis which—as in our patient—may occur despite a normal eosinophil count and serum IgE concentration.

A 27-year-old man came to our emergency department with shortness of breath, a cough, and a globus sensation, which had all started earlier in the day. He also complained of an itchy rash on his neck, chest, and arms, which had developed 2 weeks earlier. During the previous 6 weeks, he had been repeatedly exposed to tear gas while working as a photojournalist at different protests around Hong Kong; the last exposure was 11 days before he came to see us. He said he had worn a full-face respirator during recent episodes.The patient had attended our department on three previous occasions because of the rash. He had been given oral prednisolone, antihistamines, and topical steroids but his symptoms had not improved. He had a history of allergic rhinitis; he had no history of asthma or bronchitis.
On examination we found the patient to have a blanchable, maculopapular rash over his neck, upper trunk, and arms—consistent with an allergic contact dermatitis (figure). His respiratory rate was 18 breaths per min and his oxygen saturation was 100% on room air; there was no evidence of angio-edema involving the upper airway. His lung fields were clear on auscultation.
Blood investigations showed no abnormalities: the patient's absolute eosinophil count and serum IgE concentration were normal.
A chest x-ray and thoracic CT showed no abnormalities. Bronchoscopy showed mild pharyngitis but severe tracheobronchitis (figure; video). No pathogens were detected with PCR or culture of the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. We decided not to do a bronchial biopsy of the severely inflamed bronchi because we were concerned about the risk of bleeding caused by the procedure. Lung function tests showed normal spirometry but a significant bronchodilator response: an increase of 19%, 640 mL in forced expiratory volume in 1 s, and a slightly reduced oxygen diffusion capacity of 71% (normal range 75–125%).
Considering the patient's presentation in the round we believe the patient had severe tracheobronchitis and an allergic contact dermatitis due to repeated exposure to tear gas. The patient was admitted and given intravenous hydrocortisone, inhaled fluticasone and vilanterol, and 50 mg/day of oral prednisolone. His condition improved and he went home after 4 days.
At follow-up 6 weeks later, the patient's shortness of breath had improved but he still had the cough. We repeated the bronchoscopy, which showed improvement in the tracheobronchitis (figure).
Lung function tests showed a significant bronchodilator response only in small airways: an increase of 18% in forced expiratory flow between 25% and 75% of the forced vital capacity (appendix).
We recommended that he continue with the inhaled fluticasone and vilanterol. Notably, the patient's skin rash recurred following re-exposure to tear gas. He was given three more short courses of oral prednisolone. 4 months later at a follow-up appointment his dermatological and respiratory symptoms had resolved.
o-Chlorobenzylidene malononitrile (CS) has become the most commonly used tear gas agent—often deployed by producing microparticles 3–10 μm in size with pyrotechnic devices like grenades or canisters. CS is a potent agonist of the transient receptor potential cation channel A1, which is expressed in nociceptors in the skin and mucous membranes; it triggers pain and an acute inflammatory reaction. Exposure also causes immediate intense irritation of the eyes, nose, mouth, skin, respiratory tract, and gastrointestinal tract in a dose-dependent manner—these effects lead the individual to be temporarily incapacitated.
Repeated exposure has been associated with chronic bronchitis and allergic contact dermatitis which—as in our patient—may occur despite a normal eosinophil count and serum IgE concentration.

A 13-year-old boy was admitted to hospital with a low-grade fever (maximum temperature of 38°C) that had persisted for 6 months. During this time, his body temperature typically increased in the afternoon or evening and was accompanied by arthralgia, mild headache, and cough. The patient did not report any other clinical signs or symptoms. His white blood cell count, haemoglobin concentration, platelet count, C-reactive protein concentration, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were all normal. No bacterial or fungal infections were detected in the blood, bone marrow, or cerebrospinal fluid cultures. Ultrasound examination revealed multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the neck, bilateral subclavian region, abdominal cavity, and groin. The patient had previously been treated with piperacillin-tazobactam and aciclovir, but showed no improvement. His past medical history and family history were unremarkable.An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET-CT scan revealed a symmetrical increase in FDG metabolism in multiple cartilages (figure A, B). The maximum standard uptake value of the lesions was 5·4, and whole-exome sequencing revealed a pathogenic variant of the NLRP12 gene (1742G→A, Trp581*; accession number VCV001444965.2, variation ID 1444965), which has been reported in several cases associated with NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease. The pathogenicity of this mutation was assessed using InterVar, a bioinformatics software tool, which predicted very strong (PVS1), moderate (PM2), and supporting (PP3) evidence of pathogenicity. However, this mutation was classified as a variant of uncertain significance in the ClinVar database, so interpretation of the pathogenicity of this mutation should still be approached with caution. The patient was treated with 20 mg of methylprednisolone per day for 5 days and was then discharged with no fever or arthralgia. After 4 months, the 18F-FDG PET-CT scan was repeated and indicated that the polychondritis was in complete remission (figure C, D).
To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of polychondritis occurring in a patient with NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease. This result could partly explain why the patient did not have elevated inflammatory indicators, which is observed in 30% of people with autoinflammatory diseases associated with NLRP12 mutations. The clinical features of NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease differ from familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome, as only about 47% of patients with NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease have clear triggers from exposure to cold. Furthermore, the median age of onset for NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease is higher than NLRP3-related autoinflammatory disease, and headaches are an uncommon finding observed in approximately 14% of patients with NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease. Regarding this patient, we suspect that his arthralgia could indicate chondritic pain.
Most patients with NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease benefit from a short regimen of corticosteroid treatment without requiring additional interleukin-1 blocking therapy. Both NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease and polychondritis are rare diseases that are associated with immune system disorders. Due to the rarity of NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease and the diverse range of associated clinical manifestations, many clinicians have an insufficient understanding of this condition. Auxiliary diagnostic techniques, such as 18F-FDG PET-CT, can help to expand the spectrum of clinical features associated with the disease and monitor the effectiveness of treatment in conjunction with other relevant clinical data. The complete remission seen in this patient with methylprednisolone treatment supports the effectiveness of this therapy for polychondritis associated with NLRP12 mutations.

A 13-year-old boy was admitted to hospital with a low-grade fever (maximum temperature of 38°C) that had persisted for 6 months. During this time, his body temperature typically increased in the afternoon or evening and was accompanied by arthralgia, mild headache, and cough. The patient did not report any other clinical signs or symptoms. His white blood cell count, haemoglobin concentration, platelet count, C-reactive protein concentration, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were all normal. No bacterial or fungal infections were detected in the blood, bone marrow, or cerebrospinal fluid cultures. Ultrasound examination revealed multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the neck, bilateral subclavian region, abdominal cavity, and groin. The patient had previously been treated with piperacillin-tazobactam and aciclovir, but showed no improvement. His past medical history and family history were unremarkable.An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET-CT scan revealed a symmetrical increase in FDG metabolism in multiple cartilages (figure A, B). The maximum standard uptake value of the lesions was 5·4, and whole-exome sequencing revealed a pathogenic variant of the NLRP12 gene (1742G→A, Trp581*; accession number VCV001444965.2, variation ID 1444965), which has been reported in several cases associated with NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease. The pathogenicity of this mutation was assessed using InterVar, a bioinformatics software tool, which predicted very strong (PVS1), moderate (PM2), and supporting (PP3) evidence of pathogenicity. However, this mutation was classified as a variant of uncertain significance in the ClinVar database, so interpretation of the pathogenicity of this mutation should still be approached with caution. The patient was treated with 20 mg of methylprednisolone per day for 5 days and was then discharged with no fever or arthralgia. After 4 months, the 18F-FDG PET-CT scan was repeated and indicated that the polychondritis was in complete remission (figure C, D).
To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of polychondritis occurring in a patient with NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease. This result could partly explain why the patient did not have elevated inflammatory indicators, which is observed in 30% of people with autoinflammatory diseases associated with NLRP12 mutations. The clinical features of NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease differ from familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome, as only about 47% of patients with NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease have clear triggers from exposure to cold. Furthermore, the median age of onset for NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease is higher than NLRP3-related autoinflammatory disease, and headaches are an uncommon finding observed in approximately 14% of patients with NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease. Regarding this patient, we suspect that his arthralgia could indicate chondritic pain.
Most patients with NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease benefit from a short regimen of corticosteroid treatment without requiring additional interleukin-1 blocking therapy. Both NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease and polychondritis are rare diseases that are associated with immune system disorders. Due to the rarity of NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease and the diverse range of associated clinical manifestations, many clinicians have an insufficient understanding of this condition. Auxiliary diagnostic techniques, such as 18F-FDG PET-CT, can help to expand the spectrum of clinical features associated with the disease and monitor the effectiveness of treatment in conjunction with other relevant clinical data. The complete remission seen in this patient with methylprednisolone treatment supports the effectiveness of this therapy for polychondritis associated with NLRP12 mutations.

A 15-year-old male patient presented with constipation, abdominal pain, occasional non-bilious vomit, and passage of foul-smelling stool mixed with multiple gravel stones. The patient did not have oliguria, fever, rectal bleeding, or any features suggestive of peritonitis, and was not on any regular medication. He had a similar history of passage of stones 3 months previously, which had resolved spontaneously. The patient had a history of pica but no other psychiatric disorder or developmental delay.On examination, we found diffuse abdominal tenderness with normal bowel sounds. Digital rectal examination revealed a so-called colonic crunch sign. The patient's complete haemogram and blood biochemistry, including serum calcium, phosphorus, and parathyroid hormone, were within normal limits. Straight abdominal radiography revealed multiple opaque shadows of different sizes scattered throughout the colon, with a corn-on-the-cob-like appearance (figure A), consistent with a diagnosis of lithobezoars. The patient was treated conservatively with laxatives and after 5 days, repeat abdominal radiography showed a near complete resolution (figure B). A 13-year-old boy was admitted to hospital with a low-grade fever (maximum temperature of 38°C) that had persisted for 6 months. During this time, his body temperature typically increased in the afternoon or evening and was accompanied by arthralgia, mild headache, and cough. The patient did not report any other clinical signs or symptoms. His white blood cell count, haemoglobin concentration, platelet count, C-reactive protein concentration, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were all normal. No bacterial or fungal infections were detected in the blood, bone marrow, or cerebrospinal fluid cultures. Ultrasound examination revealed multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the neck, bilateral subclavian region, abdominal cavity, and groin. The patient had previously been treated with piperacillin-tazobactam and aciclovir, but showed no improvement. His past medical history and family history were unremarkable.An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET-CT scan revealed a symmetrical increase in FDG metabolism in multiple cartilages (figure A, B). The maximum standard uptake value of the lesions was 5·4, and whole-exome sequencing revealed a pathogenic variant of the NLRP12 gene (1742G→A, Trp581*; accession number VCV001444965.2, variation ID 1444965), which has been reported in several cases associated with NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease. The pathogenicity of this mutation was assessed using InterVar, a bioinformatics software tool, which predicted very strong (PVS1), moderate (PM2), and supporting (PP3) evidence of pathogenicity. However, this mutation was classified as a variant of uncertain significance in the ClinVar database, so interpretation of the pathogenicity of this mutation should still be approached with caution. The patient was treated with 20 mg of methylprednisolone per day for 5 days and was then discharged with no fever or arthralgia. After 4 months, the 18F-FDG PET-CT scan was repeated and indicated that the polychondritis was in complete remission (figure C, D).
To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of polychondritis occurring in a patient with NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease. This result could partly explain why the patient did not have elevated inflammatory indicators, which is observed in 30% of people with autoinflammatory diseases associated with NLRP12 mutations. The clinical features of NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease differ from familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome, as only about 47% of patients with NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease have clear triggers from exposure to cold. Furthermore, the median age of onset for NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease is higher than NLRP3-related autoinflammatory disease, and headaches are an uncommon finding observed in approximately 14% of patients with NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease. Regarding this patient, we suspect that his arthralgia could indicate chondritic pain.
Most patients with NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease benefit from a short regimen of corticosteroid treatment without requiring additional interleukin-1 blocking therapy. Both NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease and polychondritis are rare diseases that are associated with immune system disorders. Due to the rarity of NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease and the diverse range of associated clinical manifestations, many clinicians have an insufficient understanding of this condition. Auxiliary diagnostic techniques, such as 18F-FDG PET-CT, can help to expand the spectrum of clinical features associated with the disease and monitor the effectiveness of treatment in conjunction with other relevant clinical data. The complete remission seen in this patient with methylprednisolone treatment supports the effectiveness of this therapy for polychondritis associated with NLRP12 mutations.

The patient had a history of pica but no other psychiatric disorder or developmental delay.On examination, we found diffuse abdominal tenderness with normal bowel sounds. Digital rectal examination revealed a so-called colonic crunch sign. The patient's complete haemogram and blood biochemistry, including serum calcium, phosphorus, and parathyroid hormone, were within normal limits. Straight abdominal radiography revealed multiple opaque shadows of different sizes scattered throughout the colon, with a corn-on-the-cob-like appearance (figure A), consistent with a diagnosis of lithobezoars. The patient was treated conservatively with laxatives and after 5 days, repeat abdominal radiography showed a near complete resolution (figure B). The patient passed multiple stones (figure C), chemical analysis of which showed they were composed of aluminium silicate.
Pica is considered normal in children younger than 2 years of age, but is rare above the age of 5 years. The aetiology of pica is unknown, but is postulated to be multifactorial, including iron-deficiency anaemia and different psychiatric disorders. A bezoar is a mass found trapped in the gastrointestinal tract. Bezoars can be composed of different materials such as hair (tricobezoars), vegetable material (phytobezoars), milk (lactobezoars), sand, and, rarely, stones (lithobezoars). Other causes of colonic calcifications include phlebosclerotic colitis, lanthanum, and parasitic infections such as schistosomiasis. Absence of specific predisposing factors such as old age, history of haematochaezia, chronic renal failure, atherosclerotic vascular disease (for phlebosclerotic colitis), specific drug intake (lanthanum as a phosphate binder), and the presence of a colonic crunch sign and a typical radiological corn-on-the-cob-like appearance helped in the differential diagnosis of our patient.
