A 34-year-old woman, 22 weeks pregnant, attended the National University Hospital, Singapore, reporting asymptomatic hypertension on home blood pressure monitoring.She had a prior diagnosis of lupus membranous nephropathy and antiphospholipid syndrome with anti-cardiolipin antibodies and lupus anticoagulant, and had a deep vein thrombosis diagnosed 3 years earlier. She had been taking hydroxychloroquine, prednisolone, ciclosporin (due to azathioprine intolerance), low-dose aspirin, and therapeutic-dose enoxaparin from the first trimester of pregnancy, and had been normotensive.
On examination, the patient's blood pressure was 160/87 mm Hg; there were no neurological abnormalities or signs of fetal distress. Her serum creatinine concentration (69 μmol/L) and total urinary protein (6·4 g/day) were raised from her preadmission baseline (taken 3 months before the current presentation) of 52 μmol/L and 0·7 g/day, respectively. Her anti-double stranded DNA antibody titre was more than 800 IU/L, C3 protein concentration was 55 mg/dL (baseline 71 mg/dL), and C4 protein concentration was less than 8 mg/dL. Urinalysis showed 166 red blood cells per high power field, with casts and 25% dysmorphic red blood cells on phase-contrast microscopy. Her complete blood count was unremarkable (haemoglobin concentration 11·0 g/dL and platelet count 201 × 109/L).
Taken together, the findings suggested a lupus flare with proliferative glomerulonephritis. We started intravenous pulsed methylprednisolone (500 mg daily) and oral labetalol (200 mg thrice per day), withheld ciclosporin to avoid worsening hypertension and renal function, and continued aspirin (100 mg daily) and enoxaparin (60 mg twice per day).
48 h later, the patient developed an abrupt onset of cough and dyspnoea at rest. Her blood pressure was 175/85 mm Hg, there were coarse crackles in the lung bases, and she required supplemental oxygen with a Venturi mask with an FiO2 of 40%. Arterial blood gas measurements showed hypoxaemia and a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 237 mm Hg. Tests showed new-onset anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 8·7 g/dL) and thrombocytopenia (platelet count 126 × 109/L), an NT-proBNP concentration of 4077 pg/mL, and widespread opacities on chest x-ray (figure). We suspected superimposed pre-eclampsia with haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets (HELLP) syndrome and acute pulmonary oedema, and gave furosemide, but the dyspnoea did not improve despite diuresis. Venous thromboembolism was unlikely as she had been adequately anticoagulated with enoxaparin (anti-factor Xa activity 0·78 IU/mL [target 0·6–1·0]), and her electrocardiogram did not show abnormalities.
We intubated the patient for mechanical ventilation due to worsening respiratory distress and did a flexible bronchoscopy; sequential bronchoalveolar lavage showed fresh blood and haemosiderin-containing macrophages (figure). We diagnosed diffuse alveolar haemorrhage due to systemic lupus erythematosus. Our principal differential diagnoses were evolving catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome and antiphospholipid syndrome with microvascular features: diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, thrombocytopenia, diffuse ischaemic myocarditis, and antiphospholipid antibody-associated nephropathy.
Tests for infectious pulmonary triggers of diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, including SARS-CoV-2, were negative. We gave further pulsed methylprednisolone (1000 mg daily for 2 days) and commenced plasma exchange, but the hypoxaemia remained refractory, and we were concerned that the patient was at immediate risk of death. The pregnancy was terminated to offset competing haemodynamic demands from the gravid uterus, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and rituximab (two 1-g infusions given 14 days apart) were started urgently.
The patient stabilised, and after several weeks she was extubated and transitioned to mycophenolate mofetil (1·5 g daily). She was discharged after 9 weeks in hospital with tapering doses of prednisolone for sustained immunosuppression.
Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage is a rare but potentially fatal pulmonary manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus; patients with active lupus nephritis, positive lupus anticoagulant, C3 hypocomplementemia, and thrombocytopenia have an increased risk of diffuse alveolar haemorrhage. Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage can also occur with the microvascular phenotype of antiphospholipid syndrome, which typically presents with renal, cardiac, and pulmonary features. Antibody and immune complex-driven disruption of the alveolar–capillary basement membrane causes bleeding, dyspnoea, and a drop in haemoglobin (by at least 1·5 g/dL). Haemoptysis can be absent in a third of cases.
Pregnant patients with lupus nephritis and antiphospholipid syndrome have at least a 25% risk of pre-eclampsia. Pulmonary oedema and HELLP syndrome are subtypes of pre-eclampsia with severe features. Given the overlapping signs between diffuse alveolar haemorrhage and pre-eclampsia—anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and diffuse lung infiltrates on imaging—diffuse alveolar haemorrhage should be considered in the differential diagnosis of dyspnoea during a HELLP-like presentation in a patient with active lupus nephritis or antiphospholipid syndrome. Notably, in pre-eclampsia, complement concentrations are usually normal or elevated. Prompt bronchoscopy and multidisciplinary care, including plasmapheresis, might avoid maternal death in cases of diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, although maternal survival might require termination of the pregnancy.

input:
A 34-year-old woman, 22 weeks pregnant, attended the National University Hospital, Singapore, reporting asymptomatic hypertension on home blood pressure monitoring.She had a prior diagnosis of lupus membranous nephropathy and antiphospholipid syndrome with anti-cardiolipin antibodies and lupus anticoagulant, and had a deep vein thrombosis diagnosed 3 years earlier. She had been taking hydroxychloroquine, prednisolone, ciclosporin (due to azathioprine intolerance), low-dose aspirin, and therapeutic-dose enoxaparin from the first trimester of pregnancy, and had been normotensive.
On examination, the patient's blood pressure was 160/87 mm Hg; there were no neurological abnormalities or signs of fetal distress. Her serum creatinine concentration (69 μmol/L) and total urinary protein (6·4 g/day) were raised from her preadmission baseline (taken 3 months before the current presentation) of 52 μmol/L and 0·7 g/day, respectively. Her anti-double stranded DNA antibody titre was more than 800 IU/L, C3 protein concentration was 55 mg/dL (baseline 71 mg/dL), and C4 protein concentration was less than 8 mg/dL. Urinalysis showed 166 red blood cells per high power field, with casts and 25% dysmorphic red blood cells on phase-contrast microscopy. Her complete blood count was unremarkable (haemoglobin concentration 11·0 g/dL and platelet count 201 × 109/L).
Taken together, the findings suggested a lupus flare with proliferative glomerulonephritis. We started intravenous pulsed methylprednisolone (500 mg daily) and oral labetalol (200 mg thrice per day), withheld ciclosporin to avoid worsening hypertension and renal function, and continued aspirin (100 mg daily) and enoxaparin (60 mg twice per day).
48 h later, the patient developed an abrupt onset of cough and dyspnoea at rest. Her blood pressure was 175/85 mm Hg, there were coarse crackles in the lung bases, and she required supplemental oxygen with a Venturi mask with an FiO2 of 40%. Arterial blood gas measurements showed hypoxaemia and a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 237 mm Hg. Tests showed new-onset anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 8·7 g/dL) and thrombocytopenia (platelet count 126 × 109/L), an NT-proBNP concentration of 4077 pg/mL, and widespread opacities on chest x-ray (figure). We suspected superimposed pre-eclampsia with haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets (HELLP) syndrome and acute pulmonary oedema, and gave furosemide, but the dyspnoea did not improve despite diuresis. Venous thromboembolism was unlikely as she had been adequately anticoagulated with enoxaparin (anti-factor Xa activity 0·78 IU/mL [target 0·6–1·0]), and her electrocardiogram did not show abnormalities.
We intubated the patient for mechanical ventilation due to worsening respiratory distress and did a flexible bronchoscopy; sequential bronchoalveolar lavage showed fresh blood and haemosiderin-containing macrophages (figure). We diagnosed diffuse alveolar haemorrhage due to systemic lupus erythematosus. Our principal differential diagnoses were evolving catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome and antiphospholipid syndrome with microvascular features: diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, thrombocytopenia, diffuse ischaemic myocarditis, and antiphospholipid antibody-associated nephropathy.
Tests for infectious pulmonary triggers of diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, including SARS-CoV-2, were negative. We gave further pulsed methylprednisolone (1000 mg daily for 2 days) and commenced plasma exchange, but the hypoxaemia remained refractory, and we were concerned that the patient was at immediate risk of death. The pregnancy was terminated to offset competing haemodynamic demands from the gravid uterus, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and rituximab (two 1-g infusions given 14 days apart) were started urgently.
The patient stabilised, and after several weeks she was extubated and transitioned to mycophenolate mofetil (1·5 g daily). She was discharged after 9 weeks in hospital with tapering doses of prednisolone for sustained immunosuppression.
Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage is a rare but potentially fatal pulmonary manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus; patients with active lupus nephritis, positive lupus anticoagulant, C3 hypocomplementemia, and thrombocytopenia have an increased risk of diffuse alveolar haemorrhage. Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage can also occur with the microvascular phenotype of antiphospholipid syndrome, which typically presents with renal, cardiac, and pulmonary features. Antibody and immune complex-driven disruption of the alveolar–capillary basement membrane causes bleeding, dyspnoea, and a drop in haemoglobin (by at least 1·5 g/dL). Haemoptysis can be absent in a third of cases.
Pregnant patients with lupus nephritis and antiphospholipid syndrome have at least a 25% risk of pre-eclampsia. Pulmonary oedema and HELLP syndrome are subtypes of pre-eclampsia with severe features. Given the overlapping signs between diffuse alveolar haemorrhage and pre-eclampsia—anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and diffuse lung infiltrates on imaging—diffuse alveolar haemorrhage should be considered in the differential diagnosis of dyspnoea during a HELLP-like presentation in a patient with active lupus nephritis or antiphospholipid syndrome. Notably, in pre-eclampsia, complement concentrations are usually normal or elevated. Prompt bronchoscopy and multidisciplinary care, including plasmapheresis, might avoid maternal death in cases of diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, although maternal survival might require termination of the pregnancy.

input:
A 34-year-old woman, 22 weeks pregnant, attended the National University Hospital, Singapore, reporting asymptomatic hypertension on home blood pressure monitoring.She had a prior diagnosis of lupus membranous nephropathy and antiphospholipid syndrome with anti-cardiolipin antibodies and lupus anticoagulant, and had a deep vein thrombosis diagnosed 3 years earlier. She had been taking hydroxychloroquine, prednisolone, ciclosporin (due to azathioprine intolerance), low-dose aspirin, and therapeutic-dose enoxaparin from the first trimester of pregnancy, and had been normotensive.
On examination, the patient's blood pressure was 160/87 mm Hg; there were no neurological abnormalities or signs of fetal distress. Her serum creatinine concentration (69 μmol/L) and total urinary protein (6·4 g/day) were raised from her preadmission baseline (taken 3 months before the current presentation) of 52 μmol/L and 0·7 g/day, respectively. Her anti-double stranded DNA antibody titre was more than 800 IU/L, C3 protein concentration was 55 mg/dL (baseline 71 mg/dL), and C4 protein concentration was less than 8 mg/dL. Urinalysis showed 166 red blood cells per high power field, with casts and 25% dysmorphic red blood cells on phase-contrast microscopy. Her complete blood count was unremarkable (haemoglobin concentration 11·0 g/dL and platelet count 201 × 109/L).
Taken together, the findings suggested a lupus flare with proliferative glomerulonephritis. We started intravenous pulsed methylprednisolone (500 mg daily) and oral labetalol (200 mg thrice per day), withheld ciclosporin to avoid worsening hypertension and renal function, and continued aspirin (100 mg daily) and enoxaparin (60 mg twice per day).
48 h later, the patient developed an abrupt onset of cough and dyspnoea at rest. Her blood pressure was 175/85 mm Hg, there were coarse crackles in the lung bases, and she required supplemental oxygen with a Venturi mask with an FiO2 of 40%. Arterial blood gas measurements showed hypoxaemia and a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 237 mm Hg. Tests showed new-onset anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 8·7 g/dL) and thrombocytopenia (platelet count 126 × 109/L), an NT-proBNP concentration of 4077 pg/mL, and widespread opacities on chest x-ray (figure). We suspected superimposed pre-eclampsia with haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets (HELLP) syndrome and acute pulmonary oedema, and gave furosemide, but the dyspnoea did not improve despite diuresis. Venous thromboembolism was unlikely as she had been adequately anticoagulated with enoxaparin (anti-factor Xa activity 0·78 IU/mL [target 0·6–1·0]), and her electrocardiogram did not show abnormalities.
We intubated the patient for mechanical ventilation due to worsening respiratory distress and did a flexible bronchoscopy; sequential bronchoalveolar lavage showed fresh blood and haemosiderin-containing macrophages (figure). We diagnosed diffuse alveolar haemorrhage due to systemic lupus erythematosus. Our principal differential diagnoses were evolving catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome and antiphospholipid syndrome with microvascular features: diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, thrombocytopenia, diffuse ischaemic myocarditis, and antiphospholipid antibody-associated nephropathy.
Tests for infectious pulmonary triggers of diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, including SARS-CoV-2, were negative. We gave further pulsed methylprednisolone (1000 mg daily for 2 days) and commenced plasma exchange, but the hypoxaemia remained refractory, and we were concerned that the patient was at immediate risk of death. The pregnancy was terminated to offset competing haemodynamic demands from the gravid uterus, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and rituximab (two 1-g infusions given 14 days apart) were started urgently.
The patient stabilised, and after several weeks she was extubated and transitioned to mycophenolate mofetil (1·5 g daily). She was discharged after 9 weeks in hospital with tapering doses of prednisolone for sustained immunosuppression.
Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage is a rare but potentially fatal pulmonary manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus; patients with active lupus nephritis, positive lupus anticoagulant, C3 hypocomplementemia, and thrombocytopenia have an increased risk of diffuse alveolar haemorrhage. Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage can also occur with the microvascular phenotype of antiphospholipid syndrome, which typically presents with renal, cardiac, and pulmonary features. Antibody and immune complex-driven disruption of the alveolar–capillary basement membrane causes bleeding, dyspnoea, and a drop in haemoglobin (by at least 1·5 g/dL). Haemoptysis can be absent in a third of cases.
Pregnant patients with lupus nephritis and antiphospholipid syndrome have at least a 25% risk of pre-eclampsia. Pulmonary oedema and HELLP syndrome are subtypes of pre-eclampsia with severe features. Given the overlapping signs between diffuse alveolar haemorrhage and pre-eclampsia—anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and diffuse lung infiltrates on imaging—diffuse alveolar haemorrhage should be considered in the differential diagnosis of dyspnoea during a HELLP-like presentation in a patient with active lupus nephritis or antiphospholipid syndrome. Notably, in pre-eclampsia, complement concentrations are usually normal or elevated. Prompt bronchoscopy and multidisciplinary care, including plasmapheresis, might avoid maternal death in cases of diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, although maternal survival might require termination of the pregnancy.

Chest imaging—both x-ray and CT—showed bilateral, predominantly peripheral pulmonary infiltrates (figure).
The patient was initially treated as presumed PCR-negative COVID-19 and the antibiotics were replaced with ceftriaxone; dexamethasone was not indicated because he was not hypoxic.
On day 7, due to persisting cough, a bronchoscopy was done; examination of the washings showed an eosinophilic infiltrate. A diagnosis of acute eosinophilic pneumonitis (AEP) was established through the modified Philit criteria: a respiratory illness of less than 1 month duration, pulmonary infiltrates on chest imaging, an eosinophilia of at least 25% in bronchoscopic washings, and the exclusion of other pulmonary eosinophilic diseases such as allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis and vasculitis. Additionally, the patient had no occupational or lifestyle exposure risk factors. And finally, x-ray and CT findings were not suggestive of fungal infections or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody test was negative. The patient responded rapidly to high dose prednisolone and was allowed home 14 days after he was admitted. At follow-up 3 months later, the patient's chest x-ray was normal.
Common causes of AEP include inhaled toxins—such as smoking, inhalational drugs, and dust—medications, and parasitic and fungal infections. Daptomycin therapy is a well recognised cause of eosinophilic pneumonitis, and we believe this was the most likely cause in our case.
Notably, the patient's symptoms, biochemical, and radiological findings—including lymphopenia, raised CRP, and bilateral peripheral pulmonary infiltrates—pointed towards a diagnosis of PCR-negative COVID-19. A 21-year-old woman presented to our hospital for the first time with a history of seizures. The patient's mother had witnessed the fits and described them as lasting approximately 10 min, causing a loss of consciousness, and incontinence of urine—compatible with a tonic-clonic seizure.She had no significant medical or family history and was not taking any medication.
On examination the patient was afebrile, her blood pressure was 201/127 mm Hg, and she was drowsy. Direct fundoscopy showed no abnormal findings.
Laboratory investigations showed serum potassium concentration was 2·2 mmol/L (normal 3·5–5·1) and bicarbonate was 35 mmol/L (normal 21–31); serum creatinine concentration was normal. A screen for drugs of abuse was negative.
Chest-x ray, brain MRI, electroencephalogram, and doppler examination of the patient's renal arteries were all normal. The patient was admitted, and during her 4 day stay no further seizures were seen. Her blood pressure was slowly lowered using intravenous labetalol given at a dose of 1 mg per min; she was later started on oral amlodipine 10 mg, clonidine 0·2 mg daily, and carvedilol 12·5 mg twice a day. She continued with these medications and oral potassium chloride after leaving the hospital.
Further investigations for causes of secondary hypertension showed normal concentrations of free plasma metanephrines, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, androstenedione, dehydroepiandrosterone, dehydroepiandrosterone sulphate, and 24 h urine cortisol and creatinine. Plasma renin activity ranged from 24·48 to 30·86 μg/L per h (reference range 0·25–5·82), and serum aldosterone ranged from 1·02 to 1·39 nmol/L (reference range 0·03–0·89). An abdominal CT scan showed a solitary 11 mm central kidney mass measuring 88 Hounsfield units—arterial and venous phases—which was too dense to be a benign cyst (figure). Selective renal venous sampling demonstrated a left to right renin ratio of 1·3.
The patient underwent a partial left nephrectomy and examination after removal showed a well circumscribed, variegated, and orange to red nodule, measuring 1·6 cm × 1·5 cm × 1·3 cm surrounded by normal renal parenchyma (figure). Histological examination of a sample of the nodule showed sheets of round to oval uniform cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm (figure) and immunostaining for renin was strongly positive (figure). The diagnosis was a juxtaglomerular tumour—also known as a reninoma.
Postoperatively, the patient's blood pressure was 132/93 mm Hg, plasma renin activity ranged between 2·9 and 0·57, and serum aldosterone was 0·44 and 0·11 at 1 and 6 h, respectively. 1 h after surgery, blood pressure remained at 132/93 mm Hg without any medications. 4 weeks postoperatively, the blood pressure was 113/76 mm Hg off all medications; 16 months later, blood pressure and electrolytes remained normal. The patient was urged to check her blood pressure at regular intervals in the future and to report any persistent elevations.
Renal cell carcinomas may present with hypertension, hypokalaemia, and raised plasma renin concentrations—similarly to the presentation of the benign nodule found in our patient—and therefore need to be excluded by looking specifically for radiographic features of metastasis on imaging.
An extensive and timely work-up of secondary causes of hypertension in young people is paramount—particularly those with severe rises in blood pressure; the diagnosis and removal of a reninoma—as in this case—may save patients from a lifetime of antihypertensive medication.

A 55-year-old woman was admitted to our department with gradual onset of pain in her hands, hips, and knees, which had progressively limited her mobility over the past 6 years. She also reported feeling tired and feverish.On examination we found the patient to have skin sclerosis, microstomia, and reduced mobility in most of her joints. She also had white papules with ulcerations on the skin over her trunk, arms, and legs, but predominantly they were grouped around the large joints—hips, knees, and elbows (figure). We noted a palpable tendon friction rub on the joints of the patient's hands; there was no swelling or tenderness.
Laboratory investigations found a raised C-reactive protein concentration of 33 mg/L (normal 0–5), anaemia with a haemoglobin concentration of 8·2 g/dL, and a moderately elevated creatine kinase of 480 U/L (normal <200).
Tests for autoantibodies found increased titres for antinuclear antibodies (1:2560; normal <1:160) and highly elevated antibodies against double-stranded DNA (>200 U/L; normal <100). Anti-Sjögren's syndrome type A (SSA) and anti-Sjögren's syndrome type B (SSB) antibodies were raised and antibodies against PM/Scl-75 and PM/Scl-100 were strongly positive on immunofluorescence. Autoantibodies to rheumatoid factor (30 U/mL; normal <14) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies (19 U/mL; normal <5) were positive.
An x-ray of the patient's pelvis showed generalised massive multilocular calcinosis (figure) and an x-ray of her hands showed calcification around the tips of her fingers and thumbs (figure). MRI of the patient's thighs showed myositis and fasciitis. A CT scan of the patient's chest showed interstitial lung disease. Ultrasound scans of the patient's joints—specifically her hands and fingers—showed polyarthritis.
Taking these findings in the round, we made a diagnosis of systemic sclerosis together with polymyositis and polyarthritis. We started the patient on a combination of methotrexate, baricitinib, and intravenous immunoglobulins to modulate the immune response, and prostaglandins to cause vasodilation. Within 8 months, the ulcerative calcinosis of the patient's skin, her myositis, and her fasciitis had improved substantially; her pain had also substantially reduced.
Although calcinosis cutis is described in many diseases—including metastatic diseases, lymphomas, and metabolic diseases—it may occur secondary to medical treatments and trauma. Massive infiltrations—as in our patient—are rare and we were fortunate that our multimodal, disease-targeted pharmacological therapy combination was effective. Clinicians using such combined therapies for prolonged periods of time should remain mindful of the risk of infection (video).

A 55-year-old woman was admitted to our department with gradual onset of pain in her hands, hips, and knees, which had progressively limited her mobility over the past 6 years. She also reported feeling tired and feverish.On examination we found the patient to have skin sclerosis, microstomia, and reduced mobility in most of her joints. She also had white papules with ulcerations on the skin over her trunk, arms, and legs, but predominantly they were grouped around the large joints—hips, knees, and elbows (figure). We noted a palpable tendon friction rub on the joints of the patient's hands; there was no swelling or tenderness.
Laboratory investigations found a raised C-reactive protein concentration of 33 mg/L (normal 0–5), anaemia with a haemoglobin concentration of 8·2 g/dL, and a moderately elevated creatine kinase of 480 U/L (normal <200).
Tests for autoantibodies found increased titres for antinuclear antibodies (1:2560; normal <1:160) and highly elevated antibodies against double-stranded DNA (>200 U/L; normal <100). Anti-Sjögren's syndrome type A (SSA) and anti-Sjögren's syndrome type B (SSB) antibodies were raised and antibodies against PM/Scl-75 and PM/Scl-100 were strongly positive on immunofluorescence. Autoantibodies to rheumatoid factor (30 U/mL; normal <14) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies (19 U/mL; normal <5) were positive.
An x-ray of the patient's pelvis showed generalised massive multilocular calcinosis (figure) and an x-ray of her hands showed calcification around the tips of her fingers and thumbs (figure). MRI of the patient's thighs showed myositis and fasciitis. A CT scan of the patient's chest showed interstitial lung disease. Ultrasound scans of the patient's joints—specifically her hands and fingers—showed polyarthritis.
Taking these findings in the round, we made a diagnosis of systemic sclerosis together with polymyositis and polyarthritis. We started the patient on a combination of methotrexate, baricitinib, and intravenous immunoglobulins to modulate the immune response, and prostaglandins to cause vasodilation. Within 8 months, the ulcerative calcinosis of the patient's skin, her myositis, and her fasciitis had improved substantially; her pain had also substantially reduced.
Although calcinosis cutis is described in many diseases—including metastatic diseases, lymphomas, and metabolic diseases—it may occur secondary to medical treatments and trauma. Massive infiltrations—as in our patient—are rare and we were fortunate that our multimodal, disease-targeted pharmacological therapy combination was effective. Clinicians using such combined therapies for prolonged periods of time should remain mindful of the risk of infection (video).

An 83-year-old man was admitted to our hospital reporting a 3-week history of cough and exertional dyspnoea. At the time of admission, the patient was 4 weeks into a 6-week course of daptomycin and rifampicin because he had an infected prosthetic knee joint; he also had a history of pituitary hypoplasia and had not been vaccinated against SARS-CoV-2.On examination, he was afebrile, his vital signs were normal, and there was no sign of active infection in the prosthetic knee joint.
Laboratory investigations showed a long-standing lymphopenia of 0·7 × 109 cells per L (normal 1·5–4·0) and a raised C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration of 186·5mg/L (normal 0–5). The patient's eosinophil cell count was 0·3 × 109 per L (normal 0–0·4), haemoglobin concentration 97 g/L (normal 130–170), and platelet cell count was 322 × 109 per L (normal 150–400). RT-PCR of four consecutive nasopharyngeal swabs for SARS-CoV-2 were negative; routine sputum culture and sensitivity, tuberculosis work-up, respiratory viral screen, and HIV serology were all negative.
Chest imaging—both x-ray and CT—showed bilateral, predominantly peripheral pulmonary infiltrates (figure).
The patient was initially treated as presumed PCR-negative COVID-19 and the antibiotics were replaced with ceftriaxone; dexamethasone was not indicated because he was not hypoxic.
On day 7, due to persisting cough, a bronchoscopy was done; examination of the washings showed an eosinophilic infiltrate. A diagnosis of acute eosinophilic pneumonitis (AEP) was established through the modified Philit criteria: a respiratory illness of less than 1 month duration, pulmonary infiltrates on chest imaging, an eosinophilia of at least 25% in bronchoscopic washings, and the exclusion of other pulmonary eosinophilic diseases such as allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis and vasculitis. We thought parasitic infections were unlikely to be the cause—given the absence of a peripheral blood eosinophilia or any history of travel to a country where such infections are endemic. Additionally, the patient had no occupational or lifestyle exposure risk factors. And finally, x-ray and CT findings were not suggestive of fungal infections or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody test was negative. The patient responded rapidly to high dose prednisolone and was allowed home 14 days after he was admitted. At follow-up 3 months later, the patient's chest x-ray was normal.
Common causes of AEP include inhaled toxins—such as smoking, inhalational drugs, and dust—medications, and parasitic and fungal infections. Daptomycin therapy is a well recognised cause of eosinophilic pneumonitis, and we believe this was the most likely cause in our case.
Notably, the patient's symptoms, biochemical, and radiological findings—including lymphopenia, raised CRP, and bilateral peripheral pulmonary infiltrates—pointed towards a diagnosis of PCR-negative COVID-19. Clinicians need to be on the look out for those subtle nuances that might indicate alternative diagnoses.

A 64-year-old male physician with obstructive sleep apnoea presented for a scheduled outpatient follow-up appointment. He reported that the week before he had developed palpitations and shortness of breath, and was diagnosed with atrial fibrillation. Information downloaded from his continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) device showed excellent adherence and a residual apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI) of 2·8 events per h. Closer inspection of the information for the evening of the arrhythmia on Oct 3, 2017, showed a significant increase in the nightly residual AHI, a predominance of central sleep apnoea episodes, and a crescendo-decrescendo pattern of airflow consistent with classic Cheyne–Stokes respiration (figure). The AHI measured on the CPAP device subsequently returned to normal after successful cardioversion the following day, Oct 4.Non-hypercapnic central sleep apnoea occurs when a stimulus triggers hyperpnoea and a fall in the arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide below the apnoeic threshold, resulting in the cessation of breathing. Central sleep apnoea, specifically Cheyne–Stokes respiration, is commonly seen in heart failure, and may result from stimulation of the respiratory centres by increased left atrial pressure, which can occur acutely with the onset of atrial fibrillation.
Increasingly, medical devices such as home CPAP devices provide long-term patient monitoring. However, interpretation of resulting data presents both opportunities and challenges for clinicians.

input:
A 55-year-old woman was admitted to our department with gradual onset of pain in her hands, hips, and knees, which had progressively limited her mobility over the past 6 years. She also reported feeling tired and feverish.On examination we found the patient to have skin sclerosis, microstomia, and reduced mobility in most of her joints. She also had white papules with ulcerations on the skin over her trunk, arms, and legs, but predominantly they were grouped around the large joints—hips, knees, and elbows (figure). We noted a palpable tendon friction rub on the joints of the patient's hands; there was no swelling or tenderness.
Laboratory investigations found a raised C-reactive protein concentration of 33 mg/L (normal 0–5), anaemia with a haemoglobin concentration of 8·2 g/dL, and a moderately elevated creatine kinase of 480 U/L (normal <200).
Tests for autoantibodies found increased titres for antinuclear antibodies (1:2560; normal <1:160) and highly elevated antibodies against double-stranded DNA (>200 U/L; normal <100). Anti-Sjögren's syndrome type A (SSA) and anti-Sjögren's syndrome type B (SSB) antibodies were raised and antibodies against PM/Scl-75 and PM/Scl-100 were strongly positive on immunofluorescence. Autoantibodies to rheumatoid factor (30 U/mL; normal <14) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies (19 U/mL; normal <5) were positive.
An x-ray of the patient's pelvis showed generalised massive multilocular calcinosis (figure) and an x-ray of her hands showed calcification around the tips of her fingers and thumbs (figure). MRI of the patient's thighs showed myositis and fasciitis. A CT scan of the patient's chest showed interstitial lung disease. Ultrasound scans of the patient's joints—specifically her hands and fingers—showed polyarthritis.
Taking these findings in the round, we made a diagnosis of systemic sclerosis together with polymyositis and polyarthritis. We started the patient on a combination of methotrexate, baricitinib, and intravenous immunoglobulins to modulate the immune response, and prostaglandins to cause vasodilation. Within 8 months, the ulcerative calcinosis of the patient's skin, her myositis, and her fasciitis had improved substantially; her pain had also substantially reduced.
Although calcinosis cutis is described in many diseases—including metastatic diseases, lymphomas, and metabolic diseases—it may occur secondary to medical treatments and trauma. Massive infiltrations—as in our patient—are rare and we were fortunate that our multimodal, disease-targeted pharmacological therapy combination was effective. Clinicians using such combined therapies for prolonged periods of time should remain mindful of the risk of infection (video).

Postoperatively, the child was visually rehabilitated with aphakic glasses. Trans-scleral fixation of intraocular lens will be done after stabilisation of axial growth. A 64-year-old male physician with obstructive sleep apnoea presented for a scheduled outpatient follow-up appointment. He reported that the week before he had developed palpitations and shortness of breath, and was diagnosed with atrial fibrillation. Information downloaded from his continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) device showed excellent adherence and a residual apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI) of 2·8 events per h. Closer inspection of the information for the evening of the arrhythmia on Oct 3, 2017, showed a significant increase in the nightly residual AHI, a predominance of central sleep apnoea episodes, and a crescendo-decrescendo pattern of airflow consistent with classic Cheyne–Stokes respiration (figure). The AHI measured on the CPAP device subsequently returned to normal after successful cardioversion the following day, Oct 4.Non-hypercapnic central sleep apnoea occurs when a stimulus triggers hyperpnoea and a fall in the arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide below the apnoeic threshold, resulting in the cessation of breathing. Central sleep apnoea, specifically Cheyne–Stokes respiration, is commonly seen in heart failure, and may result from stimulation of the respiratory centres by increased left atrial pressure, which can occur acutely with the onset of atrial fibrillation.
Increasingly, medical devices such as home CPAP devices provide long-term patient monitoring. However, interpretation of resulting data presents both opportunities and challenges for clinicians.

input: A 5-year-old boy presented to our department with a 2-day history of acute febrile illness. During evaluation, his blood samples were found to be so lipaemic (figure) that it caused interference in analyte measurements. The child was born of a non-consanguineous marriage, there was no history of failure to thrive or developmental delay, and there were no reports of any previous episodes of acute pancreatitis. Neither xanthomata nor hepatosplenomegaly was found at clinical examination. Laboratory test results found a normal fasting blood glucose concentration (4·5 mmol/L). However, triglycerides were found to be very high at 21·4 mmol/L (normal level <1·7 mmol/L). Total serum cholesterol was 5·5 mmol/L (normal level <5·2 mmol/L), LDL cholesterol by direct measurement was 0·7 mmol/L (normal level <2·6 mmol/L), and HDL cholesterol was 0·5 mmol/L (normal level >1·0 mmol/L). Investigations for secondary causes of hyperlipidaemia were negative. Dilated fundus examination showed creamy white discolouration of retinal blood vessels (figure) suggestive of lipaemia retinalis; no retinal haemorrhages or exudates were seen. Fasting lipid profiles of other family members were normal. Taking into account the young age of the patient, the lipaemic plasma, the hypertriglyceridaemia, the lipaemia retinalis, and the lack of indications that his difficulties were secondary to any other diseases causing hypertriglyceridaemia, the boy was diagnosed with familial chylomicronaemia syndrome (FCS). As treatment is mainly dietary fat restriction, the child was started on a low-fat diet—less than 10% of total calories—with medium-chain triglyceride supplements.FCS is characterised by impaired or absent activity of lipoprotein lipase (LPL)—the key enzyme in catabolism of triglyceride rich lipoproteins, particularly chylomicrons. LPL is also involved in the accumulation of chylomicrons which give the milky appearance of the plasma. Bi-allelic mutations in the LPL gene account for around 80% of cases of FCS; the remainder are caused by mutations in one of four genes encoding proteins that interact with LPL. Early recognition and treatment of hyperlipidaemia are crucial to prevent systemic complications like acute pancreatitis. Many patients with elevated triglycerides do not have lipaemia retinalis for reasons that are unclear. The lipaemic appearance of the retinal blood vessels may persist after normalisation of the triglycerides on laboratory testing. Most systemic diseases have eye signs. The importance of an ophthalmological examination as a crucial component of a thorough medical examination cannot be overlooked.

input: A 5-year-old boy presented to our department with a 2-day history of acute febrile illness. During evaluation, his blood samples were found to be so lipaemic (figure) that it caused interference in analyte measurements. The child was born of a non-consanguineous marriage, there was no history of failure to thrive or developmental delay, and there were no reports of any previous episodes of acute pancreatitis. Neither xanthomata nor hepatosplenomegaly was found at clinical examination. Laboratory test results found a normal fasting blood glucose concentration (4·5 mmol/L). However, triglycerides were found to be very high at 21·4 mmol/L (normal level <1·7 mmol/L). Total serum cholesterol was 5·5 mmol/L (normal level <5·2 mmol/L), LDL cholesterol by direct measurement was 0·7 mmol/L (normal level <2·6 mmol/L), and HDL cholesterol was 0·5 mmol/L (normal level >1·0 mmol/L). Investigations for secondary causes of hyperlipidaemia were negative. Dilated fundus examination showed creamy white discolouration of retinal blood vessels (figure) suggestive of lipaemia retinalis; no retinal haemorrhages or exudates were seen. Fasting lipid profiles of other family members were normal. Taking into account the young age of the patient, the lipaemic plasma, the hypertriglyceridaemia, the lipaemia retinalis, and the lack of indications that his difficulties were secondary to any other diseases causing hypertriglyceridaemia, the boy was diagnosed with familial chylomicronaemia syndrome (FCS). As treatment is mainly dietary fat restriction, the child was started on a low-fat diet—less than 10% of total calories—with medium-chain triglyceride supplements.FCS is characterised by impaired or absent activity of lipoprotein lipase (LPL)—the key enzyme in catabolism of triglyceride rich lipoproteins, particularly chylomicrons. LPL is also involved in the accumulation of chylomicrons which give the milky appearance of the plasma. Bi-allelic mutations in the LPL gene account for around 80% of cases of FCS; the remainder are caused by mutations in one of four genes encoding proteins that interact with LPL. Early recognition and treatment of hyperlipidaemia are crucial to prevent systemic complications like acute pancreatitis. Many patients with elevated triglycerides do not have lipaemia retinalis for reasons that are unclear. The lipaemic appearance of the retinal blood vessels may persist after normalisation of the triglycerides on laboratory testing. Most systemic diseases have eye signs. The importance of an ophthalmological examination as a crucial component of a thorough medical examination cannot be overlooked.

A 47-year-old woman with well controlled HIV (CD4 >1000 cells per μL and an undetectable viral load) presented to our hospital with confusion and seizures. Results of brain MRI were unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed lymphocytosis (20 cells per μL), a high protein concentration (0·52 g/L), and a low glucose concentration (3·2 mmol/L in CSF vs 8·1 mmol/L in serum). CT chest images revealed a cavitating lesion in the left upper lobe of the lung, with surrounding tree-in-bud opacities. Tuberculosis treatment (rifabutin 150 mg per day, pyrazinamide 2 g per day, moxifloxacin 400 mg per day, isoniazid 300 mg per day) and dexamethasone (4 mg four times a day) were started, and she was followed up as an outpatient. Fully sensitive Mycobacterium tuberculosis subsequently grew from a bronchoalveolar lavage.1 month later, she presented to the emergency department with a 2 day history of fever, haemoptysis, and drowsiness. She had a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 10 (eye opening 4 points; verbal response 1 point; motor response 5 points), extension of the left big toe during the plantar response test, and a right gaze preference. Chest CT showed that the lesion in the left upper lobe of the lung had shrunk, but new lesions had appeared in the right upper lobe and left lower lobe. Multiple brain lesions were present on MRI (figure). Biopsy of the lesion in the right upper lobe of the lung revealed multiple fungal hyphae consistent with aspergillus. Liposomal amphotericin B (450 mg daily) was started. Aspergillus fumigatus subsequently grew from the biopsy sample and from a bronchoaleveolar lavage.
Her GCS score dropped to 8 the day after admission and she was intubated and ventilated. Serial CTs showed new areas of haemorrhage within the pre-existing brain lesions. 8 days after admission, her pupils became fixed and dilated, and brain CT showed herniation of the cerebellar tonsils into foramen magnum. She died 1 day later. Collateral history from a relative revealed that the patient had a history of heavy cannabis use.
Invasive aspergillosis has been reported a handful of times in association with cannabis use, usually in patients with advanced immunosuppression. Dexamethasone probably led to an immunosuppressive state in the patient despite well controlled HIV infection, in the context of repeated aspergillus exposure through regular use of aspergillus-contaminated cannabis.

During evaluation, his blood samples were found to be so lipaemic (figure) that it caused interference in analyte measurements. The child was born of a non-consanguineous marriage, there was no history of failure to thrive or developmental delay, and there were no reports of any previous episodes of acute pancreatitis. Neither xanthomata nor hepatosplenomegaly was found at clinical examination. Laboratory test results found a normal fasting blood glucose concentration (4·5 mmol/L). However, triglycerides were found to be very high at 21·4 mmol/L (normal level <1·7 mmol/L). Total serum cholesterol was 5·5 mmol/L (normal level <5·2 mmol/L), LDL cholesterol by direct measurement was 0·7 mmol/L (normal level <2·6 mmol/L), and HDL cholesterol was 0·5 mmol/L (normal level >1·0 mmol/L). Investigations for secondary causes of hyperlipidaemia were negative. Dilated fundus examination showed creamy white discolouration of retinal blood vessels (figure) suggestive of lipaemia retinalis; no retinal haemorrhages or exudates were seen. Fasting lipid profiles of other family members were normal. Taking into account the young age of the patient, the lipaemic plasma, the hypertriglyceridaemia, the lipaemia retinalis, and the lack of indications that his difficulties were secondary to any other diseases causing hypertriglyceridaemia, the boy was diagnosed with familial chylomicronaemia syndrome (FCS). As treatment is mainly dietary fat restriction, the child was started on a low-fat diet—less than 10% of total calories—with medium-chain triglyceride supplements.FCS is characterised by impaired or absent activity of lipoprotein lipase (LPL)—the key enzyme in catabolism of triglyceride rich lipoproteins, particularly chylomicrons. LPL is also involved in the accumulation of chylomicrons which give the milky appearance of the plasma. Bi-allelic mutations in the LPL gene account for around 80% of cases of FCS; the remainder are caused by mutations in one of four genes encoding proteins that interact with LPL. Early recognition and treatment of hyperlipidaemia are crucial to prevent systemic complications like acute pancreatitis. Many patients with elevated triglycerides do not have lipaemia retinalis for reasons that are unclear. The lipaemic appearance of the retinal blood vessels may persist after normalisation of the triglycerides on laboratory testing. Most systemic diseases have eye signs. The importance of an ophthalmological examination as a crucial component of a thorough medical examination cannot be overlooked.

input:
A 47-year-old woman with well controlled HIV (CD4 >1000 cells per μL and an undetectable viral load) presented to our hospital with confusion and seizures. Results of brain MRI were unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed lymphocytosis (20 cells per μL), a high protein concentration (0·52 g/L), and a low glucose concentration (3·2 mmol/L in CSF vs 8·1 mmol/L in serum). CT chest images revealed a cavitating lesion in the left upper lobe of the lung, with surrounding tree-in-bud opacities. Tuberculosis treatment (rifabutin 150 mg per day, pyrazinamide 2 g per day, moxifloxacin 400 mg per day, isoniazid 300 mg per day) and dexamethasone (4 mg four times a day) were started, and she was followed up as an outpatient. Fully sensitive Mycobacterium tuberculosis subsequently grew from a bronchoalveolar lavage.1 month later, she presented to the emergency department with a 2 day history of fever, haemoptysis, and drowsiness. She had a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 10 (eye opening 4 points; verbal response 1 point; motor response 5 points), extension of the left big toe during the plantar response test, and a right gaze preference. Chest CT showed that the lesion in the left upper lobe of the lung had shrunk, but new lesions had appeared in the right upper lobe and left lower lobe. Multiple brain lesions were present on MRI (figure). Biopsy of the lesion in the right upper lobe of the lung revealed multiple fungal hyphae consistent with aspergillus. Liposomal amphotericin B (450 mg daily) was started. Aspergillus fumigatus subsequently grew from the biopsy sample and from a bronchoaleveolar lavage.
Her GCS score dropped to 8 the day after admission and she was intubated and ventilated. Serial CTs showed new areas of haemorrhage within the pre-existing brain lesions. 8 days after admission, her pupils became fixed and dilated, and brain CT showed herniation of the cerebellar tonsils into foramen magnum. She died 1 day later. Collateral history from a relative revealed that the patient had a history of heavy cannabis use.
Invasive aspergillosis has been reported a handful of times in association with cannabis use, usually in patients with advanced immunosuppression. Dexamethasone probably led to an immunosuppressive state in the patient despite well controlled HIV infection, in the context of repeated aspergillus exposure through regular use of aspergillus-contaminated cannabis.

input:
A 47-year-old woman with well controlled HIV (CD4 >1000 cells per μL and an undetectable viral load) presented to our hospital with confusion and seizures. Results of brain MRI were unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed lymphocytosis (20 cells per μL), a high protein concentration (0·52 g/L), and a low glucose concentration (3·2 mmol/L in CSF vs 8·1 mmol/L in serum). CT chest images revealed a cavitating lesion in the left upper lobe of the lung, with surrounding tree-in-bud opacities. Tuberculosis treatment (rifabutin 150 mg per day, pyrazinamide 2 g per day, moxifloxacin 400 mg per day, isoniazid 300 mg per day) and dexamethasone (4 mg four times a day) were started, and she was followed up as an outpatient. Fully sensitive Mycobacterium tuberculosis subsequently grew from a bronchoalveolar lavage.1 month later, she presented to the emergency department with a 2 day history of fever, haemoptysis, and drowsiness. She had a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 10 (eye opening 4 points; verbal response 1 point; motor response 5 points), extension of the left big toe during the plantar response test, and a right gaze preference. Chest CT showed that the lesion in the left upper lobe of the lung had shrunk, but new lesions had appeared in the right upper lobe and left lower lobe. Multiple brain lesions were present on MRI (figure). Biopsy of the lesion in the right upper lobe of the lung revealed multiple fungal hyphae consistent with aspergillus. Liposomal amphotericin B (450 mg daily) was started. Aspergillus fumigatus subsequently grew from the biopsy sample and from a bronchoaleveolar lavage.
Her GCS score dropped to 8 the day after admission and she was intubated and ventilated. Serial CTs showed new areas of haemorrhage within the pre-existing brain lesions. 8 days after admission, her pupils became fixed and dilated, and brain CT showed herniation of the cerebellar tonsils into foramen magnum. She died 1 day later. Collateral history from a relative revealed that the patient had a history of heavy cannabis use.
Invasive aspergillosis has been reported a handful of times in association with cannabis use, usually in patients with advanced immunosuppression. Dexamethasone probably led to an immunosuppressive state in the patient despite well controlled HIV infection, in the context of repeated aspergillus exposure through regular use of aspergillus-contaminated cannabis.

input:
A 10-year-old girl with an antenatal diagnosis of Klippel–Trénaunay syndrome was referred to our institution with a 1-day history of rectal bleeding. She had stools of normal consistency and frequency, had not been on any medication recently, and had no abdominal pain or other accompanying symptoms.Her physical examination revealed extensive red–purple masses on her right lower leg. These masses on the right lower quadrant felt like a paste when palpated. Laboratory tests revealed that her haemoglobin concentration was 10·6 g/dL, white blood cell count was 9000 cells per μL, and platelet count was 221 000 cells per μL; coagulation tests were normal. D-dimer was high and thromboelastogram results were normal.
An intravenous dose of tranexamic acid 10 mg/kg was started, and colonoscopy was done, which showed continuous submucosal involvement of the rectum and sigmoid, with areas of erythema and whitish zones suggestive of lymphatic lesions, without mucosal erosions (figure, A). Large varices were observed with extensive involvement through the descending, transverse colon, hepatic angle, and ascending colon (figure, B). They extended towards the lumen, in the shape of grape clusters, leaving only a small segment towards the caecum free of disease. The ileum could not be visualised. No mucosal lesions were evident. MRI enteroclysis showed concentric mural thickening of the rectum and proximal sigmoid of the right colon, especially at the level of the caecum and the proximal aspect of the ascending colon. Concentric thickening and hyperaemia of the adjacent rectum wall were also observed. Compared with an examination done 3 years previously, there was evidence of increased involvement of the intestinal wall and adjacent tissues. Given the impossibility of surgical resection, the patient has been treated with oral rapamycin 1·5 mg per day for the past 10 months. She has presented with two episodes of self-limiting rectal bleeding since she started rapamycin, and has been undergoing strict follow-up with a paediatric multidisciplinary team (including surgery, haematology, traumatology, and endocrinology).
Klippel–Trénaunay syndrome is a congenital vascular malformation, with a pathogenesis that is not completely understood. Alteration in the fetal mesoderm has been postulated, as a result of intrauterine damage causing dilation of the arteriovenous anastomosis, deep vein obstruction with varices, or hypertrophy of the lymphatic vessels. Gastrointestinal tract involvement is observed in up to 20% of cases, usually in the rectum and sigmoid, which can manifest as gastrointestinal bleeding, usually during the first decade of life. Since most of the time the bleeding is self-limiting and the involvement of the colon is distal, the patient should be followed up and treated for anaemia if necessary. Angiographic intervention such as embolisation of the bleeding vessel can sometimes be successful. Endoscopic therapy is usually preferred for localised lesions or postoperative residual disease. Endorectal resection extending to the transverse colon has been reported in cases of more extensive disease. Involvement of the ascending colon is very unusual, and the extensive involvement of the bowel makes this particular case unique and challenging.

A 10-year-old girl with an antenatal diagnosis of Klippel–Trénaunay syndrome was referred to our institution with a 1-day history of rectal bleeding. She had stools of normal consistency and frequency, had not been on any medication recently, and had no abdominal pain or other accompanying symptoms.Her physical examination revealed extensive red–purple masses on her right lower leg. These masses on the right lower quadrant felt like a paste when palpated. Laboratory tests revealed that her haemoglobin concentration was 10·6 g/dL, white blood cell count was 9000 cells per μL, and platelet count was 221 000 cells per μL; coagulation tests were normal. D-dimer was high and thromboelastogram results were normal.
An intravenous dose of tranexamic acid 10 mg/kg was started, and colonoscopy was done, which showed continuous submucosal involvement of the rectum and sigmoid, with areas of erythema and whitish zones suggestive of lymphatic lesions, without mucosal erosions (figure, A). Large varices were observed with extensive involvement through the descending, transverse colon, hepatic angle, and ascending colon (figure, B). They extended towards the lumen, in the shape of grape clusters, leaving only a small segment towards the caecum free of disease. The ileum could not be visualised. No mucosal lesions were evident. MRI enteroclysis showed concentric mural thickening of the rectum and proximal sigmoid of the right colon, especially at the level of the caecum and the proximal aspect of the ascending colon. Concentric thickening and hyperaemia of the adjacent rectum wall were also observed. Compared with an examination done 3 years previously, there was evidence of increased involvement of the intestinal wall and adjacent tissues. Given the impossibility of surgical resection, the patient has been treated with oral rapamycin 1·5 mg per day for the past 10 months. She has presented with two episodes of self-limiting rectal bleeding since she started rapamycin, and has been undergoing strict follow-up with a paediatric multidisciplinary team (including surgery, haematology, traumatology, and endocrinology).
Klippel–Trénaunay syndrome is a congenital vascular malformation, with a pathogenesis that is not completely understood. Alteration in the fetal mesoderm has been postulated, as a result of intrauterine damage causing dilation of the arteriovenous anastomosis, deep vein obstruction with varices, or hypertrophy of the lymphatic vessels. Gastrointestinal tract involvement is observed in up to 20% of cases, usually in the rectum and sigmoid, which can manifest as gastrointestinal bleeding, usually during the first decade of life. Since most of the time the bleeding is self-limiting and the involvement of the colon is distal, the patient should be followed up and treated for anaemia if necessary. Angiographic intervention such as embolisation of the bleeding vessel can sometimes be successful. Endoscopic therapy is usually preferred for localised lesions or postoperative residual disease. Endorectal resection extending to the transverse colon has been reported in cases of more extensive disease. Involvement of the ascending colon is very unusual, and the extensive involvement of the bowel makes this particular case unique and challenging.

input: A 76-year-old woman presented to the department of ophthalmology in February, 2014, with painful unilateral exophthalmos, 5 days after undergoing couching of the right cataractous lens by a traditional healer. The following day her eye had become red and painful with reduced vision. On examination visual acuity in the right eye was light perception, the intraocular pressure was high (45 mm Hg; normal 10–20 mm Hg), and there was proptosis and ophthalmoplegia. Biomicroscopic examination showed eyelid oedema, conjunctival injection, total chemosis, abundant purulent secretions, and a greenish hypopyon occupying the anterior chamber, typical of pseudomonas infection (figure). CT showed preseptal and retroseptal cellulitis, exophthalmos grade II, and a dislocated cataractous lens in the lower vitreous. We took vitreous and aqueous humour samples and gave one injection of intravitreal antibiotics (vancomycin 1 mg/0·1 mL and ceftazidime 2·25 mg/0·1 mL). We started systemic antibiotics (intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g twice daily and levofloxacin 500 mg twice daily) and a systemic hypotonic (oral acetazolamide 250 mg twice daily). 48 h later we gave a second dose of intravitreal antibiotics and started methylprednisolone 40 mg twice daily for 5 days to reduce the inflammation. Vitreous cultures grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa. By the seventh day the patient's pain, eyelid oedema, and proptosis had resolved (figure), but she had a persistent vitreous opacity. We did pars plana vitrectomy and iris-claw intraocular lens on the posterior side of the iris to compensate for the refractive disorder caused by absence of the crystalline lens. At last follow-up in May, 2014, her best corrected visual acuity was 6/60 in the right eye and intraocular pressure had returned to normal (16 mm Hg).Lens couching is the oldest technique of cataract surgery. It was first practised by the Assyrians of Hammurabi in the 17th century BC, and then by the Hindu surgeon Sushruta around 600 BC. It consists of traumatising the zonula through the sclera using a pen so the lens falls into the vitreous and releases the visual axis, allowing the patient to see the light. The visual outcome of this technique, unfortunately still prevalent in some parts of the world, is often poor. Its complications are retinal detachment, secondary glaucoma, hyphaema, uveitis, optic atrophy, and endophthalmitis.

A 41-year-old professional hockey referee was referred to our clinic with an 8-month history of walking difficulties; previously he had consulted several orthopaedic surgeons and had undergone physical therapy—with limited benefit—for a presumed knee injury. The patient had no notable medical history, but reported two maternal aunts with Parkinson's disease which had presented at over the age of 65 years; his parents and sister were healthy. On examination he appeared generally fit and well; however, a neurological examination found that he had hypomimia, mild rigidity, and bradykinesia on motor tasks in both legs, but predominantely in the right (video). The patient's gait showed dystonic posturing of the right foot with involuntary plantar flexion and inversion, and asymmetrically reduced arm swing; his walking difficulties improved by running and walking backwards (figure; video). Additionally, despite having difficulties walking, he reported no problems while riding his bicycle (video).Laboratory investigations showed no atypical findings, imaging likewise. Molecular genetic analysis showed compound heterozygous mutations of the parkin (PRKN) gene, confirming a diagnosis of early-onset Parkinson's disease. A levodopa and carbidopa combination, which was titrated up to 100 mg three times a day, provided sustained clinical benefit. At follow-up 6 months later, the patient reported feeling better, without fluctuations of motor function; the bradykinesia had improved and there was less dystonic posturing when walking. He had resumed his professional activities.
PRKN mutations are the commonest type of autosomal recessive Parkinson's disease, accounting for between 14 and 25% of early-onset cases. A delay between symptom onset and diagnosis is often observed because dystonia and parkinsonism may be unrecognised—especially in younger patients. Important clinical clues may be overlooked; for example, people with Parkinson's disease may find running or riding a bicycle easier than walking—as in our case—despite clear motor impairment, which is suggestive of dystonia.
The combination of parkinsonism with lower-limb dystonia in a young patient should alert clinicians to the possibility of Parkinson's disease with a genetic aetiology. Early-onset Parkinson's disease, caused by PRKN mutations, is a possibility, especially if hyper-reflexia, diurnal fluctuations, and levodopa-induced lower-limb dyskinesia are present.

A 41-year-old professional hockey referee was referred to our clinic with an 8-month history of walking difficulties; previously he had consulted several orthopaedic surgeons and had undergone physical therapy—with limited benefit—for a presumed knee injury. The patient had no notable medical history, but reported two maternal aunts with Parkinson's disease which had presented at over the age of 65 years; his parents and sister were healthy. On examination he appeared generally fit and well; however, a neurological examination found that he had hypomimia, mild rigidity, and bradykinesia on motor tasks in both legs, but predominantely in the right (video). The patient's gait showed dystonic posturing of the right foot with involuntary plantar flexion and inversion, and asymmetrically reduced arm swing; his walking difficulties improved by running and walking backwards (figure; video). Additionally, despite having difficulties walking, he reported no problems while riding his bicycle (video).Laboratory investigations showed no atypical findings, imaging likewise. Molecular genetic analysis showed compound heterozygous mutations of the parkin (PRKN) gene, confirming a diagnosis of early-onset Parkinson's disease. A levodopa and carbidopa combination, which was titrated up to 100 mg three times a day, provided sustained clinical benefit. At follow-up 6 months later, the patient reported feeling better, without fluctuations of motor function; the bradykinesia had improved and there was less dystonic posturing when walking. He had resumed his professional activities.
PRKN mutations are the commonest type of autosomal recessive Parkinson's disease, accounting for between 14 and 25% of early-onset cases. A delay between symptom onset and diagnosis is often observed because dystonia and parkinsonism may be unrecognised—especially in younger patients. Important clinical clues may be overlooked; for example, people with Parkinson's disease may find running or riding a bicycle easier than walking—as in our case—despite clear motor impairment, which is suggestive of dystonia.
The combination of parkinsonism with lower-limb dystonia in a young patient should alert clinicians to the possibility of Parkinson's disease with a genetic aetiology. Early-onset Parkinson's disease, caused by PRKN mutations, is a possibility, especially if hyper-reflexia, diurnal fluctuations, and levodopa-induced lower-limb dyskinesia are present.

input: A 45-year-old man came to our emergency department in August because he experienced an abnormal, unpleasant sensation when his fingers and thumbs were touched; he also said that they were blue and felt weak. 4 h before, he had been paragliding and had flown into a tower of cumulonimbus clouds—entering a summer thunderstorm—where winds carried him rapidly upwards to more than 6000 m above sea level. At this height, the man encountered hail, rain, an air temperature of −25°C, and wind speeds of up to 100 km/h for about 45 min. Because of the worsening dysaesthesia and the paresis of his fingers, the man had been unable to properly control and steer the paraglider and had landed on a rooftop after a further 15 min descent. Notably, the patient had worn thin gloves on his hands in contrast to thick clothing on his lower legs and face. When we first examined the man's fingers, they were cyanotic, swollen, numb, and paretic (figure). We decided to initially warm his hands and then started him on intravenous iloprost 20 μg once daily, oral aspirin 100 mg once daily, subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg once daily, and topical betamethasone once daily. These treatments were continued for 10 days. 2 days after the paraglider's ordeal, blisters appeared on his fingers (figure) that were compatible with a diagnosis of grade 2 frostbite; these lesions were drained, and the dysaesthesia and paresis ameliorated. On the fifth day, erythema and desquamation of the lesions occurred (figure). The swelling reduced after 7 days—although splinter haemorrhages were seen on the tenth day (figure). After 30 days, the fingers and thumbs had fully recovered without any residual tissue damage or sensorimotor deficits.Frostbite develops as a result of thermal injury to the skin and other tissues exposed to cold temperature; it is a recognised problem seen commonly in military personnel, homeless individuals, and winter sports enthusiasts. Grade 1 lesions are characterised by numbness and erythema of the affected skin, without blister formation; when blisters filled with clear fluid are seen, the lesions should be classified as grade 2. Grade 3 lesions are characterised by a blue-grey discolouration of the skin and haemorrhagic blisters resulting in black eschars. Grade 4 lesions involve muscles, joints, and bones and result in tissue necrosis and tissue loss. For grade 4 lesions, the recommendation is that the treating physician should adopt the principle of autoamputation—whereby the damaged tissue spontaneously detaches from the body—rather than carrying out early surgical amputation. Besides rewarming, which is primarily employed to stop vasoconstriction, endothelial injury, and thrombosis caused by the cold, several adjuvant treatments should be considered; aspirin, prostaglandins, and thrombolytic agents can be given because of their antiplatelet and vasodilatory effects. Additionally, damaged tissue should be protected against further insult to avoid it becoming infected. Fortunately, frostbite among paragliders is rare.

A 41-year-old professional hockey referee was referred to our clinic with an 8-month history of walking difficulties; previously he had consulted several orthopaedic surgeons and had undergone physical therapy—with limited benefit—for a presumed knee injury. The patient had no notable medical history, but reported two maternal aunts with Parkinson's disease which had presented at over the age of 65 years; his parents and sister were healthy. On examination he appeared generally fit and well; however, a neurological examination found that he had hypomimia, mild rigidity, and bradykinesia on motor tasks in both legs, but predominantely in the right (video). The patient's gait showed dystonic posturing of the right foot with involuntary plantar flexion and inversion, and asymmetrically reduced arm swing; his walking difficulties improved by running and walking backwards (figure; video). Additionally, despite having difficulties walking, he reported no problems while riding his bicycle (video).Laboratory investigations showed no atypical findings, imaging likewise. Molecular genetic analysis showed compound heterozygous mutations of the parkin (PRKN) gene, confirming a diagnosis of early-onset Parkinson's disease. A levodopa and carbidopa combination, which was titrated up to 100 mg three times a day, provided sustained clinical benefit. At follow-up 6 months later, the patient reported feeling better, without fluctuations of motor function; the bradykinesia had improved and there was less dystonic posturing when walking. He had resumed his professional activities.
PRKN mutations are the commonest type of autosomal recessive Parkinson's disease, accounting for between 14 and 25% of early-onset cases. A delay between symptom onset and diagnosis is often observed because dystonia and parkinsonism may be unrecognised—especially in younger patients. Important clinical clues may be overlooked; for example, people with Parkinson's disease may find running or riding a bicycle easier than walking—as in our case—despite clear motor impairment, which is suggestive of dystonia.
The combination of parkinsonism with lower-limb dystonia in a young patient should alert clinicians to the possibility of Parkinson's disease with a genetic aetiology. Early-onset Parkinson's disease, caused by PRKN mutations, is a possibility, especially if hyper-reflexia, diurnal fluctuations, and levodopa-induced lower-limb dyskinesia are present.

input: A 45-year-old man came to our emergency department in August because he experienced an abnormal, unpleasant sensation when his fingers and thumbs were touched; he also said that they were blue and felt weak. 4 h before, he had been paragliding and had flown into a tower of cumulonimbus clouds—entering a summer thunderstorm—where winds carried him rapidly upwards to more than 6000 m above sea level. At this height, the man encountered hail, rain, an air temperature of −25°C, and wind speeds of up to 100 km/h for about 45 min. Because of the worsening dysaesthesia and the paresis of his fingers, the man had been unable to properly control and steer the paraglider and had landed on a rooftop after a further 15 min descent. Notably, the patient had worn thin gloves on his hands in contrast to thick clothing on his lower legs and face. When we first examined the man's fingers, they were cyanotic, swollen, numb, and paretic (figure). We decided to initially warm his hands and then started him on intravenous iloprost 20 μg once daily, oral aspirin 100 mg once daily, subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg once daily, and topical betamethasone once daily. These treatments were continued for 10 days. 2 days after the paraglider's ordeal, blisters appeared on his fingers (figure) that were compatible with a diagnosis of grade 2 frostbite; these lesions were drained, and the dysaesthesia and paresis ameliorated. On the fifth day, erythema and desquamation of the lesions occurred (figure). The swelling reduced after 7 days—although splinter haemorrhages were seen on the tenth day (figure). After 30 days, the fingers and thumbs had fully recovered without any residual tissue damage or sensorimotor deficits.Frostbite develops as a result of thermal injury to the skin and other tissues exposed to cold temperature; it is a recognised problem seen commonly in military personnel, homeless individuals, and winter sports enthusiasts. Grade 1 lesions are characterised by numbness and erythema of the affected skin, without blister formation; when blisters filled with clear fluid are seen, the lesions should be classified as grade 2. Grade 3 lesions are characterised by a blue-grey discolouration of the skin and haemorrhagic blisters resulting in black eschars. Grade 4 lesions involve muscles, joints, and bones and result in tissue necrosis and tissue loss. For grade 4 lesions, the recommendation is that the treating physician should adopt the principle of autoamputation—whereby the damaged tissue spontaneously detaches from the body—rather than carrying out early surgical amputation. Besides rewarming, which is primarily employed to stop vasoconstriction, endothelial injury, and thrombosis caused by the cold, several adjuvant treatments should be considered; aspirin, prostaglandins, and thrombolytic agents can be given because of their antiplatelet and vasodilatory effects. Additionally, damaged tissue should be protected against further insult to avoid it becoming infected. Fortunately, frostbite among paragliders is rare.

A 51-year-old woman presented to our department with a 5-year history of a loud clicking sound in her left ear. The patient said that the clicking was persistent and distressing; it disappeared during eating and talking, and she could suppress it at will for a few minutes.On examination, we found no abnormalities of the cranial nerves; eye examination was normal with no exophthalmos or conjunctival congestion. She had no involuntary movements of her mouth, face, jaw, or tongue. Fundoscopy was normal.
Laboratory investigations found no abnormalities. Otorhinolaryngological studies and tympanometry also showed no abnormalities.
However, we did find a constant, semirhythmic movement of the patient's soft palate—which had not been noticed previously—that disappeared when the patient was distracted by asking her to clap her hands (figure; video).
MRI showed no abnormalities, and we made a diagnosis of isolated palatal myoclonus—also known as essential palatal tremor or myoclonus. We treated her with 3 mg of clonazepam orally per day and her symptoms partially improved over the next 2 months.
Palatal myoclonus is an uncommon clinical finding characterised by a rhythmic contraction of the palatal muscles—including the levator veli palatini and the tensor palatini muscles. The contractions lead to the rapid opening and shutting of the Eustachian tube, which produces a clicking tinnitus that is usually audible to the examiner. Secondary or symptomatic palatal tremor is caused by lesions involving the connections between the ipsilateral red nucleus in the midbrain, the inferior olive in the medulla, and the contralateral dentate nucleus in the cerebellum—the three nuclei together being referred to as the Guillain–Mollaret triangle forming the dentato-rubro-olivary pathway (figure). In approximately 70% of cases the lesion is a vascular infarct; other causes include glial fibrillary acidic protein or mitochondrial DNA polymerase γ mutations, neuroferritinopathy, or progressive ataxia and palatal tremor.
Patients with no apparent structural lesions are considered to have isolated palatal tremor. Notably, the tensor veli palatini—innervated by the trigeminal nerve—is mostly involved in cases of isolated palatal tremor, whereas in symptomatic or secondary palatal tremor it is the levator veli palatini muscle—innervated mainly by the vagus nerve—that is affected.
Some cases of isolated palatal tremor may be considered as functional neurological disorders. Some patients report being able to suppress the clicking sound either at will or while being distracted, suggesting a functional origin.
Palatal tremor should be distinguished from middle ear myoclonus—another form of objective tinnitus. In middle ear myoclonus, the sound of the tinnitus is reported to be a buzzing rather than a clicking, and movement of the tympanic membrane rather than the palate is seen on otoscopy.
Treatment options are limited, but phenytoin, carbamazepine, clonazepam, sumatriptan, and botulinum toxin have been found to be useful in some patients.
