input: A 45-year-old man came to our emergency department in August because he experienced an abnormal, unpleasant sensation when his fingers and thumbs were touched; he also said that they were blue and felt weak. 4 h before, he had been paragliding and had flown into a tower of cumulonimbus clouds—entering a summer thunderstorm—where winds carried him rapidly upwards to more than 6000 m above sea level. At this height, the man encountered hail, rain, an air temperature of −25°C, and wind speeds of up to 100 km/h for about 45 min. Because of the worsening dysaesthesia and the paresis of his fingers, the man had been unable to properly control and steer the paraglider and had landed on a rooftop after a further 15 min descent. Notably, the patient had worn thin gloves on his hands in contrast to thick clothing on his lower legs and face. When we first examined the man's fingers, they were cyanotic, swollen, numb, and paretic (figure). We decided to initially warm his hands and then started him on intravenous iloprost 20 μg once daily, oral aspirin 100 mg once daily, subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg once daily, and topical betamethasone once daily. These treatments were continued for 10 days. 2 days after the paraglider's ordeal, blisters appeared on his fingers (figure) that were compatible with a diagnosis of grade 2 frostbite; these lesions were drained, and the dysaesthesia and paresis ameliorated. On the fifth day, erythema and desquamation of the lesions occurred (figure). The swelling reduced after 7 days—although splinter haemorrhages were seen on the tenth day (figure). After 30 days, the fingers and thumbs had fully recovered without any residual tissue damage or sensorimotor deficits.Frostbite develops as a result of thermal injury to the skin and other tissues exposed to cold temperature; it is a recognised problem seen commonly in military personnel, homeless individuals, and winter sports enthusiasts. Grade 1 lesions are characterised by numbness and erythema of the affected skin, without blister formation; when blisters filled with clear fluid are seen, the lesions should be classified as grade 2. Grade 3 lesions are characterised by a blue-grey discolouration of the skin and haemorrhagic blisters resulting in black eschars. Grade 4 lesions involve muscles, joints, and bones and result in tissue necrosis and tissue loss. For grade 4 lesions, the recommendation is that the treating physician should adopt the principle of autoamputation—whereby the damaged tissue spontaneously detaches from the body—rather than carrying out early surgical amputation. Besides rewarming, which is primarily employed to stop vasoconstriction, endothelial injury, and thrombosis caused by the cold, several adjuvant treatments should be considered; aspirin, prostaglandins, and thrombolytic agents can be given because of their antiplatelet and vasodilatory effects. Additionally, damaged tissue should be protected against further insult to avoid it becoming infected. Fortunately, frostbite among paragliders is rare.

A 51-year-old woman presented to our department with a 5-year history of a loud clicking sound in her left ear. The patient said that the clicking was persistent and distressing; it disappeared during eating and talking, and she could suppress it at will for a few minutes.On examination, we found no abnormalities of the cranial nerves; eye examination was normal with no exophthalmos or conjunctival congestion. She had no involuntary movements of her mouth, face, jaw, or tongue. Fundoscopy was normal.
Laboratory investigations found no abnormalities. Otorhinolaryngological studies and tympanometry also showed no abnormalities.
However, we did find a constant, semirhythmic movement of the patient's soft palate—which had not been noticed previously—that disappeared when the patient was distracted by asking her to clap her hands (figure; video).
MRI showed no abnormalities, and we made a diagnosis of isolated palatal myoclonus—also known as essential palatal tremor or myoclonus. We treated her with 3 mg of clonazepam orally per day and her symptoms partially improved over the next 2 months.
Palatal myoclonus is an uncommon clinical finding characterised by a rhythmic contraction of the palatal muscles—including the levator veli palatini and the tensor palatini muscles. The contractions lead to the rapid opening and shutting of the Eustachian tube, which produces a clicking tinnitus that is usually audible to the examiner. Secondary or symptomatic palatal tremor is caused by lesions involving the connections between the ipsilateral red nucleus in the midbrain, the inferior olive in the medulla, and the contralateral dentate nucleus in the cerebellum—the three nuclei together being referred to as the Guillain–Mollaret triangle forming the dentato-rubro-olivary pathway (figure). In approximately 70% of cases the lesion is a vascular infarct; other causes include glial fibrillary acidic protein or mitochondrial DNA polymerase γ mutations, neuroferritinopathy, or progressive ataxia and palatal tremor.
Patients with no apparent structural lesions are considered to have isolated palatal tremor. Notably, the tensor veli palatini—innervated by the trigeminal nerve—is mostly involved in cases of isolated palatal tremor, whereas in symptomatic or secondary palatal tremor it is the levator veli palatini muscle—innervated mainly by the vagus nerve—that is affected.
Some cases of isolated palatal tremor may be considered as functional neurological disorders. Some patients report being able to suppress the clicking sound either at will or while being distracted, suggesting a functional origin.
Palatal tremor should be distinguished from middle ear myoclonus—another form of objective tinnitus. In middle ear myoclonus, the sound of the tinnitus is reported to be a buzzing rather than a clicking, and movement of the tympanic membrane rather than the palate is seen on otoscopy.
Treatment options are limited, but phenytoin, carbamazepine, clonazepam, sumatriptan, and botulinum toxin have been found to be useful in some patients.

The Guillain-Mollaret triangle (also known as the dentato-rubro-olivary pathway) is a neural circuit involved in motor control. It consists of three anatomical structures:

*   In **Isolated Palatal Tremor** (also called Essential Palatal Tremor), there is **no structural lesion** in the Guillain-Mollaret triangle, and MRI findings are normal.

input:
In July, 2014, a healthy 1-month-old boy attended for evaluation of lesions on his back that had been present since birth. He had no relevant family history. On examination he had pink plaques on his back with central bluish colouration and depression and some prominent ectatic vessels, surrounded by a dusky halo (figure). The plaques were soft, poorly compressible, painless, and more prominent during crying. Musculoskeletal examination was normal, as were blood count, liver enzymes, renal function, and coagulation.The plaques were consistent with a vascular malformation. In infancy, such diffuse skin lesions usually result from venous malformations. Common venous malformations usually affect the muscles and joints of the lower limbs, head, and neck. Blue rubber bleb naevus syndrome usually affects the upper limbs and trunk and is associated with gastrointestinal lesions. Glomuvenous malformations affect the limbs and back, with no extracutaneous involvement. Unlike common venous malformations and blue rubber bleb naevus, glomuvenous malformations have a hyperkeratotic cobblestone-like appearance, are not completely emptied by compression, and tend to become painful. Total body MRI showed several varicosities in the subcutaneous tissue of the back but no extracutaneous lesion. The diagnosis of glomuvenous malformation was confirmed by examination of a biopsy sample, which showed dilated and irregular vascular channels lined by layers of glomus cells that stained positively for smooth muscle α-actin (figure). Laser therapy at 6 months old greatly reduced the lesions in size and colour. At last follow-up in March, 2015, the baby was well and had no new lesions.
Plaque-type glomuvenous malformation can be sporadic or familial. Relatives of the affected individual often have minor lesions, such as one small nodule. The plaques usually appear during the first month of life, grow rapidly, and enlarge to involve adjacent areas, although new lesions can present at different sites during development or after trauma in previously unaffected areas. Plaque-type glomuvenous malformations are limited to the skin, but can be a cause of concern to parents and are often a diagnostic challenge for physicians.

A 51-year-old woman presented to our department with a 5-year history of a loud clicking sound in her left ear. The patient said that the clicking was persistent and distressing; it disappeared during eating and talking, and she could suppress it at will for a few minutes.On examination, we found no abnormalities of the cranial nerves; eye examination was normal with no exophthalmos or conjunctival congestion. She had no involuntary movements of her mouth, face, jaw, or tongue. Fundoscopy was normal.
Laboratory investigations found no abnormalities. Otorhinolaryngological studies and tympanometry also showed no abnormalities.
However, we did find a constant, semirhythmic movement of the patient's soft palate—which had not been noticed previously—that disappeared when the patient was distracted by asking her to clap her hands (figure; video).
MRI showed no abnormalities, and we made a diagnosis of isolated palatal myoclonus—also known as essential palatal tremor or myoclonus. We treated her with 3 mg of clonazepam orally per day and her symptoms partially improved over the next 2 months.
Palatal myoclonus is an uncommon clinical finding characterised by a rhythmic contraction of the palatal muscles—including the levator veli palatini and the tensor palatini muscles. The contractions lead to the rapid opening and shutting of the Eustachian tube, which produces a clicking tinnitus that is usually audible to the examiner. Secondary or symptomatic palatal tremor is caused by lesions involving the connections between the ipsilateral red nucleus in the midbrain, the inferior olive in the medulla, and the contralateral dentate nucleus in the cerebellum—the three nuclei together being referred to as the Guillain–Mollaret triangle forming the dentato-rubro-olivary pathway (figure). In approximately 70% of cases the lesion is a vascular infarct; other causes include glial fibrillary acidic protein or mitochondrial DNA polymerase γ mutations, neuroferritinopathy, or progressive ataxia and palatal tremor.
Patients with no apparent structural lesions are considered to have isolated palatal tremor. Notably, the tensor veli palatini—innervated by the trigeminal nerve—is mostly involved in cases of isolated palatal tremor, whereas in symptomatic or secondary palatal tremor it is the levator veli palatini muscle—innervated mainly by the vagus nerve—that is affected.
Some cases of isolated palatal tremor may be considered as functional neurological disorders. Some patients report being able to suppress the clicking sound either at will or while being distracted, suggesting a functional origin.
Palatal tremor should be distinguished from middle ear myoclonus—another form of objective tinnitus. In middle ear myoclonus, the sound of the tinnitus is reported to be a buzzing rather than a clicking, and movement of the tympanic membrane rather than the palate is seen on otoscopy.
Treatment options are limited, but phenytoin, carbamazepine, clonazepam, sumatriptan, and botulinum toxin have been found to be useful in some patients.

In July, 2014, a healthy 1-month-old boy attended for evaluation of lesions on his back that had been present since birth. He had no relevant family history. On examination he had pink plaques on his back with central bluish colouration and depression and some prominent ectatic vessels, surrounded by a dusky halo (figure). The plaques were soft, poorly compressible, painless, and more prominent during crying. Musculoskeletal examination was normal, as were blood count, liver enzymes, renal function, and coagulation.The plaques were consistent with a vascular malformation. In infancy, such diffuse skin lesions usually result from venous malformations. Common venous malformations usually affect the muscles and joints of the lower limbs, head, and neck. Blue rubber bleb naevus syndrome usually affects the upper limbs and trunk and is associated with gastrointestinal lesions. Glomuvenous malformations affect the limbs and back, with no extracutaneous involvement. Unlike common venous malformations and blue rubber bleb naevus, glomuvenous malformations have a hyperkeratotic cobblestone-like appearance, are not completely emptied by compression, and tend to become painful. Total body MRI showed several varicosities in the subcutaneous tissue of the back but no extracutaneous lesion. The diagnosis of glomuvenous malformation was confirmed by examination of a biopsy sample, which showed dilated and irregular vascular channels lined by layers of glomus cells that stained positively for smooth muscle α-actin (figure). Laser therapy at 6 months old greatly reduced the lesions in size and colour. At last follow-up in March, 2015, the baby was well and had no new lesions.
Plaque-type glomuvenous malformation can be sporadic or familial. Relatives of the affected individual often have minor lesions, such as one small nodule. The plaques usually appear during the first month of life, grow rapidly, and enlarge to involve adjacent areas, although new lesions can present at different sites during development or after trauma in previously unaffected areas. Plaque-type glomuvenous malformations are limited to the skin, but can be a cause of concern to parents and are often a diagnostic challenge for physicians.

In July, 2014, a healthy 1-month-old boy attended for evaluation of lesions on his back that had been present since birth. He had no relevant family history. On examination he had pink plaques on his back with central bluish colouration and depression and some prominent ectatic vessels, surrounded by a dusky halo (figure). The plaques were soft, poorly compressible, painless, and more prominent during crying. Musculoskeletal examination was normal, as were blood count, liver enzymes, renal function, and coagulation.The plaques were consistent with a vascular malformation. In infancy, such diffuse skin lesions usually result from venous malformations. Common venous malformations usually affect the muscles and joints of the lower limbs, head, and neck. Blue rubber bleb naevus syndrome usually affects the upper limbs and trunk and is associated with gastrointestinal lesions. Glomuvenous malformations affect the limbs and back, with no extracutaneous involvement. Unlike common venous malformations and blue rubber bleb naevus, glomuvenous malformations have a hyperkeratotic cobblestone-like appearance, are not completely emptied by compression, and tend to become painful. Total body MRI showed several varicosities in the subcutaneous tissue of the back but no extracutaneous lesion. The diagnosis of glomuvenous malformation was confirmed by examination of a biopsy sample, which showed dilated and irregular vascular channels lined by layers of glomus cells that stained positively for smooth muscle α-actin (figure). Laser therapy at 6 months old greatly reduced the lesions in size and colour. At last follow-up in March, 2015, the baby was well and had no new lesions.
Plaque-type glomuvenous malformation can be sporadic or familial. Relatives of the affected individual often have minor lesions, such as one small nodule. The plaques usually appear during the first month of life, grow rapidly, and enlarge to involve adjacent areas, although new lesions can present at different sites during development or after trauma in previously unaffected areas. Plaque-type glomuvenous malformations are limited to the skin, but can be a cause of concern to parents and are often a diagnostic challenge for physicians.

A 15-year-old boy presented with a 2-week history of decreased vision in his right eye and a painful rash over his toes. On examination he had pallor, a vasculitic rash over the toes of both feet, and a visual acuity of 6/24 in the right eye. Fundoscopy showed vascular sheathing of the central retinal vessels, cotton wool spots, and dot haemorrhages, consistent with retinal vasculitis (figure A). Blood tests showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8 g/dL, white cell count of 1700 per μL (normal range 4000–11 000 per μL), and platelet count of 70 000 per mL (normal range 150 000–400 000 per mL). His renal and hepatic parameters were normal. Tests for antinuclear antibodies and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies were positive, and direct Coomb's test was positive. Antinuclear antibody blot test showed positivity for anti-Sjögren's-syndrome-related antigen A antibodies and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies. Complement concentrations were normal and tests for antiphospholipid antibodies were negative.He fulfilled the Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and was diagnosed as having lupus retinal vasculitis. Because of worsening visual acuity to 6/60, he was treated with pulsed intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g once a day for 3 days), followed by oral prednisolone (1 mg/kg once a day, which was tapered slowly after 1 month) and monthly doses of cyclophosphamide (0·75 mg/kg). After six doses of cyclophosphamide, his fundus showed complete resolution (figure B) and his visual acuity improved to 6/9.
Ocular manifestations of SLE include sicca syndrome, iridocyclitis, retinal vasculitis, choroidopathy, vaso-occlusive disorders, and optic neuropathy. Lupus retinopathy is attributable to an immune complex-mediated vasculopathy. The three types of retinal damage in SLE are microangiopathy, severe vaso-occlusion, and vasculitis. Microangiopathy is associated with a better visual prognosis than vaso-occlusion and vasculitis. Vascular sheathing is the classic sign of retinal vasculitis. Vision-threatening retinal involvement in SLE is associated with systemic disease, CNS involvement, and positivity for antiphospholipid antibodies. Prompt diagnosis and treatment can lead to recovery in this otherwise vision-threatening condition. Among the differential diagnoses, Behçet's disease was excluded in view of absence of orogenital ulcers. Cytomegalovirus infection is a close mimicker of SLE; it was excluded on the basis of absence of classic fundoscopic findings of cytomegalovirus retinitis and negative tests for anti-cytomegalovirus IgG and IgM.
Retinal vasculitis is an uncommon manifestation of juvenile SLE, especially as a presenting feature. A high index of suspicion and prompt initiation of immunosuppressive therapy can save the patient's vision.

A 15-year-old boy presented with a 2-week history of decreased vision in his right eye and a painful rash over his toes. On examination he had pallor, a vasculitic rash over the toes of both feet, and a visual acuity of 6/24 in the right eye. Fundoscopy showed vascular sheathing of the central retinal vessels, cotton wool spots, and dot haemorrhages, consistent with retinal vasculitis (figure A). Blood tests showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8 g/dL, white cell count of 1700 per μL (normal range 4000–11 000 per μL), and platelet count of 70 000 per mL (normal range 150 000–400 000 per mL). His renal and hepatic parameters were normal. Tests for antinuclear antibodies and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies were positive, and direct Coomb's test was positive. Antinuclear antibody blot test showed positivity for anti-Sjögren's-syndrome-related antigen A antibodies and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies. Complement concentrations were normal and tests for antiphospholipid antibodies were negative.He fulfilled the Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and was diagnosed as having lupus retinal vasculitis. Because of worsening visual acuity to 6/60, he was treated with pulsed intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g once a day for 3 days), followed by oral prednisolone (1 mg/kg once a day, which was tapered slowly after 1 month) and monthly doses of cyclophosphamide (0·75 mg/kg). After six doses of cyclophosphamide, his fundus showed complete resolution (figure B) and his visual acuity improved to 6/9.
Ocular manifestations of SLE include sicca syndrome, iridocyclitis, retinal vasculitis, choroidopathy, vaso-occlusive disorders, and optic neuropathy. Lupus retinopathy is attributable to an immune complex-mediated vasculopathy. The three types of retinal damage in SLE are microangiopathy, severe vaso-occlusion, and vasculitis. Microangiopathy is associated with a better visual prognosis than vaso-occlusion and vasculitis. Vascular sheathing is the classic sign of retinal vasculitis. Vision-threatening retinal involvement in SLE is associated with systemic disease, CNS involvement, and positivity for antiphospholipid antibodies. Prompt diagnosis and treatment can lead to recovery in this otherwise vision-threatening condition. Among the differential diagnoses, Behçet's disease was excluded in view of absence of orogenital ulcers. Cytomegalovirus infection is a close mimicker of SLE; it was excluded on the basis of absence of classic fundoscopic findings of cytomegalovirus retinitis and negative tests for anti-cytomegalovirus IgG and IgM.
Retinal vasculitis is an uncommon manifestation of juvenile SLE, especially as a presenting feature. A high index of suspicion and prompt initiation of immunosuppressive therapy can save the patient's vision.

A 15-year-old boy presented with a 2-week history of decreased vision in his right eye and a painful rash over his toes. On examination he had pallor, a vasculitic rash over the toes of both feet, and a visual acuity of 6/24 in the right eye. Fundoscopy showed vascular sheathing of the central retinal vessels, cotton wool spots, and dot haemorrhages, consistent with retinal vasculitis (figure A). Blood tests showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8 g/dL, white cell count of 1700 per μL (normal range 4000–11 000 per μL), and platelet count of 70 000 per mL (normal range 150 000–400 000 per mL). His renal and hepatic parameters were normal. Tests for antinuclear antibodies and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies were positive, and direct Coomb's test was positive. Antinuclear antibody blot test showed positivity for anti-Sjögren's-syndrome-related antigen A antibodies and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies. Complement concentrations were normal and tests for antiphospholipid antibodies were negative.He fulfilled the Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and was diagnosed as having lupus retinal vasculitis. Because of worsening visual acuity to 6/60, he was treated with pulsed intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g once a day for 3 days), followed by oral prednisolone (1 mg/kg once a day, which was tapered slowly after 1 month) and monthly doses of cyclophosphamide (0·75 mg/kg). After six doses of cyclophosphamide, his fundus showed complete resolution (figure B) and his visual acuity improved to 6/9.
Ocular manifestations of SLE include sicca syndrome, iridocyclitis, retinal vasculitis, choroidopathy, vaso-occlusive disorders, and optic neuropathy. Lupus retinopathy is attributable to an immune complex-mediated vasculopathy. The three types of retinal damage in SLE are microangiopathy, severe vaso-occlusion, and vasculitis. Microangiopathy is associated with a better visual prognosis than vaso-occlusion and vasculitis. Vascular sheathing is the classic sign of retinal vasculitis. Vision-threatening retinal involvement in SLE is associated with systemic disease, CNS involvement, and positivity for antiphospholipid antibodies. Prompt diagnosis and treatment can lead to recovery in this otherwise vision-threatening condition. Among the differential diagnoses, Behçet's disease was excluded in view of absence of orogenital ulcers. Cytomegalovirus infection is a close mimicker of SLE; it was excluded on the basis of absence of classic fundoscopic findings of cytomegalovirus retinitis and negative tests for anti-cytomegalovirus IgG and IgM.
Retinal vasculitis is an uncommon manifestation of juvenile SLE, especially as a presenting feature. A high index of suspicion and prompt initiation of immunosuppressive therapy can save the patient's vision.

Acute bacterial parotitis mostly occurs in neonates, or in elderly, or debilitated people. Non-infectious disorders associated with parotid swelling include collagen vascular disease, cystic fibrosis, sialolithiasis, diabetes, sarcoidosis, and tumours. A 26-year-old man reporting a 6-day history of fever, malaise, and a swollen cheek, was referred to our emergency room. The day before his attendance, he had been seen by his general practitioner and started on oral amoxicillin and clavulanic acid. However, his cheek continued to swell, and he developed a temperature of 39·4oC, prompting the referral.The patient had no medical history; he had all his childhood vaccinations. Additionally, he reported no sexual contacts other than with his male partner.
On examination, he did not appear acutely unwell; his vital signs were stable with his blood pressure 116/84 mm Hg, pulse 95 beats per min, and oxygen saturation 99%. The patient's left parotid gland was swollen and painful on palpitation (figure); he had no lymphadenopathy. An inspection of the oral cavity showed one ulcerative lesion on the ipsilateral lower lip (figure).
Laboratory investigations showed a mild lymphopenia (0·8 × 109 per L; normal 1·0–3·5), an elevated gamma-glutamyltransferase concentration (91 IU/L; normal <38 IU/L), and a raised C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration (76 mg/L; normal <10 mg/L). Influenza A, influenza B, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR were negative.
The antibiotics were switched to oral levofloxacin to no avail, and the parotid swelling increased and fever persisted when the patient visited the outpatient clinic, 5 days after his initial presentation; the CRP concentration had decreased to 51 mg/L, but the parotid swelling and lip ulcer were still present. Serology for mumps, HIV, and syphilis and PCRs on a throat swab for mumps, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae all tested negative, besides mumps IgG—confirming previous vaccination. However, PCRs on the throat and ulcer swabs were positive for human monkeypox (hMPX) virus: Ct-values of 18 and 22, respectively. Genomic sequencing showed a clade IIb variant clustering within the current international mpox (formerly known as monkeypox) virus outbreak (appendix). When we informed the patient of the diagnosis 7 days after initial presentation, his clinical condition had improved together with a decrease in the parotid swelling and the size of the ulcer.
Parotitis is mostly caused by a viral infection—most often mumps. Other viral causes include HIV, enteroviruses, Epstein-Barr Virus, influenza, parainfluenza, and cytomegalovirus. Acute bacterial parotitis mostly occurs in neonates, or in elderly, or debilitated people. Non-infectious disorders associated with parotid swelling include collagen vascular disease, cystic fibrosis, sialolithiasis, diabetes, sarcoidosis, and tumours. Chronic parotitis may be confused with Sjögren's syndrome. To our knowledge, this is the first described case of parotitis caused by hMPX virus.

Segmental distribution of the painful cutaneous lesions suggested haemorrhagic herpes zoster. Prednisone was stopped and the patient was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin G (1 g/kg daily for 4 days) and valacyclovir (1 g three times daily). He had a rapid increase in platelet count and uneventful recovery. Haemorrhagic herpes zoster is an atypical form of cutaneous varicella zoster virus and correlates with immunodepression, coagulopathy, or thrombocytopenia.

Segmental distribution of the painful cutaneous lesions suggested haemorrhagic herpes zoster. Prednisone was stopped and the patient was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin G (1 g/kg daily for 4 days) and valacyclovir (1 g three times daily). He had a rapid increase in platelet count and uneventful recovery. Haemorrhagic herpes zoster is an atypical form of cutaneous varicella zoster virus and correlates with immunodepression, coagulopathy, or thrombocytopenia.

input:
A 69-year-old woman who was obese presented to our emergency department with breathlessness after episodic vomiting and diarrhoea that had started the night before. She also reported right-sided pleuritic chest pain radiating to the back. She had a medical history of hyperlipidaemia and recurrent urinary tract infections.On examination she was anxious, tachycardic, tachypnoeic, and hypoxic, initially requiring supplemental oxygen, which was given through a nasal cannula. Her lungs were clear on auscultation. Arterial blood gas showed combined metabolic and respiratory acidosis. A chest x-ray was initially read as clear except for bilateral pleural effusion (figure). We decided to intubate her because she had acute hypoxic hypercarbic respiratory failure. CT of her chest showed pneumomediastinum from the thoracic inlet to the diaphragmatic hiatus, right pneumothorax, large right pleural effusion, right subcutaneous emphysema, and complete collapse of the lower lobe of the right lung (figure). On closer retrospective review of the chest x-ray, the pneumomediastinum and right subcutaneous emphysema were visible (figure). Interestingly, the subcutaneous emphysema was not palpable on physical examination.
Oesophagoscopy with minimal air inflation showed severe oesophagitis with diffuse, circumferential, black, friable mucosa that spontaneously bled from the middle to the distal third—consistent with a diagnosis of acute oesophageal necrosis (figure). We also found a slit-like perforation measuring 20 mm in the distal third of the oesophagus and put in a stent; using video-assisted thoracoscopy, we explored and washed out the mediastinum. 30 days later, when the oesophageal stent was removed, the mucosa was pink and healed. After 3 months in hospital, the patient went home.
Acute oesophageal necrosis—also known as black oesophagus—is a rare but important finding. It is associated with a high mortality and perforation is a serious complication that may lead to mediastinitis and empyema. Because of rapid clinical deterioration—especially among patients with underlying comorbidities—awareness and prompt recognition of this condition are essential for timely intervention. Vigilant chest x-ray review for any hints of pneumomediastinum or pneumothorax in any patient with significant vomiting and chest pain is essential as, initially, such findings can be subtle even to the trained eye.

input:
A 69-year-old woman who was obese presented to our emergency department with breathlessness after episodic vomiting and diarrhoea that had started the night before. She also reported right-sided pleuritic chest pain radiating to the back. She had a medical history of hyperlipidaemia and recurrent urinary tract infections.On examination she was anxious, tachycardic, tachypnoeic, and hypoxic, initially requiring supplemental oxygen, which was given through a nasal cannula. Her lungs were clear on auscultation. Arterial blood gas showed combined metabolic and respiratory acidosis. A chest x-ray was initially read as clear except for bilateral pleural effusion (figure). We decided to intubate her because she had acute hypoxic hypercarbic respiratory failure. CT of her chest showed pneumomediastinum from the thoracic inlet to the diaphragmatic hiatus, right pneumothorax, large right pleural effusion, right subcutaneous emphysema, and complete collapse of the lower lobe of the right lung (figure). On closer retrospective review of the chest x-ray, the pneumomediastinum and right subcutaneous emphysema were visible (figure). Interestingly, the subcutaneous emphysema was not palpable on physical examination.
Oesophagoscopy with minimal air inflation showed severe oesophagitis with diffuse, circumferential, black, friable mucosa that spontaneously bled from the middle to the distal third—consistent with a diagnosis of acute oesophageal necrosis (figure). We also found a slit-like perforation measuring 20 mm in the distal third of the oesophagus and put in a stent; using video-assisted thoracoscopy, we explored and washed out the mediastinum. 30 days later, when the oesophageal stent was removed, the mucosa was pink and healed. After 3 months in hospital, the patient went home.
Acute oesophageal necrosis—also known as black oesophagus—is a rare but important finding. It is associated with a high mortality and perforation is a serious complication that may lead to mediastinitis and empyema. Because of rapid clinical deterioration—especially among patients with underlying comorbidities—awareness and prompt recognition of this condition are essential for timely intervention. Vigilant chest x-ray review for any hints of pneumomediastinum or pneumothorax in any patient with significant vomiting and chest pain is essential as, initially, such findings can be subtle even to the trained eye.

input:
A 69-year-old woman who was obese presented to our emergency department with breathlessness after episodic vomiting and diarrhoea that had started the night before. She also reported right-sided pleuritic chest pain radiating to the back. She had a medical history of hyperlipidaemia and recurrent urinary tract infections.On examination she was anxious, tachycardic, tachypnoeic, and hypoxic, initially requiring supplemental oxygen, which was given through a nasal cannula. Her lungs were clear on auscultation. Arterial blood gas showed combined metabolic and respiratory acidosis. A chest x-ray was initially read as clear except for bilateral pleural effusion (figure). We decided to intubate her because she had acute hypoxic hypercarbic respiratory failure. CT of her chest showed pneumomediastinum from the thoracic inlet to the diaphragmatic hiatus, right pneumothorax, large right pleural effusion, right subcutaneous emphysema, and complete collapse of the lower lobe of the right lung (figure). On closer retrospective review of the chest x-ray, the pneumomediastinum and right subcutaneous emphysema were visible (figure). Interestingly, the subcutaneous emphysema was not palpable on physical examination.
Oesophagoscopy with minimal air inflation showed severe oesophagitis with diffuse, circumferential, black, friable mucosa that spontaneously bled from the middle to the distal third—consistent with a diagnosis of acute oesophageal necrosis (figure). We also found a slit-like perforation measuring 20 mm in the distal third of the oesophagus and put in a stent; using video-assisted thoracoscopy, we explored and washed out the mediastinum. 30 days later, when the oesophageal stent was removed, the mucosa was pink and healed. After 3 months in hospital, the patient went home.
Acute oesophageal necrosis—also known as black oesophagus—is a rare but important finding. It is associated with a high mortality and perforation is a serious complication that may lead to mediastinitis and empyema. Because of rapid clinical deterioration—especially among patients with underlying comorbidities—awareness and prompt recognition of this condition are essential for timely intervention. Vigilant chest x-ray review for any hints of pneumomediastinum or pneumothorax in any patient with significant vomiting and chest pain is essential as, initially, such findings can be subtle even to the trained eye.

He reported a history of recurrent bilateral pneumothoraces in his twenties that required bilateral pleurectomies. There was no family history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or emphysema. However, his daughter had a spontaneous pneumothorax at the age of 14 years and his younger sister had a spontaneous pneumothorax at the age of 31 years. Spirometry and the diffusion capacity of the patient's lungs for carbon monoxide were normal. His serum concentration of α1 antitrypsin was normal (concentrations of less than 11 μmol/L are considered abnormal and put the patient at high risk for the development of emphysema). A high-resolution CT scan of his chest (figure) showed numerous, thin-walled cysts in both lungs—predominantly in the bases and sub-pleural areas. These cysts were surrounded by normal lung tissue without evidence of emphysema. A high-resolution CT scan of the chest of his sister, undertaken after she had a spontaneous pneumothorax, showed two small, thin-walled cysts in the left lower lobe (appendix). Given the imaging findings and his family history, genetic testing was done. The patient was found to be heterozygous for a deletion at position 469_471 in the Folliculin (FLCN) gene—confirming a diagnosis of Birt-Hogg-Dubé (BHD) syndrome. Family screening was also done (figure) and all affected family members—the patient's father, two elder sisters, and the patient's son—had high-resolution CT scans of the thorax and MRIs of the kidneys.BHD syndrome is a rare autosomal dominant condition, caused by germline mutations in the FLCN gene. It is characterised by skin fibrofolliculomas, multiple lung cysts, spontaneous pneumothorax, and renal cancer. The cysts in BHD syndrome have several characteristics that may help distinguish them from other causes of diffuse cystic lung disease: they are basal predominant, thin-walled cysts, lentiform in shape and with a predilection for the subpleural region. The most serious complication of BHD syndrome is renal cancer, which has a prevalence of 24–37% in these patients. Once the diagnosis is made, all patients with BHD syndrome should undergo renal imaging at yearly intervals. Pneumothorax occurs in up to 25% of patients and the recurrence rate approaches 75%.

A 43-year-old man was referred to our specialist clinic for α1 antitrypsin deficiency; CT scans showed basal predominant bullae, suggestive of the disease. On review in the clinic, he had no respiratory symptoms. He was a lifelong non-smoker, without any environmental or occupational exposures of note. He reported a history of recurrent bilateral pneumothoraces in his twenties that required bilateral pleurectomies. There was no family history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or emphysema. However, his daughter had a spontaneous pneumothorax at the age of 14 years and his younger sister had a spontaneous pneumothorax at the age of 31 years. Spirometry and the diffusion capacity of the patient's lungs for carbon monoxide were normal. His serum concentration of α1 antitrypsin was normal (concentrations of less than 11 μmol/L are considered abnormal and put the patient at high risk for the development of emphysema). A high-resolution CT scan of his chest (figure) showed numerous, thin-walled cysts in both lungs—predominantly in the bases and sub-pleural areas. These cysts were surrounded by normal lung tissue without evidence of emphysema. A high-resolution CT scan of the chest of his sister, undertaken after she had a spontaneous pneumothorax, showed two small, thin-walled cysts in the left lower lobe (appendix). Given the imaging findings and his family history, genetic testing was done. The patient was found to be heterozygous for a deletion at position 469_471 in the Folliculin (FLCN) gene—confirming a diagnosis of Birt-Hogg-Dubé (BHD) syndrome. Family screening was also done (figure) and all affected family members—the patient's father, two elder sisters, and the patient's son—had high-resolution CT scans of the thorax and MRIs of the kidneys.BHD syndrome is a rare autosomal dominant condition, caused by germline mutations in the FLCN gene. It is characterised by skin fibrofolliculomas, multiple lung cysts, spontaneous pneumothorax, and renal cancer. The cysts in BHD syndrome have several characteristics that may help distinguish them from other causes of diffuse cystic lung disease: they are basal predominant, thin-walled cysts, lentiform in shape and with a predilection for the subpleural region. The most serious complication of BHD syndrome is renal cancer, which has a prevalence of 24–37% in these patients. Once the diagnosis is made, all patients with BHD syndrome should undergo renal imaging at yearly intervals. Pneumothorax occurs in up to 25% of patients and the recurrence rate approaches 75%.
Lung cysts are commonly found on CT scans of the chest and have a wide range of aetiologies including smoking and rare genetic causes such as lymphangioleiomyomatosis. Lung cysts often have distinct characteristics that help to narrow down the diagnosis. In all patients presenting with a pneumothorax, it is crucial to ask about family history and consider doing a high-resolution CT scan of the thorax.

A 50-year-old man presented to the hospital with perineal pain that had been troubling him for 5 years. He described it as a mild, dull ache that was aggravated by riding his motorcycle. The patient did not report any bothersome lower urinary tract symptoms. He was able to generate a reasonable urinary stream, and preoperative uroflowmetry showed a maximum flow rate of 11·2mL/s, a voided volume of 215 mL, and a post-void residual volume of 20 mL.In 2014, he had mild left loin pain caused by a 1·5 cm left renal calculus; this was treated with extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy. However, after the operation he still had the pain, and repeated ultrasound scans of his abdomen and cultures of his urine since that time showed nothing abnormal. He had sought help from many private practitioners and had been treated for chronic pelvic pain syndrome.
The patient came to see us in 2017 because he was still troubled by the pain. A hard swelling was felt during clinical examination of his perineum; it was palpable 4 cm above the anal verge in the midline. During urethral calibration, resistance was felt 15 cm from the urethral meatus—admitting only an infant's feeding tube of French gauge 6. A plain x-ray of the pelvis showed a radio-opaque shadow inferior to the pubic symphysis (figure), and a retrograde urethrogram showed the obstruction in the bulbar urethra, suggestive of a calculus about 2 cm in diameter (figure).
A full blood count and analysis of the patient's blood chemistry were both normal, and urine analysis showed no abnormalities. The stone was retrieved by ventral urethrotomy with a perineal approach (figure), and at subsequent follow-up appointments the patient reported that he was doing well with complete relief from his perineal pain.
Urethral stones usually present with acute urinary retention or with symptoms indicative of an obstruction of the lower urinary tract; perineal, rectal, and urethral pain, and a palpable urethral mass are uncommon presentations. Importantly, stones in the bulbar urethra—ie, outside the bony pelvis and below the perineal membrane—are likely to be missed on routine transabdominal ultrasonography, as in this case. The bulbar urethra is the widest portion of the urethra and the stone might have been retained there after crossing the sphincter. Urethroscopy performed at the time of surgery showed the stone lying in the dilated bulbar urethra with enough space at the side of the stone to allow uninterrupted urinary flow. The stone had a relatively smooth surface, which probably explained the absence of any lower urinary tract symptoms. Simple palpation of the perineum helped us to arrive at the correct diagnosis. This case highlights urethral stones as one of the causes of chronic pelvic pain syndrome and reinforces the importance of clinical examination of genitalia and perineum in the evaluation of patients.

A 64-year-old woman was referred to our department because of weakness and dizziness that had been troubling her for 3 weeks. She had a microcytic anaemia as noted by her primary care physician: her full blood count showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8·6 g/dL and a mean corpuscular volume of 62·4 fL (normal range 77–95). She said she had never had a period and she did not know why; she had never received any treatment for this problem.Physical examination showed that the patient was short in stature (1·54 m), and that the fourth digit—ring finger—on her left hand (figure) and the fourth digits on both her feet were also noticeably short (figure). She was also partly deaf. According to her medical history, she had hypertension, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, scoliosis, and osteoporosis, and had a recent compression fracture of her L2 vertebra; she had been taking diclofenac 75 mg once or twice a day for several weeks, depending on the intensity of the pain in her back.
We confirmed the patient was iron deficient: her serum iron concentration was 3·4 μmol/L (normal range 10·7–32·2), transferrin saturation was 3% (normal range 16–45), and faecal occult blood (FOB) tests were positive. We did a gastroscopy, which showed an ulcer in the gastric antrum and erosions in the fornix; a colonoscopy showed no abnormalities. We started her on treatment with pantoprazole 40 mg twice a day, and 10 days later FOB tests were negative. Serology testing for coeliac disease was negative and there were no signs of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) at endoscopy.
Considering the patient's physical signs and medical history, we suspected that she had Turner syndrome. An x-ray of her hands clearly showed a shortened left fourth metacarpal (figure) and Madelung deformity—an abnormality arising from premature arrest of growth along the medial volar aspect of the distal radius—of her left wrist, both characteristic of Turner syndrome. The diagnosis was confirmed by karyotyping, which showed the patient to have a 45,X karyotype (figure). Interestingly, 2 weeks after admission, the patient's relatives presented us with a karyotyping report dated 1980, which also showed X monosomy. We believe that the endoscopic findings and improvement after treatment with the proton pump inhibitor indicate that gastric mucosa damage was responsible for our patient's anaemia. Further, we surmise chronic low levels of oestrogen—the result of many years of no treatment—resulted in her severe osteoporosis and back pains, and prolonged use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to treat the pain then caused the gastropathy and blood loss (video).
Turner syndrome is a rare condition in women and is characterised by complete or partial loss of one X chromosome. Patients are short in stature and have ovarian dysgenesis which leads to sexual infantilism, amenorrhoea, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, and endocrine and metabolic disorders. They are at increased risk of autoimmune disorders. With regards to gastrointestinal diseases, the syndrome is associated with coeliac disease, IBD, and intestinal angiodysplasia—all of which can cause iron deficiency anaemia.
Best practice and care for Turner syndrome require a multidisciplinary approach and seeing the patient regularly throughout her life.

A 64-year-old woman was referred to our department because of weakness and dizziness that had been troubling her for 3 weeks. She had a microcytic anaemia as noted by her primary care physician: her full blood count showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8·6 g/dL and a mean corpuscular volume of 62·4 fL (normal range 77–95). She said she had never had a period and she did not know why; she had never received any treatment for this problem.Physical examination showed that the patient was short in stature (1·54 m), and that the fourth digit—ring finger—on her left hand (figure) and the fourth digits on both her feet were also noticeably short (figure). She was also partly deaf. According to her medical history, she had hypertension, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, scoliosis, and osteoporosis, and had a recent compression fracture of her L2 vertebra; she had been taking diclofenac 75 mg once or twice a day for several weeks, depending on the intensity of the pain in her back.
We confirmed the patient was iron deficient: her serum iron concentration was 3·4 μmol/L (normal range 10·7–32·2), transferrin saturation was 3% (normal range 16–45), and faecal occult blood (FOB) tests were positive. We did a gastroscopy, which showed an ulcer in the gastric antrum and erosions in the fornix; a colonoscopy showed no abnormalities. We started her on treatment with pantoprazole 40 mg twice a day, and 10 days later FOB tests were negative. Serology testing for coeliac disease was negative and there were no signs of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) at endoscopy.
Considering the patient's physical signs and medical history, we suspected that she had Turner syndrome. An x-ray of her hands clearly showed a shortened left fourth metacarpal (figure) and Madelung deformity—an abnormality arising from premature arrest of growth along the medial volar aspect of the distal radius—of her left wrist, both characteristic of Turner syndrome. The diagnosis was confirmed by karyotyping, which showed the patient to have a 45,X karyotype (figure). Interestingly, 2 weeks after admission, the patient's relatives presented us with a karyotyping report dated 1980, which also showed X monosomy. We believe that the endoscopic findings and improvement after treatment with the proton pump inhibitor indicate that gastric mucosa damage was responsible for our patient's anaemia. Further, we surmise chronic low levels of oestrogen—the result of many years of no treatment—resulted in her severe osteoporosis and back pains, and prolonged use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to treat the pain then caused the gastropathy and blood loss (video).
Turner syndrome is a rare condition in women and is characterised by complete or partial loss of one X chromosome. Patients are short in stature and have ovarian dysgenesis which leads to sexual infantilism, amenorrhoea, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, and endocrine and metabolic disorders. They are at increased risk of autoimmune disorders. With regards to gastrointestinal diseases, the syndrome is associated with coeliac disease, IBD, and intestinal angiodysplasia—all of which can cause iron deficiency anaemia.
Best practice and care for Turner syndrome require a multidisciplinary approach and seeing the patient regularly throughout her life.

A 64-year-old woman was referred to our department because of weakness and dizziness that had been troubling her for 3 weeks. She had a microcytic anaemia as noted by her primary care physician: her full blood count showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8·6 g/dL and a mean corpuscular volume of 62·4 fL (normal range 77–95). She said she had never had a period and she did not know why; she had never received any treatment for this problem.Physical examination showed that the patient was short in stature (1·54 m), and that the fourth digit—ring finger—on her left hand (figure) and the fourth digits on both her feet were also noticeably short (figure). She was also partly deaf. According to her medical history, she had hypertension, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, scoliosis, and osteoporosis, and had a recent compression fracture of her L2 vertebra; she had been taking diclofenac 75 mg once or twice a day for several weeks, depending on the intensity of the pain in her back.
We confirmed the patient was iron deficient: her serum iron concentration was 3·4 μmol/L (normal range 10·7–32·2), transferrin saturation was 3% (normal range 16–45), and faecal occult blood (FOB) tests were positive. We did a gastroscopy, which showed an ulcer in the gastric antrum and erosions in the fornix; a colonoscopy showed no abnormalities. We started her on treatment with pantoprazole 40 mg twice a day, and 10 days later FOB tests were negative. Serology testing for coeliac disease was negative and there were no signs of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) at endoscopy.
Considering the patient's physical signs and medical history, we suspected that she had Turner syndrome. An x-ray of her hands clearly showed a shortened left fourth metacarpal (figure) and Madelung deformity—an abnormality arising from premature arrest of growth along the medial volar aspect of the distal radius—of her left wrist, both characteristic of Turner syndrome. The diagnosis was confirmed by karyotyping, which showed the patient to have a 45,X karyotype (figure). Interestingly, 2 weeks after admission, the patient's relatives presented us with a karyotyping report dated 1980, which also showed X monosomy. We believe that the endoscopic findings and improvement after treatment with the proton pump inhibitor indicate that gastric mucosa damage was responsible for our patient's anaemia. Further, we surmise chronic low levels of oestrogen—the result of many years of no treatment—resulted in her severe osteoporosis and back pains, and prolonged use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to treat the pain then caused the gastropathy and blood loss (video).
Turner syndrome is a rare condition in women and is characterised by complete or partial loss of one X chromosome. Patients are short in stature and have ovarian dysgenesis which leads to sexual infantilism, amenorrhoea, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, and endocrine and metabolic disorders. They are at increased risk of autoimmune disorders. With regards to gastrointestinal diseases, the syndrome is associated with coeliac disease, IBD, and intestinal angiodysplasia—all of which can cause iron deficiency anaemia.
Best practice and care for Turner syndrome require a multidisciplinary approach and seeing the patient regularly throughout her life.

input: A rheumatology consult was taken for a 22-year-old man admitted with acute pancreatitis who developed nodular skin lesions over both shins and joint pains in the ankles, knees, and wrists. The patient had a history of mild dull aching, epigastric pain for 1 year; and presented with fever for 1 month with dyspnoea. In the hospital, blood tests showed raised amylase (1997 units per L) and lipase (889 units per L). MRI of the abdomen (figure 1A) showed diffuse enlargement of the pancreas with mild peripancreatic fat stranding and dilated main and peripheral ducts. Percutaneous drainage of the peripancreatic fluid collection was done. 2 days later he developed non-pruritic nodular erythematosus lesions over both shins and synovitis of the knees, ankles, and wrists. Skin biopsy from the nodular swellings revealed panniculitis (figure 1B). Synovial fluid aspiration showed thick white pus-like fluid, with a high neutrophil count but sterile on culture. Radiography of both ankles and feet showed multiple lytic lesions (figure 1C) and contrast-enhanced MRI of ankles showed multiple areas of altered signal intensity in multiple bones of both ankles and feet with mild joint effusion and synovitis of multiple joints of the feet (figure 1C). The patient was diagnosed as having pancreatitis panniculitis and polyarthritis syndrome. The areas of altered signal intensity on MRI of the ankle and foot were consistent with fat necrosis (figure 1D). Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography revealed pancreatic duct disruption in the head of the pancreas with opacification of upstream main pancreatic duct and tortuous course. A stent was placed in the duct across the leak to bridge the disruption. Joint pain was managed with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and intra-articular methylprednisolone in the ankle joints. The patient's symptoms improved and only mild ankle synovitis remained after 1 month. Investigation of the cause of the pancreatitis was unrevealing, with negative tests for gallstones, hypertriglyceridaemia, hypercalcaemia, hyperparathyroidism, serum IgG4, IgA tissue transglutaminase, stool for ova or cysts, and systemic vasculitis. In the absence of any identifiable cause, the disease was considered to be idiopathic chronic calcific pancreatitis (calcification on contrast-enhanced CT images).Pancreatitis panniculitis and polyarthritis syndrome is a rare extrapancreatic complication of pancreatitis. Its pathogenesis is unknown, but a role for leakage of lipase in the blood stream has been postulated. So far, about 70 case reports are available. The age at presentation varies from 6 years to 88 years, the underlying pancreatitis can be either acute or chronic, and abdominal symptoms can be mild or absent. Panniculitis can occur anywhere that fat is present; it can occur simultaneously, later, or before pancreatic disease by several weeks. Arthritis is usually symmetric and polyarticular; however, monoarticular or oligoarticular involvement has also been described; lower limb predominance is common. Synovial fluid is thick yellow because of high lipid content with neutrophilic leucocytosis; and thus mimics infectious pus. Uncommon articular manifestations in pancreatitis panniculitis and polyarthritis syndrome are pathological fractures, periostitis, destructive arthritis, and necrosis of bone and cartilage. The pathogenesis of arthritis is thought to be periarticular bone marrow lipolysis leading to increased free fatty acid, which causes synovitis and reactionary effusion. Treatment consists of treating pancreatic pathology, NSAIDs, and intra-articular steroids for symptomatic relief. However, up to half of patients might develop chronic arthritis despite resolution of pancreatitis.

Percutaneous drainage of the peripancreatic fluid collection was done. 2 days later he developed non-pruritic nodular erythematosus lesions over both shins and synovitis of the knees, ankles, and wrists. Skin biopsy from the nodular swellings revealed panniculitis (figure 1B). Synovial fluid aspiration showed thick white pus-like fluid, with a high neutrophil count but sterile on culture. Radiography of both ankles and feet showed multiple lytic lesions (figure 1C) and contrast-enhanced MRI of ankles showed multiple areas of altered signal intensity in multiple bones of both ankles and feet with mild joint effusion and synovitis of multiple joints of the feet (figure 1C). The patient was diagnosed as having pancreatitis panniculitis and polyarthritis syndrome. The areas of altered signal intensity on MRI of the ankle and foot were consistent with fat necrosis (figure 1D). Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography revealed pancreatic duct disruption in the head of the pancreas with opacification of upstream main pancreatic duct and tortuous course. A stent was placed in the duct across the leak to bridge the disruption. input: A 43-year-old woman, who was a non-smoker and who had been previously identified as having malignant pericardial effusion and a PET scan suggestive of a primary malignant tumour in the left upper lobe of the lung with mediastinal lymphadenopathy was referred to the emergency department at the University Hospital Centre Zagreb in December, 2012, because of progressive dyspnoea. Chest radiography obtained on admission showed substantial enlargement of the cardiac silhouette. Echocardiography pointed to pre-tamponade. The patient underwent pericardial drainage and 2000 mL of haemorrhagic fluid was evacuated. After 24 h, the patient had a substantial loss of red blood cells and became hypotensive. Control echocardiogram showed the tip of the drainage pericardial catheter was inside the heart, in the right ventricle, with signs of pre-tamponade still present indicating erroneous placement of the catheter. Redrainage of the pericardium was done and a preoperative CT angiography scan revealed two drainage catheters, one positioned with its tip in the pericardium and the other entering the right ventricle of the heart, going through it and into the main pulmonary artery, with its tip located in the proximal segment of left main pulmonary artery (figure). The patient underwent surgery and the incorrectly positioned drainage pericardial catheter was removed with no complications. After clinical stabilisation of the patient, further pulmonary diagnostic tests led to the diagnosis of metastatic lung adenocarcinoma. An initial test of pericardial effusion showed adenocarcinoma cells that were CK7 and TTF-1 positive and CK20 negative, which is compatible with a diagnosis of primary pulmonary adenocarcinoma. Molecular testing showed positive EGFR mutation (exon 19 deletion). The patient received 150 mg erlotinib once-daily, and her overall survival was 30 months.

input: A 43-year-old woman, who was a non-smoker and who had been previously identified as having malignant pericardial effusion and a PET scan suggestive of a primary malignant tumour in the left upper lobe of the lung with mediastinal lymphadenopathy was referred to the emergency department at the University Hospital Centre Zagreb in December, 2012, because of progressive dyspnoea. Chest radiography obtained on admission showed substantial enlargement of the cardiac silhouette. Echocardiography pointed to pre-tamponade. The patient underwent pericardial drainage and 2000 mL of haemorrhagic fluid was evacuated. After 24 h, the patient had a substantial loss of red blood cells and became hypotensive. Control echocardiogram showed the tip of the drainage pericardial catheter was inside the heart, in the right ventricle, with signs of pre-tamponade still present indicating erroneous placement of the catheter. Redrainage of the pericardium was done and a preoperative CT angiography scan revealed two drainage catheters, one positioned with its tip in the pericardium and the other entering the right ventricle of the heart, going through it and into the main pulmonary artery, with its tip located in the proximal segment of left main pulmonary artery (figure). The patient underwent surgery and the incorrectly positioned drainage pericardial catheter was removed with no complications. After clinical stabilisation of the patient, further pulmonary diagnostic tests led to the diagnosis of metastatic lung adenocarcinoma. An initial test of pericardial effusion showed adenocarcinoma cells that were CK7 and TTF-1 positive and CK20 negative, which is compatible with a diagnosis of primary pulmonary adenocarcinoma. Molecular testing showed positive EGFR mutation (exon 19 deletion). The patient received 150 mg erlotinib once-daily, and her overall survival was 30 months.

A 39-year-old man was admitted to our department with a 1-day history of pain in his left flank and dizziness. His medical history included poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and a stone in the left upper ureter. On admission to the hospital, he appeared to be in septic shock. His temperature was 38·1°C and his blood pressure was 66/35 mm Hg. Laboratory investigations showed a leucocytosis of 16·58 × 109 per L with 93·6% neutrophils. His renal function was abnormal: blood concentrations of creatinine and urea nitrogen were 0·499 mg/dL and 15·4 mmol/L, respectively. He was hyperglycaemic with a blood glucose concentration of 24·7 mmol/L.Escherichia coli were isolated in a blood culture but not in a urine culture. A CT scan of his abdomen was done immediately and showed a diffusely swollen left kidney (figure). Board-spectrum antibiotics were started empirically and 10 h later an enhanced CT scan showed that the left kidney had expanded because of gas in the parenchyma and para-renal space—especially in the renal veins. Based on these findings, we made a diagnosis of an emphysematous pyelonephritis. Because of the risk of an air embolism, an open, exploratory operation was undertaken. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit after the surgery for further resuscitation and control of his electrolytes. Repeat CT scans done 4 days and 23 days after the operation showed reducing amounts of gas in the left kidney (figure). When we repeated laboratory investigations just before he was discharged, his routine blood tests and renal function had returned to within the normal ranges: his blood creatinine concentration was 0·198 mg/dL, his blood urea nitrogen concentration was 8·6 mmol/L, and his blood glucose concentration was 4·8 mmol/L.
E coli infections in patients with diabetes and urinary tract obstruction, either occurring alone or together, are the cornerstones in the development of emphysematous pyelonephritis. In patients with poorly controlled blood glucose concentrations, the situation is complicated further by possible impairment of tissue circulation. Additionally, the high levels of blood glucose provide microorganisms with a more favourable environment in which to form gas. Mixed acid fermentation of glucose by Enterobacteriaceae is the major pathway of gas formation—carbon dioxide and hydrogen are the main components of the gas.

A 39-year-old man was admitted to our department with a 1-day history of pain in his left flank and dizziness. His medical history included poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and a stone in the left upper ureter. On admission to the hospital, he appeared to be in septic shock. His temperature was 38·1°C and his blood pressure was 66/35 mm Hg. Laboratory investigations showed a leucocytosis of 16·58 × 109 per L with 93·6% neutrophils. His renal function was abnormal: blood concentrations of creatinine and urea nitrogen were 0·499 mg/dL and 15·4 mmol/L, respectively. He was hyperglycaemic with a blood glucose concentration of 24·7 mmol/L.Escherichia coli were isolated in a blood culture but not in a urine culture. A CT scan of his abdomen was done immediately and showed a diffusely swollen left kidney (figure). Board-spectrum antibiotics were started empirically and 10 h later an enhanced CT scan showed that the left kidney had expanded because of gas in the parenchyma and para-renal space—especially in the renal veins. Based on these findings, we made a diagnosis of an emphysematous pyelonephritis. Because of the risk of an air embolism, an open, exploratory operation was undertaken. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit after the surgery for further resuscitation and control of his electrolytes. Repeat CT scans done 4 days and 23 days after the operation showed reducing amounts of gas in the left kidney (figure). When we repeated laboratory investigations just before he was discharged, his routine blood tests and renal function had returned to within the normal ranges: his blood creatinine concentration was 0·198 mg/dL, his blood urea nitrogen concentration was 8·6 mmol/L, and his blood glucose concentration was 4·8 mmol/L.
E coli infections in patients with diabetes and urinary tract obstruction, either occurring alone or together, are the cornerstones in the development of emphysematous pyelonephritis. In patients with poorly controlled blood glucose concentrations, the situation is complicated further by possible impairment of tissue circulation. Additionally, the high levels of blood glucose provide microorganisms with a more favourable environment in which to form gas. Mixed acid fermentation of glucose by Enterobacteriaceae is the major pathway of gas formation—carbon dioxide and hydrogen are the main components of the gas.

A 69-year-old woman with axial and peripheral spondyloarthritis (diagnosed in 2016) was in remission on anti-tumour necrosis factor therapy (adalimumab 40 mg every other week). She presented to our rheumatology unit with a 3-month history of inflammatory back pain and polyarthralgia associated with morning stiffness lasting more than 1 h.These symptoms were associated with asthenia, cough, and a weight loss of 10 kg in the past 3 months. On examination, restricted movement of the lumbar and dorsal spine and tenosynovitis of the first extensor compartment of the left wrist were noted. Both the Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Score (ASDAS) and the Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI) reflected active disease (ASDAS=4·7 and BASDAI=7). Her serum C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration was unusually high (24 mg/L). Because the patient was immunocompromised, we performed chest and abdominal CT scans to rule out neoplasm or infection. The chest CT revealed an intracardiac, heterogeneous, obstructive mass in the left atrium, measuring 70 mm by 49 mm suggesting a myxoma, and this was confirmed on cardiac MRI (figure, A). The mass was not present on a CT scan performed in 2017. Considering the overproduction of interleukin (IL)-6 by cardiac myxomas, we measured serum IL-6 concentration, which was 23 pg/mL (normal range <7 pg/mL).
The patient underwent surgical excision (figure, B), and the histopathological assessment confirmed the diagnosis of myxoma, which was positive for calretinin. Adalimumab was discontinued because of the infection risk during surgery. Postoperative follow-up found normalisation of CRP concentration (<3 mg/L) and a decrease in arthralgia intensity. 1 month after surgery, the patient was in remission (ASDAS <1·3, BASDAI=2·4), with a normal serum IL-6 concentration (<7 pg/mL), without reintroduction of adalimumab. Adalimumab was reintroduced 4 months after the surgery to avoid the relapse of the spondyloarthritis. 1 year after the surgery, the patient is still in remission with normal CRP concentration. Cardiac myxoma is rare with an incidence rate of 0·5 per million people, but it is the most common primary benign neoplasm of the heart. Most myxomas are asymptomatic and found incidentally; however, some can mimic systemic diseases. Because of the embolic risk and the risk of cardiac arrest, standard treatment is surgical excision.

A 69-year-old woman with axial and peripheral spondyloarthritis (diagnosed in 2016) was in remission on anti-tumour necrosis factor therapy (adalimumab 40 mg every other week). She presented to our rheumatology unit with a 3-month history of inflammatory back pain and polyarthralgia associated with morning stiffness lasting more than 1 h.These symptoms were associated with asthenia, cough, and a weight loss of 10 kg in the past 3 months. On examination, restricted movement of the lumbar and dorsal spine and tenosynovitis of the first extensor compartment of the left wrist were noted. Both the Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Score (ASDAS) and the Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI) reflected active disease (ASDAS=4·7 and BASDAI=7). Her serum C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration was unusually high (24 mg/L). Because the patient was immunocompromised, we performed chest and abdominal CT scans to rule out neoplasm or infection. The chest CT revealed an intracardiac, heterogeneous, obstructive mass in the left atrium, measuring 70 mm by 49 mm suggesting a myxoma, and this was confirmed on cardiac MRI (figure, A). The mass was not present on a CT scan performed in 2017. Considering the overproduction of interleukin (IL)-6 by cardiac myxomas, we measured serum IL-6 concentration, which was 23 pg/mL (normal range <7 pg/mL).
The patient underwent surgical excision (figure, B), and the histopathological assessment confirmed the diagnosis of myxoma, which was positive for calretinin. Adalimumab was discontinued because of the infection risk during surgery. Postoperative follow-up found normalisation of CRP concentration (<3 mg/L) and a decrease in arthralgia intensity. 1 month after surgery, the patient was in remission (ASDAS <1·3, BASDAI=2·4), with a normal serum IL-6 concentration (<7 pg/mL), without reintroduction of adalimumab. Adalimumab was reintroduced 4 months after the surgery to avoid the relapse of the spondyloarthritis. 1 year after the surgery, the patient is still in remission with normal CRP concentration. Cardiac myxoma is rare with an incidence rate of 0·5 per million people, but it is the most common primary benign neoplasm of the heart. Most myxomas are asymptomatic and found incidentally; however, some can mimic systemic diseases. Because of the embolic risk and the risk of cardiac arrest, standard treatment is surgical excision.

input:
A 46-year old nulliparous woman presented to our hospital with a 6-month history of increasing abdominal pain and pelvic pressure symptoms—including urinary frequency and overflow incontinence of faeces and dyspareunia.4 years earlier, the patient had a laparoscopic myomectomy for multiple uterine myomas: the largest myoma had only been partially excised because of its size and location (6 cm × 7 cm and abutting the rectosigmoid). It was, therefore, shredded using power morcellation—without a containment bag—into smaller pieces which were then retrieved through the laparoscopic port.
On clinical examination we found the patient to have an enlarged uterus of 20 weeks gestational size that was displaced anterosuperior by a significant pelvic mass. MRI on admission showed new uterine and extra-uterine myomas occupying the pelvis (figure). Additionally, some of the myomas were retroperitoneal, and engulfed both major vessels and bowel; these were not present at the original surgery. Following a multidisciplinary team discussion, we decided upon surgical excision to exclude possible malignancy.
En-bloc resection of the recto-sigmoid and pelvic side wall myomas, total hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (figure), omental biopsy, and end-colostomy (Hartmann's) were performed. Histopathological examination of samples obtained during the operation showed benign myomas—with no evidence of malignancy—and confirmed that they were uterine in origin.
At follow-up 3 months later, MRI showed no signs of residual intrapelvic disease; the patient remains asymptomatic and reports an improved quality of life.
We believe that the source of the retroperitoneal myomas might have been the large fibroid that was only partially excised during the first procedure 4 years earlier; the development of some of the myomas was probably independent of the surgery. However, some of the leiomyomas—both intra-uterine and retroperitoneal—might have been spread as an unintended consequence of the power morcellation being done without a containment bag resulting in seeding of cells sprayed during shredding.
Power morcellation—useful for minimally invasive surgery—has been the subject of much debate due to the risk of disseminating occult malignant tumours. While this has rightly been a focus of informed consent and the development of guidelines, the consequences of morcellation on benign tumours have been less discussed; as illustrated here by our case, although rare, these can lead to serious morbidity, and should therefore, also be discussed in shared decision making and informed consent. Furthermore, it is important to employ meticulous surgical technique and containment morcellation bags to preserve oncological hygiene—a situation frequently overlooked in benign cases (video).

She presented to our rheumatology unit with a 3-month history of inflammatory back pain and polyarthralgia associated with morning stiffness lasting more than 1 h.These symptoms were associated with asthenia, cough, and a weight loss of 10 kg in the past 3 months. On examination, restricted movement of the lumbar and dorsal spine and tenosynovitis of the first extensor compartment of the left wrist were noted. Both the Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Score (ASDAS) and the Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI) reflected active disease (ASDAS=4·7 and BASDAI=7). Her serum C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration was unusually high (24 mg/L). Because the patient was immunocompromised, we performed chest and abdominal CT scans to rule out neoplasm or infection. The chest CT revealed an intracardiac, heterogeneous, obstructive mass in the left atrium, measuring 70 mm by 49 mm suggesting a myxoma, and this was confirmed on cardiac MRI (figure, A). The mass was not present on a CT scan performed in 2017. Considering the overproduction of interleukin (IL)-6 by cardiac myxomas, we measured serum IL-6 concentration, which was 23 pg/mL (normal range <7 pg/mL).
The patient underwent surgical excision (figure, B), and the histopathological assessment confirmed the diagnosis of myxoma, which was positive for calretinin. Adalimumab was discontinued because of the infection risk during surgery. Postoperative follow-up found normalisation of CRP concentration (<3 mg/L) and a decrease in arthralgia intensity. 1 month after surgery, the patient was in remission (ASDAS <1·3, BASDAI=2·4), with a normal serum IL-6 concentration (<7 pg/mL), without reintroduction of adalimumab. Adalimumab was reintroduced 4 months after the surgery to avoid the relapse of the spondyloarthritis. 1 year after the surgery, the patient is still in remission with normal CRP concentration. Cardiac myxoma is rare with an incidence rate of 0·5 per million people, but it is the most common primary benign neoplasm of the heart. Most myxomas are asymptomatic and found incidentally; however, some can mimic systemic diseases. Because of the embolic risk and the risk of cardiac arrest, standard treatment is surgical excision.
