A 46-year old nulliparous woman presented to our hospital with a 6-month history of increasing abdominal pain and pelvic pressure symptoms—including urinary frequency and overflow incontinence of faeces and dyspareunia.4 years earlier, the patient had a laparoscopic myomectomy for multiple uterine myomas: the largest myoma had only been partially excised because of its size and location (6 cm × 7 cm and abutting the rectosigmoid). It was, therefore, shredded using power morcellation—without a containment bag—into smaller pieces which were then retrieved through the laparoscopic port.
On clinical examination we found the patient to have an enlarged uterus of 20 weeks gestational size that was displaced anterosuperior by a significant pelvic mass. MRI on admission showed new uterine and extra-uterine myomas occupying the pelvis (figure). Additionally, some of the myomas were retroperitoneal, and engulfed both major vessels and bowel; these were not present at the original surgery. Following a multidisciplinary team discussion, we decided upon surgical excision to exclude possible malignancy.
En-bloc resection of the recto-sigmoid and pelvic side wall myomas, total hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (figure), omental biopsy, and end-colostomy (Hartmann's) were performed. Histopathological examination of samples obtained during the operation showed benign myomas—with no evidence of malignancy—and confirmed that they were uterine in origin.
At follow-up 3 months later, MRI showed no signs of residual intrapelvic disease; the patient remains asymptomatic and reports an improved quality of life.
We believe that the source of the retroperitoneal myomas might have been the large fibroid that was only partially excised during the first procedure 4 years earlier; the development of some of the myomas was probably independent of the surgery. However, some of the leiomyomas—both intra-uterine and retroperitoneal—might have been spread as an unintended consequence of the power morcellation being done without a containment bag resulting in seeding of cells sprayed during shredding.
Power morcellation—useful for minimally invasive surgery—has been the subject of much debate due to the risk of disseminating occult malignant tumours. While this has rightly been a focus of informed consent and the development of guidelines, the consequences of morcellation on benign tumours have been less discussed; as illustrated here by our case, although rare, these can lead to serious morbidity, and should therefore, also be discussed in shared decision making and informed consent. Furthermore, it is important to employ meticulous surgical technique and containment morcellation bags to preserve oncological hygiene—a situation frequently overlooked in benign cases (video).

A 28-year-old man from the rural area of Tamil Nadu attended our specialist hospital, complaining of multiple, copper-coloured patches on his skin, forehead, arms, and the front and back of his torso (figure). On examination he also had bilateral thickening of his ulnar and median nerves, without any functional impairment; multiple slit skin smear tests were positive for acid-fast bacilli in most of the patches on his body. We made a diagnosis of multibacillary, or lepromatous, leprosy, and started the patient on a 12-month course of multidrug therapy (MDT)—rifampicin 600 mg once a month, dapsone 100 mg daily, and clofazimine 300 mg once a month and 50 mg daily. However, within a month, the patient developed raised erythematous lesions over the pre-existing skin patches (figure) as well as general constitutional symptoms including a fever and severe neuritis. A full blood count was normal and serological testing for any additional infections was negative. Biochemical investigations showed abnormal liver function tests (appendix). On the basis of these findings, we made a diagnosis of a severe type 1 leprosy reaction—also known as a reversal reaction—occurring alongside an adverse reaction to dapsone. The patchy, exfoliative dermatitis along with the swollen lips, fever, and hepatitis were key in reaching a diagnosis of an adverse reaction to dapsone. We stopped the MDT regimen, and started the patient on corticosteroids, beginning with a high dose and tapering over subsequent weeks—the hope was that the steroids would help both the adverse reaction to the dapsone and the reversal reaction. At follow-up visits, the patient showed improvement both clinically and biochemically, as indicated by the liver function tests (appendix). We restarted the MDT regimen but this time excluded the dapsone.5 months later the patient again showed signs of a type 1 leprosy reaction. We considered re-starting the dapsone—to see if the patient remained allergic to the drug and because it might have assisted in the treatment of the Mycobacterium leprae—but the patient was unwilling to try this. So he continued the MDT alone—rifampacin and clofazimine—without further treatment with corticosteroids as the neuritis was reasonably controlled by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and regular physiotherapy.
Leprosy has a wide range of presentations, from the lepromatous forms to the borderline forms (borderline-tuberculoid, mid-borderline, and borderline-lepromatous) to the tuberculoid forms. Type 1 or reversal reactions mostly occur in borderline-tuberculoid leprosy with a persistence of cell-mediated immunity. They are diagnosed when raised erythematous patches occur over pre-existing skin lesions in patients undergoing treatment. If the reaction is accompanied by fever, neuritis, or oedema of the hands or feet, it is categorised as a severe reaction and needs treatment with corticosteroids. Dapsone hypersensitivity affects a much smaller—and often unrecognised—population of patients: it is essentially an allergy with clinical features of a fever, skin rashes, mucosal involvement, lymphadenitis, and hepatitis. It carries a mortality of 9·9% and is probably often unrecognised because patients may not have routine blood tests in resource-poor settings. Laboratory findings show an eosinophilia, deranged liver function tests, and, rarely, renal failure. Patients with reversal reactions and hypersensitivity—as in our case—can be managed with the MDT regimen of rifampicin and clofazimine.

A 46-year old nulliparous woman presented to our hospital with a 6-month history of increasing abdominal pain and pelvic pressure symptoms—including urinary frequency and overflow incontinence of faeces and dyspareunia.4 years earlier, the patient had a laparoscopic myomectomy for multiple uterine myomas: the largest myoma had only been partially excised because of its size and location (6 cm × 7 cm and abutting the rectosigmoid). It was, therefore, shredded using power morcellation—without a containment bag—into smaller pieces which were then retrieved through the laparoscopic port.
On clinical examination we found the patient to have an enlarged uterus of 20 weeks gestational size that was displaced anterosuperior by a significant pelvic mass. MRI on admission showed new uterine and extra-uterine myomas occupying the pelvis (figure). Additionally, some of the myomas were retroperitoneal, and engulfed both major vessels and bowel; these were not present at the original surgery. Following a multidisciplinary team discussion, we decided upon surgical excision to exclude possible malignancy.
En-bloc resection of the recto-sigmoid and pelvic side wall myomas, total hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (figure), omental biopsy, and end-colostomy (Hartmann's) were performed. Histopathological examination of samples obtained during the operation showed benign myomas—with no evidence of malignancy—and confirmed that they were uterine in origin.
At follow-up 3 months later, MRI showed no signs of residual intrapelvic disease; the patient remains asymptomatic and reports an improved quality of life.
We believe that the source of the retroperitoneal myomas might have been the large fibroid that was only partially excised during the first procedure 4 years earlier; the development of some of the myomas was probably independent of the surgery. However, some of the leiomyomas—both intra-uterine and retroperitoneal—might have been spread as an unintended consequence of the power morcellation being done without a containment bag resulting in seeding of cells sprayed during shredding.
Power morcellation—useful for minimally invasive surgery—has been the subject of much debate due to the risk of disseminating occult malignant tumours. While this has rightly been a focus of informed consent and the development of guidelines, the consequences of morcellation on benign tumours have been less discussed; as illustrated here by our case, although rare, these can lead to serious morbidity, and should therefore, also be discussed in shared decision making and informed consent. Furthermore, it is important to employ meticulous surgical technique and containment morcellation bags to preserve oncological hygiene—a situation frequently overlooked in benign cases (video).

A 28-year-old man from the rural area of Tamil Nadu attended our specialist hospital, complaining of multiple, copper-coloured patches on his skin, forehead, arms, and the front and back of his torso (figure). On examination he also had bilateral thickening of his ulnar and median nerves, without any functional impairment; multiple slit skin smear tests were positive for acid-fast bacilli in most of the patches on his body. We made a diagnosis of multibacillary, or lepromatous, leprosy, and started the patient on a 12-month course of multidrug therapy (MDT)—rifampicin 600 mg once a month, dapsone 100 mg daily, and clofazimine 300 mg once a month and 50 mg daily. However, within a month, the patient developed raised erythematous lesions over the pre-existing skin patches (figure) as well as general constitutional symptoms including a fever and severe neuritis. A full blood count was normal and serological testing for any additional infections was negative. Biochemical investigations showed abnormal liver function tests (appendix). On the basis of these findings, we made a diagnosis of a severe type 1 leprosy reaction—also known as a reversal reaction—occurring alongside an adverse reaction to dapsone. The patchy, exfoliative dermatitis along with the swollen lips, fever, and hepatitis were key in reaching a diagnosis of an adverse reaction to dapsone. We stopped the MDT regimen, and started the patient on corticosteroids, beginning with a high dose and tapering over subsequent weeks—the hope was that the steroids would help both the adverse reaction to the dapsone and the reversal reaction. At follow-up visits, the patient showed improvement both clinically and biochemically, as indicated by the liver function tests (appendix). We restarted the MDT regimen but this time excluded the dapsone.5 months later the patient again showed signs of a type 1 leprosy reaction. We considered re-starting the dapsone—to see if the patient remained allergic to the drug and because it might have assisted in the treatment of the Mycobacterium leprae—but the patient was unwilling to try this. So he continued the MDT alone—rifampacin and clofazimine—without further treatment with corticosteroids as the neuritis was reasonably controlled by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and regular physiotherapy.
Leprosy has a wide range of presentations, from the lepromatous forms to the borderline forms (borderline-tuberculoid, mid-borderline, and borderline-lepromatous) to the tuberculoid forms. Type 1 or reversal reactions mostly occur in borderline-tuberculoid leprosy with a persistence of cell-mediated immunity. They are diagnosed when raised erythematous patches occur over pre-existing skin lesions in patients undergoing treatment. If the reaction is accompanied by fever, neuritis, or oedema of the hands or feet, it is categorised as a severe reaction and needs treatment with corticosteroids. Dapsone hypersensitivity affects a much smaller—and often unrecognised—population of patients: it is essentially an allergy with clinical features of a fever, skin rashes, mucosal involvement, lymphadenitis, and hepatitis. It carries a mortality of 9·9% and is probably often unrecognised because patients may not have routine blood tests in resource-poor settings. Laboratory findings show an eosinophilia, deranged liver function tests, and, rarely, renal failure. Patients with reversal reactions and hypersensitivity—as in our case—can be managed with the MDT regimen of rifampicin and clofazimine.

A 73-year-old man with a history of hypertension and diverticulosis presented to our emergency department with a 1-day history of severe, lower abdominal pain, on his left side, associated with nausea. He did not report any other symptoms: dizziness, chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, haematuria, fever, or diarrhoea.His vital signs were all normal except that he was hypertensive with a blood pressure of 187/104 mm Hg. A physical examination—including a cardiac examination—found no abnormalities. His white blood cell count was 9 × 109 per L. His blood creatinine concentration was 0·8 mg/dL, and his liver function tests were normal: aspartate aminotransaminase was 28 IU/L and alanine aminotransaminase was 20 IU/L. A urinalysis showed 1+ protein, one white blood cell, and four red blood cells— thus within normal limits. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed normal sinus rhythm with premature supraventricular complexes and variable P wave morphology in lead II with a mean duration of 133 ms and an amplitude of less than 0·25 mV. A non-contrast abdominal CT showed no calculi in the urinary tract. An urgent contrast-enhanced abdominal CT was done because of concerns about acute diverticulitis and intestinal ischaemia; this showed acute infarctions in the left kidney and spleen. Although the admission ECG was non-specific, the patient was started on anticoagulant medication, enoxaparin sodium injection 120 mg/day, because of a high index of suspicion that the infarctions were probably caused by cardioembolic events. Subsequently, continuous cardiac telemetry showed that the patient had paroxysmal atrial fibrillation—confirmed with an ECG the next morning. An echocardiogram showed that all 4 chambers of the heart were of normal sizes with a left atrium dimension of 3·8 cm. There were no signs of valvular disease, the left ventricular ejection fraction was 60%, and a bubble study was negative. Interestingly, the patient's CHA2DS2-VASc score was four based on his age, hypertension, and thromboembolic events: 1 point for age 65–74 years, 1 point for a history of hypertension, and 2 points for the current embolic event. The patient's symptoms quickly improved, and he was discharged 3 days later in normal sinus rhythm on anticoagulants enoxaparin sodium 120 mg/day injection and warfarin 7·5 mg/day. Acute renal and splenic infarctions are rare and atrial fibrillation should be suspected as the cause even in the absence of arrhythmia on ECG. Other less frequent causes of renal and splenic infarctions include cancer and subacute bacterial endocarditis. Our case demonstrates that acute renal and splenic infarctions can manifest as the first and only presentation of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation even in the absence of arrhythmia on the ECG. For patients presenting with acute renal and splenic infarction, a work-up should include exploration for underlying paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, subacute bacterial endocarditis, and an underlying malignancy.

A 73-year-old man with a history of hypertension and diverticulosis presented to our emergency department with a 1-day history of severe, lower abdominal pain, on his left side, associated with nausea. He did not report any other symptoms: dizziness, chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, haematuria, fever, or diarrhoea.His vital signs were all normal except that he was hypertensive with a blood pressure of 187/104 mm Hg. A physical examination—including a cardiac examination—found no abnormalities. His white blood cell count was 9 × 109 per L. His blood creatinine concentration was 0·8 mg/dL, and his liver function tests were normal: aspartate aminotransaminase was 28 IU/L and alanine aminotransaminase was 20 IU/L. A urinalysis showed 1+ protein, one white blood cell, and four red blood cells— thus within normal limits. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed normal sinus rhythm with premature supraventricular complexes and variable P wave morphology in lead II with a mean duration of 133 ms and an amplitude of less than 0·25 mV. A non-contrast abdominal CT showed no calculi in the urinary tract. An urgent contrast-enhanced abdominal CT was done because of concerns about acute diverticulitis and intestinal ischaemia; this showed acute infarctions in the left kidney and spleen. Although the admission ECG was non-specific, the patient was started on anticoagulant medication, enoxaparin sodium injection 120 mg/day, because of a high index of suspicion that the infarctions were probably caused by cardioembolic events. Subsequently, continuous cardiac telemetry showed that the patient had paroxysmal atrial fibrillation—confirmed with an ECG the next morning. An echocardiogram showed that all 4 chambers of the heart were of normal sizes with a left atrium dimension of 3·8 cm. There were no signs of valvular disease, the left ventricular ejection fraction was 60%, and a bubble study was negative. Interestingly, the patient's CHA2DS2-VASc score was four based on his age, hypertension, and thromboembolic events: 1 point for age 65–74 years, 1 point for a history of hypertension, and 2 points for the current embolic event. The patient's symptoms quickly improved, and he was discharged 3 days later in normal sinus rhythm on anticoagulants enoxaparin sodium 120 mg/day injection and warfarin 7·5 mg/day. Acute renal and splenic infarctions are rare and atrial fibrillation should be suspected as the cause even in the absence of arrhythmia on ECG. Other less frequent causes of renal and splenic infarctions include cancer and subacute bacterial endocarditis. Our case demonstrates that acute renal and splenic infarctions can manifest as the first and only presentation of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation even in the absence of arrhythmia on the ECG. For patients presenting with acute renal and splenic infarction, a work-up should include exploration for underlying paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, subacute bacterial endocarditis, and an underlying malignancy.

A 73-year-old man with a history of hypertension and diverticulosis presented to our emergency department with a 1-day history of severe, lower abdominal pain, on his left side, associated with nausea. He did not report any other symptoms: dizziness, chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, haematuria, fever, or diarrhoea.His vital signs were all normal except that he was hypertensive with a blood pressure of 187/104 mm Hg. A physical examination—including a cardiac examination—found no abnormalities. His white blood cell count was 9 × 109 per L. His blood creatinine concentration was 0·8 mg/dL, and his liver function tests were normal: aspartate aminotransaminase was 28 IU/L and alanine aminotransaminase was 20 IU/L. A urinalysis showed 1+ protein, one white blood cell, and four red blood cells— thus within normal limits. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed normal sinus rhythm with premature supraventricular complexes and variable P wave morphology in lead II with a mean duration of 133 ms and an amplitude of less than 0·25 mV. A non-contrast abdominal CT showed no calculi in the urinary tract. An urgent contrast-enhanced abdominal CT was done because of concerns about acute diverticulitis and intestinal ischaemia; this showed acute infarctions in the left kidney and spleen. Although the admission ECG was non-specific, the patient was started on anticoagulant medication, enoxaparin sodium injection 120 mg/day, because of a high index of suspicion that the infarctions were probably caused by cardioembolic events. Subsequently, continuous cardiac telemetry showed that the patient had paroxysmal atrial fibrillation—confirmed with an ECG the next morning. An echocardiogram showed that all 4 chambers of the heart were of normal sizes with a left atrium dimension of 3·8 cm. There were no signs of valvular disease, the left ventricular ejection fraction was 60%, and a bubble study was negative. Interestingly, the patient's CHA2DS2-VASc score was four based on his age, hypertension, and thromboembolic events: 1 point for age 65–74 years, 1 point for a history of hypertension, and 2 points for the current embolic event. The patient's symptoms quickly improved, and he was discharged 3 days later in normal sinus rhythm on anticoagulants enoxaparin sodium 120 mg/day injection and warfarin 7·5 mg/day. Acute renal and splenic infarctions are rare and atrial fibrillation should be suspected as the cause even in the absence of arrhythmia on ECG. Other less frequent causes of renal and splenic infarctions include cancer and subacute bacterial endocarditis. Our case demonstrates that acute renal and splenic infarctions can manifest as the first and only presentation of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation even in the absence of arrhythmia on the ECG. For patients presenting with acute renal and splenic infarction, a work-up should include exploration for underlying paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, subacute bacterial endocarditis, and an underlying malignancy.

input:
A 77-year-old woman presented to our department with a 2-year history of multiple, painful, purple lesions over her left breast. Physical examination showed multiple, violaceous, infiltrated papules, nodules, and plaques on her left mammary gland (figure), neck, forearms, legs, hands, and feet. She also had axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy. She had no medical history prior to this problem. Results of biochemical analyses were normal, and the patient was seronegative for HIV and cytomegalovirus. CT scans were normal, and endoscopy and colonoscopy showed no gastrointestinal tract involvement. A skin biopsy specimen taken from the left breast showed a spindle-cell neoplasm, which was positive on immunohistochemical staining for both CD34 and human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), which is known more commonly as Kaposi's sarcoma—associated with herpesvirus (figure)—thus confirming a diagnosis of Kaposi's sarcoma. The patient was referred to an oncology clinic for further treatment. However, she did not attend and was lost to follow-up.
Kaposi's sarcoma is a low-grade vascular neoplasm associated with HHV-8 infection. HHV-8 is one of the few viruses associated with tumorigenesis in humans; infection with the virus is considered necessary, although not the only factor, for the development of sarcoma. It is a multifocal disease of the endothelium—most commonly affecting the skin, oral cavity, gastrointestinal tract, or respiratory system. Breast involvement is extremely rare, but when it does occur, it can present as lesions localised just to the breast or as disseminated cutaneous lesions involving tissue beyond the breast—as in the case we describe here. All four clinical variants—classic, endemic or African, iatrogenic associated with transplantation or immunosuppression, and epidemic or HIV/AIDS-associated—have similar histological findings—namely, proliferating malignant spindle cells and ill-defined vascular channels or slits. In classic Kaposi's sarcoma—our case—originally described by Moritz Kaposi in 1872, patients affected are mainly elderly men from eastern European and Mediterranean countries. Typically, cases of classic Kaposi's sarcoma follow an indolent course; spontaneous regression has been reported. The hands and feet are usually affected initially, and later the arms and legs. Skin lesions might be asymptomatic or cause pain because of pressure exerted on underlying structures.
Treatment options are mainly determined by the type and location of the lesions. Solitary lesions can be treated by surgical excision, cryotherapy, or laser. For the patients with disseminated disease or systemic involvement, systemic treatment with interferon or liposomal doxorubicin is recommended.

A 77-year-old woman presented to our department with a 2-year history of multiple, painful, purple lesions over her left breast. Physical examination showed multiple, violaceous, infiltrated papules, nodules, and plaques on her left mammary gland (figure), neck, forearms, legs, hands, and feet. She also had axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy. She had no medical history prior to this problem. Results of biochemical analyses were normal, and the patient was seronegative for HIV and cytomegalovirus. CT scans were normal, and endoscopy and colonoscopy showed no gastrointestinal tract involvement. A skin biopsy specimen taken from the left breast showed a spindle-cell neoplasm, which was positive on immunohistochemical staining for both CD34 and human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), which is known more commonly as Kaposi's sarcoma—associated with herpesvirus (figure)—thus confirming a diagnosis of Kaposi's sarcoma. The patient was referred to an oncology clinic for further treatment. However, she did not attend and was lost to follow-up.
Kaposi's sarcoma is a low-grade vascular neoplasm associated with HHV-8 infection. HHV-8 is one of the few viruses associated with tumorigenesis in humans; infection with the virus is considered necessary, although not the only factor, for the development of sarcoma. It is a multifocal disease of the endothelium—most commonly affecting the skin, oral cavity, gastrointestinal tract, or respiratory system. Breast involvement is extremely rare, but when it does occur, it can present as lesions localised just to the breast or as disseminated cutaneous lesions involving tissue beyond the breast—as in the case we describe here. All four clinical variants—classic, endemic or African, iatrogenic associated with transplantation or immunosuppression, and epidemic or HIV/AIDS-associated—have similar histological findings—namely, proliferating malignant spindle cells and ill-defined vascular channels or slits. In classic Kaposi's sarcoma—our case—originally described by Moritz Kaposi in 1872, patients affected are mainly elderly men from eastern European and Mediterranean countries. Typically, cases of classic Kaposi's sarcoma follow an indolent course; spontaneous regression has been reported. The hands and feet are usually affected initially, and later the arms and legs. Skin lesions might be asymptomatic or cause pain because of pressure exerted on underlying structures.
Treatment options are mainly determined by the type and location of the lesions. Solitary lesions can be treated by surgical excision, cryotherapy, or laser. For the patients with disseminated disease or systemic involvement, systemic treatment with interferon or liposomal doxorubicin is recommended.

input: A 35-year-old Libyan woman was referred to us from another institution with the diagnosis of massive pericardial effusion and pericardial tamponade. On admission to us, she was hypotensive, tachycardic and tachypnoeic. Electrocardiography showed unspecific low QRS voltage and ST-T segment flattening. Chest x-ray showed cardiomegaly. We did an emergency pericardial aspiration which yielded 1500 ml of yellow coloured fluid. A transthoracic echocardiogrm showed multiple cystic formations approximately 1·5–2 cm within the pericardial cavity (figure A), and confirmed the need for surgery. We did a standard median sternotomy and thoroughly irrigated the pericardium with hypertonic saline; multiple cysts were removed from the pericardium (figures B and C). Our patient was diagnosed with a ruptured intrapericardial hydatid cyst and pericardial tamponade. We established the diagnosis based on the gross appearance of the removed cysts, the echocardiogram results, and a high ESR. Hydatid disease is endemic in Libya, a southern Mediterranean country. Serological tests were not available. After surgery she was treated with oral albendazole for 12 days. She recovered well and was discharged 12 days after surgery. Pericardial tamponade due to hydatid disease is a rare condition that has been seldom reported in the literature.

An 18-year-old man presented to our department with a 1-year history of pain in the region of his left hip and difficulty in squatting. He reported no history of any local trauma. There was no history suggestive of an autoimmune disorder. Clinical examination found a tender, hard mass in the left greater trochanteric region with painful, restricted rotation and abduction movements of the hip. Both his medical history and family history were unremarkable. Plain x-ray and CT scans of the pelvis (figure) showed bilateral—left greater than the right—and periarticular, lobulated, calcific, soft tissue masses. Serum urea, creatinine, uric acid, total calcium, alkaline phosphate, and parathyroid hormone concentrations were normal. However, serum inorganic phosphorus was elevated at 2·10 mmol/L (normal range 0·81–1·45 mmol/L). The ratio of the renal tubular maximum reabsorption rate of phosphate to corrected glomerular filtration rate was also elevated at 2·16 mmol/L (normal range 1·07–1·89 mmol/L), suggestive of increased renal tubular phosphate reabsorption. Considering the patient's age, presence of bilateral, and periarticular soft tissue, calcific masses about the hip, hyperphosphataemia with increased tubular phosphate reabsorption, and the absence of indications that the ectopic calcification was secondary to any other causes, the patient was diagnosed with hyperphosphataemic tumoral calcinosis. The symptomatic, left-sided mass was surgically excised: during the operation it appeared as a cystic mass containing chalky white material. Histological examination showed amorphous and granular calcified material surrounded by histiocytic and giant cell reaction—confirming the diagnosis. Postoperatively, attempts were made to lower the patient's blood phosphate concentration using a combination of a phosphate-restricted diet with less than 800 mg/day, tablets of the non-calcium-based phosphate binder, sevelamer hydrochloride—which binds phosphate in the intestine, and oral acetazolamide to induce phosphaturia.Hyperphosphataemic familial tumoral calcinosis—suspected but not confirmed by genetic testing in our patient—is a rare inherited disorder of dysregulated phosphate metabolism characterised by hyperphosphataemia and ectopic soft tissue calcifications—typically in periarticular sites. The disorder is caused by biallelic mutations in three genes involved in phosphate homoeostasis: GALNT3 in type 1, FGF23 in type 2, and α-Klotho in type 3. Mutations in either the FGF23 or GALNT3 genes result in reduced bioactive fibroblast growth factor-23 secretion, and mutations in the α-Klotho gene lead to resistant fibroblast growth factor receptors and the α-Klotho complex. The spectrum of tumoral calcinosis has been expanded further with the addition of a new entity known as autoimmune hyperphosphataemic tumoral calcinosis in which pathogenetic autoantibodies mediate FGF23 resistance. The differential diagnosis of tumoral calcinosis includes calcinosis of chronic kidney disease, myositis ossificans, tophaceous gout, dystrophic calcification associated with connective tissue disorders, synovial chondromatosis, and synovial sarcoma. Treatments to lower serum phosphorus—by blocking dietary phosphate absorption and increasing renal phosphate excretion—have limited effectiveness. Surgery is usually reserved for patients with significant pain or limited function. Awareness of this rare disorder is important to ensure appropriate biochemical investigations and to avoid unnecessary invasive diagnostic procedures.

An 18-year-old man presented to our department with a 1-year history of pain in the region of his left hip and difficulty in squatting. He reported no history of any local trauma. There was no history suggestive of an autoimmune disorder. Clinical examination found a tender, hard mass in the left greater trochanteric region with painful, restricted rotation and abduction movements of the hip. Both his medical history and family history were unremarkable. Plain x-ray and CT scans of the pelvis (figure) showed bilateral—left greater than the right—and periarticular, lobulated, calcific, soft tissue masses. Serum urea, creatinine, uric acid, total calcium, alkaline phosphate, and parathyroid hormone concentrations were normal. However, serum inorganic phosphorus was elevated at 2·10 mmol/L (normal range 0·81–1·45 mmol/L). The ratio of the renal tubular maximum reabsorption rate of phosphate to corrected glomerular filtration rate was also elevated at 2·16 mmol/L (normal range 1·07–1·89 mmol/L), suggestive of increased renal tubular phosphate reabsorption. Considering the patient's age, presence of bilateral, and periarticular soft tissue, calcific masses about the hip, hyperphosphataemia with increased tubular phosphate reabsorption, and the absence of indications that the ectopic calcification was secondary to any other causes, the patient was diagnosed with hyperphosphataemic tumoral calcinosis. The symptomatic, left-sided mass was surgically excised: during the operation it appeared as a cystic mass containing chalky white material. Histological examination showed amorphous and granular calcified material surrounded by histiocytic and giant cell reaction—confirming the diagnosis. Postoperatively, attempts were made to lower the patient's blood phosphate concentration using a combination of a phosphate-restricted diet with less than 800 mg/day, tablets of the non-calcium-based phosphate binder, sevelamer hydrochloride—which binds phosphate in the intestine, and oral acetazolamide to induce phosphaturia.Hyperphosphataemic familial tumoral calcinosis—suspected but not confirmed by genetic testing in our patient—is a rare inherited disorder of dysregulated phosphate metabolism characterised by hyperphosphataemia and ectopic soft tissue calcifications—typically in periarticular sites. The disorder is caused by biallelic mutations in three genes involved in phosphate homoeostasis: GALNT3 in type 1, FGF23 in type 2, and α-Klotho in type 3. Mutations in either the FGF23 or GALNT3 genes result in reduced bioactive fibroblast growth factor-23 secretion, and mutations in the α-Klotho gene lead to resistant fibroblast growth factor receptors and the α-Klotho complex. The spectrum of tumoral calcinosis has been expanded further with the addition of a new entity known as autoimmune hyperphosphataemic tumoral calcinosis in which pathogenetic autoantibodies mediate FGF23 resistance. The differential diagnosis of tumoral calcinosis includes calcinosis of chronic kidney disease, myositis ossificans, tophaceous gout, dystrophic calcification associated with connective tissue disorders, synovial chondromatosis, and synovial sarcoma. Treatments to lower serum phosphorus—by blocking dietary phosphate absorption and increasing renal phosphate excretion—have limited effectiveness. Surgery is usually reserved for patients with significant pain or limited function. Awareness of this rare disorder is important to ensure appropriate biochemical investigations and to avoid unnecessary invasive diagnostic procedures.

A 4-year old girl was admitted to our hospital after she collapsed at home while having dinner. She had a history of recurrent upper airway infections and wheezing, which were being treated with inhaled β2-adrenoceptor agonist, as an outpatient.On examination in our emergency department, the patient was tachycardic and tachypnoeic with subcostal recession and fine bilateral crackles; oxygen saturation on pulse oximetry was 85% at an oxygen flow rate of 2 L/min. Her abdomen was distended, but non-tender; her fingers were clubbed, and she had peripheral oedema in both legs.
A chest x-ray showed both cardiomegaly and hepatomegaly, bilateral pleural effusions—the right being greater than the left—and a small amount of ascitic fluid (figure). An echocardiogram showed a large circumferential pericardial effusion and reduced cardiac contractility with a shortening fraction of 20%. The patient required immediate intubation and the insertion of a pleural drain on her right side and a pericardial drain (figure) as well as inotropic support.
Once the patient was clinically stable, we carried out a comprehensive diagnostic work-up—with coeliac disease included in the list of diagnoses because of the abdominal distension; other diagnoses considered were cardiomyopathy, infections, autoimmune disorders, cystic fibrosis, and malignancies.
Anti-transglutaminase IgG concentration was 600 U/mL (reference range <7), and anti-gliadin IgG concentration was 302 U/mL (reference range <7).
Notably, the patient's IgA antibodies (<5 mg/dL; reference range 27–195) and serum albumin concentration (23 g/L; reference range 38–54) were low; aspartate aminotransferase (78 U/L; reference range 10–45) and alanine aminotransferase (78 U/L; reference range 5–25) were raised.
Upper endoscopy showed a reduction and fissuring of duodenal folds—confirming coeliac disease. Histopathology identified intraepithelial lymphocytosis, marked villous atrophy, and crypt hyperplasia: modified Marsh classification type 3b, Corazza grade B1.
The patient was started on a gluten-free diet and her abdominal distension resolved and there was no recurrence of the pericardial effusion. She was allowed home after 3 weeks when she had made a full clinical recovery. At outpatient follow-up 3 months later, she was seriously considering a career in medicine (figure).
For coeliac disease to manifest itself with cardiopulmonary symptoms at a young age—as in our patient—is unusual and while pericardial effusion is a rare presentation of the illness, it is important to consider it as a differential diagnosis. IgA deficiency is observed in approximately 2% of patients with coeliac disease, further complicating the process of establishing the correct diagnosis (video).

A 4-year old girl was admitted to our hospital after she collapsed at home while having dinner. She had a history of recurrent upper airway infections and wheezing, which were being treated with inhaled β2-adrenoceptor agonist, as an outpatient.On examination in our emergency department, the patient was tachycardic and tachypnoeic with subcostal recession and fine bilateral crackles; oxygen saturation on pulse oximetry was 85% at an oxygen flow rate of 2 L/min. Her abdomen was distended, but non-tender; her fingers were clubbed, and she had peripheral oedema in both legs.
A chest x-ray showed both cardiomegaly and hepatomegaly, bilateral pleural effusions—the right being greater than the left—and a small amount of ascitic fluid (figure). An echocardiogram showed a large circumferential pericardial effusion and reduced cardiac contractility with a shortening fraction of 20%. The patient required immediate intubation and the insertion of a pleural drain on her right side and a pericardial drain (figure) as well as inotropic support.
Once the patient was clinically stable, we carried out a comprehensive diagnostic work-up—with coeliac disease included in the list of diagnoses because of the abdominal distension; other diagnoses considered were cardiomyopathy, infections, autoimmune disorders, cystic fibrosis, and malignancies.
Anti-transglutaminase IgG concentration was 600 U/mL (reference range <7), and anti-gliadin IgG concentration was 302 U/mL (reference range <7).
Notably, the patient's IgA antibodies (<5 mg/dL; reference range 27–195) and serum albumin concentration (23 g/L; reference range 38–54) were low; aspartate aminotransferase (78 U/L; reference range 10–45) and alanine aminotransferase (78 U/L; reference range 5–25) were raised.
Upper endoscopy showed a reduction and fissuring of duodenal folds—confirming coeliac disease. Histopathology identified intraepithelial lymphocytosis, marked villous atrophy, and crypt hyperplasia: modified Marsh classification type 3b, Corazza grade B1.
The patient was started on a gluten-free diet and her abdominal distension resolved and there was no recurrence of the pericardial effusion. She was allowed home after 3 weeks when she had made a full clinical recovery. At outpatient follow-up 3 months later, she was seriously considering a career in medicine (figure).
For coeliac disease to manifest itself with cardiopulmonary symptoms at a young age—as in our patient—is unusual and while pericardial effusion is a rare presentation of the illness, it is important to consider it as a differential diagnosis. IgA deficiency is observed in approximately 2% of patients with coeliac disease, further complicating the process of establishing the correct diagnosis (video).

input: A 72-year-old man visited the surgical outpatient clinic with a spontaneous fracture of his left wrist. Physical examination suggested an additional fracture of his right wrist. Conventional radiograph showed extensive osteolytic lesions with fractures of both distal ulnae (figure). He reported no recent weight loss, night sweats, prostatic problems, or deteriorating performance status. There was no lymphadenopathy on physical examination. Positron emission tomography showed no primary tumour in the abdomen or thorax and no other skeletal lesions, nor was there any suspicion of prostate carcinoma. Microscopic and immunohistochemical analysis of a biopsy of the left ulna showed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. No malignant cells were seen in bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy. A diagnosis of primary osseous diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, stage IIE, was made. Given the striking anatomical features, treatment with three cycles of R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone) and local radiotherapy was initiated.

An 80-year-old man was admitted to our hospital with chest pain and shortness of breath.The patient had a long medical history of diabetes, ischaemic heart disease, and end-stage kidney disease requiring regular haemodialysis.
On examination we found him to be in acute distress, with bilateral ankle oedema, and basal lung crackles. An electrocardiogram showed ST segment depression over leads V2-V6 and a Q wave in lead III. Laboratory investigations showed a serum cardiac troponin T concentration of 1297 ng/L (normal <14) with an unaffected creatinine phosphate kinase level.
We made a diagnosis of an acute non-ST elevation myocardial infarction.
1 day after a percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stent insertion into the right coronary artery and mid-left anterior descending artery, he began to repeatedly vomit; he also developed a low-grade fever with a temperature of 37·8°C. An urgent chest x-ray (figure) showed a radio-opaque nodule—not seen in previous x-rays—in the right lower lung field. We initially wondered whether the patient had aspirated his denture but on review of the lesion we were unconvinced. However, on closer inspection using magnification, we found the radio-opaque object had a complex internal structure consisting of a microchip, a battery, and an electronic circuit (figure). Before the film was sent for reporting, our physician examined the patient and found a subcutaneous continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) transmitter device (FreeStyle Libre Flash Glucose Monitoring System, Abbott Laboratories, Chicago, IL) which had been displaced from deltoid muscle to the patient's back. We treated the patient as if he had a diagnosis of a nosocomial infection and his condition improved with intravenous piperacillin and tazobactam.
He was allowed home after 14 days and at follow-up 2 weeks later the patient was well with no angina or chest symptoms. However, the patient died 6 months later with a recurrent myocardial infarction.
In patients with a history of heart disease, unidentified electronic gadgets seen on chest x-ray might well be cardiac related—specifically pacemakers. Although CGM devices are typically located on the upper arm, they may slip—especially in semiconscious patients and those requiring frequent transfers—to other body parts. CGM devices may look like unexpected foreign objects on limited resolution x-rays. As CGM gains in popularity, health-care professionals should be able to identify CGM devices and be aware of their potential to move to unexpected positions where they may cause consternation on x-ray interpretation. Using appropriate magnification of x-rays may be necessary for recognising CGM devices.

A 4-year old girl was admitted to our hospital after she collapsed at home while having dinner. She had a history of recurrent upper airway infections and wheezing, which were being treated with inhaled β2-adrenoceptor agonist, as an outpatient.On examination in our emergency department, the patient was tachycardic and tachypnoeic with subcostal recession and fine bilateral crackles; oxygen saturation on pulse oximetry was 85% at an oxygen flow rate of 2 L/min. Her abdomen was distended, but non-tender; her fingers were clubbed, and she had peripheral oedema in both legs.
A chest x-ray showed both cardiomegaly and hepatomegaly, bilateral pleural effusions—the right being greater than the left—and a small amount of ascitic fluid (figure). An echocardiogram showed a large circumferential pericardial effusion and reduced cardiac contractility with a shortening fraction of 20%. The patient required immediate intubation and the insertion of a pleural drain on her right side and a pericardial drain (figure) as well as inotropic support.
Once the patient was clinically stable, we carried out a comprehensive diagnostic work-up—with coeliac disease included in the list of diagnoses because of the abdominal distension; other diagnoses considered were cardiomyopathy, infections, autoimmune disorders, cystic fibrosis, and malignancies.
Anti-transglutaminase IgG concentration was 600 U/mL (reference range <7), and anti-gliadin IgG concentration was 302 U/mL (reference range <7).
Notably, the patient's IgA antibodies (<5 mg/dL; reference range 27–195) and serum albumin concentration (23 g/L; reference range 38–54) were low; aspartate aminotransferase (78 U/L; reference range 10–45) and alanine aminotransferase (78 U/L; reference range 5–25) were raised.
Upper endoscopy showed a reduction and fissuring of duodenal folds—confirming coeliac disease. Histopathology identified intraepithelial lymphocytosis, marked villous atrophy, and crypt hyperplasia: modified Marsh classification type 3b, Corazza grade B1.
The patient was started on a gluten-free diet and her abdominal distension resolved and there was no recurrence of the pericardial effusion. She was allowed home after 3 weeks when she had made a full clinical recovery. At outpatient follow-up 3 months later, she was seriously considering a career in medicine (figure).
For coeliac disease to manifest itself with cardiopulmonary symptoms at a young age—as in our patient—is unusual and while pericardial effusion is a rare presentation of the illness, it is important to consider it as a differential diagnosis. IgA deficiency is observed in approximately 2% of patients with coeliac disease, further complicating the process of establishing the correct diagnosis (video).

A 38-year-old woman attended our hospital with a 1-week history of shortness of breath and intermittent chest pain.The patient had Down syndrome and had previously had a ventricular septal defect (VSD) repaired when she was an infant.
On examination, the patient had a blood pressure of 99/77 mm Hg, a heart rate of 98 beats per min, a respiratory rate of 35 breaths per min, and oxygen saturation of 95%. Faint crackles were heard in both lung bases and a 3/6 systolic murmur, heard best at the upper sternal border, radiated to the carotid artery.
A chest x-ray showed a large diaphragmatic hernia, which was confirmed by abdominal CT scan. Laboratory investigations showed a normocytic anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 8·0 g/dL; normal 11·5–15 and mean corpuscular volume 96 fL; normal 80–100). The blood urea nitrogen was 8·0 mg/dL (normal 6–24) and troponin concentration was 0·573 ng/mL (normal 0–0·04).
The patient had an uneventful hernia repair and was allowed home 10 days later with plans for an outpatient cardiology appointment to review the murmur. However, 3 days after leaving hospital, she developed acute respiratory failure. A cardiac CT scan, at that stage, showed a bicuspid aortic valve with calcific aortic stenosis (figure). A transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed a heavily calcified aortic valve, but we were unable to say whether it was bicuspid or unicuspid (figure); critical aortic stenosis and moderate-to-severe aortic regurgitation were present. The aortic valve area was 0·8 cm2 with mean gradient of 77 mm Hg. Additionally, the aortic root was mildly dilated, and the calculated ejection fraction was 46%.
The patient was taken to theatre and the aortic valve was replaced with a bioprosthetic valve; multiplanar reconstruction imaging from an intraoperative transoesophageal echocardiogram showed possible unicuspid aortic valve (figure). And indeed, gross pathological examination of the excised valve confirmed a unicuspid aortic valve with multifocal calcification and a single non-fenestrated raphe (figure). Microscopic examination of a sample of the valve showed moderate calcification and fibrosis.
At follow-up 3 months later, the mean systolic gradient across the prosthetic valve was 17 mm Hg, the ejection fraction had improved to 52%, and there was mild prosthetic regurgitation.
Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is commonly associated with congenital heart defects, occurring in 40–50% of patients. The most common heart defects are atrioventricular septal defects (30%), followed by atrial septum defect (25%), VSD (22%), and patent ductus arteriosus (5%), coarctation of the aorta (5%), and tetralogy of Fallot (3%).
While neonates with trisomy 21 are routinely screened for cardiovascular abnormalities, some abnormalities—such as a unicuspid aortic valve in our patient—do not manifest themselves until adolescence or adulthood. Complex aortic valve pathology can cause stenosis and regurgitation in young adults; physical examination and imaging studies are key in identifying newly developed murmurs and patients should be treated promptly. Finally, distinguishing between bicuspid and unicuspid aortic valvular morphology can be difficult: both transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiograms have clear limitations in aiding the clinician to differentiate between them.

An 80-year-old man was admitted to our hospital with chest pain and shortness of breath.The patient had a long medical history of diabetes, ischaemic heart disease, and end-stage kidney disease requiring regular haemodialysis.
On examination we found him to be in acute distress, with bilateral ankle oedema, and basal lung crackles. An electrocardiogram showed ST segment depression over leads V2-V6 and a Q wave in lead III. Laboratory investigations showed a serum cardiac troponin T concentration of 1297 ng/L (normal <14) with an unaffected creatinine phosphate kinase level.
We made a diagnosis of an acute non-ST elevation myocardial infarction.
1 day after a percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stent insertion into the right coronary artery and mid-left anterior descending artery, he began to repeatedly vomit; he also developed a low-grade fever with a temperature of 37·8°C. An urgent chest x-ray (figure) showed a radio-opaque nodule—not seen in previous x-rays—in the right lower lung field. We initially wondered whether the patient had aspirated his denture but on review of the lesion we were unconvinced. However, on closer inspection using magnification, we found the radio-opaque object had a complex internal structure consisting of a microchip, a battery, and an electronic circuit (figure). Before the film was sent for reporting, our physician examined the patient and found a subcutaneous continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) transmitter device (FreeStyle Libre Flash Glucose Monitoring System, Abbott Laboratories, Chicago, IL) which had been displaced from deltoid muscle to the patient's back. We treated the patient as if he had a diagnosis of a nosocomial infection and his condition improved with intravenous piperacillin and tazobactam.
He was allowed home after 14 days and at follow-up 2 weeks later the patient was well with no angina or chest symptoms. However, the patient died 6 months later with a recurrent myocardial infarction.
In patients with a history of heart disease, unidentified electronic gadgets seen on chest x-ray might well be cardiac related—specifically pacemakers. Although CGM devices are typically located on the upper arm, they may slip—especially in semiconscious patients and those requiring frequent transfers—to other body parts. CGM devices may look like unexpected foreign objects on limited resolution x-rays. As CGM gains in popularity, health-care professionals should be able to identify CGM devices and be aware of their potential to move to unexpected positions where they may cause consternation on x-ray interpretation. Using appropriate magnification of x-rays may be necessary for recognising CGM devices.

A 38-year-old woman attended our hospital with a 1-week history of shortness of breath and intermittent chest pain.The patient had Down syndrome and had previously had a ventricular septal defect (VSD) repaired when she was an infant.
On examination, the patient had a blood pressure of 99/77 mm Hg, a heart rate of 98 beats per min, a respiratory rate of 35 breaths per min, and oxygen saturation of 95%. Faint crackles were heard in both lung bases and a 3/6 systolic murmur, heard best at the upper sternal border, radiated to the carotid artery.
A chest x-ray showed a large diaphragmatic hernia, which was confirmed by abdominal CT scan. Laboratory investigations showed a normocytic anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 8·0 g/dL; normal 11·5–15 and mean corpuscular volume 96 fL; normal 80–100). The blood urea nitrogen was 8·0 mg/dL (normal 6–24) and troponin concentration was 0·573 ng/mL (normal 0–0·04).
The patient had an uneventful hernia repair and was allowed home 10 days later with plans for an outpatient cardiology appointment to review the murmur. However, 3 days after leaving hospital, she developed acute respiratory failure. A cardiac CT scan, at that stage, showed a bicuspid aortic valve with calcific aortic stenosis (figure). A transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed a heavily calcified aortic valve, but we were unable to say whether it was bicuspid or unicuspid (figure); critical aortic stenosis and moderate-to-severe aortic regurgitation were present. The aortic valve area was 0·8 cm2 with mean gradient of 77 mm Hg. Additionally, the aortic root was mildly dilated, and the calculated ejection fraction was 46%.
The patient was taken to theatre and the aortic valve was replaced with a bioprosthetic valve; multiplanar reconstruction imaging from an intraoperative transoesophageal echocardiogram showed possible unicuspid aortic valve (figure). And indeed, gross pathological examination of the excised valve confirmed a unicuspid aortic valve with multifocal calcification and a single non-fenestrated raphe (figure). Microscopic examination of a sample of the valve showed moderate calcification and fibrosis.
At follow-up 3 months later, the mean systolic gradient across the prosthetic valve was 17 mm Hg, the ejection fraction had improved to 52%, and there was mild prosthetic regurgitation.
Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is commonly associated with congenital heart defects, occurring in 40–50% of patients. The most common heart defects are atrioventricular septal defects (30%), followed by atrial septum defect (25%), VSD (22%), and patent ductus arteriosus (5%), coarctation of the aorta (5%), and tetralogy of Fallot (3%).
While neonates with trisomy 21 are routinely screened for cardiovascular abnormalities, some abnormalities—such as a unicuspid aortic valve in our patient—do not manifest themselves until adolescence or adulthood. Complex aortic valve pathology can cause stenosis and regurgitation in young adults; physical examination and imaging studies are key in identifying newly developed murmurs and patients should be treated promptly. Finally, distinguishing between bicuspid and unicuspid aortic valvular morphology can be difficult: both transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiograms have clear limitations in aiding the clinician to differentiate between them.

A 38-year-old woman attended our hospital with a 1-week history of shortness of breath and intermittent chest pain.The patient had Down syndrome and had previously had a ventricular septal defect (VSD) repaired when she was an infant.
On examination, the patient had a blood pressure of 99/77 mm Hg, a heart rate of 98 beats per min, a respiratory rate of 35 breaths per min, and oxygen saturation of 95%. Faint crackles were heard in both lung bases and a 3/6 systolic murmur, heard best at the upper sternal border, radiated to the carotid artery.
A chest x-ray showed a large diaphragmatic hernia, which was confirmed by abdominal CT scan. Laboratory investigations showed a normocytic anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 8·0 g/dL; normal 11·5–15 and mean corpuscular volume 96 fL; normal 80–100). The blood urea nitrogen was 8·0 mg/dL (normal 6–24) and troponin concentration was 0·573 ng/mL (normal 0–0·04).
The patient had an uneventful hernia repair and was allowed home 10 days later with plans for an outpatient cardiology appointment to review the murmur. However, 3 days after leaving hospital, she developed acute respiratory failure. A cardiac CT scan, at that stage, showed a bicuspid aortic valve with calcific aortic stenosis (figure). A transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed a heavily calcified aortic valve, but we were unable to say whether it was bicuspid or unicuspid (figure); critical aortic stenosis and moderate-to-severe aortic regurgitation were present. The aortic valve area was 0·8 cm2 with mean gradient of 77 mm Hg. Additionally, the aortic root was mildly dilated, and the calculated ejection fraction was 46%.
The patient was taken to theatre and the aortic valve was replaced with a bioprosthetic valve; multiplanar reconstruction imaging from an intraoperative transoesophageal echocardiogram showed possible unicuspid aortic valve (figure). And indeed, gross pathological examination of the excised valve confirmed a unicuspid aortic valve with multifocal calcification and a single non-fenestrated raphe (figure). Microscopic examination of a sample of the valve showed moderate calcification and fibrosis.
At follow-up 3 months later, the mean systolic gradient across the prosthetic valve was 17 mm Hg, the ejection fraction had improved to 52%, and there was mild prosthetic regurgitation.
Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is commonly associated with congenital heart defects, occurring in 40–50% of patients. The most common heart defects are atrioventricular septal defects (30%), followed by atrial septum defect (25%), VSD (22%), and patent ductus arteriosus (5%), coarctation of the aorta (5%), and tetralogy of Fallot (3%).
While neonates with trisomy 21 are routinely screened for cardiovascular abnormalities, some abnormalities—such as a unicuspid aortic valve in our patient—do not manifest themselves until adolescence or adulthood. Complex aortic valve pathology can cause stenosis and regurgitation in young adults; physical examination and imaging studies are key in identifying newly developed murmurs and patients should be treated promptly. Finally, distinguishing between bicuspid and unicuspid aortic valvular morphology can be difficult: both transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiograms have clear limitations in aiding the clinician to differentiate between them.

input: A51-year-old man presented with acute visual floaters and blurry vision in his left eye for 1 week. The patient had been diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis with positive HLA-B27 in his early 20s and had been treated with 40 mg adalimumab every 2 weeks for 1 year. A tuberculin skin test, interferon gamma release assay (QuantiFERON), and chest radiograph were checked before the initiation of adalimumab therapy, none of which revealed signs of tuberculosis. A hepatitis panel was also negative. His visual symptoms developed 5 days after the latest subcutaneous injection of adalimumab. At presentation, his best corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. There were no keratic precipitates or anterior chamber cells; however, 11–20 inflammatory vitreous cells were observed within 1 mm × 3 mm slit beam in the anterior vitreous, snowballs in vitreous, and multiple whitish retinal chorioretinitis lesions were seen in the left eye (figure A). Fluorescein angiography showed dye leakage from a local chorioretinitis lesion with segmental vascular leakage peripherally (figure B). The patient did not have any symptoms of chronic cough, fever, headache, or bodyweight loss. The cause of uveitis was then re-evaluated. CT of the chest revealed multiple tree-in-bud infiltrations in both right and left upper lobes (figure C). Positive T-spot test, acid-fast bacilli sputum smears, PCR (9·50 × 104 colony forming units per mL), and sputum culture confirmed pulmonary Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Adalimumab therapy was stopped, and the patient was treated with a full-dose anti-tuberculosis regimen. The patient achieved complete remission with no sign of recurrence after 1 year of follow-up.Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic inflammatory rheumatic disease with systemic involvement, and given that ankylosing spondylitis is commonly associated with anterior uveitis, an underlying infection could easily be missed and eventually lead to irreversible vision loss. In this unique case with posterior uveitis, the absence of respiratory symptoms posed a diagnostic challenge. Our case suggested that ocular manifestations with posterior uveitis could be the first sign of undiscovered newly developed pulmonary tuberculosis in patients with ankylosing spondylitis receiving anti-TNF therapy. The treatment strategy for typical acute anterior uveitis associated with ankylosing spondylitis usually involves intensive topical or systemic corticosteroid and immunosuppressive medications, which is divergent to that of tuberculous uveitis, and thus, an accurate diagnosis is imperative.

The patient had been diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis with positive HLA-B27 in his early 20s and had been treated with 40 mg adalimumab every 2 weeks for 1 year. A tuberculin skin test, interferon gamma release assay (QuantiFERON), and chest radiograph were checked before the initiation of adalimumab therapy, none of which revealed signs of tuberculosis. A hepatitis panel was also negative. His visual symptoms developed 5 days after the latest subcutaneous injection of adalimumab. At presentation, his best corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. There were no keratic precipitates or anterior chamber cells; however, 11–20 inflammatory vitreous cells were observed within 1 mm × 3 mm slit beam in the anterior vitreous, snowballs in vitreous, and multiple whitish retinal chorioretinitis lesions were seen in the left eye (figure A). Fluorescein angiography showed dye leakage from a local chorioretinitis lesion with segmental vascular leakage peripherally (figure B). The patient did not have any symptoms of chronic cough, fever, headache, or bodyweight loss. The cause of uveitis was then re-evaluated. CT of the chest revealed multiple tree-in-bud infiltrations in both right and left upper lobes (figure C). Positive T-spot test, acid-fast bacilli sputum smears, PCR (9·50 × 104 colony forming units per mL), and sputum culture confirmed pulmonary Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Adalimumab therapy was stopped, and the patient was treated with a full-dose anti-tuberculosis regimen. The patient achieved complete remission with no sign of recurrence after 1 year of follow-up.Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic inflammatory rheumatic disease with systemic involvement, and given that ankylosing spondylitis is commonly associated with anterior uveitis, an underlying infection could easily be missed and eventually lead to irreversible vision loss. In this unique case with posterior uveitis, the absence of respiratory symptoms posed a diagnostic challenge. Our case suggested that ocular manifestations with posterior uveitis could be the first sign of undiscovered newly developed pulmonary tuberculosis in patients with ankylosing spondylitis receiving anti-TNF therapy. The treatment strategy for typical acute anterior uveitis associated with ankylosing spondylitis usually involves intensive topical or systemic corticosteroid and immunosuppressive medications, which is divergent to that of tuberculous uveitis, and thus, an accurate diagnosis is imperative.

A 50-year-old man presented to our emergency department complaining of sudden onset of shortness of breath and pain in the back of his right shoulder. Notably, he did not report any neck pain, numbness, or weakness in his arms or legs; he had no abdominal pain or fever.In his medical history, he had C6–C7 radiculopathy treated with anterior cervical discectomy and fusion 2 years earlier; he reported no previous cardiac problems, hypertension, or alcohol use.
On examination we found the patient to have a raised body-mass index (29 kg/m2). He was not acutely distressed: his respiratory rate was 17 breaths per min, his heart rate was 64 beats per min, and his blood pressure was 130/84 mm Hg. A neurological examination found him to have full strength in both arms and legs, with normal sensation; his reflexes were normal.
A chest x-ray showed an abnormally elevated right hemidiaphragm compared to one done 2 years earlier when the patient had the cervical radiculopathy (figure).
A cervical MRI showed herniation of the C3–C4 disc with severe right C4 nerve root compression; the MRI from 2 years earlier showed a normal C3–C4 disc without stenosis (figure). Electrodiagnostic testing found right carpal tunnel syndrome—with no evidence of brachial plexopathy. ECG was normal. His vitamin B12 concentration was low at 194 pg/mL, as was his iron concentration at 40 μg/dL.
After discussion of the treatment options with the patient, he elected for surgical management—alternatives explored included conservative treatment with physiotherapy and monitoring of the diaphragm function, or surgical excision of the herniated disc, which might have resulted in additional paralysis of the diaphragm. C3–C4 anterior cervical discectomy and fusion were done, which resulted in the complete resolution of the patient's shoulder pain and shortness of breath. A follow-up x-ray showed that the problematic elevation of the right hemidiaphragm had resolved.
Shoulder pain and shortness of breath—particularly as acute presentations—are a combination of symptoms indicating a wide variety of pathologies affecting numerous organs including the heart, lungs, pancreas, gallbladder, and gastrointestinal tract. Regarding the shortness of breath, paralysis of the diaphragm can occur as a result of malignancies, cardiac surgery, cervical spine surgery, and trauma to the phrenic nerve. The diaphragm is innervated by the phrenic nerve, which originates from the C3, C4, and C5 nerve roots. However, the C4 root is the predominant origin of most function in most people. Regarding the shoulder pain, patients with C4 radiculopathy can present with pain in the axial cervical spine which can extend into the trapezial and scapular regions of the back; there is also the possibility that the pain may involve the anterior part of the chest.

input: A51-year-old man presented with acute visual floaters and blurry vision in his left eye for 1 week. The patient had been diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis with positive HLA-B27 in his early 20s and had been treated with 40 mg adalimumab every 2 weeks for 1 year. A tuberculin skin test, interferon gamma release assay (QuantiFERON), and chest radiograph were checked before the initiation of adalimumab therapy, none of which revealed signs of tuberculosis. A hepatitis panel was also negative. His visual symptoms developed 5 days after the latest subcutaneous injection of adalimumab. At presentation, his best corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. There were no keratic precipitates or anterior chamber cells; however, 11–20 inflammatory vitreous cells were observed within 1 mm × 3 mm slit beam in the anterior vitreous, snowballs in vitreous, and multiple whitish retinal chorioretinitis lesions were seen in the left eye (figure A). Fluorescein angiography showed dye leakage from a local chorioretinitis lesion with segmental vascular leakage peripherally (figure B). The patient did not have any symptoms of chronic cough, fever, headache, or bodyweight loss. The cause of uveitis was then re-evaluated. CT of the chest revealed multiple tree-in-bud infiltrations in both right and left upper lobes (figure C). Positive T-spot test, acid-fast bacilli sputum smears, PCR (9·50 × 104 colony forming units per mL), and sputum culture confirmed pulmonary Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Adalimumab therapy was stopped, and the patient was treated with a full-dose anti-tuberculosis regimen. The patient achieved complete remission with no sign of recurrence after 1 year of follow-up.Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic inflammatory rheumatic disease with systemic involvement, and given that ankylosing spondylitis is commonly associated with anterior uveitis, an underlying infection could easily be missed and eventually lead to irreversible vision loss. In this unique case with posterior uveitis, the absence of respiratory symptoms posed a diagnostic challenge. Our case suggested that ocular manifestations with posterior uveitis could be the first sign of undiscovered newly developed pulmonary tuberculosis in patients with ankylosing spondylitis receiving anti-TNF therapy. The treatment strategy for typical acute anterior uveitis associated with ankylosing spondylitis usually involves intensive topical or systemic corticosteroid and immunosuppressive medications, which is divergent to that of tuberculous uveitis, and thus, an accurate diagnosis is imperative.

A 50-year-old man presented to our emergency department complaining of sudden onset of shortness of breath and pain in the back of his right shoulder. Notably, he did not report any neck pain, numbness, or weakness in his arms or legs; he had no abdominal pain or fever.In his medical history, he had C6–C7 radiculopathy treated with anterior cervical discectomy and fusion 2 years earlier; he reported no previous cardiac problems, hypertension, or alcohol use.
On examination we found the patient to have a raised body-mass index (29 kg/m2). He was not acutely distressed: his respiratory rate was 17 breaths per min, his heart rate was 64 beats per min, and his blood pressure was 130/84 mm Hg. A neurological examination found him to have full strength in both arms and legs, with normal sensation; his reflexes were normal.
A chest x-ray showed an abnormally elevated right hemidiaphragm compared to one done 2 years earlier when the patient had the cervical radiculopathy (figure).
A cervical MRI showed herniation of the C3–C4 disc with severe right C4 nerve root compression; the MRI from 2 years earlier showed a normal C3–C4 disc without stenosis (figure). Electrodiagnostic testing found right carpal tunnel syndrome—with no evidence of brachial plexopathy. ECG was normal. His vitamin B12 concentration was low at 194 pg/mL, as was his iron concentration at 40 μg/dL.
After discussion of the treatment options with the patient, he elected for surgical management—alternatives explored included conservative treatment with physiotherapy and monitoring of the diaphragm function, or surgical excision of the herniated disc, which might have resulted in additional paralysis of the diaphragm. C3–C4 anterior cervical discectomy and fusion were done, which resulted in the complete resolution of the patient's shoulder pain and shortness of breath. A follow-up x-ray showed that the problematic elevation of the right hemidiaphragm had resolved.
Shoulder pain and shortness of breath—particularly as acute presentations—are a combination of symptoms indicating a wide variety of pathologies affecting numerous organs including the heart, lungs, pancreas, gallbladder, and gastrointestinal tract. Regarding the shortness of breath, paralysis of the diaphragm can occur as a result of malignancies, cardiac surgery, cervical spine surgery, and trauma to the phrenic nerve. The diaphragm is innervated by the phrenic nerve, which originates from the C3, C4, and C5 nerve roots. However, the C4 root is the predominant origin of most function in most people. Regarding the shoulder pain, patients with C4 radiculopathy can present with pain in the axial cervical spine which can extend into the trapezial and scapular regions of the back; there is also the possibility that the pain may involve the anterior part of the chest.

A 55-year-old woman presented with conjunctival congestion, retro-orbital pain, and diplopia. She had received her first vaccine against SARS-CoV-2—ChAdOx1 nCoV-19—10 days before admission. Both on the night after the vaccination and 7 days later, the patient reported marked flu-like symptoms and a fever. She had no medical history of visual problems, autoimmune disorders, stroke, thrombosis, thrombocytopenia, neurological disorders, or arterial disease risk factors—including hypertension, diabetes, or smoking.On examination, she had binocular diplopia at vertical and right lateral gaze, and her visual acuity was 0·85 in both eyes. MRI showed superior ophthalmic vein thrombosis (SOVT) with no contrast filling (figure) and bilateral high T2 signal intensity of the superior ophthalmic vein (figure).
Laboratory investigations on admission showed a marked isolated thrombocytopenia of 30 × 109 per L (figure). IgG antiplatelet antibodies were positive, and IgM antiplatelet antibodies were borderline; a platelet suspension immunofluorescence test and a monoclonal antibody-specific immobilisation of platelet antigens assay were positive—supporting a diagnosis of secondary immune thrombocytopenia (ITP). IgG antibodies against platelet factor 4/polyanion complexes—tested using a lateral flow immunoassay, 4 days after starting heparinisation—were negative. Other possible causes of thrombocytopenia—including antiphospholipid syndrome, thrombotic microangiopathy, and hepatitis B virus and hepatitis C virus, HIV, cytomegalovirus, hantaviruses, and Helicobacter pylori infections—were excluded.
Because we suspected ITP, intravenous dexamethasone 40 mg daily was given for 4 days which resulted in an increasing platelet count (figure). Despite the therapeutic heparinisation, 8 days after admission, the patient developed a transient, mild, right-sided hemiparesis, and aphasia. An MRI showed an ischaemic stroke in the left parietal lobe, middle cerebral artery territory, with restricted diffusion (figure), which had not been detected in the earlier scan. The patient then developed right-sided focal seizures which were controlled with levetiracetam and lacosamide; anticoagulation was switched to phenprocoumon, and 26 days after admission, she was allowed home.
That 8, 10, and 18 days after the ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccination, our previously healthy patient developed marked flu-like symptoms, two rare disorders—namely, bilateral SOVT and ITP, and an ischaemic stroke, may indicate a causal relationship. According to the European Medicines Agency review, March 18, health-care professionals should be on the alert for possible cases of thromboembolism—like cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, pulmonary embolus, and deep vein thrombosis—occurring in people who have recently received the ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccine. The thrombotic events—including bilateral SOVT as seen in our patient—may occur in the context of thrombocytopenia (video).

A 50-year-old man presented to our emergency department complaining of sudden onset of shortness of breath and pain in the back of his right shoulder. Notably, he did not report any neck pain, numbness, or weakness in his arms or legs; he had no abdominal pain or fever.In his medical history, he had C6–C7 radiculopathy treated with anterior cervical discectomy and fusion 2 years earlier; he reported no previous cardiac problems, hypertension, or alcohol use.
On examination we found the patient to have a raised body-mass index (29 kg/m2). He was not acutely distressed: his respiratory rate was 17 breaths per min, his heart rate was 64 beats per min, and his blood pressure was 130/84 mm Hg. A neurological examination found him to have full strength in both arms and legs, with normal sensation; his reflexes were normal.
A chest x-ray showed an abnormally elevated right hemidiaphragm compared to one done 2 years earlier when the patient had the cervical radiculopathy (figure).
A cervical MRI showed herniation of the C3–C4 disc with severe right C4 nerve root compression; the MRI from 2 years earlier showed a normal C3–C4 disc without stenosis (figure). Electrodiagnostic testing found right carpal tunnel syndrome—with no evidence of brachial plexopathy. ECG was normal. His vitamin B12 concentration was low at 194 pg/mL, as was his iron concentration at 40 μg/dL.
After discussion of the treatment options with the patient, he elected for surgical management—alternatives explored included conservative treatment with physiotherapy and monitoring of the diaphragm function, or surgical excision of the herniated disc, which might have resulted in additional paralysis of the diaphragm. C3–C4 anterior cervical discectomy and fusion were done, which resulted in the complete resolution of the patient's shoulder pain and shortness of breath. A follow-up x-ray showed that the problematic elevation of the right hemidiaphragm had resolved.
Shoulder pain and shortness of breath—particularly as acute presentations—are a combination of symptoms indicating a wide variety of pathologies affecting numerous organs including the heart, lungs, pancreas, gallbladder, and gastrointestinal tract. Regarding the shortness of breath, paralysis of the diaphragm can occur as a result of malignancies, cardiac surgery, cervical spine surgery, and trauma to the phrenic nerve. The diaphragm is innervated by the phrenic nerve, which originates from the C3, C4, and C5 nerve roots. However, the C4 root is the predominant origin of most function in most people. Regarding the shoulder pain, patients with C4 radiculopathy can present with pain in the axial cervical spine which can extend into the trapezial and scapular regions of the back; there is also the possibility that the pain may involve the anterior part of the chest.

- 膈神经主要来自 **C3–C5**，多数人 **C4贡献最大**；因此**C4神经根受压**可导致同侧膈肌无力/麻痹。

- 局限：操作者依赖；肥胖、气体干扰时成像受限。
