A 63-year-old woman attended our oculoplastic clinic with a 10-year history of progressive weakness of the muscles of her forehead, and drooping eyebrows and eyelids that were affecting her field of vision (figure).Notably both her mother and brother had similar symptoms. The patient had no other significant medical history.
On examination, she was generally well; she had bilateral brow ptosis, bilateral dermatochalasis, and cutis laxa. The patient had marked weakness of the muscles supplied by the temporal branches of the facial nerve and, to a lesser extent, weakness of those supplied by the zygomatic branches (figure; video). The remaining branches of the facial nerve were relatively spared. Sensation supplied by the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve was reduced, with sparing of the maxillary and mandibular branches (figure; video). She had no upper eyelid weakness, no anisocoria, and normal extraocular movements. Mild bilateral type 2 corneal lattice dystrophy was seen on slit lamp biomicroscopy (figure, appendix) and corneal sensation was reduced. The patient had good corrected visual acuities of 6/9 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left eye. We noted no lagophahalmos but a moderate Bell's phenomenon.
The patient's clinical signs and family history were consistent with a diagnosis of hereditary gelsolin amyloidosis (AGel), and previous genetic testing had confirmed a known amyloidogenic mutation in the GSN gene: c.640G>A; p.(Asp214Asn).
A conservative bilateral direct brow lift and upper eyelid blepharoplasty was done with a marked improvement in the patient's symptoms. At follow-up 1 year later, the patient remained happy with the outcome of the surgery.
Amyloidoses are a group of diseases characterised by the deposition of insoluble proteins which aggregate into distinctive fibrillar forms. Hereditary amyloid polyneuropathies are autosomal dominant in their inheritance and are defined according to the precursor protein of amyloid—transthyretin, apolipoprotein A-1, or gelsolin. AGel was first described in Finland where there are approximately 1000 carriers. The most common manifestations are ophthalmological, with lattice dystrophy; dermatological, with cutis laxa; and neurological, with cranial and peripheral neuropathies; renal amyloid deposits are also common and there may occasionally be cardiac amyloid infiltration. Facial nerve involvement has a unique presentation—it is progressive, bilateral, and starts with the temporal branches, descending to the other branches of the facial nerves over time. Severity ranges from mild involutional changes to complete bilateral facial paralysis. Patients should be counselled appropriately regarding oculoplastic facial surgery. Improved visual function must be balanced against progressive facial and trigeminal neuropathy, and ultimately corneal protection in the long term.

input: An otherwise healthy 45-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of gradual visual loss in both eyes. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/30 in both eyes. Slit-lamp examination showed bilateral—predominantly peripheral—corneal deposits of numerous minute, crystalline materials (figure A and B). The remainder of the ocular examination was unremarkable. A clinical diagnosis of monoclonal gammopathy was made on the basis of shimmering and polychromatic corneal deposits. Serum IgG concentration was 30·3 g/L (normal 8·1–16·9 g/L) and serum electrophoresis showed a monoclonal gammopathy involving IgG-kappa light chain. Our patient was referred to a haematologist and IgG-kappa multiple myeloma was diagnosed by bone marrow biopsy. Treatment was initiated with thalidomide, and no ocular-specific drugs were prescribed. During the 7-year follow-up, while maintained on a low-dose thalidomide, our patient was regularly followed up and her vision remained stable. Although still present, the amount of these corneal crystalline deposits appeared to be decreasing and migrate away from the peripheral corneas (figure C and D).

input:
A 28-year-old Egyptian woman was referred to our specialised gestational trophoblastic disease clinic for treatment. She explained that 2 years earlier, her menstrual cycle had changed and become irregular with prolonged heavy bleeding lasting between 15 and 20 days; before this, her periods had been regular, lasting 30 days with 5 days of bleeding. The woman had two children and no history of contraceptive use, hormonal therapy, or any other medications. 3 months after the irregular bleeding started, the patient visited her local gynaecologist, who reported no uterine or cervical disease and prescribed diosmin tablets. At this stage, the patient's haemoglobin concentration was 10 g/dL—importantly, her urine and serum human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels were not measured. The bleeding did not improve, and she had dilation and curettage of the uterus, during which a biopsy specimen was taken from the endometrium: histology showed a disordered proliferative endometrium. The woman was advised to take combined oral contraceptive pills, which only resulted in a reduction of the bleeding.6 months later, a transvaginal ultrasound showed focal anterior myometrial thickening, with increased blood flow seen on doppler ultrasound, which was reported as being adenomyosis (figure). Hysteroscopic endometrial resection was recommended, but the procedure was not completed because of severe bleeding during surgery. The bleeding continued postoperatively and the patient's general condition deteriorated: her haemoglobin concentration dropped to 6 g/dL. She was given a blood transfusion to stabilise her condition and then returned to theatre for a life-saving, uncomplicated abdominal hysterectomy. Histopathological examination of the uterus showed an invasive mole with no evidence of uterine perforation. The serum hCG concentration was 550 IU/L, and she was treated with two courses of methotrexate, which led to remission.
Our case illustrates that a crucial investigation of the cause of uterine bleeding—which can be attributed to numerous conditions including fibroids, adenomyosis, and an invasive mole—is a pregnancy test. An ultrasound cannot clearly differentiate between some of the causes and an endometrial biopsy might not detect lesions located deep in the myometrium.
To reiterate, hCG levels in the urine should be checked during the initial assessment of abnormal uterine bleeding because trophoblastic tumours are often easily cured with the single agent methotrexate without the need for a hysterectomy.

input:
A 28-year-old Egyptian woman was referred to our specialised gestational trophoblastic disease clinic for treatment. She explained that 2 years earlier, her menstrual cycle had changed and become irregular with prolonged heavy bleeding lasting between 15 and 20 days; before this, her periods had been regular, lasting 30 days with 5 days of bleeding. The woman had two children and no history of contraceptive use, hormonal therapy, or any other medications. 3 months after the irregular bleeding started, the patient visited her local gynaecologist, who reported no uterine or cervical disease and prescribed diosmin tablets. At this stage, the patient's haemoglobin concentration was 10 g/dL—importantly, her urine and serum human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels were not measured. The bleeding did not improve, and she had dilation and curettage of the uterus, during which a biopsy specimen was taken from the endometrium: histology showed a disordered proliferative endometrium. The woman was advised to take combined oral contraceptive pills, which only resulted in a reduction of the bleeding.6 months later, a transvaginal ultrasound showed focal anterior myometrial thickening, with increased blood flow seen on doppler ultrasound, which was reported as being adenomyosis (figure). Hysteroscopic endometrial resection was recommended, but the procedure was not completed because of severe bleeding during surgery. The bleeding continued postoperatively and the patient's general condition deteriorated: her haemoglobin concentration dropped to 6 g/dL. She was given a blood transfusion to stabilise her condition and then returned to theatre for a life-saving, uncomplicated abdominal hysterectomy. Histopathological examination of the uterus showed an invasive mole with no evidence of uterine perforation. The serum hCG concentration was 550 IU/L, and she was treated with two courses of methotrexate, which led to remission.
Our case illustrates that a crucial investigation of the cause of uterine bleeding—which can be attributed to numerous conditions including fibroids, adenomyosis, and an invasive mole—is a pregnancy test. An ultrasound cannot clearly differentiate between some of the causes and an endometrial biopsy might not detect lesions located deep in the myometrium.
To reiterate, hCG levels in the urine should be checked during the initial assessment of abnormal uterine bleeding because trophoblastic tumours are often easily cured with the single agent methotrexate without the need for a hysterectomy.

input: An otherwise healthy 45-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of gradual visual loss in both eyes. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/30 in both eyes. Slit-lamp examination showed bilateral—predominantly peripheral—corneal deposits of numerous minute, crystalline materials (figure A and B). The remainder of the ocular examination was unremarkable. A clinical diagnosis of monoclonal gammopathy was made on the basis of shimmering and polychromatic corneal deposits. Serum IgG concentration was 30·3 g/L (normal 8·1–16·9 g/L) and serum electrophoresis showed a monoclonal gammopathy involving IgG-kappa light chain. Our patient was referred to a haematologist and IgG-kappa multiple myeloma was diagnosed by bone marrow biopsy. Treatment was initiated with thalidomide, and no ocular-specific drugs were prescribed. During the 7-year follow-up, while maintained on a low-dose thalidomide, our patient was regularly followed up and her vision remained stable. Although still present, the amount of these corneal crystalline deposits appeared to be decreasing and migrate away from the peripheral corneas (figure C and D).

input:
A 40-year-old man attended our ophthalmology department reporting a gradual worsening of vision in both eyes over the previous few months.The patient had a history of sensorineural hearing loss and he had received a kidney transplant at age 19 years; he had previously been diagnosed with X-linked Alport syndrome. Genetic testing, at the time, showed a mutation in the COL4A5 gene. The kidney was donated by the patient's healthy father; the patient has one healthy brother and no children. His mother was identified as the carrier and she was also affected by the disease. The patient was prescribed sirolimus 3 mg daily and prednisolone 5 mg daily.
On general examination, he was well. Regarding his eyes, a slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment showed a clear crystalline lens with an anterior lenticonus—a subtle protrusion of the anterior surface—in both eyes (figure); the protrusion was clearly visible on anterior segment swept-source optical coherence tomography (OCT; figure) and was also detected as an oil-droplet sign with retro-illumination (figure).
Additionally, the patient showed the typical retinal findings of Alport syndrome: central fleck retinopathy—seen as scattered pigmentation irregularities around the macula, which were more obvious on red free images (figure)—temporal retinal thinning on retinal OCT (figure), and peripheral retinopathy. His best corrected vision was reduced to 20/40 (typical 20/20) in both eyes.
We implanted a toric intraocular lens with extended depth of focus in both eyes after lens removal, which improved his vision to 20/25 bilaterally. At 3 months follow-up, the patient had a full corrected distance visual acuity of 20/20.
Alport syndrome is a rare, progressive, hereditary glomerular disease characterised by haematuria, proteinuria, and progressive impairment of kidney function caused by mutations in the COL4A5, usually inherited as X-linked—as in our patient—and COL4A3 and COL4A4 genes, which are transmitted in either an autosomal recessive or dominant pattern. The mutations disrupt collagen type IV synthesis, which is a crucial component of the basal membrane in the renal glomerulus, cochlea, cornea, lens capsule, retina, and skin.
Visual impairment is mostly caused by anterior lenticonus—even if there is no cataract present; it is diagnostic for Alport syndrome, seen in 50% of patients, and can be treated effectively with lens replacement. Central and peripheral retinopathy is seen in 70% and 80% of patients, respectively, and usually does not affect vision. Lenticonus and central retinopathy are predictive for sensorineural hearing loss and renal failure before the age of 30 years. Therefore, in young men with hearing loss and haematuria, an eye examination can give helpful information in confirming the diagnosis of Alport syndrome.

A 40-year-old man attended our ophthalmology department reporting a gradual worsening of vision in both eyes over the previous few months.The patient had a history of sensorineural hearing loss and he had received a kidney transplant at age 19 years; he had previously been diagnosed with X-linked Alport syndrome. Genetic testing, at the time, showed a mutation in the COL4A5 gene. The kidney was donated by the patient's healthy father; the patient has one healthy brother and no children. His mother was identified as the carrier and she was also affected by the disease. The patient was prescribed sirolimus 3 mg daily and prednisolone 5 mg daily.
On general examination, he was well. Regarding his eyes, a slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment showed a clear crystalline lens with an anterior lenticonus—a subtle protrusion of the anterior surface—in both eyes (figure); the protrusion was clearly visible on anterior segment swept-source optical coherence tomography (OCT; figure) and was also detected as an oil-droplet sign with retro-illumination (figure).
Additionally, the patient showed the typical retinal findings of Alport syndrome: central fleck retinopathy—seen as scattered pigmentation irregularities around the macula, which were more obvious on red free images (figure)—temporal retinal thinning on retinal OCT (figure), and peripheral retinopathy. His best corrected vision was reduced to 20/40 (typical 20/20) in both eyes.
We implanted a toric intraocular lens with extended depth of focus in both eyes after lens removal, which improved his vision to 20/25 bilaterally. At 3 months follow-up, the patient had a full corrected distance visual acuity of 20/20.
Alport syndrome is a rare, progressive, hereditary glomerular disease characterised by haematuria, proteinuria, and progressive impairment of kidney function caused by mutations in the COL4A5, usually inherited as X-linked—as in our patient—and COL4A3 and COL4A4 genes, which are transmitted in either an autosomal recessive or dominant pattern. The mutations disrupt collagen type IV synthesis, which is a crucial component of the basal membrane in the renal glomerulus, cochlea, cornea, lens capsule, retina, and skin.
Visual impairment is mostly caused by anterior lenticonus—even if there is no cataract present; it is diagnostic for Alport syndrome, seen in 50% of patients, and can be treated effectively with lens replacement. Central and peripheral retinopathy is seen in 70% and 80% of patients, respectively, and usually does not affect vision. Lenticonus and central retinopathy are predictive for sensorineural hearing loss and renal failure before the age of 30 years. Therefore, in young men with hearing loss and haematuria, an eye examination can give helpful information in confirming the diagnosis of Alport syndrome.

A 28-year-old Egyptian woman was referred to our specialised gestational trophoblastic disease clinic for treatment. She explained that 2 years earlier, her menstrual cycle had changed and become irregular with prolonged heavy bleeding lasting between 15 and 20 days; before this, her periods had been regular, lasting 30 days with 5 days of bleeding. The woman had two children and no history of contraceptive use, hormonal therapy, or any other medications. 3 months after the irregular bleeding started, the patient visited her local gynaecologist, who reported no uterine or cervical disease and prescribed diosmin tablets. At this stage, the patient's haemoglobin concentration was 10 g/dL—importantly, her urine and serum human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels were not measured. The bleeding did not improve, and she had dilation and curettage of the uterus, during which a biopsy specimen was taken from the endometrium: histology showed a disordered proliferative endometrium. The woman was advised to take combined oral contraceptive pills, which only resulted in a reduction of the bleeding.6 months later, a transvaginal ultrasound showed focal anterior myometrial thickening, with increased blood flow seen on doppler ultrasound, which was reported as being adenomyosis (figure). Hysteroscopic endometrial resection was recommended, but the procedure was not completed because of severe bleeding during surgery. The bleeding continued postoperatively and the patient's general condition deteriorated: her haemoglobin concentration dropped to 6 g/dL. She was given a blood transfusion to stabilise her condition and then returned to theatre for a life-saving, uncomplicated abdominal hysterectomy. Histopathological examination of the uterus showed an invasive mole with no evidence of uterine perforation. The serum hCG concentration was 550 IU/L, and she was treated with two courses of methotrexate, which led to remission.
Our case illustrates that a crucial investigation of the cause of uterine bleeding—which can be attributed to numerous conditions including fibroids, adenomyosis, and an invasive mole—is a pregnancy test. An ultrasound cannot clearly differentiate between some of the causes and an endometrial biopsy might not detect lesions located deep in the myometrium.
To reiterate, hCG levels in the urine should be checked during the initial assessment of abnormal uterine bleeding because trophoblastic tumours are often easily cured with the single agent methotrexate without the need for a hysterectomy.

A 40-year-old man attended our ophthalmology department reporting a gradual worsening of vision in both eyes over the previous few months.The patient had a history of sensorineural hearing loss and he had received a kidney transplant at age 19 years; he had previously been diagnosed with X-linked Alport syndrome. Genetic testing, at the time, showed a mutation in the COL4A5 gene. The kidney was donated by the patient's healthy father; the patient has one healthy brother and no children. His mother was identified as the carrier and she was also affected by the disease. The patient was prescribed sirolimus 3 mg daily and prednisolone 5 mg daily.
On general examination, he was well. Regarding his eyes, a slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment showed a clear crystalline lens with an anterior lenticonus—a subtle protrusion of the anterior surface—in both eyes (figure); the protrusion was clearly visible on anterior segment swept-source optical coherence tomography (OCT; figure) and was also detected as an oil-droplet sign with retro-illumination (figure).
Additionally, the patient showed the typical retinal findings of Alport syndrome: central fleck retinopathy—seen as scattered pigmentation irregularities around the macula, which were more obvious on red free images (figure)—temporal retinal thinning on retinal OCT (figure), and peripheral retinopathy. His best corrected vision was reduced to 20/40 (typical 20/20) in both eyes.
We implanted a toric intraocular lens with extended depth of focus in both eyes after lens removal, which improved his vision to 20/25 bilaterally. At 3 months follow-up, the patient had a full corrected distance visual acuity of 20/20.
Alport syndrome is a rare, progressive, hereditary glomerular disease characterised by haematuria, proteinuria, and progressive impairment of kidney function caused by mutations in the COL4A5, usually inherited as X-linked—as in our patient—and COL4A3 and COL4A4 genes, which are transmitted in either an autosomal recessive or dominant pattern. The mutations disrupt collagen type IV synthesis, which is a crucial component of the basal membrane in the renal glomerulus, cochlea, cornea, lens capsule, retina, and skin.
Visual impairment is mostly caused by anterior lenticonus—even if there is no cataract present; it is diagnostic for Alport syndrome, seen in 50% of patients, and can be treated effectively with lens replacement. Central and peripheral retinopathy is seen in 70% and 80% of patients, respectively, and usually does not affect vision. Lenticonus and central retinopathy are predictive for sensorineural hearing loss and renal failure before the age of 30 years. Therefore, in young men with hearing loss and haematuria, an eye examination can give helpful information in confirming the diagnosis of Alport syndrome.

A 19-year-old man presented to our emergency department with abdominal pain and jaundice. He had emigrated from Senegal during infancy. He was found to be a carrier of hepatitis B virus, with a hepatitis B surface antigen serum DNA concentration persistently below 2000 IU/mL. He was negative for hepatitis B e antigen and positive for anti-hepatitis B e antibodies.Laboratory investigations showed severe hepatocellular damage: total bilirubin 35 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 23 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 544 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase 971 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase 238 U/L. He was anaemic, with a haemoglobin of 8·9 g/dL. The platelet count was slightly reduced at 144 × 109 per L (normal range 150 × 109 to 400 × 109 per L). Abdominal CT showed transient contrast-enhanced areas in the liver during the arterial phase (figure). Liver histology showed enlarged sinusoids containing sickle-cell thrombi (figure). Sickle-cell disease was confirmed by a peripheral blood smear and cellulose acetate electrophoresis with haemoglobin S making up 87% of his haemoglobin.
Additionally, a diagnosis of acute hepatitis A virus (HAV) infection was made after serum IgM anti-HAV antibodies were detected; IgG anti-HAV seroconversion followed. Serum hepatitis B virus DNA was 1520 IU/mL and hepatitis D virus—also known as hepatitis delta virus—markers were negative. The patient was treated with exchange transfusion of red cells. He made a full clinical recovery and imaging of his liver showed that it had returned to normal. He was discharged 10 days after admission; at that stage, his total bilirubin concentration was 9·3 mg/dL and direct bilirubin was 6·1 mg/dL. 3 months after the original episode, his haemoglobin was stable at a concentration above 10·5 g/dL. His direct bilirubin concentration was 0·23 mg/dL.
Life-threatening hepatic damage can result from sickle-cell sequestration in the liver. Onset of the symptoms—also known as right upper quadrant syndrome—is frequently associated with an infection, with hepatitis or tuberculosis being common causes. In this case, this was our patient's first sickling crisis—previously, he had been asymptomatic—and it is likely that it was triggered by the infection with HAV. Abnormal hepatic perfusion seen during CT scanning can be interpreted as a sign of sinusoidal obstruction. Liver disease is fairly common in sickle-cell disease and includes several intrahepatic disorders that cause occlusion of blood vessels; they can occur when the patient is not in a sickle-cell crisis. Sequestration of sickle cells occurs more frequently in the spleen, with splenic sequestration crises being the presenting symptom in up to 20% of patients with sickle-cell disease. They are more common in childhood and can cause acute anaemia or hypovolaemic shock due to the pooling of large quantities of red blood cells.

A 19-year-old man presented to our emergency department with abdominal pain and jaundice. He had emigrated from Senegal during infancy. He was found to be a carrier of hepatitis B virus, with a hepatitis B surface antigen serum DNA concentration persistently below 2000 IU/mL. He was negative for hepatitis B e antigen and positive for anti-hepatitis B e antibodies.Laboratory investigations showed severe hepatocellular damage: total bilirubin 35 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 23 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 544 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase 971 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase 238 U/L. He was anaemic, with a haemoglobin of 8·9 g/dL. The platelet count was slightly reduced at 144 × 109 per L (normal range 150 × 109 to 400 × 109 per L). Abdominal CT showed transient contrast-enhanced areas in the liver during the arterial phase (figure). Liver histology showed enlarged sinusoids containing sickle-cell thrombi (figure). Sickle-cell disease was confirmed by a peripheral blood smear and cellulose acetate electrophoresis with haemoglobin S making up 87% of his haemoglobin.
Additionally, a diagnosis of acute hepatitis A virus (HAV) infection was made after serum IgM anti-HAV antibodies were detected; IgG anti-HAV seroconversion followed. Serum hepatitis B virus DNA was 1520 IU/mL and hepatitis D virus—also known as hepatitis delta virus—markers were negative. The patient was treated with exchange transfusion of red cells. He made a full clinical recovery and imaging of his liver showed that it had returned to normal. He was discharged 10 days after admission; at that stage, his total bilirubin concentration was 9·3 mg/dL and direct bilirubin was 6·1 mg/dL. 3 months after the original episode, his haemoglobin was stable at a concentration above 10·5 g/dL. His direct bilirubin concentration was 0·23 mg/dL.
Life-threatening hepatic damage can result from sickle-cell sequestration in the liver. Onset of the symptoms—also known as right upper quadrant syndrome—is frequently associated with an infection, with hepatitis or tuberculosis being common causes. In this case, this was our patient's first sickling crisis—previously, he had been asymptomatic—and it is likely that it was triggered by the infection with HAV. Abnormal hepatic perfusion seen during CT scanning can be interpreted as a sign of sinusoidal obstruction. Liver disease is fairly common in sickle-cell disease and includes several intrahepatic disorders that cause occlusion of blood vessels; they can occur when the patient is not in a sickle-cell crisis. Sequestration of sickle cells occurs more frequently in the spleen, with splenic sequestration crises being the presenting symptom in up to 20% of patients with sickle-cell disease. They are more common in childhood and can cause acute anaemia or hypovolaemic shock due to the pooling of large quantities of red blood cells.

A 68-year-old woman with a 20-day history of exertional dyspnoea, acrocyanosis, and critical ischaemia—dry gangrene—of her fingers, presented to our rheumatology clinic (figure); she also reported the recent onset of pain in the small joints of her hands and wrists, Raynaud's phenomenon in her fingers and toes, and a feeling of general fatigue. The patient, a farmer, had been unable to carry out her daily tasks for the past 1 month. She had a medical history of well controlled hypertension treated with nebivolol; she had never smoked cigarettes.
On examination, the patient was distressed and tachypnoeic; pulse was 75 beats per min, blood pressure was 125/75 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation was 92% on 21% fraction of inspired oxygen; respiratory rate was 25 breaths per min. Her temperature was 36·0°C. Inspiratory crackles were heard on auscultation of the chest; neurological examination showed no abnormalities and proximal muscle strength of her arms and legs was within typical limits.
Laboratory investigations found antinuclear antibodies were positive with a 1:160 titre (normal range <1:80) in a speckled pattern. Anti-Jo-1 antibodies were positive and anti-Ro52 antibodies were strongly positive (range from negative to borderline to positive, and strongly positive) identified through immunoblotting. Anti-phospholipid antibodies were negative. Acute phase proteins were increased—including concentration of C-reactive protein, which was 1·7 mg/dL (normal level <0·3).
Chest CT showed a fibrotic non-specific interstitial pneumonia pattern (figure). Additionally, ulnar artery pulses were clinically absent with severely diminished blood flow observed during doppler ultrasound; CT angiography showed occlusion of the ulnar arteries bilaterally.
Considering the patient's presentation and laboratory findings, we diagnosed rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease due to antisynthetase syndrome complicated by critical ischaemia in her fingers. She was treated with three doses of pulse methylprednisolone (500 mg) followed by high dose intravenous prednisolone (1 mg/kg) and rituximab (2 × 1 g intravenous infusions, each separated by 15 days). The patient was also anticoagulated with subcutaneous enoxaparin 8000 IU/0·8 mL twice daily and aspirin 100 mg daily; intravenous iloprost—as a vasodilator—to counteract the ischaemia and to aid reperfusion was started.
The patient's condition stabilised with no further deterioration of the ischaemia in her fingers or her pulmonary function, and she was allowed home 42 days after her initial presentation. She was prescribed supplemental oxygen to use at home at a flow rate of 2 L/min.
At her last follow-up, 3 months after her initial presentation, the patient reported some progression of the digital ischaemia with gangrene up to the distal interphalangeal joints; her lung function had not changed, and a follow-up vascular ultrasound showed improved blood blow of the previously diminished pulses. The patient reported no fatigue but nevertheless still required home oxygen therapy.
Antisynthetase syndrome is one of a group of immune-mediated idiopathic inflammatory myopathies which primarily affect skeletal muscle but may also involve other organs such as the lungs, skin, and joints—as in our patient. Multimodality immunosuppressive therapy may be required to control both the muscle and pulmonary manifestations of the disease; more recently CAR T-cell treatment has been used. Early diagnosis and appropriate treatment improve outcomes.

input:
A 68-year-old woman with a 20-day history of exertional dyspnoea, acrocyanosis, and critical ischaemia—dry gangrene—of her fingers, presented to our rheumatology clinic (figure); she also reported the recent onset of pain in the small joints of her hands and wrists, Raynaud's phenomenon in her fingers and toes, and a feeling of general fatigue. The patient, a farmer, had been unable to carry out her daily tasks for the past 1 month. She had a medical history of well controlled hypertension treated with nebivolol; she had never smoked cigarettes.
On examination, the patient was distressed and tachypnoeic; pulse was 75 beats per min, blood pressure was 125/75 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation was 92% on 21% fraction of inspired oxygen; respiratory rate was 25 breaths per min. Her temperature was 36·0°C. Inspiratory crackles were heard on auscultation of the chest; neurological examination showed no abnormalities and proximal muscle strength of her arms and legs was within typical limits.
Laboratory investigations found antinuclear antibodies were positive with a 1:160 titre (normal range <1:80) in a speckled pattern. Anti-Jo-1 antibodies were positive and anti-Ro52 antibodies were strongly positive (range from negative to borderline to positive, and strongly positive) identified through immunoblotting. Anti-phospholipid antibodies were negative. Acute phase proteins were increased—including concentration of C-reactive protein, which was 1·7 mg/dL (normal level <0·3).
Chest CT showed a fibrotic non-specific interstitial pneumonia pattern (figure). Additionally, ulnar artery pulses were clinically absent with severely diminished blood flow observed during doppler ultrasound; CT angiography showed occlusion of the ulnar arteries bilaterally.
Considering the patient's presentation and laboratory findings, we diagnosed rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease due to antisynthetase syndrome complicated by critical ischaemia in her fingers. She was treated with three doses of pulse methylprednisolone (500 mg) followed by high dose intravenous prednisolone (1 mg/kg) and rituximab (2 × 1 g intravenous infusions, each separated by 15 days). The patient was also anticoagulated with subcutaneous enoxaparin 8000 IU/0·8 mL twice daily and aspirin 100 mg daily; intravenous iloprost—as a vasodilator—to counteract the ischaemia and to aid reperfusion was started.
The patient's condition stabilised with no further deterioration of the ischaemia in her fingers or her pulmonary function, and she was allowed home 42 days after her initial presentation. She was prescribed supplemental oxygen to use at home at a flow rate of 2 L/min.
At her last follow-up, 3 months after her initial presentation, the patient reported some progression of the digital ischaemia with gangrene up to the distal interphalangeal joints; her lung function had not changed, and a follow-up vascular ultrasound showed improved blood blow of the previously diminished pulses. The patient reported no fatigue but nevertheless still required home oxygen therapy.
Antisynthetase syndrome is one of a group of immune-mediated idiopathic inflammatory myopathies which primarily affect skeletal muscle but may also involve other organs such as the lungs, skin, and joints—as in our patient. Multimodality immunosuppressive therapy may be required to control both the muscle and pulmonary manifestations of the disease; more recently CAR T-cell treatment has been used. Early diagnosis and appropriate treatment improve outcomes.

input:
A 68-year-old woman with a 20-day history of exertional dyspnoea, acrocyanosis, and critical ischaemia—dry gangrene—of her fingers, presented to our rheumatology clinic (figure); she also reported the recent onset of pain in the small joints of her hands and wrists, Raynaud's phenomenon in her fingers and toes, and a feeling of general fatigue. The patient, a farmer, had been unable to carry out her daily tasks for the past 1 month. She had a medical history of well controlled hypertension treated with nebivolol; she had never smoked cigarettes.
On examination, the patient was distressed and tachypnoeic; pulse was 75 beats per min, blood pressure was 125/75 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation was 92% on 21% fraction of inspired oxygen; respiratory rate was 25 breaths per min. Her temperature was 36·0°C. Inspiratory crackles were heard on auscultation of the chest; neurological examination showed no abnormalities and proximal muscle strength of her arms and legs was within typical limits.
Laboratory investigations found antinuclear antibodies were positive with a 1:160 titre (normal range <1:80) in a speckled pattern. Anti-Jo-1 antibodies were positive and anti-Ro52 antibodies were strongly positive (range from negative to borderline to positive, and strongly positive) identified through immunoblotting. Anti-phospholipid antibodies were negative. Acute phase proteins were increased—including concentration of C-reactive protein, which was 1·7 mg/dL (normal level <0·3).
Chest CT showed a fibrotic non-specific interstitial pneumonia pattern (figure). Additionally, ulnar artery pulses were clinically absent with severely diminished blood flow observed during doppler ultrasound; CT angiography showed occlusion of the ulnar arteries bilaterally.
Considering the patient's presentation and laboratory findings, we diagnosed rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease due to antisynthetase syndrome complicated by critical ischaemia in her fingers. She was treated with three doses of pulse methylprednisolone (500 mg) followed by high dose intravenous prednisolone (1 mg/kg) and rituximab (2 × 1 g intravenous infusions, each separated by 15 days). The patient was also anticoagulated with subcutaneous enoxaparin 8000 IU/0·8 mL twice daily and aspirin 100 mg daily; intravenous iloprost—as a vasodilator—to counteract the ischaemia and to aid reperfusion was started.
The patient's condition stabilised with no further deterioration of the ischaemia in her fingers or her pulmonary function, and she was allowed home 42 days after her initial presentation. She was prescribed supplemental oxygen to use at home at a flow rate of 2 L/min.
At her last follow-up, 3 months after her initial presentation, the patient reported some progression of the digital ischaemia with gangrene up to the distal interphalangeal joints; her lung function had not changed, and a follow-up vascular ultrasound showed improved blood blow of the previously diminished pulses. The patient reported no fatigue but nevertheless still required home oxygen therapy.
Antisynthetase syndrome is one of a group of immune-mediated idiopathic inflammatory myopathies which primarily affect skeletal muscle but may also involve other organs such as the lungs, skin, and joints—as in our patient. Multimodality immunosuppressive therapy may be required to control both the muscle and pulmonary manifestations of the disease; more recently CAR T-cell treatment has been used. Early diagnosis and appropriate treatment improve outcomes.

A 19-year-old man presented to our emergency department with abdominal pain and jaundice. He had emigrated from Senegal during infancy. He was found to be a carrier of hepatitis B virus, with a hepatitis B surface antigen serum DNA concentration persistently below 2000 IU/mL. He was negative for hepatitis B e antigen and positive for anti-hepatitis B e antibodies.Laboratory investigations showed severe hepatocellular damage: total bilirubin 35 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 23 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 544 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase 971 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase 238 U/L. He was anaemic, with a haemoglobin of 8·9 g/dL. The platelet count was slightly reduced at 144 × 109 per L (normal range 150 × 109 to 400 × 109 per L). Abdominal CT showed transient contrast-enhanced areas in the liver during the arterial phase (figure). Liver histology showed enlarged sinusoids containing sickle-cell thrombi (figure). Sickle-cell disease was confirmed by a peripheral blood smear and cellulose acetate electrophoresis with haemoglobin S making up 87% of his haemoglobin.
Additionally, a diagnosis of acute hepatitis A virus (HAV) infection was made after serum IgM anti-HAV antibodies were detected; IgG anti-HAV seroconversion followed. Serum hepatitis B virus DNA was 1520 IU/mL and hepatitis D virus—also known as hepatitis delta virus—markers were negative. The patient was treated with exchange transfusion of red cells. He made a full clinical recovery and imaging of his liver showed that it had returned to normal. He was discharged 10 days after admission; at that stage, his total bilirubin concentration was 9·3 mg/dL and direct bilirubin was 6·1 mg/dL. 3 months after the original episode, his haemoglobin was stable at a concentration above 10·5 g/dL. His direct bilirubin concentration was 0·23 mg/dL.
Life-threatening hepatic damage can result from sickle-cell sequestration in the liver. Onset of the symptoms—also known as right upper quadrant syndrome—is frequently associated with an infection, with hepatitis or tuberculosis being common causes. In this case, this was our patient's first sickling crisis—previously, he had been asymptomatic—and it is likely that it was triggered by the infection with HAV. Abnormal hepatic perfusion seen during CT scanning can be interpreted as a sign of sinusoidal obstruction. Liver disease is fairly common in sickle-cell disease and includes several intrahepatic disorders that cause occlusion of blood vessels; they can occur when the patient is not in a sickle-cell crisis. Sequestration of sickle cells occurs more frequently in the spleen, with splenic sequestration crises being the presenting symptom in up to 20% of patients with sickle-cell disease. They are more common in childhood and can cause acute anaemia or hypovolaemic shock due to the pooling of large quantities of red blood cells.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal left ventricular function, a bicuspid aortic valve with fusion of the leaflets, and a severely reduced valve area of 0·8 cm2 with mean gradient of 59 mm Hg, peak gradient of 90 mm Hg, mild regurgitation, and a normal ascending aorta of 35 mm. Invasive coronary angiography showed no coronary artery disease. To investigate the valvular pathology further we did time-resolved three-dimensional phase-contrast MRI of the heart (4D flow MRI). Blood flow analysis confirmed a severely stenosed bicuspid aortic valve (figure, video) with an unusual hurricane-like flow pattern in the ascending aorta (figure, video).
Bicuspid aortic valve is the most common congenital heart defect, which occurs when two of the three leaflets fuse during development. It is present in 1–2% of the general population and is associated with other congenital malformations of the aorta (aortic coarctation and patent ductus arteriosus) leading to more deaths and morbidity than all other congenial heart malformations. The most important clinical consequences of bicuspid aortic valve disease are valvular stenosis, valvular insuffiency, infective endocarditis, and aortic complications such as aneurysm and dissection.

The mother, a 33-year-old primigravida, had conceived by in-vitro fertilisation; both parents were carriers for cystic fibrosis, and preimplantation genetic testing of the embryo was negative for aneuploidy and mutations in CFTR, the gene encoding the epithelial ion channel. No family history of birth defects, intellectual impairment, genetic disorders, or congenital anomalies was recorded. The previous second-trimester anatomy scan had shown typical growth and no fetal anomalies; and these new findings raised suspicion for a congenitally acquired infection.
Further discussion with the mother found that she had no known exposure to Toxoplasma gondii or anyone with toxoplasmosis, but she did report proximity to farm animals, feral cat exposure in the backyard of her home, and ingestion of cooked wild venison multiple times during the pregnancy.
Maternal TORCH (T gondii, cytomegalovirus, rubella virus, and herpes simplex virus) titres found elevated IgG and IgM titres for T gondii (normal range <7·2 IU/mL and less than arbitrary units per mL, respectively).
Given the late gestational age of the fetus, amniocentesis was deferred and, on discussion with the mother, it was decided to deliver the baby; an uncomplicated elective caesarean section delivered, at 38 weeks’ gestational age, a 3410 g neonate (41st percentile for gestational age). Apgar scores were 8 and 9 (typical range: between 7 and 10). Maternal and fetal cord blood samples were collected and sent to a toxoplasmosis reference laboratory. Results confirmed maternal toxoplasmosis: T gondii IgG Sabin-Feldman dye test positive 1:8000 (normal <1:16), low IgG avidity testing, T gondii IgM ELISA positive 10·0 (normal <2·0), AC/HS 400/400, IgA ELISA positive, and IgE ELISA positive, indicating a diagnosis of an acute infection with T gondii acquired during the third trimester of pregnancy.
Examination of the placenta was notable for chronic villous inflammation with multiple cysts identified within the chorionic villi and membranes with positive immunohistochemical stains for T gondii.
At delivery, the newborn presented with diffuse hypotonia. Neonatal blood samples showed T gondii IgG Sabin-Feldman dye test 1:8000 positive, T gondii IgM ELISA immunosorbent agglutination assay positive, and T gondii IgA positive. T gondii PCR on whole blood and cerebrospinal fluid were also positive, confirming congenital toxoplasmosis.
Neonatal brain MRIs showed severe dilatation bilaterally of the lateral and third ventricules, cortical thinning, aqueductal stenosis, and bilateral periventricular and basal ganglia calcifications. Ocular involvement was also noted with bilateral peripheral retinal lesions and vitritis. The infant was admitted to our neonatal intensive care unit for 45 days receiving pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine with folinic acid, steroids, supportive measures, and feeding therapy. Due to symptomatic hydrocephalus, a ventriculoperitoneal shunt was put in place after 35 days of life.
At follow-up 6 months later, the infant was recovering well, still on antiparasitic therapy with the ventriculoperitoneal shunt in place; he was meeting his milestones appropriately, although there was a concern for congenital palsy of the right upper arm.
Toxoplasmosis is an endemic disease caused by T gondii and an estimated 170 infants are born with congenital toxoplasmosis yearly in the USA. The protozoan infection is transmitted to humans by ingesting undercooked meats containing the parasite's cysts, contaminated vegetables, or by contact with cat faeces. Primary maternal infection is asymptomatic in about two-thirds of patients. When symptomatic, it typically presents with mild malaise, headache, and lymphadenopathies. The overall risk for congenital toxoplasmosis following maternal primary infection ranges from 20% to 50% without treatment. The risk of transmission increases with gestational age and can be as high as 60% if acquired by greater than 36 weeks of gestation; the earlier the infection is, the more severe the impact on the fetus. Even though most infected infants do not have clinical signs of infection at birth, up to 90% will develop sequelae later in life. Diagnosis of maternal toxoplasmosis is usually confirmed serologically. Given the high false-positive rates of commercially available IgM-based testing kits, confirmatory testing at a reference laboratory should always be done.

A 52-year-old woman was referred to our clinic with a new systolic murmur at the upper right sternal border. She reported chest pain on exertion radiating to the left arm. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal left ventricular function, a bicuspid aortic valve with fusion of the leaflets, and a severely reduced valve area of 0·8 cm2 with mean gradient of 59 mm Hg, peak gradient of 90 mm Hg, mild regurgitation, and a normal ascending aorta of 35 mm. Invasive coronary angiography showed no coronary artery disease. To investigate the valvular pathology further we did time-resolved three-dimensional phase-contrast MRI of the heart (4D flow MRI). Blood flow analysis confirmed a severely stenosed bicuspid aortic valve (figure, video) with an unusual hurricane-like flow pattern in the ascending aorta (figure, video).
Bicuspid aortic valve is the most common congenital heart defect, which occurs when two of the three leaflets fuse during development. It is present in 1–2% of the general population and is associated with other congenital malformations of the aorta (aortic coarctation and patent ductus arteriosus) leading to more deaths and morbidity than all other congenial heart malformations. The most important clinical consequences of bicuspid aortic valve disease are valvular stenosis, valvular insuffiency, infective endocarditis, and aortic complications such as aneurysm and dissection.

The mother, a 33-year-old primigravida, had conceived by in-vitro fertilisation; both parents were carriers for cystic fibrosis, and preimplantation genetic testing of the embryo was negative for aneuploidy and mutations in CFTR, the gene encoding the epithelial ion channel. No family history of birth defects, intellectual impairment, genetic disorders, or congenital anomalies was recorded. The previous second-trimester anatomy scan had shown typical growth and no fetal anomalies; and these new findings raised suspicion for a congenitally acquired infection.
Further discussion with the mother found that she had no known exposure to Toxoplasma gondii or anyone with toxoplasmosis, but she did report proximity to farm animals, feral cat exposure in the backyard of her home, and ingestion of cooked wild venison multiple times during the pregnancy.
Maternal TORCH (T gondii, cytomegalovirus, rubella virus, and herpes simplex virus) titres found elevated IgG and IgM titres for T gondii (normal range <7·2 IU/mL and less than arbitrary units per mL, respectively).
Given the late gestational age of the fetus, amniocentesis was deferred and, on discussion with the mother, it was decided to deliver the baby; an uncomplicated elective caesarean section delivered, at 38 weeks’ gestational age, a 3410 g neonate (41st percentile for gestational age). Apgar scores were 8 and 9 (typical range: between 7 and 10). Maternal and fetal cord blood samples were collected and sent to a toxoplasmosis reference laboratory. Results confirmed maternal toxoplasmosis: T gondii IgG Sabin-Feldman dye test positive 1:8000 (normal <1:16), low IgG avidity testing, T gondii IgM ELISA positive 10·0 (normal <2·0), AC/HS 400/400, IgA ELISA positive, and IgE ELISA positive, indicating a diagnosis of an acute infection with T gondii acquired during the third trimester of pregnancy.
Examination of the placenta was notable for chronic villous inflammation with multiple cysts identified within the chorionic villi and membranes with positive immunohistochemical stains for T gondii.
At delivery, the newborn presented with diffuse hypotonia. Neonatal blood samples showed T gondii IgG Sabin-Feldman dye test 1:8000 positive, T gondii IgM ELISA immunosorbent agglutination assay positive, and T gondii IgA positive. T gondii PCR on whole blood and cerebrospinal fluid were also positive, confirming congenital toxoplasmosis.
Neonatal brain MRIs showed severe dilatation bilaterally of the lateral and third ventricules, cortical thinning, aqueductal stenosis, and bilateral periventricular and basal ganglia calcifications. Ocular involvement was also noted with bilateral peripheral retinal lesions and vitritis. The infant was admitted to our neonatal intensive care unit for 45 days receiving pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine with folinic acid, steroids, supportive measures, and feeding therapy. Due to symptomatic hydrocephalus, a ventriculoperitoneal shunt was put in place after 35 days of life.
At follow-up 6 months later, the infant was recovering well, still on antiparasitic therapy with the ventriculoperitoneal shunt in place; he was meeting his milestones appropriately, although there was a concern for congenital palsy of the right upper arm.
Toxoplasmosis is an endemic disease caused by T gondii and an estimated 170 infants are born with congenital toxoplasmosis yearly in the USA. The protozoan infection is transmitted to humans by ingesting undercooked meats containing the parasite's cysts, contaminated vegetables, or by contact with cat faeces. Primary maternal infection is asymptomatic in about two-thirds of patients. When symptomatic, it typically presents with mild malaise, headache, and lymphadenopathies. The overall risk for congenital toxoplasmosis following maternal primary infection ranges from 20% to 50% without treatment. The risk of transmission increases with gestational age and can be as high as 60% if acquired by greater than 36 weeks of gestation; the earlier the infection is, the more severe the impact on the fetus. Even though most infected infants do not have clinical signs of infection at birth, up to 90% will develop sequelae later in life. Diagnosis of maternal toxoplasmosis is usually confirmed serologically. Given the high false-positive rates of commercially available IgM-based testing kits, confirmatory testing at a reference laboratory should always be done.

The mother, a 33-year-old primigravida, had conceived by in-vitro fertilisation; both parents were carriers for cystic fibrosis, and preimplantation genetic testing of the embryo was negative for aneuploidy and mutations in CFTR, the gene encoding the epithelial ion channel. No family history of birth defects, intellectual impairment, genetic disorders, or congenital anomalies was recorded. The previous second-trimester anatomy scan had shown typical growth and no fetal anomalies; and these new findings raised suspicion for a congenitally acquired infection.
Further discussion with the mother found that she had no known exposure to Toxoplasma gondii or anyone with toxoplasmosis, but she did report proximity to farm animals, feral cat exposure in the backyard of her home, and ingestion of cooked wild venison multiple times during the pregnancy.
Maternal TORCH (T gondii, cytomegalovirus, rubella virus, and herpes simplex virus) titres found elevated IgG and IgM titres for T gondii (normal range <7·2 IU/mL and less than arbitrary units per mL, respectively).
Given the late gestational age of the fetus, amniocentesis was deferred and, on discussion with the mother, it was decided to deliver the baby; an uncomplicated elective caesarean section delivered, at 38 weeks’ gestational age, a 3410 g neonate (41st percentile for gestational age). Apgar scores were 8 and 9 (typical range: between 7 and 10). Maternal and fetal cord blood samples were collected and sent to a toxoplasmosis reference laboratory. Results confirmed maternal toxoplasmosis: T gondii IgG Sabin-Feldman dye test positive 1:8000 (normal <1:16), low IgG avidity testing, T gondii IgM ELISA positive 10·0 (normal <2·0), AC/HS 400/400, IgA ELISA positive, and IgE ELISA positive, indicating a diagnosis of an acute infection with T gondii acquired during the third trimester of pregnancy.
Examination of the placenta was notable for chronic villous inflammation with multiple cysts identified within the chorionic villi and membranes with positive immunohistochemical stains for T gondii.
At delivery, the newborn presented with diffuse hypotonia. Neonatal blood samples showed T gondii IgG Sabin-Feldman dye test 1:8000 positive, T gondii IgM ELISA immunosorbent agglutination assay positive, and T gondii IgA positive. T gondii PCR on whole blood and cerebrospinal fluid were also positive, confirming congenital toxoplasmosis.
Neonatal brain MRIs showed severe dilatation bilaterally of the lateral and third ventricules, cortical thinning, aqueductal stenosis, and bilateral periventricular and basal ganglia calcifications. Ocular involvement was also noted with bilateral peripheral retinal lesions and vitritis. The infant was admitted to our neonatal intensive care unit for 45 days receiving pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine with folinic acid, steroids, supportive measures, and feeding therapy. Due to symptomatic hydrocephalus, a ventriculoperitoneal shunt was put in place after 35 days of life.
At follow-up 6 months later, the infant was recovering well, still on antiparasitic therapy with the ventriculoperitoneal shunt in place; he was meeting his milestones appropriately, although there was a concern for congenital palsy of the right upper arm.
Toxoplasmosis is an endemic disease caused by T gondii and an estimated 170 infants are born with congenital toxoplasmosis yearly in the USA. The protozoan infection is transmitted to humans by ingesting undercooked meats containing the parasite's cysts, contaminated vegetables, or by contact with cat faeces. Primary maternal infection is asymptomatic in about two-thirds of patients. When symptomatic, it typically presents with mild malaise, headache, and lymphadenopathies. The overall risk for congenital toxoplasmosis following maternal primary infection ranges from 20% to 50% without treatment. The risk of transmission increases with gestational age and can be as high as 60% if acquired by greater than 36 weeks of gestation; the earlier the infection is, the more severe the impact on the fetus. Even though most infected infants do not have clinical signs of infection at birth, up to 90% will develop sequelae later in life. Diagnosis of maternal toxoplasmosis is usually confirmed serologically. Given the high false-positive rates of commercially available IgM-based testing kits, confirmatory testing at a reference laboratory should always be done.

A 27-year-old woman came to our hospital with increasing diffuse pain around the joints of her shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, and ankles. She was well known to us because of her long history of problems due to autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1—with a mutation in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene.We first met her when she was 18 years old, after she was referred by her paediatrician for severe hypoparathyroidism, which was treated with alfacalcidol and calcium carbonate. The treatment resulted in the development of nephrocalcinosis at the age of 15 years. When she was 22 years old, she returned with a 3-month history of worsening dysphagia and vomiting because of achalasia and oesophageal candidiasis: she was unable to take her medication orally. She had also lost a substantial amount of weight—at its nadir her body mass index was 15 kg/m2. She was admitted as an emergency with a total serum calcium concentration of 1·44 mmol/L (normal range 2·20–2·55) and prolonged QTc on her electrocardiogram. We started her on replacement therapy with subcutaneous recombinant human parathyroid hormone (rhPTH; 1–34) and colecalciferol. The dose of rhPTH (1–34) varied from 20 μg once to twice a day and hypocalcaemia was adequately controlled over 5·5 years—mean albumin-adjusted serum calcium was 2·11 mmol/L.
The pain, she came to see us with, had developed after 3 years of treatment with the rhPTH (1–34) and had increased progressively. We first ruled out any inflammatory and autoimmune causes of the arthritis. Additional investigations showed that she had a low bone density of the distal radius (Z score SD −3·0, normal score SD −2) and increased markers of bone formation: alkaline phosphatase was 271 IU/L (normal range 42–98), osteocalcin was 87 ng/mL (normal range 2–12). A bone scan with whole-body early images showed precocious, intense bone uptake in the peripheral joints and in the axial skeleton, with no activity in the heart, kidneys, or bladder (figure). The images suggested that bone cells were being overstimulated by the rhPTH (1–34)—appearing like so-called super bone scans seen in patients with hyperparathyroidism. The rhPTH (1–34) was discontinued and within 48 h the patient's joint pain stopped. However, she then developed a transient hypocalcaemia requiring high doses of intravenous and oral calcium with alfacalcidol; she had concomitantly low urinary calcium excretion, indicative of hungry bone syndrome. The bone scintigraphy returned to normal 1 year after the rhPTH (1–34) was stopped (figure).
In patients with hypoparathyroidism refractory to conventional treatment, rhPTH (1–34) therapy can effectively control hypocalcaemia, but whether it is safe in the long term is unclear. Further, abnormally increased metabolic activity of the bone may occur despite adequate calcaemic control, possibly due to the pharmacokinetics of the treatment. Bone scintigraphy—including an early scan—can be useful in detecting iatrogenic hyperparathyroidism in patients receiving either rhPTH (1–34) or rhPTH (1–84) treatment (video).

A 27-year-old woman came to our hospital with increasing diffuse pain around the joints of her shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, and ankles. She was well known to us because of her long history of problems due to autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1—with a mutation in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene.We first met her when she was 18 years old, after she was referred by her paediatrician for severe hypoparathyroidism, which was treated with alfacalcidol and calcium carbonate. The treatment resulted in the development of nephrocalcinosis at the age of 15 years. When she was 22 years old, she returned with a 3-month history of worsening dysphagia and vomiting because of achalasia and oesophageal candidiasis: she was unable to take her medication orally. She had also lost a substantial amount of weight—at its nadir her body mass index was 15 kg/m2. She was admitted as an emergency with a total serum calcium concentration of 1·44 mmol/L (normal range 2·20–2·55) and prolonged QTc on her electrocardiogram. We started her on replacement therapy with subcutaneous recombinant human parathyroid hormone (rhPTH; 1–34) and colecalciferol. The dose of rhPTH (1–34) varied from 20 μg once to twice a day and hypocalcaemia was adequately controlled over 5·5 years—mean albumin-adjusted serum calcium was 2·11 mmol/L.
The pain, she came to see us with, had developed after 3 years of treatment with the rhPTH (1–34) and had increased progressively. We first ruled out any inflammatory and autoimmune causes of the arthritis. Additional investigations showed that she had a low bone density of the distal radius (Z score SD −3·0, normal score SD −2) and increased markers of bone formation: alkaline phosphatase was 271 IU/L (normal range 42–98), osteocalcin was 87 ng/mL (normal range 2–12). A bone scan with whole-body early images showed precocious, intense bone uptake in the peripheral joints and in the axial skeleton, with no activity in the heart, kidneys, or bladder (figure). The images suggested that bone cells were being overstimulated by the rhPTH (1–34)—appearing like so-called super bone scans seen in patients with hyperparathyroidism. The rhPTH (1–34) was discontinued and within 48 h the patient's joint pain stopped. However, she then developed a transient hypocalcaemia requiring high doses of intravenous and oral calcium with alfacalcidol; she had concomitantly low urinary calcium excretion, indicative of hungry bone syndrome. The bone scintigraphy returned to normal 1 year after the rhPTH (1–34) was stopped (figure).
In patients with hypoparathyroidism refractory to conventional treatment, rhPTH (1–34) therapy can effectively control hypocalcaemia, but whether it is safe in the long term is unclear. Further, abnormally increased metabolic activity of the bone may occur despite adequate calcaemic control, possibly due to the pharmacokinetics of the treatment. Bone scintigraphy—including an early scan—can be useful in detecting iatrogenic hyperparathyroidism in patients receiving either rhPTH (1–34) or rhPTH (1–84) treatment (video).

A 27-year-old woman came to our hospital with increasing diffuse pain around the joints of her shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, and ankles. She was well known to us because of her long history of problems due to autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1—with a mutation in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene.We first met her when she was 18 years old, after she was referred by her paediatrician for severe hypoparathyroidism, which was treated with alfacalcidol and calcium carbonate. The treatment resulted in the development of nephrocalcinosis at the age of 15 years. When she was 22 years old, she returned with a 3-month history of worsening dysphagia and vomiting because of achalasia and oesophageal candidiasis: she was unable to take her medication orally. She had also lost a substantial amount of weight—at its nadir her body mass index was 15 kg/m2. She was admitted as an emergency with a total serum calcium concentration of 1·44 mmol/L (normal range 2·20–2·55) and prolonged QTc on her electrocardiogram. We started her on replacement therapy with subcutaneous recombinant human parathyroid hormone (rhPTH; 1–34) and colecalciferol. The dose of rhPTH (1–34) varied from 20 μg once to twice a day and hypocalcaemia was adequately controlled over 5·5 years—mean albumin-adjusted serum calcium was 2·11 mmol/L.
The pain, she came to see us with, had developed after 3 years of treatment with the rhPTH (1–34) and had increased progressively. We first ruled out any inflammatory and autoimmune causes of the arthritis. Additional investigations showed that she had a low bone density of the distal radius (Z score SD −3·0, normal score SD −2) and increased markers of bone formation: alkaline phosphatase was 271 IU/L (normal range 42–98), osteocalcin was 87 ng/mL (normal range 2–12). A bone scan with whole-body early images showed precocious, intense bone uptake in the peripheral joints and in the axial skeleton, with no activity in the heart, kidneys, or bladder (figure). The images suggested that bone cells were being overstimulated by the rhPTH (1–34)—appearing like so-called super bone scans seen in patients with hyperparathyroidism. The rhPTH (1–34) was discontinued and within 48 h the patient's joint pain stopped. However, she then developed a transient hypocalcaemia requiring high doses of intravenous and oral calcium with alfacalcidol; she had concomitantly low urinary calcium excretion, indicative of hungry bone syndrome. The bone scintigraphy returned to normal 1 year after the rhPTH (1–34) was stopped (figure).
In patients with hypoparathyroidism refractory to conventional treatment, rhPTH (1–34) therapy can effectively control hypocalcaemia, but whether it is safe in the long term is unclear. Further, abnormally increased metabolic activity of the bone may occur despite adequate calcaemic control, possibly due to the pharmacokinetics of the treatment. Bone scintigraphy—including an early scan—can be useful in detecting iatrogenic hyperparathyroidism in patients receiving either rhPTH (1–34) or rhPTH (1–84) treatment (video).

A 34-year-old man, from sub-Saharan Africa, was referred to our hospital for short stature, when he came to France, as an actor, to play the part of a child. The patient reported that at birth he required incubator support and that his growth was blunted from early childhood.At our first evaluation, his height was 137 cm, weight was 26·4 kg, and body-mass index 14 kg/m2. He had long extremities compared to his trunk and he had signs of hypogonadism—including small intrascrotal testes (0·5 mL; typical 12–30 in adult males), absent pubic and axillary hair, micro-penis (2 cm), and a high-pitched voice.
Hormone assays showed combined pituitary hormone deficiencies with low serum morning cortisol and undetectable dehydroepiandrosterone-sulphate with low adrenocorticotropin; low thyroxine and triiodothyronine; undetectable testosterone and oestradiol; low inhibin B and low gonadotrophins; low prolactin; and growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 were both below detectable limits (appendix).
Brain MRI showed marked pituitary gland hypoplasia, absence of pituitary stalk and ectopic posterior hypophysis, and no extra-pituitary abnormalities.
The patient's bone age was 13 years, and knee MRI showed persistent growth plates at the distal femoral or proximal tibial epiphysis. Genetic testing did not identify pathogenic variants in any of the genes responsible for congenital hypopituitarism.
We commenced treatment with hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, and recombinant human growth hormone replacement for 2 months before the patient had to return to his country as his visa had expired; he was provided with growth hormone cartridges for an additional 3 months.
Figure Congenital hypopituitarism treated in adulthood
Show full caption
Figure viewer
The patient returned to France 3 years later; his height was 142 cm, but otherwise, his clinical state was unchanged. We commenced stepwise replacement with hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, growth hormone, and gonadotropins for the next 4 years. His height increased to 161 cm—an increase of 24 cm—and he achieved normal pubertal development (appendix). During the increase in height, the patient developed scoliosis which necessitated surgical correction and an arthrodesis at T2-L1 (appendix).
At baseline, cardiac MRI showed a small heart—but well-proportioned to the patient's body size—with normal contractile function; hormone treatment resulted in linear, uniform growth of the heart with a progressive increase in ventricular mass and volume. Concomitant decrease in the extracellular space indicated that the cardiac growth resulted from cardiomyocyte correction of hypotrophy; the initial rapid decrease in extracellular space, after levothyroxine and hydrocortisone were started, was mostly attributed to resorption of myxoedematous infiltration, and possibly due to inflammation.
Growth hormone—given prior to puberty induction—transiently increased ventricular contractility to supraphysiologic values, with the ejection fraction reaching 78%; it normalised during gonadotrophin therapy. Left ventricular stroke volume increased proportionally compared to end-diastolic volume, reflecting the heart's ability to enhance its contractile strength in response to increased venous return—Frank-Starling law.
We further observed a uniform increase of the cross-sectional area of the patient's femoral muscles during treatment accompanied by a progressive decrease of intramuscular fat fraction. Growth hormone induced transient glucose intolerance, which resolved during further therapy.
Congenital hypopituitarism is usually diagnosed and treated during childhood or adolescence to correct blunted growth and lack of pubertal development. Rarely is hormone replacement initiated in adulthood, and results of such cases are limited. Regarding the heart, the capacity to generate cardiomyocytes during adult life has been the subject of much debate; cardiomyogenesis is minimal in healthy humans after birth. Metachronous heart growth—as seen in our patient—from size of a child to a normal adult, has not previously been reported. In conclusion, hormone replacement, administered gradually, in an adult patient with congenital hypopituitarism can safely induce heart growth normalisation proportionate to linear growth (video).

A 25-year-old man presented to our emergency room with a sudden onset of a pulsatile headache and blurred vision. He also reported a 9-day history of a swelling in his scrotum following trauma. He had no medical history.On physical examination, a melon-sized right testicular mass was found. The patient's Glasgow Coma Scale was 15, he had a left homonymous hemianopsia, his extraocular movements were intact, and his pupils were round, equal sized, and reactive to light.
A CT scan of the patient's brain—carried out in the emergency room—showed a 6 cm haemorrhagic mass in the right occipital and posterior parietal lobes with a right to left midline shift (figure). Further CT imaging, carried out later, showed a 17·5 cm heterogeneous, necrotic mass arising from the right testicle and numerous necrotic mediastinal, pulmonary, and retroperitoneal lymph nodes (figure).
Laboratory investigations found the patient's alpha-fetoprotein serum concentration was 440 ng/mL (normal <8·5), beta-human chorionic gonadotropin was 2 mIU/mL (normal <5), and lactate dehydrogenase was 813 U/L (normal 135–225).
The patient was admitted to our neurology intensive care unit. After discussion at our tumour board and following consultation with the patient, we carried out a combined right occipital craniotomy and right radical orchiectomy. Histopathology of specimens from the patient's brain and right testis tumours was consistent with mixed malignant germ cell tumour with mature teratoma, embryonal carcinoma, and yolk sac carcinoma.
The patient was then treated with four cycles of bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin. At 3-month follow-up, repeat imaging showed a good tumour response in the mediastinum, retroperitoneum, and brain, and the tumour markers were within normal limits.
According to the National Comprehensive Cancer Network management guidelines, laboratory investigations and CT scans of the abdomen, pelvis, and chest should be done in all patients with a diagnosis of non-seminomatous germ cell tumours (NSGCT). Even though a brain MRI is not regarded as standard in the initial work-up of patients without visceral metastasis, brain imaging is imperative in patients with testicular cancer presenting with signs indicative of neurological involvement.
Treatment advances for patients with NSGCT with a poor prognosis—including personalised chemotherapy regimens and risk reclassification—have significantly improved progression-free survival. In 2019, the International Germ Cell Cancer Collaborative updated the 1997 classification system for advanced NSGCT. Despite these advances, a clear consensus on the optimal management of NSGCT patients with brain metastasis is lacking, though evidence exists for first-line chemotherapy and locoregional radiation. Surgery is of limited value when metastases are widespread. However, patients with surgically accessible, low volume, and single or oligo-metastatic brain lesions may be candidates for neurosurgical evaluation and metastasectomy, which may confer long-term survival rates of up to 60% (video).

A 34-year-old man, from sub-Saharan Africa, was referred to our hospital for short stature, when he came to France, as an actor, to play the part of a child. The patient reported that at birth he required incubator support and that his growth was blunted from early childhood.At our first evaluation, his height was 137 cm, weight was 26·4 kg, and body-mass index 14 kg/m2. He had long extremities compared to his trunk and he had signs of hypogonadism—including small intrascrotal testes (0·5 mL; typical 12–30 in adult males), absent pubic and axillary hair, micro-penis (2 cm), and a high-pitched voice.
Hormone assays showed combined pituitary hormone deficiencies with low serum morning cortisol and undetectable dehydroepiandrosterone-sulphate with low adrenocorticotropin; low thyroxine and triiodothyronine; undetectable testosterone and oestradiol; low inhibin B and low gonadotrophins; low prolactin; and growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 were both below detectable limits (appendix).
Brain MRI showed marked pituitary gland hypoplasia, absence of pituitary stalk and ectopic posterior hypophysis, and no extra-pituitary abnormalities.
The patient's bone age was 13 years, and knee MRI showed persistent growth plates at the distal femoral or proximal tibial epiphysis. Genetic testing did not identify pathogenic variants in any of the genes responsible for congenital hypopituitarism.
We commenced treatment with hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, and recombinant human growth hormone replacement for 2 months before the patient had to return to his country as his visa had expired; he was provided with growth hormone cartridges for an additional 3 months.
Figure Congenital hypopituitarism treated in adulthood
Show full caption
Figure viewer
The patient returned to France 3 years later; his height was 142 cm, but otherwise, his clinical state was unchanged. We commenced stepwise replacement with hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, growth hormone, and gonadotropins for the next 4 years. His height increased to 161 cm—an increase of 24 cm—and he achieved normal pubertal development (appendix). During the increase in height, the patient developed scoliosis which necessitated surgical correction and an arthrodesis at T2-L1 (appendix).
At baseline, cardiac MRI showed a small heart—but well-proportioned to the patient's body size—with normal contractile function; hormone treatment resulted in linear, uniform growth of the heart with a progressive increase in ventricular mass and volume. Concomitant decrease in the extracellular space indicated that the cardiac growth resulted from cardiomyocyte correction of hypotrophy; the initial rapid decrease in extracellular space, after levothyroxine and hydrocortisone were started, was mostly attributed to resorption of myxoedematous infiltration, and possibly due to inflammation.
Growth hormone—given prior to puberty induction—transiently increased ventricular contractility to supraphysiologic values, with the ejection fraction reaching 78%; it normalised during gonadotrophin therapy. Left ventricular stroke volume increased proportionally compared to end-diastolic volume, reflecting the heart's ability to enhance its contractile strength in response to increased venous return—Frank-Starling law.
We further observed a uniform increase of the cross-sectional area of the patient's femoral muscles during treatment accompanied by a progressive decrease of intramuscular fat fraction. Growth hormone induced transient glucose intolerance, which resolved during further therapy.
Congenital hypopituitarism is usually diagnosed and treated during childhood or adolescence to correct blunted growth and lack of pubertal development. Rarely is hormone replacement initiated in adulthood, and results of such cases are limited. Regarding the heart, the capacity to generate cardiomyocytes during adult life has been the subject of much debate; cardiomyogenesis is minimal in healthy humans after birth. Metachronous heart growth—as seen in our patient—from size of a child to a normal adult, has not previously been reported. In conclusion, hormone replacement, administered gradually, in an adult patient with congenital hypopituitarism can safely induce heart growth normalisation proportionate to linear growth (video).
