A 25-year-old man presented to our emergency room with a sudden onset of a pulsatile headache and blurred vision. He also reported a 9-day history of a swelling in his scrotum following trauma. He had no medical history.On physical examination, a melon-sized right testicular mass was found. The patient's Glasgow Coma Scale was 15, he had a left homonymous hemianopsia, his extraocular movements were intact, and his pupils were round, equal sized, and reactive to light.
A CT scan of the patient's brain—carried out in the emergency room—showed a 6 cm haemorrhagic mass in the right occipital and posterior parietal lobes with a right to left midline shift (figure). Further CT imaging, carried out later, showed a 17·5 cm heterogeneous, necrotic mass arising from the right testicle and numerous necrotic mediastinal, pulmonary, and retroperitoneal lymph nodes (figure).
Laboratory investigations found the patient's alpha-fetoprotein serum concentration was 440 ng/mL (normal <8·5), beta-human chorionic gonadotropin was 2 mIU/mL (normal <5), and lactate dehydrogenase was 813 U/L (normal 135–225).
The patient was admitted to our neurology intensive care unit. After discussion at our tumour board and following consultation with the patient, we carried out a combined right occipital craniotomy and right radical orchiectomy. Histopathology of specimens from the patient's brain and right testis tumours was consistent with mixed malignant germ cell tumour with mature teratoma, embryonal carcinoma, and yolk sac carcinoma.
The patient was then treated with four cycles of bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin. At 3-month follow-up, repeat imaging showed a good tumour response in the mediastinum, retroperitoneum, and brain, and the tumour markers were within normal limits.
According to the National Comprehensive Cancer Network management guidelines, laboratory investigations and CT scans of the abdomen, pelvis, and chest should be done in all patients with a diagnosis of non-seminomatous germ cell tumours (NSGCT). Even though a brain MRI is not regarded as standard in the initial work-up of patients without visceral metastasis, brain imaging is imperative in patients with testicular cancer presenting with signs indicative of neurological involvement.
Treatment advances for patients with NSGCT with a poor prognosis—including personalised chemotherapy regimens and risk reclassification—have significantly improved progression-free survival. In 2019, the International Germ Cell Cancer Collaborative updated the 1997 classification system for advanced NSGCT. Despite these advances, a clear consensus on the optimal management of NSGCT patients with brain metastasis is lacking, though evidence exists for first-line chemotherapy and locoregional radiation. Surgery is of limited value when metastases are widespread. However, patients with surgically accessible, low volume, and single or oligo-metastatic brain lesions may be candidates for neurosurgical evaluation and metastasectomy, which may confer long-term survival rates of up to 60% (video).

A 55-year-old woman who had been diagnosed with fistulising ileocolonic Crohn's disease 5 years ago presented with pain and swelling at the right hip for 2 months. For the past 3 years before presentation, the patient had not attended previous outpatient clinic appointments and had stopped using medication prescribed for Crohn's disease. On examination, the patient looked ill and cachectic. She was not able to walk without support, had a fever (38°C), her conjunctivas were pale, and she had multiple fistulas on her right inguinal region and right flank. The right inguinal fistula was active with visible faecal discharge. Her right hip was swollen, warm, and had decreased range of motion. Laboratory investigations identified iron deficiency anaemia (haemoglobin 9·8 g/dL, haematocrit 30%, mean corpuscular volume 77 fL) and leukocytosis (neutrophil count 8730 cells per mm3), elevated C-reactive protein (96 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (31 mm/h), and decreased albumin (1·5 g/dL).The patient's clinical features, including fever, monoarthritis of a large joint, short duration of presentation, and extensive intestinal involvement with a penetrating disease phenotype, suggested an alternative diagnosis to inflammatory arthritis. Furthermore, a CT of the abdomen showed effusion and narrowing of the right coxofemoral joint space adjacent to the diseased ileal segment that was consistent with septic arthritis. To investigate the fistula route, a fistulogram was obtained by injecting contrast through the orifice of the right inguinal fistula, which showed that the tract was extending from the terminal ileum to the right hip joint and right pararenal space (figure). Intravenous vancomycin and meropenem were commenced for septic arthritis. The patient improved clinically with resolution of fever within the first 2 weeks of antibiotic therapy and nutritional support. A follow-up CT showed reduced inflammation at the right hip; however, the patient had fever after 4 weeks of antibiotic therapy. Surgical management was decided by the multidisciplinary team due to fever and the active fistula. During surgery, an enteroenteric fistula located 15 cm proximal to the ileocaecal valve was detected, which necessitated an ileocaecal resection and diverting ileostomy. After surgery, the patient received 2 more weeks of intravenous antibiotics for septic arthritis (total 6 weeks). We treated the patient with infliximab plus immunomodulator therapy after the antibiotic therapy, which achieved clinical remission at 12 weeks of treatment and endoscopic remission at 24 weeks.
Patients with Crohn's disease can develop intestinal and extraintestinal complications. Although inflammatory arthritis is a common extraintestinal manifestation of Crohn's disease, septic arthritis should be considered in patients with a penetrating disease phenotype and requires a tailored approach to management.

A 25-year-old man presented to our emergency room with a sudden onset of a pulsatile headache and blurred vision. He also reported a 9-day history of a swelling in his scrotum following trauma. He had no medical history.On physical examination, a melon-sized right testicular mass was found. The patient's Glasgow Coma Scale was 15, he had a left homonymous hemianopsia, his extraocular movements were intact, and his pupils were round, equal sized, and reactive to light.
A CT scan of the patient's brain—carried out in the emergency room—showed a 6 cm haemorrhagic mass in the right occipital and posterior parietal lobes with a right to left midline shift (figure). Further CT imaging, carried out later, showed a 17·5 cm heterogeneous, necrotic mass arising from the right testicle and numerous necrotic mediastinal, pulmonary, and retroperitoneal lymph nodes (figure).
Laboratory investigations found the patient's alpha-fetoprotein serum concentration was 440 ng/mL (normal <8·5), beta-human chorionic gonadotropin was 2 mIU/mL (normal <5), and lactate dehydrogenase was 813 U/L (normal 135–225).
The patient was admitted to our neurology intensive care unit. After discussion at our tumour board and following consultation with the patient, we carried out a combined right occipital craniotomy and right radical orchiectomy. Histopathology of specimens from the patient's brain and right testis tumours was consistent with mixed malignant germ cell tumour with mature teratoma, embryonal carcinoma, and yolk sac carcinoma.
The patient was then treated with four cycles of bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin. At 3-month follow-up, repeat imaging showed a good tumour response in the mediastinum, retroperitoneum, and brain, and the tumour markers were within normal limits.
According to the National Comprehensive Cancer Network management guidelines, laboratory investigations and CT scans of the abdomen, pelvis, and chest should be done in all patients with a diagnosis of non-seminomatous germ cell tumours (NSGCT). Even though a brain MRI is not regarded as standard in the initial work-up of patients without visceral metastasis, brain imaging is imperative in patients with testicular cancer presenting with signs indicative of neurological involvement.
Treatment advances for patients with NSGCT with a poor prognosis—including personalised chemotherapy regimens and risk reclassification—have significantly improved progression-free survival. In 2019, the International Germ Cell Cancer Collaborative updated the 1997 classification system for advanced NSGCT. Despite these advances, a clear consensus on the optimal management of NSGCT patients with brain metastasis is lacking, though evidence exists for first-line chemotherapy and locoregional radiation. Surgery is of limited value when metastases are widespread. However, patients with surgically accessible, low volume, and single or oligo-metastatic brain lesions may be candidates for neurosurgical evaluation and metastasectomy, which may confer long-term survival rates of up to 60% (video).

A 55-year-old woman who had been diagnosed with fistulising ileocolonic Crohn's disease 5 years ago presented with pain and swelling at the right hip for 2 months. For the past 3 years before presentation, the patient had not attended previous outpatient clinic appointments and had stopped using medication prescribed for Crohn's disease. On examination, the patient looked ill and cachectic. She was not able to walk without support, had a fever (38°C), her conjunctivas were pale, and she had multiple fistulas on her right inguinal region and right flank. The right inguinal fistula was active with visible faecal discharge. Her right hip was swollen, warm, and had decreased range of motion. Laboratory investigations identified iron deficiency anaemia (haemoglobin 9·8 g/dL, haematocrit 30%, mean corpuscular volume 77 fL) and leukocytosis (neutrophil count 8730 cells per mm3), elevated C-reactive protein (96 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (31 mm/h), and decreased albumin (1·5 g/dL).The patient's clinical features, including fever, monoarthritis of a large joint, short duration of presentation, and extensive intestinal involvement with a penetrating disease phenotype, suggested an alternative diagnosis to inflammatory arthritis. Furthermore, a CT of the abdomen showed effusion and narrowing of the right coxofemoral joint space adjacent to the diseased ileal segment that was consistent with septic arthritis. To investigate the fistula route, a fistulogram was obtained by injecting contrast through the orifice of the right inguinal fistula, which showed that the tract was extending from the terminal ileum to the right hip joint and right pararenal space (figure). Intravenous vancomycin and meropenem were commenced for septic arthritis. The patient improved clinically with resolution of fever within the first 2 weeks of antibiotic therapy and nutritional support. A follow-up CT showed reduced inflammation at the right hip; however, the patient had fever after 4 weeks of antibiotic therapy. Surgical management was decided by the multidisciplinary team due to fever and the active fistula. During surgery, an enteroenteric fistula located 15 cm proximal to the ileocaecal valve was detected, which necessitated an ileocaecal resection and diverting ileostomy. After surgery, the patient received 2 more weeks of intravenous antibiotics for septic arthritis (total 6 weeks). We treated the patient with infliximab plus immunomodulator therapy after the antibiotic therapy, which achieved clinical remission at 12 weeks of treatment and endoscopic remission at 24 weeks.
Patients with Crohn's disease can develop intestinal and extraintestinal complications. Although inflammatory arthritis is a common extraintestinal manifestation of Crohn's disease, septic arthritis should be considered in patients with a penetrating disease phenotype and requires a tailored approach to management.

A 67-year-old woman, who had a 4-month history of a sudden onset of intermittent jerking movements with contortions of her head and right arm, attended our specialist unit. She had been seen earlier at another hospital where neuroimaging and electroencephalography were reported as normal. And after the patient was told the diagnosis was probably “psychogenic spells”, she sought a further consultation.She had no notable medical history; she was previously fit and well.
On examination, we found the patient to have paroxysmal retrocollis with rotational head movements accompanied by intermittent contractions of the platysma muscle. The movements were variable in amplitude and frequency, and briefly suppressed while she tried to perform complex finger tapping tasks; they occasionally synchronised to the frequency of finger tapping (video). During walking, the patient had a variable step length and width—astasia-abasia—and additional variations to her head movements (figure). She had an exaggerated response to the pull test. The patient's neurological examination was otherwise normal.
We did no laboratory investigations or imaging since the clinical presentation met the pillars of inconsistence and incongruence, rendering a definitive diagnosis of functional movement disorder (FMD). With explanation and reassurance that unrecognised maladaptive thoughts and beliefs can predispose to the development of FMD, the patient relayed to us that she had a diminished sense of self-worth; she was eager to address this issue with a cognitive behavioural therapist.
After 2 months of therapy, the patient's atypical movements ceased (video).
FMD is not a diagnosis of exclusion and can be established by clearly demonstrating the two clinical pillars of the disorder: inconsistency (or variability or distractibility) of the amplitude, distribution, and severity of the phenotype; and incongruence with the wide spectrum of manifestations of other neurological disorders.
Features suggestive of psychological difficulties are neither necessary nor sufficient to make the diagnosis. Historical details (eg, the way the condition started) are also unnecessary in concluding that the patient has FMD. Additionally, laboratory or neuroimaging investigations are not needed.
Finally, delivering and explaining the diagnosis to the patient is a critical step in the care pathway.
Patients receiving reassurance and a clear appreciation and understanding of FMD increases the possibility of successful resolution of symptoms and concordance with cognitive, physical, and occupational therapies.

A 55-year-old woman who had been diagnosed with fistulising ileocolonic Crohn's disease 5 years ago presented with pain and swelling at the right hip for 2 months. For the past 3 years before presentation, the patient had not attended previous outpatient clinic appointments and had stopped using medication prescribed for Crohn's disease. On examination, the patient looked ill and cachectic. She was not able to walk without support, had a fever (38°C), her conjunctivas were pale, and she had multiple fistulas on her right inguinal region and right flank. The right inguinal fistula was active with visible faecal discharge. Her right hip was swollen, warm, and had decreased range of motion. Laboratory investigations identified iron deficiency anaemia (haemoglobin 9·8 g/dL, haematocrit 30%, mean corpuscular volume 77 fL) and leukocytosis (neutrophil count 8730 cells per mm3), elevated C-reactive protein (96 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (31 mm/h), and decreased albumin (1·5 g/dL).The patient's clinical features, including fever, monoarthritis of a large joint, short duration of presentation, and extensive intestinal involvement with a penetrating disease phenotype, suggested an alternative diagnosis to inflammatory arthritis. Furthermore, a CT of the abdomen showed effusion and narrowing of the right coxofemoral joint space adjacent to the diseased ileal segment that was consistent with septic arthritis. To investigate the fistula route, a fistulogram was obtained by injecting contrast through the orifice of the right inguinal fistula, which showed that the tract was extending from the terminal ileum to the right hip joint and right pararenal space (figure). Intravenous vancomycin and meropenem were commenced for septic arthritis. The patient improved clinically with resolution of fever within the first 2 weeks of antibiotic therapy and nutritional support. A follow-up CT showed reduced inflammation at the right hip; however, the patient had fever after 4 weeks of antibiotic therapy. Surgical management was decided by the multidisciplinary team due to fever and the active fistula. During surgery, an enteroenteric fistula located 15 cm proximal to the ileocaecal valve was detected, which necessitated an ileocaecal resection and diverting ileostomy. After surgery, the patient received 2 more weeks of intravenous antibiotics for septic arthritis (total 6 weeks). We treated the patient with infliximab plus immunomodulator therapy after the antibiotic therapy, which achieved clinical remission at 12 weeks of treatment and endoscopic remission at 24 weeks.
Patients with Crohn's disease can develop intestinal and extraintestinal complications. Although inflammatory arthritis is a common extraintestinal manifestation of Crohn's disease, septic arthritis should be considered in patients with a penetrating disease phenotype and requires a tailored approach to management.

A 67-year-old woman, who had a 4-month history of a sudden onset of intermittent jerking movements with contortions of her head and right arm, attended our specialist unit. She had been seen earlier at another hospital where neuroimaging and electroencephalography were reported as normal. And after the patient was told the diagnosis was probably “psychogenic spells”, she sought a further consultation.She had no notable medical history; she was previously fit and well.
On examination, we found the patient to have paroxysmal retrocollis with rotational head movements accompanied by intermittent contractions of the platysma muscle. The movements were variable in amplitude and frequency, and briefly suppressed while she tried to perform complex finger tapping tasks; they occasionally synchronised to the frequency of finger tapping (video). During walking, the patient had a variable step length and width—astasia-abasia—and additional variations to her head movements (figure). She had an exaggerated response to the pull test. The patient's neurological examination was otherwise normal.
We did no laboratory investigations or imaging since the clinical presentation met the pillars of inconsistence and incongruence, rendering a definitive diagnosis of functional movement disorder (FMD). With explanation and reassurance that unrecognised maladaptive thoughts and beliefs can predispose to the development of FMD, the patient relayed to us that she had a diminished sense of self-worth; she was eager to address this issue with a cognitive behavioural therapist.
After 2 months of therapy, the patient's atypical movements ceased (video).
FMD is not a diagnosis of exclusion and can be established by clearly demonstrating the two clinical pillars of the disorder: inconsistency (or variability or distractibility) of the amplitude, distribution, and severity of the phenotype; and incongruence with the wide spectrum of manifestations of other neurological disorders.
Features suggestive of psychological difficulties are neither necessary nor sufficient to make the diagnosis. Historical details (eg, the way the condition started) are also unnecessary in concluding that the patient has FMD. Additionally, laboratory or neuroimaging investigations are not needed.
Finally, delivering and explaining the diagnosis to the patient is a critical step in the care pathway.
Patients receiving reassurance and a clear appreciation and understanding of FMD increases the possibility of successful resolution of symptoms and concordance with cognitive, physical, and occupational therapies.

A 51-year-old woman with a 2-month history of exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, and low-grade fever presented to our rheumatology clinic. She had a medical history of well controlled hypertension, and had mechanic's hands (scaly, hyperkeratoic rash) and 3 out of 5 according to the Oxford scale for strength in deltoids and biceps.
Laboratory investigations found a creatine kinase concentration of 3193 IU/L (normal range 26–200 IU/L) and creatinine concentration of 90·2 μmol/L (normal range 35–106 μmol/L). Antinuclear antibodies were positive with a 1:160 titre (normal range <1:80) in a cytoplasmic pattern, anti-EJ antibody was positive (identified through immunoblotting), and a chest CT showed a fibrotic non-specific interstitial pneumonia pattern (figure A).
Considering the patient's presentation and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of anti-synthetase syndrome was made. She was treated with methylprednisolone (40 mg per day) and cyclosporine (50 mg twice per day) for five days, and monitored at regular intervals as an inpatient. Over 2 weeks after the initial treatment the patient's creatine kinase concentration decreased gradually; however, she began to show decreased urine output, her creatinine concentration increased to 600·3 μmol/L, her haemoglobin concentration dropped from 87 g/L to 73 g/L, and her platelet count gradually decreased from 266 × 109 per L to 78 × 109 per L. Furthermore, the patient developed abdominal pain with bloody stools 3 weeks after the initial treatment. Abdominal enhanced CT showed swelling of the small intestine wall, suggesting ischemic bowel disease (figure B). The patient had percutaneous renal biopsy, and the pathological results showed microthrombus formation in the glomerular capillary lumen, disintegration and shedding of tubular epithelial cells, and renal tubular cast formation (figure C–F), indicating thrombotic microangiopathy with acute renal tubular injury.
The patient continued glucocorticoid therapy but stopped cyclosporine (due to deteriorating kidney function and the risk of kidney damage caused by cyclosporine itself). Meanwhile, continuous renal replacement therapy, plasma exchange, and immunoglobulin infusion were performed, and rituximab was tried (2 × 500 mg intravenous infusions, each separated by 15 days) to treat both thrombotic microangiopathy and anti-synthetase syndrome. The patient's symptoms of ischemic bowel disease and changes in the blood system were improved; however, her impaired renal function did not recover and regular haemodialysis was performed during follow-up for 3 months.
Anti-synthetase syndrome is a subtype of idiopathic inflammatory myopathy, and has clinical features including interstitial lung disease, myositis, Raynaud's phenomenon, arthritis, mechanic's hands, and fever. Thrombotic microangiopathy rarely accompanies anti-synthetase syndrome; only about six cases of anti-synthetase syndrome with thrombotic microangiopathy have been reported, of which two cases had no or only mild kidney injury. However, the pathogenetic mechanisms that link anti-synthetase syndrome and thrombotic microangiopathy remain obscure. One hypothesis is that activation of the complement system might play a role in promoting anti-synthetase syndrome and thrombotic microangiopathy simultaneously. Other studies have suggested that, under certain circumstances, circulating autoantibodies in patients with autoimmune inflammatory muscle diseases (including anti-synthetase syndrome) might inhibit plasma von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease activity, which is another pathogenesis of thrombotic microangiopathy. Patients could need combination therapy to treat anti-synthetase syndrome with thrombotic microangiopathy, including plasma exchange, glucocorticoids, and immunosuppressive drugs. However, the combination of anti-synthetase syndrome with thrombotic microangiopathy is still difficult to treat and as such is associated with a poor survival rate.

A 67-year-old woman, who had a 4-month history of a sudden onset of intermittent jerking movements with contortions of her head and right arm, attended our specialist unit. She had been seen earlier at another hospital where neuroimaging and electroencephalography were reported as normal. And after the patient was told the diagnosis was probably “psychogenic spells”, she sought a further consultation.She had no notable medical history; she was previously fit and well.
On examination, we found the patient to have paroxysmal retrocollis with rotational head movements accompanied by intermittent contractions of the platysma muscle. The movements were variable in amplitude and frequency, and briefly suppressed while she tried to perform complex finger tapping tasks; they occasionally synchronised to the frequency of finger tapping (video). During walking, the patient had a variable step length and width—astasia-abasia—and additional variations to her head movements (figure). She had an exaggerated response to the pull test. The patient's neurological examination was otherwise normal.
We did no laboratory investigations or imaging since the clinical presentation met the pillars of inconsistence and incongruence, rendering a definitive diagnosis of functional movement disorder (FMD). With explanation and reassurance that unrecognised maladaptive thoughts and beliefs can predispose to the development of FMD, the patient relayed to us that she had a diminished sense of self-worth; she was eager to address this issue with a cognitive behavioural therapist.
After 2 months of therapy, the patient's atypical movements ceased (video).
FMD is not a diagnosis of exclusion and can be established by clearly demonstrating the two clinical pillars of the disorder: inconsistency (or variability or distractibility) of the amplitude, distribution, and severity of the phenotype; and incongruence with the wide spectrum of manifestations of other neurological disorders.
Features suggestive of psychological difficulties are neither necessary nor sufficient to make the diagnosis. Historical details (eg, the way the condition started) are also unnecessary in concluding that the patient has FMD. Additionally, laboratory or neuroimaging investigations are not needed.
Finally, delivering and explaining the diagnosis to the patient is a critical step in the care pathway.
Patients receiving reassurance and a clear appreciation and understanding of FMD increases the possibility of successful resolution of symptoms and concordance with cognitive, physical, and occupational therapies.

A 51-year-old woman with a 2-month history of exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, and low-grade fever presented to our rheumatology clinic. She had a medical history of well controlled hypertension, and had mechanic's hands (scaly, hyperkeratoic rash) and 3 out of 5 according to the Oxford scale for strength in deltoids and biceps.
Laboratory investigations found a creatine kinase concentration of 3193 IU/L (normal range 26–200 IU/L) and creatinine concentration of 90·2 μmol/L (normal range 35–106 μmol/L). Antinuclear antibodies were positive with a 1:160 titre (normal range <1:80) in a cytoplasmic pattern, anti-EJ antibody was positive (identified through immunoblotting), and a chest CT showed a fibrotic non-specific interstitial pneumonia pattern (figure A).
Considering the patient's presentation and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of anti-synthetase syndrome was made. She was treated with methylprednisolone (40 mg per day) and cyclosporine (50 mg twice per day) for five days, and monitored at regular intervals as an inpatient. Over 2 weeks after the initial treatment the patient's creatine kinase concentration decreased gradually; however, she began to show decreased urine output, her creatinine concentration increased to 600·3 μmol/L, her haemoglobin concentration dropped from 87 g/L to 73 g/L, and her platelet count gradually decreased from 266 × 109 per L to 78 × 109 per L. Furthermore, the patient developed abdominal pain with bloody stools 3 weeks after the initial treatment. Abdominal enhanced CT showed swelling of the small intestine wall, suggesting ischemic bowel disease (figure B). The patient had percutaneous renal biopsy, and the pathological results showed microthrombus formation in the glomerular capillary lumen, disintegration and shedding of tubular epithelial cells, and renal tubular cast formation (figure C–F), indicating thrombotic microangiopathy with acute renal tubular injury.
The patient continued glucocorticoid therapy but stopped cyclosporine (due to deteriorating kidney function and the risk of kidney damage caused by cyclosporine itself). Meanwhile, continuous renal replacement therapy, plasma exchange, and immunoglobulin infusion were performed, and rituximab was tried (2 × 500 mg intravenous infusions, each separated by 15 days) to treat both thrombotic microangiopathy and anti-synthetase syndrome. The patient's symptoms of ischemic bowel disease and changes in the blood system were improved; however, her impaired renal function did not recover and regular haemodialysis was performed during follow-up for 3 months.
Anti-synthetase syndrome is a subtype of idiopathic inflammatory myopathy, and has clinical features including interstitial lung disease, myositis, Raynaud's phenomenon, arthritis, mechanic's hands, and fever. Thrombotic microangiopathy rarely accompanies anti-synthetase syndrome; only about six cases of anti-synthetase syndrome with thrombotic microangiopathy have been reported, of which two cases had no or only mild kidney injury. However, the pathogenetic mechanisms that link anti-synthetase syndrome and thrombotic microangiopathy remain obscure. One hypothesis is that activation of the complement system might play a role in promoting anti-synthetase syndrome and thrombotic microangiopathy simultaneously. Other studies have suggested that, under certain circumstances, circulating autoantibodies in patients with autoimmune inflammatory muscle diseases (including anti-synthetase syndrome) might inhibit plasma von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease activity, which is another pathogenesis of thrombotic microangiopathy. Patients could need combination therapy to treat anti-synthetase syndrome with thrombotic microangiopathy, including plasma exchange, glucocorticoids, and immunosuppressive drugs. However, the combination of anti-synthetase syndrome with thrombotic microangiopathy is still difficult to treat and as such is associated with a poor survival rate.

A 76-year-old man who had a 2-day history being unwell—starting with sweating and a fever that then developed into delirium—was admitted to the emergency room of a local general hospital; he then had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure without recovering consciousness. The patient was transferred to our intensive care unit after orotracheal intubation and initiation of invasive mechanical ventilation.
1 month earlier, the patient had radiofrequency catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation refractory to both medication and electrical cardioversion. The patient had a medical history of atrial fibrillation, hypertension, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease; he was prescribed apixaban, bisoprolol, dapagliflozin, furosemide, and metformin.
On examination, the patient was in a coma—Glasgow Coma Score 6; pupils were reactive and symmetrical. He had no sensory or motor deficits or focal neurological signs. Blood pressure was 113/52 mm Hg, heart rate 83 beats per min, oxygen saturation was in typical range, and temperature was 39·6°C.
Laboratory investigations found a biological inflammatory syndrome (C-reactive protein concentration was 177 mg/L [typical range <10]; white blood cell count was 15 000 per mm [typical range 4000–10 000]; and troponin was 3309 ng/L [typical range <5]).
A CT scan of the patient's brain showed diffuse pneumocephalus (figure); brain ischaemia was confirmed by hyperintense signals on MRI FLAIR T2-weighted sequences (figure).
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy was immediately started which effectively dissolved the cerebral air embolism (appendix); the patient had two sessions, 24 h apart, in our hyperbaric chamber receiving invasive mechanical ventilation—3 atmospheres of pressure with the fraction of inspired oxygen at 100% for 2 h.
We suspected the cerebral air embolism had come from an atrio-oesophageal fistula by a process of elimination: none of the common sources of pneumocephalus—including an intravenous line, or a recent endoscopy or laparoscopy—were identified in our patient. The absence of any abnormalities on clinical examination and the recent history of catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation further added to our conviction of an atrio-oesophageal fistula.
A chest CT angiogram showed a filiform hypodense signal within the left atrium anterior to the opening of the right inferior pulmonary vein and extending to the posterior wall of the left atrium communicating with the oesophagus, suggestive of an atrio-oesophageal fistula (figure). Delayed phase contrast-enhanced CT scanning showed recurrence of an air bubble in the left atrium—confirming air leakage (figure).
The patient had surgery to close the fistula with oesophagostomy immediately on completion of the hyperbaric oxygen therapy and more than 24 h after the onset of symptoms. However, due to the presence of diffuse brain ischaemia seen on MRI done prior to the hyperbaric oxygen therapy and following discussion with the patient's relatives, active treatment was withdrawn. The patient died 1 week after admission to the intensive care unit.
Atrio-oesophageal fistula complicating catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation can—as in our patient—result in air embolism. Cerebral air embolism can result in acute ischaemia and cerebral oedema that may mimic the presentation of other stroke syndromes; prompt hyperbaric oxygen therapy is the mainstay of treatment.
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy decreases the size of bubbles because of an increase in ambient pressure and a rapid lowering of nitrogen levels that optimises oxygenation of poorly perfused brain tissue; it remains the gold standard treatment for cerebral air embolism with excellent results when initiated immediately.

input:
A 76-year-old man who had a 2-day history being unwell—starting with sweating and a fever that then developed into delirium—was admitted to the emergency room of a local general hospital; he then had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure without recovering consciousness. The patient was transferred to our intensive care unit after orotracheal intubation and initiation of invasive mechanical ventilation.
1 month earlier, the patient had radiofrequency catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation refractory to both medication and electrical cardioversion. The patient had a medical history of atrial fibrillation, hypertension, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease; he was prescribed apixaban, bisoprolol, dapagliflozin, furosemide, and metformin.
On examination, the patient was in a coma—Glasgow Coma Score 6; pupils were reactive and symmetrical. He had no sensory or motor deficits or focal neurological signs. Blood pressure was 113/52 mm Hg, heart rate 83 beats per min, oxygen saturation was in typical range, and temperature was 39·6°C.
Laboratory investigations found a biological inflammatory syndrome (C-reactive protein concentration was 177 mg/L [typical range <10]; white blood cell count was 15 000 per mm [typical range 4000–10 000]; and troponin was 3309 ng/L [typical range <5]).
A CT scan of the patient's brain showed diffuse pneumocephalus (figure); brain ischaemia was confirmed by hyperintense signals on MRI FLAIR T2-weighted sequences (figure).
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy was immediately started which effectively dissolved the cerebral air embolism (appendix); the patient had two sessions, 24 h apart, in our hyperbaric chamber receiving invasive mechanical ventilation—3 atmospheres of pressure with the fraction of inspired oxygen at 100% for 2 h.
We suspected the cerebral air embolism had come from an atrio-oesophageal fistula by a process of elimination: none of the common sources of pneumocephalus—including an intravenous line, or a recent endoscopy or laparoscopy—were identified in our patient. The absence of any abnormalities on clinical examination and the recent history of catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation further added to our conviction of an atrio-oesophageal fistula.
A chest CT angiogram showed a filiform hypodense signal within the left atrium anterior to the opening of the right inferior pulmonary vein and extending to the posterior wall of the left atrium communicating with the oesophagus, suggestive of an atrio-oesophageal fistula (figure). Delayed phase contrast-enhanced CT scanning showed recurrence of an air bubble in the left atrium—confirming air leakage (figure).
The patient had surgery to close the fistula with oesophagostomy immediately on completion of the hyperbaric oxygen therapy and more than 24 h after the onset of symptoms. However, due to the presence of diffuse brain ischaemia seen on MRI done prior to the hyperbaric oxygen therapy and following discussion with the patient's relatives, active treatment was withdrawn. The patient died 1 week after admission to the intensive care unit.
Atrio-oesophageal fistula complicating catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation can—as in our patient—result in air embolism. Cerebral air embolism can result in acute ischaemia and cerebral oedema that may mimic the presentation of other stroke syndromes; prompt hyperbaric oxygen therapy is the mainstay of treatment.
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy decreases the size of bubbles because of an increase in ambient pressure and a rapid lowering of nitrogen levels that optimises oxygenation of poorly perfused brain tissue; it remains the gold standard treatment for cerebral air embolism with excellent results when initiated immediately.

input:
A 76-year-old man who had a 2-day history being unwell—starting with sweating and a fever that then developed into delirium—was admitted to the emergency room of a local general hospital; he then had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure without recovering consciousness. The patient was transferred to our intensive care unit after orotracheal intubation and initiation of invasive mechanical ventilation.
1 month earlier, the patient had radiofrequency catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation refractory to both medication and electrical cardioversion. The patient had a medical history of atrial fibrillation, hypertension, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease; he was prescribed apixaban, bisoprolol, dapagliflozin, furosemide, and metformin.
On examination, the patient was in a coma—Glasgow Coma Score 6; pupils were reactive and symmetrical. He had no sensory or motor deficits or focal neurological signs. Blood pressure was 113/52 mm Hg, heart rate 83 beats per min, oxygen saturation was in typical range, and temperature was 39·6°C.
Laboratory investigations found a biological inflammatory syndrome (C-reactive protein concentration was 177 mg/L [typical range <10]; white blood cell count was 15 000 per mm [typical range 4000–10 000]; and troponin was 3309 ng/L [typical range <5]).
A CT scan of the patient's brain showed diffuse pneumocephalus (figure); brain ischaemia was confirmed by hyperintense signals on MRI FLAIR T2-weighted sequences (figure).
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy was immediately started which effectively dissolved the cerebral air embolism (appendix); the patient had two sessions, 24 h apart, in our hyperbaric chamber receiving invasive mechanical ventilation—3 atmospheres of pressure with the fraction of inspired oxygen at 100% for 2 h.
We suspected the cerebral air embolism had come from an atrio-oesophageal fistula by a process of elimination: none of the common sources of pneumocephalus—including an intravenous line, or a recent endoscopy or laparoscopy—were identified in our patient. The absence of any abnormalities on clinical examination and the recent history of catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation further added to our conviction of an atrio-oesophageal fistula.
A chest CT angiogram showed a filiform hypodense signal within the left atrium anterior to the opening of the right inferior pulmonary vein and extending to the posterior wall of the left atrium communicating with the oesophagus, suggestive of an atrio-oesophageal fistula (figure). Delayed phase contrast-enhanced CT scanning showed recurrence of an air bubble in the left atrium—confirming air leakage (figure).
The patient had surgery to close the fistula with oesophagostomy immediately on completion of the hyperbaric oxygen therapy and more than 24 h after the onset of symptoms. However, due to the presence of diffuse brain ischaemia seen on MRI done prior to the hyperbaric oxygen therapy and following discussion with the patient's relatives, active treatment was withdrawn. The patient died 1 week after admission to the intensive care unit.
Atrio-oesophageal fistula complicating catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation can—as in our patient—result in air embolism. Cerebral air embolism can result in acute ischaemia and cerebral oedema that may mimic the presentation of other stroke syndromes; prompt hyperbaric oxygen therapy is the mainstay of treatment.
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy decreases the size of bubbles because of an increase in ambient pressure and a rapid lowering of nitrogen levels that optimises oxygenation of poorly perfused brain tissue; it remains the gold standard treatment for cerebral air embolism with excellent results when initiated immediately.

input:
A 51-year-old woman with a 2-month history of exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, and low-grade fever presented to our rheumatology clinic. She had a medical history of well controlled hypertension, and had mechanic's hands (scaly, hyperkeratoic rash) and 3 out of 5 according to the Oxford scale for strength in deltoids and biceps.
Laboratory investigations found a creatine kinase concentration of 3193 IU/L (normal range 26–200 IU/L) and creatinine concentration of 90·2 μmol/L (normal range 35–106 μmol/L). Antinuclear antibodies were positive with a 1:160 titre (normal range <1:80) in a cytoplasmic pattern, anti-EJ antibody was positive (identified through immunoblotting), and a chest CT showed a fibrotic non-specific interstitial pneumonia pattern (figure A).
Considering the patient's presentation and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of anti-synthetase syndrome was made. She was treated with methylprednisolone (40 mg per day) and cyclosporine (50 mg twice per day) for five days, and monitored at regular intervals as an inpatient. Over 2 weeks after the initial treatment the patient's creatine kinase concentration decreased gradually; however, she began to show decreased urine output, her creatinine concentration increased to 600·3 μmol/L, her haemoglobin concentration dropped from 87 g/L to 73 g/L, and her platelet count gradually decreased from 266 × 109 per L to 78 × 109 per L. Furthermore, the patient developed abdominal pain with bloody stools 3 weeks after the initial treatment. Abdominal enhanced CT showed swelling of the small intestine wall, suggesting ischemic bowel disease (figure B). The patient had percutaneous renal biopsy, and the pathological results showed microthrombus formation in the glomerular capillary lumen, disintegration and shedding of tubular epithelial cells, and renal tubular cast formation (figure C–F), indicating thrombotic microangiopathy with acute renal tubular injury.
The patient continued glucocorticoid therapy but stopped cyclosporine (due to deteriorating kidney function and the risk of kidney damage caused by cyclosporine itself). Meanwhile, continuous renal replacement therapy, plasma exchange, and immunoglobulin infusion were performed, and rituximab was tried (2 × 500 mg intravenous infusions, each separated by 15 days) to treat both thrombotic microangiopathy and anti-synthetase syndrome. The patient's symptoms of ischemic bowel disease and changes in the blood system were improved; however, her impaired renal function did not recover and regular haemodialysis was performed during follow-up for 3 months.
Anti-synthetase syndrome is a subtype of idiopathic inflammatory myopathy, and has clinical features including interstitial lung disease, myositis, Raynaud's phenomenon, arthritis, mechanic's hands, and fever. Thrombotic microangiopathy rarely accompanies anti-synthetase syndrome; only about six cases of anti-synthetase syndrome with thrombotic microangiopathy have been reported, of which two cases had no or only mild kidney injury. However, the pathogenetic mechanisms that link anti-synthetase syndrome and thrombotic microangiopathy remain obscure. One hypothesis is that activation of the complement system might play a role in promoting anti-synthetase syndrome and thrombotic microangiopathy simultaneously. Other studies have suggested that, under certain circumstances, circulating autoantibodies in patients with autoimmune inflammatory muscle diseases (including anti-synthetase syndrome) might inhibit plasma von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease activity, which is another pathogenesis of thrombotic microangiopathy. Patients could need combination therapy to treat anti-synthetase syndrome with thrombotic microangiopathy, including plasma exchange, glucocorticoids, and immunosuppressive drugs. However, the combination of anti-synthetase syndrome with thrombotic microangiopathy is still difficult to treat and as such is associated with a poor survival rate.

A 34-year-old woman with a 2-year history of progressively worsening difficulties in walking, eating and swallowing, presented to our department. Additionally, the patient's sister reported observing unusual behaviours over the past 6 months: she said her sister had been taking her meals to eat alone in the bathroom and had crafted a doll from leaves gathered from local trees, referring to it as her son (figure). The patient had no previous medical history or family history of similar difficulties.
On examination, the patient was cachectic, drooling her saliva, and had multiple injuries and scars on her tongue, lower lips, and arms caused by self-biting (figure); she had abnormal—primarily choreatic—movements of her trunk and oromandibular region, involuntary vocalisations, and vocal tics (video 1). She also had involuntary jaw opening and dystonia—particularly during feeding (video 2). Limb examination showed mild bradykinesia, hypotonia, mild motor weakness, and reduced reflexes in all extremities.
Laboratory investigations found urea and electrolyte levels within normal range; liver enzymes were slightly elevated with alanine aminotransferase at 43 U/L (normal range 4–36 U/L) and aspartate aminotransferase at 74 U/L (normal range 8–33 U/L). Thyroid function was normal. Haemoglobin concentration was within the normal range at 12·1 g/dL (normal 11·0–14·0). The serum creatinine kinase level was elevated at 1 344 U/L (normal range for a woman is 26–192), and lactate dehydrogenase was raised at 269 UI/L (normal range for a woman is 100–240 UI/L). A blood smear showed that 15% of the red blood cells were acanthocytes (normal < 3%) (figure).
An MRI brain showed bilateral atrophy in the caudate nucleus and cortical atrophy in the frontal-parietal and occipital regions (figure). Nerve conduction studies showed axonal neuropathy affecting both sensory and motor neurons. Whole exome sequencing showed the patient to be a compound heterozygous carrier of two novel pathogenic loss-of-function variants in the VPS13A gene, namely: NM_033305.3(VPS13A): c.2425C>T (p. Gln809*) and NM_033305.3(VPS13A): c.5072delA (p.Asp1691fs). No other pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were found in any genes previously associated with adult-onset dystonia, chorea, or related movement disorders. Considering the findings together, we diagnosed VPS13A disease. Initially, we prescribed oral haloperidol with no response; she was switched to oral risperidone and tetrabenazine resulting in some improvement in both psychiatric and motor symptoms.
After 1 month, the patient was allowed home and followed up every 4 weeks as an outpatient. The patient's condition continued to deteriorate, with significant weight loss and worsening of both motor and psychiatric symptoms. At last review, she was receiving palliative care.
VPS13A disease—previously known as Chorea-acanthocytosis—is an autosomal recessive condition resulting from mutations in the VPS13A gene, which encodes a lipid transfer protein. Patients typically have progressive symptoms of chorea, oromandibular dyskinesia, Parkinsonism, neuropsychiatric issues, diminished or absent tendon deep reflexes and seizures. Symptoms usually begin around 30 years of age. Prognosis is poor, and the disease is ultimately fatal. Additional features indicative of VSP13A disease include elevated creatinine kinase levels, transaminitis, acanthocytocytosis, and caudate atrophy. The differential diagnoses include XK disease—also known as McLeod syndrome. Both VSP13A and XK disease fall under the umbrella of neuroacanthocytosis syndrome: XK disease is an X-linked disorder predominantly affecting middle-aged men.
Huntington's disease, Huntington's disease-like 2, Wilson's disease, and other rare adult-onset choreatic disorders, including neuroferritinopathy, aceruloplasminaemia, and c9orf72-related disorders, should also be considered as other possible differential diagnoses.
In Africa, choreatic movement disorders—seen in our patient, which we believe is the first genetically confirmed case of VPS13A disease in a black patient from sub-Saharan Africa—are often underdiagnosed; many cases are referred to traditional healers and customary medicine.

A 34-year-old woman with a 2-year history of progressively worsening difficulties in walking, eating and swallowing, presented to our department. Additionally, the patient's sister reported observing unusual behaviours over the past 6 months: she said her sister had been taking her meals to eat alone in the bathroom and had crafted a doll from leaves gathered from local trees, referring to it as her son (figure). The patient had no previous medical history or family history of similar difficulties.
On examination, the patient was cachectic, drooling her saliva, and had multiple injuries and scars on her tongue, lower lips, and arms caused by self-biting (figure); she had abnormal—primarily choreatic—movements of her trunk and oromandibular region, involuntary vocalisations, and vocal tics (video 1). She also had involuntary jaw opening and dystonia—particularly during feeding (video 2). Limb examination showed mild bradykinesia, hypotonia, mild motor weakness, and reduced reflexes in all extremities.
Laboratory investigations found urea and electrolyte levels within normal range; liver enzymes were slightly elevated with alanine aminotransferase at 43 U/L (normal range 4–36 U/L) and aspartate aminotransferase at 74 U/L (normal range 8–33 U/L). Thyroid function was normal. Haemoglobin concentration was within the normal range at 12·1 g/dL (normal 11·0–14·0). The serum creatinine kinase level was elevated at 1 344 U/L (normal range for a woman is 26–192), and lactate dehydrogenase was raised at 269 UI/L (normal range for a woman is 100–240 UI/L). A blood smear showed that 15% of the red blood cells were acanthocytes (normal < 3%) (figure).
An MRI brain showed bilateral atrophy in the caudate nucleus and cortical atrophy in the frontal-parietal and occipital regions (figure). Nerve conduction studies showed axonal neuropathy affecting both sensory and motor neurons. Whole exome sequencing showed the patient to be a compound heterozygous carrier of two novel pathogenic loss-of-function variants in the VPS13A gene, namely: NM_033305.3(VPS13A): c.2425C>T (p. Gln809*) and NM_033305.3(VPS13A): c.5072delA (p.Asp1691fs). No other pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were found in any genes previously associated with adult-onset dystonia, chorea, or related movement disorders. Considering the findings together, we diagnosed VPS13A disease. Initially, we prescribed oral haloperidol with no response; she was switched to oral risperidone and tetrabenazine resulting in some improvement in both psychiatric and motor symptoms.
After 1 month, the patient was allowed home and followed up every 4 weeks as an outpatient. The patient's condition continued to deteriorate, with significant weight loss and worsening of both motor and psychiatric symptoms. At last review, she was receiving palliative care.
VPS13A disease—previously known as Chorea-acanthocytosis—is an autosomal recessive condition resulting from mutations in the VPS13A gene, which encodes a lipid transfer protein. Patients typically have progressive symptoms of chorea, oromandibular dyskinesia, Parkinsonism, neuropsychiatric issues, diminished or absent tendon deep reflexes and seizures. Symptoms usually begin around 30 years of age. Prognosis is poor, and the disease is ultimately fatal. Additional features indicative of VSP13A disease include elevated creatinine kinase levels, transaminitis, acanthocytocytosis, and caudate atrophy. The differential diagnoses include XK disease—also known as McLeod syndrome. Both VSP13A and XK disease fall under the umbrella of neuroacanthocytosis syndrome: XK disease is an X-linked disorder predominantly affecting middle-aged men.
Huntington's disease, Huntington's disease-like 2, Wilson's disease, and other rare adult-onset choreatic disorders, including neuroferritinopathy, aceruloplasminaemia, and c9orf72-related disorders, should also be considered as other possible differential diagnoses.
In Africa, choreatic movement disorders—seen in our patient, which we believe is the first genetically confirmed case of VPS13A disease in a black patient from sub-Saharan Africa—are often underdiagnosed; many cases are referred to traditional healers and customary medicine.

A 31-year-old woman reporting a headache and epigastric pain for the past 12 h attended our unit. She had a history of gestational hypertension and 5 days earlier had a caesarean section at term; there had been no post-partum haemorrhage and she had been allowed home. The patient's haemoglobin concentration had been 11·7 g/dL (normal >10 post partum), and the serum creatinine concentration 48 μmol/L (normal <90); she was normotensive and on no medication.On examination, we found the patient to be lethargic: her blood pressure was 193/102 mm Hg, and she had hyper-reflexia and bilateral clonus. A spot urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio was 57 mg/mol (normal <30), her haemoglobin concentration was 9·5 g/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 764 mIU/L (normal <600), alanine transaminase 127 IU/L (normal <70), and the serum creatinine concentration 115·0 μmol/L were raised: indicating possible post-partum pre-eclampsia with partial HELLP—Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets—syndrome and acute kidney injury.
We started the patient on fluids, and intravenous labetalol and magnesium sulphate. Over the next 24 h, she passed 10·9 L of clear urine despite a total fluid intake of 3·7 L. Laboratory investigations for polyuria (appendix) excluded osmotic diuresis and post-partum hypopituitarism; however, her urine osmolality was 228 mOsmol/kg (normal >600), suggestive of diabetes insipidus causing pure-water loss.
A water deprivation test showed an inability to concentrate urine fully: the plasma osmolality reached 301 mOsmol/kg—maximum endogenous antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release occurs above the threshold of 295 mOsmol/kg—and her urine osmolality failed to rise sufficiently (figure). A desmopressin test with a vasopressinase-resistant ADH analogue found urine osmolality increased by 13% to 426 mOsmol/kg (figure). We did not assess plasma ADH or copeptin levels because the polyuria resolved when liver function recovered. She was allowed home 4 days later; her blood pressure and urine were normal.
Taken together, the findings suggested a partial central diabetes insipidus (DI) due to a transient deficiency in ADH caused by an excess of vasopressinase resulting from impaired liver function because of the HELLP syndrome. The polyuria abated when the transaminitis resolved. Further, we believe the increase in urine concentration after desmopressin was small because of wash-out of the renal medullary concentrating gradient from water diuresis.
DI is characterised by a failure of the kidneys to conserve water due either to ADH deficiency (central DI) or resistance (nephrogenic DI) resulting in hypotonic polyuria. In pregnancy, DI occurs when the breakdown of ADH by placental vasopressinase is enhanced because of either increased production in multiple pregnancy or—as in our patient—decreased hepatic catabolism. Gestational DI commonly occurs in the third trimester, coinciding with peak placental vasopressinase synthesis, and rarely in the early post-partum period.
Given pre-eclampsia—the most frequent cause of acute kidney injury in pregnancy—typically results in oliguria, a good urine output in such patients may be falsely reassuring: if the urine output is above 3L per day and urine osmolality is less than 300 mOsmol/kg, gestational DI should be considered.
Finally, if gestational DI is missed, patients are at high risk of severe hypernatraemia resulting from the standard pre-eclampsia management of fluid restriction, and seizures, as the magnesium sulphate will be rapidly excreted. Therefore, in the context of polyuria, it might be necessary to increase fluids; the magnesium sulphate infusion rate might also need to be increased and levels monitored for toxicity (video).

A 34-year-old woman with a 2-year history of progressively worsening difficulties in walking, eating and swallowing, presented to our department. Additionally, the patient's sister reported observing unusual behaviours over the past 6 months: she said her sister had been taking her meals to eat alone in the bathroom and had crafted a doll from leaves gathered from local trees, referring to it as her son (figure). The patient had no previous medical history or family history of similar difficulties.
On examination, the patient was cachectic, drooling her saliva, and had multiple injuries and scars on her tongue, lower lips, and arms caused by self-biting (figure); she had abnormal—primarily choreatic—movements of her trunk and oromandibular region, involuntary vocalisations, and vocal tics (video 1). She also had involuntary jaw opening and dystonia—particularly during feeding (video 2). Limb examination showed mild bradykinesia, hypotonia, mild motor weakness, and reduced reflexes in all extremities.
Laboratory investigations found urea and electrolyte levels within normal range; liver enzymes were slightly elevated with alanine aminotransferase at 43 U/L (normal range 4–36 U/L) and aspartate aminotransferase at 74 U/L (normal range 8–33 U/L). Thyroid function was normal. Haemoglobin concentration was within the normal range at 12·1 g/dL (normal 11·0–14·0). The serum creatinine kinase level was elevated at 1 344 U/L (normal range for a woman is 26–192), and lactate dehydrogenase was raised at 269 UI/L (normal range for a woman is 100–240 UI/L). A blood smear showed that 15% of the red blood cells were acanthocytes (normal < 3%) (figure).
An MRI brain showed bilateral atrophy in the caudate nucleus and cortical atrophy in the frontal-parietal and occipital regions (figure). Nerve conduction studies showed axonal neuropathy affecting both sensory and motor neurons. Whole exome sequencing showed the patient to be a compound heterozygous carrier of two novel pathogenic loss-of-function variants in the VPS13A gene, namely: NM_033305.3(VPS13A): c.2425C>T (p. Gln809*) and NM_033305.3(VPS13A): c.5072delA (p.Asp1691fs). No other pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were found in any genes previously associated with adult-onset dystonia, chorea, or related movement disorders. Considering the findings together, we diagnosed VPS13A disease. Initially, we prescribed oral haloperidol with no response; she was switched to oral risperidone and tetrabenazine resulting in some improvement in both psychiatric and motor symptoms.
After 1 month, the patient was allowed home and followed up every 4 weeks as an outpatient. The patient's condition continued to deteriorate, with significant weight loss and worsening of both motor and psychiatric symptoms. At last review, she was receiving palliative care.
VPS13A disease—previously known as Chorea-acanthocytosis—is an autosomal recessive condition resulting from mutations in the VPS13A gene, which encodes a lipid transfer protein. Patients typically have progressive symptoms of chorea, oromandibular dyskinesia, Parkinsonism, neuropsychiatric issues, diminished or absent tendon deep reflexes and seizures. Symptoms usually begin around 30 years of age. Prognosis is poor, and the disease is ultimately fatal. Additional features indicative of VSP13A disease include elevated creatinine kinase levels, transaminitis, acanthocytocytosis, and caudate atrophy. The differential diagnoses include XK disease—also known as McLeod syndrome. Both VSP13A and XK disease fall under the umbrella of neuroacanthocytosis syndrome: XK disease is an X-linked disorder predominantly affecting middle-aged men.
Huntington's disease, Huntington's disease-like 2, Wilson's disease, and other rare adult-onset choreatic disorders, including neuroferritinopathy, aceruloplasminaemia, and c9orf72-related disorders, should also be considered as other possible differential diagnoses.

A 31-year-old woman reporting a headache and epigastric pain for the past 12 h attended our unit. She had a history of gestational hypertension and 5 days earlier had a caesarean section at term; there had been no post-partum haemorrhage and she had been allowed home. The patient's haemoglobin concentration had been 11·7 g/dL (normal >10 post partum), and the serum creatinine concentration 48 μmol/L (normal <90); she was normotensive and on no medication.On examination, we found the patient to be lethargic: her blood pressure was 193/102 mm Hg, and she had hyper-reflexia and bilateral clonus. A spot urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio was 57 mg/mol (normal <30), her haemoglobin concentration was 9·5 g/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 764 mIU/L (normal <600), alanine transaminase 127 IU/L (normal <70), and the serum creatinine concentration 115·0 μmol/L were raised: indicating possible post-partum pre-eclampsia with partial HELLP—Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets—syndrome and acute kidney injury.
We started the patient on fluids, and intravenous labetalol and magnesium sulphate. Over the next 24 h, she passed 10·9 L of clear urine despite a total fluid intake of 3·7 L. Laboratory investigations for polyuria (appendix) excluded osmotic diuresis and post-partum hypopituitarism; however, her urine osmolality was 228 mOsmol/kg (normal >600), suggestive of diabetes insipidus causing pure-water loss.
A water deprivation test showed an inability to concentrate urine fully: the plasma osmolality reached 301 mOsmol/kg—maximum endogenous antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release occurs above the threshold of 295 mOsmol/kg—and her urine osmolality failed to rise sufficiently (figure). A desmopressin test with a vasopressinase-resistant ADH analogue found urine osmolality increased by 13% to 426 mOsmol/kg (figure). We did not assess plasma ADH or copeptin levels because the polyuria resolved when liver function recovered. She was allowed home 4 days later; her blood pressure and urine were normal.
Taken together, the findings suggested a partial central diabetes insipidus (DI) due to a transient deficiency in ADH caused by an excess of vasopressinase resulting from impaired liver function because of the HELLP syndrome. The polyuria abated when the transaminitis resolved. Further, we believe the increase in urine concentration after desmopressin was small because of wash-out of the renal medullary concentrating gradient from water diuresis.
DI is characterised by a failure of the kidneys to conserve water due either to ADH deficiency (central DI) or resistance (nephrogenic DI) resulting in hypotonic polyuria. In pregnancy, DI occurs when the breakdown of ADH by placental vasopressinase is enhanced because of either increased production in multiple pregnancy or—as in our patient—decreased hepatic catabolism. Gestational DI commonly occurs in the third trimester, coinciding with peak placental vasopressinase synthesis, and rarely in the early post-partum period.
Given pre-eclampsia—the most frequent cause of acute kidney injury in pregnancy—typically results in oliguria, a good urine output in such patients may be falsely reassuring: if the urine output is above 3L per day and urine osmolality is less than 300 mOsmol/kg, gestational DI should be considered.
Finally, if gestational DI is missed, patients are at high risk of severe hypernatraemia resulting from the standard pre-eclampsia management of fluid restriction, and seizures, as the magnesium sulphate will be rapidly excreted. Therefore, in the context of polyuria, it might be necessary to increase fluids; the magnesium sulphate infusion rate might also need to be increased and levels monitored for toxicity (video).

input: An 85-year-old man was admitted to hospital with a 5-day history of fever and neck pain. He had a 12-year history of chronic kidney disease and gouty arthritis; however, the patient did not take urate lowering drugs. On admission to hospital, physical examination revealed neck pain and stiffness. He had a blood pressure of 140/102 mm Hg, pulse rate of 95 per min, respiration rate of 18 breaths per min, and body temperature of 38°C. Laboratory results revealed a white blood cell count of 11 200 cells per mm3 (reference 4 000–10 000) and C-reactive protein level of 12·26 mg/dL (reference 0·0–0·3). MRI findings suggested cervical osteomyelitis and meningitis (figure A). Cervical spine CT revealed curvilinear calcifications of the transverse ligament of the atlas (figure B). After assessing blood cultures, ceftriaxone (2 g every 12 h) and vancomycin (1750 mg loading, followed by 750 mg every 48 h) were administered intravenously as empirical antibiotic treatments. On the second day of admission, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis did not reveal meningitis (white blood cell count 8 cells per μL, glucose concentration 79 mg/dL, and protein concentration 168 mg/dL), and CSF culture and molecular tests were negative for bacteria and mycobacteria. The patient was diagnosed with crowned dens syndrome and administered 20 mg prednisolone, and his symptoms dramatically improved. However, CSF examination under polarising microscopy revealed monosodium urate crystals (figure C). Dual-energy CT confirmed the calcifications to be monosodium urate crystals (figure D). The patient's uric acid concentration was 10·4 mg/dL (reference 0–7·0) and subcutaneous tophi were not apparent on physical examination 9 days after hospital admission. Crowned dens syndrome is a rare finding in calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease and could be clinically similar to meningitis, so it should be suspected when the evidence for infection is unclear. Our patient had a history of gout, and monosodium urate crystals were confirmed by CSF analysis and dual-energy CT, suggesting that the symptoms were caused by gout flare in the cervical spine. Thus, physicians should consider that intrathecal monosodium urate crystal formation can cause meningitis-like symptoms in patients with gout history.

A 31-year-old woman reporting a headache and epigastric pain for the past 12 h attended our unit. She had a history of gestational hypertension and 5 days earlier had a caesarean section at term; there had been no post-partum haemorrhage and she had been allowed home. The patient's haemoglobin concentration had been 11·7 g/dL (normal >10 post partum), and the serum creatinine concentration 48 μmol/L (normal <90); she was normotensive and on no medication.On examination, we found the patient to be lethargic: her blood pressure was 193/102 mm Hg, and she had hyper-reflexia and bilateral clonus. A spot urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio was 57 mg/mol (normal <30), her haemoglobin concentration was 9·5 g/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 764 mIU/L (normal <600), alanine transaminase 127 IU/L (normal <70), and the serum creatinine concentration 115·0 μmol/L were raised: indicating possible post-partum pre-eclampsia with partial HELLP—Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets—syndrome and acute kidney injury.
We started the patient on fluids, and intravenous labetalol and magnesium sulphate. Over the next 24 h, she passed 10·9 L of clear urine despite a total fluid intake of 3·7 L. Laboratory investigations for polyuria (appendix) excluded osmotic diuresis and post-partum hypopituitarism; however, her urine osmolality was 228 mOsmol/kg (normal >600), suggestive of diabetes insipidus causing pure-water loss.
A water deprivation test showed an inability to concentrate urine fully: the plasma osmolality reached 301 mOsmol/kg—maximum endogenous antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release occurs above the threshold of 295 mOsmol/kg—and her urine osmolality failed to rise sufficiently (figure). A desmopressin test with a vasopressinase-resistant ADH analogue found urine osmolality increased by 13% to 426 mOsmol/kg (figure). We did not assess plasma ADH or copeptin levels because the polyuria resolved when liver function recovered. She was allowed home 4 days later; her blood pressure and urine were normal.
Taken together, the findings suggested a partial central diabetes insipidus (DI) due to a transient deficiency in ADH caused by an excess of vasopressinase resulting from impaired liver function because of the HELLP syndrome. The polyuria abated when the transaminitis resolved. Further, we believe the increase in urine concentration after desmopressin was small because of wash-out of the renal medullary concentrating gradient from water diuresis.
DI is characterised by a failure of the kidneys to conserve water due either to ADH deficiency (central DI) or resistance (nephrogenic DI) resulting in hypotonic polyuria. In pregnancy, DI occurs when the breakdown of ADH by placental vasopressinase is enhanced because of either increased production in multiple pregnancy or—as in our patient—decreased hepatic catabolism. Gestational DI commonly occurs in the third trimester, coinciding with peak placental vasopressinase synthesis, and rarely in the early post-partum period.
Given pre-eclampsia—the most frequent cause of acute kidney injury in pregnancy—typically results in oliguria, a good urine output in such patients may be falsely reassuring: if the urine output is above 3L per day and urine osmolality is less than 300 mOsmol/kg, gestational DI should be considered.
Finally, if gestational DI is missed, patients are at high risk of severe hypernatraemia resulting from the standard pre-eclampsia management of fluid restriction, and seizures, as the magnesium sulphate will be rapidly excreted. Therefore, in the context of polyuria, it might be necessary to increase fluids; the magnesium sulphate infusion rate might also need to be increased and levels monitored for toxicity (video).

input: An 85-year-old man was admitted to hospital with a 5-day history of fever and neck pain. He had a 12-year history of chronic kidney disease and gouty arthritis; however, the patient did not take urate lowering drugs. On admission to hospital, physical examination revealed neck pain and stiffness. He had a blood pressure of 140/102 mm Hg, pulse rate of 95 per min, respiration rate of 18 breaths per min, and body temperature of 38°C. Laboratory results revealed a white blood cell count of 11 200 cells per mm3 (reference 4 000–10 000) and C-reactive protein level of 12·26 mg/dL (reference 0·0–0·3). MRI findings suggested cervical osteomyelitis and meningitis (figure A). Cervical spine CT revealed curvilinear calcifications of the transverse ligament of the atlas (figure B). After assessing blood cultures, ceftriaxone (2 g every 12 h) and vancomycin (1750 mg loading, followed by 750 mg every 48 h) were administered intravenously as empirical antibiotic treatments. On the second day of admission, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis did not reveal meningitis (white blood cell count 8 cells per μL, glucose concentration 79 mg/dL, and protein concentration 168 mg/dL), and CSF culture and molecular tests were negative for bacteria and mycobacteria. The patient was diagnosed with crowned dens syndrome and administered 20 mg prednisolone, and his symptoms dramatically improved. However, CSF examination under polarising microscopy revealed monosodium urate crystals (figure C). Dual-energy CT confirmed the calcifications to be monosodium urate crystals (figure D). The patient's uric acid concentration was 10·4 mg/dL (reference 0–7·0) and subcutaneous tophi were not apparent on physical examination 9 days after hospital admission. Crowned dens syndrome is a rare finding in calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease and could be clinically similar to meningitis, so it should be suspected when the evidence for infection is unclear. Our patient had a history of gout, and monosodium urate crystals were confirmed by CSF analysis and dual-energy CT, suggesting that the symptoms were caused by gout flare in the cervical spine. Thus, physicians should consider that intrathecal monosodium urate crystal formation can cause meningitis-like symptoms in patients with gout history.

Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography showed a normal appearing liver with four prominent retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Laboratory tests on follow-up 6 weeks later showed an AST concentration of 144 U/L, an ALT concentration of 222 U/L, a total bilirubin concentration of 15·0 mg/dL, a direct bilirubin concentration of 9·1 mg/dL, and an ALP concentration of 866 U/L with a positive antimitochondrial antibody (AMA) at 1:320. Percutaneous liver biopsy showed organising microabscesses, mild mixed portal inflammation with bile duct damage, endotheliitis of portal veins, and mild lobular mixed inflammation (figure A, B). After biopsy, she developed a hyperpigmented papulosquamous rash affecting bilateral palms and forearms (figure C). Serum rapid plasma reagin titre was 1:32768 with a positive serum test for syphilis IgG and a negative HIV serological test. She was treated with a 2-week course of continuous intravenous benzylpenicillin 24 million units per day, with resolution of liver chemistries 1 month later. Although Warthin-Starry stain of her liver biopsy was negative for spirochaetes, the Centers for Diseases Control and Prevention reported positive Treponema spp immunohistochemistry confirming syphilitic hepatitis.Liver abnormalities characterised by a disproportionally elevated ALP concentration and normal or mildly increased bilirubin and aminotransferases are reported in 30–40% of early syphilis cases, and rapidly return to normal with antibiotic treatment. Understanding of the pathophysiology of syphilitic hepatitis is hampered by an inability to culture the organism, but it might be due to dissemination of spirochaetes in the liver, as shown by its presence on biopsy samples. Syphilis should be considered in the evaluation of hepatic disease, especially in patients with HIV, because of high rates of co-infection. Notably, AMA positivity that clears with antibiotic treatment has previously been reported in syphilitic hepatitis. There are nine distinct mitochondrial autoantigens (M1–9), of which M2 is specific for primary biliary cholangitis. In syphilis, autoantibodies against cardiolipin (M1) explain the positive AMA results. The M1 and M2 autoantibodies can be distinguished with an M2-specific ELISA test, if needed, to rule out a diagnosis of primary biliary cholangitis.

input:
An 18-year-old man was referred to our hospital for a planned total hip replacement. He had a long history of reduced mobility and pain in his left hip because of a developmental bone disorder, dysplasia epiphysealis hemimelica (DEH). The teenager was first suspected of having DEH following a consultation when he was 10 years old, but because of his young age, the medical team at the time decided to manage his condition conservatively. They were concerned a more interventionist approach was inappropriate at a young age as he had manageable symptoms and delaying hip replacement surgery would allow him to reach skeletal maturity.We recommended that he have the surgery because he had stopped growing and he had reached his maximum height. Also, investigations of his hip had shown that the joint had become progressively more damaged with the result that both his pain and mobility had become significantly worse. During the surgery, the head of the patient's femur was found to be extremely enlarged with concomitant stretching of the joint capsule and surrounding muscles. The implant required appropriate increased offset to avoid instability of the joint. Postoperatively, he was given analgesia and venous thromboembolic prophylaxis. He was also given information on precautions to take to minimise the risk of dislocating the hip joint while the capsule healed. Pleasingly, at follow-up, the patient reported an improvement in both his quality of life and mobility.
DEH is a rare childhood osteochondroma characterised by asymmetrical enlargement of the epiphyseal cartilage of the long bones, usually involving the lower limbs and most commonly occurring in the ankle region. Patients present with painless swelling on one side of the joint, a limitation of movement, angular deformity, regional muscle wasting, and occasionally recurrent locking of the joint.
When assessing any child presenting with chronic hip pain, a careful examination is mandatory with attention being paid to any deformity, asymmetry, and discrepancy between the length of the affected and unaffected limbs. It is also crucial to obtain images of the affected area. Even though it is rare—DEH, must be considered as a differential diagnosis in anyone presenting with chronic hip pain. Other important conditions to consider include Perthes disease, skeletal dysplasias, tumours, and septic and inflammatory disorders.
Assessment of the extent of a patient's pain and the need to wait until skeletal maturity is necessary as often the only feasible long-term solution is total hip replacement. In our case, the patient's pain leading up to surgery was still manageable conservatively and rushing to surgery would not have been beneficial in the long term.
