Full viral hepatitis serological tests and anti-smooth muscle antibodies were negative but anti-nuclear antibodies were positive at 1:640 with a normal IgG concentration. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography showed a normal appearing liver with four prominent retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Laboratory tests on follow-up 6 weeks later showed an AST concentration of 144 U/L, an ALT concentration of 222 U/L, a total bilirubin concentration of 15·0 mg/dL, a direct bilirubin concentration of 9·1 mg/dL, and an ALP concentration of 866 U/L with a positive antimitochondrial antibody (AMA) at 1:320. Percutaneous liver biopsy showed organising microabscesses, mild mixed portal inflammation with bile duct damage, endotheliitis of portal veins, and mild lobular mixed inflammation (figure A, B). After biopsy, she developed a hyperpigmented papulosquamous rash affecting bilateral palms and forearms (figure C). Serum rapid plasma reagin titre was 1:32768 with a positive serum test for syphilis IgG and a negative HIV serological test. She was treated with a 2-week course of continuous intravenous benzylpenicillin 24 million units per day, with resolution of liver chemistries 1 month later. Although Warthin-Starry stain of her liver biopsy was negative for spirochaetes, the Centers for Diseases Control and Prevention reported positive Treponema spp immunohistochemistry confirming syphilitic hepatitis.Liver abnormalities characterised by a disproportionally elevated ALP concentration and normal or mildly increased bilirubin and aminotransferases are reported in 30–40% of early syphilis cases, and rapidly return to normal with antibiotic treatment. Understanding of the pathophysiology of syphilitic hepatitis is hampered by an inability to culture the organism, but it might be due to dissemination of spirochaetes in the liver, as shown by its presence on biopsy samples. Syphilis should be considered in the evaluation of hepatic disease, especially in patients with HIV, because of high rates of co-infection. Notably, AMA positivity that clears with antibiotic treatment has previously been reported in syphilitic hepatitis. There are nine distinct mitochondrial autoantigens (M1–9), of which M2 is specific for primary biliary cholangitis. In syphilis, autoantibodies against cardiolipin (M1) explain the positive AMA results. The M1 and M2 autoantibodies can be distinguished with an M2-specific ELISA test, if needed, to rule out a diagnosis of primary biliary cholangitis.

An 18-year-old man was referred to our hospital for a planned total hip replacement. He had a long history of reduced mobility and pain in his left hip because of a developmental bone disorder, dysplasia epiphysealis hemimelica (DEH). The teenager was first suspected of having DEH following a consultation when he was 10 years old, but because of his young age, the medical team at the time decided to manage his condition conservatively. They were concerned a more interventionist approach was inappropriate at a young age as he had manageable symptoms and delaying hip replacement surgery would allow him to reach skeletal maturity.We recommended that he have the surgery because he had stopped growing and he had reached his maximum height. Also, investigations of his hip had shown that the joint had become progressively more damaged with the result that both his pain and mobility had become significantly worse. During the surgery, the head of the patient's femur was found to be extremely enlarged with concomitant stretching of the joint capsule and surrounding muscles. The implant required appropriate increased offset to avoid instability of the joint. Postoperatively, he was given analgesia and venous thromboembolic prophylaxis. He was also given information on precautions to take to minimise the risk of dislocating the hip joint while the capsule healed. Pleasingly, at follow-up, the patient reported an improvement in both his quality of life and mobility.
DEH is a rare childhood osteochondroma characterised by asymmetrical enlargement of the epiphyseal cartilage of the long bones, usually involving the lower limbs and most commonly occurring in the ankle region. Patients present with painless swelling on one side of the joint, a limitation of movement, angular deformity, regional muscle wasting, and occasionally recurrent locking of the joint.
When assessing any child presenting with chronic hip pain, a careful examination is mandatory with attention being paid to any deformity, asymmetry, and discrepancy between the length of the affected and unaffected limbs. It is also crucial to obtain images of the affected area. Even though it is rare—DEH, must be considered as a differential diagnosis in anyone presenting with chronic hip pain. Other important conditions to consider include Perthes disease, skeletal dysplasias, tumours, and septic and inflammatory disorders.
Assessment of the extent of a patient's pain and the need to wait until skeletal maturity is necessary as often the only feasible long-term solution is total hip replacement. In our case, the patient's pain leading up to surgery was still manageable conservatively and rushing to surgery would not have been beneficial in the long term.

A 50-year-old woman attended our emergency department with a 3-day history of severe back pain and a severe headache. 10 days earlier she had received the first dose of vaccine against SARS-CoV-2—ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 (AstraZeneca). The patient had no significant medical history—specifically no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism. She was not pregnant, she did not take an oral contraceptive, and did not have a hormone-eluting intrauterine device in situ.On examination, the patient was afebrile, her peripheral oxygen saturation was 99% (with a 21% fraction of inspired oxygen), blood pressure was 130/80 mm Hg, heart rate was 80 beats per min, and body-mass index was 20 kg/m2. She had no obvious haematomas or petechial haemorrhages; she reported no chest pain, shortness of breath, swelling, redness, pallor, or cold in any limb.
Laboratory investigations showed a severe thrombocytopenia of 27 × 109 per L (normal 140–440). 3 days earlier it had been 163 × 109 per L. Serum D-dimer concentration was significantly elevated at greater than 33 mg/L (normal <0·5), fibrinogen concentration was 121 mg/dL (normal 210–400), coagulation factor XIII activity was 63% (normal >70%), and both prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) were normal. Haemoglobin concentration was 10·8 g/dL (normal 12·0–15·3); microcytic–hypochromic red blood cell indices, a low ferritin concentration of 12 ng/mL (normal 22–112), and a soluble transferrin receptor concentration of 10·1 mg/L (normal 1·78–4·59) indicated an iron deficiency anaemia. No schistocytes were detected. A thrombophilia screen—including resistance to activated protein C, and protein C and protein S activity—was negative; no antibodies to platelet factor 4 were found and genetic testing for prothrombin mutations was negative.
Creatinine, electrolytes, lactate dehydrogenase, aspartate aminotransferase, and alanine aminotransferase concentrations were within normal range. SARS-CoV-2 antigen and RT-PCR were negative on a nasopharyngeal swab. Tests for hantaviruses, HIV, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, and antiphospholipid antibodies (cardiolipin, β2 glycoprotein, and lupus) were negative.
We undertook consecutive thrombelastography, which indicated a stable clot pattern—despite the low platelet count and low fibrinogen concentration, and excluded fibrinolysis—both primary and secondary.
Contrast-enhanced MRI of the patient's abdomen and pelvis showed multifocal thrombus formations in the pelvic region—including bilateral thrombi in the parauterine venous plexus, a superficial vein of the left gluteus maximus muscle, and left presacral and lumbar veins (figure; appendix).
CT pulmonary angiography showed a subsegmental embolus in the posterior–basal right lower lobe (figure). CT cerebral venography and compression ultrasound of both legs showed no abnormalities—neither cerebral venous sinus thrombosis nor deep vein thrombosis.
We assumed the diagnosis was a vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia and administered high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) followed by a second dose 24 h later, together with dexamethasone 40 mg orally for 4 days to avoid allergic reactions to IVIG. Simultaneously, anticoagulant therapy with intravenous argatroban—a direct thrombin inhibitor—was started at a dose of 2 μg per kg bodyweight per min; the dose was adjusted to obtain a steady state aPTT of between 1·5 to three times baseline.
The patient's condition rapidly improved; her pain subsided and her platelet count reached 91 × 109 per L 48 h after starting treatment. Additionally, concentrations of fibrinogen and coagulation factor XIII also steadily increased as D-dimer concentrations dropped (appendix). After 4 days, we switched argatroban to oral dabigatran 150 mg twice a day, and 6 days after her admission, the patient's platelets, fibrinogen, and coagulation factor XIII levels were within normal range (video).

input:
A 50-year-old woman attended our emergency department with a 3-day history of severe back pain and a severe headache. 10 days earlier she had received the first dose of vaccine against SARS-CoV-2—ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 (AstraZeneca). The patient had no significant medical history—specifically no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism. She was not pregnant, she did not take an oral contraceptive, and did not have a hormone-eluting intrauterine device in situ.On examination, the patient was afebrile, her peripheral oxygen saturation was 99% (with a 21% fraction of inspired oxygen), blood pressure was 130/80 mm Hg, heart rate was 80 beats per min, and body-mass index was 20 kg/m2. She had no obvious haematomas or petechial haemorrhages; she reported no chest pain, shortness of breath, swelling, redness, pallor, or cold in any limb.
Laboratory investigations showed a severe thrombocytopenia of 27 × 109 per L (normal 140–440). 3 days earlier it had been 163 × 109 per L. Serum D-dimer concentration was significantly elevated at greater than 33 mg/L (normal <0·5), fibrinogen concentration was 121 mg/dL (normal 210–400), coagulation factor XIII activity was 63% (normal >70%), and both prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) were normal. Haemoglobin concentration was 10·8 g/dL (normal 12·0–15·3); microcytic–hypochromic red blood cell indices, a low ferritin concentration of 12 ng/mL (normal 22–112), and a soluble transferrin receptor concentration of 10·1 mg/L (normal 1·78–4·59) indicated an iron deficiency anaemia. No schistocytes were detected. A thrombophilia screen—including resistance to activated protein C, and protein C and protein S activity—was negative; no antibodies to platelet factor 4 were found and genetic testing for prothrombin mutations was negative.
Creatinine, electrolytes, lactate dehydrogenase, aspartate aminotransferase, and alanine aminotransferase concentrations were within normal range. SARS-CoV-2 antigen and RT-PCR were negative on a nasopharyngeal swab. Tests for hantaviruses, HIV, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, and antiphospholipid antibodies (cardiolipin, β2 glycoprotein, and lupus) were negative.
We undertook consecutive thrombelastography, which indicated a stable clot pattern—despite the low platelet count and low fibrinogen concentration, and excluded fibrinolysis—both primary and secondary.
Contrast-enhanced MRI of the patient's abdomen and pelvis showed multifocal thrombus formations in the pelvic region—including bilateral thrombi in the parauterine venous plexus, a superficial vein of the left gluteus maximus muscle, and left presacral and lumbar veins (figure; appendix).
CT pulmonary angiography showed a subsegmental embolus in the posterior–basal right lower lobe (figure). CT cerebral venography and compression ultrasound of both legs showed no abnormalities—neither cerebral venous sinus thrombosis nor deep vein thrombosis.
We assumed the diagnosis was a vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia and administered high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) followed by a second dose 24 h later, together with dexamethasone 40 mg orally for 4 days to avoid allergic reactions to IVIG. Simultaneously, anticoagulant therapy with intravenous argatroban—a direct thrombin inhibitor—was started at a dose of 2 μg per kg bodyweight per min; the dose was adjusted to obtain a steady state aPTT of between 1·5 to three times baseline.
The patient's condition rapidly improved; her pain subsided and her platelet count reached 91 × 109 per L 48 h after starting treatment. Additionally, concentrations of fibrinogen and coagulation factor XIII also steadily increased as D-dimer concentrations dropped (appendix). After 4 days, we switched argatroban to oral dabigatran 150 mg twice a day, and 6 days after her admission, the patient's platelets, fibrinogen, and coagulation factor XIII levels were within normal range (video).

An 18-year-old man was referred to our hospital for a planned total hip replacement. He had a long history of reduced mobility and pain in his left hip because of a developmental bone disorder, dysplasia epiphysealis hemimelica (DEH). The teenager was first suspected of having DEH following a consultation when he was 10 years old, but because of his young age, the medical team at the time decided to manage his condition conservatively. They were concerned a more interventionist approach was inappropriate at a young age as he had manageable symptoms and delaying hip replacement surgery would allow him to reach skeletal maturity.We recommended that he have the surgery because he had stopped growing and he had reached his maximum height. Also, investigations of his hip had shown that the joint had become progressively more damaged with the result that both his pain and mobility had become significantly worse. During the surgery, the head of the patient's femur was found to be extremely enlarged with concomitant stretching of the joint capsule and surrounding muscles. The implant required appropriate increased offset to avoid instability of the joint. Postoperatively, he was given analgesia and venous thromboembolic prophylaxis. He was also given information on precautions to take to minimise the risk of dislocating the hip joint while the capsule healed. Pleasingly, at follow-up, the patient reported an improvement in both his quality of life and mobility.
DEH is a rare childhood osteochondroma characterised by asymmetrical enlargement of the epiphyseal cartilage of the long bones, usually involving the lower limbs and most commonly occurring in the ankle region. Patients present with painless swelling on one side of the joint, a limitation of movement, angular deformity, regional muscle wasting, and occasionally recurrent locking of the joint.
When assessing any child presenting with chronic hip pain, a careful examination is mandatory with attention being paid to any deformity, asymmetry, and discrepancy between the length of the affected and unaffected limbs. It is also crucial to obtain images of the affected area. Even though it is rare—DEH, must be considered as a differential diagnosis in anyone presenting with chronic hip pain. Other important conditions to consider include Perthes disease, skeletal dysplasias, tumours, and septic and inflammatory disorders.
Assessment of the extent of a patient's pain and the need to wait until skeletal maturity is necessary as often the only feasible long-term solution is total hip replacement. In our case, the patient's pain leading up to surgery was still manageable conservatively and rushing to surgery would not have been beneficial in the long term.

A 50-year-old woman attended our emergency department with a 3-day history of severe back pain and a severe headache. 10 days earlier she had received the first dose of vaccine against SARS-CoV-2—ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 (AstraZeneca). The patient had no significant medical history—specifically no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism. She was not pregnant, she did not take an oral contraceptive, and did not have a hormone-eluting intrauterine device in situ.On examination, the patient was afebrile, her peripheral oxygen saturation was 99% (with a 21% fraction of inspired oxygen), blood pressure was 130/80 mm Hg, heart rate was 80 beats per min, and body-mass index was 20 kg/m2. She had no obvious haematomas or petechial haemorrhages; she reported no chest pain, shortness of breath, swelling, redness, pallor, or cold in any limb.
Laboratory investigations showed a severe thrombocytopenia of 27 × 109 per L (normal 140–440). 3 days earlier it had been 163 × 109 per L. Serum D-dimer concentration was significantly elevated at greater than 33 mg/L (normal <0·5), fibrinogen concentration was 121 mg/dL (normal 210–400), coagulation factor XIII activity was 63% (normal >70%), and both prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) were normal. Haemoglobin concentration was 10·8 g/dL (normal 12·0–15·3); microcytic–hypochromic red blood cell indices, a low ferritin concentration of 12 ng/mL (normal 22–112), and a soluble transferrin receptor concentration of 10·1 mg/L (normal 1·78–4·59) indicated an iron deficiency anaemia. No schistocytes were detected. A thrombophilia screen—including resistance to activated protein C, and protein C and protein S activity—was negative; no antibodies to platelet factor 4 were found and genetic testing for prothrombin mutations was negative.
Creatinine, electrolytes, lactate dehydrogenase, aspartate aminotransferase, and alanine aminotransferase concentrations were within normal range. SARS-CoV-2 antigen and RT-PCR were negative on a nasopharyngeal swab. Tests for hantaviruses, HIV, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, and antiphospholipid antibodies (cardiolipin, β2 glycoprotein, and lupus) were negative.
We undertook consecutive thrombelastography, which indicated a stable clot pattern—despite the low platelet count and low fibrinogen concentration, and excluded fibrinolysis—both primary and secondary.
Contrast-enhanced MRI of the patient's abdomen and pelvis showed multifocal thrombus formations in the pelvic region—including bilateral thrombi in the parauterine venous plexus, a superficial vein of the left gluteus maximus muscle, and left presacral and lumbar veins (figure; appendix).
CT pulmonary angiography showed a subsegmental embolus in the posterior–basal right lower lobe (figure). CT cerebral venography and compression ultrasound of both legs showed no abnormalities—neither cerebral venous sinus thrombosis nor deep vein thrombosis.
We assumed the diagnosis was a vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia and administered high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) followed by a second dose 24 h later, together with dexamethasone 40 mg orally for 4 days to avoid allergic reactions to IVIG. Simultaneously, anticoagulant therapy with intravenous argatroban—a direct thrombin inhibitor—was started at a dose of 2 μg per kg bodyweight per min; the dose was adjusted to obtain a steady state aPTT of between 1·5 to three times baseline.
The patient's condition rapidly improved; her pain subsided and her platelet count reached 91 × 109 per L 48 h after starting treatment. Additionally, concentrations of fibrinogen and coagulation factor XIII also steadily increased as D-dimer concentrations dropped (appendix). After 4 days, we switched argatroban to oral dabigatran 150 mg twice a day, and 6 days after her admission, the patient's platelets, fibrinogen, and coagulation factor XIII levels were within normal range (video).

input: A 65-year-old hypertensive man presented to the Government Medical College Associated Superspeciality Hospital (Srinagar, India) with a 3-month history of progressive fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, and dull abdominal pain. On evaluation, he was found to have hypochromic, microcytic anaemia, and renal dysfunction (blood urea of 147 mg/dL and serum creatinine of 4·2 mg/dL). He had microscopic haematuria with dysmorphic red blood cells, 3+ proteinuria on dipstick analysis (300 mg/dL), and a 24-h urinary protein concentration of 1300 mg. His upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and colonoscopy were normal. A high-resolution CT of the man's chest showed a diffuse ground glass appearance. A CT angiography of his abdomen revealed diffuse aortitis of the abdominal aorta and both iliac arteries, without any luminal narrowing (figure A–C) or radiological evidence of extension of the inflammatory process into the periaortic space. A CT angiography of the man's thorax did not reveal any involvement of the thoracic aorta or subclavian arteries. A Doppler ultrasound of his temporal arteries was normal. Other blood tests showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 80 mm/h and a C-reactive protein concentration of 111 mg/L. Hepatitis B, C, and HIV serologies were negative. Tests for antinuclear and antiglomerular basement membrane antibodies were negative. An antimyeloperoxidase antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) ELISA was positive (121 U/mL [typical<5 U/mL]). Over the next few days, the man developed haemoptysis and a worsening estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) requiring several sessions of dialysis. A kidney biopsy was done, which revealed pauci-immune necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis (figure D). A diagnosis of ANCA-associated large vessel vasculitis of the abdominal aorta and iliacae communis, and small vessel vasculitis with necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis, and pulmonary capillaritis, causing an aorto-pulmonary-renal syndrome, was made. This was managed with intravenous methylprednisone followed by oral prednisone and intravenous cyclophosphamide, which led to an improvement in his symptoms and estimated GFR. The man died of a massive pulmonary haemorrhage at home, a few weeks post discharge, after having discontinued his immunosuppressants against medical advice.ANCA-associated vasculitis is a small vessel vasculitis, encompassing granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Large vessel vasculitis, comprises giant cell arteritis and Takayasu's arteritis, notably without ANCA and pauci-immune necrotising crescentic nephritis. The prevalence of large vessel vasculitis in people with ANCA-associated vasculitis is higher than in the general population, especially in those with granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Whether this aortitis in ANCA-associated vasculitis represents the so-called polyangiitis overlap or an independent entity is a matter of debate. Some experts regard ANCA-associated small vessel vasculitis with large vessel vasculitis as a separate entity because, according to a few case series, the appearance of ANCA precedes aortitis, and the aortic disease is characterised by an inceptive intimal lesion, possibly secondary to the vasculitis and fibrinoid necrosis of the vasa vasorum interna, and the subsequent spread of inflammation into the media and adventitia. Conversely, in large vessel vasculitis, both subsequent stenosis (especially in medium-sized arteries) and dilatation (especially in the aorta) can occur. ANCA-associated large vessel vasculitis of the aorta can be complicated by aortic aneurysms and dissection. The treatment of ANCA-associated large vessel vasculitis has not been clearly defined but, according to case reports, glucocorticoids, cyclophosphamide, rituximab, plasmapheresis, and surgery in cases of aneurysms and dissection have been found to be successful. The case presented in this Clinical Picture highlights the key concept that vasculitis of all three categories (large vessel vasculitis, medium vessel vasculitis, and small vessel vasculitis) can affect arteries of any size.

input: A 65-year-old hypertensive man presented to the Government Medical College Associated Superspeciality Hospital (Srinagar, India) with a 3-month history of progressive fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, and dull abdominal pain. On evaluation, he was found to have hypochromic, microcytic anaemia, and renal dysfunction (blood urea of 147 mg/dL and serum creatinine of 4·2 mg/dL). He had microscopic haematuria with dysmorphic red blood cells, 3+ proteinuria on dipstick analysis (300 mg/dL), and a 24-h urinary protein concentration of 1300 mg. His upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and colonoscopy were normal. A high-resolution CT of the man's chest showed a diffuse ground glass appearance. A CT angiography of his abdomen revealed diffuse aortitis of the abdominal aorta and both iliac arteries, without any luminal narrowing (figure A–C) or radiological evidence of extension of the inflammatory process into the periaortic space. A CT angiography of the man's thorax did not reveal any involvement of the thoracic aorta or subclavian arteries. A Doppler ultrasound of his temporal arteries was normal. Other blood tests showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 80 mm/h and a C-reactive protein concentration of 111 mg/L. Hepatitis B, C, and HIV serologies were negative. Tests for antinuclear and antiglomerular basement membrane antibodies were negative. An antimyeloperoxidase antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) ELISA was positive (121 U/mL [typical<5 U/mL]). Over the next few days, the man developed haemoptysis and a worsening estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) requiring several sessions of dialysis. A kidney biopsy was done, which revealed pauci-immune necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis (figure D). A diagnosis of ANCA-associated large vessel vasculitis of the abdominal aorta and iliacae communis, and small vessel vasculitis with necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis, and pulmonary capillaritis, causing an aorto-pulmonary-renal syndrome, was made. This was managed with intravenous methylprednisone followed by oral prednisone and intravenous cyclophosphamide, which led to an improvement in his symptoms and estimated GFR. The man died of a massive pulmonary haemorrhage at home, a few weeks post discharge, after having discontinued his immunosuppressants against medical advice.ANCA-associated vasculitis is a small vessel vasculitis, encompassing granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Large vessel vasculitis, comprises giant cell arteritis and Takayasu's arteritis, notably without ANCA and pauci-immune necrotising crescentic nephritis. The prevalence of large vessel vasculitis in people with ANCA-associated vasculitis is higher than in the general population, especially in those with granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Whether this aortitis in ANCA-associated vasculitis represents the so-called polyangiitis overlap or an independent entity is a matter of debate. Some experts regard ANCA-associated small vessel vasculitis with large vessel vasculitis as a separate entity because, according to a few case series, the appearance of ANCA precedes aortitis, and the aortic disease is characterised by an inceptive intimal lesion, possibly secondary to the vasculitis and fibrinoid necrosis of the vasa vasorum interna, and the subsequent spread of inflammation into the media and adventitia. Conversely, in large vessel vasculitis, both subsequent stenosis (especially in medium-sized arteries) and dilatation (especially in the aorta) can occur. ANCA-associated large vessel vasculitis of the aorta can be complicated by aortic aneurysms and dissection. The treatment of ANCA-associated large vessel vasculitis has not been clearly defined but, according to case reports, glucocorticoids, cyclophosphamide, rituximab, plasmapheresis, and surgery in cases of aneurysms and dissection have been found to be successful. The case presented in this Clinical Picture highlights the key concept that vasculitis of all three categories (large vessel vasculitis, medium vessel vasculitis, and small vessel vasculitis) can affect arteries of any size.

A 37-year-old man attended our clinic after his occupational health physician had found his blood pressure to be abnormally high during his annual check-up at his workplace. The patient, whose job was mainly office work, had a 20-year history of tobacco use—although he had quit 1 month before the annual examination; he had no history of hypertension and was not prescribed any regular medications. The patient's father had hypertension and his mother had a history of renal failure; details about whether she had hypertension were unavailable.
On examination he was generally well; his BMI was 27·1 kg/m2 (normal range 18·5–24·9) and his blood pressure was 230/140 mm Hg. Urinalysis showed more than 300 mg/dL of protein (normal <15). Fundoscopy showed grade IV hypertensive retinopathy with papilloedema, flame-shaped haemorrhages, exudates, and arteriovenous nipping: features typical of malignant hypertension (figure 1).
Laboratory investigations on admission found an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 21·4 mL/min/1·73m2 (normal >90) and a serum B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) concentration of 263 pg/mL (normal <18·4), indicating possible damage to the kidneys and heart; additional tests and examinations—including an echocardiogram, and brain and adrenal CTs—were normal, thereby ruling out any cerebral or cardiovascular emergencies that may have caused the raised blood pressure. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit and commenced on antihypertensive medication: initially a continuous intravenous infusion of nicaldipine. 6 h later he was started on oral amlodipine and the nicaldipine was gradually discontinued.
After 20 days of treatment, the averages of multiple blood pressure measurements and serum BNP concentrations were close to normal. The hypertensive retinopathy findings had improved compared with those seen on admission (appendix). The patient was allowed home with a plan for regular outpatient care.
After 40 days of treatment, the patient's blood pressure had returned to normal and fundoscopy showed considerable improvement of the retinopathy—indicating amelioration of microvascular endothelial function in the retina (figure 1). However, the improvement in the retina contrasted starkly with assessment of flow-mediated dilation—a non-invasive index of vascular endothelial function measured in the brachial artery—which remained low at 3·2% (normal >6), indicative of persistent impairment (figure 2; appendix).
After 90 days of treatment, the flow-mediated dilation was 7·5%, indicating significant improvement (figure 2; appendix). Moreover, the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio—measured to complement assessment of vascular endothelial damage—showed a significant decrease to 44·7 mg/g (normal <30); on admission the ratio had been 411·6 mg/g. The eGFR also showed a gradual recovery, from the rate on admission to 28·3 mL/min/1·73m2 at day 90, to 32·4 mL/min/1·73m2 at day 360; blood pressure was 128/80 mm Hg (appendix).
Malignant hypertension is a term used for patients with elevated blood pressure and multiple complications; hypertensive crisis describes patients with systolic blood pressure >180 mm Hg and diastolic >120 mm Hg. Hypertensive emergency is severe elevation in blood pressure with end-organ damage. Hypertensive urgency is severe hypertension without end-organ damage. Prompt diagnosis and treatment with appropriate antihypertensive treatments is vital since the prognosis is poor. Patients may have loss of vision, cerebral oedema, cerebral haemorrhage, acute kidney injury, and cardiovascular disorders. Vascular endothelial function damage caused by malignant hypertension—as seen in our patient—may be reversed by antihypertensive treatments, although improvement may occur at differing rates in different organs.
Causes include essential hypertension, poor concordance to antihypertensive medications, excessive dietary sodium, acute stroke, acute decompensated heart failure, acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection, acute kidney injury, renovascular stenosis, phaeochromocytoma, and primary aldosteronism. However, in some cases—as in our patient—the exact cause is unclear.

On evaluation, he was found to have hypochromic, microcytic anaemia, and renal dysfunction (blood urea of 147 mg/dL and serum creatinine of 4·2 mg/dL). He had microscopic haematuria with dysmorphic red blood cells, 3+ proteinuria on dipstick analysis (300 mg/dL), and a 24-h urinary protein concentration of 1300 mg. His upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and colonoscopy were normal. A high-resolution CT of the man's chest showed a diffuse ground glass appearance. A CT angiography of his abdomen revealed diffuse aortitis of the abdominal aorta and both iliac arteries, without any luminal narrowing (figure A–C) or radiological evidence of extension of the inflammatory process into the periaortic space. A CT angiography of the man's thorax did not reveal any involvement of the thoracic aorta or subclavian arteries. A Doppler ultrasound of his temporal arteries was normal. Other blood tests showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 80 mm/h and a C-reactive protein concentration of 111 mg/L. Hepatitis B, C, and HIV serologies were negative. Tests for antinuclear and antiglomerular basement membrane antibodies were negative. An antimyeloperoxidase antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) ELISA was positive (121 U/mL [typical<5 U/mL]). Over the next few days, the man developed haemoptysis and a worsening estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) requiring several sessions of dialysis. A kidney biopsy was done, which revealed pauci-immune necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis (figure D). A diagnosis of ANCA-associated large vessel vasculitis of the abdominal aorta and iliacae communis, and small vessel vasculitis with necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis, and pulmonary capillaritis, causing an aorto-pulmonary-renal syndrome, was made. This was managed with intravenous methylprednisone followed by oral prednisone and intravenous cyclophosphamide, which led to an improvement in his symptoms and estimated GFR. The man died of a massive pulmonary haemorrhage at home, a few weeks post discharge, after having discontinued his immunosuppressants against medical advice.ANCA-associated vasculitis is a small vessel vasculitis, encompassing granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Large vessel vasculitis, comprises giant cell arteritis and Takayasu's arteritis, notably without ANCA and pauci-immune necrotising crescentic nephritis. The prevalence of large vessel vasculitis in people with ANCA-associated vasculitis is higher than in the general population, especially in those with granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Whether this aortitis in ANCA-associated vasculitis represents the so-called polyangiitis overlap or an independent entity is a matter of debate. Some experts regard ANCA-associated small vessel vasculitis with large vessel vasculitis as a separate entity because, according to a few case series, the appearance of ANCA precedes aortitis, and the aortic disease is characterised by an inceptive intimal lesion, possibly secondary to the vasculitis and fibrinoid necrosis of the vasa vasorum interna, and the subsequent spread of inflammation into the media and adventitia. Conversely, in large vessel vasculitis, both subsequent stenosis (especially in medium-sized arteries) and dilatation (especially in the aorta) can occur. ANCA-associated large vessel vasculitis of the aorta can be complicated by aortic aneurysms and dissection. The treatment of ANCA-associated large vessel vasculitis has not been clearly defined but, according to case reports, glucocorticoids, cyclophosphamide, rituximab, plasmapheresis, and surgery in cases of aneurysms and dissection have been found to be successful. The case presented in this Clinical Picture highlights the key concept that vasculitis of all three categories (large vessel vasculitis, medium vessel vasculitis, and small vessel vasculitis) can affect arteries of any size.

A 37-year-old man attended our clinic after his occupational health physician had found his blood pressure to be abnormally high during his annual check-up at his workplace. The patient, whose job was mainly office work, had a 20-year history of tobacco use—although he had quit 1 month before the annual examination; he had no history of hypertension and was not prescribed any regular medications. The patient's father had hypertension and his mother had a history of renal failure; details about whether she had hypertension were unavailable.
On examination he was generally well; his BMI was 27·1 kg/m2 (normal range 18·5–24·9) and his blood pressure was 230/140 mm Hg. Urinalysis showed more than 300 mg/dL of protein (normal <15). Fundoscopy showed grade IV hypertensive retinopathy with papilloedema, flame-shaped haemorrhages, exudates, and arteriovenous nipping: features typical of malignant hypertension (figure 1).
Laboratory investigations on admission found an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 21·4 mL/min/1·73m2 (normal >90) and a serum B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) concentration of 263 pg/mL (normal <18·4), indicating possible damage to the kidneys and heart; additional tests and examinations—including an echocardiogram, and brain and adrenal CTs—were normal, thereby ruling out any cerebral or cardiovascular emergencies that may have caused the raised blood pressure. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit and commenced on antihypertensive medication: initially a continuous intravenous infusion of nicaldipine. 6 h later he was started on oral amlodipine and the nicaldipine was gradually discontinued.
After 20 days of treatment, the averages of multiple blood pressure measurements and serum BNP concentrations were close to normal. The hypertensive retinopathy findings had improved compared with those seen on admission (appendix). The patient was allowed home with a plan for regular outpatient care.
After 40 days of treatment, the patient's blood pressure had returned to normal and fundoscopy showed considerable improvement of the retinopathy—indicating amelioration of microvascular endothelial function in the retina (figure 1). However, the improvement in the retina contrasted starkly with assessment of flow-mediated dilation—a non-invasive index of vascular endothelial function measured in the brachial artery—which remained low at 3·2% (normal >6), indicative of persistent impairment (figure 2; appendix).
After 90 days of treatment, the flow-mediated dilation was 7·5%, indicating significant improvement (figure 2; appendix). Moreover, the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio—measured to complement assessment of vascular endothelial damage—showed a significant decrease to 44·7 mg/g (normal <30); on admission the ratio had been 411·6 mg/g. The eGFR also showed a gradual recovery, from the rate on admission to 28·3 mL/min/1·73m2 at day 90, to 32·4 mL/min/1·73m2 at day 360; blood pressure was 128/80 mm Hg (appendix).
Malignant hypertension is a term used for patients with elevated blood pressure and multiple complications; hypertensive crisis describes patients with systolic blood pressure >180 mm Hg and diastolic >120 mm Hg. Hypertensive emergency is severe elevation in blood pressure with end-organ damage. Hypertensive urgency is severe hypertension without end-organ damage. Prompt diagnosis and treatment with appropriate antihypertensive treatments is vital since the prognosis is poor. Patients may have loss of vision, cerebral oedema, cerebral haemorrhage, acute kidney injury, and cardiovascular disorders. Vascular endothelial function damage caused by malignant hypertension—as seen in our patient—may be reversed by antihypertensive treatments, although improvement may occur at differing rates in different organs.
Causes include essential hypertension, poor concordance to antihypertensive medications, excessive dietary sodium, acute stroke, acute decompensated heart failure, acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection, acute kidney injury, renovascular stenosis, phaeochromocytoma, and primary aldosteronism. However, in some cases—as in our patient—the exact cause is unclear.

A 63-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of an insidious fever with chills and a non-productive cough. He had lost 5 kg in weight. He also had type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidaemia. He was a farmer involved in rice cultivation and palm oil plantation in the central region of Sarawak, Malaysia.On examination, we found no abnormalities. Initial laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 12·6 g/dL, a platelet count of 399 × 109 per L, and total white blood cell count of 11·4 × 109 per L; neutrophils 66·2%, lymphocytes 22·5%, and eosinophils 1·7%. Renal and liver function tests showed no abnormalities.
Plain chest x-ray showed a left hilar mass with blunted left costophrenic angle. Sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli were negative.
The patient's fever persisted—despite a week of empirical treatment with oral antimicrobial agents—and we carried out a CT of the thorax which showed an enhancing, 2·5 cm × 4·1 cm × 2·5 cm mass at the aorto-pulmonary window abutting the left main bronchus and descending thoracic aorta (figure).
A primary lung malignancy was suspected because of the constitutional symptoms with negative tuberculosis work-up, and the CT finding.
White light flexible bronchoscopy showed a grossly abnormal and stenotic left main bronchus with an endobronchial nodule (appendix); narrow band imaging showed the mucosa to be diffusely thickened (appendix). An endobronchial biopsy was taken, and bronchial brushings were collected. The bronchoscopy findings reinforced our working diagnosis of a lung malignancy.
Despite the development of a low-grade temperature post procedure, the patient's blood investigations remained normal and microbiological analyses remained negative. We therefore let the patient go home with a 2-week course of oral amoxicillin and clavulanic acid, while awaiting the histopathological and microbiological analysis.
2 weeks later, the patient attended our outpatient clinic for review: the endobronchial biopsy showed inflamed granulation tissue with underlying stroma infiltrated by neutrophils, lymphocytes, and plasma cells, with proliferation of small blood vessels lined by benign endothelial cells. There were no granuloma or multinucleated giant cells seen. Periodic acid–Schiff and Ziehl–Neelsen stains showed no fungal elements or acid-fast bacilli. Analysis of the bronchial brushings was negative for bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterium.
However, the patient was found to be febrile and unwell: pulse rate 139 beats per min, blood pressure 114/64 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and temperature 38°C.
He was immediately admitted to hospital, but he developed septic shock requiring mechanical ventilation and vasopressor support in the intensive care unit. We empirically gave the patient intravenous meropenem (25 mg/kg per day). Blood cultures grew Gram-negative bacilli with a safety pin appearance and confirmed as Burkholderia pseudomallei by conventional biochemical testing and mass spectrometry. The patient gradually improved and was allowed home after a month of intensive care. He completed 6 months of eradication therapy with oral co-trimoxazole; a CT scan after 3 months of treatment showed resolution of the left hilar mass (appendix).
Melioidosis is a common infectious disease in southeast Asia, usually presenting as an acute febrile illness with pneumonia or chronic illness. It may present atypically—as in our case where we found an isolated mediastinal mass—representing a lethal trap for the unwary (video).

A 37-year-old man attended our clinic after his occupational health physician had found his blood pressure to be abnormally high during his annual check-up at his workplace. The patient, whose job was mainly office work, had a 20-year history of tobacco use—although he had quit 1 month before the annual examination; he had no history of hypertension and was not prescribed any regular medications. The patient's father had hypertension and his mother had a history of renal failure; details about whether she had hypertension were unavailable.
On examination he was generally well; his BMI was 27·1 kg/m2 (normal range 18·5–24·9) and his blood pressure was 230/140 mm Hg. Urinalysis showed more than 300 mg/dL of protein (normal <15). Fundoscopy showed grade IV hypertensive retinopathy with papilloedema, flame-shaped haemorrhages, exudates, and arteriovenous nipping: features typical of malignant hypertension (figure 1).
Laboratory investigations on admission found an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 21·4 mL/min/1·73m2 (normal >90) and a serum B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) concentration of 263 pg/mL (normal <18·4), indicating possible damage to the kidneys and heart; additional tests and examinations—including an echocardiogram, and brain and adrenal CTs—were normal, thereby ruling out any cerebral or cardiovascular emergencies that may have caused the raised blood pressure. A 63-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of an insidious fever with chills and a non-productive cough. He had lost 5 kg in weight. He also had type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidaemia. He was a farmer involved in rice cultivation and palm oil plantation in the central region of Sarawak, Malaysia.On examination, we found no abnormalities. Initial laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 12·6 g/dL, a platelet count of 399 × 109 per L, and total white blood cell count of 11·4 × 109 per L; neutrophils 66·2%, lymphocytes 22·5%, and eosinophils 1·7%. Renal and liver function tests showed no abnormalities.
Plain chest x-ray showed a left hilar mass with blunted left costophrenic angle. Sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli were negative.
The patient's fever persisted—despite a week of empirical treatment with oral antimicrobial agents—and we carried out a CT of the thorax which showed an enhancing, 2·5 cm × 4·1 cm × 2·5 cm mass at the aorto-pulmonary window abutting the left main bronchus and descending thoracic aorta (figure).
A primary lung malignancy was suspected because of the constitutional symptoms with negative tuberculosis work-up, and the CT finding.
White light flexible bronchoscopy showed a grossly abnormal and stenotic left main bronchus with an endobronchial nodule (appendix); narrow band imaging showed the mucosa to be diffusely thickened (appendix). An endobronchial biopsy was taken, and bronchial brushings were collected. The bronchoscopy findings reinforced our working diagnosis of a lung malignancy.
Despite the development of a low-grade temperature post procedure, the patient's blood investigations remained normal and microbiological analyses remained negative. We therefore let the patient go home with a 2-week course of oral amoxicillin and clavulanic acid, while awaiting the histopathological and microbiological analysis.
2 weeks later, the patient attended our outpatient clinic for review: the endobronchial biopsy showed inflamed granulation tissue with underlying stroma infiltrated by neutrophils, lymphocytes, and plasma cells, with proliferation of small blood vessels lined by benign endothelial cells. There were no granuloma or multinucleated giant cells seen. Periodic acid–Schiff and Ziehl–Neelsen stains showed no fungal elements or acid-fast bacilli. Analysis of the bronchial brushings was negative for bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterium.
However, the patient was found to be febrile and unwell: pulse rate 139 beats per min, blood pressure 114/64 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and temperature 38°C.
He was immediately admitted to hospital, but he developed septic shock requiring mechanical ventilation and vasopressor support in the intensive care unit. We empirically gave the patient intravenous meropenem (25 mg/kg per day). Blood cultures grew Gram-negative bacilli with a safety pin appearance and confirmed as Burkholderia pseudomallei by conventional biochemical testing and mass spectrometry. The patient gradually improved and was allowed home after a month of intensive care. He completed 6 months of eradication therapy with oral co-trimoxazole; a CT scan after 3 months of treatment showed resolution of the left hilar mass (appendix).
Melioidosis is a common infectious disease in southeast Asia, usually presenting as an acute febrile illness with pneumonia or chronic illness. It may present atypically—as in our case where we found an isolated mediastinal mass—representing a lethal trap for the unwary (video).

A 63-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of an insidious fever with chills and a non-productive cough. He had lost 5 kg in weight. He also had type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidaemia. He was a farmer involved in rice cultivation and palm oil plantation in the central region of Sarawak, Malaysia.On examination, we found no abnormalities. Initial laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 12·6 g/dL, a platelet count of 399 × 109 per L, and total white blood cell count of 11·4 × 109 per L; neutrophils 66·2%, lymphocytes 22·5%, and eosinophils 1·7%. Renal and liver function tests showed no abnormalities.
Plain chest x-ray showed a left hilar mass with blunted left costophrenic angle. Sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli were negative.
The patient's fever persisted—despite a week of empirical treatment with oral antimicrobial agents—and we carried out a CT of the thorax which showed an enhancing, 2·5 cm × 4·1 cm × 2·5 cm mass at the aorto-pulmonary window abutting the left main bronchus and descending thoracic aorta (figure).
A primary lung malignancy was suspected because of the constitutional symptoms with negative tuberculosis work-up, and the CT finding.
White light flexible bronchoscopy showed a grossly abnormal and stenotic left main bronchus with an endobronchial nodule (appendix); narrow band imaging showed the mucosa to be diffusely thickened (appendix). An endobronchial biopsy was taken, and bronchial brushings were collected. The bronchoscopy findings reinforced our working diagnosis of a lung malignancy.
Despite the development of a low-grade temperature post procedure, the patient's blood investigations remained normal and microbiological analyses remained negative. We therefore let the patient go home with a 2-week course of oral amoxicillin and clavulanic acid, while awaiting the histopathological and microbiological analysis.
2 weeks later, the patient attended our outpatient clinic for review: the endobronchial biopsy showed inflamed granulation tissue with underlying stroma infiltrated by neutrophils, lymphocytes, and plasma cells, with proliferation of small blood vessels lined by benign endothelial cells. There were no granuloma or multinucleated giant cells seen. Periodic acid–Schiff and Ziehl–Neelsen stains showed no fungal elements or acid-fast bacilli. Analysis of the bronchial brushings was negative for bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterium.
However, the patient was found to be febrile and unwell: pulse rate 139 beats per min, blood pressure 114/64 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and temperature 38°C.
He was immediately admitted to hospital, but he developed septic shock requiring mechanical ventilation and vasopressor support in the intensive care unit. We empirically gave the patient intravenous meropenem (25 mg/kg per day). Blood cultures grew Gram-negative bacilli with a safety pin appearance and confirmed as Burkholderia pseudomallei by conventional biochemical testing and mass spectrometry. The patient gradually improved and was allowed home after a month of intensive care. He completed 6 months of eradication therapy with oral co-trimoxazole; a CT scan after 3 months of treatment showed resolution of the left hilar mass (appendix).
Melioidosis is a common infectious disease in southeast Asia, usually presenting as an acute febrile illness with pneumonia or chronic illness. It may present atypically—as in our case where we found an isolated mediastinal mass—representing a lethal trap for the unwary (video).

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of having swollen and red eyelids. The problem was not associated with pruritus or pain. She had been previously treated with topical steroids and antibiotics but with little effect. Her past medical history was unremarkable. During physical examination, she was found to have scaly, atrophic, erythematous plaques—with the loss of eyelashes on the lateral aspects—on both lower eyelids (figure). Additionally, the scaly erythema was accompanied by hyperpigmentation on the left lateral canthus (figure). There were no other skin or mucosal lesions. Histological examination of the lesions showed follicular plugging, epidermal atrophy, liquefaction degeneration of epidermal basal cells, and dermal perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltration. Direct immunofluorescence revealed linear deposition of immunoglobulin M (IgM) at the dermo-epidermal junction. She was diagnosed as having discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE); she did not meet the criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). She was advised to avoid ultraviolet light by wearing sunglasses and sunscreen. She was also treated with oral hydroxychloroquine 300 mg/day for 16 weeks. The DLE lesions completely remitted without the improvement of the madarosis.DLE is the most common form of chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus, accounting for up to 80% of all cases. As many as 28% of DLE patients may go on to develop SLE. Specific risk factors for progression to SLE include female gender, widespread DLE lesions, positive antinuclear antibodies, and increased numbers of SLE criteria.
Ocular complications can occur in DLE. Eyelid involvement is seen in 6% of patients. The lesion usually develops bilaterally on the lower eyelids. It may be asymptomatic; however, some patients complain of photosensitivity, burning, or swelling. Ocular DLE is commonly accompanied by facial DLE lesions—but it can be the initial or sole manifestation.
DLE management begins by protecting the skin from sunlight. First-line medications are oral antimalarials such as hydroxychloroquine. Topical corticosteroids, intralesional corticosteroids, and topical calcineurin inhibitors may be effective for isolated manifestations. Early treatment is important to prevent poor cosmetic results, cicatricial dysfunction, and rarely the development of squamous cell carcinoma on the DLE lesion.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of having swollen and red eyelids. The problem was not associated with pruritus or pain. She had been previously treated with topical steroids and antibiotics but with little effect. Her past medical history was unremarkable. During physical examination, she was found to have scaly, atrophic, erythematous plaques—with the loss of eyelashes on the lateral aspects—on both lower eyelids (figure). Additionally, the scaly erythema was accompanied by hyperpigmentation on the left lateral canthus (figure). There were no other skin or mucosal lesions. Histological examination of the lesions showed follicular plugging, epidermal atrophy, liquefaction degeneration of epidermal basal cells, and dermal perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltration. Direct immunofluorescence revealed linear deposition of immunoglobulin M (IgM) at the dermo-epidermal junction. She was diagnosed as having discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE); she did not meet the criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). She was advised to avoid ultraviolet light by wearing sunglasses and sunscreen. She was also treated with oral hydroxychloroquine 300 mg/day for 16 weeks. The DLE lesions completely remitted without the improvement of the madarosis.DLE is the most common form of chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus, accounting for up to 80% of all cases. As many as 28% of DLE patients may go on to develop SLE. Specific risk factors for progression to SLE include female gender, widespread DLE lesions, positive antinuclear antibodies, and increased numbers of SLE criteria.
Ocular complications can occur in DLE. Eyelid involvement is seen in 6% of patients. The lesion usually develops bilaterally on the lower eyelids. It may be asymptomatic; however, some patients complain of photosensitivity, burning, or swelling. Ocular DLE is commonly accompanied by facial DLE lesions—but it can be the initial or sole manifestation.
DLE management begins by protecting the skin from sunlight. First-line medications are oral antimalarials such as hydroxychloroquine. Topical corticosteroids, intralesional corticosteroids, and topical calcineurin inhibitors may be effective for isolated manifestations. Early treatment is important to prevent poor cosmetic results, cicatricial dysfunction, and rarely the development of squamous cell carcinoma on the DLE lesion.

On March 11, 2017, a 59-year-old woman came to our hospital's emergency department. She had been unwell for 7 days, with recurrent epigastric pain of acute onset that radiated into her right hemithorax, intensified during respiratory movements, and was accompanied by mild dyspnoea. Vomiting and dysphagia were absent. She had presented to our hospital because of the same symptoms 4 days before admission, but she was discharged after examination and investigations had shown no notable abnormalities: chest radiograph and electrocardiogram (ECG) were normal, as were C-reactive protein and troponin concentrations. She smoked 20 cigarettes daily, did not drink alcohol, and took atorvastatin.On admission, a chest radiograph revealed a right pleural effusion (figure, A). Considering her symptoms and her increased concentrations of serum D-dimer, a CT of the chest was done to rule out a pulmonary embolism, within 3 h of her arrival at the hospital. However, the chest CT unexpectedly showed a mediastinal collection (figure, B), arising from the oesophagus through an orifice that was about 1 cm in diameter. She was started on meropenem. A subsequent endoscopic assessment showed a distal oesophageal perforation communicating with a para-oesophageal abscess (figure, C,D), which was drained in the same procedure. The fluoroscopy after the drainage did not show any mediastinal leakage from the abscess; 24 h after the fluoroscopy, a right thoracic tube was placed because dyspnoea was worsening, and the increased pleural effusion fulfilled the criteria for diagnosis of empyema. The existence of an oesophago-pleural fistula was later suspected because there was a high pleural fluid-serum amylase gradient (pleural amylase concentration 5050 IU/L, concomitant blood amylase level 76 IU/L), and methylene blue was present in pleural fluid after its administration into the abscess cavity. In addition to these observations, the patient also had unremittent fever and bilateral lung opacities, consistent with acute respiratory distress syndrome, so she underwent right thoracoscopy for debridement, drainage, and urokinase instillation. Culture from a mediastinal abscess sample grew Streptococcus oralis and Candida glabrata, thus clindamycin and anidulafungin were added to her treatment regimen.
Eventually, her respiratory insufficiency worsened, so an oesophagectomy was done 7 days after the right thoracoscopy. The patient's condition between the two surgical procedures was characterised by malaise, intermitent fever, and slowly worsening dyspnoea. A new chest CT chest had revealed a right multiloculated pleural empyema. The oesophagectomy involved gastric tubulisation, cervical oesophagogastric anastomosis, and splenectomy. Pathological evaluation showed acute and chronic oesophageal inflammatory changes, multinucleated foreign body giant cells on the abscess wall, and no evidence of neoplasia. The patient was discharged 30 days after admission, and was prescribed atorvastatin, omeprazole, and paracetamol at discharge. Six follow-ups have been made as of June, 2018. She was well in her last follow-up in March, 2018; chest and abdominal CT showed no new, clincally significant abnormalities. The patient was able to eat all kinds of food, and presented with no odynophagia, dysphagia, vomiting, chest pain, abdominal pain, or dyspnoea.
Oesophageal perforation is an uncommon but potentially life-threatening condition. More than 50% of cases are iatrogenic and most of them occur during endoscopy. Other causes of oesophageal perforation include spontaneous perforation (typically resulting from vomiting, called Boerhaave's syndrome), ingestion of a foreign body, trauma, and malignancy. Diagnosis and treatment are often delayed because symptoms might mimic other more frequent disorders. A multidisciplinary approach in specialised centres is strongly recommended to minimise the high morbidity and mortality associated with this complex and challenging condition.

On March 11, 2017, a 59-year-old woman came to our hospital's emergency department. She had been unwell for 7 days, with recurrent epigastric pain of acute onset that radiated into her right hemithorax, intensified during respiratory movements, and was accompanied by mild dyspnoea. Vomiting and dysphagia were absent. She had presented to our hospital because of the same symptoms 4 days before admission, but she was discharged after examination and investigations had shown no notable abnormalities: chest radiograph and electrocardiogram (ECG) were normal, as were C-reactive protein and troponin concentrations. She smoked 20 cigarettes daily, did not drink alcohol, and took atorvastatin.On admission, a chest radiograph revealed a right pleural effusion (figure, A). Considering her symptoms and her increased concentrations of serum D-dimer, a CT of the chest was done to rule out a pulmonary embolism, within 3 h of her arrival at the hospital. However, the chest CT unexpectedly showed a mediastinal collection (figure, B), arising from the oesophagus through an orifice that was about 1 cm in diameter. She was started on meropenem. A subsequent endoscopic assessment showed a distal oesophageal perforation communicating with a para-oesophageal abscess (figure, C,D), which was drained in the same procedure. The fluoroscopy after the drainage did not show any mediastinal leakage from the abscess; 24 h after the fluoroscopy, a right thoracic tube was placed because dyspnoea was worsening, and the increased pleural effusion fulfilled the criteria for diagnosis of empyema. The existence of an oesophago-pleural fistula was later suspected because there was a high pleural fluid-serum amylase gradient (pleural amylase concentration 5050 IU/L, concomitant blood amylase level 76 IU/L), and methylene blue was present in pleural fluid after its administration into the abscess cavity. In addition to these observations, the patient also had unremittent fever and bilateral lung opacities, consistent with acute respiratory distress syndrome, so she underwent right thoracoscopy for debridement, drainage, and urokinase instillation. Culture from a mediastinal abscess sample grew Streptococcus oralis and Candida glabrata, thus clindamycin and anidulafungin were added to her treatment regimen.
Eventually, her respiratory insufficiency worsened, so an oesophagectomy was done 7 days after the right thoracoscopy. The patient's condition between the two surgical procedures was characterised by malaise, intermitent fever, and slowly worsening dyspnoea. A new chest CT chest had revealed a right multiloculated pleural empyema. The oesophagectomy involved gastric tubulisation, cervical oesophagogastric anastomosis, and splenectomy. Pathological evaluation showed acute and chronic oesophageal inflammatory changes, multinucleated foreign body giant cells on the abscess wall, and no evidence of neoplasia. The patient was discharged 30 days after admission, and was prescribed atorvastatin, omeprazole, and paracetamol at discharge. Six follow-ups have been made as of June, 2018. She was well in her last follow-up in March, 2018; chest and abdominal CT showed no new, clincally significant abnormalities. The patient was able to eat all kinds of food, and presented with no odynophagia, dysphagia, vomiting, chest pain, abdominal pain, or dyspnoea.
Oesophageal perforation is an uncommon but potentially life-threatening condition. More than 50% of cases are iatrogenic and most of them occur during endoscopy. Other causes of oesophageal perforation include spontaneous perforation (typically resulting from vomiting, called Boerhaave's syndrome), ingestion of a foreign body, trauma, and malignancy. Diagnosis and treatment are often delayed because symptoms might mimic other more frequent disorders. A multidisciplinary approach in specialised centres is strongly recommended to minimise the high morbidity and mortality associated with this complex and challenging condition.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of having swollen and red eyelids. The problem was not associated with pruritus or pain. She had been previously treated with topical steroids and antibiotics but with little effect. Her past medical history was unremarkable. During physical examination, she was found to have scaly, atrophic, erythematous plaques—with the loss of eyelashes on the lateral aspects—on both lower eyelids (figure). Additionally, the scaly erythema was accompanied by hyperpigmentation on the left lateral canthus (figure). There were no other skin or mucosal lesions. Histological examination of the lesions showed follicular plugging, epidermal atrophy, liquefaction degeneration of epidermal basal cells, and dermal perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltration. Direct immunofluorescence revealed linear deposition of immunoglobulin M (IgM) at the dermo-epidermal junction. She was diagnosed as having discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE); she did not meet the criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). She was advised to avoid ultraviolet light by wearing sunglasses and sunscreen. She was also treated with oral hydroxychloroquine 300 mg/day for 16 weeks. The DLE lesions completely remitted without the improvement of the madarosis.DLE is the most common form of chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus, accounting for up to 80% of all cases. As many as 28% of DLE patients may go on to develop SLE. Specific risk factors for progression to SLE include female gender, widespread DLE lesions, positive antinuclear antibodies, and increased numbers of SLE criteria.
Ocular complications can occur in DLE. Eyelid involvement is seen in 6% of patients. The lesion usually develops bilaterally on the lower eyelids. It may be asymptomatic; however, some patients complain of photosensitivity, burning, or swelling. Ocular DLE is commonly accompanied by facial DLE lesions—but it can be the initial or sole manifestation.
DLE management begins by protecting the skin from sunlight. First-line medications are oral antimalarials such as hydroxychloroquine. Topical corticosteroids, intralesional corticosteroids, and topical calcineurin inhibitors may be effective for isolated manifestations. Early treatment is important to prevent poor cosmetic results, cicatricial dysfunction, and rarely the development of squamous cell carcinoma on the DLE lesion.

An 80-year-old man with a 6-month-history of shortness of breath on minimal exertion and fatigue was admitted to our unit for a planned operation to replace his stenotic aortic valve. The surgery was uneventful and a temporary ventricular epicardial pacing lead was placed on the free wall of the right ventricle. The patient remained haemodynamically stable in sinus rhythm post-surgery and was extubated 8 h later. The following day he was transferred from intensive care to our high dependency unit with the temporary epicardial pacemaker in VVI mode: stimulation amplitude 10 V, sensitivity 1 mV, and back-up pacing rate of 44 beats per min. A pacing check at that time showed no problems.2 days after the operation the patient had a cardiac arrest during mobilisation and physiotherapy; chest compressions were started, and the patient was re-intubated. The defibrillator showed ventricular fibrillation and he was shocked into sinus rhythm using 200 joules biphasic.
A telemetry review showed a spike on a T wave as a possible cause of the cardiac arrest: sinus rhythm was present during the first two cardiac cycles—heart rate 76 beats per min—followed by a premature pacing spike which produced a paced cardiac cycle. Another intrinsic cardiac cycle then followed. However, during the repolarisation phase of this cycle, a second pacing spike was seen falling on the T wave; this spike triggered polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that apparently degenerated into ventricular fibrillation (figure).
The patient was stabilised post-resuscitation and extubated 4 h later; he recovered well and was allowed home 12 days later. 1 month later he was well and asymptomatic when reviewed in our outpatient clinic.
Indications for temporary cardiac pacing include the management of bradyarrhythmias—specifically atrioventricular block—and both atrial and ventricular tachyarrhythmias. In cardiac surgery, insertion of temporary epicardial pacing wires is common practice; it both optimises myocardial function in patients, who postoperatively develop haemodynamically significant arrhythmias, and helps maintain a stable cardiac rhythm.
However, placement of epicardial pacing leads is not without risk. In the short term, function deteriorates mainly due to the inflammation around the surfaces of the myocardium and the leads. Daily checking of the pacemaker's pacing (the depolarisation of the atria or ventricles resulting from an impulse delivered from the generator down a lead to the heart) and sensing (the detection by the generator of intrinsic atrial or ventricular depolarisation signals) parameters after cardiac surgery is therefore paramount.
Pacemaker under-sensing occurs when the pacemaker fails to detect spontaneous myocardial depolarisation—as probably happened in our patient—and is a common reason for the appearance of inappropriate ventricular pacing spikes. When the spikes fall on the T wave, then the patient may develop a tachyarrhythmia—including polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Increasing the pacemaker rate above that of the intrinsic heart rate may reduce the possibility of production of inappropriate ventricular pacing spikes.

A 41-year-old woman with a 6-day history of worsening shortness of breath and 4 syncopal episodes, which were preceded by coughing spells, attended our hospital; she reported no chest pain or palpitations.
The patient had a medical history of recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP), diagnosed when she was aged 36 years; at the time a chest CT showed nodules in the trachea—RRP was confirmed after bronchoscopy and biopsy. Serotyping was positive for human papillomavirus (HPV) serotypes 6 and 7, and negative for all other serotypes, specifically oncogenic serotypes 16 and 18. She had also been diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus, migraines, asthma, and pneumonia 1 year before admission caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. She reported no history of seizures and said she was concordant with medication prescribed for her asthma—specifically, albuterol, which she used when needed, and ipratropium bromide combined with albuterol.
On examination she appeared uncomfortable; her pulse rate was 79 beats per min, respiratory rate was 20 breaths per min, blood pressure was 128/84 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. Chest examination found diminished breath sounds at the bases with no appreciable jugular venous distention. An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with left axis deviation, unchanged from a previous recording.
Laboratory investigations showed a typical complete blood count, and urea and electrolytes within normal range. A respiratory virus infection panel was negative for influenza, rhinovirus, SARS COV-2, respiratory syncytial virus, rhinovirus, and parainfluenza.
The patient was treated empirically with intravenous cefepime, and inhaled tobramycin given the history of P aeruginosa pneumonia; the asthma medications were continued.
CT angiogram, compared with previous images, showed that the pathological findings of the RRP had progressed: multiple cavitary opacities and a lesion located in the right main-stem bronchus. Pulmonary emboli were not seen (figure).
On the third day after admission, the patient developed worsening shortness of breath and required 1 L of oxygen overnight, raising concerns of pulmonary oedema secondary to airway obstruction. She was given 40 mg of furosemide intravenously which improved her respiratory status, and she was weaned off the supplemental oxygen. Bronchoscopy confirmed a partially obstructing mass in the middle portion of the right main-stem bronchus (figure); the abnormal tissue was ablated by cryotherapy. Histopathological analysis of a sample obtained from a biopsy of the lesion, showed squamous papilloma with focal low-grade squamous dysplasia.
The patient reported improvement in shortness of breath following the procedure. Bronchoalveolar lavage was also done which later showed negative cultures for aerobic, anaerobic, fungal, and mycobacterial organisms. Given the unlikelihood of an infection after the negative preliminary cultures plus improvement of the symptoms after the ablation, the antibiotics were stopped.
The patient went home 8 days after admission at her baseline respiratory status without the need for supplemental oxygen; at follow-up 1 month later she was relatively well and reported no further syncopal episodes or shortness of breath.
RRP is managed by removal of the papillomas, which because of recurrence, may require repeated attention. The 9-valent HPV (Gardasil 9; Merk & Co., Inc., Rahway, NJ, USA) vaccine protects against serotypes 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58; serotypes 6 and 11 have a known association with greater than 90% of cases with RRP. The vaccine prevents new cases of HPV and in patients who have RRP, it may increase the interval time between the need for surgical removal of the papillomas.
Patients with RRP express vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) in both the papillomas and the nearby blood vessels. Bevacizumab—an antibody inhibiting VEGF—is emerging as a promising treatment for the disease; studies have indicated that systemic treatment with bevacizumab increases the time required between surgical removal and, in some cases, with remission of papilloma development and need for future surgical debridement.
RRP may present with coughing, wheezing, and shortness of breath—as in our patient. HPV rarely transforms into malignancy; for patients with pulmonary involvement, there is a 32-times increased risk. RRP lesions are typically of varying sizes, bilateral, and located posteriorly in the chest; diagnosis is made with CT imaging and either a laryngoscopy or bronchoscopy.
