A 41-year-old woman with a 6-day history of worsening shortness of breath and 4 syncopal episodes, which were preceded by coughing spells, attended our hospital; she reported no chest pain or palpitations.
The patient had a medical history of recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP), diagnosed when she was aged 36 years; at the time a chest CT showed nodules in the trachea—RRP was confirmed after bronchoscopy and biopsy. Serotyping was positive for human papillomavirus (HPV) serotypes 6 and 7, and negative for all other serotypes, specifically oncogenic serotypes 16 and 18. She had also been diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus, migraines, asthma, and pneumonia 1 year before admission caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. She reported no history of seizures and said she was concordant with medication prescribed for her asthma—specifically, albuterol, which she used when needed, and ipratropium bromide combined with albuterol.
On examination she appeared uncomfortable; her pulse rate was 79 beats per min, respiratory rate was 20 breaths per min, blood pressure was 128/84 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. Chest examination found diminished breath sounds at the bases with no appreciable jugular venous distention. An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with left axis deviation, unchanged from a previous recording.
Laboratory investigations showed a typical complete blood count, and urea and electrolytes within normal range. A respiratory virus infection panel was negative for influenza, rhinovirus, SARS COV-2, respiratory syncytial virus, rhinovirus, and parainfluenza.
The patient was treated empirically with intravenous cefepime, and inhaled tobramycin given the history of P aeruginosa pneumonia; the asthma medications were continued.
CT angiogram, compared with previous images, showed that the pathological findings of the RRP had progressed: multiple cavitary opacities and a lesion located in the right main-stem bronchus. Pulmonary emboli were not seen (figure).
On the third day after admission, the patient developed worsening shortness of breath and required 1 L of oxygen overnight, raising concerns of pulmonary oedema secondary to airway obstruction. She was given 40 mg of furosemide intravenously which improved her respiratory status, and she was weaned off the supplemental oxygen. Bronchoscopy confirmed a partially obstructing mass in the middle portion of the right main-stem bronchus (figure); the abnormal tissue was ablated by cryotherapy. Histopathological analysis of a sample obtained from a biopsy of the lesion, showed squamous papilloma with focal low-grade squamous dysplasia.
The patient reported improvement in shortness of breath following the procedure. Bronchoalveolar lavage was also done which later showed negative cultures for aerobic, anaerobic, fungal, and mycobacterial organisms. Given the unlikelihood of an infection after the negative preliminary cultures plus improvement of the symptoms after the ablation, the antibiotics were stopped.
The patient went home 8 days after admission at her baseline respiratory status without the need for supplemental oxygen; at follow-up 1 month later she was relatively well and reported no further syncopal episodes or shortness of breath.
RRP is managed by removal of the papillomas, which because of recurrence, may require repeated attention. The 9-valent HPV (Gardasil 9; Merk & Co., Inc., Rahway, NJ, USA) vaccine protects against serotypes 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58; serotypes 6 and 11 have a known association with greater than 90% of cases with RRP. The vaccine prevents new cases of HPV and in patients who have RRP, it may increase the interval time between the need for surgical removal of the papillomas.
Patients with RRP express vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) in both the papillomas and the nearby blood vessels. Bevacizumab—an antibody inhibiting VEGF—is emerging as a promising treatment for the disease; studies have indicated that systemic treatment with bevacizumab increases the time required between surgical removal and, in some cases, with remission of papilloma development and need for future surgical debridement.
RRP may present with coughing, wheezing, and shortness of breath—as in our patient. HPV rarely transforms into malignancy; for patients with pulmonary involvement, there is a 32-times increased risk. RRP lesions are typically of varying sizes, bilateral, and located posteriorly in the chest; diagnosis is made with CT imaging and either a laryngoscopy or bronchoscopy.

A 41-year-old woman with a 6-day history of worsening shortness of breath and 4 syncopal episodes, which were preceded by coughing spells, attended our hospital; she reported no chest pain or palpitations.
The patient had a medical history of recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP), diagnosed when she was aged 36 years; at the time a chest CT showed nodules in the trachea—RRP was confirmed after bronchoscopy and biopsy. Serotyping was positive for human papillomavirus (HPV) serotypes 6 and 7, and negative for all other serotypes, specifically oncogenic serotypes 16 and 18. She had also been diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus, migraines, asthma, and pneumonia 1 year before admission caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. She reported no history of seizures and said she was concordant with medication prescribed for her asthma—specifically, albuterol, which she used when needed, and ipratropium bromide combined with albuterol.
On examination she appeared uncomfortable; her pulse rate was 79 beats per min, respiratory rate was 20 breaths per min, blood pressure was 128/84 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. Chest examination found diminished breath sounds at the bases with no appreciable jugular venous distention. An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with left axis deviation, unchanged from a previous recording.
Laboratory investigations showed a typical complete blood count, and urea and electrolytes within normal range. A respiratory virus infection panel was negative for influenza, rhinovirus, SARS COV-2, respiratory syncytial virus, rhinovirus, and parainfluenza.
The patient was treated empirically with intravenous cefepime, and inhaled tobramycin given the history of P aeruginosa pneumonia; the asthma medications were continued.
CT angiogram, compared with previous images, showed that the pathological findings of the RRP had progressed: multiple cavitary opacities and a lesion located in the right main-stem bronchus. Pulmonary emboli were not seen (figure).
On the third day after admission, the patient developed worsening shortness of breath and required 1 L of oxygen overnight, raising concerns of pulmonary oedema secondary to airway obstruction. She was given 40 mg of furosemide intravenously which improved her respiratory status, and she was weaned off the supplemental oxygen. Bronchoscopy confirmed a partially obstructing mass in the middle portion of the right main-stem bronchus (figure); the abnormal tissue was ablated by cryotherapy. Histopathological analysis of a sample obtained from a biopsy of the lesion, showed squamous papilloma with focal low-grade squamous dysplasia.
The patient reported improvement in shortness of breath following the procedure. Bronchoalveolar lavage was also done which later showed negative cultures for aerobic, anaerobic, fungal, and mycobacterial organisms. Given the unlikelihood of an infection after the negative preliminary cultures plus improvement of the symptoms after the ablation, the antibiotics were stopped.
The patient went home 8 days after admission at her baseline respiratory status without the need for supplemental oxygen; at follow-up 1 month later she was relatively well and reported no further syncopal episodes or shortness of breath.
RRP is managed by removal of the papillomas, which because of recurrence, may require repeated attention. The 9-valent HPV (Gardasil 9; Merk & Co., Inc., Rahway, NJ, USA) vaccine protects against serotypes 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58; serotypes 6 and 11 have a known association with greater than 90% of cases with RRP. The vaccine prevents new cases of HPV and in patients who have RRP, it may increase the interval time between the need for surgical removal of the papillomas.
Patients with RRP express vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) in both the papillomas and the nearby blood vessels. Bevacizumab—an antibody inhibiting VEGF—is emerging as a promising treatment for the disease; studies have indicated that systemic treatment with bevacizumab increases the time required between surgical removal and, in some cases, with remission of papilloma development and need for future surgical debridement.
RRP may present with coughing, wheezing, and shortness of breath—as in our patient. HPV rarely transforms into malignancy; for patients with pulmonary involvement, there is a 32-times increased risk. RRP lesions are typically of varying sizes, bilateral, and located posteriorly in the chest; diagnosis is made with CT imaging and either a laryngoscopy or bronchoscopy.

A 40-year-old woman with a history of chronic pancreatitis and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease presented with fatigue, malaise, dizziness, difficulty ambulating, diarrhoea, easy bruising, and a diffuse rash involving her extremities and trunk that had been present for several days. She explained that she had limited her diet to consist mostly of bread, rice, dumplings, and the occasional egg white to reduce the symptoms she suffered from her gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. Her diet was also devoid of red meat, fish, chicken, fruits, and vegetables.On physical examination, she had extensive, non-palpable, perifollicular haemorrhages involving her extremities (figure), ecchymosis (figure), and gingival bleeding. Corkscrew hairs, visible with the unaided eye, were seen all over her skin—although they were much more apparent with dermoscopy (figure). Her laboratory results showed haemoglobin 8·3 mg/dL, haematocrit 25·2%, and a plasma vitamin C concentration of <5 μmol/L (normal range 23–50 μmol/L). Endoscopy of the upper gastrointestinal tract and colonoscopy of the lower bowel did not find a source of bleeding.
A biopsy of the skin from her right lower leg showed a corkscrew shaped profile of the hair follicle, and histopathological examination showed follicular hyperkeratosis and plugging (figure). Taken together, the clinical, laboratory, and histopathological findings were consistent with a diagnosis of scurvy. Vitamin C must be obtained from dietary sources and it is essential for hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues for the synthesis of collagen. It is also important for immune system function and iron absorption. Scurvy rarely affects adults but may be seen in some individuals with malnutrition or malabsorption. Signs and symptoms usually occur by the third month of inadequate consumption, and treatment is with vitamin C supplementation. Early diagnosis and treatment of scurvy can be life-saving, so recognition of the physical findings is important. This patient was given intravenous vitamin C followed by daily oral supplementation and her symptoms resolved within a few weeks.

A 40-year-old woman with a history of chronic pancreatitis and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease presented with fatigue, malaise, dizziness, difficulty ambulating, diarrhoea, easy bruising, and a diffuse rash involving her extremities and trunk that had been present for several days. She explained that she had limited her diet to consist mostly of bread, rice, dumplings, and the occasional egg white to reduce the symptoms she suffered from her gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. Her diet was also devoid of red meat, fish, chicken, fruits, and vegetables.On physical examination, she had extensive, non-palpable, perifollicular haemorrhages involving her extremities (figure), ecchymosis (figure), and gingival bleeding. Corkscrew hairs, visible with the unaided eye, were seen all over her skin—although they were much more apparent with dermoscopy (figure). A 27-year-old man presented to an emergency department with vomiting and an altered mental state. He had a history of possible Gilbert's syndrome as a child and previous opiate use disorder, but with no evidence of recent use. He gave a family history of a maternal grandfather who had developed seizures during a hospital admission for asthma. The patient had otherwise been fit and well and physically active—including playing hockey. While in the emergency department he became combative and left the hospital against medical advice.Laboratory investigations taken just before he left showed a raised blood ammonia concentration of 155 μmol/L (normal 16–60).
4 days before attending the hospital, he had epidural injections of the corticosteroid triamcinolone at two spinal levels because of chronic back pain. Soon after the procedure, the patient reported a headache and feeling unwell.
The day after his presentation to an emergency department, the patient's father called 911 saying that the patient was behaving strangely and having violent outbursts; he also said that the day before, he and his son had an episode of vomiting after eating a takeaway meal.
When the patient attended the emergency department for the second time, he immediately had a seizure. He was intubated and transferred to our university hospital. A screen for drugs of abuse was negative.
On examination, the patient had bilateral, fixed, dilated pupils, and he made minimal response to physical stimulation.
Investigations showed that the ammonia concentration had increased further to 591 μmol/L; serum creatinine kinase concentration was 299 units per L (normal 20–200), aspartate aminotransferase 26 units per L (normal <40), alanine aminotransferase 65 units per L (normal <41), alkaline phosphatase 84 units per L (normal 40–129), and total bilirubin concentration was 3 mg/dL (normal <1·2), and screening for paracetamol, salicylates, valproic acid, and serum ethanol was negative.
A CT scan of the patient's head showed diffuse cerebral oedema with effacement of both lateral ventricles (figure).
Despite treatment, including intravenous 3% hypertonic saline, levocarnitine, lactulose, and mannitol, the patient's condition continued to deteriorate, and 3 days after he arrived at our hospital, he was pronounced brain dead.
Further investigations into the cause of death—including genetic testing for urea cycle disorders—showed a mutation indicative of X-linked ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency. The patient's family members have been advised to have genetic screening.
The commonest cause of hyperammonaemia in adults is liver disease—specifically cirrhosis. However, congenital disorders—such as urea cycle defects—should also be considered, even later in life.
OTC deficiency is the commonest urea cycle disorder and it can present at any age; late-onset disease is usually seen in heterozygous females. Adult-onset presentations can be triggered by infection, stress, fasting, surgery, increased protein intake, and medications—including glucocorticoids. Our case emphasises the need for timely recognition of unexplained life-threatening hyperammonaemia and the prompt employment of treatment with ammonia scavengers, arginine and citrulline supplements, and haemodialysis. Liver transplantation is also an option in the management of patients with severe urea cycle disorders.

A 27-year-old man presented to an emergency department with vomiting and an altered mental state. He had a history of possible Gilbert's syndrome as a child and previous opiate use disorder, but with no evidence of recent use. He gave a family history of a maternal grandfather who had developed seizures during a hospital admission for asthma. The patient had otherwise been fit and well and physically active—including playing hockey. While in the emergency department he became combative and left the hospital against medical advice.Laboratory investigations taken just before he left showed a raised blood ammonia concentration of 155 μmol/L (normal 16–60).
4 days before attending the hospital, he had epidural injections of the corticosteroid triamcinolone at two spinal levels because of chronic back pain. Soon after the procedure, the patient reported a headache and feeling unwell.
The day after his presentation to an emergency department, the patient's father called 911 saying that the patient was behaving strangely and having violent outbursts; he also said that the day before, he and his son had an episode of vomiting after eating a takeaway meal.
When the patient attended the emergency department for the second time, he immediately had a seizure. He was intubated and transferred to our university hospital. A screen for drugs of abuse was negative.
On examination, the patient had bilateral, fixed, dilated pupils, and he made minimal response to physical stimulation.
Investigations showed that the ammonia concentration had increased further to 591 μmol/L; serum creatinine kinase concentration was 299 units per L (normal 20–200), aspartate aminotransferase 26 units per L (normal <40), alanine aminotransferase 65 units per L (normal <41), alkaline phosphatase 84 units per L (normal 40–129), and total bilirubin concentration was 3 mg/dL (normal <1·2), and screening for paracetamol, salicylates, valproic acid, and serum ethanol was negative.
A CT scan of the patient's head showed diffuse cerebral oedema with effacement of both lateral ventricles (figure).
Despite treatment, including intravenous 3% hypertonic saline, levocarnitine, lactulose, and mannitol, the patient's condition continued to deteriorate, and 3 days after he arrived at our hospital, he was pronounced brain dead.
Further investigations into the cause of death—including genetic testing for urea cycle disorders—showed a mutation indicative of X-linked ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency. The patient's family members have been advised to have genetic screening.
The commonest cause of hyperammonaemia in adults is liver disease—specifically cirrhosis. However, congenital disorders—such as urea cycle defects—should also be considered, even later in life.
OTC deficiency is the commonest urea cycle disorder and it can present at any age; late-onset disease is usually seen in heterozygous females. Adult-onset presentations can be triggered by infection, stress, fasting, surgery, increased protein intake, and medications—including glucocorticoids. Our case emphasises the need for timely recognition of unexplained life-threatening hyperammonaemia and the prompt employment of treatment with ammonia scavengers, arginine and citrulline supplements, and haemodialysis. Liver transplantation is also an option in the management of patients with severe urea cycle disorders.

A 27-year-old man presented to an emergency department with vomiting and an altered mental state. He had a history of possible Gilbert's syndrome as a child and previous opiate use disorder, but with no evidence of recent use. He gave a family history of a maternal grandfather who had developed seizures during a hospital admission for asthma. The patient had otherwise been fit and well and physically active—including playing hockey. While in the emergency department he became combative and left the hospital against medical advice.Laboratory investigations taken just before he left showed a raised blood ammonia concentration of 155 μmol/L (normal 16–60).
4 days before attending the hospital, he had epidural injections of the corticosteroid triamcinolone at two spinal levels because of chronic back pain. Soon after the procedure, the patient reported a headache and feeling unwell.
The day after his presentation to an emergency department, the patient's father called 911 saying that the patient was behaving strangely and having violent outbursts; he also said that the day before, he and his son had an episode of vomiting after eating a takeaway meal.
When the patient attended the emergency department for the second time, he immediately had a seizure. He was intubated and transferred to our university hospital. A screen for drugs of abuse was negative.
On examination, the patient had bilateral, fixed, dilated pupils, and he made minimal response to physical stimulation.
Investigations showed that the ammonia concentration had increased further to 591 μmol/L; serum creatinine kinase concentration was 299 units per L (normal 20–200), aspartate aminotransferase 26 units per L (normal <40), alanine aminotransferase 65 units per L (normal <41), alkaline phosphatase 84 units per L (normal 40–129), and total bilirubin concentration was 3 mg/dL (normal <1·2), and screening for paracetamol, salicylates, valproic acid, and serum ethanol was negative.
A CT scan of the patient's head showed diffuse cerebral oedema with effacement of both lateral ventricles (figure).
Despite treatment, including intravenous 3% hypertonic saline, levocarnitine, lactulose, and mannitol, the patient's condition continued to deteriorate, and 3 days after he arrived at our hospital, he was pronounced brain dead.
Further investigations into the cause of death—including genetic testing for urea cycle disorders—showed a mutation indicative of X-linked ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency. The patient's family members have been advised to have genetic screening.
The commonest cause of hyperammonaemia in adults is liver disease—specifically cirrhosis. However, congenital disorders—such as urea cycle defects—should also be considered, even later in life.
OTC deficiency is the commonest urea cycle disorder and it can present at any age; late-onset disease is usually seen in heterozygous females. Adult-onset presentations can be triggered by infection, stress, fasting, surgery, increased protein intake, and medications—including glucocorticoids. Our case emphasises the need for timely recognition of unexplained life-threatening hyperammonaemia and the prompt employment of treatment with ammonia scavengers, arginine and citrulline supplements, and haemodialysis. Liver transplantation is also an option in the management of patients with severe urea cycle disorders.

A 48-year-old man came to our eye clinic because his vision had been deteriorating over the previous 3 weeks; he had no pain and no other eye symptoms.In his medical history, he had been diagnosed with advanced stage, aggressive B-cell lymphoma—with no indication of CNS involvement: his cerebrospinal fluid had shown no cancer cells. He had been treated with systemic chemotherapy, with rituximab and intrathecal methotrexate prophylaxis for six cycles over a 110-day period, resulting in a complete remission; his last dose of his treatment was given 88 days before the onset of his vision problems.
On examination, we found his visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/60 in the left. Intraocular pressures were elevated in both eyes—43 mm Hg in the right and 52 mm Hg in the left (normal range 10–21). Both eyes showed mild conjunctival injection and corneal oedema, and the anterior chamber of both eyes contained a high concentration of cells—grade 4, severe cellularity—a layered pseudohypopyon, but no signs of flare or protein transudate (figure). The vitreous humour showed no cellularity or haze, and the patient's retina and choroid were normal.
We were concerned that he might have ocular metastasis—given the recent history of B-cell lymphoma—and a sample of aqueous humour confirmed our suspicions (appendix). The patient was again treated with rituximab and high-dose methotrexate. At follow-up, 2 months later, his vision was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left. The pseudohypopyon had completely resolved in the right eye and was much reduced in the left; his intraocular pressures returned to within normal range using topical therapy (appendix). Neuroimaging and CSF studies remained unremarkable throughout the course of treatment. However, the lymphoma recurred—involving the CNS—and 15 months after the onset of his visual symptoms, he died.
A hypopyon—also known as sterile pus—is produced because of toxins, which are usually produced by pathogens, causing the collection of leucocytes in the anterior chamber of the eye. It can occur with a corneal ulcer, Behçet's disease, endophthalmitis, and as an adverse reaction to some drugs—including rifabutin.
Pseudohypopyons can be caused by metastatic cells: they have been reported with leukaemias, lymphomas, and retinoblastomas. Patients with pseudohypopyons—unlike eye infections—typically have no pain or redness. Metastatic diseases in the eye can involve infiltration of the aqueous or vitreous humour, retina, or choroid. Mechanical blocking of the aqueous humour outflow by metastatic cells can result in increased intraocular pressures—as occurred in our patient. As is well known, but cannot be repeated often enough, eye problems should prompt a thorough history and an investigation for a primary cancer or for referral for further treatment in a patient with a known malignancy.

input:
A 48-year-old man came to our eye clinic because his vision had been deteriorating over the previous 3 weeks; he had no pain and no other eye symptoms.In his medical history, he had been diagnosed with advanced stage, aggressive B-cell lymphoma—with no indication of CNS involvement: his cerebrospinal fluid had shown no cancer cells. He had been treated with systemic chemotherapy, with rituximab and intrathecal methotrexate prophylaxis for six cycles over a 110-day period, resulting in a complete remission; his last dose of his treatment was given 88 days before the onset of his vision problems.
On examination, we found his visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/60 in the left. Intraocular pressures were elevated in both eyes—43 mm Hg in the right and 52 mm Hg in the left (normal range 10–21). Both eyes showed mild conjunctival injection and corneal oedema, and the anterior chamber of both eyes contained a high concentration of cells—grade 4, severe cellularity—a layered pseudohypopyon, but no signs of flare or protein transudate (figure). The vitreous humour showed no cellularity or haze, and the patient's retina and choroid were normal.
We were concerned that he might have ocular metastasis—given the recent history of B-cell lymphoma—and a sample of aqueous humour confirmed our suspicions (appendix). The patient was again treated with rituximab and high-dose methotrexate. At follow-up, 2 months later, his vision was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left. The pseudohypopyon had completely resolved in the right eye and was much reduced in the left; his intraocular pressures returned to within normal range using topical therapy (appendix). Neuroimaging and CSF studies remained unremarkable throughout the course of treatment. However, the lymphoma recurred—involving the CNS—and 15 months after the onset of his visual symptoms, he died.
A hypopyon—also known as sterile pus—is produced because of toxins, which are usually produced by pathogens, causing the collection of leucocytes in the anterior chamber of the eye. It can occur with a corneal ulcer, Behçet's disease, endophthalmitis, and as an adverse reaction to some drugs—including rifabutin.
Pseudohypopyons can be caused by metastatic cells: they have been reported with leukaemias, lymphomas, and retinoblastomas. Patients with pseudohypopyons—unlike eye infections—typically have no pain or redness. Metastatic diseases in the eye can involve infiltration of the aqueous or vitreous humour, retina, or choroid. Mechanical blocking of the aqueous humour outflow by metastatic cells can result in increased intraocular pressures—as occurred in our patient. As is well known, but cannot be repeated often enough, eye problems should prompt a thorough history and an investigation for a primary cancer or for referral for further treatment in a patient with a known malignancy.

input:
A 48-year-old man came to our eye clinic because his vision had been deteriorating over the previous 3 weeks; he had no pain and no other eye symptoms.In his medical history, he had been diagnosed with advanced stage, aggressive B-cell lymphoma—with no indication of CNS involvement: his cerebrospinal fluid had shown no cancer cells. He had been treated with systemic chemotherapy, with rituximab and intrathecal methotrexate prophylaxis for six cycles over a 110-day period, resulting in a complete remission; his last dose of his treatment was given 88 days before the onset of his vision problems.
On examination, we found his visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/60 in the left. Intraocular pressures were elevated in both eyes—43 mm Hg in the right and 52 mm Hg in the left (normal range 10–21). Both eyes showed mild conjunctival injection and corneal oedema, and the anterior chamber of both eyes contained a high concentration of cells—grade 4, severe cellularity—a layered pseudohypopyon, but no signs of flare or protein transudate (figure). The vitreous humour showed no cellularity or haze, and the patient's retina and choroid were normal.
We were concerned that he might have ocular metastasis—given the recent history of B-cell lymphoma—and a sample of aqueous humour confirmed our suspicions (appendix). The patient was again treated with rituximab and high-dose methotrexate. At follow-up, 2 months later, his vision was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left. The pseudohypopyon had completely resolved in the right eye and was much reduced in the left; his intraocular pressures returned to within normal range using topical therapy (appendix). Neuroimaging and CSF studies remained unremarkable throughout the course of treatment. However, the lymphoma recurred—involving the CNS—and 15 months after the onset of his visual symptoms, he died.
A hypopyon—also known as sterile pus—is produced because of toxins, which are usually produced by pathogens, causing the collection of leucocytes in the anterior chamber of the eye. It can occur with a corneal ulcer, Behçet's disease, endophthalmitis, and as an adverse reaction to some drugs—including rifabutin.
Pseudohypopyons can be caused by metastatic cells: they have been reported with leukaemias, lymphomas, and retinoblastomas. Patients with pseudohypopyons—unlike eye infections—typically have no pain or redness. Metastatic diseases in the eye can involve infiltration of the aqueous or vitreous humour, retina, or choroid. Mechanical blocking of the aqueous humour outflow by metastatic cells can result in increased intraocular pressures—as occurred in our patient. As is well known, but cannot be repeated often enough, eye problems should prompt a thorough history and an investigation for a primary cancer or for referral for further treatment in a patient with a known malignancy.

A 24-year-old woman was referred to our specialist unit with a 3-month history of 15·8 kg weight loss, increasing abdominal pain and bloating, fatigue, night sweats, difficulty passing urine, amenorrhoea, and trouble walking. She was nulligravida and had a copper intrauterine device (IUD) in situ for the past 4 years. She was a non-smoker, drank alcohol socially, and had no history of recent travel. She stated she was allergic to penicillin.On examination, the patient was pale and cachexic—body-mass index 20·15 kg/m2—and afebrile, with normal vital signs (appendix). She had an abdominopelvic mass of approximately 18-week gestation that was continuous with the cervix, uterus, and anterior abdominal wall.
Investigations showed her human chorionic gonadotropin serum concentration pregnancy test was negative, haemoglobin concentration was 68 g/L (normal 120–160), CA-125 antigen concentration was 152 IU/mL (normal <35 IU/mL) and C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration was 146 mg/L (normal 0–5). All other blood tests were unremarkable.
Ultrasound, CT, and MRI of the pelvis showed an 18 week-sized uterine mass invading the anterior abdominal wall, bladder, colon, ileum, and enlarged pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes (figure). 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET–CT showed extensive hypermetabolic abnormalities below the diaphragm (appendix). The IUD had partially perforated into the myometrium.
We considered uterine lymphoma, sarcoma, and actinomycosis as differential diagnoses. However, histopathological examination of core biopsies of the mass from two different sites on two separate occasions only showed inflammation—with no histological evidence of malignancy, actinomyces, tuberculosis, or fungal infection.
Culture of core tissue samples, endocervical swabs, and the IUD—which was removed—had no bacterial or fungal growth. Despite this, given the IUD perforation into the myometrium, extensive and contiguous crossing of tissue boundaries, and lack of histological evidence of malignancy, we started treatment for actinomycosis. Initially, we used intravenous ceftriaxone but switched to penicillin—the antibiotic of choice—after hypersensitivity skin testing was negative. To facilitate ambulatory management, treatment was subsequently changed to oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times a day. The patient's symptoms improved significantly within a week, and 3 months later her CRP concentration had dropped to 0·7 mg/L; imaging showed complete resolution of actinomycosis and her return to good health (appendix).
Actinomycosis is caused by a filamentous, Gram-positive, anaerobic bacteria, Actinomyces spp, which is of low virulence and unable to cross normal mucosal barriers. However, once trauma breaches the mucosa, the organism spreads contiguously, disregarding anatomical planes.
Clinicians should consider the diagnosis of actinomycosis when there is either progression across tissue boundaries or the development of sinus tracts. Confirmation by culture and or histological findings of sulphur granules may be negative; newer techniques such as 16S ribosomal RNA sequencing and matrix-assisted laser desorption ionisation time-of-flight can facilitate the diagnosis. Treatment for 6–12 months is key to preventing relapse. Actinomyces-like organisms are found in the pap smears of approximately 7% of IUD users and pose no risk if there are no signs or symptoms of infection. Injury to myometrium and IUDs left in situ for prolonged periods are risk factors for an actinomycosis infection which, if suspected, warrants removal of the IUD and prompt treatment (video).

She was nulligravida and had a copper intrauterine device (IUD) in situ for the past 4 years. She was a non-smoker, drank alcohol socially, and had no history of recent travel. She stated she was allergic to penicillin.On examination, the patient was pale and cachexic—body-mass index 20·15 kg/m2—and afebrile, with normal vital signs (appendix). She had an abdominopelvic mass of approximately 18-week gestation that was continuous with the cervix, uterus, and anterior abdominal wall.
Investigations showed her human chorionic gonadotropin serum concentration pregnancy test was negative, haemoglobin concentration was 68 g/L (normal 120–160), CA-125 antigen concentration was 152 IU/mL (normal <35 IU/mL) and C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration was 146 mg/L (normal 0–5). All other blood tests were unremarkable.
Ultrasound, CT, and MRI of the pelvis showed an 18 week-sized uterine mass invading the anterior abdominal wall, bladder, colon, ileum, and enlarged pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes (figure). 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET–CT showed extensive hypermetabolic abnormalities below the diaphragm (appendix). The IUD had partially perforated into the myometrium.
We considered uterine lymphoma, sarcoma, and actinomycosis as differential diagnoses. However, histopathological examination of core biopsies of the mass from two different sites on two separate occasions only showed inflammation—with no histological evidence of malignancy, actinomyces, tuberculosis, or fungal infection.
Culture of core tissue samples, endocervical swabs, and the IUD—which was removed—had no bacterial or fungal growth. Despite this, given the IUD perforation into the myometrium, extensive and contiguous crossing of tissue boundaries, and lack of histological evidence of malignancy, we started treatment for actinomycosis. Initially, we used intravenous ceftriaxone but switched to penicillin—the antibiotic of choice—after hypersensitivity skin testing was negative. The patient's symptoms improved significantly within a week, and 3 months later her CRP concentration had dropped to 0·7 mg/L; imaging showed complete resolution of actinomycosis and her return to good health (appendix).
Actinomycosis is caused by a filamentous, Gram-positive, anaerobic bacteria, Actinomyces spp, which is of low virulence and unable to cross normal mucosal barriers. However, once trauma breaches the mucosa, the organism spreads contiguously, disregarding anatomical planes.

In December, 2015, an 18-month-old boy with an unremarkable medical history was admitted to the paediatric emergency room for left leg trauma following a fall. A clinical examination showed a leg deformity and total functional impairment of the limb. A radiograph of the leg (figure) revealed a diaphyseal tibial and fibular fracture, with condensed cortical bone and anterolateral bowing (Crawford type I). Café au lait spots were noticed on the child's trunk (figure). After 3 months of immobilisation in an above-knee cast, there were still no signs of bone healing. A clinical examination of the boy's mother revealed multiple café au lait spots and cutaneous neurofibromas, and confirmed the presence of a hitherto undiagnosed case of familial neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). The course of the boy's disease confirmed that he was suffering from NF1-associated congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia (CPT). No cutaneous or visceral neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, or optic gliomas were observed. No other skeletal manifestations were noted. Surgical treatment (resection of the pseudarthrosis area and an induced membrane technique) was initiated 5 months after the fracture. 1 year after surgery, persistent non-union at the distal end of the tibia prompted surgical revision with a second induced membrane technique.Although up to 55% of cases of CPT are associated with NF1, only 3% of patients with NF1 have CPT. Young children often develop CPT long before the appearance of other signs. Most cases are unilateral. Cystic forms (as in the present case) show condensed cortical and thickened bone in the concavity of the deformity, together with a narrow medullary canal. Progression of the deformity can result in a transverse fracture. Crawford's classification is most frequently applied. Surgical treatment of CPT remains a challenge because of refracture, delayed union, non-union, and persistent lower limb disorders. Several surgical options have been described, such as resection and nailing, fibular vascularised grafting, and the induced membrane technique.
This case report demonstrates the importance of diagnosis of pathological fractures in children, since they can reveal NF1.

In December, 2015, an 18-month-old boy with an unremarkable medical history was admitted to the paediatric emergency room for left leg trauma following a fall. A clinical examination showed a leg deformity and total functional impairment of the limb. A radiograph of the leg (figure) revealed a diaphyseal tibial and fibular fracture, with condensed cortical bone and anterolateral bowing (Crawford type I). Café au lait spots were noticed on the child's trunk (figure). After 3 months of immobilisation in an above-knee cast, there were still no signs of bone healing. A clinical examination of the boy's mother revealed multiple café au lait spots and cutaneous neurofibromas, and confirmed the presence of a hitherto undiagnosed case of familial neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). The course of the boy's disease confirmed that he was suffering from NF1-associated congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia (CPT). No cutaneous or visceral neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, or optic gliomas were observed. No other skeletal manifestations were noted. Surgical treatment (resection of the pseudarthrosis area and an induced membrane technique) was initiated 5 months after the fracture. 1 year after surgery, persistent non-union at the distal end of the tibia prompted surgical revision with a second induced membrane technique.Although up to 55% of cases of CPT are associated with NF1, only 3% of patients with NF1 have CPT. Young children often develop CPT long before the appearance of other signs. Most cases are unilateral. Cystic forms (as in the present case) show condensed cortical and thickened bone in the concavity of the deformity, together with a narrow medullary canal. Progression of the deformity can result in a transverse fracture. Crawford's classification is most frequently applied. Surgical treatment of CPT remains a challenge because of refracture, delayed union, non-union, and persistent lower limb disorders. Several surgical options have been described, such as resection and nailing, fibular vascularised grafting, and the induced membrane technique.
This case report demonstrates the importance of diagnosis of pathological fractures in children, since they can reveal NF1.

input:
A 44-year-old woman who had been diagnosed with diabetes at age 21 years presented with a three-day history of oligoarthritis involving both knees and wrists, and primary amenorrhea. Physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness in the affected joints. Pelvic examination showed a blind-ending vaginal pouch without the cervix. Radiographs of the knees and wrists showed calcification of the cartilage in both knees (figure A), both ulnocarpal joints, and right trapeziometacarpal joint (figure B), suggesting calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease.
Further laboratory investigations revealed hypomagnesemia (serum magnesium 1·15 mg/dL) with renal magnesium wasting (fractional excretion of magnesium 19·3%) and hypocalciuria. Serum calcium, urate, ferritin, alkaline phosphatase, rheumatoid factor, and intact parathyroid hormone concentrations were within normal limits. There were no clinical or historical features suggestive of alternative causes of arthritis, such as psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, palmoplantar lesions, or recent genitourinary or gastrointestinal infections. Genetic testing was performed and a complete deletion of the HNF1B coding sequence was identified. This finding confirmed a diagnosis of HNF1B-related disease, characterised by maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 5, Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome, and secondary CPPD disease due to hypomagnesaemia.
An abdominal CT scan was performed to look for structural atypicalities commonly associated with HNF1B mutations, including renal cysts, pancreatic atrophy, and uterine anomalies. Although none of these findings were present, the CT scan revealed calcification involving the pubic symphysis and bilateral hips (figure C). The diffuse distribution of calcifications in CPPD disease is often linked to genetic or metabolic disturbances. Although hypomagnesaemia is a recognised feature of HNF1B-related disease, the association between HNF1B-related disease and CPPD remains uncommon.
This case highlights the importance of thorough evaluation in patients presenting with extensive CPPD disease and multisystem involvement. HNF1B encodes a transcription factor that is crucial for pancreatic and genitourinary development and plays a key role in magnesium homoeostasis through the regulation of basolateral magnesium transport in the distal convoluted tubule. The triad of hypomagnesaemia, diabetes, and Müllerian anomalies (associated with Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome) should prompt consideration of HNF1B-related disease. The patient's arthritis was managed with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and magnesium supplementation was initiated. She was given a combination of glipizide and insulin for her diabetes, with the addition of empagliflozin for improved glycaemic control and to mitigate renal magnesium loss—potentially by enhancing transcellular magnesium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule through upregulation of the transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily M member 6, and increasing paracellular reabsorption in the loop of Henle.

input:
A 44-year-old woman who had been diagnosed with diabetes at age 21 years presented with a three-day history of oligoarthritis involving both knees and wrists, and primary amenorrhea. Physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness in the affected joints. Pelvic examination showed a blind-ending vaginal pouch without the cervix. Radiographs of the knees and wrists showed calcification of the cartilage in both knees (figure A), both ulnocarpal joints, and right trapeziometacarpal joint (figure B), suggesting calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease.
Further laboratory investigations revealed hypomagnesemia (serum magnesium 1·15 mg/dL) with renal magnesium wasting (fractional excretion of magnesium 19·3%) and hypocalciuria. Serum calcium, urate, ferritin, alkaline phosphatase, rheumatoid factor, and intact parathyroid hormone concentrations were within normal limits. There were no clinical or historical features suggestive of alternative causes of arthritis, such as psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, palmoplantar lesions, or recent genitourinary or gastrointestinal infections. Genetic testing was performed and a complete deletion of the HNF1B coding sequence was identified. This finding confirmed a diagnosis of HNF1B-related disease, characterised by maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 5, Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome, and secondary CPPD disease due to hypomagnesaemia.
An abdominal CT scan was performed to look for structural atypicalities commonly associated with HNF1B mutations, including renal cysts, pancreatic atrophy, and uterine anomalies. Although none of these findings were present, the CT scan revealed calcification involving the pubic symphysis and bilateral hips (figure C). The diffuse distribution of calcifications in CPPD disease is often linked to genetic or metabolic disturbances. Although hypomagnesaemia is a recognised feature of HNF1B-related disease, the association between HNF1B-related disease and CPPD remains uncommon.
This case highlights the importance of thorough evaluation in patients presenting with extensive CPPD disease and multisystem involvement. HNF1B encodes a transcription factor that is crucial for pancreatic and genitourinary development and plays a key role in magnesium homoeostasis through the regulation of basolateral magnesium transport in the distal convoluted tubule. The triad of hypomagnesaemia, diabetes, and Müllerian anomalies (associated with Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome) should prompt consideration of HNF1B-related disease. The patient's arthritis was managed with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and magnesium supplementation was initiated. She was given a combination of glipizide and insulin for her diabetes, with the addition of empagliflozin for improved glycaemic control and to mitigate renal magnesium loss—potentially by enhancing transcellular magnesium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule through upregulation of the transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily M member 6, and increasing paracellular reabsorption in the loop of Henle.

A 44-year-old woman who had been diagnosed with diabetes at age 21 years presented with a three-day history of oligoarthritis involving both knees and wrists, and primary amenorrhea. Physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness in the affected joints. Pelvic examination showed a blind-ending vaginal pouch without the cervix. Radiographs of the knees and wrists showed calcification of the cartilage in both knees (figure A), both ulnocarpal joints, and right trapeziometacarpal joint (figure B), suggesting calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease.
Further laboratory investigations revealed hypomagnesemia (serum magnesium 1·15 mg/dL) with renal magnesium wasting (fractional excretion of magnesium 19·3%) and hypocalciuria. Serum calcium, urate, ferritin, alkaline phosphatase, rheumatoid factor, and intact parathyroid hormone concentrations were within normal limits. There were no clinical or historical features suggestive of alternative causes of arthritis, such as psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, palmoplantar lesions, or recent genitourinary or gastrointestinal infections. Genetic testing was performed and a complete deletion of the HNF1B coding sequence was identified. This finding confirmed a diagnosis of HNF1B-related disease, characterised by maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 5, Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome, and secondary CPPD disease due to hypomagnesaemia.
An abdominal CT scan was performed to look for structural atypicalities commonly associated with HNF1B mutations, including renal cysts, pancreatic atrophy, and uterine anomalies. Although none of these findings were present, the CT scan revealed calcification involving the pubic symphysis and bilateral hips (figure C). The diffuse distribution of calcifications in CPPD disease is often linked to genetic or metabolic disturbances. Although hypomagnesaemia is a recognised feature of HNF1B-related disease, the association between HNF1B-related disease and CPPD remains uncommon.
This case highlights the importance of thorough evaluation in patients presenting with extensive CPPD disease and multisystem involvement. HNF1B encodes a transcription factor that is crucial for pancreatic and genitourinary development and plays a key role in magnesium homoeostasis through the regulation of basolateral magnesium transport in the distal convoluted tubule. The triad of hypomagnesaemia, diabetes, and Müllerian anomalies (associated with Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome) should prompt consideration of HNF1B-related disease. The patient's arthritis was managed with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and magnesium supplementation was initiated. She was given a combination of glipizide and insulin for her diabetes, with the addition of empagliflozin for improved glycaemic control and to mitigate renal magnesium loss—potentially by enhancing transcellular magnesium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule through upregulation of the transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily M member 6, and increasing paracellular reabsorption in the loop of Henle.

A 3-month-old boy was brought by his mother to our clinic who had noticed that her child had developed several round red lesions on his face (figure). She said that the problem had begun 3 weeks post partum. The baby had been born at full term following an uncomplicated pregnancy. The patient's mother was fit and well with no medical history of note—specifically she did not report any previous infections, or dermatological or autoimmune diseases.The baby had been seen by another dermatologist when he was 10 weeks old and given topical antifungal treatment—miconazole cream—and a low potency topical corticosteroid cream—hydrocortisone—which had no effect after a 2-week trial.
On examination, we found six, well defined, erythematous annular plaques, with indurated borders, on the baby's face. We found no other abnormalities: the baby's temperature was normal, his heart rate was 138 beats per min, and the respiratory rate was 36 breaths per min.
Histopathological examination of a biopsy sample of the plaque on the face showed a vacuolar interface dermatitis with dermal oedema and a periadnexal infiltrate of lymphocytes (figure). Laboratory blood tests showed that both the mother and child were positive for antibodies against extractable nuclear antigen. They were also positive for anti-Sjögren's syndrome type A (SSA) and anti-Sjögren's syndrome type B (SSB) antibodies. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 11 mm per h, the C-reactive protein concentration was 0·6 mg/L. The white cell count was 13·85 × 109 per L—the neutrophil count was 1·47 × 109 per L, eosinophils 0·18 × 109 per L, basophils 0·02 × 109 per L, lymphocytes 10·58 × 109 per L, and monocytes 1·60 × 109 per L. Both liver and kidney function tests were normal.
Taken together with the findings of the biopsy, we diagnosed neonatal lupus erythematosus.
Given that heart abnormalities are associated with the condition, we referred the baby to a paediatric cardiologist who requested an electrocardiogram which showed findings consistent with first-degree atrioventricular block.
3 months later at a follow-up appointment, all the baby's skin lesions had resolved without any scarring.
Finally, again given the diagnosis and the positive antinuclear antibodies, we referred the patient's mother to a rheumatologist who diagnosed Sjögren's syndrome.
Neonatal lupus erythematosus is a passively acquired, self-limiting, autoimmune disease thought to be caused by the transplacental passage of anti-SSA and anti-SSB antibodies from mother to fetus: the skin—and more importantly—the heart are particularly affected. In approximately half the cases, the mothers are asymptomatic at time of presentation. The cutaneous manifestations in the baby usually develop within the first few weeks of life—typically appearing on the scalp and periorbital areas. The association of the skin lesions with positive anti-SSA and anti-SSB tests in both mother and baby is well recognised, and a skin biopsy is not necessarily required to make the diagnosis. The important complication of congenital heart block—which usually develops in utero and generally resolves—is rare and found in approximately 2% of pregnant women with anti-SSA or anti-SSB antibodies. The skin manifestations in neonatal lupus spontaneously resolve after 4–6 months (video).

input:
A 3-month-old boy was brought by his mother to our clinic who had noticed that her child had developed several round red lesions on his face (figure). She said that the problem had begun 3 weeks post partum. The baby had been born at full term following an uncomplicated pregnancy. The patient's mother was fit and well with no medical history of note—specifically she did not report any previous infections, or dermatological or autoimmune diseases.The baby had been seen by another dermatologist when he was 10 weeks old and given topical antifungal treatment—miconazole cream—and a low potency topical corticosteroid cream—hydrocortisone—which had no effect after a 2-week trial.
On examination, we found six, well defined, erythematous annular plaques, with indurated borders, on the baby's face. We found no other abnormalities: the baby's temperature was normal, his heart rate was 138 beats per min, and the respiratory rate was 36 breaths per min.
Histopathological examination of a biopsy sample of the plaque on the face showed a vacuolar interface dermatitis with dermal oedema and a periadnexal infiltrate of lymphocytes (figure). Laboratory blood tests showed that both the mother and child were positive for antibodies against extractable nuclear antigen. They were also positive for anti-Sjögren's syndrome type A (SSA) and anti-Sjögren's syndrome type B (SSB) antibodies. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 11 mm per h, the C-reactive protein concentration was 0·6 mg/L. The white cell count was 13·85 × 109 per L—the neutrophil count was 1·47 × 109 per L, eosinophils 0·18 × 109 per L, basophils 0·02 × 109 per L, lymphocytes 10·58 × 109 per L, and monocytes 1·60 × 109 per L. Both liver and kidney function tests were normal.
Taken together with the findings of the biopsy, we diagnosed neonatal lupus erythematosus.
Given that heart abnormalities are associated with the condition, we referred the baby to a paediatric cardiologist who requested an electrocardiogram which showed findings consistent with first-degree atrioventricular block.
3 months later at a follow-up appointment, all the baby's skin lesions had resolved without any scarring.
Finally, again given the diagnosis and the positive antinuclear antibodies, we referred the patient's mother to a rheumatologist who diagnosed Sjögren's syndrome.
Neonatal lupus erythematosus is a passively acquired, self-limiting, autoimmune disease thought to be caused by the transplacental passage of anti-SSA and anti-SSB antibodies from mother to fetus: the skin—and more importantly—the heart are particularly affected. In approximately half the cases, the mothers are asymptomatic at time of presentation. The cutaneous manifestations in the baby usually develop within the first few weeks of life—typically appearing on the scalp and periorbital areas. The association of the skin lesions with positive anti-SSA and anti-SSB tests in both mother and baby is well recognised, and a skin biopsy is not necessarily required to make the diagnosis. The important complication of congenital heart block—which usually develops in utero and generally resolves—is rare and found in approximately 2% of pregnant women with anti-SSA or anti-SSB antibodies. The skin manifestations in neonatal lupus spontaneously resolve after 4–6 months (video).

input:
In December, 2015, an 18-month-old boy with an unremarkable medical history was admitted to the paediatric emergency room for left leg trauma following a fall. A clinical examination showed a leg deformity and total functional impairment of the limb. A radiograph of the leg (figure) revealed a diaphyseal tibial and fibular fracture, with condensed cortical bone and anterolateral bowing (Crawford type I). Café au lait spots were noticed on the child's trunk (figure). After 3 months of immobilisation in an above-knee cast, there were still no signs of bone healing. A clinical examination of the boy's mother revealed multiple café au lait spots and cutaneous neurofibromas, and confirmed the presence of a hitherto undiagnosed case of familial neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). The course of the boy's disease confirmed that he was suffering from NF1-associated congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia (CPT). No cutaneous or visceral neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, or optic gliomas were observed. No other skeletal manifestations were noted. Surgical treatment (resection of the pseudarthrosis area and an induced membrane technique) was initiated 5 months after the fracture. 1 year after surgery, persistent non-union at the distal end of the tibia prompted surgical revision with a second induced membrane technique.Although up to 55% of cases of CPT are associated with NF1, only 3% of patients with NF1 have CPT. Young children often develop CPT long before the appearance of other signs. Most cases are unilateral. Cystic forms (as in the present case) show condensed cortical and thickened bone in the concavity of the deformity, together with a narrow medullary canal. Progression of the deformity can result in a transverse fracture. Crawford's classification is most frequently applied. Surgical treatment of CPT remains a challenge because of refracture, delayed union, non-union, and persistent lower limb disorders. Several surgical options have been described, such as resection and nailing, fibular vascularised grafting, and the induced membrane technique.
This case report demonstrates the importance of diagnosis of pathological fractures in children, since they can reveal NF1.

input: A 46-year-old man visited the ophthalmology department because of a fleshy pink-orange lesion, located temporally on the iris of his left eye (figure). Histopathological examination showed monotonous proliferation of small blue round cells, strong membranous CD99 positivity, and EWSR1-rearrangement, characteristic for Ewing sarcoma. Another primary tumour was excluded. This is the first report of a primary Ewing sarcoma of the iris. The patient was treated with six cycles of vincristin, ifosfamide, doxorubicin, and etoposide, followed by local radiation therapy with ruthenium-106 plaque brachytherapy (advantageous for functional eye preservation over surgery), and eight cycles of vincristin, actinomycine D, and ifosfamide, leading to complete remission of the sarcoma (figure). Because of the patient's advanced age in terms of developing Ewing sarcoma, doxorubicin and etoposide were administered with 25% dose reduction, and pegfilgrastim was administered after each cycle. He did not have severe adverse effects from the treatment.

A 3-month-old boy was brought by his mother to our clinic who had noticed that her child had developed several round red lesions on his face (figure). She said that the problem had begun 3 weeks post partum. The baby had been born at full term following an uncomplicated pregnancy. The patient's mother was fit and well with no medical history of note—specifically she did not report any previous infections, or dermatological or autoimmune diseases.The baby had been seen by another dermatologist when he was 10 weeks old and given topical antifungal treatment—miconazole cream—and a low potency topical corticosteroid cream—hydrocortisone—which had no effect after a 2-week trial.
On examination, we found six, well defined, erythematous annular plaques, with indurated borders, on the baby's face. We found no other abnormalities: the baby's temperature was normal, his heart rate was 138 beats per min, and the respiratory rate was 36 breaths per min.
Histopathological examination of a biopsy sample of the plaque on the face showed a vacuolar interface dermatitis with dermal oedema and a periadnexal infiltrate of lymphocytes (figure). Laboratory blood tests showed that both the mother and child were positive for antibodies against extractable nuclear antigen. They were also positive for anti-Sjögren's syndrome type A (SSA) and anti-Sjögren's syndrome type B (SSB) antibodies. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 11 mm per h, the C-reactive protein concentration was 0·6 mg/L. The white cell count was 13·85 × 109 per L—the neutrophil count was 1·47 × 109 per L, eosinophils 0·18 × 109 per L, basophils 0·02 × 109 per L, lymphocytes 10·58 × 109 per L, and monocytes 1·60 × 109 per L. Both liver and kidney function tests were normal.
Taken together with the findings of the biopsy, we diagnosed neonatal lupus erythematosus.
Given that heart abnormalities are associated with the condition, we referred the baby to a paediatric cardiologist who requested an electrocardiogram which showed findings consistent with first-degree atrioventricular block.
3 months later at a follow-up appointment, all the baby's skin lesions had resolved without any scarring.
Finally, again given the diagnosis and the positive antinuclear antibodies, we referred the patient's mother to a rheumatologist who diagnosed Sjögren's syndrome.
Neonatal lupus erythematosus is a passively acquired, self-limiting, autoimmune disease thought to be caused by the transplacental passage of anti-SSA and anti-SSB antibodies from mother to fetus: the skin—and more importantly—the heart are particularly affected. In approximately half the cases, the mothers are asymptomatic at time of presentation. The cutaneous manifestations in the baby usually develop within the first few weeks of life—typically appearing on the scalp and periorbital areas. The association of the skin lesions with positive anti-SSA and anti-SSB tests in both mother and baby is well recognised, and a skin biopsy is not necessarily required to make the diagnosis. The important complication of congenital heart block—which usually develops in utero and generally resolves—is rare and found in approximately 2% of pregnant women with anti-SSA or anti-SSB antibodies. The skin manifestations in neonatal lupus spontaneously resolve after 4–6 months (video).

input: A 46-year-old man visited the ophthalmology department because of a fleshy pink-orange lesion, located temporally on the iris of his left eye (figure). Histopathological examination showed monotonous proliferation of small blue round cells, strong membranous CD99 positivity, and EWSR1-rearrangement, characteristic for Ewing sarcoma. Another primary tumour was excluded. This is the first report of a primary Ewing sarcoma of the iris. The patient was treated with six cycles of vincristin, ifosfamide, doxorubicin, and etoposide, followed by local radiation therapy with ruthenium-106 plaque brachytherapy (advantageous for functional eye preservation over surgery), and eight cycles of vincristin, actinomycine D, and ifosfamide, leading to complete remission of the sarcoma (figure). Because of the patient's advanced age in terms of developing Ewing sarcoma, doxorubicin and etoposide were administered with 25% dose reduction, and pegfilgrastim was administered after each cycle. He did not have severe adverse effects from the treatment.

input:
A 68-year-old man diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) was referred to our specialised team. The patient had noticed increasing difficulty speaking and swallowing, followed by excessive weight loss and sialorrhoea, for 1 year before the diagnosis. A feeding tube had been inserted to support nutritional intake 2 weeks after the patient had first been diagnosed.During the following months, treatment was delivered by our multidisciplinary team composed of a rehabilitation physician, occupational therapist, physiotherapist, speech therapist, dietitian, psychologist, social worker, and spiritual counsellor, according to international ALS care guidelines. The aim was to optimise quality of life through symptom management and psychological support. Particularly important for the patient was his ability to communicate and the management of the sialorrhoea—both relevant for continued social interaction. The sialorrhoea was initially managed with glycopyrronium and dextromethorphan combined quinidine, and then with botulin toxin A injections into the salivary glands. As the disease progressed, a second round of botulinum injections failed to adequately relieve his symptoms; the patient decided against radiotherapy of the salivary glands—the next line of treatment.
The ALS-care team provided support—including psychological—to reduce both the patient's and his partner's struggle with the impact of ALS on their lives.
6 months after being diagnosed, his general practitioner started regular conversations with the patient about his values in life, his needs, and goals—considering the progressive course of his disease: advance care planning. End-of-life practices were explored.
9 months after being diagnosed, the patient developed progressive weakness in his hands; he reported that the symptom burden of dysphagia, excessive sialorrhoea, and uncontrollable coughing was exhausting.
10 months after being diagnosed, the patient's respiratory function had decreased to a point where options for respiratory support had to be discussed; he agreed to nocturnal non-invasive ventilation (NIV) to reduce symptom burden. Continuous, invasive ventilation—through a tracheostoma—had been discussed before starting NIV, but the patient felt that this would not allow him to continue being, and wanting to remain, an autonomous, independent person.
13 months after being diagnosed, the patient started to contemplate how his life would end; both he and his wife attended sessions with the spiritual counsellor to assist him in coming to terms with the last phase of his life.
14 months after being diagnosed, the patient spoke to his general practitioner and requested euthanasia. An independent physician was consulted to confirm that the patient's request was voluntary and well considered, and to substantiate that there was unbearable suffering without the prospect of improvement. The request was also discussed between the general practitioner and the ALS-care team. The patient died peacefully, in the presence of his family and general practitioner, 15 months after being diagnosed with ALS.

A 68-year-old man diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) was referred to our specialised team. The patient had noticed increasing difficulty speaking and swallowing, followed by excessive weight loss and sialorrhoea, for 1 year before the diagnosis. A feeding tube had been inserted to support nutritional intake 2 weeks after the patient had first been diagnosed.During the following months, treatment was delivered by our multidisciplinary team composed of a rehabilitation physician, occupational therapist, physiotherapist, speech therapist, dietitian, psychologist, social worker, and spiritual counsellor, according to international ALS care guidelines. The aim was to optimise quality of life through symptom management and psychological support. Particularly important for the patient was his ability to communicate and the management of the sialorrhoea—both relevant for continued social interaction. The sialorrhoea was initially managed with glycopyrronium and dextromethorphan combined quinidine, and then with botulin toxin A injections into the salivary glands. As the disease progressed, a second round of botulinum injections failed to adequately relieve his symptoms; the patient decided against radiotherapy of the salivary glands—the next line of treatment.
The ALS-care team provided support—including psychological—to reduce both the patient's and his partner's struggle with the impact of ALS on their lives.
6 months after being diagnosed, his general practitioner started regular conversations with the patient about his values in life, his needs, and goals—considering the progressive course of his disease: advance care planning. End-of-life practices were explored.
9 months after being diagnosed, the patient developed progressive weakness in his hands; he reported that the symptom burden of dysphagia, excessive sialorrhoea, and uncontrollable coughing was exhausting.
10 months after being diagnosed, the patient's respiratory function had decreased to a point where options for respiratory support had to be discussed; he agreed to nocturnal non-invasive ventilation (NIV) to reduce symptom burden. Continuous, invasive ventilation—through a tracheostoma—had been discussed before starting NIV, but the patient felt that this would not allow him to continue being, and wanting to remain, an autonomous, independent person.
13 months after being diagnosed, the patient started to contemplate how his life would end; both he and his wife attended sessions with the spiritual counsellor to assist him in coming to terms with the last phase of his life.
14 months after being diagnosed, the patient spoke to his general practitioner and requested euthanasia. An independent physician was consulted to confirm that the patient's request was voluntary and well considered, and to substantiate that there was unbearable suffering without the prospect of improvement. The request was also discussed between the general practitioner and the ALS-care team. The patient died peacefully, in the presence of his family and general practitioner, 15 months after being diagnosed with ALS.

A 35-year-old woman presented to our emergency room with a 3-day history of dizziness, nausea, and fatigue. The patient said she had been diagnosed with a brain tumour 2 years earlier; at that time, she reported having diplopia as well as dizziness and fatigue. A stereotactic tumour biopsy was considered, but not done because she made a full recovery with high-dose steroid treatment.On examination, we found no neurological abnormalities, but she had a low blood pressure of 83/39 mm Hg.
Laboratory investigations showed severe hyponatraemia: sodium concentration was 109 mmol/L (normal 135–145). Urine osmolality was 336 mmol/kg (normal 200–1200)—suggesting impaired water excretion—and the urine sodium excretion was 44 mmol/L (normal 60–140)—indicating syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) secretion.
Further endocrine testing confirmed impaired production of corticotropin-releasing hormone: the patient's basal cortisol concentration was 52 nmol/L (normal 166–507) and her adrenocorticotropic hormone concentration was inadequately low 8·2 ng/L (normal <46·0).
A brain MRI showed a contrast-enhancing subthalamic tumefactive lesion, several periventricular lesions, and a lesion adjacent to the midbrain tectum (figure; video); the MRI of the spinal cord was normal.
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed eight leukocytes per μL (normal <5) and a CSF:serum albumin ratio of 6·5 (normal <6·3) with no oligoclonal bands. Further testing showed serum anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies (titre 1:32; normal <1:10), indicating neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD). After 3% saline bolus, fluid restriction, and high-dose steroid treatment, the patient recovered and a further brain MRI, 1 month later, showed marked regression of the subthalamic lesion (figure; video). Off-label rituximab treatment was started 2 months after the patient presented initially, and she remained asymptomatic over the following 6 months while having continuous hydrocortisone replacement.
Retrospective chart analyses reported a SIADH secretion prevalence of about 15% in NMOSD; tertiary adrenal insufficiency due to inflammatory and demyelinating processes affecting the hypothalamus is rare and has mostly been described in multiple sclerosis. The brain circumventricular organs have osmoregulatory functions and are enriched with aquaporin-4 water channels; every patient with SIADH secretion and lesions affecting these organs should be tested for NMOSD. Notably, routine CSF analysis in NMOSD can be normal (video).

input:
A 35-year-old woman presented to our emergency room with a 3-day history of dizziness, nausea, and fatigue. The patient said she had been diagnosed with a brain tumour 2 years earlier; at that time, she reported having diplopia as well as dizziness and fatigue. A stereotactic tumour biopsy was considered, but not done because she made a full recovery with high-dose steroid treatment.On examination, we found no neurological abnormalities, but she had a low blood pressure of 83/39 mm Hg.
Laboratory investigations showed severe hyponatraemia: sodium concentration was 109 mmol/L (normal 135–145). Urine osmolality was 336 mmol/kg (normal 200–1200)—suggesting impaired water excretion—and the urine sodium excretion was 44 mmol/L (normal 60–140)—indicating syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) secretion.
Further endocrine testing confirmed impaired production of corticotropin-releasing hormone: the patient's basal cortisol concentration was 52 nmol/L (normal 166–507) and her adrenocorticotropic hormone concentration was inadequately low 8·2 ng/L (normal <46·0).
A brain MRI showed a contrast-enhancing subthalamic tumefactive lesion, several periventricular lesions, and a lesion adjacent to the midbrain tectum (figure; video); the MRI of the spinal cord was normal.
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed eight leukocytes per μL (normal <5) and a CSF:serum albumin ratio of 6·5 (normal <6·3) with no oligoclonal bands. Further testing showed serum anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies (titre 1:32; normal <1:10), indicating neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD). After 3% saline bolus, fluid restriction, and high-dose steroid treatment, the patient recovered and a further brain MRI, 1 month later, showed marked regression of the subthalamic lesion (figure; video). Off-label rituximab treatment was started 2 months after the patient presented initially, and she remained asymptomatic over the following 6 months while having continuous hydrocortisone replacement.
Retrospective chart analyses reported a SIADH secretion prevalence of about 15% in NMOSD; tertiary adrenal insufficiency due to inflammatory and demyelinating processes affecting the hypothalamus is rare and has mostly been described in multiple sclerosis. The brain circumventricular organs have osmoregulatory functions and are enriched with aquaporin-4 water channels; every patient with SIADH secretion and lesions affecting these organs should be tested for NMOSD. Notably, routine CSF analysis in NMOSD can be normal (video).

input:
A 68-year-old man diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) was referred to our specialised team. The patient had noticed increasing difficulty speaking and swallowing, followed by excessive weight loss and sialorrhoea, for 1 year before the diagnosis. A feeding tube had been inserted to support nutritional intake 2 weeks after the patient had first been diagnosed.During the following months, treatment was delivered by our multidisciplinary team composed of a rehabilitation physician, occupational therapist, physiotherapist, speech therapist, dietitian, psychologist, social worker, and spiritual counsellor, according to international ALS care guidelines. The aim was to optimise quality of life through symptom management and psychological support. Particularly important for the patient was his ability to communicate and the management of the sialorrhoea—both relevant for continued social interaction. The sialorrhoea was initially managed with glycopyrronium and dextromethorphan combined quinidine, and then with botulin toxin A injections into the salivary glands. As the disease progressed, a second round of botulinum injections failed to adequately relieve his symptoms; the patient decided against radiotherapy of the salivary glands—the next line of treatment.
The ALS-care team provided support—including psychological—to reduce both the patient's and his partner's struggle with the impact of ALS on their lives.
6 months after being diagnosed, his general practitioner started regular conversations with the patient about his values in life, his needs, and goals—considering the progressive course of his disease: advance care planning. End-of-life practices were explored.
9 months after being diagnosed, the patient developed progressive weakness in his hands; he reported that the symptom burden of dysphagia, excessive sialorrhoea, and uncontrollable coughing was exhausting.
10 months after being diagnosed, the patient's respiratory function had decreased to a point where options for respiratory support had to be discussed; he agreed to nocturnal non-invasive ventilation (NIV) to reduce symptom burden. Continuous, invasive ventilation—through a tracheostoma—had been discussed before starting NIV, but the patient felt that this would not allow him to continue being, and wanting to remain, an autonomous, independent person.
13 months after being diagnosed, the patient started to contemplate how his life would end; both he and his wife attended sessions with the spiritual counsellor to assist him in coming to terms with the last phase of his life.
14 months after being diagnosed, the patient spoke to his general practitioner and requested euthanasia. An independent physician was consulted to confirm that the patient's request was voluntary and well considered, and to substantiate that there was unbearable suffering without the prospect of improvement. The request was also discussed between the general practitioner and the ALS-care team. The patient died peacefully, in the presence of his family and general practitioner, 15 months after being diagnosed with ALS.
