input:
A 35-year-old woman presented to our emergency room with a 3-day history of dizziness, nausea, and fatigue. The patient said she had been diagnosed with a brain tumour 2 years earlier; at that time, she reported having diplopia as well as dizziness and fatigue. A stereotactic tumour biopsy was considered, but not done because she made a full recovery with high-dose steroid treatment.On examination, we found no neurological abnormalities, but she had a low blood pressure of 83/39 mm Hg.
Laboratory investigations showed severe hyponatraemia: sodium concentration was 109 mmol/L (normal 135–145). Urine osmolality was 336 mmol/kg (normal 200–1200)—suggesting impaired water excretion—and the urine sodium excretion was 44 mmol/L (normal 60–140)—indicating syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) secretion.
Further endocrine testing confirmed impaired production of corticotropin-releasing hormone: the patient's basal cortisol concentration was 52 nmol/L (normal 166–507) and her adrenocorticotropic hormone concentration was inadequately low 8·2 ng/L (normal <46·0).
A brain MRI showed a contrast-enhancing subthalamic tumefactive lesion, several periventricular lesions, and a lesion adjacent to the midbrain tectum (figure; video); the MRI of the spinal cord was normal.
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed eight leukocytes per μL (normal <5) and a CSF:serum albumin ratio of 6·5 (normal <6·3) with no oligoclonal bands. Further testing showed serum anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies (titre 1:32; normal <1:10), indicating neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD). After 3% saline bolus, fluid restriction, and high-dose steroid treatment, the patient recovered and a further brain MRI, 1 month later, showed marked regression of the subthalamic lesion (figure; video). Off-label rituximab treatment was started 2 months after the patient presented initially, and she remained asymptomatic over the following 6 months while having continuous hydrocortisone replacement.
Retrospective chart analyses reported a SIADH secretion prevalence of about 15% in NMOSD; tertiary adrenal insufficiency due to inflammatory and demyelinating processes affecting the hypothalamus is rare and has mostly been described in multiple sclerosis. The brain circumventricular organs have osmoregulatory functions and are enriched with aquaporin-4 water channels; every patient with SIADH secretion and lesions affecting these organs should be tested for NMOSD. Notably, routine CSF analysis in NMOSD can be normal (video).

input:
A 66-year-old man collapsed at home with chest pain. He was found by paramedics to be in ventricular fibrillation leading to a cardiac arrest. A post-resuscitation electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm and inferolateral ST-segment elevation. On arrival at our department he had an emergency invasive coronary angiogram which showed an occluded left circumflex artery, confirming myocardial infarction (MI). We opened the artery using a balloon, and following recanalisation, we identified a substantial filling defect indicative of a large thrombus (figure). Following stent implantation, normal coronary artery flow was restored and the patient made an uneventful recovery—although brief paroxysms of atrial fibrillation were noted on cardiac monitoring in the ensuing 24 h.The patient enrolled in a research study (NCT03943966) of PET/CT angiography using a novel radiotracer, 18F-GP1, which binds to activated platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors and provides an assessment of thrombus formation. CT angiography confirmed a patent stent that co-localised with intense 18F-GP1 uptake on the PET/CT images, consistent with acute thrombus trapped behind the stent (figure).
Incomplete contrast opacification in the left atrial appendage made assessment on CT challenging. However, the presence of a separate and discrete filling defect raised the possibility of an in-situ appendage thrombus, which was confirmed on the 18F-GP1 PET/CT scan (figure). The clinical diagnosis was therefore changed from type 1 MI—caused by an atherosclerotic plaque rupture—to a type 2 MI—caused by a coronary embolism arising from a left atrial appendage thrombus in the context of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.
The patient was commenced on apixaban 5 mg twice a day, aspirin 75 mg daily, and clopidogrel 75 mg daily. The patient was allowed home after 2 days and made a full recovery.
Differentiation between type 1 and type 2 MIs is important because different therapeutic interventions are required to prevent recurrence. Most MIs—type 1—are due to acute coronary occlusion from a thrombus forming on a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque. In type 2, MIs are caused by a mismatch between the supply and demand of myocardial oxygen in the context of another disease—including coronary embolism—as seen in our patient. Adjunctive invasive or non-invasive imaging can often help clarify the clinical diagnosis and guide management (appendix; video).

A 66-year-old man collapsed at home with chest pain. He was found by paramedics to be in ventricular fibrillation leading to a cardiac arrest. A post-resuscitation electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm and inferolateral ST-segment elevation. On arrival at our department he had an emergency invasive coronary angiogram which showed an occluded left circumflex artery, confirming myocardial infarction (MI). We opened the artery using a balloon, and following recanalisation, we identified a substantial filling defect indicative of a large thrombus (figure). Following stent implantation, normal coronary artery flow was restored and the patient made an uneventful recovery—although brief paroxysms of atrial fibrillation were noted on cardiac monitoring in the ensuing 24 h.The patient enrolled in a research study (NCT03943966) of PET/CT angiography using a novel radiotracer, 18F-GP1, which binds to activated platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors and provides an assessment of thrombus formation. CT angiography confirmed a patent stent that co-localised with intense 18F-GP1 uptake on the PET/CT images, consistent with acute thrombus trapped behind the stent (figure).
Incomplete contrast opacification in the left atrial appendage made assessment on CT challenging. However, the presence of a separate and discrete filling defect raised the possibility of an in-situ appendage thrombus, which was confirmed on the 18F-GP1 PET/CT scan (figure). The clinical diagnosis was therefore changed from type 1 MI—caused by an atherosclerotic plaque rupture—to a type 2 MI—caused by a coronary embolism arising from a left atrial appendage thrombus in the context of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.
The patient was commenced on apixaban 5 mg twice a day, aspirin 75 mg daily, and clopidogrel 75 mg daily. The patient was allowed home after 2 days and made a full recovery.
Differentiation between type 1 and type 2 MIs is important because different therapeutic interventions are required to prevent recurrence. Most MIs—type 1—are due to acute coronary occlusion from a thrombus forming on a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque. In type 2, MIs are caused by a mismatch between the supply and demand of myocardial oxygen in the context of another disease—including coronary embolism—as seen in our patient. Adjunctive invasive or non-invasive imaging can often help clarify the clinical diagnosis and guide management (appendix; video).

A 66-year-old man collapsed at home with chest pain. He was found by paramedics to be in ventricular fibrillation leading to a cardiac arrest. A post-resuscitation electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm and inferolateral ST-segment elevation. On arrival at our department he had an emergency invasive coronary angiogram which showed an occluded left circumflex artery, confirming myocardial infarction (MI). We opened the artery using a balloon, and following recanalisation, we identified a substantial filling defect indicative of a large thrombus (figure). Following stent implantation, normal coronary artery flow was restored and the patient made an uneventful recovery—although brief paroxysms of atrial fibrillation were noted on cardiac monitoring in the ensuing 24 h.The patient enrolled in a research study (NCT03943966) of PET/CT angiography using a novel radiotracer, 18F-GP1, which binds to activated platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors and provides an assessment of thrombus formation. CT angiography confirmed a patent stent that co-localised with intense 18F-GP1 uptake on the PET/CT images, consistent with acute thrombus trapped behind the stent (figure).
Incomplete contrast opacification in the left atrial appendage made assessment on CT challenging. However, the presence of a separate and discrete filling defect raised the possibility of an in-situ appendage thrombus, which was confirmed on the 18F-GP1 PET/CT scan (figure). The clinical diagnosis was therefore changed from type 1 MI—caused by an atherosclerotic plaque rupture—to a type 2 MI—caused by a coronary embolism arising from a left atrial appendage thrombus in the context of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.
The patient was commenced on apixaban 5 mg twice a day, aspirin 75 mg daily, and clopidogrel 75 mg daily. The patient was allowed home after 2 days and made a full recovery.
Differentiation between type 1 and type 2 MIs is important because different therapeutic interventions are required to prevent recurrence. Most MIs—type 1—are due to acute coronary occlusion from a thrombus forming on a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque. In type 2, MIs are caused by a mismatch between the supply and demand of myocardial oxygen in the context of another disease—including coronary embolism—as seen in our patient. Adjunctive invasive or non-invasive imaging can often help clarify the clinical diagnosis and guide management (appendix; video).

A 50-year-old woman reporting chest discomfort and found to have ventricular tachycardia (VT) on electrocardiogram (ECG) with a reduced ejection fraction on echocardiogram was transferred to our hospital (figure). The patient had no significant medical history.On examination in our emergency department, she appeared well: her blood pressure was 114/79 mm Hg and her oxygen saturation was 97% breathing room air. She was afebrile.
We repeated the echocardiogram which showed a 20% ejection fraction, global hypokinesis of the left ventricle, and biventricular dilation—notably the patient was not in VT during the procedure (figure). Coronary artery angiography showed no significant stenosis and a repeat ECG demonstrated right bundle branch block and features suggestive of an acute anteroseptal infarct (figure).
Laboratory investigations showed an elevated N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide concentration of 2922 pg/mL (normal 0–125) and a troponin T concentration of 0·17 ng/mL (normal 0·01–0·03).
The patient returned to normal sinus rhythm after intravenous amiodarone and oral metoprolol; a cardioverter defibrillator was implanted for secondary prevention.
Cardiac MRI after cardioversion showed features of a transmural myocardial infarction of the anterior aspect of the interventricular septum and basal anterior wall (figure).
Our differential diagnosis at this time included inflammatory conditions—infectious or autoimmune—and ischaemic cardiomyopathies. No definitive clinical, laboratory, or radiographic findings entirely supported any specific aetiology. An endomyocardial biopsy provided little clarification of the diagnosis as it did not include any myocardium. The patient was then allowed home.
One month later, she presented in respiratory distress; she was hypoxic, had acute kidney injury, and worsening of her reduced ejection fraction. The patient required extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and an intra-aortic balloon pump; 2 weeks later she had a heart transplant.
Pathological examination of the explanted native heart showed giant cell myocarditis centred around the interventricular septum; the relatively localised lesion had both active inflammation and cardiomyocyte injury, as well as chronic features of interstitial fibrosis (figure).
Approximately 5 months after transplantation, the patient's postoperative course was complicated by Klebsiella aerogenes pneumonia and transient evidence of acute cellular and active antibody-mediated rejection with donor specific antibodies—although recent biopsies showed no evidence of rejection and donor specific antibodies were undetectable. Endomyocardial biopsies since have shown no recurrence of giant cell myocarditis.
The finding of giant cell myocarditis was unexpected in our case: very few cases present with acute ischaemia and heart block. Most patients present with congestive heart failure and a small percentage with ventricular arrhythmias. Various immunosuppression regimens, albeit without consensus recommendations, have been shown to prolong time before transplantation or death, compared to patients receiving no immunosuppression. In cases that proceeded to cardiac transplantation, mortality is the same as patients having transplants for both dilated and ischaemic cardiomyopathy (video).

A 50-year-old woman reporting chest discomfort and found to have ventricular tachycardia (VT) on electrocardiogram (ECG) with a reduced ejection fraction on echocardiogram was transferred to our hospital (figure). The patient had no significant medical history.On examination in our emergency department, she appeared well: her blood pressure was 114/79 mm Hg and her oxygen saturation was 97% breathing room air. She was afebrile.
We repeated the echocardiogram which showed a 20% ejection fraction, global hypokinesis of the left ventricle, and biventricular dilation—notably the patient was not in VT during the procedure (figure). Coronary artery angiography showed no significant stenosis and a repeat ECG demonstrated right bundle branch block and features suggestive of an acute anteroseptal infarct (figure).
Laboratory investigations showed an elevated N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide concentration of 2922 pg/mL (normal 0–125) and a troponin T concentration of 0·17 ng/mL (normal 0·01–0·03).
The patient returned to normal sinus rhythm after intravenous amiodarone and oral metoprolol; a cardioverter defibrillator was implanted for secondary prevention.
Cardiac MRI after cardioversion showed features of a transmural myocardial infarction of the anterior aspect of the interventricular septum and basal anterior wall (figure).
Our differential diagnosis at this time included inflammatory conditions—infectious or autoimmune—and ischaemic cardiomyopathies. No definitive clinical, laboratory, or radiographic findings entirely supported any specific aetiology. An endomyocardial biopsy provided little clarification of the diagnosis as it did not include any myocardium. The patient was then allowed home.
One month later, she presented in respiratory distress; she was hypoxic, had acute kidney injury, and worsening of her reduced ejection fraction. The patient required extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and an intra-aortic balloon pump; 2 weeks later she had a heart transplant.
Pathological examination of the explanted native heart showed giant cell myocarditis centred around the interventricular septum; the relatively localised lesion had both active inflammation and cardiomyocyte injury, as well as chronic features of interstitial fibrosis (figure).
Approximately 5 months after transplantation, the patient's postoperative course was complicated by Klebsiella aerogenes pneumonia and transient evidence of acute cellular and active antibody-mediated rejection with donor specific antibodies—although recent biopsies showed no evidence of rejection and donor specific antibodies were undetectable. Endomyocardial biopsies since have shown no recurrence of giant cell myocarditis.
The finding of giant cell myocarditis was unexpected in our case: very few cases present with acute ischaemia and heart block. Most patients present with congestive heart failure and a small percentage with ventricular arrhythmias. Various immunosuppression regimens, albeit without consensus recommendations, have been shown to prolong time before transplantation or death, compared to patients receiving no immunosuppression. In cases that proceeded to cardiac transplantation, mortality is the same as patients having transplants for both dilated and ischaemic cardiomyopathy (video).

input:
A 33-year-old man was referred to our specialist clinic with a 6-month history of a rapid purple discolouration of his legs on standing; he reported that his legs would progressively feel heavy, tingly, itchy, and become dusky in colour. Additionally, he said a petechial rash would occasionally appear over his feet (figure). The patient said his legs would return to their usual colour and the other symptoms would abate if he lay down.He had a mild SARS-CoV-2 infection, confirmed by PCR, 18 months before we saw him, with a suspected further SARS-CoV-2 infection 6 months later. He had been diagnosed with post-COVID-19 condition (also known as long COVID) in a specialist clinic 3 months before we saw him—reporting a 12-month history of disabling and delayed post-exertional exhaustion, disproportionate to the effort made; he also reported muscular pain, sleep disturbance, visual difficulties, sexual dysfunction, and brain fog. The patient had been diagnosed with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) 2 months before we saw him, by a cardiologist.
Regarding his medical history, he had been diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome aged 18 years and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder aged 31 years. He also had joint hypermobility—he scored 7 out of 9 on the Beighton Score after being assessed by a rheumatologist at age 32 years. He reported pelvic pain since the age of 21 years. He was prescribed sertraline and an oral solution of amitriptyline.
On examination when lying down, his pulse was 68 beats per min and blood pressure was 138/85 mm Hg; on standing for 8 min, his pulse increased to a maximum of 127 beats per min and his blood pressure remained stable at 125/97 mm Hg. He reported accompanying symptoms of feeling foggy and shaky, having tingling, itchiness, and heaviness in his legs: findings consistent with a diagnosis of POTS.
Laboratory investigations showed normal C-reactive protein concentration, normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and negative antinuclear antibodies, anti-neutrophil cytoplasm autoantibody, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies, and normal immunoglobulin levels.
Considering the patient's signs and symptoms, we diagnosed dysautonomia secondary to SARS-CoV-2 infection and associated with long COVID. We explained that the leg discolouration was due to venous pooling and cutaneous ischaemia; we recommended he increase his fluid intake, increase his salt intake, and do muscle strengthening exercises.
Dysautonomia is a diverse group of disorders affecting either the central or peripheral autonomic nervous system or both. Dysautonomia can be primary, due to a disease of the autonomic nervous system, or secondary, due to a disease that causes secondary damage to the autonomic nervous system.
POTS is a dysautonomia syndrome where patients have orthostatic intolerance with an excessive increase in heart rate and symptoms of light-headedness, non-vertiginous dizziness, and palpitations when standing, but they maintain their blood pressure. They may also report low energy, headache, cognitive impairment, muscle fatigue, chest pain, non-specific weakness, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Onset of POTS may be precipitated by a viral infection, physical trauma, menarche, pregnancy, or surgery; it may co-occur with other conditions, including migraine, hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and chronic fatigue syndrome.
Long COVID is a multisystem syndrome with an array of symptoms and disabilities in daily activities; evidence is growing of a link between long COVID and POTS dysautonomia. In children with long COVID, Bier anaemic spots—not obvious in our patient—and cyanosis with urticarial-like eruption (known as BASCULE) syndrome has been reported.

A 50-year-old woman reporting chest discomfort and found to have ventricular tachycardia (VT) on electrocardiogram (ECG) with a reduced ejection fraction on echocardiogram was transferred to our hospital (figure). The patient had no significant medical history.On examination in our emergency department, she appeared well: her blood pressure was 114/79 mm Hg and her oxygen saturation was 97% breathing room air. She was afebrile.
We repeated the echocardiogram which showed a 20% ejection fraction, global hypokinesis of the left ventricle, and biventricular dilation—notably the patient was not in VT during the procedure (figure). Coronary artery angiography showed no significant stenosis and a repeat ECG demonstrated right bundle branch block and features suggestive of an acute anteroseptal infarct (figure).
Laboratory investigations showed an elevated N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide concentration of 2922 pg/mL (normal 0–125) and a troponin T concentration of 0·17 ng/mL (normal 0·01–0·03).
The patient returned to normal sinus rhythm after intravenous amiodarone and oral metoprolol; a cardioverter defibrillator was implanted for secondary prevention.
Cardiac MRI after cardioversion showed features of a transmural myocardial infarction of the anterior aspect of the interventricular septum and basal anterior wall (figure).
Our differential diagnosis at this time included inflammatory conditions—infectious or autoimmune—and ischaemic cardiomyopathies. No definitive clinical, laboratory, or radiographic findings entirely supported any specific aetiology. An endomyocardial biopsy provided little clarification of the diagnosis as it did not include any myocardium. The patient was then allowed home.
One month later, she presented in respiratory distress; she was hypoxic, had acute kidney injury, and worsening of her reduced ejection fraction. The patient required extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and an intra-aortic balloon pump; 2 weeks later she had a heart transplant.
Pathological examination of the explanted native heart showed giant cell myocarditis centred around the interventricular septum; the relatively localised lesion had both active inflammation and cardiomyocyte injury, as well as chronic features of interstitial fibrosis (figure).
Approximately 5 months after transplantation, the patient's postoperative course was complicated by Klebsiella aerogenes pneumonia and transient evidence of acute cellular and active antibody-mediated rejection with donor specific antibodies—although recent biopsies showed no evidence of rejection and donor specific antibodies were undetectable. Endomyocardial biopsies since have shown no recurrence of giant cell myocarditis.
The finding of giant cell myocarditis was unexpected in our case: very few cases present with acute ischaemia and heart block. Most patients present with congestive heart failure and a small percentage with ventricular arrhythmias. Various immunosuppression regimens, albeit without consensus recommendations, have been shown to prolong time before transplantation or death, compared to patients receiving no immunosuppression. In cases that proceeded to cardiac transplantation, mortality is the same as patients having transplants for both dilated and ischaemic cardiomyopathy (video).

A 35-year-old woman complaining of weakness of her left arm and leg was admitted to our hospital. She said the problem started 25 h earlier, soon after liposuction on her left thigh and a filler injection of the fat into her face in a beauty salon. The woman was previously healthy with no medical history. On physical examination we found hemiplegia of the left limbs: muscle strength was 1/5 in the arm and 3/5 in the leg. She had left central facial palsy and clear speech, and was cognitively intact. Bilateral Babinski signs were negative and there were no features of meningeal irritation. The patient's blood pressure, pulse rate, and temperature were in the normal ranges. Routine blood tests, blood lipids, glucose concentration, and electrolytes were also normal. An electrocardiogram and a transthoracic echocardiogram showed no abnormalities.A CT scan of the woman's brain showed a low-density strip (appendix) in the right middle cerebral artery (MCA) that was hyperintense on T1, T2, and T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery weighted MRIs (figure; appendix). Additionally, the MRI showed an area of infarction in the region supplied by the right MCA. Magnetic resonance angiography (appendix) showed an occlusion of part of the right MCA and a low-density filling defect in the initial segment of the right external carotid artery—which, on an ultrasound scan, was hyperechoic—indicative of an embolus (figure).
Considering all the information in the round, we decided that the patient had a cerebral fat embolism (CFE) following the injection into her face of autologous fat. We decided to treat her conservatively with oral aspirin 0·2 g once daily, oral atorvastatin 40 mg once daily, and intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg once daily. After 1 week, the patient's symptoms began to resolve and after 2 weeks she was transferred to the rehabilitation department. 3 months after she came into hospital, she was able to walk unaided.
A stroke in a young person can be caused by emboli, atherosclerotic disease, vasculopathies, or subarachnoid or intraparenchymal bleeding. Other causes particularly important in the younger age group are oral contraceptive use, pregnancy and postpartum states, substance use, trauma, and migraine. CFE—a thankfully rarely reported complication of cosmetic procedures—more usually occurs after fractures of the long bones.
How the fat from an autologous facial filler reaches the arterial network is unclear. It may be that during the injection the needle penetrates a small artery. Then, possibly due to continuous pressure applied during the injection, the fat travels, against the normal blood flow, up the small artery, through the facial artery and the external carotid artery, into the internal carotid artery.
CFE is usually self-limiting. The key with a presentation of rapid onset of left-sided weakness—such as in our patient—is to make the right diagnosis as soon as possible.

A 35-year-old woman complaining of weakness of her left arm and leg was admitted to our hospital. She said the problem started 25 h earlier, soon after liposuction on her left thigh and a filler injection of the fat into her face in a beauty salon. The woman was previously healthy with no medical history. On physical examination we found hemiplegia of the left limbs: muscle strength was 1/5 in the arm and 3/5 in the leg. She had left central facial palsy and clear speech, and was cognitively intact. Bilateral Babinski signs were negative and there were no features of meningeal irritation. The patient's blood pressure, pulse rate, and temperature were in the normal ranges. Routine blood tests, blood lipids, glucose concentration, and electrolytes were also normal. An electrocardiogram and a transthoracic echocardiogram showed no abnormalities.A CT scan of the woman's brain showed a low-density strip (appendix) in the right middle cerebral artery (MCA) that was hyperintense on T1, T2, and T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery weighted MRIs (figure; appendix). Additionally, the MRI showed an area of infarction in the region supplied by the right MCA. Magnetic resonance angiography (appendix) showed an occlusion of part of the right MCA and a low-density filling defect in the initial segment of the right external carotid artery—which, on an ultrasound scan, was hyperechoic—indicative of an embolus (figure).
Considering all the information in the round, we decided that the patient had a cerebral fat embolism (CFE) following the injection into her face of autologous fat. We decided to treat her conservatively with oral aspirin 0·2 g once daily, oral atorvastatin 40 mg once daily, and intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg once daily. After 1 week, the patient's symptoms began to resolve and after 2 weeks she was transferred to the rehabilitation department. 3 months after she came into hospital, she was able to walk unaided.
A stroke in a young person can be caused by emboli, atherosclerotic disease, vasculopathies, or subarachnoid or intraparenchymal bleeding. Other causes particularly important in the younger age group are oral contraceptive use, pregnancy and postpartum states, substance use, trauma, and migraine. CFE—a thankfully rarely reported complication of cosmetic procedures—more usually occurs after fractures of the long bones.
How the fat from an autologous facial filler reaches the arterial network is unclear. It may be that during the injection the needle penetrates a small artery. Then, possibly due to continuous pressure applied during the injection, the fat travels, against the normal blood flow, up the small artery, through the facial artery and the external carotid artery, into the internal carotid artery.
CFE is usually self-limiting. The key with a presentation of rapid onset of left-sided weakness—such as in our patient—is to make the right diagnosis as soon as possible.

input:
A 33-year-old man was referred to our specialist clinic with a 6-month history of a rapid purple discolouration of his legs on standing; he reported that his legs would progressively feel heavy, tingly, itchy, and become dusky in colour. Additionally, he said a petechial rash would occasionally appear over his feet (figure). The patient said his legs would return to their usual colour and the other symptoms would abate if he lay down.He had a mild SARS-CoV-2 infection, confirmed by PCR, 18 months before we saw him, with a suspected further SARS-CoV-2 infection 6 months later. He had been diagnosed with post-COVID-19 condition (also known as long COVID) in a specialist clinic 3 months before we saw him—reporting a 12-month history of disabling and delayed post-exertional exhaustion, disproportionate to the effort made; he also reported muscular pain, sleep disturbance, visual difficulties, sexual dysfunction, and brain fog. The patient had been diagnosed with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) 2 months before we saw him, by a cardiologist.
Regarding his medical history, he had been diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome aged 18 years and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder aged 31 years. He also had joint hypermobility—he scored 7 out of 9 on the Beighton Score after being assessed by a rheumatologist at age 32 years. He reported pelvic pain since the age of 21 years. He was prescribed sertraline and an oral solution of amitriptyline.
On examination when lying down, his pulse was 68 beats per min and blood pressure was 138/85 mm Hg; on standing for 8 min, his pulse increased to a maximum of 127 beats per min and his blood pressure remained stable at 125/97 mm Hg. He reported accompanying symptoms of feeling foggy and shaky, having tingling, itchiness, and heaviness in his legs: findings consistent with a diagnosis of POTS.
Laboratory investigations showed normal C-reactive protein concentration, normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and negative antinuclear antibodies, anti-neutrophil cytoplasm autoantibody, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies, and normal immunoglobulin levels.
Considering the patient's signs and symptoms, we diagnosed dysautonomia secondary to SARS-CoV-2 infection and associated with long COVID. We explained that the leg discolouration was due to venous pooling and cutaneous ischaemia; we recommended he increase his fluid intake, increase his salt intake, and do muscle strengthening exercises.
Dysautonomia is a diverse group of disorders affecting either the central or peripheral autonomic nervous system or both. Dysautonomia can be primary, due to a disease of the autonomic nervous system, or secondary, due to a disease that causes secondary damage to the autonomic nervous system.
POTS is a dysautonomia syndrome where patients have orthostatic intolerance with an excessive increase in heart rate and symptoms of light-headedness, non-vertiginous dizziness, and palpitations when standing, but they maintain their blood pressure. They may also report low energy, headache, cognitive impairment, muscle fatigue, chest pain, non-specific weakness, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Onset of POTS may be precipitated by a viral infection, physical trauma, menarche, pregnancy, or surgery; it may co-occur with other conditions, including migraine, hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and chronic fatigue syndrome.
Long COVID is a multisystem syndrome with an array of symptoms and disabilities in daily activities; evidence is growing of a link between long COVID and POTS dysautonomia. In children with long COVID, Bier anaemic spots—not obvious in our patient—and cyanosis with urticarial-like eruption (known as BASCULE) syndrome has been reported.

An 87-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 3-day history of dyspnoea on exertion. She had a history of chronic kidney disease, pulmonary embolism, and recent right-sided ischaemic stroke causing aphasia and hemiparesis. She was taking aspirin, clopidogrel, and atorvastatin.On examination we found the patient to be well and afebrile. Her blood pressure was 134/86 mm Hg, oxygen saturation was 95% on room air, and she had bilateral rhonchi prominent in her lung bases.
Laboratory investigations found a normocytic anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 11·4 g/dL; normal 12–16), serum creatinine concentration was 1·34 mg/dL (normal 0·6–1·5), and the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was 36 mL/min per 1·73 m2. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with no signs of ischaemia and chest x-ray showed patchy multifocal airspace opacities in both lungs—indicating possible pneumonia. A chest CT with intravenous contrast showed no abnormalities—ruling out the possibility of a pulmonary embolus—and the upper parts of the patient's kidneys, seen on the same image, also showed no obvious lesions, and notably no intraparenchymal contrast medium (figure). The lung windows of the CT showed ground glass changes.
Over the next 48 h, the patient became oliguric and her serum creatinine concentration increased to 2·4 mg/dL. A non-contrast CT of the patient's abdomen and pelvis (figure) showed renal parenchymal enhancement from retained intravenous contrast medium 53 h after administration. The patient's urine sodium concentration was 36 mEq/L and the fractional excretion of sodium was 0·7%. Considering the findings, we made a diagnosis of contrast-associated acute kidney injury (AKI) in the context of a viral lower respiratory tract infection.
The patient was started on supportive AKI care—including adjustment of medication doses, avoidance of nephrotoxins, and judicious administration of fluids—and antitussives and paracetamol for the chest infection. Her dyspnoea improved and her serum creatinine concentration peaked at 3·7 mg/dL, with an eGFR of 10 mL/min per 1·73 m2, 4 days after the administration of the contrast. 7 days after the initial contrast CT, the serum creatinine concentration returned to the preadmission baseline of 1·3 mg/dL. The patient was then transferred to a nursing facility and seen again 3 weeks later; at that time her kidney function was stable.
Retained intravenous contrast can be seen on a plain radiograph or a non-contrasted CT study of the abdomen more than 24 h after the administration in situations of significant renal impairment—including end stage renal disease or AKI—when the glomerular filtration rate is 45 mL/min per 1·73 m2 or less. Retained contrast accompanied by an acute rise in the serum creatinine concentration—in the absence of other causes of AKI—is highly suggestive of contrast-associated nephropathy. Oliguria and a low fractional excretion of sodium are also typical features. Contrast may be retained in the kidneys for several days—although is it usually cleared within 24–72 h after the injury.
In patients with residual renal function, management is conservative, and outcomes are usually favourable. In patients receiving renal replacement therapy, contrast is cleared through dialysis.
Intravenous contrast used in any clinical setting can result in contrast-associated AKI and debate continues over the level of toxicity of currently used materials. In patients with severe chronic kidney disease or receiving renal replacement therapy risks are greater: here the benefits of imaging should be weighed against the potential harm of the contrast (video).

Additionally, the MRI showed an area of infarction in the region supplied by the right MCA. Magnetic resonance angiography (appendix) showed an occlusion of part of the right MCA and a low-density filling defect in the initial segment of the right external carotid artery—which, on an ultrasound scan, was hyperechoic—indicative of an embolus (figure).

An 87-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 3-day history of dyspnoea on exertion. She had a history of chronic kidney disease, pulmonary embolism, and recent right-sided ischaemic stroke causing aphasia and hemiparesis. She was taking aspirin, clopidogrel, and atorvastatin.On examination we found the patient to be well and afebrile. Her blood pressure was 134/86 mm Hg, oxygen saturation was 95% on room air, and she had bilateral rhonchi prominent in her lung bases.
Laboratory investigations found a normocytic anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 11·4 g/dL; normal 12–16), serum creatinine concentration was 1·34 mg/dL (normal 0·6–1·5), and the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was 36 mL/min per 1·73 m2. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with no signs of ischaemia and chest x-ray showed patchy multifocal airspace opacities in both lungs—indicating possible pneumonia. A chest CT with intravenous contrast showed no abnormalities—ruling out the possibility of a pulmonary embolus—and the upper parts of the patient's kidneys, seen on the same image, also showed no obvious lesions, and notably no intraparenchymal contrast medium (figure). The lung windows of the CT showed ground glass changes.
Over the next 48 h, the patient became oliguric and her serum creatinine concentration increased to 2·4 mg/dL. A non-contrast CT of the patient's abdomen and pelvis (figure) showed renal parenchymal enhancement from retained intravenous contrast medium 53 h after administration. The patient's urine sodium concentration was 36 mEq/L and the fractional excretion of sodium was 0·7%. Considering the findings, we made a diagnosis of contrast-associated acute kidney injury (AKI) in the context of a viral lower respiratory tract infection.
The patient was started on supportive AKI care—including adjustment of medication doses, avoidance of nephrotoxins, and judicious administration of fluids—and antitussives and paracetamol for the chest infection. Her dyspnoea improved and her serum creatinine concentration peaked at 3·7 mg/dL, with an eGFR of 10 mL/min per 1·73 m2, 4 days after the administration of the contrast. 7 days after the initial contrast CT, the serum creatinine concentration returned to the preadmission baseline of 1·3 mg/dL. The patient was then transferred to a nursing facility and seen again 3 weeks later; at that time her kidney function was stable.
Retained intravenous contrast can be seen on a plain radiograph or a non-contrasted CT study of the abdomen more than 24 h after the administration in situations of significant renal impairment—including end stage renal disease or AKI—when the glomerular filtration rate is 45 mL/min per 1·73 m2 or less. Retained contrast accompanied by an acute rise in the serum creatinine concentration—in the absence of other causes of AKI—is highly suggestive of contrast-associated nephropathy. Oliguria and a low fractional excretion of sodium are also typical features. Contrast may be retained in the kidneys for several days—although is it usually cleared within 24–72 h after the injury.
In patients with residual renal function, management is conservative, and outcomes are usually favourable. In patients receiving renal replacement therapy, contrast is cleared through dialysis.
Intravenous contrast used in any clinical setting can result in contrast-associated AKI and debate continues over the level of toxicity of currently used materials. In patients with severe chronic kidney disease or receiving renal replacement therapy risks are greater: here the benefits of imaging should be weighed against the potential harm of the contrast (video).

7 years earlier, she had an episode of left flank pain caused by a stone in her distal left ureter, which was evacuated after insertion of a single-J splint.
On examination, we found the patient to be generally well; microscopy of a sample of fresh urine sediment showed multiple amorphous ovoid crystals (figure). Laboratory investigations—including full blood count, glucose and lipid metabolism, liver function tests, muscle enzymes, parathyroid and thyroid function tests, and inflammatory and immunological markers—found no abnormalities suggestive of primary or secondary glomerular diseases. Additionally, despite renal impairment, the patient had profound hypouricemia (serum uric acid concentration <0·5 mg/dL; typical range in an adult post-menopausal woman is 3·4–7·0).
A CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed two normal kidneys without nephro-urolithiasis.
Urinary excretion of uric acid was abnormally low (<3 mmol/mol creatinine; normal 443–695); urinary excretion of hypoxanthine was slightly elevated (16 mmol/mol creatinine; normal 7–13); and urinary excretion of xanthine was high (135 mmol/mol creatinine; normal 9–14); indicating a possible diagnosis of either type I or type II xanthinuria. Molecular genetic sequencing found two mutations in the XDH gene on chromosome 2, which encodes for the enzyme xanthine dehydrogenase (OMIM 278300: heterozygous mutations c.3847C>T [p.Arg1283*] and c.3520-69_*3432delinsCAGTCGCT); no mutations were found in the MOCOS gene on chromosome 18, which encodes for molybdenum cofactor sulferase, corroborating the diagnosis of hereditary xanthinuria type I.
The patient was informed of the diagnosis and advised to follow a low-purine diet and drink plenty of fluids; she was counselled about possible genetic testing of her siblings.
At follow-up 6 months later, the patient was clinically well and her renal function was stable.
Hereditary xanthinuria is characterised by high levels of xanthine in the urine; uric acid is much reduced in the serum and urine—compared with gout where an increased concentration of serum urate (hyperuricaemia) is the important risk factor. Two clinically similar forms of xanthinuria are found: type I—our patient—where there is an isolated deficiency of xanthine dehydrogenase, and type II, with a deficiency of both xanthine dehydrogenase and aldehyde oxidase (appendix).
Xanthinuria may occur in molybdenum cofactor sulferase deficiency; type II xanthinuria is caused by a mutation in the MOCOS gene. Excess xanthine can accumulate in the kidneys and other tissues; in the kidneys it may lead to stones and in the muscles, pain and cramping. Apart from a low-purine diet and high fluid intake, which prevent xanthine accumulation, no specific therapies are available for this rare autosomal recessive disorder of purine metabolism. Symptoms may occur at any age, with approximately 50% of patients presenting with urinary tract infections, haematuria, renal colic, acute renal failure, crystalluria, or urolithiasis. Rarely patients’ renal disease may result in failure.

An 87-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 3-day history of dyspnoea on exertion. She had a history of chronic kidney disease, pulmonary embolism, and recent right-sided ischaemic stroke causing aphasia and hemiparesis. She was taking aspirin, clopidogrel, and atorvastatin.On examination we found the patient to be well and afebrile. Her blood pressure was 134/86 mm Hg, oxygen saturation was 95% on room air, and she had bilateral rhonchi prominent in her lung bases.
Laboratory investigations found a normocytic anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 11·4 g/dL; normal 12–16), serum creatinine concentration was 1·34 mg/dL (normal 0·6–1·5), and the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was 36 mL/min per 1·73 m2. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with no signs of ischaemia and chest x-ray showed patchy multifocal airspace opacities in both lungs—indicating possible pneumonia. A chest CT with intravenous contrast showed no abnormalities—ruling out the possibility of a pulmonary embolus—and the upper parts of the patient's kidneys, seen on the same image, also showed no obvious lesions, and notably no intraparenchymal contrast medium (figure). The lung windows of the CT showed ground glass changes.
Over the next 48 h, the patient became oliguric and her serum creatinine concentration increased to 2·4 mg/dL. A non-contrast CT of the patient's abdomen and pelvis (figure) showed renal parenchymal enhancement from retained intravenous contrast medium 53 h after administration. The patient's urine sodium concentration was 36 mEq/L and the fractional excretion of sodium was 0·7%. Considering the findings, we made a diagnosis of contrast-associated acute kidney injury (AKI) in the context of a viral lower respiratory tract infection.
The patient was started on supportive AKI care—including adjustment of medication doses, avoidance of nephrotoxins, and judicious administration of fluids—and antitussives and paracetamol for the chest infection. Her dyspnoea improved and her serum creatinine concentration peaked at 3·7 mg/dL, with an eGFR of 10 mL/min per 1·73 m2, 4 days after the administration of the contrast. 7 days after the initial contrast CT, the serum creatinine concentration returned to the preadmission baseline of 1·3 mg/dL. The patient was then transferred to a nursing facility and seen again 3 weeks later; at that time her kidney function was stable.
Retained intravenous contrast can be seen on a plain radiograph or a non-contrasted CT study of the abdomen more than 24 h after the administration in situations of significant renal impairment—including end stage renal disease or AKI—when the glomerular filtration rate is 45 mL/min per 1·73 m2 or less. Retained contrast accompanied by an acute rise in the serum creatinine concentration—in the absence of other causes of AKI—is highly suggestive of contrast-associated nephropathy. Oliguria and a low fractional excretion of sodium are also typical features. Contrast may be retained in the kidneys for several days—although is it usually cleared within 24–72 h after the injury.
In patients with residual renal function, management is conservative, and outcomes are usually favourable. In patients receiving renal replacement therapy, contrast is cleared through dialysis.
Intravenous contrast used in any clinical setting can result in contrast-associated AKI and debate continues over the level of toxicity of currently used materials. In patients with severe chronic kidney disease or receiving renal replacement therapy risks are greater: here the benefits of imaging should be weighed against the potential harm of the contrast (video).

7 years earlier, she had an episode of left flank pain caused by a stone in her distal left ureter, which was evacuated after insertion of a single-J splint.
On examination, we found the patient to be generally well; microscopy of a sample of fresh urine sediment showed multiple amorphous ovoid crystals (figure). Laboratory investigations—including full blood count, glucose and lipid metabolism, liver function tests, muscle enzymes, parathyroid and thyroid function tests, and inflammatory and immunological markers—found no abnormalities suggestive of primary or secondary glomerular diseases. Additionally, despite renal impairment, the patient had profound hypouricemia (serum uric acid concentration <0·5 mg/dL; typical range in an adult post-menopausal woman is 3·4–7·0).
A CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed two normal kidneys without nephro-urolithiasis.
Urinary excretion of uric acid was abnormally low (<3 mmol/mol creatinine; normal 443–695); urinary excretion of hypoxanthine was slightly elevated (16 mmol/mol creatinine; normal 7–13); and urinary excretion of xanthine was high (135 mmol/mol creatinine; normal 9–14); indicating a possible diagnosis of either type I or type II xanthinuria. Molecular genetic sequencing found two mutations in the XDH gene on chromosome 2, which encodes for the enzyme xanthine dehydrogenase (OMIM 278300: heterozygous mutations c.3847C>T [p.Arg1283*] and c.3520-69_*3432delinsCAGTCGCT); no mutations were found in the MOCOS gene on chromosome 18, which encodes for molybdenum cofactor sulferase, corroborating the diagnosis of hereditary xanthinuria type I.
The patient was informed of the diagnosis and advised to follow a low-purine diet and drink plenty of fluids; she was counselled about possible genetic testing of her siblings.
At follow-up 6 months later, the patient was clinically well and her renal function was stable.
Hereditary xanthinuria is characterised by high levels of xanthine in the urine; uric acid is much reduced in the serum and urine—compared with gout where an increased concentration of serum urate (hyperuricaemia) is the important risk factor. Two clinically similar forms of xanthinuria are found: type I—our patient—where there is an isolated deficiency of xanthine dehydrogenase, and type II, with a deficiency of both xanthine dehydrogenase and aldehyde oxidase (appendix).
Xanthinuria may occur in molybdenum cofactor sulferase deficiency; type II xanthinuria is caused by a mutation in the MOCOS gene. Excess xanthine can accumulate in the kidneys and other tissues; in the kidneys it may lead to stones and in the muscles, pain and cramping. Apart from a low-purine diet and high fluid intake, which prevent xanthine accumulation, no specific therapies are available for this rare autosomal recessive disorder of purine metabolism. Symptoms may occur at any age, with approximately 50% of patients presenting with urinary tract infections, haematuria, renal colic, acute renal failure, crystalluria, or urolithiasis. Rarely patients’ renal disease may result in failure.

A 61-year-old woman with a 4-day history of asthenia, fever, and a rash was seen by our team in the hospital intensive care unit.
The patient had clear cell renal cell carcinoma with tumoral thrombosis of the right renal vein and inferior vena cava. She was being treated with a checkpoint inhibitor, pembrolizumab—a PD-1 inhibitor—and the endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGF-R) tyrosine kinase inhibitor, axitinib, before re-assessment for surgery, in the oncology day hospital unit. 3 days after the third infusion of pembrolizumab, the patient had been admitted to the intensive care unit because she had become haemodynamically unstable; she had developed heart failure, and purpura fulminans (figure; appendix) over her arms and legs, which had initially appeared as livedo racemose a few hours before. She had also been found to have an ascending sensory motor deficit of her lower limbs.
On examination, we found the patient to be unwell; her blood pressure was 90/60 mm Hg, pulse 30 beats per min, oxygen saturation was 100% on 15 L/min oxygen, and temperature was 32°C. She was confused, with a Glasgow Coma Score of 8 (eye opening response 2, verbal response 2, and motor response 4). She needed both noradrenaline and dobutamine because of her cardiac failure. Additionally, the patient was being treated with meropenem and amikacin; axitinib had been stopped at the point of admission to the intensive care unit.
Laboratory investigations showed high concentrations of N-terminal-pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (10 518 pg/mL; typical level <125 in people younger than 75 years) and troponin (109 ng/L; typical level <14). Concentrations of liver enzymes and thyroid-stimulating hormone were elevated; C-reactive protein concentration was 36 mg/L (typical range 8–10). Analysis of a sample of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed an elevated protein concentration (0·52 g/L; typical level <0·4) and a normal white blood cell count; cultures of blood, CSF, urine, and skin showed no abnormalities.
PCR skin swab testing was negative for Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae, resulting in the cessation of antibiotics treatment.
A CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed diffuse thickening of the wall of the colon; echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 25% (normal range 50–70). MRIs of brain and spinal cord showed no abnormalities. An electromyogram showed severe sensory-motor neurogenic damage compatible with axonal length-dependent processes without demyelination.
Histopathological analysis of a sample of a skin biopsy showed thrombosis with leukocytoclastic vasculitis, which, considering the patient's presentation, investigations, and history in the round, led us to conclude she had developed an immune-induced myocarditis, acute motor and sensory axonal polyneuropathy, colitis, hypothyroidism, hepatitis, and purpura fulminans.
The patient was commenced on pulse methylprednisolone (1 g per day for 5 days) and intravenous immunoglobulin (2 g per kg over 4 days), which resulted in the improvement of her general condition. She had three separate plasma exchanges to clear the pembrolizumab and surgery of the deepest wounds with skin grafts.
The corticosteroids were gradually tapered down over the next 4 months, and at follow-up 6 months later the skin lesions had completely healed. The patient's neoplastic disease was under control—despite discontinuation of the pembrolizumab and axitinib.
Immune checkpoint inhibitors have become established treatments for several cancers including malignant melanoma and renal cell carcinoma. Such developments have, in some patients resulted, in treatment-related adverse effects of variable severity. Immune-related purpura fulminans associated with pembrolizumab has been reported previously in a patient treated for lung carcinoma.

The patient had clear cell renal cell carcinoma with tumoral thrombosis of the right renal vein and inferior vena cava. She was being treated with a checkpoint inhibitor, pembrolizumab—a PD-1 inhibitor—and the endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGF-R) tyrosine kinase inhibitor, axitinib, before re-assessment for surgery, in the oncology day hospital unit. 3 days after the third infusion of pembrolizumab, the patient had been admitted to the intensive care unit because she had become haemodynamically unstable; she had developed heart failure, and purpura fulminans (figure; appendix) over her arms and legs, which had initially appeared as livedo racemose a few hours before. She had also been found to have an ascending sensory motor deficit of her lower limbs.
On examination, we found the patient to be unwell; her blood pressure was 90/60 mm Hg, pulse 30 beats per min, oxygen saturation was 100% on 15 L/min oxygen, and temperature was 32°C. She was confused, with a Glasgow Coma Score of 8 (eye opening response 2, verbal response 2, and motor response 4). She needed both noradrenaline and dobutamine because of her cardiac failure. Additionally, the patient was being treated with meropenem and amikacin; axitinib had been stopped at the point of admission to the intensive care unit.
Laboratory investigations showed high concentrations of N-terminal-pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (10 518 pg/mL; typical level <125 in people younger than 75 years) and troponin (109 ng/L; typical level <14). Concentrations of liver enzymes and thyroid-stimulating hormone were elevated; C-reactive protein concentration was 36 mg/L (typical range 8–10). Analysis of a sample of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed an elevated protein concentration (0·52 g/L; typical level <0·4) and a normal white blood cell count; cultures of blood, CSF, urine, and skin showed no abnormalities.
PCR skin swab testing was negative for Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae, resulting in the cessation of antibiotics treatment.
A CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed diffuse thickening of the wall of the colon; echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 25% (normal range 50–70). MRIs of brain and spinal cord showed no abnormalities. An electromyogram showed severe sensory-motor neurogenic damage compatible with axonal length-dependent processes without demyelination.
Histopathological analysis of a sample of a skin biopsy showed thrombosis with leukocytoclastic vasculitis, which, considering the patient's presentation, investigations, and history in the round, led us to conclude she had developed an immune-induced myocarditis, acute motor and sensory axonal polyneuropathy, colitis, hypothyroidism, hepatitis, and purpura fulminans.
The patient was commenced on pulse methylprednisolone (1 g per day for 5 days) and intravenous immunoglobulin (2 g per kg over 4 days), which resulted in the improvement of her general condition. She had three separate plasma exchanges to clear the pembrolizumab and surgery of the deepest wounds with skin grafts.
The corticosteroids were gradually tapered down over the next 4 months, and at follow-up 6 months later the skin lesions had completely healed. The patient's neoplastic disease was under control—despite discontinuation of the pembrolizumab and axitinib.
Immune checkpoint inhibitors have become established treatments for several cancers including malignant melanoma and renal cell carcinoma. Such developments have, in some patients resulted, in treatment-related adverse effects of variable severity. Immune-related purpura fulminans associated with pembrolizumab has been reported previously in a patient treated for lung carcinoma.

A 61-year-old woman with a 4-day history of asthenia, fever, and a rash was seen by our team in the hospital intensive care unit.
The patient had clear cell renal cell carcinoma with tumoral thrombosis of the right renal vein and inferior vena cava. She was being treated with a checkpoint inhibitor, pembrolizumab—a PD-1 inhibitor—and the endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGF-R) tyrosine kinase inhibitor, axitinib, before re-assessment for surgery, in the oncology day hospital unit. 3 days after the third infusion of pembrolizumab, the patient had been admitted to the intensive care unit because she had become haemodynamically unstable; she had developed heart failure, and purpura fulminans (figure; appendix) over her arms and legs, which had initially appeared as livedo racemose a few hours before. She had also been found to have an ascending sensory motor deficit of her lower limbs.
On examination, we found the patient to be unwell; her blood pressure was 90/60 mm Hg, pulse 30 beats per min, oxygen saturation was 100% on 15 L/min oxygen, and temperature was 32°C. She was confused, with a Glasgow Coma Score of 8 (eye opening response 2, verbal response 2, and motor response 4). She needed both noradrenaline and dobutamine because of her cardiac failure. Additionally, the patient was being treated with meropenem and amikacin; axitinib had been stopped at the point of admission to the intensive care unit.
Laboratory investigations showed high concentrations of N-terminal-pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (10 518 pg/mL; typical level <125 in people younger than 75 years) and troponin (109 ng/L; typical level <14). Concentrations of liver enzymes and thyroid-stimulating hormone were elevated; C-reactive protein concentration was 36 mg/L (typical range 8–10). Analysis of a sample of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed an elevated protein concentration (0·52 g/L; typical level <0·4) and a normal white blood cell count; cultures of blood, CSF, urine, and skin showed no abnormalities.
PCR skin swab testing was negative for Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae, resulting in the cessation of antibiotics treatment.
A CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed diffuse thickening of the wall of the colon; echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 25% (normal range 50–70). MRIs of brain and spinal cord showed no abnormalities. An electromyogram showed severe sensory-motor neurogenic damage compatible with axonal length-dependent processes without demyelination.
Histopathological analysis of a sample of a skin biopsy showed thrombosis with leukocytoclastic vasculitis, which, considering the patient's presentation, investigations, and history in the round, led us to conclude she had developed an immune-induced myocarditis, acute motor and sensory axonal polyneuropathy, colitis, hypothyroidism, hepatitis, and purpura fulminans.
The patient was commenced on pulse methylprednisolone (1 g per day for 5 days) and intravenous immunoglobulin (2 g per kg over 4 days), which resulted in the improvement of her general condition. She had three separate plasma exchanges to clear the pembrolizumab and surgery of the deepest wounds with skin grafts.
The corticosteroids were gradually tapered down over the next 4 months, and at follow-up 6 months later the skin lesions had completely healed. The patient's neoplastic disease was under control—despite discontinuation of the pembrolizumab and axitinib.
Immune checkpoint inhibitors have become established treatments for several cancers including malignant melanoma and renal cell carcinoma. Such developments have, in some patients resulted, in treatment-related adverse effects of variable severity. Immune-related purpura fulminans associated with pembrolizumab has been reported previously in a patient treated for lung carcinoma.

A 13-year-old boy presented to the paediatrics outpatient department with recurrent fever and abdominal pain that started 8 months before presentation. He was admitted to the paediatric nephrology unit for evaluation following a generalised seizure, persistent stage 2 hypertension, and melaena for one week requiring packed red cell transfusion. Significant examination findings included severe thinness (BMI-for-age –5·2 standard deviation score), stage 2 hypertension (blood pressure 136/110 mm Hg), pallor, and generalised muscle tenderness. Investigations identified normocytic normochromic anaemia (haemoglobin 85 g/L), acute kidney injury (serum creatinine 353·6 μmol/L), and elevated inflammatory markers (serum ferritin 3312 pmol/L, serum C-reactive protein 146 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 50 mm/h). Urinalysis revealed proteinuria (2+ on dipstick) and haematuria (4–5 red blood cells per high power field).
On diagnostic evaluation, serum antinuclear antibodies and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative and C3 and C4 complement protein concentrations were normal. Serum hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C virus, and HIV antibodies were also absent. A non-reactive tuberculin skin test excluded tuberculosis infection. Malignant lesions were excluded after a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen. Worsening gastrointestinal bleeding prompted a CT angiogram. The beaded appearance of medium-sized arteries, alternating stenosis and dilatation, and microaneurysms, particularly along the coeliac–mesenteric axis, was consistent with polyarteritis nodosa (figure 1A, B, C). MRI with angiography showed similar abnormalities in intracranial vessels (figure 1D). Vasculitis-induced end-organ ischaemia was evident in both scans. Considering the characteristic angiographic findings, multisystem presentation (fever, myalgia, hypertension, and central nervous system, gastrointestinal, and renal involvement) and laboratory features of inflammation, the patient was diagnosed with childhood-onset polyarteritis nodosa. Clinical exome sequencing excluded inherited deficiency of adenosine deaminase 2 (DADA2 mutation).
Therapy with intravenous methylprednisolone pulses (30 mg/kg per day for 3 days) was followed by oral prednisolone at 1 mg/kg per day for 4 weeks, gradually tapered to 5 mg/day over the next 16 weeks. The day after finishing the three methylprednisolone pulses, intravenous cyclophosphamide pulses (500 mg/m2 per dose) were started once a month for 6 months. Vasculitis-induced ischemia resulted in generalised myalgia, anuric acute kidney injury requiring maintenance haemodialysis, stage 2 hypertension that was controlled on concomitant therapy with five oral antihypertensive medications (amlodipine, 0·6 mg/kg per day; prazocin, 0·6 mg/kg per day; enalapril, 0·6 mg/kg per day; metoprolol, 3·0 mg/kg per day; and clonidine, 5·0 mcg/kg per day), and nervous system involvement with seizures requiring two oral antiseizure medications (initially phenytoin, 5·0 mg/kg per day; which was changed to levetiracetam, 20·0 mg/kg per day). During treatment initiation with intravenous methylprednisolone pulses and the first cyclophosphamide pulse, mesenteric ischaemia deteriorated into gut perforation, requiring bowel resection and re-anastomosis. Post-operative peritonitis and septicaemia required intravenous broad-spectrum antimicrobials (renal-modified doses; piperacillin–tazobactam, 210 mg/kg per day; teicoplanin, 5 mg/kg per day; metronidazole, 30 mg/kg per day; and caspofungin, 50 mg/m2 per day) and intravenous vasopressors (adrenaline and noradrenaline, titrated to 1 μg/kg per min). The overall disease was severe, reflected by a Factor-Five Score of 3. Discharged under multidisciplinary follow-up, the patient was receiving oral prednisolone (0·5 mg/kg per day, on tapering), oral mycophenolate mofetil (500 mg/m2 per day), and maintenance haemodialysis (done locally) at the last teleconsultation.
Childhood-onset polyarteritis nodosa is a rare, severe condition that requires prompt recognition and management. Patients with Factor-Five Scores exceeding 2 have a fulminant course of polyarteritis nodosa with a high risk of mortality and long-term morbidities. This case illustrates the role of early diagnosis and treatment in preventing mortality and improving outcomes.

input:
A 13-year-old boy presented to the paediatrics outpatient department with recurrent fever and abdominal pain that started 8 months before presentation. He was admitted to the paediatric nephrology unit for evaluation following a generalised seizure, persistent stage 2 hypertension, and melaena for one week requiring packed red cell transfusion. Significant examination findings included severe thinness (BMI-for-age –5·2 standard deviation score), stage 2 hypertension (blood pressure 136/110 mm Hg), pallor, and generalised muscle tenderness. Investigations identified normocytic normochromic anaemia (haemoglobin 85 g/L), acute kidney injury (serum creatinine 353·6 μmol/L), and elevated inflammatory markers (serum ferritin 3312 pmol/L, serum C-reactive protein 146 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 50 mm/h). Urinalysis revealed proteinuria (2+ on dipstick) and haematuria (4–5 red blood cells per high power field).
On diagnostic evaluation, serum antinuclear antibodies and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative and C3 and C4 complement protein concentrations were normal. Serum hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C virus, and HIV antibodies were also absent. A non-reactive tuberculin skin test excluded tuberculosis infection. Malignant lesions were excluded after a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen. Worsening gastrointestinal bleeding prompted a CT angiogram. The beaded appearance of medium-sized arteries, alternating stenosis and dilatation, and microaneurysms, particularly along the coeliac–mesenteric axis, was consistent with polyarteritis nodosa (figure 1A, B, C). MRI with angiography showed similar abnormalities in intracranial vessels (figure 1D). Vasculitis-induced end-organ ischaemia was evident in both scans. Considering the characteristic angiographic findings, multisystem presentation (fever, myalgia, hypertension, and central nervous system, gastrointestinal, and renal involvement) and laboratory features of inflammation, the patient was diagnosed with childhood-onset polyarteritis nodosa. Clinical exome sequencing excluded inherited deficiency of adenosine deaminase 2 (DADA2 mutation).
Therapy with intravenous methylprednisolone pulses (30 mg/kg per day for 3 days) was followed by oral prednisolone at 1 mg/kg per day for 4 weeks, gradually tapered to 5 mg/day over the next 16 weeks. The day after finishing the three methylprednisolone pulses, intravenous cyclophosphamide pulses (500 mg/m2 per dose) were started once a month for 6 months. Vasculitis-induced ischemia resulted in generalised myalgia, anuric acute kidney injury requiring maintenance haemodialysis, stage 2 hypertension that was controlled on concomitant therapy with five oral antihypertensive medications (amlodipine, 0·6 mg/kg per day; prazocin, 0·6 mg/kg per day; enalapril, 0·6 mg/kg per day; metoprolol, 3·0 mg/kg per day; and clonidine, 5·0 mcg/kg per day), and nervous system involvement with seizures requiring two oral antiseizure medications (initially phenytoin, 5·0 mg/kg per day; which was changed to levetiracetam, 20·0 mg/kg per day). During treatment initiation with intravenous methylprednisolone pulses and the first cyclophosphamide pulse, mesenteric ischaemia deteriorated into gut perforation, requiring bowel resection and re-anastomosis. Post-operative peritonitis and septicaemia required intravenous broad-spectrum antimicrobials (renal-modified doses; piperacillin–tazobactam, 210 mg/kg per day; teicoplanin, 5 mg/kg per day; metronidazole, 30 mg/kg per day; and caspofungin, 50 mg/m2 per day) and intravenous vasopressors (adrenaline and noradrenaline, titrated to 1 μg/kg per min). The overall disease was severe, reflected by a Factor-Five Score of 3. Discharged under multidisciplinary follow-up, the patient was receiving oral prednisolone (0·5 mg/kg per day, on tapering), oral mycophenolate mofetil (500 mg/m2 per day), and maintenance haemodialysis (done locally) at the last teleconsultation.
Childhood-onset polyarteritis nodosa is a rare, severe condition that requires prompt recognition and management. Patients with Factor-Five Scores exceeding 2 have a fulminant course of polyarteritis nodosa with a high risk of mortality and long-term morbidities. This case illustrates the role of early diagnosis and treatment in preventing mortality and improving outcomes.

7 years earlier, she had an episode of left flank pain caused by a stone in her distal left ureter, which was evacuated after insertion of a single-J splint.
On examination, we found the patient to be generally well; microscopy of a sample of fresh urine sediment showed multiple amorphous ovoid crystals (figure). Laboratory investigations—including full blood count, glucose and lipid metabolism, liver function tests, muscle enzymes, parathyroid and thyroid function tests, and inflammatory and immunological markers—found no abnormalities suggestive of primary or secondary glomerular diseases. Additionally, despite renal impairment, the patient had profound hypouricemia (serum uric acid concentration <0·5 mg/dL; typical range in an adult post-menopausal woman is 3·4–7·0).
A CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed two normal kidneys without nephro-urolithiasis.
Urinary excretion of uric acid was abnormally low (<3 mmol/mol creatinine; normal 443–695); urinary excretion of hypoxanthine was slightly elevated (16 mmol/mol creatinine; normal 7–13); and urinary excretion of xanthine was high (135 mmol/mol creatinine; normal 9–14); indicating a possible diagnosis of either type I or type II xanthinuria. Molecular genetic sequencing found two mutations in the XDH gene on chromosome 2, which encodes for the enzyme xanthine dehydrogenase (OMIM 278300: heterozygous mutations c.3847C>T [p.Arg1283*] and c.3520-69_*3432delinsCAGTCGCT); no mutations were found in the MOCOS gene on chromosome 18, which encodes for molybdenum cofactor sulferase, corroborating the diagnosis of hereditary xanthinuria type I.
The patient was informed of the diagnosis and advised to follow a low-purine diet and drink plenty of fluids; she was counselled about possible genetic testing of her siblings.
At follow-up 6 months later, the patient was clinically well and her renal function was stable.
Hereditary xanthinuria is characterised by high levels of xanthine in the urine; uric acid is much reduced in the serum and urine—compared with gout where an increased concentration of serum urate (hyperuricaemia) is the important risk factor. Two clinically similar forms of xanthinuria are found: type I—our patient—where there is an isolated deficiency of xanthine dehydrogenase, and type II, with a deficiency of both xanthine dehydrogenase and aldehyde oxidase (appendix).
Xanthinuria may occur in molybdenum cofactor sulferase deficiency; type II xanthinuria is caused by a mutation in the MOCOS gene. Excess xanthine can accumulate in the kidneys and other tissues; in the kidneys it may lead to stones and in the muscles, pain and cramping. Apart from a low-purine diet and high fluid intake, which prevent xanthine accumulation, no specific therapies are available for this rare autosomal recessive disorder of purine metabolism. Symptoms may occur at any age, with approximately 50% of patients presenting with urinary tract infections, haematuria, renal colic, acute renal failure, crystalluria, or urolithiasis. Rarely patients’ renal disease may result in failure.

A 30-year-old woman was seen in our outpatient clinic reporting a 1-month history of fatigue and breathlessness on exertion. She reported having heavy menstrual bleeding.Notably in her medical history, the patient had a similar episode of fatigue and dyspnoea 2 years earlier. At that time, her full blood count showed a haemoglobin concentration of 7·9 g/dL and a mean corpuscular volume of 68 fL (normal range 83–98). The platelet count was 148 × 109 per L and the white cell count 4·1 × 109 per L. The serum ferritin level was 3·9 ng/mL (normal for a woman 12–150). A physical examination, at that stage, was unremarkable. Iron-deficiency anaemia caused by heavy periods was thought to be the most likely diagnosis; the patient was treated with oral iron and no further investigations were done.
When we saw the patient, a full physical examination was unremarkable except for a non-tender, firm, fixed, well circumscribed mass in the lower abdomen. She was not pale and there were no signs of iron deficiency anaemia—including angular cheilitis or defects in the nail beds.
A full blood count showed a microcytic anaemia: the patient's haemoglobin concentration was 7·8 g/dL and the mean corpuscular volume was 70 fL. The platelet count was 118 × 109 per L and the white cell count 3·1 × 109 per L. The C-reactive protein concentration was 0·2 mg/L. The serum ferritin level was low (1·9 ng/mL). There was no clinical evidence of overt bleeding from the gastrointestinal tract. An abdominal ultrasound and a contrast-enhanced CT scan showed an enlarged ectopic spleen 11·3 cm × 6·2 cm × 11·8 cm (figure).
Our working diagnoses were the unusual combination of an iron deficiency anaemia related to menstrual bleeding, and thrombocytopenia and leucopenia caused by hypersplenism in the context of splenomegaly.
We opted to manage the patient conservatively. After 2 months of oral iron supplementation, the patient's anaemia had been corrected: the haemoglobin concentration was 13 g/dL and the mean corpuscular volume was 84 fL. However, the patient remained thrombocytopenic at 82 × 109 platelets per L and leucopenic—white cell count was 2·21 × 109 per L.
An ectopic or so-called wandering spleen is rare. Normally, the spleen is fixed by several ligaments in the left upper quadrant; if the ligaments are congenitally absent or lax, it may be ectopic—being usually located in the pelvis. Elongation of the splenic vascular pedicle may predispose to torsion and splenic infarction: patients may then have recurrent episodes of chronic abdominal pain or a life-threatening acute abdomen requiring immediate splenectomy, or detorsion, or splenopexy in the absence of splenic infarction. Episodic torsions are thought to result in splenomegaly secondary to venous congestion with subsequent features of hypersplenism. Laparoscopic splenopexy or splenectomy may be considered. However, the risk of sepsis after splenectomy and the lack of long-term outcome data in patients treated by splenopexy—where secondary splenic infarction, recurrent splenic pedicle torsion, and asplenia may occur—add weight to watchful waiting in asymptomatic patients (video).

A 13-year-old boy presented to the paediatrics outpatient department with recurrent fever and abdominal pain that started 8 months before presentation. He was admitted to the paediatric nephrology unit for evaluation following a generalised seizure, persistent stage 2 hypertension, and melaena for one week requiring packed red cell transfusion. Significant examination findings included severe thinness (BMI-for-age –5·2 standard deviation score), stage 2 hypertension (blood pressure 136/110 mm Hg), pallor, and generalised muscle tenderness. Investigations identified normocytic normochromic anaemia (haemoglobin 85 g/L), acute kidney injury (serum creatinine 353·6 μmol/L), and elevated inflammatory markers (serum ferritin 3312 pmol/L, serum C-reactive protein 146 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 50 mm/h). Urinalysis revealed proteinuria (2+ on dipstick) and haematuria (4–5 red blood cells per high power field).
On diagnostic evaluation, serum antinuclear antibodies and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative and C3 and C4 complement protein concentrations were normal. Serum hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C virus, and HIV antibodies were also absent. A non-reactive tuberculin skin test excluded tuberculosis infection. Malignant lesions were excluded after a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen. Worsening gastrointestinal bleeding prompted a CT angiogram. The beaded appearance of medium-sized arteries, alternating stenosis and dilatation, and microaneurysms, particularly along the coeliac–mesenteric axis, was consistent with polyarteritis nodosa (figure 1A, B, C). MRI with angiography showed similar abnormalities in intracranial vessels (figure 1D). Vasculitis-induced end-organ ischaemia was evident in both scans. Considering the characteristic angiographic findings, multisystem presentation (fever, myalgia, hypertension, and central nervous system, gastrointestinal, and renal involvement) and laboratory features of inflammation, the patient was diagnosed with childhood-onset polyarteritis nodosa. Clinical exome sequencing excluded inherited deficiency of adenosine deaminase 2 (DADA2 mutation).
