A 30-year-old woman was seen in our outpatient clinic reporting a 1-month history of fatigue and breathlessness on exertion. She reported having heavy menstrual bleeding.Notably in her medical history, the patient had a similar episode of fatigue and dyspnoea 2 years earlier. At that time, her full blood count showed a haemoglobin concentration of 7·9 g/dL and a mean corpuscular volume of 68 fL (normal range 83–98). The platelet count was 148 × 109 per L and the white cell count 4·1 × 109 per L. The serum ferritin level was 3·9 ng/mL (normal for a woman 12–150). A physical examination, at that stage, was unremarkable. Iron-deficiency anaemia caused by heavy periods was thought to be the most likely diagnosis; the patient was treated with oral iron and no further investigations were done.
When we saw the patient, a full physical examination was unremarkable except for a non-tender, firm, fixed, well circumscribed mass in the lower abdomen. She was not pale and there were no signs of iron deficiency anaemia—including angular cheilitis or defects in the nail beds.
A full blood count showed a microcytic anaemia: the patient's haemoglobin concentration was 7·8 g/dL and the mean corpuscular volume was 70 fL. The platelet count was 118 × 109 per L and the white cell count 3·1 × 109 per L. The C-reactive protein concentration was 0·2 mg/L. The serum ferritin level was low (1·9 ng/mL). There was no clinical evidence of overt bleeding from the gastrointestinal tract. An abdominal ultrasound and a contrast-enhanced CT scan showed an enlarged ectopic spleen 11·3 cm × 6·2 cm × 11·8 cm (figure).
Our working diagnoses were the unusual combination of an iron deficiency anaemia related to menstrual bleeding, and thrombocytopenia and leucopenia caused by hypersplenism in the context of splenomegaly.
We opted to manage the patient conservatively. After 2 months of oral iron supplementation, the patient's anaemia had been corrected: the haemoglobin concentration was 13 g/dL and the mean corpuscular volume was 84 fL. However, the patient remained thrombocytopenic at 82 × 109 platelets per L and leucopenic—white cell count was 2·21 × 109 per L.
An ectopic or so-called wandering spleen is rare. Normally, the spleen is fixed by several ligaments in the left upper quadrant; if the ligaments are congenitally absent or lax, it may be ectopic—being usually located in the pelvis. Elongation of the splenic vascular pedicle may predispose to torsion and splenic infarction: patients may then have recurrent episodes of chronic abdominal pain or a life-threatening acute abdomen requiring immediate splenectomy, or detorsion, or splenopexy in the absence of splenic infarction. Episodic torsions are thought to result in splenomegaly secondary to venous congestion with subsequent features of hypersplenism. Laparoscopic splenopexy or splenectomy may be considered. However, the risk of sepsis after splenectomy and the lack of long-term outcome data in patients treated by splenopexy—where secondary splenic infarction, recurrent splenic pedicle torsion, and asplenia may occur—add weight to watchful waiting in asymptomatic patients (video).

Additionally, she reported having chest pain brought on by exertion for the past 2 months. She had no medical history suggesting malabsorption, recurrent epigastric pain suggesting a hookworm infestation, or blood loss. She said her diet was strictly vegetarian, as advised by the local Ayurvedic practitioner, and mainly comprised chapattis and dhal, with no fruit, milk, or vegetables. A physical examination confirmed deep brownish-black pigmentation over her fingers and toes, and on the palms of her hands, and soles of her feet (figure). Her scalp hair was brittle, her tongue was bald with brown pigmented spots, and she had brown pigmented spots all around the inside of her mouth. Examination of her cardiovascular system found a soft systolic murmur at the apex and a fourth heart sound. Neurological examination found diminished deep tendon reflexes with intact peripheral sensation. Romberg's sign was absent. Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8 g/dL, macrocytosis (mean corpuscular volume 107·9 fL), and white cell count 3·4 × 109 per L. A peripheral blood smear showed oval macrocytes, fragmented and teardrop shaped red blood cells, and hypersegmented neutrophils (figure). Serum folate concentration was 14·2 ng/mL (normal range 3–17), serum B12 concentration was less than 83 pg/mL (normal range 174–878), and serum homocysteine concentration was 34·69 μmol/L (normal range <15). A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed biphasic T waves in leads V1–V3. A coronary angiogram showed critical proximal stenosis in the left anterior descending coronary artery. The patient was treated with oral B12 supplements, statins, and antiplatelets, and advised to have a protein rich diet, with fruits and vegetables. 3 months later, her symptoms had greatly improved: the pigmentation of her skin was markedly reduced (figure) and her haemoglobin concentration had increased to 10·4 g/dL, with improvement in all red blood cell indices.Pigmentation of skin and nail beds is a sign of malnutrition often seen in patients with tropical sprue, strict vegetarians, and tropical megaloblastic anaemia caused by vitamin B12 deficiency. The mechanism underlying the hyperpigmentation is thought to be a decrease in glutathione levels—responsible for the activation of tyrosinase and the transfer of melanin to melanosomes. A defect in the melanin transfer between melanocytes and keratinocytes leads to hyperpigmentation.
Demonstration of macrocytes, abnormal shaped red blood cells—including teardrop shaped cells—and hypersegmented neutrophils is a cheap and easily available way of confirming vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia: the blood film remains an important, simple, and speedy investigation in outpatient departments in rural India.

A 30-year-old woman was seen in our outpatient clinic reporting a 1-month history of fatigue and breathlessness on exertion. She reported having heavy menstrual bleeding.Notably in her medical history, the patient had a similar episode of fatigue and dyspnoea 2 years earlier. At that time, her full blood count showed a haemoglobin concentration of 7·9 g/dL and a mean corpuscular volume of 68 fL (normal range 83–98). The platelet count was 148 × 109 per L and the white cell count 4·1 × 109 per L. The serum ferritin level was 3·9 ng/mL (normal for a woman 12–150). A physical examination, at that stage, was unremarkable. Iron-deficiency anaemia caused by heavy periods was thought to be the most likely diagnosis; the patient was treated with oral iron and no further investigations were done.
When we saw the patient, a full physical examination was unremarkable except for a non-tender, firm, fixed, well circumscribed mass in the lower abdomen. She was not pale and there were no signs of iron deficiency anaemia—including angular cheilitis or defects in the nail beds.
A full blood count showed a microcytic anaemia: the patient's haemoglobin concentration was 7·8 g/dL and the mean corpuscular volume was 70 fL. The platelet count was 118 × 109 per L and the white cell count 3·1 × 109 per L. The C-reactive protein concentration was 0·2 mg/L. The serum ferritin level was low (1·9 ng/mL). There was no clinical evidence of overt bleeding from the gastrointestinal tract. An abdominal ultrasound and a contrast-enhanced CT scan showed an enlarged ectopic spleen 11·3 cm × 6·2 cm × 11·8 cm (figure).
Our working diagnoses were the unusual combination of an iron deficiency anaemia related to menstrual bleeding, and thrombocytopenia and leucopenia caused by hypersplenism in the context of splenomegaly.
We opted to manage the patient conservatively. After 2 months of oral iron supplementation, the patient's anaemia had been corrected: the haemoglobin concentration was 13 g/dL and the mean corpuscular volume was 84 fL. However, the patient remained thrombocytopenic at 82 × 109 platelets per L and leucopenic—white cell count was 2·21 × 109 per L.
An ectopic or so-called wandering spleen is rare. Normally, the spleen is fixed by several ligaments in the left upper quadrant; if the ligaments are congenitally absent or lax, it may be ectopic—being usually located in the pelvis. Elongation of the splenic vascular pedicle may predispose to torsion and splenic infarction: patients may then have recurrent episodes of chronic abdominal pain or a life-threatening acute abdomen requiring immediate splenectomy, or detorsion, or splenopexy in the absence of splenic infarction. Episodic torsions are thought to result in splenomegaly secondary to venous congestion with subsequent features of hypersplenism. Laparoscopic splenopexy or splenectomy may be considered. However, the risk of sepsis after splenectomy and the lack of long-term outcome data in patients treated by splenopexy—where secondary splenic infarction, recurrent splenic pedicle torsion, and asplenia may occur—add weight to watchful waiting in asymptomatic patients (video).

A 40-year-old woman attended our hospital complaining of excessive darkening over her fingers and toes, and on the palms of her hands, and the soles of her feet: she also said she got tired easily, had a burning sensation in her mouth, and had become increasingly forgetful over the past 12 months. Additionally, she reported having chest pain brought on by exertion for the past 2 months. She had no medical history suggesting malabsorption, recurrent epigastric pain suggesting a hookworm infestation, or blood loss. She said her diet was strictly vegetarian, as advised by the local Ayurvedic practitioner, and mainly comprised chapattis and dhal, with no fruit, milk, or vegetables. A physical examination confirmed deep brownish-black pigmentation over her fingers and toes, and on the palms of her hands, and soles of her feet (figure). Her scalp hair was brittle, her tongue was bald with brown pigmented spots, and she had brown pigmented spots all around the inside of her mouth. Examination of her cardiovascular system found a soft systolic murmur at the apex and a fourth heart sound. Neurological examination found diminished deep tendon reflexes with intact peripheral sensation. Romberg's sign was absent. Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8 g/dL, macrocytosis (mean corpuscular volume 107·9 fL), and white cell count 3·4 × 109 per L. A peripheral blood smear showed oval macrocytes, fragmented and teardrop shaped red blood cells, and hypersegmented neutrophils (figure). Serum folate concentration was 14·2 ng/mL (normal range 3–17), serum B12 concentration was less than 83 pg/mL (normal range 174–878), and serum homocysteine concentration was 34·69 μmol/L (normal range <15). A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed biphasic T waves in leads V1–V3. A coronary angiogram showed critical proximal stenosis in the left anterior descending coronary artery. The patient was treated with oral B12 supplements, statins, and antiplatelets, and advised to have a protein rich diet, with fruits and vegetables. 3 months later, her symptoms had greatly improved: the pigmentation of her skin was markedly reduced (figure) and her haemoglobin concentration had increased to 10·4 g/dL, with improvement in all red blood cell indices.Pigmentation of skin and nail beds is a sign of malnutrition often seen in patients with tropical sprue, strict vegetarians, and tropical megaloblastic anaemia caused by vitamin B12 deficiency. The mechanism underlying the hyperpigmentation is thought to be a decrease in glutathione levels—responsible for the activation of tyrosinase and the transfer of melanin to melanosomes. A defect in the melanin transfer between melanocytes and keratinocytes leads to hyperpigmentation.
Demonstration of macrocytes, abnormal shaped red blood cells—including teardrop shaped cells—and hypersegmented neutrophils is a cheap and easily available way of confirming vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia: the blood film remains an important, simple, and speedy investigation in outpatient departments in rural India.

A 32-year-old woman presented to our department for an evaluation of possible cardiac manifestations of tuberous sclerosis complex.The patient had been diagnosed with tuberous sclerosis complex in her early childhood when she started having daily focal seizures. Genetic analysis when she was 16 years old confirmed a TSC1 (Q783X) de novo mutation. During adolescence, she had continued anticonvulsant medication—a combination of carbamazepine and valproate—and remained free from further seizures. However, after the initial diagnosis, regular follow-up imaging was not performed.
1 year before the assessment in our department, the patient was diagnosed with a papillary thyroid carcinoma for which she underwent a right hemi-thyroidectomy with lymphadenectomy. Following the operation, she reported an increase of the focal seizures—thought to be provoked by stress. A neurological examination, at the time, was unremarkable and no dermatological signs specific to tuberous sclerosis complex were found—such as hypomelanotic macules, or facial angiofibromas. Further, because of the lack of regular follow-up over the previous 17 years, extensive additional investigations were requested by the neurologist who saw her: brain MRI showed typical cortical tubers (figure) and a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma adjacent to the foramen of Monro—without any signs of obstruction (figure). Compared to an MRI from 17 years earlier, the giant cell astrocytoma showed no significant increase in size. Abdominal MRI showed cyst-like lesions in the patient's left kidney, which was thought to be a fat-poor angiomyolipoma (figure).
For completeness and because screening for the cardiac manifestations of tuberous sclerosis complex had not been done previously, the patient was referred to our department: cardiac MRI showed myocardial fatty foci (figure) with no cardiac rhabdomyomas. We concluded that in the absence of cardiac rhabdomyomas no further follow-up cardiac imaging was indicated; cardiac magnetic resonance and an electrocardiogram were normal.
The patient was continued on anticonvulsant medication—a combination of carbamazepine and lamotrigine—and she remained seizure-free. Surgery and medical treatment with everolimus were considered for the subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, but because the lesion had remained stable, the neurologist decided to simply keep the patient under active surveillance. Diagnostic imaging of the patient's kidneys is also planned to be repeated regularly to monitor possible growth of the lesions.
Tuberous sclerosis complex is a protean disease. Regarding the heart, cardiac rhabdomyomas usually appear in the fetus and almost always regress in infancy. Although the presence of myocardial fatty foci—as seen in our patient—is not one of the clinical diagnostic criteria of tuberous sclerosis complex, they are strongly associated with the disease and can be useful in making the initial clinical diagnosis; the number of lesions correlates with the degree of extra cardiac involvement.

Additionally, she reported having chest pain brought on by exertion for the past 2 months. She had no medical history suggesting malabsorption, recurrent epigastric pain suggesting a hookworm infestation, or blood loss. She said her diet was strictly vegetarian, as advised by the local Ayurvedic practitioner, and mainly comprised chapattis and dhal, with no fruit, milk, or vegetables. A physical examination confirmed deep brownish-black pigmentation over her fingers and toes, and on the palms of her hands, and soles of her feet (figure). Her scalp hair was brittle, her tongue was bald with brown pigmented spots, and she had brown pigmented spots all around the inside of her mouth. Examination of her cardiovascular system found a soft systolic murmur at the apex and a fourth heart sound. Neurological examination found diminished deep tendon reflexes with intact peripheral sensation. Romberg's sign was absent. Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8 g/dL, macrocytosis (mean corpuscular volume 107·9 fL), and white cell count 3·4 × 109 per L. A peripheral blood smear showed oval macrocytes, fragmented and teardrop shaped red blood cells, and hypersegmented neutrophils (figure). A 49-year-old man with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus was referred for an internal medicine consultation because of worsening heartburn for the past 3 months. The patient regularly ate pickled anchovies (raw anchovies in vinegar sauce). His overall health was good, and findings from physical examination were unexceptional. Laboratory results showed peripheral eosinophilia (1·7 × 103 cells per μL, normal 0·5 × 103 cells per μL) but were otherwise unremarkable. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed characteristic findings of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and Barrett's oesophagus (confirmed by pathological study); an isolated, thickened gastric fold (which was biopsied; figure); and no macroscopic evidence of erythema, oedema, erosive gastritis, ulcerations, tumour-like nodules, or worms. Nevertheless, histological assessment showed a striking eosinophilic inflammatory infiltrate and a sectioned larva of the nematode Anisakis simplex embedded in the gastric mucosa (figure). Additionally, serum IgE specific for A simplex was increased. We gave the patient omeprazole to treat his gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and specific preventive recommendations to avoid ingestion of potentially contaminated seafood (eg, by freezing or suitably heating fish) and decrease the risk of anaphylaxis due to A simplex. 10 months after the diagnosis of anisakidosis was made, his blood eosinophil count was within normal limits, and both gastroscopy and examination of gastric biopsy samples showed no abnormalities.
Anisakidosis, a disease caused by any member of the family Anisakidae that occurs worldwide, usually results from consumption of raw or undercooked marine fish or squid contaminated with the larvae of A simplex or Pseudoterranova decipiens. Although symptomatic gastro-oesophageal, intestinal, ectopic, and allergic diseases are the most common clinical presentations in human beings, this case shows that symptomless eosinophilic gastritis with secondary eosinophilia can also develop. In view of the popularity of raw seafood consumption, clinicians should keep anisakidosis high on their list of differential diagnoses for a wide range of disorders, especially in patients known to have these dietary habits.

A 32-year-old woman presented to our department for an evaluation of possible cardiac manifestations of tuberous sclerosis complex.The patient had been diagnosed with tuberous sclerosis complex in her early childhood when she started having daily focal seizures. Genetic analysis when she was 16 years old confirmed a TSC1 (Q783X) de novo mutation. During adolescence, she had continued anticonvulsant medication—a combination of carbamazepine and valproate—and remained free from further seizures. However, after the initial diagnosis, regular follow-up imaging was not performed.
1 year before the assessment in our department, the patient was diagnosed with a papillary thyroid carcinoma for which she underwent a right hemi-thyroidectomy with lymphadenectomy. Following the operation, she reported an increase of the focal seizures—thought to be provoked by stress. A neurological examination, at the time, was unremarkable and no dermatological signs specific to tuberous sclerosis complex were found—such as hypomelanotic macules, or facial angiofibromas. Further, because of the lack of regular follow-up over the previous 17 years, extensive additional investigations were requested by the neurologist who saw her: brain MRI showed typical cortical tubers (figure) and a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma adjacent to the foramen of Monro—without any signs of obstruction (figure). Compared to an MRI from 17 years earlier, the giant cell astrocytoma showed no significant increase in size. Abdominal MRI showed cyst-like lesions in the patient's left kidney, which was thought to be a fat-poor angiomyolipoma (figure).
For completeness and because screening for the cardiac manifestations of tuberous sclerosis complex had not been done previously, the patient was referred to our department: cardiac MRI showed myocardial fatty foci (figure) with no cardiac rhabdomyomas. We concluded that in the absence of cardiac rhabdomyomas no further follow-up cardiac imaging was indicated; cardiac magnetic resonance and an electrocardiogram were normal.
The patient was continued on anticonvulsant medication—a combination of carbamazepine and lamotrigine—and she remained seizure-free. Surgery and medical treatment with everolimus were considered for the subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, but because the lesion had remained stable, the neurologist decided to simply keep the patient under active surveillance. Diagnostic imaging of the patient's kidneys is also planned to be repeated regularly to monitor possible growth of the lesions.
Tuberous sclerosis complex is a protean disease. Regarding the heart, cardiac rhabdomyomas usually appear in the fetus and almost always regress in infancy. Although the presence of myocardial fatty foci—as seen in our patient—is not one of the clinical diagnostic criteria of tuberous sclerosis complex, they are strongly associated with the disease and can be useful in making the initial clinical diagnosis; the number of lesions correlates with the degree of extra cardiac involvement.

A 49-year-old man with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus was referred for an internal medicine consultation because of worsening heartburn for the past 3 months. The patient regularly ate pickled anchovies (raw anchovies in vinegar sauce). His overall health was good, and findings from physical examination were unexceptional. Laboratory results showed peripheral eosinophilia (1·7 × 103 cells per μL, normal 0·5 × 103 cells per μL) but were otherwise unremarkable. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed characteristic findings of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and Barrett's oesophagus (confirmed by pathological study); an isolated, thickened gastric fold (which was biopsied; figure); and no macroscopic evidence of erythema, oedema, erosive gastritis, ulcerations, tumour-like nodules, or worms. Nevertheless, histological assessment showed a striking eosinophilic inflammatory infiltrate and a sectioned larva of the nematode Anisakis simplex embedded in the gastric mucosa (figure). Additionally, serum IgE specific for A simplex was increased. We gave the patient omeprazole to treat his gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and specific preventive recommendations to avoid ingestion of potentially contaminated seafood (eg, by freezing or suitably heating fish) and decrease the risk of anaphylaxis due to A simplex. 10 months after the diagnosis of anisakidosis was made, his blood eosinophil count was within normal limits, and both gastroscopy and examination of gastric biopsy samples showed no abnormalities.
Anisakidosis, a disease caused by any member of the family Anisakidae that occurs worldwide, usually results from consumption of raw or undercooked marine fish or squid contaminated with the larvae of A simplex or Pseudoterranova decipiens. Although symptomatic gastro-oesophageal, intestinal, ectopic, and allergic diseases are the most common clinical presentations in human beings, this case shows that symptomless eosinophilic gastritis with secondary eosinophilia can also develop. In view of the popularity of raw seafood consumption, clinicians should keep anisakidosis high on their list of differential diagnoses for a wide range of disorders, especially in patients known to have these dietary habits.

A 27-year-old Asian man presented with erythematous, violaceous, and photosensitive lesions on the face, upper chest, and scalp, which had developed over 6 months (figure A). The patient had previously consulted a private practitioner for malar and heliotrope rash with photosensitivity and periorbital puffiness, who prescribed him methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine. However, the lesions progressed with ulceration over bilateral malar areas and the left mandibular angle (figure B–C), associated with non-scarring alopecia, oral ulcers, and violaceous papules on the dorsal aspect of metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints (Gottron's papules). There were no other comorbidities. On examination, the patient's blood pressure was 146/96 mm Hg and he had facial ulcers, as described (figure B–C). Investigations revealed he had mild elevation of alanine aminotransferase and gamma-glutamyl transferase, both elevated up to 2 × the upper limit of normal.
Based on the patient's history and symptoms, a number of differential diagnoses were considered, including dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus, lupus vulgaris (tuberculosis), granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and sarcoidosis. Buruli ulcer, which might also have a similar presentation, has yet to be reported in India. He had no clinical, radiological, or laboratory evidence of myositis, interstitial lung disease, neuropathy, nephritis, or arthritis. Serum creatine kinase, nerve conduction study results, and urine analysis were within normal limits and a high-resolution chest CT showed no abnormalities. Histopathological examination of a skin biopsy sample from the ulcer edge from the left mandibular angle revealed perivascular and periadnexal lymphoid infiltrates, vacuolar interface dermatitis, and basement membrane zone thickening (figure D). Direct immunofluorescence was negative for IgA, IgG, IgM, C1q, and C3. Ziehl–Neelsen staining was negative for acid-fast bacillus, and there was no evidence of malignancy. Serology for antinuclear antibody (Hep-2 cell by indirect immunofluorescence assay) was negative; although, an immunoblot was strongly positive for anti-MDA5. A diagnosis of anti-MDA5 amyopathic dermatomyositis was made.
Treatment with a combination of oral prednisolone (30 mg per day for 2 weeks, tapered over 2 months), mycophenolate mofetil (2 g per day), and topical tacrolimus healed his facial ulcers completely and dramatically reduced facial erythema, oral ulcers, heliotrope rash, and Gottron's papules over 7 months (figure E–F). The patient was followed up initially on a monthly basis for 3 months and then once every 3 months subsequently. Residual post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation was noted at 1 year after starting mycophenolate mofetil and prednisolone (figure E–F). The patient also remained hypertensive during the first 2 months of treatment, which was managed and controlled with lifestyle modifications alone. The patient has been under follow-up for 18 months with no additional symptoms, and continues to be treated with mycophenolate mofetil.
Anti-MDA5, a myositis-specific antibody, is typically associated with ulcers on the digits and extensor surfaces and facial ulcerations have not been reported previously. Progressive facial ulcers without accompanying myositis make for a diagnostic challenge.

A 49-year-old man with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus was referred for an internal medicine consultation because of worsening heartburn for the past 3 months. The patient regularly ate pickled anchovies (raw anchovies in vinegar sauce). His overall health was good, and findings from physical examination were unexceptional. Laboratory results showed peripheral eosinophilia (1·7 × 103 cells per μL, normal 0·5 × 103 cells per μL) but were otherwise unremarkable. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed characteristic findings of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and Barrett's oesophagus (confirmed by pathological study); an isolated, thickened gastric fold (which was biopsied; figure); and no macroscopic evidence of erythema, oedema, erosive gastritis, ulcerations, tumour-like nodules, or worms. Nevertheless, histological assessment showed a striking eosinophilic inflammatory infiltrate and a sectioned larva of the nematode Anisakis simplex embedded in the gastric mucosa (figure). Additionally, serum IgE specific for A simplex was increased. We gave the patient omeprazole to treat his gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and specific preventive recommendations to avoid ingestion of potentially contaminated seafood (eg, by freezing or suitably heating fish) and decrease the risk of anaphylaxis due to A simplex. 10 months after the diagnosis of anisakidosis was made, his blood eosinophil count was within normal limits, and both gastroscopy and examination of gastric biopsy samples showed no abnormalities.
Anisakidosis, a disease caused by any member of the family Anisakidae that occurs worldwide, usually results from consumption of raw or undercooked marine fish or squid contaminated with the larvae of A simplex or Pseudoterranova decipiens. Although symptomatic gastro-oesophageal, intestinal, ectopic, and allergic diseases are the most common clinical presentations in human beings, this case shows that symptomless eosinophilic gastritis with secondary eosinophilia can also develop. In view of the popularity of raw seafood consumption, clinicians should keep anisakidosis high on their list of differential diagnoses for a wide range of disorders, especially in patients known to have these dietary habits.

A 27-year-old Asian man presented with erythematous, violaceous, and photosensitive lesions on the face, upper chest, and scalp, which had developed over 6 months (figure A). The patient had previously consulted a private practitioner for malar and heliotrope rash with photosensitivity and periorbital puffiness, who prescribed him methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine. However, the lesions progressed with ulceration over bilateral malar areas and the left mandibular angle (figure B–C), associated with non-scarring alopecia, oral ulcers, and violaceous papules on the dorsal aspect of metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints (Gottron's papules). There were no other comorbidities. On examination, the patient's blood pressure was 146/96 mm Hg and he had facial ulcers, as described (figure B–C). Investigations revealed he had mild elevation of alanine aminotransferase and gamma-glutamyl transferase, both elevated up to 2 × the upper limit of normal.
Based on the patient's history and symptoms, a number of differential diagnoses were considered, including dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus, lupus vulgaris (tuberculosis), granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and sarcoidosis. Buruli ulcer, which might also have a similar presentation, has yet to be reported in India. He had no clinical, radiological, or laboratory evidence of myositis, interstitial lung disease, neuropathy, nephritis, or arthritis. Serum creatine kinase, nerve conduction study results, and urine analysis were within normal limits and a high-resolution chest CT showed no abnormalities. Histopathological examination of a skin biopsy sample from the ulcer edge from the left mandibular angle revealed perivascular and periadnexal lymphoid infiltrates, vacuolar interface dermatitis, and basement membrane zone thickening (figure D). Direct immunofluorescence was negative for IgA, IgG, IgM, C1q, and C3. Ziehl–Neelsen staining was negative for acid-fast bacillus, and there was no evidence of malignancy. Surgical resection of large epiglottic cysts should be considered in patients with either dysphagia or dyspnoea. VFSS, also known as a modified barium swallowing examination, is considered the gold standard-method of investigating dysphagia. Investigations revealed he had mild elevation of alanine aminotransferase and gamma-glutamyl transferase, both elevated up to 2 × the upper limit of normal.

The patient has been under follow-up for 18 months with no additional symptoms, and continues to be treated with mycophenolate mofetil.

A 49-year-old man with Wernicke's encephalopathy visited our hospital because of generalised weakness. He had lost more than 10 kg in weight in recent months and he reported dysphagia with a feeling of something being stuck in his throat. He also had symptoms caused by aspiration. He was referred to our dysphagia clinic for a videofluoroscopic swallowing study (VFSS). An initial visual inspection of the mouth showed a large cystic mass behind the tongue (figure). The lesion was also seen in the vallecula on a lateral fluoroscopic view (figure). Laryngoscopy and neck CT showed a giant cyst on the lingual surface of the epiglottis (figure). However, it was VFSS that unequivocally proved the cyst was the cause of the patient's dysphagia: the mass was seen to move through the upper oesophageal sphincter and enter the oesophagus itself, preventing the passage of food. It interfered with folding of the epiglottis, resulting in residue build up in the vallecula, and it caused aspiration during swallowing (video 1).We performed laryngeal microsurgery using a carbon dioxide laser to resect the 40 mm diameter cyst. The VFSS was repeated 4 days postoperatively and it showed almost normal oropharyngeal movement during swallowing (video 2). When the patient was discharged, he had no difficulty swallowing whatsoever and had begun to gain weight.
Epiglottic cysts are often found in adults. Most laryngeal cysts are asymptomatic and rarely large enough to cause symptoms. However, large laryngeal cysts may present with patients complaining of a sensation of having a foreign body in their throat, voice change, dysphagia, or dyspnoea. Surgical resection of large epiglottic cysts should be considered in patients with either dysphagia or dyspnoea. VFSS, also known as a modified barium swallowing examination, is considered the gold standard-method of investigating dysphagia. It allows for real-time observation of bolus flow in relation to structural movement throughout the whole of the upper aerodigestive tract.

A 49-year-old man with Wernicke's encephalopathy visited our hospital because of generalised weakness. He had lost more than 10 kg in weight in recent months and he reported dysphagia with a feeling of something being stuck in his throat. He also had symptoms caused by aspiration. He was referred to our dysphagia clinic for a videofluoroscopic swallowing study (VFSS). An initial visual inspection of the mouth showed a large cystic mass behind the tongue (figure). The lesion was also seen in the vallecula on a lateral fluoroscopic view (figure). Laryngoscopy and neck CT showed a giant cyst on the lingual surface of the epiglottis (figure). However, it was VFSS that unequivocally proved the cyst was the cause of the patient's dysphagia: the mass was seen to move through the upper oesophageal sphincter and enter the oesophagus itself, preventing the passage of food. It interfered with folding of the epiglottis, resulting in residue build up in the vallecula, and it caused aspiration during swallowing (video 1).We performed laryngeal microsurgery using a carbon dioxide laser to resect the 40 mm diameter cyst. The VFSS was repeated 4 days postoperatively and it showed almost normal oropharyngeal movement during swallowing (video 2). When the patient was discharged, he had no difficulty swallowing whatsoever and had begun to gain weight.
Epiglottic cysts are often found in adults. Most laryngeal cysts are asymptomatic and rarely large enough to cause symptoms. However, large laryngeal cysts may present with patients complaining of a sensation of having a foreign body in their throat, voice change, dysphagia, or dyspnoea. Surgical resection of large epiglottic cysts should be considered in patients with either dysphagia or dyspnoea. VFSS, also known as a modified barium swallowing examination, is considered the gold standard-method of investigating dysphagia. It allows for real-time observation of bolus flow in relation to structural movement throughout the whole of the upper aerodigestive tract.

A 46-year-old man presented to our hospital with abdominal pain and fever. In his medical history he reported three previous episodes of varicella zoster. On examination, he had a temperature of 38·3°C, small cervical lymph nodes, and some right upper quadrant tenderness.A CT of the patient's abdomen showed bilateral adrenalitis (figure). Laboratory investigations showed marked cholestatic hepatitis—including a raised alkaline phosphatase (1 995 U/mL; normal 30–135).
12 days later he developed thrombocytopenia (29 × 109 per L; normal 150–400), markedly elevated acute phase reactants—C-reactive protein concentration 266 mg/L (<3·1), D-dimer 12 696 μg/L (<500), ferritin 8 626 μg/L (<300), and soluble interleukin-2 receptor 2 481 U/mL (<846). We found him to have anasarca with pleural effusions, ascites, and subcutaneous oedema (figure).
Serum creatinine was 44 μmol/L, and urine microalbumin: creatinine ratio 387 (normal <2·0). Serum protein electrophoresis showed albumin 14 g/L, normal gamma globulins, and no monoclonal proteins. Interleukin-6 concentration was 39·6 pg/mL (<1·8) and vascular endothelial growth factor 212 pg/mL (31–86). SARS-CoV-2 nasal swabs, HIV, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) serology were negative.
18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT showed diffuse enlarged lymphadenopathy up to 3 cm, mild hepatosplenomegaly, and ascites, pleural effusions, and subcutaneous oedema. Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy were normal; biopsy specimens taken from along the gastrointestinal tract were normal. Bone marrow biopsy showed moderate haemophagocytosis with no fibrosis.
Excisional biopsy of the largest cervical lymph node showed many regressed germinal centres, prominent vascularity, very prominent follicular dendritic cells, and marked plasmacytosis (appendix); immunohistochemical stain for HHV-8 was negative.
Considering the patient in the round—thrombocytopenia, anasarca, reticulin fibrosis of the bone marrow, renal dysfunction, and organomegaly, acronymed to TAFRO—we diagnosed a variant of idiopathic multicentric Castleman's disease.
The patient was treated with numerous agents and ultimately responded to a combination of bortezomib, dexamethasone, baricitinib, siltuximab, and ciclosporin.
TAFRO is an aggressive variant of idiopathic multicentric Castleman's disease. The diagnosis is elusive; patients are often initially thought to have viral illness or haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. The lymphadenopathy and organomegaly are typically mild, and gamma globulins often normal. Patients decline rapidly and may be refractory to initial therapy, so early diagnosis is essential. Adrenalitis can be an important early clue, but because an adrenal biopsy is often unhelpful, clinical recognition is essential (video).

A 46-year-old man presented to our hospital with abdominal pain and fever. In his medical history he reported three previous episodes of varicella zoster. On examination, he had a temperature of 38·3°C, small cervical lymph nodes, and some right upper quadrant tenderness.A CT of the patient's abdomen showed bilateral adrenalitis (figure). Laboratory investigations showed marked cholestatic hepatitis—including a raised alkaline phosphatase (1 995 U/mL; normal 30–135).
12 days later he developed thrombocytopenia (29 × 109 per L; normal 150–400), markedly elevated acute phase reactants—C-reactive protein concentration 266 mg/L (<3·1), D-dimer 12 696 μg/L (<500), ferritin 8 626 μg/L (<300), and soluble interleukin-2 receptor 2 481 U/mL (<846). We found him to have anasarca with pleural effusions, ascites, and subcutaneous oedema (figure).
Serum creatinine was 44 μmol/L, and urine microalbumin: creatinine ratio 387 (normal <2·0). Serum protein electrophoresis showed albumin 14 g/L, normal gamma globulins, and no monoclonal proteins. Interleukin-6 concentration was 39·6 pg/mL (<1·8) and vascular endothelial growth factor 212 pg/mL (31–86). SARS-CoV-2 nasal swabs, HIV, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) serology were negative.
18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT showed diffuse enlarged lymphadenopathy up to 3 cm, mild hepatosplenomegaly, and ascites, pleural effusions, and subcutaneous oedema. Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy were normal; biopsy specimens taken from along the gastrointestinal tract were normal. Bone marrow biopsy showed moderate haemophagocytosis with no fibrosis.
Excisional biopsy of the largest cervical lymph node showed many regressed germinal centres, prominent vascularity, very prominent follicular dendritic cells, and marked plasmacytosis (appendix); immunohistochemical stain for HHV-8 was negative.
Considering the patient in the round—thrombocytopenia, anasarca, reticulin fibrosis of the bone marrow, renal dysfunction, and organomegaly, acronymed to TAFRO—we diagnosed a variant of idiopathic multicentric Castleman's disease.
The patient was treated with numerous agents and ultimately responded to a combination of bortezomib, dexamethasone, baricitinib, siltuximab, and ciclosporin.
TAFRO is an aggressive variant of idiopathic multicentric Castleman's disease. The diagnosis is elusive; patients are often initially thought to have viral illness or haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. The lymphadenopathy and organomegaly are typically mild, and gamma globulins often normal. Patients decline rapidly and may be refractory to initial therapy, so early diagnosis is essential. Adrenalitis can be an important early clue, but because an adrenal biopsy is often unhelpful, clinical recognition is essential (video).

A 44-year-old night porter presented to our clinic with difficulty walking, instability, and stiffness—particularly in the muscles of his face—which had developed over the previous 3 weeks. His wife said that he had also been tired and lethargic for about 1 year.He had been seen in our hepatology outpatient clinic 12 months earlier because of a raised aspartate aminotransaminase (AST) of 43 IU/L (normal 11–34) and gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) of 301 IU/L (normal 12–68); his alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and bilirubin were normal. Investigations showed no evidence of active viral hepatitis, haemochromatosis, α1 antitrypsin deficiency, or autoimmune liver disease. Serum ceruloplasmin concentration was reduced at 0·11 g/L (normal 0·2–0·6). Ultrasound and transient elastography showed signs of fibrosis and a liver biopsy specimen showed microvesicular steatosis, bilirubinostasis, and severe fibrosis with incomplete cirrhosis. Rhodanine staining for copper was negative. The patient's mother had been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease at age 70 years (see appendix for full family tree).
On examination we found him to have symmetrical cog-wheel muscle rigidity and hypokinetic movements bilaterally. He had diminished arm swing, he was unstable, and when he walked he episodically had short, accelerating steps. He had a mask-like facial expression with a fixed smile—risus sardonicus (figure; video). Investigations found an AST of 128 IU/L, ALT of 131 IU/L, GGT of 497 IU/L, and bilirubin of 64·4 μmol/L (normal <24).
The patient's symptoms deteriorated significantly over the following weeks: he was barely able to walk, he was bradykinetic with episodes of freezing, and he was very unstable on his feet (video). A single photon emission CT DaTSCAN (GE Healthcare, Amersham, UK), 5 weeks after his symptoms began, showed bilaterally reduced presynaptic dopamine transporter in the striatum (figure). Slit-lamp examination of his eyes was normal. The patient's serum ceruloplasmin concentration was again low 0·13 g/L and his urine copper excretion was markedly increased at 5·81 μmol per 24 h (normal <0·95). Histological examination of a biopsy specimen of his liver showed severe progressive chronic hepatitis with cholestasis and fibrosis with complete cirrhosis. Rhodanine staining for copper was again negative. However, analysis using atomic absorption spectrometry showed increased hepatic copper concentrations of 325 μg/g (normal 10–35). We confirmed a diagnosis of Wilson's disease by DNA sequencing, which showed that the patient was homozygous for a missense variant of the ATP7B, gene 2998G →A leading to Gly1000Arg substitution.
We started chelation therapy—8 weeks after his neurological symptoms began—with penicillamine. However, the patient's extrapyramidal motor symptoms worsened—probably because of mobilisation of the excess copper and deposition into the basal ganglia. So we switched penicillamine to trientine. The patient's symptoms—apart from the risus sardonicus—showed considerable improvement after 5 months of treatment.
Wilson's disease is an important and treatable differential diagnosis of rapidly developing extra-pyramidal or atypical Parkinsonian symptoms. Even if the patient is over 40 years of age, there are no eye signs—eg Kayser-Fleischer rings, or sunflower cataracts, and conventional histopathological analysis of a liver biopsy with rhodanine stain was negative.

A 46-year-old man presented to our hospital with abdominal pain and fever. In his medical history he reported three previous episodes of varicella zoster. On examination, he had a temperature of 38·3°C, small cervical lymph nodes, and some right upper quadrant tenderness.A CT of the patient's abdomen showed bilateral adrenalitis (figure). Laboratory investigations showed marked cholestatic hepatitis—including a raised alkaline phosphatase (1 995 U/mL; normal 30–135).
12 days later he developed thrombocytopenia (29 × 109 per L; normal 150–400), markedly elevated acute phase reactants—C-reactive protein concentration 266 mg/L (<3·1), D-dimer 12 696 μg/L (<500), ferritin 8 626 μg/L (<300), and soluble interleukin-2 receptor 2 481 U/mL (<846). We found him to have anasarca with pleural effusions, ascites, and subcutaneous oedema (figure).
Serum creatinine was 44 μmol/L, and urine microalbumin: creatinine ratio 387 (normal <2·0). Serum protein electrophoresis showed albumin 14 g/L, normal gamma globulins, and no monoclonal proteins. Interleukin-6 concentration was 39·6 pg/mL (<1·8) and vascular endothelial growth factor 212 pg/mL (31–86). SARS-CoV-2 nasal swabs, HIV, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) serology were negative.
18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT showed diffuse enlarged lymphadenopathy up to 3 cm, mild hepatosplenomegaly, and ascites, pleural effusions, and subcutaneous oedema. Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy were normal; biopsy specimens taken from along the gastrointestinal tract were normal. Bone marrow biopsy showed moderate haemophagocytosis with no fibrosis.
Excisional biopsy of the largest cervical lymph node showed many regressed germinal centres, prominent vascularity, very prominent follicular dendritic cells, and marked plasmacytosis (appendix); immunohistochemical stain for HHV-8 was negative.
Considering the patient in the round—thrombocytopenia, anasarca, reticulin fibrosis of the bone marrow, renal dysfunction, and organomegaly, acronymed to TAFRO—we diagnosed a variant of idiopathic multicentric Castleman's disease.
The patient was treated with numerous agents and ultimately responded to a combination of bortezomib, dexamethasone, baricitinib, siltuximab, and ciclosporin.
TAFRO is an aggressive variant of idiopathic multicentric Castleman's disease. The diagnosis is elusive; patients are often initially thought to have viral illness or haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. The lymphadenopathy and organomegaly are typically mild, and gamma globulins often normal. Patients decline rapidly and may be refractory to initial therapy, so early diagnosis is essential. Adrenalitis can be an important early clue, but because an adrenal biopsy is often unhelpful, clinical recognition is essential (video).

A 44-year-old night porter presented to our clinic with difficulty walking, instability, and stiffness—particularly in the muscles of his face—which had developed over the previous 3 weeks. His wife said that he had also been tired and lethargic for about 1 year.He had been seen in our hepatology outpatient clinic 12 months earlier because of a raised aspartate aminotransaminase (AST) of 43 IU/L (normal 11–34) and gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) of 301 IU/L (normal 12–68); his alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and bilirubin were normal. Investigations showed no evidence of active viral hepatitis, haemochromatosis, α1 antitrypsin deficiency, or autoimmune liver disease. Serum ceruloplasmin concentration was reduced at 0·11 g/L (normal 0·2–0·6). Ultrasound and transient elastography showed signs of fibrosis and a liver biopsy specimen showed microvesicular steatosis, bilirubinostasis, and severe fibrosis with incomplete cirrhosis. Rhodanine staining for copper was negative. The patient's mother had been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease at age 70 years (see appendix for full family tree).
On examination we found him to have symmetrical cog-wheel muscle rigidity and hypokinetic movements bilaterally. He had diminished arm swing, he was unstable, and when he walked he episodically had short, accelerating steps. He had a mask-like facial expression with a fixed smile—risus sardonicus (figure; video). Investigations found an AST of 128 IU/L, ALT of 131 IU/L, GGT of 497 IU/L, and bilirubin of 64·4 μmol/L (normal <24).
The patient's symptoms deteriorated significantly over the following weeks: he was barely able to walk, he was bradykinetic with episodes of freezing, and he was very unstable on his feet (video). A single photon emission CT DaTSCAN (GE Healthcare, Amersham, UK), 5 weeks after his symptoms began, showed bilaterally reduced presynaptic dopamine transporter in the striatum (figure). Slit-lamp examination of his eyes was normal. The patient's serum ceruloplasmin concentration was again low 0·13 g/L and his urine copper excretion was markedly increased at 5·81 μmol per 24 h (normal <0·95). Histological examination of a biopsy specimen of his liver showed severe progressive chronic hepatitis with cholestasis and fibrosis with complete cirrhosis. Rhodanine staining for copper was again negative. However, analysis using atomic absorption spectrometry showed increased hepatic copper concentrations of 325 μg/g (normal 10–35). We confirmed a diagnosis of Wilson's disease by DNA sequencing, which showed that the patient was homozygous for a missense variant of the ATP7B, gene 2998G →A leading to Gly1000Arg substitution.
We started chelation therapy—8 weeks after his neurological symptoms began—with penicillamine. However, the patient's extrapyramidal motor symptoms worsened—probably because of mobilisation of the excess copper and deposition into the basal ganglia. So we switched penicillamine to trientine. The patient's symptoms—apart from the risus sardonicus—showed considerable improvement after 5 months of treatment.
Wilson's disease is an important and treatable differential diagnosis of rapidly developing extra-pyramidal or atypical Parkinsonian symptoms. Even if the patient is over 40 years of age, there are no eye signs—eg Kayser-Fleischer rings, or sunflower cataracts, and conventional histopathological analysis of a liver biopsy with rhodanine stain was negative.

A 44-year-old night porter presented to our clinic with difficulty walking, instability, and stiffness—particularly in the muscles of his face—which had developed over the previous 3 weeks. His wife said that he had also been tired and lethargic for about 1 year.He had been seen in our hepatology outpatient clinic 12 months earlier because of a raised aspartate aminotransaminase (AST) of 43 IU/L (normal 11–34) and gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) of 301 IU/L (normal 12–68); his alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and bilirubin were normal. Investigations showed no evidence of active viral hepatitis, haemochromatosis, α1 antitrypsin deficiency, or autoimmune liver disease. Serum ceruloplasmin concentration was reduced at 0·11 g/L (normal 0·2–0·6). Ultrasound and transient elastography showed signs of fibrosis and a liver biopsy specimen showed microvesicular steatosis, bilirubinostasis, and severe fibrosis with incomplete cirrhosis. Rhodanine staining for copper was negative. The patient's mother had been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease at age 70 years (see appendix for full family tree).
On examination we found him to have symmetrical cog-wheel muscle rigidity and hypokinetic movements bilaterally. He had diminished arm swing, he was unstable, and when he walked he episodically had short, accelerating steps. He had a mask-like facial expression with a fixed smile—risus sardonicus (figure; video). Investigations found an AST of 128 IU/L, ALT of 131 IU/L, GGT of 497 IU/L, and bilirubin of 64·4 μmol/L (normal <24).
The patient's symptoms deteriorated significantly over the following weeks: he was barely able to walk, he was bradykinetic with episodes of freezing, and he was very unstable on his feet (video). A single photon emission CT DaTSCAN (GE Healthcare, Amersham, UK), 5 weeks after his symptoms began, showed bilaterally reduced presynaptic dopamine transporter in the striatum (figure). Slit-lamp examination of his eyes was normal. The patient's serum ceruloplasmin concentration was again low 0·13 g/L and his urine copper excretion was markedly increased at 5·81 μmol per 24 h (normal <0·95). Histological examination of a biopsy specimen of his liver showed severe progressive chronic hepatitis with cholestasis and fibrosis with complete cirrhosis. Rhodanine staining for copper was again negative. However, analysis using atomic absorption spectrometry showed increased hepatic copper concentrations of 325 μg/g (normal 10–35). We confirmed a diagnosis of Wilson's disease by DNA sequencing, which showed that the patient was homozygous for a missense variant of the ATP7B, gene 2998G →A leading to Gly1000Arg substitution.
We started chelation therapy—8 weeks after his neurological symptoms began—with penicillamine. However, the patient's extrapyramidal motor symptoms worsened—probably because of mobilisation of the excess copper and deposition into the basal ganglia. So we switched penicillamine to trientine. The patient's symptoms—apart from the risus sardonicus—showed considerable improvement after 5 months of treatment.
Wilson's disease is an important and treatable differential diagnosis of rapidly developing extra-pyramidal or atypical Parkinsonian symptoms. Even if the patient is over 40 years of age, there are no eye signs—eg Kayser-Fleischer rings, or sunflower cataracts, and conventional histopathological analysis of a liver biopsy with rhodanine stain was negative.

A 68-year-old Polish man was admitted to our hospital because of continued, painless, and worsening jaundice, and malaise. 2 months earlier he had a Whipple's pancreaticoduodenectomy for suspected carcinoma of the pancreas. He initially presented with mild weight loss and pain in the epigastric area. He did not use alcohol above recommended limits and had not travelled abroad recently. On examination his skin and sclera were jaundiced, and he had excoriations on all four limbs and his torso. There was no ascites, oedema, lymphadenopathy, or orbitopathy. Investigations done before the operation showed total bilirubin was 6·4 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 62 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 39 IU/L, gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) 312 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 426 IU/L. Serum tumour markers were within normal limits, and tests for hepatitis B and C were negative. A CT scan showed a mass in the head of the pancreas, normal liver parenchyma, and dilated extrahepatic and intrahepatic bile ducts and pancreatic duct proximally to the pancreatic head, and stricture of the pancreatic part of the common bile duct. Lymph nodes and abdominal vessels were normal.When we saw the patient, his total bilirubin (8·36 mg/dL), AST (89 IU/L), ALT (51 IU/L), GGT (443 IU/L), and ALP (712 IU/L) were increased. Antinuclear antibodies were detected at a titre of 1:1 280, with grainy fluorescence, but other antibodies—namely, antimitochondrial antibodies, smooth muscle antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, or liver–kidney microsome antibodies—were not found. An abdominal ultrasound scan showed dilatation of both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, and stricture of the common bile duct. Magnetic resonance cholangio-pancreatography (MRCP) showed multiple strictures of the patient's bile ducts (figure). A percutaneous liver biopsy specimen showed mixed inflammatory infiltration surrounding neocholangioles, with IgG4 in plasmocytes—approximately 60 per large field view, an IgG4:IgG ratio of more than 40%, mild fibrosis (grade 2 on the Batts-Ludwig scale), and cholestasis. The patient's serum IgG4 concentration was elevated at 380 mg/dL (normal 10–140). Looking at the presentation and the results in the round, we made a diagnosis of IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis and pancreatitis.
We therefore started treatment with prednisone 40 mg once daily for 2 months, followed by azathioprine 2·0 mg/kg once a day. After 2 months, a repeat MRCP showed that the stenosis of the bile ducts had reduced (figure). Also, the patient's total bilirubin concentration and liver enzyme levels normalised, and his malaise improved.
A post-factum analysis of the head of the pancreas removed at the initial operation stained positively for IgG4, and a mixed inflammatory infiltration with IgG4 plasmocytes was seen.
Sclerosing cholangitis and pancreatitis are mani-festations of IgG4-related disease, characterised by an abundance of IgG4-positive plasma cells in affected tissues. Patients with IgG4-related disease are often misdiagnosed as having a malignancy because of the non-specific signs and pseudotumour-like lesions; they may—as in our case—have unnecessary surgical procedures and investigations. A full clinical assessment of any patient presenting with jaundice and a pancreatic mass must include measurement of IgG4 concentrations and a biopsy before surgeons put knife to skin.

A 68-year-old Polish man was admitted to our hospital because of continued, painless, and worsening jaundice, and malaise. 2 months earlier he had a Whipple's pancreaticoduodenectomy for suspected carcinoma of the pancreas. He initially presented with mild weight loss and pain in the epigastric area. He did not use alcohol above recommended limits and had not travelled abroad recently. On examination his skin and sclera were jaundiced, and he had excoriations on all four limbs and his torso. There was no ascites, oedema, lymphadenopathy, or orbitopathy. Investigations done before the operation showed total bilirubin was 6·4 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 62 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 39 IU/L, gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) 312 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 426 IU/L. Serum tumour markers were within normal limits, and tests for hepatitis B and C were negative. A CT scan showed a mass in the head of the pancreas, normal liver parenchyma, and dilated extrahepatic and intrahepatic bile ducts and pancreatic duct proximally to the pancreatic head, and stricture of the pancreatic part of the common bile duct. Lymph nodes and abdominal vessels were normal.When we saw the patient, his total bilirubin (8·36 mg/dL), AST (89 IU/L), ALT (51 IU/L), GGT (443 IU/L), and ALP (712 IU/L) were increased. Antinuclear antibodies were detected at a titre of 1:1 280, with grainy fluorescence, but other antibodies—namely, antimitochondrial antibodies, smooth muscle antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, or liver–kidney microsome antibodies—were not found. An abdominal ultrasound scan showed dilatation of both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, and stricture of the common bile duct. Magnetic resonance cholangio-pancreatography (MRCP) showed multiple strictures of the patient's bile ducts (figure). A percutaneous liver biopsy specimen showed mixed inflammatory infiltration surrounding neocholangioles, with IgG4 in plasmocytes—approximately 60 per large field view, an IgG4:IgG ratio of more than 40%, mild fibrosis (grade 2 on the Batts-Ludwig scale), and cholestasis. The patient's serum IgG4 concentration was elevated at 380 mg/dL (normal 10–140). Looking at the presentation and the results in the round, we made a diagnosis of IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis and pancreatitis.
We therefore started treatment with prednisone 40 mg once daily for 2 months, followed by azathioprine 2·0 mg/kg once a day. After 2 months, a repeat MRCP showed that the stenosis of the bile ducts had reduced (figure). Also, the patient's total bilirubin concentration and liver enzyme levels normalised, and his malaise improved.
A post-factum analysis of the head of the pancreas removed at the initial operation stained positively for IgG4, and a mixed inflammatory infiltration with IgG4 plasmocytes was seen.
Sclerosing cholangitis and pancreatitis are mani-festations of IgG4-related disease, characterised by an abundance of IgG4-positive plasma cells in affected tissues. Patients with IgG4-related disease are often misdiagnosed as having a malignancy because of the non-specific signs and pseudotumour-like lesions; they may—as in our case—have unnecessary surgical procedures and investigations. A full clinical assessment of any patient presenting with jaundice and a pancreatic mass must include measurement of IgG4 concentrations and a biopsy before surgeons put knife to skin.

A 41-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 1-month history of worsening abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The patient gave no history of recent travel, previous abdominal surgery, or adverse reactions to any allergens. She had no past medical problems. However, 2 days before we saw her, the patient had a gastrointestinal endoscopy which found no abnormalities; gastroduodenal and colonic mucosal biopsies had also been reported as healthy.On examination we found the patient to be generally well; heart rate was 92 beats per min, blood pressure 110/60 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 98%. She was afebrile. Her abdomen was tender and distended with bulging flanks and shifting dullness: indicative of ascites.
Laboratory investigations showed leukocytosis (19·54 × 109 per L; normal 4·5–11·0) associated with a significant eosinophilia of 8·94 × 109 per L (normal 0–0·5), a raised IgE concentration (208 IU/mL; normal 1·5–144), and a slightly elevated C-reactive protein concentration (43 mg/L; normal <3·1). CA125 concentration was elevated (83 units/mL; normal 0–35); no other tumour marker was positive. Serum tryptase concentration was normal and tests screening for autoimmune diseases—including antinuclear antibodies for systemic lupus erythematosus or scleroderma—found nothing abnormal.
A CT scan excluded any visceral lesions. A diagnostic paracentesis showed eosinophilic ascites (figure). Blood, stool, and ascites analyses, including specific serological examinations and cultures, excluded viral, bacterial, and parasitic infections. That some parasitic infections, such as Strongyloides stercoralis, can be hard to diagnose based on one stool sample, led us to do repeated parasitological examinations of different stool samples, which all showed no positive results.
Lymphocytic and myeloproliferative forms of hypereosinophilic syndrome were excluded: a bone marrow biopsy showed no abnormalities. Using RT-PCR, no FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion gene was found, and T-cell-receptor gene rearrangement testing of the patient's peripheral blood was negative. A QuantiFERON-TB test was also negative.
We suspected a case of eosinophilic gastroenteritis, but to rule out any intra-abdominal neoplasm and to collect biopsies from the caecum serosa, we did a laparoscopy. Histopathological analysis of biopsy specimens confirmed our suspicions: significant eosinophilic infiltration with greater than 20 eosinophiles per high-power field; the small vessels were not involved, ruling out an associated vasculitis (figure). The patient was started on oral methylprednisolone and her symptoms rapidly improved; the serum eosinophilia returned to a typical level.
Three patterns of eosinophilic gastroenteritis are described: mucosal, mural, and serosal. Diagnosis of the serosal form is often considered a challenge as clinical and radiological presentations can be atypical. Likewise, histological findings can be misleading, as mucosal biopsies in the serosal form of eosinophilic gastroenteritis may appear normal, unlike those of the serosal layers which can confirm the diagnosis.
The diagnosis is usually made based on the combined biological, radiological, and histological findings. Finally, a good response to oral corticosteroids—as happened in our patient—adds weight to making a correct diagnosis of eosinophilic gastroenteritis.

A 68-year-old Polish man was admitted to our hospital because of continued, painless, and worsening jaundice, and malaise. 2 months earlier he had a Whipple's pancreaticoduodenectomy for suspected carcinoma of the pancreas. He initially presented with mild weight loss and pain in the epigastric area. He did not use alcohol above recommended limits and had not travelled abroad recently. On examination his skin and sclera were jaundiced, and he had excoriations on all four limbs and his torso. There was no ascites, oedema, lymphadenopathy, or orbitopathy. Investigations done before the operation showed total bilirubin was 6·4 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 62 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 39 IU/L, gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) 312 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 426 IU/L. Serum tumour markers were within normal limits, and tests for hepatitis B and C were negative. A CT scan showed a mass in the head of the pancreas, normal liver parenchyma, and dilated extrahepatic and intrahepatic bile ducts and pancreatic duct proximally to the pancreatic head, and stricture of the pancreatic part of the common bile duct. Lymph nodes and abdominal vessels were normal.When we saw the patient, his total bilirubin (8·36 mg/dL), AST (89 IU/L), ALT (51 IU/L), GGT (443 IU/L), and ALP (712 IU/L) were increased. Antinuclear antibodies were detected at a titre of 1:1 280, with grainy fluorescence, but other antibodies—namely, antimitochondrial antibodies, smooth muscle antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, or liver–kidney microsome antibodies—were not found. An abdominal ultrasound scan showed dilatation of both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, and stricture of the common bile duct. Magnetic resonance cholangio-pancreatography (MRCP) showed multiple strictures of the patient's bile ducts (figure). A percutaneous liver biopsy specimen showed mixed inflammatory infiltration surrounding neocholangioles, with IgG4 in plasmocytes—approximately 60 per large field view, an IgG4:IgG ratio of more than 40%, mild fibrosis (grade 2 on the Batts-Ludwig scale), and cholestasis. The patient's serum IgG4 concentration was elevated at 380 mg/dL (normal 10–140). Looking at the presentation and the results in the round, we made a diagnosis of IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis and pancreatitis.
We therefore started treatment with prednisone 40 mg once daily for 2 months, followed by azathioprine 2·0 mg/kg once a day. After 2 months, a repeat MRCP showed that the stenosis of the bile ducts had reduced (figure). Also, the patient's total bilirubin concentration and liver enzyme levels normalised, and his malaise improved.
A post-factum analysis of the head of the pancreas removed at the initial operation stained positively for IgG4, and a mixed inflammatory infiltration with IgG4 plasmocytes was seen.
Sclerosing cholangitis and pancreatitis are mani-festations of IgG4-related disease, characterised by an abundance of IgG4-positive plasma cells in affected tissues. Patients with IgG4-related disease are often misdiagnosed as having a malignancy because of the non-specific signs and pseudotumour-like lesions; they may—as in our case—have unnecessary surgical procedures and investigations. A full clinical assessment of any patient presenting with jaundice and a pancreatic mass must include measurement of IgG4 concentrations and a biopsy before surgeons put knife to skin.

A 41-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 1-month history of worsening abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The patient gave no history of recent travel, previous abdominal surgery, or adverse reactions to any allergens. She had no past medical problems. However, 2 days before we saw her, the patient had a gastrointestinal endoscopy which found no abnormalities; gastroduodenal and colonic mucosal biopsies had also been reported as healthy.On examination we found the patient to be generally well; heart rate was 92 beats per min, blood pressure 110/60 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 98%. She was afebrile. Her abdomen was tender and distended with bulging flanks and shifting dullness: indicative of ascites.
Laboratory investigations showed leukocytosis (19·54 × 109 per L; normal 4·5–11·0) associated with a significant eosinophilia of 8·94 × 109 per L (normal 0–0·5), a raised IgE concentration (208 IU/mL; normal 1·5–144), and a slightly elevated C-reactive protein concentration (43 mg/L; normal <3·1). CA125 concentration was elevated (83 units/mL; normal 0–35); no other tumour marker was positive. Serum tryptase concentration was normal and tests screening for autoimmune diseases—including antinuclear antibodies for systemic lupus erythematosus or scleroderma—found nothing abnormal.
A CT scan excluded any visceral lesions. A diagnostic paracentesis showed eosinophilic ascites (figure). Blood, stool, and ascites analyses, including specific serological examinations and cultures, excluded viral, bacterial, and parasitic infections. That some parasitic infections, such as Strongyloides stercoralis, can be hard to diagnose based on one stool sample, led us to do repeated parasitological examinations of different stool samples, which all showed no positive results.
Lymphocytic and myeloproliferative forms of hypereosinophilic syndrome were excluded: a bone marrow biopsy showed no abnormalities. Using RT-PCR, no FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion gene was found, and T-cell-receptor gene rearrangement testing of the patient's peripheral blood was negative. A QuantiFERON-TB test was also negative.
We suspected a case of eosinophilic gastroenteritis, but to rule out any intra-abdominal neoplasm and to collect biopsies from the caecum serosa, we did a laparoscopy. Histopathological analysis of biopsy specimens confirmed our suspicions: significant eosinophilic infiltration with greater than 20 eosinophiles per high-power field; the small vessels were not involved, ruling out an associated vasculitis (figure). The patient was started on oral methylprednisolone and her symptoms rapidly improved; the serum eosinophilia returned to a typical level.
Three patterns of eosinophilic gastroenteritis are described: mucosal, mural, and serosal. Diagnosis of the serosal form is often considered a challenge as clinical and radiological presentations can be atypical. Likewise, histological findings can be misleading, as mucosal biopsies in the serosal form of eosinophilic gastroenteritis may appear normal, unlike those of the serosal layers which can confirm the diagnosis.
The diagnosis is usually made based on the combined biological, radiological, and histological findings. Finally, a good response to oral corticosteroids—as happened in our patient—adds weight to making a correct diagnosis of eosinophilic gastroenteritis.

In 2012, an 84-year-old Chinese man presented with progressive, chronic left atraumatic knee pain and swelling. His medical history was notable for pulmonary tuberculosis treated in China in 1951 and rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed in 2006. His joint pain progressed despite use of disease modifying drugs and steroid injections. Antitumor necrosis factor inhibitors were not used because of concerns of tuberculosis reactivation. Clinical examination showed he had antalgic gait, knee effusion, stiffness, and joint-line tenderness. Laboratory results included erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 88 mm/h and C-reactive protein of 205 mg/L. Radiographs showed severe tri-compartmental degenerative arthritis (figure A).The patient underwent total knee arthroplasty in August, 2012 (figure B). Extensive synovitis was noted and pathological examination showed granulomatous inflammation (figure C). Staining of synovial tissue for acid-fast bacilli and tuberculosis PCR were negative. input:
A 41-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 1-month history of worsening abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The patient gave no history of recent travel, previous abdominal surgery, or adverse reactions to any allergens. She had no past medical problems. However, 2 days before we saw her, the patient had a gastrointestinal endoscopy which found no abnormalities; gastroduodenal and colonic mucosal biopsies had also been reported as healthy.On examination we found the patient to be generally well; heart rate was 92 beats per min, blood pressure 110/60 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 98%. She was afebrile. Her abdomen was tender and distended with bulging flanks and shifting dullness: indicative of ascites.
Laboratory investigations showed leukocytosis (19·54 × 109 per L; normal 4·5–11·0) associated with a significant eosinophilia of 8·94 × 109 per L (normal 0–0·5), a raised IgE concentration (208 IU/mL; normal 1·5–144), and a slightly elevated C-reactive protein concentration (43 mg/L; normal <3·1). CA125 concentration was elevated (83 units/mL; normal 0–35); no other tumour marker was positive. Serum tryptase concentration was normal and tests screening for autoimmune diseases—including antinuclear antibodies for systemic lupus erythematosus or scleroderma—found nothing abnormal.
A CT scan excluded any visceral lesions. A diagnostic paracentesis showed eosinophilic ascites (figure). Blood, stool, and ascites analyses, including specific serological examinations and cultures, excluded viral, bacterial, and parasitic infections. That some parasitic infections, such as Strongyloides stercoralis, can be hard to diagnose based on one stool sample, led us to do repeated parasitological examinations of different stool samples, which all showed no positive results.
Lymphocytic and myeloproliferative forms of hypereosinophilic syndrome were excluded: a bone marrow biopsy showed no abnormalities. Using RT-PCR, no FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion gene was found, and T-cell-receptor gene rearrangement testing of the patient's peripheral blood was negative. A QuantiFERON-TB test was also negative.
We suspected a case of eosinophilic gastroenteritis, but to rule out any intra-abdominal neoplasm and to collect biopsies from the caecum serosa, we did a laparoscopy. Histopathological analysis of biopsy specimens confirmed our suspicions: significant eosinophilic infiltration with greater than 20 eosinophiles per high-power field; the small vessels were not involved, ruling out an associated vasculitis (figure). The patient was started on oral methylprednisolone and her symptoms rapidly improved; the serum eosinophilia returned to a typical level.
Three patterns of eosinophilic gastroenteritis are described: mucosal, mural, and serosal. Diagnosis of the serosal form is often considered a challenge as clinical and radiological presentations can be atypical. Likewise, histological findings can be misleading, as mucosal biopsies in the serosal form of eosinophilic gastroenteritis may appear normal, unlike those of the serosal layers which can confirm the diagnosis.
The diagnosis is usually made based on the combined biological, radiological, and histological findings. Finally, a good response to oral corticosteroids—as happened in our patient—adds weight to making a correct diagnosis of eosinophilic gastroenteritis.

In 2012, an 84-year-old Chinese man presented with progressive, chronic left atraumatic knee pain and swelling. His medical history was notable for pulmonary tuberculosis treated in China in 1951 and rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed in 2006. His joint pain progressed despite use of disease modifying drugs and steroid injections. Antitumor necrosis factor inhibitors were not used because of concerns of tuberculosis reactivation. Clinical examination showed he had antalgic gait, knee effusion, stiffness, and joint-line tenderness. Laboratory results included erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 88 mm/h and C-reactive protein of 205 mg/L. Radiographs showed severe tri-compartmental degenerative arthritis (figure A).The patient underwent total knee arthroplasty in August, 2012 (figure B). Extensive synovitis was noted and pathological examination showed granulomatous inflammation (figure C). Staining of synovial tissue for acid-fast bacilli and tuberculosis PCR were negative. The patient's knee symptoms initially improved, but 5 months after total knee arthroplasty he developed a draining sinus from the knee incision. He underwent irrigation and debridement of the knee with exchange of the polyethylene tibial insert. Initial synovial tissue fluid cultures were negative, but subsequent acid-fast bacilli cultures from synovial tissue and joint fluid grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Sputum cultures were negative for pulmonary tuberculosis. He started a course of antituberculosis therapy including rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for treatment of tuberculosis prosthetic joint infection in February, 2013. He was advised to undergo a two-stage resection-revision arthroplasty but declined further surgery and thus an implant retention strategy was pursued. The patient completed 12 months of antituberculosis therapy in February, 2014. He has since continued rifampicin and isoniazid treatment with a plan for long-term suppressive therapy in the setting of retained prosthesis. At his latest follow-up, 2 years after initial diagnosis of tuberculous prosthetic joint infection, the incision had healed without clinical sign of infection and his knee has a pain-free range of motion from 0–95°.
Tuberculous arthritis accounts for 1–5% of people with tuberculosis. Scarce data are available for optimum management of tuberculous prosthetic joint infection. This case illustrates an unusual reactivation of tuberculosis in an isolated extra-pulmonary site after joint replacement surgery. Prompt initiation of antituberculosis therapy might enable implant retention, although continuation of suppressive therapy might be needed. In the setting of globalisation and the increasing use of immunomodulatory therapies and joint replacement surgeries, this case illustrates the need for tuberculosis to be thought about early in the differential diagnosis for culture-negative prosthetic joint infection in patients with previous exposures or epidemiological risk factors.
