A 62-year-old man with a parastomal hernia at the site of a urinary conduit and symptoms of urinary obstruction lasting several months presented to our hospital.
The patient previously had a radical cysto-prostatectomy with formation of an ileal conduit ileostomy—involving the interposition of a segment of small bowel between the distal end of the ureters and the skin resulting in urine being collected in a stoma bag—because of a high grade transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder 7 years earlier.
Additionally, he had a history of Child-Pugh A cirrhosis secondary to hepatitis C, which had been successfully treated, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; he used tiotropium bromide and fluticasone inhalers and was prescribed methadone.
On examination, the patient was generally well; his blood pressure was 135/77 mm Hg, pulse was 87 beats per min, and oxygen saturation was 96% on room air. Some deformity and asymmetry were seen on inspection of his abdomen: a bulge was visible inferior and lateral to the conduit; overall the abdomen was soft with some mild tenderness noted at the stoma site. Bowel sounds were normal. The conduit ileostomy was pink and warm. The patient reported that only a small amount of urine had been collected in the past few days and we noted little urine output. Regarding the hernia, we found that it was partially reducible with some incarceration, and we concluded that the ileal conduit had obstructed acutely secondary to a parastomal hernia.
Laboratory investigations found an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 26 mL/min/1·73 m2 (normal >90) and creatinine concentration of 223 μmol/L (normal 61·9–114·9); C-reactive protein concentration was 132 mg/L (normal <5).
Percutaneous nephrostomies—urinary drains placed directly in the lumbar region connecting the renal calices to drainage bags which allow alternative urine drainage from the kidneys—were inserted under CT imaging guidance and urine began flowing normally. Ureteric stents were then passed through the percutaneous nephrostomies with proximal ends in the renal calyces and distal ends in the deep end of the conduit.
The patient was then taken to theatre and had a parastomal hernia repair using the Pauli technique which involved tunnelling the stoma through the retro-muscular space and offsetting the trephine in the peritoneum and the anterior sheath. Notably—as always occurs with this technique—the procedure resulted in the bowel changing direction as it traversed the abdominal wall (figures 1, 2). Postoperatively, the patient was well; the urinary obstruction was resolved and urine flowed, as expected, through the conduit. The nephrostomy tubes were capped, and renal function remained normal.
2 weeks later, endoscopic removal of the stents was attempted but it had to be abandoned due to, what was thought to be, a stricture in the conduit caused by the surgery at the time of the hernia repair; the result was a micro perforation of the stoma at the anterior sheath where the bowel changed direction.

Parastomal hernias are a common and challenging surgical problem; patients present with chronic pain, bowel obstruction and ischaemia, and difficulties in keeping stoma appliances adequately sited.

A 62-year-old man with a parastomal hernia at the site of a urinary conduit and symptoms of urinary obstruction lasting several months presented to our hospital.
The patient previously had a radical cysto-prostatectomy with formation of an ileal conduit ileostomy—involving the interposition of a segment of small bowel between the distal end of the ureters and the skin resulting in urine being collected in a stoma bag—because of a high grade transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder 7 years earlier.
Additionally, he had a history of Child-Pugh A cirrhosis secondary to hepatitis C, which had been successfully treated, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; he used tiotropium bromide and fluticasone inhalers and was prescribed methadone.
On examination, the patient was generally well; his blood pressure was 135/77 mm Hg, pulse was 87 beats per min, and oxygen saturation was 96% on room air. Some deformity and asymmetry were seen on inspection of his abdomen: a bulge was visible inferior and lateral to the conduit; overall the abdomen was soft with some mild tenderness noted at the stoma site. Bowel sounds were normal. The conduit ileostomy was pink and warm. The patient reported that only a small amount of urine had been collected in the past few days and we noted little urine output. Regarding the hernia, we found that it was partially reducible with some incarceration, and we concluded that the ileal conduit had obstructed acutely secondary to a parastomal hernia.
Laboratory investigations found an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 26 mL/min/1·73 m2 (normal >90) and creatinine concentration of 223 μmol/L (normal 61·9–114·9); C-reactive protein concentration was 132 mg/L (normal <5).
Percutaneous nephrostomies—urinary drains placed directly in the lumbar region connecting the renal calices to drainage bags which allow alternative urine drainage from the kidneys—were inserted under CT imaging guidance and urine began flowing normally. Ureteric stents were then passed through the percutaneous nephrostomies with proximal ends in the renal calyces and distal ends in the deep end of the conduit.
The patient was then taken to theatre and had a parastomal hernia repair using the Pauli technique which involved tunnelling the stoma through the retro-muscular space and offsetting the trephine in the peritoneum and the anterior sheath. Notably—as always occurs with this technique—the procedure resulted in the bowel changing direction as it traversed the abdominal wall (figures 1, 2). Postoperatively, the patient was well; the urinary obstruction was resolved and urine flowed, as expected, through the conduit. The nephrostomy tubes were capped, and renal function remained normal.
2 weeks later, endoscopic removal of the stents was attempted but it had to be abandoned due to, what was thought to be, a stricture in the conduit caused by the surgery at the time of the hernia repair; the result was a micro perforation of the stoma at the anterior sheath where the bowel changed direction.
The patient was treated conservatively and the perforation healed, and he was allowed home. At follow-up 2 weeks later, the stoma was patent; the ureteric stents were removed via the nephrostomy tubes which were then also removed.
Parastomal hernias are a common and challenging surgical problem; patients present with chronic pain, bowel obstruction and ischaemia, and difficulties in keeping stoma appliances adequately sited.
Recurrence rates are high and there are risks of surgical site complications. The Pauli technique of parastomal hernia repair is increasingly being adopted by specialists because of improved outcomes; key has been the use of synthetic mesh in the retro-muscular or preperitoneal plane.
Crucially, patients who have had a parastomal hernia repaired using a Pauli technique have a stomal course through the abdominal wall that may be unexpected; it is similar to a Sugarbaker repair, but in the retro-muscular or preperitoneal plane. Essentially, the bowel lumen changes direction twice—firstly at the deep peritoneal position it travels anteriorly at a right angle to the abdominal wall, then in the intramural retro-muscular position it is parallel to the abdominal wall, and finally at the superficial anterior sheet it moves through the abdominal wall anteriorly through the skin to end in the stoma (figures 1, 2). Furthermore, the segment of bowel contained within the abdominal wall is unusually long and looks different on imaging; other common parastomal hernia repair techniques—including direct suture, mesh keyhole, or cruciate repairs—do not have these specific anatomical changes. Enhanced clinician awareness of these anatomical aspects will minimise the risk of complications during instrumentation of the stoma and avoid unnecessary concerns over successfully repaired hernias.

A 26-year-old man with an 8-year history of breathlessness on exertion was referred to our hospital for assessment. Previously, he had been noted to have clubbing of his toes and a heart murmur.On examination, we found the patient to be peripherally and centrally cyanosed; he had grade 3 clubbing of his toes but not of his fingers (figure); his pulse was 82 beats per min, blood pressure was 110/72 mm Hg, and, notably, oxygen saturations were 98% in his hands and 86% in his toes while breathing room air, and he had grade 2 dyspnoea. He had a parasternal heave with a palpable second heart sound; on auscultation, the pulmonary component of the second heart sound was accentuated and closely split.
Laboratory investigations showed a raised haemoglobin concentration (20·0 g/dL; normal 13·2–16·6 in men) and haematocrit (52%; normal 38–48 for men).
An electrocardiogram showed right ventricular hypertrophy with right axis deviation; a chest x-ray showed a dilated main pulmonary artery with peripheral pruning (appendix). A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a 7 mm patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) with right-to-left shunting (appendix).
Catheterisation showed an elevated pulmonary artery pressure of 120/68 mm Hg (normal 18/8–25/15) and a mean pressure of 108 mm Hg (normal 12–16) and an indexed pulmonary vascular resistance of 20·1 Wood units per m2 (normal 1–3; figure).
Because of the supra-systemic pulmonary artery pressures, we believed surgery was not feasible and therefore started the patient on oral sildenafil and bosentan.
During follow-up over the past 10 years, the patient presented on two occasions reporting blurred vision, tinnitus, and tingling in his hands and feet—symptoms of hyperviscosity. He was treated with phlebotomy on both occasions and his symptoms improved. At his last follow-up, he remains on sildenafil and bosentan and continues to have grade 2 dyspnoea.
Clubbing usually involves both the upper and lower limbs in congenital heart diseases. Differential clubbing, characterised by the involvement of the toes with sparing of the fingers, is a distinctive feature of PDA with reversed shunt from right to left: Eisenmenger syndrome.
Cyanosis and clubbing may also involve the left upper limb if the left subclavian artery arises distal to the PDA. The treatment of severe pulmonary arterial hypertension with sildenafil, a phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor, and bosentan, an endothelin receptor antagonist, has been shown to have some beneficial effects: offering hope to patients—like ours—whose PDAs are inoperable (video).

A 26-year-old man with an 8-year history of breathlessness on exertion was referred to our hospital for assessment. Previously, he had been noted to have clubbing of his toes and a heart murmur.On examination, we found the patient to be peripherally and centrally cyanosed; he had grade 3 clubbing of his toes but not of his fingers (figure); his pulse was 82 beats per min, blood pressure was 110/72 mm Hg, and, notably, oxygen saturations were 98% in his hands and 86% in his toes while breathing room air, and he had grade 2 dyspnoea. He had a parasternal heave with a palpable second heart sound; on auscultation, the pulmonary component of the second heart sound was accentuated and closely split.
Laboratory investigations showed a raised haemoglobin concentration (20·0 g/dL; normal 13·2–16·6 in men) and haematocrit (52%; normal 38–48 for men).
An electrocardiogram showed right ventricular hypertrophy with right axis deviation; a chest x-ray showed a dilated main pulmonary artery with peripheral pruning (appendix). A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a 7 mm patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) with right-to-left shunting (appendix).
Catheterisation showed an elevated pulmonary artery pressure of 120/68 mm Hg (normal 18/8–25/15) and a mean pressure of 108 mm Hg (normal 12–16) and an indexed pulmonary vascular resistance of 20·1 Wood units per m2 (normal 1–3; figure).
Because of the supra-systemic pulmonary artery pressures, we believed surgery was not feasible and therefore started the patient on oral sildenafil and bosentan.
During follow-up over the past 10 years, the patient presented on two occasions reporting blurred vision, tinnitus, and tingling in his hands and feet—symptoms of hyperviscosity. He was treated with phlebotomy on both occasions and his symptoms improved. At his last follow-up, he remains on sildenafil and bosentan and continues to have grade 2 dyspnoea.
Clubbing usually involves both the upper and lower limbs in congenital heart diseases. Differential clubbing, characterised by the involvement of the toes with sparing of the fingers, is a distinctive feature of PDA with reversed shunt from right to left: Eisenmenger syndrome.
Cyanosis and clubbing may also involve the left upper limb if the left subclavian artery arises distal to the PDA. The treatment of severe pulmonary arterial hypertension with sildenafil, a phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor, and bosentan, an endothelin receptor antagonist, has been shown to have some beneficial effects: offering hope to patients—like ours—whose PDAs are inoperable (video).

A 26-year-old man with an 8-year history of breathlessness on exertion was referred to our hospital for assessment. Previously, he had been noted to have clubbing of his toes and a heart murmur.On examination, we found the patient to be peripherally and centrally cyanosed; he had grade 3 clubbing of his toes but not of his fingers (figure); his pulse was 82 beats per min, blood pressure was 110/72 mm Hg, and, notably, oxygen saturations were 98% in his hands and 86% in his toes while breathing room air, and he had grade 2 dyspnoea. He had a parasternal heave with a palpable second heart sound; on auscultation, the pulmonary component of the second heart sound was accentuated and closely split.
Laboratory investigations showed a raised haemoglobin concentration (20·0 g/dL; normal 13·2–16·6 in men) and haematocrit (52%; normal 38–48 for men).
An electrocardiogram showed right ventricular hypertrophy with right axis deviation; a chest x-ray showed a dilated main pulmonary artery with peripheral pruning (appendix). A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a 7 mm patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) with right-to-left shunting (appendix).
Catheterisation showed an elevated pulmonary artery pressure of 120/68 mm Hg (normal 18/8–25/15) and a mean pressure of 108 mm Hg (normal 12–16) and an indexed pulmonary vascular resistance of 20·1 Wood units per m2 (normal 1–3; figure).
Because of the supra-systemic pulmonary artery pressures, we believed surgery was not feasible and therefore started the patient on oral sildenafil and bosentan.
During follow-up over the past 10 years, the patient presented on two occasions reporting blurred vision, tinnitus, and tingling in his hands and feet—symptoms of hyperviscosity. He was treated with phlebotomy on both occasions and his symptoms improved. At his last follow-up, he remains on sildenafil and bosentan and continues to have grade 2 dyspnoea.
Clubbing usually involves both the upper and lower limbs in congenital heart diseases. Differential clubbing, characterised by the involvement of the toes with sparing of the fingers, is a distinctive feature of PDA with reversed shunt from right to left: Eisenmenger syndrome.
Cyanosis and clubbing may also involve the left upper limb if the left subclavian artery arises distal to the PDA. The treatment of severe pulmonary arterial hypertension with sildenafil, a phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor, and bosentan, an endothelin receptor antagonist, has been shown to have some beneficial effects: offering hope to patients—like ours—whose PDAs are inoperable (video).

A 42-year-old woman was reviewed by our team after a right femoral artery endarterectomy for acute ischaemia of her leg which developed following coronary angiography using femoral access. The patient had a history of type 1 diabetes—managed by insulin pump therapy—and diabetic-hypertensive kidney disease which had required maintenance haemodialysis for the previous 9 months.
Post-surgery, the patient's blood glucose concentration had increased to 21·7 mmol/L (typical range 3·9–5·6) or 391 mg/dL (typical range 70–100); capillary blood ketones were so high that they were unmeasurable (>8 mmol/L; typical level <0·6). An arterial blood gas showed metabolic acidosis with pH at 7·26 (typical range 7·35−7·45), pCO2 23·8 mm Hg (typical range 35−45), bicarbonates 10·05 mmol/L (typical range 22−26), lactate 2·55 mmol/L (typical range <2), and an anion gap of 28·1 mmol/L (typical range 5−12). The insulin pump was functioning well. We concluded the findings compatible with a diagnosis of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).
Haemodialysis and intravenous insulin, plus glucose supplementation, were started with careful monitoring of potassium and glucose levels; ketone levels reduced within 24 h.
A review of data from the patient's continuous glucose monitoring system showed chronically elevated monthly mean blood glucose concentrations, between 13·95−17·25 mmol/L (251–311 mg/dL); with low glycaemic levels and frequent hypoglycaemias on days the patient had dialysis and elevated glycaemic levels on days she did not have dialysis (figure; appendix). Additionally, we noticed a surprisingly high level of bicarbonate on the routine protocol of chronic haemodialysis; it had progressively increased from 30 mmol/L to 38 mmol/L over the previous 9 months to maintain a normal (>22 mmol/L) pre-dialysis serum bicarbonate concentration, as recommended by the latest guidelines (appendix).
Furthermore, we found the anion gap to be surprisingly high, which we thought unlikely to be caused by chronic kidney disease alone. Therefore, given the high level of ketones before and after dialysis, we concluded that the excessive need for bicarbonates was due to the DKA.
We excluded lactic acidosis since the lactate was only slightly increased at 2·55 mmol/L (typical level ≤2). And based on clinical history, we also ruled out salicylate intoxication, ingestion of toxic substances, and small intestine bacterial overgrowth.
The duration of the DKA was indicated by the progressive increase in bicarbonate in the dialysate, which, combined with the high glucose clearance during haemodialysis, had been responsible for maintaining metabolic stability without marked acidosis (appendix). However, ketones had increased to high levels because of limited clearance during successive haemodialysis sessions.
In conclusion then, the high ketonaemia with an exceptionally high anion gap—despite partial clearance—together with relatively moderate decreases in bicarbonate and pH, in a patient with end-stage kidney disease, suggested chronic DKA partially masked by alkalinisation of the dialysis baths.
In cases of high anion gap metabolic acidosis with end-stage kidney disease, necessitating bicarbonate-enriched dialysate, physicians must search for a cause of metabolic acidosis. In diabetic patients, the diagnosis of DKA should be considered first, especially with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes under pump therapy.Diagnosing DKA in dialysis patients is challenging. Relying solely on glycated haemoglobin or blood glucose levels during dialysis is insufficient to assess glucose control. As patients with end-stage kidney disease present with a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, both the anion gap and the bicarbonate may not be the most reliable diagnostic parameters for DKA; therefore, the measurement of plasma β-hydroxybutyrate is key.
Although the optimal concentration of bicarbonate in dialysate for haemodialysis is uncertain, the presence of a high dialysate bicarbonate concentration (≥38 mmol/L) has been reported to be associated with poorer outcomes: all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalisation (appendix).
Regarding glucose variation in patients having dialysis, the lowest glycaemic level—on days of dialysis—is due to glucose loss to the dialysate and diffusion of glucose into erythrocytes. After dialysis, a paradoxical rebound hyperglycaemia occurs due to increased secretion of counter-regulatory hormones—specifically glucagon, adrenocorticotropic hormone, and cortisol—and partial clearance of negligible amounts of insulin during dialysis, even though the insulin resistance is diminished after dialysis (appendix). The lack of glucose clearance then maintains hyperglycaemia on days between dialysis.

A 42-year-old woman was reviewed by our team after a right femoral artery endarterectomy for acute ischaemia of her leg which developed following coronary angiography using femoral access. The patient had a history of type 1 diabetes—managed by insulin pump therapy—and diabetic-hypertensive kidney disease which had required maintenance haemodialysis for the previous 9 months.
Post-surgery, the patient's blood glucose concentration had increased to 21·7 mmol/L (typical range 3·9–5·6) or 391 mg/dL (typical range 70–100); capillary blood ketones were so high that they were unmeasurable (>8 mmol/L; typical level <0·6). An arterial blood gas showed metabolic acidosis with pH at 7·26 (typical range 7·35−7·45), pCO2 23·8 mm Hg (typical range 35−45), bicarbonates 10·05 mmol/L (typical range 22−26), lactate 2·55 mmol/L (typical range <2), and an anion gap of 28·1 mmol/L (typical range 5−12). The insulin pump was functioning well. We concluded the findings compatible with a diagnosis of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).
Haemodialysis and intravenous insulin, plus glucose supplementation, were started with careful monitoring of potassium and glucose levels; ketone levels reduced within 24 h.
A review of data from the patient's continuous glucose monitoring system showed chronically elevated monthly mean blood glucose concentrations, between 13·95−17·25 mmol/L (251–311 mg/dL); with low glycaemic levels and frequent hypoglycaemias on days the patient had dialysis and elevated glycaemic levels on days she did not have dialysis (figure; appendix). Additionally, we noticed a surprisingly high level of bicarbonate on the routine protocol of chronic haemodialysis; it had progressively increased from 30 mmol/L to 38 mmol/L over the previous 9 months to maintain a normal (>22 mmol/L) pre-dialysis serum bicarbonate concentration, as recommended by the latest guidelines (appendix).
Furthermore, we found the anion gap to be surprisingly high, which we thought unlikely to be caused by chronic kidney disease alone. Therefore, given the high level of ketones before and after dialysis, we concluded that the excessive need for bicarbonates was due to the DKA.
We excluded lactic acidosis since the lactate was only slightly increased at 2·55 mmol/L (typical level ≤2). And based on clinical history, we also ruled out salicylate intoxication, ingestion of toxic substances, and small intestine bacterial overgrowth.
The duration of the DKA was indicated by the progressive increase in bicarbonate in the dialysate, which, combined with the high glucose clearance during haemodialysis, had been responsible for maintaining metabolic stability without marked acidosis (appendix). However, ketones had increased to high levels because of limited clearance during successive haemodialysis sessions.
In conclusion then, the high ketonaemia with an exceptionally high anion gap—despite partial clearance—together with relatively moderate decreases in bicarbonate and pH, in a patient with end-stage kidney disease, suggested chronic DKA partially masked by alkalinisation of the dialysis baths.
In cases of high anion gap metabolic acidosis with end-stage kidney disease, necessitating bicarbonate-enriched dialysate, physicians must search for a cause of metabolic acidosis. In diabetic patients, the diagnosis of DKA should be considered first, especially with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes under pump therapy.Diagnosing DKA in dialysis patients is challenging. Relying solely on glycated haemoglobin or blood glucose levels during dialysis is insufficient to assess glucose control. As patients with end-stage kidney disease present with a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, both the anion gap and the bicarbonate may not be the most reliable diagnostic parameters for DKA; therefore, the measurement of plasma β-hydroxybutyrate is key.
Although the optimal concentration of bicarbonate in dialysate for haemodialysis is uncertain, the presence of a high dialysate bicarbonate concentration (≥38 mmol/L) has been reported to be associated with poorer outcomes: all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalisation (appendix).
Regarding glucose variation in patients having dialysis, the lowest glycaemic level—on days of dialysis—is due to glucose loss to the dialysate and diffusion of glucose into erythrocytes. After dialysis, a paradoxical rebound hyperglycaemia occurs due to increased secretion of counter-regulatory hormones—specifically glucagon, adrenocorticotropic hormone, and cortisol—and partial clearance of negligible amounts of insulin during dialysis, even though the insulin resistance is diminished after dialysis (appendix). The lack of glucose clearance then maintains hyperglycaemia on days between dialysis.

A 41-year-old woman presented to our clinic because of the sudden appearance of erosions on and swelling of her lips. On clinical examination, diffuse erythema of the labial mucosae with small vesicles and crusted erosions on both the superior and inferior vermillion borders were noted (figure). Further inspection of her mouth showed erythema and erosions on the inner cheek and mild focal desquamated gingivitis. The patient was otherwise healthy, with good oral hygiene. No other lesions were seen on the rest of her body. She had been taking paracetamol and amoxicillin for 3 days for a sore throat and fever. Based on the clinical symptoms and medical history, we diagnosed erythema multiforme (EM) major. She was treated with prednisolone 60 mg/day, with dramatic improvement of her symptoms.EM is an inflammatory condition that can affect the skin, the mucosa, or both. It is characterised by acute onset of symptoms and is divided into major or minor depending on the presence or absence of mucosal involvement, respectively. Infections with herpes simplex viruses and Mycoplasma pneumoniae (M pneumoniae-induced rash mucositis) have been thought to be pathogenetic factors—along with several drugs, including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, allopurinol, and some antibiotics. EM is no longer considered to be on the spectrum of severe cutaneous adverse reactions, which include Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), and SJS/TEN overlap. It differs in that it occurs in younger people and is associated with frequent recurrences. Also, patients tend to be free of comorbidities such as HIV infection or cancer, and when they have systemic symptoms, they are usually mild.
In our patient, herpes simplex virus infection was excluded, both as a primary phenomenon in the mouth and as a secondary phenomenon causing EM. The exclusive involvement of the oral mucosa in EM is uncommon and may be challenging diagnostically in the differentiation from various inflammatory and autoimmune disorders—including lichen planus, pemphigus vulgaris, and herpetic gingivostomatitis.

A 42-year-old woman was reviewed by our team after a right femoral artery endarterectomy for acute ischaemia of her leg which developed following coronary angiography using femoral access. The patient had a history of type 1 diabetes—managed by insulin pump therapy—and diabetic-hypertensive kidney disease which had required maintenance haemodialysis for the previous 9 months.
Post-surgery, the patient's blood glucose concentration had increased to 21·7 mmol/L (typical range 3·9–5·6) or 391 mg/dL (typical range 70–100); capillary blood ketones were so high that they were unmeasurable (>8 mmol/L; typical level <0·6). An arterial blood gas showed metabolic acidosis with pH at 7·26 (typical range 7·35−7·45), pCO2 23·8 mm Hg (typical range 35−45), bicarbonates 10·05 mmol/L (typical range 22−26), lactate 2·55 mmol/L (typical range <2), and an anion gap of 28·1 mmol/L (typical range 5−12). The insulin pump was functioning well. We concluded the findings compatible with a diagnosis of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).
Haemodialysis and intravenous insulin, plus glucose supplementation, were started with careful monitoring of potassium and glucose levels; ketone levels reduced within 24 h.
A review of data from the patient's continuous glucose monitoring system showed chronically elevated monthly mean blood glucose concentrations, between 13·95−17·25 mmol/L (251–311 mg/dL); with low glycaemic levels and frequent hypoglycaemias on days the patient had dialysis and elevated glycaemic levels on days she did not have dialysis (figure; appendix). Additionally, we noticed a surprisingly high level of bicarbonate on the routine protocol of chronic haemodialysis; it had progressively increased from 30 mmol/L to 38 mmol/L over the previous 9 months to maintain a normal (>22 mmol/L) pre-dialysis serum bicarbonate concentration, as recommended by the latest guidelines (appendix).
Furthermore, we found the anion gap to be surprisingly high, which we thought unlikely to be caused by chronic kidney disease alone. Therefore, given the high level of ketones before and after dialysis, we concluded that the excessive need for bicarbonates was due to the DKA.
We excluded lactic acidosis since the lactate was only slightly increased at 2·55 mmol/L (typical level ≤2). And based on clinical history, we also ruled out salicylate intoxication, ingestion of toxic substances, and small intestine bacterial overgrowth.
The duration of the DKA was indicated by the progressive increase in bicarbonate in the dialysate, which, combined with the high glucose clearance during haemodialysis, had been responsible for maintaining metabolic stability without marked acidosis (appendix). However, ketones had increased to high levels because of limited clearance during successive haemodialysis sessions.
In conclusion then, the high ketonaemia with an exceptionally high anion gap—despite partial clearance—together with relatively moderate decreases in bicarbonate and pH, in a patient with end-stage kidney disease, suggested chronic DKA partially masked by alkalinisation of the dialysis baths.
In cases of high anion gap metabolic acidosis with end-stage kidney disease, necessitating bicarbonate-enriched dialysate, physicians must search for a cause of metabolic acidosis. In diabetic patients, the diagnosis of DKA should be considered first, especially with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes under pump therapy.Diagnosing DKA in dialysis patients is challenging. Relying solely on glycated haemoglobin or blood glucose levels during dialysis is insufficient to assess glucose control. As patients with end-stage kidney disease present with a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, both the anion gap and the bicarbonate may not be the most reliable diagnostic parameters for DKA; therefore, the measurement of plasma β-hydroxybutyrate is key.
Although the optimal concentration of bicarbonate in dialysate for haemodialysis is uncertain, the presence of a high dialysate bicarbonate concentration (≥38 mmol/L) has been reported to be associated with poorer outcomes: all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalisation (appendix).
Regarding glucose variation in patients having dialysis, the lowest glycaemic level—on days of dialysis—is due to glucose loss to the dialysate and diffusion of glucose into erythrocytes. After dialysis, a paradoxical rebound hyperglycaemia occurs due to increased secretion of counter-regulatory hormones—specifically glucagon, adrenocorticotropic hormone, and cortisol—and partial clearance of negligible amounts of insulin during dialysis, even though the insulin resistance is diminished after dialysis (appendix). The lack of glucose clearance then maintains hyperglycaemia on days between dialysis.

A 41-year-old woman presented to our clinic because of the sudden appearance of erosions on and swelling of her lips. On clinical examination, diffuse erythema of the labial mucosae with small vesicles and crusted erosions on both the superior and inferior vermillion borders were noted (figure). Further inspection of her mouth showed erythema and erosions on the inner cheek and mild focal desquamated gingivitis. The patient was otherwise healthy, with good oral hygiene. No other lesions were seen on the rest of her body. She had been taking paracetamol and amoxicillin for 3 days for a sore throat and fever. Based on the clinical symptoms and medical history, we diagnosed erythema multiforme (EM) major. She was treated with prednisolone 60 mg/day, with dramatic improvement of her symptoms.EM is an inflammatory condition that can affect the skin, the mucosa, or both. It is characterised by acute onset of symptoms and is divided into major or minor depending on the presence or absence of mucosal involvement, respectively. Infections with herpes simplex viruses and Mycoplasma pneumoniae (M pneumoniae-induced rash mucositis) have been thought to be pathogenetic factors—along with several drugs, including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, allopurinol, and some antibiotics. EM is no longer considered to be on the spectrum of severe cutaneous adverse reactions, which include Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), and SJS/TEN overlap. It differs in that it occurs in younger people and is associated with frequent recurrences. Also, patients tend to be free of comorbidities such as HIV infection or cancer, and when they have systemic symptoms, they are usually mild.
In our patient, herpes simplex virus infection was excluded, both as a primary phenomenon in the mouth and as a secondary phenomenon causing EM. The exclusive involvement of the oral mucosa in EM is uncommon and may be challenging diagnostically in the differentiation from various inflammatory and autoimmune disorders—including lichen planus, pemphigus vulgaris, and herpetic gingivostomatitis.

A 41-year-old woman presented to our clinic because of the sudden appearance of erosions on and swelling of her lips. On clinical examination, diffuse erythema of the labial mucosae with small vesicles and crusted erosions on both the superior and inferior vermillion borders were noted (figure). Further inspection of her mouth showed erythema and erosions on the inner cheek and mild focal desquamated gingivitis. The patient was otherwise healthy, with good oral hygiene. No other lesions were seen on the rest of her body. She had been taking paracetamol and amoxicillin for 3 days for a sore throat and fever. Based on the clinical symptoms and medical history, we diagnosed erythema multiforme (EM) major. She was treated with prednisolone 60 mg/day, with dramatic improvement of her symptoms.EM is an inflammatory condition that can affect the skin, the mucosa, or both. It is characterised by acute onset of symptoms and is divided into major or minor depending on the presence or absence of mucosal involvement, respectively. Infections with herpes simplex viruses and Mycoplasma pneumoniae (M pneumoniae-induced rash mucositis) have been thought to be pathogenetic factors—along with several drugs, including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, allopurinol, and some antibiotics. EM is no longer considered to be on the spectrum of severe cutaneous adverse reactions, which include Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), and SJS/TEN overlap. It differs in that it occurs in younger people and is associated with frequent recurrences. Also, patients tend to be free of comorbidities such as HIV infection or cancer, and when they have systemic symptoms, they are usually mild.
In our patient, herpes simplex virus infection was excluded, both as a primary phenomenon in the mouth and as a secondary phenomenon causing EM. The exclusive involvement of the oral mucosa in EM is uncommon and may be challenging diagnostically in the differentiation from various inflammatory and autoimmune disorders—including lichen planus, pemphigus vulgaris, and herpetic gingivostomatitis.

input:
A 40-year-old woman presented with 1 week of worsening pharyngalgia and neck swelling in October, 2013. Her only medical history was tonsillectomy and appendectomy in adolescence, and she had no history of foreign body ingestion or pharyngeal injury. Fibre optic pharyngolaryngoscopy showed nothing more than swelling of the posterior wall of the pharynx. A plain cervical radiograph, however, showed gas in the retropharyngeal space, and CT showed a large abscess between the pharyngoesophagus and the prevertebral muscles extending from the upper neck region to the lower mediastinum (figure). She had a raised white cell count (30·3 × 109 cells per L; normal 3·9–9·0 × 109 cells per L) and C-reactive protein (3106·73 nmol/L; normal ≤28·57 nmol/L). We diagnosed descending necrotising mediastinitis. We drained and debrided the area transcervically and transthoracically with video-assisted guidance. Cultures of the purulent fluid drained from the abscess grew Streptococcus constellatus, Streptococcus anginosus, Prevotella intermedia, Prevotella buccae, Anaerococcus prevotii, Peptostreptococcus anaerobius, and Finegoldia magna. The patient recovered well and was discharged after 4 weeks of intravenous antibiotics. At last follow-up visit in August, 2014, she was well, with only a slight sensation of shortness of breath on exertion.
Although descending necrotising mediastinitis is rare, high mortality is still reported. Early transcervical and transthoracic surgery is recommended in cases that involve the lower part of the mediastinum. Acute retropharyngeal abscesses are reported more frequently in children than in adults because of the development of retropharyngeal lymph nodes in childhood. The reason why the infection progressed so dramatically in our patient, a non-immunocompromised otherwise healthy adult, remains unclear.

A 40-year-old woman presented with 1 week of worsening pharyngalgia and neck swelling in October, 2013. Her only medical history was tonsillectomy and appendectomy in adolescence, and she had no history of foreign body ingestion or pharyngeal injury. Fibre optic pharyngolaryngoscopy showed nothing more than swelling of the posterior wall of the pharynx. A plain cervical radiograph, however, showed gas in the retropharyngeal space, and CT showed a large abscess between the pharyngoesophagus and the prevertebral muscles extending from the upper neck region to the lower mediastinum (figure). She had a raised white cell count (30·3 × 109 cells per L; normal 3·9–9·0 × 109 cells per L) and C-reactive protein (3106·73 nmol/L; normal ≤28·57 nmol/L). We diagnosed descending necrotising mediastinitis. We drained and debrided the area transcervically and transthoracically with video-assisted guidance. Cultures of the purulent fluid drained from the abscess grew Streptococcus constellatus, Streptococcus anginosus, Prevotella intermedia, Prevotella buccae, Anaerococcus prevotii, Peptostreptococcus anaerobius, and Finegoldia magna. The patient recovered well and was discharged after 4 weeks of intravenous antibiotics. At last follow-up visit in August, 2014, she was well, with only a slight sensation of shortness of breath on exertion.
Although descending necrotising mediastinitis is rare, high mortality is still reported. Early transcervical and transthoracic surgery is recommended in cases that involve the lower part of the mediastinum. Acute retropharyngeal abscesses are reported more frequently in children than in adults because of the development of retropharyngeal lymph nodes in childhood. The reason why the infection progressed so dramatically in our patient, a non-immunocompromised otherwise healthy adult, remains unclear.

input:
A 31-year-old man with Wilson's disease presented with a pruritic rash across the neck of 12 months' duration. His disease had been well controlled on penicillamine (500 mg twice daily) with pyridoxine (25 mg daily) for many years. There had been no new medications, trauma, animal contact, or change in detergents, clothing, or environment before rash onset. Physical examination revealed two annular lesions on the ventral and posterior neck, which were well demarcated with serpiginous, raised borders and central clearing (figure, A and B). There were no other lesions present. Full blood count, liver function tests, and inflammatory markers were within normal limits aside from a chronically increased alkaline phosphatase concentration (179 U/L, reference range 40–130 U/L). Coeliac serology was negative. The rash had not resolved with previous empirical courses of systemic and topical antifungal medication for presumed dermatophyte infection (tinea corporis). A 2-mm punch biopsy of the rash was done and the histology results are shown (figure, C and D).Elastosis perforans serpiginosa is a rare complication of penicillamine therapy for Wilson's disease and might also be seen in association with systemic diseases such as Ehlers Danlos and Down's syndrome. It is a chronic dermatosis characterised by extrusion of elastic fibre aggregates through the epidermis. The exact mechanism of pencillamine-related elastosis perforans serpiginosa is unclear, but has been postulated to occur indirectly as a result of impairment of lysyl oxidase, a copper-dependent enzyme, which has an important role in dermal elastic fibre cross-linking, as well as directly through formation of complexes with elastic fibre precursors, leading to impaired elastic fibre maturation. The diagnosis is made clinically and histologically with the characteristic findings illustrated in the figures.
As seen in our case, this chronic dermatosis is often seen in the second decade of life, following prolonged use of penicillamine. The rash distribution is variable, involving the neck and upper limbs most commonly. Although regression is possible with cessation of penicillamine, scarring and atrophy could persist indefinitely. Misdiagnosis is common and continued use of penicillamine risks progression of rash and permanent scarring. In this case, penicillamine was changed to trientene as an alternative chelating agent to manage the Wilson's disease. Despite its similar mechanism of action to penicillamine, there have been no published case reports of trientene-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa to our knowledge. 4 weeks after cessation of penicillamine, the rash persisted unchanged.

input: A 15-year-old girl presented to our outpatient clinic with a 10-year history of two band-like atrophic grooves located on the left part of the forehead (figure A, B). Within the previous 2 years, the lesions had considerably progressed and resulted in a marked atrophy of subcutaneous tissue and bone structures on the left side of the face (figure C). There was no history of preceding trauma, but the patient had experienced several episodes of focal seizures and recurrent hemiplegic migraine in the past 6 months. Cerebral MRI showed a dense area of gliosis in the ipsilateral frontal region (figure D). Further physical examination showed no pathological findings. Laboratory tests, including screening for auto-antibodies, showed increased antinuclear antibody titres (1:2560 [normal value <1:160]) and a raised C-reactive protein concentration of 24 mg/L (normal value <5 mg/L). Extractable nuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, anticyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies, and Borrelia-specific antibodies were negative. On the basis of these findings, a diagnosis of bilateral linear scleroderma “en coup de sabre” with transition into progressive facial hemiatrophy was made. We initiated a combination of pulsed intravenous methylprednisolone (1000 mg for 3 consecutive days monthly) and low-dose methotrexate (10 mg per m2, resulting in 15 mg cumulative dose weekly) for a total of 6 months, followed by methotrexate monotherapy (15 mg weekly) for a further 6 months. Additionally, focal seizures were treated with carbamazepine (200 mg daily). This combination therapy prevented further progression of facial hemiatrophy. At age 22 years, the patient underwent autologous fat transplantation to correct her facial atrophy, with good cosmetic outcome (figure E).Progressive facial hemiatrophy, also known as Parry Romberg syndrome, is a rare craniofacial disease characterised by a slowly progressive atrophy of the facial skin, subcutaneous tissue, muscle, and bone. Disease onset is typically within the first two decades of life, and it affects females more often than males. Progressive facial hemiatrophy might be associated with ipsilateral brain lesions, various neurological symptoms, and ophthalmological or oral complications. Linear scleroderma “en coup de sabre” and progressive facial hemiatrophy are considered to be two variants of localised scleroderma involving the frontoparietal face and skull. The prevalence of localised scleroderma ranges from 0·4 to 2·7 cases per 100 000 people and occurs 2–6 times more frequently in femals than in males. Linear subtypes, as shown here, mostly affect children aged between 2 and 14 years.

Within the previous 2 years, the lesions had considerably progressed and resulted in a marked atrophy of subcutaneous tissue and bone structures on the left side of the face (figure C). There was no history of preceding trauma, but the patient had experienced several episodes of focal seizures and recurrent hemiplegic migraine in the past 6 months. Cerebral MRI showed a dense area of gliosis in the ipsilateral frontal region (figure D). Further physical examination showed no pathological findings. Laboratory tests, including screening for auto-antibodies, showed increased antinuclear antibody titres (1:2560 [normal value <1:160]) and a raised C-reactive protein concentration of 24 mg/L (normal value <5 mg/L). Extractable nuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, anticyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies, and Borrelia-specific antibodies were negative. On the basis of these findings, a diagnosis of bilateral linear scleroderma “en coup de sabre” with transition into progressive facial hemiatrophy was made. We initiated a combination of pulsed intravenous methylprednisolone (1000 mg for 3 consecutive days monthly) and low-dose methotrexate (10 mg per m2, resulting in 15 mg cumulative dose weekly) for a total of 6 months, followed by methotrexate monotherapy (15 mg weekly) for a further 6 months. Additionally, focal seizures were treated with carbamazepine (200 mg daily). This combination therapy prevented further progression of facial hemiatrophy. At age 22 years, the patient underwent autologous fat transplantation to correct her facial atrophy, with good cosmetic outcome (figure E).Progressive facial hemiatrophy, also known as Parry Romberg syndrome, is a rare craniofacial disease characterised by a slowly progressive atrophy of the facial skin, subcutaneous tissue, muscle, and bone. Disease onset is typically within the first two decades of life, and it affects females more often than males. Progressive facial hemiatrophy might be associated with ipsilateral brain lesions, various neurological symptoms, and ophthalmological or oral complications. Linear scleroderma “en coup de sabre” and progressive facial hemiatrophy are considered to be two variants of localised scleroderma involving the frontoparietal face and skull. The prevalence of localised scleroderma ranges from 0·4 to 2·7 cases per 100 000 people and occurs 2–6 times more frequently in femals than in males. Linear subtypes, as shown here, mostly affect children aged between 2 and 14 years.

input: A 15-year-old girl presented to our outpatient clinic with a 10-year history of two band-like atrophic grooves located on the left part of the forehead (figure A, B). Within the previous 2 years, the lesions had considerably progressed and resulted in a marked atrophy of subcutaneous tissue and bone structures on the left side of the face (figure C). There was no history of preceding trauma, but the patient had experienced several episodes of focal seizures and recurrent hemiplegic migraine in the past 6 months. Cerebral MRI showed a dense area of gliosis in the ipsilateral frontal region (figure D). Further physical examination showed no pathological findings. Laboratory tests, including screening for auto-antibodies, showed increased antinuclear antibody titres (1:2560 [normal value <1:160]) and a raised C-reactive protein concentration of 24 mg/L (normal value <5 mg/L). Extractable nuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, anticyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies, and Borrelia-specific antibodies were negative. On the basis of these findings, a diagnosis of bilateral linear scleroderma “en coup de sabre” with transition into progressive facial hemiatrophy was made. We initiated a combination of pulsed intravenous methylprednisolone (1000 mg for 3 consecutive days monthly) and low-dose methotrexate (10 mg per m2, resulting in 15 mg cumulative dose weekly) for a total of 6 months, followed by methotrexate monotherapy (15 mg weekly) for a further 6 months. Additionally, focal seizures were treated with carbamazepine (200 mg daily). This combination therapy prevented further progression of facial hemiatrophy. At age 22 years, the patient underwent autologous fat transplantation to correct her facial atrophy, with good cosmetic outcome (figure E).Progressive facial hemiatrophy, also known as Parry Romberg syndrome, is a rare craniofacial disease characterised by a slowly progressive atrophy of the facial skin, subcutaneous tissue, muscle, and bone. Disease onset is typically within the first two decades of life, and it affects females more often than males. Progressive facial hemiatrophy might be associated with ipsilateral brain lesions, various neurological symptoms, and ophthalmological or oral complications. Linear scleroderma “en coup de sabre” and progressive facial hemiatrophy are considered to be two variants of localised scleroderma involving the frontoparietal face and skull. The prevalence of localised scleroderma ranges from 0·4 to 2·7 cases per 100 000 people and occurs 2–6 times more frequently in femals than in males. Linear subtypes, as shown here, mostly affect children aged between 2 and 14 years.

A 34-year-old woman who collapsed during a mountain trek in northern Spain was initially assessed at an emergency rescue centre. She was unresponsive, asystolic, and pulseless, had unreactive dilated pupils, and had a tympanic temperature of 18°C. Advanced life support was started, and the woman was transferred to our hospital. She arrived 2 h and 25 min after the first evaluation—she was still in asystole, had unreactive dilated pupils, and had a core temperature of 20·2°C. An arterial blood sample showed a pH of 6·81, a lactate concentration of 10·3 mmol/L (normal 0·5–1), and a potassium concentration of 4·4 mmol/L (normal 3·5–5). Peripheral venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) support was started and a fine ventricular fibrillation rhythm was immediately seen on an electrocardiogram (ECG). The patient also started gasping, ventilator asynchronies appeared, and a burst suppression pattern was seen on a bispectral index monitor; these difficulties disappeared after she was given sedatives.During the first few hours of extracorporeal support, the patient had coagulopathy, bleeding, lung oedema (figure), and a highly variable ECMO flow. However, once the woman was stable, her body temperature was progressively increased at a rate of 3°C per h. The patient regained pupillary reactivity after 3 h of extracorporeal support. When her temperature reached 30°C, coarse ventricular fibrillation was observed. She was then defibrillated, which resulted in a posterior effective rhythm—meaning that 6 h and 10 min after the initial assessment there was return of spontaneous circulation. When her temperature was 32°C, an ECG showed sinus rhythm with classic Osborn—or J–waves, seen clearly in lead V3 (figure). The patient's neuron-specific enolase was found to be 93·4 ng/mL (normal range 1·5–13·5) on day 1 in the intensive care unit (ICU); by day 2 it had fallen to 55·1 ng/mL; other laboratory investigations normalised during the patient's recovery (appendix).
The heating process was continued until the patient's temperature was 35°C. ECMO was stopped after 45 h and 40 min. The patient was successfully extubated on day 2 of her stay in the ICU.
A neurological evaluation at the end of day 2 found no abnormalities, and the patient was moved from the ICU on day 6. She was allowed home on day 11. A month after the episode, she had resumed her normal activities of daily living.
Neurological sequelae are common after prolonged periods of cardiac arrest. The maintenance of extracorporeal support and neuroprotection along with regimented temperature management until adequate biventricular function is recovered—as in our case—may be key in preventing brain damage. We kept the patient on extracorporeal support for a total of 45 h and 40 min, which is substantially longer than previuously reported times (appendix). In cases of hypothermia and asystole, resuscitation using ECMO as a means of oxygen redistribution and temperature management should be considered.

A 34-year-old woman who collapsed during a mountain trek in northern Spain was initially assessed at an emergency rescue centre. She was unresponsive, asystolic, and pulseless, had unreactive dilated pupils, and had a tympanic temperature of 18°C. Advanced life support was started, and the woman was transferred to our hospital. She arrived 2 h and 25 min after the first evaluation—she was still in asystole, had unreactive dilated pupils, and had a core temperature of 20·2°C. An arterial blood sample showed a pH of 6·81, a lactate concentration of 10·3 mmol/L (normal 0·5–1), and a potassium concentration of 4·4 mmol/L (normal 3·5–5). Peripheral venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) support was started and a fine ventricular fibrillation rhythm was immediately seen on an electrocardiogram (ECG). The patient also started gasping, ventilator asynchronies appeared, and a burst suppression pattern was seen on a bispectral index monitor; these difficulties disappeared after she was given sedatives.During the first few hours of extracorporeal support, the patient had coagulopathy, bleeding, lung oedema (figure), and a highly variable ECMO flow. However, once the woman was stable, her body temperature was progressively increased at a rate of 3°C per h. The patient regained pupillary reactivity after 3 h of extracorporeal support. When her temperature reached 30°C, coarse ventricular fibrillation was observed. She was then defibrillated, which resulted in a posterior effective rhythm—meaning that 6 h and 10 min after the initial assessment there was return of spontaneous circulation. When her temperature was 32°C, an ECG showed sinus rhythm with classic Osborn—or J–waves, seen clearly in lead V3 (figure). The patient's neuron-specific enolase was found to be 93·4 ng/mL (normal range 1·5–13·5) on day 1 in the intensive care unit (ICU); by day 2 it had fallen to 55·1 ng/mL; other laboratory investigations normalised during the patient's recovery (appendix).
The heating process was continued until the patient's temperature was 35°C. ECMO was stopped after 45 h and 40 min. The patient was successfully extubated on day 2 of her stay in the ICU.
A neurological evaluation at the end of day 2 found no abnormalities, and the patient was moved from the ICU on day 6. She was allowed home on day 11. A month after the episode, she had resumed her normal activities of daily living.
Neurological sequelae are common after prolonged periods of cardiac arrest. The maintenance of extracorporeal support and neuroprotection along with regimented temperature management until adequate biventricular function is recovered—as in our case—may be key in preventing brain damage. We kept the patient on extracorporeal support for a total of 45 h and 40 min, which is substantially longer than previuously reported times (appendix). In cases of hypothermia and asystole, resuscitation using ECMO as a means of oxygen redistribution and temperature management should be considered.

A 77-year-old woman presented to our emergency department in Brescia, Italy with fever, altered conscious state, and neck stiffness. She was a heavy smoker, with hypertension and dyslipidaemia, and had had right-sided back pain for the previous 3 days.
Head CT and chest radiograph were normal, whereas lumbar puncture and blood cultures revealed pneumococcal meningitis with bacteraemia. Antibiotic therapy with ceftriaxone (2 g twice daily) was started. The patient rapidly improved, with resolution of fever and substantial reduction of inflammatory markers (white blood cell count dropped from 19·7 cells per mL to 14·9 cells per mL, and C-reactive protein dropped from 225 mg/L to 108 mg/L). However, 12 days after the patient was admitted to hospital, and less than a week after the initial clinical and biochemical improvement, she reported worsening backache, and the inflammatory markers rebounded (white blood cell count to 19·8 cells per mL and C-reactive protein to 171 mg/L). Lumbar spine CT showed no signs of spondylodiscitis, but an enlarged abdominal aorta with signs of perianeurysmal inflammation. The CT angiography done straight afterwards confirmed the presence of an abdominal aortic aneurysm with signs of impending rupture (figure A).Mycotic aneurysm and microbial aortitis are uncommon entities that usually occur in people with underlying atherosclerotic vascular disease as a consequence of bacteraemic seeding on the abnormal aortic surface. The clinical presentation is often subacute, and the diagnosis often delayed or not made until after death. Streptococcus pneumoniae, despite being a common cause of bacteraemia, is seldom responsible for vascular seeding. Yet, pneumococcal aortitis should be ruled out in patients with sepsis at high risk of cardiovascular diseases presenting with typical symptoms of abdominal aortic aneurysm.
The patient promptly underwent aorto-aortic homograft substitution. The patient recovered after surgery without any complications and returned home shortly thereafter. CT angiography done after 1 month, however, revealed the presence of an initial disease progression (figure B), but the patient refused any surgery. Since then, she has had strict clinical and radiological follow-up examinations without evidence of further worsening. After almost 12 months she is still alive and in a good clinical condition.

A 34-year-old woman who collapsed during a mountain trek in northern Spain was initially assessed at an emergency rescue centre. She was unresponsive, asystolic, and pulseless, had unreactive dilated pupils, and had a tympanic temperature of 18°C. Advanced life support was started, and the woman was transferred to our hospital. She arrived 2 h and 25 min after the first evaluation—she was still in asystole, had unreactive dilated pupils, and had a core temperature of 20·2°C. An arterial blood sample showed a pH of 6·81, a lactate concentration of 10·3 mmol/L (normal 0·5–1), and a potassium concentration of 4·4 mmol/L (normal 3·5–5). Peripheral venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) support was started and a fine ventricular fibrillation rhythm was immediately seen on an electrocardiogram (ECG). The patient also started gasping, ventilator asynchronies appeared, and a burst suppression pattern was seen on a bispectral index monitor; these difficulties disappeared after she was given sedatives.During the first few hours of extracorporeal support, the patient had coagulopathy, bleeding, lung oedema (figure), and a highly variable ECMO flow. However, once the woman was stable, her body temperature was progressively increased at a rate of 3°C per h. The patient regained pupillary reactivity after 3 h of extracorporeal support. When her temperature reached 30°C, coarse ventricular fibrillation was observed. She was then defibrillated, which resulted in a posterior effective rhythm—meaning that 6 h and 10 min after the initial assessment there was return of spontaneous circulation. When her temperature was 32°C, an ECG showed sinus rhythm with classic Osborn—or J–waves, seen clearly in lead V3 (figure). The patient's neuron-specific enolase was found to be 93·4 ng/mL (normal range 1·5–13·5) on day 1 in the intensive care unit (ICU); by day 2 it had fallen to 55·1 ng/mL; other laboratory investigations normalised during the patient's recovery (appendix).
The heating process was continued until the patient's temperature was 35°C. ECMO was stopped after 45 h and 40 min. The patient was successfully extubated on day 2 of her stay in the ICU.
A neurological evaluation at the end of day 2 found no abnormalities, and the patient was moved from the ICU on day 6. She was allowed home on day 11. A month after the episode, she had resumed her normal activities of daily living.
Neurological sequelae are common after prolonged periods of cardiac arrest. The maintenance of extracorporeal support and neuroprotection along with regimented temperature management until adequate biventricular function is recovered—as in our case—may be key in preventing brain damage. We kept the patient on extracorporeal support for a total of 45 h and 40 min, which is substantially longer than previuously reported times (appendix). In cases of hypothermia and asystole, resuscitation using ECMO as a means of oxygen redistribution and temperature management should be considered.

A 77-year-old woman presented to our emergency department in Brescia, Italy with fever, altered conscious state, and neck stiffness. She was a heavy smoker, with hypertension and dyslipidaemia, and had had right-sided back pain for the previous 3 days.
Head CT and chest radiograph were normal, whereas lumbar puncture and blood cultures revealed pneumococcal meningitis with bacteraemia. Antibiotic therapy with ceftriaxone (2 g twice daily) was started. The patient rapidly improved, with resolution of fever and substantial reduction of inflammatory markers (white blood cell count dropped from 19·7 cells per mL to 14·9 cells per mL, and C-reactive protein dropped from 225 mg/L to 108 mg/L). However, 12 days after the patient was admitted to hospital, and less than a week after the initial clinical and biochemical improvement, she reported worsening backache, and the inflammatory markers rebounded (white blood cell count to 19·8 cells per mL and C-reactive protein to 171 mg/L). Lumbar spine CT showed no signs of spondylodiscitis, but an enlarged abdominal aorta with signs of perianeurysmal inflammation. The CT angiography done straight afterwards confirmed the presence of an abdominal aortic aneurysm with signs of impending rupture (figure A).Mycotic aneurysm and microbial aortitis are uncommon entities that usually occur in people with underlying atherosclerotic vascular disease as a consequence of bacteraemic seeding on the abnormal aortic surface. The clinical presentation is often subacute, and the diagnosis often delayed or not made until after death. Streptococcus pneumoniae, despite being a common cause of bacteraemia, is seldom responsible for vascular seeding. Yet, pneumococcal aortitis should be ruled out in patients with sepsis at high risk of cardiovascular diseases presenting with typical symptoms of abdominal aortic aneurysm.
The patient promptly underwent aorto-aortic homograft substitution. The patient recovered after surgery without any complications and returned home shortly thereafter. CT angiography done after 1 month, however, revealed the presence of an initial disease progression (figure B), but the patient refused any surgery. Since then, she has had strict clinical and radiological follow-up examinations without evidence of further worsening. After almost 12 months she is still alive and in a good clinical condition.

A 77-year-old woman presented to our emergency department in Brescia, Italy with fever, altered conscious state, and neck stiffness. She was a heavy smoker, with hypertension and dyslipidaemia, and had had right-sided back pain for the previous 3 days.
Head CT and chest radiograph were normal, whereas lumbar puncture and blood cultures revealed pneumococcal meningitis with bacteraemia. Antibiotic therapy with ceftriaxone (2 g twice daily) was started. The patient rapidly improved, with resolution of fever and substantial reduction of inflammatory markers (white blood cell count dropped from 19·7 cells per mL to 14·9 cells per mL, and C-reactive protein dropped from 225 mg/L to 108 mg/L). However, 12 days after the patient was admitted to hospital, and less than a week after the initial clinical and biochemical improvement, she reported worsening backache, and the inflammatory markers rebounded (white blood cell count to 19·8 cells per mL and C-reactive protein to 171 mg/L). Lumbar spine CT showed no signs of spondylodiscitis, but an enlarged abdominal aorta with signs of perianeurysmal inflammation. The CT angiography done straight afterwards confirmed the presence of an abdominal aortic aneurysm with signs of impending rupture (figure A).Mycotic aneurysm and microbial aortitis are uncommon entities that usually occur in people with underlying atherosclerotic vascular disease as a consequence of bacteraemic seeding on the abnormal aortic surface. The clinical presentation is often subacute, and the diagnosis often delayed or not made until after death. Streptococcus pneumoniae, despite being a common cause of bacteraemia, is seldom responsible for vascular seeding. Yet, pneumococcal aortitis should be ruled out in patients with sepsis at high risk of cardiovascular diseases presenting with typical symptoms of abdominal aortic aneurysm.
The patient promptly underwent aorto-aortic homograft substitution. The patient recovered after surgery without any complications and returned home shortly thereafter. CT angiography done after 1 month, however, revealed the presence of an initial disease progression (figure B), but the patient refused any surgery. Since then, she has had strict clinical and radiological follow-up examinations without evidence of further worsening. After almost 12 months she is still alive and in a good clinical condition.

A 53-year-old man presented to the emergency department of our hospital in January, 2014, after a syncopal episode. He was a regular smoker and recreational drug user, and had taken heroin, cannabis, and benzodiazepine during that week. He had a history of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. On examination he had grey pallor and was dyspnoeic at rest (respiratory rate 23 breaths per minute). His oxygen saturation was 70% on 100% inspired oxygen and his blood sample, which showed anaemia (haemoglobin 54 g/L; normal 130–180 g/L), was chocolate brown (figure). Arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7·40 (7·35–7·45) and methaemoglobin 26% (<2%).
Oxidant agents like benzocaine or novocaine, which are sometimes added to street heroin and cocaine, oxidise haemoglobin from its ferrous (Fe2+) to ferric state (Fe3+), and can cause methaemoglobinaemia. This altered form of haemoglobin loses its ability to transport oxygen, and can cause hypoxaemia. Chocolate-coloured blood is typical of methaemoglobinaemia. Unlike deoxyhaemoglobin, methaemoglobin does not brighten on exposure to atmospheric oxygen. In our patient, haemolysis associated with G6PD deficiency caused release of the methaemoglobin from within the red blood cells into the serum.

He was a regular smoker and recreational drug user, and had taken heroin, cannabis, and benzodiazepine during that week. He had a history of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. On examination he had grey pallor and was dyspnoeic at rest (respiratory rate 23 breaths per minute). His oxygen saturation was 70% on 100% inspired oxygen and his blood sample, which showed anaemia (haemoglobin 54 g/L; normal 130–180 g/L), was chocolate brown (figure). Arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7·40 (7·35–7·45) and methaemoglobin 26% (<2%).
Oxidant agents like benzocaine or novocaine, which are sometimes added to street heroin and cocaine, oxidise haemoglobin from its ferrous (Fe2+) to ferric state (Fe3+), and can cause methaemoglobinaemia. This altered form of haemoglobin loses its ability to transport oxygen, and can cause hypoxaemia. Chocolate-coloured blood is typical of methaemoglobinaemia. Unlike deoxyhaemoglobin, methaemoglobin does not brighten on exposure to atmospheric oxygen. In our patient, haemolysis associated with G6PD deficiency caused release of the methaemoglobin from within the red blood cells into the serum.

A 53-year-old man presented to the emergency department of our hospital in January, 2014, after a syncopal episode. He was a regular smoker and recreational drug user, and had taken heroin, cannabis, and benzodiazepine during that week. He had a history of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. On examination he had grey pallor and was dyspnoeic at rest (respiratory rate 23 breaths per minute). His oxygen saturation was 70% on 100% inspired oxygen and his blood sample, which showed anaemia (haemoglobin 54 g/L; normal 130–180 g/L), was chocolate brown (figure). Arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7·40 (7·35–7·45) and methaemoglobin 26% (<2%).
Oxidant agents like benzocaine or novocaine, which are sometimes added to street heroin and cocaine, oxidise haemoglobin from its ferrous (Fe2+) to ferric state (Fe3+), and can cause methaemoglobinaemia. This altered form of haemoglobin loses its ability to transport oxygen, and can cause hypoxaemia. Chocolate-coloured blood is typical of methaemoglobinaemia. Unlike deoxyhaemoglobin, methaemoglobin does not brighten on exposure to atmospheric oxygen. In our patient, haemolysis associated with G6PD deficiency caused release of the methaemoglobin from within the red blood cells into the serum.

input: A 27-year-old man was admitted to Shinshu University hospital with overt jaundice and ascites 8 days after long exposure to sunlight. He had been diagnosed with erythropoietic protoporphyria 6 years previously and was prescribed cimetidine (800 mg/day) at that time to downregulate Δ-aminolevulinic acid synthase-2 activity and reduce free protoporphyrin concentrations. Lactulose was also given to promote defaecation and to limit re-absorption of protoporphyrin, although its role in the management of erythropoietic protoporphyria has not been established. The patient was observed to have hallucinations, prolonged prothrombin time (international normalised ratio of 2·1), and elevation of serum total bilirubin (9·5 mg/dL) after admission; as a result, we diagnosed acute liver failure and did two rounds of plasma exchange. Acute viral hepatitis, Wilson's disease, and autoimmune hepatitis were ruled out by blood tests. His plasma looked icteric under regular white light, but turned red under ultraviolet A in the intensive care unit, suggestive of very high concentrations of porphyrins (figure, A). Ascites drained from the patient also turned red under ultraviolet A (figure, B). Erythrocyte protoporphyrin was markedly increased at the time of admission (5727 μg/dL red blood cells; compared with the normal range of 30–86 μg/dL red blood cells), which supported the diagnosis of rapid aggravation of erythropoietic protoporphyria. After two rounds of plasma exchange, the patient's hepatic function slowly recovered.Hepatopathy induced by erythropoietic protoporphyria can show fulminant aggravation. Since plasma protoporphyrin is very sensitive to light and rapidly declines during sample preparation, erythrocyte protoporphyrin measurement is recommended to detect erythropoietic protoporphyria activity. However, this measurement is uncommon and takes time to assess, which can delay accurate diagnosis. Ultraviolet A has increasingly been used in hospitals to check the quality of handwashing. When we encounter patients with acute liver failure of unknown cause, direct examination of body fluids—eg, plasma and ascites—under ultraviolet A could be a simple and useful method to screen for erythropoietic protoporphyria. Samples should therefore be protected from light when a porphyrin measurement is ordered.

A 65-year-old man attended our hospital with a 15-day history of fever, fatigue, and anorexia. He had been seen at his local hospital before coming to us and had been given a variety of different anti-infective agents and antipyretic drugs to no avail. The patient was previously fit and well. He lived in the rural Henan province, China, and gave no history of recent travel.On examination, apart from an enlarged spleen—measuring on ultrasound 70 mm thick and 175 mm long—and a temperature of 39·6°C, we found no abnormalities.
Laboratory investigations showed decreased white blood cell count of 2·15 × 109 per L (normal 3·5–9·5), red blood cell count of 3·75 × 1012 per L (normal 4·3–5·8), haemoglobin concentration of 9·95 g/dL, platelet count of 78 × 109 per L (normal 125–350), absolute neutrophil count of 1·57 × 109 per L (normal 1·8–6·3), albumin concentration of 31·6 g/L (normal 35–55), and HDL concentration 0·55 mmol/L (normal >0·91). The patient's triglyceride (1·83 mmol/L; normal 1·7), D-dimer (37·58 mg/L; normal 0–0·55), procalcitonin (0·455 ng/mL; normal 0–0·046), ferritin (2508·5 ng/mL; normal 30–400), and 1,3-β-D-glucan (166·50 pg/mL; normal 0–100) levels were raised.
The patient's globulin (27·0 g/L; normal 20–35), fibrinogen (2·75 g/L; normal 2–4), and aspergillus-antigen test for serum galactomannan (0·27 μg/L; normal 0–0·85) were in the normal ranges. The T-SPOT.TB (Oxford Immunotec, Oxford, UK) test was negative. Tests for HIV and tumour markers were negative; blood and bone marrow cultures were also both negative.
On day 2 of the admission, we did a bone marrow aspiration; marrow cytology showed an extremely low myelodysplasia and several haemophagocytic cells.
Our working diagnoses at this stage included malignant lymphoma, haemophagocytic syndrome, or an unidentified infectious disease. We decided to treat the patient with intravenous penciclovir, biapenem, and oral voriconazole, but his condition did not improve.
On day 5 of the admission, metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS; Illumina NextSeq 550, San Diego, CA, USA) was done and 1791 sequence readings of both Leishmania infantum and Leishmania donovani were detected in peripheral blood within 24 h—accounting for 0·671% of genome coverage. We then did a rK39 test (InBios International, Seattle, WA, USA) which was positive.
A second bone marrow aspiration showed the Leishmania spp amastigotes (figure)—confirming the mNGS result. The patient was diagnosed as having visceral leishmaniasis and started on intravenous amphotericin B at a dose of 50 mg daily. After 8 days of treatment, the patient's fever had remitted; mNGS was repeated—this time using peripheral blood—showing 1226 sequence readings of L infantum and L donovani. After leaving hospital, he was further treated with sodium stibogluconate intramuscularly at a dose of 1·9 g daily for 10 days. At follow-up 1 month later, the fever, fatigue, and anorexia had fully resolved. As an emerging method of pathogen-detection, mNGS—also known as shotgun sequencing—is an unbiased and hypothesis-free way of diagnosing a variety of different organisms simultaneously and rapidly. It may be particularly useful when the organism is difficult to culture and where—as in the case of leishmaniasis—detection sensitivity depends upon the tissue (video).

A 65-year-old man attended our hospital with a 15-day history of fever, fatigue, and anorexia. He had been seen at his local hospital before coming to us and had been given a variety of different anti-infective agents and antipyretic drugs to no avail. The patient was previously fit and well. He lived in the rural Henan province, China, and gave no history of recent travel.On examination, apart from an enlarged spleen—measuring on ultrasound 70 mm thick and 175 mm long—and a temperature of 39·6°C, we found no abnormalities.
Laboratory investigations showed decreased white blood cell count of 2·15 × 109 per L (normal 3·5–9·5), red blood cell count of 3·75 × 1012 per L (normal 4·3–5·8), haemoglobin concentration of 9·95 g/dL, platelet count of 78 × 109 per L (normal 125–350), absolute neutrophil count of 1·57 × 109 per L (normal 1·8–6·3), albumin concentration of 31·6 g/L (normal 35–55), and HDL concentration 0·55 mmol/L (normal >0·91). The patient's triglyceride (1·83 mmol/L; normal 1·7), D-dimer (37·58 mg/L; normal 0–0·55), procalcitonin (0·455 ng/mL; normal 0–0·046), ferritin (2508·5 ng/mL; normal 30–400), and 1,3-β-D-glucan (166·50 pg/mL; normal 0–100) levels were raised.
The patient's globulin (27·0 g/L; normal 20–35), fibrinogen (2·75 g/L; normal 2–4), and aspergillus-antigen test for serum galactomannan (0·27 μg/L; normal 0–0·85) were in the normal ranges. The T-SPOT.TB (Oxford Immunotec, Oxford, UK) test was negative. Tests for HIV and tumour markers were negative; blood and bone marrow cultures were also both negative.
On day 2 of the admission, we did a bone marrow aspiration; marrow cytology showed an extremely low myelodysplasia and several haemophagocytic cells.
Our working diagnoses at this stage included malignant lymphoma, haemophagocytic syndrome, or an unidentified infectious disease. We decided to treat the patient with intravenous penciclovir, biapenem, and oral voriconazole, but his condition did not improve.
On day 5 of the admission, metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS; Illumina NextSeq 550, San Diego, CA, USA) was done and 1791 sequence readings of both Leishmania infantum and Leishmania donovani were detected in peripheral blood within 24 h—accounting for 0·671% of genome coverage. We then did a rK39 test (InBios International, Seattle, WA, USA) which was positive.
A second bone marrow aspiration showed the Leishmania spp amastigotes (figure)—confirming the mNGS result. The patient was diagnosed as having visceral leishmaniasis and started on intravenous amphotericin B at a dose of 50 mg daily. After 8 days of treatment, the patient's fever had remitted; mNGS was repeated—this time using peripheral blood—showing 1226 sequence readings of L infantum and L donovani. After leaving hospital, he was further treated with sodium stibogluconate intramuscularly at a dose of 1·9 g daily for 10 days. At follow-up 1 month later, the fever, fatigue, and anorexia had fully resolved. As an emerging method of pathogen-detection, mNGS—also known as shotgun sequencing—is an unbiased and hypothesis-free way of diagnosing a variety of different organisms simultaneously and rapidly. It may be particularly useful when the organism is difficult to culture and where—as in the case of leishmaniasis—detection sensitivity depends upon the tissue (video).
