A 55-year-old woman with a 3-day history of abdominal pain and vomiting was admitted to our hospital. 7 days earlier she had a subtotal gastrectomy for poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma—stage T2N1M0.
24 h after admission, the patient was transferred to the cardiology ward for the management of chest pain associated with a raised high-sensitivity Troponin I concentration (342 ng/L; normal range <14).
The patient had a history of previous surgical operations—she had been diagnosed with Lynch syndrome with a confirmed MLH1 gene mutation. At the age of 48 years, she had a moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the colon and had a right hemicolectomy, prophylactic salpingo-oophorectomy, and adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy. 2 years later, she had a laparoscopic proctocolectomy and end ileostomy. She had a thalamic stroke aged 51 years; she was treated for hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. She had recently stopped smoking, which she had done for more than 30 years.
In her family history, her paternal uncle had bowel and stomach cancer and his daughter had bowel and breast cancer.
On examination, we found the patient to be unwell and reporting abdominal pain; she was hypotensive with a blood pressure of 92/57 mm Hg—she had managed to drink only small amounts of fluid prior to coming to hospital. Her pulse rate was 92 beats per min and her oxygen saturation was 97%.
After intravenous fluid replacement the patient's vital signs stabilised. An electrocardiogram showed a biphasic P wave in lead V1 and isoelectric T waves in the limb leads (appendix). Transthoracic echocardiography showed apical ballooning and a small thrombus in the dyskinetic apical segment with basal hyperkinesis (figure); the patient was started on dalteparin and dual antiplatelet therapy, and high-intensity statin treatment. Because we considered the patient to be too frail to have coronary angiography, she was treated with guideline-directed medical therapy for left ventricular systolic dysfunction. The patient's condition stabilised and she reported no further chest pain.
2 weeks later, transthoracic echocardiography showed full recovery of the left ventricular apical dyskinesis, and the ejection fraction had increased from 45% to a range of 55–60% (normal range 50–70%; figure). Additionally, the small left ventricular thrombus had almost completely resolved.
Considering the patient's presenting symptoms, transient left ventricular dysfunction—dyskinetic apical segment with basal hyperkinesis—we established a diagnosis of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (figure; video).
The patient remained stable and continued to be prescribed clopidogrel, bisoprolol, dapagliflozin, ramipril, and warfarin.
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is a clinical syndrome that typically presents as chest pain mimicking acute coronary syndrome; the term was originally used to describe apical ballooning of the left ventricle. Incidence is higher in postmenopausal women due to low levels of oestradiol. Additionally, a chronic inflammatory state, major surgical intervention, chemotherapy, as well as the emotional stress, are potential risk factors in oncology patients—notably present in our patient—that may result in the development of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy.
The development of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy in someone with Lynch syndrome has not, as far as we are aware, previously been described. Compared with Lynch syndrome, the genetic mechanism of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is still poorly understood. However, variants of adrenergic receptors and epigenetic changes in their expression are thought to be contributory; no evidence of a genetic overlap between Takotsubo cardiomyopathy and Lynch syndrome is apparent.

A 55-year-old woman with a 3-day history of abdominal pain and vomiting was admitted to our hospital. 7 days earlier she had a subtotal gastrectomy for poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma—stage T2N1M0.
24 h after admission, the patient was transferred to the cardiology ward for the management of chest pain associated with a raised high-sensitivity Troponin I concentration (342 ng/L; normal range <14).
The patient had a history of previous surgical operations—she had been diagnosed with Lynch syndrome with a confirmed MLH1 gene mutation. At the age of 48 years, she had a moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the colon and had a right hemicolectomy, prophylactic salpingo-oophorectomy, and adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy. 2 years later, she had a laparoscopic proctocolectomy and end ileostomy. She had a thalamic stroke aged 51 years; she was treated for hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. She had recently stopped smoking, which she had done for more than 30 years.
In her family history, her paternal uncle had bowel and stomach cancer and his daughter had bowel and breast cancer.
On examination, we found the patient to be unwell and reporting abdominal pain; she was hypotensive with a blood pressure of 92/57 mm Hg—she had managed to drink only small amounts of fluid prior to coming to hospital. Her pulse rate was 92 beats per min and her oxygen saturation was 97%.
After intravenous fluid replacement the patient's vital signs stabilised. An electrocardiogram showed a biphasic P wave in lead V1 and isoelectric T waves in the limb leads (appendix). Transthoracic echocardiography showed apical ballooning and a small thrombus in the dyskinetic apical segment with basal hyperkinesis (figure); the patient was started on dalteparin and dual antiplatelet therapy, and high-intensity statin treatment. Because we considered the patient to be too frail to have coronary angiography, she was treated with guideline-directed medical therapy for left ventricular systolic dysfunction. The patient's condition stabilised and she reported no further chest pain.
2 weeks later, transthoracic echocardiography showed full recovery of the left ventricular apical dyskinesis, and the ejection fraction had increased from 45% to a range of 55–60% (normal range 50–70%; figure). Additionally, the small left ventricular thrombus had almost completely resolved.
Considering the patient's presenting symptoms, transient left ventricular dysfunction—dyskinetic apical segment with basal hyperkinesis—we established a diagnosis of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (figure; video).
The patient remained stable and continued to be prescribed clopidogrel, bisoprolol, dapagliflozin, ramipril, and warfarin.
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is a clinical syndrome that typically presents as chest pain mimicking acute coronary syndrome; the term was originally used to describe apical ballooning of the left ventricle. Incidence is higher in postmenopausal women due to low levels of oestradiol. Additionally, a chronic inflammatory state, major surgical intervention, chemotherapy, as well as the emotional stress, are potential risk factors in oncology patients—notably present in our patient—that may result in the development of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy.
The development of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy in someone with Lynch syndrome has not, as far as we are aware, previously been described. Compared with Lynch syndrome, the genetic mechanism of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is still poorly understood. However, variants of adrenergic receptors and epigenetic changes in their expression are thought to be contributory; no evidence of a genetic overlap between Takotsubo cardiomyopathy and Lynch syndrome is apparent.

A 55-year-old woman with a 3-day history of abdominal pain and vomiting was admitted to our hospital. 7 days earlier she had a subtotal gastrectomy for poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma—stage T2N1M0.
24 h after admission, the patient was transferred to the cardiology ward for the management of chest pain associated with a raised high-sensitivity Troponin I concentration (342 ng/L; normal range <14).
The patient had a history of previous surgical operations—she had been diagnosed with Lynch syndrome with a confirmed MLH1 gene mutation. At the age of 48 years, she had a moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the colon and had a right hemicolectomy, prophylactic salpingo-oophorectomy, and adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy. 2 years later, she had a laparoscopic proctocolectomy and end ileostomy. She had a thalamic stroke aged 51 years; she was treated for hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. She had recently stopped smoking, which she had done for more than 30 years.
In her family history, her paternal uncle had bowel and stomach cancer and his daughter had bowel and breast cancer.
On examination, we found the patient to be unwell and reporting abdominal pain; she was hypotensive with a blood pressure of 92/57 mm Hg—she had managed to drink only small amounts of fluid prior to coming to hospital. Her pulse rate was 92 beats per min and her oxygen saturation was 97%.
After intravenous fluid replacement the patient's vital signs stabilised. An electrocardiogram showed a biphasic P wave in lead V1 and isoelectric T waves in the limb leads (appendix). Transthoracic echocardiography showed apical ballooning and a small thrombus in the dyskinetic apical segment with basal hyperkinesis (figure); the patient was started on dalteparin and dual antiplatelet therapy, and high-intensity statin treatment. Because we considered the patient to be too frail to have coronary angiography, she was treated with guideline-directed medical therapy for left ventricular systolic dysfunction. The patient's condition stabilised and she reported no further chest pain.
2 weeks later, transthoracic echocardiography showed full recovery of the left ventricular apical dyskinesis, and the ejection fraction had increased from 45% to a range of 55–60% (normal range 50–70%; figure). Additionally, the small left ventricular thrombus had almost completely resolved.
Considering the patient's presenting symptoms, transient left ventricular dysfunction—dyskinetic apical segment with basal hyperkinesis—we established a diagnosis of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (figure; video).
The patient remained stable and continued to be prescribed clopidogrel, bisoprolol, dapagliflozin, ramipril, and warfarin.
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is a clinical syndrome that typically presents as chest pain mimicking acute coronary syndrome; the term was originally used to describe apical ballooning of the left ventricle. Incidence is higher in postmenopausal women due to low levels of oestradiol. Additionally, a chronic inflammatory state, major surgical intervention, chemotherapy, as well as the emotional stress, are potential risk factors in oncology patients—notably present in our patient—that may result in the development of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy.
The development of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy in someone with Lynch syndrome has not, as far as we are aware, previously been described. Compared with Lynch syndrome, the genetic mechanism of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is still poorly understood. However, variants of adrenergic receptors and epigenetic changes in their expression are thought to be contributory; no evidence of a genetic overlap between Takotsubo cardiomyopathy and Lynch syndrome is apparent.

A 50-year-old man with a 2-year history of a dry cough and mild exertional dyspnoea was referred to our lung disease clinic. The patient—who was originally from Turkey—had a significant cigarette smoking history but no relevant occupational exposures.Physical examination was unremarkable. A chest x-ray was normal and lung function testing showed a moderate reduction in diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide: 72% predicted. A high-resolution CT scan of the patient's chest demonstrated extensive septal thickening and ground glass abnormalities in a crazy-paving pattern (figure; appendix).
Differential diagnoses we considered at this stage included organising pneumonia, lymphangitic spread of a tumour, lipoid pneumonia, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and atypical infections such as Pneumocystis jirovecii.
A bronchoscopy and transbronchial biopsies were performed. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was normal in appearance and no pathogens were identified. Transbronchial biopsy showed architecturally preserved alveoli filled with amorphous material positive for periodic acid-Schiff, granular material, and foamy alveolar macrophages (figure).
Immunohistochemistry showed surfactant protein B proprotein in the intra-alveolar material and cytoplasmic staining in the adjacent alveolar epithelial type II pneumocytes (appendix). Surfactant protein C proprotein was also expressed in alveolar epithelial type II pneumocytes but absent in the intra-alveolar material (appendix).
Taken together, the findings were consistent with a diagnosis of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) syndrome. Serum concentration of antibodies to granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) was raised at 33 μg/mL (normal <5), confirming the diagnosis. Over the subsequent 12 months, the patient reported increasing dyspnoea on exertion and his pulmonary function tests declined. He is under consideration for whole lung lavage or inhaled recombinant GM-CSF therapy.
PAP is a rare syndrome characterised by alveolar surfactant accumulation resulting in progressive dyspnoea and hypoxaemic respiratory failure. Autoimmune PAP accounts for 90–95% of cases; notably dust exposure, infection, and myelodysplastic syndrome are among several secondary causes of PAP.
An important clinical feature of PAP is a discrepancy between the severity of chest CT findings and patients' symptoms—as seen in our patient whose symptoms were mild despite a markedly abnormal chest CT. GM-CSF autoantibody levels in serum are reported to be close to 100% sensitive and specific for autoimmune PAP, and their measurement can prevent delay in the diagnosis. Surgical lung biopsy and transbronchial lung biopsy are often non-diagnostic due to the patchy distribution of the disease and are associated with potential morbidity; additionally, they do not provide further understanding of the underlying cause of PAP. Identifying the cause of PAP is important as new, targeted therapies—including aerosolised GM-CSF in autoimmune PAP—are emerging for this rare but underdiagnosed condition (video).

A 50-year-old man with a 2-year history of a dry cough and mild exertional dyspnoea was referred to our lung disease clinic. The patient—who was originally from Turkey—had a significant cigarette smoking history but no relevant occupational exposures.Physical examination was unremarkable. A chest x-ray was normal and lung function testing showed a moderate reduction in diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide: 72% predicted. A high-resolution CT scan of the patient's chest demonstrated extensive septal thickening and ground glass abnormalities in a crazy-paving pattern (figure; appendix).
Differential diagnoses we considered at this stage included organising pneumonia, lymphangitic spread of a tumour, lipoid pneumonia, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and atypical infections such as Pneumocystis jirovecii.
A bronchoscopy and transbronchial biopsies were performed. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was normal in appearance and no pathogens were identified. Transbronchial biopsy showed architecturally preserved alveoli filled with amorphous material positive for periodic acid-Schiff, granular material, and foamy alveolar macrophages (figure).
Immunohistochemistry showed surfactant protein B proprotein in the intra-alveolar material and cytoplasmic staining in the adjacent alveolar epithelial type II pneumocytes (appendix). Surfactant protein C proprotein was also expressed in alveolar epithelial type II pneumocytes but absent in the intra-alveolar material (appendix).
Taken together, the findings were consistent with a diagnosis of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) syndrome. Serum concentration of antibodies to granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) was raised at 33 μg/mL (normal <5), confirming the diagnosis. Over the subsequent 12 months, the patient reported increasing dyspnoea on exertion and his pulmonary function tests declined. He is under consideration for whole lung lavage or inhaled recombinant GM-CSF therapy.
PAP is a rare syndrome characterised by alveolar surfactant accumulation resulting in progressive dyspnoea and hypoxaemic respiratory failure. Autoimmune PAP accounts for 90–95% of cases; notably dust exposure, infection, and myelodysplastic syndrome are among several secondary causes of PAP.
An important clinical feature of PAP is a discrepancy between the severity of chest CT findings and patients' symptoms—as seen in our patient whose symptoms were mild despite a markedly abnormal chest CT. GM-CSF autoantibody levels in serum are reported to be close to 100% sensitive and specific for autoimmune PAP, and their measurement can prevent delay in the diagnosis. Surgical lung biopsy and transbronchial lung biopsy are often non-diagnostic due to the patchy distribution of the disease and are associated with potential morbidity; additionally, they do not provide further understanding of the underlying cause of PAP. Identifying the cause of PAP is important as new, targeted therapies—including aerosolised GM-CSF in autoimmune PAP—are emerging for this rare but underdiagnosed condition (video).

A 50-year-old man with a 2-year history of a dry cough and mild exertional dyspnoea was referred to our lung disease clinic. The patient—who was originally from Turkey—had a significant cigarette smoking history but no relevant occupational exposures.Physical examination was unremarkable. A chest x-ray was normal and lung function testing showed a moderate reduction in diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide: 72% predicted. A high-resolution CT scan of the patient's chest demonstrated extensive septal thickening and ground glass abnormalities in a crazy-paving pattern (figure; appendix).
Differential diagnoses we considered at this stage included organising pneumonia, lymphangitic spread of a tumour, lipoid pneumonia, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and atypical infections such as Pneumocystis jirovecii.
A bronchoscopy and transbronchial biopsies were performed. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was normal in appearance and no pathogens were identified. Transbronchial biopsy showed architecturally preserved alveoli filled with amorphous material positive for periodic acid-Schiff, granular material, and foamy alveolar macrophages (figure).
Immunohistochemistry showed surfactant protein B proprotein in the intra-alveolar material and cytoplasmic staining in the adjacent alveolar epithelial type II pneumocytes (appendix). Surfactant protein C proprotein was also expressed in alveolar epithelial type II pneumocytes but absent in the intra-alveolar material (appendix).
Taken together, the findings were consistent with a diagnosis of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) syndrome. Serum concentration of antibodies to granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) was raised at 33 μg/mL (normal <5), confirming the diagnosis. Over the subsequent 12 months, the patient reported increasing dyspnoea on exertion and his pulmonary function tests declined. He is under consideration for whole lung lavage or inhaled recombinant GM-CSF therapy.
PAP is a rare syndrome characterised by alveolar surfactant accumulation resulting in progressive dyspnoea and hypoxaemic respiratory failure. Autoimmune PAP accounts for 90–95% of cases; notably dust exposure, infection, and myelodysplastic syndrome are among several secondary causes of PAP.
An important clinical feature of PAP is a discrepancy between the severity of chest CT findings and patients' symptoms—as seen in our patient whose symptoms were mild despite a markedly abnormal chest CT. GM-CSF autoantibody levels in serum are reported to be close to 100% sensitive and specific for autoimmune PAP, and their measurement can prevent delay in the diagnosis. Surgical lung biopsy and transbronchial lung biopsy are often non-diagnostic due to the patchy distribution of the disease and are associated with potential morbidity; additionally, they do not provide further understanding of the underlying cause of PAP. Identifying the cause of PAP is important as new, targeted therapies—including aerosolised GM-CSF in autoimmune PAP—are emerging for this rare but underdiagnosed condition (video).

The patient was on anticoagulation therapy with dabigatran because of atrial fibrillation and had a history of a deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism 7 years ago. Additionally, the patient was also receiving treatment for hypertension (bisoprolol, amlodipine, and ramipril). As a consequence, a thromboembolic accident or a cerebral haemorrhage was initially discussed. Furthermore, a potential adverse event of the recent influenza vaccination was considered as a differential diagnosis.
Physical examination revealed hypoglossal paresis on the left side (figure, A). No other neurological abnormalities could be found. Blood pressure was 174/103 mmHg at admission. No abnormalities were recorded in routine cellular blood cell count and blood chemistry; in particular, no signs of infection or inflammation were noted. No specific cerebrovascular risk factors were apparent. An initial cranial CT scan ruled out any bleeding or infarction. Doppler sonography of the cranial vessels was unremarkable.However, a left-sided, stage I primary breast tumour was documented in the patient's medical history. This tumour had been diagnosed 9 years ago. At that time, the patient was treated with breast-conserving surgery, radiotherapy of the left breast, and adjuvant endocrine treatment with tamoxifen for 1 year. Tamoxifen therapy was stopped after 1 year as a consequence of deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
During further examination of the acute hypoglossal paresis, cerebral MRI detected a solitary tumoral lesion at the basal skull (figure, B), affecting the left hypoglossal nerve. Except for this solitary lesion, none of the other staging procedures used, including CT scan of the chest and abdomen and bone scan, found any additional metastatic lesions. Therefore, a secondary, solitary metastatic breast tumour at the basal skull was assumed. The patient was treated with locoregional radiotherapy, antiresorptive treatment with zoledronate, and first-line endocrine therapy with an aromatase inhibitor. Furthermore, the patient subsequently received speech therapy. As a result of all these therapeutic measures, the hypoglossal paresis soon regressed completely and the patient is currently without any symptoms 8 months after primary treatment.
Solitary breast cancer metastases are rare, but affected patients often have a good chance of achieving long-term remission. In our case, the work-up to investigate an acute, uncommon clinical finding led to the diagnosis.

A 76-year-old female patient was admitted to the neurological department of our institution in October, 2016, because of acute dysarthria. Her symptoms started 2 weeks ago at the same time as a severe cold that had developed immediately after she received an influenza vaccine.
The patient was on anticoagulation therapy with dabigatran because of atrial fibrillation and had a history of a deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism 7 years ago. Additionally, the patient was also receiving treatment for hypertension (bisoprolol, amlodipine, and ramipril). As a consequence, a thromboembolic accident or a cerebral haemorrhage was initially discussed. Furthermore, a potential adverse event of the recent influenza vaccination was considered as a differential diagnosis.
Physical examination revealed hypoglossal paresis on the left side (figure, A). No other neurological abnormalities could be found. Blood pressure was 174/103 mmHg at admission. No abnormalities were recorded in routine cellular blood cell count and blood chemistry; in particular, no signs of infection or inflammation were noted. No specific cerebrovascular risk factors were apparent. An initial cranial CT scan ruled out any bleeding or infarction. Doppler sonography of the cranial vessels was unremarkable.However, a left-sided, stage I primary breast tumour was documented in the patient's medical history. This tumour had been diagnosed 9 years ago. At that time, the patient was treated with breast-conserving surgery, radiotherapy of the left breast, and adjuvant endocrine treatment with tamoxifen for 1 year. Tamoxifen therapy was stopped after 1 year as a consequence of deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
During further examination of the acute hypoglossal paresis, cerebral MRI detected a solitary tumoral lesion at the basal skull (figure, B), affecting the left hypoglossal nerve. Except for this solitary lesion, none of the other staging procedures used, including CT scan of the chest and abdomen and bone scan, found any additional metastatic lesions. Therefore, a secondary, solitary metastatic breast tumour at the basal skull was assumed. The patient was treated with locoregional radiotherapy, antiresorptive treatment with zoledronate, and first-line endocrine therapy with an aromatase inhibitor. Furthermore, the patient subsequently received speech therapy. As a result of all these therapeutic measures, the hypoglossal paresis soon regressed completely and the patient is currently without any symptoms 8 months after primary treatment.
Solitary breast cancer metastases are rare, but affected patients often have a good chance of achieving long-term remission. In our case, the work-up to investigate an acute, uncommon clinical finding led to the diagnosis.

A 76-year-old female patient was admitted to the neurological department of our institution in October, 2016, because of acute dysarthria. Her symptoms started 2 weeks ago at the same time as a severe cold that had developed immediately after she received an influenza vaccine.
The patient was on anticoagulation therapy with dabigatran because of atrial fibrillation and had a history of a deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism 7 years ago. Additionally, the patient was also receiving treatment for hypertension (bisoprolol, amlodipine, and ramipril). As a consequence, a thromboembolic accident or a cerebral haemorrhage was initially discussed. Furthermore, a potential adverse event of the recent influenza vaccination was considered as a differential diagnosis.
Physical examination revealed hypoglossal paresis on the left side (figure, A). No other neurological abnormalities could be found. Blood pressure was 174/103 mmHg at admission. No abnormalities were recorded in routine cellular blood cell count and blood chemistry; in particular, no signs of infection or inflammation were noted. No specific cerebrovascular risk factors were apparent. An initial cranial CT scan ruled out any bleeding or infarction. Doppler sonography of the cranial vessels was unremarkable.However, a left-sided, stage I primary breast tumour was documented in the patient's medical history. This tumour had been diagnosed 9 years ago. At that time, the patient was treated with breast-conserving surgery, radiotherapy of the left breast, and adjuvant endocrine treatment with tamoxifen for 1 year. Tamoxifen therapy was stopped after 1 year as a consequence of deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
During further examination of the acute hypoglossal paresis, cerebral MRI detected a solitary tumoral lesion at the basal skull (figure, B), affecting the left hypoglossal nerve. Except for this solitary lesion, none of the other staging procedures used, including CT scan of the chest and abdomen and bone scan, found any additional metastatic lesions. Therefore, a secondary, solitary metastatic breast tumour at the basal skull was assumed. The patient was treated with locoregional radiotherapy, antiresorptive treatment with zoledronate, and first-line endocrine therapy with an aromatase inhibitor. Furthermore, the patient subsequently received speech therapy. As a result of all these therapeutic measures, the hypoglossal paresis soon regressed completely and the patient is currently without any symptoms 8 months after primary treatment.
Solitary breast cancer metastases are rare, but affected patients often have a good chance of achieving long-term remission. In our case, the work-up to investigate an acute, uncommon clinical finding led to the diagnosis.

We aimed to adopt a fertility sparing strategy—neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by conservative surgery of the body of the uterus—since biopsy samples of both pelvic sentinel lymph nodes showed no signs of metastatic spread.The patient had no previous medical history of note.
She received three courses of a cisplatin and paclitaxel regimen. Abdominopelvic ultrasonography was carried out during the first cycle of chemotherapy because of moderate liver cytolysis; at that time, the uterine corpus was 48 mm and endometrial thickness 4 mm. MRI post-chemotherapy showed a partial tumour response, but most notably, there was a clear decrease in the size of the uterine body of nearly 20 mm—from 47 mm to 28 mm. The shrinkage began early after the third course of chemotherapy (figure).
A trachelectomy was then performed and the patient was allowed home after 3 days. She had no postoperative complications. At follow-up 36 months later, the uterus was measured at 27 mm on MRI.
Uterine atrophy has—as far as we are aware—not previously been described in patients undergoing chemotherapy; we have been unable to find a clear explanation for its aetiology in this case. However, on review of our patient's history, she said that for the few weeks before starting the treatment, she had adhered to a strict ketogenic diet—with no slow or fast sugars.
Recently, uterine atrophy and osteoporosis was reported in mice after food restriction by reducing an insulin-like growth factor. The uterine atrophy seen in our patient might therefore have been due to a radical change in the patient's diet combined with the chemotherapy regimen—although we appreciate this is highly speculative. Alternatively, the cisplatin, which has been reported to induce atrophy of striated skeletal muscle, may have been responsible—although a similar effect on smooth muscle has not been documented.

In patients with tumours below 2 cm in size, surgery—in the form of a simple or radical trachelectomy, depending on local prognostic factors—are standard. A 41-year-old woman presented to our hospital complaining of breathlessness and pain in the right side of her chest. She said that the problem was not new and that it happened every time she had her period: she had begun menstruating 24 h earlier.On examination she had reduced breath sounds and dullness to percussion on the right side of her chest. In her medical history, it was noted that she had been diagnosed with catamenial pneumothorax 9 years earlier for which she was treated with the gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist buserelin 1200 μg/day; she stopped taking it after 6 months.
A CT scan of her chest showed a moderately sized pneumothorax on the right side. A blood test showed a serum concentration of the tumour marker cancer antigen 125 of 2219 U/mL (normal level <35·0 U/mL). Considering the history and the current presentation, we concluded that our patient had again had a catamenial pneumothorax. We therefore decided to do a thoracoscopy, during which a red lesion was seen in the pleura of the superior segment of the right lower lobe (figure) and two black lesions were seen in the pleura of the right middle lobe: the lesions were resected. Additionally, several small defects—known as blueberry spots—ranging between 2-3 mm in diameter, were seen on the right side of the diaphragm (figure), through which the liver was visible. Histopathological examination of both the diaphragmatic and the pulmonary lesions showed endometrial stroma, which was oestrogen and progesterone receptor positive and CD10 positive.
The lesions were cut out and resected areas were covered with sheets of polyglycolic acid and fibrin glue. The patient recovered well postoperatively, and no further lesions were identified; however, 72 days after the surgery, she had a further pneumothorax. She was re-started on buserelin.
Catamenial pneumothorax is a rare condition and has a mean age of onset of 32–35 years. The pneumothorax usually occurs within 72 h before or after the start of menstruation. The lesions are classically on the right side and endometriosis might also be present. The actual cause is unknown, but three theories have been proposed as underlying mechanisms: retrograde regurgitation of endometrial cells through the ovarian duct into the pelvis and then into the diaphragm; metastatic spread of endometrial cells through lymphatic or venous dissemination; and müllerian cell metaplasia of the coelomic epithelium.
Menstruation has a clear association with the worsening of several other diseases including migraine, epilepsy, and some psychological disorders. Questions about the relationship of any symptoms to the menstrual cycle can sometimes provide an important clue to the precise diagnosis.

input:
A 31-year-old nulliparous woman attended our hospital for treatment of squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix. She had previously presented with vaginal bleeding and a 28 mm lesion had been found on clinical examination and shown on MRI. We aimed to adopt a fertility sparing strategy—neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by conservative surgery of the body of the uterus—since biopsy samples of both pelvic sentinel lymph nodes showed no signs of metastatic spread.The patient had no previous medical history of note.
She received three courses of a cisplatin and paclitaxel regimen. Abdominopelvic ultrasonography was carried out during the first cycle of chemotherapy because of moderate liver cytolysis; at that time, the uterine corpus was 48 mm and endometrial thickness 4 mm. MRI post-chemotherapy showed a partial tumour response, but most notably, there was a clear decrease in the size of the uterine body of nearly 20 mm—from 47 mm to 28 mm. The shrinkage began early after the third course of chemotherapy (figure).
A trachelectomy was then performed and the patient was allowed home after 3 days. She had no postoperative complications. At follow-up 36 months later, the uterus was measured at 27 mm on MRI.
Uterine atrophy has—as far as we are aware—not previously been described in patients undergoing chemotherapy; we have been unable to find a clear explanation for its aetiology in this case. However, on review of our patient's history, she said that for the few weeks before starting the treatment, she had adhered to a strict ketogenic diet—with no slow or fast sugars.
Recently, uterine atrophy and osteoporosis was reported in mice after food restriction by reducing an insulin-like growth factor. The uterine atrophy seen in our patient might therefore have been due to a radical change in the patient's diet combined with the chemotherapy regimen—although we appreciate this is highly speculative. Alternatively, the cisplatin, which has been reported to induce atrophy of striated skeletal muscle, may have been responsible—although a similar effect on smooth muscle has not been documented.
Fertility sparing management should be offered to a select group of young patients requiring treatment for early stage I cervical cancer located in the cervix, without evidence of extracervical metastasis, and of conventional histopathological types. In patients with tumours below 2 cm in size, surgery—in the form of a simple or radical trachelectomy, depending on local prognostic factors—are standard. In patients with tumours between 2 cm and 4 cm, two options should be considered: a radical trachelectomy using an abdominal approach or neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by conservative surgery. The assessment of the oncological safety of both strategies is still currently unclear—although results of an exploration of the different options are pending; either way the aim is to obtain a uterine corpus of at least 40 mm so as to allow a potential at term pregnancy. Finally, removal of the uterus after childbearing is not necessary in patients that are diligently followed up (video).

A 41-year-old woman presented to our hospital complaining of breathlessness and pain in the right side of her chest. She said that the problem was not new and that it happened every time she had her period: she had begun menstruating 24 h earlier.On examination she had reduced breath sounds and dullness to percussion on the right side of her chest. In her medical history, it was noted that she had been diagnosed with catamenial pneumothorax 9 years earlier for which she was treated with the gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist buserelin 1200 μg/day; she stopped taking it after 6 months.
A CT scan of her chest showed a moderately sized pneumothorax on the right side. A blood test showed a serum concentration of the tumour marker cancer antigen 125 of 2219 U/mL (normal level <35·0 U/mL). Considering the history and the current presentation, we concluded that our patient had again had a catamenial pneumothorax. We therefore decided to do a thoracoscopy, during which a red lesion was seen in the pleura of the superior segment of the right lower lobe (figure) and two black lesions were seen in the pleura of the right middle lobe: the lesions were resected. Additionally, several small defects—known as blueberry spots—ranging between 2-3 mm in diameter, were seen on the right side of the diaphragm (figure), through which the liver was visible. Histopathological examination of both the diaphragmatic and the pulmonary lesions showed endometrial stroma, which was oestrogen and progesterone receptor positive and CD10 positive.
The lesions were cut out and resected areas were covered with sheets of polyglycolic acid and fibrin glue. The patient recovered well postoperatively, and no further lesions were identified; however, 72 days after the surgery, she had a further pneumothorax. She was re-started on buserelin.
Catamenial pneumothorax is a rare condition and has a mean age of onset of 32–35 years. The pneumothorax usually occurs within 72 h before or after the start of menstruation. The lesions are classically on the right side and endometriosis might also be present. The actual cause is unknown, but three theories have been proposed as underlying mechanisms: retrograde regurgitation of endometrial cells through the ovarian duct into the pelvis and then into the diaphragm; metastatic spread of endometrial cells through lymphatic or venous dissemination; and müllerian cell metaplasia of the coelomic epithelium.
Menstruation has a clear association with the worsening of several other diseases including migraine, epilepsy, and some psychological disorders. Questions about the relationship of any symptoms to the menstrual cycle can sometimes provide an important clue to the precise diagnosis.

A woman aged 24 years with a history of cerebral infarction presented with eruptions on the acral regions that had relapsed in winter since her childhood. On examination, we observed brownish erythema and dark red scaly papules on the fingers and toes (figure A, B). The patient's younger sister, mother, and maternal grandfather had similar eruptions (figure D, E, F). Magnetic resonance angiography showed multiple cerebral aneurysms in the patient (figure H, I, J). There was no evidence of intellectual disability or basal ganglia calcification. Laboratory tests showed normal blood cell counts and complement: positive for antinuclear antibodies at 1:80, positive for anticardiolipin antibodies at 27·1 IU/mL, and negative for antidouble-stranded DNA antibodies and cryoglobulins. Multiple enlarging cerebral aneurysms and a previous cerebral infarction were found in the patient's younger sister (figure L), although neither anticardiolipin antibodies nor other coagulation abnormalities were detected. The previously reported heterozygous TREX1 (pAsp18Asn) mutation 53G→A was identified in the family and familial chilblain lupus was diagnosed.Chilblain lupus erythematosus is a rare and unique form of chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus that is characterised by chilblains, which are cold-induced eruptions on the acral regions. A familial form of chilblain lupus erythematosus, related to heterozygous mutations in TREX1 and SAMHD1, has been previously reported. To date, there have been two case reports of familial chilblain lupus that have included cerebral vasculopathy presenting as multiple cerebral aneurysms, narrowing cerebral arteries, or cerebral infarction. Chilblains with family history and systemic symptoms might suggest the presence of hereditary autoinflammatory diseases.
Avoiding cold exposure, applying topical corticosteroid, or taking systemic immunosuppressive agents can be therapeutic options. In this case, administration of systemic prednisolone (1·0 mg/kg per day) improved the acral eruptions and the cerebral aneurysms. Because of the occurrence of hyperlipidaemia, the prednisolone dose was gradually tapered to 5 mg/day. Both the skin and the cerebral lesions have remained stable for 6 months. Familial chilblain lupus can present with various symptoms in a family with identical gene mutations. Recognising that cerebral infarctions and aneurysms can occur in familial chilblain lupus cases is important. Further investigation is needed to better understand the pathomechanisms and to prevent such severe complications.

A 41-year-old woman presented to our hospital complaining of breathlessness and pain in the right side of her chest. She said that the problem was not new and that it happened every time she had her period: she had begun menstruating 24 h earlier.On examination she had reduced breath sounds and dullness to percussion on the right side of her chest. In her medical history, it was noted that she had been diagnosed with catamenial pneumothorax 9 years earlier for which she was treated with the gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist buserelin 1200 μg/day; she stopped taking it after 6 months.
A CT scan of her chest showed a moderately sized pneumothorax on the right side. A blood test showed a serum concentration of the tumour marker cancer antigen 125 of 2219 U/mL (normal level <35·0 U/mL). Considering the history and the current presentation, we concluded that our patient had again had a catamenial pneumothorax. We therefore decided to do a thoracoscopy, during which a red lesion was seen in the pleura of the superior segment of the right lower lobe (figure) and two black lesions were seen in the pleura of the right middle lobe: the lesions were resected. Additionally, several small defects—known as blueberry spots—ranging between 2-3 mm in diameter, were seen on the right side of the diaphragm (figure), through which the liver was visible. Histopathological examination of both the diaphragmatic and the pulmonary lesions showed endometrial stroma, which was oestrogen and progesterone receptor positive and CD10 positive.
The lesions were cut out and resected areas were covered with sheets of polyglycolic acid and fibrin glue. The patient recovered well postoperatively, and no further lesions were identified; however, 72 days after the surgery, she had a further pneumothorax. She was re-started on buserelin.
Catamenial pneumothorax is a rare condition and has a mean age of onset of 32–35 years. The pneumothorax usually occurs within 72 h before or after the start of menstruation. The lesions are classically on the right side and endometriosis might also be present. The actual cause is unknown, but three theories have been proposed as underlying mechanisms: retrograde regurgitation of endometrial cells through the ovarian duct into the pelvis and then into the diaphragm; metastatic spread of endometrial cells through lymphatic or venous dissemination; and müllerian cell metaplasia of the coelomic epithelium.
Menstruation has a clear association with the worsening of several other diseases including migraine, epilepsy, and some psychological disorders. Questions about the relationship of any symptoms to the menstrual cycle can sometimes provide an important clue to the precise diagnosis.

A woman aged 24 years with a history of cerebral infarction presented with eruptions on the acral regions that had relapsed in winter since her childhood. On examination, we observed brownish erythema and dark red scaly papules on the fingers and toes (figure A, B). The patient's younger sister, mother, and maternal grandfather had similar eruptions (figure D, E, F). Magnetic resonance angiography showed multiple cerebral aneurysms in the patient (figure H, I, J). There was no evidence of intellectual disability or basal ganglia calcification. Laboratory tests showed normal blood cell counts and complement: positive for antinuclear antibodies at 1:80, positive for anticardiolipin antibodies at 27·1 IU/mL, and negative for antidouble-stranded DNA antibodies and cryoglobulins. Multiple enlarging cerebral aneurysms and a previous cerebral infarction were found in the patient's younger sister (figure L), although neither anticardiolipin antibodies nor other coagulation abnormalities were detected. The previously reported heterozygous TREX1 (pAsp18Asn) mutation 53G→A was identified in the family and familial chilblain lupus was diagnosed.Chilblain lupus erythematosus is a rare and unique form of chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus that is characterised by chilblains, which are cold-induced eruptions on the acral regions. A familial form of chilblain lupus erythematosus, related to heterozygous mutations in TREX1 and SAMHD1, has been previously reported. To date, there have been two case reports of familial chilblain lupus that have included cerebral vasculopathy presenting as multiple cerebral aneurysms, narrowing cerebral arteries, or cerebral infarction. Chilblains with family history and systemic symptoms might suggest the presence of hereditary autoinflammatory diseases.
Avoiding cold exposure, applying topical corticosteroid, or taking systemic immunosuppressive agents can be therapeutic options. In this case, administration of systemic prednisolone (1·0 mg/kg per day) improved the acral eruptions and the cerebral aneurysms. Because of the occurrence of hyperlipidaemia, the prednisolone dose was gradually tapered to 5 mg/day. Both the skin and the cerebral lesions have remained stable for 6 months. Familial chilblain lupus can present with various symptoms in a family with identical gene mutations. Recognising that cerebral infarctions and aneurysms can occur in familial chilblain lupus cases is important. Further investigation is needed to better understand the pathomechanisms and to prevent such severe complications.

A woman aged 24 years with a history of cerebral infarction presented with eruptions on the acral regions that had relapsed in winter since her childhood. On examination, we observed brownish erythema and dark red scaly papules on the fingers and toes (figure A, B). The patient's younger sister, mother, and maternal grandfather had similar eruptions (figure D, E, F). Magnetic resonance angiography showed multiple cerebral aneurysms in the patient (figure H, I, J). There was no evidence of intellectual disability or basal ganglia calcification. Laboratory tests showed normal blood cell counts and complement: positive for antinuclear antibodies at 1:80, positive for anticardiolipin antibodies at 27·1 IU/mL, and negative for antidouble-stranded DNA antibodies and cryoglobulins. Multiple enlarging cerebral aneurysms and a previous cerebral infarction were found in the patient's younger sister (figure L), although neither anticardiolipin antibodies nor other coagulation abnormalities were detected. The previously reported heterozygous TREX1 (pAsp18Asn) mutation 53G→A was identified in the family and familial chilblain lupus was diagnosed.Chilblain lupus erythematosus is a rare and unique form of chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus that is characterised by chilblains, which are cold-induced eruptions on the acral regions. A familial form of chilblain lupus erythematosus, related to heterozygous mutations in TREX1 and SAMHD1, has been previously reported. To date, there have been two case reports of familial chilblain lupus that have included cerebral vasculopathy presenting as multiple cerebral aneurysms, narrowing cerebral arteries, or cerebral infarction. Chilblains with family history and systemic symptoms might suggest the presence of hereditary autoinflammatory diseases.
Avoiding cold exposure, applying topical corticosteroid, or taking systemic immunosuppressive agents can be therapeutic options. In this case, administration of systemic prednisolone (1·0 mg/kg per day) improved the acral eruptions and the cerebral aneurysms. Because of the occurrence of hyperlipidaemia, the prednisolone dose was gradually tapered to 5 mg/day. Both the skin and the cerebral lesions have remained stable for 6 months. Familial chilblain lupus can present with various symptoms in a family with identical gene mutations. Recognising that cerebral infarctions and aneurysms can occur in familial chilblain lupus cases is important. Further investigation is needed to better understand the pathomechanisms and to prevent such severe complications.

A 32-year-old woman, who was 12 weeks pregnant, was referred to our emergency department feeling generally unwell after recurrent vomiting. She had no notable medical history.On arrival at the hospital, she was mildly confused and reported polyuria. On clinical examination she was unwell and showed signs of dehydration; her pulse was 119 beats per min and her blood pressure was 100/60 mm Hg, and temperature 37°C. An electrocardiogram showed a prolonged PR interval and repolarisation was abnormal.
Laboratory investigations found a serum potassium concentration of 3 mmol/L (normal range 3·5–5·1) and a serum creatine concentration of 43 μmol/L (normal range 64–104); the patient's thyroid hormone concentrations were normal. Total serum calcium and phosphorus concentrations were 4·15 mmol/L (normal range 2·20–2·55) and 1·02 mmol/L (normal range 0·8–1·5), respectively; serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) concentration was 992 pg/mL (normal range 6–50).
We made a working diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism presenting as a hypercalcaemic crisis. The patient was rehydrated with a saline infusion of 5 L given over 24 h and an intravenous infusion of calcitonin—100 U over 8 h—under cardiac monitoring. After 48 h, as the patient's serum calcium had reduced to 3·89 mmol/L, but still above normal range, cinacalcet was added at a dose of 30 mg every 8 h. The clinical condition of the patient improved, but after 72 h, severe hypercalcaemia (3·40 mmol/L) persisted. Two sessions of dialysis using a low-calcium dialysate transiently lowered the serum calcium level; the patient's albumin-adjusted serum calcium concentration remained stable at 3·1 mmol/L, while she was given a saline infusion, calcitonin, and cinacalcet.
A cervical ultrasound showed a 27 mm × 12 mm × 8 mm, highly hypoechoic oval thyroid nodule vascularised in the periphery of the right thyroid lobe—suggestive of a malignant lesion—which we graded 5 on the European Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (figure). No lesions in the usual parathyroid sites were seen. A cervicothoracic CT scan confirmed the intrathyroid lesion and showed no evidence of parathyroid adenoma in the usual or ectopic sites (figure). We did a fine needle aspiration and PTH concentration—measured in the evacuated aspirate—was found to be very high (1495 pg/mL), indicative of a parathyroid adenoma. Notably, PTH is normally undetectable in non-parathyroid tissue. Additionally, parathyroid scintigraphy, which would have helped localise the lesion, is currently unavailable in French Guiana. The patient had an emergency operation to remove the intrathyroid lesion (figure). Serum PTH and calcium concentrations reduced from preoperative levels of 1465 pg/mL and 3·22 mmol/L, respectively to 103 pg/mL and 3·06 mmol/L intraoperatively, and to 16 pg/mL and 2·7 mmol/L immediately postoperatively. Histopathological examination of a sample of the excised lesion confirmed a parathyroid adenoma (figure). Postoperatively, the patient's general condition markedly improved; a fetal ultrasound showed no abnormalities, and the remainder of the patient's pregnancy was uneventful.
Diagnosing hypercalcaemia during pregnancy can be difficult. Symptoms—including nausea, vomiting, and fatigue—are like those of early pregnancy. Furthermore, long-standing hypercalcaemia may lead to preeclampsia, which in early pregnancy can lead to shortness of breath, tachycardia, and confusion; both mother and child's needs must be considered during management and treatment. Primary hyperparathyroidism is the commonest cause, and adenomas may be difficult to find. Fine needle aspiration and PTH measurement in the aspirate may be an alternative method of diagnosis—particularly in resource-limited settings.

We made a working diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism presenting as a hypercalcaemic crisis. The patient was rehydrated with a saline infusion of 5 L given over 24 h and an intravenous infusion of calcitonin—100 U over 8 h—under cardiac monitoring. After 48 h, as the patient's serum calcium had reduced to 3·89 mmol/L, but still above normal range, cinacalcet was added at a dose of 30 mg every 8 h. The clinical condition of the patient improved, but after 72 h, severe hypercalcaemia (3·40 mmol/L) persisted. Two sessions of dialysis using a low-calcium dialysate transiently lowered the serum calcium level; the patient's albumin-adjusted serum calcium concentration remained stable at 3·1 mmol/L, while she was given a saline infusion, calcitonin, and cinacalcet.

A 32-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 3-week history of fever, cough, and general fatigue; he also reported a 1-month history of night sweats. The patient had no significant medical history; he had been previously fit and well and was prescribed no medications.
On examination he was generally unwell looking; his temperature was 38·8°C, his blood pressure 82/49 mm Hg, and he had a sinus tachycardia of 130 beats per min.
CT scans of the patient's chest and abdomen showed multiple pulmonary nodules and bilateral adrenal masses—in the left adrenal gland the lesion was 61 mm × 36 mm and in the right 90 mm × 63 mm (figure). 18fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT scan showed an increase in tracer uptake in the multiple pulmonary nodules, the bilateral adrenal masses, and the thyroid gland (figure).Laboratory investigations showed hyponatremia (128 mEq/L; typical range 135–145), and elevated lactate dehydrogenase concentration (903 IU/L; typical range 124–222), soluble interleukin-2 receptor concentration (2140 U/mL; typical range 157–474), adrenocorticotropic hormone concentration (177 pg/mL; typical range 7·2–63·3), and low cortisol level (1·9 μg/dL; typical range 6·2–19). The plasma renin activity was markedly elevated at 16 ng/mL/h (typical range 0·3–2·9) with an aldosterone level at the lower end of the normal range (66·3 pg/mL; typical range 30–159).
Lung cancer markers—including pro-gastrin-releasing peptide, serum carcinoembryonic antigen, and cytokeratin fraction 21-1—were within normal limits. Cosyntropin stimulation testing demonstrated no response in plasma cortisol concentrations: at 0 min the concentration was 1·7 μg/dL; at 30 min it was 2·6 μg/dL; and at 60 min it was 1·8 μg/dL, confirming primary adrenal insufficiency.
Oral hydrocortisone improved the patient's general fatigue; his blood pressure returned to normal range and the hyponatremia resolved.
Histopathological examination of a sample of tissue obtained from a biopsy specimen of one of the adrenal masses showed lymphocytic infiltration with atypical and enlarged cells; immunohistochemical staining showed CD3 positive T-cell infiltration and CD20 positive B-cell infiltration. Epstein-Barr virus—using in situ hybridisation—was identified; CD20 positive B-cells showed Epstein-Barr virus positivity, indicating that B cells were infected with the virus. Additionally, Epstein-Barr virus was detected in a sample of blood using PCR: 2400 copies of Epstein-Barr virus DNA to 106 white blood cells (reference range <200 copies to 106). Considering the findings and the presentation in the round, we diagnosed grade 2 lymphomatoid granulomatosis.
Therapy with cyclophosphamide, hydroxydaunorubicin, oncovin, and prednisone—acronymed to CHOP—was initiated and then switched to rituximab, etoposide, prednisone, oncovin, cyclophosphamide, and hydroxydaunorubicin (R-EPOCH) therapy. However, invasion of the liver by lymphoproliferative tissue was detected, and the bilateral adrenal tumours had increased in size; the patient developed liver and renal failure and died 2 months after the diagnosis of lymphomatoid granulomatosis was made.
The differential diagnoses of pulmonary lesions with bilateral adrenal masses and adrenal insufficiency includes malignant lymphoma, granulomatous infections—tuberculosis and histoplasmosis—and lung cancer with adrenal metastases.
Lymphomatoid granulomatosis is a rare lymphoproliferative disorder driven by Epstein-Barr virus which occurs mainly in patients with no overt immune deficiency. Presenting complaints include fever, sweating, and weight loss; patients typically have pulmonary nodules, skin nodules, and other extranodal sites—including the CNS. The disease is challenging to diagnose and treat mainly because of its heterogeneous clinical presentations, rarity, and sparsity of data about treatment.

A 32-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 3-week history of fever, cough, and general fatigue; he also reported a 1-month history of night sweats. The patient had no significant medical history; he had been previously fit and well and was prescribed no medications.
On examination he was generally unwell looking; his temperature was 38·8°C, his blood pressure 82/49 mm Hg, and he had a sinus tachycardia of 130 beats per min.
CT scans of the patient's chest and abdomen showed multiple pulmonary nodules and bilateral adrenal masses—in the left adrenal gland the lesion was 61 mm × 36 mm and in the right 90 mm × 63 mm (figure). 18fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT scan showed an increase in tracer uptake in the multiple pulmonary nodules, the bilateral adrenal masses, and the thyroid gland (figure).Laboratory investigations showed hyponatremia (128 mEq/L; typical range 135–145), and elevated lactate dehydrogenase concentration (903 IU/L; typical range 124–222), soluble interleukin-2 receptor concentration (2140 U/mL; typical range 157–474), adrenocorticotropic hormone concentration (177 pg/mL; typical range 7·2–63·3), and low cortisol level (1·9 μg/dL; typical range 6·2–19). The plasma renin activity was markedly elevated at 16 ng/mL/h (typical range 0·3–2·9) with an aldosterone level at the lower end of the normal range (66·3 pg/mL; typical range 30–159).
Lung cancer markers—including pro-gastrin-releasing peptide, serum carcinoembryonic antigen, and cytokeratin fraction 21-1—were within normal limits. Cosyntropin stimulation testing demonstrated no response in plasma cortisol concentrations: at 0 min the concentration was 1·7 μg/dL; at 30 min it was 2·6 μg/dL; and at 60 min it was 1·8 μg/dL, confirming primary adrenal insufficiency.
Oral hydrocortisone improved the patient's general fatigue; his blood pressure returned to normal range and the hyponatremia resolved.
Histopathological examination of a sample of tissue obtained from a biopsy specimen of one of the adrenal masses showed lymphocytic infiltration with atypical and enlarged cells; immunohistochemical staining showed CD3 positive T-cell infiltration and CD20 positive B-cell infiltration. Epstein-Barr virus—using in situ hybridisation—was identified; CD20 positive B-cells showed Epstein-Barr virus positivity, indicating that B cells were infected with the virus. Additionally, Epstein-Barr virus was detected in a sample of blood using PCR: 2400 copies of Epstein-Barr virus DNA to 106 white blood cells (reference range <200 copies to 106). Considering the findings and the presentation in the round, we diagnosed grade 2 lymphomatoid granulomatosis.
Therapy with cyclophosphamide, hydroxydaunorubicin, oncovin, and prednisone—acronymed to CHOP—was initiated and then switched to rituximab, etoposide, prednisone, oncovin, cyclophosphamide, and hydroxydaunorubicin (R-EPOCH) therapy. However, invasion of the liver by lymphoproliferative tissue was detected, and the bilateral adrenal tumours had increased in size; the patient developed liver and renal failure and died 2 months after the diagnosis of lymphomatoid granulomatosis was made.
The differential diagnoses of pulmonary lesions with bilateral adrenal masses and adrenal insufficiency includes malignant lymphoma, granulomatous infections—tuberculosis and histoplasmosis—and lung cancer with adrenal metastases.
Lymphomatoid granulomatosis is a rare lymphoproliferative disorder driven by Epstein-Barr virus which occurs mainly in patients with no overt immune deficiency. Presenting complaints include fever, sweating, and weight loss; patients typically have pulmonary nodules, skin nodules, and other extranodal sites—including the CNS. The disease is challenging to diagnose and treat mainly because of its heterogeneous clinical presentations, rarity, and sparsity of data about treatment.

A 32-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 3-week history of fever, cough, and general fatigue; he also reported a 1-month history of night sweats. The patient had no significant medical history; he had been previously fit and well and was prescribed no medications.
On examination he was generally unwell looking; his temperature was 38·8°C, his blood pressure 82/49 mm Hg, and he had a sinus tachycardia of 130 beats per min.
CT scans of the patient's chest and abdomen showed multiple pulmonary nodules and bilateral adrenal masses—in the left adrenal gland the lesion was 61 mm × 36 mm and in the right 90 mm × 63 mm (figure). 18fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT scan showed an increase in tracer uptake in the multiple pulmonary nodules, the bilateral adrenal masses, and the thyroid gland (figure).Laboratory investigations showed hyponatremia (128 mEq/L; typical range 135–145), and elevated lactate dehydrogenase concentration (903 IU/L; typical range 124–222), soluble interleukin-2 receptor concentration (2140 U/mL; typical range 157–474), adrenocorticotropic hormone concentration (177 pg/mL; typical range 7·2–63·3), and low cortisol level (1·9 μg/dL; typical range 6·2–19). The plasma renin activity was markedly elevated at 16 ng/mL/h (typical range 0·3–2·9) with an aldosterone level at the lower end of the normal range (66·3 pg/mL; typical range 30–159).
Lung cancer markers—including pro-gastrin-releasing peptide, serum carcinoembryonic antigen, and cytokeratin fraction 21-1—were within normal limits. Cosyntropin stimulation testing demonstrated no response in plasma cortisol concentrations: at 0 min the concentration was 1·7 μg/dL; at 30 min it was 2·6 μg/dL; and at 60 min it was 1·8 μg/dL, confirming primary adrenal insufficiency.
Oral hydrocortisone improved the patient's general fatigue; his blood pressure returned to normal range and the hyponatremia resolved.
Histopathological examination of a sample of tissue obtained from a biopsy specimen of one of the adrenal masses showed lymphocytic infiltration with atypical and enlarged cells; immunohistochemical staining showed CD3 positive T-cell infiltration and CD20 positive B-cell infiltration. Epstein-Barr virus—using in situ hybridisation—was identified; CD20 positive B-cells showed Epstein-Barr virus positivity, indicating that B cells were infected with the virus. Additionally, Epstein-Barr virus was detected in a sample of blood using PCR: 2400 copies of Epstein-Barr virus DNA to 106 white blood cells (reference range <200 copies to 106). Considering the findings and the presentation in the round, we diagnosed grade 2 lymphomatoid granulomatosis.
Therapy with cyclophosphamide, hydroxydaunorubicin, oncovin, and prednisone—acronymed to CHOP—was initiated and then switched to rituximab, etoposide, prednisone, oncovin, cyclophosphamide, and hydroxydaunorubicin (R-EPOCH) therapy. However, invasion of the liver by lymphoproliferative tissue was detected, and the bilateral adrenal tumours had increased in size; the patient developed liver and renal failure and died 2 months after the diagnosis of lymphomatoid granulomatosis was made.
The differential diagnoses of pulmonary lesions with bilateral adrenal masses and adrenal insufficiency includes malignant lymphoma, granulomatous infections—tuberculosis and histoplasmosis—and lung cancer with adrenal metastases.
Lymphomatoid granulomatosis is a rare lymphoproliferative disorder driven by Epstein-Barr virus which occurs mainly in patients with no overt immune deficiency. Presenting complaints include fever, sweating, and weight loss; patients typically have pulmonary nodules, skin nodules, and other extranodal sites—including the CNS. The disease is challenging to diagnose and treat mainly because of its heterogeneous clinical presentations, rarity, and sparsity of data about treatment.

A 7-month-old boy presented to Osaka City General Hospital, Osaka, Japan, with persistent thrombocytopenia since birth. Despite treatments including intravenous immunoglobulin, prednisolone, romiplostim, and rituximab (details provided in the appendix p 1), platelet counts remained at approximately 20–30 × 109 platelets per L (normal range 158–348 × 109 platelets per L). A blood transfusion was administered when the platelet count fell below 5 × 109 platelets per L. After platelet transfusions, the platelet count could be maintained for several days. Physical examination at age 7 months showed purpura without dysmorphic features, and he had no history of severe bleeding or immunodeficiency. Peripheral blood smears showed microthrombocytes with a mean platelet diameter of 1·9 μm (SD 0·4; normal range 2–4 μm; figure) and an immature platelet fraction of 1·1% (normal range 0·8–6·8%).Family history (obtained at birth in Osaka City General Hospital) revealed that the patient's mother carried a known WAS variant (168C→T), and his maternal uncle had diagnosed X-linked thrombocytopenia. On the paternal side, both his father and grandfather had a history of chronic thrombocytopenia, not thoroughly studied. Genetic analyses were performed on the patient, his father, his mother, and his paternal grandfather, identfying both the WAS variant (inherited maternally) and a pathogenic ANKRD26 variant (134G→A; inherited paternally) in the patient. The patient's father (now identified with the ANKRD26 variant) had a platelet count of 57 × 109 platelets per L, and the paternal grandfather had 37 × 109 platelets per L. The patient's mother had 186 × 109 platelets per L, and the patient's maternal uncle had 16 × 109 platelets per L. The patient had one female sibling without thrombocytopenia, in whom the presence of the ANKRD26 variant is considered unlikely as she does not have thrombocytopenia; however, carrier status for the WAS variant cannot be excluded as WAS follows an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern.
The co-occurrence of pathogenic variants in WAS and ANKRD26—two genes independently associated with congenital thrombocytopenia—suggests multilocus inheritance of thrombocytopenia in this patient. Whereas WAS variants typically cause X-linked thrombocytopenia with microthrombocytopenia and immune dysregulation, ANKRD26 variants in the 5′-untranslated region (including the 134G→A variant) lead to autosomal dominant thrombocytopenia with normal-sized platelets and have a predisposition to haematological malignancy. As there is no established treatment for congenital thrombocytopenia, management is tailored to clinical symptoms. This patient presented only with purpura; therefore, watchful waiting without active treatment was chosen.
This patient exemplifies the diagnostic challenges in congenital thrombocytopenia and highlights the importance of considering digenic or multilocus inheritance in patients with atypical clinical features or complex family histories. The presence of multiple causative genes in congenital thrombocytopenia might exacerbate clinical manifestations, including pronounced bleeding symptoms, highlighting the importance of vigilant disease monitoring. As high throughput sequencing becomes more widespread, such patients might become increasingly recognised.

input: A 48-year-old woman presented with asymmetric vision loss: the right eye being more affected than the left eye. She had a history of uncontrolled type 2 diabetes, 100% occlusion of the right carotid artery, and transient ischaemic attacks. She also had a history of proliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes, and had undergone multiple retinal surgeries for repair of retinopathy-related traction retinal detachments in her right eye. Diabetic macular oedema was present in the left eye. Examination of the right eye showed traction of the pupillary edge by a fibrovascular membrane (figure A, arrow). Cataracts were present in both eyes: however, the cataract in the left eye was milder than the cataract in the right eye. Pathological iris neovascularisation extended onto the cataractous lens (figure A, B, arrowheads). Vascular leakage was confirmed by iris angiography (blurred hyperfluorescence; figure C, arrowhead). Ultrasonography did not show a tumour or retinal detachment. We diagnosed ocular ischaemic syndrome secondary to right carotid artery occlusion, related to systemic type 2 diabetes. Insufficient view was available for pan-retinal photocoagulation—the standard treatment for iris neovascularisation—because of the cataract. The patient received a subconjunctival injection of bevacizumab 2·5 mg (Genentech, South San Francisco, CA, USA), an antibody against vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF; figure D, asterisk). 5 weeks later, regression of iris neovascularisation was observed (figure E–G, arrowheads). The patient was referred to a primary-care physician to assist with control of diabetes and systemic anticoagulation. The anti-angiogenic effect was temporary, and the patient received three injections in the following 6 months to maintain regression and normal intraocular pressure. The patient continues to receive treatment. To date, no corneal epitheliopathy, conjunctival injection, or other toxic effects have been reported.

input: A 48-year-old woman presented with asymmetric vision loss: the right eye being more affected than the left eye. She had a history of uncontrolled type 2 diabetes, 100% occlusion of the right carotid artery, and transient ischaemic attacks. She also had a history of proliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes, and had undergone multiple retinal surgeries for repair of retinopathy-related traction retinal detachments in her right eye. Diabetic macular oedema was present in the left eye. Examination of the right eye showed traction of the pupillary edge by a fibrovascular membrane (figure A, arrow). Cataracts were present in both eyes: however, the cataract in the left eye was milder than the cataract in the right eye. Pathological iris neovascularisation extended onto the cataractous lens (figure A, B, arrowheads). Vascular leakage was confirmed by iris angiography (blurred hyperfluorescence; figure C, arrowhead). Ultrasonography did not show a tumour or retinal detachment. We diagnosed ocular ischaemic syndrome secondary to right carotid artery occlusion, related to systemic type 2 diabetes. Insufficient view was available for pan-retinal photocoagulation—the standard treatment for iris neovascularisation—because of the cataract. The patient received a subconjunctival injection of bevacizumab 2·5 mg (Genentech, South San Francisco, CA, USA), an antibody against vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF; figure D, asterisk). 5 weeks later, regression of iris neovascularisation was observed (figure E–G, arrowheads). The patient was referred to a primary-care physician to assist with control of diabetes and systemic anticoagulation. The anti-angiogenic effect was temporary, and the patient received three injections in the following 6 months to maintain regression and normal intraocular pressure. The patient continues to receive treatment. To date, no corneal epitheliopathy, conjunctival injection, or other toxic effects have been reported.

input: A 48-year-old woman presented with asymmetric vision loss: the right eye being more affected than the left eye. She had a history of uncontrolled type 2 diabetes, 100% occlusion of the right carotid artery, and transient ischaemic attacks. She also had a history of proliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes, and had undergone multiple retinal surgeries for repair of retinopathy-related traction retinal detachments in her right eye. Diabetic macular oedema was present in the left eye. Examination of the right eye showed traction of the pupillary edge by a fibrovascular membrane (figure A, arrow). Cataracts were present in both eyes: however, the cataract in the left eye was milder than the cataract in the right eye. Pathological iris neovascularisation extended onto the cataractous lens (figure A, B, arrowheads). Vascular leakage was confirmed by iris angiography (blurred hyperfluorescence; figure C, arrowhead). Ultrasonography did not show a tumour or retinal detachment. We diagnosed ocular ischaemic syndrome secondary to right carotid artery occlusion, related to systemic type 2 diabetes. Insufficient view was available for pan-retinal photocoagulation—the standard treatment for iris neovascularisation—because of the cataract. The patient received a subconjunctival injection of bevacizumab 2·5 mg (Genentech, South San Francisco, CA, USA), an antibody against vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF; figure D, asterisk). 5 weeks later, regression of iris neovascularisation was observed (figure E–G, arrowheads). The patient was referred to a primary-care physician to assist with control of diabetes and systemic anticoagulation. The anti-angiogenic effect was temporary, and the patient received three injections in the following 6 months to maintain regression and normal intraocular pressure. The patient continues to receive treatment. To date, no corneal epitheliopathy, conjunctival injection, or other toxic effects have been reported.

input:
A man aged 19 years attended the rheumatology clinic with a 7-year history of finger swelling. He referred to occasional mild arthralgia without weakness, limitations of activity, or morning stiffness. On further questioning, he referred to habitual knuckle cracking of the affected hand. Physical examination revealed swelling around the first, second, third, and fourth proximal interphalangeal joints of the left hand with hyperkeratosis (figure). Examination of the right hand was typical. Complete blood-cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein were within normal range and rheumatoid factor was negative. An x-ray of both hands showed soft-tissue swelling of the left hand without joint alterations. The patient was diagnosed with pachydermodactyly and advised to cease knuckle cracking. At follow-up 1 year after diagnosis, he was asymptomatic with improvement of the swelling and hyperkeratosis.
Pachydermodactyly is a rare and benign condition usually seen in young adults as painless swelling and growth around the lateral and dorsum regions of the proximal interphalangeal joints with unspecified cause. It regularly affects the second, third, and fourth fingers. Case reports and case series suggest repetitive mechanical movements and behavioural disorders (eg, obsessive-compulsive disorder or generalised anxiety disorder) as risk factors. This condition can be a diagnostic challenge. Differential diagnoses include juvenile idiopathic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, knuckle pads, juvenile fibromatosis, pachydermoperiostosis, and thyroid acropachy. Image findings on radiography are important to diagnose pachydermodactyly and usually show soft-tissue swelling without joint involvement, erosions, or subchondral sclerosis. Skin biopsy or MRI are helpful but usually not necessary for the diagnosis. Treatment is not required and behavioural modification with avoidance of repetitive mechanical stress is recommended.
Inflammation and swelling of hands in young adults has a broad differential diagnosis and could be the first expression of systemic autoimmune diseases or be secondary to repeated mechanical stress. Timely diagnosis of this condition can avoid unnecessary diagnosis testing, worriedness, and treatment.
