A 50-year-old woman with a sudden onset of chest pain, diaphoresis, and nausea was admitted to our hospital; additionally, she reported a 1-month history of shortness of breath and chest pain brought on by moderate activity. She had hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and type 2 diabetes of gestational origin; she was prescribed subcutaneous insulin, dulaglutide, empagliflozin, metformin, rosuvastatin and ezetimibe, fenofibrate, ramipril, aspirin, and omeprazole.
On examination she was generally well; she had a blood pressure of 154/72 mm Hg, pulse of 82 beats per min, and oxygen saturation of 96%. Laboratory investigations showed blood glucose concentration of 138 mg/dL (reference range 70·0–105·0), creatinine concentration 0·9 mg/dL (reference range 0·5–1·0), haemoglobin concentration 10·5 g/dL (reference range 12·0–14·0), and ultrasensitive troponin I 417 pg/mL (reference range 0–12).
An electrocardiogram showed ST-segment depression and T-wave inversion in inferolateral leads; a bedside echocardiogram indicated marked hypokinesia in mid-basal segments of the inferior and inferolateral walls. The patient was taken to the catheterisation laboratory for an early invasive strategy. The coronary angiogram (figure 1) and optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging (figure 2) showed a critical stenosis in the distal right coronary artery due to an occlusive atherosclerotic plaque.We decided to do a percutaneous coronary intervention: after effective pre-dilatation of the lesion (figure 1), we did a coronary angioplasty using a crystalline sirolimus butylated hydroxytoluene drug-coated balloon (DCB; B Braun Melsungen, Melsungen, Germany) in a single 45 sec inflation, resulting in a good final angiographic result (figure 1).
OCT imaging after angioplasty showed hyperechoic particles in the endothelium of the DCB-treated segment (figure 2), in a variety of different patterns (figure 3); notably, the particles caused shadowing effects like those generated by the struts of metallic drug-eluting stents (figure 3).Follow-up coronary angiography 28 days later showed continued patency of the previously stenotic segment—indicative of a favourable angiographic result (figure 1); OCT imaging showed that in some sections of the artery most of the strut-like shadowing and the particles had disappeared (figure 2). In some parts of the artery, however, a few particles remained embedded in the endothelium (figure 2)—suggesting that while most particles had been absorbed, a few continued to be endothelialised and in the process of absorption.
DCBs treat atherosclerotic plaques with antiproliferative agents, similarly to drug-eluting stents but without leaving any permanent metallic stent scaffold—a strategy also known as leave nothing behind. We believe this case shows how sirolimus is deposited and subsequently absorbed within the coronary endothelium after DCB angioplasty (video; appendix).

A 50-year-old woman with a sudden onset of chest pain, diaphoresis, and nausea was admitted to our hospital; additionally, she reported a 1-month history of shortness of breath and chest pain brought on by moderate activity. She had hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and type 2 diabetes of gestational origin; she was prescribed subcutaneous insulin, dulaglutide, empagliflozin, metformin, rosuvastatin and ezetimibe, fenofibrate, ramipril, aspirin, and omeprazole.
On examination she was generally well; she had a blood pressure of 154/72 mm Hg, pulse of 82 beats per min, and oxygen saturation of 96%. Laboratory investigations showed blood glucose concentration of 138 mg/dL (reference range 70·0–105·0), creatinine concentration 0·9 mg/dL (reference range 0·5–1·0), haemoglobin concentration 10·5 g/dL (reference range 12·0–14·0), and ultrasensitive troponin I 417 pg/mL (reference range 0–12).
An electrocardiogram showed ST-segment depression and T-wave inversion in inferolateral leads; a bedside echocardiogram indicated marked hypokinesia in mid-basal segments of the inferior and inferolateral walls. The patient was taken to the catheterisation laboratory for an early invasive strategy. The coronary angiogram (figure 1) and optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging (figure 2) showed a critical stenosis in the distal right coronary artery due to an occlusive atherosclerotic plaque.We decided to do a percutaneous coronary intervention: after effective pre-dilatation of the lesion (figure 1), we did a coronary angioplasty using a crystalline sirolimus butylated hydroxytoluene drug-coated balloon (DCB; B Braun Melsungen, Melsungen, Germany) in a single 45 sec inflation, resulting in a good final angiographic result (figure 1).
OCT imaging after angioplasty showed hyperechoic particles in the endothelium of the DCB-treated segment (figure 2), in a variety of different patterns (figure 3); notably, the particles caused shadowing effects like those generated by the struts of metallic drug-eluting stents (figure 3).Follow-up coronary angiography 28 days later showed continued patency of the previously stenotic segment—indicative of a favourable angiographic result (figure 1); OCT imaging showed that in some sections of the artery most of the strut-like shadowing and the particles had disappeared (figure 2). In some parts of the artery, however, a few particles remained embedded in the endothelium (figure 2)—suggesting that while most particles had been absorbed, a few continued to be endothelialised and in the process of absorption.
DCBs treat atherosclerotic plaques with antiproliferative agents, similarly to drug-eluting stents but without leaving any permanent metallic stent scaffold—a strategy also known as leave nothing behind. We believe this case shows how sirolimus is deposited and subsequently absorbed within the coronary endothelium after DCB angioplasty (video; appendix).

A 50-year-old woman with a sudden onset of chest pain, diaphoresis, and nausea was admitted to our hospital; additionally, she reported a 1-month history of shortness of breath and chest pain brought on by moderate activity. She had hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and type 2 diabetes of gestational origin; she was prescribed subcutaneous insulin, dulaglutide, empagliflozin, metformin, rosuvastatin and ezetimibe, fenofibrate, ramipril, aspirin, and omeprazole.
On examination she was generally well; she had a blood pressure of 154/72 mm Hg, pulse of 82 beats per min, and oxygen saturation of 96%. Laboratory investigations showed blood glucose concentration of 138 mg/dL (reference range 70·0–105·0), creatinine concentration 0·9 mg/dL (reference range 0·5–1·0), haemoglobin concentration 10·5 g/dL (reference range 12·0–14·0), and ultrasensitive troponin I 417 pg/mL (reference range 0–12).
An electrocardiogram showed ST-segment depression and T-wave inversion in inferolateral leads; a bedside echocardiogram indicated marked hypokinesia in mid-basal segments of the inferior and inferolateral walls. The patient was taken to the catheterisation laboratory for an early invasive strategy. The coronary angiogram (figure 1) and optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging (figure 2) showed a critical stenosis in the distal right coronary artery due to an occlusive atherosclerotic plaque.We decided to do a percutaneous coronary intervention: after effective pre-dilatation of the lesion (figure 1), we did a coronary angioplasty using a crystalline sirolimus butylated hydroxytoluene drug-coated balloon (DCB; B Braun Melsungen, Melsungen, Germany) in a single 45 sec inflation, resulting in a good final angiographic result (figure 1).
OCT imaging after angioplasty showed hyperechoic particles in the endothelium of the DCB-treated segment (figure 2), in a variety of different patterns (figure 3); notably, the particles caused shadowing effects like those generated by the struts of metallic drug-eluting stents (figure 3).Follow-up coronary angiography 28 days later showed continued patency of the previously stenotic segment—indicative of a favourable angiographic result (figure 1); OCT imaging showed that in some sections of the artery most of the strut-like shadowing and the particles had disappeared (figure 2). In some parts of the artery, however, a few particles remained embedded in the endothelium (figure 2)—suggesting that while most particles had been absorbed, a few continued to be endothelialised and in the process of absorption.
DCBs treat atherosclerotic plaques with antiproliferative agents, similarly to drug-eluting stents but without leaving any permanent metallic stent scaffold—a strategy also known as leave nothing behind. We believe this case shows how sirolimus is deposited and subsequently absorbed within the coronary endothelium after DCB angioplasty (video; appendix).

A preterm baby—delivered by caesarean section at 36 weeks and 5 days due to pathological trace on cardiotocography—presented immediately after birth with tachypnoea, and sternal, intercostal, and subcostal recessions.The pregnancy had been normal, the baby's birthweight was 2825 g and the Apgar scores were 7, 8, and 9 at 1, 5, and 10 min.
The baby was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit and after he was initially stabilised using continuous positive airway pressure, he required nasal continuous positive airway pressure of 7 mbar. During the first day of life, the fraction of inspired oxygen increased from 0·3 to 0·6.
At this stage, we thought the most likely diagnosis was respiratory distress syndrome, transient tachypnoea of the newborn, neonatal sepsis, or pneumothorax.
Laboratory investigations found normal C-reactive protein (0·5 mg/dL; normal <1·5) and interleukin-6 concentrations (90·1 pg/mL; normal <100); there was no leukopenia or leukocytosis. A raised bilirubin concentration (16·48 mg/L; normal 0·0–14·6) was effectively treated with light emitting diode phototherapy using a fibre optic phototherapy blanket for 14 h.
A lung ultrasound showed no signs of respiratory distress syndrome, transient tachypnoea of the newborn, or pneumothorax. However, in the parasternal view—usually a helpful window for the assessment of the tracheal tube position and where the great vessels are visible below the thymus in the healthy infant—a stairway-like set of horizontal hyperechogenic reflections was seen instead of the great vessels indicating the presence of trapped air below the thymus (figure; video).
A chest x-ray confirmed that the patient did not have respiratory distress syndrome or a pneumothorax, and showed a large, clearly defined radiolucent structure above the heart—known as the spinnaker sign—indicative of pneumomediastinum and affirming the findings and diagnosis made using the lung ultrasound (figure).
The patient was successfully weaned off respiratory support within 5 days and was allowed home after 8 days; no drainage was necessary.
We believe that—based upon the current literature and our findings in this case—a lung ultrasound can differentiate between some of the key causes of acute respiratory conditions in the neonate—namely, respiratory distress syndrome, transient tachypnoea of the newborn, pneumonia, pneumothorax, and pneumomediastinum. We would like to propose that the distinctive finding of a set of horizontal hyperechogenic reflections below the thymus—indicating pneumomediastinum—be known as the stairway sign.
Pneumomediastinum after birth is an uncommon condition—defined as air trapped in the mediastinum—presenting with signs of respiratory distress, uneven chest expansion, and muffling of cardiac sounds. Resolution usually occurs within 1–2 days and, in most cases, no specific treatment is needed. Risk factors associated with pneumomediastinum include prematurity, the need for positive pressure ventilation, pneumonia, and meconium aspiration. Patients need to be closely observed—depending upon the severity of the air leak and the ability of the infant to compensate for the respiratory distress—due to the risk of further deterioration, and possible pneumothorax or emphysema.

A preterm baby—delivered by caesarean section at 36 weeks and 5 days due to pathological trace on cardiotocography—presented immediately after birth with tachypnoea, and sternal, intercostal, and subcostal recessions.The pregnancy had been normal, the baby's birthweight was 2825 g and the Apgar scores were 7, 8, and 9 at 1, 5, and 10 min.
The baby was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit and after he was initially stabilised using continuous positive airway pressure, he required nasal continuous positive airway pressure of 7 mbar. During the first day of life, the fraction of inspired oxygen increased from 0·3 to 0·6.
At this stage, we thought the most likely diagnosis was respiratory distress syndrome, transient tachypnoea of the newborn, neonatal sepsis, or pneumothorax.
Laboratory investigations found normal C-reactive protein (0·5 mg/dL; normal <1·5) and interleukin-6 concentrations (90·1 pg/mL; normal <100); there was no leukopenia or leukocytosis. A raised bilirubin concentration (16·48 mg/L; normal 0·0–14·6) was effectively treated with light emitting diode phototherapy using a fibre optic phototherapy blanket for 14 h.
A lung ultrasound showed no signs of respiratory distress syndrome, transient tachypnoea of the newborn, or pneumothorax. However, in the parasternal view—usually a helpful window for the assessment of the tracheal tube position and where the great vessels are visible below the thymus in the healthy infant—a stairway-like set of horizontal hyperechogenic reflections was seen instead of the great vessels indicating the presence of trapped air below the thymus (figure; video).
A chest x-ray confirmed that the patient did not have respiratory distress syndrome or a pneumothorax, and showed a large, clearly defined radiolucent structure above the heart—known as the spinnaker sign—indicative of pneumomediastinum and affirming the findings and diagnosis made using the lung ultrasound (figure).
The patient was successfully weaned off respiratory support within 5 days and was allowed home after 8 days; no drainage was necessary.
We believe that—based upon the current literature and our findings in this case—a lung ultrasound can differentiate between some of the key causes of acute respiratory conditions in the neonate—namely, respiratory distress syndrome, transient tachypnoea of the newborn, pneumonia, pneumothorax, and pneumomediastinum. We would like to propose that the distinctive finding of a set of horizontal hyperechogenic reflections below the thymus—indicating pneumomediastinum—be known as the stairway sign.
Pneumomediastinum after birth is an uncommon condition—defined as air trapped in the mediastinum—presenting with signs of respiratory distress, uneven chest expansion, and muffling of cardiac sounds. Resolution usually occurs within 1–2 days and, in most cases, no specific treatment is needed. Risk factors associated with pneumomediastinum include prematurity, the need for positive pressure ventilation, pneumonia, and meconium aspiration. Patients need to be closely observed—depending upon the severity of the air leak and the ability of the infant to compensate for the respiratory distress—due to the risk of further deterioration, and possible pneumothorax or emphysema.

A preterm baby—delivered by caesarean section at 36 weeks and 5 days due to pathological trace on cardiotocography—presented immediately after birth with tachypnoea, and sternal, intercostal, and subcostal recessions.The pregnancy had been normal, the baby's birthweight was 2825 g and the Apgar scores were 7, 8, and 9 at 1, 5, and 10 min.
The baby was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit and after he was initially stabilised using continuous positive airway pressure, he required nasal continuous positive airway pressure of 7 mbar. During the first day of life, the fraction of inspired oxygen increased from 0·3 to 0·6.
At this stage, we thought the most likely diagnosis was respiratory distress syndrome, transient tachypnoea of the newborn, neonatal sepsis, or pneumothorax.
Laboratory investigations found normal C-reactive protein (0·5 mg/dL; normal <1·5) and interleukin-6 concentrations (90·1 pg/mL; normal <100); there was no leukopenia or leukocytosis. A raised bilirubin concentration (16·48 mg/L; normal 0·0–14·6) was effectively treated with light emitting diode phototherapy using a fibre optic phototherapy blanket for 14 h.
A lung ultrasound showed no signs of respiratory distress syndrome, transient tachypnoea of the newborn, or pneumothorax. However, in the parasternal view—usually a helpful window for the assessment of the tracheal tube position and where the great vessels are visible below the thymus in the healthy infant—a stairway-like set of horizontal hyperechogenic reflections was seen instead of the great vessels indicating the presence of trapped air below the thymus (figure; video).
A chest x-ray confirmed that the patient did not have respiratory distress syndrome or a pneumothorax, and showed a large, clearly defined radiolucent structure above the heart—known as the spinnaker sign—indicative of pneumomediastinum and affirming the findings and diagnosis made using the lung ultrasound (figure).
The patient was successfully weaned off respiratory support within 5 days and was allowed home after 8 days; no drainage was necessary.
We believe that—based upon the current literature and our findings in this case—a lung ultrasound can differentiate between some of the key causes of acute respiratory conditions in the neonate—namely, respiratory distress syndrome, transient tachypnoea of the newborn, pneumonia, pneumothorax, and pneumomediastinum. We would like to propose that the distinctive finding of a set of horizontal hyperechogenic reflections below the thymus—indicating pneumomediastinum—be known as the stairway sign.
Pneumomediastinum after birth is an uncommon condition—defined as air trapped in the mediastinum—presenting with signs of respiratory distress, uneven chest expansion, and muffling of cardiac sounds. Resolution usually occurs within 1–2 days and, in most cases, no specific treatment is needed. Risk factors associated with pneumomediastinum include prematurity, the need for positive pressure ventilation, pneumonia, and meconium aspiration. Patients need to be closely observed—depending upon the severity of the air leak and the ability of the infant to compensate for the respiratory distress—due to the risk of further deterioration, and possible pneumothorax or emphysema.

A 52-year-old builder with a 6-year history of neck pain and dysphagia was referred to our rheumatology unit by a spinal neurosurgeon who was concerned the patient might have axial spondyloarthritis.
A review of the patient's history found that at age 45 years, he had been referred to the spinal surgeons; an x-ray and CT scan of the cervical spine showed osteophytosis at C5-C7 (figure). The radiologist had noted elongation of the styloid processes and calcification of the stylohyoid ligaments, suggestive of Eagle's syndrome.
Aged 47 years, new osteophytosis within mid and lower cervical spine were noted after the patient had a work-related injury.
Aged 50 years, the patient had been referred to both the neurosurgeons due to persistent neck symptoms, and to the Ear, Nose, and Throat (ENT) department because of ongoing dysphagia. The conclusion at that time was that the main reason for his dysphagia was laryngospasm and that his cervical osteophytosis was unlikely to be a contributing factor.
Additionally, the patient had a history of long-standing rosacea and folliculitis, a metallic heart valve, hypertension, a stroke, and gout; he was prescribed medication which included warfarin, atorvastatin, bisoprolol, allopurinol, and isotretinoin. The prescription of isotretinoin, which had been started 13 years earlier to treat the rosacea, necessitated the patient remaining under the care of the dermatology department. He was an ex-smoker.
On examination, we found the patient to be well; his BMI was 29·0 kg/m2 (typical range 18·5–24·9), his blood pressure was 142/82 mm Hg, and he had limited movement in his cervical spine, brisk reflexes, and some paraesthesia, which we considered to be related to his previous stroke. The patient had reduced movement in his left hip—consistent with advanced osteoarthritis. He had no skin rashes or peripheral synovitis.
Laboratory investigations found a typical C-reactive protein concentration (<0·5 mg/dL; normal range 0·3–1·0), total vitamin D concentration of 85 nmol/L (typical range 50–100), alkaline phosphatase concentration of 79 IU/L (typical range 30–130), parathyroid hormone concentration of 7·2 pmol/L (typical range 1·5–7·6), HbA1c concentration of 35 mmol/mol (typical range 20–41), estimated glomerular filtration rate of 82 mL/min/1·73 m2, and triglycerides concentration of 1·2 mmol/L (typical range <2·3). Testing for HLA-B27 was negative.
A review of previous x-rays showed progressive ossification of the patient's cervical spine, which impinged on adjacent soft-tissue structures—including the oesophagus (figure). An MRI confirmed multi-level spinal ossification consistent with a degenerative, rather than an inflammatory process; no evidence of axial spondyloarthritis or radiographic axial spondyloarthritis—which is also termed ankylosing spondylitis—was seen.
Furthermore, even though our patient had features of the metabolic syndrome—associated with diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis—the relatively young age at which his symptoms began, and the speed of progression of the symptoms indicated an alternative diagnosis. Considering the x-ray and MRI findings together with the absence of any markers of inflammation—ruling out diagnoses of axial spondyloarthritis or any other inflammatory arthropathies—and the history of isotretinoin treatment, we concluded the patient had retinoid-induced diffuse skeletal hyperostosis. We recommended that the isotretinoin was stopped, and the patient was again referred to the spinal surgeons for consideration of surgery to improve his dysphagia. input:
A 52-year-old builder with a 6-year history of neck pain and dysphagia was referred to our rheumatology unit by a spinal neurosurgeon who was concerned the patient might have axial spondyloarthritis.
A review of the patient's history found that at age 45 years, he had been referred to the spinal surgeons; an x-ray and CT scan of the cervical spine showed osteophytosis at C5-C7 (figure). The radiologist had noted elongation of the styloid processes and calcification of the stylohyoid ligaments, suggestive of Eagle's syndrome.
Aged 47 years, new osteophytosis within mid and lower cervical spine were noted after the patient had a work-related injury.
Aged 50 years, the patient had been referred to both the neurosurgeons due to persistent neck symptoms, and to the Ear, Nose, and Throat (ENT) department because of ongoing dysphagia. The conclusion at that time was that the main reason for his dysphagia was laryngospasm and that his cervical osteophytosis was unlikely to be a contributing factor.
Additionally, the patient had a history of long-standing rosacea and folliculitis, a metallic heart valve, hypertension, a stroke, and gout; he was prescribed medication which included warfarin, atorvastatin, bisoprolol, allopurinol, and isotretinoin. The prescription of isotretinoin, which had been started 13 years earlier to treat the rosacea, necessitated the patient remaining under the care of the dermatology department. He was an ex-smoker.
On examination, we found the patient to be well; his BMI was 29·0 kg/m2 (typical range 18·5–24·9), his blood pressure was 142/82 mm Hg, and he had limited movement in his cervical spine, brisk reflexes, and some paraesthesia, which we considered to be related to his previous stroke. The patient had reduced movement in his left hip—consistent with advanced osteoarthritis. He had no skin rashes or peripheral synovitis.
Laboratory investigations found a typical C-reactive protein concentration (<0·5 mg/dL; normal range 0·3–1·0), total vitamin D concentration of 85 nmol/L (typical range 50–100), alkaline phosphatase concentration of 79 IU/L (typical range 30–130), parathyroid hormone concentration of 7·2 pmol/L (typical range 1·5–7·6), HbA1c concentration of 35 mmol/mol (typical range 20–41), estimated glomerular filtration rate of 82 mL/min/1·73 m2, and triglycerides concentration of 1·2 mmol/L (typical range <2·3). Testing for HLA-B27 was negative.
A review of previous x-rays showed progressive ossification of the patient's cervical spine, which impinged on adjacent soft-tissue structures—including the oesophagus (figure). An MRI confirmed multi-level spinal ossification consistent with a degenerative, rather than an inflammatory process; no evidence of axial spondyloarthritis or radiographic axial spondyloarthritis—which is also termed ankylosing spondylitis—was seen.
Furthermore, even though our patient had features of the metabolic syndrome—associated with diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis—the relatively young age at which his symptoms began, and the speed of progression of the symptoms indicated an alternative diagnosis. Considering the x-ray and MRI findings together with the absence of any markers of inflammation—ruling out diagnoses of axial spondyloarthritis or any other inflammatory arthropathies—and the history of isotretinoin treatment, we concluded the patient had retinoid-induced diffuse skeletal hyperostosis. We recommended that the isotretinoin was stopped, and the patient was again referred to the spinal surgeons for consideration of surgery to improve his dysphagia. At follow-up aged 53 years the patient was seen again by the ENT and spinal neurosurgeons and was listed for excision of his cervical osteophytosis.
Arthralgia and new bone formation have been recognised as side-effects of isotretinoin since it was first licensed for treatment of disorders of keratinisation—including severe cystic acne. Osteophytes involving the anterior margin of the cervical vertebrae may cause dysphonia, dyspnoea, or dysphagia. Clinicians need to be aware that the effects of retinoid-associated skeletal toxicity can be seen within 6 months of initiating treatment—although prompt withdrawal of the drug can prevent irreversible ossification.

A 67-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 2-month history of a low-grade fever and progressive weakness in the muscles of his face. He also reported drooling and slurred speech.He had a 10-year history of hypertension that was treated with antihypertensives.
On examination we found that he could not close his eyes, wrinkle his forehead, or raise his eyebrows and that the nasolabial folds of his face were flattened—indicating a bilateral lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy (figure). We found no other abnormalities on physical examination.
Laboratory investigations showed a mild anaemia, with a haemoglobin concentration of 11·6 g/dL, a leucocytosis of 17·2 × 109 per L, and a monocytosis of 2·14 × 109 per L. The patient's erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 22 mm/h and C-reactive protein concentration was 10 mg/L. Infectious diseases—including Lyme disease, HIV, syphilis, and herpes zoster—were excluded. Neoplasms—particularly head and neck tumours—were ruled out, and granulomatous diseases, like sarcoidosis, and metabolic and autoimmune diseases—including Guillain–Barré syndrome, systemic autoimmune diseases, and vasculitis were excluded.
A peripheral blood smear showed excessive monocytosis with left shift, dysplastic granulocytes, promonocytes, and blasts (figure). A bone marrow aspiration confirmed the diagnosis of chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia (CMML).
Cytogenetic analysis found trisomy of chromosome 8; DNA sequencing showed mutations in the RUNX1, SF3B1, and CBL genes. Nerve conduction studies found an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy—affecting the facial nerves and the peripheral nerves in the patient's arms and legs. We decided to treat the patient using corticosteroids and intravenous immunoglobulin. He remained afebrile with no improvement of his facial nerve palsy. We decided against using hypomethylating agents because in Europe azacitidine has been approved only for CMML patients with white blood cell counts of less than 13 × 109 per L.
2 months later, while still on steroid therapy, the patient was admitted with a fever, aphthous stomatitis, and arthralgias. Physical examination found an aphthous ulceration on the right side of the tongue, synovitis of the wrists and right knee, and bilateral facial nerve palsy. Soon after admission, the patient complained of an acute onset abdominal pain; he was hypotensive and tachycardic, and had tenderness and rigidity of the right upper quadrant. Multiphase CT scan of the abdomen showed a large haematoma of the right kidney with active bleeding; he also had multiple disseminated microaneurysms—up to 1 cm in diameter—of both interlobar arteries, indicative of a medium-vessel vasculitis (figure). He underwent urgent right radical nephrectomy.
Histology showed a focal necrotising arteritis with mixed inflammatory infiltration and fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls and intramural thrombosis of medium-size vessels—resembling polyarteritis nodosa. We decided to start him on cyclophosphamide and continue with the steroids: this led to a significant decline of acute phase reactants. 10 days later, an aneurysm in the remaining kidney ruptured and we had to do a further radical nephrectomy, resulting in the patient requiring haemodialysis. However, 3 weeks after the cyclophosphamide was started, we noted a significant improvement in his facial nerve palsies.
CMML is a myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative neoplasm, sometimes associated with extrahaematological manifestations: autoimmune inflammatory phenomena can cause a systemic vasculitis, connective tissue diseases, relapsing polychondritis, and a seronegative arthritis. High clinical suspicion for such atypical manifestations should be considered in all patients with CMML (video).

A 52-year-old builder with a 6-year history of neck pain and dysphagia was referred to our rheumatology unit by a spinal neurosurgeon who was concerned the patient might have axial spondyloarthritis.
A review of the patient's history found that at age 45 years, he had been referred to the spinal surgeons; an x-ray and CT scan of the cervical spine showed osteophytosis at C5-C7 (figure). The radiologist had noted elongation of the styloid processes and calcification of the stylohyoid ligaments, suggestive of Eagle's syndrome.
Aged 47 years, new osteophytosis within mid and lower cervical spine were noted after the patient had a work-related injury.
Aged 50 years, the patient had been referred to both the neurosurgeons due to persistent neck symptoms, and to the Ear, Nose, and Throat (ENT) department because of ongoing dysphagia. The conclusion at that time was that the main reason for his dysphagia was laryngospasm and that his cervical osteophytosis was unlikely to be a contributing factor.
Additionally, the patient had a history of long-standing rosacea and folliculitis, a metallic heart valve, hypertension, a stroke, and gout; he was prescribed medication which included warfarin, atorvastatin, bisoprolol, allopurinol, and isotretinoin. The prescription of isotretinoin, which had been started 13 years earlier to treat the rosacea, necessitated the patient remaining under the care of the dermatology department. He was an ex-smoker.
On examination, we found the patient to be well; his BMI was 29·0 kg/m2 (typical range 18·5–24·9), his blood pressure was 142/82 mm Hg, and he had limited movement in his cervical spine, brisk reflexes, and some paraesthesia, which we considered to be related to his previous stroke. The patient had reduced movement in his left hip—consistent with advanced osteoarthritis. He had no skin rashes or peripheral synovitis.
Laboratory investigations found a typical C-reactive protein concentration (<0·5 mg/dL; normal range 0·3–1·0), total vitamin D concentration of 85 nmol/L (typical range 50–100), alkaline phosphatase concentration of 79 IU/L (typical range 30–130), parathyroid hormone concentration of 7·2 pmol/L (typical range 1·5–7·6), HbA1c concentration of 35 mmol/mol (typical range 20–41), estimated glomerular filtration rate of 82 mL/min/1·73 m2, and triglycerides concentration of 1·2 mmol/L (typical range <2·3). Testing for HLA-B27 was negative.
A review of previous x-rays showed progressive ossification of the patient's cervical spine, which impinged on adjacent soft-tissue structures—including the oesophagus (figure). An MRI confirmed multi-level spinal ossification consistent with a degenerative, rather than an inflammatory process; no evidence of axial spondyloarthritis or radiographic axial spondyloarthritis—which is also termed ankylosing spondylitis—was seen.
Furthermore, even though our patient had features of the metabolic syndrome—associated with diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis—the relatively young age at which his symptoms began, and the speed of progression of the symptoms indicated an alternative diagnosis. Considering the x-ray and MRI findings together with the absence of any markers of inflammation—ruling out diagnoses of axial spondyloarthritis or any other inflammatory arthropathies—and the history of isotretinoin treatment, we concluded the patient had retinoid-induced diffuse skeletal hyperostosis. We recommended that the isotretinoin was stopped, and the patient was again referred to the spinal surgeons for consideration of surgery to improve his dysphagia. At follow-up aged 53 years the patient was seen again by the ENT and spinal neurosurgeons and was listed for excision of his cervical osteophytosis.
Arthralgia and new bone formation have been recognised as side-effects of isotretinoin since it was first licensed for treatment of disorders of keratinisation—including severe cystic acne. Osteophytes involving the anterior margin of the cervical vertebrae may cause dysphonia, dyspnoea, or dysphagia. Clinicians need to be aware that the effects of retinoid-associated skeletal toxicity can be seen within 6 months of initiating treatment—although prompt withdrawal of the drug can prevent irreversible ossification.

A 67-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 2-month history of a low-grade fever and progressive weakness in the muscles of his face. He also reported drooling and slurred speech.He had a 10-year history of hypertension that was treated with antihypertensives.
On examination we found that he could not close his eyes, wrinkle his forehead, or raise his eyebrows and that the nasolabial folds of his face were flattened—indicating a bilateral lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy (figure). We found no other abnormalities on physical examination.
Laboratory investigations showed a mild anaemia, with a haemoglobin concentration of 11·6 g/dL, a leucocytosis of 17·2 × 109 per L, and a monocytosis of 2·14 × 109 per L. The patient's erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 22 mm/h and C-reactive protein concentration was 10 mg/L. Infectious diseases—including Lyme disease, HIV, syphilis, and herpes zoster—were excluded. Neoplasms—particularly head and neck tumours—were ruled out, and granulomatous diseases, like sarcoidosis, and metabolic and autoimmune diseases—including Guillain–Barré syndrome, systemic autoimmune diseases, and vasculitis were excluded.
A peripheral blood smear showed excessive monocytosis with left shift, dysplastic granulocytes, promonocytes, and blasts (figure). A bone marrow aspiration confirmed the diagnosis of chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia (CMML).
Cytogenetic analysis found trisomy of chromosome 8; DNA sequencing showed mutations in the RUNX1, SF3B1, and CBL genes. Nerve conduction studies found an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy—affecting the facial nerves and the peripheral nerves in the patient's arms and legs. We decided to treat the patient using corticosteroids and intravenous immunoglobulin. He remained afebrile with no improvement of his facial nerve palsy. We decided against using hypomethylating agents because in Europe azacitidine has been approved only for CMML patients with white blood cell counts of less than 13 × 109 per L.
2 months later, while still on steroid therapy, the patient was admitted with a fever, aphthous stomatitis, and arthralgias. Physical examination found an aphthous ulceration on the right side of the tongue, synovitis of the wrists and right knee, and bilateral facial nerve palsy. Soon after admission, the patient complained of an acute onset abdominal pain; he was hypotensive and tachycardic, and had tenderness and rigidity of the right upper quadrant. Multiphase CT scan of the abdomen showed a large haematoma of the right kidney with active bleeding; he also had multiple disseminated microaneurysms—up to 1 cm in diameter—of both interlobar arteries, indicative of a medium-vessel vasculitis (figure). He underwent urgent right radical nephrectomy.
Histology showed a focal necrotising arteritis with mixed inflammatory infiltration and fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls and intramural thrombosis of medium-size vessels—resembling polyarteritis nodosa. We decided to start him on cyclophosphamide and continue with the steroids: this led to a significant decline of acute phase reactants. 10 days later, an aneurysm in the remaining kidney ruptured and we had to do a further radical nephrectomy, resulting in the patient requiring haemodialysis. However, 3 weeks after the cyclophosphamide was started, we noted a significant improvement in his facial nerve palsies.
CMML is a myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative neoplasm, sometimes associated with extrahaematological manifestations: autoimmune inflammatory phenomena can cause a systemic vasculitis, connective tissue diseases, relapsing polychondritis, and a seronegative arthritis. High clinical suspicion for such atypical manifestations should be considered in all patients with CMML (video).

A 67-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 2-month history of a low-grade fever and progressive weakness in the muscles of his face. He also reported drooling and slurred speech.He had a 10-year history of hypertension that was treated with antihypertensives.
On examination we found that he could not close his eyes, wrinkle his forehead, or raise his eyebrows and that the nasolabial folds of his face were flattened—indicating a bilateral lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy (figure). We found no other abnormalities on physical examination.
Laboratory investigations showed a mild anaemia, with a haemoglobin concentration of 11·6 g/dL, a leucocytosis of 17·2 × 109 per L, and a monocytosis of 2·14 × 109 per L. The patient's erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 22 mm/h and C-reactive protein concentration was 10 mg/L. Infectious diseases—including Lyme disease, HIV, syphilis, and herpes zoster—were excluded. Neoplasms—particularly head and neck tumours—were ruled out, and granulomatous diseases, like sarcoidosis, and metabolic and autoimmune diseases—including Guillain–Barré syndrome, systemic autoimmune diseases, and vasculitis were excluded.
A peripheral blood smear showed excessive monocytosis with left shift, dysplastic granulocytes, promonocytes, and blasts (figure). A bone marrow aspiration confirmed the diagnosis of chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia (CMML).
Cytogenetic analysis found trisomy of chromosome 8; DNA sequencing showed mutations in the RUNX1, SF3B1, and CBL genes. Nerve conduction studies found an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy—affecting the facial nerves and the peripheral nerves in the patient's arms and legs. We decided to treat the patient using corticosteroids and intravenous immunoglobulin. He remained afebrile with no improvement of his facial nerve palsy. We decided against using hypomethylating agents because in Europe azacitidine has been approved only for CMML patients with white blood cell counts of less than 13 × 109 per L.
2 months later, while still on steroid therapy, the patient was admitted with a fever, aphthous stomatitis, and arthralgias. Physical examination found an aphthous ulceration on the right side of the tongue, synovitis of the wrists and right knee, and bilateral facial nerve palsy. Soon after admission, the patient complained of an acute onset abdominal pain; he was hypotensive and tachycardic, and had tenderness and rigidity of the right upper quadrant. Multiphase CT scan of the abdomen showed a large haematoma of the right kidney with active bleeding; he also had multiple disseminated microaneurysms—up to 1 cm in diameter—of both interlobar arteries, indicative of a medium-vessel vasculitis (figure). He underwent urgent right radical nephrectomy.
Histology showed a focal necrotising arteritis with mixed inflammatory infiltration and fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls and intramural thrombosis of medium-size vessels—resembling polyarteritis nodosa. We decided to start him on cyclophosphamide and continue with the steroids: this led to a significant decline of acute phase reactants. 10 days later, an aneurysm in the remaining kidney ruptured and we had to do a further radical nephrectomy, resulting in the patient requiring haemodialysis. However, 3 weeks after the cyclophosphamide was started, we noted a significant improvement in his facial nerve palsies.
CMML is a myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative neoplasm, sometimes associated with extrahaematological manifestations: autoimmune inflammatory phenomena can cause a systemic vasculitis, connective tissue diseases, relapsing polychondritis, and a seronegative arthritis. High clinical suspicion for such atypical manifestations should be considered in all patients with CMML (video).

A 66-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 5-year history of recurrent episodes of epigastric burning pain, bloating, and constipation. In the past 3 months, the patient reported that his symptoms had resulted in him losing 4·5 kg in weight.He had a medical history of hypertension, but reported he was not taking any medications—specifically aspirin or any non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
On examination the patient was generally well; his blood pressure was 147/91 mm Hg, and his pulse rate was 95 beats per min. The patient had mild epigastric and right upper quadrant abdominal distention; hypoactive bowel sounds were heard in the right upper quadrant region.
Laboratory investigations found a positive test for Helicobacter pylori using the 13C-urea breath test.
CT of the patient's abdomen showed gastric dilation above the junction between the gastric antrum and the duodenum where the calibre of the gastric antrum reduced substantially in diameter (figure).
The patient initially underwent gastric decompression using a nasogastric tube; he was then prescribed a 14-day course of H pylori triple therapy—consisting of a proton pump inhibitor (pantoprazole), and the antibiotics clarithromycin and amoxicillin.
An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, done for further diagnostic evaluation, showed gastric stenosis and chronic gastritis. Immunohistopathological examination of a sample of biopsied tissue section confirmed the presence of H pylori with no evidence of gastric dysplasia.
The patient's symptoms were alleviated within 2 days, and after a successful oral food challenge with a regular diet, he was allowed home.
At 3-month follow-up, the patient remained asymptomatic; a repeat upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed stenotic gastric regions—without any visible obstruction—and chronic inactive gastritis; further immunohistopathological examination of a sample of biopsied tissue was negative for H pylori, indicating successful eradication. The patient will be followed up episodically for the foreseeable future primarily to monitor for signs of gastric outlet obstruction recurrence.
Gastric outlet obstruction occurs in both acute and chronic peptic ulcer disease. Repeated episodes of acute peptic ulcer disease can cause progressive stenosis of the gastric antrum—as probably occurred in our patient—and subsequent gastric outlet obstruction.
Risk factors for peptic ulcer disease include poor diet and hygiene, reduced physical activity, use of NSAIDs and infection with H pylori. Notably, recurrent rates of obstruction due to peptic ulcer disease are variable; and interestingly, rates appear reduced in cases associated with H pylori. Endoscopic balloon dilation of the pylorus or more invasive surgical intervention is reserved for cases of gastric outlet obstruction that are not resolved with medical treatments.
Gastric outlet obstruction is a rare, but important, complication of peptic ulcer disease and identification of any risk factors—specifically infection with H pylori—aids diagnosis and treatment regimens.

A 66-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 5-year history of recurrent episodes of epigastric burning pain, bloating, and constipation. In the past 3 months, the patient reported that his symptoms had resulted in him losing 4·5 kg in weight.He had a medical history of hypertension, but reported he was not taking any medications—specifically aspirin or any non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
On examination the patient was generally well; his blood pressure was 147/91 mm Hg, and his pulse rate was 95 beats per min. The patient had mild epigastric and right upper quadrant abdominal distention; hypoactive bowel sounds were heard in the right upper quadrant region.
Laboratory investigations found a positive test for Helicobacter pylori using the 13C-urea breath test.
CT of the patient's abdomen showed gastric dilation above the junction between the gastric antrum and the duodenum where the calibre of the gastric antrum reduced substantially in diameter (figure).
The patient initially underwent gastric decompression using a nasogastric tube; he was then prescribed a 14-day course of H pylori triple therapy—consisting of a proton pump inhibitor (pantoprazole), and the antibiotics clarithromycin and amoxicillin.
An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, done for further diagnostic evaluation, showed gastric stenosis and chronic gastritis. Immunohistopathological examination of a sample of biopsied tissue section confirmed the presence of H pylori with no evidence of gastric dysplasia.
The patient's symptoms were alleviated within 2 days, and after a successful oral food challenge with a regular diet, he was allowed home.
At 3-month follow-up, the patient remained asymptomatic; a repeat upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed stenotic gastric regions—without any visible obstruction—and chronic inactive gastritis; further immunohistopathological examination of a sample of biopsied tissue was negative for H pylori, indicating successful eradication. The patient will be followed up episodically for the foreseeable future primarily to monitor for signs of gastric outlet obstruction recurrence.
Gastric outlet obstruction occurs in both acute and chronic peptic ulcer disease. Repeated episodes of acute peptic ulcer disease can cause progressive stenosis of the gastric antrum—as probably occurred in our patient—and subsequent gastric outlet obstruction.
Risk factors for peptic ulcer disease include poor diet and hygiene, reduced physical activity, use of NSAIDs and infection with H pylori. Notably, recurrent rates of obstruction due to peptic ulcer disease are variable; and interestingly, rates appear reduced in cases associated with H pylori. Endoscopic balloon dilation of the pylorus or more invasive surgical intervention is reserved for cases of gastric outlet obstruction that are not resolved with medical treatments.
Gastric outlet obstruction is a rare, but important, complication of peptic ulcer disease and identification of any risk factors—specifically infection with H pylori—aids diagnosis and treatment regimens.

A 66-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 5-year history of recurrent episodes of epigastric burning pain, bloating, and constipation. In the past 3 months, the patient reported that his symptoms had resulted in him losing 4·5 kg in weight.He had a medical history of hypertension, but reported he was not taking any medications—specifically aspirin or any non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
On examination the patient was generally well; his blood pressure was 147/91 mm Hg, and his pulse rate was 95 beats per min. The patient had mild epigastric and right upper quadrant abdominal distention; hypoactive bowel sounds were heard in the right upper quadrant region.
Laboratory investigations found a positive test for Helicobacter pylori using the 13C-urea breath test.
CT of the patient's abdomen showed gastric dilation above the junction between the gastric antrum and the duodenum where the calibre of the gastric antrum reduced substantially in diameter (figure).
The patient initially underwent gastric decompression using a nasogastric tube; he was then prescribed a 14-day course of H pylori triple therapy—consisting of a proton pump inhibitor (pantoprazole), and the antibiotics clarithromycin and amoxicillin.
An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, done for further diagnostic evaluation, showed gastric stenosis and chronic gastritis. Immunohistopathological examination of a sample of biopsied tissue section confirmed the presence of H pylori with no evidence of gastric dysplasia.
The patient's symptoms were alleviated within 2 days, and after a successful oral food challenge with a regular diet, he was allowed home.
At 3-month follow-up, the patient remained asymptomatic; a repeat upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed stenotic gastric regions—without any visible obstruction—and chronic inactive gastritis; further immunohistopathological examination of a sample of biopsied tissue was negative for H pylori, indicating successful eradication. The patient will be followed up episodically for the foreseeable future primarily to monitor for signs of gastric outlet obstruction recurrence.
Gastric outlet obstruction occurs in both acute and chronic peptic ulcer disease. Repeated episodes of acute peptic ulcer disease can cause progressive stenosis of the gastric antrum—as probably occurred in our patient—and subsequent gastric outlet obstruction.
Risk factors for peptic ulcer disease include poor diet and hygiene, reduced physical activity, use of NSAIDs and infection with H pylori. Notably, recurrent rates of obstruction due to peptic ulcer disease are variable; and interestingly, rates appear reduced in cases associated with H pylori. Endoscopic balloon dilation of the pylorus or more invasive surgical intervention is reserved for cases of gastric outlet obstruction that are not resolved with medical treatments.
Gastric outlet obstruction is a rare, but important, complication of peptic ulcer disease and identification of any risk factors—specifically infection with H pylori—aids diagnosis and treatment regimens.

Drosophila is its vector host, and it tends to infect individuals residing in poor communities in Asia, particularly in China.

A 57-year-old man with a 2-day history of a fever and sudden onset of bilateral hearing loss was admitted to our local infectious diseases unit. The patient had no medical history.
On examination, the patient's temperature was 39·0°C, pulse was 65 beats per min, blood pressure 130/80 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation was 97%. He had rigor nucalis and Kernig's sign was present.
Laboratory investigations found a white blood cell count of 26·31 × 103 per μL (typical range 4·0–11·0) and platelet count of 150 × 103 per μL (typical range 140–440). A lumbar puncture showed turbid cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with 4300 × 106 white blood cells per L (typical range <5 × 106 white blood cells per L), mainly neutrophils; raised protein concentration of 391·6 mg/L (typical range 15·0–45·0); and an elevated lactate concentration (13·9 mmol/L; typical range 1·2–2·4), indicative of a bacterial meningitis.
The patient was treated empirically with intravenous ceftriaxone at a dose of 2 g every 12 h. Real-time PCR testing of a sample of CSF was positive for serotype B Neisseria meningitidis.
Contrast-enhanced MRIs showed pia-subarachnoid space enhancement of the frontal lobes; purulent material in the lateral ventricles, basal cisterns, and around the cerebral sulci and faint enhancement of the cochleae and inner ears was also seen (appendix).
Audiological tests—including auditory brainstem evoked potentials—showed that the patient had bilateral anacusis. During his stay in the hospital, the antibiotic treatment was changed to levofloxacin 500 mg every 12 h because of a transaminitis. The patient was allowed home after 12 days with planned rehabilitation with cochlear implantation.
1 month after leaving hospital, the patient attended our unit and had simultaneous bilateral cochlear implantation (Advanced Bionics CI-1601-05, Valencia, CA, USA). The intervention bilaterally involved mastoidectomy, posterior tympanotomy, and insertion of the cochlear implant array through the cochleostomy—at the level of the round window—into the tympanic scale of the cochlea. The intraoperative electrophysiological measurements showed a correct function of both cochlear implants, and the postoperative course was uneventful. Skull x-rays, on the first postoperative day to check the placement of the cochlear implants, showed both arrays were correctly located within the cochleae (figure).
At a follow-up appointment 9 months after the operation, the cochlear implants provided the patient with a pure-tone average of 35 dB—indicating mild hearing loss. Speech audiometry found a speech discrimination score of 100% at 50 dB (typically in people with normal hearing the score is 100% at 30 dB).
Bacterial meningitis can cause acquired profound sensorineural hearing loss—especially in children—with permanent hearing loss occurring in up to 35% of patients after the infection. The risk of deafness after meningitis varies depending upon the cause of the infection: with Streptococcus pneumoniae the risk is 22% compared with 8% with N. meningitidis. Deafness results after spread of the infection from the meninges to perilymphatic spaces of the inner ear. Although rarely described in adults with profound sensorineural hearing loss after bacterial meningitis, simultaneous bilateral cochlear implantation is feasible and clinically effective, providing good functional results with few major complications—as demonstrated in our patient. Compared with sequential implantation, simultaneous implantation may reduce the number of hospital admissions and operations, and the time needed to regain binaural hearing.

A 57-year-old man with a 2-day history of a fever and sudden onset of bilateral hearing loss was admitted to our local infectious diseases unit. The patient had no medical history.
On examination, the patient's temperature was 39·0°C, pulse was 65 beats per min, blood pressure 130/80 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation was 97%. He had rigor nucalis and Kernig's sign was present.
Laboratory investigations found a white blood cell count of 26·31 × 103 per μL (typical range 4·0–11·0) and platelet count of 150 × 103 per μL (typical range 140–440). A lumbar puncture showed turbid cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with 4300 × 106 white blood cells per L (typical range <5 × 106 white blood cells per L), mainly neutrophils; raised protein concentration of 391·6 mg/L (typical range 15·0–45·0); and an elevated lactate concentration (13·9 mmol/L; typical range 1·2–2·4), indicative of a bacterial meningitis.
The patient was treated empirically with intravenous ceftriaxone at a dose of 2 g every 12 h. Real-time PCR testing of a sample of CSF was positive for serotype B Neisseria meningitidis.
Contrast-enhanced MRIs showed pia-subarachnoid space enhancement of the frontal lobes; purulent material in the lateral ventricles, basal cisterns, and around the cerebral sulci and faint enhancement of the cochleae and inner ears was also seen (appendix).
Audiological tests—including auditory brainstem evoked potentials—showed that the patient had bilateral anacusis. During his stay in the hospital, the antibiotic treatment was changed to levofloxacin 500 mg every 12 h because of a transaminitis. The patient was allowed home after 12 days with planned rehabilitation with cochlear implantation.
1 month after leaving hospital, the patient attended our unit and had simultaneous bilateral cochlear implantation (Advanced Bionics CI-1601-05, Valencia, CA, USA). The intervention bilaterally involved mastoidectomy, posterior tympanotomy, and insertion of the cochlear implant array through the cochleostomy—at the level of the round window—into the tympanic scale of the cochlea. The intraoperative electrophysiological measurements showed a correct function of both cochlear implants, and the postoperative course was uneventful. Skull x-rays, on the first postoperative day to check the placement of the cochlear implants, showed both arrays were correctly located within the cochleae (figure).
At a follow-up appointment 9 months after the operation, the cochlear implants provided the patient with a pure-tone average of 35 dB—indicating mild hearing loss. Speech audiometry found a speech discrimination score of 100% at 50 dB (typically in people with normal hearing the score is 100% at 30 dB).
Bacterial meningitis can cause acquired profound sensorineural hearing loss—especially in children—with permanent hearing loss occurring in up to 35% of patients after the infection. The risk of deafness after meningitis varies depending upon the cause of the infection: with Streptococcus pneumoniae the risk is 22% compared with 8% with N. meningitidis. Deafness results after spread of the infection from the meninges to perilymphatic spaces of the inner ear. Although rarely described in adults with profound sensorineural hearing loss after bacterial meningitis, simultaneous bilateral cochlear implantation is feasible and clinically effective, providing good functional results with few major complications—as demonstrated in our patient. Compared with sequential implantation, simultaneous implantation may reduce the number of hospital admissions and operations, and the time needed to regain binaural hearing.

A 57-year-old man with a 2-day history of a fever and sudden onset of bilateral hearing loss was admitted to our local infectious diseases unit. The patient had no medical history.
On examination, the patient's temperature was 39·0°C, pulse was 65 beats per min, blood pressure 130/80 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation was 97%. He had rigor nucalis and Kernig's sign was present.
Laboratory investigations found a white blood cell count of 26·31 × 103 per μL (typical range 4·0–11·0) and platelet count of 150 × 103 per μL (typical range 140–440). A lumbar puncture showed turbid cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with 4300 × 106 white blood cells per L (typical range <5 × 106 white blood cells per L), mainly neutrophils; raised protein concentration of 391·6 mg/L (typical range 15·0–45·0); and an elevated lactate concentration (13·9 mmol/L; typical range 1·2–2·4), indicative of a bacterial meningitis.
The patient was treated empirically with intravenous ceftriaxone at a dose of 2 g every 12 h. Real-time PCR testing of a sample of CSF was positive for serotype B Neisseria meningitidis.
Contrast-enhanced MRIs showed pia-subarachnoid space enhancement of the frontal lobes; purulent material in the lateral ventricles, basal cisterns, and around the cerebral sulci and faint enhancement of the cochleae and inner ears was also seen (appendix).
Audiological tests—including auditory brainstem evoked potentials—showed that the patient had bilateral anacusis. During his stay in the hospital, the antibiotic treatment was changed to levofloxacin 500 mg every 12 h because of a transaminitis. The patient was allowed home after 12 days with planned rehabilitation with cochlear implantation.
1 month after leaving hospital, the patient attended our unit and had simultaneous bilateral cochlear implantation (Advanced Bionics CI-1601-05, Valencia, CA, USA). The intervention bilaterally involved mastoidectomy, posterior tympanotomy, and insertion of the cochlear implant array through the cochleostomy—at the level of the round window—into the tympanic scale of the cochlea. The intraoperative electrophysiological measurements showed a correct function of both cochlear implants, and the postoperative course was uneventful. Skull x-rays, on the first postoperative day to check the placement of the cochlear implants, showed both arrays were correctly located within the cochleae (figure).
At a follow-up appointment 9 months after the operation, the cochlear implants provided the patient with a pure-tone average of 35 dB—indicating mild hearing loss. Speech audiometry found a speech discrimination score of 100% at 50 dB (typically in people with normal hearing the score is 100% at 30 dB).
Bacterial meningitis can cause acquired profound sensorineural hearing loss—especially in children—with permanent hearing loss occurring in up to 35% of patients after the infection. The risk of deafness after meningitis varies depending upon the cause of the infection: with Streptococcus pneumoniae the risk is 22% compared with 8% with N. meningitidis. Deafness results after spread of the infection from the meninges to perilymphatic spaces of the inner ear. Although rarely described in adults with profound sensorineural hearing loss after bacterial meningitis, simultaneous bilateral cochlear implantation is feasible and clinically effective, providing good functional results with few major complications—as demonstrated in our patient. Compared with sequential implantation, simultaneous implantation may reduce the number of hospital admissions and operations, and the time needed to regain binaural hearing.

A 58-year-old man was admitted to our hospital with a 2-week history of persistent fever and pancytopenia. Physical examination showed no other abnormal findings. However, a septic screen isolated Mycobacterium abscessus from his blood and bone marrow. An 18fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT scan showed an area of increased uptake in the patient's prostate (figure). Prostate specific antigen was 8·06 ng/mL—previously, it had been measured and reported to be 0·8 ng/mL. A transrectal biopsy of his prostate showed granulomatous inflammation. Tissue cultures grew M abscessus. He said he had never had prostatic manipulation before. However, he had been previously diagnosed with benign prostatic enlargement and, 1 year before start of current symptoms, he had surgical resection of a neuroendocrine intestinal tumour.Recently, despite no evidence of residual disease, he had become worried about the possibility of recurrence. He decided to respond to an advertisement he had heard on the radio extolling the benefits of stem cell treatments—including cancer prevention or recurrence. A 58-year-old man was admitted to our hospital with a 2-week history of persistent fever and pancytopenia. Physical examination showed no other abnormal findings. However, a septic screen isolated Mycobacterium abscessus from his blood and bone marrow. An 18fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT scan showed an area of increased uptake in the patient's prostate (figure). Prostate specific antigen was 8·06 ng/mL—previously, it had been measured and reported to be 0·8 ng/mL. A transrectal biopsy of his prostate showed granulomatous inflammation. Tissue cultures grew M abscessus. He said he had never had prostatic manipulation before. However, he had been previously diagnosed with benign prostatic enlargement and, 1 year before start of current symptoms, he had surgical resection of a neuroendocrine intestinal tumour.Recently, despite no evidence of residual disease, he had become worried about the possibility of recurrence. He decided to respond to an advertisement he had heard on the radio extolling the benefits of stem cell treatments—including cancer prevention or recurrence. He said the clinic told him that the treatment was a type of “immunotherapy” that would allow his own stem cells to recognise any cancer cells as abnormal and destroy them. Further, he said they explained that the procedure entailed extracting his blood which would then be “stimulated to produce abundant stem cells” and these would then be injected into him intravenously.
A few hours after the infusion, the patient developed profuse vomiting and high-grade fever. He was given intravenous hydration and antibiotics, without resolution. He then attended our hospital.
Initially, we ruled out immunodeficiency—a hallmark of disseminated non-tuberculous mycobacteria—and only after repeat questioning of other possible risk factors did he disclose details of the “stem cell treatment”. We believe the “stem cells” had been contaminated with mycobacteria prior to being transfused into the patient. The infusion—into the blood stream—enabled dissemination and seeding of the mycobacteria in the previously diseased prostate.
The field of stem cell therapy has grown substantially. However, unregulated, unscientifically proven, and irresponsible use has also increased worldwide leading to rising numbers of cases of patients being infected from products contaminated with a variety of different bacteria including Escherichia coli, Enterococcus faecalis, Proteus mirabilis, Enterobacter cloacae, and Citrobacter freundii.

input: After 8 years of levothyroxine therapy, a male patient who underwent thyroidectomy at the age of 47 years for Graves' disease developed a 3 cm mass on his left hallux. The lesion was removed and diagnosed as localised myxoedema. Two years later, at the age of 57 years, the patient presented to our sarcoma service with a local recurrence. On physical examination, he had orbitopathy and no sign of pretibial myxoedema; the recurrence presented as a soft, mobile lump of the dorsal aspect of the hallux (figure). MRI showed a suprafascial mass with hyperintense T2-weighted signal and poorly defined margins (figure). To confirm the dermopathy and to exclude a soft tissue neoplasm, tissue slides of the previous surgery were reviewed. Haematoxylin and eosin stain showed a diffuse widening of the reticular dermis by a faintly basophilic acellular material, associated with isolated lymphocytes, that was dissecting collagen fibres and diffusing in perivascular and periadnexal spaces (figure). These microscopic features were consistent with an extracellular mucopolysaccharides deposit (ie, myxoedema). The original diagnosis was thus confirmed, the present lesion considered a recurrence, and the patient referred for conservative management.Graves' disease manifests with infiltrative orbitopathy in around 25% of patients, and with thyroid dermopathy in less than 5% of patients. Although usually located on the anterolateral aspect of the lower leg (pretibial myxoedema), it can occur elsewhere, especially after trauma. Dermopathy and orbitopathy can also occur after thyroid surgery, radioiodine therapy, or in clinically euthyroid patients. Myxoedema usually does not require treatment, and surgical excision is not advised due to recurrence (as in this patient). In case of cosmetic issues or interference with shoe fitting, topical glucocorticoids under occlusive dressing might be beneficial. Localised nodular myxoedema is a rare form of Graves' dermopathy, and although this mass-forming condition might cause concern about a soft tissue neoplasm, clinical presentation and histology warrant a conservative approach.

input: After 8 years of levothyroxine therapy, a male patient who underwent thyroidectomy at the age of 47 years for Graves' disease developed a 3 cm mass on his left hallux. The lesion was removed and diagnosed as localised myxoedema. Two years later, at the age of 57 years, the patient presented to our sarcoma service with a local recurrence. On physical examination, he had orbitopathy and no sign of pretibial myxoedema; the recurrence presented as a soft, mobile lump of the dorsal aspect of the hallux (figure). MRI showed a suprafascial mass with hyperintense T2-weighted signal and poorly defined margins (figure). To confirm the dermopathy and to exclude a soft tissue neoplasm, tissue slides of the previous surgery were reviewed. Haematoxylin and eosin stain showed a diffuse widening of the reticular dermis by a faintly basophilic acellular material, associated with isolated lymphocytes, that was dissecting collagen fibres and diffusing in perivascular and periadnexal spaces (figure). These microscopic features were consistent with an extracellular mucopolysaccharides deposit (ie, myxoedema). The original diagnosis was thus confirmed, the present lesion considered a recurrence, and the patient referred for conservative management.Graves' disease manifests with infiltrative orbitopathy in around 25% of patients, and with thyroid dermopathy in less than 5% of patients. Although usually located on the anterolateral aspect of the lower leg (pretibial myxoedema), it can occur elsewhere, especially after trauma. Dermopathy and orbitopathy can also occur after thyroid surgery, radioiodine therapy, or in clinically euthyroid patients. Myxoedema usually does not require treatment, and surgical excision is not advised due to recurrence (as in this patient). In case of cosmetic issues or interference with shoe fitting, topical glucocorticoids under occlusive dressing might be beneficial. Localised nodular myxoedema is a rare form of Graves' dermopathy, and although this mass-forming condition might cause concern about a soft tissue neoplasm, clinical presentation and histology warrant a conservative approach.

There was faecal loading without features of mechanical obstruction.The patient was thought to have a perforated peptic ulcer and was booked for emergency surgery. Diagnostic laparoscopy, however, revealed faeculent peritonitis and a sigmoid colonic perforation (figure C). Extensive laparoscopic washout, sigmoid colectomy, and colostomy formation were done. Postoperatively, the patient had no major complications. She underwent successful reversal of her stoma 9 months later.
Histopathology assessment showed an 11 mm, full-thickness, rounded antimesenteric defect with no evidence of diverticular disease or a malignant process. The diagnosis was consistent with stercoral perforation. Subsequent colonoscopy confirmed the absence of diverticula and malignancy in the remaining colon and rectum.
Approximately 15% of the population have constipation, although most improve with lifestyle measures and aperients. However, a rare and unusual life-threatening complication of chronic constipation is stercoral perforation. Stercoral perforation is the reported cause of 3·4% of colonic perforations. The pathology is characterised by an antimesenteric, round colonic perforation larger than 10 mm, faecal contamination exuding through the perforation, necrosis, and an inflammatory reaction around the perforation in the absence of tumours, diverticular disease, and trauma. Risk factors for stercoral perforation in patients with chronic constipation include older age (median age 62 years) and smoking. Stercoral perforation has a high mortality of approximately 30–40% and is a devastating sequela of chronic constipation. Many clinicians are sceptical of the diagnosis of stercoral perforation, citing other predisposing bowel pathology, such as diverticulitis, inflammatory bowel disease, and malignancy, as the main pathology, with inspissated stool as a disease-modifier. A 72-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with sudden onset crampy, generalised abdominal pain. She had a history of peptic ulcer disease, chronic constipation, and heavy smoking. She was tachycardic and febrile, and had generalised peritonism. Her white cell count was 13·6 × 109 cells per L. CT showed pneumoperitoneum in the upper abdomen and pelvic free fluid without oral contrast extravasation (figure A, B). There was faecal loading without features of mechanical obstruction.The patient was thought to have a perforated peptic ulcer and was booked for emergency surgery. Diagnostic laparoscopy, however, revealed faeculent peritonitis and a sigmoid colonic perforation (figure C). Extensive laparoscopic washout, sigmoid colectomy, and colostomy formation were done. Postoperatively, the patient had no major complications. She underwent successful reversal of her stoma 9 months later.
Histopathology assessment showed an 11 mm, full-thickness, rounded antimesenteric defect with no evidence of diverticular disease or a malignant process. The diagnosis was consistent with stercoral perforation. Subsequent colonoscopy confirmed the absence of diverticula and malignancy in the remaining colon and rectum.
Approximately 15% of the population have constipation, although most improve with lifestyle measures and aperients. However, a rare and unusual life-threatening complication of chronic constipation is stercoral perforation. Stercoral perforation is the reported cause of 3·4% of colonic perforations. The pathology is characterised by an antimesenteric, round colonic perforation larger than 10 mm, faecal contamination exuding through the perforation, necrosis, and an inflammatory reaction around the perforation in the absence of tumours, diverticular disease, and trauma. Risk factors for stercoral perforation in patients with chronic constipation include older age (median age 62 years) and smoking. Stercoral perforation has a high mortality of approximately 30–40% and is a devastating sequela of chronic constipation. Many clinicians are sceptical of the diagnosis of stercoral perforation, citing other predisposing bowel pathology, such as diverticulitis, inflammatory bowel disease, and malignancy, as the main pathology, with inspissated stool as a disease-modifier. However, this case suggests that stercoral perforation is a true entity independent of other disease processes.

A 4-year-old boy in a collision with a speeding motorcycle as he crossed the road was referred to our hospital from a peripheral clinic. The child had injuries to his left leg, left arm, chest, and head; there was no history of loss of consciousness.
On examination, the patient was distressed and fractious; his blood pressure was 90/65 mm Hg, pulse was 142 beats per min, and oxygen saturation was 89%; his injured leg and arm had been splinted. He was in pain and had difficulty breathing; his respiratory rate was 43 breaths per min; an intercostal drain, which did not appear to be working, had been inserted for a suspected haemothorax at the clinic. High-pitched bowel sounds were audible all over the left side of the patient's chest and an inward concavity of the anterior abdominal wall—known as a scaphoid abdomen—was seen; no tenderness was found on palpation of the abdomen.
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 9·9 g/dL (normal range 9·5–14); serum sodium concentration was 138·5 mmol/L (normal range 136·0–145·0) and potassium concentration was 3·7 mmol/L (normal range 3·5–5·2).
Chest x-rays showed an opacity of the left hemithorax, loss of normal contour of the left hemidiaphragm, a large intrathoracic air fluid level, and contralateral tracheal deviation indicating the presence of abdominal viscera in the chest (figure). We made a diagnosis of a traumatic diaphragmatic hernia. And because the patient showed both respiratory and haemodynamic compromise, he was supported by 2 L per min oxygen therapy delivered by face mask. He was given fentanyl and paracetamol, both intravenously, because of pain before being intubated in the operating theatre. An emergency thoracotomy was done through a posterolateral approach, during which we found a herniated stomach, spleen, and small bowel, and a central diaphragmatic rupture close to the pericardium and extending anteriorly. Additionally, owing to viability of the visceral contents, reduction and primary repair of the diaphragmatic rupture was done using a non-absorbable suture; he was transfused 150 mL of packed red blood cells intraoperatively.
The patient made a good recovery after the operation and stayed on the ward for a further 6 weeks for management of the femoral shaft fractures. The fractures of the left femur and left humerus were managed using skin traction and sling and swathe, respectively.
At 6 weeks, the child's respiratory and cardiovascular symptoms had abated and skin traction was discontinued and a cast applied for management of the femoral shaft fracture; the patient was then allowed home.
Traumatic diaphragmatic hernia is a rare complication of thoracoabdominal injury that is commonly incorrectly diagnosed yet it carries high mortality. Blunt traumatic diaphragmatic hernia occurs because of a sudden rise in intrabdominal pressure that causes a tear in the diaphragm, leading to the migration of intrabdominal viscera into the thoracic cavity; patients have varying degrees of respiratory and cardiovascular compromise.
The Carter's scheme categorises traumatic diaphragmatic hernia into acute, latent, and obstructive phases. In the acute phase the diagnosis is usually missed in up to 66% of cases due to associated abdominal and musculoskeletal injuries—as happened in our patient; the latent phase comprises non-specific respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms due to herniation of contents in the chest; and finally, the obstructive phase, which is associated with bowel obstruction that may proceed to ischaemia and strangulation.
A CT scan is the gold standard method for diagnosing traumatic diaphragmatic hernia but is not commonly available in many trauma centres in low-resource settings; a chest x-ray is more routinely done. While laparoscopic repair remains the recommended method of treating patients with traumatic diaphragmatic hernia, open surgical repair with or without a mesh is an option in haemodynamically unstable patients and in a low-resource setting where expertise and laparoscopic services are often unavailable. Clinicians assessing patients after traumatic injury should have a high index of suspicion for diaphragmatic hernia with attention paid to radiographic and chest auscultation findings to avoid complications of delayed diagnosis.

About 92% of these road-related fatalities occur in low-income and middle-income countries, for which African countries take the greatest burden due to the young population. Resulting morbidities and disabilities lead to an average 4–5% loss of gross domestic product due to loss of productivity of those killed or disabled.
Uganda—according to WHO—ranks among those countries with the highest traffic death rates at 29 deaths per 100 000 people compared to 24·1 deaths per 100 000 in the African region and globally to 18·1 deaths per 100 000 people.
According to the Uganda police annual traffic report, mortality from road crashes was as high as 19·4% (4806 deaths of 24 728 casualties of road traffic accidents) in 2023. Collisions with pedestrians—as in our patient—constitute 20% of all traffic crashes and 37% of all those pedestrians die.
