A 4-year-old boy in a collision with a speeding motorcycle as he crossed the road was referred to our hospital from a peripheral clinic. The child had injuries to his left leg, left arm, chest, and head; there was no history of loss of consciousness.
On examination, the patient was distressed and fractious; his blood pressure was 90/65 mm Hg, pulse was 142 beats per min, and oxygen saturation was 89%; his injured leg and arm had been splinted. He was in pain and had difficulty breathing; his respiratory rate was 43 breaths per min; an intercostal drain, which did not appear to be working, had been inserted for a suspected haemothorax at the clinic. High-pitched bowel sounds were audible all over the left side of the patient's chest and an inward concavity of the anterior abdominal wall—known as a scaphoid abdomen—was seen; no tenderness was found on palpation of the abdomen.
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 9·9 g/dL (normal range 9·5–14); serum sodium concentration was 138·5 mmol/L (normal range 136·0–145·0) and potassium concentration was 3·7 mmol/L (normal range 3·5–5·2).
Chest x-rays showed an opacity of the left hemithorax, loss of normal contour of the left hemidiaphragm, a large intrathoracic air fluid level, and contralateral tracheal deviation indicating the presence of abdominal viscera in the chest (figure). We made a diagnosis of a traumatic diaphragmatic hernia. And because the patient showed both respiratory and haemodynamic compromise, he was supported by 2 L per min oxygen therapy delivered by face mask. He was given fentanyl and paracetamol, both intravenously, because of pain before being intubated in the operating theatre. An emergency thoracotomy was done through a posterolateral approach, during which we found a herniated stomach, spleen, and small bowel, and a central diaphragmatic rupture close to the pericardium and extending anteriorly. Additionally, owing to viability of the visceral contents, reduction and primary repair of the diaphragmatic rupture was done using a non-absorbable suture; he was transfused 150 mL of packed red blood cells intraoperatively.
The patient made a good recovery after the operation and stayed on the ward for a further 6 weeks for management of the femoral shaft fractures. The fractures of the left femur and left humerus were managed using skin traction and sling and swathe, respectively.
At 6 weeks, the child's respiratory and cardiovascular symptoms had abated and skin traction was discontinued and a cast applied for management of the femoral shaft fracture; the patient was then allowed home.
Traumatic diaphragmatic hernia is a rare complication of thoracoabdominal injury that is commonly incorrectly diagnosed yet it carries high mortality. Blunt traumatic diaphragmatic hernia occurs because of a sudden rise in intrabdominal pressure that causes a tear in the diaphragm, leading to the migration of intrabdominal viscera into the thoracic cavity; patients have varying degrees of respiratory and cardiovascular compromise.
The Carter's scheme categorises traumatic diaphragmatic hernia into acute, latent, and obstructive phases. In the acute phase the diagnosis is usually missed in up to 66% of cases due to associated abdominal and musculoskeletal injuries—as happened in our patient; the latent phase comprises non-specific respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms due to herniation of contents in the chest; and finally, the obstructive phase, which is associated with bowel obstruction that may proceed to ischaemia and strangulation.
A CT scan is the gold standard method for diagnosing traumatic diaphragmatic hernia but is not commonly available in many trauma centres in low-resource settings; a chest x-ray is more routinely done. While laparoscopic repair remains the recommended method of treating patients with traumatic diaphragmatic hernia, open surgical repair with or without a mesh is an option in haemodynamically unstable patients and in a low-resource setting where expertise and laparoscopic services are often unavailable. An autoimmune antibody screen was negative and microbiology tests—including serum antibodies for hepatitis A, B, and C, and HIV, QuantiFERON-TB Gold In-Tube test and urine PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Aspergillus fumigatus serum antigen, and blood cultures for aerobic and anaerobic bacteria—were not positive. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a severe pericardial effusion with thickening of the myocardium on the roof of the right atrium suggestive of a cardiac mass. An MRI also confirmed an effusion causing cardiac tamponade (figure). We stopped the digoxin and the patient's condition improved immediately. We also did a pericardiocentesis, which drained 800 mL of serous fluid—also negative on microbiological tests and showed no malignant cells. The cardiac MRI was repeated, and the images showed a thickening of the right atrial roof, interatrial septum, and atrioventricular sulcus. Further investigations—which did not show any metastatic neoplasia—were key in steering us towards a diagnosis of a multisystem disorder—namely, Erdheim–Chester disease. A CT scan and MRI of the abdomen showed bilateral dilatation of the renal pelvises and retroperitoneal fibrosis—known as hairy kidneys. Additionally, the MRI showed periadventitial thickening of the abdominal aorta—yet another pathognomonic sign of Erdheim–Chester disease—known as coated aorta. We also found the patient had a mutation of the BRAF gene, specifically BRAFV600E. Soon after admission she became lethargic and confused, so we did an MRI of her brain, which showed a parenchymal lesion of the left trigone of the lateral ventricle. Our patient died 4 weeks after admission.
Erdheim–Chester disease, a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis, is a rare multisystem disorder of adulthood. It is characterised by excessive production and accumulation of histiocytes in multiple tissues and organs. Prognosis is poor—especially when the heart and brain are affected. Diagnosis is challenging and should be suspected in the presence of indicators of a multisystem disease.

input:
A 59-year-old woman was admitted to our emergency department for asthenia and swollen ankles. 1 week earlier she began to feel tired while walking. On clinical examination, we found peripheral oedema but no other signs suggestive of heart failure. Her blood pressure was 150/70 mm Hg. An electrocardiogram showed junctional bradycardia (35 beats per min): P waves were absent and the QRS complexes were regular and narrow. In her medical history, it was noted that she had recently been treated with ibuprofen and colchicine for acute idiopathic pericarditis: the patient had chest pain and paroxysmal atrial flutter. After this episode she had travelled to the Philippines and had further cardiac problems so was started on digoxin 0·25 mg/day.Our laboratory investigations showed a high digoxin concentration (3·97 ng/mL) and a raised concentration of C-reactive protein (12 mg/L) in her serum. An autoimmune antibody screen was negative and microbiology tests—including serum antibodies for hepatitis A, B, and C, and HIV, QuantiFERON-TB Gold In-Tube test and urine PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Aspergillus fumigatus serum antigen, and blood cultures for aerobic and anaerobic bacteria—were not positive. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a severe pericardial effusion with thickening of the myocardium on the roof of the right atrium suggestive of a cardiac mass. An MRI also confirmed an effusion causing cardiac tamponade (figure). We stopped the digoxin and the patient's condition improved immediately. We also did a pericardiocentesis, which drained 800 mL of serous fluid—also negative on microbiological tests and showed no malignant cells. The cardiac MRI was repeated, and the images showed a thickening of the right atrial roof, interatrial septum, and atrioventricular sulcus. Further investigations—which did not show any metastatic neoplasia—were key in steering us towards a diagnosis of a multisystem disorder—namely, Erdheim–Chester disease. A CT scan and MRI of the abdomen showed bilateral dilatation of the renal pelvises and retroperitoneal fibrosis—known as hairy kidneys. Additionally, the MRI showed periadventitial thickening of the abdominal aorta—yet another pathognomonic sign of Erdheim–Chester disease—known as coated aorta. An endomyocardial biopsy specimen provided histological evidence of the diagnosis, showing an infiltration with non-Langerhans histiocytes: immunohistochemical analysis was positive for CD68 but negative for CD1a and S100. We also found the patient had a mutation of the BRAF gene, specifically BRAFV600E. Soon after admission she became lethargic and confused, so we did an MRI of her brain, which showed a parenchymal lesion of the left trigone of the lateral ventricle. Our patient died 4 weeks after admission.
Erdheim–Chester disease, a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis, is a rare multisystem disorder of adulthood. It is characterised by excessive production and accumulation of histiocytes in multiple tissues and organs. Prognosis is poor—especially when the heart and brain are affected. Diagnosis is challenging and should be suspected in the presence of indicators of a multisystem disease.

A 59-year-old woman was admitted to our emergency department for asthenia and swollen ankles. 1 week earlier she began to feel tired while walking. On clinical examination, we found peripheral oedema but no other signs suggestive of heart failure. Her blood pressure was 150/70 mm Hg. An electrocardiogram showed junctional bradycardia (35 beats per min): P waves were absent and the QRS complexes were regular and narrow. In her medical history, it was noted that she had recently been treated with ibuprofen and colchicine for acute idiopathic pericarditis: the patient had chest pain and paroxysmal atrial flutter. After this episode she had travelled to the Philippines and had further cardiac problems so was started on digoxin 0·25 mg/day.Our laboratory investigations showed a high digoxin concentration (3·97 ng/mL) and a raised concentration of C-reactive protein (12 mg/L) in her serum. An autoimmune antibody screen was negative and microbiology tests—including serum antibodies for hepatitis A, B, and C, and HIV, QuantiFERON-TB Gold In-Tube test and urine PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Aspergillus fumigatus serum antigen, and blood cultures for aerobic and anaerobic bacteria—were not positive. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a severe pericardial effusion with thickening of the myocardium on the roof of the right atrium suggestive of a cardiac mass. An MRI also confirmed an effusion causing cardiac tamponade (figure). We stopped the digoxin and the patient's condition improved immediately. We also did a pericardiocentesis, which drained 800 mL of serous fluid—also negative on microbiological tests and showed no malignant cells. The cardiac MRI was repeated, and the images showed a thickening of the right atrial roof, interatrial septum, and atrioventricular sulcus. Further investigations—which did not show any metastatic neoplasia—were key in steering us towards a diagnosis of a multisystem disorder—namely, Erdheim–Chester disease. A CT scan and MRI of the abdomen showed bilateral dilatation of the renal pelvises and retroperitoneal fibrosis—known as hairy kidneys. Additionally, the MRI showed periadventitial thickening of the abdominal aorta—yet another pathognomonic sign of Erdheim–Chester disease—known as coated aorta. An endomyocardial biopsy specimen provided histological evidence of the diagnosis, showing an infiltration with non-Langerhans histiocytes: immunohistochemical analysis was positive for CD68 but negative for CD1a and S100. We also found the patient had a mutation of the BRAF gene, specifically BRAFV600E. Soon after admission she became lethargic and confused, so we did an MRI of her brain, which showed a parenchymal lesion of the left trigone of the lateral ventricle. Our patient died 4 weeks after admission.
Erdheim–Chester disease, a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis, is a rare multisystem disorder of adulthood. It is characterised by excessive production and accumulation of histiocytes in multiple tissues and organs. Prognosis is poor—especially when the heart and brain are affected. Diagnosis is challenging and should be suspected in the presence of indicators of a multisystem disease.

input:
A 91-year-old man was referred to our cancer centre for assessment and treatment of pulmonary metastases from a previously diagnosed colorectal cancer. The patient had a 2-week history of occasional haemoptysis and mild dyspnoea.The diagnosis of colorectal cancer had been made 2 years earlier after the patient presented with a large persistent peri-anal abscess and obstructive symptoms. An abdominal CT scan had shown rectosigmoid thickening, and a colonoscopy confirmed near complete bowel obstruction. The patient had a Hartmann's resection with end colostomy, and the diagnosis was confirmed as Grade 2 adenocarcinoma of the rectum, stage pT3N1; he did not have an adjuvant treatment due to his advanced age and preference. 2 months later, the patient was found to have biopsy-proven recurrence of the malignancy after a colonoscopy. Restaging CT scans found new bilateral pulmonary nodules, considered to be metastases.
When we saw the patient, he was stable. He was breathing comfortably with a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per min, blood pressure was 114/75 mm Hg, heart rate 89 beats per min, oxygen saturation was 96% on room air. He was not cyanotic, and his BMI was 23·5 kg/m2.
On chest auscultation, bowel sounds were audible in the mid and lower posterior thorax bilaterally, but not audible when auscultated from the anterior thorax. Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 15·0 g/dL (normal 12·9–16·5), mean corpuscular volume 104 fL (normal 80–98), leukocyte count 9·0 × 109 per L (normal 3·2–9·4), platelet count 301 × 109 per L (normal 155–371). A CT scan of the patient's chest showed two metastatic pulmonary deposits in the right and left lobes and a large hiatal hernia—reaching the level of the aortic arch—containing the stomach, and small and large intestines; importantly, a segment of bowel was adjacent to one of the metastatic deposits (figure).
Upon reviewing previous imaging, we found that the hiatal hernia had been present 17 years ago and that it had increased in size since that time. Additionally, the patient, on further questioning, did recall occasionally having regurgitation and dysphagia without—until recently—any bleeding, abdominal discomfort, or dyspnoea. Due to the radiation tolerance limit of the bowel adjacent to the metastatic lesions, we decided that it was unsafe for the patient to have ablative-dose stereotactic radiotherapy. Instead, we treated him with lower-dose palliative radiotherapy to control his haemoptysis. At follow-up 2 and ½ weeks after the radiation, the patient reported resolution of the haemoptysis, and stability in terms of his dyspnoea and cough.
Hiatal hernias are common with an estimated prevalence of 15–20% in western populations; large hiatal hernias—often referred to as upside-down stomach—are rare, and may cause heartburn, postprandial discomfort, dysphagia, and anaemia from chronic bleeding. They are often surgically corrected on an elective basis due to perceived risks of unpredictable complications such as gastric volvulus, oesophageal and gastric obstruction, incarceration, strangulation, and infarction of the herniated organs. However, they can also be asymptomatic—as was the case with our patient.
Stereotactic ablative radiotherapy delivers precise, high doses of radiation, and is often used in metastasis-directed treatment of oligometastatic colorectal cancer. The small bowel is one of the most radiosensitive organs, and the presence of a loop of bowel adjacent to a target lesion—as was the case in our patient—risks stereotactic ablative radiotherapy causing enteritis, perforation, stricture, and fistula. Lower-dose palliative radiation is effective for controlling haemoptysis from metastatic lesions and has a lower risk of toxicity to nearby organs, but it is inferior to stereotactic radiation in terms of tumour control and in producing a sustained response.

A 91-year-old man was referred to our cancer centre for assessment and treatment of pulmonary metastases from a previously diagnosed colorectal cancer. The patient had a 2-week history of occasional haemoptysis and mild dyspnoea.The diagnosis of colorectal cancer had been made 2 years earlier after the patient presented with a large persistent peri-anal abscess and obstructive symptoms. An abdominal CT scan had shown rectosigmoid thickening, and a colonoscopy confirmed near complete bowel obstruction. The patient had a Hartmann's resection with end colostomy, and the diagnosis was confirmed as Grade 2 adenocarcinoma of the rectum, stage pT3N1; he did not have an adjuvant treatment due to his advanced age and preference. 2 months later, the patient was found to have biopsy-proven recurrence of the malignancy after a colonoscopy. Restaging CT scans found new bilateral pulmonary nodules, considered to be metastases.
When we saw the patient, he was stable. He was breathing comfortably with a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per min, blood pressure was 114/75 mm Hg, heart rate 89 beats per min, oxygen saturation was 96% on room air. He was not cyanotic, and his BMI was 23·5 kg/m2.
On chest auscultation, bowel sounds were audible in the mid and lower posterior thorax bilaterally, but not audible when auscultated from the anterior thorax. Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 15·0 g/dL (normal 12·9–16·5), mean corpuscular volume 104 fL (normal 80–98), leukocyte count 9·0 × 109 per L (normal 3·2–9·4), platelet count 301 × 109 per L (normal 155–371). A CT scan of the patient's chest showed two metastatic pulmonary deposits in the right and left lobes and a large hiatal hernia—reaching the level of the aortic arch—containing the stomach, and small and large intestines; importantly, a segment of bowel was adjacent to one of the metastatic deposits (figure).
Upon reviewing previous imaging, we found that the hiatal hernia had been present 17 years ago and that it had increased in size since that time. Additionally, the patient, on further questioning, did recall occasionally having regurgitation and dysphagia without—until recently—any bleeding, abdominal discomfort, or dyspnoea. Due to the radiation tolerance limit of the bowel adjacent to the metastatic lesions, we decided that it was unsafe for the patient to have ablative-dose stereotactic radiotherapy. Instead, we treated him with lower-dose palliative radiotherapy to control his haemoptysis. At follow-up 2 and ½ weeks after the radiation, the patient reported resolution of the haemoptysis, and stability in terms of his dyspnoea and cough.
Hiatal hernias are common with an estimated prevalence of 15–20% in western populations; large hiatal hernias—often referred to as upside-down stomach—are rare, and may cause heartburn, postprandial discomfort, dysphagia, and anaemia from chronic bleeding. They are often surgically corrected on an elective basis due to perceived risks of unpredictable complications such as gastric volvulus, oesophageal and gastric obstruction, incarceration, strangulation, and infarction of the herniated organs. However, they can also be asymptomatic—as was the case with our patient.
Stereotactic ablative radiotherapy delivers precise, high doses of radiation, and is often used in metastasis-directed treatment of oligometastatic colorectal cancer. The small bowel is one of the most radiosensitive organs, and the presence of a loop of bowel adjacent to a target lesion—as was the case in our patient—risks stereotactic ablative radiotherapy causing enteritis, perforation, stricture, and fistula. Lower-dose palliative radiation is effective for controlling haemoptysis from metastatic lesions and has a lower risk of toxicity to nearby organs, but it is inferior to stereotactic radiation in terms of tumour control and in producing a sustained response.

A 91-year-old man was referred to our cancer centre for assessment and treatment of pulmonary metastases from a previously diagnosed colorectal cancer. The patient had a 2-week history of occasional haemoptysis and mild dyspnoea.The diagnosis of colorectal cancer had been made 2 years earlier after the patient presented with a large persistent peri-anal abscess and obstructive symptoms. An abdominal CT scan had shown rectosigmoid thickening, and a colonoscopy confirmed near complete bowel obstruction. The patient had a Hartmann's resection with end colostomy, and the diagnosis was confirmed as Grade 2 adenocarcinoma of the rectum, stage pT3N1; he did not have an adjuvant treatment due to his advanced age and preference. 2 months later, the patient was found to have biopsy-proven recurrence of the malignancy after a colonoscopy. Restaging CT scans found new bilateral pulmonary nodules, considered to be metastases.
When we saw the patient, he was stable. He was breathing comfortably with a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per min, blood pressure was 114/75 mm Hg, heart rate 89 beats per min, oxygen saturation was 96% on room air. He was not cyanotic, and his BMI was 23·5 kg/m2.
On chest auscultation, bowel sounds were audible in the mid and lower posterior thorax bilaterally, but not audible when auscultated from the anterior thorax. Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 15·0 g/dL (normal 12·9–16·5), mean corpuscular volume 104 fL (normal 80–98), leukocyte count 9·0 × 109 per L (normal 3·2–9·4), platelet count 301 × 109 per L (normal 155–371). A CT scan of the patient's chest showed two metastatic pulmonary deposits in the right and left lobes and a large hiatal hernia—reaching the level of the aortic arch—containing the stomach, and small and large intestines; importantly, a segment of bowel was adjacent to one of the metastatic deposits (figure).
Upon reviewing previous imaging, we found that the hiatal hernia had been present 17 years ago and that it had increased in size since that time. Additionally, the patient, on further questioning, did recall occasionally having regurgitation and dysphagia without—until recently—any bleeding, abdominal discomfort, or dyspnoea. Due to the radiation tolerance limit of the bowel adjacent to the metastatic lesions, we decided that it was unsafe for the patient to have ablative-dose stereotactic radiotherapy. Instead, we treated him with lower-dose palliative radiotherapy to control his haemoptysis. At follow-up 2 and ½ weeks after the radiation, the patient reported resolution of the haemoptysis, and stability in terms of his dyspnoea and cough.
Hiatal hernias are common with an estimated prevalence of 15–20% in western populations; large hiatal hernias—often referred to as upside-down stomach—are rare, and may cause heartburn, postprandial discomfort, dysphagia, and anaemia from chronic bleeding. They are often surgically corrected on an elective basis due to perceived risks of unpredictable complications such as gastric volvulus, oesophageal and gastric obstruction, incarceration, strangulation, and infarction of the herniated organs. However, they can also be asymptomatic—as was the case with our patient.
Stereotactic ablative radiotherapy delivers precise, high doses of radiation, and is often used in metastasis-directed treatment of oligometastatic colorectal cancer. The small bowel is one of the most radiosensitive organs, and the presence of a loop of bowel adjacent to a target lesion—as was the case in our patient—risks stereotactic ablative radiotherapy causing enteritis, perforation, stricture, and fistula. Lower-dose palliative radiation is effective for controlling haemoptysis from metastatic lesions and has a lower risk of toxicity to nearby organs, but it is inferior to stereotactic radiation in terms of tumour control and in producing a sustained response.

input: A 55-year-old woman presented with a non-healing, painless pigmented macule with a superficial ulceration on the left planta, which she said had been there for 6 months. She could not recall any history of trauma and did not report any family history of cutaneous diseases. On physical examination, an irregular pigmented macule with a superficial ulceration and brown haemorrhagic crusts was observed on the left plantar near the heel (figures). A skin biopsy showed a malignant melanoma and immunohistochemical examination of biopsied tissue sections showed positive staining for melanoma associated antigens using the antibodies HMB-45, Melan-A, and S100. The patient was diagnosed with an acral lentiginous melanoma (ALM). She underwent a wide local excision with a sufficiently large margin from the lesion's border. A sentinel lymph node biopsy of the inguinal nodes was negative. Fortunately, there was no evidence of recurrence during 5 years of follow-up.ALM is the least common (accounting for 4–10% of all melanoma diagnoses) of the four major subtypes of cutaneous malignant melanoma that typically occur on the palms, the soles of the feet, and the nail beds. However, even though they are uncommon, it is the commonest subtype of melanoma among people with darker skin types—including those of Asian or African descent. Patients with ALM tend to have a poor prognosis, mainly because of the delay in diagnosis and the advanced state of the disease at presentation. Previous research has shown that 25–33% of melanomas on the feet are incorrectly diagnosed when they are first seen by a doctor. Melanomas presenting as an ulcer on the foot can be challenging because the list of differential diagnoses for such a lesion is long. Therefore, even though ALM is a rare cause of ulceration on the foot, it must be considered when examining atypical acral lesions or ulcers that fail to heal.

A chest x-ray showed bilateral infiltrates—pulmonary oedema—and she was treated with furosemide and nitroglycerin and transferred to our intensive care unit.She was not taking any medication, but she did have an etonogestrel—a progestagen only—contraceptive implant put in 6 months earlier. Around the time the implant was put in, she also had a lump in her right breast; a biopsy found it to be benign proliferative breast tissue. She had no significant medical or social history and there was no history of breast or ovarian cancer in her family.
On examination, we found the patient's breasts were asymmetrical; both were erythematous, tender, and had focal, palpable, mobile masses (figure). The skin of both breasts had a peau d'orange pattern. We found no axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. At this initial assessment, we were concerned for possible inflammatory breast cancer; a diagnostic mammogram and an ultrasound (figure) showed large bilateral masses. Given the skin findings, the rapid growth, and the large, irregular, and heterogeneous nature of the masses, our radiologist assigned a Breast Imaging-Reporting and Data System category of 5—indicating that we considered the lesion highly suspicious of malignancy.
Histopathological examination of samples taken from both breasts, using core-needle biopsies, showed prominent pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia (PASH) and mammary hamartomas.
We then removed the implant, and 1 week later, the patient reported significant reduction in breast size, pain, pressure, and erythema. We advised her against future use of exogenous hormonal therapies with the aim of reducing the likelihood of recurrence. She is planning to have both masses excised and oncoplastic reconstructive surgery carried out.
PASH masses can resemble breast cancer both on examination and at imaging, and tissue sampling is imperative for diagnosis. PASH is a hormone-sensitive process and rapid progression can occur with sudden hormonal changes, which given the timeline we believe was the case with our patient—the contraceptive implant being the source of the excess hormone. PASH should be considered as an important differential diagnosis of breast hypertrophy in a premenopausal patient, particularly in the context of changes to the hormonal milieu.
The risk of developing breast cancer is not increased with PASH, and so follow-up using standard mammographic screening is recommended (video).

A 24-week pregnant 18-year-old woman was seen at her local health-care centre where she was found to have a respiratory rate of 38 breaths per min, a blood pressure of 250/90 mm Hg, and a heart rate of 39 beats per min. She collapsed and required intubation and ventilation. A chest x-ray showed bilateral infiltrates—pulmonary oedema—and she was treated with furosemide and nitroglycerin and transferred to our intensive care unit.She was not taking any medication, but she did have an etonogestrel—a progestagen only—contraceptive implant put in 6 months earlier. Around the time the implant was put in, she also had a lump in her right breast; a biopsy found it to be benign proliferative breast tissue. She had no significant medical or social history and there was no history of breast or ovarian cancer in her family.
On examination, we found the patient's breasts were asymmetrical; both were erythematous, tender, and had focal, palpable, mobile masses (figure). The skin of both breasts had a peau d'orange pattern. We found no axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. At this initial assessment, we were concerned for possible inflammatory breast cancer; a diagnostic mammogram and an ultrasound (figure) showed large bilateral masses. Given the skin findings, the rapid growth, and the large, irregular, and heterogeneous nature of the masses, our radiologist assigned a Breast Imaging-Reporting and Data System category of 5—indicating that we considered the lesion highly suspicious of malignancy.
Histopathological examination of samples taken from both breasts, using core-needle biopsies, showed prominent pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia (PASH) and mammary hamartomas.
We then removed the implant, and 1 week later, the patient reported significant reduction in breast size, pain, pressure, and erythema. We advised her against future use of exogenous hormonal therapies with the aim of reducing the likelihood of recurrence. She is planning to have both masses excised and oncoplastic reconstructive surgery carried out.
PASH masses can resemble breast cancer both on examination and at imaging, and tissue sampling is imperative for diagnosis. PASH is a hormone-sensitive process and rapid progression can occur with sudden hormonal changes, which given the timeline we believe was the case with our patient—the contraceptive implant being the source of the excess hormone. PASH should be considered as an important differential diagnosis of breast hypertrophy in a premenopausal patient, particularly in the context of changes to the hormonal milieu.
The risk of developing breast cancer is not increased with PASH, and so follow-up using standard mammographic screening is recommended (video).

input:
A 24-week pregnant 18-year-old woman was seen at her local health-care centre where she was found to have a respiratory rate of 38 breaths per min, a blood pressure of 250/90 mm Hg, and a heart rate of 39 beats per min. She collapsed and required intubation and ventilation. A chest x-ray showed bilateral infiltrates—pulmonary oedema—and she was treated with furosemide and nitroglycerin and transferred to our intensive care unit.She was not taking any medication, but she did have an etonogestrel—a progestagen only—contraceptive implant put in 6 months earlier. Around the time the implant was put in, she also had a lump in her right breast; a biopsy found it to be benign proliferative breast tissue. She had no significant medical or social history and there was no history of breast or ovarian cancer in her family.
On examination, we found the patient's breasts were asymmetrical; both were erythematous, tender, and had focal, palpable, mobile masses (figure). The skin of both breasts had a peau d'orange pattern. We found no axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. At this initial assessment, we were concerned for possible inflammatory breast cancer; a diagnostic mammogram and an ultrasound (figure) showed large bilateral masses. Given the skin findings, the rapid growth, and the large, irregular, and heterogeneous nature of the masses, our radiologist assigned a Breast Imaging-Reporting and Data System category of 5—indicating that we considered the lesion highly suspicious of malignancy.
Histopathological examination of samples taken from both breasts, using core-needle biopsies, showed prominent pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia (PASH) and mammary hamartomas.
We then removed the implant, and 1 week later, the patient reported significant reduction in breast size, pain, pressure, and erythema. We advised her against future use of exogenous hormonal therapies with the aim of reducing the likelihood of recurrence. She is planning to have both masses excised and oncoplastic reconstructive surgery carried out.
PASH masses can resemble breast cancer both on examination and at imaging, and tissue sampling is imperative for diagnosis. PASH is a hormone-sensitive process and rapid progression can occur with sudden hormonal changes, which given the timeline we believe was the case with our patient—the contraceptive implant being the source of the excess hormone. PASH should be considered as an important differential diagnosis of breast hypertrophy in a premenopausal patient, particularly in the context of changes to the hormonal milieu.
The risk of developing breast cancer is not increased with PASH, and so follow-up using standard mammographic screening is recommended (video).

A 58-year-old man attended our hospital with a 3-month history of bloody diarrhoea, proctalgia, arthralgia, and weight loss. The patient said that when his symptoms began, he had noticed a rash that had recently become more conspicuous. Accompanying the change in the rash, he said he had developed a high fever.3 weeks before we saw him, the patient had been admitted to the surgical ward for treatment of an anal fistula; he was given oral antibiotics and the fistula was surgically debrided.
Additionally, in his medical history, he had type 2 diabetes, arterial hypertension, and dyslipidaemia: he was prescribed metformin, gliclazide, enalapril, a thiazide diuretic, and simvastatin.
On examination, the patient looked unwell: he had pale mucous membranes and a temperature of 37·5°C. He had extensive, well-delineated, erythematous, and mildly tender plaques on the upper part of his back, arms, and hands (figure); he had multiple non-tender mouth ulcers. His abdomen was generally mildly tender with no specific area of localisation. We found no other atypicalities.
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 7·6 g/dL (normal 13·0–16·5), white blood cell count of 7·6 × 109 per L (normal 4·5–11·0), neutrophil count of 6·0 × 109 per L (normal 2·0–7·0), and elevated acute phase reactants: ferritin concentration was 533 ng/mL (normal 25–400), erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 120 mm/h (normal 1–10), and C-reactive protein concentration was 15 mg/dL (normal <5).
Histopathological analysis of a sample of a skin biopsy showed a rich, diffuse, predominantly neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate (figure). At colonoscopy we found multiple star-shaped ulcers scattered throughout the colon with areas of preserved mucosa between them (figure); histological analysis showed active chronic colitis with crypt inflammatory destruction and abscesses.
Considering the myriad of clinical and histopathological findings, we concluded that the patient had Crohn's disease with an acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis—also known as Sweet's syndrome. The patient was given systemic corticosteroids and his gastrointestinal symptoms improved. His skin lesions significantly improved over the next 14 days, at which point he was started on adalimumab and allowed to go home.
Bloody stools and significant unintentional weight loss should raise the possibility of a serious systemic disease. The presence of a fever and skin lesions suggests an inflammatory, infectious, or paraneoplastic disorder. Mouth ulcers and a recent history of a perianal pathology—as seen in our patient—would suggest an inflammatory bowel disease: Crohn's disease. Sweet's syndrome should be considered in the case of a fever and neutrophilic dermal nodular plaques with a neutrophilia.
Sweet's syndrome represents a group of autoinflammatory skin lesions or neutrophilic dermatoses, associated with a wide variety of infections, haematological malignancies, and autoimmune and inflammatory disorders. The concurrence of Sweet's syndrome and Crohn's disease is rare. And in reality, Sweet's syndrome should be considered as an extraintestinal manifestation of Crohn's disease. Differentiation from the other inflammatory diseases accompanying Crohn's disease—including erythema nodosum and pyoderma gangrenosum—is key.

A 22-year-old woman with a history of gradually worsening headache, who had developed nausea, vomiting, and diplopia within the past month, was referred to the Department of Neurosurgery of Hospital de Santo António (Porto, Portugal) in June, 2017. Initial neurological examination and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies were unremarkable. Lumbar puncture opening pressure was elevated. The patient had no lesions evoking a congenital phakomatosis or neurocutaneous melanosis, including no nevus of Ota. MRI of the neuroaxis showed mild hydrocephalus and discrete disperse leptomeningeal enhancement of the cranial and spinal nerves (figure, A). Complete physical examination, including observation by ophthalmology and dermatology, followed by whole-body CT scan and scintigraphy, excluded the presence of other lesions. She was proposed for ventricle–peritoneal shunt placement and open brain biopsy. Biopsy analysis showed leptomeningeal thickening, with melanin-containing cells, low mitotic count, and no cellular atypia or brain invasion. Staining was positive for HMB45 and Melan-A, but she tested negative for the BRAFV600E mutation. These findings were consistent with meningeal melanocytosis. Her symptoms improved with shunting.3 months later, she was admitted to the hospital with shunt obstruction, and CSF collected during shunt revision showed cells with nuclear atypia, dark macronucleoli, and positive for melanic pigment, suggestive of melanoma. Off-label treatment with immune checkpoint blockade was considered in combination with radiotherapy, but rapid progression with biplegia and sphincter anomalies, followed by tetraplegia and respiratory depression, ensued. MRI at this stage showed syringobulbia, strong leptomeningeal enhancement of the cranial and spinal nerves, with exuberant filling of the spinal subarachnoid spaces and lumbar cistern (figure, B). She died 4 months after disease presentation.
Primary CNS malignant melanoma is a rare disease. It can be divided into nodular intraparenchymal and diffuse leptomeningeal patterns. The differential diagnosis for a diffusely disseminated leptomeningeal disease includes leptomeningeal carcinomatosis; disseminated primary brain tumours, such as diffuse leptomeningeal glioneuronal tumour; lymphoma; infectious meningitis; and inflammatory conditions, including sarcoidosis. Primary leptomeningeal melanocytosis is an extremely rare and aggressive type of primary CNS melanoma, and few published reports exist. Classically described treatments include radiotherapy and chemotherapy, but recent successes with BRAF inhibitors and immune checkpoint inhibitors in metastatic CNS melanoma suggest the potential of these drugs to treat CNS melanoma.
Clinical awareness of this condition and its aggressive course is fundamental for prompt discussion and expeditious initiation of treatments.

A 22-year-old woman with a history of gradually worsening headache, who had developed nausea, vomiting, and diplopia within the past month, was referred to the Department of Neurosurgery of Hospital de Santo António (Porto, Portugal) in June, 2017. Initial neurological examination and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies were unremarkable. Lumbar puncture opening pressure was elevated. The patient had no lesions evoking a congenital phakomatosis or neurocutaneous melanosis, including no nevus of Ota. MRI of the neuroaxis showed mild hydrocephalus and discrete disperse leptomeningeal enhancement of the cranial and spinal nerves (figure, A). Complete physical examination, including observation by ophthalmology and dermatology, followed by whole-body CT scan and scintigraphy, excluded the presence of other lesions. She was proposed for ventricle–peritoneal shunt placement and open brain biopsy. Biopsy analysis showed leptomeningeal thickening, with melanin-containing cells, low mitotic count, and no cellular atypia or brain invasion. Staining was positive for HMB45 and Melan-A, but she tested negative for the BRAFV600E mutation. These findings were consistent with meningeal melanocytosis. Her symptoms improved with shunting.3 months later, she was admitted to the hospital with shunt obstruction, and CSF collected during shunt revision showed cells with nuclear atypia, dark macronucleoli, and positive for melanic pigment, suggestive of melanoma. Off-label treatment with immune checkpoint blockade was considered in combination with radiotherapy, but rapid progression with biplegia and sphincter anomalies, followed by tetraplegia and respiratory depression, ensued. MRI at this stage showed syringobulbia, strong leptomeningeal enhancement of the cranial and spinal nerves, with exuberant filling of the spinal subarachnoid spaces and lumbar cistern (figure, B). She died 4 months after disease presentation.
Primary CNS malignant melanoma is a rare disease. It can be divided into nodular intraparenchymal and diffuse leptomeningeal patterns. The differential diagnosis for a diffusely disseminated leptomeningeal disease includes leptomeningeal carcinomatosis; disseminated primary brain tumours, such as diffuse leptomeningeal glioneuronal tumour; lymphoma; infectious meningitis; and inflammatory conditions, including sarcoidosis. Primary leptomeningeal melanocytosis is an extremely rare and aggressive type of primary CNS melanoma, and few published reports exist. Classically described treatments include radiotherapy and chemotherapy, but recent successes with BRAF inhibitors and immune checkpoint inhibitors in metastatic CNS melanoma suggest the potential of these drugs to treat CNS melanoma.
Clinical awareness of this condition and its aggressive course is fundamental for prompt discussion and expeditious initiation of treatments.

A 22-year-old woman with a history of gradually worsening headache, who had developed nausea, vomiting, and diplopia within the past month, was referred to the Department of Neurosurgery of Hospital de Santo António (Porto, Portugal) in June, 2017. Initial neurological examination and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies were unremarkable. Lumbar puncture opening pressure was elevated. The patient had no lesions evoking a congenital phakomatosis or neurocutaneous melanosis, including no nevus of Ota. MRI of the neuroaxis showed mild hydrocephalus and discrete disperse leptomeningeal enhancement of the cranial and spinal nerves (figure, A). Complete physical examination, including observation by ophthalmology and dermatology, followed by whole-body CT scan and scintigraphy, excluded the presence of other lesions. She was proposed for ventricle–peritoneal shunt placement and open brain biopsy. Biopsy analysis showed leptomeningeal thickening, with melanin-containing cells, low mitotic count, and no cellular atypia or brain invasion. Staining was positive for HMB45 and Melan-A, but she tested negative for the BRAFV600E mutation. These findings were consistent with meningeal melanocytosis. Her symptoms improved with shunting.3 months later, she was admitted to the hospital with shunt obstruction, and CSF collected during shunt revision showed cells with nuclear atypia, dark macronucleoli, and positive for melanic pigment, suggestive of melanoma. Off-label treatment with immune checkpoint blockade was considered in combination with radiotherapy, but rapid progression with biplegia and sphincter anomalies, followed by tetraplegia and respiratory depression, ensued. MRI at this stage showed syringobulbia, strong leptomeningeal enhancement of the cranial and spinal nerves, with exuberant filling of the spinal subarachnoid spaces and lumbar cistern (figure, B). She died 4 months after disease presentation.
Primary CNS malignant melanoma is a rare disease. It can be divided into nodular intraparenchymal and diffuse leptomeningeal patterns. The differential diagnosis for a diffusely disseminated leptomeningeal disease includes leptomeningeal carcinomatosis; disseminated primary brain tumours, such as diffuse leptomeningeal glioneuronal tumour; lymphoma; infectious meningitis; and inflammatory conditions, including sarcoidosis. Primary leptomeningeal melanocytosis is an extremely rare and aggressive type of primary CNS melanoma, and few published reports exist. Classically described treatments include radiotherapy and chemotherapy, but recent successes with BRAF inhibitors and immune checkpoint inhibitors in metastatic CNS melanoma suggest the potential of these drugs to treat CNS melanoma.
Clinical awareness of this condition and its aggressive course is fundamental for prompt discussion and expeditious initiation of treatments.

A 64-year-old man with a history of atrial fibrillation with portal vein and superior mesenteric vein thrombosis was admitted to hospital with haematemesis. He was diagnosed with non-cirrhotic portal hypertension leading to variceal bleeding. He had two endoscopies with variceal banding and gastric variceal glue injection within 1 month that were unsuccessful; hence, he was referred to a tertiary unit for further management. Given his performance status and comorbidities, he was neither a candidate for surgery nor transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt; therefore, after careful counselling, glue embolisation of the culprit vein was performed via an endovascular approach. Post-procedure, the patient developed left homonymous hemianopia, which gradually worsened, leading to cortical blindness. The visual disturbance was further investigated with a CT scan (figure A). The CT images showed a right occipital infarct and multiple, scattered, high-density foci in subarachnoid space. Further MRI and MR angiogram (figures B–E) supported right distal posterior cerebral artery occlusion, probably due to glue embolisation.Unfortunately, our patient did not consent to further investigations to determine the mechanism, although a non-contrast echocardiogram did not show any cardiac sequelae of septal defects. After appropriate specialist consultation, his stroke has been managed with lifelong anticoagulation due to portal vein and superior mesenteric vein thrombosis and he had conservative management for the neurological symptoms, leading to partial improvement of his vision.
Glue embolisation acts as definitive treatment of gastric varices in selected cases, although complications do occur in 0·5–4·3% of patients. In a large retrospective case series (n=753), distant glue embolisation complications were reported in five patients (0·7%, one pulmonary, one brain, and three splenic). Embolisation to the right atrium and beyond has been reported in previous case studies, including systemic arterial embolisation due to septal defects. However, cerebral embolisation is uncommon but can present with cortical blindness, similarly to our case. Therefore, informed procedural consent must include glue embolisation and a high index of suspicion must be shown if a patient develops acute respiratory or neurological complications after the intervention.

A 64-year-old man with a history of atrial fibrillation with portal vein and superior mesenteric vein thrombosis was admitted to hospital with haematemesis. He was diagnosed with non-cirrhotic portal hypertension leading to variceal bleeding. He had two endoscopies with variceal banding and gastric variceal glue injection within 1 month that were unsuccessful; hence, he was referred to a tertiary unit for further management. Given his performance status and comorbidities, he was neither a candidate for surgery nor transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt; therefore, after careful counselling, glue embolisation of the culprit vein was performed via an endovascular approach. Post-procedure, the patient developed left homonymous hemianopia, which gradually worsened, leading to cortical blindness. The visual disturbance was further investigated with a CT scan (figure A). The CT images showed a right occipital infarct and multiple, scattered, high-density foci in subarachnoid space. Further MRI and MR angiogram (figures B–E) supported right distal posterior cerebral artery occlusion, probably due to glue embolisation.Unfortunately, our patient did not consent to further investigations to determine the mechanism, although a non-contrast echocardiogram did not show any cardiac sequelae of septal defects. After appropriate specialist consultation, his stroke has been managed with lifelong anticoagulation due to portal vein and superior mesenteric vein thrombosis and he had conservative management for the neurological symptoms, leading to partial improvement of his vision.
Glue embolisation acts as definitive treatment of gastric varices in selected cases, although complications do occur in 0·5–4·3% of patients. In a large retrospective case series (n=753), distant glue embolisation complications were reported in five patients (0·7%, one pulmonary, one brain, and three splenic). Embolisation to the right atrium and beyond has been reported in previous case studies, including systemic arterial embolisation due to septal defects. However, cerebral embolisation is uncommon but can present with cortical blindness, similarly to our case. Therefore, informed procedural consent must include glue embolisation and a high index of suspicion must be shown if a patient develops acute respiratory or neurological complications after the intervention.

A 26-year-old woman presented at week 20 of pregnancy with a 3-month history of fever, cough, and breathlessness. She had hearing loss, epistaxis, nasal crusting, haemoptysis, and a purpuric rash over her legs. No significant weight loss was reported. Chest x-ray (with abdominal shield) showed bilateral cannonball opacities, and contrast-enhanced chest CT (with abdominal shield) revealed multiple nodules, without pleural effusion or lymphadenopathy (figure). Ultrasound of the patient's abdomen and pelvis showed a single live fetus and no abnormalities. Her haemoglobin concentration was 8·3 g/dL, total leucocyte count was 8·6 × 109/L, platelet count was 600 × 109/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 65 mm/h, and C-reactive protein concentration was 186 mg/L. The patient's serum anti-proteinase 3 antibody concentration was 102 U/mL. Sputum acid-fast bacilli and fungal smear, serum β-D-glucan and galactomannan, and Mantoux test results were all negative. A diagnosis of granulomatosis with polyangiitis was made.
The patient commenced remission induction therapy with intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g once daily for 3 days) and rituximab (1000 mg, two doses 2 weeks apart). She showed substantial improvement over the next 2–3 days and delivered a healthy baby girl at term. The patient commenced oral prednisolone immediately after induction therapy, starting at 60 mg/day for 1 month followed by taper every two weeks. She has received remission maintenance therapy with oral prednisolone (5 mg/day) and intravenous rituximab (500 mg every 6 months) for 1 year, and is planned to continue this treatment for at least 2 years total duration. A follow-up chest x-ray 6 months after the initial treatment showed complete resolution of lung nodules.
Cannonball opacities on chest x-ray usually suggest metastatic malignancies such as choriocarcinoma, lung carcinoma, renal cell cancer, or endometrial carcinoma, but, less frequently, can be due to other conditions, such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis, fungal infections, and tuberculosis. The most common chest radiological finding at presentation in patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis is bilateral nodules or masses (reported in up to 90% of patients in case series). In the current case, hearing loss, purpuric rash, and upper respiratory symptoms led us to suspect granulomatosis with polyangiitis. The absence of pleural effusion or lymphadenopathy on chest radiology made a diagnosis of malignancy or infection less likely, the normal pelvic ultrasound helped to rule out choriocarcinoma, and the negative Mantoux test, sputum workup, and fungal serology helped to rule out infection. Elevated concentrations of anti-proteinase 3 antibodies and the patient's rapid response to immunosuppression contributed to confirmation of the diagnosis. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a small-vessel vasculitis that can mimic malignancy and infections. This diagnosis should be suspected in patients with lung nodules when there are accompanying upper respiratory tract symptoms, rash, neuropathy, or eye, ear, or renal involvement.

input:
A 26-year-old woman presented at week 20 of pregnancy with a 3-month history of fever, cough, and breathlessness. She had hearing loss, epistaxis, nasal crusting, haemoptysis, and a purpuric rash over her legs. No significant weight loss was reported. Chest x-ray (with abdominal shield) showed bilateral cannonball opacities, and contrast-enhanced chest CT (with abdominal shield) revealed multiple nodules, without pleural effusion or lymphadenopathy (figure). Ultrasound of the patient's abdomen and pelvis showed a single live fetus and no abnormalities. Her haemoglobin concentration was 8·3 g/dL, total leucocyte count was 8·6 × 109/L, platelet count was 600 × 109/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 65 mm/h, and C-reactive protein concentration was 186 mg/L. The patient's serum anti-proteinase 3 antibody concentration was 102 U/mL. Sputum acid-fast bacilli and fungal smear, serum β-D-glucan and galactomannan, and Mantoux test results were all negative. A diagnosis of granulomatosis with polyangiitis was made.
The patient commenced remission induction therapy with intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g once daily for 3 days) and rituximab (1000 mg, two doses 2 weeks apart). A 64-year-old woman presented with multiple asymptomatic, erythematosus papulopustular facial lesions (figure, A). The patient had been diagnosed with rosacea, and received oral doxycycline, 100 mg twice daily for 3 weeks as first-line therapy by her family doctor. Because of the poor response to therapy, she had been referred to our dermatology clinic for further evaluation. On clinical examination, the eruptions, which were practically asymptomatic, had a rosacea-like appearance. They had emerged and gradually worsened over a period of 5 weeks. There were no pathological findings on physical examination and routine laboratory test results were normal. Microscopic examination of specimens collected from the patient's skin by epidermal scraping showed many Demodex folliculorum mites (figure, B, magnification ×100). The patient showed substantial improvement after treatment with oral metronidazole (250 mg three times daily for 2 weeks) and subsequent weekly topical permethrin (cream 5%).
Demodex spp are common saprophytic vermiform mites, which asymptomatically parasitise the hair follicles and the pilosebaceous glands of mammals. In human beings, two species of acarid mite have been identified: Demodex folliculorum and Demodex brevis. Sites favoured by Demodex spp mites include the scalp, forehead, and chin, and areas around the orbit, nose, and mouth. Demodex spp have been implicated in the development of various facial conditions, including pityriasis folliculorum, rosacea-like demodicidosis (also known as demodicosis), pustular folliculitis, demodectic blepharitis, and so-called “demodicidosis gravis”. Clinical features of Demodex spp infestation include erythematopapulous and pustulous skin lesions together with erythematodesquamative changes of the face. Furthermore, demodicidosis should also be considered in any patient with rosacea-like dermatitis resistant to conventional rosacea therapies.
Although there is no consensus to how and what degree infestation with Demodex spp mites contributes to skin pathology, there is evidence that demodicidosis is a condition distinct from common rosacea. The prevalence of Demodex spp carriers increases with age. It is possible that large numbers of demodex mites can stimulate inflammatory or allergic reactions by mechanical blockage of follicles, or by acting as vectors for microorganisms, which ultimately results in connective tissue damage and telangiectasia. Another interesting hypothesis is that inflammatory response may be stimulated by antigenic proteins related to a bacterium (Bacillus oleronius) isolated from D folliculorum.

A 51-year-old man attended our outpatient clinic complaining of repeated bouts of pain in his left groin. He said he had a lump that appeared intermittently in the area, and because of this, he regularly wore firm underwear. In his medical history, it was noted that 9 years earlier he had undergone an open flat mesh repair of a left inguinal hernia. 14 months later, however, the problem had recurred; at this stage, he was managed by a different surgeon—who had not been involved in the original operation—who did a further open mesh repair. The second repair was also unsuccessful and the hernia recurred. 9 months later, the patient had another operation to repair the problem: this time, another surgeon did a laparoscopic total extraperitoneal (TEP) repair. Unfortunately, this too was unsuccessful, and the patient's problem recurred 3 months later. At this stage, the patient said he had lost hope in the possibility of his problem being resolved and he decided not to seek further help for some time.On clinical examination, two oblique scars were visible in the left groin area and there was also a palpable ridge above them—suggestive of the mesh used in the previous laparoscopic inguinal repair. We found no evidence of a further hernia despite the patient repeatedly pointing out that the area of the medial groin below the scars was the source of his symptoms.
Given the rather complex history, we decided we needed to do an MRI of the groin while the patient was repeatedly putting the area under strain by increasing his intra-abdominal pressure—in a similar way that coughing, bending over, or lifting a heavy object does. This showed a femoral hernia that contained omentum (figure). We decided to repair the hernia by using a prosthetic mesh plug through an infrainguinal approach to avoid the previously scarred areas. At follow-up 6 months later, the patient was free of symptoms and the problem had not recurred.
A femoral hernia is a protrusion of a peritoneal sac through the femoral ring or canal below the inguinal ligament. It is relatively uncommon in men but more frequent in women. About 5000 femoral hernia repairs are done in the UK each year; 30–40% of cases present acutely with an associated ten-fold increase in risk of mortality. By contrast with a femoral hernia, an inguinal hernia is essentially a defect due to weak connective tissue. As traditional sutured repairs are associated with high recurrence rates, the repair of both femoral and inguinal hernias is often augmented with synthetic prosthetic mesh by using either an open or laparoscopic (colloquially called a keyhole) technique. Laparoscopic approaches include a TEP—as with our patient—or a transabdominal preperitoneal repair. The ideal approach to a successful outcome is dependent on the patient's fitness, informed consent, and the surgeon's skill.
The key message here is that patients presenting with a history suggestive of an earlier recurrence of an inguinal hernia might actually have another problem altogether—in our patient's case, a primary femoral hernia. We believe that ultrasound scans are unreliable in the assessment of such cases, especially when the groin area is disfigured. And we would suggest that an MRI, done with provocation or straining to increase pressure in the affected area during scanning, can be very useful. Furthermore, additional pathology—including indurated lymph nodes, lobulated lipomas, and saphena varix—in the absence of classic diagnostic clinical signs, may be detected.

A 64-year-old woman presented with multiple asymptomatic, erythematosus papulopustular facial lesions (figure, A). The patient had been diagnosed with rosacea, and received oral doxycycline, 100 mg twice daily for 3 weeks as first-line therapy by her family doctor. Because of the poor response to therapy, she had been referred to our dermatology clinic for further evaluation. On clinical examination, the eruptions, which were practically asymptomatic, had a rosacea-like appearance. They had emerged and gradually worsened over a period of 5 weeks. There were no pathological findings on physical examination and routine laboratory test results were normal. Microscopic examination of specimens collected from the patient's skin by epidermal scraping showed many Demodex folliculorum mites (figure, B, magnification ×100). The patient showed substantial improvement after treatment with oral metronidazole (250 mg three times daily for 2 weeks) and subsequent weekly topical permethrin (cream 5%).
Demodex spp are common saprophytic vermiform mites, which asymptomatically parasitise the hair follicles and the pilosebaceous glands of mammals. In human beings, two species of acarid mite have been identified: Demodex folliculorum and Demodex brevis. Sites favoured by Demodex spp mites include the scalp, forehead, and chin, and areas around the orbit, nose, and mouth. Demodex spp have been implicated in the development of various facial conditions, including pityriasis folliculorum, rosacea-like demodicidosis (also known as demodicosis), pustular folliculitis, demodectic blepharitis, and so-called “demodicidosis gravis”. Clinical features of Demodex spp infestation include erythematopapulous and pustulous skin lesions together with erythematodesquamative changes of the face. Furthermore, demodicidosis should also be considered in any patient with rosacea-like dermatitis resistant to conventional rosacea therapies.
Although there is no consensus to how and what degree infestation with Demodex spp mites contributes to skin pathology, there is evidence that demodicidosis is a condition distinct from common rosacea. The prevalence of Demodex spp carriers increases with age. It is possible that large numbers of demodex mites can stimulate inflammatory or allergic reactions by mechanical blockage of follicles, or by acting as vectors for microorganisms, which ultimately results in connective tissue damage and telangiectasia. Another interesting hypothesis is that inflammatory response may be stimulated by antigenic proteins related to a bacterium (Bacillus oleronius) isolated from D folliculorum.

A 51-year-old man attended our outpatient clinic complaining of repeated bouts of pain in his left groin. He said he had a lump that appeared intermittently in the area, and because of this, he regularly wore firm underwear. In his medical history, it was noted that 9 years earlier he had undergone an open flat mesh repair of a left inguinal hernia. 14 months later, however, the problem had recurred; at this stage, he was managed by a different surgeon—who had not been involved in the original operation—who did a further open mesh repair. The second repair was also unsuccessful and the hernia recurred. 9 months later, the patient had another operation to repair the problem: this time, another surgeon did a laparoscopic total extraperitoneal (TEP) repair. Unfortunately, this too was unsuccessful, and the patient's problem recurred 3 months later. At this stage, the patient said he had lost hope in the possibility of his problem being resolved and he decided not to seek further help for some time.On clinical examination, two oblique scars were visible in the left groin area and there was also a palpable ridge above them—suggestive of the mesh used in the previous laparoscopic inguinal repair. We found no evidence of a further hernia despite the patient repeatedly pointing out that the area of the medial groin below the scars was the source of his symptoms.
Given the rather complex history, we decided we needed to do an MRI of the groin while the patient was repeatedly putting the area under strain by increasing his intra-abdominal pressure—in a similar way that coughing, bending over, or lifting a heavy object does. This showed a femoral hernia that contained omentum (figure). We decided to repair the hernia by using a prosthetic mesh plug through an infrainguinal approach to avoid the previously scarred areas. At follow-up 6 months later, the patient was free of symptoms and the problem had not recurred.
A femoral hernia is a protrusion of a peritoneal sac through the femoral ring or canal below the inguinal ligament. It is relatively uncommon in men but more frequent in women. About 5000 femoral hernia repairs are done in the UK each year; 30–40% of cases present acutely with an associated ten-fold increase in risk of mortality. By contrast with a femoral hernia, an inguinal hernia is essentially a defect due to weak connective tissue. As traditional sutured repairs are associated with high recurrence rates, the repair of both femoral and inguinal hernias is often augmented with synthetic prosthetic mesh by using either an open or laparoscopic (colloquially called a keyhole) technique. Laparoscopic approaches include a TEP—as with our patient—or a transabdominal preperitoneal repair. The ideal approach to a successful outcome is dependent on the patient's fitness, informed consent, and the surgeon's skill.
The key message here is that patients presenting with a history suggestive of an earlier recurrence of an inguinal hernia might actually have another problem altogether—in our patient's case, a primary femoral hernia. We believe that ultrasound scans are unreliable in the assessment of such cases, especially when the groin area is disfigured. And we would suggest that an MRI, done with provocation or straining to increase pressure in the affected area during scanning, can be very useful. Furthermore, additional pathology—including indurated lymph nodes, lobulated lipomas, and saphena varix—in the absence of classic diagnostic clinical signs, may be detected.

A 51-year-old man attended our outpatient clinic complaining of repeated bouts of pain in his left groin. He said he had a lump that appeared intermittently in the area, and because of this, he regularly wore firm underwear. In his medical history, it was noted that 9 years earlier he had undergone an open flat mesh repair of a left inguinal hernia. 14 months later, however, the problem had recurred; at this stage, he was managed by a different surgeon—who had not been involved in the original operation—who did a further open mesh repair. The second repair was also unsuccessful and the hernia recurred. 9 months later, the patient had another operation to repair the problem: this time, another surgeon did a laparoscopic total extraperitoneal (TEP) repair. Unfortunately, this too was unsuccessful, and the patient's problem recurred 3 months later. At this stage, the patient said he had lost hope in the possibility of his problem being resolved and he decided not to seek further help for some time.On clinical examination, two oblique scars were visible in the left groin area and there was also a palpable ridge above them—suggestive of the mesh used in the previous laparoscopic inguinal repair. We found no evidence of a further hernia despite the patient repeatedly pointing out that the area of the medial groin below the scars was the source of his symptoms.
Given the rather complex history, we decided we needed to do an MRI of the groin while the patient was repeatedly putting the area under strain by increasing his intra-abdominal pressure—in a similar way that coughing, bending over, or lifting a heavy object does. This showed a femoral hernia that contained omentum (figure). We decided to repair the hernia by using a prosthetic mesh plug through an infrainguinal approach to avoid the previously scarred areas. At follow-up 6 months later, the patient was free of symptoms and the problem had not recurred.
A femoral hernia is a protrusion of a peritoneal sac through the femoral ring or canal below the inguinal ligament. It is relatively uncommon in men but more frequent in women. About 5000 femoral hernia repairs are done in the UK each year; 30–40% of cases present acutely with an associated ten-fold increase in risk of mortality. By contrast with a femoral hernia, an inguinal hernia is essentially a defect due to weak connective tissue. As traditional sutured repairs are associated with high recurrence rates, the repair of both femoral and inguinal hernias is often augmented with synthetic prosthetic mesh by using either an open or laparoscopic (colloquially called a keyhole) technique. Laparoscopic approaches include a TEP—as with our patient—or a transabdominal preperitoneal repair. The ideal approach to a successful outcome is dependent on the patient's fitness, informed consent, and the surgeon's skill.
The key message here is that patients presenting with a history suggestive of an earlier recurrence of an inguinal hernia might actually have another problem altogether—in our patient's case, a primary femoral hernia. We believe that ultrasound scans are unreliable in the assessment of such cases, especially when the groin area is disfigured. And we would suggest that an MRI, done with provocation or straining to increase pressure in the affected area during scanning, can be very useful. Furthermore, additional pathology—including indurated lymph nodes, lobulated lipomas, and saphena varix—in the absence of classic diagnostic clinical signs, may be detected.

A 65-year-old man attended our outpatient clinic for diagnostic evaluation of abnormal blood tests detected during a routine check requested by his cardiologist. The investigations showed a raised serum gamma-glutamyl transferase (406 U/L; normal <60) and a raised serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration of 99·20 μIU/mL (normal 0·27–4·20). The patient's free thyroxine and free tri-iodothyronine were low at 0·67 ng/dL (normal 0·93–1·70) and 1·5 pg/mL (normal 2·0–4·4) respectively. Anti-thyroid antibodies—including thyroid peroxidase antibodies and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies—were not detected.The patient did not report any symptoms indicative of hypothyroidism—specifically fatigue, constipation, or an increased sensitivity to cold. He had no history of thyroid disease.
On general physical examination, the patient did not have a goitre, and his cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes were not enlarged or tender.
Thyroid sonography showed a destructive thyroiditis with a heterogeneous, hypoechoic sonographic pattern and slightly increased vascularisation in both thyroid lobes—without circumscribed nodules (figure; appendix).
In the absence of specific anti-thyroid antibodies, our considered differential diagnoses were: a subacute or infectious thyroiditis, a seronegative autoimmune thyroiditis, or a drug-induced thyroiditis.
Infectious thyroiditis is commonly associated with thyroid pain and elevated inflammatory markers; both of which were not present in our patient. Regarding autoimmune thyroiditis, approximately 5% of cases are seronegative—without detectable autoantibodies—and display a hypoechoic sonographic pattern akin to a destructive thyroiditis; biochemical abnormalities are mild with slight TSH elevation and minimally reduced concentrations of the peripheral hormones. We considered a diagnosis of seronegative autoimmune thyroiditis unlikely in our patient. That left us with the possibility of a drug-induced thyroiditis.
The patient reported that he had been started on amiodarone, because of symptomatic episodes of ventricular tachycardia, 5 months ago. We therefore immediately started oral levothyroxine at a dose of 1·5 μg/kg bodyweight per day, which led to the rapid normalisation of the patient's thyroid hormone levels.
The prevalence of amiodarone-induced overt hypothyroidism is reported to be approximately 5% of amiodarone-treated patients, with subclinical manifestations five times as frequent. In the absence of autoimmunity, the withdrawal of amiodarone can be considered in subclinical cases.
Even though thyrotoxicosis is the most feared endocrinological side-effect of amiodarone—posing diagnostic and therapeutic challenges—the importance of hypothyroidism caused by the drug should not be underestimated, despite its relatively easy clinical management (video).

A 65-year-old man attended our outpatient clinic for diagnostic evaluation of abnormal blood tests detected during a routine check requested by his cardiologist. The investigations showed a raised serum gamma-glutamyl transferase (406 U/L; normal <60) and a raised serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration of 99·20 μIU/mL (normal 0·27–4·20). The patient's free thyroxine and free tri-iodothyronine were low at 0·67 ng/dL (normal 0·93–1·70) and 1·5 pg/mL (normal 2·0–4·4) respectively. Anti-thyroid antibodies—including thyroid peroxidase antibodies and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies—were not detected.The patient did not report any symptoms indicative of hypothyroidism—specifically fatigue, constipation, or an increased sensitivity to cold. He had no history of thyroid disease.
On general physical examination, the patient did not have a goitre, and his cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes were not enlarged or tender.
Thyroid sonography showed a destructive thyroiditis with a heterogeneous, hypoechoic sonographic pattern and slightly increased vascularisation in both thyroid lobes—without circumscribed nodules (figure; appendix).
In the absence of specific anti-thyroid antibodies, our considered differential diagnoses were: a subacute or infectious thyroiditis, a seronegative autoimmune thyroiditis, or a drug-induced thyroiditis.
Infectious thyroiditis is commonly associated with thyroid pain and elevated inflammatory markers; both of which were not present in our patient. Regarding autoimmune thyroiditis, approximately 5% of cases are seronegative—without detectable autoantibodies—and display a hypoechoic sonographic pattern akin to a destructive thyroiditis; biochemical abnormalities are mild with slight TSH elevation and minimally reduced concentrations of the peripheral hormones. We considered a diagnosis of seronegative autoimmune thyroiditis unlikely in our patient. That left us with the possibility of a drug-induced thyroiditis.
The patient reported that he had been started on amiodarone, because of symptomatic episodes of ventricular tachycardia, 5 months ago. We therefore immediately started oral levothyroxine at a dose of 1·5 μg/kg bodyweight per day, which led to the rapid normalisation of the patient's thyroid hormone levels.
The prevalence of amiodarone-induced overt hypothyroidism is reported to be approximately 5% of amiodarone-treated patients, with subclinical manifestations five times as frequent. In the absence of autoimmunity, the withdrawal of amiodarone can be considered in subclinical cases.
Even though thyrotoxicosis is the most feared endocrinological side-effect of amiodarone—posing diagnostic and therapeutic challenges—the importance of hypothyroidism caused by the drug should not be underestimated, despite its relatively easy clinical management (video).

input:
A 65-year-old man attended our outpatient clinic for diagnostic evaluation of abnormal blood tests detected during a routine check requested by his cardiologist. The investigations showed a raised serum gamma-glutamyl transferase (406 U/L; normal <60) and a raised serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration of 99·20 μIU/mL (normal 0·27–4·20). The patient's free thyroxine and free tri-iodothyronine were low at 0·67 ng/dL (normal 0·93–1·70) and 1·5 pg/mL (normal 2·0–4·4) respectively. Anti-thyroid antibodies—including thyroid peroxidase antibodies and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies—were not detected.The patient did not report any symptoms indicative of hypothyroidism—specifically fatigue, constipation, or an increased sensitivity to cold. He had no history of thyroid disease.
On general physical examination, the patient did not have a goitre, and his cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes were not enlarged or tender.
Thyroid sonography showed a destructive thyroiditis with a heterogeneous, hypoechoic sonographic pattern and slightly increased vascularisation in both thyroid lobes—without circumscribed nodules (figure; appendix).
In the absence of specific anti-thyroid antibodies, our considered differential diagnoses were: a subacute or infectious thyroiditis, a seronegative autoimmune thyroiditis, or a drug-induced thyroiditis.
Infectious thyroiditis is commonly associated with thyroid pain and elevated inflammatory markers; both of which were not present in our patient. Regarding autoimmune thyroiditis, approximately 5% of cases are seronegative—without detectable autoantibodies—and display a hypoechoic sonographic pattern akin to a destructive thyroiditis; biochemical abnormalities are mild with slight TSH elevation and minimally reduced concentrations of the peripheral hormones. We considered a diagnosis of seronegative autoimmune thyroiditis unlikely in our patient. That left us with the possibility of a drug-induced thyroiditis.
The patient reported that he had been started on amiodarone, because of symptomatic episodes of ventricular tachycardia, 5 months ago. We therefore immediately started oral levothyroxine at a dose of 1·5 μg/kg bodyweight per day, which led to the rapid normalisation of the patient's thyroid hormone levels.
The prevalence of amiodarone-induced overt hypothyroidism is reported to be approximately 5% of amiodarone-treated patients, with subclinical manifestations five times as frequent. In the absence of autoimmunity, the withdrawal of amiodarone can be considered in subclinical cases.
Even though thyrotoxicosis is the most feared endocrinological side-effect of amiodarone—posing diagnostic and therapeutic challenges—the importance of hypothyroidism caused by the drug should not be underestimated, despite its relatively easy clinical management (video).
