12 years earlier, the patient had a right colectomy with resection of liver metastases for a mucinous adenocarcinoma of the colon, stage pT3N2aM1; the tumour was of a hypermutant phenotype referred to as microsatellite instability high (MSI-H) and deficient mismatch repair (dMMR). At the time, the patient had been diagnosed with Lynch syndrome after DNA sequencing showed a pathogenic variant in MSH2. After the patient had the surgery, he was treated with adjuvant chemotherapy—folinic acid, fluorouracil, and oxaliplatin, also known as FOLFOX. 3 months later, the disease had progressed in the liver and coeliac and periaortic lymph nodes; he was treated with folinic acid, fluorouracil, irinotecan, and cetuximab.
Notably, a family history showed the patient's mother had carcinoma of the uterus and colon, and his sister had malignancy in the uterus.
5 years after his initial diagnosis, the patient was enrolled in a clinical trial and given combined treatment with the immune-checkpoint inhibitors—including nivolumab for 24 months and 4 injections for induction therapy of ipilumumab; the disease went into remission.
9 years after the initial presentation, a CT scan showed a new metastatic lesion in the left adrenal gland which was treated by stereotaxic radiotherapy.
When we first assessed the patient, a transthoracic echocardiogram showed a mass extending from the inferior vena cava into the right atrium causing obstruction of the tricuspid valve (appendix); contrast-enhancement showed some opacification of the mass (appendix). A 18fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT showed no metabolic activity in the right atrium nor in the inferior vena cava.
After assessment and discussion with the patient—considering firstly his generally good physical state, secondly the response of the disease to immune-checkpoint inhibitors, and thirdly, the obstruction of the tricuspid valve—we excised the right atrial mass during beating-heart surgery with partial cardiopulmonary bypass (appendix).
Gross macroscopic evaluation of the excised mass showed a small amount of thrombus with mostly tissue consistent with a metastatic process (appendix); histopathological analysis of a sample of the lesion confirmed mucinous adenocarcinoma. The patient continued solely on nivolumab, and his general condition improved.
5 months after the heart surgery, the patient was well; a transthoracic echocardiogram and a cardiac CT scan showed no residual or recurrence of the right atrium metastatic mass (appendix). A CT scan confirmed partial response of the metastases in the lymph nodes.
Lynch syndrome, with a pathogenic germline variant in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, or EPCAM, is the most common hereditary colorectal cancer predisposition syndrome. Diagnosis—necessitating input from both oncology and genetics—as well as follow-up involving colonoscopy surveillance is key. In addition, the efficacy of immune checkpoint immunotherapy, specifically anti-PD-1 and anti-CTLA4 antibodies, has resulted in an unprecedented improvement in the number of patients with Lynch syndrome-associated cancers having a successful outcome. The benefits of a multidisciplinary management approach—illustrated by the different teams involved in the treatment of our patient—are clearly apparent.

12 years earlier, the patient had a right colectomy with resection of liver metastases for a mucinous adenocarcinoma of the colon, stage pT3N2aM1; the tumour was of a hypermutant phenotype referred to as microsatellite instability high (MSI-H) and deficient mismatch repair (dMMR). At the time, the patient had been diagnosed with Lynch syndrome after DNA sequencing showed a pathogenic variant in MSH2. After the patient had the surgery, he was treated with adjuvant chemotherapy—folinic acid, fluorouracil, and oxaliplatin, also known as FOLFOX. 3 months later, the disease had progressed in the liver and coeliac and periaortic lymph nodes; he was treated with folinic acid, fluorouracil, irinotecan, and cetuximab.
Notably, a family history showed the patient's mother had carcinoma of the uterus and colon, and his sister had malignancy in the uterus.
5 years after his initial diagnosis, the patient was enrolled in a clinical trial and given combined treatment with the immune-checkpoint inhibitors—including nivolumab for 24 months and 4 injections for induction therapy of ipilumumab; the disease went into remission.
9 years after the initial presentation, a CT scan showed a new metastatic lesion in the left adrenal gland which was treated by stereotaxic radiotherapy.
When we first assessed the patient, a transthoracic echocardiogram showed a mass extending from the inferior vena cava into the right atrium causing obstruction of the tricuspid valve (appendix); contrast-enhancement showed some opacification of the mass (appendix). A 18fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT showed no metabolic activity in the right atrium nor in the inferior vena cava.
After assessment and discussion with the patient—considering firstly his generally good physical state, secondly the response of the disease to immune-checkpoint inhibitors, and thirdly, the obstruction of the tricuspid valve—we excised the right atrial mass during beating-heart surgery with partial cardiopulmonary bypass (appendix).
Gross macroscopic evaluation of the excised mass showed a small amount of thrombus with mostly tissue consistent with a metastatic process (appendix); histopathological analysis of a sample of the lesion confirmed mucinous adenocarcinoma. The patient continued solely on nivolumab, and his general condition improved.
5 months after the heart surgery, the patient was well; a transthoracic echocardiogram and a cardiac CT scan showed no residual or recurrence of the right atrium metastatic mass (appendix). A CT scan confirmed partial response of the metastases in the lymph nodes.
Lynch syndrome, with a pathogenic germline variant in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, or EPCAM, is the most common hereditary colorectal cancer predisposition syndrome. Diagnosis—necessitating input from both oncology and genetics—as well as follow-up involving colonoscopy surveillance is key. In addition, the efficacy of immune checkpoint immunotherapy, specifically anti-PD-1 and anti-CTLA4 antibodies, has resulted in an unprecedented improvement in the number of patients with Lynch syndrome-associated cancers having a successful outcome. The benefits of a multidisciplinary management approach—illustrated by the different teams involved in the treatment of our patient—are clearly apparent.

input: A 26-year-old man was referred to our orthopaedics department with left thigh pain. Radiography and CT revealed a cortical mass unilaterally on the medial side of the distal femoral diaphysis (figure A, B). The lesion extended with osteoblastic and osteolytic changes that accompany a periosteal reaction. MRI revealed a contrast-enhanced soft tissue mass surrounding the cortical lesion (figure C–E). No major blood vessel or bone marrow infiltration was observed. Our primary differential diagnosis was malignancy, particularly periosteal osteosarcoma, followed by fracture, osteomyelitis, or periostitis. A periosteal biopsy did not show malignancy but did reveal neutrophilic inflammation (figure F, G). Additional testing showed elevated inflammatory markers and arterial wall thickening in the aortic arch and its common branches (figure H) but not in the left femoral artery. At follow-up 2 months after the first visit, the patient reported general fatigue. Carotid bruits and blood pressure differences between the arms were observed. The patient was diagnosed with Takayasu arteritis based on the American College of Rheumatology–European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology classification criteria. Treatment of Takayasu arteritis was initiated using daily oral prednisolone (initial dose of 80 mg followed by decreasing dose thereafter) followed by subcutaneous tocilizumab (162 mg/week), after which the left thigh pain disappeared and periostitis subsided on imaging (figure I–K). The patient's Indian Takayasu Clinical Activity Score decreased from 6 to 2. We concluded that the femoral lesions were associated with Takayasu arteritis. Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel vasculitis that presents with non-specific symptoms and signs, but periostitis is a rare manifestation. Isolated bone lesions incline the diagnosis more towards malignancy than systemic disease; however, several previous reports have shown isolated Takayasu arteritis-associated periostitis. Local inflammation of the periosteum might create a malignancy-like mass and periosteal osteosarcoma is suspected when the mass affects the femoral diaphysis in young adults. As patient presentation and imaging findings of Takayasu arteritis-associated periostitis might mimic periosteal osteosarcoma, it is imperative to rule out malignancy and maintain a broad differential diagnosis.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a chronic history of constipation, abdominal pain, and bloating. There was no history of weight loss or haematochezia. She had anorexia nervosa for which she was engaged with psychiatric care. She was a non-smoker and consumed minimal alcohol. She used glycerine suppositories as required. Initial treatment with polyethylene glycol improved the symptoms. Blood tests revealed a normocytic anaemia of 103 g/L and normal haematinics; faecal calprotectin was negative. A colonoscopy was done that showed significant discolouration of the bowel mucosa from caecum (figure, A) to distal descending colon (figure, B). The terminal ileum (figure, C) and rectum (figure, D) were of normal colour. Biopsy samples confirmed normal gland architecture with abundant pigment laden macrophages in keeping with melanosis coli (figure, E).Melanosis coli is a brown discolouration of the colonic mucosa, caused by the accumulation of pigment in macrophages within the lamina propria. The pigment was initially thought to be melanin, but was later identified as lipofuscin deposited in macrophages due to apoptosis. The pigment accumulation is reversible within 6–12 months of withdrawal of the offending agent, usually anthraquinone-containing laxatives. In this case, the patient denied laxative use. Melanosis typically is most intense in the caecum and diminishes in intensity down the length of the colon. This relates to the highest concentration of the active form of the drug, which is chemically inert until it reaches the caecum. Characteristically, the terminal ileum is devoid of any pigment uptake, as seen here, despite the high macrophage concentration. This might be due to the structural differences or the bacterial flora.
Although unlikely in the context of the clinical presentation, the diagnostic dilemma for clinicians is differentiating between benign melanosis coli and severe consequences of ischaemic colitis in the emergency setting. Endoscopically and intraoperatively this differentiation is problematic especially as both conditions can coexist, although the distribution of mucosal changes and the patient's symptomology are able to support decision making.

input: A 26-year-old man was referred to our orthopaedics department with left thigh pain. Radiography and CT revealed a cortical mass unilaterally on the medial side of the distal femoral diaphysis (figure A, B). The lesion extended with osteoblastic and osteolytic changes that accompany a periosteal reaction. MRI revealed a contrast-enhanced soft tissue mass surrounding the cortical lesion (figure C–E). No major blood vessel or bone marrow infiltration was observed. Our primary differential diagnosis was malignancy, particularly periosteal osteosarcoma, followed by fracture, osteomyelitis, or periostitis. A periosteal biopsy did not show malignancy but did reveal neutrophilic inflammation (figure F, G). Additional testing showed elevated inflammatory markers and arterial wall thickening in the aortic arch and its common branches (figure H) but not in the left femoral artery. At follow-up 2 months after the first visit, the patient reported general fatigue. Carotid bruits and blood pressure differences between the arms were observed. The patient was diagnosed with Takayasu arteritis based on the American College of Rheumatology–European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology classification criteria. Treatment of Takayasu arteritis was initiated using daily oral prednisolone (initial dose of 80 mg followed by decreasing dose thereafter) followed by subcutaneous tocilizumab (162 mg/week), after which the left thigh pain disappeared and periostitis subsided on imaging (figure I–K). The patient's Indian Takayasu Clinical Activity Score decreased from 6 to 2. We concluded that the femoral lesions were associated with Takayasu arteritis. Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel vasculitis that presents with non-specific symptoms and signs, but periostitis is a rare manifestation. Isolated bone lesions incline the diagnosis more towards malignancy than systemic disease; however, several previous reports have shown isolated Takayasu arteritis-associated periostitis. Local inflammation of the periosteum might create a malignancy-like mass and periosteal osteosarcoma is suspected when the mass affects the femoral diaphysis in young adults. As patient presentation and imaging findings of Takayasu arteritis-associated periostitis might mimic periosteal osteosarcoma, it is imperative to rule out malignancy and maintain a broad differential diagnosis.

input: A 26-year-old man was referred to our orthopaedics department with left thigh pain. Radiography and CT revealed a cortical mass unilaterally on the medial side of the distal femoral diaphysis (figure A, B). The lesion extended with osteoblastic and osteolytic changes that accompany a periosteal reaction. MRI revealed a contrast-enhanced soft tissue mass surrounding the cortical lesion (figure C–E). No major blood vessel or bone marrow infiltration was observed. Our primary differential diagnosis was malignancy, particularly periosteal osteosarcoma, followed by fracture, osteomyelitis, or periostitis. A periosteal biopsy did not show malignancy but did reveal neutrophilic inflammation (figure F, G). Additional testing showed elevated inflammatory markers and arterial wall thickening in the aortic arch and its common branches (figure H) but not in the left femoral artery. At follow-up 2 months after the first visit, the patient reported general fatigue. Carotid bruits and blood pressure differences between the arms were observed. The patient was diagnosed with Takayasu arteritis based on the American College of Rheumatology–European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology classification criteria. Treatment of Takayasu arteritis was initiated using daily oral prednisolone (initial dose of 80 mg followed by decreasing dose thereafter) followed by subcutaneous tocilizumab (162 mg/week), after which the left thigh pain disappeared and periostitis subsided on imaging (figure I–K). The patient's Indian Takayasu Clinical Activity Score decreased from 6 to 2. We concluded that the femoral lesions were associated with Takayasu arteritis. Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel vasculitis that presents with non-specific symptoms and signs, but periostitis is a rare manifestation. Isolated bone lesions incline the diagnosis more towards malignancy than systemic disease; however, several previous reports have shown isolated Takayasu arteritis-associated periostitis. Local inflammation of the periosteum might create a malignancy-like mass and periosteal osteosarcoma is suspected when the mass affects the femoral diaphysis in young adults. As patient presentation and imaging findings of Takayasu arteritis-associated periostitis might mimic periosteal osteosarcoma, it is imperative to rule out malignancy and maintain a broad differential diagnosis.

Over a period of approxinately 1 year, it extended onto the scalp, resulting in a linear non-scarring alopecia, seemingly following the lines of Blaschko (figure). Initial therapy with topical glucocorticoids failed, and a skin biopsy was taken. Histopathological examination showed a normal epidermis, accumulation of mucin in the dermis, and lymphocytic panniculitis (figure). Linear cutaneous lupus profundus was diagnosed. Laboratory tests were normal, apart from positive antinuclear antibodies (1:200) and slightly increased C3d complement. Under oral hydroxychloroquine therapy the disorder resolved within 12 weeks, followed by complete regrowth of hair. No relapse occurred during 1 year of maintenance treatment. The face and scalp are predilection sites of cutaneous lupus erythematosus profundus. This can result in an alopecia areata-like clinical picture or non-scarring linear alopecia, which has thus far mainly been reported in east Asians.

And from about one year of age, her parents had difficulty combing her hair.On clinical examination of the patient's scalp hair, we found the patient had blonde, dry, and glistening hair (figure); her eyebrows and eyelashes were unaffected.
Examination of the hair using light microscopy showed irregular triangle-shaped hair shafts and atypical canals along the hair shaft axis.
Molecular genetic analysis showed the homozygous pathogenic variant c.881C>T (p.Ala294Val) in exon 8 of the PADI3 gene.
Considering together the findings from clinical examination, light microscopy, and genetic analysis, we made a diagnosis of uncombable hair syndrome: a rare hair shaft anomaly that presents in early childhood with blond, glistening, and frizzy hair.
Patients’ scalp hair grows in thick bundles that project out in different directions which makes combing impossible. Additionally, in some cases the rate of hair growth may be slow. Under light microscopy, the hair shafts may appear unaffected, and scanning electron microscopy may be necessary to confirm the presence of triangulated hair shafts and longitudinal grooves along the hair shaft axis. No definitive treatment is yet available, but oral biotin supplementation has been reported to make clinical improvement in some cases. The prognosis is promising as hair texture improves during puberty. In some cases, the condition is associated with brachydactyly, ectodermal dysplasia, juvenile cataract, and oligodontia.
Most cases of uncombable hair syndrome—a condition depicted in the 1845 German children's book Der Struwwelpeter, which translates as “Shock-headed Peter”—are sporadic and autosomal recessive; the responsible pathogenic variants are in the PADI3, TCHH, and TGM3 genes, which encode for proteins involved in hair shaft formation. Employment of molecular genetics in diagnosing this syndrome must now be considered the gold standard. Generally, when diagnosing hair and skin disorders, molecular genetics has the advantage of confirming the clinical diagnosis with greater certainty; risks of family members may also be identified. Additionally, molecular genetic analysis usually only requires saliva or an EDTA blood sample, thus avoiding the employment of more invasive investigations.

A 3-year-old girl was referred to the dermatology department with blonde, straw-like, and unruly hair. The child's parents reported that since birth her hair had been sparse and slow growing. And from about one year of age, her parents had difficulty combing her hair.On clinical examination of the patient's scalp hair, we found the patient had blonde, dry, and glistening hair (figure); her eyebrows and eyelashes were unaffected.
Examination of the hair using light microscopy showed irregular triangle-shaped hair shafts and atypical canals along the hair shaft axis.
Molecular genetic analysis showed the homozygous pathogenic variant c.881C>T (p.Ala294Val) in exon 8 of the PADI3 gene.
Considering together the findings from clinical examination, light microscopy, and genetic analysis, we made a diagnosis of uncombable hair syndrome: a rare hair shaft anomaly that presents in early childhood with blond, glistening, and frizzy hair.
Patients’ scalp hair grows in thick bundles that project out in different directions which makes combing impossible. Additionally, in some cases the rate of hair growth may be slow. Under light microscopy, the hair shafts may appear unaffected, and scanning electron microscopy may be necessary to confirm the presence of triangulated hair shafts and longitudinal grooves along the hair shaft axis. No definitive treatment is yet available, but oral biotin supplementation has been reported to make clinical improvement in some cases. The prognosis is promising as hair texture improves during puberty. In some cases, the condition is associated with brachydactyly, ectodermal dysplasia, juvenile cataract, and oligodontia.
Most cases of uncombable hair syndrome—a condition depicted in the 1845 German children's book Der Struwwelpeter, which translates as “Shock-headed Peter”—are sporadic and autosomal recessive; the responsible pathogenic variants are in the PADI3, TCHH, and TGM3 genes, which encode for proteins involved in hair shaft formation. Employment of molecular genetics in diagnosing this syndrome must now be considered the gold standard. Generally, when diagnosing hair and skin disorders, molecular genetics has the advantage of confirming the clinical diagnosis with greater certainty; risks of family members may also be identified. Additionally, molecular genetic analysis usually only requires saliva or an EDTA blood sample, thus avoiding the employment of more invasive investigations.

input:
A 3-year-old girl was referred to the dermatology department with blonde, straw-like, and unruly hair. The child's parents reported that since birth her hair had been sparse and slow growing. And from about one year of age, her parents had difficulty combing her hair.On clinical examination of the patient's scalp hair, we found the patient had blonde, dry, and glistening hair (figure); her eyebrows and eyelashes were unaffected.
Examination of the hair using light microscopy showed irregular triangle-shaped hair shafts and atypical canals along the hair shaft axis.
Molecular genetic analysis showed the homozygous pathogenic variant c.881C>T (p.Ala294Val) in exon 8 of the PADI3 gene.
Considering together the findings from clinical examination, light microscopy, and genetic analysis, we made a diagnosis of uncombable hair syndrome: a rare hair shaft anomaly that presents in early childhood with blond, glistening, and frizzy hair.
Patients’ scalp hair grows in thick bundles that project out in different directions which makes combing impossible. Additionally, in some cases the rate of hair growth may be slow. Under light microscopy, the hair shafts may appear unaffected, and scanning electron microscopy may be necessary to confirm the presence of triangulated hair shafts and longitudinal grooves along the hair shaft axis. No definitive treatment is yet available, but oral biotin supplementation has been reported to make clinical improvement in some cases. The prognosis is promising as hair texture improves during puberty. In some cases, the condition is associated with brachydactyly, ectodermal dysplasia, juvenile cataract, and oligodontia.
Most cases of uncombable hair syndrome—a condition depicted in the 1845 German children's book Der Struwwelpeter, which translates as “Shock-headed Peter”—are sporadic and autosomal recessive; the responsible pathogenic variants are in the PADI3, TCHH, and TGM3 genes, which encode for proteins involved in hair shaft formation. Employment of molecular genetics in diagnosing this syndrome must now be considered the gold standard. Generally, when diagnosing hair and skin disorders, molecular genetics has the advantage of confirming the clinical diagnosis with greater certainty; risks of family members may also be identified. Additionally, molecular genetic analysis usually only requires saliva or an EDTA blood sample, thus avoiding the employment of more invasive investigations.

A baby girl delivered vaginally at full-term at a local hospital was found to have a global decrease in tone which was predominately in her arms. She had been born after an induction of labour because of decreased movements and oligohydramnios seen at 39 weeks of gestation on ultrasound.An ultrasound of the baby's head soon after birth demonstrated no obvious abnormalities. However, a T1-gadolinium enhanced MRI of the brain and spine showed an enhancing, intramedullary lesion extending from the medulla down to the upper thoracic spinal cord—indicating a possible high-grade neoplasm (figure). The patient was transferred to our quaternary referral hospital and comprehensive cancer centre.
On examination, the baby was awake and alert, with a flat fontanelle, normal head circumference, and global hypotonia. Over the next 2 weeks, her quadriparesis became progressively worse—the cervical spine showed signs of compression because of the expansile tumour in the spinal canal. We decompressed the cervical spine by doing a laminoplasty; we used electrostimulation, neuromonitoring, and intraoperative ultrasound to locate a safe midline entry point to obtain a biopsy and partially debulk the tumour. Histopathological analysis of a biopsy sample confirmed the suspected diagnosis of congenital spinal cord glioblastoma WHO grade IV.
Next generation sequencing showed a gene fusion involving the neurotrophin tropomyosin receptor kinase (NTRK) 1 gene: an inversion on chromosome 1q. No other pathogenic mutations, amplifications, deletions, or rearrangements were identified. Additionally, the tumour showed diffuse tropomyosin receptor kinase (TRK) positivity; she was treated with induction chemotherapy and the oral TRK inhibitor, larotrectinib, starting at a 50% dose of 50 mg/m2 twice a day for the first week to monitor for possible signs of toxicity because of the concurrent chemotherapy. The full dose of 100 mg/m2 twice a day was started in week 2 and continued. The patient tolerated the treatment well, and following cycle 1 of only conventional chemotherapy, a small reduction in size of the spinal cord tumour was seen.
2 weeks after the addition of larotrectinib, we observed a significant decrease in the size and enhancement on MRI of the lesion, with improvement in the patient's quadriparesis.
8 weeks into treatment with the oral TRK inhibitor and 4 cycles of carboplatin and etoposide, the tumour had completely regressed and was no longer visible with imaging (figure). 17 months after starting treatment, the patient was crawling and progressing toward walking; she continues treatment on the oral TRK inhibitor only, and there was no evidence of recurrence of the tumour.
The NTRK genes—NTRK1, NTRK2, and NTRK3 which produce TRK proteins—are affected by oncogenic fusions leading to a wide range of both paediatric and adult neoplasms. Small molecule TRK inhibitors have shown efficacy in treating a diverse array of TRK-positive tumours. In clinical trials of TRK inhibitors for tumours—in both adult and paediatric patients with a variety of different primary tumour types with NTRK gene fusions—response rates ranged from 75–93%. The first generation TRK inhibitors appear, on the whole, to be well tolerated in terms of adverse events: most are low grade—including neurotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, anaemia and neutropenia, and nausea and vomiting.
Aided by histopathological examination findings, next generation sequencing can uncover NTRK fusions that may change the clinical course for patients with many primary tumours. While we could not entirely rule out a response to chemotherapy alone resulting in the improvement seen in our patient, the prognosis for congenital glioblastomas treated with chemotherapy alone remains very poor (video).

A baby girl delivered vaginally at full-term at a local hospital was found to have a global decrease in tone which was predominately in her arms. She had been born after an induction of labour because of decreased movements and oligohydramnios seen at 39 weeks of gestation on ultrasound.An ultrasound of the baby's head soon after birth demonstrated no obvious abnormalities. However, a T1-gadolinium enhanced MRI of the brain and spine showed an enhancing, intramedullary lesion extending from the medulla down to the upper thoracic spinal cord—indicating a possible high-grade neoplasm (figure). The patient was transferred to our quaternary referral hospital and comprehensive cancer centre.
On examination, the baby was awake and alert, with a flat fontanelle, normal head circumference, and global hypotonia. Over the next 2 weeks, her quadriparesis became progressively worse—the cervical spine showed signs of compression because of the expansile tumour in the spinal canal. We decompressed the cervical spine by doing a laminoplasty; we used electrostimulation, neuromonitoring, and intraoperative ultrasound to locate a safe midline entry point to obtain a biopsy and partially debulk the tumour. Histopathological analysis of a biopsy sample confirmed the suspected diagnosis of congenital spinal cord glioblastoma WHO grade IV.
Next generation sequencing showed a gene fusion involving the neurotrophin tropomyosin receptor kinase (NTRK) 1 gene: an inversion on chromosome 1q. No other pathogenic mutations, amplifications, deletions, or rearrangements were identified. Additionally, the tumour showed diffuse tropomyosin receptor kinase (TRK) positivity; she was treated with induction chemotherapy and the oral TRK inhibitor, larotrectinib, starting at a 50% dose of 50 mg/m2 twice a day for the first week to monitor for possible signs of toxicity because of the concurrent chemotherapy. The full dose of 100 mg/m2 twice a day was started in week 2 and continued. The patient tolerated the treatment well, and following cycle 1 of only conventional chemotherapy, a small reduction in size of the spinal cord tumour was seen.
2 weeks after the addition of larotrectinib, we observed a significant decrease in the size and enhancement on MRI of the lesion, with improvement in the patient's quadriparesis.
8 weeks into treatment with the oral TRK inhibitor and 4 cycles of carboplatin and etoposide, the tumour had completely regressed and was no longer visible with imaging (figure). 17 months after starting treatment, the patient was crawling and progressing toward walking; she continues treatment on the oral TRK inhibitor only, and there was no evidence of recurrence of the tumour.
The NTRK genes—NTRK1, NTRK2, and NTRK3 which produce TRK proteins—are affected by oncogenic fusions leading to a wide range of both paediatric and adult neoplasms. Small molecule TRK inhibitors have shown efficacy in treating a diverse array of TRK-positive tumours. In clinical trials of TRK inhibitors for tumours—in both adult and paediatric patients with a variety of different primary tumour types with NTRK gene fusions—response rates ranged from 75–93%. The first generation TRK inhibitors appear, on the whole, to be well tolerated in terms of adverse events: most are low grade—including neurotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, anaemia and neutropenia, and nausea and vomiting.
Aided by histopathological examination findings, next generation sequencing can uncover NTRK fusions that may change the clinical course for patients with many primary tumours. While we could not entirely rule out a response to chemotherapy alone resulting in the improvement seen in our patient, the prognosis for congenital glioblastomas treated with chemotherapy alone remains very poor (video).

A baby girl delivered vaginally at full-term at a local hospital was found to have a global decrease in tone which was predominately in her arms. She had been born after an induction of labour because of decreased movements and oligohydramnios seen at 39 weeks of gestation on ultrasound.An ultrasound of the baby's head soon after birth demonstrated no obvious abnormalities. However, a T1-gadolinium enhanced MRI of the brain and spine showed an enhancing, intramedullary lesion extending from the medulla down to the upper thoracic spinal cord—indicating a possible high-grade neoplasm (figure). The patient was transferred to our quaternary referral hospital and comprehensive cancer centre.
On examination, the baby was awake and alert, with a flat fontanelle, normal head circumference, and global hypotonia. Over the next 2 weeks, her quadriparesis became progressively worse—the cervical spine showed signs of compression because of the expansile tumour in the spinal canal. We decompressed the cervical spine by doing a laminoplasty; we used electrostimulation, neuromonitoring, and intraoperative ultrasound to locate a safe midline entry point to obtain a biopsy and partially debulk the tumour. Histopathological analysis of a biopsy sample confirmed the suspected diagnosis of congenital spinal cord glioblastoma WHO grade IV.
Next generation sequencing showed a gene fusion involving the neurotrophin tropomyosin receptor kinase (NTRK) 1 gene: an inversion on chromosome 1q. No other pathogenic mutations, amplifications, deletions, or rearrangements were identified. Additionally, the tumour showed diffuse tropomyosin receptor kinase (TRK) positivity; she was treated with induction chemotherapy and the oral TRK inhibitor, larotrectinib, starting at a 50% dose of 50 mg/m2 twice a day for the first week to monitor for possible signs of toxicity because of the concurrent chemotherapy. The full dose of 100 mg/m2 twice a day was started in week 2 and continued. The patient tolerated the treatment well, and following cycle 1 of only conventional chemotherapy, a small reduction in size of the spinal cord tumour was seen.
2 weeks after the addition of larotrectinib, we observed a significant decrease in the size and enhancement on MRI of the lesion, with improvement in the patient's quadriparesis.
8 weeks into treatment with the oral TRK inhibitor and 4 cycles of carboplatin and etoposide, the tumour had completely regressed and was no longer visible with imaging (figure). 17 months after starting treatment, the patient was crawling and progressing toward walking; she continues treatment on the oral TRK inhibitor only, and there was no evidence of recurrence of the tumour.
The NTRK genes—NTRK1, NTRK2, and NTRK3 which produce TRK proteins—are affected by oncogenic fusions leading to a wide range of both paediatric and adult neoplasms. Small molecule TRK inhibitors have shown efficacy in treating a diverse array of TRK-positive tumours. In clinical trials of TRK inhibitors for tumours—in both adult and paediatric patients with a variety of different primary tumour types with NTRK gene fusions—response rates ranged from 75–93%. The first generation TRK inhibitors appear, on the whole, to be well tolerated in terms of adverse events: most are low grade—including neurotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, anaemia and neutropenia, and nausea and vomiting.
Aided by histopathological examination findings, next generation sequencing can uncover NTRK fusions that may change the clinical course for patients with many primary tumours. While we could not entirely rule out a response to chemotherapy alone resulting in the improvement seen in our patient, the prognosis for congenital glioblastomas treated with chemotherapy alone remains very poor (video).

A 25-year-old woman presented to our hospital with sudden onset of blurred vision in her right eye. The patient had a history of Graves' disease and had started methimazole 20 mg daily 2 months earlier: investigations at that time had found her free tri-iodothyronine concentration at 13·60 pg/mL (normal 1·71–3·71), free thyroxine 2·93 ng/dL (normal 0·70–1·48), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) of 0·01 μU/mL (normal 0·35–4·94), and TSH-receptor antibody of 11·4 IU/L (normal 0·0–1·9).On examination, we found the patient to be well; she reported no tiredness, she had no tremor or tachycardia, but she did have mild bilateral exophthalmos—with normal eye movements.
Slit lamp and fundus examinations showed cellular infiltrates in the anterior chamber and vitreous opacity (figure) in the right eye. Fluorescein angiography showed retinal vascular leakage in the right eye: retinal vasculitis (figure).
Laboratory investigations showed an improvement in her thyroid function tests: free tri-iodothyronine concentration was 2·74 pg/mL, free thyroxine was 1·01 ng/dL, TSH was 0·01 μU/mL, and TSH-receptor antibody was 6·0 IU/L. Additional tests—to exclude autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and sarcoidosis—were negative. However, the patient was found to be seropositive for human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1); tests for other infections—including cytomegalovirus and tuberculosis—were negative. Real-time PCR analysis indicated a relatively low HTLV-1 provirus load of 1·90 copies per 100 peripheral blood mononuclear cells.
A neurological assessment—specifically looking for HTLV-1-associated myelopathy or tropical spastic paraparesis—found no signs of progressive spastic weakness in the patient's legs, no lower back pain, and she reported no bowel or bladder dysfunction.
Considering the systemic and ocular findings, we made a diagnosis of HTLV-1 uveitis and started the patient on topical 0·1% betamethasone 4 times daily applied to her right eye and oral prednisolone 0·5 mg per kg daily.
The HTLV-1 uveitis gradually improved and after 10 months, the patient had normal vision with no abnormalities on examination of her eye. The dose of the systemic corticosteroid was tapered down after 1 month and discontinued after 10 months.
Evaluation of the patient's family found her parents and two siblings to be HTLV-1 seropositive: indicating that our patient probably acquired the infection by vertical transmission from her mother.
Notably, the patient's sister had developed HTLV-1 uveitis 6 years earlier, aged 24 years; the course of the disease was similar to our case with the diagnosis of HTLV-1 being made after the diagnosis and treatment of Graves' disease with methimazole.
HTLV-1 infection is associated with an increased risk of premature death independent of the more well known associated diseases of adult T-cell leukaemia-lymphoma and HTLV-1-associated myelopathy or tropical spastic paraparesis. HTLV-1 infection is also associated with a range of morbidities including inflammatory conditions such as Sjogren's syndrome, bronchiectasis, infections—including tuberculosis and urinary tract infections—other malignancies such as cervical cancer. HTLV-1 uveitis should be excluded during evaluation of the ophthalmic complications of Graves' disease in patients where HTLV-1 is endemic or where there is a family history of HTLV-1-associated diseases (video).

A 20-year-old daycare teacher presented to our hospital reporting a generalised erythematous maculopapular rash. The patient also had a fever, myalgia, nausea, reduced urine output, peripheral oedema, and dyspnoea on exertion. She reported that the rash had rapidly increased in size over the past 72 h—coinciding with a doubling of the dose of her lamotrigine which she was prescribed for bipolar affective disorder.Apart from her mental health condition, she had no other significant medical history.
On examination, we found the patient to be feverish with a temperature of 40·3°C and bradycardic with a heart rate of 42 beats per min. She had a morbilliform rash—prominently seen over her trunk and extremities; there was no mucosal or genital involvement (figure). Hepatosplenomegaly and mild oedema of both the patient's legs were also noted.
An electrocardiogram showed sinus bradycardia (figure). Laboratory investigations showed a leukocytosis of 14·03 × 109 per L (normal 4·5–11) with an eosinophilia of 1·08 × 109 per L (normal 0–0·5). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated at 24 mm/h (normal 0–29).
The patient's aspartate aminotransferase was 42 units per L (normal 8–33) and alanine aminotransferase was 79 units per L (normal 7–55): indicating a transaminitis. The blood urea nitrogen concentration was 50 mg/dL (normal 6–21) and creatine concentration was 5·6 mg/dL (normal 0·5–1·2).
Screening for hepatitis A, B, and C viruses was reactive only for hepatitis A virus IgG. An autoimmune panel was negative for antinuclear and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies. However, a Monospot test was positive; a cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgG test was also positive.
Considering the findings in the round—the transaminitis and acute renal failure showed multiorgan involvement, the positive Monospot test indicated active Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection, and the positive IgG test suggested previous CMV infection—we made a diagnosis of drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome induced by lamotrigine with a concomitant infection. We considered that the EBV was either a new infection or a reactivation of a previous infection with the virus.
We stopped the lamotrigine and gave the patient a course of pulse steroids which gradually led to an improvement in her symptoms and renal function.
DRESS syndrome is an idiosyncratic drug-induced delayed type IV hypersensitivity severe multisystemic reaction that typically develops within 2–8 weeks of exposure. The proposed pathogenesis is a reactivation of latent herpesviruses which can be triggered by certain medications—including lamotrigine; a cross-reaction is thought to occur between the virus-specific T lymphocytes and the medications. In our case, the underlying cause of DRESS syndrome could be explained two ways: firstly, the concurrent lamotrigine use and a primary EBV infection or, secondly, lamotrigine-induced reactivation of EBV which then caused DRESS syndrome. Whatever the sequence of events, the treatment remains the same: immediate cessation of the drug causing the problem, systemic corticosteroids, or other immunosuppressants—including intravenous immuno-globulin in steroid-resistant cases (video).

A 20-year-old daycare teacher presented to our hospital reporting a generalised erythematous maculopapular rash. The patient also had a fever, myalgia, nausea, reduced urine output, peripheral oedema, and dyspnoea on exertion. She reported that the rash had rapidly increased in size over the past 72 h—coinciding with a doubling of the dose of her lamotrigine which she was prescribed for bipolar affective disorder.Apart from her mental health condition, she had no other significant medical history.
On examination, we found the patient to be feverish with a temperature of 40·3°C and bradycardic with a heart rate of 42 beats per min. She had a morbilliform rash—prominently seen over her trunk and extremities; there was no mucosal or genital involvement (figure). Hepatosplenomegaly and mild oedema of both the patient's legs were also noted.
An electrocardiogram showed sinus bradycardia (figure). Laboratory investigations showed a leukocytosis of 14·03 × 109 per L (normal 4·5–11) with an eosinophilia of 1·08 × 109 per L (normal 0–0·5). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated at 24 mm/h (normal 0–29).
The patient's aspartate aminotransferase was 42 units per L (normal 8–33) and alanine aminotransferase was 79 units per L (normal 7–55): indicating a transaminitis. The blood urea nitrogen concentration was 50 mg/dL (normal 6–21) and creatine concentration was 5·6 mg/dL (normal 0·5–1·2).
Screening for hepatitis A, B, and C viruses was reactive only for hepatitis A virus IgG. An autoimmune panel was negative for antinuclear and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies. However, a Monospot test was positive; a cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgG test was also positive.
Considering the findings in the round—the transaminitis and acute renal failure showed multiorgan involvement, the positive Monospot test indicated active Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection, and the positive IgG test suggested previous CMV infection—we made a diagnosis of drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome induced by lamotrigine with a concomitant infection. We considered that the EBV was either a new infection or a reactivation of a previous infection with the virus.
We stopped the lamotrigine and gave the patient a course of pulse steroids which gradually led to an improvement in her symptoms and renal function.
DRESS syndrome is an idiosyncratic drug-induced delayed type IV hypersensitivity severe multisystemic reaction that typically develops within 2–8 weeks of exposure. The proposed pathogenesis is a reactivation of latent herpesviruses which can be triggered by certain medications—including lamotrigine; a cross-reaction is thought to occur between the virus-specific T lymphocytes and the medications. In our case, the underlying cause of DRESS syndrome could be explained two ways: firstly, the concurrent lamotrigine use and a primary EBV infection or, secondly, lamotrigine-induced reactivation of EBV which then caused DRESS syndrome. Whatever the sequence of events, the treatment remains the same: immediate cessation of the drug causing the problem, systemic corticosteroids, or other immunosuppressants—including intravenous immuno-globulin in steroid-resistant cases (video).

A 47-year-old woman presented to our institution with a 1-month history of swelling and a painless skin plaque on her left breast. 6 years earlier, the patient had been treated for luminal A invasive ductal carcinoma in the superomedial quadrant of the left breast; she had neoadjuvant chemotherapy, breast-conserving surgery, radiation therapy—a whole breast dose of 50 Gy plus a 10 Gy boost to the tumour bed—and oral tamoxifen. The patient had been found to have no recurrence of the tumour at any subsequent follow-up appointments. She had no history of breast trauma or lymphoedema.
On physical examination, we found the patient was generally well; she had a 1 cm purple plaque on the inferolateral quadrant of her left breast, approximately 1·5 cm from the areola (figure).Breast ultrasound examination showed skin thickening, subcutaneous oedema, and a predominantly hypoechoic nonmass finding in the inferomedial quadrant of the left breast with irregular borders, regional distribution, and central hypervascularity on power Doppler (figure). Diagnostic mammogram showed a developing asymmetry in the inferomedial quadrant of the left breast, as well as skin thickening and parenchymal oedema that were more pronounced compared with her previous mammograms (figure). Histological examination of a sample obtained by ultrasound-guided core biopsy showed solid epithelial proliferation with marked cellular atypia—initially deemed suspicious for recurrence of the carcinoma (figure). Immunohistochemistry results were positive for CD31, ERG, and D2-40 on most target cells and for CD34 in subgroups of target cells (appendix), along with very high Ki67 expression (90% of target cells), findings compatible with post radiation angiosarcoma.
On post-biopsy follow-up—54 days after the first ultrasound examination—the previously 1 cm wide skin lesion had progressed to a 4 cm irregular violaceous plaque with subtle areas of yellowish discoloration on adjacent skin (figure). On ultrasound examination, the lesion appeared as an irregular, hypoechoic mass with thick echogenic rind; the high central vascularity on power Doppler remained visible (appendix).
The findings, diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment options were discussed with the patient and together the decision was made to proceed to mastectomy of the affected breast.
On the day of mastectomy—60 days after the first ultrasound examination—additional satellite lesions and morphological changes in the nipple-areola complex were seen adjacent to the irregular violaceous plaque, with progression of the areas of yellowish skin discoloration (figure).
Histopathological analysis of a sample of the surgical specimen, which measured 9·0 cm × 7·0 cm X 6·0 cm and invaded the nipple, dermis, and parenchymal breast tissue, confirmed the diagnosis of post-radiation angiosarcoma. CT scans of the patient's head, chest, and abdomen showed no evidence of metastases.
The patient made an uneventful recovery from the operation and was allowed home 24 h later. At follow-up 3 months after the mastectomy, a new 1 cm violaceous skin lesion surrounded by a yellowish halo appeared in the mastectomy scar (appendix); recurrence of the post-radiation angiosarcoma was confirmed by histopathological analysis of a sample obtained from surgically excised tissue.
Post-radiation angiosarcoma is an uncommon aggressive complication of radiotherapy for breast cancer, with a median latency period of 5–6 years. About one in every 1000 patients treated with radiotherapy for breast cancer may be at risk of developing the condition, and global incidence is expected to rise as the number of patients undergoing breast-preserving surgery plus radiotherapy increases. Typically, the tumour arises within the skin and subcutaneous tissues previously included in the irradiation field—this is unlike primary breast angiosarcomas which usually originate deep within the breast parenchyma. Patients with post-radiation angiosarcomas may develop breast swelling, erythema, skin thickening, and painless erythematous patches or plaques in previously irradiated areas, as well as areas of yellowish discoloration on circumjacent skin which is related to haemoglobin degradation products. Lymph node involvement is uncommon. Imaging findings, when present, are often non-specific and include skin and trabecular thickening, developing asymmetry on mammogram, and solid, irregular masses on breast ultrasound examination.
Surgical excision with negative margins is considered the standard treatment; prognosis is poor even with complete tumour resection, with 5-year survival rates of about 40%.

A 20-year-old daycare teacher presented to our hospital reporting a generalised erythematous maculopapular rash. The patient also had a fever, myalgia, nausea, reduced urine output, peripheral oedema, and dyspnoea on exertion. She reported that the rash had rapidly increased in size over the past 72 h—coinciding with a doubling of the dose of her lamotrigine which she was prescribed for bipolar affective disorder.Apart from her mental health condition, she had no other significant medical history.
On examination, we found the patient to be feverish with a temperature of 40·3°C and bradycardic with a heart rate of 42 beats per min. She had a morbilliform rash—prominently seen over her trunk and extremities; there was no mucosal or genital involvement (figure). Hepatosplenomegaly and mild oedema of both the patient's legs were also noted.
An electrocardiogram showed sinus bradycardia (figure). Laboratory investigations showed a leukocytosis of 14·03 × 109 per L (normal 4·5–11) with an eosinophilia of 1·08 × 109 per L (normal 0–0·5). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated at 24 mm/h (normal 0–29).
The patient's aspartate aminotransferase was 42 units per L (normal 8–33) and alanine aminotransferase was 79 units per L (normal 7–55): indicating a transaminitis. The blood urea nitrogen concentration was 50 mg/dL (normal 6–21) and creatine concentration was 5·6 mg/dL (normal 0·5–1·2).
Screening for hepatitis A, B, and C viruses was reactive only for hepatitis A virus IgG. An autoimmune panel was negative for antinuclear and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies. However, a Monospot test was positive; a cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgG test was also positive.
Considering the findings in the round—the transaminitis and acute renal failure showed multiorgan involvement, the positive Monospot test indicated active Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection, and the positive IgG test suggested previous CMV infection—we made a diagnosis of drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome induced by lamotrigine with a concomitant infection. We considered that the EBV was either a new infection or a reactivation of a previous infection with the virus.
We stopped the lamotrigine and gave the patient a course of pulse steroids which gradually led to an improvement in her symptoms and renal function.
DRESS syndrome is an idiosyncratic drug-induced delayed type IV hypersensitivity severe multisystemic reaction that typically develops within 2–8 weeks of exposure. The proposed pathogenesis is a reactivation of latent herpesviruses which can be triggered by certain medications—including lamotrigine; a cross-reaction is thought to occur between the virus-specific T lymphocytes and the medications. In our case, the underlying cause of DRESS syndrome could be explained two ways: firstly, the concurrent lamotrigine use and a primary EBV infection or, secondly, lamotrigine-induced reactivation of EBV which then caused DRESS syndrome. Whatever the sequence of events, the treatment remains the same: immediate cessation of the drug causing the problem, systemic corticosteroids, or other immunosuppressants—including intravenous immuno-globulin in steroid-resistant cases (video).

A 47-year-old woman presented to our institution with a 1-month history of swelling and a painless skin plaque on her left breast. 6 years earlier, the patient had been treated for luminal A invasive ductal carcinoma in the superomedial quadrant of the left breast; she had neoadjuvant chemotherapy, breast-conserving surgery, radiation therapy—a whole breast dose of 50 Gy plus a 10 Gy boost to the tumour bed—and oral tamoxifen. The patient had been found to have no recurrence of the tumour at any subsequent follow-up appointments. She had no history of breast trauma or lymphoedema.
On physical examination, we found the patient was generally well; she had a 1 cm purple plaque on the inferolateral quadrant of her left breast, approximately 1·5 cm from the areola (figure).Breast ultrasound examination showed skin thickening, subcutaneous oedema, and a predominantly hypoechoic nonmass finding in the inferomedial quadrant of the left breast with irregular borders, regional distribution, and central hypervascularity on power Doppler (figure). Diagnostic mammogram showed a developing asymmetry in the inferomedial quadrant of the left breast, as well as skin thickening and parenchymal oedema that were more pronounced compared with her previous mammograms (figure). Histological examination of a sample obtained by ultrasound-guided core biopsy showed solid epithelial proliferation with marked cellular atypia—initially deemed suspicious for recurrence of the carcinoma (figure). Immunohistochemistry results were positive for CD31, ERG, and D2-40 on most target cells and for CD34 in subgroups of target cells (appendix), along with very high Ki67 expression (90% of target cells), findings compatible with post radiation angiosarcoma.
On post-biopsy follow-up—54 days after the first ultrasound examination—the previously 1 cm wide skin lesion had progressed to a 4 cm irregular violaceous plaque with subtle areas of yellowish discoloration on adjacent skin (figure). On ultrasound examination, the lesion appeared as an irregular, hypoechoic mass with thick echogenic rind; the high central vascularity on power Doppler remained visible (appendix).
The findings, diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment options were discussed with the patient and together the decision was made to proceed to mastectomy of the affected breast.
On the day of mastectomy—60 days after the first ultrasound examination—additional satellite lesions and morphological changes in the nipple-areola complex were seen adjacent to the irregular violaceous plaque, with progression of the areas of yellowish skin discoloration (figure).
Histopathological analysis of a sample of the surgical specimen, which measured 9·0 cm × 7·0 cm X 6·0 cm and invaded the nipple, dermis, and parenchymal breast tissue, confirmed the diagnosis of post-radiation angiosarcoma. CT scans of the patient's head, chest, and abdomen showed no evidence of metastases.
The patient made an uneventful recovery from the operation and was allowed home 24 h later. At follow-up 3 months after the mastectomy, a new 1 cm violaceous skin lesion surrounded by a yellowish halo appeared in the mastectomy scar (appendix); recurrence of the post-radiation angiosarcoma was confirmed by histopathological analysis of a sample obtained from surgically excised tissue.
Post-radiation angiosarcoma is an uncommon aggressive complication of radiotherapy for breast cancer, with a median latency period of 5–6 years. About one in every 1000 patients treated with radiotherapy for breast cancer may be at risk of developing the condition, and global incidence is expected to rise as the number of patients undergoing breast-preserving surgery plus radiotherapy increases. Typically, the tumour arises within the skin and subcutaneous tissues previously included in the irradiation field—this is unlike primary breast angiosarcomas which usually originate deep within the breast parenchyma. Patients with post-radiation angiosarcomas may develop breast swelling, erythema, skin thickening, and painless erythematous patches or plaques in previously irradiated areas, as well as areas of yellowish discoloration on circumjacent skin which is related to haemoglobin degradation products. Lymph node involvement is uncommon. Imaging findings, when present, are often non-specific and include skin and trabecular thickening, developing asymmetry on mammogram, and solid, irregular masses on breast ultrasound examination.
Surgical excision with negative margins is considered the standard treatment; prognosis is poor even with complete tumour resection, with 5-year survival rates of about 40%.

A 37-year-old woman with a 1-month history of fatigue, weight loss, palpitations, and dyspnoea, attended our clinic for investigation.
12 months earlier, the patient had embolisation of pelvic varicose veins, using glue and lipiodised oil, for pelvic venous disorder; she had reported a history of pelvic congestion syndrome with chronic pelvic pain beginning after a pregnancy 5 years earlier. The pain worsened just before the onset of menstruation. She also had symptomatic varicose veins in her legs. Venograms had confirmed abdominal-pelvic venous insufficiency with reflux in a dilated left ovarian vein, tortuous pelvic varicosities near the uterus, and bilateral dilated utero-vaginal venous plexuses.
The patient had no history of recent viral infection or neck pain; she was prescribed no medication.
On examination the patient was generally unwell; her blood pressure was 132/70 mm Hg, her pulse was 97 beats per min, and her BMI was 20·7 kg/m2. She had a firm, hard moderate-sized goitre but no signs of Graves’ orbitopathy.
Laboratory investigations showed hyperthyroidism; the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration was biologically undetectable, the free thyroxine (FT4) concentration was above 100·0 pmol/L (typical range 12·0–22·0), and the free triiodothyroxine (FT3) concentration was 36·0 pmol/L (typical range 3·1–6·8). Tests for TSH-receptor antibodies were negative. Thyroglobulin concentration was 1143 ng/mL (typical range 3·5–77·0); C-reactive protein concentration was within typical range (<5 mg/L). Thyroid peroxidase antibodies were also within the normal range. Urinary iodine concentration was raised at 10·01 μmol/L (typical range 0·35–1·60).
123Iodine thyroid scintigraphy showed no significant uptake with a blunted measured value of 0·4% at 120 min (average value 12% at 120 min for a mean TSH of 1·2 mIU/L in France; appendix).
Considering the findings in the round, we ruled out thyrotoxicosis factitia because of the raised thyroglobulin concentration and concluded the most likely diagnosis was an iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis. As stated above, the patient was not prescribed amiodarone—a recognised cause of iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis—or any other drugs associated with thyroiditis and thyrotoxicosis, and she had no history of recent radiographic contrast exposure. However, an unenhanced abdominal CT scan showed lipiodised oil in the ovarian veins (figure 1); additionally, an unenhanced CT scan of the patient's neck, which we requested to give further weight to our conclusion that the patient had thyrotoxicosis secondary to the lipiodised oil, showed a very high density of the thyroid (147 Hounsfield units [HU]; typical range 80–100; figure 2).
The patient was commenced on oral prednisone at a dose of 1 mg/kg per day until laboratory investigations showed she was euthyroid; the corticosteroids were gradually reduced over 5 months.
At follow-up 18 months later, she was well with normal thyroid function.
Excessive intake of iodine can cause hyperthyroidism; mainly this occurs after exposure to iodinated radiographic material or treatment with amiodarone. Interestingly, a study proposed a cutoff level of 117 HU for the density of the thyroid seen on unenhanced CT scan to distinguish patients with amiodarone-induced hyperthyroidism from healthy controls and from euthyroid amiodarone-treated patients (appendix). With this in mind, we suggest that a hyperdense thyroid, seen on an unenhanced CT scan—with a density level above 120 HU—should raise the possibility of iodine overload and subsequent testing of the serum TSH concentration.

input:
A 37-year-old woman with a 1-month history of fatigue, weight loss, palpitations, and dyspnoea, attended our clinic for investigation.
12 months earlier, the patient had embolisation of pelvic varicose veins, using glue and lipiodised oil, for pelvic venous disorder; she had reported a history of pelvic congestion syndrome with chronic pelvic pain beginning after a pregnancy 5 years earlier. The pain worsened just before the onset of menstruation. She also had symptomatic varicose veins in her legs. Venograms had confirmed abdominal-pelvic venous insufficiency with reflux in a dilated left ovarian vein, tortuous pelvic varicosities near the uterus, and bilateral dilated utero-vaginal venous plexuses.
The patient had no history of recent viral infection or neck pain; she was prescribed no medication.
On examination the patient was generally unwell; her blood pressure was 132/70 mm Hg, her pulse was 97 beats per min, and her BMI was 20·7 kg/m2. She had a firm, hard moderate-sized goitre but no signs of Graves’ orbitopathy.
Laboratory investigations showed hyperthyroidism; the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration was biologically undetectable, the free thyroxine (FT4) concentration was above 100·0 pmol/L (typical range 12·0–22·0), and the free triiodothyroxine (FT3) concentration was 36·0 pmol/L (typical range 3·1–6·8). Tests for TSH-receptor antibodies were negative. Thyroglobulin concentration was 1143 ng/mL (typical range 3·5–77·0); C-reactive protein concentration was within typical range (<5 mg/L). Thyroid peroxidase antibodies were also within the normal range. Urinary iodine concentration was raised at 10·01 μmol/L (typical range 0·35–1·60).
123Iodine thyroid scintigraphy showed no significant uptake with a blunted measured value of 0·4% at 120 min (average value 12% at 120 min for a mean TSH of 1·2 mIU/L in France; appendix).
Considering the findings in the round, we ruled out thyrotoxicosis factitia because of the raised thyroglobulin concentration and concluded the most likely diagnosis was an iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis. As stated above, the patient was not prescribed amiodarone—a recognised cause of iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis—or any other drugs associated with thyroiditis and thyrotoxicosis, and she had no history of recent radiographic contrast exposure. However, an unenhanced abdominal CT scan showed lipiodised oil in the ovarian veins (figure 1); additionally, an unenhanced CT scan of the patient's neck, which we requested to give further weight to our conclusion that the patient had thyrotoxicosis secondary to the lipiodised oil, showed a very high density of the thyroid (147 Hounsfield units [HU]; typical range 80–100; figure 2).
The patient was commenced on oral prednisone at a dose of 1 mg/kg per day until laboratory investigations showed she was euthyroid; the corticosteroids were gradually reduced over 5 months.
At follow-up 18 months later, she was well with normal thyroid function.
Excessive intake of iodine can cause hyperthyroidism; mainly this occurs after exposure to iodinated radiographic material or treatment with amiodarone. Interestingly, a study proposed a cutoff level of 117 HU for the density of the thyroid seen on unenhanced CT scan to distinguish patients with amiodarone-induced hyperthyroidism from healthy controls and from euthyroid amiodarone-treated patients (appendix). With this in mind, we suggest that a hyperdense thyroid, seen on an unenhanced CT scan—with a density level above 120 HU—should raise the possibility of iodine overload and subsequent testing of the serum TSH concentration.

input:
A 37-year-old woman with a 1-month history of fatigue, weight loss, palpitations, and dyspnoea, attended our clinic for investigation.
12 months earlier, the patient had embolisation of pelvic varicose veins, using glue and lipiodised oil, for pelvic venous disorder; she had reported a history of pelvic congestion syndrome with chronic pelvic pain beginning after a pregnancy 5 years earlier. The pain worsened just before the onset of menstruation. She also had symptomatic varicose veins in her legs. Venograms had confirmed abdominal-pelvic venous insufficiency with reflux in a dilated left ovarian vein, tortuous pelvic varicosities near the uterus, and bilateral dilated utero-vaginal venous plexuses.
The patient had no history of recent viral infection or neck pain; she was prescribed no medication.
On examination the patient was generally unwell; her blood pressure was 132/70 mm Hg, her pulse was 97 beats per min, and her BMI was 20·7 kg/m2. She had a firm, hard moderate-sized goitre but no signs of Graves’ orbitopathy.
Laboratory investigations showed hyperthyroidism; the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration was biologically undetectable, the free thyroxine (FT4) concentration was above 100·0 pmol/L (typical range 12·0–22·0), and the free triiodothyroxine (FT3) concentration was 36·0 pmol/L (typical range 3·1–6·8). Tests for TSH-receptor antibodies were negative. Thyroglobulin concentration was 1143 ng/mL (typical range 3·5–77·0); C-reactive protein concentration was within typical range (<5 mg/L). Thyroid peroxidase antibodies were also within the normal range. Urinary iodine concentration was raised at 10·01 μmol/L (typical range 0·35–1·60).
123Iodine thyroid scintigraphy showed no significant uptake with a blunted measured value of 0·4% at 120 min (average value 12% at 120 min for a mean TSH of 1·2 mIU/L in France; appendix).
Considering the findings in the round, we ruled out thyrotoxicosis factitia because of the raised thyroglobulin concentration and concluded the most likely diagnosis was an iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis. As stated above, the patient was not prescribed amiodarone—a recognised cause of iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis—or any other drugs associated with thyroiditis and thyrotoxicosis, and she had no history of recent radiographic contrast exposure. However, an unenhanced abdominal CT scan showed lipiodised oil in the ovarian veins (figure 1); additionally, an unenhanced CT scan of the patient's neck, which we requested to give further weight to our conclusion that the patient had thyrotoxicosis secondary to the lipiodised oil, showed a very high density of the thyroid (147 Hounsfield units [HU]; typical range 80–100; figure 2).
The patient was commenced on oral prednisone at a dose of 1 mg/kg per day until laboratory investigations showed she was euthyroid; the corticosteroids were gradually reduced over 5 months.
At follow-up 18 months later, she was well with normal thyroid function.
Excessive intake of iodine can cause hyperthyroidism; mainly this occurs after exposure to iodinated radiographic material or treatment with amiodarone. Interestingly, a study proposed a cutoff level of 117 HU for the density of the thyroid seen on unenhanced CT scan to distinguish patients with amiodarone-induced hyperthyroidism from healthy controls and from euthyroid amiodarone-treated patients (appendix). With this in mind, we suggest that a hyperdense thyroid, seen on an unenhanced CT scan—with a density level above 120 HU—should raise the possibility of iodine overload and subsequent testing of the serum TSH concentration.

A 74-year-old female patient presented in November, 2017, with a 3-month history of pain in the upper left thigh. X-ray revealed three osteolytic lesions of the left femur, one of which was breaking the cortical bone. No organomegaly was noted on physical examination. Blood counts and biochemical tests were normal except for mild hypergammaglobulinemia (16·9%) with positive immunofixation for monoclonal immunoglobulin A (0·2 g/dL in the serum, but urine negative).Multiple myeloma was suspected, and whole-body PET scan documented increased fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in several bone sites (SUVmax 4·9–10·9): at the head of humeri, sacrum, iliac wings, right acetabulum, and proximal femurs (figure, A), with extension into the soft tissues surrounding the broken cortex of the left femur.
A routine marrow biopsy from the iliac crest was unexpectedly normal on immunohistology for the plasma cell marker CD138 and the B-cell marker CD20. However, a core biopsy of the left femural neck documented a massive infiltration by mature lymphoid cells with ample cytoplasm and hairy projections positive for CD20, annexin-1 (figure, B), and BRAFV600E, thereby establishing a diagnosis of hairy cell leukaemia.
Morphological and flow-cytometric analyses of peripheral blood did not show any hairy cells, and a sensitive allele-specific PCR assay for BRAFV600E was also negative in both the blood and iliac marrow aspirate.
The patient received chemotherapy with cladribine (0·14 mg/kg per day for 5 consecutive days subcutaneously) and her pain gradually subsided. A PET scan 8 weeks later showed substantially decreased uptake of fluorodeoxyglucose at multiple bone lesions.
Although skeletal involvement can occur in hairy cell leukaemia (in around 3% of cases), patients with hairy cell leukaemia, who are mostly males, usually also present with cytopenias, splenomegaly, circulating hairy cells, and diffuse leukaemic infiltration of the bone marrow. Focal bone lesions accompanied by none of these characteristic features, but rather by a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance as occurred in this woman, represent a challenging differential diagnosis with more frequent neoplasms, especially multiple myeloma.

input:
A 40-year-old-woman presented to our outpatient clinic with a 6-month history of pain in her throat and a feeling that she had a foreign body in the submandibular region. She said the pain was pricking, intermittent, bilateral, non-radiating, aggravated by eating solid food, and moderate to severe in intensity. She reported no history of trauma or previous operations—specifically a tonsillectomy. The patient was previously fit and well and had no medical history.At examination, on bimanual palpation—tolerated by the patient without the use of any anaesthetic spray—we found tender bony prominences in both tonsillar fossa; bilateral grade 1 tonsillar hypertrophy was also present. We found no other physical abnormalities and all laboratory investigations were normal. CT showed bilaterally elongated styloid processes; with three-dimensional reconstruction the abnormalities were clearly seen, and the enlarged styloid processes measured—3·9 cm on the left side and 3·5 cm on the right side (reference range 2·5–3 cm; figure).
Initially, we decided to treat the patient conservatively with analgesics and neuropathic pain medications; this had no effect. We then carried out a bilateral transoral tonsillectomy with styloidectomy; both the elongated styloid processes were visualised during surgery and about 1 cm and 2 cm of the elongated styloid processes were resected from right and left sides respectively, bringing their lengths down to within the reference range.
Notably, the foreign body sensation resolved following surgery. At 3 months' follow-up, the patient was symptom-free.
Eagle syndrome, also known as styloid or stylohyoid syndrome, is a very rare entity which was first described in 1937. Watt Weems Eagle, born in Statesville, North Carolina, was the first chief of the ear, nose and throat division at Duke Medical Center. Classically, the syndrome is characterised by orofacial pain, dysphagia, and the sensation of a foreign body in the throat. The condition is usually seen in women older than 30 years and can be confused with a wide array of head and neck disorders—including trigeminal neuralgia, glossopharyngeal neuralgia, temporal arteritis, migraine, and cervical arthritis—hence its presentation to dentists, neurologists, and otolaryngologists. The exact pathophysiology behind this syndrome is still unknown. However, it is associated with a history of neck trauma, tonsillectomy, and the presence of an arcuate foramen. Most cases can be managed conservatively but surgery may be indicated in unresponsive cases (video).

input:
A 40-year-old-woman presented to our outpatient clinic with a 6-month history of pain in her throat and a feeling that she had a foreign body in the submandibular region. She said the pain was pricking, intermittent, bilateral, non-radiating, aggravated by eating solid food, and moderate to severe in intensity. She reported no history of trauma or previous operations—specifically a tonsillectomy. The patient was previously fit and well and had no medical history.At examination, on bimanual palpation—tolerated by the patient without the use of any anaesthetic spray—we found tender bony prominences in both tonsillar fossa; bilateral grade 1 tonsillar hypertrophy was also present. We found no other physical abnormalities and all laboratory investigations were normal. CT showed bilaterally elongated styloid processes; with three-dimensional reconstruction the abnormalities were clearly seen, and the enlarged styloid processes measured—3·9 cm on the left side and 3·5 cm on the right side (reference range 2·5–3 cm; figure).
Initially, we decided to treat the patient conservatively with analgesics and neuropathic pain medications; this had no effect. We then carried out a bilateral transoral tonsillectomy with styloidectomy; both the elongated styloid processes were visualised during surgery and about 1 cm and 2 cm of the elongated styloid processes were resected from right and left sides respectively, bringing their lengths down to within the reference range.
Notably, the foreign body sensation resolved following surgery. At 3 months' follow-up, the patient was symptom-free.
Eagle syndrome, also known as styloid or stylohyoid syndrome, is a very rare entity which was first described in 1937. Watt Weems Eagle, born in Statesville, North Carolina, was the first chief of the ear, nose and throat division at Duke Medical Center. Classically, the syndrome is characterised by orofacial pain, dysphagia, and the sensation of a foreign body in the throat. The condition is usually seen in women older than 30 years and can be confused with a wide array of head and neck disorders—including trigeminal neuralgia, glossopharyngeal neuralgia, temporal arteritis, migraine, and cervical arthritis—hence its presentation to dentists, neurologists, and otolaryngologists. The exact pathophysiology behind this syndrome is still unknown. However, it is associated with a history of neck trauma, tonsillectomy, and the presence of an arcuate foramen. Most cases can be managed conservatively but surgery may be indicated in unresponsive cases (video).

input: In March, 2020, a 59-year-old man presented to Hospital Universitario 12 de Octubre, Madrid, Spain, with a 15-day history of fever, headache, leg myalgia, and weight loss (4 kg). Physical examination showed no pathological findings. Initial diagnostic workup showed an increased concentration of C-reactive protein (16 mg/dL) and lymphopenia (700 lymphocytes per μL). White blood cell count and concentrations of creatine kinase were normal (52 units per L; reference range: 34–171 units per L). Nasopharyngeal exudate was negative for influenza A and B, respiratory syncytial virus, and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). A chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. Symptomatic treatment with oral analgesics and antipyretics (paracetamol 650 mg every 8 h, alternating every 4 h with dipyrone 575 mg every 8 h) was initiated, and the patient showed clinical improvement 4 days after admission. The patient was discharged and scheduled for a follow-up 3 weeks later. At 7 days after discharge, the fever and headache recurred. The patient did not seek medical attention and was not evaluated by a physician until the 3-week follow-up. During this follow-up, the patient reported the fever and headache recurrence, and analysis indicated increased concentrations of inflammatory markers (14 mg/dL of C-reactive protein and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 46 mm per h). The patient was readmitted to the hospital and a PET scan was done, which showed an increase in metabolic activity on the vascular walls of small and medium vessels. A subsequent visceral arteriography showed multiple microaneurysms in the small arteries of the digestive visceral territory and both renal arteries, which suggested polyarteritis nodosa vasculitis (figure). Tests for antinuclear antibodies and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. Hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, and HIV serological tests were negative. There was no evidence to suggest the involvement of other organs (five factor score=0). The patient received treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone bolus for 2 days (120 mg daily). The patient was discharged and received oral azathioprine (100 mg daily for 1 week, followed by 150 mg daily indefinitely) and a tapering regimen of oral prednisone (30 mg daily for 1 week, followed by 20 mg daily for 1 week, 1 week off, 10 mg daily for 2 weeks, alternate daily doses of 10 mg and 7·5 mg for 2 weeks, and 7·5 mg daily indefinitely). At the 3-week follow-up, fever, headache, and myalgia had resolved.Polyarteritis nodosa is a rare necrotising vasculitis of medium and small arteries, with substantial associated morbidity and mortality. Clinical features are highly variable; symptoms at onset are usually unspecific, and the differential diagnosis is often broad. Because the patient was admitted during the COVID-19 pandemic, the possibility of an infection with SARS-CoV-2 was initially considered; however, the poor clinical and analytical improvement prompted us to look for other causes of the symptoms and laboratory abnormalities. Accurate diagnosis of polyarteritis nodosa allowed for early initiation of immunosuppressive treatment.
