A 40-year-old-woman presented to our outpatient clinic with a 6-month history of pain in her throat and a feeling that she had a foreign body in the submandibular region. She said the pain was pricking, intermittent, bilateral, non-radiating, aggravated by eating solid food, and moderate to severe in intensity. She reported no history of trauma or previous operations—specifically a tonsillectomy. The patient was previously fit and well and had no medical history.At examination, on bimanual palpation—tolerated by the patient without the use of any anaesthetic spray—we found tender bony prominences in both tonsillar fossa; bilateral grade 1 tonsillar hypertrophy was also present. We found no other physical abnormalities and all laboratory investigations were normal. CT showed bilaterally elongated styloid processes; with three-dimensional reconstruction the abnormalities were clearly seen, and the enlarged styloid processes measured—3·9 cm on the left side and 3·5 cm on the right side (reference range 2·5–3 cm; figure).
Initially, we decided to treat the patient conservatively with analgesics and neuropathic pain medications; this had no effect. We then carried out a bilateral transoral tonsillectomy with styloidectomy; both the elongated styloid processes were visualised during surgery and about 1 cm and 2 cm of the elongated styloid processes were resected from right and left sides respectively, bringing their lengths down to within the reference range.
Notably, the foreign body sensation resolved following surgery. At 3 months' follow-up, the patient was symptom-free.
Eagle syndrome, also known as styloid or stylohyoid syndrome, is a very rare entity which was first described in 1937. Watt Weems Eagle, born in Statesville, North Carolina, was the first chief of the ear, nose and throat division at Duke Medical Center. Classically, the syndrome is characterised by orofacial pain, dysphagia, and the sensation of a foreign body in the throat. The condition is usually seen in women older than 30 years and can be confused with a wide array of head and neck disorders—including trigeminal neuralgia, glossopharyngeal neuralgia, temporal arteritis, migraine, and cervical arthritis—hence its presentation to dentists, neurologists, and otolaryngologists. The exact pathophysiology behind this syndrome is still unknown. However, it is associated with a history of neck trauma, tonsillectomy, and the presence of an arcuate foramen. Most cases can be managed conservatively but surgery may be indicated in unresponsive cases (video).

input: In March, 2020, a 59-year-old man presented to Hospital Universitario 12 de Octubre, Madrid, Spain, with a 15-day history of fever, headache, leg myalgia, and weight loss (4 kg). Physical examination showed no pathological findings. Initial diagnostic workup showed an increased concentration of C-reactive protein (16 mg/dL) and lymphopenia (700 lymphocytes per μL). White blood cell count and concentrations of creatine kinase were normal (52 units per L; reference range: 34–171 units per L). Nasopharyngeal exudate was negative for influenza A and B, respiratory syncytial virus, and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). A chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. Symptomatic treatment with oral analgesics and antipyretics (paracetamol 650 mg every 8 h, alternating every 4 h with dipyrone 575 mg every 8 h) was initiated, and the patient showed clinical improvement 4 days after admission. The patient was discharged and scheduled for a follow-up 3 weeks later. At 7 days after discharge, the fever and headache recurred. The patient did not seek medical attention and was not evaluated by a physician until the 3-week follow-up. During this follow-up, the patient reported the fever and headache recurrence, and analysis indicated increased concentrations of inflammatory markers (14 mg/dL of C-reactive protein and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 46 mm per h). The patient was readmitted to the hospital and a PET scan was done, which showed an increase in metabolic activity on the vascular walls of small and medium vessels. A subsequent visceral arteriography showed multiple microaneurysms in the small arteries of the digestive visceral territory and both renal arteries, which suggested polyarteritis nodosa vasculitis (figure). Tests for antinuclear antibodies and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. Hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, and HIV serological tests were negative. There was no evidence to suggest the involvement of other organs (five factor score=0). The patient received treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone bolus for 2 days (120 mg daily). The patient was discharged and received oral azathioprine (100 mg daily for 1 week, followed by 150 mg daily indefinitely) and a tapering regimen of oral prednisone (30 mg daily for 1 week, followed by 20 mg daily for 1 week, 1 week off, 10 mg daily for 2 weeks, alternate daily doses of 10 mg and 7·5 mg for 2 weeks, and 7·5 mg daily indefinitely). At the 3-week follow-up, fever, headache, and myalgia had resolved.Polyarteritis nodosa is a rare necrotising vasculitis of medium and small arteries, with substantial associated morbidity and mortality. Clinical features are highly variable; symptoms at onset are usually unspecific, and the differential diagnosis is often broad. input: In March, 2020, a 59-year-old man presented to Hospital Universitario 12 de Octubre, Madrid, Spain, with a 15-day history of fever, headache, leg myalgia, and weight loss (4 kg). Physical examination showed no pathological findings. Initial diagnostic workup showed an increased concentration of C-reactive protein (16 mg/dL) and lymphopenia (700 lymphocytes per μL). White blood cell count and concentrations of creatine kinase were normal (52 units per L; reference range: 34–171 units per L). Nasopharyngeal exudate was negative for influenza A and B, respiratory syncytial virus, and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). A chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. Symptomatic treatment with oral analgesics and antipyretics (paracetamol 650 mg every 8 h, alternating every 4 h with dipyrone 575 mg every 8 h) was initiated, and the patient showed clinical improvement 4 days after admission. The patient was discharged and scheduled for a follow-up 3 weeks later. At 7 days after discharge, the fever and headache recurred. The patient did not seek medical attention and was not evaluated by a physician until the 3-week follow-up. During this follow-up, the patient reported the fever and headache recurrence, and analysis indicated increased concentrations of inflammatory markers (14 mg/dL of C-reactive protein and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 46 mm per h). The patient was readmitted to the hospital and a PET scan was done, which showed an increase in metabolic activity on the vascular walls of small and medium vessels. A subsequent visceral arteriography showed multiple microaneurysms in the small arteries of the digestive visceral territory and both renal arteries, which suggested polyarteritis nodosa vasculitis (figure). Tests for antinuclear antibodies and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. Hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, and HIV serological tests were negative. There was no evidence to suggest the involvement of other organs (five factor score=0). The patient received treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone bolus for 2 days (120 mg daily). The patient was discharged and received oral azathioprine (100 mg daily for 1 week, followed by 150 mg daily indefinitely) and a tapering regimen of oral prednisone (30 mg daily for 1 week, followed by 20 mg daily for 1 week, 1 week off, 10 mg daily for 2 weeks, alternate daily doses of 10 mg and 7·5 mg for 2 weeks, and 7·5 mg daily indefinitely). At the 3-week follow-up, fever, headache, and myalgia had resolved.Polyarteritis nodosa is a rare necrotising vasculitis of medium and small arteries, with substantial associated morbidity and mortality. Clinical features are highly variable; symptoms at onset are usually unspecific, and the differential diagnosis is often broad. Because the patient was admitted during the COVID-19 pandemic, the possibility of an infection with SARS-CoV-2 was initially considered; however, the poor clinical and analytical improvement prompted us to look for other causes of the symptoms and laboratory abnormalities. Accurate diagnosis of polyarteritis nodosa allowed for early initiation of immunosuppressive treatment.

A 23-year-old woman with a 1-week history of a rash, fever, diffuse arthralgia, sore throat, and oral oedema attended our hospital. The patient had previously been fit and well; she had no medical history and was prescribed no medications.
On examination she was unwell; she was febrile with a temperature of 40·1°C, hypotensive (blood pressure 82/56 mm Hg), and she had a widespread, symmetrical distribution of erythematous papules and macules coalescing into patches on her trunk and extremities (figure).
The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for vasopressor support; her leukocyte count was 15·9 × 109 per L (normal range 4·5–11·0; neutrophils were 88% [normal range 40–60] and lymphocytes 1·5% [normal range 20–40]), and she was treated empirically for sepsis. An infectious diseases workup was negative; she continued to decompensate haemodynamically, developing pleural and pericardial effusions, and requiring veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Serum troponin concentration rose to 550 ng/L (normal level <14) and an echocardiogram showed biventricular dilation and reduced function, suggestive of a myocarditis that was confirmed on epi-myocardial biopsy.
Additional laboratory investigations showed a raised serum C-reactive protein concentration (228·6 mg/L; normal value < 3·1 mg/L), a raised D-dimer concentration (5307 μg/L; normal value <500), and a raised ferritin concentration (3655 μg/L; normal value <300); soluble CD25 was 229 U/mL (normal value < 852). Tests for anti-nuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibody were negative.
CT scan showed enlarged lymph nodes—some 1·2 cm in diameter—in the neck and thorax.
Considering the patient's presentation, laboratory findings, and results of other investigations (appendix), we concluded she met Yamaguchi criteria for the diagnosis of Still's disease—although the severity of the illness necessitated consideration of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and COVID-19 associated multisystem inflammatory syndrome as differential diagnoses.
Histopathological examination of the skin demonstrated dyskeratotic keratinocytes within the superficial epidermis and cornified layer. Vacuolar interface change and apoptotic keratinocytes were present at the dermoepidermal junction and a sparse perivascular inflammatory infiltrate was seen (figure); notably, these findings have not been reported in either haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis or multisystem inflammatory syndrome. Repeatedly negative COVID-19 tests, blood cultures, and tests for viral loads for Epstein–Barr virus and cytomegalovirus reinforced our conclusion of a diagnosis of severe Still's disease and we commenced treatment with subcutaneous anakinra 100 mg given twice daily and intravenous methylprednisolone 500 mg daily for 3 days with a subsequent taper.
2 weeks later, the patient left intensive care and, after 2 months of rehabilitation, she went home. At follow-up 1 year later, she was well and treated with subcutaneous anakinra 100 mg daily.
Still's disease is characterised by a fever, arthritis, and skin rash; it was formerly considered as two separate entities—systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis in children and adult-onset Still's disease in adults.
Dyskeratosis and apoptotic keratinocytes in the superficial epidermis and cornified layer are characteristic of Still's disease and help to differentiate it from other cytokine storm syndromes—including haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, sepsis, and multisystem inflammatory syndrome. Although histological findings are not included in current classification criteria for Still's disease, they can be a useful diagnostic clue, particularly in the subset of patients with catastrophic disease.

A 23-year-old woman with a 1-week history of a rash, fever, diffuse arthralgia, sore throat, and oral oedema attended our hospital. The patient had previously been fit and well; she had no medical history and was prescribed no medications.
On examination she was unwell; she was febrile with a temperature of 40·1°C, hypotensive (blood pressure 82/56 mm Hg), and she had a widespread, symmetrical distribution of erythematous papules and macules coalescing into patches on her trunk and extremities (figure).
The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for vasopressor support; her leukocyte count was 15·9 × 109 per L (normal range 4·5–11·0; neutrophils were 88% [normal range 40–60] and lymphocytes 1·5% [normal range 20–40]), and she was treated empirically for sepsis. An infectious diseases workup was negative; she continued to decompensate haemodynamically, developing pleural and pericardial effusions, and requiring veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Serum troponin concentration rose to 550 ng/L (normal level <14) and an echocardiogram showed biventricular dilation and reduced function, suggestive of a myocarditis that was confirmed on epi-myocardial biopsy.
Additional laboratory investigations showed a raised serum C-reactive protein concentration (228·6 mg/L; normal value < 3·1 mg/L), a raised D-dimer concentration (5307 μg/L; normal value <500), and a raised ferritin concentration (3655 μg/L; normal value <300); soluble CD25 was 229 U/mL (normal value < 852). Tests for anti-nuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibody were negative.
CT scan showed enlarged lymph nodes—some 1·2 cm in diameter—in the neck and thorax.
Considering the patient's presentation, laboratory findings, and results of other investigations (appendix), we concluded she met Yamaguchi criteria for the diagnosis of Still's disease—although the severity of the illness necessitated consideration of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and COVID-19 associated multisystem inflammatory syndrome as differential diagnoses.
Histopathological examination of the skin demonstrated dyskeratotic keratinocytes within the superficial epidermis and cornified layer. Vacuolar interface change and apoptotic keratinocytes were present at the dermoepidermal junction and a sparse perivascular inflammatory infiltrate was seen (figure); notably, these findings have not been reported in either haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis or multisystem inflammatory syndrome. Repeatedly negative COVID-19 tests, blood cultures, and tests for viral loads for Epstein–Barr virus and cytomegalovirus reinforced our conclusion of a diagnosis of severe Still's disease and we commenced treatment with subcutaneous anakinra 100 mg given twice daily and intravenous methylprednisolone 500 mg daily for 3 days with a subsequent taper.
2 weeks later, the patient left intensive care and, after 2 months of rehabilitation, she went home. At follow-up 1 year later, she was well and treated with subcutaneous anakinra 100 mg daily.
Still's disease is characterised by a fever, arthritis, and skin rash; it was formerly considered as two separate entities—systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis in children and adult-onset Still's disease in adults.
Dyskeratosis and apoptotic keratinocytes in the superficial epidermis and cornified layer are characteristic of Still's disease and help to differentiate it from other cytokine storm syndromes—including haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, sepsis, and multisystem inflammatory syndrome. Although histological findings are not included in current classification criteria for Still's disease, they can be a useful diagnostic clue, particularly in the subset of patients with catastrophic disease.

A 23-year-old woman with a 1-week history of a rash, fever, diffuse arthralgia, sore throat, and oral oedema attended our hospital. The patient had previously been fit and well; she had no medical history and was prescribed no medications.
On examination she was unwell; she was febrile with a temperature of 40·1°C, hypotensive (blood pressure 82/56 mm Hg), and she had a widespread, symmetrical distribution of erythematous papules and macules coalescing into patches on her trunk and extremities (figure).
The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for vasopressor support; her leukocyte count was 15·9 × 109 per L (normal range 4·5–11·0; neutrophils were 88% [normal range 40–60] and lymphocytes 1·5% [normal range 20–40]), and she was treated empirically for sepsis. An infectious diseases workup was negative; she continued to decompensate haemodynamically, developing pleural and pericardial effusions, and requiring veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Serum troponin concentration rose to 550 ng/L (normal level <14) and an echocardiogram showed biventricular dilation and reduced function, suggestive of a myocarditis that was confirmed on epi-myocardial biopsy.
Additional laboratory investigations showed a raised serum C-reactive protein concentration (228·6 mg/L; normal value < 3·1 mg/L), a raised D-dimer concentration (5307 μg/L; normal value <500), and a raised ferritin concentration (3655 μg/L; normal value <300); soluble CD25 was 229 U/mL (normal value < 852). Tests for anti-nuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibody were negative.
CT scan showed enlarged lymph nodes—some 1·2 cm in diameter—in the neck and thorax.
Considering the patient's presentation, laboratory findings, and results of other investigations (appendix), we concluded she met Yamaguchi criteria for the diagnosis of Still's disease—although the severity of the illness necessitated consideration of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and COVID-19 associated multisystem inflammatory syndrome as differential diagnoses.
Histopathological examination of the skin demonstrated dyskeratotic keratinocytes within the superficial epidermis and cornified layer. Vacuolar interface change and apoptotic keratinocytes were present at the dermoepidermal junction and a sparse perivascular inflammatory infiltrate was seen (figure); notably, these findings have not been reported in either haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis or multisystem inflammatory syndrome. Repeatedly negative COVID-19 tests, blood cultures, and tests for viral loads for Epstein–Barr virus and cytomegalovirus reinforced our conclusion of a diagnosis of severe Still's disease and we commenced treatment with subcutaneous anakinra 100 mg given twice daily and intravenous methylprednisolone 500 mg daily for 3 days with a subsequent taper.
2 weeks later, the patient left intensive care and, after 2 months of rehabilitation, she went home. At follow-up 1 year later, she was well and treated with subcutaneous anakinra 100 mg daily.
Still's disease is characterised by a fever, arthritis, and skin rash; it was formerly considered as two separate entities—systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis in children and adult-onset Still's disease in adults.
Dyskeratosis and apoptotic keratinocytes in the superficial epidermis and cornified layer are characteristic of Still's disease and help to differentiate it from other cytokine storm syndromes—including haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, sepsis, and multisystem inflammatory syndrome. Although histological findings are not included in current classification criteria for Still's disease, they can be a useful diagnostic clue, particularly in the subset of patients with catastrophic disease.

input:
A 25-year-old man presented to our department with a 5-year history of an insidious, progressive weakness in his right hand. Despite being right-handed, he had recently become reliant on his left hand to carry out tasks needing manual dexterity. Clinical examination showed muscular atrophy without fasciculations of the first dorsal interosseous muscle and weakness of both the thenar and hypothenar muscles of the right hand; he also had atrophy but no fasciculation of the lumbrical and interosseous muscles. He complained of bilateral, electric shock-like sensations throughout his body when we examined the range of movements of his neck—Lhermitte's sign. Laboratory investigations showed a serum B12 concentration of 648 pg/mL (normal range 174–878) and the serum panel for heavy metal toxicity—including arsenic, mercury, and lead—was negative. Investigations for rheumatoid arthritis—including antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor (less than 14 IU/mL)—were within the normal ranges and his erythrocyte sedimentation rate was normal at 2 mm/h.An MRI of the patient's brain showed no abnormalities; however, an MRI of his cervical spine showed myelomalacia of the spinal cord but no other features that might give a clue as to the underlying cause of his problems (figure). The association of the patient's electric shock-like sensations prompted us to do a dynamic cervical spine MRI study with the neck in positions of flexion and extension: MRI showed that the spinal cord was being compressed—most noticeably at the level of the fifth cervical vertebral body—and that the dorsal epidural space was abnormally expanding while in a flexed position (figure). Such radiographic findings are pathognomonic of Hirayama disease and so clinched the diagnosis.
To prevent further neurological injury, we did a two-level anterior cervical spine fusion at C4/C5 and C5/C6 using synthetic interbody grafts between the vertebral bodies after removal of the intervertebral disc material; these were secured with a titanium plate from C4 to C6. A further dynamic cervical spine MRI done 6 weeks after the operation showed that the spinal cord was no longer being compressed when the patient flexed his neck (figure). Dexterity in his right hand had subjectively improved at follow-up 6 months later.
Hirayama disease—first described by Keizo Hirayama in 1959 as a juvenile, unilateral, muscular atrophy of the upper limb—predominantly affects adolescent men and is thought to be caused by dynamic mechanical or ischaemic injury to the ventral cervical motor neurons. Our case shows the importance of doing a dynamic flexion and extension MRI in young patients with otherwise unexplained progressive neuronal dysfunction. The imaging findings are key to differentiating the disease from more common disorders—such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis, cervical spondylotic myelopathy, tabes dorsalis, spinal muscular atrophy, or syringomyelia—and allowing for appropriate surgical action, as in our patient.

A 25-year-old man presented to our department with a 5-year history of an insidious, progressive weakness in his right hand. Despite being right-handed, he had recently become reliant on his left hand to carry out tasks needing manual dexterity. Clinical examination showed muscular atrophy without fasciculations of the first dorsal interosseous muscle and weakness of both the thenar and hypothenar muscles of the right hand; he also had atrophy but no fasciculation of the lumbrical and interosseous muscles. He complained of bilateral, electric shock-like sensations throughout his body when we examined the range of movements of his neck—Lhermitte's sign. Laboratory investigations showed a serum B12 concentration of 648 pg/mL (normal range 174–878) and the serum panel for heavy metal toxicity—including arsenic, mercury, and lead—was negative. Investigations for rheumatoid arthritis—including antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor (less than 14 IU/mL)—were within the normal ranges and his erythrocyte sedimentation rate was normal at 2 mm/h.An MRI of the patient's brain showed no abnormalities; however, an MRI of his cervical spine showed myelomalacia of the spinal cord but no other features that might give a clue as to the underlying cause of his problems (figure). The association of the patient's electric shock-like sensations prompted us to do a dynamic cervical spine MRI study with the neck in positions of flexion and extension: MRI showed that the spinal cord was being compressed—most noticeably at the level of the fifth cervical vertebral body—and that the dorsal epidural space was abnormally expanding while in a flexed position (figure). Such radiographic findings are pathognomonic of Hirayama disease and so clinched the diagnosis.
To prevent further neurological injury, we did a two-level anterior cervical spine fusion at C4/C5 and C5/C6 using synthetic interbody grafts between the vertebral bodies after removal of the intervertebral disc material; these were secured with a titanium plate from C4 to C6. A further dynamic cervical spine MRI done 6 weeks after the operation showed that the spinal cord was no longer being compressed when the patient flexed his neck (figure). Dexterity in his right hand had subjectively improved at follow-up 6 months later.
Hirayama disease—first described by Keizo Hirayama in 1959 as a juvenile, unilateral, muscular atrophy of the upper limb—predominantly affects adolescent men and is thought to be caused by dynamic mechanical or ischaemic injury to the ventral cervical motor neurons. Our case shows the importance of doing a dynamic flexion and extension MRI in young patients with otherwise unexplained progressive neuronal dysfunction. The imaging findings are key to differentiating the disease from more common disorders—such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis, cervical spondylotic myelopathy, tabes dorsalis, spinal muscular atrophy, or syringomyelia—and allowing for appropriate surgical action, as in our patient.

input:
A man aged 42 years with alcohol use disorder and of no fixed abode was admitted to hospital for acute abdominal pain that started 12 h previously. Blood tests showed a high lipase concentration (745 IU/L), and an abdominal CT scan confirmed the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis with one acute necrotic collection, characterised as moderately severe acute pancreatitis according to the Atlanta classification.2 days later, the man presented with acute pain in both legs and local examination showed multiple purpuric erythematous macular lesions. On day 4, these lesions were characterised as subcutaneous erythematous nodules associated with inflammatory oedema of the left ankle although both legs were affected (figure, A).
A punch biopsy was performed and histology showed cytosteatonecrosis in the superficial part of the hypoderm (figure, B), characterised by lobular panniculitis with dense inflammation, and necrosis together with foaming macrophages and so-called ghost adipocytes (without nuclei). No lesions that would suggest vasculitis or T-cell lymphoma were reported. Blood tests ruled out autoimmune disease or vasculitis and the concentration of α1-antitrypsin was normal. Bacteriological and mycobacteriological cultures were negative. Skin lesions, oedema, and pain in the lower limbs resolved spontaneously after 7 days, confirming the diagnosis of pancreatic panniculitis.
Systemic panniculitis is caused by the release of pancreatic enzymes, leading to necrosis of hypodermic fat tissue and sometimes bone tissue. Systemic panniculitis mainly affects men aged 40–70 years who have a history of chronic alcohol use disorder. Lesions are typically dermo-hypodermic inflammatory nodules or plaques, predominantly on the lower limbs and fingers. In case of chronic pancreatitis or pancreatic carcinoma, dermatological lesions might precede the usual manifestations of underlying pancreatic disease by several weeks to several months. Systemic symptoms can occur, such as fever, arthralgia, or bone pain due to intraosseous fat necrosis. Histologically, a predominantly lobular pattern with fat necrosis and ghost adipocytes is pathognomonic. Treatment with glucocorticoids and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs is usually ineffective. Apart from the usual spontaneous resolution of skin lesions with the treatment of pancreatitis, octreotide has been proposed as an option due to an inhibitory effect on lipase activity, and tetracycline has also been proposed in the treatment of panniculitis.

input:
A man aged 42 years with alcohol use disorder and of no fixed abode was admitted to hospital for acute abdominal pain that started 12 h previously. Blood tests showed a high lipase concentration (745 IU/L), and an abdominal CT scan confirmed the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis with one acute necrotic collection, characterised as moderately severe acute pancreatitis according to the Atlanta classification.2 days later, the man presented with acute pain in both legs and local examination showed multiple purpuric erythematous macular lesions. On day 4, these lesions were characterised as subcutaneous erythematous nodules associated with inflammatory oedema of the left ankle although both legs were affected (figure, A).
A punch biopsy was performed and histology showed cytosteatonecrosis in the superficial part of the hypoderm (figure, B), characterised by lobular panniculitis with dense inflammation, and necrosis together with foaming macrophages and so-called ghost adipocytes (without nuclei). No lesions that would suggest vasculitis or T-cell lymphoma were reported. Blood tests ruled out autoimmune disease or vasculitis and the concentration of α1-antitrypsin was normal. Bacteriological and mycobacteriological cultures were negative. Skin lesions, oedema, and pain in the lower limbs resolved spontaneously after 7 days, confirming the diagnosis of pancreatic panniculitis.
Systemic panniculitis is caused by the release of pancreatic enzymes, leading to necrosis of hypodermic fat tissue and sometimes bone tissue. Systemic panniculitis mainly affects men aged 40–70 years who have a history of chronic alcohol use disorder. Lesions are typically dermo-hypodermic inflammatory nodules or plaques, predominantly on the lower limbs and fingers. In case of chronic pancreatitis or pancreatic carcinoma, dermatological lesions might precede the usual manifestations of underlying pancreatic disease by several weeks to several months. Systemic symptoms can occur, such as fever, arthralgia, or bone pain due to intraosseous fat necrosis. Histologically, a predominantly lobular pattern with fat necrosis and ghost adipocytes is pathognomonic. Treatment with glucocorticoids and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs is usually ineffective. Apart from the usual spontaneous resolution of skin lesions with the treatment of pancreatitis, octreotide has been proposed as an option due to an inhibitory effect on lipase activity, and tetracycline has also been proposed in the treatment of panniculitis.

A man aged 42 years with alcohol use disorder and of no fixed abode was admitted to hospital for acute abdominal pain that started 12 h previously. Blood tests showed a high lipase concentration (745 IU/L), and an abdominal CT scan confirmed the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis with one acute necrotic collection, characterised as moderately severe acute pancreatitis according to the Atlanta classification.2 days later, the man presented with acute pain in both legs and local examination showed multiple purpuric erythematous macular lesions. On day 4, these lesions were characterised as subcutaneous erythematous nodules associated with inflammatory oedema of the left ankle although both legs were affected (figure, A).
A punch biopsy was performed and histology showed cytosteatonecrosis in the superficial part of the hypoderm (figure, B), characterised by lobular panniculitis with dense inflammation, and necrosis together with foaming macrophages and so-called ghost adipocytes (without nuclei). No lesions that would suggest vasculitis or T-cell lymphoma were reported. Blood tests ruled out autoimmune disease or vasculitis and the concentration of α1-antitrypsin was normal. Bacteriological and mycobacteriological cultures were negative. Skin lesions, oedema, and pain in the lower limbs resolved spontaneously after 7 days, confirming the diagnosis of pancreatic panniculitis.
Systemic panniculitis is caused by the release of pancreatic enzymes, leading to necrosis of hypodermic fat tissue and sometimes bone tissue. Systemic panniculitis mainly affects men aged 40–70 years who have a history of chronic alcohol use disorder. Lesions are typically dermo-hypodermic inflammatory nodules or plaques, predominantly on the lower limbs and fingers. In case of chronic pancreatitis or pancreatic carcinoma, dermatological lesions might precede the usual manifestations of underlying pancreatic disease by several weeks to several months. Systemic symptoms can occur, such as fever, arthralgia, or bone pain due to intraosseous fat necrosis. Histologically, a predominantly lobular pattern with fat necrosis and ghost adipocytes is pathognomonic. Treatment with glucocorticoids and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs is usually ineffective. Apart from the usual spontaneous resolution of skin lesions with the treatment of pancreatitis, octreotide has been proposed as an option due to an inhibitory effect on lipase activity, and tetracycline has also been proposed in the treatment of panniculitis.

A 23-year-old man was admitted to our hospital in status epilepticus—he had been having repeated episodes of generalised tonic-clonic seizures without gaining consciousness between them. He was in a wheelchair. He was intubated and the seizures were controlled with midazolam and he was then transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU). On examination his blood pressure (BP) was 220/110 mm Hg, and his heart rate was 120 beats per min. He was given labetalol and his blood pressure lowered.In his medical history, it was noted that he had experienced recurrent episodes of hypertension and tachycardia, intractable epilepsy, psychiatric problems—specifically depression and anorexia nervosa—and episodic abdominal pain for the past 10 years; he was reportedly pain free during the time between relapses. He had been prescribed phenytoin, sodium valproate, and levetiracetam for the seizures—although his level of concordance was unclear. He had been in a wheelchair for some time because of a weakness in his arms and legs which nerve conduction studies showed a pattern consistent with motor axonal polyneuropathy; he had previously been admitted to hospital with pneumonia and respiratory failure, and it had been difficult to wean him off the prolonged ventilation he had required.
Laboratory investigations—including thyroid profile, autoimmune profile, HIV testing, urinary catecholamines and metanephrines were negative (appendix). An electrocardiogram and an echocardiogram were normal apart from the sinus tachycardia. An electroencephalogram showed bursts of alpha waves without any epileptic activity. A CT of the patient's brain was normal, but an MRI showed bilateral asymmetric vasogenic oedema within both occipital and parietal regions—a picture typical of so-called posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (figure).
A Hoesch bedside screening test was positive for urinary porphobilinogen and further testing of a urine sample found a porphobilinogen concentration of 1490 μmol/L (normal <8·8). We therefore made a diagnosis of acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) and treated the patient with a high carbohydrate diet, delivered by a nasogastric tube, and a continuous intravenous infusion of 10% dextrose solution.
Within 2 weeks, the patient's symptoms had resolved, and he was extubated and discharged from the ICU fully conscious and with his BP controlled. The anticonvulsants were stopped, and he was started on haematin therapy.
The classic triad of AIP is abdominal pain, psychosis, and neuropathy. Patients may have a tachycardia and seizures will be seen in about 20% of cases. Patients with porphyric neuropathy may be a source of confusion in practice, and the diagnosis—as in our patient—may be delayed. Porphyric neuropathy looks to all intents and purposes like acute Guillain–Barré syndrome. However, the presence of psychological features, a proximal, asymmetric weakness, and electrodiagnostic findings indicative of an axonal polyradiculopathy or neuronopathy point the way to a diagnosis of porphyria (video).

He had been in a wheelchair for some time because of a weakness in his arms and legs which nerve conduction studies showed a pattern consistent with motor axonal polyneuropathy; he had previously been admitted to hospital with pneumonia and respiratory failure, and it had been difficult to wean him off the prolonged ventilation he had required.
Laboratory investigations—including thyroid profile, autoimmune profile, HIV testing, urinary catecholamines and metanephrines were negative (appendix). An electrocardiogram and an echocardiogram were normal apart from the sinus tachycardia. An electroencephalogram showed bursts of alpha waves without any epileptic activity. A CT of the patient's brain was normal, but an MRI showed bilateral asymmetric vasogenic oedema within both occipital and parietal regions—a picture typical of so-called posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (figure).
A Hoesch bedside screening test was positive for urinary porphobilinogen and further testing of a urine sample found a porphobilinogen concentration of 1490 μmol/L (normal <8·8). Within 2 weeks, the patient's symptoms had resolved, and he was extubated and discharged from the ICU fully conscious and with his BP controlled. The anticonvulsants were stopped, and he was started on haematin therapy.

Porphyric neuropathy looks to all intents and purposes like acute Guillain–Barré syndrome. However, the presence of psychological features, a proximal, asymmetric weakness, and electrodiagnostic findings indicative of an axonal polyradiculopathy or neuronopathy point the way to a diagnosis of porphyria (video).

A 51-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital for investigation of blackouts occurring in the context of worsening breathlessness (New York Heart Association [NYHA] class IV) and swelling of her legs. 14 months earlier she had a gastric banding operation.The patient had a history of systemic lupus erythematosus for which she had been taking oral azathioprine 50 mg twice a day, prednisolone 5 mg daily, and hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice a day for 5 days a week for the past 19 years; she had no significant family history.
On examination, the patient's body-mass index had fallen from 46 kg/m2 pre-gastric bypass to 25 kg/m2; her jugular venous pressure was elevated, heart sounds were normal, and her chest was clear. She had bilateral peripheral oedema to her ankles and abdominal distension. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed right bundle branch block with evidence of right ventricular hypertrophy.
Laboratory investigations showed renal impairment with creatinine 99 μmol/L and estimated glomerular filtration rate 51 mL/min per 1·73 m2. High-sensitivity troponin I was 251 ng/L (normal <32) and plasma concentration of N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) was raised at 32 208 ng/L (normal <400).
Transthoracic echocardiography showed left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) with small cavity, normal ejection fraction, and impaired longitudinal function; and right ventricular dysfunction and bi-atrial dilatation. A cardiac MRI (figure) confirmed LVH with 16 mm maximal wall thickness and non-coronary late gadolinium enhancement. Myocardial T1 relaxation time was normal; a high-resolution CT showed fibrotic changes in the lungs.
Considering the findings in the round, we suspected hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy and stopped this medication. Right heart catheterisation confirmed pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease. Right ventricular biopsy demonstrated marked vacuolation—shown on electron microscopy to be an excess of lysosomes (figure) containing electron-dense, phospholipid-rich lamellar bodies: features that are common to Fabry's disease and hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy. A normal α-galactosidase A level, a normal T1 relaxation time on MRI, and negative genetic tests for abnormalities of the GLA gene excluded the former.
We decided that the patient was not eligible for cardiac transplantation due to her frailty and comorbidities. However, within 12 months after stopping the hydroxychloroquine, her condition was much better: the breathlessness had improved—NYHA class III—and the concentration of NT-proBNP had reduced to 5337 ng/L. In retrospect, we found evidence of LVH and ECG changes before gastric surgery, but we believe that the rapid weight loss may have accelerated the damage to the heart by altering the absorption of the hydroxychloroquine.
Hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy is rare—although the true prevalence is unknown—and related to perturbed lysosomal autophagy. Risk factors—relevant to our case—include older age, female sex, and a high cumulative dose of hydroxychloroquine; we calculated the dose to have been greater than or equal to 2774 g over 19 years. Hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy should be considered in patients with LVH and restrictive cardiomyopathy, as it may be partially reversible after medication withdrawal (video).

A 51-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital for investigation of blackouts occurring in the context of worsening breathlessness (New York Heart Association [NYHA] class IV) and swelling of her legs. 14 months earlier she had a gastric banding operation.The patient had a history of systemic lupus erythematosus for which she had been taking oral azathioprine 50 mg twice a day, prednisolone 5 mg daily, and hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice a day for 5 days a week for the past 19 years; she had no significant family history.
On examination, the patient's body-mass index had fallen from 46 kg/m2 pre-gastric bypass to 25 kg/m2; her jugular venous pressure was elevated, heart sounds were normal, and her chest was clear. She had bilateral peripheral oedema to her ankles and abdominal distension. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed right bundle branch block with evidence of right ventricular hypertrophy.
Laboratory investigations showed renal impairment with creatinine 99 μmol/L and estimated glomerular filtration rate 51 mL/min per 1·73 m2. High-sensitivity troponin I was 251 ng/L (normal <32) and plasma concentration of N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) was raised at 32 208 ng/L (normal <400).
Transthoracic echocardiography showed left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) with small cavity, normal ejection fraction, and impaired longitudinal function; and right ventricular dysfunction and bi-atrial dilatation. A cardiac MRI (figure) confirmed LVH with 16 mm maximal wall thickness and non-coronary late gadolinium enhancement. Myocardial T1 relaxation time was normal; a high-resolution CT showed fibrotic changes in the lungs.
Considering the findings in the round, we suspected hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy and stopped this medication. Right heart catheterisation confirmed pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease. Right ventricular biopsy demonstrated marked vacuolation—shown on electron microscopy to be an excess of lysosomes (figure) containing electron-dense, phospholipid-rich lamellar bodies: features that are common to Fabry's disease and hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy. A normal α-galactosidase A level, a normal T1 relaxation time on MRI, and negative genetic tests for abnormalities of the GLA gene excluded the former.
We decided that the patient was not eligible for cardiac transplantation due to her frailty and comorbidities. However, within 12 months after stopping the hydroxychloroquine, her condition was much better: the breathlessness had improved—NYHA class III—and the concentration of NT-proBNP had reduced to 5337 ng/L. In retrospect, we found evidence of LVH and ECG changes before gastric surgery, but we believe that the rapid weight loss may have accelerated the damage to the heart by altering the absorption of the hydroxychloroquine.
Hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy is rare—although the true prevalence is unknown—and related to perturbed lysosomal autophagy. Risk factors—relevant to our case—include older age, female sex, and a high cumulative dose of hydroxychloroquine; we calculated the dose to have been greater than or equal to 2774 g over 19 years. Hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy should be considered in patients with LVH and restrictive cardiomyopathy, as it may be partially reversible after medication withdrawal (video).

A 51-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital for investigation of blackouts occurring in the context of worsening breathlessness (New York Heart Association [NYHA] class IV) and swelling of her legs. 14 months earlier she had a gastric banding operation.The patient had a history of systemic lupus erythematosus for which she had been taking oral azathioprine 50 mg twice a day, prednisolone 5 mg daily, and hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice a day for 5 days a week for the past 19 years; she had no significant family history.
On examination, the patient's body-mass index had fallen from 46 kg/m2 pre-gastric bypass to 25 kg/m2; her jugular venous pressure was elevated, heart sounds were normal, and her chest was clear. She had bilateral peripheral oedema to her ankles and abdominal distension. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed right bundle branch block with evidence of right ventricular hypertrophy.
Laboratory investigations showed renal impairment with creatinine 99 μmol/L and estimated glomerular filtration rate 51 mL/min per 1·73 m2. High-sensitivity troponin I was 251 ng/L (normal <32) and plasma concentration of N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) was raised at 32 208 ng/L (normal <400).
Transthoracic echocardiography showed left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) with small cavity, normal ejection fraction, and impaired longitudinal function; and right ventricular dysfunction and bi-atrial dilatation. A cardiac MRI (figure) confirmed LVH with 16 mm maximal wall thickness and non-coronary late gadolinium enhancement. Myocardial T1 relaxation time was normal; a high-resolution CT showed fibrotic changes in the lungs.
Considering the findings in the round, we suspected hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy and stopped this medication. Right heart catheterisation confirmed pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease. Right ventricular biopsy demonstrated marked vacuolation—shown on electron microscopy to be an excess of lysosomes (figure) containing electron-dense, phospholipid-rich lamellar bodies: features that are common to Fabry's disease and hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy. A normal α-galactosidase A level, a normal T1 relaxation time on MRI, and negative genetic tests for abnormalities of the GLA gene excluded the former.
We decided that the patient was not eligible for cardiac transplantation due to her frailty and comorbidities. However, within 12 months after stopping the hydroxychloroquine, her condition was much better: the breathlessness had improved—NYHA class III—and the concentration of NT-proBNP had reduced to 5337 ng/L. In retrospect, we found evidence of LVH and ECG changes before gastric surgery, but we believe that the rapid weight loss may have accelerated the damage to the heart by altering the absorption of the hydroxychloroquine.
Hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy is rare—although the true prevalence is unknown—and related to perturbed lysosomal autophagy. Risk factors—relevant to our case—include older age, female sex, and a high cumulative dose of hydroxychloroquine; we calculated the dose to have been greater than or equal to 2774 g over 19 years. Hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy should be considered in patients with LVH and restrictive cardiomyopathy, as it may be partially reversible after medication withdrawal (video).

A 37-year-old female patient was referred to the rheumatology department at Treliske Hospital (Truro, UK) in April, 2015, following 8 months of rib pain, initially thought to be costochondritis. She had isolated hypophosphataemia (serum phosphate level 0·50 mmol/L) and a pelvic MRI identified stress fractures (figure, A). 14 months after her presentation she had a persistently low serum phosphate concentration, with normal parathyroid hormone and serum calcium levels, and a 25(OH) vitamin D concentration of 32ng/mL. It was concluded that she had subclinical vitamin D deficiency, and she was prescribed cholecalciferol 20 000 units per week and Phosphate Sandoz (HK Pharma Ltd, Bedford UK), given as two tablets twice daily. In March, 2016, still symptomatic, she was referred to the UCL Centre for Nephrology (University College London, London, UK) to investigate a possible renal cause for her hypophosphataemia.There, her calculated urinary fractional excretion of phosphate was raised at 42%, confirming hyperphosphaturia. Her sex and age weighed against X-linked, autosomal dominant, or recessive hypophosphatemic rickets; and normal excretion of low-molecular-weight protein, urate, and glucose ruled out the renal Fanconi syndrome. Her serum concentration of FGF23 was 180 relative units (RU) per mL (normal range is 0–150 RU/mL). Previous standard practice protocolled a first-line FDG PET/CT scan, which identified a nasal cavity mass that was avid on a subsequent 68Ga DOTATATE PET/CT scan (figure B). The tumour was excised and pathology confirmed as sinonasal mucosa with evidence of phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour; her serum phosphate and FCF23 returned to normal following surgery.
Oncogenic osteomalacia is a paraneoplastic syndrome usually associated with mesenchymal tumours, although somatic mutations in adenocarcinomas causing this syndrome have been reported. Phosphatonins (eg, FGF23) decrease renal resorption of phosphate, leading to hypophosphataemia, muscle weakness, and osteomalacia. Most such tumours are located in the bone and soft tissue, are solitary, and rarely cause local symptoms, often making the diagnosis long and difficult. Use of radiolabelled somatostatin analogues (such as octreotate, as in a 68GA-DOTATATE scan) is the most sensitive and specific functional imaging.
The only definitive management is removal of the phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour; recurrence is rare but has been described in some cases.

input:
A 37-year-old female patient was referred to the rheumatology department at Treliske Hospital (Truro, UK) in April, 2015, following 8 months of rib pain, initially thought to be costochondritis. She had isolated hypophosphataemia (serum phosphate level 0·50 mmol/L) and a pelvic MRI identified stress fractures (figure, A). 14 months after her presentation she had a persistently low serum phosphate concentration, with normal parathyroid hormone and serum calcium levels, and a 25(OH) vitamin D concentration of 32ng/mL. It was concluded that she had subclinical vitamin D deficiency, and she was prescribed cholecalciferol 20 000 units per week and Phosphate Sandoz (HK Pharma Ltd, Bedford UK), given as two tablets twice daily. In March, 2016, still symptomatic, she was referred to the UCL Centre for Nephrology (University College London, London, UK) to investigate a possible renal cause for her hypophosphataemia.There, her calculated urinary fractional excretion of phosphate was raised at 42%, confirming hyperphosphaturia. Her sex and age weighed against X-linked, autosomal dominant, or recessive hypophosphatemic rickets; and normal excretion of low-molecular-weight protein, urate, and glucose ruled out the renal Fanconi syndrome. Her serum concentration of FGF23 was 180 relative units (RU) per mL (normal range is 0–150 RU/mL). Previous standard practice protocolled a first-line FDG PET/CT scan, which identified a nasal cavity mass that was avid on a subsequent 68Ga DOTATATE PET/CT scan (figure B). The tumour was excised and pathology confirmed as sinonasal mucosa with evidence of phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour; her serum phosphate and FCF23 returned to normal following surgery.
Oncogenic osteomalacia is a paraneoplastic syndrome usually associated with mesenchymal tumours, although somatic mutations in adenocarcinomas causing this syndrome have been reported. Phosphatonins (eg, FGF23) decrease renal resorption of phosphate, leading to hypophosphataemia, muscle weakness, and osteomalacia. Most such tumours are located in the bone and soft tissue, are solitary, and rarely cause local symptoms, often making the diagnosis long and difficult. Use of radiolabelled somatostatin analogues (such as octreotate, as in a 68GA-DOTATATE scan) is the most sensitive and specific functional imaging.
The only definitive management is removal of the phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour; recurrence is rare but has been described in some cases.

input:
A 37-year-old female patient was referred to the rheumatology department at Treliske Hospital (Truro, UK) in April, 2015, following 8 months of rib pain, initially thought to be costochondritis. She had isolated hypophosphataemia (serum phosphate level 0·50 mmol/L) and a pelvic MRI identified stress fractures (figure, A). 14 months after her presentation she had a persistently low serum phosphate concentration, with normal parathyroid hormone and serum calcium levels, and a 25(OH) vitamin D concentration of 32ng/mL. It was concluded that she had subclinical vitamin D deficiency, and she was prescribed cholecalciferol 20 000 units per week and Phosphate Sandoz (HK Pharma Ltd, Bedford UK), given as two tablets twice daily. In March, 2016, still symptomatic, she was referred to the UCL Centre for Nephrology (University College London, London, UK) to investigate a possible renal cause for her hypophosphataemia.There, her calculated urinary fractional excretion of phosphate was raised at 42%, confirming hyperphosphaturia. Her sex and age weighed against X-linked, autosomal dominant, or recessive hypophosphatemic rickets; and normal excretion of low-molecular-weight protein, urate, and glucose ruled out the renal Fanconi syndrome. Her serum concentration of FGF23 was 180 relative units (RU) per mL (normal range is 0–150 RU/mL). Previous standard practice protocolled a first-line FDG PET/CT scan, which identified a nasal cavity mass that was avid on a subsequent 68Ga DOTATATE PET/CT scan (figure B). The tumour was excised and pathology confirmed as sinonasal mucosa with evidence of phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour; her serum phosphate and FCF23 returned to normal following surgery.
Oncogenic osteomalacia is a paraneoplastic syndrome usually associated with mesenchymal tumours, although somatic mutations in adenocarcinomas causing this syndrome have been reported. Phosphatonins (eg, FGF23) decrease renal resorption of phosphate, leading to hypophosphataemia, muscle weakness, and osteomalacia. Most such tumours are located in the bone and soft tissue, are solitary, and rarely cause local symptoms, often making the diagnosis long and difficult. Use of radiolabelled somatostatin analogues (such as octreotate, as in a 68GA-DOTATATE scan) is the most sensitive and specific functional imaging.
The only definitive management is removal of the phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour; recurrence is rare but has been described in some cases.

input: A 41-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of progressive vision loss and headaches. MRI revealed a large sellar tumour with suprasellar extension, which was deemed a probable pituitary macroadenoma (figure A, B). The patient underwent transsphenoidal surgery because of visual field defects and headaches. Histological analysis after surgery revealed a giant cell tumour of bone (GCTB) and symptoms improved; however, 2 months later the large sellar–clival remnant compressing the optic chiasm (figure C, D) motivated a second surgery by pterional craniotomy. After surgery, tumour regrowth occurred (figure E, F), causing diplopia and blurred vision. A third decompressing operation aiming for maximal debulking before denosumab commencement was done endoscopically; however, only partial tumour removal was achieved (figure G, H). Denosumab (120 mg subcutaneously every 28 days) was initiated, and a marked response was noted after 6 months of treatment (figure I, J). After 14 months of denosumab, the patient remained symptom-free without needing further operations (figure K, L).GCTB represent 5–10% of bone tumours, classically affect long bones (<1% of all GCTB have a cranial location) and, although benign, can be locally aggressive. GCTB are histologically characterised by large multinucleated giant cells, but the clinical or radiological differential diagnosis can be challenging. Denosumab, an inhibitor of receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL), can be used to treat GCTB, because RANKL is overexpressed by mononuclear neoplastic stromal cells. As shown here, denosumab should also be considered in the early management of sellar–clival GCTB. This case also highlights the sustained reduction in tumour mass achieved by denosumab, sparing the patient from further operations. If feasible, surgical resection is still preferable as the definitive treatment, because the effect of denosumab wears off after stopping treatment and tumour regrowth can occur. Lifelong denosumab treatment will thus be likely required in this case; however, increasing the intervals between denosumab administration can be attempted to prevent or minimise adverse events, such as osteonecrosis of the jaw or atypical femoral fractures. Although GCTB is usually managed by rheumatologists, oncologists, or orthopaedics, sellar or parasellar GCTB might be first seen by endocrinologists, ophthalmologists, or neurosurgeons, who should be aware of this entity and the potential role of denosumab in its management.

input: A 41-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of progressive vision loss and headaches. MRI revealed a large sellar tumour with suprasellar extension, which was deemed a probable pituitary macroadenoma (figure A, B). The patient underwent transsphenoidal surgery because of visual field defects and headaches. Histological analysis after surgery revealed a giant cell tumour of bone (GCTB) and symptoms improved; however, 2 months later the large sellar–clival remnant compressing the optic chiasm (figure C, D) motivated a second surgery by pterional craniotomy. After surgery, tumour regrowth occurred (figure E, F), causing diplopia and blurred vision. A third decompressing operation aiming for maximal debulking before denosumab commencement was done endoscopically; however, only partial tumour removal was achieved (figure G, H). Denosumab (120 mg subcutaneously every 28 days) was initiated, and a marked response was noted after 6 months of treatment (figure I, J). After 14 months of denosumab, the patient remained symptom-free without needing further operations (figure K, L).GCTB represent 5–10% of bone tumours, classically affect long bones (<1% of all GCTB have a cranial location) and, although benign, can be locally aggressive. GCTB are histologically characterised by large multinucleated giant cells, but the clinical or radiological differential diagnosis can be challenging. Denosumab, an inhibitor of receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL), can be used to treat GCTB, because RANKL is overexpressed by mononuclear neoplastic stromal cells. As shown here, denosumab should also be considered in the early management of sellar–clival GCTB. This case also highlights the sustained reduction in tumour mass achieved by denosumab, sparing the patient from further operations. If feasible, surgical resection is still preferable as the definitive treatment, because the effect of denosumab wears off after stopping treatment and tumour regrowth can occur. Lifelong denosumab treatment will thus be likely required in this case; however, increasing the intervals between denosumab administration can be attempted to prevent or minimise adverse events, such as osteonecrosis of the jaw or atypical femoral fractures. Although GCTB is usually managed by rheumatologists, oncologists, or orthopaedics, sellar or parasellar GCTB might be first seen by endocrinologists, ophthalmologists, or neurosurgeons, who should be aware of this entity and the potential role of denosumab in its management.

A 61-year-old Japanese man with a history of cord-blood transplantation for acute myeloid leukaemia 15 years previously, and chronic graft-versus-host disease of the skin, was admitted for bleeding due to a duodenal ulcer. A maintenance dose of 5 mg prednisone was administered daily. The patient was successfully treated with a combination of endoscopic clipping and proton-pump inhibitor. 7 days after the episode of gastrointestinal bleeding, the patient underwent repeated oesophagogastroduodenoscopies, which showed multiple, newly developed, shallow ulcers in the oesophagus. Some of the lesions were circumscribed and discrete (figure).An oesophageal biopsy of the lesions was done, and histopathology of the oesophagus showed ballooning degeneration and multinucleated epithelial giant cells with eosinophilic intracellular inclusion bodies (figure). The biopsy samples showed neither malignancy nor graft-versus-host disease. Immunohistochemical staining of the specimens was also positive for herpes simplex virus, but negative for cytomegalovirus. On the basis of the gross and histopathological findings, herpes simplex oesophagitis was diagnosed. After the patient completed a 10 day course of intravenous aciclovir, repeat oesophagogastroduodenoscopies showed no abnormalities.
Herpes simplex virus is one of the most common pathogens causing infective oesophagitis. Herpes simplex oesophagitis is commonly seen in patients with immunosuppressive status, including after bone marrow transplantation, but has also been reported in immunocompetent individuals. In some patients, oesophagitis due to other pathogens such as cytomegalovirus or Candidia spp has been reported. Diagnosis is often confirmed by a combination of the gross oesophagogastroduodenoscopy findings, a histopathological examination, and an immunohistochemical stain of the biopsied specimen. Oesophageal herpes simplex lesions detected by oesophagogastroduodenoscopy are typically referred to as volcano ulcers, and appear as discrete, diffusely scattered shallow ulcers. The Cowdry type-A inclusion body is a classic histopathological finding in biopsy specimens of herpes simplex oesopohagitis as seen in this case, and is observed in up to 70% of biopsy specimens.

A 61-year-old Japanese man with a history of cord-blood transplantation for acute myeloid leukaemia 15 years previously, and chronic graft-versus-host disease of the skin, was admitted for bleeding due to a duodenal ulcer. A maintenance dose of 5 mg prednisone was administered daily. The patient was successfully treated with a combination of endoscopic clipping and proton-pump inhibitor. 7 days after the episode of gastrointestinal bleeding, the patient underwent repeated oesophagogastroduodenoscopies, which showed multiple, newly developed, shallow ulcers in the oesophagus. Some of the lesions were circumscribed and discrete (figure).An oesophageal biopsy of the lesions was done, and histopathology of the oesophagus showed ballooning degeneration and multinucleated epithelial giant cells with eosinophilic intracellular inclusion bodies (figure). The biopsy samples showed neither malignancy nor graft-versus-host disease. Immunohistochemical staining of the specimens was also positive for herpes simplex virus, but negative for cytomegalovirus. On the basis of the gross and histopathological findings, herpes simplex oesophagitis was diagnosed. After the patient completed a 10 day course of intravenous aciclovir, repeat oesophagogastroduodenoscopies showed no abnormalities.
Herpes simplex virus is one of the most common pathogens causing infective oesophagitis. Herpes simplex oesophagitis is commonly seen in patients with immunosuppressive status, including after bone marrow transplantation, but has also been reported in immunocompetent individuals. In some patients, oesophagitis due to other pathogens such as cytomegalovirus or Candidia spp has been reported. Diagnosis is often confirmed by a combination of the gross oesophagogastroduodenoscopy findings, a histopathological examination, and an immunohistochemical stain of the biopsied specimen. Oesophageal herpes simplex lesions detected by oesophagogastroduodenoscopy are typically referred to as volcano ulcers, and appear as discrete, diffusely scattered shallow ulcers. The Cowdry type-A inclusion body is a classic histopathological finding in biopsy specimens of herpes simplex oesopohagitis as seen in this case, and is observed in up to 70% of biopsy specimens.

A 61-year-old Japanese man with a history of cord-blood transplantation for acute myeloid leukaemia 15 years previously, and chronic graft-versus-host disease of the skin, was admitted for bleeding due to a duodenal ulcer. A maintenance dose of 5 mg prednisone was administered daily. The patient was successfully treated with a combination of endoscopic clipping and proton-pump inhibitor. 7 days after the episode of gastrointestinal bleeding, the patient underwent repeated oesophagogastroduodenoscopies, which showed multiple, newly developed, shallow ulcers in the oesophagus. Some of the lesions were circumscribed and discrete (figure).An oesophageal biopsy of the lesions was done, and histopathology of the oesophagus showed ballooning degeneration and multinucleated epithelial giant cells with eosinophilic intracellular inclusion bodies (figure). The biopsy samples showed neither malignancy nor graft-versus-host disease. Immunohistochemical staining of the specimens was also positive for herpes simplex virus, but negative for cytomegalovirus. On the basis of the gross and histopathological findings, herpes simplex oesophagitis was diagnosed. After the patient completed a 10 day course of intravenous aciclovir, repeat oesophagogastroduodenoscopies showed no abnormalities.
Herpes simplex virus is one of the most common pathogens causing infective oesophagitis. Herpes simplex oesophagitis is commonly seen in patients with immunosuppressive status, including after bone marrow transplantation, but has also been reported in immunocompetent individuals. In some patients, oesophagitis due to other pathogens such as cytomegalovirus or Candidia spp has been reported. Diagnosis is often confirmed by a combination of the gross oesophagogastroduodenoscopy findings, a histopathological examination, and an immunohistochemical stain of the biopsied specimen. Oesophageal herpes simplex lesions detected by oesophagogastroduodenoscopy are typically referred to as volcano ulcers, and appear as discrete, diffusely scattered shallow ulcers. The Cowdry type-A inclusion body is a classic histopathological finding in biopsy specimens of herpes simplex oesopohagitis as seen in this case, and is observed in up to 70% of biopsy specimens.

input: A 62-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital because she had been having involuntary movement of her right arm and leg for the previous month. In her medical history, she had developed type 2 diabetes approximately 10 years ago, which was treated with metformin and glimepiride. However, her blood glucose had been poorly controlled. A physical examination showed involuntary, unilateral, choreiform movements affecting only her right side (video). Further neurological examination showed her cranial nerves to be intact, ocular examination was normal, and there were no abnormal pyramidal signs—specifically, muscle strength was normal, and tone and reflexes were normal. Sensory neurological examination also found no abnormalities. Laboratory examination showed an elevated fasting blood glucose, with values ranging from 7·9 to 17·7 mmol/L. Her serum glycosylated haemoglobin was 13·6%. She had no ketones in her urine, and an unenhanced cranial CT scan showed a mild hyperdense lesion in the left basal ganglia. A cranial MRI showed lesions of hyperintensity in both the putamen and caudate nucleus on the left side (figure). A T2-weighted MRI also showed mild hyperintensity in the left corpus striatum (figure), which led us to consider the possibility of an ischaemic infarct. However, hyperintensity was also shown in a T1-weighted MRI sequences, which reassured us that it was not ischaemic damage. The patient was diagnosed with hemichorea with non-ketotic hyperglycaemia. Subcutaneous injections of insulin were added to the patient's diabetic medications in an effort to improve the control of her blood glucose. And haloperidol and clonazepam were prescribed to control the chorea. Within 2 weeks, the choreiform movements were much reduced.Neurological complications of diabetes are common; however, so-called diabetic striatopathy is relatively rare. When it does occur, it is usually in the context of non-ketotic hyperglycaemia and in patients with type 2 diabetes—although it may occur in patients with type 1 disease. It was previously described only in Asian women, but nowadays it is known to also affect other populations as well. Patients with diabetic striatopathy have a characteristic T1 hyperintensity signal in basal ganglia with sparing of the internal capsule. Hyperglycaemic injury to the basal ganglia is thought to be responsible for the hyperkinetic movements—usually manifesting as hemichorea or hemiballismus—which mostly resolve after glycaemic control has been achieved.

input: A 62-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital because she had been having involuntary movement of her right arm and leg for the previous month. In her medical history, she had developed type 2 diabetes approximately 10 years ago, which was treated with metformin and glimepiride. However, her blood glucose had been poorly controlled. A physical examination showed involuntary, unilateral, choreiform movements affecting only her right side (video). Further neurological examination showed her cranial nerves to be intact, ocular examination was normal, and there were no abnormal pyramidal signs—specifically, muscle strength was normal, and tone and reflexes were normal. Sensory neurological examination also found no abnormalities. Laboratory examination showed an elevated fasting blood glucose, with values ranging from 7·9 to 17·7 mmol/L. Her serum glycosylated haemoglobin was 13·6%. She had no ketones in her urine, and an unenhanced cranial CT scan showed a mild hyperdense lesion in the left basal ganglia. A cranial MRI showed lesions of hyperintensity in both the putamen and caudate nucleus on the left side (figure). A T2-weighted MRI also showed mild hyperintensity in the left corpus striatum (figure), which led us to consider the possibility of an ischaemic infarct. However, hyperintensity was also shown in a T1-weighted MRI sequences, which reassured us that it was not ischaemic damage. The patient was diagnosed with hemichorea with non-ketotic hyperglycaemia. Subcutaneous injections of insulin were added to the patient's diabetic medications in an effort to improve the control of her blood glucose. And haloperidol and clonazepam were prescribed to control the chorea. Within 2 weeks, the choreiform movements were much reduced.Neurological complications of diabetes are common; however, so-called diabetic striatopathy is relatively rare. When it does occur, it is usually in the context of non-ketotic hyperglycaemia and in patients with type 2 diabetes—although it may occur in patients with type 1 disease. It was previously described only in Asian women, but nowadays it is known to also affect other populations as well. Patients with diabetic striatopathy have a characteristic T1 hyperintensity signal in basal ganglia with sparing of the internal capsule. Hyperglycaemic injury to the basal ganglia is thought to be responsible for the hyperkinetic movements—usually manifesting as hemichorea or hemiballismus—which mostly resolve after glycaemic control has been achieved.

input: A 62-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital because she had been having involuntary movement of her right arm and leg for the previous month. In her medical history, she had developed type 2 diabetes approximately 10 years ago, which was treated with metformin and glimepiride. However, her blood glucose had been poorly controlled. A physical examination showed involuntary, unilateral, choreiform movements affecting only her right side (video). Further neurological examination showed her cranial nerves to be intact, ocular examination was normal, and there were no abnormal pyramidal signs—specifically, muscle strength was normal, and tone and reflexes were normal. Sensory neurological examination also found no abnormalities. Laboratory examination showed an elevated fasting blood glucose, with values ranging from 7·9 to 17·7 mmol/L. Her serum glycosylated haemoglobin was 13·6%. She had no ketones in her urine, and an unenhanced cranial CT scan showed a mild hyperdense lesion in the left basal ganglia. A cranial MRI showed lesions of hyperintensity in both the putamen and caudate nucleus on the left side (figure). A T2-weighted MRI also showed mild hyperintensity in the left corpus striatum (figure), which led us to consider the possibility of an ischaemic infarct. However, hyperintensity was also shown in a T1-weighted MRI sequences, which reassured us that it was not ischaemic damage. The patient was diagnosed with hemichorea with non-ketotic hyperglycaemia. Subcutaneous injections of insulin were added to the patient's diabetic medications in an effort to improve the control of her blood glucose. And haloperidol and clonazepam were prescribed to control the chorea. Within 2 weeks, the choreiform movements were much reduced.Neurological complications of diabetes are common; however, so-called diabetic striatopathy is relatively rare. When it does occur, it is usually in the context of non-ketotic hyperglycaemia and in patients with type 2 diabetes—although it may occur in patients with type 1 disease. It was previously described only in Asian women, but nowadays it is known to also affect other populations as well. Patients with diabetic striatopathy have a characteristic T1 hyperintensity signal in basal ganglia with sparing of the internal capsule. Hyperglycaemic injury to the basal ganglia is thought to be responsible for the hyperkinetic movements—usually manifesting as hemichorea or hemiballismus—which mostly resolve after glycaemic control has been achieved.

A 37-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of episodic pain, swelling, and redness of her left ear. She said the problem had re-occurred three to four times each year and had either resolved spontaneously or after she took non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) which she had bought over the counter. She also reported infrequent episodes of redness of her eyes.In the 2 months before we saw her, she said she had been increasingly fatigued and that she had lost her appetite; in the week before presenting, she said she believed she had been passing less urine compared to before—though, of course, we could not verify this.
On examination, the patient had a raised blood pressure of 160/90 mm Hg. She had a markedly tender and inflamed left ear pinna—sparing the ear lobe, the auditory canal, and tympanic membrane, which were all normal (figure). No discharge or cervical lymphadenopathy was found, and the right ear, both eyes, and nose were unremarkable. She had 1+ bilateral pitting oedema in her legs: barely detectable impression when finger is pressed into the skin. A chest x-ray was normal.
Urinalysis showed ten to 20 dysmorphic erythrocytes per high power field and 1+ proteinuria. Laboratory investigations showed a serum creatinine concentration of 4·2 mg/dL (normal 0·51–0·95), which had increased from 0·9 mg/dL 1 year earlier. The patient's complement levels were normal, and an anti-nuclear antibody test was negative. However, she tested positive for both anti-myeloperoxidase antibodies and perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies. A random plasma glucose concentration was 99 mg/dL (normal 70–140), and the patient's serum albumin concentration was 4·1 mg/dL (normal 3·4–5·4).
Histopathological examination of a sample taken from a biopsy of the patient's kidney showed active cellular crescents (figure) with a ruptured glomerular basement membrane (figure) and marked tubulointerstitial inflammation; no endocapillary proliferation or duplication of the glomerular basement membrane was found, and immunofluorescence staining was negative for IgG, IgA, IgM, C1q, C3, and kappa and lambda light chains.
We diagnosed pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis with relapsing polychondritis.
2 days after admission, the patient's serum creatinine concentration rose to 5·6 mg/dL, which required seven sessions of plasmapheresis. She was given both oral cyclophosphamide at a dose of 2 mg per kg per day and intravenous methylprednisolone at a dose of 500 mg a day for 3 days followed by oral prednisolone 1 mg per kg per day, which induced clinical remission of the polychondritis and reduced the serum creatinine concentration to 2·4 mg/dL at day 25. After 4 months, the oral cyclophosphamide was replaced with azathioprine and the patient has not had any recurrence of the problems during 2 years of follow-up.
The differential diagnosis of a patient positive for anti-myeloperoxidase antibodies and crescentic glomerulonephritis are microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis—the former was more likely in our patient because of the absence of asthma, peripheral neuropathy, and eosinophilia.
Relapsing polychondritis is a rare condition; renal involvement is unusual but has been reported in association with crescentic glomerulonephritis. Unlike isolated relapsing polychondritis—which may resolve either spontaneously or with steroids or NSAID monotherapy—renal involvement needs prompt investigation and immunosuppression to halt illness progression and prevent end-stage kidney disease (video).
