A 37-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of episodic pain, swelling, and redness of her left ear. She said the problem had re-occurred three to four times each year and had either resolved spontaneously or after she took non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) which she had bought over the counter. She also reported infrequent episodes of redness of her eyes.In the 2 months before we saw her, she said she had been increasingly fatigued and that she had lost her appetite; in the week before presenting, she said she believed she had been passing less urine compared to before—though, of course, we could not verify this.
On examination, the patient had a raised blood pressure of 160/90 mm Hg. She had a markedly tender and inflamed left ear pinna—sparing the ear lobe, the auditory canal, and tympanic membrane, which were all normal (figure). No discharge or cervical lymphadenopathy was found, and the right ear, both eyes, and nose were unremarkable. She had 1+ bilateral pitting oedema in her legs: barely detectable impression when finger is pressed into the skin. A chest x-ray was normal.
Urinalysis showed ten to 20 dysmorphic erythrocytes per high power field and 1+ proteinuria. Laboratory investigations showed a serum creatinine concentration of 4·2 mg/dL (normal 0·51–0·95), which had increased from 0·9 mg/dL 1 year earlier. The patient's complement levels were normal, and an anti-nuclear antibody test was negative. However, she tested positive for both anti-myeloperoxidase antibodies and perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies. A random plasma glucose concentration was 99 mg/dL (normal 70–140), and the patient's serum albumin concentration was 4·1 mg/dL (normal 3·4–5·4).
Histopathological examination of a sample taken from a biopsy of the patient's kidney showed active cellular crescents (figure) with a ruptured glomerular basement membrane (figure) and marked tubulointerstitial inflammation; no endocapillary proliferation or duplication of the glomerular basement membrane was found, and immunofluorescence staining was negative for IgG, IgA, IgM, C1q, C3, and kappa and lambda light chains.
We diagnosed pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis with relapsing polychondritis.
2 days after admission, the patient's serum creatinine concentration rose to 5·6 mg/dL, which required seven sessions of plasmapheresis. She was given both oral cyclophosphamide at a dose of 2 mg per kg per day and intravenous methylprednisolone at a dose of 500 mg a day for 3 days followed by oral prednisolone 1 mg per kg per day, which induced clinical remission of the polychondritis and reduced the serum creatinine concentration to 2·4 mg/dL at day 25. After 4 months, the oral cyclophosphamide was replaced with azathioprine and the patient has not had any recurrence of the problems during 2 years of follow-up.
The differential diagnosis of a patient positive for anti-myeloperoxidase antibodies and crescentic glomerulonephritis are microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis—the former was more likely in our patient because of the absence of asthma, peripheral neuropathy, and eosinophilia.
Relapsing polychondritis is a rare condition; renal involvement is unusual but has been reported in association with crescentic glomerulonephritis. Unlike isolated relapsing polychondritis—which may resolve either spontaneously or with steroids or NSAID monotherapy—renal involvement needs prompt investigation and immunosuppression to halt illness progression and prevent end-stage kidney disease (video).

A 37-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of episodic pain, swelling, and redness of her left ear. She said the problem had re-occurred three to four times each year and had either resolved spontaneously or after she took non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) which she had bought over the counter. She also reported infrequent episodes of redness of her eyes.In the 2 months before we saw her, she said she had been increasingly fatigued and that she had lost her appetite; in the week before presenting, she said she believed she had been passing less urine compared to before—though, of course, we could not verify this.
On examination, the patient had a raised blood pressure of 160/90 mm Hg. She had a markedly tender and inflamed left ear pinna—sparing the ear lobe, the auditory canal, and tympanic membrane, which were all normal (figure). No discharge or cervical lymphadenopathy was found, and the right ear, both eyes, and nose were unremarkable. She had 1+ bilateral pitting oedema in her legs: barely detectable impression when finger is pressed into the skin. A chest x-ray was normal.
Urinalysis showed ten to 20 dysmorphic erythrocytes per high power field and 1+ proteinuria. Laboratory investigations showed a serum creatinine concentration of 4·2 mg/dL (normal 0·51–0·95), which had increased from 0·9 mg/dL 1 year earlier. The patient's complement levels were normal, and an anti-nuclear antibody test was negative. However, she tested positive for both anti-myeloperoxidase antibodies and perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies. A random plasma glucose concentration was 99 mg/dL (normal 70–140), and the patient's serum albumin concentration was 4·1 mg/dL (normal 3·4–5·4).
Histopathological examination of a sample taken from a biopsy of the patient's kidney showed active cellular crescents (figure) with a ruptured glomerular basement membrane (figure) and marked tubulointerstitial inflammation; no endocapillary proliferation or duplication of the glomerular basement membrane was found, and immunofluorescence staining was negative for IgG, IgA, IgM, C1q, C3, and kappa and lambda light chains.
We diagnosed pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis with relapsing polychondritis.
2 days after admission, the patient's serum creatinine concentration rose to 5·6 mg/dL, which required seven sessions of plasmapheresis. She was given both oral cyclophosphamide at a dose of 2 mg per kg per day and intravenous methylprednisolone at a dose of 500 mg a day for 3 days followed by oral prednisolone 1 mg per kg per day, which induced clinical remission of the polychondritis and reduced the serum creatinine concentration to 2·4 mg/dL at day 25. After 4 months, the oral cyclophosphamide was replaced with azathioprine and the patient has not had any recurrence of the problems during 2 years of follow-up.
The differential diagnosis of a patient positive for anti-myeloperoxidase antibodies and crescentic glomerulonephritis are microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis—the former was more likely in our patient because of the absence of asthma, peripheral neuropathy, and eosinophilia.
Relapsing polychondritis is a rare condition; renal involvement is unusual but has been reported in association with crescentic glomerulonephritis. Unlike isolated relapsing polychondritis—which may resolve either spontaneously or with steroids or NSAID monotherapy—renal involvement needs prompt investigation and immunosuppression to halt illness progression and prevent end-stage kidney disease (video).

input: A 66-year-old, left-handed man was seen in our specialist clinic, complaining of difficulty reading, counting coins, using his mobile phone, and getting dressed. Otherwise, he was managing at home alone and going out independently, albeit with difficulty using stairs and walking on uneven ground. His problems had started 6 years earlier with difficulty reading and fastening his buttons and zips. At that stage, having seen opticians, he was referred to an ophthalmologist and underwent cataract surgery; however, his visual problems continued and got worse. He had no medical or family history of neurological disease. On physical examination, we noticed he had difficulty locating objects in space in the left lower hemifield. Visual acuity, fundi, pupillary responses, and extraocular movements were normal. We also noticed bilateral finger myoclonus and symmetrically brisk reflexes with flexor plantars. Tone, power, and sensation of all limbs and his trunk were normal. On cognitive testing, he scored 25/30 on the Mini-Mental State Examination, losing points for recall of three words, writing, reading, and drawing intersecting pentagons. He also struggled to perform simple calculations and had limb dyspraxia even after we accounted for his visual problems. In view of these findings, we suspected an underlying neurodegenerative disorder. Blood investigations for reversible causes of dementia were either negative or normal. An MRI of his brain showed extensive atrophy of the parietal and occipital lobes with so-called knife-like thinning of the gyri (figure). We made a diagnosis of posterior cortical atrophy (PCA), on the basis of the clinical presentation and the findings on imaging. The patient was offered cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis and amyloid PET—to investigate further the underlying cause of the PCA—but he decided he did not want any additional tests.PCA is a syndrome characterised by progressive impairment of visual processing and other functions of the occipital and parietal lobes including praxis, calculation, and spelling. Typically patients present to health professionals with PCA symptoms before the age of 65 years. PCA is usually caused by Alzheimer's disease, and is not thought to occur with an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. Other causes of PCA include dementia with Lewy bodies, corticobasal degeneration, and, very rarely, prion disease. CSF analysis—to look for amyloid and tau proteins—or amyloid PET imaging can provide evidence to corroborate the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease. Patients with PCA are often referred to optometrists and ophthalmologists in the belief that they have a primary ocular abnormality, leading to a delay in diagnosis of the syndrome. It is therefore important that PCA is considered in late middle-aged patients presenting with progressive visual symptoms and normal visual acuity. Our case illustrates the need for awareness that visual problems in patients might not have a cause within the eye.

input: A 66-year-old, left-handed man was seen in our specialist clinic, complaining of difficulty reading, counting coins, using his mobile phone, and getting dressed. Otherwise, he was managing at home alone and going out independently, albeit with difficulty using stairs and walking on uneven ground. His problems had started 6 years earlier with difficulty reading and fastening his buttons and zips. At that stage, having seen opticians, he was referred to an ophthalmologist and underwent cataract surgery; however, his visual problems continued and got worse. He had no medical or family history of neurological disease. On physical examination, we noticed he had difficulty locating objects in space in the left lower hemifield. Visual acuity, fundi, pupillary responses, and extraocular movements were normal. We also noticed bilateral finger myoclonus and symmetrically brisk reflexes with flexor plantars. Tone, power, and sensation of all limbs and his trunk were normal. On cognitive testing, he scored 25/30 on the Mini-Mental State Examination, losing points for recall of three words, writing, reading, and drawing intersecting pentagons. He also struggled to perform simple calculations and had limb dyspraxia even after we accounted for his visual problems. In view of these findings, we suspected an underlying neurodegenerative disorder. Blood investigations for reversible causes of dementia were either negative or normal. An MRI of his brain showed extensive atrophy of the parietal and occipital lobes with so-called knife-like thinning of the gyri (figure). We made a diagnosis of posterior cortical atrophy (PCA), on the basis of the clinical presentation and the findings on imaging. The patient was offered cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis and amyloid PET—to investigate further the underlying cause of the PCA—but he decided he did not want any additional tests.PCA is a syndrome characterised by progressive impairment of visual processing and other functions of the occipital and parietal lobes including praxis, calculation, and spelling. Typically patients present to health professionals with PCA symptoms before the age of 65 years. PCA is usually caused by Alzheimer's disease, and is not thought to occur with an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. Other causes of PCA include dementia with Lewy bodies, corticobasal degeneration, and, very rarely, prion disease. CSF analysis—to look for amyloid and tau proteins—or amyloid PET imaging can provide evidence to corroborate the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease. Patients with PCA are often referred to optometrists and ophthalmologists in the belief that they have a primary ocular abnormality, leading to a delay in diagnosis of the syndrome. It is therefore important that PCA is considered in late middle-aged patients presenting with progressive visual symptoms and normal visual acuity. Our case illustrates the need for awareness that visual problems in patients might not have a cause within the eye.

A 79-year-old woman was referred to our department with a sudden onset of dyspnoea. She had end-stage kidney disease secondary to IgA nephropathy and, 6 months earlier, had started peritoneal dialysis. The patient did not report a cough, fever, or chills.On examination, her blood pressure was 154/93 mm Hg, heart rate 58 beats per min, oxygen saturation 91% room air, temperature 36·8°C. She had no oedema, nor any symptoms of right-sided heart failure. She had no abdominal pain. On chest auscultation, we found no breath sounds on the right side. Her weight had been stable.
A chest x-ray showed a new large right pleural effusion—a previous x-ray, done 11 months earlier, had been reported as clear.
Analysis of a sample of pleural fluid showed a clear yellow liquid with a cell count of 113 cells per mm3, composed of 2% neutrophils and 45% lymphocytes. The protein concentration of the pleural fluid was 5 g/L, glucose concentration was 7·9 mmol/L, and creatinine concentration was 498 μmol/L, indicating a likely transudate.
Blood tests showed a white blood count of 8·67 × 109 per L (normal 4·5–11·0), a C-reactive protein concentration of 0·8 mg/L (normal <5), glucose concentration of 5·4 mmol/L (normal 4·1–6·0), plasma protein concentration of 69 g/L (normal 66–87), albumin concentration of 32 g/L (normal 36–44), and a creatinine concentration of 512 μmol/L (normal range 45–84). Electrolytes and liver function tests were unremarkable.
The peritoneal dialysis fluid was clear and showed a glucose concentration of 7·8 g/L and creatinine of 484 μmol/L.
Peritoneal scintigraphy, combined with a single-photon-emission CT and CT (SPECT/CT) scan, showed radioactive tracer in the pleural cavity after infusion into the peritoneal cavity, confirming pleuro-peritoneal communication (figure, video). The patient's symptoms completely resolved on cessation of peritoneal dialysis. The recurrence of a pleural effusion, immediately on recommencing peritoneal dialysis, led us to decide on a definitive transfer to haemodialysis. After 8 months of follow-up, she remains asymptomatic, without any recurrence of a pleural effusion.
Pleuro-peritoneal communication is an uncommon complication of peritoneal dialysis, occurring in 1–2% of patients. The communication usually appears less than 3 months after initiating dialysis, but may also occur months to years later.
In 88% of cases, the pleural effusion is on the right side of the chest; left-sided defects are often covered by the heart and pericardium, making leakage on the left side less likely.
Pleuro-peritoneal communication takes place via congenital or acquired diaphragmatic defects and occurs when intra-abdominal pressure is increased by the administration of the peritoneal dialysis fluid.
A rapidly developed transudative unilateral pleural efffusion, with a high glucose concentration—dextrose being the most commonly used osmotic agent in peritoneal dialysis—accompanied by a high creatinine level, close to the dialysate composition, is highly suggestive of a leak of dialysate into the pleural cavity.
Dynamic imaging, such as SPECT/CT, shows the transfer of the radioactive tracer from the peritoneal to the pleural cavity and facilitates location of the site of the leak. Conservative treatment—temporary interruption of the peritoneal dialysis for 2–6 weeks—is effective in half of cases. Chemical pleurodesis or surgical interventions should be considered as second-line treatments, and the pros and cons of an invasive treatment should be weighed up against a definitive transfer to haemodialysis.

input: A 66-year-old, left-handed man was seen in our specialist clinic, complaining of difficulty reading, counting coins, using his mobile phone, and getting dressed. Otherwise, he was managing at home alone and going out independently, albeit with difficulty using stairs and walking on uneven ground. His problems had started 6 years earlier with difficulty reading and fastening his buttons and zips. At that stage, having seen opticians, he was referred to an ophthalmologist and underwent cataract surgery; however, his visual problems continued and got worse. He had no medical or family history of neurological disease. On physical examination, we noticed he had difficulty locating objects in space in the left lower hemifield. Visual acuity, fundi, pupillary responses, and extraocular movements were normal. We also noticed bilateral finger myoclonus and symmetrically brisk reflexes with flexor plantars. Tone, power, and sensation of all limbs and his trunk were normal. On cognitive testing, he scored 25/30 on the Mini-Mental State Examination, losing points for recall of three words, writing, reading, and drawing intersecting pentagons. He also struggled to perform simple calculations and had limb dyspraxia even after we accounted for his visual problems. In view of these findings, we suspected an underlying neurodegenerative disorder. Blood investigations for reversible causes of dementia were either negative or normal. An MRI of his brain showed extensive atrophy of the parietal and occipital lobes with so-called knife-like thinning of the gyri (figure). We made a diagnosis of posterior cortical atrophy (PCA), on the basis of the clinical presentation and the findings on imaging. The patient was offered cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis and amyloid PET—to investigate further the underlying cause of the PCA—but he decided he did not want any additional tests.PCA is a syndrome characterised by progressive impairment of visual processing and other functions of the occipital and parietal lobes including praxis, calculation, and spelling. Typically patients present to health professionals with PCA symptoms before the age of 65 years. PCA is usually caused by Alzheimer's disease, and is not thought to occur with an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. Other causes of PCA include dementia with Lewy bodies, corticobasal degeneration, and, very rarely, prion disease. CSF analysis—to look for amyloid and tau proteins—or amyloid PET imaging can provide evidence to corroborate the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease. Patients with PCA are often referred to optometrists and ophthalmologists in the belief that they have a primary ocular abnormality, leading to a delay in diagnosis of the syndrome. It is therefore important that PCA is considered in late middle-aged patients presenting with progressive visual symptoms and normal visual acuity. Our case illustrates the need for awareness that visual problems in patients might not have a cause within the eye.

A 79-year-old woman was referred to our department with a sudden onset of dyspnoea. She had end-stage kidney disease secondary to IgA nephropathy and, 6 months earlier, had started peritoneal dialysis. The patient did not report a cough, fever, or chills.On examination, her blood pressure was 154/93 mm Hg, heart rate 58 beats per min, oxygen saturation 91% room air, temperature 36·8°C. She had no oedema, nor any symptoms of right-sided heart failure. She had no abdominal pain. On chest auscultation, we found no breath sounds on the right side. Her weight had been stable.
A chest x-ray showed a new large right pleural effusion—a previous x-ray, done 11 months earlier, had been reported as clear.
Analysis of a sample of pleural fluid showed a clear yellow liquid with a cell count of 113 cells per mm3, composed of 2% neutrophils and 45% lymphocytes. The protein concentration of the pleural fluid was 5 g/L, glucose concentration was 7·9 mmol/L, and creatinine concentration was 498 μmol/L, indicating a likely transudate.
Blood tests showed a white blood count of 8·67 × 109 per L (normal 4·5–11·0), a C-reactive protein concentration of 0·8 mg/L (normal <5), glucose concentration of 5·4 mmol/L (normal 4·1–6·0), plasma protein concentration of 69 g/L (normal 66–87), albumin concentration of 32 g/L (normal 36–44), and a creatinine concentration of 512 μmol/L (normal range 45–84). Electrolytes and liver function tests were unremarkable.
The peritoneal dialysis fluid was clear and showed a glucose concentration of 7·8 g/L and creatinine of 484 μmol/L.
Peritoneal scintigraphy, combined with a single-photon-emission CT and CT (SPECT/CT) scan, showed radioactive tracer in the pleural cavity after infusion into the peritoneal cavity, confirming pleuro-peritoneal communication (figure, video). The patient's symptoms completely resolved on cessation of peritoneal dialysis. The recurrence of a pleural effusion, immediately on recommencing peritoneal dialysis, led us to decide on a definitive transfer to haemodialysis. After 8 months of follow-up, she remains asymptomatic, without any recurrence of a pleural effusion.
Pleuro-peritoneal communication is an uncommon complication of peritoneal dialysis, occurring in 1–2% of patients. The communication usually appears less than 3 months after initiating dialysis, but may also occur months to years later.
In 88% of cases, the pleural effusion is on the right side of the chest; left-sided defects are often covered by the heart and pericardium, making leakage on the left side less likely.
Pleuro-peritoneal communication takes place via congenital or acquired diaphragmatic defects and occurs when intra-abdominal pressure is increased by the administration of the peritoneal dialysis fluid.
A rapidly developed transudative unilateral pleural efffusion, with a high glucose concentration—dextrose being the most commonly used osmotic agent in peritoneal dialysis—accompanied by a high creatinine level, close to the dialysate composition, is highly suggestive of a leak of dialysate into the pleural cavity.
Dynamic imaging, such as SPECT/CT, shows the transfer of the radioactive tracer from the peritoneal to the pleural cavity and facilitates location of the site of the leak. Conservative treatment—temporary interruption of the peritoneal dialysis for 2–6 weeks—is effective in half of cases. Chemical pleurodesis or surgical interventions should be considered as second-line treatments, and the pros and cons of an invasive treatment should be weighed up against a definitive transfer to haemodialysis.

A 37-year-old woman presented to our emergency room reporting chest pain and palpitations which had woken her up in the early hours of the morning. She was known to be homozygous for a rare and severe form of cystic fibrosis with a mutation, described among Jewish people of Georgian descent, in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane regulator gene: Q359K/T360K. The patient had previous multisystem complications related to her cystic fibrosis—namely pancreatic insufficiency, chronic rhinosinusitis, and advanced bronchiectasis in the upper lung lobes (figure). In the year before her presentation at the emergency room, the patient had experienced a single episode of a pulmonary exacerbation and had been treated with oral antibiotics. She had a history of iron deficiency anaemia attributed to excessive menstrual bleeding and was prescribed iron supplementation.At interview in the emergency room, the patient reported no periods of lengthy immobilisation—such as a long-haul flight—and said she had not used any hormonal contraceptives. She had no risk factors for venous thromboembolism.
On examination, the patient was distressed: her pulse rate was 80 beats per min; she had a prolonged expiration time.
An electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia with incomplete right bundle branch block. Laboratory investigation demonstrated a microcytic anaemia with a haemoglobin concentration of 10·1 mg/dL (normal 12·0–16·0) and a raised cardiac troponin T concentration (123 ng/L; normal 0–14).
A pulmonary CT angiogram showed areas of uneven contrast filling in the right pulmonary artery—indicating a possible pulmonary embolus (figure). We therefore decided to give the patient a single dose of low molecular weight heparin.
However, upon review of the CT scan, we suspected that the filling defects were due to abnormal flow in the pulmonary arteries of the right upper lobe, rather than a pulmonary embolus.
2 days later, a repeat pulmonary CT angiogram showed normal filling of the right pulmonary artery (figure) and coronary CT angiography, with enhanced contrast flow, showed normal coronary arteries. Sonography showed no venous thrombosis, and an echocardiogram was normal. A repeat troponin T test, done later the same day, showed a decreased concentration of 34·9 ng/L, and 3 days later, it was found to be <13 ng/L. The patient was then allowed home with a prescription for her usual medications.
At review 11 months later, she had experienced no further chest pain or cardiac events. The cause of chest pain and elevated troponin T remains unclear—although, we believe that the anaemia and tachycardia, causing an increased myocardial oxygen demand, might have played a role.
Misdiagnosis of pulmonary emboli in contrast CT angiograms has been described before and attributed to various effects—including motion artifacts from breathing or cardiac pulsation. In advanced cystic fibrosis, severe lung involvement typically results in upper lobe bronchiectasis with dilated bronchial arteries in affected areas. Abnormal vessel anastomoses may occur between bronchial and pulmonary arteries. The systemic pressure in the bronchial arteries may cause slowing and even reversal of blood flow in the lower pressure pulmonary arteries leading to affected regions, with uneven contrast filling on imaging. Typically, the filling defect of an intraluminal clot has a sharp interface—not the case in our patient—with the bright contrast material.
Increasing the contrast flow and concentration may help to visualise the artery; when in question, a vascular MRI with serial scanning may demonstrate normal blood flow. Clinicians should be aware of the difficulty in diagnosing a pulmonary embolism in cystic fibrosis complicated by bronchiectasis.

A 37-year-old woman presented to our emergency room reporting chest pain and palpitations which had woken her up in the early hours of the morning. She was known to be homozygous for a rare and severe form of cystic fibrosis with a mutation, described among Jewish people of Georgian descent, in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane regulator gene: Q359K/T360K. The patient had previous multisystem complications related to her cystic fibrosis—namely pancreatic insufficiency, chronic rhinosinusitis, and advanced bronchiectasis in the upper lung lobes (figure). In the year before her presentation at the emergency room, the patient had experienced a single episode of a pulmonary exacerbation and had been treated with oral antibiotics. She had a history of iron deficiency anaemia attributed to excessive menstrual bleeding and was prescribed iron supplementation.At interview in the emergency room, the patient reported no periods of lengthy immobilisation—such as a long-haul flight—and said she had not used any hormonal contraceptives. She had no risk factors for venous thromboembolism.
On examination, the patient was distressed: her pulse rate was 80 beats per min; she had a prolonged expiration time.
An electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia with incomplete right bundle branch block. Laboratory investigation demonstrated a microcytic anaemia with a haemoglobin concentration of 10·1 mg/dL (normal 12·0–16·0) and a raised cardiac troponin T concentration (123 ng/L; normal 0–14).
A pulmonary CT angiogram showed areas of uneven contrast filling in the right pulmonary artery—indicating a possible pulmonary embolus (figure). We therefore decided to give the patient a single dose of low molecular weight heparin.
However, upon review of the CT scan, we suspected that the filling defects were due to abnormal flow in the pulmonary arteries of the right upper lobe, rather than a pulmonary embolus.
2 days later, a repeat pulmonary CT angiogram showed normal filling of the right pulmonary artery (figure) and coronary CT angiography, with enhanced contrast flow, showed normal coronary arteries. Sonography showed no venous thrombosis, and an echocardiogram was normal. A repeat troponin T test, done later the same day, showed a decreased concentration of 34·9 ng/L, and 3 days later, it was found to be <13 ng/L. The patient was then allowed home with a prescription for her usual medications.
At review 11 months later, she had experienced no further chest pain or cardiac events. The cause of chest pain and elevated troponin T remains unclear—although, we believe that the anaemia and tachycardia, causing an increased myocardial oxygen demand, might have played a role.
Misdiagnosis of pulmonary emboli in contrast CT angiograms has been described before and attributed to various effects—including motion artifacts from breathing or cardiac pulsation. In advanced cystic fibrosis, severe lung involvement typically results in upper lobe bronchiectasis with dilated bronchial arteries in affected areas. Abnormal vessel anastomoses may occur between bronchial and pulmonary arteries. The systemic pressure in the bronchial arteries may cause slowing and even reversal of blood flow in the lower pressure pulmonary arteries leading to affected regions, with uneven contrast filling on imaging. Typically, the filling defect of an intraluminal clot has a sharp interface—not the case in our patient—with the bright contrast material.
Increasing the contrast flow and concentration may help to visualise the artery; when in question, a vascular MRI with serial scanning may demonstrate normal blood flow. Clinicians should be aware of the difficulty in diagnosing a pulmonary embolism in cystic fibrosis complicated by bronchiectasis.

A 37-year-old man attended our hospital with a 1-week history of fever, chills, headaches, sore throat, generalised malaise, and a rash on his arms, legs, trunk, and in his groin. The patient also reported significant pain and discomfort in his rectum when defecating. He had a history of HIV and metastatic Kaposi sarcoma; secondary syphilis, which had been treated; and hypertension. He was prescribed the following medications: emtricitabine-tenofovir, doravarine, darunavir-cobicistat, and hydrochlorothiazide.The patient reported no recent travel or contact with human or animal with a similar rash or illnesses. He reported no history of varicella zoster virus infection as a child and said he had received all childhood vaccinations. The patient reported no sexual activity for the past 6 months.
On examination, the patient was afebrile: temperature 37·3°C. He appeared uncomfortable and had several scattered, pink, umbilicated papules, vesicles, and pustules on the trunk, upper and lower extremities, groin, and peri-anal region (figure).
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 12·7 g/dL (normal 13·3–16·3), CD4+ T-helper cell count of 262 cells per mcL (normal 490–1740), HIV-1 RNA PCR less than 20 copies per mL, and an absolute lymphocyte count of 3·01 per uL (normal 1·1–2·7). Serology was negative for Bartonella henselae, Aspergillus spp, hepatitis A, B, and C, cryptococcal antigen, herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), and (1→3)-β-D-glucan.
Immunohistochemical analysis of a biopsy sample of one of the truncal papules was negative for HSV-1, HSV-2, and Treponema pallidum. Warthin-Starry staining was negative for spirochetes and periodic-acid-Schiff staining was negative for fungal organisms. Histopathological analysis of the biopsy sample showed focal epidermal necrosis with underlying acute inflammation in the superficial dermis and individually necrotic keratinocytes at the periphery. A Dacron swab of one of the truncal lesions was positive for human monkeypox virus.
Considering our patient's history of immunosuppression, we prescribed doxycycline, ceftriaxone, and valacyclovir; we subsequently gave him a 2-week course of 600 mg of tecovirimat twice a day. He reported no significant adverse effects and the skin lesions healed rapidly. At follow-up one month later, the patient reported areas of hyperpigmentation at the sites of the healed lesions and said he was doing well.
Monkeypox is caused by the monkeypox virus, a member of the Poxviridae family and Orthopoxvirus genus. The virus is transmitted via large respiratory droplets, direct or indirect contact with bodily fluids or lesion material, or contact with fomites—including bedding or towels. Malaise, lymphadenopathy, headache, myalgia, and cutaneous symptoms can occur within 1–3 days of the onset of fever. Lesions may initially appear as macules progressing to papules, vesicles, and pustules that dry up and fall off. The development of skin lesions, in addition to viral prodromal symptoms, in immunocompromised patients should raise the possibility of other diagnosis, such as primary or secondary infection with varicella zoster virus or other organisms such as Cryptococcus neoformans, Histoplasma capsulatum, or Bartonella henselae; we considered this unlikely in our patient given his presentation. Molluscum contagiosum also presents with umbilicated papules, but usually without systemic symptoms. Notably, proctitis has recently been recognised as being associated with a human monkeypox infection. Tecovirimat is approved for treating human smallpox disease. Treatment in cases of human monkeypox should be considered in severe cases, immunocompromised patients, paediatric populations, pregnant or breastfeeding women, and people with concurrent disease or other comorbidities.

input:
A 37-year-old man attended our hospital with a 1-week history of fever, chills, headaches, sore throat, generalised malaise, and a rash on his arms, legs, trunk, and in his groin. The patient also reported significant pain and discomfort in his rectum when defecating. He had a history of HIV and metastatic Kaposi sarcoma; secondary syphilis, which had been treated; and hypertension. He was prescribed the following medications: emtricitabine-tenofovir, doravarine, darunavir-cobicistat, and hydrochlorothiazide.The patient reported no recent travel or contact with human or animal with a similar rash or illnesses. He reported no history of varicella zoster virus infection as a child and said he had received all childhood vaccinations. The patient reported no sexual activity for the past 6 months.
On examination, the patient was afebrile: temperature 37·3°C. He appeared uncomfortable and had several scattered, pink, umbilicated papules, vesicles, and pustules on the trunk, upper and lower extremities, groin, and peri-anal region (figure).
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 12·7 g/dL (normal 13·3–16·3), CD4+ T-helper cell count of 262 cells per mcL (normal 490–1740), HIV-1 RNA PCR less than 20 copies per mL, and an absolute lymphocyte count of 3·01 per uL (normal 1·1–2·7). Serology was negative for Bartonella henselae, Aspergillus spp, hepatitis A, B, and C, cryptococcal antigen, herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), and (1→3)-β-D-glucan.
Immunohistochemical analysis of a biopsy sample of one of the truncal papules was negative for HSV-1, HSV-2, and Treponema pallidum. Warthin-Starry staining was negative for spirochetes and periodic-acid-Schiff staining was negative for fungal organisms. Histopathological analysis of the biopsy sample showed focal epidermal necrosis with underlying acute inflammation in the superficial dermis and individually necrotic keratinocytes at the periphery. A Dacron swab of one of the truncal lesions was positive for human monkeypox virus.
Considering our patient's history of immunosuppression, we prescribed doxycycline, ceftriaxone, and valacyclovir; we subsequently gave him a 2-week course of 600 mg of tecovirimat twice a day. He reported no significant adverse effects and the skin lesions healed rapidly. At follow-up one month later, the patient reported areas of hyperpigmentation at the sites of the healed lesions and said he was doing well.
Monkeypox is caused by the monkeypox virus, a member of the Poxviridae family and Orthopoxvirus genus. The virus is transmitted via large respiratory droplets, direct or indirect contact with bodily fluids or lesion material, or contact with fomites—including bedding or towels. Malaise, lymphadenopathy, headache, myalgia, and cutaneous symptoms can occur within 1–3 days of the onset of fever. Lesions may initially appear as macules progressing to papules, vesicles, and pustules that dry up and fall off. The development of skin lesions, in addition to viral prodromal symptoms, in immunocompromised patients should raise the possibility of other diagnosis, such as primary or secondary infection with varicella zoster virus or other organisms such as Cryptococcus neoformans, Histoplasma capsulatum, or Bartonella henselae; we considered this unlikely in our patient given his presentation. Molluscum contagiosum also presents with umbilicated papules, but usually without systemic symptoms. Notably, proctitis has recently been recognised as being associated with a human monkeypox infection. Tecovirimat is approved for treating human smallpox disease. Treatment in cases of human monkeypox should be considered in severe cases, immunocompromised patients, paediatric populations, pregnant or breastfeeding women, and people with concurrent disease or other comorbidities.

input:
A 37-year-old man attended our hospital with a 1-week history of fever, chills, headaches, sore throat, generalised malaise, and a rash on his arms, legs, trunk, and in his groin. The patient also reported significant pain and discomfort in his rectum when defecating. He had a history of HIV and metastatic Kaposi sarcoma; secondary syphilis, which had been treated; and hypertension. He was prescribed the following medications: emtricitabine-tenofovir, doravarine, darunavir-cobicistat, and hydrochlorothiazide.The patient reported no recent travel or contact with human or animal with a similar rash or illnesses. He reported no history of varicella zoster virus infection as a child and said he had received all childhood vaccinations. The patient reported no sexual activity for the past 6 months.
On examination, the patient was afebrile: temperature 37·3°C. He appeared uncomfortable and had several scattered, pink, umbilicated papules, vesicles, and pustules on the trunk, upper and lower extremities, groin, and peri-anal region (figure).
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 12·7 g/dL (normal 13·3–16·3), CD4+ T-helper cell count of 262 cells per mcL (normal 490–1740), HIV-1 RNA PCR less than 20 copies per mL, and an absolute lymphocyte count of 3·01 per uL (normal 1·1–2·7). Serology was negative for Bartonella henselae, Aspergillus spp, hepatitis A, B, and C, cryptococcal antigen, herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), and (1→3)-β-D-glucan.
Immunohistochemical analysis of a biopsy sample of one of the truncal papules was negative for HSV-1, HSV-2, and Treponema pallidum. Warthin-Starry staining was negative for spirochetes and periodic-acid-Schiff staining was negative for fungal organisms. Histopathological analysis of the biopsy sample showed focal epidermal necrosis with underlying acute inflammation in the superficial dermis and individually necrotic keratinocytes at the periphery. A Dacron swab of one of the truncal lesions was positive for human monkeypox virus.
Considering our patient's history of immunosuppression, we prescribed doxycycline, ceftriaxone, and valacyclovir; we subsequently gave him a 2-week course of 600 mg of tecovirimat twice a day. He reported no significant adverse effects and the skin lesions healed rapidly. At follow-up one month later, the patient reported areas of hyperpigmentation at the sites of the healed lesions and said he was doing well.
Monkeypox is caused by the monkeypox virus, a member of the Poxviridae family and Orthopoxvirus genus. The virus is transmitted via large respiratory droplets, direct or indirect contact with bodily fluids or lesion material, or contact with fomites—including bedding or towels. Malaise, lymphadenopathy, headache, myalgia, and cutaneous symptoms can occur within 1–3 days of the onset of fever. Lesions may initially appear as macules progressing to papules, vesicles, and pustules that dry up and fall off. The development of skin lesions, in addition to viral prodromal symptoms, in immunocompromised patients should raise the possibility of other diagnosis, such as primary or secondary infection with varicella zoster virus or other organisms such as Cryptococcus neoformans, Histoplasma capsulatum, or Bartonella henselae; we considered this unlikely in our patient given his presentation. Molluscum contagiosum also presents with umbilicated papules, but usually without systemic symptoms. Notably, proctitis has recently been recognised as being associated with a human monkeypox infection. Tecovirimat is approved for treating human smallpox disease. Treatment in cases of human monkeypox should be considered in severe cases, immunocompromised patients, paediatric populations, pregnant or breastfeeding women, and people with concurrent disease or other comorbidities.

input:
A 60-year-old male active smoker visited Hunan Cancer Hospital (Changsha, China) on Jan 3, 2018, with a swollen upper lip and lower cheek for the past 3 months. According to the patient, his swelling had increased in size during the previous few weeks. No other specific symptoms were reported and his blood tests were normal. On examination, he had a tender palpable mass measuring approximately 3·5 × 4·7cm on the upper lip and 5·6 × 3·2 cm on the lower cheek (figure, A). The skin surface covering the masses appeared normal. He had neither a history of an injury nor tumour.The differential diagnosis based on the preliminary findings included primary tumour of the head and neck, metastasis from the thyroid or lung, lymphoma, or inflammation. An ultrasound-guided biopsy was done on the cheek and lip. The histopathological diagnosis was poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma (cytokeratin [CK]5/6+++, CK7–, p63+++, thyroid transcription factor [TTF]-1+/–, Epstein-Barr virus [EBV]–). To further evaluate the primary tumour, a PET-CT scan was done; this scan showed a nodule in the upper lobe of his left lung measuring 3·7 × 4·7 cm and pleural invasion. A CT-guided biopsy of the left lung nodule was done and showed well-differentiated squamous carcinoma (CK5/6+++, CK7-, p63+++, TTF-1+/–, EBV–; figure, B). The patient was diagnosed with squamous cell lung carcinoma and transferred to a lung cancer unit in the hospital to receive chemotherapy (gemcitabine 1250 mg/m2 on days 1 and 8 plus cisplatin 75 mg/m2 on day 1, every 21 days). The patient was evaluated with CT scans of the head, neck, and chest after every two cycles of chemotherapy (ie, every 2 months) and subsequently achieved a partial response to treatment.
Malignancy involving metastasis to the lip and cheek is a rare clinical event. To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of squamous cell lung carcinoma presenting with lip and cheek metastasis.
Squamous cell lung carcinoma grows rapidly. However, when it presents with lip and cheek metastasis, it can easily be misdiagnosed as squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck. The physician must be able to recognise this disease, to have an adequate degree of suspicion to consider this option in the differential diagnosis with other tumours or inflammatory diseases through biopsy of multiple lesions and immunohistochemistry, and to provide suitable treatment strategies.

input:
A 60-year-old male active smoker visited Hunan Cancer Hospital (Changsha, China) on Jan 3, 2018, with a swollen upper lip and lower cheek for the past 3 months. According to the patient, his swelling had increased in size during the previous few weeks. No other specific symptoms were reported and his blood tests were normal. On examination, he had a tender palpable mass measuring approximately 3·5 × 4·7cm on the upper lip and 5·6 × 3·2 cm on the lower cheek (figure, A). The skin surface covering the masses appeared normal. He had neither a history of an injury nor tumour.The differential diagnosis based on the preliminary findings included primary tumour of the head and neck, metastasis from the thyroid or lung, lymphoma, or inflammation. An ultrasound-guided biopsy was done on the cheek and lip. The histopathological diagnosis was poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma (cytokeratin [CK]5/6+++, CK7–, p63+++, thyroid transcription factor [TTF]-1+/–, Epstein-Barr virus [EBV]–). To further evaluate the primary tumour, a PET-CT scan was done; this scan showed a nodule in the upper lobe of his left lung measuring 3·7 × 4·7 cm and pleural invasion. A CT-guided biopsy of the left lung nodule was done and showed well-differentiated squamous carcinoma (CK5/6+++, CK7-, p63+++, TTF-1+/–, EBV–; figure, B). The patient was diagnosed with squamous cell lung carcinoma and transferred to a lung cancer unit in the hospital to receive chemotherapy (gemcitabine 1250 mg/m2 on days 1 and 8 plus cisplatin 75 mg/m2 on day 1, every 21 days). The patient was evaluated with CT scans of the head, neck, and chest after every two cycles of chemotherapy (ie, every 2 months) and subsequently achieved a partial response to treatment.
Malignancy involving metastasis to the lip and cheek is a rare clinical event. To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of squamous cell lung carcinoma presenting with lip and cheek metastasis.
Squamous cell lung carcinoma grows rapidly. However, when it presents with lip and cheek metastasis, it can easily be misdiagnosed as squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck. The physician must be able to recognise this disease, to have an adequate degree of suspicion to consider this option in the differential diagnosis with other tumours or inflammatory diseases through biopsy of multiple lesions and immunohistochemistry, and to provide suitable treatment strategies.

A 60-year-old male active smoker visited Hunan Cancer Hospital (Changsha, China) on Jan 3, 2018, with a swollen upper lip and lower cheek for the past 3 months. According to the patient, his swelling had increased in size during the previous few weeks. No other specific symptoms were reported and his blood tests were normal. On examination, he had a tender palpable mass measuring approximately 3·5 × 4·7cm on the upper lip and 5·6 × 3·2 cm on the lower cheek (figure, A). The skin surface covering the masses appeared normal. He had neither a history of an injury nor tumour.The differential diagnosis based on the preliminary findings included primary tumour of the head and neck, metastasis from the thyroid or lung, lymphoma, or inflammation. An ultrasound-guided biopsy was done on the cheek and lip. The histopathological diagnosis was poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma (cytokeratin [CK]5/6+++, CK7–, p63+++, thyroid transcription factor [TTF]-1+/–, Epstein-Barr virus [EBV]–). To further evaluate the primary tumour, a PET-CT scan was done; this scan showed a nodule in the upper lobe of his left lung measuring 3·7 × 4·7 cm and pleural invasion. A CT-guided biopsy of the left lung nodule was done and showed well-differentiated squamous carcinoma (CK5/6+++, CK7-, p63+++, TTF-1+/–, EBV–; figure, B). The patient was diagnosed with squamous cell lung carcinoma and transferred to a lung cancer unit in the hospital to receive chemotherapy (gemcitabine 1250 mg/m2 on days 1 and 8 plus cisplatin 75 mg/m2 on day 1, every 21 days). The patient was evaluated with CT scans of the head, neck, and chest after every two cycles of chemotherapy (ie, every 2 months) and subsequently achieved a partial response to treatment.
Malignancy involving metastasis to the lip and cheek is a rare clinical event. To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of squamous cell lung carcinoma presenting with lip and cheek metastasis.
Squamous cell lung carcinoma grows rapidly. However, when it presents with lip and cheek metastasis, it can easily be misdiagnosed as squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck. The physician must be able to recognise this disease, to have an adequate degree of suspicion to consider this option in the differential diagnosis with other tumours or inflammatory diseases through biopsy of multiple lesions and immunohistochemistry, and to provide suitable treatment strategies.

input: A 27-year-old woman presented to our department for evaluation and treatment of dysphagia with recently diagnosed oesophageal stenosis. The patient had progressive difficulty in swallowing during the previous 2 years, first with solids then with liquids. The medical history showed that the patient was admitted to our clinic 5 months earlier for fatigue and she was diagnosed with severe iron deficiency anaemia. 2 months before presenting to our department, the patient underwent an oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD), which revealed a 3-mm marked narrowing due to an eccentric oesophageal web 14 cm from the incisors preventing passage of either an adult or a paediatric endoscope (figure A). Biopsies taken from the oesophageal web showed that the mucosa had no substantial alterations. Physical examination showed that the patient was emaciated (BMI 16·9 kg/m2) and had bilateral angular cheilitis and koilonychia (ie, spoon-shaped nails). We completed the evaluation with a barium swallow (figure B) and a CT of the neck to assess the extent of the stenosis and to exclude extraluminal process. The examinations showed a focal stenosis in the upper oesophagus at the C6 level, without signs of malignancy. The EGD and the barium swallow findings with the history of severe iron deficiency anaemia led to a final diagnosis of an oesophageal web associated with Plummer-Vinson syndrome. The oesophageal web was managed by oesophageal dilation, which was done gradually multiple times over 6 weeks with a through-the-scope balloon to 18 mm in diameter (figure C). The patient reported complete resolution of dysphagia symptoms and is planned for regular surveillance of malignant transformation of the hypopharynx or the upper oesophagus with upper endoscopy.Plummer-Vinson syndrome, also known as Paterson-Brown Kelly syndrome, is a rare condition characterised by the triad of dysphagia, iron deficiency anaemia, and proximal oesophageal webs. The majority of reported cases (90%) are middle-aged female individuals. Although the exact pathogenesis of this condition is not fully understood, iron deficiency anaemia represents the most accepted hypothesis. Iron deficiency is postulated to especially affect the epithelial cells of the gastrointestinal tract due to their rapid turnover. Low iron concentrations lead to reduction in the activity of iron-dependent oxidative enzymes, which is speculated to cause mucosal atrophy and degeneration, eventually leading to the development of oesophageal webs after repeated injury. Although mucosal changes probably occur throughout the oesophagus, the postcricoid region incurs the most damage during the swallowing of solid food due to its restrictive skeletal surroundings, and is thus more susceptible to web formation. Barium swallow and EGD have high sensitivity to detect oesophageal webs. Many patients with mild dysphagia might have improved swallowing function through iron therapy alone, which restores impaired oesophageal contraction and the integrity of the oesophageal mucosa. However, long-standing dysphagia is unlikely to respond to iron therapy, necessitating the use of endoscopic oesophageal dilation. The recognition of this syndrome is crucial as it signifies a precancerous condition, with an estimated 4–16% increased risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma of the postcricoid pharynx and the upper oesophageal region. Annual EGD is recommended for the early detection of prematurely malignant transformation.

input: A 27-year-old woman presented to our department for evaluation and treatment of dysphagia with recently diagnosed oesophageal stenosis. The patient had progressive difficulty in swallowing during the previous 2 years, first with solids then with liquids. The medical history showed that the patient was admitted to our clinic 5 months earlier for fatigue and she was diagnosed with severe iron deficiency anaemia. 2 months before presenting to our department, the patient underwent an oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD), which revealed a 3-mm marked narrowing due to an eccentric oesophageal web 14 cm from the incisors preventing passage of either an adult or a paediatric endoscope (figure A). Biopsies taken from the oesophageal web showed that the mucosa had no substantial alterations. Physical examination showed that the patient was emaciated (BMI 16·9 kg/m2) and had bilateral angular cheilitis and koilonychia (ie, spoon-shaped nails). We completed the evaluation with a barium swallow (figure B) and a CT of the neck to assess the extent of the stenosis and to exclude extraluminal process. The examinations showed a focal stenosis in the upper oesophagus at the C6 level, without signs of malignancy. The EGD and the barium swallow findings with the history of severe iron deficiency anaemia led to a final diagnosis of an oesophageal web associated with Plummer-Vinson syndrome. The oesophageal web was managed by oesophageal dilation, which was done gradually multiple times over 6 weeks with a through-the-scope balloon to 18 mm in diameter (figure C). The patient reported complete resolution of dysphagia symptoms and is planned for regular surveillance of malignant transformation of the hypopharynx or the upper oesophagus with upper endoscopy.Plummer-Vinson syndrome, also known as Paterson-Brown Kelly syndrome, is a rare condition characterised by the triad of dysphagia, iron deficiency anaemia, and proximal oesophageal webs. The majority of reported cases (90%) are middle-aged female individuals. Although the exact pathogenesis of this condition is not fully understood, iron deficiency anaemia represents the most accepted hypothesis. Iron deficiency is postulated to especially affect the epithelial cells of the gastrointestinal tract due to their rapid turnover. Low iron concentrations lead to reduction in the activity of iron-dependent oxidative enzymes, which is speculated to cause mucosal atrophy and degeneration, eventually leading to the development of oesophageal webs after repeated injury. Although mucosal changes probably occur throughout the oesophagus, the postcricoid region incurs the most damage during the swallowing of solid food due to its restrictive skeletal surroundings, and is thus more susceptible to web formation. Barium swallow and EGD have high sensitivity to detect oesophageal webs. Many patients with mild dysphagia might have improved swallowing function through iron therapy alone, which restores impaired oesophageal contraction and the integrity of the oesophageal mucosa. However, long-standing dysphagia is unlikely to respond to iron therapy, necessitating the use of endoscopic oesophageal dilation. The recognition of this syndrome is crucial as it signifies a precancerous condition, with an estimated 4–16% increased risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma of the postcricoid pharynx and the upper oesophageal region. Annual EGD is recommended for the early detection of prematurely malignant transformation.

input: A 27-year-old woman presented to our department for evaluation and treatment of dysphagia with recently diagnosed oesophageal stenosis. The patient had progressive difficulty in swallowing during the previous 2 years, first with solids then with liquids. The medical history showed that the patient was admitted to our clinic 5 months earlier for fatigue and she was diagnosed with severe iron deficiency anaemia. 2 months before presenting to our department, the patient underwent an oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD), which revealed a 3-mm marked narrowing due to an eccentric oesophageal web 14 cm from the incisors preventing passage of either an adult or a paediatric endoscope (figure A). Biopsies taken from the oesophageal web showed that the mucosa had no substantial alterations. Physical examination showed that the patient was emaciated (BMI 16·9 kg/m2) and had bilateral angular cheilitis and koilonychia (ie, spoon-shaped nails). We completed the evaluation with a barium swallow (figure B) and a CT of the neck to assess the extent of the stenosis and to exclude extraluminal process. The examinations showed a focal stenosis in the upper oesophagus at the C6 level, without signs of malignancy. The EGD and the barium swallow findings with the history of severe iron deficiency anaemia led to a final diagnosis of an oesophageal web associated with Plummer-Vinson syndrome. The oesophageal web was managed by oesophageal dilation, which was done gradually multiple times over 6 weeks with a through-the-scope balloon to 18 mm in diameter (figure C). The patient reported complete resolution of dysphagia symptoms and is planned for regular surveillance of malignant transformation of the hypopharynx or the upper oesophagus with upper endoscopy.Plummer-Vinson syndrome, also known as Paterson-Brown Kelly syndrome, is a rare condition characterised by the triad of dysphagia, iron deficiency anaemia, and proximal oesophageal webs. The majority of reported cases (90%) are middle-aged female individuals. Although the exact pathogenesis of this condition is not fully understood, iron deficiency anaemia represents the most accepted hypothesis. Iron deficiency is postulated to especially affect the epithelial cells of the gastrointestinal tract due to their rapid turnover. Low iron concentrations lead to reduction in the activity of iron-dependent oxidative enzymes, which is speculated to cause mucosal atrophy and degeneration, eventually leading to the development of oesophageal webs after repeated injury. Although mucosal changes probably occur throughout the oesophagus, the postcricoid region incurs the most damage during the swallowing of solid food due to its restrictive skeletal surroundings, and is thus more susceptible to web formation. Barium swallow and EGD have high sensitivity to detect oesophageal webs. Many patients with mild dysphagia might have improved swallowing function through iron therapy alone, which restores impaired oesophageal contraction and the integrity of the oesophageal mucosa. However, long-standing dysphagia is unlikely to respond to iron therapy, necessitating the use of endoscopic oesophageal dilation. The recognition of this syndrome is crucial as it signifies a precancerous condition, with an estimated 4–16% increased risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma of the postcricoid pharynx and the upper oesophageal region. Annual EGD is recommended for the early detection of prematurely malignant transformation.

input: A 40-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 4-year history of recurrent central chest pain. The pain was unrelated to food or exertion, and occurred intermittently during both day and night. The patient had no medical history of diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia or hypothyroidism. She did, however, give a history of having a prolonged fever for about 3 months accompanied by arthralgia at the age of 13 years. She said that at the time she had extensive investigations for infections and possible malignancies—but the fever resolved gradually without any cause being identified. She said that she had had no further problems until the current complaint began 4 years ago. On clinical examination, her blood pressure was 130/90 mm Hg in both upper limbs, pulses were easily palpable, and there were no bruits or murmurs heard on auscultation. A chest x-ray showed calcification of the wall of the aortic arch and descending thoracic aorta, with narrowing at the level of the diaphragmatic hiatus (figure). Full blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, lipid profile, and parathyroid hormone levels were normal. MRI angiograms showed narrowing of the aorta in the post-subclavian area, in the descending thoracic aorta at the level of the diaphragm, and at the level just above the origin of the left renal artery (figure); T2-weighted images showed a thickened and oedematous thoracic aorta, suggesting active inflammation (figure), and a CT angiogram showed extensive calcification (figure). Taken together these findings led us to making a diagnosis of aorta arteritis type III with active disease. Takayasu arteritis or aorto-arteritis is a large vessel vasculitis of the aorta and its branches. The disease may manifest itself with only non-specific features like fever, myalgia, arthritis, and malaise during the acute phase, which can last for several months. In the chronic phase, in the absence of clinical features secondary to vessel occlusion or ischaemia, the diagnosis maybe further delayed. However, disease activity may persist in the aortic wall despite the patient being asymptomatic and all inflammatory markers remaining within normal limits. A high index of suspicion is required to make the diagnosis during the acute phase, and regular monitoring is necessary to avoid serious long-term complications. The disease takes its name from Mikito Takayasu, who described the first case in 1908 at the Annual Meeting of the Japan Ophthalmology Society.

Taken together these findings led us to making a diagnosis of aorta arteritis type III with active disease. Takayasu arteritis or aorto-arteritis is a large vessel vasculitis of the aorta and its branches. The disease may manifest itself with only non-specific features like fever, myalgia, arthritis, and malaise during the acute phase, which can last for several months. A 64-year-old man with a 2-month history of breathlessness, reduced effort tolerance, and a worsening cough, attended our clinic. The patient was a non-smoker, and he had no relevant history of occupational exposures nor severe viral infections; he reported that none of his family had lung disease. No consanguinity was noted.On examination, we found the patient to be hypoxic and he needed supplementary oxygen; his respiratory rate was 22 breaths per min. He had no finger clubbing. Mild crepitation was detected bilaterally in the mid to lower lung zones.
Plain chest x-ray showed a diffuse sandstorm-like, micro-nodular pattern throughout both lung fields (figure). High resolution chest CT showed a crazy-paving pattern characterised by thickened interlobular septa (figure). Punctiform calcifications were also seen along the interlobular septa and pleural line in a circumferential pattern—including the mediastinal pleura (figure). An echocardiography showed no evidence of pulmonary hypertension.
Pulmonary function tests showed a restrictive ventilatory defect with forced vital capacity of 2·18 L (66% predicted) and transfer factor—also known as the diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon dioxide—of 24% predicted.
Considering the patient in the round, we made a provisional diagnosis of pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis (PAM). However, as genetic testing was not available to us and bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for microliths, we decided, with the patient's consent, to do transbronchial cryobiopsy to confirm our clinical diagnosis. Therefore, under total intravenous anaesthesia with endotracheal intubation, transbronchial cryobiopsy was done, with no complications, using a 1·7 mm flexible cryoprobe and a prophylactic balloon blocker, guided by fluoroscopy, with a single 5-sec activation in the lateral segment of the right lower lobe.
Histological examination of a sample of the cryobiopsy specimen showed alveolated lung parenchyma and thickened interstitial walls with numerous calcified bodies present within the airspaces, occasionally exhibiting concentric laminations (figure); findings that were overall consistent with PAM.
Despite counselling regarding a potential lung transplant referral, the patient, after lengthy discussion with his family, decided against further treatment. He was allowed home with long-term oxygen therapy and supportive care.
PAM is a rare hereditary lung disease characterised by autosomal recessive inheritance, resulting from a loss-of-function mutation in the SLC34A2 gene that causes an abnormal accumulation of calcium phosphate deposits in the lungs. The current PAM-diagnostic algorithm suggests lung biopsy as a reasonable option if the patient has no family history of lung disease, microliths are not seen in bronchoalveolar lavage, and genetic testing is not available. Conventional approaches for biopsy in PAM cases have involved transbronchial forceps biopsy and surgical lung biopsy. Transbronchial cryobiopsy—used in our patient—has, so far, been reported in a few cases as a possible diagnostic method for PAM; it allows acquisition of high-quality lung tissue samples that gives accurate histopathological assessment, with an acceptable level of risk, compared to surgical lung biopsy, for this rare disease.

However, as genetic testing was not available to us and bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for microliths, we decided, with the patient's consent, to do transbronchial cryobiopsy to confirm our clinical diagnosis. Therefore, under total intravenous anaesthesia with endotracheal intubation, transbronchial cryobiopsy was done, with no complications, using a 1·7 mm flexible cryoprobe and a prophylactic balloon blocker, guided by fluoroscopy, with a single 5-sec activation in the lateral segment of the right lower lobe.

A 12-day-old baby was admitted to our hospital with a fever, irritability, and poor feeding. His temperature was 39° C. On physical examination, he was irritable but consolable. His anterior fontanelle was full but not bulging. Laboratory tests included a complete blood cell count, which showed a white blood cell count of 4·8 × 109 per L, with 72% neutrophils. Analysis of the infant's cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed 3 050 white blood cells per μL, with 94% neutrophils, protein concentration was 110 mg/dL, and glucose concentration 49 mg/dL (normal 60–80).CSF showed Gram-negative coccobacilli, not typical of an enteric pathogen—eg, Escherichia coli. Treatment with two antibiotics was commenced: intravenous ampicillin 50 mg/kg every 6 h and intravenous ceftazidime 50 mg/kg every 6 h. 2 days later, the infant was afebrile and improving clinically. Blood and CSF cultures grew Pasteurella multocida (figure). Further history revealed that the family had no cats but did have two dogs—a Maltese Poodle and a Bichon Shih Tzu. The dogs loved the new addition to the family—the baby—and showed their delight and affection by licking his face. The infant was treated for 14 days with intravenous ampicillin 50 mg/kg every 6 h. At follow-up, 1 year later, he was well and developing normally. And more specifically, he had no hearing deficits.
P multocida is a small, Gram-negative coccobacillus, first recognised in 1881 by Louis Pasteur. It is present in the oral microbiota of 70–90% of cats and 50–66% of dogs and is a common pathogen associated with bites. Infection can also result from simple mucosal contact with saliva and from vertical transmission from a colonised mother. P multocida meningitis, with or without sepsis, is rare; most cases occur in infants, especially neonates, and immunocompromised patients. So far, 30 cases of P multocida meningitis have been reported in neonates. Most were linked to exposure to saliva without bites or vertical transmission from an asymptomatic mother colonised with P multocida. The mortality rate for neonatal P multocida meningitis, with or without sepsis, is 20%. Increased neonatal mortality is associated with disease onset occurring within 72 h of birth, a birthweight less than 2500 g, and infection due to vertical transmission. Sequelae, commonly hearing loss, occur in 20–30% of survivors. Household pets can harbour zoonotic pathogens capable of being spread by multiple mechanisms. Contact with dog or cat saliva through a bite or lick risks exposure to oral cavity commensal organisms such as Capnocytophaga canimorsus and P multocida. Allowing pets to show such affection for a newborn baby is best avoided.

His anterior fontanelle was full but not bulging. Laboratory tests included a complete blood cell count, which showed a white blood cell count of 4·8 × 109 per L, with 72% neutrophils. Analysis of the infant's cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed 3 050 white blood cells per μL, with 94% neutrophils, protein concentration was 110 mg/dL, and glucose concentration 49 mg/dL (normal 60–80).CSF showed Gram-negative coccobacilli, not typical of an enteric pathogen—eg, Escherichia coli. Treatment with two antibiotics was commenced: intravenous ampicillin 50 mg/kg every 6 h and intravenous ceftazidime 50 mg/kg every 6 h. 2 days later, the infant was afebrile and improving clinically. Blood and CSF cultures grew Pasteurella multocida (figure). Further history revealed that the family had no cats but did have two dogs—a Maltese Poodle and a Bichon Shih Tzu. The dogs loved the new addition to the family—the baby—and showed their delight and affection by licking his face. The infant was treated for 14 days with intravenous ampicillin 50 mg/kg every 6 h. At follow-up, 1 year later, he was well and developing normally. And more specifically, he had no hearing deficits.
P multocida is a small, Gram-negative coccobacillus, first recognised in 1881 by Louis Pasteur. It is present in the oral microbiota of 70–90% of cats and 50–66% of dogs and is a common pathogen associated with bites. Infection can also result from simple mucosal contact with saliva and from vertical transmission from a colonised mother. P multocida meningitis, with or without sepsis, is rare; most cases occur in infants, especially neonates, and immunocompromised patients. So far, 30 cases of P multocida meningitis have been reported in neonates. Most were linked to exposure to saliva without bites or vertical transmission from an asymptomatic mother colonised with P multocida. The mortality rate for neonatal P multocida meningitis, with or without sepsis, is 20%. Increased neonatal mortality is associated with disease onset occurring within 72 h of birth, a birthweight less than 2500 g, and infection due to vertical transmission. Sequelae, commonly hearing loss, occur in 20–30% of survivors. Household pets can harbour zoonotic pathogens capable of being spread by multiple mechanisms. Contact with dog or cat saliva through a bite or lick risks exposure to oral cavity commensal organisms such as Capnocytophaga canimorsus and P multocida. Allowing pets to show such affection for a newborn baby is best avoided.

A 54-year-old man presented to our emergency department reporting several weeks of diffuse abdominal pain. He had no medical history of note.On physical examination we found his abdomen was soft with some slight tenderness and there were diffuse petechiae on his hands and feet. The patient was afebrile and his vital signs were stable.
Laboratory investigations showed a raised serum C-reactive protein concentration of 12·2 mg/dL (normal <0·6).
An abdominal CT scan showed signs of occult ileocecal perforation and segmented small bowel wall thickening. During an explorative laparotomy, we found multiple 5–10 cm haemorrhagic small bowel skip lesions (figure) without any perforations; we did not resect any of the affected segments because they showed active peristalsis.
Further laboratory testing showed the presence of antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies against proteinase 3 of 241 IU/mL (normal <10), haematuria, proteinuria, urinary casts, and normal serum creatinine concentration. Urine output was unremarkable.
We made a diagnosis of granulomatosis with polyangiitis presenting with intestinal manifestations; treatment with prednisolone significantly relieved the patient's abdominal pain and he was allowed home.
1 month later, the patient attended again with acute abdominal pain and peritonitis. A CT scan showed free intra-abdominal air. We undertook a further explorative laparotomy and found several ileal perforations; we carried out a small bowel resection and constructed an ileostomy.
Histopathological work-up of the excised bowel showed necrotic tissue with severe peritonitis and some small vessels with microthrombi and partially enhanced infiltrating granulocytes in the vessel walls; a renal biopsy sample confirmed granulomatosis with polyangiitis. At regular follow-up visits on treatment with prednisolone and cyclophosphamide, no new manifestations of systemic vasculitis were detected.
Skip lesions of the bowel are usually seen in inflammatory bowel disease, distal thromboembolic mesenteric ischaemia, and lupus enteritis.
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a small to medium vessel necrotising vasculitis whose exact aetiology is unclear; it mostly affects the respiratory tract and kidneys and there is a potential for multiorgan involvement. First intestinal manifestations leading to surgical complications are extremely rare and depending on the extent of involvement, granulomatosis with polyangiitis may be treated with immunosuppressive agents—including glucocorticoids, cyclophosphamide, or rituximab—the caveat being that such therapies might increase the risk of intestinal perforation (video).

input:
A 54-year-old man presented to our emergency department reporting several weeks of diffuse abdominal pain. He had no medical history of note.On physical examination we found his abdomen was soft with some slight tenderness and there were diffuse petechiae on his hands and feet. The patient was afebrile and his vital signs were stable.
Laboratory investigations showed a raised serum C-reactive protein concentration of 12·2 mg/dL (normal <0·6).
An abdominal CT scan showed signs of occult ileocecal perforation and segmented small bowel wall thickening. During an explorative laparotomy, we found multiple 5–10 cm haemorrhagic small bowel skip lesions (figure) without any perforations; we did not resect any of the affected segments because they showed active peristalsis.
Further laboratory testing showed the presence of antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies against proteinase 3 of 241 IU/mL (normal <10), haematuria, proteinuria, urinary casts, and normal serum creatinine concentration. Urine output was unremarkable.
We made a diagnosis of granulomatosis with polyangiitis presenting with intestinal manifestations; treatment with prednisolone significantly relieved the patient's abdominal pain and he was allowed home.
1 month later, the patient attended again with acute abdominal pain and peritonitis. A CT scan showed free intra-abdominal air. We undertook a further explorative laparotomy and found several ileal perforations; we carried out a small bowel resection and constructed an ileostomy.
Histopathological work-up of the excised bowel showed necrotic tissue with severe peritonitis and some small vessels with microthrombi and partially enhanced infiltrating granulocytes in the vessel walls; a renal biopsy sample confirmed granulomatosis with polyangiitis. At regular follow-up visits on treatment with prednisolone and cyclophosphamide, no new manifestations of systemic vasculitis were detected.
Skip lesions of the bowel are usually seen in inflammatory bowel disease, distal thromboembolic mesenteric ischaemia, and lupus enteritis.
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a small to medium vessel necrotising vasculitis whose exact aetiology is unclear; it mostly affects the respiratory tract and kidneys and there is a potential for multiorgan involvement. First intestinal manifestations leading to surgical complications are extremely rare and depending on the extent of involvement, granulomatosis with polyangiitis may be treated with immunosuppressive agents—including glucocorticoids, cyclophosphamide, or rituximab—the caveat being that such therapies might increase the risk of intestinal perforation (video).

input: A 20-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of swollen gums. Her medical history included seizures for the past 19 years and a macular patch on the right side of her face since birth. She was taking phenytoin for her seizures. Intraoral examination showed extension of the macular patch on the right side of the oral cavity and generalised gingival enlargement. On the basis of her history and clinical presentation she was diagnosed with Sturge-Weber angiomatosis and drug-induced gingival enlargement. Extraoral skull radiographs showed tramline calcification because of angiomas affecting the leptomeninges. The patient was given meticulous oral treatment and her antiepileptic medication was changed. The angiomas present in our patient are malformations of blood vessels in the pia mater causing the calcification and loss of nerve cells in the cerebral cortex. These sequelae of the malformations give rise to the clinical symptom of seizures and radiological sign of tramline calcification.

She was taking phenytoin for her seizures. Intraoral examination showed extension of the macular patch on the right side of the oral cavity and generalised gingival enlargement. On the basis of her history and clinical presentation she was diagnosed with Sturge-Weber angiomatosis and drug-induced gingival enlargement. Extraoral skull radiographs showed tramline calcification because of angiomas affecting the leptomeninges. The patient was given meticulous oral treatment and her antiepileptic medication was changed. The angiomas present in our patient are malformations of blood vessels in the pia mater causing the calcification and loss of nerve cells in the cerebral cortex. These sequelae of the malformations give rise to the clinical symptom of seizures and radiological sign of tramline calcification.
