A 69-year-old woman was admitted to our ward with fever and respiratory failure. 3 weeks earlier she had been treated with ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection, caused by Escherichia coli; she had a history of diabetes.On examination she was oriented in time, place, and person; her blood pressure was 130/70 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats per min, respiratory rate was 15 breaths per min, temperature 37·1°C, and oxygen saturation 94%. She had harsh vesicular breath sounds that were diffusely reduced with no added noises.
Laboratory investigations showed the patient's white blood cell count was 15·2 × 109 per L (normal 3·84–10·0), neutrophils 83%, C-reactive protein concentration (CRP)was 9·97 mg/dL (normal <0·5), procalcitonin concentration was 0·5 ng/mL (normal 0–0·5), and D-dimer concentration was 3490 ng/mL (normal 0–500).
A CT angiogram showed bronchopneumonia and bilateral pulmonary nodules—raising the suspicion of metastases (figure). A full-body CT, with contrast medium, showed thrombosis of the left renal vein and homolateral thickening of calyces’ walls and renal pelvis. Urine cytology was negative for any urothelial malignancy. Our working diagnosis at this stage was septic emboli from a nephritic focus. However, despite 8 days of ceftazidime and clarithromycin, and enoxaparin, the patient's condition worsened. Given the working diagnosis, we did a transoesophageal echocardiography and broncho-alveolar lavage. The echocardiogram showed some thickening of the free margin of the aortic valve cusps with normal function; the mitral valve flaps showed some thickening with mild insufficiency. A set of blood and urine cultures were done which were negative for any infection and malignancy. At this stage, we suspected the patient had an autoimmune disease and we decided to start methylprednisolone empirically. The patient's condition improved, and she was able to go home 11 days later. At follow-up 1 month later, she reported rusty sputum, a persistent cough, and back pain; investigations showed a raised white blood cell count of 16·76 × 109 per L, neutrophils 90·5%, CRP concentration 15·2 mg/dL. An autoimmune screen showed no atypical results. An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT of the chest showed three excavated lesions with hypermetabolic perimeters; we suspected either an inflammatory or an infectious process and the patient was readmitted.
A CT scan of the chest confirmed the pulmonary lesions and indicated that they were probably septic emboli (figure); arterial blood gas analysis indicated respiratory failure. Cultures of blood, urine, broncho-alveolar lavage fluid, and a sample of a lung biopsy showed non-extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing strain E coli, mucoid phenotype, characterised by a thick polysaccharide wall impervious to antibiotics. We started the patient on voriconazole and—according to culture antibiogram—ceftazidime and ampicillin combined with sulbactam. The methylprednisolone was gradually reduced over the next 8 weeks; the two largest chest lesions were drained. After 38 days of antibiotic treatment, the patient's symptoms had improved; she was no longer in respiratory failure and cultures of blood, urine, broncho-alveolar lavage fluid, and pleural fluid were negative. A chest CT scan showed a decrease in the size of the pulmonary lesions.
Although rare, an E coli urinary tract infection can spread to the lungs, causing a pneumonia. Mucoid phenotypes have been shown to be associated with advanced disease states—specifically in Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii infections. A mucoid phenotype has never been shown to underlie the development of invasive disease after an E coli urinary tract infection, but such a possibility cannot be ruled out.

input:
A 69-year-old woman was admitted to our ward with fever and respiratory failure. 3 weeks earlier she had been treated with ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection, caused by Escherichia coli; she had a history of diabetes.On examination she was oriented in time, place, and person; her blood pressure was 130/70 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats per min, respiratory rate was 15 breaths per min, temperature 37·1°C, and oxygen saturation 94%. She had harsh vesicular breath sounds that were diffusely reduced with no added noises.
Laboratory investigations showed the patient's white blood cell count was 15·2 × 109 per L (normal 3·84–10·0), neutrophils 83%, C-reactive protein concentration (CRP)was 9·97 mg/dL (normal <0·5), procalcitonin concentration was 0·5 ng/mL (normal 0–0·5), and D-dimer concentration was 3490 ng/mL (normal 0–500).
A CT angiogram showed bronchopneumonia and bilateral pulmonary nodules—raising the suspicion of metastases (figure). A full-body CT, with contrast medium, showed thrombosis of the left renal vein and homolateral thickening of calyces’ walls and renal pelvis. Urine cytology was negative for any urothelial malignancy. Our working diagnosis at this stage was septic emboli from a nephritic focus. However, despite 8 days of ceftazidime and clarithromycin, and enoxaparin, the patient's condition worsened. Given the working diagnosis, we did a transoesophageal echocardiography and broncho-alveolar lavage. The echocardiogram showed some thickening of the free margin of the aortic valve cusps with normal function; the mitral valve flaps showed some thickening with mild insufficiency. A set of blood and urine cultures were done which were negative for any infection and malignancy. At this stage, we suspected the patient had an autoimmune disease and we decided to start methylprednisolone empirically. The patient's condition improved, and she was able to go home 11 days later. At follow-up 1 month later, she reported rusty sputum, a persistent cough, and back pain; investigations showed a raised white blood cell count of 16·76 × 109 per L, neutrophils 90·5%, CRP concentration 15·2 mg/dL. An autoimmune screen showed no atypical results. An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT of the chest showed three excavated lesions with hypermetabolic perimeters; we suspected either an inflammatory or an infectious process and the patient was readmitted.
A CT scan of the chest confirmed the pulmonary lesions and indicated that they were probably septic emboli (figure); arterial blood gas analysis indicated respiratory failure. Cultures of blood, urine, broncho-alveolar lavage fluid, and a sample of a lung biopsy showed non-extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing strain E coli, mucoid phenotype, characterised by a thick polysaccharide wall impervious to antibiotics. We started the patient on voriconazole and—according to culture antibiogram—ceftazidime and ampicillin combined with sulbactam. The methylprednisolone was gradually reduced over the next 8 weeks; the two largest chest lesions were drained. After 38 days of antibiotic treatment, the patient's symptoms had improved; she was no longer in respiratory failure and cultures of blood, urine, broncho-alveolar lavage fluid, and pleural fluid were negative. A chest CT scan showed a decrease in the size of the pulmonary lesions.
Although rare, an E coli urinary tract infection can spread to the lungs, causing a pneumonia. Mucoid phenotypes have been shown to be associated with advanced disease states—specifically in Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii infections. A mucoid phenotype has never been shown to underlie the development of invasive disease after an E coli urinary tract infection, but such a possibility cannot be ruled out.

A 69-year-old woman was admitted to our ward with fever and respiratory failure. 3 weeks earlier she had been treated with ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection, caused by Escherichia coli; she had a history of diabetes.On examination she was oriented in time, place, and person; her blood pressure was 130/70 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats per min, respiratory rate was 15 breaths per min, temperature 37·1°C, and oxygen saturation 94%. She had harsh vesicular breath sounds that were diffusely reduced with no added noises.
Laboratory investigations showed the patient's white blood cell count was 15·2 × 109 per L (normal 3·84–10·0), neutrophils 83%, C-reactive protein concentration (CRP)was 9·97 mg/dL (normal <0·5), procalcitonin concentration was 0·5 ng/mL (normal 0–0·5), and D-dimer concentration was 3490 ng/mL (normal 0–500).
A CT angiogram showed bronchopneumonia and bilateral pulmonary nodules—raising the suspicion of metastases (figure). A full-body CT, with contrast medium, showed thrombosis of the left renal vein and homolateral thickening of calyces’ walls and renal pelvis. Urine cytology was negative for any urothelial malignancy. Our working diagnosis at this stage was septic emboli from a nephritic focus. However, despite 8 days of ceftazidime and clarithromycin, and enoxaparin, the patient's condition worsened. Given the working diagnosis, we did a transoesophageal echocardiography and broncho-alveolar lavage. The echocardiogram showed some thickening of the free margin of the aortic valve cusps with normal function; the mitral valve flaps showed some thickening with mild insufficiency. A set of blood and urine cultures were done which were negative for any infection and malignancy. At this stage, we suspected the patient had an autoimmune disease and we decided to start methylprednisolone empirically. The patient's condition improved, and she was able to go home 11 days later. At follow-up 1 month later, she reported rusty sputum, a persistent cough, and back pain; investigations showed a raised white blood cell count of 16·76 × 109 per L, neutrophils 90·5%, CRP concentration 15·2 mg/dL. An autoimmune screen showed no atypical results. An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT of the chest showed three excavated lesions with hypermetabolic perimeters; we suspected either an inflammatory or an infectious process and the patient was readmitted.
A CT scan of the chest confirmed the pulmonary lesions and indicated that they were probably septic emboli (figure); arterial blood gas analysis indicated respiratory failure. Cultures of blood, urine, broncho-alveolar lavage fluid, and a sample of a lung biopsy showed non-extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing strain E coli, mucoid phenotype, characterised by a thick polysaccharide wall impervious to antibiotics. We started the patient on voriconazole and—according to culture antibiogram—ceftazidime and ampicillin combined with sulbactam. The methylprednisolone was gradually reduced over the next 8 weeks; the two largest chest lesions were drained. After 38 days of antibiotic treatment, the patient's symptoms had improved; she was no longer in respiratory failure and cultures of blood, urine, broncho-alveolar lavage fluid, and pleural fluid were negative. A chest CT scan showed a decrease in the size of the pulmonary lesions.
Although rare, an E coli urinary tract infection can spread to the lungs, causing a pneumonia. Mucoid phenotypes have been shown to be associated with advanced disease states—specifically in Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii infections. A mucoid phenotype has never been shown to underlie the development of invasive disease after an E coli urinary tract infection, but such a possibility cannot be ruled out.

A 43-year-old man attended our hospital with a 2-day history of gradually worsening left-sided abdominal pain 6 months after he had a deceased-donor renal transplant—both native kidneys were left in place—because of end-stage kidney disease due to diabetes mellitus. The patient had a history of coronary artery disease and had previously had coronary artery bypass surgery; he was prescribed tacrolimus (2 mg twice a day), mycophenolate mofetil (500 mg twice a day), prednisolone (5 mg daily), carvedilol (25 mg twice a day), acetylsalicylate (81 mg daily), and fluconazole (200 mg daily); he smoked 20 packets of cigarettes per year—he quit 1 year before the kidney transplant and restarted 2 months after the transplant smoking ten cigarettes a day.
On examination, the patient was generally well; his blood pressure was 145/90 mm Hg, heart rate was 96 beats per min and regular. We found left-sided abdominal tenderness with no rebound or guarding.
Laboratory investigations found a leucocytosis (12·8 × 109 per L; typical range 4·0–11·0), and elevated haemoglobin concentration (19·8 g/dL; typical range 14·0–18·0); haematocrit was 60% (typical range 41–50); serum creatinine concentration was 1.38 mg/dL (typical range 0·7–1·3).
x-rays of chest and abdomen were within normal limits. An electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia and normal left ventricular systolic function, with an ejection fraction of 55% shown on an echocardiogram. CT angiogram of the abdomen showed complete occlusion of the left renal artery—by thrombosis and calcific atherosclerosis—and a non-vascularised atrophic left native kidney; the transplant kidney, in the pelvis, attached to healthy iliac vessels, was functioning well and had a good blood flow (figure). A hypercoagulable workup—including measurement of prothrombin G20210a and Factor V Leiden mutations, anticardiolipin, and anti-β2 glycoprotein Ib antibodies—found no causes indicating a prothrombotic state; genetic screening showed no JAK2 mutations.
The patient was diagnosed with left renal artery thrombosis due to post-transplant erythrocytosis. Aspirin, apixaban, and monthly phlebotomy were initiated with the aim to reduce the haemoglobin concentration to <17 g/dL. After a repeat negative hypercoagulable workup—including measurement of protein C, protein S, and antithrombin III levels, which were negative—at 6 months, the apixaban was stopped and the angiotensin-receptor blocker, losartan, was started and increased to optimum level. Additionally, the patient continued to have therapeutic phlebotomy to keep his haemoglobin concentration below 17 g/dL. The patient had continued to smoke tobacco after the transplant. We counselled him on the need to quit smoking, which he managed to do. At follow-up 2 years later, the patient had excellent kidney function, and he had not needed any phlebotomy in the previous 4 months.
Post-transplant erythrocytosis is common after kidney transplant occurring in about 10–15% of the transplanted population. Myeloproliferative disorders can present with erythrocytosis in the post-transplant patients and need to be excluded along with other malignancies—including breast cancer and hepatocellular carcinoma. Renal artery stenosis—present in our patient's left kidney due to calcification—and sleep apnoea may cause erythrocytosis. In patients with post-transplant erythrocytosis, a smoking history should be taken; screening for acquired cystic renal disease and renal cell cancer in native kidneys should also be done.
Post-transplant erythrocytosis can occur at any time between 8 months and 2 years after kidney transplantation; thromboembolic events—including cerebrovascular accidents, deep venous thrombosis, and pulmonary embolism—may occur; notably, native renal arterial thrombosis is unusual after a kidney transplant. Aspirin and angiotensin receptor blockade are the key strategies to manage post-transplant erythrocytosis; phlebotomy and theophylline may also be used.

The patient had recently been given a course of Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy with no improvement in his symptoms. Additionally, he had sought help from traditional healers who superficially cut the skin over his abdomen with a sharp blade—a process known as scarification—with the aim of relieving the pain.He was a non-smoker and drank alcohol occasionally; he had no medical history and no family history of malignancy, liver disease, or viral hepatitis.
On examination, we found the patient to be cachectic but comfortable at rest; blood pressure was 99/60 mm Hg, heart rate 96 beats per min, temperature 35·0°C, respiratory rate was 18 breaths per min, peripheral oxygen saturation was 96% on room air, and he was not jaundiced. He had a mass in the right upper quadrant of his abdomen which was firm and palpable 8 cm below the subcostal margin; several scarification marks were observed (figure).
Abdominal ultrasound showed a heterogeneous mass within the right liver lobe which measured 11·8 cm; it had invaded the right portal vein (figure).

Rapid tests for HIV and anti-hepatitis C antibody were negative but positive for HBsAg.
We diagnosed hepatocellular carcinoma, commenced regular morphine sulphate for pain relief, and referred the patient to the palliative care. He was allowed home after 3 days; 3 months after admission, he died from the effects of progressive malignant disease.
In sub-Saharan Africa, hepatocellular carcinoma is the cancer reported to have the second highest mortality among men and the fourth highest among women, according to the Global Cancer Observatory. Late diagnosis is common due to referral delay and initial care seeking from traditional healers. In southern Africa, hepatitis B virus infection is estimated to be the attributable cause of 29% of liver cancers with a median age of onset of 46 years.
In 2016, a strategic plan to reduce mortality from chronic hepatitis B virus by 2030 was approved at the World Health Assembly. However, modelling data show that without implementation of additional public health measures—including community-based screening and treatment programmes, birth dose vaccination rather than vaccination schedules starting at 6 weeks, and antenatal antiviral therapy for highly viraemic pregnant women—mortality will continue to rise beyond 2030 in sub-Saharan Africa.
The effective public health tools to tackle mortality from hepatitis B virus associated hepatocellular carcinoma in sub-Saharan Africa—delineated above—are available now. A 43-year-old man attended our hospital with a 2-day history of gradually worsening left-sided abdominal pain 6 months after he had a deceased-donor renal transplant—both native kidneys were left in place—because of end-stage kidney disease due to diabetes mellitus. The patient had a history of coronary artery disease and had previously had coronary artery bypass surgery; he was prescribed tacrolimus (2 mg twice a day), mycophenolate mofetil (500 mg twice a day), prednisolone (5 mg daily), carvedilol (25 mg twice a day), acetylsalicylate (81 mg daily), and fluconazole (200 mg daily); he smoked 20 packets of cigarettes per year—he quit 1 year before the kidney transplant and restarted 2 months after the transplant smoking ten cigarettes a day.
On examination, the patient was generally well; his blood pressure was 145/90 mm Hg, heart rate was 96 beats per min and regular. We found left-sided abdominal tenderness with no rebound or guarding.
Laboratory investigations found a leucocytosis (12·8 × 109 per L; typical range 4·0–11·0), and elevated haemoglobin concentration (19·8 g/dL; typical range 14·0–18·0); haematocrit was 60% (typical range 41–50); serum creatinine concentration was 1.38 mg/dL (typical range 0·7–1·3).
x-rays of chest and abdomen were within normal limits. An electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia and normal left ventricular systolic function, with an ejection fraction of 55% shown on an echocardiogram. CT angiogram of the abdomen showed complete occlusion of the left renal artery—by thrombosis and calcific atherosclerosis—and a non-vascularised atrophic left native kidney; the transplant kidney, in the pelvis, attached to healthy iliac vessels, was functioning well and had a good blood flow (figure). A hypercoagulable workup—including measurement of prothrombin G20210a and Factor V Leiden mutations, anticardiolipin, and anti-β2 glycoprotein Ib antibodies—found no causes indicating a prothrombotic state; genetic screening showed no JAK2 mutations.
The patient was diagnosed with left renal artery thrombosis due to post-transplant erythrocytosis. Aspirin, apixaban, and monthly phlebotomy were initiated with the aim to reduce the haemoglobin concentration to <17 g/dL. After a repeat negative hypercoagulable workup—including measurement of protein C, protein S, and antithrombin III levels, which were negative—at 6 months, the apixaban was stopped and the angiotensin-receptor blocker, losartan, was started and increased to optimum level. Additionally, the patient continued to have therapeutic phlebotomy to keep his haemoglobin concentration below 17 g/dL. The patient had continued to smoke tobacco after the transplant. We counselled him on the need to quit smoking, which he managed to do. At follow-up 2 years later, the patient had excellent kidney function, and he had not needed any phlebotomy in the previous 4 months.
Post-transplant erythrocytosis is common after kidney transplant occurring in about 10–15% of the transplanted population. Myeloproliferative disorders can present with erythrocytosis in the post-transplant patients and need to be excluded along with other malignancies—including breast cancer and hepatocellular carcinoma. Renal artery stenosis—present in our patient's left kidney due to calcification—and sleep apnoea may cause erythrocytosis. In patients with post-transplant erythrocytosis, a smoking history should be taken; screening for acquired cystic renal disease and renal cell cancer in native kidneys should also be done.
Post-transplant erythrocytosis can occur at any time between 8 months and 2 years after kidney transplantation; thromboembolic events—including cerebrovascular accidents, deep venous thrombosis, and pulmonary embolism—may occur; notably, native renal arterial thrombosis is unusual after a kidney transplant. Aspirin and angiotensin receptor blockade are the key strategies to manage post-transplant erythrocytosis; phlebotomy and theophylline may also be used.

A 34-year-old man presented to our department with a 4-month history of constant, progressive epigastric abdominal pain. He also reported that he had lost a substantial amount of weight and that his clothes no longer fitted him. The patient had recently been given a course of Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy with no improvement in his symptoms. Additionally, he had sought help from traditional healers who superficially cut the skin over his abdomen with a sharp blade—a process known as scarification—with the aim of relieving the pain.He was a non-smoker and drank alcohol occasionally; he had no medical history and no family history of malignancy, liver disease, or viral hepatitis.
On examination, we found the patient to be cachectic but comfortable at rest; blood pressure was 99/60 mm Hg, heart rate 96 beats per min, temperature 35·0°C, respiratory rate was 18 breaths per min, peripheral oxygen saturation was 96% on room air, and he was not jaundiced. He had a mass in the right upper quadrant of his abdomen which was firm and palpable 8 cm below the subcostal margin; several scarification marks were observed (figure).
Abdominal ultrasound showed a heterogeneous mass within the right liver lobe which measured 11·8 cm; it had invaded the right portal vein (figure).
Laboratory investigations showed haemoglobin concentration of 9·1 g/dL with mean corpuscular volume of 72·1 fL, white cell count of 2·61  × 109 per L (normal 3·5–9·5), platelet count of 742  × 109 per L (normal 125–350), bilirubin concentration was 4·5 μmol/L, alanine aminotransferase was 41 units per L, gamma-glutamyl transferase was 168·8 units per L, albumin concentration was 18·6 g/L, and creatinine concentration was 52·1 μmol/L. Rapid tests for HIV and anti-hepatitis C antibody were negative but positive for HBsAg.
We diagnosed hepatocellular carcinoma, commenced regular morphine sulphate for pain relief, and referred the patient to the palliative care. He was allowed home after 3 days; 3 months after admission, he died from the effects of progressive malignant disease.
In sub-Saharan Africa, hepatocellular carcinoma is the cancer reported to have the second highest mortality among men and the fourth highest among women, according to the Global Cancer Observatory. Late diagnosis is common due to referral delay and initial care seeking from traditional healers. In southern Africa, hepatitis B virus infection is estimated to be the attributable cause of 29% of liver cancers with a median age of onset of 46 years.
In 2016, a strategic plan to reduce mortality from chronic hepatitis B virus by 2030 was approved at the World Health Assembly. However, modelling data show that without implementation of additional public health measures—including community-based screening and treatment programmes, birth dose vaccination rather than vaccination schedules starting at 6 weeks, and antenatal antiviral therapy for highly viraemic pregnant women—mortality will continue to rise beyond 2030 in sub-Saharan Africa.
The effective public health tools to tackle mortality from hepatitis B virus associated hepatocellular carcinoma in sub-Saharan Africa—delineated above—are available now. That patients—as illustrated by our case—continue to present late with hepatocellular carcinoma, when the prognosis is poor, demands awareness and action from both clinicians and policy makers alike (video).

A 61-year-old man was admitted to our hospital with a 5-day history of sudden-onset, persistent myocloni in his left leg and the left side of his abdomen. Previously, the patient had been fit and well. He reported no recent fever, headache, or trauma.
14 months before admission, the patient had an allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for acute myeloid leukaemia with mutated nucleophosmin 1 which resulted in full remission.
On examination, we found the patient generally well; he had painless, rhythmic myocloni, with a frequency of 0·5–1·0 per s, of the proximal left leg and abdomen. The movements were continuous and would not be triggered or suppressed by any specific movements. The patient had no other atypical findings and cognitively was fully alert and conscious.
Laboratory investigations—apart from a previously described macrocytosis—were within typical range.
On day 1 after admission, an MRI of the patient's brain showed multiple cortico-subcortical fluid-attenuated-inversion-recovery hyperintense lesions without diffusion restrictions or contrast-enhancement (figure).On day 2 after admission, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analyses showed normal cell and protein count; microbial multiplex PCR testing and cytology tests for malignancies were negative.
On day 3, a scalp electroencephalogram (EEG) showed no epileptiform discharges that correlated with the myocloni. Further investigations found no neoplasms.
On day 5, the myocloni extended to the proximal part of the left arm despite the patient being given multiple antiseizure medications.
On day 8 after admission, a biopsy of the brain was done and histopathological analysis of a sample of the biopsy showed T-cell-dominated perivascular lymphocyte infiltrates and endothelial proliferations without evidence of viral infection, demyelination, graft-versus-host disease, or neoplasia.
From day 9 after admission, the patient's condition deteriorated; he became disorientated and confused, then drowsy and stuporous; the myocloni continued.
Repeated MRIs, from days 5 to 12 after admission, showed progression of the multiple cortico-subcortical lesions (figure); the EEG showed right-hemispheric temporo-parietal focal slowing independent of the worsening of the patient's condition.
On day 15 after admission, he developed electroclinical super-refractory status epilepticus, which was finally terminated by continuous intravenous thiopental. At this stage autoimmune encephalitis was suspected and immunosuppressive treatment with prednisolone, plasmapheresis, intravenous immunoglobulins, and rituximab started; serum and CSF—collected prior to initiation of the treatments—was subsequently found to be positive for GABAA receptor antibodies (serum titre 1:320; normal <1:20; CSF titre 1:1), confirming the diagnosis of anti-GABAA receptor encephalitis.
On day 33 and day 185, MRIs showed improvement (figure) with concomitant decreases in serum antibody titres (day 79, 1:20; day 186, <1:20) and serum neurofilament light chain concentrations—day 34, 511·5 pg/mL (99·995 percentile); day 233, 25·4 pg/mL (97·20 percentile).
During the period of hospitalisation, the patient experienced multiple complications, including asystole, which required resuscitation, and critical-illness poly-neuromyopathy. After a prolonged stay in the intensive care unit, the patient was transferred to a neurorehabilitation unit.
At outpatient follow-up, the patient was ambulatory and had mild, residual paresis of his left leg (video); his neurological deficits continued to improve.
Autoantibodies against GABAA receptor cause an encephalitis characterised by seizures, cognitive impairment, psychiatric symptoms, and movement disorders. Underlying pathogenic mechanisms are, in most cases, unclear; associations between haematological malignancies and allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplants—as in our case—causing immune dysregulation may indicate possible aetiologies. Studies have reported a range of 9 to 43 months from completion of allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplant to the development of GABAA receptor encephalitis.
Typical MRI changes, in conjunction with the patient's history and symptoms, should prompt consideration of anti-GABAA receptor encephalitis; confirmatory autoantibody results—often available only after a significant length of time—should not delay treatment initiation.

input:
A 61-year-old man was admitted to our hospital with a 5-day history of sudden-onset, persistent myocloni in his left leg and the left side of his abdomen. Previously, the patient had been fit and well. He reported no recent fever, headache, or trauma.
14 months before admission, the patient had an allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for acute myeloid leukaemia with mutated nucleophosmin 1 which resulted in full remission.
On examination, we found the patient generally well; he had painless, rhythmic myocloni, with a frequency of 0·5–1·0 per s, of the proximal left leg and abdomen. The movements were continuous and would not be triggered or suppressed by any specific movements. The patient had no other atypical findings and cognitively was fully alert and conscious.
Laboratory investigations—apart from a previously described macrocytosis—were within typical range.
On day 1 after admission, an MRI of the patient's brain showed multiple cortico-subcortical fluid-attenuated-inversion-recovery hyperintense lesions without diffusion restrictions or contrast-enhancement (figure).On day 2 after admission, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analyses showed normal cell and protein count; microbial multiplex PCR testing and cytology tests for malignancies were negative.
On day 3, a scalp electroencephalogram (EEG) showed no epileptiform discharges that correlated with the myocloni. Further investigations found no neoplasms.
On day 5, the myocloni extended to the proximal part of the left arm despite the patient being given multiple antiseizure medications.
On day 8 after admission, a biopsy of the brain was done and histopathological analysis of a sample of the biopsy showed T-cell-dominated perivascular lymphocyte infiltrates and endothelial proliferations without evidence of viral infection, demyelination, graft-versus-host disease, or neoplasia.
From day 9 after admission, the patient's condition deteriorated; he became disorientated and confused, then drowsy and stuporous; the myocloni continued.
Repeated MRIs, from days 5 to 12 after admission, showed progression of the multiple cortico-subcortical lesions (figure); the EEG showed right-hemispheric temporo-parietal focal slowing independent of the worsening of the patient's condition.
On day 15 after admission, he developed electroclinical super-refractory status epilepticus, which was finally terminated by continuous intravenous thiopental. At this stage autoimmune encephalitis was suspected and immunosuppressive treatment with prednisolone, plasmapheresis, intravenous immunoglobulins, and rituximab started; serum and CSF—collected prior to initiation of the treatments—was subsequently found to be positive for GABAA receptor antibodies (serum titre 1:320; normal <1:20; CSF titre 1:1), confirming the diagnosis of anti-GABAA receptor encephalitis.
On day 33 and day 185, MRIs showed improvement (figure) with concomitant decreases in serum antibody titres (day 79, 1:20; day 186, <1:20) and serum neurofilament light chain concentrations—day 34, 511·5 pg/mL (99·995 percentile); day 233, 25·4 pg/mL (97·20 percentile).
During the period of hospitalisation, the patient experienced multiple complications, including asystole, which required resuscitation, and critical-illness poly-neuromyopathy. After a prolonged stay in the intensive care unit, the patient was transferred to a neurorehabilitation unit.
At outpatient follow-up, the patient was ambulatory and had mild, residual paresis of his left leg (video); his neurological deficits continued to improve.
Autoantibodies against GABAA receptor cause an encephalitis characterised by seizures, cognitive impairment, psychiatric symptoms, and movement disorders. Underlying pathogenic mechanisms are, in most cases, unclear; associations between haematological malignancies and allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplants—as in our case—causing immune dysregulation may indicate possible aetiologies. Studies have reported a range of 9 to 43 months from completion of allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplant to the development of GABAA receptor encephalitis.
Typical MRI changes, in conjunction with the patient's history and symptoms, should prompt consideration of anti-GABAA receptor encephalitis; confirmatory autoantibody results—often available only after a significant length of time—should not delay treatment initiation.

A 61-year-old man was admitted to our hospital with a 5-day history of sudden-onset, persistent myocloni in his left leg and the left side of his abdomen. Previously, the patient had been fit and well. He reported no recent fever, headache, or trauma.
14 months before admission, the patient had an allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for acute myeloid leukaemia with mutated nucleophosmin 1 which resulted in full remission.
On examination, we found the patient generally well; he had painless, rhythmic myocloni, with a frequency of 0·5–1·0 per s, of the proximal left leg and abdomen. The movements were continuous and would not be triggered or suppressed by any specific movements. The patient had no other atypical findings and cognitively was fully alert and conscious.
Laboratory investigations—apart from a previously described macrocytosis—were within typical range.
On day 1 after admission, an MRI of the patient's brain showed multiple cortico-subcortical fluid-attenuated-inversion-recovery hyperintense lesions without diffusion restrictions or contrast-enhancement (figure).On day 2 after admission, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analyses showed normal cell and protein count; microbial multiplex PCR testing and cytology tests for malignancies were negative.
On day 3, a scalp electroencephalogram (EEG) showed no epileptiform discharges that correlated with the myocloni. Further investigations found no neoplasms.
On day 5, the myocloni extended to the proximal part of the left arm despite the patient being given multiple antiseizure medications.
On day 8 after admission, a biopsy of the brain was done and histopathological analysis of a sample of the biopsy showed T-cell-dominated perivascular lymphocyte infiltrates and endothelial proliferations without evidence of viral infection, demyelination, graft-versus-host disease, or neoplasia.
From day 9 after admission, the patient's condition deteriorated; he became disorientated and confused, then drowsy and stuporous; the myocloni continued.
Repeated MRIs, from days 5 to 12 after admission, showed progression of the multiple cortico-subcortical lesions (figure); the EEG showed right-hemispheric temporo-parietal focal slowing independent of the worsening of the patient's condition.
On day 15 after admission, he developed electroclinical super-refractory status epilepticus, which was finally terminated by continuous intravenous thiopental. At this stage autoimmune encephalitis was suspected and immunosuppressive treatment with prednisolone, plasmapheresis, intravenous immunoglobulins, and rituximab started; serum and CSF—collected prior to initiation of the treatments—was subsequently found to be positive for GABAA receptor antibodies (serum titre 1:320; normal <1:20; CSF titre 1:1), confirming the diagnosis of anti-GABAA receptor encephalitis.
On day 33 and day 185, MRIs showed improvement (figure) with concomitant decreases in serum antibody titres (day 79, 1:20; day 186, <1:20) and serum neurofilament light chain concentrations—day 34, 511·5 pg/mL (99·995 percentile); day 233, 25·4 pg/mL (97·20 percentile).
During the period of hospitalisation, the patient experienced multiple complications, including asystole, which required resuscitation, and critical-illness poly-neuromyopathy. After a prolonged stay in the intensive care unit, the patient was transferred to a neurorehabilitation unit.
At outpatient follow-up, the patient was ambulatory and had mild, residual paresis of his left leg (video); his neurological deficits continued to improve.
Autoantibodies against GABAA receptor cause an encephalitis characterised by seizures, cognitive impairment, psychiatric symptoms, and movement disorders. Underlying pathogenic mechanisms are, in most cases, unclear; associations between haematological malignancies and allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplants—as in our case—causing immune dysregulation may indicate possible aetiologies. Studies have reported a range of 9 to 43 months from completion of allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplant to the development of GABAA receptor encephalitis.
Typical MRI changes, in conjunction with the patient's history and symptoms, should prompt consideration of anti-GABAA receptor encephalitis; confirmatory autoantibody results—often available only after a significant length of time—should not delay treatment initiation.

A 41-year-old man presented to our rheumatology clinic with a 2-month history of symmetric inflammatory polyarthralgia and pleuritic chest pain. 1 year before, he had visited another hospital reporting a dry cough; 2 months later he returned to the same institution complaining of breathlessness and fatigue; at that time, pulmonary tuberculosis and heart failure had been ruled out.Notably, in his occupational history, 11 years before his current health difficulties, he had finished 6 years of employment in a factory producing glass and fibreglass, in Medellin, Colombia. The patient's main tasks had been in the blending process: mixing sand and soda ash, cutting, polishing, and repairing flat glass and fibreglass. He worked 9-h days in a poorly ventilated workspace and used personal protection equipment for less than 30 min per h. The patient had smoked one to two cigarettes daily for the past 26 years and stopped 4 months before his current presentation.
On examination he was well looking and not distressed; he had bilateral effusions in his wrist, metacarpophalangeal, and knee joints. Crackles were audible at the apex of his right lung.
Laboratory investigations showed positive antinuclear antibodies—at a titre of 1:320, homogeneous pattern—and raised anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies (ACPAs; 37 UI/ml; reference value <5). Rheumatoid factor was negative.
A digital chest x-ray showed scattered and tiny lung nodules, cavitation in the right upper lobe, and consolidation at the left upper lobe (figure). A CT scan showed cavitation and numerous nodules between 1 mm and 5 mm in size, with some confluent areas, randomly distributed throughout the lungs (figure).
Ziehl-Neelsen staining, nucleic acid amplification test, and culture for Mycobacterium tuberculosis of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid were negative. Histopathological analysis of a sample obtained by thoracoscopically guided open lung biopsy showed multiple granulomas with a central necrotic area, surrounded by layers of crystal silica and mononuclear infiltrate, without neoplasm or acid-fast bacteria (appendix). Considering the patient's occupational history, signs, and symptoms, and findings on investigation, we diagnosed accelerated silicosis complicated by Caplan syndrome—mimicking a miliary pattern and cavitary disease. At 6 months’ follow-up, spirometry testing showed FEV1/FVC (%) 95% (0,77), FVC 145·0% (7,14 L), and FEV1 138% (5,5 L).
At 12 months’ follow-up, the patient continued to report a dry cough and dyspnoea on exertion; original x-ray findings remained unchanged. However, treatment with rituximab, methotrexate, and prednisolone had improved the condition of the patient's painful, swollen knee and hand joints.
Caplan syndrome is a rare complication of silicosis—incidence between 0·75% and 0·89%—characterised by pulmonary nodules and rheumatoid arthritis in patients with pneumoconiosis.
The relationship between silicosis and rheumatoid arthritis development has been the subject of much debate. Disease development begins when respirable crystalline silica dust is engulfed by macrophages producing lysosomal dysfunction. Cell death results in exposure of sequestered antigens, NALP3 inflammasome activation, production of proinflammatory cytokines (eg, IL-1β and TNF-α), and activation of T and B cells (eg, T-reg with production of IL-10 and TGF-β which produces fibrosis, and T-helper CD4+ cell responses). These changes lead to the formation of autoantibodies and immune complexes—including rheumatoid factor and ACPAs—which ultimately lead to synovial cell activation, infiltration, inflammation, neoangiogenesis, and joint tissue destruction.
Tuberculosis and lung cancer—at high risk in patients with silicosis—need to be excluded before diagnosing Caplan syndrome since all three can produce cavity lung lesions and miliary pattern on imaging.

A 34-year-old man presented to our department with a 4-month history of constant, progressive epigastric abdominal pain. He also reported that he had lost a substantial amount of weight and that his clothes no longer fitted him. The patient had recently been given a course of Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy with no improvement in his symptoms. Additionally, he had sought help from traditional healers who superficially cut the skin over his abdomen with a sharp blade—a process known as scarification—with the aim of relieving the pain.He was a non-smoker and drank alcohol occasionally; he had no medical history and no family history of malignancy, liver disease, or viral hepatitis.
On examination, we found the patient to be cachectic but comfortable at rest; blood pressure was 99/60 mm Hg, heart rate 96 beats per min, temperature 35·0°C, respiratory rate was 18 breaths per min, peripheral oxygen saturation was 96% on room air, and he was not jaundiced. He had a mass in the right upper quadrant of his abdomen which was firm and palpable 8 cm below the subcostal margin; several scarification marks were observed (figure).
Abdominal ultrasound showed a heterogeneous mass within the right liver lobe which measured 11·8 cm; it had invaded the right portal vein (figure).
Laboratory investigations showed haemoglobin concentration of 9·1 g/dL with mean corpuscular volume of 72·1 fL, white cell count of 2·61  × 109 per L (normal 3·5–9·5), platelet count of 742  × 109 per L (normal 125–350), bilirubin concentration was 4·5 μmol/L, alanine aminotransferase was 41 units per L, gamma-glutamyl transferase was 168·8 units per L, albumin concentration was 18·6 g/L, and creatinine concentration was 52·1 μmol/L. Rapid tests for HIV and anti-hepatitis C antibody were negative but positive for HBsAg.
We diagnosed hepatocellular carcinoma, commenced regular morphine sulphate for pain relief, and referred the patient to the palliative care. He was allowed home after 3 days; 3 months after admission, he died from the effects of progressive malignant disease.
In sub-Saharan Africa, hepatocellular carcinoma is the cancer reported to have the second highest mortality among men and the fourth highest among women, according to the Global Cancer Observatory. Late diagnosis is common due to referral delay and initial care seeking from traditional healers. In southern Africa, hepatitis B virus infection is estimated to be the attributable cause of 29% of liver cancers with a median age of onset of 46 years.
In 2016, a strategic plan to reduce mortality from chronic hepatitis B virus by 2030 was approved at the World Health Assembly. However, modelling data show that without implementation of additional public health measures—including community-based screening and treatment programmes, birth dose vaccination rather than vaccination schedules starting at 6 weeks, and antenatal antiviral therapy for highly viraemic pregnant women—mortality will continue to rise beyond 2030 in sub-Saharan Africa.
The effective public health tools to tackle mortality from hepatitis B virus associated hepatocellular carcinoma in sub-Saharan Africa—delineated above—are available now. That patients—as illustrated by our case—continue to present late with hepatocellular carcinoma, when the prognosis is poor, demands awareness and action from both clinicians and policy makers alike (video).

A 41-year-old man presented to our rheumatology clinic with a 2-month history of symmetric inflammatory polyarthralgia and pleuritic chest pain. 1 year before, he had visited another hospital reporting a dry cough; 2 months later he returned to the same institution complaining of breathlessness and fatigue; at that time, pulmonary tuberculosis and heart failure had been ruled out.Notably, in his occupational history, 11 years before his current health difficulties, he had finished 6 years of employment in a factory producing glass and fibreglass, in Medellin, Colombia. The patient's main tasks had been in the blending process: mixing sand and soda ash, cutting, polishing, and repairing flat glass and fibreglass. He worked 9-h days in a poorly ventilated workspace and used personal protection equipment for less than 30 min per h. The patient had smoked one to two cigarettes daily for the past 26 years and stopped 4 months before his current presentation.
On examination he was well looking and not distressed; he had bilateral effusions in his wrist, metacarpophalangeal, and knee joints. Crackles were audible at the apex of his right lung.
Laboratory investigations showed positive antinuclear antibodies—at a titre of 1:320, homogeneous pattern—and raised anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies (ACPAs; 37 UI/ml; reference value <5). Rheumatoid factor was negative.
A digital chest x-ray showed scattered and tiny lung nodules, cavitation in the right upper lobe, and consolidation at the left upper lobe (figure). A CT scan showed cavitation and numerous nodules between 1 mm and 5 mm in size, with some confluent areas, randomly distributed throughout the lungs (figure).
Ziehl-Neelsen staining, nucleic acid amplification test, and culture for Mycobacterium tuberculosis of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid were negative. Histopathological analysis of a sample obtained by thoracoscopically guided open lung biopsy showed multiple granulomas with a central necrotic area, surrounded by layers of crystal silica and mononuclear infiltrate, without neoplasm or acid-fast bacteria (appendix). Considering the patient's occupational history, signs, and symptoms, and findings on investigation, we diagnosed accelerated silicosis complicated by Caplan syndrome—mimicking a miliary pattern and cavitary disease. At 6 months’ follow-up, spirometry testing showed FEV1/FVC (%) 95% (0,77), FVC 145·0% (7,14 L), and FEV1 138% (5,5 L).
At 12 months’ follow-up, the patient continued to report a dry cough and dyspnoea on exertion; original x-ray findings remained unchanged. However, treatment with rituximab, methotrexate, and prednisolone had improved the condition of the patient's painful, swollen knee and hand joints.
Caplan syndrome is a rare complication of silicosis—incidence between 0·75% and 0·89%—characterised by pulmonary nodules and rheumatoid arthritis in patients with pneumoconiosis.
The relationship between silicosis and rheumatoid arthritis development has been the subject of much debate. Disease development begins when respirable crystalline silica dust is engulfed by macrophages producing lysosomal dysfunction. Cell death results in exposure of sequestered antigens, NALP3 inflammasome activation, production of proinflammatory cytokines (eg, IL-1β and TNF-α), and activation of T and B cells (eg, T-reg with production of IL-10 and TGF-β which produces fibrosis, and T-helper CD4+ cell responses). These changes lead to the formation of autoantibodies and immune complexes—including rheumatoid factor and ACPAs—which ultimately lead to synovial cell activation, infiltration, inflammation, neoangiogenesis, and joint tissue destruction.
Tuberculosis and lung cancer—at high risk in patients with silicosis—need to be excluded before diagnosing Caplan syndrome since all three can produce cavity lung lesions and miliary pattern on imaging.

A 17-year-old transgender man attended our hospital with a 2-month history of intermittent right-sided abdominal pain, nausea, early satiety, profuse night sweats, and 14 kg weight loss.For the past 14 months, he had been undergoing hormonal gender reassignment—female to male—with weekly intramuscular injections of 32 mg of testosterone cypionate.
On examination he showed secondary male sexual characteristics: he had a deep voice and he had facial hair and acne. He was thin with a body-mass index of 18·5 kg/m2. On deep palpation he had increased mild tenderness of the right upper abdominal quadrant, compared to the left side.
MRI of the patient's abdomen showed a 17·5 cm × 7·2 cm × 8·0 cm enhancing mass in the left hemiliver with numerous small surrounding satellite lesions and tumour thrombi in the main, right, and left portal veins (figure). Core needle biopsy of the liver mass showed hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) with clear cell change (figure); androgen receptor (AR) nuclear staining was seen in 40% of the cells (figure). Liver tissue outside the tumour was normal—confirmed on staining with trichrome, reticulin, periodic acid-Schiff, and iron.
The patient's serum alpha-fetoprotein concentration was 4320 ng/mL (normal less than 8·3) with a non-reactive hepatitis serology panel—including hepatitis A virus IgM, HBsAg, HBcAg IgM, and hepatitis C virus antibody.
We treated him initially with yttrium-90 (90Y)-loaded glass microspheres (TheraSphere, Boston Scientific, Marlborough, MA, USA) at a dose of 160 Gray (Gy), delivered by intra-arterial injection to the involved segments of his liver, 1·48 gigabecquerel (GBq) to segment 4 and 1·87 GBq to segments 2 and 3.
MRI of the patient's abdomen 2 months after the treatment showed new lesions in the right hemiliver (figure) and his alpha-fetoprotein concentration had increased to 10 933 ng/mL. The patient stopped taking the exogenous testosterone after we discussed with him the possible effects it might be having upon the tumour. He was then started on intramuscular injections of leuprolide—a synthetic gonadotropin-releasing hormone—at a dose of 30 mg every 30 days to prevent the development of secondary female sexual characteristics.
He returned for a second treatment of 90Y-loaded glass microspheres to the right hemiliver at a dose of 151 Gy: 4·42 GBq to segments 5–8. He was found to have partial radiographic response in both the right and left hemiliver lesions and subsequently received additional 90Y-loaded glass microsphere treatment. The patient continues to be monitored for progression of the disease. Future treatment—if necessary—may include systemic targeted therapy or immunotherapy in a clinical trial.
HCC is mostly found in men and studies have linked the AR to development of the disease. AR expression and its role in HCC remains unclear. AR is overexpressed in the nuclei of approximately 74% of HCCs in men and 38% in women; it is associated with advanced disease and poor survival. Preclinical work suggests AR may play a role in the early development of HCC, but knocking out AR signalling in the later stages of the disease does not attenuate tumour growth. AR staining is not routinely obtained in patients with HCC and antiandrogen therapy is not indicated.
The relationship between exogenous testosterone and development and progression of HCC in peripubertal transgender patients is unknown. Further, it is unknown whether continuation of testosterone in patients positive for AR nuclear staining affects the outcome of the disease (video).

A 17-year-old transgender man attended our hospital with a 2-month history of intermittent right-sided abdominal pain, nausea, early satiety, profuse night sweats, and 14 kg weight loss.For the past 14 months, he had been undergoing hormonal gender reassignment—female to male—with weekly intramuscular injections of 32 mg of testosterone cypionate.
On examination he showed secondary male sexual characteristics: he had a deep voice and he had facial hair and acne. He was thin with a body-mass index of 18·5 kg/m2. On deep palpation he had increased mild tenderness of the right upper abdominal quadrant, compared to the left side.
MRI of the patient's abdomen showed a 17·5 cm × 7·2 cm × 8·0 cm enhancing mass in the left hemiliver with numerous small surrounding satellite lesions and tumour thrombi in the main, right, and left portal veins (figure). Core needle biopsy of the liver mass showed hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) with clear cell change (figure); androgen receptor (AR) nuclear staining was seen in 40% of the cells (figure). Liver tissue outside the tumour was normal—confirmed on staining with trichrome, reticulin, periodic acid-Schiff, and iron.
The patient's serum alpha-fetoprotein concentration was 4320 ng/mL (normal less than 8·3) with a non-reactive hepatitis serology panel—including hepatitis A virus IgM, HBsAg, HBcAg IgM, and hepatitis C virus antibody.
We treated him initially with yttrium-90 (90Y)-loaded glass microspheres (TheraSphere, Boston Scientific, Marlborough, MA, USA) at a dose of 160 Gray (Gy), delivered by intra-arterial injection to the involved segments of his liver, 1·48 gigabecquerel (GBq) to segment 4 and 1·87 GBq to segments 2 and 3.
MRI of the patient's abdomen 2 months after the treatment showed new lesions in the right hemiliver (figure) and his alpha-fetoprotein concentration had increased to 10 933 ng/mL. The patient stopped taking the exogenous testosterone after we discussed with him the possible effects it might be having upon the tumour. He was then started on intramuscular injections of leuprolide—a synthetic gonadotropin-releasing hormone—at a dose of 30 mg every 30 days to prevent the development of secondary female sexual characteristics.
He returned for a second treatment of 90Y-loaded glass microspheres to the right hemiliver at a dose of 151 Gy: 4·42 GBq to segments 5–8. He was found to have partial radiographic response in both the right and left hemiliver lesions and subsequently received additional 90Y-loaded glass microsphere treatment. The patient continues to be monitored for progression of the disease. Future treatment—if necessary—may include systemic targeted therapy or immunotherapy in a clinical trial.
HCC is mostly found in men and studies have linked the AR to development of the disease. AR expression and its role in HCC remains unclear. AR is overexpressed in the nuclei of approximately 74% of HCCs in men and 38% in women; it is associated with advanced disease and poor survival. Preclinical work suggests AR may play a role in the early development of HCC, but knocking out AR signalling in the later stages of the disease does not attenuate tumour growth. AR staining is not routinely obtained in patients with HCC and antiandrogen therapy is not indicated.
The relationship between exogenous testosterone and development and progression of HCC in peripubertal transgender patients is unknown. Further, it is unknown whether continuation of testosterone in patients positive for AR nuclear staining affects the outcome of the disease (video).

input:
A 17-year-old transgender man attended our hospital with a 2-month history of intermittent right-sided abdominal pain, nausea, early satiety, profuse night sweats, and 14 kg weight loss.For the past 14 months, he had been undergoing hormonal gender reassignment—female to male—with weekly intramuscular injections of 32 mg of testosterone cypionate.
On examination he showed secondary male sexual characteristics: he had a deep voice and he had facial hair and acne. He was thin with a body-mass index of 18·5 kg/m2. On deep palpation he had increased mild tenderness of the right upper abdominal quadrant, compared to the left side.
MRI of the patient's abdomen showed a 17·5 cm × 7·2 cm × 8·0 cm enhancing mass in the left hemiliver with numerous small surrounding satellite lesions and tumour thrombi in the main, right, and left portal veins (figure). Core needle biopsy of the liver mass showed hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) with clear cell change (figure); androgen receptor (AR) nuclear staining was seen in 40% of the cells (figure). Liver tissue outside the tumour was normal—confirmed on staining with trichrome, reticulin, periodic acid-Schiff, and iron.
The patient's serum alpha-fetoprotein concentration was 4320 ng/mL (normal less than 8·3) with a non-reactive hepatitis serology panel—including hepatitis A virus IgM, HBsAg, HBcAg IgM, and hepatitis C virus antibody.
We treated him initially with yttrium-90 (90Y)-loaded glass microspheres (TheraSphere, Boston Scientific, Marlborough, MA, USA) at a dose of 160 Gray (Gy), delivered by intra-arterial injection to the involved segments of his liver, 1·48 gigabecquerel (GBq) to segment 4 and 1·87 GBq to segments 2 and 3.
MRI of the patient's abdomen 2 months after the treatment showed new lesions in the right hemiliver (figure) and his alpha-fetoprotein concentration had increased to 10 933 ng/mL. The patient stopped taking the exogenous testosterone after we discussed with him the possible effects it might be having upon the tumour. He was then started on intramuscular injections of leuprolide—a synthetic gonadotropin-releasing hormone—at a dose of 30 mg every 30 days to prevent the development of secondary female sexual characteristics.
He returned for a second treatment of 90Y-loaded glass microspheres to the right hemiliver at a dose of 151 Gy: 4·42 GBq to segments 5–8. He was found to have partial radiographic response in both the right and left hemiliver lesions and subsequently received additional 90Y-loaded glass microsphere treatment. The patient continues to be monitored for progression of the disease. Future treatment—if necessary—may include systemic targeted therapy or immunotherapy in a clinical trial.
HCC is mostly found in men and studies have linked the AR to development of the disease. AR expression and its role in HCC remains unclear. AR is overexpressed in the nuclei of approximately 74% of HCCs in men and 38% in women; it is associated with advanced disease and poor survival. Preclinical work suggests AR may play a role in the early development of HCC, but knocking out AR signalling in the later stages of the disease does not attenuate tumour growth. AR staining is not routinely obtained in patients with HCC and antiandrogen therapy is not indicated.
The relationship between exogenous testosterone and development and progression of HCC in peripubertal transgender patients is unknown. Further, it is unknown whether continuation of testosterone in patients positive for AR nuclear staining affects the outcome of the disease (video).

input: A 71-year-old man with renal cell carcinoma with symptomatic bilateral lung metastases and multiple subpleural lesions started second-line cabozantinib (60 mg orally daily) after disease progression on pazopanib. After 3 months of therapy, in May, 2018, the patient presented at the emergency department and complained of a worsening of his dyspnoea, leading us to suppose that disease progression had occurred. However, a CT scan revealed an impressive volumetric reduction of the lung nodules but the onset of an apical grade 3 left pneumothorax (figure). The patient was admitted to hospital at the University Hospital of Verona (Verona, Italy) and was treated with thorax drainage with complete pneumothorax resolution and no further sequelae. Given this excellent response, cabozantinib treatment was continued. So far, the patient remains on cabozantinib treatment, with a treatment duration of 5 months. A second case of pneumothorax was observed in a 69-year-old woman with metastatic renal cell carcinoma 1 month after beginning second-line cabozantinib at a dose of 60 mg daily. The patient had one subpleural lung lesion 5 cm in size. In May, 2018, the patient presented at the emergency department with a sudden worsening of dyspnoea, which led to a diagnosis of grade 3 pneumothorax, admission to the Oncological Department of the University Hospital of Verona, and treatment with drainage of the pneumothorax, which was ipsilateral to the pulmonary metastasis. Treatment with cabozantinib was continued, with a partial response recorded at subsequent disease evaluations. Cabozantinib therapy is still ongoing in this patient 6 months since the start of treatment.Tumour necrosis—as a result of a rapid, dramatic response to cabozantinib—of subpleural lung metastases might explain the pathogenesis of the pneumothorax in both these cases. Cabozantinib is the only approved tyrosine kinase inhibitor that has been shown to increase overall survival, progression-free survival, and overall responses compared with everolimus in previously treated patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma. Only two grade 3 and one grade 4 pneumothorax were reported with cabozantinib in the pivotal METEOR phase 3 trial. Pneumothorax, potentially related to the outstanding clinical activity of cabozantinib, is therefore an adverse event that must be considered in patients with peripheral lung or pleural metastases and unexpected onset of dyspnoea.

input: A 71-year-old man with renal cell carcinoma with symptomatic bilateral lung metastases and multiple subpleural lesions started second-line cabozantinib (60 mg orally daily) after disease progression on pazopanib. After 3 months of therapy, in May, 2018, the patient presented at the emergency department and complained of a worsening of his dyspnoea, leading us to suppose that disease progression had occurred. However, a CT scan revealed an impressive volumetric reduction of the lung nodules but the onset of an apical grade 3 left pneumothorax (figure). The patient was admitted to hospital at the University Hospital of Verona (Verona, Italy) and was treated with thorax drainage with complete pneumothorax resolution and no further sequelae. Given this excellent response, cabozantinib treatment was continued. So far, the patient remains on cabozantinib treatment, with a treatment duration of 5 months. A second case of pneumothorax was observed in a 69-year-old woman with metastatic renal cell carcinoma 1 month after beginning second-line cabozantinib at a dose of 60 mg daily. The patient had one subpleural lung lesion 5 cm in size. In May, 2018, the patient presented at the emergency department with a sudden worsening of dyspnoea, which led to a diagnosis of grade 3 pneumothorax, admission to the Oncological Department of the University Hospital of Verona, and treatment with drainage of the pneumothorax, which was ipsilateral to the pulmonary metastasis. Treatment with cabozantinib was continued, with a partial response recorded at subsequent disease evaluations. Cabozantinib therapy is still ongoing in this patient 6 months since the start of treatment.Tumour necrosis—as a result of a rapid, dramatic response to cabozantinib—of subpleural lung metastases might explain the pathogenesis of the pneumothorax in both these cases. Cabozantinib is the only approved tyrosine kinase inhibitor that has been shown to increase overall survival, progression-free survival, and overall responses compared with everolimus in previously treated patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma. Only two grade 3 and one grade 4 pneumothorax were reported with cabozantinib in the pivotal METEOR phase 3 trial. Pneumothorax, potentially related to the outstanding clinical activity of cabozantinib, is therefore an adverse event that must be considered in patients with peripheral lung or pleural metastases and unexpected onset of dyspnoea.

A 6-year-old boy with Ewing's sarcoma presented with generalised skin rash, low grade fever (38°C), and red eyes. Itchiness in the hands and feet preceded the rash. The child received chemotherapy (vincristine, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide) and blood transfusion 1 week before the onset of symptoms. Examination revealed purplish discoloration of both palms and soles in a glove and socks pattern (figure, A–C). Lesions resembled petechiae over the trunk, hands and feet, and face. Oral mucosa was erythematous with the rash including both pinnae (figure, D). The boy was neutropenic (haemoglobin 11·5 g/dL, total leucocyte count 0·5 × 106/L, and platelet count 20 × 109/L).
The striking glove and socks distribution of the rash prompted the diagnosis of papular purpuric gloves and socks syndrome (PPGSS) related to parvoviral infection. Parvovirus serology showed immunoglobulin M positivity. Skin biopsy revealed lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate with red-blood-cell extravasation. The boy was initiated on antibiotics (cefoperazone–sulbactam and amikacin, as per unit guidelines for febrile neutropenia), which were stopped 2 days later because he was afebrile and the blood cultures were sterile. Rash resolved with desquamation over the next 2 weeks. Blood counts also normalised after 1 week.
In children, parvovirus B19 infection usually presents as erythema infectiosum. Although uncommon, infection can manifest itself as PPGSS, which is an acute self-limited dermatosis characterised by fever, acral pruritus, oedema, petechiae, and oral lesions. The distinguishing feature is the symmetric erythema of hands and feet, with sharp margins at wrists and ankles. Other causes of PPGSS include cytomegalovirus, Coxsackie virus, and measles virus. The disease is mostly self-limited with a benign prognosis.
Febrile neutropenia is an oncological emergency that needs prompt initiation of antibacterial treatment. Recognition of such a classic manifestation, especially in an immunocompromised host, is essential to avoid aggressive treatment. Unlike patients with erythema infectiosum, individuals with PPGSS are regarded as infectious and should be isolated. Further, immunocompromised children need to be monitored for red-cell aplasia as a manifestation of persistent parvovirus infection. The index child has been well since illness, and completed his chemotherapy in June 2013.

input: A 71-year-old man with renal cell carcinoma with symptomatic bilateral lung metastases and multiple subpleural lesions started second-line cabozantinib (60 mg orally daily) after disease progression on pazopanib. After 3 months of therapy, in May, 2018, the patient presented at the emergency department and complained of a worsening of his dyspnoea, leading us to suppose that disease progression had occurred. However, a CT scan revealed an impressive volumetric reduction of the lung nodules but the onset of an apical grade 3 left pneumothorax (figure). The patient was admitted to hospital at the University Hospital of Verona (Verona, Italy) and was treated with thorax drainage with complete pneumothorax resolution and no further sequelae. Given this excellent response, cabozantinib treatment was continued. So far, the patient remains on cabozantinib treatment, with a treatment duration of 5 months. A second case of pneumothorax was observed in a 69-year-old woman with metastatic renal cell carcinoma 1 month after beginning second-line cabozantinib at a dose of 60 mg daily. The patient had one subpleural lung lesion 5 cm in size. In May, 2018, the patient presented at the emergency department with a sudden worsening of dyspnoea, which led to a diagnosis of grade 3 pneumothorax, admission to the Oncological Department of the University Hospital of Verona, and treatment with drainage of the pneumothorax, which was ipsilateral to the pulmonary metastasis. Treatment with cabozantinib was continued, with a partial response recorded at subsequent disease evaluations. Cabozantinib therapy is still ongoing in this patient 6 months since the start of treatment.Tumour necrosis—as a result of a rapid, dramatic response to cabozantinib—of subpleural lung metastases might explain the pathogenesis of the pneumothorax in both these cases. Cabozantinib is the only approved tyrosine kinase inhibitor that has been shown to increase overall survival, progression-free survival, and overall responses compared with everolimus in previously treated patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma. Only two grade 3 and one grade 4 pneumothorax were reported with cabozantinib in the pivotal METEOR phase 3 trial. Pneumothorax, potentially related to the outstanding clinical activity of cabozantinib, is therefore an adverse event that must be considered in patients with peripheral lung or pleural metastases and unexpected onset of dyspnoea.

A 6-year-old boy with Ewing's sarcoma presented with generalised skin rash, low grade fever (38°C), and red eyes. Itchiness in the hands and feet preceded the rash. The child received chemotherapy (vincristine, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide) and blood transfusion 1 week before the onset of symptoms. Examination revealed purplish discoloration of both palms and soles in a glove and socks pattern (figure, A–C). Lesions resembled petechiae over the trunk, hands and feet, and face. Oral mucosa was erythematous with the rash including both pinnae (figure, D). The boy was neutropenic (haemoglobin 11·5 g/dL, total leucocyte count 0·5 × 106/L, and platelet count 20 × 109/L).
The striking glove and socks distribution of the rash prompted the diagnosis of papular purpuric gloves and socks syndrome (PPGSS) related to parvoviral infection. Parvovirus serology showed immunoglobulin M positivity. Skin biopsy revealed lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate with red-blood-cell extravasation. The boy was initiated on antibiotics (cefoperazone–sulbactam and amikacin, as per unit guidelines for febrile neutropenia), which were stopped 2 days later because he was afebrile and the blood cultures were sterile. Rash resolved with desquamation over the next 2 weeks. Blood counts also normalised after 1 week.
In children, parvovirus B19 infection usually presents as erythema infectiosum. Although uncommon, infection can manifest itself as PPGSS, which is an acute self-limited dermatosis characterised by fever, acral pruritus, oedema, petechiae, and oral lesions. The distinguishing feature is the symmetric erythema of hands and feet, with sharp margins at wrists and ankles. Other causes of PPGSS include cytomegalovirus, Coxsackie virus, and measles virus. The disease is mostly self-limited with a benign prognosis.
Febrile neutropenia is an oncological emergency that needs prompt initiation of antibacterial treatment. Recognition of such a classic manifestation, especially in an immunocompromised host, is essential to avoid aggressive treatment. Unlike patients with erythema infectiosum, individuals with PPGSS are regarded as infectious and should be isolated. Further, immunocompromised children need to be monitored for red-cell aplasia as a manifestation of persistent parvovirus infection. The index child has been well since illness, and completed his chemotherapy in June 2013.

input:
A 6-year-old boy with Ewing's sarcoma presented with generalised skin rash, low grade fever (38°C), and red eyes. Itchiness in the hands and feet preceded the rash. The child received chemotherapy (vincristine, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide) and blood transfusion 1 week before the onset of symptoms. Examination revealed purplish discoloration of both palms and soles in a glove and socks pattern (figure, A–C). Lesions resembled petechiae over the trunk, hands and feet, and face. Oral mucosa was erythematous with the rash including both pinnae (figure, D). The boy was neutropenic (haemoglobin 11·5 g/dL, total leucocyte count 0·5 × 106/L, and platelet count 20 × 109/L).
The striking glove and socks distribution of the rash prompted the diagnosis of papular purpuric gloves and socks syndrome (PPGSS) related to parvoviral infection. Parvovirus serology showed immunoglobulin M positivity. Skin biopsy revealed lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate with red-blood-cell extravasation. The boy was initiated on antibiotics (cefoperazone–sulbactam and amikacin, as per unit guidelines for febrile neutropenia), which were stopped 2 days later because he was afebrile and the blood cultures were sterile. Rash resolved with desquamation over the next 2 weeks. Blood counts also normalised after 1 week.
In children, parvovirus B19 infection usually presents as erythema infectiosum. Although uncommon, infection can manifest itself as PPGSS, which is an acute self-limited dermatosis characterised by fever, acral pruritus, oedema, petechiae, and oral lesions. The distinguishing feature is the symmetric erythema of hands and feet, with sharp margins at wrists and ankles. Other causes of PPGSS include cytomegalovirus, Coxsackie virus, and measles virus. The disease is mostly self-limited with a benign prognosis.
Febrile neutropenia is an oncological emergency that needs prompt initiation of antibacterial treatment. Recognition of such a classic manifestation, especially in an immunocompromised host, is essential to avoid aggressive treatment. Unlike patients with erythema infectiosum, individuals with PPGSS are regarded as infectious and should be isolated. Further, immunocompromised children need to be monitored for red-cell aplasia as a manifestation of persistent parvovirus infection. The index child has been well since illness, and completed his chemotherapy in June 2013.

A 52-year-old right-handed woman was referred to our clinic reporting a 4-year history of spontaneous unpredictable episodes of dizziness. The patient was seen remotely due to restrictions imposed because of the COVID-19 pandemic. She described the episodes as a sudden sensation of feeling like the room was spinning for 5–40 s; they were happening approximately three times a day and she could identify no triggers. Occasionally, the episodes were associated with nausea and vomiting; they had also caused her to fall but did not result in any impairment of consciousness. The patient reported no visual symptoms, tinnitus, or headache. She was otherwise in good health and took no regular medication.The referral, from the otorhinolaryngology clinic via the family doctor, reported a negative Dix-Hallpike test and failure to improve the patient's symptoms with the Epley manoeuvre. The referrer diagnosed Ménière's disease—a triad of tinnitus, vertigo, and hearing loss—and prescribed the patient a trial of betahistine, bendroflumethiazide, and prochlorperazine with no benefit.
On remote examination the patient appeared well, although further examination was limited as there was no opportunity to test for nystagmus.
Laboratory investigations, previously arranged by the family doctor, had shown no atypical findings—full blood count, renal profile, and liver function were all within normal range. A brain MRI, which had been done 1 year before our consultation, as part of the initial work-up, showed normal brain parenchyma and ventricular system. We requested a further MRI to include high-resolution axial T2-weighted sequences of the posterior fossa; this showed a prominent left-sided vascular loop extending into the internal auditory meatus and causing compression of the left eighth cranial nerve—consistent with our suspected diagnosis of vestibular paroxysmia (figure). We prescribed the patient carbamazepine and she reported that her symptoms had resolved completely soon after commencing the treatment.
Vestibular paroxysmia is a rare cause of spontaneous, brief, and recurrent attacks of vertigo; episodes can be significantly disabling. The diagnosis—as in our patient—often goes unrecognised for many years. The key features differentiating vestibular paroxysmia from more common causes of vertigo are the spontaneity, the brevity, and the frequency. Regarding spontaneity, attacks are not typically triggered by head movement; syndromes to consider if attacks are triggered by head movement include benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, central positional nystagmus (caused by cerebellar and brainstem lesions), and bow hunter syndrome (vertebrobasilar insufficiency resulting from vertebral artery occlusion during neck rotation, usually from cervical spondylosis). Regarding brevity, attacks are usually < 1min; syndromes to consider if episodes are longer include Ménière's disease (typically attacks last 20 min to 12 h) and vestibular migraine (5 min to 72 h). And finally, regarding frequency, attacks occur up to 30 or more times per day; syndromes where episodes are less frequently include vertebrobasilar transient ischaemic attacks and epileptic vertigo.
Although infrequently encountered, vestibular paroxysmia is a condition to be aware of since it is an eminently treatable cause of dizziness and could very easily be mistaken for more common causes. MRIs typically show neurovascular compression of the eighth cranial nerve—radiologists should be asked to specifically look for this.
